en: Preface to the Collected Works of the Elder Zibo, composed by the Recluse of Kuangshan, the Chan Monk Deqing. The Great Void is vast and expansive;
when the long wind blows, the myriad apertures roar in fury. These diverse sounds and manifold echoes are all but the resonance of a single vital energy.

Furthermore, how could that which is proclaimed be subject to distinctions? One cannot claim that there are gaps in the spiritual faculties based on whether things are great or small, refined or coarse.
It is only our Buddha who, through inconceivable wisdom, emanates all dhāraṇīs of sound; therefore, even the words of worldly convention [partake of this].

All of these manifest the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). If even the dust speaks, the lands speak, and the blazing flames speak—such that flowing water and moving winds all intone the perfect sound (*paripūrṇa-svara*)—how much more so for one whose universe is in profound stillness, who illuminates the myriad conditions and responds to every encounter without thought, like an echo in a valley?
For this reason, the successive patriarchs of old were those who realized the untaught, spontaneous wisdom (*asat-kāra-jñāna*).
Thus, whether by raising an eyebrow, blinking an eye, or through angry rebukes and scathing criticisms, they all directly revealed the great meaning of the Western Arrival.
Furthermore, how could one ever attempt to grasp its true form through ordinary consciousness, emotions, or language?

Therefore, although Bodhidharma came from the West without establishing written texts, Caoxi possessed the *Platform Sūtra*. And while the two lineages and five schools of Chan, though pointing directly to the ultimate, all—

These were composed for the present age. Whether ascending the hall or entering the room, when he addressed the assembly and raised up the Dharma, his spiritual resonance was like thunder and lightning.
Whenever he bestowed a single word, it was invariably compiled into a record. For the most part, these were merely provisional gateways;

those such as Dahui, Zhongfeng, and even my own Ming-dynasty predecessor Chushi, all belonged to this category. Indeed, they borrowed words to transmit the mind and relied on speech to reveal the Way, thereby expressing that which is beyond words.

Thus it was said. Now, more than two hundred years after Chu-shih, the Chan Master Da-guan appeared. At a time when the Chan school had already fallen into decline, he rose up and vigorously revitalized it.
Having attained teacherless wisdom (*asatya-jñāna*) and wielding a vajra-like mind, his resolve to shoulder the burden of the Dharma was like that of Pa-rang in his bloody battles;
even though he wielded only empty fists, they were still capable of halting the sun. Although he had not yet...

He plowed the enemy’s court and swept out their lairs; yet his solitary loyalty in a single thought cannot be ranked as superior or inferior to those who bit through snow and swallowed felt in terms of life or death.
He was truly a great, heroic, and courageous man of the Dharma-ending age! However, the Master’s nature did not harmonize with worldly sentiments;
until his old age, he never once raised a hand in greeting when seeing a guest. Although he never sat upon the Flower Throne to strike the ritual mallet, [his spirit remained unyielding].

He swept away all delusions. Yet, wherever his footsteps reached, half the world was moved; whether they were high officials or lay devotees, those who turned their hearts in devotion upon seeing his shadow, or those who humbled themselves upon beholding his form, were beyond counting.

Because he had mastered the principle of the self-nature school, his spontaneous discourse—like a crossbow bolt weighing a thousand catties released—struck down its targets as soon as the string was drawn.
Every word was nothing other than a pointing toward the intent of the Western Land, spoken directly from the mouth in accordance with the nature of reality. Never...
There was no deliberate effort to compose this text; it was finished with a single spittle. My disciples transcribed and preserved about one-tenth of it.
When the Master first traveled between Jinsha and Qu’a, he shared a profound karmic affinity with the various gentlemen, including Yu Wanghe.
He heard the most from them; for instance, Layman Ru’an, Mr. Yu, served him with great diligence and obtained a few words [of his teaching].
Not even a single word was omitted, as if it were a precious treasure; anyone who followed the Master’s staff and sandals would surely search for and find them.
Whenever the Master went to Mount Kuanglu, he invariably stayed at the Changsong Pavilion of Mr. Xing Lai-ci, a distinguished scholar of Jiangzhou, where he spoke much.
After the Master’s passing, his disciples Zhonggao and Runfu compiled [the writings] into a volume.
Having long been submerged in the miasmic sea, I was recently at Shuangjing to attend to the Master’s final affairs; on my way, I first passed through Dongchan at Jinsha.

These two gentlemen, considering that I shared a profound karmic affinity with the Master within the Dharma-gate, presented me with their manuscript and bowed their heads in request that I edit and publish it.

I read his words three times and sighed deeply, saying: "Alas! In this age of the Dharma’s decline, to subdue the mind and exert the strength to uproot the very source of birth and death is like a single man facing ten thousand enemies. I see that the Master alone is such a person.
Beholding his vigorous, resolute, and courageous spirit, it often reveals itself at the tip of a single hair, like the Great Spirit wielding his axe. Truly.
This refers to one who has waged war against the Māra of afflictions, the Māra of desire, and the Māra of death, and has ultimately transcended birth and death as if casting off worn-out sandals;
such a person may be called a victor of great merit. Therefore, how could that which he has vomited forth be sought through words, language, sounds, or forms?
The Buddha taught that desire is the root of birth and death; this is what the Master has cited.
One must certainly express this intention three times. To prick at the painful spot with a needle is precisely to seek the total eradication of the life-root;
this alone may serve as a golden probe. What need is there for the formal arrangements of the gate?
Formerly, Master Juefan’s wondrous realization was transcendent and his language was skillful and canonical; he termed his own writings "Literary Chan. Therefore, I have titled this work *Purple*.
The Collected Works of Old Man Bai. This is certainly not something that falls within the realm of worldly conventions. Those who observe it should possess the adamantine eye of right view;
if they look beyond the words, they will have grasped more than half the meaning.
Written on the first day of the first month of spring in the year of Xinyou, the first year of the Tianqi era, at Wuyufeng on Mount Kuang.
Preface to the Collected Works of Master Zibo from the Hermitage of Wood and Stone:
Zhuangzi said, "Buliang Yi possesses the talent of a sage but lacks his Way; I possess the Way of a sage but lack his talent."
"He lacks talent. Now, he was a sage; how could there be any distinction between his talent and the Way? It is said:
"If it is not the right person, the Way will not manifest in vain. Talent belongs to the person. I once examined the ancestral portraits of successive generations at Shaoshi Mountain;
among them, there were none who were not stalwart and possessed extraordinary features, which left me privately amazed. Subsequently, I encountered the Great Master Zibo and observed his...
With a face as broad as a cubit and a waist that encompasses a fathom, he sits like a crouching bear and walks with the gait of an elephant.

When scholars and officials receive his audience, their presumptuous thoughts vanish without a word being spoken; when disciples look up to him for guidance, their spirits are already cowed even before he has applied a staff or a shout.
Were one to encounter him now, it would seem as though they were seeing those ancient patriarchs depicted in the portraits previously viewed—truly, he is such a man.
During the Wuzi and Jichou years of the Divine Temple era, the Great Master took up residence in our land.

He engaged in profound discussions on the Non-dual [Dharma] with the late Minister Lu Zhuangjian and my former teacher, Mr. Feng Juqu. Consequently, he constructed a hermitage on the ruins of the Lengyan Temple;
at that time, the site was overgrown with weeds as far as the eye could see. Yet, the Great Master’s preaching of the Dharma was like clouds and rain, and the faithful of the southeast heard it.
The winds of fortune blew favorably, and offerings poured in from all directions. Before long, the halls were adorned with cypress and paulownia wood and painted in brilliant colors;

towering and resplendent, they were restored to their former glory beyond mere repair. The Great Master, together with his eminent disciple Master Kai, established a set of regulations intended to be preserved for a hundred generations.
From south of the Yangtze to north of the sea, among the hundreds of monasteries, none could match the elegance and clarity of these pure rules as they were observed here.

Those who tread the path without overstepping even a single inch must first take the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* as their guide. The Great Master crossed the surging Yangtze River to pay homage at the King-Nurturing Temple;

he ascended the snowy ladders to behold Mount Emei and stepped upon the icy ravines to visit the Five Peaks. His footprints spanned the entire world before he proceeded to the imperial capital to propagate the Dharma.

He manifested his passing within the prison gates for the sake of the Dharma. Whether it be those who were enlightened or obscured, great or small, dull or sharp—his various capacities were all benefited.
Extensive and vast, his language is even more scattered. The Dharma he expounds is recorded as it issues from his mouth upon contact with objects;
grasped by his hand, it is utterly free of artifice. While following the traces of the narrow paths and threads, his waves overflow in all directions;

rising and submerging with sovereign ease, he possesses the power to swallow the heavens and drench the sun, surging tumultuously across the pages of paper. Such a thing has not been seen in recent times.
Among his peers, I have sought for an example in antiquity; perhaps the "Miraculous Joy" (Miaoxi) and "Illusory Abiding" (Huanzhu) [of the Linji masters] come close to it.
The Great Officer Yu Runfu of Jinsha acted with a sincere heart, mingling with the mundane world while upholding the Great Teaching. He was of the same lineage as the ancient Vimalakīrti and Pangyun;

his understanding of the Great Master was the most profound, and his bond of friendship the most steadfast. Whenever he encountered the Master’s instructions or expositions, he would immediately record them and preserve them. This continued until—
He returned to stillness. Whenever he heard that a manuscript by hand had fallen into someone's possession, he would travel no less than a thousand *li* to ensure its recovery by all means.

Over more than twenty years, these were gathered into a massive volume. Recently, he carefully transcribed and had them exquisitely engraved to honor his fellow students. Yet, after a while, he suddenly changed his mind, saying:
"Among all the scriptures upon which the Great Master rested his life and focused his contemplation, none is like the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. What he brought forth..."
Among the vast aspirations for the propagation of the Dharma, there is none more primary than the compilation of the scriptural treasury (*dharmapiṭaka*).

The task of carving the woodblocks has recently been undertaken at Mount Shuangjing, located only five or six *shè* from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. This record ought to be appended to the *Śūraṅgama* so that it may be carved and circulated;

its proceeds should be used to support the carving of the entire canon. This would surely be a source of joy within the Master’s realm of tranquil light. Furthermore, it will serve to propagate the Dharma.

The person Wei Ren, the presiding official of Lingyan, addressed the Dharma Master: "As a son who has truly inherited the legacy of his great master, you have exerted every effort in restoring what was ruined and reviving what had fallen into ruin.
This record ought to be included within your burden of upholding the Dharma.

Thereupon, in the month of Jia-ping during the Xin-wei year of the current Emperor’s Chongzhen reign, he placed the wooden boards upon the hall; the Dharma Master accepted them and dispatched a messenger to announce it.
I said to him, "The intention of you, Great Officer, is indeed noble. Let us try, for your sake, to burn a piece of sandalwood and go before the portrait hall of the Great Master;
there, as we read through the meaning of his instructions, there will surely be something that transcends the paper and ink."

These words are truly worthy of savoring; such a person is truly worthy of emulation. Therefore, I value their harmony. Furthermore, as for the Master’s words and deeds, they capture the essential framework of the Dharma.
If the Master’s vows are fulfilled and the teachings of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are fully implemented, then one will penetrate to the very source and bottom of the Dharma.
One cannot say that this is not the time when the sun of the Buddha is setting behind the Yanzhi Mountains. Strive with all your might!
This is the *Gē* (spear) of Luyang. You, my fellow disciples, must surely exert yourselves. Do not fail the Great Master;
do not fail the Great Master! Written by the layman Li Zhulan, Li Rihua, with hands washed in reverence:
The Great Master’s preaching of the Dharma in response to circumstances was spontaneous and extemporaneous, without any artificial arrangement, all arising from the very first thought-moment.
These were written out as they flowed forth, with the sole intention of clarifying this matter for others; originally, there was no concern for literary style or language.

Whenever he gave instruction to someone, he would have that person write it down on his behalf. As soon as the writing was finished, the Master would take it away with him, never casting even a single glance back at it.
Consequently, the meaning within these texts often contains repetitions, and even the accumulation of characters and overlapping phrases is likewise [redundant].
Not a few. Alas, at that time there was no one specifically entrusted with recording them; thus, subtle words and wondrous meanings were scattered in all directions in great abundance.

This collection has been obtained in its entirety from three individuals—Zhou Zongjie of Wujiang, Xing Laici of Jiujiang, and Wang Zhongtao of the same prefecture—who each recorded them with slight variations in detail. I, along with two or three friends, have examined these with an open mind.

Revised. As for those points that remain doubtful, I have provisionally set them aside before daring to commit this work to print. Regarding other fragments that have been lost or scattered, I am unable to seek out and recover each one individually.

May all my fellow students who wish to repay the kindness of the Dharma-milk and extend the universal salvation of the Compassionate Vessel, if they possess even a single word or half a verse of the teachings, [contribute them].
Without sparing the effort of distributing them from afar, I have collected them all together to continue the *Transmission of the Lamp*. This is truly a source of great joy for the Dharma-gate.
Recorded with reverent hands by the disciple Sanju in the autumn of the Dingmao year of the Tianqi era.
Epilogue to the Collected Works of the Great Master Zibo:
For a long time, the Dharma seat has been obscured by dust and the ancestral lamp has lacked flame.

In seeking those who could shoulder the Great Dharma, uphold the school’s tradition, vanquish the demons of emotion in a hundred battles, and dry up the ocean of consciousness through a thousand streams, there appeared...
It is clear that since the time of Chu-shih, there has been only one person, the Great Master Zi-bai.
The Great Master had a profound and penetrating realization of his own mind, which shone forth with solitary brilliance.
Words and letters overflowed naturally from within the light of his mind; once he raised a finger, the fundamental wondrousness was revealed before him.

As for his compassionate and earnest heart—its fervor and intensity—are nothing other than a desire to cause the ignorance of students accumulated over kalpas to melt away instantly, so as to investigate this great matter of cause and condition.
Alas! The First Patriarch did not establish written words, yet he pointed directly to the human mind;
the Great Master did not depart from written words, yet he likewise pointed to the human mind. Their principles are one and the same. —Huanglang.
I once saw an attendant standing by, grasping his brush, while the Great Master spoke spontaneously. The attendant raised his wrist and wrote with great speed, yet he still found it insufficient;
when one sheet was filled, he changed to another. It was like a spring gushing from the earth, resonant and unceasing.
Were it not for a perfectly clear realization of the ground of reality, free from all stagnation, how could such a thing be achieved? Alas! There is indeed such a thing as literary brilliance.
Regarding characters: there has never been anything that exists [independently]. Those who study characters awaken through characters;

yet, where there have never been characters, the exquisite flavors of sublime delicacies fill everyone. This is like merely understanding it as characters—how is this different from pointing at food and saying one is full?
How could this cure hunger? Nevertheless, as long as the ordinary mind has not been unlocked, the realization of the Sage is difficult to perceive. Therefore, I request that you...

The Great Master applied his attention to daily activities. From within his collected works, he extracted a single verse by Vipaśyin Buddha, claiming it encompassed the entire Tripitaka and penetrated the very source of Chan.
He maintained this practice for fifteen years of winter and summer without ceasing in his devotion.
He said that whenever he encountered circumstances of adversity or favor, or of love or hatred, he invariably took this verse as his vanguard to "overthrow armies and slay enemies."

I do not know how many such as he there have been. Alas! That one who has attained such total penetration as Master [Zhaozhou] should still remain so steadfast, sharp, fierce, and decisive—this is why his singular style is peerless and his companions non-existent, and why the intent of the Buddhas and the marrow of the patriarchs find their source everywhere.

Even when confined within the prison cell at the end of his life, he was serene and at ease; matters of birth and death, profit and harm, were like shaking empty space. Such was the subtlety of his illumination and function.
The virtuous ones of antiquity were indeed peerless. Yet every person originally possesses the luminosity of the mind; failing to recognize its illuminating function leads to its loss and decline.
The Great Master, moved by urgent compassion, acted as a guide for us all. Every fragmentary phrase and single word serves as an aid to wipe away the grime and restore the light.
Only when one captures the essential message herein can one truly be called a descendant of Zibo. This is the ultimate sharp faculty.
This gentleman, having merely touched upon a few drops, immediately witnessed the surging winds and steaming clouds;

his soaring transformations were so transcendent that he attained silent resonance, utterly transcending thought and language. Thus, not a single word of this collection of recorded sayings can be found.
Master Yican discussed this for several years and took sole responsibility for its dissemination, causing the heart-light of Zibo to shine like the brilliance of the sun and the radiance of the moon.
The needle penetrates through the ages; the radiance of the Master shines forth. How could these not reflect one another, mutually encompassing and merging into a single whole?
With deepest reverence, the disciple He Liang bows and writes this letter.

The Master of Song inscribed this himself for this master:
His mind is straightforward and his speech is swift; He has traveled throughout the world, Moving with ease within the monastic circle.
In the summer of the Renyin year of the Wanli era, [he] inscribed this at Cibiao in Heyan Huiyanqing Temple.
In the winter of the following year, the Guiyou year, he indeed entered parinirvāṇa within the monastery. This was a clear manifestation of his prior knowledge. Thus it is said.
The disciple Sanju, having washed his hands, bows and writes this eulogy for the portrait of the Great Master Zibo.

The net of the Dharma-realm has been torn asunder and its cords no longer held; it was only upon the birth of this Great Master that he exerted the strength to restore its framework, sitting majestically within the lion’s den.
He fells the sandalwood tree; though his prowess is not yet fully displayed, his claws and fangs are already bared. He beats the drum smeared with lethal poison and pours out the nectar of ambrosia;

those who drink it become intoxicated, and those who hear it go mad. Within the nature of quiescent emptiness, he unleashes a tongue like a crashing thunderclap—like rushing lightning that rolls across the heavens.
To encounter him is to be struck dumb with awe. With the mind of the great earth, he erects the vajra-bones; within his eyes there are sinews, and within his breast there is nothing.
Linji does not die, and Huangbo still lives. Who knows that the Great Master did not accept such a title? He strides across the vast expanse with wide steps.
Without abiding by conventional rules, he turned his body and hurled it beyond the peak of Mount Sumeru; with a single punch, he shattered the realm of non-arising.
Hanzhan Deqing praises Qian Bozi of Shanyin, who holds the small portrait of Master Daguan and requests that I compose a eulogy for it. At this time, I—
My illness is now severe; I have been unable to exert my thoughts. I have instead composed these Zen words offhand to send to you.
Ha ha ha! This is Daguan. In the past, my beard and hair remained as they were; today, my eyebrows have not changed.
Facing each other as before, his compassionate countenance and vows remain. People say this old man passed away within the meditation hall, yet he is actually right here.
Unfolding and rolling up, he has always acted through skillful means. If you wish to know the Master’s true self, you might try to glimpse his features here;
however, even so, you will only obtain half of it. If you wish for full manifestation, you must burn even this [text] away; only then will you truly meet him. Why?
Therefore, within the Great Ming realm, this man could not be overlooked.
I first met the Master in the year of Guisi (1593) at the He family garden in Jinling, when I was serving as a Lang in the Department of the Imperial Carriages.

It had been many years since I had requested an audience with him. I recall previously meeting him at the residence of Qu Dongguan, the Vice Minister of Rites, and at the home of Fu [surname], the Grand Music Master.

The two gentlemen, [Wang] Heng and [Wang] Qi, accompanied by their disciples, went there several times; yet upon arrival, they would turn back again. How many times did they urge their horses home in vain?
Consequently, the two gentlemen ceased further requests for an audience. However, my own desire had not yet been satisfied, and so it was that we finally met at this time.

The Master’s beard and hair were unshorn, and he wore a simple headcloth like a woodcutter. His physical frame was robust and imposing; whether sitting or standing, he was as steady as a mountain. This was as Master Hei-weng had described...

It was said that these were all men of imposing stature and heroic excellence. Upon seeing one another, their faces were filled with expressions of compassion, and they behaved with courtesy as before.
Within the hall were several scholars dressed in scholar’s robes and caps, holding pens and lost in deep thought, as solemn as if they were taking an examination.
I took my seat. The attendant laid out mats before me, prepared ink and brushes, and unfurled paper.

I asked for the reason, and he replied, "I request that you compose a commentary on a certain four-line passage from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* together with these disciples; a verse would also be acceptable.
I agreed and accepted this without hesitation. As we proceeded to discuss other doctrines with the Master, after one or two turns of conversation had not yet concluded, the Master—
He immediately called to his attendant, saying, "Pass the paper and brush before Old Master Zhou.

After discussing it for another turn or two, the Master said, "He is stubbornly struggling; he is stubbornly struggling. A short while later, the attendant brought a visitor's card to announce the arrival of Mr.
Xuezhai Xu, the Director of the Court of State Ceremonial. One of the disciples rose and said, "The Master is physically weary today; let Mr. Xu see you [at ease]."
"I shall wait for another time to request his return. He was about to depart when the Master said, "That will not do;
you must see him as soon as you arrive. Previously, Mr. Xu had sought an audience with the Master but knew it would not be granted.
Consequently, he would follow me wherever I went. Thus, having now managed to gain entry because I was present at the gate, he was able to reach the Master’s presence.
I was staying in a room. My disciples requested that I attend the assembly, saying, "If you are not present, we fear the Master will have no way of knowing [the proceedings].
On that day, I took my midday meal with Xu Gong and then dispersed. The next day, the sky began to grow light.
The streets were deserted as people walked about. Just then, there was a knock at my office door. Upon inquiry, I learned it was the master with two disciples.

I went out to welcome them; they said the Great Master was coming to pay his respects. After a short while, he arrived, holding a staff and walking with broad strides and long steps, escorted by several disciples.
He lingered until evening before departing. At that time, Zhou Shuzong was accompanying me, who recorded this for me.
[He] consented. I have forgotten his other name and surname. An attendant said, "The Great Master has never visited anyone before;

therefore, to bestow this upon you is an extraordinary honor. I sighed inwardly at that time, for my mind was not yet entirely settled and I could not reach a definitive conclusion through deliberation.
Subsequently, I wished to record this as evidence, but had no opportunity. It is regrettable that people say the Master is strange; I have witnessed it clearly myself.
It is thus. Is it strange? Is it difficult? That anyone who sees this for the first time should consider it difficult is entirely due to the influence of their peers.

One can infer this from the single episode of Master Xu, which I witnessed firsthand. Nevertheless, what illness did the Master suffer from? The world was not broad, and the eyes of the people of that time were not large enough;
in the end, they could not tolerate this old man. Some even took his entry into the capital gates as his "illness," yet—
His compassionate vows are profound and far-reaching, almost beyond measure. I have already composed a eulogy for his portrait as a son of the Qian family;
I now further record the details of our first meeting and, moved by emotion, offer these words of lament.
On the eighth day of the twelfth month in the Bingwu year, Zhou Rude of Shan City prostrates himself upon the ground and respectfully records these words:
Opening the empty mouth to speak of east and west; using the Dharma of compassion to strike with blind fists and shout with blind eyes; cold in countenance yet warm at heart.
The Lotus Flower Society: cold debts repaid with warmth. Twenty blows from the bamboo staff; the bird flies away, leaving behind its cry. Fragrance wafts as the embers fall.
Truly, this is a master whom Zhi Dao could not capture in his painting.
For a long time, I have looked toward Master Zibo with devotion. In the year of Xinchou, I entered the capital, while the Master was residing at West Mountain.
I was filled with joy, wishing to meet him by offering the fragrant incense of my devotion. However, several fellow students all disparaged the Master; their doubts caused me to desist.

Later, reading his posthumous writings, I examined his lifelong authentic realization and secret practices, his profound compassion and lofty integrity, which were unrivaled among the monastic communities of the time.

The Master’s seat was truly rare in its peerless quality; yet, one still regrets that the Master did not depart earlier, ultimately meeting with misfortune—a fate that does not accord with the Way of the luminous and wise.
Upon seeing the portrait sent by Mr. Wu Xianxi, I tasted the words of his own eulogy, which resembled a prophecy.
Could it be that the Master, like the Second Patriarch, possessed such primordial knowledge from of old? I have often...
When the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging saw people bowing to him, he would say, "You shall all become Buddhas.
The people would then chase after him, beating, throwing, and reviling him. Yuan Jingqian said: "In a certain country there was a 'mad spring. Anyone who drank from it went mad."
Only the king drew water from the well and was thus saved, yet the entire nation regarded the king as mad. They seized him together, binding and branding him;

unable to endure the suffering, he rushed to drink from the spring, acting like a madman. The people of the land rejoiced, saying, "The king’s illness has been cured," and only then did they cease their persecution.
Zibo regarded the multitude as Buddhas and could not help but deliver them; so it was with the multitude.
To view the purple cypress as madness is to be compelled to die. Alas! What is there to regret?

On the first day of the bright fortnight of the first month of the year Dingwei, Tao Wangling of Kuaiji respectfully inscribed this upon the flying whiskers, the furrowed brows, the bald pate, the upturned eyes, the clenched fists, and the bared chest—wherein the divine and wondrous wisdom is fully present.

Sufficient. Celestial beings, dragons, humans, and ghosts are all subdued. His voice shakes the mountains and peaks, filling the empty valleys. He drew his sword at Tiger Hill and buried it at Heaven’s Eye.
Eight facets of majestic wind are depicted on a single scroll. Six times six is originally thirty-six.
Yusheng Huang Ruheng’s eulogy:
His two eyes gaze loftily; his two cheeks sag with age. The Milky Way is his mouth, and wind and thunder are his tongue.

Busily and tirelessly he ferries others across, whether great or small, never failing in his response. How profoundly compassionate! How truly heroic! Between the worthy and the ignorant, he remains eternally so.
Without rest, how can one distinguish between a prince, a king, and a high official? If you lack even a moment’s reflection, I shall apply the staff and shout.
Such a burning heart is difficult to compose; this composing cannot be described. Do not ask about those on paper; try looking at the inscription of Jing Mountain.
Inscribed by the disciple Li Peijing of Changshui.

During his lifetime, his teaching style was stern and rigorous; at the time of his passing, the staff and shouts were intermingled. With a single thought, he constantly contemplated Avalokiteśvara; for him, heaven and hell made no difference.
While others speak of causes, conditions, and karmic retribution, I speak of the master of one's own fundamental share. There is only this: when opposition comes...
In accordance with what is received. From the illusory shadows and empty flowers of others, Yao Shishen of Changshui respectfully inscribes this preface.

Formerly, my late grandfather, the Jianshan [Duke], was a golden fortress for the Dharma; he widely sought out the "dragons and elephants" (great masters) to serve as bridges and rafts for the Dharma. Having encountered our Master, [he found his purpose].

He is called the True Dharma King. I take refuge in him and seek his instruction. In my advanced age, I am filled with awe; through the grace of loyalty, I have gained the opportunity to serve by his side, providing his water and towel.

He is a lamp of wisdom for the dark paths and a compassionate vessel for the sea of suffering. A paternal elder in this world and a guiding teacher beyond it, he inspires reverence when approached closely.

Gazing from afar, I contemplated it further; seeing it for the first time, I was struck with wonder. As I approached, my heart turned toward compassion. You have revealed the essentials of the Way and awakened me from my delusion.

In the space of a finger-snap, I realized the errors of my past. Having abandoned the ocean to identify with a bubble, I have only now come to understand that it is through the Master that one knows the Buddha.

Because the Buddha knew Confucianism, its spiritual luminosity is vast and penetrating; thus there are stages and steps. The Master said, "Alas! Alas! These stages and steps are not it. One must take responsibility right beneath one's feet;
lift your foot and you arrive immediately. I have often reflected upon this profound compassion, moved to tears of gratitude. The milk of the Dharma is difficult to repay.
Death is certain, there is no doubt; yet how could I have expected that our karmic affinity were so deep? To personally witness the passing of my teacher—alas for the man of wisdom!

His light of precepts and insight blazed ever more intensely upon meeting with the right conditions. Now dwelling in the Hall of Blessings, he performs the great Dharma-gift, having traversed through all manner of suffering and affliction.

His mind was tranquil; having fulfilled his royal duties, he declared that his karmic conditions from former lives were exhausted. With palms joined and legs crossed in the lotus posture, his single sandal slipped away gracefully.

For six days he remained in a prison cell, exposed to the wind and dust in the open air, yet he stood firm as a mountain, a radiant light overflowing from his cheeks. He was buried in the summer at Xiyuan.

Floods overflowed to form rivers; the city was tilted and houses swept away. Nothing remained firm as they were violently tossed about. Thinking that this earthen mound would be gnawed by rain and pierced by wind, he moved southward to open the stupa and beheld the Master’s countenance once more.
His marks and signs were majestic and solemn, as if he were still alive. Thus it is said of the ancient sages: [they remain as they were].
He comes and goes at will through the power of meditative concentration and wisdom; he forms śarīra relics and enters fire and water without his physical body being destroyed.

It was not to be expected that one so ignorant and deluded would witness such wonders; indeed, as the Master said, the evidence lies in his closed eyes upon the ground—he is no flesh-and-blood Buddha.
How could it be otherwise?
This is the eulogy by Lu Jizhong on the portraits of the Venerable Zibo and the Great Master Daguan Ke.
There is a Great King of Physicians who cures the disease of delusive darkness. Entering the mud and the water, he beats and strikes to bring about transformation;
he calls out to awaken those in their dream-houses, sustaining the life-force of wisdom. For the sake of the Dharma, he forgets his own body, loftily upholding the ancestral seal.

The Layman Xiangguang Dong Qichang praised this: "Do not view falsely, and the eyes will not be impaired. Do not listen falsely, and the ears will not be impaired. Do not speak falsely, and the tongue will not be impaired.
Do not act falsely, and the body will not be impaired. Do not play with the vital spirit nor feign eccentricity. Only now can one truly verify the authentic observance of the precepts."
I must plant a marker for humans and devas; what harm is there in returning some debts to the hells? *Pah!* The debt is already repaid—what more is there to wait for?
Sitting upright and waiting for the old fool to arrive, he shatters his former worn-out skin-sack.
A single ray of divine light flashes like fire and lightning; this elegant iron man is now free and unencumbered.
The Layman Wenwen Chen Jiru’s Epitaph for the Great Master Daguan:
Now, throughout the great earth, birth and death constitute a long night of delusion; because the gate of emotion is firmly closed, the shackles of consciousness are difficult to open.
There are those capable of springing up and shattering it with a single blow, or turning their sleeves and proceeding alone;
unless one is a heroic and valiant man, possessing a capacity that transcends the world, such a feat is not easily achieved.
Looking back through the various elders of the *Chuan Deng Lu*, they were all such individuals. For a long time, no one has done so again, until recently, when I beheld it in Master Daguan.
The Master’s name was Zhēn Kě; his courtesy name was Dàguān, and he later styled himself Zǐbó. His disciple, Zhòng Zuǒzūn, adopted this title out of reverence for the Dharma.
His ancestors were from Jùqū. His father was Shěn Lián, the youngest son of [a certain] Ji. They had resided for generations at Tānquē on Lake Tàihú in Wújiāng.
His mother dreamed that a strange person gave her a large, fresh peach with its leaves still attached; upon waking, she was filled with fragrance.
The mother subsequently conceived. When the Master was five years old, he did not speak.

At that time, a strange monk passed by his gate, rubbed the child’s head, and said to his father, "This boy shall leave the household life and become a teacher of gods and men. Having spoken these words, he suddenly vanished.
Thereupon, the Master was able to speak. Previously, the footprints of a giant had been seen descending into the courtyard; from that time on, [he continued to grow].
Furthermore, it was seen that since childhood, the Master’s disposition had been heroic and fierce, noble and intense, and his appearance magnificent beyond the common.
As a youth, he did not enjoy playing; he disliked seeing women. He would not permit anyone to bathe before him.

One day, his elder sister happened to enter the bath first by mistake; the Master was greatly incensed. From then on, from his relatives down to ordinary women, none dared to approach him. His great resolve grew daily.
He grew increasingly bold; his parents could no longer restrain him. He once wrote a poem that said: "The heroic ambition of one who has slaughtered dogs is not easily extinguished.
At the age of seventeen, he finally took up his sword and traveled far to the northern borders. Upon reaching the Changmen Gate of Suzhou, it began to rain heavily and he could not proceed.
There he happened to meet the monk Mingjue of Tiger Hill (Huaqiu). As they looked at one another, Mingjue marveled at his appearance and recognized [his potential].
The youth was extraordinary; [the Master] felt he was different from others and shielded him with an umbrella. He then returned to the temple with him and prepared an evening meal;
they were so delighted that they found great affinity with one another. Hearing the monk recite the names of the Eighty-eight Buddhas at night, the Master’s heart was filled with great joy.
At dawn, he entered the meditation hall and said, "We two possess a great treasure; why is it defiled here?"

"Is it sufficient? [Hui] asked. He immediately untied the ten-plus pieces of gold wrapped at his waist and gave them to Huìjué, instructing him to prepare a vegetarian feast and requesting that [Huìjué] shave his head.
He then took Huìjué as his teacher. That night, he sat upright until dawn. Whenever he spoke to himself in private, he sighed three times, saying:
"Looking at it, there is no meat; eating it, there is flavor. At that time, Huìjué wished to melt down ten thousand catties of iron to cast a great bell. The Master...
He said, "I shall assist you. He then went to the gate of a wealthy household in Píhú and sat cross-legged.

When the master of the house saw him, he offered him food, but the Master would not eat. The master asked what he required; the Master replied, "I need ten thousand catties of iron to cast a great bell."
He accepted the food immediately. The host went outside and set up ten thousand catties of iron at the gate. The Master smiled. When he had finished eating, he drove the cart straight back to Huqiu.
Upon returning, he closed his door and devoted himself to reading. For half a year he did not step beyond the threshold.
He once saw a monk who was drinking wine and eating meat, and the Master said, "For an ordained person to act like this is truly deplorable. At that time—

He knelt down to observe the work, and after a long while, sighed and said, "If people like us were able to do this, it would have been sufficient. Thereupon, he...
He went to Jingde Temple in Wutang and remained there for three years behind closed doors.
He then returned to Wumen, where one day he took leave of his teacher Jue, saying, "I shall now go on pilgrimage to various regions to visit spiritual teachers and investigate the Great Matter.
Thereupon, he departed with staff in hand. One day, he heard a monk reciting the verse by Zhang Zhuo on realizing the Way, which reached the line: "Severing deluded thoughts..."
His illness increased even further. [The monk] said, "To incline toward True Suchness (tathatā) is also erroneous.

The Master said, "That is wrong. You should say that only when one is free from illness is it not erroneous. The monk said, "You are wrong; he is not. The Master was greatly perplexed by this, and whenever he went to a place...

One day during a meal, he suddenly attained awakening; his head and face immediately subsided. From then on, he traveled through various regions, often saying:

Zong’ao traveled twenty *li* in a single day; his feet became sore, so the Master ground the soles of his feet with stone until he could travel two hundred *li* before stopping.
While the Master was traveling to Mount Wutai, he reached a steep cliff and a hollow cavern where an elderly practitioner sat alone.
The Master paid his respects and asked, "What is it like when not a single thought has yet arisen? The elder held up a finger.
[The Master] pointed his finger. He asked again, "What about after birth? [The Master] extended both hands. The Teacher (Huairang) attained the essential meaning beneath these words.
He followed his tracks, but lost his whereabouts. The Teacher arrived at the capital and visited the great elder Bianrong. Bianrong asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Jiangnan.

Rong said, "You must preach the Dharma with purity. The Master said, "Right now, I am not stained by a single speck of dust. Rong ordered his attendant to strip the Master of his *zhiduo* (monastic robe).
As he looked at the Master, he said, "If you shed one layer, return it to me. The Master smiled and nodded, whereupon Rong left him.

He was received as a resident monk. At that time, his spiritual mentors, including the Dharma Master Xiaoyan and the various great elders such as Xianli, were all among those who had entered his door.
Nine years later, he returned to Huqiu to visit Jue. He then went to Songjiang and remained in seclusion behind closed doors for one hundred days.
Upon going to Wuxian, it happened that Fu Jun Guangzhe of Liaocheng was serving as the county magistrate; his son, Ligen, commanded him to pay his respects.

Ming heard these words and held him in deep esteem. The Master then took up a single cluster of roses with two blossoms and asked the Master [Gong]:

Because he had been penalized by being excluded from one offering at the vegetarian feast, they subsequently became inseparable friends.

"I order you to be severely reprimanded with thirty blows; if you are light, double that. The administrator was startled, not knowing who it was.
