The current state of affairs had reached this point. If eunuchs were to kill a virtuous high official and even his wife, what would become of the world?
He therefore took up his staff and crossed the gates of the capital. Wu was imprisoned, and the Master arrived to provide extensive protection for him.

He bestowed upon Lord Wu half a verse of the *Vipaśyin Buddha* and instructed him to recite it until it reached one hundred thousand times, at which point he would be released from prison. Wu held fast to this.

When [the number of years] reached eighty thousand, he received the Master’s instruction on the meaning of the teachings and attained the stage of final diminution (*antya-kṣaya*). Upon returning to Wu, he would shed tears whenever he thought of his teacher.
Before my own return to lay life, the Master frequently lamented, saying: "The Dharma-gate is without people; if we sit idly by while the banner of the Dharma collapses..."

Thus, where should one who seeks to uphold and flourish the Triple Gem direct their efforts? If this old man [Hanshan] does not return [to the source], it will be a great failure for me in bringing forth into the world;
if the mining taxes do not cease, it will be a great failure for me in saving the world;

and if the transmission of the lamp is not continued, it will be a great failure for me regarding the life of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*). If these three failures are resolved, then [the task] shall no longer remain.

He departed for Rājagṛha. In the autumn of the *guimao* year, while I was at Caoxi, I dispatched a letter to one of my disciples who was traveling to the capital with the imperial examination, requesting that he invite the Master into the mountains.
In my reply, I wrote directly: "I shall cast aside this single set of poor bones."

Not long after he had settled there, suddenly a seditious book was circulated, causing a great upheaval both at court and throughout the realm. At that time, those who harbored resentment took advantage of the situation to impeach the Master with a formal indictment.
Ultimately, the Master met his end because of this.

Previously, His Majesty, as a Cakravartin King moved by the power of his vows, had revered the Great Dharma and transcribed the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. By chance, a drop of sweat [fell upon it].
The paper beneath was soaked through; suspecting it would soon need to be replaced, he urgently sent his close attendant, Cao Gongzhi, to consult the Master.

The Master offered this verse in response: "A single drop of imperial sweat, A bridge and raft for ten thousand generations. From this point on, the inexhaustible Dharma-treasury Shall radiate its light."
The Emperor read this and was greatly pleased; from that time on, he paid close attention to him. Just as he saw the memorial, he felt great compassion for him.
Since he could not escape the law, he was consequently arrested.

When the imperial decree was issued, it stated only that he should undergo a thorough investigation. During his interrogation by the Golden Watch (Jinwu), he answered regarding the three matters of his failure, and [the case] was concluded.

There were no other words [of protest]. He was sent to the Minister of Justice (Sikou). Previously, the Censor-in-Chief, Mr. Cao Xuecheng, had been arrested for submitting a memorial and had been in prison for a long time;

he had questioned the Master about the Way, and their conversations were recorded as the *Yuanzhong yulu* (Records of Words within the Circular Prison). At that time, the administrators of the government wished to put the Master to death.
Upon hearing this, the Master said, "The ways of the world are such as this; what is the use of staying for long?
He then requested a bath, and upon its completion, he instructed his attendant, the novice Xing Tian, saying, "I am departing. Please convey my thanks to all the Dharma protectors in Jiangnan.
The novice wept, and the Master rebuked him, saying, "You have served me for twenty years, yet you still behave in such a manner."
"Yes. He then spoke a verse, the words of which are recorded in the chronicles. Having finished speaking, he sat upright and passed away peacefully.
When Lord Cao heard of this, he hurried there and patted him, saying, "The Master has departed well. The Master opened his eyes again, smiled, and took his leave.
This was the seventeenth day of the twelfth month of the Gui-mao year. The Master was born in the sixth [month] of the Gui-mao year.
On the twelfth day of the month, at the age of sixty-one and with over forty years of Dharma seniority, the Master passed away. Alas!

Regarding the Master’s conduct throughout his life, doubt and faith were equally present; yet as for this final, decisive act, everyone from high to low who heard of it could not help but sigh in admiration.
Oh, how the Master viewed birth and death, regarding the four great elements as if casting off worn-out clothes!
[The Master] Xi. By what dharma was this brought about? The Master constantly used the verse of Vipaśyin Buddha to instruct people.
I asked him, "Does the Master also uphold it? The Master replied, "I have upheld it for over twenty years; I am already familiar with half a stanza.
If I were to master two stanzas, I would have no anxiety regarding birth and death. Could this be a sign of its efficacy? After the Master passed away, [I waited...]
His life span was said to be six days, yet his complexion did not change. When he emerged, his body was left to float and be buried outside Cihui Temple.
Subsequently, during the spring and summer rains and into autumn, Mr. Lu Changgong of Xiyuan wished to transport the Master’s physical body back to the south.
The coffin was opened, yet it remained peaceful and unmoving. Just then, my disciple Dayi arrived and immediately escorted the Master’s reliquary shrine here.
While crossing the Luhe River, the Imperial Censor Ma Jinglun, deeply moved by the matter concerning the Master and Li Zhuowu, felt the greatest sorrow in his heart.

He opened the sarcophagus and brushed the face [of the Master], weeping bitterly. Upon arriving at Jinshui, Qu'e, and other locations, his disciples there escorted him back to Mount Jing, where he was enshrined in Jizhao Monastery.
Because of the circumstances surrounding the carving of the Tripitaka, they further urged Shen Zhongcheng to rebuild the main hall, in accordance with the Master’s final instructions.
For the Master had uttered a verse at the time of his death which said: "It is strange that..."
The two peaks serve as the twin trees; the palm leaves are like clouds, and the sun naturally gathers there. It was for this reason.
It was the ninth month of autumn in the year Jiachen. Eleven years later, in the year Yimao, my disciple first interred the master’s entire remains behind Mount Shuangjing.
It happened that Lord Zhushi Cheng Wenning came to pay respects at the master’s stupa and discovered that there was water.
He urgently instructed his disciple Fakai to open it, and indeed it was as he had said. They then moved the reliquary shrine to Kaishan.
There, he consulted with his lay disciple Miu Xiuyong and secured a site within Wufeng, to the left of the second-generation patriarch’s tomb behind the Dahui Pagoda;
this place was called Wenshu Terrace. They selected the nineteenth day of the eleventh month of the Bingchen year for the interment.
The cremation took place on the [blank] day. On the twenty-third day, the remains were enshrined in a stupa here.

When I was first among the traveling monks, I heard the news of the Master’s passing and immediately wished to go in person to offer my condolences; however, due to procrastination over the course of twelve years, I failed to fulfill my original intention.

Recently, having come from Nanyue over several thousand li, I had no prior intention of meeting with him, yet the date for the memorial service was already fixed—this was surely due to the power of his spirit.
How extraordinary was his response to my sincerity! As for the Master’s later affairs, I was fortunate enough to witness them personally and was thus able to devote some measure of my heart to them.
Alas! How could the Master’s lifelong conduct and practice ever be easily emulated? From the moment he left the household life, his side never touched his mat for over forty years.
His nature was fierce and resolute in its diligence, and he disciplined himself with the utmost severity; even those close to him could not...
Trembling in the cold, he frequently sat in the open air, avoiding neither wind nor frost. From his youth, he followed his mother’s instruction not to sit upon the threshold;
thus, throughout his life, he did not stand near the door-sill. Maintaining a diamond-like mind, he alone took it as his heart's resolve to shoulder the Great Dharma.
Whenever he saw ancient monasteries falling into ruin, he was determined to restore them.
Beginning with Lingyan and continuing through Guizong, Yunju, and others, he revitalized fifteen Buddhist temples.

Aside from carving the Tripitaka, he also collected all the recorded sayings of renowned masters of antiquity, as well as the various commentaries on the sutras and treatises composed by the Venerable Jiyin.
Those works that had not been heard of in the world, he searched out entirely and carved for publication. Later, he obtained Su Dongpo’s commentary on the *Yi Jing* and was greatly delighted by it.
Whenever he showed it to his disciples in his quarters, he invariably required them to engage in personal investigation (*zichen*) so as to trigger their own awakening.
He continued in this until the very roots of his doubt were completely uprooted.

Nevertheless, as the principles of loyalty and filial piety toward sovereign and parent are of paramount importance, he would invariably pay his respects upon entering a Buddha hall to see the "Ten-Thousand-Year" tablet, and he would invariably raise his hands to his forehead before reading the imperial calendar. Thus it was with the Master in Yangxian.
While casually reading the *Changsha Zhi*, I saw the account of the loyal minister Li Bei. As the city was on the verge of falling, he did not wish to die at the hands of the rebels;

he bestowed a sword upon his subordinate general, ordering him to slaughter his entire family. The subordinate general wept bitterly as he received the command, and having applied the blade, he then took his own life.
When the Master reached this point, tears gushed forth directly from his eyes. A disciple was attending by his side.
The man did not weep. The Master rebuked him, saying, "I shall push you down over a cliff! His loyalty and righteousness were moving in this manner.
The Master possessed a majestic spirit and a robust physique, yet his countenance was stern and cold; his heart, however, was most compassionate.
He did not employ ordinary sentiments as the standard for receiving others; he sought out people like a hawk seizing a rabbit, desiring to give birth to [awaken] them the moment he saw them.
He captured them. Thus, whenever anyone entered his room without attaining harmony with him, his heart grew all the more compassionate while their resentment deepened;

beneath a single blow, he sought only to sever their life-root instantly. Therefore, those who drew near to him were rare. Whether in desolation or in warmth, the Master truly possessed these qualities.
By nature the Master was fond of mountains and waters; throughout his life he moved like clouds and birds, possessing nothing beyond a single robe. There was no other.
Dwelling on the ground of steadfastness, he observed that the Chan lineage of the Southern School had fallen into decline.

Desiring to seek out the机缘 (ji-yuan—critical encounters) of the various venerable masters from the beginning of the dynasty to continue the *Lamp of the Dharma*, he was unable to fulfill his original vow.
Carrying this resolve with him, he set forth. Alas! How could the Master be an ordinary man? His realization was direct, unimpeded, stable, and profound. It should...

He emulated the ancients of old; his compassionate vows to benefit sentient beings and his vast protection of the Triple Gem made him what is called a Great Being (Mahāsattva) of the Response Body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
I once wrote a letter in response to an old friend who asked what kind of person this Master was. I replied:
"In the Age of True Dharma, Linji and Deshan might have been dispensed with, but in the Age of Decline, we cannot do without this elder. This Master often lamented the five houses [of Chan].

The fundamental principles have not flourished; [the Master] constantly held this up to show others. I have often sighed, saying: "If the fundamental principles do not flourish, what will become of the life-force of wisdom?
Tracing back to the Cao-Dong school, they exclusively maintained the Shaolin tradition. The circular diagrams (yuanxiang) of the Guiyang school had long been obscured.
As for the Yunmen school, after Han Daobei, it has been difficult to find anyone worthy of its lineage. Only the Fayan school was greatly flourishing.
During the Yongming era, it subsequently flowed into Goryeo; however, only the Linji lineage spread throughout the world.
Reaching the Song dynasty, Dahui revitalized its teachings.
Furthermore, from the founding of our own country, masters such as Chushik and Munam transmitted them, until the end of the Hongje and Jeongdo reigns, when there appeared the master Jigwan.
The regulations established by his former master, Master Yungu, still survive. Yet, for some fifty years now, the lion’s lute has fallen silent.
Recently, there have been those whose sitting cushions remain unsteady and whose true eye remains unclarified, yet they arrogantly claim to be the several dozen generations of the Linji lineage.
Alas! That demons and devils should thus disrupt the Dharma—is this not tragic?
From my own perspective as a teacher, [this master] is fully capable of tracing his lineage far back to Linji and ascending to inherit the tradition of Dahui.
However, as he belongs to a school that has no prior masters, I have not dared to make such a bold attribution.

If we rely on the Way of Yao and Shun, which was transmitted to Confucius and Mencius—after Mencius died, the transmission was lost until the two Cheng brothers of the Song dynasty directly continued its pulse. By this same logic...
This serves as proof that the Master did not fail his duty as a true son of the Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin).
I have recorded these general outlines here to await future masters of clear vision; let those who continue the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Transmission of the Lamp) gather them therein.

Since the Master had not yet appeared in the world, there are no records of his formal ascending to the hall (*shang tang*), general discourses (*pushe*), or instructions to the assembly (*shizhong*); however, I have compiled what remains from the机缘 (jiyuan—opportunities for inquiry and response).
[The Master] showed [the manuscript]. His disciples compiled it; there are several volumes of the collection, which have been carved into woodblocks and circulated in the world.

Among his disciples who entered the inner chamber, both monastics and laypeople were very numerous, and among them, officials and lay practitioners (*upāsaka*) were especially many. The Master’s life and conduct cannot be recorded in full;
there is a separate biography. Therefore, I have composed this inscription for him. The inscription says:
Before the Buddha appeared in the world, and before the Patriarch came from the West—who was it that struck the drum of lethal poison?
At Vulture Peak, the flower was held up; at Shaoshi, the wall was faced. These were merely called "expedient means," yet they resulted only in disorder. At midnight at Huangmei—
Old Lu stole away; who would have thought that in Lingnan there was such a wild barbarian?
At Nanyue and Qingyuan, what a lot of foolish people were deceived by these fellows who wipe away their own pus and snot! Five houses, swift-handed as they play the zither of Shun.
The southern breeze suddenly arrives; those who discern know its sound. The children and grandchildren are fierce and hot-tempered; whoever touches them perishes first.
If you grant but a single thread of leniency, the family will prosper forever. The household stands alone and solitary; life hangs by a single thread. If there is one who can save it—
He is certainly the legitimate son. Like Zhang Liang of the Han, who sought vengeance for the state of Han; even though the kingdom was destroyed, the ancestral line could still be restored.
This man gave birth to my teacher; like a bamboo shoot bursting from a stone, once it emerges, it soars toward the heavens—who would know its origin?
He fought for the Dharma with such vigor that his entire body was drenched in blood, much like Li Ling. Though empty-handed, he remained undaunted;
though his body fell captive to the enemy, his mind did not perish. After a thousand years, he shall ultimately return to the King. You must take this as your adamantine resolve.
All have been transformed into bones, filling the void of space; how could they remain at the foot of this mountain? You, Master, do not know me;
who then shall know you? In one death and one birth, spring resides within the flower branches.
Written on the first day of the month of Jia in the forty-fourth year of the Wanli era,
by the mountain-dwelling śramaṇa Deqing of Haiyin, who humbly received these instructions; prostrations.
The Memorial Inscription:
In the forty-fourth year of the Wanli era, the cyclical year being Bingchen, on the tenth day of the eleventh month, the first day of which was Gengzi. Beyond this...

On the ninth day, Bingxu, the former Sha-men Haiyin, humbled himself by requesting the virtue of Deqing to respectfully present an offering from the Gandharva’s Kitchen (Xiangji) to offer a sacrifice to the spirit of the Venerable Zibo and the Great Master Daguan, saying: "Alas! Regarding the birth of our Master..."
He was born by the power of his vows and has come here. At the Master’s death, he did not die; he departed in accordance with liberation.
His coming and going do not fall within the realm of ordinary sentiment; how could birth and death be the same as worldly truth?
During the Master’s stay in this world, he maintained the adamantine mind and sat upon the firm ground for over thirty years. Amidst the daily meals of the household, his backbone remained pure.
Steel. One thousand seven hundred cases. Withered old vines. Residual mucus from the nostrils. Overthrowing Maitreya and Śākyamuni, he did not yield to Deshan or Linji.
In his dealings with others, he exhausted all compassion; in responding to the moment, he was utterly without inhibition.
He vowed to protect the Dharma as if guarding his own eyes, and sought the Great Matter as if mourning a deceased parent. He did not conform to the world...
The harmony of mind and circumstances is itself the true practice. He sat serenely amidst the moonlight upon the water and walked alone within the shadows of flowers in the void.
When he first visited me at the Eastern Sea, he immediately cast off his physical form;
when we met again at the Western Mountain, he had thoroughly exhausted the very marrow of his bones. Even before my misfortune had taken shape, he informed me of it in full detail.
Regarding these hidden and subtle matters, now that my objections have been raised, you intend to clear my name and fulfill our long-standing agreement at Caoxi.

You would then proceed to knock at the palace gates in the imperial capital, braving the scorching heat upon the road while watching for signs of approval to determine whether to advance or retreat; thus, you have established this method.
By various means, you hoped to deliver me from the nine deaths. Alas! In your role as a Dharma teacher, you truly harbored the hearts of Cheng Ying and Chu Ji;
in your being a true friend, you were surely beyond the comparison of Guan Zhong and Bao Shuya, or Chen Lin and Lei Hu.
I am deeply indebted to you.
The imperial benevolence is slight in its punishment, yet the Master’s heart remains unyielding. While I was exiled to the southern borders, the Master waited for me upon the river isles.
At our first meeting, our joy was as if we had returned to life, like rising again from the Nine Original Plains.
As I bid my Master eternal farewell, I would willingly become a restless spirit in this torrid land. The Master entrusted me with his charge:
With my will stilled, I hope that the dark door shall open once more. As I wipe away my tears and face the long road ahead, the Master takes my hand, filled with sorrow and remaining silent.
At this moment, separated by mountains and passes, days and months pass like arrows;
though I know in my heart that the Master does not forget me, he repeatedly urges me with earnest instructions, saying, "Do not [grieve]," for he wishes—
Supported by this power, I vow never to betray my original source. Thus, I withdraw the radiant flames of the Great Aśoka sword, refusing to cast my body among the dregs of the mundane world.
Hoping for the absolute sincerity of the He-bi jade, I do not begrudge the easy sacrifice of the Sui-zhu pearl. I shall now strike—
The gates of the sovereign’s court are ninefold deep; suddenly, a gale arises from all sides. Land and sea surge with waves; dragons and snakes scatter in disarray.
Jade and stone are burned together; the banner of the Dharma collapses. The Master ascends the broad highway of the Eightfold Path.

Suddenly encountering a long serpent and a great boar, the August Heaven truly beholds his inner sincerity; yet it sees only the indulgence of the vulgar and base. Fortunate that this heart remains pure, I shall briefly unfold its hidden depths.
You, Master, are truly vast and open—what cause for worry or joy? Whether encountering the adverse or the favorable, follow along as they come.
It was fitting. He played with life and death as if in sport. Why did the traces of past burdens follow him so closely? Truly, prior karmic conditions were indeed firm.
The Master grieved that the five turbidities were unbearable; he relied solely upon the single practice of *ekayāna*.
Then, having rinsed his mouth and sat in the lotus posture, he passed away into stillness. Alas, how painful! The Master, having already not regarded [this body] as a calamity...
Suffering from the affliction of seeking "serene repose," how could one take coming and going as a matter? Therefore, he cast off his hands and simply walked on, entirely without deliberation.
It was only because the Master took the Vajra as his heart that he left behind this indestructible body.
When my disciple escorted the Master southward and settled at Shuangjing, I heard the news of his passing and my heart was shattered.
Alas! Gazing at the vast expanse of the sky, my tears fall. I long to pay my respects in person at the reliquary chamber, yet I am bound by the shackles of karmic constraints.
I intended to return to life to comfort the spirit of the Master, but suddenly years have passed like the shifting of stars and frost.

It is not that this heart finds temporary peace; rather, it is simply that the conditions for such a meeting were not granted to me. Recently, however, I have fortunately been able to fulfill my original aspiration.
Ah! Only now have I been able to arrange my words and offer this eulogy. Alas, how painful it is! Why has the Master died while I remain alive?
Because I did not come, the Master could not find peace. Though our physical forms are different, we share this same heart. Though separated by the realm of darkness, we shall ultimately be united.
We vow to return together and fulfill our profound covenant. In the radiant light of the silent illumination, the Master dwells in peace.
I prostrate, expressing my sorrowful longing; I present incense from the Accumulated Fragrance and sprinkle nectar.
Master, as you respond to the occasion, I pray that you will come. Your radiance shines forth; with uplifted devotion, I wait expectantly. Alas! May you partake of this offering.
Raising the flame-nature: fire is true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is true fire. Meeting on a narrow path, there is surely no place to hide.
I pay my respects to the Venerable Master Zibo and the Great Monk Daguan. You have come to the human world by chance and, by error, fallen into the mundane realm. With naked strength...
With power, he strips away the cloth shirt of his natural birth; it shines brilliantly, revealing his original face.
Shouldering the True Dharma, his shoulders are forged from pure steel; acting thoroughly for the sake of others, his liver and gall are cast from raw iron.
On the path of birth and death, one goes straight ahead and comes straight back. At the gateway of the present moment, it is half-open and half-closed.
For over sixty years, my breast has held the spirit of pines, waters, wind, and moon; for seventeen hundred cases, I have used the rabbit’s horn and tortoise hair as a staff.
"Even if he were to be as elegant as possible in the end, he could not avoid hiding his head and showing his tail.

Having left behind his private spoils, who would have thought they would fall into the hands of this monk from Mount Han? Today, before this assembly of humans and devas, I shall bring them forth openly.
Does the great assembly see them? (With a torch, he draws a circle and says: "The staff lifts open the clouds of the Double Peak."
A treasury of radiance surges forth from his entire body; I urge you all to look with eyes of deep attention. Only now do I truly believe there are no obstructions.
In Praise of the Stupa Containing the Sarīra Relics of the Great Master Zibo, with Preface.
All religions do not depart from the verses of the Seven Buddhas as their fundamental origin. The verse of Viśvabhū Buddha says:
"The body is borrowed from the four great elements; the mind is originally unborn, arising only because of objects.

This half-verse alone already encompasses the Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of the canon, the five thousand and forty-eight volumes, and the seventeen hundred cases of entanglement—all filling one's mouth.
The Way emerges; there is nothing further to conceal. Those who awaken to it are called Chan Patriarchs; those who realize it attain the fruit of the Tathāgata.
Master Zibo held this half-verse and universally sealed the various kinds of minds of sentient beings.

For forty years, his side did not touch his mat, and his hand never ceased its movement. For beginners, he discoursed on the meaning of *dharmalakṣaṇa*; for those of long-standing practice, he opened [the way].
The Gate of Prajñā. For the sake of those with sharp faculties, it points toward the mind of nirvāṇa and reveals the treasury of the *dharmadhātu*.
At times, it thunders like a clap of lightning, severing all currents; at other times, it wades through water and drags through mud, with all four wheels firmly planted upon the ground.

Responding to conditions according to the capacity of beings, it has never produced even half a verse within the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) that is as sharp as the point of a needle. Thus did my Dharma friend, Master Hanshan, say: "I uphold..."
Regarding this verse: having already attained half a line which manifested before him, he further attained the remaining half-line, attaining clear and constant awareness.

He declared that his lifelong pursuit of study was complete. More than ten years later, by the power of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and the power of his roots of goodness, he moved freely and at ease through the mountains of blades and peaks of swords;
with his supernatural powers and the residual influence of his precepts and meditative concentration, his physical body remained unimpaired. This is possible.

This refers to the merging of emptiness and the provisional, where mind and object are of one suchness. Using the sensory faculties and their objects—dusts analyzed from the four great elements—he expounds the wondrous intent of the half-verse of the Double Mystery.
With his *vibhu* tongue, he covers the three thousandfold world system; both the Dharma upheld and the upholder are simultaneously quiescent.

Who would say that the Master was not an emanation sent by the Seven Buddhas? Guangyue beheld his countenance yet was stingy with the conditions for it; hearing his name, one plants the seeds [of liberation].

Matured. Your pure and clear instructions have been privately studied by me for many years. In the middle month of autumn in the year of Jiayin, I completed my studies of your bequeathed teachings, which further increased my hearing and reflection.
Although I had no leisure to look up as the waters swirled and the waves surged, the royal seal was in my hand and the handle of the Dipper pointed toward heaven;

thus, whether in the practice of dissemination or the realization of perfect fusion, there was nothing that did not dissolve back into this half-verse. My only regret is that I have not yet been able to use this half-verse to dissolve into the stillness of dry meditation (*kucan*).

Returning to myself, I have long been a destitute son, failing to repay the compassionate heart [of my teacher]. I have composed these verses as a modest offering to fill the stūpa—a most inferior gift.

Beneath the Seven Golden Mountains, there is the marvel of feathers and down sharing the same color; from the tip of the tongue of the Two-footed One, the taste of poison is transformed into the flavor of *amṛta*.
By this root of goodness, may it be self-infused to form a seed, so that in some future life or subsequent world, [I may not...]
"O Master of the Half-Gāthā, your eyebrows have fallen to the ground! The verse says:
The four elements are both provisional and real; Mind and objects are neither two nor one.
When the duality of both is transcended, even oneness perishes; Awakening to the provisional, one realizes that the Real is all-pervasive.
Hair, body hair, nails, teeth, as well as mucus and saliva, The warmth, the movements, and all the floating sense organs— I declare these to be the Vajra King;
Illusory transformations and empty bodies are all the true mark.
Earth, water, fire, and wind combine and aggregate; Brightness and darkness, form and emptiness, depend upon one another and shift.
The conscious mind absorbs and gathers the traces upon the mirror; if one part is deficient, there can never be two.
The ten directions and the three periods of time are fundamentally void and mysterious; without form, without name, and without limit, they enter into a single mote of dust at all times and places.
Half a verse, layer upon layer, forms a celestial net (*indrajāla*).
Zi-ber attained this gate of samādhi; From Great Nirvāṇa he manifested in the realm of birth and death, Proclaiming half a verse with the light of his mouth.
The wind-swept forest and the walls all resounded with thunderous sound;
Like pouring from a jar, clouds of word-dhyāna arose, And from every single pore of every sentient being, he roared.
He departed, proclaiming half a verse with the light of his body;
He played amidst the eternal and the impermanent, fully understanding that what is a mere composite is itself solid. Within this skin-sack, the kalpa-fire is ever tranquil;
Moving through coming and going in both direct and reverse order, he enters the dreams of others' minds to awaken them from their dreaming.
Compassion and wisdom intermingled within Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya; The half-verse was expounded without remainder.
Majestic is the stupa at Mount Shuangjing; Within it the Master sat, preaching the Buddha’s verses with blazing intensity.
The Master is the verse, and the verse is the Master; They pervade the thoughts and minds of all sentient beings.
From these neglected remains, I have obtained the crest-jewel; Without traversing a hundred cities, I have upheld it as an offering.
The transmission of half a verse from the Master was followed by the transmission of the robe; All Tathāgatas share the same nostrils.
On the seventh day of the final autumn month of the Bingchen year of the Wanli era, I, Wu Guangyue—an upāsaka and humble disciple who studies in private at Xuanzhou—[record this].
Yingbin bows respectfully and humbly composes this preface to the *Record of Sayings from the Meditation Cell* of the Elder Zibo.

The *Record of Sayings from the Meditation Cell* is a compilation of the words spoken by the Dharma Master Zibo while he resided within his meditation cell. As for the compiler of these words, it is the youth Wu of Western Zhejiang.

This is Yanxian. Yanxian is a Confucian scholar; why does he harbor such admiration for this [Buddhism]? We Confucians take Kongzi and Mengzi as our masters, and we repeatedly speak of "expelling" (pí) Buddhism and Daoism. This is not because we hate their teachings as being entirely wrong, but because we hate those who are immersed in what is wrong, leading one another to the point of destroying human relations and violating the Way. If [these teachings] can indeed assist the spiritual nature, broaden learning and insight, and supplement what our sagely teachings do not cover— The provided text ends abruptly. A complete translation would require the remainder of the passage. However, based on the fragment, the translation is as follows: ...then there is no reason to reject them. Yanxian’s intent is likely similar to this. As for the Master [Huiyuan], his purpose was to clarify the principles of our own school and to refute those who slander it. He did not seek to destroy the Buddha, but rather to protect the Dharma. If one examines the words of Yanxian and the Master, they are both consistent with the intent of the sages. How could they be considered heterodox? If one were to say that Yanxian and the Master were heterodox, then all the sages of the past would likewise be heterodox. If one were to say that the sages of the past were heterodox, then how could one possibly avoid being a heterodox person oneself? Therefore, I say: the principles of the sages are one; the Way of the Buddhas is also one. It is only when people are deluded that they create distinctions between them. If one can understand this, then the two teachings will naturally harmonize.

If one cannot, then even if one studies extensively, one will only end up increasing one's confusion. Thus, I have written this to inform those who are confused. May those who possess wisdom examine it and judge it for themselves. I am merely a humble person of the present day, seeking only to follow the path of the ancients. What fault could there be in this? I hope you will not consider me a heterodox person. I humbly submit this. Your disciple, Liu Xiaobiao, respectfully addresses you. (Note: The final sentence is a standard closing formula used by Liu Xiaobiao in his correspondence.)
The word "and" (*ji*) refers to the words of actors and widows, as well as the transformations of insects, plants, and trees; there is nothing that does not participate in the Way (*dào*).
Officials of minor bureaus (*bàiguān*) and scholars (*bōshì*) often did not discard such matters, even collecting them from folk songs to provide for study and observation.

How much more so for our Confucians, who compete with the two other schools (Buddhism and Daoism) and stand as a trinity in the present age! Formerly, Han Changli was hailed as a great Confucian scholar of his time.
He forcefully rejected divergent views; his essay "On the Origin of the Way" (*Yuandao*) is truly majestic, vying with the sun and moon in its brilliance.
Yet, when he resided in Chao, he sent several scrolls of letters to Dadian, even leaving behind inscriptions and garments—how inconsistent this is!
Those for whom he held such disapproval were not those who had fallen into heterodoxy; those whom he approved of were those who approximated the correct path.

Therefore, it is said that only one who is thoroughly versed in Confucianism may be discussed with regarding Buddhism and Daoism. The man known as the Purple Cypress Hermit (Zibai Daoren) had the style name Daguan.

Having lost his parents at an early age, he entered the monastic life at twenty. Being illiterate, he practiced *zhi chan* (seated meditation) for three years, engaging in ascetic practices and observing the precepts.

One day, he attained sudden enlightenment; consequently, the Buddhist scriptures and secular classics became perfectly clear to him. He traveled extensively throughout the land, resting [only] on his side...
For thirty years he did not attend formal banquets. His countenance was like that of Maitreya; his mind was like a cold, clear pool; his voice was like a great bell;

and his eloquence was like a cascading river. His tranquil wisdom was profound and luminous, and his fame eclipsed all within the realm. Even those of high rank and noble status always bowed their heads and humbled themselves before him.
This man of the Way possesses great compassion within and strictly observes the precepts without. It is said that he is like the venerable master Linji appearing once more;
toward people, regardless of whether they are noble or humble, great or small, he maintains a mind of equanimity.

Thus, the humble and the small rejoice in his welcoming presence, while the noble and the great perceive him as arrogant. Those who find the gateway and enter it all take refuge in him; those who do not... [cannot].
Those who entered through his gate were frequently subjected to his refutations and criticisms; thus did the Master gain his reputation, yet it was also for this that he incurred misfortune.
The Master himself claimed that a sense of righteousness and destiny resided therein. I know not whether he possessed fame or substance, nor do I know whether he encountered fortune or calamity;
this may serve as a general summary of his life. In the year Gengzi, the Master Yuzhi and Nan...

Nankangzi and I were detained together at Futang. We engaged in leisurely discussions on renowned principles. Nankangzi delighted in reciting Buddhist scriptures, whereas I alone did not delight in reciting them;
I would often mock him, saying: "Is the mind itself the Buddha? Or is the mouth itself the Buddha?

Although Nankangzi had never met a Daoist master face-to-face, his heart held the masters in profound reverence, and he frequently exchanged letters with them. He once presented me with one of their writings.
Yinzan showed this to the two of us, and we composed verses in response to one another. The Daoist felt it resonated with his mind;
consequently, Liaojiezi sent tea to me and presented me with a half-verse. I composed a verse in return, and he further wrote for me the "Record of the Stone Buddha Crossing the Sea."
In every word, he clarified the mind and revealed the nature. He further presented four verses on tea, fans, incense, and flowers, each with its own response and exchange.
I regretted that we could not meet once to satisfy my long-cherished wish. Before long, false rumors were fabricated and a great persecution arose;

it spread among the virtuous, causing both the central government and the provinces to tremble with fear. The Master was also unjustly implicated and brought before the law. Alas, the two of us were unfortunate to have met so late in life.
When the practitioner was being interrogated, his countenance remained composed and his principles were most upright. With this aged and infirm body, he endured every form of flogging and torture;
until death, he did not yield, possessing the spirit of a true hero. At that time, the weather was bitterly cold, yet the practitioner was both freezing and starving.
I gave him a bowl of rice, a rush mat, and a patched robe. Day and night, the practitioner sat in the full lotus posture without sleeping, surrounded by a casket of accumulated [relics].

As for those who are bound [by worldly ties], he would engage them; according to the person’s capacity for enlightenment, his every interaction was aimed at guiding them toward goodness. He did not employ hollow talk or illusory words to delude others.
It is fitting that the worthy and eminent men of the age should take great pleasure in associating with him extensively. On the fifth day of the twelfth month of the Gui-mao year, he entered prison.
On the seventeenth day, he passed away while sitting peacefully without illness. His lifespan was but sixty-one years. Prior to this, the practitioner...

He bestowed verses upon Yanxian. If he had foreknowledge that his transformation [death] was imminent, he further discussed with me the chapter on "Hearing the Way at Dawn," reaching profound states of liberation.
On the day of his transformation, he recited several verses. At the fifth watch of the night, he told people that he would enter parinirvāṇa.
No one understood. At dawn, when the door opened, he called for Jiang to rinse his mouth and made the sound of reciting the Buddha’s name.
He went out and sat on the ground; the assembly was startled and helped him onto a couch. He closed his eyes and remained silent. The assembly ran to report, "The practitioner has passed away.
When I went to see him, he called out loudly, "It is well that the practitioner has departed! Do you remember? The practitioner then opened his eyes and looked at me. From—
He opened his hands and supported both feet, sitting in the full lotus posture until he passed away. They carried him out to an open space, where he remained for six days and nights.

Though buffeted by whirlwinds and exposed to the sun, shrouded in shadows and struck by severe frost, and subjected to flying sand and falling filth that caused him to crumble and break in every way, he sat upright and composed.

His spirit was radiant and brilliant, manifesting a state of luminosity. Among those of us within the enclosure, there was none who did not witness this with their own eyes and marvel at it; we all burned incense and prostrated ourselves in worship.
The Buddha’s voice was resonant and vast. When he was interred within an earthen pit, seven months passed;

when his remains were exhumed and moved southward, his illusory body remained as if alive, uncorrupted—a marvel never before seen in the world. This was personally witnessed by Lu Xi-yuan of Ping-hu. Alas, how extraordinary!
Was it that the Great Spirit (Juling) protected him, or did the Master himself possess a divine power of self-protection? [Signed by] a scholar of Jiangnan, [Name Redacted].

Tang praised his divine anomalies and had a niche carved to enshrine his remains, returning them for burial at the mountain temple he had originally founded. When the practitioner was imprisoned, Yanxian attended him with unremitting devotion from beginning to end.
He further transcribed by hand the dialogues and verses exchanged within the prison and presented them to those who had been his former associates.
Yanxian claimed that he shared a karmic affinity with the practitioner from a previous life and requested a word from me to commemorate this. I, for my part, reflect upon the Buddha’s teaching:
He did not rely on written words. This record is insufficient to determine whether this person exists or not. Regarding the great matter of birth and death, he had foreknowledge of its causes;
at the time of his passing, his nature remained undisturbed and his body remained uncorrupted. His traces are clearly manifest, and his spiritual wonders are such as these.
This is not something that can be attained through practice in a single lifetime, nor could it ever be approximated even in its slightest degree by the monastics of this degenerate age.
Recorded by Yu Zhizi Cao Xuecheng of Xiangyuan,
as the Elder Zibo spoke within his circular prison cell to the monastic community of Tanzhe Temple.

Water causes moisture to dry out; mountains collapse due to their height. These things are brought about by causes. To bring merit leads to calamity; to commit evil leads to auspiciousness—what is the cause of this?
It arises from one's own many past lives; it is simply that ordinary people do not perceive it. I am old and frail, yet I have come out of the mountains and the mountain gate remains unharmed.
I wish not to wait for an invitation, so I shall go there first. They will surely burden you with other matters; wait for now.
Do not be alarmed when you encounter such circumstances; this is because the causes do not belong to you. Even a snowstorm and cold wind in a thatched hut are not unpleasant;
the boiling cauldrons and burning coals, the agonizing screams of suffering—all are entirely the samādhi of mental delight.
If you do not believe me, test it for yourself upon my deathbed.
Having been arrested, I replied to my patrons:

"Now that I have been taken into custody, there are those among the worldly scholars and the clever who, filled with indignation, said to me: 'The Master has grown weary of and sought transcendence from the realm of dust;

you ought to have been carefree and free from entanglements. Why, then, have you encountered these official charges? You still linger with longing for the capital, leading to this present situation.'"
"Is it not painful? [The Master] replied, "Lay brother, what do you consider to be the realm of dust, and what do you consider to be suffering?
In deep mountains and vast marshes dwell tigers, leopards, dragons, and snakes; these serpents and beasts have never failed to cause pain to people.
Yet, those who probe the abyss obtain pearls, and those who quarry the mountains acquire jade. This is because they see the profit in the pearls and jade, and thus they are unaware of the danger."
[They are like] dragons, snakes, tigers, and leopards. We Mahāyāna śramaṇas take the salvation of others as our task;

we venture into hardships to provide rescue, so how could we know that the dust and toil [of saṃsāra] can be escaped? The unsurpassed great treasure was lost to the impoverished son, who has now spent vast kalpas in pursuit of it;
how could he have known that his [original] portion was precious? My only concern is that the parable of the jewel in the garment has not yet been understood.
I do not worry about my clothes changing frequently. I have used this understanding to liberate my physical shell;
how could it be merely about liberating myself from foul-smelling, tattered rags? The pearl within my inner garment is not obtained from without. What suffering is there?
When you, donor, speak of suffering, it is different from the kind of suffering I experience.
While conversing with Official Cao at night, Official Cao cited Su Shi’s *Eulogy on the Arhat*: "The right hand holds a staff, the left hand strokes a rock.
Is it the hand that holds the staff, or the staff that holds the hand? Sitting in repose upon the rock, what use is there for a staff? This is the use of the useless. Worldly...
No one knew [the meaning]. The Venerable One said: "The pivot for entering the Way—when the pivot penetrates the subtle, and the subtle is penetrated, then both the hand and the staff are abandoned.
Therefore it is said: 'Leaving the subtle to enter the Way' is the true pivot. Zhizhi said: "Dongpo, Dongpo! What about the hand and the staff?
Sometimes they are used; sometimes they are discarded. Why do you ask? The Venerable One said: "To support the heavens and prop up the earth."
"First one uses the hook of desire to lead them forward, and later causes them to enter the Buddha-wisdom. This is what Vimalakīrti taught. "Plan for the difficult while it is still easy;
act for the great while it is still small. This is what Laozi taught. Using these two teachings as a ball upon which to reflect, if one observes why they are so, it does not go beyond this:
the Perfect Man’s illumination is complete, while the common person’s illumination is partial. Being partial leads to stagnation; being complete leads to freedom.
Then there is penetration (*tong*). Once it is called penetration, then regardless of whether matters are great or small, or principles are shallow or deep, as sounds enter, the mind penetrates;
what room is there for doubt? Nevertheless, the penetration of principle begins with the examination of names (*ming*). Therefore, if names are not examined, reality (*shi*) cannot be attained.
If reality is not attained, the meaning (*yi*) will not be refined. If the meaning is not refined, the principle cannot be fully exhausted. If the principle is not...
If one is in such a state of exhaustion, how can the study of nature and destiny (xing-ming) possibly find entry? Therefore, those who aspire to the study of nature and destiny,
if they do not know how to value themselves and allow the desires for food, drink, and sexual union to disturb their true essence,
then even worldly fame, achievement, and enterprise will not come to them at all— how much less that which is greater than these?

(Gengzi year of the Wanli era, the Master sent this from Yuanshan to Zhongkangzi. The inscription for the Stone Buddha of Suzhou reads: "The prison cell is named the Hall of Blessings; examine the name and its reality, and you will understand it clearly for yourself. Through suffering, awakening-insight arises; once awakened, self and others are forgotten.
What is now being discussed seems to be a reiteration of this same meaning. Recorded by the disciple Li Lin.)
To Ruyuan Xian:

Observe that the arising of fame and profit is not without its foundation. If one contemplates the body through the four great elements and contemplates the mind through the objects before one, then how would the body and mind differ from the sprout of a scorched seed or the son of a barren woman? It is because the multitude do not know this.
Contemplate this: if one is not intoxicated by fame, then one is intoxicated by profit. Yet one does not realize that by relying on fame and profit, one should look back upon the body and mind;
and by relying on the body and mind, one should look back further upon what precedes the body and mind—is it fame? Is it profit? Or is it the body?
"Is it the mind? I cannot know. I showed this to the literary scholar Chou of Yingzhou, who exclaimed, 'Alas!
Why do you sleep? You creatures of the snail, the mussel, and the clam—sleeping for a thousand years, never hearing the name of the Buddha.'"
This verse was spoken by Śākyamuni for his disciple Aniruddha while he was listening to the sutra;
it was taught to awaken him from his drowsiness and lethargy as his eyes grew heavy with sleep. Alas! Among the five desires, none is more weighty than sleep.

Thus, when one is overcome by deep slumber, even if West Lake’s Xi Shi were to press her lips against one’s own, or the spring thunder were to roar from the earth, one would not know what sound or form they are.
Now, sound and form are the common objects of habitual experience for all people.

Yet when one is asleep and sound and form present themselves before them, there are those who do not see with their eyes and those who do not hear with their ears. Viewed from this perspective, the intoxication of sleep and alcohol is far more pervasive than other forms of intoxication.
Therefore it is said: "If the demon of darkness is not severed, the demons of distraction will gather without being summoned. This is because...
Obscurity and dissipation must both be rooted in thought; thought is rooted in sensation. Knowing that thought is rooted in sensation, one realizes that thought is fundamentally without self.
Since the self is non-existent, who is it that receives sensations? To know this belongs to contemplation (*guan*); to have no recipient belongs to stillness (*zhi*).

Contemplation is sufficient to cast out obscurity; stillness is sufficient to purge dissipation. When obscurity is cast out, there is clarity; when dissipation is purged, there is tranquility. Clarity and tranquility inherently possess [the Way].

This is the nature’s virtue (*xing-de*). When nature transforms into emotion (*qing*), obscuration and distraction arise. If this is so, then clarity is not inherently possessed, and thus obscuration has no source;
stillness is not inherently possessed, and thus distraction has no ground. The multitude do not realize that they treat obscuration/distraction and clarity/stillness as two separate things;
for this reason, the restoration of emotion to nature ultimately remains difficult to achieve.

He cautioned the assembly of ball-players, saying: "One must not neglect the present moment. To neglect it for even a moment is to darken the mind; if the mind is darkened, what task will not be neglected?
From negligence arises indolence, and once the habit of indolence grows, the vital energy (*qi*) becomes the master and the mind becomes its slave. Therefore, he [instructed them] regarding sleep.
"Tasting the gallwood" is not a hollow precept; it was said because Goujian could do it, whereas I cannot, failing to know how to value myself.
If one knew how to value oneself, then heaven, earth, and the myriad things would all be secondary, while the self would be the primary essence.

Nevertheless, once the nature has changed into emotion, one spontaneously moves from being independent to being dependent. When one is dependent, the distinction between "thing" and "self" becomes prominent. If one follows this habit...
Joy arises from favorable conditions, while anger arises from adverse ones; when these emotions predominate, the fundamental nature becomes obscured.
The nature, however, is such that its wisdom encompasses all things without toil, and its form fills the eight directions without entanglement. Thus, it is able to unify all things within itself.

When one is unified with all things, there is nothing external to oneself, and outside of things, there is no self. Because there is no self outside of things, the functioning of the self is simply the functioning of things.

Since there is nothing external to oneself, the functioning of things is itself the functioning of oneself. Thus, knowledge is all-pervasive without toil, and the physical form is full without entanglement.

What cause for doubt remains? The Scripture further states: "If one can transform things, one is identical to the Tathāgata. Judging by this, when I am able to transform things, I am called the Tathāgata;
when I am transformed by things, I am called the Tathāgata-gata (the Thus-Gone). The Tathāgata-gata is precisely the multitude [of beings].
Man is a human being. The Tathāgata is the Sage among humans. The Sage is without self and is spiritual; the ordinary person possesses a self and is deluded.
To be deluded is to neglect the present moment. One who neglects the present moment does not grieve deeply, does not contemplate far-reaching matters, and fails to know how to value themselves.
Man is the most spiritual of all things; yet, if one does not know how to value oneself, what more can be said of "Piqiu"? (The Master’s pen-name was Piqiu.)
On the twenty-ninth day of the eleventh month, I was arrested and separated from Tanzhe Temple.
A verse: A cold pond and ancient *zhè* trees reflect the blue lotus; The wild elder has wandered here for thirty years.
Leaving this verse as we part, I charge through the snow to depart, Seeking to ride the crisp air and break through the profound mystery.
A Verse on Leaving Tanzhe to Show the Assembly of Monks:
The old fellow Daguan is going out of the mountains; The Chan practitioners within the hall may set their minds at ease. Upon their heads is the Heaven’s Open True Eye;
In the moment of action, fortune and calamity are both prior causes.

On the fifth day of the first lunar month, passing from the Imperial Guard (Jin-yi-wei) through the Ministry of Punishments (Xing-bu), a great merchant burst into the Hall of Blessings (Fu-tang). How many fish and dragons have changed their bones and wombs!
Amidst the terrifying sea, they sleep soundly once more; yet with a sudden turn, there comes a clap of thunder.
Hearing the watchman’s rattle, King Ajātaśatru suddenly questioned the Dharma; he had previously thought that as he gazed at the river, he saw no change.
Now, with my faculty of sight listening to the night watch, I cast aside the thick veil of ignorance and feel even more profoundly clear.

The sound of the wooden clapper has not ceased when the sound of the bell continues. Who is the sound, and who is the listener? Recalling the tolling of the bells and drums in the Dharma Hall, one finds that from ancient times, the realm of dreams and spirits has been ever more chaotic.
Together with Attendant Cáo and various literary scholars, we gathered for a night talk with Wú Yànxian on the White Dharma (Buddhism).

As we dissected the subtlest particles, emerald waves rose as we swallowed our spittle. What prevents the true from mingling with the mundane? Let us gamble through the deep night, staking both sides.
Upon first glance, it turns out to be an old acquaintance. Why must those of one heart share the same body? Who determines the weight of this burden?
These two eyebrows possess a spirit that is truly remarkable.
Our canopies were tilted together as we grew old, yet we were no two people; it was simply because our divergent thoughts were always of one body.
Between heaven and earth, who is capable of bearing this burden? This person has possessed a single point of spirit from birth. (Cao He)
To Wu Yanxian:
Intellectuals in Jiangnan are separated by wind and dust; how can a solitary figure find intimacy in the shadows?
A single long啸 shatters the empty realm—whom would have known that the "needle and magnet" affinity lay within this wanderer?
A wanderer dares not presume to be entirely without fault; one must recognize that the mechanism of life is itself the mechanism of death.
When one perceives that birth and death are fundamentally one and the same, then wings return to their flight and feet resume their running.

Meeting you, there is no need to inquire into past causes; like a mirror polished free from dust, the myriad phenomena are newly bright. The flowers and fruits of the old garden must surely be flourishing of their own accord;
the sounds of the stream and the hues of the mountains are all pleasing to the spirit.
The sun is three *zhang* high, yet I still sleep soundly; this is far superior to the "nose-contemplation" (*nigan*) Chan of Yunlin. Now I am disturbed awake by the idle monk;
there is no place left for my dream-soul to linger.
I entrust this to you, Fami:
Is Yanluo truly the Commander-in-Chief? Are the fires, cauldrons, ice, and mountains real or not? I ask you, Master Mi, what do you understand?
This wretched body of six feet is but equal to a clump of reeds.
The Verse on the Emptiness of Form for Yang Zhongjuan:
Dwelling in seclusion, you merely accompany the flowers in sleep. Who would say that the spirit of the flowers explains Chan?
Unable to remain within the two barriers of emptiness and form, the spring breeze and the secluded birds grasp the Three Mysteries.
A Verse on Adding Beads to the Rosary:
A single thread passes through one hundred and eight beads; if by chance one bead should fall away, why seek it beyond the phenomenal world?
Simply take that which awakens from delusion and add it back.
On the eleventh day of the twelfth month, I was flogged during the judicial review;

thirty strokes with the bamboo rakes settled my karmic debts from the past. How could the gravity of such a charge even be compared? This pain is for the sake of the Dharma-realm—who can offer it as a memorial?
A single laugh in response fills the great void.
Sitting here, I have often suffered as lice invade my skin; whether the events of those years were real or not, who can say?
One might say that the bamboo comb could cause pain, but try using this withered thigh to support your cross-legged posture.
On the fourteenth day, I heard the verse regarding the proposed sentence:

past karma meets present conditions; surely there is a capacity for faith. From the Lotus Society in the south to the prison cell in the north—should anyone on a distant peak inquire after me, tell them that the Lion of old has truly cast off his robes.
Recalling Master Jie—who could have thought you would go forth braving the cold? There is no divine spirit that pulls the marionette’s strings. Do not speak of posthumous wishes for a long farewell;
instead, skillfully dissect the subtle dust of the present moment.
I recall how Master Zhuo wept last year for those who burned the scriptures; today, as we discuss the sutras, not a single word remains. There is no need to debate good and evil after death;
the samādhi of tranquil light is permitted to be shared by us alike.
On the fifteenth day, the Dharma-administrator adjudicated the case and spoke this verse:

"The origin of the 'Single Smile' has a cause distinct from the ordinary. Who would have known that the Great Mass of Matter cannot tolerate a speck of dust? From now on, I shall gather in my mother-born feet;
the iron stake shall blossom without waiting for spring."
On the sixteenth day, as he approached the end of his life, he spoke this verse:
"Only now, at the moment of transformation, do we see the heroic bones. Did Master Da and Mr. Wu share a karmic affinity from past lives? I shall return to the West while you remain in the North;
our conversations over many lifetimes shall become even more ethereal."
He traveled north and south for thirty years; those of dull faculties still fall behind the point of the arrow. Do not say there is no news from this journey:
on a snowy night, the lotus first blossomed within the fire.
Everyone calls old Da a stirrer of wind and waves; what is this matter of wind and waves today like? Try looking at Old Da again next year:
wind and waves will fill the earth, and he himself will be laughing and humming along.
The twin green peaks of Tan and Zha are but empty talk of dragons; we dwell together in this prison-like retreat with greater ease. When the master returns, the fragrant clouds will grow cold;
it would be well to lie amidst a thousand peaks and ten thousand crags.

I know that illusory bones possess no Buddha-nature; what has been called "stone" from the beginning is entirely hollow and insubstantial. Deep in the night, the cold moon shines upon the gates of Wu;
I cannot help but laugh at Master Sheng as he nodded his head in the dark.
The dark barrier lies silent, its lock difficult to open; that Way-seeking śramaṇa comes through the snow. What prevents a starving rat from partaking in the joy of the Dharma?
Let frozen pus be cast early into the yellow dust.

My lifelong vow has not been easily fulfilled; the vast scriptures lie shrouded in deep darkness. It is no wonder that the Twin Peaks have become like the twin trees under which the Buddha passed away;
the palm-leaf manuscripts gather like clouds as the sun itself withdraws.
When opening the shrine, one must remember the time of closing it; pain and itchiness, life and death—they are but this. There is no need for lingering attachment to Yan and Yun;
this body has been granted to the stone and is permitted to remain as it is.
The mountain ghosts need not be propitiated; how can the water deities be appeased? Amidst withered trees and heavy, cold clouds, I see only the attendant Tianshi.

How could human life suddenly end in death? The dead are the very treasury of the living. What have I heard regarding the gates of Dharma? I entrust them all to the "poison-coated drum" (as known from the prophecy).
I, Shouzi, address the various dharma-heirs and associates in Jiangnan: each of you should firmly maintain your faith.
I am old and weary; we shall not meet again. This is my final farewell. I entrust this to the young monk to hold and show to others. Protect and uphold the Triple Gem.
Regarding the project to carve the Tripitaka at Lingyan and Jingshan: proceed if it is feasible, otherwise desist. The year of Gui Mao.
On the sixteenth day of the twelfth month, this unworthy one has long been engaged with brush and inkstone, traveling in the company of various renowned worthies.

From them, I have heard the widespread renown of the Venerable Zibo’s virtuous influence, regarding him as a great Bodhisattva in human form; yet, I am ultimately ashamed that my own efforts have been as frantic as a galloping horse.

Alas! Within this world, there has been no opportunity to behold the blue lotus beyond the kalpas. In the year of Renyin, Yan was struck by the white indictment and was detained in the prison of the Department of Comparisons.
In the winter of the following year, Gui Mao—

The Sovereign, enraged by a seditious book, launched a great search throughout the land. The Venerable One, whose propagation of the Dharma had incurred suspicion, was likewise implicated in the indictment.
Upon hearing of these troubles, the entire assembly trembled with fear; yet the Master remained composed, speaking and laughing as if all were normal.
He then used the Buddha-dharma to provide analogies for the monks and, with an air of equanimity, departed the mountain to proceed to the imperial prison. Before long, he entered.
Xi Cao Yan was fortunate enough to obtain refuge [in the Master]. Initially, he had heard that the Master was stern and cold, difficult to approach;

yet upon meeting him, he found his deep compassion and universal pity to penetrate to the very marrow of his bones. Yan then lit incense and sought the essential points of the mind, whereupon the Master recited half a verse of the Buddha Vipaśyin:
"Provisionally borrowing the four elements to form a body, The mind is fundamentally unborn, arising only due to objects."

There is. To cause [the student] to recite this for a long time, let us first resolve its essential meaning: This body has no origin; it is a composite formed from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
This mind has no origin; it arises conditioned by preceding objects. If one examines these four great elements and their objects, from what else could they possibly originate?

Ordinary people do not understand the principle that the nature transforms into emotion; following after emotion, they give rise to attachments, and thus the cycle of birth and death becomes vast and boundless.
However, when the Sage uses principle to subdue emotion, the nature (*xing*) returns to its original state. When the nature returns and emotion becomes empty, what birth and death could there be?

Yanwei, it was like hearing thunder in the dead of night; I reflect upon how the ancients sought the Dharma to the point of standing in the snow and cutting off their own arms, yet I, burdened by the sins of an ordinary fool, remained submerged in the prison of delusion, until suddenly I heard that after ten thousand kalpas, I have finally emerged.
The cause of suffering is profound; the grace of the Dharma-milk is deep, such that even sacrificing one’s head and limbs would be insufficient to express gratitude for it.
After the Master had resided in seclusion for a long time, Yan frequently visited him in leisure, along with Cao Zhizhi, Magistrate Shen, and various literary scholars from Yingcheng.

Together they explored the profound mysteries of the nature and destiny of both Confucianism and Buddhism, like the bursting of a river or the flowing of its tributaries, as they spontaneously expounded verses according to the occasion.

He spoke spontaneously as it arose. When he was interrogated, though his body was worn out and decrepit and he endured various forms of torture, all his attendants felt their hearts sink with despair;

yet the Master remained as calm as drifting clouds and still waters, appearing entirely unperturbed by anything. As soon as he entered the prison cell, he would earnestly exhort the assembly on the Buddha-dharma.
Such was his profound concentration and wisdom, standing firm and unshakable like a wall ten thousand fathoms high.
On the full moon of the twelfth month, he joined his palms and recited a verse. He then spoke softly to Yan, saying, "The practitioner is about to depart.

Yan was startled and said, "Does the Master not care for the Dharma and the Way? Does the Master not care for sentient beings? He entreated him earnestly, but the Master looked at him and smiled, saying:
He departed swiftly and arrived swiftly. He immediately sang a song on rebirth for Master He of Zhejiang; however, Yan did not record it because he was in such a state of haste.
Two days later, at dawn, the prison gates opened. The Master hurriedly stepped out of his cell and looked up, saying, "It is the hour of the morning watch.
He then called for ginger tea to cleanse his mouth and sat upon the ground, chanting the name of Vairocana repeatedly.
He uttered the sound "Vairocana Buddha" several times. The assembly was startled and supported him onto his sitting platform, whereupon he closed his eyes.
When Zhizhi heard this, he hurriedly reached the foot of the platform and cried out, "Well done! Do you remember? The Master then cast a subtle glance at Zhizhi;

with hands opened and feet drawn in, he passed away with a sudden, expansive movement. This was precisely at the hour of the Dragon (7–9 a.m. on the seventeenth day. He was carried forth while still seated.
In an open space, exposed to frost, wind, dust, and sand, he suffered various forms of erosion for six days and nights; yet his spiritual radiance overflowed as if he had not yet passed away.
After he emerged from the prison, following the master’s final instruction not to enshroud him, they merely surrounded him with a wicker basket and buried him in the western suburbs.
It happened that during the Jiachen year, the capital was struck by a great flood, and the city gates and walls all collapsed, leaving the four suburbs like [a vast expanse].

The sea. The disciples, mindful that their master was within the vast waters, instructed the attendant Tian to summon those in authority so that they might retrieve the remains to the reliquary stupa.
Li Biyu Xiyuan personally went to inspect the site on the thirteenth day of the first month of autumn;

the earth covering the seven-foot mound had not yet dried, leading him to suspect that the master had perhaps undergone "water-transformation" (dissolution). However, upon breaking the seal, he found the master sitting upright as if alive, unmoving.
He remained unchanging. The entire assembly cried out in unison, exclaiming in wonder at what had never before occurred: "Alas!

Is this not the Great Being of physical form, whose radiance is vast and magnificent, who transcends all categories and measures, and who is inconceivable? Having encountered the Master late in life, I have yet to attain realization within the principles of the essential vehicle (zongcheng).
Day and night I carry the heavens upon my head and tread the earth beneath my feet, yet its height and thickness remain beyond my grasp.
This is beyond the capacity of ordinary knowledge to comprehend. Yet he regards calamities as a mere game and treats birth and death as equal to coming and going.

When he attains nirvana, even his illusory body is not destroyed; yet while he remains for a single breath, though he is exhausted by punishments and torments that do not trouble his mind, he remains earnest and sincere, exhorting and guiding anyone he meets, desiring nothing more than to deliver them.
In the ocean of suffering, there are those who are like rescuers of drowning men or those who extinguish fires; their eyes do not blink, yet their hands cannot reach to offer aid.
To say that such people are not great practitioners of the Way or true sages and worthies would mean that all the sages and worthies of antiquity are likewise unworthy of trust.
When the Master entered the prison, he bestowed the Dharma freely according to the place, the time, and the person, speaking spontaneously as if—
The ocean-treasury of the definitive teachings flows on, vast and surging; whether it be the great fragrant elephant or the tiny mouse, all fill their bellies.
Each person records what they encounter and carries it away with them. Yet, that which Master Yan has seen and heard is contained entirely within these volumes.
