Śākyamuni Buddha established his teachings through words; therefore, Mañjuśrī, by means of the Samādhi of Words, assisted Śākyamuni in exercising the power of discernment.

At the assembly of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he advanced and withdrew twenty-five sages, uniquely selecting Avalokiteśvara as the one suited to the occasion, such that none dared to question his private judgment. Although Avalokiteśvara was an assistant to Amitābha, [he served Śākyamuni].
The assistant also enters through hearing, reflection, and cultivation, drawing near to the Samādhi of Words and Letters.
Therefore, Śākyamuni Buddha withdrew thirty-two billion *Ganges*-sands of Bodhisattvas and advanced only Avalokiteśvara;

was this not because the true essence of the teaching in this land is that purity resides in sound and hearing? If the Samādhi of Words and Letters did not take sound and hearing as its essence, it would be like—
A flower does not take spring as its essence; how could it truly be a flower? For characters are rooted in sound-hearing (*śruta*);
sound-hearing is rooted in applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*); and applied and sustained thought are, in turn, rooted in that which is without applied or sustained thought.

The Buddha’s intention is for all sentient beings, by means of their discriminating minds, to enter the samādhi of characters, and by means of the samādhi of characters, to enter [the samādhi of] sound-hearing.

The "faculty" (ki): it is the faculty that hears through sound. Upon entering the state of being without vitarka (no-thought) and without vicāra (no-discrimination), once one has entered this state of no-vitarka and no-vicāra, the initial mind of discrimination is no longer termed "discriminative"; rather, it is termed "no-vitarka and no-vicāra.

Now, this state of no-vitarka and no-vicāra is what is called the "True Cause Buddha-nature" (zhengyin foxing). Once this True Cause Buddha-nature transforms and becomes emotion (qing), [the subsequent process unfolds].
If one does not accord with it through the *nirvedha-hetu* (the cause of penetration), then the *dharmatā-hetu* (the true cause) can ultimately never be realized.

Although the *nirvedha-hetu* is capable of acceding to the *dharmatā-hetu*, if it is not stimulated by the subtle influence of the *pratyaya-hetu* (the causal condition), then the *nirvedha-hetu* likewise cannot ultimately manifest itself.
The *pratyaya-hetu* is an alternative name for the samādhi of letters; the *nirvedha-hetu* is an alternative name for the faculty of auditory reception.

Thus it is. If a student can touch upon one principle and extend it to all others, then the Mañjuśrī-mantra-samādhi and the Avalokiteśvara-śabda-śravaṇa-samādhi are neither found in Mañjuśrī, nor in Avalokiteśvara, nor even in Śākyamuni Buddha;
they are found only within our daily activities. Therefore, the Elder Pang said: "In daily affairs there is no distinction; only I myself find harmony. Spiritual powers and wondrous functions..."
Using water and carrying firewood—this is Old Pang’s samādhi of words and letters. His supernormal powers are his faculty of hearing sounds.

"Only I alone am in harmony with them" refers to Old Pang’s realization of the *nidāna-hetu* (the cause of understanding) and his accord with the *samyak-hetu* (the correct cause), which is Buddha-nature.
Viewed from this perspective, any disciple of the Buddha who does not penetrate the *prajñā* of words and letters is [not yet complete].
One must attain the prajñā of contemplative observation; without penetrating the prajñā of contemplative observation, one will certainly be unable to realize the prajñā of the true mark.
The prajñā of the true mark is the Buddha-nature as the direct cause, while the prajñā of contemplative observation is the Buddha-nature as the revealing cause.

The Prajñā of Words is precisely the Buddha-nature as the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*). Those who study the Buddha’s teachings today invariably seek to cast aside words and texts, wishing to transcend directly and enter the stage of the Tathāgata.
Their ambition is indeed lofty; yet I fear that painted cakes cannot satisfy hunger.
Moreover, words are the Buddha’s speech, and contemplative observation is the Buddha’s mind. It is through the Buddha’s speech that one reaches the Buddha’s mind.
This is the process by which one proceeds from the state of an ordinary person to that of a sage.

Proceeding from the Buddha-mind to reach the Buddha-word, the Sage emerges from the Samādhi of Immeasurable Meanings and emits light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, forming an ocean of written characters.

This enables all sentient beings to receive a drop from this ocean, whereby they all enter the stream and lose the sense of a subjective locus, until their realization of emptiness becomes perfectly complete and quiescent extinction manifests.
To proceed only to the beginning and stop at the end—if this were so, then language and written characters would be like flowers in spring.
For one who would surely discard the flowers to seek the spring, they would be either a fool or a madman.

Those with the aspiration to enter the stream where there is no locus of attainment should deeply contemplate the intent behind why our Śākyamuni used written characters to establish his teachings. If one understands this clearly, then the written characters themselves—
It may be that words are permissible; it may be that departing from words and language is permissible.
Yet, if one has not yet attained clarity, then both employing words and departing from words are impermissible. Even "neither employing nor departing" is impermissible.
The Master said: "The Sahā world and the worlds of sentient beings in the ten directions are both rooted in emptiness; emptiness, in turn, is rooted in the mind. Therefore, a sutra says:
'Emptiness arises within the Great Awakening, like a single bubble emerging from the ocean. Within it lie the lands of conditioned dust.'"
All things arise dependent upon emptiness. However, sentient beings are deeply attached to the habitual tendencies of the sense bases (*āyatana*) and their objects (*viṣaya*).

Having accumulated these over a long time, they have become solidified and are ultimately difficult to shatter. Therefore, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas first employ the medicine of emptiness to treat the disease of this hardened existence.
Those in the world who do not understand the intent of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, seeing them speak so fervently of emptiness within the sūtras and śāstras, consequently claim that the Buddhas—

To take emptiness as the Way, they label their gate the "Gate of Emptiness. Yet they do not realize that once the illness of sentient beings is cured, the empty medicine of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas has no further application.
When the medicine of emptiness can no longer be applied, one must instead use the wondrous medicine to treat the illness of emptiness itself.
However, because sentient beings are firmly adhered to the habits of sense-bases and sense-objects, although they rely on the medicine of emptiness for treatment, [they remain bound by] emptiness...
Illness arises throughout one's life. If one does not rely on the wondrous medicine of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, then the harm caused by this emptiness of illness will be no small matter.
As for those in the world who refer to the Buddha-dharma as the "Gate of Emptiness," do they truly understand the Buddha’s mind?
Some take the words of Caoxi, "Originally there was not a single thing; where could dust and grime cling? and recklessly fix them in their minds, claiming, "I am originally nothing."
There is not a single thing. Furthermore, what dust or defilement could there be to stain it? Please examine this for yourself.
Since I have originally possessed not a single thing, when someone raises their hand to bow to me, I rejoice; when someone thrusts their hand at me, I am provoked to anger.
What substance is there in these manifest joys and angers? If you cannot shatter such things right here and now, they will remain as a blockage in the breast throughout long kalpas.
I venture to say that those who harbor perverse calculations originally possess not a single thing. Is this not the "originally not a single thing" of Caoxi?
When Buddhas and Bodhisattvas preach the Dharma, they are like a skilled physician dispensing medicine or a capable general employing troops; how could the medicine or the troops have a fixed nature?
It depends entirely on observing the patient or the enemy to see where their condition lies. If one simply attains what is appropriate, [the purpose is achieved].

When one understands the reality of things, medicine and weapons are like the butcher Ding’s skillful dissection of an ox. Thus, the world regards the Buddhist gate as the "Gate of Emptiness" (*kōmon*).
Consequently, those who appropriate Caoxi’s “originally there was not a single thing” to claim for themselves that they "originally have nothing" [are merely grasping at shadows].
In all these cases, the blade has broken while the ox remains unslain. Buddhas and Bodhisattvas know that sentient beings are deluded regarding the mind, and thus there is emptiness;

they are deluded regarding emptiness, and thus there is the body and mind; they are deluded regarding the body and mind, and thus there are the external objects (*viṣaya*). These external objects comprise the world and its contents.
Body and mind are the very category of sentient beings. Yet, both the world and sentient beings have no foundation apart from emptiness (*śūnyatā*);

likewise, emptiness has no foundation apart from the awakened mind. Therefore, Buddhas and Bodhisattvas teach sentient beings by first leading them to understand emptiness and finally to awaken to the mind.
When the mind awakens, emptiness, the world, and sentient beings are all found to be ungraspable—this is what is called the Great Awakened Mind.
It is like the vanishing of drifting clouds: before one even lifts one's eyes, the bright moon is already before one. Drifting clouds are a metaphor for that which exists through conditions;
the bright moon is a metaphor for the constant radiance that is inherently possessed. Someone stepped forward and said: "From the objects of sense one reaches the faculties;
from the body and mind one reaches emptiness; from emptiness one reaches the mind. I beg the Master to point this out to me right now."
"Where is the mind? The Master smiled and said, "If you have no mind, what is this that poses such a question? The questioner was at a loss.
The Master said, "To take the mind and ask the mind—pointing to the mind while not knowing the mind—is your fault, or is it my fault?
[The student] said, "It is the student's fault. [The Master] said, "If you truly knew your own fault, then whether walking or sitting, when you are hungry..."

Within the interior of cold; within the conditions and circumstances of favorability, adversity, right, and wrong—if you can never forget this error, then emptiness arises from within Great Awakening, like a single bubble surfacing upon the ocean.
The minute, conditioned lands of the dust-motes all depend upon emptiness for their birth. You will know this for yourself one day:
not only are sentient beings and their lands, but even empty space itself, all contained within your own mind—that is, the mind of Great Awakening. Apart from it, there is nothing.
“Your mind, too, cannot be apprehended. Thereupon, Jin bowed his head and withdrew.
Now, principle (*li*) is the pervasion of nature (*xing*); emotion (*qing*) is the obstruction of nature. Nevertheless, both principle and emotion belong to the mind, which governs them.
Therefore it is said that the mind governs both nature and emotion. Viewed from this perspective, the mind is that which stands alone between nature and emotion.
Thus, when the mind awakens, emotion can be transformed into principle; when the mind is deluded, principle changes into emotion.
As for that which precedes the mind, it is called "nature" (xing). When nature is able to respond to things, it is called "mind" (xin).
When responding to things without entanglement, it is called "principle" (li). When responding to things with entanglement, it is first termed "sentiment" (qing). Therefore, it is said:
To be without self and yet be unobstructed is the principle (*li*); to have a self and yet be obstructed is emotion (*qing*).
The dynamic of obstruction and unobstruction naturally and inevitably stands in opposition to one another. As it is said, "Natures are similar, but habits lead to divergence.
To be similar means that one returns before long; to diverge means that one does not know how to return. Not returning for long is the root [of delusion].
In the awakening of the mind, one does not know what constitutes returning [to the source]; in the delusion of the mind, it is rooted in the failure to realize this.
Thus, whether there is penetration or obstruction, distance or proximity, awakening or delusion, all are initially impermanent. When the mind awakens, there is no obstruction that is not penetrated;
when the mind is deluded, there is nothing near that does not become distant. Alas! What indeed is this thing called "mind"? It can cause a person to become a sage, and yet it can also cause...
Humans are part of the multitude; even sages and the common people alike are subject to impermanence. It is simply a matter of whether one applies the mind skillfully or unskillfully.
As for the nature of the mind, it cannot be sought within or without, nor can it be measured in terms of existence or non-existence.
To seek it within is inevitably to calculate the mind as being inside the body; to seek it without is inevitably to calculate the mind as being outside.

Beyond the body, if one has desires, one cannot avoid calculating the mind with respect to sounds, forms, and physical appearances; if one is without desires, one cannot avoid calculating the mind with respect to quiescence and empty space.
Thus, those who seek awakening of the mind in such ways are all those who do not seek well. Therefore it is said: "Investigate apart from mind, intellect, and consciousness.
If this is so, as long as the攀缘心 (攀緣心, *pān-yuán xīn*—the攀緣心, the mind that grasps at conditions) does not cease, the faculties of emotion will never wither.

If the faculty of feeling does not wither, then the mind, intellect, and consciousness can never be transcended. If the mind, intellect, and consciousness cannot be transcended, then the spirit (shen) does not coalesce.
If the spirit does not coalesce, then there is no unity. Without unity, one cannot stand independently.

If one cannot stand independently, then there is an "external. Where there is an external, there is dependence. Where there is dependence, then self and object stand in opposition. Thus, one encounters matters that are contrary to one's will.

One cannot help but become suddenly enraged; when encountering things that please the mind, one unconsciously becomes joyfully delighted. Joy and anger battle within, ceasing neither in waking nor in sleep.
To speak briefly, it is nothing more than the fact that one has been ruined by the manipulations of the mind, intellect, and consciousness.

Therefore, a true student of the Way does not know cold when it is cold, nor hunger when they are hungry; toil and ease are forgotten, and the body is like withered wood while the mind is like extinguished ashes.
At such a time, one knows that there is no place for the mind, intellect, or consciousness to settle.

After practicing thus for a long duration, all at once the sense faculties and their objects are completely detached, and the constant radiance manifests before one.
