There is nothing. It is neither internal nor external, neither existent nor non-existent. Everything relies upon my speaking of "feminine" and my speaking of "yellow";
all naturally accord with the *Sūtras*. This is what is meant by the saying: "Building a carriage inside the door; when one goes out, it fits the tracks. An ancient worthy said:

"If one does not undergo a transformation that brings life from within death, one will always remain like quicksilver in medicine—when touched by fire, it will surely fly away. He further said: "It is not..."

It is most piercingly cold to the very marrow of one's bones. How can one obtain the fragrance of plum blossoms that strikes the nose? These are all manifestations of personal realization and authentic awakening.

In recent years, those who study Chan and those who study the Way have initially no idea what the "mind" is; they immediately speak of Chan with reckless abandon and lecture on the Way with superficiality.
Yet, as soon as they encounter danger or doubt, their courage fails and their spirits vanish; they are blown away by the winds of external conditions.
It is ruined. One’s nostrils, born of one's mother, cannot exercise even a modicum of mastery over them.
This is truly not as good as the people in a village of three households, who know nothing and understand nothing, yet simply till the land to earn their daily bread.

Nāgārjuna was a Bodhisattva of the ninth stage (*bhūmi*). Regarding his refutation of the four modes of arising (*catur-utpāda*), he stated: "All phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another;

they do not arise from both, nor without cause. Therefore, they are said to be unarisen. This is like one whose worldly desires are shallow and whose celestial faculties are profound: upon hearing it once, they are able to contemplate it;
through contemplation, they are able to refine it; through refinement, they transcend hearing. What is transcended by the abandonment of hearing is that which is liberated.

Once liberated, one is able to dissolve [the seeds]. When both subject and object have been swept away, even while dwelling amidst circumstances that are favorable or adverse, one responds without entanglement;
thus, the seeds and active manifestations of many lifetimes diminish day by day. Diminishing them again and again, they finally reach a state of no further diminution.
Suddenly, there is a realization of sameness. Viewed from this perspective, what was previously called the "dissolution of the faculties and their objects" is [identical to this].
Now, as for this sudden realization of identity: is it one or two? If it is one, then the former is not the latter; if it is two, then there is no latter apart from the former.
Yet scholars do not feel shame in failing to refine their understanding of the fourfold nature (*catuskoṭi*), but instead doubt that Nāgārjuna’s verses are verified by experience.
This is like a person whose illness is grave yet who cannot bear to take medicine; seeing the disease not depart, they become violently angry and revile the medicine.

This is unproven. For one who treats physical illness, one must necessarily take Shen Nong as the physician; likewise, for one who treats mental illness, one must necessarily take Nāgārjuna as the physician.
If one discards the *Shennong Bencao*, then even Hua Tuo and Bian Que would be unable to cure physical ailments.

Yet, when scholars wish to cure the disease of the mind, if they do not employ Nāgārjuna’s verse on the refutation of the four modes of existence (*catuskoṭi*) to treat it, there has never been one whose illness was healed.
When I first heard this verse, I was startled; subsequently, I doubted it. Thereupon, I reflected upon it with intense persistence.
As I applied it to the circumstances of my life—both favorable and adverse—I frequently met with failure. The more I failed, the more vigorously I fought. From then on...
This is what it means to dare to fight and face death; thus, I have finally achieved victory. Alas! One must know that every grain of food on one's plate was earned through bitter toil.
If these are people who farm the land, they will surely shed tears upon hearing this. Those who are later-born youths, deluded in principle and flighty of mind, do not know shame;

their karma will certainly not be extinguished, and their illness will be difficult to cure even while sitting. Furthermore, upon hearing this instruction, they give rise to a heart that refuses to accept the good.
To willfully act as a golden fortress for protecting one's own shortcomings—alas, how tragic! I know that Nāgārjuna has been reborn; he instructs me directly, face to face.
That I should not encounter the spittle and abuse of the sick is simply impossible.

Now, when a sharp blade emerges from its scabbard, its radiance outshines the sun; it cuts iron as if it were mud. Whatever timber—whether paulownia, cypress, pine, or cedar—is subjected to its slicing and carving will inevitably become a functional vessel.
This is one who skillfully employs the blade. Yet there are certain foolish people who, though their blades are swift and keen, [fail to do so].
"He uses it only to cut mud. Yet the mud cannot form a vessel, and his blade is worn away daily; this is one who does not know how to use a knife well.

It is like the nature of sentient beings, which is fundamentally wondrous, yet they do not employ meditative concentration and wisdom to observe and illuminate it. Instead, they merely indulge in clinging to external conditions, rushing toward the dust of the world without returning.
Wandering through birth and death, their illusory suffering grows ever deeper, with no prospect of escape. How can this be called skillful application of the mind?"

Ah! Like those of sharp faculties and superior wisdom, they use the light of the mind-nature to illuminate and shatter both the sense organs and their objects, revealing that both are devoid of intrinsic nature.

When the powers of concentration and wisdom are perfected, one attains liberation within the very midst of worldly afflictions (*kleśa*) and reaches the light of wisdom within the very midst of emotional consciousness.

Using the "knife" in this manner is not for the purpose of cleaving gold or carving jade; whatever vessel is thus formed will be solid and indestructible, filled to the brim with nectar and pervading everywhere.
Sprinkle it everywhere; even a mere drop that touches anything will cool all feverish afflictions, and one will attain immeasurable hundreds of thousands of samādhis.
These do not come from outside, for they are inherently present within the nature of the mind. Therefore, it is said: "Skillfully employ the mind.
The eighty-four thousand afflictions are themselves the eighty-four thousand samādhis; if one does not skillfully employ the mind, the eighty-four thousand samādhis are themselves [the afflictions].
There are eighty-four thousand afflictions. Alas! A blade is fundamentally non-dual; used skillfully, there is nothing it cannot cut.
Used unskillfully, the blade is worn away day by day.
Now, light possesses both the true and the false. The true illuminates ten thousand ages without dependence; the false clings to the six sense-objects to emit its radiance. Therefore it is said:
detached from darkness and detached from light, there is no essence of seeing; detached from motion and detached from stillness, there is no substance of hearing.

When openness and obstruction are detached from one another and the fluctuations of tranquility and change are lost, then smelling and tasting are like fragrance within excrement or fire within ice—merging and parting, yet detached from all.
The arising and ceasing of awakening and discrimination are merely names without reality. Nevertheless, the sense objects and the sense organs must exist in mutual dependence;
they arise together and cease together. Thus, the mind arises because of external conditions, which is called "the manifestation of light through the adhesion to delusion.
When the mind does not arise because of conditions but shines with solitary clarity and perfect illumination, it is first called "light that is independent. Being independent, then—
The conditions of the internal and external are empty. When there is dependence, the conditions of the internal and external become obstructed.
When conditions are empty, the nature returns; when conditions arise, the nature is deluded. Therefore, that which can turn things is itself a resource for entering the Way;

thus, conditions are not laboriously dispelled, yet they are empty. Master Lao Pang said: "When I saw Shitou, I first attained the state where the myriad phenomena before my eyes were all fused together. He also said:
"Daily activities are no different; it is only that I alone am in harmony with them. This old man takes thorough understanding as fire to burn away the empty faculties and sense objects.

When there is dependence, they are discarded; when there is no dependence, they are complete. Being complete means there is nothing external. When there is nothing external, there is not even a speck of dust remaining.

These are what constitute obstacles for me. When Caoqi heard a guest reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, upon hearing the passage, "One should give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere," his sense organs and their objects were immediately liberated and his numinous light became perfect. This is called "having seen the Way" (*darśanamārga*), yet not yet having fully clarified the Way.
Therefore it is said: "To honor what one knows makes one lofty and brilliant; to practice what one knows makes one vast and great. Lately...
In studying the Way, one loses its fundamental essence. When discussing the "seeing of the Way" and the "illumination of the Way," these are often conflated and not clearly distinguished;
at times, this even leads to the failure to avoid identifying emotional states as the true nature (*xing*). Therefore, the Great Master Changsha Cen uttered a verse in lamentation:

"Those who study the Way do not recognize the Real, Simply because they have long been attached to consciousness and spirit. The root of birth and death throughout immeasurable eons— Fools call it the mind."
"The person of original nature" is truly a needle at the crown of the head for those throughout the world who mistake emotional sentiment for their true nature.
Now, "fú-fú" (夫夫) is a designation for a man; yet while possessing this designation of a man, one lacks the reality of a man—what is called a "false man."

Yet, in reality, she was but a woman. Like that poor wood-seller of Caoxi, who upon first hearing the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, immediately attained certainty without hesitation—he was truly a remarkable man.
When Jiashan turned his head back, the Boatman’s life came to an end; thus, while the son harbored doubts toward the father, the father could not help but capsize the boat.
Guangfu, since you have already resolved to uphold the *Vajracchedikā*, [you must likewise resolve your doubts].

When hatred and love, honor and disgrace confront one another, if you cannot sternly subdue their active manifestations with that which Caoqi realized, then your dependent emotions will ultimately find it difficult to return to their original nature.

If the nature does not return, then the five thousand kalpas of a single retribution within the three miserable realms are precisely what Guangfu ought to worry about. Guangfu, exert yourself! (Shown to Guangfu)
Shu Guang, Grand Tutor of the Han, submitted a memorial requesting to retire from office. The Emperor granted him twenty *jin* of gold, and the Crown Prince presented him with fifty *jin*.
Upon returning to his native village, Guang ordered his household daily to prepare wine and food, inviting his kinsmen, old friends, and guests to enjoy themselves together.
After more than a year, his gold was nearly exhausted. Guang’s descendants urged him to establish a permanent estate, to which Guang replied: "I—"
How could I, an old and deluded man, fail to consider my descendants? I already possess ancestral fields and dwellings;

if I instruct my descendants to labor diligently within them, it will suffice to provide for their food and clothing. To now further increase these so as to produce a surplus would do nothing but teach my descendants idleness.
Moreover, if the worthy possess great wealth, it diminishes their ambition; if the foolish possess great wealth, it increases their transgressions. Furthermore—
"Indeed, wealth is a source of resentment for the multitude. Since I have no means to instruct my descendants, I do not wish to increase their transgressions and thereby breed resentment.
Consequently, his kinsmen were pleased and submitted to him. Furthermore, while Pang Degong was plowing on the ridges, his wife and children were weeding before him.
Liu Biao, the Imperial Protector of Jingzhou, pointed at them and asked, "Sir, why do you toil so hard living in these furrows?"
He was unwilling to accept a salary, asking, "How can I leave anything for my descendants in future generations? Master De replied, "The people of this world all leave behind danger;
I alone leave behind peace. Although what we leave behind differs, it is not that I have left nothing at all.
Wang Biao sighed and departed. Both elders were sages of the mundane world (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and their insight was as lofty and brilliant as [the following].
This is so. We are those who have left the household life; yet we do not seek alms to sustain ourselves, but instead covet the offerings of others and unwarrantedly accept what is improper.
If one investigates the source of this fault, it does not go beyond scheming to obtain ready-made clothing and eating ready-made food.
Now, to loathe labor and love ease is the common sentiment of humanity. Yet clothing does not descend from heaven, nor does food spring up from the earth. For every garment and every meal—
All things must arise from diligent labor. If others labor while I enjoy the fruits in peace, yet I desire to enjoy them for a long time without misfortune, such a thing is impossible.

Lord Shu Zhong was originally a veteran minister of the Han court; though he was granted gold, he did not dare to enjoy it alone, but shared it with his clansmen, and even his descendants were not permitted to possess it.
Since we belong to one of the four classes of society, [we must likewise share our gains].
Aside from this, I beg for alms to sustain my remaining breath; among the four classes of the common people outside, who then would act as my donor?
Although donors differ according to whether they are scholars, farmers, artisans, or merchants, every inch of silk and every grain of rice results from diligent labor.
They obtained this through diligent toil, yet they joyfully bestowed it upon me; this was because they wished to seek the expiation of their own transgressions and to increase their merit.
If I bear the name of a monk but lack the substance of one, I will certainly be unable to benefit myself or others.
In future lives and other worlds, I shall have to change my head and face to take the body of an animal in order to repay the kindness of their almsgiving.

If someone like Old Man Yama were to grant you the license to be jocular, soft-natured, and stubborn, and thus manage to deceive him, then the teachings regarding heaven and hell, the five blessings and the six calamities, would all be false words. Would the Tathāgata, a holy being, ever deceive sentient beings with such falsehoods?
Furthermore, food, drink, sex, and wealth are the great desires of humanity; among these four, if indeed...
Having established the stability of one's own footing, why must one avoid cities to dwell in mountain forests? This is said regarding the highest class of monks;
for it is because their Buddha-knowledge and vision have already been opened and their Buddha’s compassionate vows have already been awakened.
For such a kind of monk, how could there be any offering that cannot cleanse their transgressions and increase their benefit? If, however, their Buddha-knowledge and vision have not yet...
The Great Opening. Although their compassionate vows have not yet been fully awakened, they are able to recite the words of the Buddha and understand their meaning to some extent;

practicing in accordance with that understanding, this type is called the "Middle-Rank Monks. Those who merely recite the words of the Buddha but cannot understand their meaning, fearing only to bring disgrace upon the Dharma-gate, and who strive to maintain the precepts—this type is called the "Lower-Rank Monks. Although these three types of monks are shallow...

Their depths differ; none of them are those who possess the name but lack the reality. If one reveres and makes offerings to them, their offenses will surely be extinguished and their merit increased—of this, why should there be any doubt?
Apart from these three, they are all merely shaven-headed commoners and not monks.

Although you have shaved your hair as you have done hitherto, have you ever reflected upon the true nature of a monk to feel no shame? If you truly feel ashamed before the Sangha, then you will not suffer external contempt.

Come. You must take this for yourself. Therefore, I have specifically cited Shu Zhongweng of the Western Han and Pang Degong of the Eastern Han, while also presenting the three types of monastics—superior, middling, and inferior—to show you. You should hollow out your heart and forget your physical form;
weep bitterly and read this twenty or thirty times. Only then will you be able to become a true monk from this day forward. (Shown to Long Dong at Huaian Temple Liaofan)
I read Dongpo’s *Praise of Guanyin* and thereby realized that Dongpo was not someone whom a pedantic scholar could even approximate.
Dongpo held that when this single body is beset by the eight hardships, how is it any different from a single thread suspending the Nine Cauldrons?
At such a time, the body is forgotten of its own accord without waiting to be forgotten; yet while the body is forgotten, the world alone does not forget it—this is impossible.

When one dwells in this state and forgets both body and world, the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) are simultaneously lost and become without counterpart. When the organs and objects have no counterpart, consciousness itself becomes wisdom (*jñāna*).

This wisdom illuminates the numinous source, into which all that was forgotten flows back in. As for what were previously called the fiery pits, mountains of knives, fierce beasts, and poisonous drugs—[they are now transformed].

"All these various sufferings—the teachers through whom I have entered the stream—are present here. Therefore, entering the stream is not difficult; it is difficult to understand that there is neither pain nor non-pain.
At the very moment of experiencing pain, one must investigate this pain: does it arise from the sense organ? Yet, externally, the object has no organ.
Does it arise from the external object? Yet, externally, the organ has no object. Externally, the object has no organ; the organ is..."
The roots of the house of dust—how could these roots belong to me? As for external roots, they are devoid of dust; yet dust is the dust of the house of the roots, and is non-dual with the roots.
Where there is no duality, there is oneness. Where there is oneness, there is no exterior. Where there is no exterior, there is no dependence. Reaching this point, what can be called "pain"?
If one has not fully realized this, and perceives even a hair’s breadth of pain, how can that truly be without dependence? It is merely...
Sentient beings do not thoroughly understand this; thus, their "independent" life-force (wu-dai xue-mai) is severed.

When the independent life-force is severed, the "dependent" life-force (you-dai xue-mai) continues of its own accord. Once the dependent life-force has continued, they erroneously perceive phenomena as existing externally to the mind.
This is not because sentient beings possess duality; otherwise, would one body alone undergo all manner of suffering? When suffering reaches its ultimate limit, the light returns and shines directly.
There is no dependence. Where there is no dependence, there is no self; how much less could there be external objects? When object and self are forgotten, the illumination does not wither;
thus the wondrously profound fountain of spirit universally drenches the parched and withered. As the withered are moistened by the nectar of immortality, they sprout and flourish.
Is this not the true non-duality? Is this not Avalokiteśvara himself?

Birth and death revolve in a cycle, with love and hatred as their root. Therefore, when I am without a mind, the heavens, earth, people, and things within my dreams do not require effort to be dispelled;
they are empty of themselves. "Emptiness" is a name that awaits the existence of heavens, earth, people, and things. When I am without a mind, though there is emptiness, there is also no earth.
Humans are the most spiritually intelligent among the myriad things; if one does not know this and instead seeks knowledge elsewhere, then that which is truly spiritual remains obscured.
As cold and heat alternate, and antiquity and the present succeed one another; as honor and disgrace, death and birth—all these are capable of plundering me.
If the spiritual essence (*ling*) is not obscured, then the false mind is empty. When the false mind is empty, how could those who plunder me wait for me to raise banners and drums before they flee?
If a person understands this, then amidst a thousand deprivations and ten thousand transformations, I shall respond to them.
And thus one does not weary oneself.
Now, to eat when hungry and to wear clothes when cold is the common nature of humanity.

If, all at once, one were to abstain from grain and subsist on water—unless there were something greater than life and death that one desired to seek and obtain—then even if such a thing were obtained, though life and death [might be transcended],...
It is fierce, yet it cannot bring calamity or fortune upon me. If this were so, then water could indeed be "consumed.
However, even if one avoids food and consumes water, if the roots of the passions do not wither and one merely endures the delusions of hunger, then consuming water is no better than eating rice.
I have heard that the source of this practice of consuming water originates with the Bodhisattva Jñānakūṭa. This Bodhisattva [considered] that sentient beings could not...
The Way is hindered by dullness and distraction. To consume water leads to hunger; hunger prevents sleep. When one cannot sleep, wakefulness is frequent and slumber is scarce.
When wakefulness is frequent and slumber is scarce, the mind may uphold even half a verse; with resolve focused and the spirit concentrated, delusive thoughts will not arise.
When delusive thoughts do not arise, the grasping of body and mind will ultimately find no ground. Therefore it is said:
The moon is high above; all things are tranquil. Holding half a verse in mind, ten thousand conditions are empty. When conditions are empty, the self has no counterpart.
Since the self has no counterpart, how could conditions alone have a counterpart? Alas! Reaching this point, there is naturally the constant radiance;
why wait for the arising of a thought for it to manifest? Guishan said: "The numinous light shines alone, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects. Its essence reveals the truth."
It is constant. It does not depend on written words; written words are merely the roots and dust of the senses. To observe this directly is like abstaining from food and drinking only water:

at first it may seem a minor matter, yet the achievement it brings is vast. If one has not yet encountered the One who is Alone, it is difficult to speak with them (this is shown as the "Water-Abstaining Fast").
The Buddha said: "In general, any place where food and drink are prepared as offerings to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha is called a 'Fragrant Accumulation Kitchen' (xiāngjī chú).

Therefore, if those who prepare the food do not understand the three virtues, cannot distinguish the six flavors, and furthermore possess impurity in their own three karmas of body, speech, and mind, then that place where food is prepared shall not be called a Fragrant Accumulation Kitchen; it is called 'filth'."

The kitchen was already prepared. What are called the "three virtues"? They are purity, softness, and being in accordance with the Dharma. What are called the "six flavors"? They are bland, salty, sour, pungent, sweet, and bitter.
These are the foods offered to the Buddha and provided for the Sangha; if they are not refined and clean, and if one does not distinguish against pungent or impure things, [it is improper].
If it lacks purity, one loses the quality of clarity. If it is not refined and sweetly blended, but possesses even slight coarseness or astringency, one loses the quality of softness.

If it is not prepared at the proper time, not manufactured appropriately, handled with negligence and indulgence, and furthermore not offered with saliva flowing [in anticipation], one loses the quality of being in accordance with the Dharma.
Moreover, if these three qualities lack the harmonization of the six flavors, they will likewise not be perfected; for indeed, flavor is essential.
It constitutes the essence of all tastes. Saline taste is moist by nature and can nourish the skin; therefore, among harmonized flavors, salt is invariably primary.
Pungent taste is hot by nature and can warm the coldness of the internal organs; therefore, that which has a sharp flavor is called pungent.
Sour taste is cool by nature and can neutralize the toxins of other flavors; therefore, that which has a fermented sour flavor is called... [sour].
Sourness. Sweetness is harmonious in its nature; it can harmonize the spleen and stomach, therefore that which tastes sweet is called "sweet. Bitterness is cold in its nature;
it can dispel the heat of the viscera, therefore that which tastes astringent is called "bitter. You [should understand] these as the three virtues and six flavors.
One should examine this with careful discernment to understand the reason for its merit and the reason for its flavor.

Furthermore, with a mind free from the notions of self, person, sentient being, or life-span, one should lead the six sense faculties and the four limbs with diligent vigor and skillful means to prepare food and drink to offer to the Buddha and provide for the Sangha. As for the merit of such a person, even if one were to fill the void...

Even if one were to fill the world with the seven treasures and practice such giving for immeasurable eons, without ever giving rise to weariness, aversion, or a stingy mind—were this compared to [the merit of offering] these foods, its virtue would not equal even a ten-thousandth part of the latter. Why is this? Because these foods lack nothing in their three qualities and fail in nothing regarding their six flavors;
when such food touches the Buddha’s nose or enters the mouths of the Sangha, it is like smelling sandalwood or drinking nectar. Five.

Internally harmonized, the hundred hairs are refreshed and joyful; the body is at ease and the mind is peaceful. It provides manifest support for physical vitality and secret support for mental power.

When physical vitality receives this support, the body becomes healthy and robust; when mental power receives this support, the spirit is free from disturbance. When the body is healthy and robust, there is support for advancing on the Path;
when the spirit is free from disturbance, contemplative wisdom is easily perfected. If one’s eating and drinking do not accord with the Dharma, the body will suffer much...
When one is ill, the mind is greatly disturbed. When both body and mind are ill and disturbed, it is impossible for one to achieve diligent progress and awakening.
Judging from this, the very life of a practitioner truly depends upon the hands of the kitchen staff.

Therefore, if those in the kitchen do not discern the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) and fail to prepare the six flavors (*ṣad-rasa*) with refinement, they are called ox-headed *āpāda* demons; they kill people without [mercy].
Externally, as explained in the *Tri-dharmaka*, one uses the six exquisite flavors.

Furthermore, with a mind free of self, person, sentient being, or life-span, one leads the six sense organs and the four limbs to prepare food and drink according to the Dharma to offer to the Buddhas and serve the Sangha;

such a person is called a Bodhisattva of Great Compassion. Therefore it is said: "The Buddhas of the three thousandfold world system all emerge from within the kitchen. Moreover, this is considered the constant practice.
Abiding in stinginess, one does not honor the worthy or respect the noble; in the future, one will receive the retribution of a hungry ghost.

Constantly squandering wealth without examining the hardships from which it was obtained, one will receive the retribution of poverty in the future. Furthermore, when preparing food and drink, if the six sense faculties are not guarded, [the same result follows].
The nine orifices are unrestrained, and the four limbs are impure; one shall receive the retribution of being a dung-worm or a stinking insect in the future, as described above.
All of this was spoken by the Tathāgata. Whether you hear it or see it, you should give rise to a sense of shame and follow it in practice.

Thus, ignorance will surely be shattered, Prajñā will surely be opened, all transgressions will surely be extinguished, and myriad blessings will surely gather. In the present, body and mind will be at peace and secure. When...
They shall attain the Unsurpassed Way and ascend to the rank of Bodhisattva. The Buddha’s word is not deceptive. You sons of the Buddha in the kitchen should embody the Buddha-mind;
you possess the capacity to emerge from suffering. (Pointing to the kitchen.)
Now, that which is fundamentally pure and quiescent has no spatial location. How is it that after this sudden arising, the mountains, rivers, and worlds are arrayed?
From this point on, there are spatial locations. Once there are locations, there must be names for the east, west, south, and north. Where there is a name, there must be a corresponding reality;

thus, the West belongs to Dui (the trigram of the lake), the East belongs to Zhen (the trigram of the thunder), the North belongs to Kan (the trigram of the water), and the South belongs to Li (the trigram of the fire). [Flowers...]
The youth Sudhana visited spiritual friends everywhere; why did he omit the three other directions and inquire only about the south?
Is it not because the south corresponds to the hexagram Li? The center of Li is empty; being empty, it is luminous; being luminous, it is patterned.
Thus, Li is said to be the symbol of "civilized brilliance. Now, written characters and speech must be rooted in sound, and sound, in turn, is rooted in...
Within the vacuous and numinous clarity of one’s own mind, the forty-two characters of the *Avataṃsaka* each contain inexhaustible meanings and principles.
This is because characters are rooted in sound, and sound is rooted in the mind; the mind is precisely this innate, vacuous, and numinous clarity of ours.
Furthermore, these forty-two characters encompass the forty-two stages of the Dharma-body Bodhisattvas, for all these Great Beings reside therein.

Therefore, Sudhana did not shrink from the smoke and waters of a hundred cities; whether the winds of his environment were adverse or favorable, he vowed to advance another hundred paces from atop a hundred-foot pole.
This was surely because he desired to exhaustively traverse the courtyards of all the Great Beings (Mahāsattvas). Alas!
How easy is it to traverse the courtyards of these Great Beings? If one cannot use principle to subdue emotion, then [one remains bound by] birth and death, calamity and fortune.
This barrier is truly not easy to break through. It refers to the fifty-five stages of true Bodhi on the path of Śūraṅgama, from the first stage of faith up to Equal Enlightenment.
Following the Diamond Path, one undergoes repeated refinement through the forty-two grades of ignorance.
When ignorance is completely smelted away, wondrous enlightenment finally becomes perfect. This, too, does not go beyond the four characters "using principle to subdue emotion.
This is because principle is without self, while emotion possesses a self. One who skillfully cultivates the Way can use non-self to subdue the self;

thus, the sense of self diminishes day by day, while the light of non-self increases day by day. When there is light, there is clarity; when there is clarity, there is emptiness; when there is emptiness, there is spiritual vitality; when there is spiritual vitality, there is penetration. Once this is achieved—
When one penetrates and attains spiritual illumination, our quest for the Unsurpassed Way reaches its consummation.
Thus, when Sudhana did not inquire of other directions but inquired only of the South, it was a metaphor for the mind; it is because there is no phenomenon outside the mind.
Once one knows that there is no phenomenon outside the mind, the myriad objects before one suddenly melt away. When the myriad objects have melted away, yet one says "I"—
If it exists as something solitary, then how does this "self" differ from the fur of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit?

When you, Master Zang, present it in this way, you will finally understand that asking about the South is not asking about the South; it is asking about detachment. Asking about detachment is not asking about detachment; it is truly asking about the mind.
Alas! When the mind does not see the mind, how can one use the mind to question the mind? If you have realized it, do not ask; if you doubt it, seek another teacher.

Reading the verse of Chan Master Changsha Cen, I first learned that those who identify the perceiving consciousness as the Buddha-nature and take empty space as their homeland were not only present in recent times, but already existed during the late Tang dynasty. Indeed, this...
These people merely take the conscious spirit—vivid and alert in daily life—to be the Buddha-nature.

They do not realize that for one who has seen their nature, the conscious spirit is itself the Buddha-nature; yet for one who has not seen their nature, the Buddha-nature is merely the conscious spirit.
If one examines this directly: the consciousness-spirit (*vijñāna*) and the Buddha-nature (*buddhatā*) are certainly not two separate things.

However, as long as one has not yet seen one's nature, the consciousness-spirit remains the consciousness-spirit and the Buddha-nature remains the Buddha-nature; they must by no means be treated as a single, indistinct entity.

To speak of them as a confused whole would mean that the holy and the ordinary are not distinguished, and awakening and delusion are not discerned. If the holy and the ordinary are not distinguished, then laypeople might falsely claim to be seated [in enlightenment].
Regarding the offense of the dragon bed: if one fails to distinguish between awakening and delusion, then sentient beings will not discern the heterodox from the orthodox.

Therefore, within the gate of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, the Teachings (Jiao) comprise both Nature (Xing) and Characteristics (Xiang), while the School (Zong) comprises both Illumination (Zhao) and Function (Yong). If one believes in Nature but does not believe in Characteristics, one will ultimately fall into the pit of nihilism.

If one believes in the signs but does not believe in the nature, one will inevitably fall into the pit of eternalism. If one believes in illumination but does not employ it in practice, then the roots of the emotional mind will be difficult to uproot;
one will merely perversely indulge in verbal explanations. Thus, Mount Gui (Huishan) rebuked Yangshan, saying: "Son of Silence, do not rely on verbal explanations."

If one merely places trust in [the teachings] without relying on their illumination, then mad demons will enter the mind. One will treat cause and effect as mere scraps of paper, view birth and death with contempt, and mistake this for true understanding;
it will be utterly devoid of even a hair’s breadth of practical utility. The essential point is that whatever degree of realization one attains through practice, that much alone is real.
To boast merely of intellectual understanding is of no avail at the critical juncture of birth and death; one can ultimately rely on it not in the slightest.

Little do they realize that while it is certainly a sickness to boast of understanding without being able to practice, it is equally a sickness to act recklessly and arbitrarily without any understanding at all.
Thus their illness becomes even greater. Therefore, the old man of Changsha, out of compassion for such people, spoke this verse:

"The student of the Way does not recognize the Real, Simply because they have recognized the spirit from of old. The root of birth and death throughout immeasurable kalpas— The deluded person calls it the 'original person.'"
Su Zizhan said: "The hearts of both the gentleman and the petty person are upright; the kidneys of both the gentleman and the petty person are depraved.
However, the gentleman is able to nourish the heart through principle; thus, the heart acts and the kidneys follow it. The petty person cannot nourish the heart through principle;
thus, the kidneys act and the heart follows them. When the heart acts and the kidneys follow, this is [the state of] depravity."
It follows what is correct. When the kidneys act and the heart follows them, this is the correct following the depraved.
When the depraved follows the correct, then emotion is eliminated and principle gradually becomes clear. When the correct follows the depraved, then principle is obscured and emotion gradually flows.

When emotion is eliminated and principle is clear, the mind will return to its nature. When principle is obscured and emotion flows, the mind gradually becomes burdened by external things. The mind will...

Furthermore, regarding the nature (*xing*): when *kun* returns to *qian*, there will be days [of light]. When the mind gradually becomes burdened by external objects, then *kun* will ultimately be unable to return to *qian*.
For *qian* is principle (*li*), while *kun* is emotion (*qing*). As for the mind as a thing:
if it is nourished by principle, it will ultimately return to its nature; if it is not nourished by principle, it will gradually flow toward emotion. Emotion is like water; therefore—

Gravity is its nature; as its principle is like fire, it takes flame as its nature. That which falls must descend into the turbid darkness, while that which flames must ascend toward the lofty brightness.
Thus, the turbid darkness is the domain of the *ki* (vital energy) of the kidneys, and the lofty brightness is the domain of the *ki* of the heart.
The heart is always close to principle (*li*), while the kidneys are always close to emotion (*qing*). It is only the nature (*xing*) that dwells between principle and emotion.
If one irrigates it with the water of orthodox learning, the spiritual sprouts will flourish daily;

unfortunately, if one irrigates it with the water of heterodox learning, the weeds and tares will grow daily. "Spiritual sprouts" is a metaphor for the mind; "weeds and tares" is an analogy for the kidneys.
As an ancient said: "Take the solid core from the center of the Kan position, and transform the internal yin within the Li palace."
From this, it transforms into a firm and vigorous body; whether hidden or soaring, leaping or bounding, all proceeds from the mind.
The meaning of this poem is that nature transforms into emotion: Qian (Heaven) transforms into Li (Fire), and Kun (Earth) transforms into Kan (Water).
Thus, the single Yang of Qian becomes submerged within the two Yins of Kun, while the single Yin of Kun comes to reside within the two Yangs of Qian. Li is the symbol of the mind.
*Kan* (the trigram for water) is the image of the kidneys. The Perfected Person, knowing this to be so, exhausts principle and fully realizes their nature;
thus, the single Yang line of *Kan* can be restored to become *Qian*, and the single Yin line of *Li* likewise returns to its place as *Kun*.
When I observe this through principle, the doctrine of the mutual completion of *Kan* and *Li*, and the mechanism of the reversal of *Qian* and *Kun*, are fundamentally self-evident.
Why must one harbor doubts and hesitations? As for those of the Daoist school, some designate [the elixir] by the names lead and mercury;

others use various terms such as dragon and tiger, pear and jujube, infant and maiden. These are merely ways of encouraging people toward this Way. If one possesses the sincere resolve, one will naturally not weary of these trivial names and forms.
If one seeks it while constrained by difficulties, one will approach forgetfulness; once forgotten, the mind runs wild.

Seeking ceases of its own accord. Once the mind of frantic seeking has ceased, one may, amidst a single cough or sneeze from a True Person, attain awakening upon hearing it once—a thousand insights at once.
Thus one realizes: if nature can be transformed into emotion, why should emotion alone not be able to be transformed back into nature?
If emotion can indeed be transformed into nature, then for an ordinary person to seek to become a True Person is likewise no matter beyond their capacity.

From this point on, emotional habits gradually diminish and the aspiration for the Way becomes ever more firm. When emotional habits are eliminated, the single yin line within the hexagram Zhong (the Central) will revert to Kun;
when the aspiration for the Way is ever more firm, the single yang line within Kan will ultimately restore Qian.
When pure yin is entirely extinguished and pure yang is fully restored, one can enter water without drowning and enter fire without being burned; even metal and stone may be [penetrated].
One passes directly through; the void can be traversed at will. Therefore it is said: "From this, one transforms into a body of firm vigor (*k'ien-kan*);
whether hidden or soaring, leaping or flying, all depends on the mind. Although this is easy to understand, it is truly difficult to practice.

For the emotional habits of sentient beings are thoroughly ingrained, like oil mixed into flour. Unless one is supremely wise and courageous, how could one wish for the oil to emerge from the flour? It is not so easy.
How difficult this is!
If the world were truly existent, it could never be shattered; if atoms were truly existent, they could never be joined together.
Yet now, one joins atoms to form the world and shatters the world to form atoms; thus, their contraction and expansion are impermanent. And...
When combined and fragmented, it is not obscured. In impermanence, many emotions reach their end; when not obscured, the mechanism of combination and fragmentation persists.

When emotions are exhausted, the principle exists but the path is blocked; when the mechanism persists, emotions wither and phenomena become manifest. Therefore, although the great earth is solid, [it is subject to these transformations].
Contemplating these as being like light clouds, one realizes that the attachment to this single body is as insubstantial as a mass of foam.

When the form is cast off, the spirit becomes whole; when the spirit is whole, discursive thought ceases. When discursive thought ceases, the mind exists yet is without birth. When the form is cast off, the body is empty yet possesses utility.
Being without birth, it is numinous yet without self; possessing utility, it is without self yet numinous. Taking what is near at hand from within one's own person, it may be called intimate.
To seek [the answer] from distant objects may be called superficial. Therefore, clothing and food are more intimate than the chamber; the chamber is more intimate than the fields;
and the fields are more intimate than the vast expanse of the earth. Now, the Elder Kāśyapa called upon Subhūti and asked him:
"If one were to shatter the great trichiliocosm into fine motes of dust, would they be many? When Subhūti heard this—
I do not yet know the root. I consider that although dust has the name of being manifold and fragmented, it originally lacks the reality of being manifold and fragmented.
For there are no subtle particles within the external world; thus, one contemplates subtle particles through the lens of the world, yet the particles are fundamentally no-particles.
One contemplates the world through the lens of subtle particles, yet the world is fundamentally no-world. Alas! The world may be said to be remote from me, yet a single body—within [the world]...

I may be called "intimate. If one can awaken to intimacy by means of what is distant, then why wait until one has dissected the body and mind and exerted every effort to cast them aside before desire for food, drink, and sex becomes pure and free from entanglement?

Nevertheless, since beginningless time, sentient beings have reckoned this body—a mere provisional conglomeration of the four great elements—as necessarily belonging to themselves, and they have reckoned the combination of the four aggregates...
When these [views] converge upon the mind, they inevitably become my own; if one clings to them without transformation, they become as firm as the great earth, like oil permeating flour.
To desire that what is perceived as solid become fragile, and that what is viewed as existent be seen as non-existent—this is certainly not easy for those of shallow celestial faculties.
It was only because Xu Wugui, upon seeing Marquis Wu once, was able to overturn his habitual perceptions, that he caused the Marquis’s five desires to blaze forth.

Within this, immeasurable heat and affliction are suddenly transformed into refreshing coolness. This is not because I have forgotten or neglected anything; for one whose spirit merges with the Dao and whose physical form is liberated, who could fail to reach such a state?
Yet, it is better to perceive the distant and thereby awaken to the intimate, so that one may reflect upon the gasping breaths of those who have wounded their blades and gashed their hands.
Viewed from this perspective, the depth of one’s celestial mechanism determines whether awakening comes sooner or later; thus, one perceives the errors.
Thus, in this litigation, he yielded to the Yan family. Furthermore, it is said that "to know others is wisdom; to know oneself is clarity.

Had the Yan family not possessed the clarity of self-knowledge, their transgression would not have been easily seen; had they not possessed the courage of diligent practice, their transgression would not have been easily contested.
We, along with you, my fellow disciples, have long shared the karmic affinity for *prajñā*. It is fitting that we have gathered here now. As the autumn wind rises high, let us put this into practice.

The physical form wavers and decays; yet after this separation, may your resolve each remain firm and steadfast. To ferry yourselves across and to ferry others across—like launching a boat upon raging waves, one call and you ascend;
who among you is not a hero? If three calls go unanswered, my tears will soak my robes. Remembering that we share the same essence, there is no harm even as slight as a hair’s breadth.
Yet those who turn their backs on the root to pursue the branches become solitary, wandering, and withered. (I instruct my disciples thus.)

When knowledge is discarded, awakening is complete; when knowledge is established, awakening is obscured. When obscured, one is deluded; when deluded, there is nowhere one goes that is not an obstruction.

This extends to the way form obstructs the eye, sound obstructs the ear, fragrance and stench obstruct the nose, flavor obstructs the tongue, touch obstructs the body, and mental objects obstruct the mind.
Thus, the sense faculties and their objects are turbidly agitated, perpetually murky and never clear.

Alas! The numinous tower of my mind (*lingtai*) is originally empty and pure. Because it is obstructed by various hindrances, that which is empty is no longer empty, and that which is pure is no longer pure.
Since the empty is no longer empty, one falsely asserts the existence of form where there is no form; one falsely asserts the existence of touch where there is no touch;
one falsely asserts the existence of a body where there is no body; and one falsely asserts the existence of a mind where there is no mind.

When body and mind are fully prepared, then death and life, likes and dislikes, will arrive without being summoned. Why is this so? It is because knowledge establishes awakening as its hidden foundation.

Now, "knowledge" (*zhi*) is that which has already been manifested yet remains obscure in its core; "awakening" (*jue*) is that which is manifested in accordance with the measure (*jie*), without the core remaining obscure.
If the core is obscure, there is disharmony; if there is disharmony, then what destination would not be [a place of conflict]?
This is to follow one's feelings. Feelings possess private attachments, whereas nature (*xing*) is without self. Therefore, if one follows nature, where could one go that is not spiritual?

An ancient worthy said: "That which is without self yet spiritual is nature. Since it is said to be without self yet spiritual, then as for these twelve factors—form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and phenomena;
and the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—are they truly obstructive? Or are they truly unobstructive?
Indeed. Where there is obstruction, there is a self; where there is a self, there is no spiritual efficacy. Thus, every faculty and every object of perception becomes an obstacle to the self.
Only one who perceives their true nature understands that outside of this nature there is no mind, and outside of the mind there are no phenomena.

Therefore, as for all manner of things that act as obstacles to the self, there is no need to laboriously contemplate emptiness for them to become empty, nor to strive for clarity for them to become clear. This is what is meant by "original."
"Emptiness and clarity are like the vast heavens when clouds disperse; they have never failed to be manifest. Awakening and Compassion, come forward. I shall speak to you:
if you can truly awaken, then there will be nowhere you do not act with compassion. When one is compassionate, one regards the birth of all things as one's own birth.
If one does not awaken, then one's own birth is not the birth of things, and the birth of things is not one's own birth; they stand in opposition as two separate entities."
When duality is established, discrimination arises. When discrimination arises, likes and dislikes become private without being sought, yet they are indeed private.
Being private, one holds that one's own life is noble while the lives of other things are base; thus, the mind to harm other things arises without anyone knowing why.
Is this mind the fruit of compassion? Or is it not the fruit of compassion? If you understand this, you will realize that you are complete, and know that you were previously deficient.
To realize completeness is to have nothing that is not illuminated; to know one's former deficiency is to have nothing that is not impartial. Being impartial, there is naturally no self.
To practice compassion without a self—this is what is called "awakened compassion. Strive for awakened compassion! (This is the instruction on awakened compassion.)
Now, between the multitude of people and the sage, they are fundamentally not two different kinds of beings. The sage is human; the multitude are also human.
Yet, while the sage in every action follows his nature, the multitude in every action follow their emotions.
If one follows one's nature, then alertness and stillness flow as one; if one follows one's emotions, then dullness and distraction gallop together.

When alertness and stillness flow as one, the sense bases and objects are empty, yet the functions of subject and object are not abandoned. When dullness and distraction gallop together, the sense bases and objects create obstructions, obscuring the essence of the single truth.
Therefore, our Great Master Yongjia, within the gateless state, opened these ten gates. Although the gates—
The stages are, in truth, a single thread. To use an analogy: although there may be many beads, the string is fundamentally one.

Thus, for those whose minds penetrate and whose principles are mastered, there is no gate they do not pass through; though their levels of depth differ, in the final analysis, they do not transcend the principle of suchness.
The Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai established the classification of the "six identities": first, identity in principle; second, identity in name;
third, identity in contemplative practice; fourth, identity in semblance; fifth, identity in partial realization; and sixth, ultimate identity.

If these six identities are refined and clarified, then the fifty-five stages of the true path to Bodhi in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* can be understood without the trouble of exhaustive investigation, as their essential points are thereby grasped.
"It rests with me. Juepi, come forward; I shall speak to you. You must listen attentively. This collection is the very heart-essence of the Ancestral Teacher of Yongjia.
It begins with reading, then reciting; through recitation one maintains it, and through maintenance one refines it. When refined, there is oneness; when one, there is independence.
When independent, self and object are equal, and past and present become a single thread. Alas! Man is the pinnacle of all things."
If one’s spirit does not focus on this essence but instead focuses on something else, one is either ignorant or insane. I urge Juepi to be mindful of this (I show Juepi the *Yongjia ji*).
Now, there are three kinds of Prajñā: namely, the Prajñā of Words and Letters, the Prajñā of Contemplative Insight, and the Prajñā of Ultimate Reality.

Furthermore, these three Prajñās are called the Three Buddha-natures: the Buddha-nature of the Contributory Cause, the Buddha-nature of the Revealing Cause, and the Buddha-nature of the Primary Cause.
Alas! In the Dharma-body of the Sahā world, what is precious is hearing through sound; only after there is sound can [the teaching be realized].
There are words. Only after there are words does there arise the conditional cause for Buddha-nature.

Once there is the conditional cause for Buddha-nature, one is then able to permeate and awaken the light that is inherently possessed. When this inherent light opens, one can finally come to understand the direct cause of Buddha-nature.

It does not increase by even a fraction in the presence of the Buddhas, nor does it decrease by even a fraction in the presence of sentient beings. Understanding this thus, one should seal the mind with the Seal of Reality (*tattvamudrā*).

Thereafter, amidst the impact of favorable and adverse conditions regarding objects, and at the juncture where honor and disgrace intersect, one uses the light of this seal to break through all phenomena.
When the sense faculties and their objects are liberated, the eternal light manifests. Then, holding this eternal light, one illuminates all things universally.
When self-benefit and the benefit of others are accomplished and the wheel of vows is inexhaustible, the bodhisattva’s duties are complete.

Viewing it from this perspective, within the Sahā world, if there were no *prajñā* of words and letters (*vyañjana-prajñā*), then the *prajñā* of contemplative observation (*darśana-prajñā*) would not be developed.
If the *prajñā* of contemplative observation is not developed, by what means could one comprehend the *prajñā* of the true cause (*dharmatā-prajñā*)? Therefore, the *Vajra*...
The Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra consists of more than five thousand words; every character emits light, and every sentence is like the sun and moon, or like a bright lamp.
Where the light of the sun and moon cannot reach, the lamp can provide continuity.
Therefore, if a person can uphold the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, they will ultimately realize their nature, just as the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi was originally a poor wood-seller who—
Upon hearing the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he attained immediate awakening, realizing that one should give rise to the mind without abiding anywhere.

Furthermore, the Buddha-nature as the direct cause (*yuan-yin*) is like fire latent within wood; the Buddha-nature as the revealing cause (*liao-yin*) is like the fire that has been ignited and is able to burn the wood.
The Buddha-nature as the conditional cause is like wood used for drilling fire. Although fire exists within the wood, if one does not employ the act of drilling, smoke will ultimately not arise.
If smoke does not arise, how can fire be ignited? If fire is not ignited, with what could the wood be burned? If the wood is not burned...
In the end, it is difficult for them to return to the earth. That which is called "wood" is a thing that desires to ascend but cannot complete its ascent.
Yet, without subtle soil there would be no wood; wood arises because of soil. When fire breaks out, the wood transforms and its essence returns to the soil; this is the end of the wood. Alas!
The transformation of nature (*xing*) into emotion (*qing*) is like soil giving rise to wood. The permeation of emotion to restore nature is like wood [returning to soil].
This is returning to the fundamental substance. One awakens through sound to know this; one diligently upholds this sutra until it reaches ten million recitations.

When the upholding becomes mature, afflictions are extinguished; when afflictions are extinguished, clouds vanish. Then the celestial sky of the nature (dharmatā) unfolds vast and wide. How could one wait for the awakening sound to open one's eyes before finally seeing?
Jue-sheng was encouraged [to recite] this (it is shown that Jue-sheng held the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*):

"If the world before one's eyes were truly existent, then before True Suchness had responded to conditions, the world and its sentient beings would have been fundamentally non-existent from the start.
Because they were fundamentally non-existent at the beginning, they will likewise be non-existent in the end. Since both the beginning and the end are non-existent,"
To insist that this perception exists only when it is directly present before one is an irrational sentiment. It is like the mirage seen during the heat of the day;
when the sun has not yet risen or has already set, this mirage is entirely absent, yet one insists it is water and calculates that it will quench one's thirst—this is the delusion of the deer.
If the deer were not deluded, how could it have fled in pursuit? If sentient beings were not deluded, how could they engage in conceptual discrimination?

Therefore, the Dharma and the metaphor are observed as identical. Since there is nothing at either end, how could there be anything in the middle? The principle is like a box and its lid fitting together. In the present, what is there to discriminate?
Since discrimination does not arise, light vanishes and shadows are extinguished. When observing the moment of discrimination in reverse, subject and object are like snow in a dream. [Open.]
The sun of the eye is in the window; snow in a dream cannot be grasped. Both the measure and that which is measured are empty; the faculties and their objects were never originally defiled.
This is the principle; it is not a matter of emotion. (Shown by Kaixian)
The Master said: "From the single essence of brilliance, it is divided into the six harmonious aggregates.
Thus, the eyes and the other faculties harmonize with the six objects; from beginningless time, I have not been able to leave them for even a moment.

This is because when the eyes are open, they harmonize with the objects of form during the waking state, and when the eyes are closed, they harmonize with the objects of form during the dreaming state. Viewed in this light, the six sense-faculties..."
It is in conjunction with the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). Whether awake or dreaming, they mutually receive one another in every single object.
It is evident that from beginningless time until this very day, there has not been a single moment when they were not in conjunction.

Furthermore, the vision of the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) in conjunction with the object of form (*rūpaviṣaya*) is called "vision dependent on conditions. The vision of the eye-faculty when it is not in conjunction with the object of form—
This is called vision that is independent; as for vision that is dependent, it necessarily exists in reliance upon light, and when light ceases, one cannot see.
Vision that is independent does not exist in reliance upon light; even within a dark chamber, it is no different than being in broad daylight.

Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Vision depends on light; in darkness, it becomes non-vision. If clarity arises spontaneously from within, then all appearances of darkness can never again obscure it.

When the Chan Master Chushi Qi of our dynasty read this passage in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he attained great enlightenment, realizing that the sense faculties and their objects do not initially reach one another;
it is only because sentient beings' horizontal conceptualizations have not been eliminated that they remain in the darkness of ignorance.

In the midst [of this], one perceives brightness and darkness horizontally. In the teachings, this is called *aparāmāṇa* (non-valid cognition); it is neither inference (*anumāna*) nor direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
This horizontal perception functions as non-valid cognition because the sixth consciousness cannot examine names or verify reality.

Rather than entering the subtle essence of the refined meaning, it follows the knowledge that arises from the sensory objects; thus, the knowing faculty rushes toward external realms and is turned by the beautiful and the ugly. It is just like this.

Know this: if one can understand that the shadows of light and darkness, which possess characteristics due to the sense organs, are themselves fundamentally without intrinsic nature from the very beginning;

and having understood that these shadows of light and darkness are fundamentally without intrinsic nature, then how could the cognition that arises from the objects (dharmas) have any intrinsic nature of its own?
If a practitioner can perform such an investigation during daily activities and analyze it through principle, [they will realize this].

This is what is called *anumāna* (inference) in this land. When one observes in this manner for a long time, it gradually matures. Once matured, the afflictions of view and thought burst forth and fall away;
then the practitioner first enters the stage of semblance (*pratirūpa-bhūmi*). This stage of semblance pertains to both the *Hīnayāna* (Treasury) and *Mahāyāna* (Penetration) teachings.
These are all the stages of Buddhahood, not the stages of Bodhisattvas or Arhats. In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), they are merely called the "stage of semblance.
In the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao), they correspond to the seventh stage of abiding (the Seventh Bhūmi).

When a practitioner reaches this stage, the eye can perceive sounds, the ear can perceive forms, and the nose, tongue, and body can all function interchangeably with one another. If this is so, then the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue— [...]* *Note: The source text appears to be truncated here.*
Regarding the body: when the five sense organs perceive their respective objects, if the sixth consciousness has not yet arisen, the essence of the five organs is like the light of a mirror;
although beauty and ugliness are clearly perceived, there is no discrimination. This absence of discrimination is called *pratyakṣa* (direct perception). Thus Yongming said:
"At first, one abides within the direct perception of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), before the sensory dust has arisen; later, one falls into the clarity of mental cognition."
The "ground of the faculties" refers externally to the submerged forms; both the "floating dust" (the sensory objects) and the "mental faculty" (manas-indriya) refer to the sixth consciousness.
Furthermore, "non-inferential cognition" (aprāmāṇa) means to indulge one's whims and hold arbitrary views, being unable to subdue the emotions through principle.

"Inferential cognition" (anumāna) means that the practitioner is able to examine names and verify reality within the ocean of the Buddha-nature as the causal condition for enlightenment. When reality is verified, the meaning becomes refined; when the meaning is refined, [one attains realization].

Thus, the principle is penetrated. When the principle is penetrated, the emotions can no longer remain obscured. I am then able to employ analogies to apply it; reaching this stage is called "observation with mind.
Because one uses the principle to subdue the emotions, it is designated as "inference" (anumāna). Inference is precisely the wisdom that is free from objective dust (*nirnimitta-jñāna*).
Only when this wisdom free from dust is mature does one attain a semblance of "mindlessness" (*acittaka*); it is not yet true mindlessness. This is the principle.
Those who have even a slight understanding of teaching and contemplation can all comprehend this clearly, without needing the old fellow’s biased and prolix prattle.
Nevertheless, there are those great icchantikas who naturally know the depths of this old fellow’s warm-heartedness. Furthermore, regarding the seeing that arises from the cause of seeing:
although it is called "dependent seeing," it is able to give rise to cognition through objects and manifest characteristics through the faculties, such that they mutually negate one another.
If one contemplates this with deep pain, and through contemplation enters [the truth], then there is nothing that need be forgotten, and nothing that can ever further burden the essence of vision.

However, because the practitioner’s contemplation of this is not yet mature, their emotions suppress the principle; the principle cannot be trusted, and thus the faith of penetrating wisdom does not open.
Consequently, they cannot transcend the faith of mundane supernormal powers and remain perpetually suppressed by their emotions. It is like...
Observe this well: you will know that light and darkness mutually usurp one another, yet they fundamentally have no contact whatsoever with the essence of seeing.
Thus Yongjia said: "All numerical phrases are not numerical phrases; what contact do they have with my numinous awareness?
I, the old man, say: "All light and darkness are not light and darkness; what contact do they have with my essence of seeing? This was spoken at the assembly of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra.
The Buddha commanded Rāhula to strike the bell to test for permanence; this is also according to that principle.

For it is heard that the essence does not arise because of the sound of the bell, nor does it cease because of the sound of the bell. The movement and stillness of the sensory object of sound merely contend with one another as their own characteristics.

Furthermore, the faculty of hearing has never had any interaction with the essence of hearing (*śrotra-vid*). However, because Ānanda was calculating based on the present mind that can investigate and discriminate, he had not yet broken through the essence of seeing;
thus, the faculty of hearing could not suddenly become clearly manifest. For this reason, the Buddha specifically commanded Rāhula to strike the bell.
The Buddha’s intention was to use the movement and stillness, the arising and ceasing, of the auditory object (*śabda-viṣaya*) to cause Ānanda to immediately perceive the arising and...
The place of cessation. It is where there is fundamentally no movement or stillness, nor arising or ceasing. For example, when Xiangyan saw Guishan, Guishan said:
"I have heard that you can provide ten answers for every single question. Now I ask you: before your parents were born, try to utter a single word."
Xiangyan answered several times, yet none of his responses could match the pivotal opportunity of Muzhou’s intent.
He then requested that Muzhou provide a single word on his behalf. Muzhou said, "What I can say is merely my own samādhi; what business does it have with you?
Thereupon, Xiangyan cast away all he had learned and departed in tears, saying, "I shall spend the rest of my life as a long-term provider of rice gruel."
The assembly dispersed, and when Yan returned to his hermitage, he cleared away the debris and rubble. Just then, he heard the sound of bamboo being struck;

at that moment, all that he had known was suddenly forgotten, and he attained a profound realization of his own mind. Thereupon, he went before Master Muzhou and prostrated himself fully, saying, "If you, O Master, had explained this to me back then, how could there be a 'today'?
Yan had a verse which says: "One strike and all knowledge is forgotten; no further cultivation is required."
Maintain it! A movement of the countenance reveals the ancient road; do not fall into the trap of silent stillness. Alas!

One such as Xiangyan is what is called "attaining realization through conditions," one who shall never again suffer loss or regression. Viewed from this perspective, that which Xiangyan knows is precisely the mind with which Ānanda was able to investigate and pursue [the source].
This mind is the very awareness that arises from the dust; this awareness— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]
If one does not forget [this], then the faith of penetrating wisdom can ultimately never enter.

Once the faith of penetrating wisdom cannot enter, even if you discourse on the profound and explain the subtle, with eloquence equal to that of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, it will be nothing more than the faith of functional penetration.
Furthermore, this "knowledge arising from objects" was the state of subject and object in Xiangyan before he had seen Muzhou; this is the duality of subject and object.
The mind—though Guishan was renowned as a great spiritual friend (mahā-kalyāṇamitra), he could ultimately not cause [his student] to forget it.
It was only upon hearing the sound of the bamboo being struck by Yan that he was able to forget it of his own accord. Therefore, this matter can certainly not be sought through emotional sentiment.

For seeking through sentiment does not transcend the deluded thoughts of the sense bases (indriya) and their objects (viṣaya). If one can thoroughly realize that the sense bases and their objects have no inherent nature, then from the objects...
Such knowledge can also be forgotten. Furthermore, Xiangyan called this "becoming enlightened through sincerity" (*zicheng er ming*).
If one enters the Way by relying on the teachings and principles to subdue the emotions and treat habitual tendencies, it is called "becoming sincere through enlightenment" (*ziming er cheng*).

Formerly, there was a patriarch who asked a monk, "Hearing the sound of hairpins and bracelets from the next room constitutes breaking the precepts; how do you maintain the precepts? The monk replied, "What a fine..."
The path of entry. Does the entry of this monk truly coincide with that of Xiangyan, or is it different?

If they are the same, then the sound of hairpins and bracelets is not the sound of striking bamboo. If they are different, then the sound of hairpins and bracelets is certainly not the sound of striking bamboo.
Yet, in the end, there are no two [realities]. If a practitioner can discern the male and female at this point, then the one refined spirit is divided into the six harmonies.
Combine them. The six harmonies combine again to form a single, brilliant spirit. Squeeze it together and release it; let yourself act as you will.
If you cannot discern this, there is a verse from an ancient master for you all to chew upon once more.
If you can indeed break through it by chewing, it will not be too late to come see this old man again. The verse says: "Who else could it be but you? The remaining crimson is left on the hook..."
The Fish Pier: The sun slants and the wind has stilled; no one sweeps it. Swallows carry [the dust] away as they fly toward the water’s edge (shown to Kaixian).
