Ming Dynasty: Han-shan Deqing reads the *Fayu* (Discourses on the Dharma).
Now, although the paths of the sages and the ordinary are many, to speak of them in essence, they do not, in total, transcend the Four Noble Truths. "Truth" (*di*) means to examine with precision.

This is indeed not erroneous. Therefore, when the Sage speaks of suffering, it is necessarily suffering; when he speaks of its origin, it is necessarily its origin; when he speaks of the path, it is necessarily the path;

and when he speaks of cessation, it is necessarily cessation. Furthermore, regarding the Four Noble Truths, there are the Four Truths of Arising and Ceasing, the Four Truths of Non-arising, and the Immeasurable Four Truths.

There are the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*) Four Noble Truths. Therefore, for both the Śrāvaka Four Noble Truths and the Pratyekabuddha Four Noble Truths, Suffering and its Origin come first, while Cessation and the Path follow later.
This is because the aspirations of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas lie solely in the Two Vehicles; they seek only their own welfare and lack the vow to bring universal benefit to others.
As for the Immeasurable Four Noble Truths and the Unconditioned Four Noble Truths, although the Separate and Perfect [teachings] are indeed distinct...

Although they differ, both possess the aspiration for universal goodness; therefore, it is called a "great vow" (*mahāpraṇidhāna*). Viewed from this perspective, it is clear that the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas possess the [Four] Truths but lack the vows.
Thus it is said: "That which possesses vows is called the Mahāyāna; that which lacks vows is called the Two Vehicles. What are the immeasurable Four Truths?
They are cultivated through the sequential practice of the three contemplations—emptiness (*śūnyatā*), provisional existence (*upāya*), and the Middle Way (*madhyamā*)—beginning first with emptiness.
One contemplates and shatters the afflictions of views and thought; next, one uses the contemplation of the provisional to shatter the afflictions of the "dust-sands";

finally, one uses the contemplation of the Middle Way to shatter fundamental ignorance. When views and thought are shattered, one attains the virtue of *prajñā*; when the dust-sands are shattered, one attains the virtue of *vimukti*;
when fundamental ignorance is shattered, one attains the virtue of the *dharmakāya*. These three virtues are the innate, natural virtues of one's nature. They reside in...
It is not that there is a deficiency in the ordinary person, nor an excess in the sage; therefore it is said, "Natures are nearly alike.

When the nature transforms into emotion (*qing*), the gateway of coarse compliance opens. Once the gateway of coarse compliance opens, those who were nearly alike become accustomed to what is distant.
If one becomes accustomed to the distant and does not return, one will sink into suffering without end. Therefore it is said, "Practices lead to great divergence. Thus, first...
The Awakened One pities this and strives to cause those who are distant to practice what is near. Thus, within the gate of compliance with the coarse, he first opens the gate of reversal.

"Reversal" means, essentially, to flow upstream against the current. To ascend to the ultimate limit—wherein there is no difference between a sage and the common person—is what I have fully realized. If I have realized it while others have not, then as for the sages...
Furthermore, being unable to bear [the suffering of others], one therefore rides upon that wholeness to travel extensively amidst the myriad transformations.

One opens up things and accomplishes tasks so that those who have not yet recognized their own wholeness may all attain it. Thus, after the stage of "contrary" (ni), there is "wondrous compliance" (miao-shun).
However, this wondrous compliance exists only for Bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching (bie-jiao) and the Perfect Teaching (yuan-jiao); for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, there is only contrariety.
It is not yet sublime or compliant. This is because it lacks the Four Great Vows and fails to give rise to the compassion of the same essence (*sahaja-karuṇā*).

What is meant by the compassion of the same essence? It means that while I am in the midst of coarse non-compliance, I undergo immeasurable suffering. Amidst this immeasurable suffering, when the pain reaches its peak, one contemplates the source.
To contemplate the source is to draw near to awakening; when one draws near to awakening, it is easy to cultivate and manifest [the seeds]. At this time, first—
The Awakened One knows that I am capable of being perfumed. He then discerns by what causes and conditions I may be perfumed, and immediately perfumes me by those very causes and conditions.
It is like the meeting of arrowheads or the simultaneous snapping of a beak; skillful power cannot intervene, for it is known not how it happens, yet they naturally accord with one another.
Alas! This is not a matter of examining names, scrutinizing reality, or refining meaning—it enters the divine.
In that case, how could the perfumer and the perfumed fail to forget their roles as subject and object, thereby attaining a non-conceptual accord?

Nevertheless, Wu Yuan and Gou Jian were able to overcome their coarse resentment for their enemies; they both scorched their bodies and tormented their minds for over twenty years until they finally achieved their desires.
Now, we seek the Unsurpassed Way within the supramundane Dharma to emerge from immeasurable suffering—surely we shall attain the fruit.
If one can endure the hardship of withering the body through diligent practice for a thousand days, then that which I desire will surely be accomplished without doubt. Why is this?

It is because Wu Yuan and Gou Jian pursued their affairs by following their emotions; they were not close to the fundamental nature (*xing*), and thus required long-term suffering before their desires could be fulfilled.
We, however, set our will upon restoring the nature and seek the method for transcending emotion; we must persevere with diligence.
The goodness of nature contains within it the way of the filial son. Thus, the merit of a thousand days can be exchanged for more than twenty years of arduous toil.
This is the natural principle; this is the inevitable trend. Why, then, should I harbor any doubt?
Following these Four Great Vows, I shall now set forth the essence and the details of the Four Noble Truths, as well as the exposition of the Three Virtues and the Two Submissions.

A general summary of the first transgression is this: I fear that when you resolve to attain enlightenment, you may fail to distinguish between the shallow and deep teachings of the *Zang*, *Tong*, *Bie*, and *Yuan* [Tripitaka].
If your resolve lacks a guiding principle—where "principle" refers to the fundamental school—then your ultimate destination will lack a foundation. You must know this fundamental principle.

Within the Great Canon, there is the *Tiantai Sijiaoyi* (The Ritual of the Four Teachings of Tiantai), which consists of approximately ten thousand characters. If you seek it out and obtain it, you must vow to read it.

Once you have mastered the recitation and gained a general understanding of its meaning, then the relative depth of the four teachings and the fundamental source of the resolve for enlightenment will reside within you,
rather than in the book alone.
When a horse forgets the leather thong and the compass and square, yet remains within the compass and square, the horse will never fail.

If it were to gallop while not having forgotten the leather thong and the compass and square, there would be no horse that does not fail. Therefore, when the feet forget the shoes, one first attains true comfort.
When one forgets the waist-belt, it becomes comfortable; there has never been anything that is not comfortable when forgotten. Thus, comfort begins with forgetting.

Observing this, when the body is forgotten, the mind’s function becomes all-pervasive; when the mind is forgotten, that which has never failed to be pervasive pervades the myriad things without ever becoming weary.
Because it is never weary, it is able to labor for the myriad things, yet it does not labor for the myriad things itself. Therefore it is said: "Only..."
To forget even forgetting—such that there is nothing left to forget—is possible only for one who has fully exhausted [all conceptualization] and knows how to adapt to change.
The *Jing-shan Jie-yao* (Essential Passages from Jing-shan) edited by the Śramaṇa Mingxiu of Ezhou is indeed clear, lucid, and precise. However, the verse he composed says:
"When movement and stillness participate in the essential pivot, the path devised by artifice is further astray. Now, departing from the place of emotional views, there is something else."
What a fine life! I do not know what these emotional views (*qingjian*) are that one wishes to leave behind.

One fails to realize that those whom one intends to leave behind—those very emotional views—are they themselves emotional views? Or are they not emotional views? If they are emotional views, then the subsequent departure is the initial departure.
If they are not emotional views, then the subsequent departure is likewise not [the departure from] emotional views. Alas! The essential point is indeed subtle and refined.
"It has arrived! How could you know that the point where the essential principles reach their ultimate refinement is precisely the tea and rice of Mount Jing;

it is not the food and drink of Master Xiu. Master Xiu, speak quickly, speak quickly! If you cannot produce a word, it will not be that Master Xiu is defining the standard for Mount Jing, but rather that Mount Jing is defining the standard for Master Xiu."
Regarding the principle that dependent origination is non-arising, those who have even a slight mastery of the *prajñā* of words are generally able to speak of it.
Yet they fail to realize that knowing dependent origination as non-arising is merely like using a painted cake to stave off hunger; how could it ever be able to plunder the bandit of birth and death?
Only when one knows can one act; when one acts can one contend; when one contends can one triumph. To triumph is to realize it. Alas!
If one realizes it yet cannot forget it, then the Great Function will not manifest.

If the Great Function does not manifest, then the wondrous principle of "carrying the fruit while practicing the cause," as well as the ever-present conduct of Samantabhadra, will almost come to an end. By this I know that it is easy to clarify the Way, but difficult to practice it.
That the Way is difficult to apply is by no means a hollow statement;

we must strive in this. Nature is like water, while emotion is like ice. Ice has substance and obstruction, whereas water is fluid and pervasive. When there is fluidity and pervasion, there is fundamentally no subject or object;

when there is substantiality and obstruction, the sense organs and their objects stand in opposition. This principle involves both knowing and perceiving; yet though the mind may be clear through such knowing, it remains conceptual.
When encountering phenomena while still deluded, one remains confused; when awakened, one realizes the principle upon encountering phenomena, and the dust of emotional attachments naturally vanishes.
Delusion is the burden of emotion; awakening is the resonance with the nature. Burden implies duality; resonance implies unity. Duality entails dependence; unity is non-arising.

Non-arising is the constancy of nature; having conditions is the transformation of nature. Constancy implies being without self yet spiritual; transformation implies having emotions and being obscured.
Thus, within obscuration, knowledge cannot overcome the obscuration; this is why the Way cannot oppose habitual tendencies.
Spirituality means that habitual tendencies cannot overcome awakening; this is why one can advance toward Bodhi while sitting without relying on formal cultivation. To act otherwise is the reverse.
Although one may sacrifice body and life as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it merely increases the karma of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

This is because awakening (*bodhi*) pertains to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), whereas knowledge (*jñāna*) pertains to inference (*anumāna*); thus, there is a distinction between the accomplishment of awakening and that of knowledge.
If the object contains the subject, the object is not established as such; if the subject contains the object, the subject is likewise not established.
This is because if there is no subject within the object, the subject is identical to the object; and if there is no object within the subject, the object is identical to the subject.

This is simply because the subject and object do not encounter one another. If they were to encounter, then both subject and object would fail to be established. That neither is established is not [the case].

The Buddha-dharma: because its nature is not obscured by intellect, both [nature and intellect] are fully realized. Although the intellect may not be obscured, if the nature has severed the "bloodline" (the continuity of realization), it is likewise not the Buddha-dharma.
Only when the bloodline is not severed and the intellect is also unobscured can one know this through direct personal realization alone.
Now, the eye dreams of forms, the ear dreams of sounds, the nose dreams of fragrances, the tongue dreams of flavors, the body dreams of tangibles, and the mind dreams of dharmas.
Within this single body, the six sense organs are all dreaming; if there were none among them who could awaken, then one dream would be an eternal dream.

Thereupon, this Bodhisattva of Great Compassion instructed him to observe with the eye, listen to forms with the ear, taste flavors with the nose, smell fragrances with the tongue, grasp objects with the body, and perceive contacts with the mind. Thus, the six dreams were suddenly awakened, and the overturned basin was instantly enlightened.
Viewed from this perspective, if one employs the six sense faculties in accordance with the flow [of worldly existence], then the six sense-objects are all mediators for dreams.
When the six faculties are employed to flow against the current, the six sense objects all become the thunder of awakening.

This is as described in the twenty-five methods of perfect penetration (*vimalakīrti-sūtra*), wherein the six faculties, the six objects, the six consciousnesses, and furthermore earth, water, fire, wind, space, sight, and cognition, mutually serve as thunder to startle and awaken the dreamer.
Lately, however, the ways of the world have fallen into ruin; people take thunder for dreams and dreams for thunder, not knowing which is which.
The awakened one—what, then, is the dreamer? Since one cannot distinguish between dreaming and awakening, one will not stop until even jade and stone are burned together.

Now, although the School of the Way (Daoxue) has its defects, it is far superior to vulgar learning; although the School of Chan (Chanxue) has its defects, it is far superior to the School of the Way.
Yet today, some regard the School of the Way as a mire of fame and profit, and thus they mutually attack it; and regarding the School of Chan...
It has become a marsh and thicket for fugitives and runaways, and they have even mutually excluded one another. Yet they fail to realize that customs are not fixed:
if the wind of Daoist learning is fanned, a custom of Daoist learning is formed; if the wind of Chan learning is fanned, a custom of Chan learning is likewise formed.
Once the customs of Daoist and Chan learning are established, naturally those who are lofty and enlightened will increase day by day. And...
Those who are defiled and obscured are few. This may include those who falsely adopt Daoist learning or Chan Buddhism;
such people exist among the defiled and obscured. These, too, are merely tares and weeds amidst excellent grain. It must be that the grain is abundant while the weeds are few.
If one hates the few weeds and wishes to utterly eliminate the abundant grain, how could this be the intent of a benevolent person? (Daoist learning and Chan Buddhism)
I, the Elder of Great Enlightenment, preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* at the assembly on Vulture Peak.

Although the work consists of twenty-eight chapters in total, and though its teachings and parables are extensively elaborated and mutually clarifying, they do not exceed the principle of attaining the subtle through the coarse.
As for the comparison of the relative merits of the six sense faculties, it is as brilliant as the sun and stars; such is the case with the three faculties of the eyes, nose, and body.
The three faculties of ear, tongue, and mind each possess one thousand two hundred merits.
To speak according to reality, when compared with the nose and body, the tongue faculty also possesses only eight hundred merits;
however, in its expounding of the wondrous Dharma, its merit surpasses that of all other faculties. Thus, the reason the Tathāgata added four hundred merits to it was to reward it.

If one cannot preach the Dharma, yet engages in frivolous speech, false speech, untruthful speech, double-tongued speech, and abusive language, then the retribution for such sins will likewise exceed that of the sense organs.
Therefore it is said: "When a gentleman dwells in his chamber, if he utters one word of goodness, it will be responded to from a thousand li away;
if he utters one word of evil, it will likewise be responded to from a thousand li away. It is further said: "Speech is the source of both fortune and calamity."
It is a ladder. As it is the master of both honor and disgrace, how can one not be cautious? Furthermore, the two faculties of eye and ear apprehend their objects from a distance;

the three faculties of nose, tongue, and body apprehend their objects through contact; and the mental faculty merely presides over the shadows left behind when the first five faculties have ceased their activity.
The actual objects of the five sensory realms are all governed by the first five consciousnesses. However, at the assembly of the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra*, the Tathāgata commanded—

Mañjuśrī selected the faculty of the perfect penetration; among those twenty-four sages, he rejected them all and chose only the ear-faculty, which precisely accords with the capacities of beings in this Sahā world.
This is why Avalokiteśvara is placed first and the other sages follow; it is simply a matter of causes, conditions, and timing.
How could it be that the other sages possess any sense of shame? Long ago, a Chan master asked a monk: "Do you hear what is happening next door?"
The sound of her hairpins and bracelets falling was itself a breaking of the precepts. The son asked, "How then does one maintain the precepts? He replied, "What an excellent way of entry!
The Chan Master said, "In the future, you shall become the provider of food for fifteen hundred spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).
If this is so, then how could even the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra—whose mental hearing penetrates the ten directions—not feel a sense of shame before this monk? Indeed," [it was] when...
As for the spiritual capacity of those in this region, Samantabhadra is not as well-suited as Avalokiteśvara;

yet in other regions, Avalokiteśvara is likewise not as well-suited as Samantabhadra—it is impossible to say. This is because when a sage preaches the Dharma, it is like casting a luminous pearl into a golden platter:
its horizontal, diagonal, and winding movements, its collisions and free transitions, are entirely spontaneous. Even though [the Buddha] was as holy as Kāśyapa...

Wen: "I do not know this myself either. Nevertheless, I have one further question: When the mind-hearing penetrates the ten directions, is it because the directions are outside the mind that it can hear?
Or is it because the directions are inside the mind that it can hear? If it can hear while they are outside—"
To hear it internally is impossible when examined through reason; this is known only by those who have personally heard it and realized it for themselves.

Therefore, regarding the study that exhausts principle and perfects nature, if one sets aside the Tathāgata, who else could investigate the superiority and inferiority of the six sense faculties, such that their functions are complete and their principles are thoroughly penetrated?
How fortunate I am, a youth, to have entered the house of the Tathāgata and cultivated the unsurpassed seed. Slightly...
To not contemplate repaying the profound kindness of the Buddha is to be no human being at all. May you, my son, exert yourself with poignant diligence.

(Shown to Dongwen) The long wind wanders through the great void, and ten thousand apertures clamor and howl in competition. The common person hears this with their ears; the Bodhisattva observes it with their eyes.
If this fruit of sound were permanent, the gate of perfect penetration would be difficult to open. Alas! When sound comes to the ear, who is the subject at the time of its arrival?

When the ear goes to the place of the sound, what is it that can hear? Investigating this coming and going, if the natures of the sense-faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) exist, then subject and object are difficult to discard;
if they do not exist, one is as withered as dead wood. Since both paths are exhausted, how could the center stand in isolation? Therefore, it is said: "Wisdom enters."
The three periods of time have no coming or going; this is the constancy of the fundamental light. That consciousness traverses the three periods is the transformation of the fundamental light.
When the fundamental light transforms, the faculties and objects become obstructed; sentient beings, in their profound ignorance, sleep in a dense dream.

At twilight, one prostrates before the Buddha—who strikes the chime? The sound enters the ear: is it empty or not empty? If it is empty, there is no hearing; if it is not empty, it is an obstruction. Hearing the resonance, its weight increases.
For their sake, he explained the perfect penetration (*yuantong*). Since sound is thus, form is no different; how profound are scent, flavor, touch, and phenomena!
The single word "knowing" is the gateway to all wonders. To establish a knowing within seeing and knowing is a calamity of great magnitude. To follow feelings and to follow nature are worlds apart.
How many who meet realize the ultimate point? These two have always been one yet two; their application depends on whether one is enlightened or deluded.

Upon awakening, joy and anger follow only the nature; following the nature enables one to penetrate the sentiments of all under heaven. When sentiments are penetrated, things are opened up and affairs are accomplished.
It is like the bending and extending of a single finger: if one does not follow the nature but follows the sentiments, one is doubly deluded—a pitiable being indeed.
Using oneself to communicate with others gives rise to discrimination; at the critical juncture of opposition and compliance, love and hatred abound. Therefore it is said: "The Ultimate Way..."

There is no difficulty; it is simply a matter of avoiding discrimination. Just do not harbor love or hatred, and all will be transparently clear. It is also said: "To follow one's nature is called the Way;
to follow one's emotions is called perversion. Alas! Does the Sage have no emotions? It is simply that his emotions are pervasive yet not obscured; he possesses emotion without being burdened by it.
Because he has emotion, there is nothing he does not penetrate; because he is without burden, he is fundamentally free from love and hatred. Therefore, in all things—
Great Bodhisattvas, in years of famine, transform their bodies into mountains of fish, rice, and meat; in ages of pestilence, they transform their bodies into all manner of medicinal herbs.
Are these sentient or non-sentient? If they were non-sentient, they would be the same as wood and stone; if they were sentient, they would not differ from ordinary beings.
Therefore, one who can hear sounds with the eyes is a sage; one who hears sounds with the ears is an ordinary person.
Furthermore, when Zhongni reached the age of sixty, his ears became attuned to all sounds. Commentators have taken this to mean that sounds entered his ears and were understood by his mind.
This is a constant source of affliction for practitioners of the Way. For what reason? When the ears are attuned, there is neither compliance nor resistance toward sounds;

they all become conduits for following one’s nature. To follow one’s nature is to be without self. To be without self is to be without internal or external. Since internal and external no longer exist, who is it that enters and exits? Alas! Not... [text ends]
To go out and not come back in is like painting eyebrows on a formless void; how much more so for those who go out and in again and again! Awaken the emotions, awaken the emotions:

when awakened, the nature is luminous, without distinction between hatred and love. Wherever one touches it, it is fundamentally radiant and numinous. Self-awakening and further awakening others—when they meet, their true nature begins to incline toward clarity.
In the direct encounter, there is no lingering existence; after parting, one remains ever more alert and aware.
Viśvabhū Buddha—this means "Self-Mastering Awakened One" (*svayambhū*). This is because this Buddha has awakened to and realized liberation in both body and mind.
Through liberation of the body, there is no obstruction of birth and death; through liberation of the mind, there is no obstruction of afflictions.
Liberation (vimukti) carries the meaning of mastery (vaśitā). Yet, all sentient beings are unable to awaken to and understand the body and the mind;

therefore, they cannot liberate themselves from the obstructions of birth-and-death and afflictions (kleśa). If one can awaken to and shatter the grasping and attachment to body and mind, [liberation is attained].
Sentient beings and Buddhas are no different. If one cannot awaken to and shatter the grasping and attachment to body and mind, then even the Buddhas could never attain true sovereignty.
Now tell me, how does one awaken to and shatter the body? One should observe minutely:
from where did the skin, flesh, sinews, and bones of my body—everything that is solid—first arise? From where did the mucus, saliva, phlegm, blood, and urine of my body come?
Regarding all things of the moist category, from what did they first arise? Regarding the warmth of my body, regarding all things of the hot category, from what did they first arise?

Regarding my body’s four limbs and hundred bones, its eighty-four thousand pores, the unimpeded circulation of the blood vessels, and that which enables movement and motion—where did these first arise?
Once the contemplation of the body has matured, one should next contemplate the mind. I...

Does this presently manifesting discriminating mind exist because of another, or does it exist because of itself? If it existed because of another, then love and hatred would not arise when one has not yet contacted an object.
If it existed because of itself, then even in the absence of contact with an object, the mind would still possess love and hatred.
One repeatedly investigates both with respect to oneself and with respect to others, considering whether [the mind] arises dependent on another or whether it arises dependent on itself.

When one analyzes this through reasoning, the notions of self and other wither away until no ground remains. Once the notions of self and other have withered, by what means could a mind arise in conjunction?
Since the notion of arising in conjunction has withered, how could a mind arise without a cause? If there were none...
"If causes can produce things, why is there no water within fire? Why do stones not grow grass? Why is there no sweetness in salt?
Why does a rabbit have no horns? And why does a tortoise have no hair? Nāgārjuna replied: "All phenomena are not produced from themselves, nor are they produced from another;

they are not produced from both, nor are they produced without a cause. Therefore, it is said that they are unproduced. This verse by Nāgārjuna is, moreover, a commentary on the verses of the Buddha Vipaśyin.
(An explanation of the verse of Vipaśyin Buddha:
I have often reflected in stillness upon this: from the beginning, there has never been such a thing as fortune or misfortune in the world.

The arising of fortune and misfortune arises merely from slander and praise. Therefore, when one slanders me, others suffer misfortune while I enjoy fortune; when one praises me, others enjoy fortune...
I am unlucky. Furthermore, praise and blame arise from likes and dislikes, and likes and dislikes arise from that which has never begun to like or dislike.

Therefore, I say: the world has never begun to have good fortune or misfortune. Nevertheless, when I observe the good and bad fortune of the world through the perspective of that which has never begun to like or dislike, they are all like the hair on a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit. If one were to observe that which has never begun [to exist] through the lens of good and bad fortune...
As for the existence of good fortune and misfortune, there has never been anything that is inherently good or bad; there is nowhere one goes that is not characterized by good or bad fortune.
If this is so, then good and bad fortune originally have no source; they depend entirely upon how I perceive them.

Thus, when an arrow pierces a stone tiger or fish leap from beneath the ice of a river, if it were not for that which has never had good or bad fortune to move the ice and the stone, then the fish and the [pierced] object would not exist.
How could Shi Hu possibly change along with me? It is precisely this principle that the gentleman does not harbor anger in his heart for long.
However, the multitude is ignorant of this truth and gives rein to their passions; thus, at first, things and the self appear as utterly distinct.
Furthermore, likes and dislikes cannot arise of themselves; they must arise because of external objects. Since they arise because of external objects, then the "self" is manifest...
The likes and dislikes previously experienced were originally the likes and dislikes of external objects; they had no prior connection with me.

It is like having a mind that is equanimous toward those who are close or distant; yet when such close or distant persons suddenly appear, my feelings of liking or disliking arise spontaneously, beyond my own restraint.
This suggests that these feelings already exist within my mind and are merely manifested through being drawn out by external conditions.
Thus, in my true mind, even birth does not exist; how, then, could there be a self? To have a self is to be dependent;
to be dependent is to be subject to verbal description. When the mind and its objects pull upon one another, this emotion arises.

If one says that my mind is unborn yet can produce this emotion, is it not then produced without a cause? Whether it is produced from itself, from another, or from both—when analyzed through reason, none of these hold.
If [things] can arise from conditions, how much more so from no cause? An ancient said, "To be absent for even a moment is to be the same as a dead man.

This refers to the mind's flight toward sensory objects while its underlying principle remains obscured. Caoxi also said, "If one is a true practitioner of the Way, they do not see the faults of the world.
From this I know that those who perceive faults in the world have not yet forgotten their own minds; thus, external things...
"Wait for me! If I am without mind, then all things will likewise transform along with my lack of mind. Why should one trouble oneself to repeatedly cast them aside before they can be dissolved?
If you disciples can observe adverse and favorable circumstances and conditions in this way, then these very circumstances and conditions are truly my great teacher.
How could I dare to oppose or resist my great teacher? (Taught to his disciples.)
If the affairs of sentient beings were permanent, then the affairs of the Buddha would also be permanent.

Since the affairs of sentient beings are impermanent, the affairs of the Buddha are likewise impermanent. For example, when sentient beings suffer from the affliction of famine, the Buddha provides fragrant food as medicine;
or when sentient beings suffer from the affliction of cold and frost, the Buddha provides padded robes as medicine. When sentient beings have...

Taking darkness as the illness, the Buddha takes radiance as the medicine. Thus, while the illnesses committed by sentient beings are immeasurable, the medicines bestowed by the Buddha are likewise immeasurable.
For example, at the assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, the Buddha emitted the light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows.
It illuminates eighteen thousand lands in the eastern direction. The verse by the Venerable Xuansha Shibei on deceased monks says:

"Myriad miles of divine light is the mark behind the head. Linji said: "All of you, upon this ball of red flesh, each possesses a true person of no rank who emits great radiance from the gates of the six sense organs. Judging from this, it is clear that this light emerges [from there].
It has no fixed location. The *Lotus Sūtra* states that when the Buddha emits light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, it illuminates eighteen thousand lands in the eastern direction.
Thus, this light appears to have a fixed location. Why? Because while the light illuminates the eastern direction, it does not illuminate the other directions.
Nevertheless, although the light illuminates the eastern direction and does not illuminate the other directions, it is not that it fails to illuminate the others.

This is indeed the case. It is likely the intention of the Tathāgata to take up one direction and thereby cause the other nine directions to respond. Some have said that the "True Person of No Station" in Linji’s teaching has light that has no fixed location, whereas in Xuansha and Fahua’s teachings, the light has a before and after.

To this, I replied: [The text continues with the response: "The light of the True Person of No Station is like the light of the sun and moon; it is not something that can be grasped by the mind or intellect. It is simply that when the conditions for seeing are met, there is seeing; when the conditions for seeing are absent, there is no seeing. This is not a matter of the light having a before and after, nor is it a matter of the light being without a fixed location. It is simply that the light of the True Person of No Station is originally non-dual with the light of all phenomena."
Since the sutra cites one direction while the other nine directions are its opposite, the light between the eyebrows has never failed to illuminate the ten directions in their entirety.
You call the light between the eyebrows the "front light," and you call the light behind the crown of the head the "rear light."
This is merely the disciple’s groundless fabrication; it is not that the light of the Buddhas and Patriarchs has any distinction of before or after.

However, as for the intent of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, if sentient beings were to enter through even a single ray of light, the radiance that perfectly illumines the ten directions would never have been different.

When objects again give rise to the mind, the fire of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*) blazes intensely; when the mind again gives rise to objects, the realm of mental discourse arises.

The Bodhisattva thoroughly understands that all objective spheres arise through the transformations of mental discourse (*manojalpa*), yet mental discourse has no intrinsic substance; it does not transcend mere consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*).

Mere consciousness has no intrinsic substance; it does not transcend the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Therefore, by observing mere consciousness through the Dharma-realm, mere consciousness is itself the Dharma-realm.
By observing mental discourse through mere consciousness, mental discourse is itself mere consciousness. By observing external objects through mental discourse—[one realizes they are] false.
[Answer: It is attachment. Attachment to external objects is precisely mental verbalization (*manojalpa*). This is why one can transform things rather than being transformed by things.
As when Wang of Boling asked Niu-tou Rong: "When conditions for objects arise from form, you do not say that they arise conditioned by form.

How then can one know the conditions? One wishes to bring their arising to rest. Wang of Boling believed that the objects of mental verbalization are conditioned by the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).

It arises. It does not say, "I arise conditioned by the external object. Nor does the external object say, "I am able to trigger the mind that produces speech. To say it does not speak is not to say it lacks cognition;

rather, it means that where there is cognition, one can speak, and where there is no cognition, one cannot speak. Therefore, both the subject (the cognizer) and the object (the cognized) are devoid of cognition.
Being devoid of cognition, they are devoid of self. Being devoid of self, they are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Since both subject and object are thus...

If there is no intrinsic nature, then between the object and form, which is the subject that perceives and which is the object perceived? Is this non-arising through conditions not itself non-arising?
Since arising through conditions is itself non-arising, whom would you teach to know conditions? And why would you wish to cause them to cease?
Therefore, Niutou immediately followed up on Boling’s line of thought and replied: "When the objective form first arises, this is precisely dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

That the two natures of form and object are empty is precisely non-arising (*anutpāda*). Fundamentally, there is no one who cognizes conditions; the mental measure (*cittamātra*) is identical with cognition.
Since both subject and object are fundamentally without arising, whom could one instruct to cognize conditions? Since there is no one who cognizes conditions, then mind and its measure—"

Together with cognition, all are without arising. For if one does not illumine the source, subject and object remain distinct; if one illumines the source, the sense organs and their objects are stilled and extinguished.
Thus it is said: "Illuminating the source, what arises does not arise. At that time, arising is itself cessation. Clutching at darkness gives rise to the conditions for awakening;

yet when the mind is present, these conditions are not pursued. This means that awakening arises because of darkness, and as awakening arises, darkness fades away. When darkness fades, awakening becomes limpid and still, and the mind has nothing upon which to rest.

Condition. Since the object of perception (*ālambana*) is absent, even profound stillness has no place to rest. Prior to arising, there was fundamentally no form or mind to nourish; it is simply vast emptiness without thought.
All notions of form, mind, nourishment, and sensation are said to arise from thought. Yet, this arising is in truth non-arising; therefore, it is said that what is initiated has never been initiated.
At such a time, not only do sentient beings have no ground, but even a Buddha finds it difficult to find a mooring. This is because...
Principle subdues emotion; it integrates phenomena into principle.
A whirlwind does not last the morning; a torrential rain does not last the day.

Even such winds and rains, wrought by Heaven and Earth, cannot preserve their duration or permanence—how much less so that which exists beneath Heaven and Earth? Yet, the Way of Heaven and Earth remains unfathomed.
Yet these transformations are subtle and hidden. Thus, although all things dwell within the realm of change and transformation, they themselves do not perceive it.
It is like the course of a year: before winter has ended, it changes into spring; before spring has ended, it changes into summer; before summer has ended, it changes into autumn;
and before autumn has ended, it changes into winter. Winter is the conclusion; "conclusion" means reaching the ultimate limit. Long ago, there was a man who saw the sun rise from the sea.
The lines, "The waning night; the river spring enters the old year," also represent one who knows change before being exhausted by it.
It is like the way of the single body: before life is exhausted, it changes into youth; before youth is exhausted, it changes into maturity; before maturity is exhausted, it changes into old age;
and before old age is exhausted, one comes to know death. Once one knows death, death cannot exhaust me. Death cannot exhaust [me].
As for me, how could life possibly bring me joy? Since death cannot exhaust me, life likewise cannot please me.
I take birth and death as my vessel to navigate the sea of calamity and fortune;

when I encounter the alarms of sudden gales and torrential rain, these may indeed startle the common crowd, but how could they startle me? Indeed, the Three Sovereigns transformed the world through the Way.

When the Way reached its limit, it changed into Virtue (*de*). The Five Emperors governed the world through Virtue. When Virtue reached its limit, it changed into Benevolence and Righteousness (*ren-yi*).
The Three Kings governed the world through Benevolence and Righteousness, yet they did not know how to change; thus, they were exhausted by Benevolence and Righteousness.
Once Benevolence and Righteousness were exhausted, the Five Hegemons exploited the resulting gaps, using their power and intelligence to coerce the world—a state of affairs that is truly unspeakable.
Therefore, those who possess a body, a family, or a state—if they do not understand this, they will be unable to cultivate their bodies, bring order to their families, or govern their states.
Yet, it is only the sage who, without exhausting his efforts, knows how to adapt to change.
Now, the principles of the hidden and the manifest, the discourse on ghosts and spirits, and the way of life and death are all matters that follow transformation.
Yet worldly people are often bewildered by them, like the people of Dian and Yue who speak of the affairs within the Han Yuandian Palace;

regarding ghosts and spirits, they harbor even deeper doubts, failing only because they do not apply their minds to investigate them. Indeed, it is through ghosts and spirits that one may exhaustively investigate the nature and emotions of humanity. By...

The nature and disposition reach their ultimate limit in the *hun* and *po* spirits. Now that they have reached this ultimate limit, we know that governing the emotions with principle constitutes the *hun*, while indulging the emotions to destroy the nature constitutes the *po*.
Thus, all matters concerning the hidden and the manifest, death and life, become perfectly clear.

Although birth and death are rooted in the possession of a body, and the hidden and manifest realms of ghosts and spirits are rooted in the existence of a mind, the multitude are merely ignorant of these roots;
thus, nothing is more intense than their preoccupation with life and death, and they remain complacent and indulgent in them, taking suffering for pleasure.

For this reason, the Elder of Great Enlightenment took pity on them and rescued them, teaching them to analyze the body through the four great elements and to analyze the mind through the four aggregates. Having analyzed them...
For a long time, when the body is exhausted and the mind is understood, then the body is fundamentally no-body and the mind is fundamentally no-mind.
When the body is no-body, one forever transcends great suffering; when the mind is no-mind, there is no hidden darkness that it does not illuminate.
Thus, at this point, Nāgārjuna strikes another singular blow, his verse saying: "If birth were to exist first, and old age and death later, then there would be birth without old age and death."

If it is truly as the saying goes—that there is no old age and death apart from birth—then when one exhausts the body after the four elements have combined and seeks the mind prior to the four aggregates, it is like a revolving wheel;
who can determine its beginning or end? Regarding Viśvabhū Buddha, this may be called "each dreaming while sharing the same bed.
Thus, concerning what are called the hidden and the manifest, spirits and ghosts, death and life, all are encompassed by the mark of the broad and long tongue. Now...
This verse consists of twenty-eight characters in total. Within the first half of the verse lies the point of entry.

Once one has entered this state, amidst the intersection of good and evil and within the field of right and wrong, favor and adversity, one can maintain an uninterrupted mindfulness, deeply contemplating non-arising (*anutpāda*).

When the practice of non-arising becomes familiar, the arising of conditions gradually thins out. As the coarse is transformed into the refined, body and mind can no longer confine it; one immediately perceives the Great.

Thus, one awakens to sovereign mastery. Indeed, clouds gather and disperse; water rises and sinks. The sun and moon shift and alternate; the seasons succeed one another in turn. Good and evil contend with each other; prosperity and decline pass on in succession.

There are a thousand manners and ten thousand forms, changing without end. To investigate the explanation of why this is so: [The original text concludes here, as the provided fragment ends mid-sentence.]
Thus, those various and extraordinary transformations, whose divine wisdom is unfathomable, are no different from what is seen in a dream.

If one traces the origin of the dream, it is formed by daytime thoughts; if one traces the origin of those daytime thoughts, they have no dependence on the ears or eyes, and no root in sounds or forms.
This is what is called "arising where it is and ceasing where it is. How could the Sage deceive me?

Ah! Thus, when the common people hear of birth, they rejoice; when they hear of death, they grieve. Yet there are those who act contrary to this norm: hearing of death, they rejoice; hearing of birth, they grieve.

All such cases arise because they are obscured by emotion and have not yet attained understanding of the underlying principle. When the Perfected One establishes his teachings, it is difficult for them to be identical in every respect.
Once one reaches the root and forgets emotion, then a thousand paths lead to the same destination. As I read of the Great Being Nāgārjuna’s death...
The *Jāti-gāthā* suddenly reveals the purport of the *I Ching* regarding the beginning and end of things. The verse says:
"If birth were to exist first, and old age and death later, then there would be birth without old age and death; birth would not possess old age and death.
If old age and death existed first, and birth later, this would be without cause; there would be old age and death without birth. The meaning of this verse is as clear as the sun and stars.

It does not require exhaustive searching or the exhaustion of one’s thoughts; yet, when one asks people to explain how it is so, they often stare with eyes wide open as if seeing their father’s taboo name.
If one infers what obscures them, it is simply that they cannot trace the origin back to the end.

If they were able to do so, they would know that the beginning does not originate from the end—where then would the beginning begin? And that the end does not originate from the beginning—where then would the end end? Where, then, is the beginning?
As for what begins, it has never begun by beginning; as for where it ends, it has never ended by ending.

When one is not deluded regarding beginning and end, then as for joy and anger, love and hate, good fortune and misfortune, calamity and blessing, birth and death, success and failure—do these truly arise because there is a cause that makes them so?
Or do they truly arise because there is no cause that makes them so? Reaching this point, that which is called "the ultimate of all under heaven"—
That which is difficult to clarify is as follows: it is like a bright mirror or still water; when one sees one's own beard and eyebrows therein, what obscuration could there be?

Now, where there is no desire, there is no birth; where there is no birth, there is no need for the sustenance that causes vexation. Therefore, wherever there is birth, there must necessarily be that from which it arises.
The means of sustaining life also have their source. Thus, the paths of filial piety toward one’s parents and loyalty toward one’s sovereign are opened.

However, if one realizes that the body itself is a source of suffering and that the means of sustenance are the medium for that suffering, then by contemplating the body through the lens of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), the root of suffering can be uprooted.

If the root of suffering is indeed uprooted, what reliance would there be on the means of sustaining life? For this reason, though parents may be most compassionate and a sovereign may be most stern, both must be relinquished.

Disregarding this, it was only with [Vimalakīrti] that compassion first became expansive, and with [Śāriputra] that reverence first became paramount. Nevertheless, emotion is the mother of transformation, and all sentient beings are its children.

If one can attain the mother by means of the child, and attain the father of the mother by means of the mother, then the expansion of compassion and the heightening of reverence are not contrary to the natural order.
Now, even a person of the utmost stupidity, if made to tread upon boiling water or fire, will fear being burned or cooked; though driven by force, they would not willingly enter.
Yet the boiling water and fire of the five desires burn and cook the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom of sentient beings, not merely for a morning or an evening.
Yet people willingly tread upon it and ultimately do not fear it; is this not because they have lost their minds and gone mad?

It is likely because they reckon this stinking skin-bag to be a pure vessel and reckon the mind of ignorance to be the root of life, and thus are unable to contemplate the body as the four great elements or the mind as the four aggregates.
Nowadays, when people are lying down to sleep, if their pillow is even slightly uncomfortable, they—

One can sleep, but it is essential to ensure one is secure before doing so. Birth and death are matters of great consequence for humanity, yet everyone openly takes them for granted and fails to plan for them at all. Why is this?

Tracing back to the ultimate source of the constant radiance, from the beginning there has been no ground of distinction between the holy and the ordinary. Because there is internal awareness without external objects, one creates the conditions for dreams oneself.

These conditions are truly without origin; that which is independent becomes dependent. Beginning with the three subtle stages and ending with the six coarse stages, these coarse and subtle levels possess a constant nature.
How could sentient beings have a path of awakening? The constant radiance is unchanging; how could the mechanism of delusion and movement arise?

Therefore it is said: "Arising is only the dharma arising; ceasing is only the dharma ceasing. Although arising and ceasing differ, the dharma is fundamentally non-dual. It is like bubbles arising from water.
Outside the bubble there is no water; the bubble arises from water. Outside the water there is no bubble. Furthermore, it is like beating a bellows in the wind or picking out brightness within light:
who is the one who picks, and what is that which is picked? What constitutes the internal wind, and what the external wind?
What is this water, and what is not water? Therefore, this dharma is truly inconceivable. Now, that which is inconceivable is not—
It is inconceivable. This is because, beyond the inconceivable, there is no separate dharma that can be called "inconceivable.

Nevertheless, when all sentient beings skillfully contemplate this inconceivable Dharma, they are able to enter meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) within a single atom and arise from the samādhi of all atoms.
Therefore, it is said that it is not "inconceivable. Viewed in this light, all performance of Buddha-work is accomplished through non-...
To benefit others is the true benefit; there is no benefit greater than this. To regard the benefit of benefiting others as the ultimate benefit is a benefit that is most subtle and minute.
Why is this? The benefit of non-benefit arises in accordance with the nature (*dharmatā*); the benefit of benefiting others is bestowed according to emotional conditions (*saṃjñā*).

That which arises in accordance with the nature perfectly accords with non-arising (*anutpāda*); that which is bestowed according to emotional conditions is born of the conditions of intoxication and delusion. Although it perfectly accords with non-arising...

A subtle gift brings merit equal to empty space. That which arises from conditions is like intoxication or a dream; even if one gives away an entire kingdom, cities, wife, and children, the benefit gained is extremely small.

This is because that which is unborn has no dependence, whereas that which arises from conditions has abiding. That which has no dependence has nothing external; that which has abiding has something external.
Since there is nothing external, there is nothing capable of destroying that which has no externality. Since there is something external, there is the capacity [for destruction].

If that which is destroyed is its object, then its capacity is likewise destroyed accordingly. Therefore, one who dwells upon form while generating the mind will ultimately suffer the destruction of form;

one who does not dwell upon form while generating the mind cannot be carried away by form. However, this wondrous state of non-destruction can be realized through the spirit but is difficult to seek through mundane affairs;
it can be schemed and measured where there is a mind of attachment, and it is easy to calculate and estimate. Formerly, there was a monk who cast a great bronze [image].

The bell weighed several *jin*. As he was leaving the gate, he happened to encounter a poor woman. She asked the monk where he was going, and the monk replied, "I am going to beg for copper to cast a bell.
The poor woman, reaching out her hand, offered him a single broken coin. The monk accepted it with some reluctance, yet he found it too thin and immediately threw it into the river at the temple.
Later, when the monk’s collection of copper reached the required amount and the bell had been cast seven times, there appeared [a flaw] at the very vital spot of the bell.
There was a single hole. The monk said in anger, "My intention in casting this bell was sincere. After seven firings, a hole appeared in the bell;
if it were cast again and the hole remains unfilled, I shall surely throw myself into molten copper and be transformed along with it—I would accept that with a willing heart.
At that time, a man of extraordinary character enlightened the monk, saying, "The bell is not perfect for no other reason than that you have obscured its original donor."
"This is because his gift was made with a lack of faith. The monk reflected deeply for a long time and said, "I understand now.

When I first went to beg for copper, I encountered a poor woman who gave me a single coin. At that time, I despised its smallness and threw it into the river at the temple. Thereupon, the river's flow was cut off and it began to suck up water;
when the water receded, I found the broken coin and cast it into the molten bronze for the seven-fire furnace, where it fused into one piece in a single firing."
How perfect! How tragic! A gift made without a [self-centered] mind accords with the inconceivable; to carve [blocks] and then discard them is to place ignorance at the vanguard.
Regarding the carving of the Great Canon at Mount Jing, there were those who calculated profit rather than the Dharma, thinking:
"Rather than having the Master carve it, it would be better to carve it myself. The expense will be less and it will be completed more easily, and furthermore, I shall obtain the benefit."
All of you are my kinsmen and servants. Among you, there may be those who calculate the Dharma rather than the profit;

they should consider that I am merely giving money to the Master to carve the Tripitaka. He is truly carving the scriptures for me. I might mistake what is non-existent for what exists, yet I shall certainly accept this with joy.
Furthermore, the Buddha’s words are not false; I shall surely rely on the conditions created by carving the Tripitaka to borrow from these conditions to plant the seeds of the Unconditioned.

This is the cause for rebirth; in the end, one shall surely emerge from suffering. Is this not truly magnificent? Some may say that those who calculate profit are not equal to those who calculate the Dharma.
To the person who observes with penetrating insight, this is not so. While calculating the Dharma is indeed superior to calculating profit, both still arise from a state of mind.
How can they compare to when the woman Pimpa heard the sound of a monk begging for money before it had even finished; she simply reached out her hand and offered a single broken coin as alms?
To give while thinking of it is called having a mind; when Pindola does not initially form a thought to calculate the amount of merit gained, it is called being without a mind.
Thus, a wooden puppet does not understand giving. At the assembly on Vulture Peak, our Great Awakened Elder held up a flower to show the multitude;
only Kāśyapa broke into a smile. The Wayman Daguan acted as a judge in a place where there was no public path.
The path is severed. One should consider that the *poṇava* and the *dhūta* should be investigated together and their confessions recorded.
In this way, those who calculate the Dharma and calculate profit will themselves realize they have fallen into transgression.

The Great Dharma of the Golden Fortress does not transcend the two gates of *she* (refutation) and *she* (gathering). As for refutation, even Buddhas and Patriarchs have things to criticize and reject;
how much more so others? Only the single gate of gathering exhaustively encompasses the capacities of those who are timid and weak.

Nevertheless, if one has not attained the mind of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, then even Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot easily be reviled—just as Deshan used the Great Canon as a cloth for wiping his feet.

"Scrap paper! As for the monk who placed Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra between the legs of his cotton trousers—since none of the venerable elders with true insight from all quarters have heard of anyone rebuking him, it must be that he has not yet attained the mind of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; who else would be willing to nod in agreement?

Lately, the Great Beings no longer appear, and demons and heretics abound. Regardless of whether they are 'black' or 'white,' as soon as they possess a modicum of intellectual understanding, they claim to have already realized the truth."
Among the recorded encounters of the ancient worthies, the essential principles were no different; yet those who remain in doubt regarding clarity and obscurity merely acquire empty fame.
They willfully obscure their own minds and arrogantly pass judgment, indulging their momentary passions and binding themselves with karma for long kalpas.
This is what is meant by "if the ground is not true, the fruit will be circuitous. It is like a paper flower that can never bear fruit. I know this well.
Pursuing empty fame will ultimately only lead to one’s own ruin; it is better to join the ranks of the timid and weak.

Though you may not yet have attained the mind of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, if you can simply trust their words and practice them with rigorous discipline, I can guarantee that there will be no failure whatsoever.
If you cannot yet crawl, do not attempt to walk; how much more secure this is! To force yourself to walk before you can crawl—I know such a person will surely fall.

Falling into pits or trenches—there will surely come a day for that. Only when the Yellow Dragon’s mind first realizes this matter can his brush-tip samādhi wield life and death with ease, and exercise mastery over both subduing and gathering.
Greed and hatred are both certainly poisons; yet none is more virulent than the poison of delusion. Why is this?
If my mind were not deluded, greed and hatred would have no basis from which to arise. Once greed and hatred have arisen, it is because of delusion that one fails to perceive them.

Greed is like the ocean swallowing rivers; hatred is like fire burning mountains. One creates immeasurable dark karma and undergoes suffering for long kalpas, which is difficult even to illustrate by the analogy of mustard seeds or stones.
Having investigated the reason why suffering arises, one sees that apart from ignorance (*moha*), there is no greed or hatred.
From where, then, would suffering come? Furthermore, the arising of ignorance results from non-awakening (*abodha*); non-awakening, in turn, results from awakening (*bodha*). Once awakening...

Regarding *benjue* (original enlightenment): on what basis does delusion arise? Because there is no awakening outside of awakening that can awaken original awakening, original awakening likewise cannot awaken itself.

If original awakening were able to awaken itself, it could be called "commencement-awakening" (*shijue*), but it could not be called "original awakening," for in that case, there would be an awakening external to awakening.
Where, then, would the meaning of original awakening reside? Viewed in this light, only...
Innate awakening cannot awaken itself; therefore, ignorance arises. From the arising of ignorance, greed and hatred are produced.

When greed and hatred reach their extreme, the retribution of suffering will inevitably be severe. Being severe, it is difficult to endure. Because it is difficult to endure, one must investigate the origin of this bitter poison.
Only then does one come to understand that greed and hatred originally stem from ignorance, and that ignorance, in turn, is rooted in innate awakening. Innate awakening, however, is without [origin].

This is the fundamental basis. In the fundamental state, there is neither middle nor edge; how could there be inner or outer? It is numinous yet without self. If there is no self, who is it that receives the poison?

Being numinous, ignorance is fundamentally non-existent from the start. Once this principle is realized, one governs the emotions with that principle. When the emotions are exhausted, one returns to the source.

Having returned to the source, one feels compassion for all those who have not yet returned, and thus mounts the wheel of wisdom and vow to thoroughly transform all things, crushing them [into liberation].
To sever the root of ignorance and ascend together to the Unsurpassed, only then will there be true joy; such is the mind of the Sage. Therefore it is said:
"The body of the Pure Dharma-realm fundamentally has no appearing or disappearing; through the power of great compassion and vows, it manifests birth."
When thoughts cease and the dust of delusion is forgotten, one forgets and thus there is no effort. When the dust of delusion is forgotten and thoughts cease, one rests and thus there is no exertion.

Because there is neither effort nor exertion, the Way is accomplished through non-action. This non-active action brings liberation from both opposition and compliance. Through this liberation from opposition and compliance, [the Way is realized].
The faculties and objects blaze forth without dependence. Because they blaze forth, one purifies buddha-lands and brings sentient beings to maturity;
thus, even the merit of giving a single needle or a single thread, though minute, is not obscure.

Because there is no dependence, this merit—minute yet non-obscure—is equal to the blessings of the Dharma-realm as vast as space. Viewed from this perspective, if subject and object are not forgotten, then the faculties...
Dust (objects) is the teacher of the ghost-hells. When the faculties and their objects fall away, then subject and object become the guide to non-arising. Why is this?

If one cultivates in accordance with the nature, though I do not wish to forget, subject and object forget themselves. If one exerts effort through emotional attachment, though I wish to forget, the faculties and objects become further entangled.
Thus, one attains the essential meaning. The feverish afflictions of ordinary people are no different from being on the road.
The sages have lost their essential intent. Those who seek to transcend desire mock those who preceded them.
Therefore, one who aspires to transcend the world must first gain knowledge and then act; only then will their efforts not be wasted in vain.
To act without such knowledge—even if one were to sacrifice a body and life as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges—will ultimately result only in the suffering of karma.
It is through functioning that it responds; outside of number there is no cognition. Thus, apart from number there is no cognition, and apart from cognition there is no number.
Number has never numbered, so what number is not cognition? Cognition has never cognized, so what cognition is not number?

To understand in this way, subject and object naturally do not arise, yet functioning is not obscured. Therefore it is said: "it is through functioning that it responds. From the beginning, there have been neither sages nor ordinary beings. Functioning...

In this state of non-doubt, although one may traverse the field of birth and death, likes and dislikes, one knows that the source is not entangled by them; for if there were entanglement, it would not be true function.
Therefore, the Gate of the Patriarchs values that function not be obscured. When function is unobscured, it is simply a matter of reaching through to illumination.

Responding according to the teachings, even those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment still possess two kinds of ignorance regarding what is known, which they cannot exhaustively shatter; only upon reaching Sublime Enlightenment is there no ignorance left to be shattered.
This refers to what is said in the treatises; it does not depend on practical application. If you are a clever practitioner, when he asks a question, extend a finger and counter-question him:
"Do you know this finger? When he says, "I know," you say: "Knowing this one thing, all matters are finished."
I asked further about the number of those who were "even-headed" and the number of those who were not. If he had not realized it, I would have simply stepped aside and left.
The above is the "Old Woman’s Chan" spoken by the Elder Zibo, used to deceive and intimidate fledgling Chan practitioners; I do not know what kind of mental activity this is.
If one has doubts, one should take from various sources.
The Dharma is beyond metaphor; if the Dharma were amenable to metaphor, then the Dharma itself would be a metaphor.

Only the Sage knows that the Dharma cannot be metaphorized, yet the employment of various metaphors is nothing more than a temporary expedient (*upāya*). If one were to use "emptiness" as a metaphor, although emptiness is without...
It reaches the limit, yet it cannot give birth to all things. If it is compared to the earth, although the earth can produce [things], it has boundaries.
If it is compared to water, although water is pervasive and flowing, it can run dry.

If it is compared to wind, although the wind animates and stirs the myriad things, it eventually ceases. If it is compared to fire, although fire’s brilliance can dispel darkness, it must not be touched.
Contact arises when it adheres to an object and ceases as soon as it is separated from that object. To use a tree as an analogy:

although a tree can produce various flowers and fruits, its roots have no support if it is removed from the earth. To use a lotus flower as an analogy: although its flowers and fruits appear simultaneously, [it cannot exist apart from its source].
Yet it does not exist apart from water. If it were compared to the *campaka* flower, although the *campaka* is fragrant, its scent vanishes as soon as the autumn wind arises.

If it were compared to the *ma-mu-ya* (māṇikya) gem, although both are extraordinary treasures that surpass all others, they do not equal the emptiness, transparency, and spiritual penetration of the Dharma. As for comparing it to a dragon, to a lion, to a great man, or to...
By means of the king, it is illustrated by the father, the mother, the great, the small, the long, the broad, the square, the round, and the curved.

It is illustrated by the straight; it is illustrated by the moving; it is illustrated by the still; it is illustrated by the contracting; it is illustrated by the extending; it is illustrated by dependence; it is illustrated by non-dependence.

To speak briefly, even with hundreds or thousands of illustrations, the Dharma cannot be fully illustrated. Therefore, I say: an illustration is merely a skillful means (*upāya*) employed by the Sage at a particular time to respond to sentient beings.
Thus, those who cling to the illustration and challenge the Dharma do not understand the Dharma.

Now, the sense faculties and their objects are from the outset not two separate things; yet ordinary people fail to understand this and recklessly calculate them as such, thereby falling into delusion.
If one observes with the eye of wisdom, although the tree is not the seeing, there is no tree apart from the seeing; although the seeing is not the tree, there is no seeing apart from the tree.
Because there is no tree apart from the seeing, the tree exists but does not truly subsist; because there is no seeing apart from the tree, the seeing exists but is non-existent.
The self does not exist within the trees; though the myriad phenomena spread out in all directions, there is no thing that corresponds to the mind.

Seeing that there is no self, one sees that even amidst the blazing activity of conceptual discrimination, there is no self that corresponds to things. When one repeatedly examines both the sense faculties and their objects, neither is found to have any correspondence.
Yet, in this field where neither has any correspondence, the multitude distinguishes between the beautiful and the ugly, and their minds harbor love and hatred. Myriad...
To die without knowing this—is it not to dream with one's eyes open?
Now, the habit of lust is not difficult to overcome; the difficulty lies in understanding why lust arises as it does.
Once the "why" is clarified, one can follow the current to reach its source. The current is like the mind; the water is a metaphor for the nature (prakṛti). Water is inherently still, yet it flows.

The eye-light illuminates objects; from the outset, it possesses neither aversion nor attachment. It does not shine first upon sandalwood, nor does it shine later upon dog dung.

This is called the light of equality. This fragment of the light of equality, within the realm of Buddhas and patriarchs—whether in joy or anger, in sorrow or pleasure—there is nowhere it does not manifest as the fundamental light.
Within the realm of ordinary beings, amidst the clouds of feverish affliction, [it likewise shines].

At that moment, one [aspect] suddenly breaks through and manifests; yet because the power of active conduct (*saṃskāra*) is fierce, it immediately obscures it once more. Thus it is said: "Within the shadows of colored clouds, a divine immortal appears;
in hand he holds a red silk fan to shield his face. One must urgently turn one's eyes to behold the immortal; do not look at the fan in the immortal’s hand.
What are called the "clouds" and the "fan" are, in fact, the afflictions and attachments within the pit of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Therefore, one who is skilled in cultivating the Path is able, at the critical juncture when likes and dislikes are difficult to overcome and when this light suddenly flashes forth, to fix their gaze and penetrate through to the core, remaining unswayed by active defilements (*saṃmukhībhāva*).
Such a person is called a hero. Those who lack brilliance from the start find that delusive clouds suddenly close in;
when they first attempt contemplation, they must expend great effort to dispel them, like a single man facing ten thousand—how many among them can hope for victory?
Ah! At the moment of light and dew, as it passes over one shoulder, the ignorance accumulated over kalpas shall instantly melt away like ice.
It is like soldiers not shedding blood upon their blades; the world is at peace.
The King of Xiangzhi in South India offered a priceless jewel as an offering to the Venerable Prajñātāra.
At that time, the king had three sons, the youngest of whom was a bodhisattva. Desiring to test what they had attained, the Venerable took the offered jewel and asked the three princes:
"This jewel is perfectly round and luminous; is there anything that can equal it? The first son—
Candraprabhāvatī and her second son, Guṇavatī, both said, "This jewel is the most honored among the seven treasures;
truly, nothing surpasses it. Were it not for the power of the Venerable One's path, who could receive it? Then her third son, Bodhivatī, said:
These are worldly treasures, yet they are not supreme; among all treasures, the treasure of the Dharma is supreme.
These are worldly lights, yet they are not supreme; among all lights, the light of wisdom is supreme. These are worldly illuminations, yet they are not supreme.
Among all forms of luminosity, the light of wisdom is supreme. This jewel’s radiance cannot illuminate itself; it must rely upon the light of wisdom for its manifestation.
Once this has been discerned, one knows it to be a jewel; knowing it to be a jewel, one then recognizes its preciousness.
If one clarifies its treasure, the treasure is not itself the treasure; if one discerns its pearl, the pearl is not itself the pearl.

That a pearl is not itself the pearl means that it must rely upon the wisdom-pearl to discern worldly pearls. That a treasure is not itself the treasure means that it must rely upon the wisdom-treasure to clarify the Dharma-treasure.
Thus, when a teacher possesses the Way, his treasure immediately manifests; when sentient beings possess the Way, their mental treasure is likewise so.
The Venerable One praised his eloquence and wisdom. Furthermore, among the feudal lords of the Warring States period, those who regarded "treasure" as nothing more than pearls and jade were few;
it was only King Wei of Qi and Marquis Sun Yu of Chu who truly knew what constitutes true treasure. King Wei did not value even a single-inch pearl...

Jewels are considered treasures. Yet, when the Grandson of the King of Chu, Sun Yu, did not regard the white jade pendant as his treasure, it was known that what is truly treasured lies here and not there.
Although China and India differ in their outward splendor, the fundamental character of their national customs has never been different.

Thus, while one who treasures jewels may have illumination reaching only ten feet, one who treasures people possesses illumination that extends for a thousand li. The Patriarch of the Buddha-dharma in Zhendan...

Tiduo realized that outside of the Jewel there is no Way, and outside of the Way there is no Jewel; it is only according to the time that there is penetration or obstruction, and through its use that there is manifestation or concealment.
Subsequently, after nine years of wall-gazing at Shaolin, he attained the Divine Light. Like flowers linked in a string of pearls, he took form as sound and listened with his eyes;

suddenly, the essence of mind abandoned hearing, and the substance of the pearl was revealed alone. The spiritual flame became a lamp, its light— *Note: The source text appears to be a fragment of a poetic or prose commentary on Zen practice, likely from a work such as the *Liuzu Tanjing* (Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch) or a related collection of kōans and commentaries.*

The transmission is inexhaustible. Before the image appeared, it was not yet radiant; after the painting was made, it shone with perfect illumination. Non-radiance suggests obscurity; perfect illumination suggests wisdom.
When this is further sustained by compassion, the lamp is transformed once more into a high, vast, and great vehicle.

This vehicle extends vertically through the three periods of time and spans horizontally across the ten directions; it carries both the ordinary and the holy, encompassing all things from antiquity to the present. Viewed from this perspective, then—
As for King Wei’s carriage, how could its smallness or greatness matter? Therefore it is said: "One who transforms a family into a state does not know the Way;
one who transforms the mind into the Way can simultaneously forget the world. By this I know that the myriad things are but one thing, and the myriad spirits are but one spirit.
Only for those who skillfully employ their minds is there nothing that is not spirit; for those who act contrary to this, what spirit is not a thing? What...?
Objects are not the spirit; though clouds and mountains may be layered one upon another, the eye remains free from even the slightest speck of dust.

How could the spirit not be the object? Though it may be silent and as clear as a deep pool, the mind is often beset by obstructions. It is further said: "Is the Way far away? It is true in every encounter. Is the Sage far away?
To embody it is to be the spirit. And again: "Within there is a treasure, hidden within the mountain of the physical form. Yet this treasure also has its "treasure-explanation."
There are those who practice the jewel, those who realize the jewel, and those who forget the jewel; only he who understands the jewel knows how to honor that which is known.

For one who practices the jewel, the radiance of that jewel will gradually become complete. For one who realizes the jewel, although the jewel is already complete, if they forget it, its utility will not be full.
Therefore, it is only by forgetting the treasure that one can truly employ it. Alas! How easy is it to understand why this is so?
If one knows it but cannot practice it, or practices it but cannot realize it, the Middle Way falls into neglect.
If one realizes it but cannot forget it, one is like a person trapped in a jar or a fish stranded on dry land; such a person cannot even utilize themselves, let alone utilize external things.
All things float and sink, emerging from and submerging in the sea of suffering. Although there are differences between humans and devas, their horizontal and vertical states are inconsistent;
