for long kalpas they have wandered in delusion and fallen, with the emotions serving as the root. The arising of these emotions stems from being deluded by one's own mind. When the self-mind is spiritually penetrating, its illumination reaches the ultimate and follows movement.
Movement leads to obscurity, and obscurity gives rise to movement again. Obscurity and movement intermingle like a waterwheel rising and falling, without end.
This is the ultimate conclusion. To speak of the reality of the matter: emotion is rooted in attachment; attachment nourishes the sickness of greed.

When greed is insatiable, dissatisfaction arises. Liking and disliking are inconstant, arising and ceasing in alternation. Toward objects that accord with one's desires, one becomes bound by longing and immersed in indulgence, as if intoxicated or deluded.
Though harm may strike in an instant, one still remains in a state of merriment, simply because one has forgotten [the danger]. For the most part, if one does not forget, then...

When the one essence gives rise to differentiation, forgetting that differentiation causes diverse entities to become as one. Where there are two, there is opposition; where there is opposition, there is a standing-off against one another.

At the moment of this standoff, "self" and "other" stand in stark contrast; yet with even a slight reversal of perspective, one realizes this truth. It is only within favorable conditions that the ultimate state of mutual forgetting occurs, wherein diversity becomes as one.
When there is oneness, there is no opposition; when there is no opposition, it is difficult to perceive. Furthermore, when sentient beings first undergo birth, it arises from craving.

When favorable conditions arise, they nourish [the mind], and one becomes spontaneously and unconsciously merged with them. This is why adverse conditions are easily perceived, while favorable conditions constantly lead to delusion.

If one can illuminate favorable conditions so that the light does not grow dim, then the source of craving will gradually dry up and the waves of anger will also cease. One will no longer be angry with oneself.
It is born from craving; once craving is gradually eliminated, how could hatred not be extinguished? It is like felling a tree:
once its root is severed, the branches and twigs fall of their own accord. The mutual destruction of hatred and craving is likewise so.
The earth has no boundaries; all is trodden by my feet. Sound has no boundaries; all is heard by my mind. The earth is that which is trodden; the mind is that which can hear.
That which is trodden is dead—it can remain still but cannot move. That which can hear is alive and constant.

Because it is alive, the myriad sounds do not obscure one another; great and small are clearly perceived. Because it is constant, sounds arise and perish of their own accord, yet the hearer does not shift. This is like...
All precious mirrors possess a perfect radiance; when an elephant touches them, they reflect it immediately, such that beauty and ugliness cannot be concealed.

It is precisely because they reflect without sentiment that they respond to all things without leaving a trace. This wondrous state of tracelessness means that their response does not flow as a lingering image. Thus, from antiquity to the present, the more they reflect, the more they remain serene.
My own mind is fundamentally luminous, universally responding to the myriad phenomena; yet these phenomena have never obstructed it. This is the walking of one who is already complete. Its...

It is likewise so. When I speak of the "earth" and "death," these are merely expedient means used to point toward things. Since the faculty of hearing is subtle and the faculty of the body is perfect, the feet do not manifest themselves independently, but are revealed by means of the earth;
the earth does not reveal itself independently, but is known by means of the feet. It is like two hollow reeds leaning against one another:
when one suddenly realizes the nature of the feet and the earth, the same applies to the capacity for hearing.

The reason why sentient beings undergo birth and death is simply that their views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi* and *kleśa*) have not been severed. "Views" refers to the five sharp fetters (*pañca-tīkṣṇa-saṃyojana*), while "afflictions" refers to the five dull fetters (*pañca-mṛdu-saṃyojana*).
These are categorized according to the three realms and nine stages; thus, there is an opening and closing [of categories]. The five sharp fetters are:

the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), false views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*), the attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and the attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
It is so. The five dull messengers refer to greed, anger, ignorance, pride, and doubt. These ten are spoken of collectively;

if they are expanded, they may be found in detail within the *Tiantai sijiao yi zhu* (Commentary on the Ritual of the Four Teachings of Tiantai). When these ten are completely severed, this is the stage of the fruition in the Tripitaka Teaching (*zangjiao*).

In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), it is the stage of semblance-realization at the level of the seventh faith. Thus, the noble ones (*xiasheng*) of both the fruition and the seventh-faith stages [attain this].

Being able to exercise the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) with total mastery and without hindrance, one passes straight through mountains and walls by means of them. One cuts off these ten delusions (daśakleśa).

First, one cultivates the contemplation of emptiness (śūnyatā-vipaśyanā), which negates the dualistic grasping at self and phenomena (ātma-dharma-dvaya-grāha). These two types of grasping are precisely the ten delusions; they differ only in their mode of opening and closing.

Only the cultivation and progress of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) is far removed from ordinary paths; its single mind and threefold contemplation (ekacitta-trivipaśyanā) constitute a perfect cultivation and full advancement. This is supreme.

For the beginner, the intent is focused on directly breaking through fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), rather than on the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) or the delusions of dust and sand (*rajas*).
Nevertheless, when the resolve for contemplation is firm and fierce, one advances spontaneously; the coarse delusions of views and thoughts are then cast off along the way.

This is like a strong man entering a battle: he shoots at the horse before shooting at the man, and captures the leader before capturing the common thieves. However, where the blade is drawn... [the King].
Among those who are harmed by their own spontaneous actions, there have never been any exceptions. The "sovereign" refers to fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*);

the "attendants" refer to the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *saṃjñā-kleśa*). When the afflictions of views and thoughts are exhausted, one will then shatter the "dust and sand" [afflictions]. However, this cannot be shattered through the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*);
it is only by employing the contemplation of the provisional (*parikalpita-vipaśyanā*) that these afflictions can be destroyed. As for the term "dust and sand," it describes their [infinite] nature.
Those who possess clarity are many. What are the dharmas of those who lack clarity? They are the mundane and supramundane dharmas.

The mundane refers to the governance of kings and hegemons, astronomy and geography, yin-yang and mathematics, the waxing and waning of fortune and misfortune, the various arts of civil and military affairs, and the fundamental origins of all things—knowing them all thoroughly.
The supramundane refers to the three trainings and the six perfections, as well as the Buddha-lands throughout the dust-motes of the ten directions; or it is explained as follows:

The tracks of the Dharma, the rituals for delivering sentient beings, the various skillful means, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the eighty thousand dharma-gates—all these he thoroughly penetrates;

thus, the dust-like ignorance is severed. This Bodhisattva, having first severed these delusions, travels extensively through the lands of the ten directions, serving all Buddhas of the ten directions, inquiring about the clarities of each, and receiving the seal of authentication for each, until he attains full realization.
There is no further doubt. From this point forward, whether a crow is black or a crane is white, there is nothing that will not be known.

This method of provisional contemplation (*prajñā*) is simply a matter of extensively consulting those who have already awakened; thus, there is nothing one does not know. To speak of "ignorance" (*avidyā*) is to say that one faces a wall when encountering any matter.
Once the "dust-sands" [of delusion] are shattered, one will proceed to shatter fundamental ignorance. As for the term "fundamental," it means...
This is because it serves as the fundamental cause of the delusions and karma of all sentient beings. This fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*) is originally pure;

yet, due to original non-awakening (*anabodha*), it becomes deluded and moves in accordance with conditions, whereby the three subtle states arise. These three subtle states constitute the root of the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and the dust-sands of afflictions (*pāramitā-āvaraṇa*).
The views and thoughts, as well as the dust-sands, are their branches and twigs. Although these branches and twigs may be severed first, the root—
The root still remains. At this juncture, the practitioner must use the axe of Madhyamaka to break it down.
Furthermore, these three subtle states are divided into forty-two categories for refutation within the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. These forty-two stages refer to the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*).

The ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*), and Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*) [the final mind], together with the preceding sands-of-the-Ganges-like ignorance (*avidyā*), are thus called the forty-two grades.
By the power of the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*), a Bodhisattva in the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) severs the very first grade of ignorance among these forty-two grades and enters the first stage;
at that moment, they are able to become the sovereign over the territories of a hundred Buddha-lands. One Buddha-land constitutes a single territory.
This is what constitutes a great trichiliocosm. A great trichiliocosm consists of one thousand worlds of heaven and earth;
this is called a small chiliocosm. One thousand small chiliocosms constitute a medium chiliocosm. One thousand medium chiliocosms constitute a great trichiliocosm.
Yet a Bodhisattva in the first stage can exercise sovereignty over as many as one hundred such great thousandfold Buddha-lands.
Now, food, drink, men, and women, sounds, forms, wealth, and profit have never been obstacles to the Way; rather, that which truly obstructs the Way is [the following].
It is merely one's own body and one's own mind. Thus, an ancient said: "Among labors, none precedes having wisdom;
among great afflictions, none is like having a body. Wisdom here refers to the deluded mind; the body refers to the deluded body.
Now, the deluded mind arises by relying upon objects, and the deluded body is accomplished by borrowing from objects. Yet, it is only the true mind that is not produced by objects.
It is not born; when things perish, it does not perish. It is the true body. When the vital breath gathers, it does not gather;
when the vital breath disperses, it does not disperse. What are "things"? They refer to the sensory objects (*viṣaya*). What is "vital breath"? It refers to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

That which is called the deluded mind gives rise to emotion upon contacting objects; likes and dislikes alternate and shift. From birth to old age, and from old age to death, it continues incessantly, amidst impurity.
They dwell in these states, becoming addicted and attached as if to their own marrow and brain, clinging to them with such parsimony that they will not let go.

Even when there are excellent teachers, elder brothers, or virtuous friends who seek to awaken them through their words, not only are they unable to suddenly abandon [their attachments], reform their evils, and transform toward the good;

indeed, there are not a few who even harbor resentment. This is because they follow their own reckless emotions and consciousness: they are joyful when things accord with them, but displeased when they oppose them.

Such are those who are called "human-headed oxen. Furthermore, there are those who toil and strive with deep schemes and far-reaching considerations, making the preservation of life their primary concern.
When poor, they hope for wealth; when wealthy, they hope for nobility; when noble, they hope for longevity; and when long-lived, they hope for immortality.
The waves of their passions surge vast and boundless. These are what are called deluded sentient beings. To investigate this thoroughly, it is as follows:

This deluded thought flows turbulently from morning until night; throughout one’s entire life of toil and hardship, it is nothing more than the failure to empty that initial single point of deluded mind.
Therefore, I say that food, drink, men, women, sounds, colors, wealth, and profit do not obstruct the Way.
That which obstructs the Way is solely this deluded mind. Why is this deluded mind also called "wisdom"? It is because it is skilled at scheming.

This is because [the mind] is capable of painting [these delusions). If one can abandon this deluded mind, all the various labors performed previously will dissolve and vanish like ice melting in hot water.
However, one who is truly able to abandon this mind is not merely someone concerned with birth and death;
such an extraordinary and heroic individual is not easily found. In the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Subhūti first raised the question regarding the subduing of the mind.
This is because one understands that this mind is the source of the ocean of suffering and the root of birth and death.
Once this mind is set aside, intellectual consciousness dissolves and merges. What is called the "True Mind" is like the bright moon revealed when drifting clouds disperse.

When the bright moon illuminates the world, its reflection appears everywhere—in high and low places, far and near, across the four seas and a hundred rivers, even in puddles and hoofprints—yet it has never [been divided].
There is a mind. Only those who awaken to this mind are Buddhas, even if they are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); if they do not awaken, even a Buddha is but an ordinary being.
Here, the deluded mind and the true mind are presented side by side. Those with the aspiration to transcend the world should pay close attention to this;
there is no time to speak further of the deluded body and the true body.
Regarding the division of subject and object without interruption: it is because the subject is fundamentally not the object, and the object is fundamentally not the subject.

Thus, the subject is not self-sufficient as subject, and the object is not self-sufficient as object. The subject is not self-sufficient as subject because it is a subject by virtue of the object; the object is not self-sufficient as object because it is an object by virtue of the subject.
Since the subject is a subject by virtue of the object, the merit belongs to the object; since the object is an object by virtue of the subject, the merit likewise returns to the subject.
When the function belongs to the "object" (*yǒu*), then that which stands alone is the object. When the function returns to the "capacity" (*néng*), then that which stands alone is the capacity.
Generally speaking, that which is called "standing alone" is independent; therefore, it is said to be undifferentiated. That which does not stand alone is dependent.
Therefore, it is called "differentiation. To know this is to attain the function of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). The true mark refers to that which is entirely without leakage or deviation.

An ancient said: "The difficult and the easy are mutually constitutive; thus, the difficult is precisely the mechanism of the easy. Therefore, those who fear the difficult are called... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].
Since the mechanism of the *Yī* was blocked, the term "change" (*yì*) refers to that which is spiritually numinous and eternally penetrating. Penetration is change; change is transformation;
transformation is the divine.
The man of great wisdom often instructed people, saying: "Among those deluded in the world, none are more extreme than those driven by greed and desire. And as for greed and desire...
Their arising originates from the objects before one. Although such objects are numerous, the physical forms of men and women are the most seductive.

Men, craving the beauty of women, view them as flowers; women, craving the appearance of men, view them as jewels. Becoming deeply attached, they give rise to lust, such that they would not hesitate to step upon white blades or rush into boiling water and fire.
They do not even have time to consider the ruin of their reputation, the loss of their virtue, the defilement of social customs, or the destruction of their own lives.

Yet you do not realize that if one were to strip away the adornments and look at it within the midst of the four crossroads, with hair disheveled and ugliness exposed, not only would no attachment arise, but one could hardly refrain from retching.
If one were to strip away the skin and look further, it would not merely cause retching.
Furthermore, one cannot help but feel terror. If one were to remove the flesh and observe it, there would be nothing but white bones lying in decay;
how could one not feel more than mere terror? Only then does one realize that from emptiness comes bone, from bone comes flesh, and from flesh comes skin.
When these four are assembled and further adorned, they are able to delude people. Today, the world is in a state of turmoil—like ascending a spring terrace, like beholding something beautiful.
Flowers! To die without awakening—how lamentable this is! How does it compare to outwardly adorning oneself to observe the skin;
observing the flesh and bone beneath the skin; observing the emptiness beneath the flesh and bone; and observing non-arising beyond that emptiness?
Now, non-arising is the abode of all sages and the origin of all spirits. Therefore it is said: "Only by attaining the Origin can one [attain liberation]."
A "good end. If one dies without having exhausted the beginning, even if they are interred in an auspicious place within a golden coffin and silver outer casing, can this be called a good end?
If there is activity, how can there be cessation? If there is cessation, how could there be further spontaneity? If there is spontaneity...

How could there be extinction? It is precisely because it does not act, does not cease, does not take up, and does not extinguish, that it is able to act and act, cease and cease, take up and take up, and extinguish and extinguish.
If someone realizes this, then throughout the three periods of time and the ten directions, the five aggregates and the eighteen realms—
Pick up even a mere hair’s breadth and cast it before people; I fear that even the Yellow-Faced Gautama would have no sharp hand for it.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "When wondrous touch is proclaimed and made clear. These words fully reveal the fundamental light without remainder.
Yet students, their realization being not yet subtle, often miss it right before their faces. Formerly, there was a Head Monk who asked a monk, "Listen from next door."

"The sound of hairpins and bracelets is itself the breaking of the precepts. How, then, are the precepts maintained? The monk said, "What an excellent point of entry! Observing it from this perspective:

when it pertains to the body, it is the sublime touch that proclaims clarity; when it pertains to the ear, it is the sublime sound that proclaims clarity. Since this is so for one faculty, it is so for all.

Why would the faculties not be so? Furthermore, when the Fourth Patriarch met Master Xinxin at the age of fourteen, he said to Master Can, "I pray that the Honored One will grant me a Dharma-gate of liberation.
Can replied, "As for liberation, let it rest for now; who is binding you right now?"
Xìn attained great enlightenment beneath these words. An ancient worthy said, "To strike it and to bump into it—there is nothing that is not the entrance.
Truly, he did not deceive me.
The Master said: "There are three grades of sitting in stillness: inferior sitting, equal sitting, and superior sitting.

As for inferior sitting, one merely presses the tongue against the palate, keeps the teeth and lips tightly closed, clenches both hands into fists and clasps them against the spine, and holds the neck straight and upright without leaning, taking the power of faith as the primary focus.
One may recite half a verse, or maintain the Buddha’s name and mantras. Above this—
The teacher is stern yet compassionate and protective; below him, there are fellow practitioners who provide support. This is called the "inferior sitting.

As for the "equal sitting," one first takes the discernment that penetrates the faculties, objects, and consciousness as the primary focus of the three realms. One thoroughly understands the beginning and end of these three realms without any doubt.
When sitting, view the body as a cloud-shadow and the mind as wind through a net. There is no separate agent of action.

If you can remain steadfast and firm, drowsiness, distraction, pain, and itching will naturally fall away. Whether one sits for half a day or two or three days, even if food and drink are not taken, one's physical strength remains as before;
this is called "equanimous sitting" (*pingdeng zuo*). As for "superior sitting" (*zengshang zuo*), it is by means of thorough penetration.

When one takes the fundamental mind as the object of activity, or when one uses the kōans and机缘 (ji-yuan) of ancient worthies to scratch an itch, [the mind] naturally coagulates and fails to transform.
It is as if one were bearing a shared-enemy-with-heaven resentment; though I do not wish for anger or vexation, the anger and vexation block and break through empty space.
One must truly reach the point where both the primary and secondary realms, as well as all holy and ordinary beings, are simultaneously overturned from their very foundations.
Possessing such resolve and strength, one plants one’s feet upon the meditation cushion and strives to transcend kalpas in every moment, yet remains without the thought of transcending kalpas.

When one reaches this state, dullness and distraction find no place to lodge; the entirety of the ten directions and three periods of time is, in its totality, a single *huatou*, standing vividly and unobstructedly before one.
Block the eyes and eyebrows. Suddenly, there is a mechanism like the bursting of beans within the mind; do not give rise to joy. Why?
Because it was already possessed by me, and now we have merely met with it—what is so extraordinary about this? This is called the "Superior Seat" (Agraśayana).
When a petty person dwells with a superior man, there is always something that does not satisfy the mind of the superior man; this is precisely the nature of the petty person.

If the petty person were fortunately to recognize this disposition and strive with all their might to overcome it, then without wasting years or months, they would realize that dwelling with a superior man brings them joy, whereas dwelling among the common crowd brings them anxiety. From [this point on...]

This clarifies that courage is the vanguard; one must cultivate this self-mastery without ceasing. When one reaches this stage, one feels a sense of ease when dwelling among the common people, yet a sense of alertness when dwelling among the noble.
If one reaches this point and continues to cultivate self-mastery without rest, it will no longer be possible for anyone who has not deeply awakened to their own mind.

When one’s celestial faculties (*deva-indriya*) are coarse and dull, even the Buddha’s words become an obstruction; myriad sufferings then converge. Yet those whose celestial faculties are profound are all guides. Thus it is said:
"If one skillfully employs the mind, every encounter provides the causal conditions; if one does not skillfully employ the mind, every instance becomes an obstacle.
This is like the time before Vipaśyin Buddha had appeared, when there was no ground for causes and conditions; thus, the teacher of Vipaśyin, in the end...
Who is it? One does not realize that suffering itself is the guide; why seek anything else?

Yet, since the time of Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, [the Buddha] has manifested through a mixture of suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure to condition various capacities, which differ in ten thousand ways.
Only those who are not tormented by the heat of suffering, though their celestial faculties may be profound, find it difficult for awakening to open. Once awakening opens, all is one.
All conditions and causes flow forth from within this; this is the functional manifestation of the fruition of Vipaśyin.
Reflect upon this, and whatever doubts or obstructions you may have will be resolved by applying this principle to similar cases.
The knowledge of ordinary people is limited to the span of six feet; the knowledge of sages, however, leaves nothing outside its scope uncomprehended.
Yet, if the knowledge of ordinary people were divorced from this all-encompassing knowledge, their cognition would have no foundation.
To call the consciousness limited to six feet "one's own mind" is to limit the mind to those six feet, such that there is absolutely nothing known beyond them—like washing away everything else.
This knowing—then there would be no external object that is not known, yet ultimately it cannot be attained.

Likewise, if this knowing is not cleansed away, there would be no external object that is not known, yet ultimately it cannot be attained. Therefore it is said: "Even though one is capable of knowing, one cannot attain universal knowledge."
Apart from the knower, universal knowledge cannot be attained; apart from both "is" and "is not," universal knowledge cannot be attained;
even through both "is" and "is not," universal knowledge cannot be attained. This is the word of the Sage, which will never deceive for ten thousand ages.
Generally speaking, the capacities of sentient beings do not exceed the four modes of examination (*catuḥ-prayoga*). There are those who can rise high but cannot descend;

those who can descend but cannot rise high; those who can neither rise nor descend; and those who can both rise high and descend. A skillful teacher guides and receives them according to their respective capacities.

Now, the true mind is luminous and pure; it is fundamentally and spontaneously radiant. When this radiance reaches its limit, darkness arises, and in an instant, the marks of karma (*karmalakṣaṇa*) are formed.

From this, the evolving manifestations (*nirmāṇa*) suddenly emerge, shrouded in a state where subject and object are indistinguishable. Yet, at this stage, the marks of cognition (*jñānalakṣaṇa*) have not yet arisen, and there is still no discrimination.

Because one fails to understand that these manifesting marks arise from the mind itself, false discrimination is produced. This discrimination is precisely the mark of cognition. The mark of cognition is...
The mental consciousness manifests in various forms of love and hatred, undergoing thousands of transformations and myriad changes in a state of impermanence, falsely dividing up boundaries.

If there were no mental consciousness, then although the five consciousnesses of the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body each rely upon their respective faculties and each maintains its own limited scope, they would all lack discernment.
Since they lack discernment, the five are fundamentally not five; thus, the consciousnesses of the eyes, ears, and so forth could even be called one.

It may be so. One may also say there are five [senses]. The six faculties cannot function interchangeably; this is entirely due to the arbitrary conceptualization of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

The eye can see, the ear can hear, and so forth. If the mental consciousness were empty, then although the visual and auditory consciousnesses see and hear all day long, they would never truly see or hear, because there would be no discrimination (*vikalpa*).
Wherever there is discrimination, there is the subject and the object; that which performs the discrimination is the [mental] faculty.
This is the mind. That which is discriminated by it is the object. Mind and objects stand in opposition; things and self are in chaotic confusion.
Thus, one becomes deluded regarding that luminous purity, whereby a single essence of clarity is divided into six functions. The eye then sees forms, and the ear hears sounds.
As the sensory faculties and their objects interact, delusions arise and vanish without end. Therefore, when the eye is separated from light and darkness, its faculty of seeing has no substance.

The same applies to the other five [senses]. Since the substance of seeing does not exist, who can perceive the characteristics of objects? Since the characteristics of objects do not exist, the substance of seeing also does not exist.
When both object and seeing are simultaneously absent, there is originally but one true mind. This very true mind, when stirred by emotion, transforms into the faculties and objects;

when emotion is emptied, the faculties and objects are seen to be originally the true mind. The faculties and objects and the true mind—when deluded, they become two; when awakened, they are originally one.
This "one" exists only in dependence upon "two. If "two" did not exist, where would "one" be based? For example, one speaks of "the unobtainable" in dependence upon "the obtainable";
only when there is this "unobtainable" does the "obtainable" first come to be. If the "unobtainable" did not exist, where would the "obtainable" be based?
Thus, as for the previously mentioned three phases of karma—evolving, evolving-manifesting, and manifesting—as well as the phase of cognition...
Returning to the true source: it is because one is deluded regarding the true source that these [phenomena] arise; by awakening to these very phenomena, the true source is revealed.

These phenomena and the true source are not two separate things. It is like a person who has been awake: even if they momentarily experience a state of confusion, though they hear external sounds, [they remain aware].
Furthermore, it is not yet clear. Although it is not clear, when one hears external sounds, it is called "awakening"; yet when it is truly not clear, it is called "swooning.
Again, hearing external sounds, one reaches a state where it is said that swooning and awakening are half-and-half.
If someone calls out, one follows the side of awakening; if no one calls out, one follows the side of swooning. Since one follows the side of swooning, externally—

Having fully cognized the object, internally it does not dream; it remains in a state of profound stillness where neither subject nor object has yet been established. After a short while, it enters the dream state, and subject and object then come into being.

The first is called the *svasaṃvittivijñāna* (the self-cognizing portion). The second is called the *svasaṃvittivijñāna* (the self-cognizing portion). Upon entering the dream, it divides into two parts:
that which sees is called the *darśanabhāga* (the seeing portion), and that which is seen is called the *nimittabhāga* (the image portion). This is the union of principle and metaphor.
This is consistent. The principle is naturally clear:
the place where form arises is precisely where emptiness arises; the place where emptiness arises is precisely where form arises. Although the myriad dharmas are vast, none exceed emptiness and form.

If one can thoroughly penetrate the nature of form and emptiness, then there is nothing obstructed that is not permeable, and nothing permeable that is not perfect. When perfect, this is the principle.
When affairs are thoroughly understood to their ultimate limit, Buddhas, patriarchs, sages, and worthies may breathe through a single nostril.

The sense organs and their objects are not substantial entities; delusion is formed by false thoughts. False thoughts are fundamentally empty, yet the sense organs and their objects become obstructions.

Through this, I know that the sense organs and their objects do not exist apart from false thoughts, and false thoughts are not inherently existent apart from the sense organs and their objects. Since they do not exist [independently], the mountains...
Rivers are not obstructions. If they were originally non-existent, then thoughts would not be cognition. Mountains and rivers are not obstructions;

thus, there is nowhere that is not the body. Thoughts are not cognition; thus, there is nowhere that is not the mind. Wherever there is nothing that is not the body, every speck of dust and every world-system is a gathering of merit.
Wherever there is nothing that is not the mind, every thought and every moment of mind is the mechanism of wondrous response.
Sentient beings and the insentient are fundamentally one and the same; Buddhas and sentient beings have never been two distinct things.
Therefore, the laughter and speech of sentient beings are the perfectly consummate discourse of the Tathāgata, and the Brahma-voices of all Buddhas are the humorous chatter of sentient beings.
Some say that when I merely press my finger, the Sea-Seal emits light; others say that my clearing my throat, sneezing, or spitting are all the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West.
Truly, they do not deceive me. It is simply that sentient beings do not understand their own minds, whereby the non-illusory becomes illusory.

If one realizes the point of return directly, it has been manifest from the very beginning. Although such profound depths are reached, the merit derives from the power of wisdom. This is like contemplating words as reality itself.

As for "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*): investigate the origin of speech. If it arises from discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*), yet there is no external framework, then the melodic resonance cannot be formed.

If it arises from the sense organs (*indriya*), yet there is no internal discursive thought, then there is no means by which it can be struck forth. Investigating and tracing it back repeatedly, neither of these two extremes exists.
Since both do not exist, how could a middle arise? When its very substance is found to have no dependence, it is suddenly and starkly revealed. Thus it is.
How could this be fathomed by the five eyes or measured by the four wisdoms? (To my disciples: It is easy to practice cultivation, but difficult to awaken to the mind.
It is easy to awaken to the mind, but difficult to discipline the mind. It is easy to discipline the mind, but difficult to reach the state of no-mind.
It is easy to abide in no-mind, but difficult to employ the mind [skillfully]. Those who merely lean against the gate or stand beside the door cannot be spoken to regarding this.
Those who study Buddhism rely upon Śākyamuni; those who study Confucianism rely upon Confucius; those who study the Way rely upon Laozi.

To cast off such reliance and stand firmly upon the open ground—like a lion king moving back and forth, leaping and bounding with sovereign ease, entirely without dependence—if one has thoroughly awakened to the light of the mind, they will use it spontaneously at hand, just as Ding Shàngzuò did.
Coming from Linji, when someone asked, "How is it that a Chan practitioner reaches the ultimate bottom? Xuedou seized him by the collar and threw him over the bridge.

A fellow practitioner who was traveling with him tried to intervene, but Xuedou said, "If it were not for this old, frozen lump of filth, I would have driven this Chan practitioner right to the bottom.
Xuedou can truly be called one who employs his hand spontaneously; such is his way of acting upon leaving the world.
When they are called "Buddha," they are Confucians in the secular world; when they practice the preservation of life, they are called Laoists.

Those who lean against gates and lurk beside doors are like merchants on a boat: having no power of their own, they falsely assume the authority of others and brand their foreheads with titles such as "Some Imperial Secretariat."

Whether it be officials of certain ministries or palaces, or those of the Censorate and Remonstrance Bureau, they deceive all who are ignorant; few fail to collapse at the mere sight of their reputation.
Yet, were they to suddenly encounter a true lord, then that which they have falsely assumed would not only dare not be flaunted, but they would find themselves with no leisure even to conceal it.
Alas! A man of spirit stands firm under heaven and upon earth, with brows arched and eyes bulging, loftily—
In broad conversation and expansive discourse, who among us does not claim to be a sage, a worthy, or a hero?
Yet, when one suddenly encounters this faceless fellow, who strikes with a seamless iron mallet, there is none whose eyes do not flicker and whose defenses fail.
How, then, can one hope that such a person can understand the meaning of the "Four Difficulties"?
Piqiuzi said: "Externally there is no separation without union; externally there is no union without separation. Separation arises from union, and union originates from separation.
If one examines union through separation, union has no source; if one examines separation through union, separation has no origin.

The Perfected One knows that separation and union have no self, and thus he traces them back to the realization that the near and far are impermanent, and the ancient and modern are mutually dependent. Therefore, he precedes Heaven."
Thus, being born does not constitute old age; descending after Heaven does not constitute youth. Taking what is near, from one's own person, it is already so;

taking what is distant, from external objects, there has never been two different principles. Within the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), if one investigates them through the object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*) in this manner, one finds that those who receive the blows of a staff or a whip cannot fathom the beginning or end of their pain; consequently, they cannot avoid their souls being startled and their bones trembling.

Alarming! A bitter anguish enters the heart. Although the breath has ceased and the form has dissolved, and the spirit wanders while the vital energies disperse, those who are still capable of knowing continue to harbor this pain as they take birth.
Though that birth is separated from the previous world by an entire lifetime, the pain remains vividly present. Sometimes it is transmitted from grandfather to father, and from father to son;
as sons and grandsons succeed one another, the pain only begins to fade after five generations have passed. Alas, O sentient beings!

Emotions accumulate; when emotions accumulate, they become solid. Thus, it reaches the point where a virtuous woman transforms into a stone of chastity, and the blood-light of Chang Hong becomes azure jade.
If one investigates the reason why this occurs, it begins with the deluded nature giving rise to emotion; as emotion accumulates, the myriad transformations become constantless.
Therefore, transformation does not go beyond that which is dependent. "Dependence" is merely another name for the distinction between beginning and end.

The wise person, knowing this, directly extends their inquiry to the point before pain arises and to the time after it has ceased; at these points of beginning and end, there is absolutely no locus where pain is experienced.
Precisely when the pain is occurring, they ride upon clarity with courage, transforming pain into joy in an instant. Pain is thus transformed.
Thus, while existing, one can be non-existent; when delighting in existence, one can exist within non-existence.

Being able to be non-existent while existing, one can roll up or expand out the dust-motes and lands within a single pore. Being able to exist while non-existent, one can unfold a single pore to emit mountains and rivers.
Therefore it is said: "The skillful observer enters the Buddha-wisdom through a single mote of dust," and thus now [the practitioner] touches upon it.
This single speck of dust begins with the mutual displacement of separation and union; extending to the far and the near, the ancient and the modern, there is nowhere it does not reach.
How much more so for one who enters the samādhi of every speck of dust!
In all instances of waking, one perceives forms in places where there are forms, but does not perceive forms in places where there are no forms;
this is the common experience of the world. In all instances of dreaming, one perceives forms in places where there are no forms, but does not perceive forms in places where there are forms;
this too is the common experience of the world. Only those who have realized the Way [understand that] during dreams there is no...
When one perceives forms within the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*), the delusion of perceiving forms during the waking state is as clear as the sun and stars;
what further confusion could there be?
For when doubt and discursive thought proliferate, the emotions become increasingly stagnant and delusion grows deeper; yet when the mind is focused on clarity, it becomes a limpid mirror.
Shining brightly, it reaches the ultimate limit of density. The mind is like water or fire: when it is gathered and concentrated, its function becomes more complete;
when it is dispersed and scattered, its momentum becomes more attenuated. Thus, a treatise says: "If the substance is subtle, the momentum is heavy; if the substance is heavy, the momentum is subtle.

For instance, because the substance of earth is heavy, its momentum is not as great as that of water; because the nature of water is heavy, its power is not as great as that of fire; and so it is with fire.
It is not like the wind; the wind is not like the mind. The mind has no form, and thus its power is unsurpassed.
Its supernatural transformations and entry into the inconceivable are the power of the mind. Once the power of the mind is perfected, one can turn from darkness into light.

Although light is superior to non-light, light itself is not yet complete. The perfection of light lies in the forgetting of illumination. Only when illumination is forgotten is there no longer any darkness.
It is clarity; there is nothing that is not clarity. This is nearly equivalent to cessation. That which is nearly equivalent to cessation is the function of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Thus, the Sūtra says: "Without dhyāna there is no wisdom; without wisdom there is no dhyāna. Therefore, dhyāna does not illuminate without wisdom, and illumination is not accomplished without dhyāna.
How great is the practice of dhyāna and wisdom! How can one not apply oneself to them?
A monk asked, "When Linji returned from seeing Dayu, how did Huangbo immediately know that his great matter had been thoroughly realized?
The Master said, "One who is cold gains wine, and their face blooms with spring. One who is hungry gains food, and their spirit becomes joyful.
How much more so for one who has drunk the unsurpassed nectar of *amṛta*!"
That which encompasses all things is Heaven and Earth. That which encompasses Heaven and Earth is Great Purity (*Taiching*).
As for that which encompasses Great Purity, who knows what it is? If it were a thing, it could not support that which has form;

if it were nothing, where would its function reside? To know is to have no doubt; to doubt is not to know. If one does not know and yet does not seek to know, one will never know. Man is but one among the myriad things.
It knows the ignorant and the wise; it knows cold and heat; it knows fragrance and stench; it knows the past and the present.
Regarding these things, it alone does not know [the nature of] man. Is man, then, truly spiritual? Or is he not spiritual?
Prajñā is the fire of true wisdom. It exists within both ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles, yet they do not all employ it skillfully.

Some cling to existence, while others cling to non-existence; such knowing of existence and non-existence is not what is called "true knowledge. When the fire of true wisdom encounters existence, existence is destroyed;
when it encounters non-existence, non-existence is destroyed.
The mind that exists because of objects exists for ordinary beings but not for sages. Only the unborn mind is shared by both sages and ordinary beings.
That which exists for ordinary beings but not for sages is a shadow dependent on conditions; that which is shared by both sages and ordinary beings is the light that is independent of conditions.
The upward path is such that it can neither be said to be without dependence nor to depend on conditions;

it can only be approximated by those true sons of the robe who hold the nostrils in their own hands. Thus, they exercise mastery over life and death, where the holy and the ordinary intersect and race against one another. In bestowing, they take away;
in killing, they give life. Like a luminous pearl upon a platter, its winding, horizontal, and diagonal movements, its collisions and revolutions, cannot be grasped through the intellect alone.

It is thus. That which cannot be attained through the conceptual mind cannot be sought by means of immediate cognition (*jñāna*). It is not sought apart from cognition, nor is it sought both by being attached to it and by being detached from it.
While escorting the remains of a deceased monk into the universal stupa (*pūtong ta*), he asked the assembly: "These handfuls of bones—compared to those of Tianjie..."

"The Buddha’s tooth relic at the temple—tell me, are they the same or different? If they are the same, then ordinary people and sages are not distinguished; if they are different, then there are phenomena outside the mind.

Speak quickly! Speak quickly! The assembly had no reply. After a long silence, he said: "Once one has entered the universal sea of the Sangha, the waves of compassion splash like incense reaching the heavens."

When hunger and thirst burn the heart, causing a person such heat and affliction that they nearly die, obtaining even a small amount of food and drink to relieve them makes one feel boundless coolness;
one is satisfied without having sought it. Yet one does not realize that within the very beginning of hunger and thirst, there exists that which is neither hungry nor thirsty.
If you are merely willing to observe slowly and attentively, it will be like a pond opening up and filling with water until the moon suddenly appears before you;

how could you wait for someone else to point it out before you see it? Nevertheless, while ordinary people give rise to hunger and thirst through food, drink, and sex, those above the level of the common folk give rise to hunger and thirst through fame and achievement, or through righteousness, principle, virtue, and the nature and destiny of life.
Although there is a difference between the lofty and enlightened and the lowly and ignorant, before hunger and thirst, they have never been different.
Therefore, the gentleman makes it his priority to hear the Way as his vanguard.

Now, emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and form (*rūpa*) constitute a single thread, yet they are sometimes divided into two. Those who divide them do so because of their own dualistic minds. As for that which is called "one," is it truly dual?

If the one were not dual, from what source would the myriad things arise? If duality were not unified by the one, then the multitude of beings would be severed from the ladder leading to the stage of the Sage.
Therefore it is said: "I only wish to empty all that exists; I am careful not to let things fill what is non-existent."
There is none.
The *wutong* tree excels in the wind; the *bajiao* plant excels in the rain. Though the *wutong* and *bajiao* are produced from the earth, the wind and rain come from heaven.
If the wind and rain did not rely on the excellence of these two for their intensity, then one would not perceive the force of the gale or the torrential downpour.
When it is majestic yet subtle, even the *tóng* and *jiāo* trees exist as if they do not. Therefore it is said: "If Heaven does not assist Earth, there is nothing by which life can be produced;
if Earth does not assist Heaven, there is nothing by which things can grow. Now, among all things that possess form, none exceed Heaven and Earth;
yet even these must depend upon one another to constitute their very substance. Thus, if the hairy insects and winged insects were to lack either male or female, their transformation would cease.
It is also easy to reach an impasse. Suppose there is a person here who advances toward the Way and its Virtue while retreating from power and profit;

yet they fail to realize that if there is even a slight advance, the retreat lacks its source, and if there is even a slight retreat, the advance lacks its foundation. If this is so, then the Way and its Virtue and power and profit are fundamentally not two separate things.

It is only those who employ them skillfully for whom power and influence are entirely the Way and its Virtue; if they do not employ them skillfully, then the Way and its Virtue— [The text ends abruptly.]
It flows secretly into the pursuit of power and profit, yet those who are ignorant do not perceive it. Therefore, when the Way is insufficient, one must supplement it with Virtue;
when Virtue is insufficient, one must rely upon Benevolence and Righteousness; and when Benevolence and Righteousness are insufficient, one inevitably flows toward Legalism and Nominalism.
Only when sage succeeds sage does this downward drift not occur—this is something I cannot know.
Those who lamented for the world in antiquity regarded food, drink, and sexual desire as the great cravings;
they sought to govern them, yet were unaware that they were grieving over one while neglecting the other. Indeed, if one were incapable of understanding food, drink, and sexual desire—

This is the ground of mutual delight; it is impossible for the essence of sweetness to arise otherwise. One who can know this does not grieve, yet to grieve over what one knows is to fail to understand the categories of things.
However, that which can be known is difficult to shatter; it is like oil entering flour, for through long habituation it has become one's nature.
If one cannot penetrate and clarify the fundamental mind and govern it with the spiritual state of non-self, then the oil will never depart.
It has emerged! Today, those throughout the world who claim to lecture on the Way do not know that they can recognize this thief.
They provide for it with no law, and moreover, exert their strength to nurture it. What is called "the spiritual self that is without ego" will, in the end, remain stunted and never flourish.
Worse still, some identify this capacity for knowing as the "host," as "seeing one's nature," or as "innate knowledge. Alas! To call a slave the master—this is truly lamentable.
Young sir, why is it so extreme? Now, the knowledge of an ant can encompass the space of a mustard seed, while the knowledge of a Kunpeng can encompass thousands of miles.
Yet, when one investigates their origins, though their names differ in magnitude, their capacity is one and the same. Thus it is said:
"To cleave a single atom and reveal a great thousand-fold world-system sutra—none but those who have heard the Way can do this. It is like a dragon hearing with its spirit, as opposed to a snake.
The eye hears; the ox’s nose hears. The faculties differ, yet what is heard is no different. Thus, that which can know may be inferred by analogy.

In the nine contemplations of the body, at first all are forceful observations. When the power of forceful observation becomes mature, one sees [the objects] spontaneously as soon as they are brought to mind. Seeing them bloated, one finds them loathsome.

Seeing its decay, one fears it; fearing it, one finds evil unbearable. One calculates the abandonment of this body as one loathes a dead snake—foul-smelling and offensive to the nose, causing one’s soul to tremble even in dreams, let alone when beheld with the eyes.
When the practitioner reaches this point, seeking the mind of lust, it is like searching for sprouts from parched grain.
It is like the son of a barren woman; one searches throughout the ten directions, ransacks the five internal organs, and investigates every single pore again and again.
Foul stench wafts everywhere—where could lustful thoughts exist? To contemplate death once is enough to satisfy my mind; by the power of a single thought, the ocean of desire is instantly dried up.
If all such [purifying] thoughts were to be realized one by one, what filth would not be cleansed? Since this is true for foul thoughts, it is likewise so for others.
The cause of pure perceptions has, from the beginning, no fixed characteristics. A single atom arises suddenly; having arisen suddenly, it flows along with the current, flowing without returning.

One reckons what is foul as fragrant. From a sudden moment, moments accumulate into instants; from instants, they accumulate into hours; from hours, they accumulate into days; from days, they accumulate into months.
Months accumulate into years; years accumulate into kalpas; and kalpas accumulate into delusion. Like oil absorbed into flour, the mind no longer returns to its original nature;

as it is difficult to extract oil from flour, once deluded, one remains forever deluded. The path to awakening is shrouded in darkness, and with craving and desire as one's lifeblood, one rises and falls in myriad ways.

The six realms are like a site under construction; the three miserable paths are familiar through long habituation. There, one is subjected to the burning of knives and blood and the scorching of fire, while food, drink, and clothing become causes of immeasurable suffering that penetrates the heart and reaches the very marrow of the bones.
The Sages take pity on them and thus teach this visualization: one must forcibly contemplate impurity. When the merit of contemplating impurity is perfected, [one attains liberation].
Through the transformative cultivation of overturning delusions, one becomes a dragon from a snake and a sage from an ordinary person. One takes a long farewell to the realms of suffering;
the bonds of birth and death are severed. In the bliss of non-self, joy is inexhaustible. Tracing back its merit, it begins with a single thought.

To give full expression to discourse is the *prajñā* of words and letters (*vyañjana-prajñā*). To be able to thoroughly penetrate the deluded attachments of body and mind is the *prajñā* of contemplative observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-prajñā*).
That Buddhas and sentient beings share the same essence is the *prajñā* of ultimate reality (*dharmatā-prajñā*).
This mind, from the beginning, cannot be called "consciousness" (vijñāna), nor can it be called "wisdom" (jñāna). Therefore it is said: "To speak of it as a single entity is incorrect.

Yet, how can it be that it lacks intrinsic nature and yet follows conditions? When a single thought flickers into being, from that point onward, the three subtleties and six coarsenesses arise in succession.
That which is called the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna) is the functioning of the Dharma-body; the Wisdom of Equality (samatā-jñāna) exists within ordinary beings.
Now, this so-called "defiled consciousness" is defiled not by external factors; rather, it refers to the reckoning of the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) of the eight consciousnesses as the self.
To speak according to the ultimate principle, the *darśana-bhāga* is in reality not the self; it is only through horizontal attachment that one reckons it to be so.

This constitutes the substance of this consciousness. This substance of consciousness takes the "self" as its primary focus, thereby giving rise to delusion, views, pride, and craving—these are called the four afflictions (*kleśas*).
These four afflictions do not compare to those of the six consciousnesses; they move the mind and arise through the activation of thought. They simply occur without knowing why.
Whenever encountering an object, one naturally feels aversion and naturally feels hatred. This habituation is most subtle. Furthermore...
This is called "innate ignorance" (*sahaja-avidyā*); this is spoken from the perspective of defilement. If one speaks from the perspective of purity:

when the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) practice the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), the seventh consciousness (*manas*) naturally subdues its attachment to phenomena. Just as when the six consciousnesses have long practiced the contemplation of the two-fold emptiness (*dvaya-śūnyatā*), the six consciousnesses themselves transform into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*).
Through long-term diligence, the power of contemplation gradually becomes intense; at that point, the two [attachments] of self and phenomena in the seventh consciousness—

Grasping dissolves like ice melting, becoming the Wisdom of Equality. As for the eighth consciousness and the first five consciousnesses, they are transformed into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom and the Wisdom of Accomplishing What is Done.
These two wisdoms exist at the stage of fruition and manifest when there is a momentary correspondence.
This does not involve hierarchical gradations. What were previously termed the "three subtleties" and "six coarsenesses" are alternative designations for the eight consciousnesses (*vijñāna*).

Viewed from this perspective, there is no need to worry that the eighth consciousness will not become the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), nor that the five sensory consciousnesses will not become the All-Accomplishing Wisdom (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).

It simply requires that one gains mastery over the sixth consciousness and sees through its nature clearly. Through gradual accumulation over months and years, it will naturally undergo transformation.

Consciousness is transformed into wisdom. Once the six consciousnesses have been transformed into wisdom, one does not fall from the summit. By continuing to apply effort without ceasing, the seventh consciousness naturally transforms into the Wisdom of Equality.
These two wisdoms exist within ordinary beings at the very first moment of generating the resolve for enlightenment, that single thought-moment of transcending the world.

Upon reaching the seventh stage, one achieves the fruition of their practice. From the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages, up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), all proceed through the effortless application of non-action (anābhoga).

This is the great affliction of the Buddha-dharma that has come upon us. This affliction does not lie with celestial Māras or non-Buddhist paths; rather, it lies in the seven great errors of blind teachers and disciples.

The first is the belief that the *gong'an* (critical phrases) and encounters of the ancient masters of the Chan school can bring about awakening, and that awakening is absolutely not to be found within the scriptural teachings (*śāsana*).
I shall ask you this: did Master An of Anzhou attain awakening by reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* with broken syntax? Or was it Master Yongjia?
Master Puan Su of Ying in Shaowu attained enlightenment by reading the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, and both he and [Master] Huaigan attained enlightenment by reading the *Avataṃsaka-śāstra*.
If you claim that only the karmic conditions of the Chan school can lead to enlightenment while the scriptural teachings (*jiao-cheng*) cannot, is this not a great error?
Second, you believe that the pathways of intellectual understanding and views obstruct the gate of self-enlightenment, and that the Way does not enter through the eyes or ears; you must...

Seclude yourself from all distractions. Wait until the beans crackle in the cold ashes; only when you have clarified this Great Matter will it be truly settled and finalized, attained once and for all.
Now I ask you: among the black and white of this world, who possesses true insight and the path of principle?
If you can indeed discern even one or two such people, I shall not concern myself with whether they have realized the Way or not.
To realize the Way, one must not fail to cherish it; yet I fear such realization is not easily attained.
One day, Wang Jiefu asked Chan Master Yuan of Jiangshan, "May I hear about the 'separate transmission outside the teachings'? Yuan replied, "You have obstructions.
For now, nourish your sprouting spiritual roots with the ocean of the teachings; only after another one or two lifetimes will you be able to do so. People today are far removed from Jiefu.
To learn to walk before one has even learned to crawl—is this not a great error?

Thirdly, you consider that seeking rebirth in the Pure Land through the recitation of the Buddha's name is easy and not difficult, and that compared to investigating Zen or studying the teachings, this alone is the most stable and reliable path.
I shall ask you this: does a person with a defiled mind take birth in the Pure Land, or does a person with a pure mind take birth there, or is it a person who is half-pure and half-defiled?

Is it those who are entirely pure in mind who are born there? If those with defiled minds could be born in the Pure Land, then name and reality would be at odds, and cause and effect would be divorced.
If it were those with both defilement and purity who are born in the Pure Land, I recall an ancient master saying: [text continues]
If, at the moment of death, a person possesses even a mustard-seed’s worth of consciousness that still clings to the Sahā world, they will absolutely be unable to be born in the Pure Land.
If one’s mind is entirely pure, then since the mind is already wholly pure, where could one go that is not the Pure Land? What further need would there be for a "Pure Land"?
Thus, this single point of nianfo (recitation of the Buddha's name) can surpass both the practice of Zen meditation and the study of the scriptures—is this not so?
A great error. Fourth: there are those like blind roosters who, upon hearing a true cock crow or a false cock crow, imitate them by making all manner of sounds.
To think that movement of thought immediately deviates from the original substance, or that deliberation falls into the livelihood of ghosts—how much more so when there are words?
Let me ask you: as for these kinds of views and knowledge, are they understanding (*jñāna*) or are they practice (*caryā*)? If they are understanding...

How can there be any deviation from the movement of thought? What illness is there in deliberation? An ancient said that after five *dǔ* of rice had been cooked, he was finally able to respond with a single turning word;
yet this did not deviate from the fundamental essence, and all the great Chan elders granted him the realization of thorough penetration.

Furthermore, it is said: "Deliberate upon it, deliberate upon it; then spirits and ghosts will communicate it to you. It is not that spirits and ghosts communicate it, but rather that the mind opens and becomes clear through deliberation. Deliberation!

What harm is there? The three wisdoms of hearing, contemplation, and cultivation of Avalokiteśvara permeate and transform all beings. For you to take pervasive discursive thought as your illness is surely a great error.
Fifth, it is not that human beings are necessarily without desire; yet, one who possesses desire and can restrain it rather than follow it is no ordinary person.
Furthermore, there are those who indulge their desires without restraint, who must have relied upon the seeds of wisdom from many lifetimes to have even slightly engaged in such study.

Regarding the teachings and vehicles, some may obtain a mere partial understanding and immediately regard everything as empty before their eyes, thinking that the ancients' realization of principle did not go beyond this.
Believing there is fundamentally nothing to do, why should one seek further investigation?

Amidst the winds of favorable and adverse circumstances, they drift eastward and westward, unable to exercise even a hair’s breadth of mastery. I ask you: when the ancients attained such vision, how did they act?
"You have attained [a superficial understanding], yet you are so lacking in intelligence that you fail to see its true application.
You have not even dreamed of it, yet you dare to be shameless and unashamed, speaking such reckless, grandiose words. This will only invite bitter retribution—is this not a great error?

Sixth, those among the followers of the Three Teachings each lack settled views; having failed to master Confucianism, they abandon it to study Buddhism; having failed to master Buddhism, they abandon it."
Those who study Laozi: having not mastered the study of Laozi, they drift into heterodox paths, reaching everywhere.
Let me ask you: have you truly reached the realm of Confucius and Mencius? If you had, you certainly would not act with such conduct as this.

If you have not yet reached that, you have not even mastered Confucianism; how then can you study Buddhism? If you have not even mastered Buddhism, what leisure do you have to study Laozi? Furthermore, there is another class...
People say that the principles of the Buddha’s house are already difficult to understand at the very threshold of their meaning and benefit; how much more so is the Holy Path?
Furthermore, those scriptures are vast and sprawling, such that one can never grasp their furthest reaches.

It would be better for each person to simply maintain their own way, rather than complicating matters further. Let me ask you this: have you realized the Buddha-mind? If you have realized the Buddha-mind, then the mind itself—

There is no doubt. Without doubt, there is no regret; without regret, one enters into faith. Now you have no cause for shame before yourself, yet with your shallow and limited faculties, you instead doubt the Buddhist scriptures—is this not a great error?
Seventh, when comparing those who are lay and those who have left the home-life to the "black" and "white" [sects] of the Tang and Song dynasties, they are as different as heaven and abyss.
As for the people of the Tang and Song, such as Pei Xiu and Su Shi, regarding both religion and doctrine—
Throughout these paths, all have attained realization and entry. Whether through a single phrase or a single verse, they praise and extol our Way;
like the light of a torch illuminating a carriage at night, their radiance cannot be obscured for a thousand ages. It shines brilliantly, vying in brilliance with the Sun of the Buddha.

Thus, when members of our own school engage in dialogue with them—such as when Master Taoguang answered the verses of Bai Juyi, or when Venerable Jiyin responded to Chen [Ziming]—[the same principle applies].
The ancient poems by Yingzhong also possess a refined elegance in abundance.

As for his inscriptions and prefaces to the sutras—though they vary in length from long compositions to brief accounts—they accord with the *sūtras* as if fitting together like two halves of a tally. Were it not for one who had truly grasped the Buddha’s mind, who could have attained such perfection?
In our own dynasty, since the time of Song Lian, there have been those capable of extolling [the Dharma] through language and writing.

Regarding my Way: it is not that it is entirely absent, nor can I say it is even slight. It is simply that the various worthies of the Tang and Song dynasties, who associated with those outside the secular world, were all able to transcend emotion and leave behind views;
they tore asunder the mundane net and cast gain and loss, honor and disgrace into the midst of empty flowers.
Their hearts shone upon one another like two mirrors reflecting each other’s light. Therefore, their lingering influence and remaining legacy have been passed down by later generations.
One cannot attach anything superfluous to this oneself. Alas! To seek the Way through emotions is like trying to reach Yan by traveling north from Shou.
To seek the Way by discarding emotions is like seeking water apart from the waves.

If there were a person who, between these two, possessed a separate path for their own emergence—one that does not involve taboos—I would guarantee that such a person need not practice Zen and need not study the teachings; they would surely attain enlightenment.
The Way has its days. It is like standing with both heels planted between two things; it is not as good as being a simple person who eats long rows of gruel and rice—would that not be excellent?
Furthermore, when monks and laypeople today go to visit teachers or friends, they do not yet possess the true heart of a student visiting a teacher or a friend;
instead, they immediately begin to speculate and calculate, thinking, "Such-and-such a teacher is nothing more than this," or "Such-and-such a friend is likewise nothing more than this."
It is thus. Once this mind has arisen, even if a Tathāgata were to appear once more, he could not benefit that person; how much less could anyone else?
Whenever one visits a teacher or seeks out a friend, it is like picking peaches: who has time to concern themselves with whether the tree is crooked or straight?

It lies solely in the beauty of the peach. If this is so, then for one who visits teachers and seeks friends yet strives to seek the Way through mere emotional consciousness—is this not a great error?
Thus are the seven errors; I too have spoken these words impulsively, unaware of their implications. How will the wise and noble—whether black or white—regard them?
Yet these seven errors are both the finest cream (*amṛta*) and also poison. One must be skillful [in their application].
When used properly, even poison has never failed to be *amṛta* (clarified butter). When not used properly, even *amṛta* has never failed to be poison.
I ask you again: when these seven errors have not yet arisen in a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), where do they abide? When that single thought-moment has already arisen, where do they abide?
If anyone can discern this, I, this old man, shall one day carry his shoes and hold his water-pitcher for him.
To remain thus, as previously distinguished, is not to emerge from it; one must not be careless, lest you provoke the laughter of those with clear eyes.
To think that mindfulness does not cease because of the non-forgetfulness of objects is to fail to understand that mindfulness and objects are like form and shadow.

If one were to say that form precedes shadow or that shadow precedes form, such a view fails to see that form and shadow are fundamentally neither subject nor object. All of this stems from not yet having realized that there is nothing outside the mind.
This is impossible; it is merely to follow one's own whims and engage in forced interpretation. Indeed, there is no dharma apart from the mind, and no mind apart from dharmas.

Yet, why is it that mind and dharmas appear as if they were two? This is simply because when one illuminates them with principle (*li*), there is no dharma outside the mind and no mind outside dharmas;

but when one discriminates them with sentiment (*qing*), then subject and object stand in opposition, making it difficult to resolve. To arbitrarily claim that one perceives [duality] before oneself—[is this not a delusion?]
As for "distinction," why should my own mind harbor doubt? As for "the objects" perceived by the aforementioned discrimination, why should they harbor doubt?

Object and self are held to crosswise; these accumulated attachments become solid. This solidity blocks the ten directions; where could one go that is not occupied by attachment? It is like honey: originally it has no center or periphery.
Alas! This clinging has burdened me. Tracing back the current to its source from the beginningless past until this very day, it is like pouring water onto ice:
as the days pass, the ice grows ever thicker; what is hard does not melt, and what is thick becomes even harder.

Through such accumulated habituation, it becomes firmer than the great earth and thicker than Mount Sumeru. If one wishes to shatter and dissolve it, it cannot be done unless one realizes the fundamental mind.
At present, he has no reliance. Amidst the circumstances of favorable or adverse conditions, he uses the light of non-reliance with great intensity;
the power of his blazing wisdom-fire is profound. Thus, even if a thousand Buddhas were to appear in the world, this habit would ultimately be difficult to transform.
When Master Lingrun was surrounded on all sides by wild fires with no place to flee and his companions scattered, Master Run immediately countered it by practicing the contemplation of Mind-Only.

One considers that the fire actually arises from within the mind; yet how could there be any principle by which the mind could burn the mind? As this contemplation enters slightly deeper, the fire immediately subsides and vanishes.
This is the model for breaking through and dissolving deep-seated habitual tendencies. In this way, sensory objects are naturally forgotten and mental discursive thoughts naturally dissolve.

When objects are forgotten and thoughts dissolve, the fundamental mind first becomes complete. Responding to things with this completeness, there is nothing that does not accord with it. There is nothing that...

It is not compliant. Although there should be compliance, there is no compliance; though there is compliance, it is without compliance. Thus, throughout past and present, East and West, who is the "other" and who is the "self"?
It is just as when the self revolves within the self—what "thing" exists outside the self? And when a thing revolves within a thing—what "self" exists outside that thing?
Therefore it is said: "When one stills the back, one does not perceive one's own body; when one walks in the courtyard, one does not see the other person. This is because...

It is the duty of one who has practiced from afar to become familiar with what is near. If one attains this familiarity and employs it to engage with things, then this Way will shine with great brilliance. (This is shown to the student.)
Those with rounded heads and square-cut robes, wearing crowns and girdles, are called the followers of the Black and White [teachings].

These two types of people may have entered Buddhism from Confucianism, or entered Confucianism from Buddhism; they may never have intersected at all, or having intersected, their transformations may be infinite.
Whether as Confucians or as Buddhists—tracing these various manifestations back to their origin—how could they have suddenly arisen?
Previously, it was likened to a great mass of fire upon which nothing can rest; were anything to rest there, it would be scorched and consumed before one could turn back.
Therefore it is said: the攀緣 (pān-yuán) mind of sentient beings is able to take objects everywhere, yet alone it cannot take as its object the Prajñā.
Viewed from this perspective, if one uses the攀緣 mind to study the supramundane Dharma, then the supramundane Dharma becomes nothing but攀緣 itself.
With a mind free from攀緣 (*pāra-ālambana*, grasping at objects), one studies worldly dharmas; all worldly dharmas are *prajñā*.

Now, there are those who claim that written words and language are insufficient for seeing the Way, and that only the practice of *chan* (Zen) and investigating the *huatou* (critical phrase) is sufficient for seeing the Way.
If written words and language were insufficient for seeing the Way, then Master Yongjia would not have attained awakening while reading the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*.
The Sixth Patriarch attained enlightenment upon hearing the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*; Pupan Xiu attained enlightenment by studying Fazang’s commentary on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*;
and the Tiantai Master Zhiyi attained the *āvartanī-dhāraṇī* samādhi while reading the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. Such examples are too numerous to cite exhaustively.
Furthermore, the kōans of the Chan school are all established precedents from past patriarchs; if one encounters the right person, they will handle these cases with authority and precision.
Punishment may be meted out; rewards and penalties may be applied. Illumination and function are unconfused, and the fundamental principles are held firmly in hand.
Amidst the silent roars and shouts of the dark, and beneath the thunderous strikes of staff and shout, the thieving mind dies instantly, and the living word flows freely in all directions.

Were it not for the right person, these so-called seventeen hundred cases of entanglement would instead become a demonic snare; once caught in their coils, liberation would be difficult even after ten thousand kalpas.
[The Master] said, "Understood. Why is this? Because the thorn has pierced the heart. An ancient worthy once said: "Written characters and spoken language are merely tools for entanglement;
fundamentally, they possess neither life nor death. Life and death depend on the person. When a living person employs them, there is nowhere they do not bring life;
when a dead person employs them, there is nowhere they do not bring death. The trouble does not lie in the language, the writing, or the entanglements, but rather in the person who regards them."

It is simply a matter of how one employs them. Furthermore, those who seek the Way by relying on external speech and written words—those who seek the Way through speech and writing—are what the world calls "religion" (zōngjiào).

Once religion is thus divided, each side disparages the other as being incorrect. One side maintains that the "sect" (zōng) can awaken the mind, whereas the "teaching" (jiào) is merely a path of meaning;
they argue that a path of meaning is insufficient to clarify one's own mind. This is utterly not so.

To know the refined meaning (*jingyi*) is to be able to enter the divine (*ru shen*). To enter the divine is to be able to bring forth function (*zhiyong*). Awakening the mind is another name for knowing the refined meaning.
Therefore, when the great elders of the Gate of the Patriarchs possess great capacity and great function, if they do not enter the divine, from where would such capacity and function arise?
Hence it is said: "Once one understands the words of the Buddhas, the words of the Patriarchs naturally manifest before one. This is truly a famous saying for all eternity. Always.
