Black and white are indistinct; beans and wheat cannot be distinguished; male and female are not yet recognized. To falsely claim that these are "texts" and "language"—I have no need to seek them out.
To suddenly transcend language and depart from texts: only then will my heart be satisfied. Of those who follow such a path, I have personally examined them with my own eyes;
of ten, there are five pairs. All harbor this view without transformation; take it for granted that they [will encounter] the Buddha.

Their speech never reached refinement, and their understanding of the Buddha-mind never attained clarity. Since neither of these two paths had entered their being, they continued to search peripherally and inquire circuitously, casting aspersions upon various quarters:
"How is such-and-such a virtuous teacher? "Such-and-such a virtuous teacher is not like that.

Yet, when matters of profit and loss came head-on, or when the urgency of life and death confronted them, they could no longer even recall whether he was "like this" or "not like that," let alone be able to...
One attains mastery over birth and death. Therefore it is said: "If one's sorrow is not deep, one cannot avoid negligence; if one's ailments are many, one is overly fastidious.

When seeking with excessive fineness, one harbors suspicion and carves at the ghost within. I wish that all—whether of the clergy or the laity, the worthy or the eminent—would realize that the teachings must be refined and the fundamental principle (zong) must be clear.
If the teachings are refined, then the Buddha’s words are my own words. If the principle is clear, then the Patriarch’s mind is my own mind. Reaching this field...
The ground is such that entering Buddhism is entering Confucianism, and entering Confucianism is entering Buddhism; yet in the end, they do not truly merge. There is neither "can" nor "cannot.
Know for yourself where to apply this, and who can shake you? Nevertheless, this is still the toil of the path; as for the one step beyond, you have not even dreamed of it yet.
(This is shown for those belonging to the Dharma.)

The Dharma discourse asks: "Before you were one year old, how many years had passed? You answer: "Before I was one year old, my parents' yin and yang were in union.
[The Master asks: "If they had not been in union, what then? He further asks: "When the minds of both your parents' families were unmoving, then the yin and yang—"

Regarding the realm of union: furthermore, in what place does it reside? If you can understand the state when the thoughts of the father and mother have not yet arisen, then regardless of how many years you have lived, you will certainly know where this falls.

If you do not understand this single point, it is like purchasing sandalwood to carve a Buddha; the Buddha within it will not emit light. If you thoroughly penetrate this single point, then even a dog [is the Buddha].
The dung-sculpted Buddha also emits light, shattering the darkness of your overturned basin. Furthermore, how long is human life? Suffering is much and joy is little;
if you do not clarify the nature of birth and death, with a single breath yet to come, you will once again collide headlong into the wombs of donkeys and horses.
"How tragic! An ancient worthy said: 'In the three realms of suffering, a single retribution lasts five thousand kalpas;
when will one emerge from it? I would say: 'Once you have emerged, there is no need to ask; within those five thousand kalpas, reflect deeply. (He showed Zhongsheng.
The Master asked, "This present body of yours—how could it exist? He replied, "It exists by borrowing the four great elements."
Question: Before the four great elements had yet gathered, where was your body? Answer: Fundamentally, there was no body. Question:
After the four great elements have dispersed, where is your body? Answer: There is likewise none. The Master laughed heartily and said:
"You sought your body before the four great elements had gathered, and after they had dispersed; in both cases it was non-existent. It appears alone."
The body exists by borrowing from the four great elements. If one examines this through reason, could it not be that there is nothing at either end, yet something exists in the middle?
Since there is nothing at either end, while something exists alone in the middle, I fear such a thing cannot be.
You should examine this thoroughly: does the middle exist first, and then the two ends? Or do the two ends exist first, and then the middle? If you examine this with precision—

When it is ripe, the wisdom of contemplation splits it open, and only then does the "seed" emerge. For the sake of this seed, one must investigate with great intensity: where, furthermore, is the mind of this seed?

If the investigation of the body is not yet thorough, one then investigates the mind; yet the mind will ultimately not be thoroughly understood. Therefore it is said: "Examine the names in order to refine the meanings."
Refining one's principles leads to the divine; entering the divine enables practical application. This is the path that both the sages of the East and the sages of the West must necessarily follow.
Thus, Yanzi sought to dissolve his physical frame and cast aside his cleverness; Laozi likewise said, "I have a great affliction, which is that I have a body.
If I had no body, what affliction would there be? He further said, "It exists with a distinct presence; when it acts..."
Regarding the Great Way, it is only this [teaching] that inspires awe. Laozi was likewise a sage of the East;

yet if one investigates where his path ultimately leads, its fundamental source is the same as that of Confucianism. An ancient said: "The origin of Laozi’s learning lies in the hexagram Qian (Humility) of the *I Ching*.

Nevertheless, to exhaust the causes of birth and death and to investigate the ultimate limit of the spiritual nature, if one does not study Buddhism, one will ultimately find it difficult to achieve complete penetration. Why is this so?

Indeed, the study that exhausts the spiritual and reaches the ultimate in numerical analysis—if one has not personally realized the full verification within one's own mind and attained the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle—will ultimately be difficult to clarify.
Phenomena belong to the realm of numbers; principle is rooted in the spiritual. To exhaust the principle while neglecting the numbers is called "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*).
To reach the ultimate in numbers while remaining ignorant of the principle is called "neglecting the root. As for *yoga* and *vijñapti-mātra*...
The *Shi* (The Book of Numerical Categories) is the ultimate treatise on calculation. The *Avataṃsaka* and *Śūraṅgama* Sūtras are the scriptures that exhaustively investigate principles.

When both calculation and principle are refined, yet one does not penetrate the Chan school, it is like Lord Ye’s painted dragon; how could it produce clouds or lightning? Therefore, for those who study the body and mind:
if the body is not refined, there will be the burdens of birth-and-death and honor-and-dishonor; if the mind is not refined, there will be...
One is thus attacked by likes and dislikes, and by right and wrong. Therefore, it is said that one must investigate nature (*xing*) and destiny (*ming*) starting from one's own body and mind.

If one neglects the body and mind without investigating them, then even if one has read the five carriages of books and the Tripitaka, what benefit will it ultimately bring to the body and mind? (To Ruan Jianzhi)
Between the sage and the ordinary person, there is no gate; yet the gate opens for both delusion and awakening. Delusion and awakening have no root; they are rooted in one’s own mind.

When the self-mind is not clear, one believes when hearing sounds with the ears, but doubts when observing sounds with the eyes. Nevertheless, when hearing sounds with the ears, likes and dislikes are vividly apparent;
yet when observing sounds with the eyes, where do likes and dislikes exist? To understand this clearly is to be entirely free of doubt.
Only then did he come to believe that it is not only the Great Being who can perceive with the ear, but that all people can likewise perceive with the ear.
Alas! If the external object is not transformed yet is fused, and the internal faculty is not liberated yet is detached—this is but a partial understanding.
If the function of hearing and liberation is not obscured, then the object and the faculty have never ceased to be the fundamental source. If, however, this function can be obscured, then...
Furthermore, if the holy and the mundane are not distinguished, then initial awakening would be without merit. How could such a thing be possible?

(To Li Shengfeng) The Bhagavān entered the Great Treasury of Supernatural Penetration and Radiance, in accord with non-duality, manifesting all pure lands together with one hundred thousand great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. Their names were Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, Samantanetra, and Suvarṇa... [and so forth].

Vajragarbha, Maitreya, Viśuddhamati, Vīryendra, Ghoṣavati, Karmāvaraṇaviśodhani, Samantabodhi, Pariniṣpannabodhi, Bhadraśrī, and other Dharma Bodhisattvas, together entered the Great Radiance Treasury of Supernatural Power. Alas!
Is this Great Radiance Treasury possessed solely by the Bhagavat and these great Bodhisattvas? It belongs to all sentient beings as well.

Is it that there are no fruits? Nevertheless, all sentient beings are deluded regarding the selfless, numinous awareness, and instead take the攀緣 (pān-yuán) [grasping] awareness of a self to be their own mind.

Consequently, like the treasure storehouse within a poor woman’s house or the bright pearl within a destitute son’s garment, though these exist in the present, they cannot be utilized. All sentient beings have realized perfect enlightenment; this is my Bhagavān.

This is the speech of a "Ba" (a term for a fool). In the past, people used the character *ju* (to possess) as a means of easy proof. Chan Master Zhenjing Wen called such a person a "stinking sheep-bleater," for they obstruct their own fundamental mind with words and doctrines.
Even regarding the Buddha’s words, they remain doubtful and do not believe them; they recklessly alter the sacred scriptures.
Thus, what they have realized can be known. Therefore it is said: "Without involving emotional understanding, it manifests right where one is;
the paths of ordinary and sage are cut off. Then, as for what is called the Bhagavān and the great Bodhisattvas—at that time, where would they be situated?
Yongguang once attended upon a man of the Way at the Changsong Hermitage, and he himself vowed to uphold the *Mahāvaipulya-samyak-saṃbodhi-vajra-cakra-nirvāṇa-sūtra*.

One begins by reading the *Yijing*. Having read it, one achieves its recitation. Once the recitation is mastered, one maintains it without relying on scrolls or volumes, thereby illuminating the capacity to trace back and ascend.
Initially, one relies on scrolls and volumes; subsequently, one discards the scrolls and volumes to achieve recitation.
Through recitation, one attains retention; through retention, one attains refinement; through refinement, one attains entry—this is what is called the "Treasury of Great Radiant Supernatural Powers."
When one bows one's head until it strikes the ground before the Bhagavān and the great Bodhisattvas, is there truly any discrimination?

If you can discern this through careful investigation, then in the future, whether amidst flowing waters and wild clouds, or in the Peach Blossom Spring and the bustling city, you may suddenly encounter [the truth] and finally be able to deliberate upon the words of the old fellow Xianshanshou for their circulation.
How much time remains? Sound and form— (Note: The final phrase "shengse" (sound and form) appears to be an incomplete thought or fragment of the original text.)
This is a critical juncture. If the treasury of spiritual powers (*abhijñā*) were to be buried and lost, then it would be as if they had never been born at all.
Yongguang, you must exert yourself and embody this—[this is addressed to] Xing Yongguang.

Now, although the Avataṃsaka Mahā-śāstra is vast in its phrasing and expansive in its meaning—truly surpassing other sūtras—its great principles do not exceed four divisions, namely, the four dharma-realms (dharmadhātu).
When not a single thought arises, it is called the principle dharma-realm (li-fajie). Once a thought has arisen, it is called the phenomenon dharma-realm (shi-fajie).
That the unarisen does not obstruct the already arisen, and the already arisen does not obstruct the unarisen, is called the phenomenon... [dharma-realm].
The Dharma-realm of Non-obstruction of Principle is like taking up and using something as it comes, without involving emotional attachments or intellectual interpretations;

it is perfected right where it is. It cannot be sought through principle, nor can it be exhausted through phenomena. This is provisionally called the Dharma-realm of Non-obstruction of Phenomenon-to-Phenomenon.
The practitioner is able to believe this, understand this, practice this, and realize this; these are collectively termed the four divisions.
Furthermore, regarding the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle, nearly a thousand years have passed since the Great Canon arrived from the East.

Among both the ordained and the laity, as well as all the eminent figures, there has been none who did not regard this sutra as the fundamental wheel of the Dharma, all of whom have refined their skills and exhausted their thoughts to annotate and comment upon it. As for...
The Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomena (shishi wuai fajie) is like a son who, upon hearing his father's name, would never dare to utter it himself;

even if one were to forcefully expound it, it would merely be a matter of using principle to harmonize phenomena so that phenomena finally become unobstructed. If this is the case, then as for the Great Hero (the Buddha):
Apart from the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle, if one were to posit this "Dharma-realm," would it not be in vain?
Furthermore, regarding the sayings of Dixin and Shanhui—such as "The ox in Huaizhou eats the grain; the horse in Yizhou has a bloated belly;
the world seeks a physician to cauterize the left shoulder of a pig"—these are nothing more than indirect provocations (*pángqiāo*). Now, both Dixin and Shanhui...

Mañjuśrī and Maitreya have returned; yet even those two great Bodhisattvas, regarding the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*dharmadhātu-dharmatā-pratītyasamutpāda*), could only hint at it from the side and did not dare speak of it directly.
Now, that you have transcribed this sutra amidst green mountains and white clouds, it may be said that you possess most excellent karmic conditions.
Know that the three preceding dharma-realms can be comprehended through intellectual cognition, but as for the final one—
There is but one realm. If you seek it while remaining apart from wisdom-consciousness (*jñāna-vijñāna*), you will never enter it.
Furthermore, if it could be sought apart from wisdom-consciousness, then one might as well seek it in earthenware or wooden puppets; why wait for you to seek it?
If you seek it and do not yet penetrate it, at that very point where penetration has not occurred, you must exert your utmost brilliance and risk your life to seek it, as if it were your very life.
If the root suddenly severs, then the sutras written by the disciple are like a drum smeared with poison;

when struck and its sound issues forth, whether one has a mind or is mindless, all who hear it die before their feet can even turn back. Though they die, they may revive, and it will not be too late for them to come again and receive certification (addressed to Zen practitioner Lin).
While it is certainly benevolent to save a person’s body, nothing is more inconceivable than saving a person’s mind. One saves a person’s body with medicine;

one saves a person’s mind with the Dharma. Medicine is subject to the uncertainty of presence or absence, whereas the Dharma is identical to one’s own mind from the very beginning—it cannot be limited by existence or non-existence.
Furthermore, the mind does not save the mind, just as water does not [wash itself].
Washing away the water. How can one bring it back to life? To be able to awaken to this is precisely the Buddha-physician. If there is doubt, one must not let go of it;
if doubt reaches its peak, one doubts even further. Only when that doubt suddenly breaks through can one speak of the physician (referring to Master Chen, the physician).
Now, as for hunger and cold compared to honor and disgrace, or poverty and low status compared to life and death—there is no one in the world who does not consider these to be afflictions.
Alas! To know they are afflictions yet not know from whence the affliction arises—this is called delusion. In delusion, one lacks awareness;
lacking awareness, one cannot return [to the source]. Since one does not return, then from birth until death, everything is nothing but a turning away from the root.
One acts, yet remains unaware that one has been背离 (divergent from) the fundamental source for an entire lifetime, and even for immeasurable lifetimes.

If one can directly reflect back and realize the fundamental source, thereby forgetting emotional attachments—when attachments are forgotten, the root of affliction is uprooted; when the root of affliction is uprooted, the "suffering" mentioned previously will naturally manifest.
Once it manifests, one treats it: then the superficial afflictions (the skin) will instantly give way as the root is pulled out, and only then can one treat the fleshly afflictions.

The afflictions of the flesh, the afflictions of the bones, and the afflictions of the skin—when these are extracted, the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) are exercised with ease within the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), and one passes straight through mountains and walls.

This is called the exhaustion of the ignorance of the branches and twigs. If the spiritual function [of the mind] is already such when the ignorance of the branches and twigs is exhausted, how much more so when the afflictions of the flesh and bones are exhausted? These three types of affliction are names that people of the world do not even know.
How can one know its meaning? Since the meaning is not known, how can one know its principle? Since the principle is not known, how can one know the Way?
As for what is called "virtue," that is even less understood. Now, names are the traps for meaning; meaning is the fish.
Meanings are manifold; to synthesize and penetrate them is called principle (*li*). To embody and practice that principle is called the Way (*dao*).

To practice until even the merit is forgotten is called virtue (*de*). Now, you wish to regulate the body and mind, yet if you do not distinguish these names and meanings, will you not be merely laboring under their names in vain?
If you labor in vain under their names, yet calculate that regulating [the self] has produced results—is this not folly? For instance, since there is a body, there is...
The pressure of hunger and cold follows next; after that, honor and disgrace; nothing is greater than birth and death.
Furthermore, where there is a mind, there are likes and dislikes: one rejoices when things accord with oneself and becomes angry when they oppose oneself.
From this point onward, there are consequences beyond description. Therefore, our Great Enlightened Sage showed us the verse of Viśvabhū Buddha; if you read it as follows—

Recite it thoroughly; having recited it, investigate its meaning. Having investigated the meaning, one accords with the principle. When the principle is mastered, it can be put into practice. To practice is to attain realization (as shown by Master Bin).
Now, the poor long for wealth; the wealthy long for nobility; the noble long for ease and leisure; and those who enjoy ease and leisure long for immortality.
Little do people realize that from volition arises birth; from birth arise wealth and honor, poverty and low status, toil and ease, and even all manner of suffering, which are beyond counting.
Therefore, those who wish to cross the sea of suffering must take non-volition as their boat and oars.
Thus, one finally ascends to the other shore. Yet, thought cannot simply cease of its own accord; it must rely on hearing the Way to bring it to cessation.
The Way cannot manifest itself through hearing alone; it must further rely on conditions and causes to draw it forth, only then can it be heard.

Now, these conditions and causes are truly the mother of all Buddhas and the sustenance of all sentient beings. To take the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) as conditions and causes is like contemplating their virtues.

Regarding the human countenance, it refers to those for whom base and stingy thoughts naturally vanish; regarding sound as a contributory cause, it refers to those whose minds are opened and enlightened by a single word;

furthermore, it refers to taking the holy teachings as a contributory cause, great spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) as a contributory cause, virtuous companions and fellow practitioners as a contributory cause, and even adverse conditions as a contributory cause.

Favorable conditions serve as the causal conditions (*pratyaya-hetu*). Alternatively, through diligent and courageous effort, one may use flayed skin as paper, split bones as pens, and draw blood as ink to transcribe the Mahāyāna scriptures;
thus, these serve as causal conditions. Therefore it is said: "The seed of the Buddha arises from conditions.
Although all such various causal conditions are aids for hearing the Way, only the final one—using blood as ink to write the sutras—is the [definitive] causal condition.

This cause is most preeminent and supreme. Yet, sentient beings cling so heavily to their physical forms that even when a mosquito or a fly—so minute—bites them, they cannot overcome their anger and brush it away, refusing to let it go until it has finished.
How much more so when pricked by a sharp needle, causing blood to flow and the heart to tremble;

only one who can stand firm and endure the pain can attain the ultimate favorable condition. If it were not for a long-standing faith that is steadfast and profound, the consciousness [could not endure].
To see one who transcends the crowd is surely no easy feat. The Venerable Tang Guànxiū inscribed this upon Master Chǔyún’s *Lotus Sūtra* written in his own blood:

"Shaving the skin and piercing the flesh—how bitter the suffering! For the sake of transcribing the ninefold scriptures of Vulture Peak, The ten fingers were drained dry to complete these seven fascicles;
Henceforth, those seeking the Dharma shall find no peer like you. Fǎdēng, you ought to sing this poem with great intensity dozens of times.

Once pervasion is achieved, the attachment to the body naturally lightens. When attachment to the body has lightened, this sutra—consisting of no more than five thousand words—is not difficult to transcribe (referring to Layman Shifa Deng’s transcription of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* by drawing blood).

Now, among us, if we do not use the light of "I," "me," and "mine" to pierce through the entangled realms of hatred and love during our daily lives, then even though we dwell on the shores of seclusion and solitude, it will be no different from the places where horse hooves and carriage dust swirl.
Therefore it is said: "If you simply forget your own mind, there is nowhere that is not wondrous" (from the *Biyun si* [Blue Cloud Temple], by Yu Ruqi and others).
I read the *Amitābha Sūtra* translated by Zhi Qian of Eastern Wu and first learned that the light from the crowns of the Buddhas’ heads varies in size;
there is light seven *zhang* high, light one *li* high, light one hundred *li* high, and even light reaching thousands of millions of *li*.
Only the Buddha Amitābha possesses a crown-light that is exceptionally sublime and immeasurable. At Mount She, at Xiqia Temple...
On its back is Thousand-Buddha Ridge. Upon this ridge are rock grottoes, like honeycombs or anthills, arranged in tiers and winding patterns.
The dimensions of the Buddha figures therein also vary in size. Previously, this was the site of the Qi-era Master Ming Sengshao.
He invited Dhyāna Master Fadu to lecture on the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*. Moved by this, the heavens rained down four kinds of flowers, and he beheld the countenance of the Buddha in a dream.
Thereupon, the Retired Scholar, based on what he had seen in his dream, ordered the carving of several images into the mountain immediately after waking.

Before the work was half-finished, the Retired Scholar passed away. His son, [Name], who served as the Magistrate of Linyi, fulfilled his father’s ambition and completed the task. From the Qi dynasty until...
It has been nearly a thousand years. During this time, the rise and fall of temples and the completion or destruction of Buddha images have all been matters of coincidental causes and conditions.

When the Jin general Wuzhu occupied the Ch’epyeong Ridge and was about to go to war, he prayed for the Buddha’s hidden protection. When his army suffered defeat, he grew enraged and commanded his generals, saying:
"Since the Buddha does not bless me but aids the rebels, the Buddha is himself a rebel! I must destroy him to vent my indignation. For this reason—

The images enshrined within the rock caves—regardless of their size—have all suffered damage; some have had their bodies and heads mutilated, while others have had their eyes, ears, mouths, noses, arms, and wrists disfigured or destroyed.
Those who see them are moved to grief. Though I am not gifted, I venture to rely upon the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, the Chan master Suan-an, having received the praise and affection of the Abbot Cang, wished to restore it.
When the Abbot’s grandson, named Hai-yin, heard my words, he immediately vowed to sacrifice his efforts to undertake the project. Alas! Such was the Master Zhengjun’s devotion to the Buddha.

Wu-ju’s destruction of the Buddha was an act of his own mind; his destruction of the Buddha was likewise an act of his own mind. If he had employed it for good, its radiance would have flowed through ten thousand generations.
Had he done the opposite, his evil would have filled the void. Even if the void were to perish, his ill repute would not vanish. Be cautious! Be cautious!
Furthermore, there is no Buddha outside the mind, and no mind outside the Buddha. When the conceptualizations of "mind" and "Buddha" are extinguished, the constant radiance is revealed alone.

This is what is meant by "affirming oneself with a willing heart. As for this light—whether it extends seven fathoms, or up to ten million fathoms, or throughout immeasurable lands—it is not that the Way of the Buddhas differs;
rather, these differences all arise from the varying vows made during their causal practice. Haiyin, come forward! I [am facing] east, west, south, and north.
A person of the North, departing for the impermanence [of death], has briefly written this to leave behind. May you exert yourself accordingly (this letter was shown to Haiyin).
A single louse on the ear makes a sound like a peal of thunder; a single flea in the bosom causes a restless itching as it bites.

How much more so when the four great poisonous snakes coil and entwine around one’s body? That a person does not know fear is nothing short of being mentally deranged or a mere wooden or earthen form.
Who could endure this? As for the four snakes fighting one another, their strength varies in intensity and their influence varies in gravity.
When the fire-snake gains the upper hand, the heart and bones are steamed and scorched; when the wind-snake suffers defeat, the four limbs cannot be raised; and the earth-snake is heavy by nature.
The nature of the water-snake is cold. Once it enters within me, there is cold pain, aching, and numbness; the spirit becomes dazed and confused, and the suffering takes myriad forms.
Though one is called a human, one is no different from a ghost. Reflecting on this after the illness has passed, it is truly fearsome and startling.

For this reason, in the city of Vaiśālī, the layman Vimalakīrti manifested illness to preach the Dharma, pointing out that the four snakes are a great affliction and calling the five desires [the source of suffering].

The poison of the *hen* bird. To refute the partial and disparage the small, to praise the Great and extol the Perfect, and to harmonize the coarse to enter the subtle—through hundreds of thousands of skillful means, one purifies Buddha-lands and brings sentient beings to maturity.
If this is so, then whether one is ill or not depends entirely on how that person employs their mind.
If one skillfully employs the mind, even the great affliction of *hen* poison becomes the mark of the broad and long tongue; what, then, could be called "illness"? (From the *Wen*)
My son traveled more than several thousand *li* to reach the capital of Yan. Suddenly he fell ill, appearing as though he would not survive.

By relying upon the pervasive light of the Triple Gem, he found the path to rebirth. Although his illness has gradually improved, as he returns south on this long journey, the autumn is high and the trees have fallen;
the cold winds are mournful and desolate, and the traveler lingers with lingering sorrow. At such a time, one can truly reflect upon the sufferings endured during illness, compared to what is now.

The autumnal scenery fills the eyes; staff and sandals are light and carefree. Yet, within this state, one does not seek a prescription for freedom from illness, nor become a person who is autonomous and free from affliction.
I have long been ashamed before the old man Vimalakīrti. When Wenzi came forward, I asked him, "At the very moment of being ill, is there anyone who is not ill?
Wenzi was unable to answer. The Daoist master rebuked him, saying: [Note: The original text ends abruptly with the master's rebuke. A full translation would require the subsequent dialogue.]
Seeing the reflection across the river, he turns and departs; before and after, there is no mind to discriminate others. Wenzi attained the four great poisonous snakes;
from the beginning, they were nothing other than the four immeasurable compassions (as shown in the words of Shiji).

The body of the pure Dharma-realm is fundamentally without birth or death. When the mind stirs for a mere instant, the ten realms become manifest. From the coarse to the refined, and from suffering to joy:
the cause for the hell realm is what is evoked by the ten non-virtuous actions; the cause for the hungry ghost realm is what is evoked by stinginess and envy;
the cause for the animal realm is what is evoked by delusion and lust; the cause for the human realm is what is evoked by observing the five precepts; [the cause for] the asura realm...

The cause for the [human] realm is the cultivation of virtue combined with anger and deceit. The cause for the celestial realm is the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*). These six realms are called the "six mundane states" (*ṣaḍpṛthagjana*).

The cause for the realm of the *śrāvakas* is the realization of the Four Noble Truths. The cause for the realm of the *pratyekabuddhas* is the cultivation of the cessation of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda*).

The cause for the realm of the *bodhisattvas* is the cultivation of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*). The cause for the realm of the Buddhas is the cultivation of unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttarabodhi*).

These four realms are called the Four Noble Ones. If, by proceeding from the refined to the coarse and from pleasure to suffering, one cannot enter the Buddha-realm, one remains in the Bodhisattva-realm;
if one cannot enter the Bodhisattva-realm, one falls into the Pratyekabuddha-realm.
Those who cannot enter the realm of the *pratyekabuddhas* fall into the realm of the *śrāvakas*. Those who cannot enter the realm of the *śrāvakas* fall into the celestial realms.

Those who cannot enter the celestial realms fall into the realm of the *asuras*. If those in the realm of the *asuras* do not turn their minds back [toward enlightenment], they will fall into the realms of animals, hungry ghosts, and hell.
If those in the human realm do not turn their minds back, they likewise fall into the realms of animals, hungry ghosts, and [hell].
The hells and the three realms—alas! When the single mind has not yet arisen, neither ordinary beings nor sages can be found;

there is only the body of the pure Dharma-realm, perfect and without deficiency. Once the single mind has arisen, the distinction between the sage and the ordinary being becomes clear and cannot be obscured by even a hair’s breadth.
Therefore, the practitioner should use the ten realms as a mirror for the mind; wherever an ordinary thought arises, one should know that this is where one has entered.

The realms into which one falls are as clearly visible as the lines on the palm of one's hand. If a mind arises toward the objects of the ten unwholesome actions, one immediately knows this to be the cause for the hell realm.
If a mind arises toward the objects of stinginess and envy, one immediately knows this to be the cause for the hungry ghost realm.
If a mind arises toward the objects of delusion and lust, one immediately knows this to be the cause for the animal realm. Regarding the five precepts...

When a mind arises toward the realm of sensory objects, one knows this is the cause for the realm of humans. When a mind arises toward the realm of anger or feigned goodness, one knows this is the cause for the realm of asuras.
When a mind arises toward the realm of the ten wholesome actions, one knows this is the cause for the realm of devas.

When a mind arises toward the realm of the Four Noble Truths, one knows this is the cause for the realm of śrāvakas. When a mind arises toward the realm of the twelve links of dependent origination...

If one gives rise to a mind directed toward the realm of the pratyekabuddhas, one knows that this is the cause for the pratyekabuddha-element. If one gives rise to a mind directed toward the objects of the six perfections, one knows that this is the cause for the bodhisattva-element.
If one gives rise to a mind directed toward the realm of unsurpassed enlightenment, one knows that this is the cause for the Buddha-element.

Nevertheless, the sufferings of hell vary in their lightness and heaviness; the hunger of hungry ghosts varies in its shallowness and depth; the ignorance and lust of animals vary in their thickness and thinness; and so it is with the human realm.
There are the noble and the wealthy, the poor and the lowly; among asuras there are the strong and the weak; among devas and humans there are the superior and the inferior;
among śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas there are the skillful and the clumsy; and among bodhisattvas and buddhas there are degrees of distinction.

All of these are induced by the karmic power of sentient beings' daily activities, just as a mirror reflects the face, making beauty and ugliness appear exactly as they are. Yet, sentient beings in the hells long for the realm of hungry ghosts, and hungry ghosts long for the realm of animals.
Beings in the animal realm long for the human realm; those in the human realm long for the celestial realms;
those in the celestial realms long for the *śrāvakas*; the *śrāvakas* long for the *pratyekabuddhas*; the *pratyekabuddhas* long for the *bodhisattvas*; and the *bodhisattvas* long for the Buddhas.
This is no less than a dragon coiled in the mud longing for the clouds and sky, or an insect in a puddle longing for the vast ocean. Now, there is a certain kind of...

Foolish people, weary of the limited nature of this floating life and the impermanence of its pleasures and longevity, aspire to the Way of the Immortals in order to plan for long life and enjoy eternal bliss.
Yet they do not realize that a single thought of a sentient being in hell can give rise to the unsurpassed mind of Bodhi.
This applies even up to the point of directly transcending the realm of Bodhisattvas; how much more so for devas and humans, or asuras and immortals?

If one within the human realm cannot give rise to the unsurpassed mind and cultivate the seeds of Buddhahood, they are far inferior to those sentient beings in hell who can, in a single thought-moment, give rise to the bodhicitta. Furthermore, the suffering of hell is not the ultimate limit.

Suffering. The suffering of the female body is the most extreme of all sufferings. Though you are the mother of a Son of Heaven and consider yourself to have received unsurpassed blessings, you do not realize that there are far more impoverished and lowly men who seek the Way on famous mountains and study Zen within the ocean of the Buddhas.
Why is this? Because women face immeasurable obstacles and manifold suspicions; whether moving or still, whether going out or—
[The wealthy] enter [a state of bondage]. In all their hundred activities, they are constrained by others and cannot act as they wish. It is not so for a poor and lowly man.

Should he simply give rise to a resolute mind, whether visiting sacred mountains to seek the Way depends on him; whether attending a Chan master depends on him; whether traveling thousands of miles depends on him;
whether sitting in meditation in deep mountains depends on him; and even whether chanting the Buddha’s name aloud depends on him.
Rejoicing in the Way and finding joy in it, even a few loud laughs come from me; I move with sovereign ease, coming and going as I please.
Considering this, it is clear that even the most noble woman is not equal to a poor and humble man. Furthermore, it is not difficult to escape the female body;
one need only have sufficient faith in the words of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), thoroughly penetrate them, turn away from the heterodox, and return to the orthodox. Side by side—

At every gate and narrow path, sweep them all at once. Whether coming in the morning or returning in the evening, whether joy or affliction, busyness or leisure, movement or stillness, dullness or distraction—at every such critical juncture, do not let even a hair’s breadth slip away. Take only the verse of Viśvabhū Buddha as your fundamental *huatou*.
Amidst all circumstances, whether adverse or favorable, maintain it continuously without interruption, remaining vividly clear and unclouded, reciting it thus.

I am about to depart. If you practice in this manner for three or five years and yet see no results—if in the future you still do not escape the female body—not only shall my own tongue be split asunder, but the broad and long tongues of all the Buddhas of the ten directions shall also be split asunder.
I utter these words of sincere truth; yet you are unable to believe and accept them, nor can you...

The ten realms illuminate the mind, serving as a whip and spur for daily life. To fall into the great hells and encounter suffering in the present is entirely due to failing to rely upon a *kalyāṇamitra*.
Alas! A single retribution in the three miserable realms lasts five thousand kalpas; when will you emerge from them? (This is shown by Faden).
Now, when the single mind does not arise, existence and non-existence have no basis upon which to depend; how much less could there be those who hear or see?
Nevertheless, once the single mind has arisen and the six sense organs are already complete, there has never been anyone who attained entry by means other than these.

When people everywhere preach the Dharma, they may expound it through the faculty of the tongue and enter it through the faculty of the ear, or they may initiate it through the faculty of the body and the faculty of the eye.
Enter into it. Extending this to the nose and all the sense organs, circulate through them to elucidate their subtleties; though they are impermanent, therein one receives their wondrous essence.

If one is thus, then whether it be sorrowful songs and lamentations, spitting insults and derisive rebukes; thorny thickets and jade trees; robes, caps, rites, and music; the beating of drums and the playing of flutes;
food, drink, men, and women; right and wrong, likes and dislikes; or the clashing of spears and halberds—when these are stirred up and advanced, [the sage remains unmoved].

Whether it be the golden halls or the seclusion of forested clouds, whether it be the clamor of the marketplace or the silence of the wilderness, all are the *prabhūta-tanujihvā* (long and broad tongue) of the Tathāgata.
Whether one enters [the path] or not depends solely upon the nature of the listener.

On the eleventh day of the third month of spring in the year of Wuli (Gui-si), the setting sun rested upon the peaks, the incense smoke in the burner coalesced into emerald green, the empty hall was like a mirror, and the eye of the mind was clarified.

Ting. At that time, Ka-lang hurried in, performed a solemn prostration, and stood aside. Within the chamber of purification, the faculty of the body (*kāyendriya*) preached the Dharma, the faculty of the eye (*cakṣurindriya*) listened and received it, the faculty of the tongue (*jihvendriya*) preached the Dharma, and the faculty of the ear (*śrotrendriya*) saw and accepted these words.
Unconsciously, I was filled with great joy and said: "My son may truly be called one who understands speech. Thereupon, I took up my brush and wrote this to broaden its meaning. (Shown to Dao-kai).
The Sage established the precepts in order to prevent villainy and depravity; the ancestral regulations and fundamental principles were established in order to ward off demons and heretics.
Therefore, whether one is ordinary or a sage, if one cannot pass through this very circle, then even if one possesses some slight insight, [it remains incomplete].
None of these are the true cause. Thus, Chan Master Yantou Quanhuo said: "Simply understand the fundamental principle that, fundamentally, there is no substantial dharma.
In recent years, those who are far removed from the Buddhas have emerged as 'true sons' everywhere, following in crowds and shouting wildly and confusedly.
If they encounter a true master, he will take up a single article of the Great Vinaya and interrogate them on their crimes based on the evidence; even if you were a Buddha of antiquity returning..."
Come! You must also submit your surrender; how much more so for a demonic child of inferior capacity? Nevertheless, tell me: how will you finally explain this?
"The pleasures of heaven have an end; the sufferings of the human world are inexhaustible. A hundred years are like a morning dream;
do not wait until you have awakened to find it empty."
This old man has been lodging in Mount Qingliang. One day, the practitioner Xuan said to me: "I have suffered from a fever for nearly three months.
During this time, my mother attended to my illness until she was utterly exhausted and distressed. In her resentment, she prayed, 'Why does this fellow not die soon?
At that moment, I realized that my mother's compassion far exceeds that of the Buddha. Hearing this, the old man could not help but feel deep sorrow for a long while.
He then said to Washerman Lang, "You understand what I have said; yet, even so, you have not reached the ultimate excellence.

The Buddha’s compassion for sentient beings is such that even the heavens covering above and the earth supporting below, or the void encompassing all existence, would find it difficult to serve as a metaphor for it—how much more so the case of parents who harbor affection?
Even when parents cause one extreme provocation and distress, resentment still arises within them; yet when sentient beings provoke the Tathāgata..."
Having passed through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, they still employ skillful means with such grace that they are never weary of protecting others with compassion;
they will not cease until one attains Buddhahood. Viewed from this perspective, how can the compassion of the Buddha and the compassion of a mother be compared? (Shown to the Chan practitioner Xuan).
On the third day of the second month of autumn in the *xinmao* year of the Wanli era, the old fellow Daguan was blown by the winds of karma to a place named Huayan Hermitage.
Before the hermitage flows a stream; behind the hermitage rises a green mountain. The green mountains and flowing waters chill the mark of the broad and long tongue.
At that time, the old fellow asked the Chan practitioner Xuan: "What is the name of this hermitage? He replied: "Huayan."
Yan’an, the old fellow calmly pressed him further: "I have heard that the Avataṃsaka Sūtra speaks of four dharma-realms:
first, the dharma-realm of principle; second, the dharma-realm of phenomena; third, the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena;
and fourth, the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena. Now, when the dharma-realm of principle manifests before one, where is the dharma-realm of phenomena?"
When the dharma-realm of principle manifests before one, where is the dharma-realm of phenomena?

When the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena manifests before one, where is the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena? If you claim that the dharma-realm of principle is identical to the dharma-realm of phenomena...

The phenomenal dharma-realm (*dharma-dhātu*) is itself the noumenal dharma-realm. This effectively subsumes the previous two levels of dharma-realms, resulting only in a dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomenon and noumenon (*shili wuai*).

If one were to claim that the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomenon and noumenon is itself the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai*), then it would mean that the Elder Śākyamuni merely opened up the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena to create something that has a name.
There is no real going away. Furthermore, among the four dharma-realms, the first three serve merely as precursors to the final one.

Therefore, even if you have thoroughly penetrated the first three dharma-realms, if you cannot pass through the fourth stage, you will inevitably encounter various obstacles whenever you meet with conditions or touch upon objects. These various obstacles are also not...
It does not descend from heaven, nor does it gush forth from the earth; it is neither bestowed by humans, nor is it obstructed by external objects.

The root of this illness lies simply in the fact that one has been unable to pass with a casual wave of the hand through the pivot of the Dharma-realm—the very point where all things are unimpeded. This is that pivotal point.
It is not only students of the present day who cannot penetrate this; long ago there was a presiding master (zhǔzǔ) whose learning was profound both within and without.
Regarding the Great Canon of teachings spoken by the Yellow-Faced Old Man (the Buddha), there was nothing he did not understand as clearly as pointing at his palm;

regarding Confucius, Laozi, and the hundred schools of thought, there was likewise nothing to which he had not attained the ultimate depth. He considered himself fully competent in both worldly and world-transcending matters. Furthermore, he possessed one particular...

I have long felt a burning indignation toward those who afflict the three schools of Tiantai, Xianshou, and Cien, as well as those outside the teachings who insult and disparage the Buddha-dharma, causing them to be as opposed as ice and charcoal.
I intended to compose a work to adjudicate between these three schools and establish a defensive wall for the inner scriptures.
Just then, a Chan practitioner asked me: "I have heard that the Master intends to adjudicate the three schools; I do not know whose lineage the Master belongs to."
The Disciple: "Our school is that of Xianshou. The Zen Practitioner: "As for Dushun, which patriarch of the Huayan school was he?
The Scholar: "He was the third patriarch. The Zen Practitioner: "This old man had a verse that says: 'An ox in Huaizhou eats the grain; a horse in Yizhou has a bloated belly.
The world seeks a physician, yet he applies moxibustion to the left shoulder of a pig. May I ask you, Master, what does this mean?"
"How do you understand this? The Master of the Seat (Zezhu) had a large tongue yet could not answer. The Chan practitioner said, "This is the very pivot of your own school;
if you cannot even penetrate it, how dare you attempt to arbitrate another school? Thereupon, the Master of the Seat resolved to leave and travel to various quarters for study.
Old Man Daguan now provides another commentary for the assembly here and now, so that everyone may—
You must certainly attain thorough penetration right now. Dafa Shi of Shuanglin was an emanation of Maitreya Bodhisattva;
he also had a verse that said: "Empty-handed, I hold a hoe; walking, I ride a water buffalo. A person passes over the bridge."

The bridge flows, but the water does not flow. If one were to say that the verses of Master Fu Da Shi are identical to those of the old man Du Shun, then Maitreya Bodhisattva would be the founding ancestor of Ci’en Monastery, and Du Shun would likewise be an emanation of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.
He was the third patriarch of the Huayan school. Now, the Cien school is the School of Characteristics (Lakṣaṇayāna), while the Huayan school is the School of Nature (Dharmatā).
Since nature and characteristics have traditionally been as incompatible as ice and fire, how can they be said to be the same? If one were to say they are different...

The School of Characteristics (Lakṣaṇayāna) is like the waves; the School of Nature (Dharmatāyāna) is like the water. Waves do not exist apart from water, and water does not manifest apart from waves.
How could there be any divergent explanations? Furthermore, Linji has the "Fourfold Critical Examination": first, taking away the person but not the environment;
second, taking away the environment but not the person; third, taking away both person and environment; and fourth, taking away neither person nor environment. You—
"Great assembly, tell me: are the Four Selective Judgments the same as or different from the Four Dharma Realms?

If you say they are the same, then even if you have thoroughly and repeatedly penetrated the four dharma realms of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, you will still fail to pass through the Four Selective Judgments of Linji."
This refers to "difference," which is the Buddha-mind transmitted by Linji. The four dharma-realms of the *Avataṃsaka* are the Buddha’s words that they expound.
How could the Buddha-mind and the Buddha’s words be mutually contradictory? This old man has never been able to tolerate entangling complications in his life;
today, however, for the sake of the assembly present here, I shall [explore] the four dharma-realms of the *Avataṃsaka* like a blind man feeling his way with his hands.
It is like an elephant that has been thoroughly exhausted; such is the state of this old woman. Nevertheless, Master Yongjia said: "Alas for the Dharma of the Final Age! Alas for this evil world!
Sentient beings have meager merit and are difficult to discipline. Hearing the teachings of the Tathāgata’s sudden school, they lament that they cannot destroy them so that not even a tile remains.
Alas! How can the compassionate heart of the Sage be described as merely covering the heavens and supporting the earth?
It is not merely that they are like a compassionate father or mother; rather, it is because sentient beings do not awaken to their own minds that they do not know the Buddha-mind.

Since they do not know the Buddha-mind, how can they know the Buddha’s words? It is only natural, then, that within the four dharma-realms they strike their heads and smash their brains, left blocked and right hindered;
the fault lies simply in their failure to clarify their own minds. But tell me, what is this "own mind"? [Huihai: "To harbor..."
A cow from the province eats the grain; a horse from Yizhou has a bloated belly. The whole world searches for a physician to apply moxibustion upon the left shoulder of a pig.
*Du!* Do not say this is a double case; if you have doubts, investigate it with painful intensity. (To Upāsaka Huan).

Now, as for kindness and benevolence versus humility and prudence; inclusiveness and vastness versus refinement and diligence; profound stillness versus luminosity; cruelty and harshness versus pride and arrogance;
narrow-minded haste versus procrastination; and frivolity versus ignorance and incompetence—these six qualities on one side and those six on the other:
are they truly one and the same thing? Or are they many distinct things? Alas! Good and evil are not fixed.
The coarse and the subtle are like illusions; only those who have fully realized their own minds are able to practice them skillfully and employ them well.

To such a person, even that which appears cruel is compassionate and benevolent. Conversely, for those who still harbor a sense of self and have not forgotten it, even that which appears compassionate and benevolent is actually cruel.
Viewed in this light, are compassion and benevolence and cruelty one and the same thing? Or are they two distinct things? It depends entirely upon the person.
It depends merely on whether one’s practice is coarse or subtle. Thus it is said: "One who skillfully cultivates the Way does not require the labor of a thousand days;
there is nothing in which they do not attain its subtlety. How could this not be believed? (Shown to Attendant Kai).
The Master asked Master Ben: "Ordinary people say that while the physical body (rūpakāya) is subject to decay, the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) is indestructible.
Tell me, is the Dharma-body present during a dream? Ben replied, "It is. The Master said, "Is the body in a dream the same as the body when awake? Ben replied, "They are the same."
[The Master] asked: "Does the body perish during the waking state? [The disciple] replied: "It perishes. [The Master] asked: "Does the body perish during the dream state?
[The disciple] replied: "It does not perish. [The Master] said: "If the body indeed perishes during the waking state, then the body during the dream state should likewise perish.

If the body does not perish during the dream state, then the body during the waking state should likewise not perish. If this is not so, then one cannot say they are the same. How then can you distinguish between them?"

The Master asked Master Ben, “If one were to write a single character and omit even one stroke, would it still constitute that character? Ben replied, “It would not. The Master asked, “Would it have meaning?
Ben said, “Since the character is not formed, how could there be meaning? The Master asked, “If all the strokes are complete, does it form the character?

Ben said, “It does. The Master asked, “Does it have meaning? Ben said, “It has meaning. The Master said, “Take the character for ‘body’ (shen), for instance; how many strokes does it have? Ben said, “Six.”

[The Master] drew a line and said, "The meaning lies in which stroke? [The student] had no words. After a short while, he stepped forward and said, "The meaning lies in the sixth stroke. The Master said, "Are the six strokes equal, or are the six strokes unequal?
It is by means of them being unequal that their meaning is formed. [The student] said, "They are equal. [The Master] asked, "Is it collectively equal or individually equal?

If they were collectively equal, then the meaning would reside entirely in the first stroke, and the remaining five would have no meaning. If they are individually equal, then each stroke possesses [the meaning]."
Meaning: If scattered, it is not accomplished. Fundamentally, there are no words [to express this] (these two sections both demonstrate the person of fundamental dhyāna).
Food, drink, and sexual intercourse are the great desires of humanity; therefore, one who can restrain these great desires may be spoken to regarding the path of unsurpassed awakening.
Indeed, the difficulty of restraining desire is greater than that of a venomous dragon or a fierce tiger. Thereupon, the Lord of Awakening turned his gaze and issued a mandate.
At that time, Ānanda asked: "After the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, what shall the fourfold assembly take as their teacher?
The Tathāgata commanded, saying: "After my parinirvāṇa, all my disciples shall take the Prātimokṣa as their Great Teacher."

If one can be thus, it is no different from my remaining in the world. Viewed from this perspective, since you have become a son of the Buddha through the Prātimokṣa, how could you dare not to revere and uphold it?
Lately, as the time since the Buddha’s passing has grown distant, it is not only in remote mountain fastnesses and coastal corners that the monastic community fails to follow the precepts;
even at famous mountains and sacred sites, they do not know what the Prātimokṣa actually is.
Dong. Alas! When the self-mind is pure, the root of precepts is pristine. When the self-mind is empty and still, the water of concentration is fundamentally clear.
When the self-mind is luminous and penetrating, the light of wisdom is perfect and complete. Yet, in a single moment of negligence, one forcibly subjects oneself to delusive illumination;

what was originally endowed as precept, concentration, and wisdom becomes, through delusion, greed, anger, and ignorance. From birth to death, and from death to birth, [one continues this cycle]. Death...

Death leads to birth; one is entangled in the net of karma, rising and sinking without constancy. Whether manifesting as scales and shells or feathers and fur, or wearing celestial crowns or human robes, the myriad varieties of suffering and joy are all termed "ignorance" (*avidyā*).
Thus it is said: "By following along with ignorance, one falls into the various realms of existence (*bhava*). If one does not follow along, the various realms of existence are severed.

If this is so, then ignorance and wisdom are like the bending and extending of a single finger. I— (Note: The final character "予" (I) appears to be a fragment of a signature or personal note appended to the text.)
All deprivation arises from one's own mind; why rely on the power of others? It depends entirely on whether that person is willing or not.

If they truly become willing to resolve their mind, then even the most foolish person will know what to drink when thirsty, what to eat when hungry, and a man will know a woman while a woman will know a man.
Once the willing mind is established, one shall immediately use this very knowledge to know that the body does not exist, and to know the mind.
It is merely a name. When body and mind are liberated, then the myriad differences of favorable and adverse conditions and circumstances are all the manifestation of the light of my own mind.
At such a stage, even wisdom has no place to lodge, let alone ignorance. By this I know that among people there is neither the foolish nor the wise;
it depends only on whether one gives rise to the aspiration [for enlightenment] or not. Therefore, for a person of wisdom...
If the sincere resolve has not yet arisen, one is no different from oxen or horses. As for the assembly present here and the deeds of the past, let us leave them aside for now.
Since the drawing of lots has already taken place, we must resolutely abide by the Buddha’s injunctions. We must strictly prohibit women from entering the monastery.
Once women do not enter the monastery, the fragrance of virtue will naturally become pure and far-reaching, the springs and rocks will radiate light, and the deceased—

Those who are born shall attain birth in a favorable realm; those born together shall all obtain auspicious signs. Should you even slightly violate the Buddha’s command, the deceased will fall further into ruin and the living will meet with extinction.
The great assembly present here must each clearly distinguish between good and evil. You must take the *Prātimokṣa* as your Great Teacher;
do not be negligent, lest you bring yourself future suffering. (Addressed to the monastic community of Mount Jue Temple.)
The Chan Master Wenli, known as Mingtong Mie’eng of Siming, went to Jingci Temple to study under Huyen but did not find resonance there.
He then visited Chan Master Foguo Guang of Yuyang. Guang asked, "For one who comes like this, who is your true host? The Master suddenly attained realization of the meaning.
On another day, Guang again asked about the monk who said, "It is the wind moving; it is the banner moving. The Master replied: [He was right.]
[Zhaozhou] said, "When an object meets its master, the eyes stand out straight. He asked again, "It is neither the wind moving nor the banner moving;
where do you see the Patriarch? The Master [Zhaozhou] said, "Lift off the skull-cap! Zhaoxi was delighted by his brilliance and loftiness.

Later, when Songyuan was propagating the Way at Jianfu Temple in Rao, he questioned a monk in his room, "It is neither the wind moving nor the banner moving. As the monk hesitated, Songyuan struck him with his staff and drove him out.

Upon hearing this, the Master [Zhaozhou] immediately forgot his previous understanding and went to visit him. He received the seal of approval. The Master ascended the hall and, citing the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, said:

"All things that can be returned belong naturally to others; that which cannot be returned—since it is not you, who else could it be? He then offered this verse: "That which cannot be returned—who else could it be?
Fading red petals remain upon the fishing pier. The sun sets and the wind dies down; no one is there to sweep them up."
The swallow carries it off, flying toward the water’s edge. Alas! Behold this old man, the Extinction-Master: at the age of six, he already knew that such a thing existed.

He saw its manifestation in Fozhao; he realized its essence in Songyuan. When he appeared in the world as a teacher, with every single movement and situation, every fragmentary word and phrase, his mastery over life and death was absolute;
both demons and Buddhas were struck with terror. It was like the General of Huaiyin leading his armies forth.

When Huo Guang presided over the court, his regulations and legal codes were so precise that one could close the door and build a carriage, only to find its tracks perfectly aligned upon opening it. Thus it is said:
"If you study, you must study in reality; if you awaken, you must awaken in reality; if you act, you must act in reality.
Since you three have all severed worldly ties and travel together with one mind, although I, an old man, am not quick-witted, I shall offer you a few plain words for your journey ahead.
Even when holding a staff, one must know good from evil before it can be used.

If the first phrase is severed completely, the second phrase is realized thoroughly, and the third phrase is passed through as appropriate, then if you can penetrate the first phrase, not only will you be able to serve as a teacher to the Buddhas and Patriarchs, but it will also not be difficult to see the true face of Old Man Xie. Second.
If you can realize it through the third phrase, you may take it for granted that you will experience great happiness in both the heavens and the human world.

Furthermore, if you can realize it through the third phrase, it would be just as well to simply face the present moment and pass your days according to conditions; why must you travel ten thousand miles across the waters and clouds?
The pursuit was exceedingly exhausting. Nevertheless, as the ancient masters have said: "If you possess your own staff, I give it back to you;
if you lack your own staff, I take it away from you. But tell me, why is it so?
*Pah!* "Leaving my abode at Miaode, you depart from me; for whom do these two rows of hot tears flow?"
These three are the karmic conditions; they are all the temporary shelters (*jūru*) used by the ancients when they had fully realized the Great Matter.
Nevertheless, while traveling on the path, if a sudden gale and torrential rain were to arrive, they could still serve as a makeshift shelter to avoid having one's head and face drenched.
Since you three have completely mastered the first phrase, [you may proceed].
Then, practices such as mindfulness of the Buddha, the recitation of mantras, and the chanting of sutras all belong to the second phrase [of the verse].
If you do not understand this, how can you ever reach a definitive conclusion? I ask you: as you wander aimlessly on your pilgrimage, what exactly do you take as your staff of reliance?
It is like a woodcutter entering the mountains without an axe, or a fisherman entering the sea without a net—what will you do?
Carrying firewood, what do you use to catch fish? You fellows are as ignorant as black-clad barbarians; you go on like this without ever realizing it yourselves—truly laughable and pitiable.
Out of compassion for your foolishness and negligence, I, an old man, have specially had the Head of the House take three instances of karmic conditions and transmit them to you.
They shall serve as a staff of mastery for you on the road ahead; you must know them well.
Regarding likes and dislikes: it is like sandalwood that does not know its own fragrance, or dog dung that does not know its own stench;

failing to recognize patience in adverse conditions, failing to recognize weary detachment in favorable conditions, failing to recognize that loyal words are for one's benefit, and failing to recognize that flattery is harmful to oneself—walking the path of practice in such a manner, even if one travels until one’s hair is white and one dies of old age, what benefit could there possibly be? Viewed from this perspective...
It would be better not to go out the gate at all. Nevertheless, a man of spirit naturally possesses aspirations that soar to the heavens;
how could he be content to fall among the ranks of the mediocre? Ultimately, if one does not penetrate these three karmic conditions, life is no better than death.
The workings of the mind are without constancy; as for the arising of sages and ordinary beings, everything depends upon what one relies upon.
If one relies upon purity, then persons and dharmas are seen to be like dreams and empty; the sense organs and their objects are utterly detached, and one's own mind becomes whole and luminous.

Were it otherwise, the three miserable realms would open up before one, all phenomena would sink into delusion, and myriad sufferings would entwine one another, binding one for eternity. How can a man who possesses this numinous spirit not be cautious? Herein lies [the work of] Lu...

Life is difficult to purify when defiled by habitual afflictions. Relying on the path of victory, he reverently prostrated within the light of the Triple Gem. Piercing his finger, he drew blood to transcribe the text of the precepts;
this may be called governing oneself with rigor and being prudent regarding that upon which one relies.

Intending to lead others from the mundane to the sacred and to extensively deliver all sentient beings—this is the blood-covenant vow of a man of the Way, which Lu Sheng (Shi Lu Jigao) shall never forget.
I have heard the words of the ancient sage, the Great Sovereign: "In general, when things are burdened by attachments, their power is diminished.
It is as if the eye is burdened by forms, the ear by sounds, the nose by fragrances, the tongue by flavors, the body by tactile sensations, and the mind by mental objects.
When the six sense-objects (ṣaḍviṣaya) enclose and obscure them, the light of the single mind is shrouded. Thus, the great earth is composed of these four gross elements."
Thus, it can support sentient beings. That which is composed of three elements of the great water can support the great earth;
that which is composed of two elements of the great fire can support the great water; and that which is composed of one element of the great wind can support the great fire.
Viewed from this perspective, even a single atom cannot be established as independent, yet its power is inconceivably great. We humans are shrouded by six layers of ignorance.

Dust clouds [the mind], yet one remains unaware and unawakened; from time immemorial it has been like a long night. Though one inherently possesses the power of wisdom, one does not know how to employ it—is this not truly painful?
(Shown to Chan practitioner Chuguang).
Now, the Dao-heart is solely subtle; the human heart is solely precarious. When subtlety rides upon precariousness, precariousness topples subtlety.
If one lacks the will to sustain it, then that which is subtle may well never be restored. Nevertheless, is subtlety not indeed precarious?
Is precariousness not indeed subtle? Subtle yet precarious! Precarious yet subtle! Suppose there were a person here who truly possesses the will for the Dao.

Within the realm of virtue, achievement, and fame, one cannot honor that which is called "subtle. Not only will one fail to attain what they desire, but there will be nothing to which they do not fall short.

Alas! Among the myriad species of beings, only man is most spiritually gifted; yet if one cannot value this [the human spirit] while valuing that [external things], one is no true gentleman (mianmada zhi).

Now, fire does not spread without oil, and oil does not blaze without fuel. Some take fire to represent the spirit (*shen*), oil to represent the essence (*jing*), and fuel to represent the physical form (*xing*).
Thus, when the essence is exhausted and the form decays, the spirit does not remain. If this is so, fire is never absent;
yet without oil and fuel, its characteristics cannot be manifested. Therefore it is said: "The characteristic of fire is the skin of fire."
It is merely a matter of the skin. As for what is called "nature-fire," how could it be exhausted by what is heard or seen through the ears and eyes?
It simply requires that one value it and clarify it through the spirit.
The ancients would wear coarse clothing and eat poor food, calling this being able to find sweetness in simplicity and detachment.
Generally speaking, "coarse clothing" does not exceed garments made of birch bark or hemp; "poor food" does not exceed dregs and husks.

Although I lack virtue, in summer I take pleasure in wearing birch bark, and in winter I enjoy donning cloth robes. As for food, I consume dregs, husks, vegetable roots, and bean sprouts—there is nothing [I do not accept].
I am not satisfied. As for fasting, whether for one day, two days, or three days, I have practiced it until it became habitual, almost without giving it a second thought.
Alas! Although I have acted thus, I do not know if those who dwell in this Joyful and Auspicious Monastery in the future will truly be able to fulfill my aspirations.
If they can, then the monastic groves will naturally flourish and the phoenixes and peacocks will naturally flock and settle there. The Dharma...
The Way naturally flourishes; the mountain gate naturally becomes free of affairs. Alas! The green mountains and flowing waters can delight the ears and eyes;
the palm-leaf scriptures and butter lamps can clarify the body and mind.

That neither the Son of Heaven may enslave one as a subject nor the feudal lords may treat one as a friend—that even a single commoner should be able to attain this state is entirely due to the radiance of the Buddha’s light. It may be so.
Do you not value yourselves? (To the assembly of Xixifu Temple).
Since the Buddha-dharma came from the East, the world has known only that there is a Buddha, followed by the Dharma, and only after the Dharma is there the Sangha.
Yet they fail to realize that there are the Buddhas of the past, the Buddhas of the present, and the Buddhas of the future, as well as the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
The sutras all take the Sangha as their fundamental source. Thus it is said: "The Sangha is that from which the Buddha and the Dharma emerge.

If the source is not pure, then the Buddha and the Dharma may as well not exist. Now, the source of the Sangha is further based upon the two types of precepts: the natural precepts (*dharmatā-śīla*) and the circumstantial precepts (*prajñapti-śīla*). As for the natural precepts:
to penetrate and clarify one's own nature (*svabhāva*), reaching a definitive understanding free from doubt—this is what is called the natural precept. Regarding the circumstantial [precepts]...
Regarding the precepts: initially, there are the five fundamental precepts; in the middle, there are the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera;

and finally, there are the two hundred and fifty precepts of a bhikṣu. As for the five precepts: they are not killing, not stealing, not engaging in sexual misconduct, not speaking falsely, and not drinking intoxicants. As for the ten precepts:
following the five precepts, one further adds not anointing the body with fragrant oils, not sitting on high or wide beds, and not intentionally going [to see entertainments].
Listening to music; not grasping gold, silver, raw or wrought precious objects, and so forth; and not eating past midday—these two hundred and fifty precepts cannot be described here at length.

These are called the precepts of ritual conduct (*śīla*). Lately, as the ways of the world have declined, those who act as monks are utterly ignorant of these precepts of ritual conduct, let alone the hope that they might thoroughly understand the precepts of intrinsic nature (*dharmatā-śīla*). At Shijing Mountain in Zhuozhou, for Heaven...

Descending to the Sea of Dharma: Since the time of the Sui dynasty’s Master Wan, the "dragons and elephants" [great masters] have trodden the path, propagating the teachings and traditions without fail from generation to generation.
Yet by our Ming dynasty, the Pearl Forest had been reduced to overgrown weeds, and its golden and azure halls had turned to mud and mire. If one investigates the root cause of this ailment:
It is simply because our nature lacks clarity regarding the precepts of character and we fail to maintain the precepts of conduct.
This old man truly has a profound karmic affinity with this mountain; moved by the contrast between past and present, I could not bear to sit idly by.

Thereupon, I instructed the various donors to redeem the pagoda and temple grounds of Master Wan, and further to redeem more than two hundred bone-pagodas of eminent monks dating back to the Sui dynasty. Having done so, I reflected once more upon my karma.
Having already lost it and returned to it, yet having returned, there is nothing to be maintained; it would be better not to have returned at all.

Thereupon, the abbots of the two monasteries, Dongyunju and Xiyunju, together with the administrative monks and others, struck the great bell and beat the Dharma drum to announce to the Buddhas of the ten directions, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, all the worthy and holy Saṃghas, the Venerable Dashi, and the Venerable Master Wan.

All you guardians of the Dharma, spirits of intelligence, and guardian deities of this monastery, have been granted the *Dharmapada* verses of Vipaśyin Buddha, which open the fundamental source of the precepts of nature (*dharmatā-śīla*).
Next, the fundamental five precepts have been proclaimed to you, which cultivate the foundation for the precepts of phenomena (*saṃvṛti-śīla*).
From this day forward, each of you should repent of past transgressions, reform your ways, and cultivate yourselves for the future. At [this time],...
The verse of Vipaśyin Buddha can first be read; once read, it can be recited; once recited, there is no distinction between leisure and haste.

If one’s innate precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*) become daily more luminous, and one can strenuously uphold the five fundamental precepts without transgression for a thousand days, then they may be maintained for the remainder of one’s life.
Alas! I look up to the compassionate majesty of the Buddha and the great spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), who have compassionately and exhaustively uplifted me.
The precepts of nature and the precepts of practice are like the two wheels of a chariot or the two wings of a bird.

If you cherish and preserve them without loss, what difficulty could there be in traveling far or soaring through the air? Alas! An eighty-year-old has come onto the stage; this is by no means a child’s play.
You must also know the difference between good and evil, so that the Buddha’s source may wither and then flourish again, and run dry and then overflow once more.
The crux lies precisely here (addressing the monastic community of Dongxi Yunju Monastery).

If you wish to travel elsewhere, it is truly a commendable endeavor. Look back to the ancients: among those who achieved great potential in their time, there was not a single one who did not emerge from the practice of traveling on pilgrimage (*xingjiao*).
If one does not roam extensively at the gates of spiritual mentors (*zhishishi*) and undergo refinement through the crucible of experience, [one cannot attain realization].
Under the hammer, it is impossible for one to produce a vessel [if one does not act].

Nevertheless, it is not necessarily that one must always act and never abide, nor is it necessarily that one must always abide and never act. One should simply act when it is time to act, and abide when it is time to abide.

As for those times when one ought to act—whether it be after a full meal or while dwelling in leisure—to remain inactive and abide while indulging the passions and following one's desires; would this be permissible? When it is time to...
As for "abiding": if you encounter a master of piercing skill or a true spiritual friend, would it be appropriate not to abide but instead to practice?
According to what you perceive, you consider worldly conditions to be distracting and incompatible with the Buddha-dharma, and thus intend to abandon them to seek elsewhere.
Little do they realize that both Buddhist Dharma and worldly conditions are merely secondary matters; in relation to one's own fundamental nature, they are entirely irrelevant.
It would be better to turn back and look within amidst the turmoil to see what it ultimately is.
One must not rely on worldly conditions as support, nor should one interpret them through the lens of the Buddha-dharma. After a long time, when one suddenly attains self-awakening, then its—

One’s skill will improve twofold. Even if one wishes to travel on foot, seeking the mind without ceasing, yet thoughts remain in disarray—thinking today of a certain prefecture and tomorrow of a certain county, rushing south and running north, eyes gazing and heart racing until one reaches old age—it will ultimately yield no accomplishment.
One must simply press down the clouds upon the head, cast away life and limb, traverse hardships and perils, and let the skin of the face grow anew.
It is forged from iron. Meeting with music and encountering joy, the mind and will are as if forged from pure steel.
