When the mind does not reach the境 (object) and the object does not reach the mind, then there is a slight measure of the life of a wandering monk (addressed to Attendant Cihang Yun).
Now, when profit is weighed against fame, fame is more exalted than profit; when fame is weighed against the body, the body is closer than fame;
when the body is weighed against the mind, the mind is more intimate than the body; and when the mind is weighed against nature (*xing*), nature is the fundamental source of all those various things.
Hence it is said: "To exhaust principle and fully realize nature. Alas! If nature could be exhausted, then what indeed would that thing be which one desires to exhaust? Its...
As for desire, what indeed is its fruit? It is like a diamond rubbing the back of a clay figure;
the sensation of pain and itch is most extraordinary, yet no one perceives it. This is truly a matter of regret for the earth. (Shown to Lu Jigao)

Now, the fact that "black and yellow" (the phenomenal world) are without fault means that fault arises from emotion (*qing*). If emotion does not arise, then everything encountered by the eyes is the Way (*Dao*).
Therefore, when there is principle (*li*) but no emotion, the Sage empties it; when there is emotion but no principle, the multitude is deluded by it. An ancient worthy said:
"When the one mind does not arise, the myriad things are without fault. He also said: "The self-mind grasps the self-mind; what is not illusory becomes an illusory dharma. Because of this...
Viewed in this light, those who have attained the mind find that all myriad differences are as such; whereas those who adhere to objective realms find even the single reality to be turbulent. Alas!
The myriad phenomena of the universe are the seal of a single dharma. Now, as for this so-called single dharma, does it exist inherently within the mind?
Does the fruit exist apart from the mind? Does the fruit exist as neither identical to nor apart from the mind?

If a student can here examine this with earnest scrutiny and, through long-term contemplation, suddenly experience the mind opening wide, then being apart is suchness, being identical is suchness, and being neither identical nor apart is suchness.
If it is so, there is nowhere that is not suchness. How could it ever be exhausted by the myriad things?
Ah! Wanyu, you must earnestly uphold the pearl of the precepts, lest it be buried and lost amidst the filth of the five colors.
Exert yourself, exert yourself! (To the Zen practitioner Wanyu).
Now, that which is called "mind" (*citta*) refers to the state before emotions have undergone change; that which precedes the mind is called "nature" (*prakṛti*).

The essence of nature inherently possesses the two virtues of clarity and stillness. Because the essence of nature has no external boundaries, it cannot achieve self-awareness on its own; therefore, forced illumination arises.
Once forced illumination arises, the virtues of clarity and stillness transform into turbidity and movement. When turbidity and movement have emerged, the myriad phenomena (*dharmas*) arise. And...

Its transformations are inexhaustible; therefore, it is called that which lacks cognition and perception. This is termed the "dependent retribution" (*niśraya-vipāka*) and the "receptacle world" (*bhājana-loka*).
That which possesses cognition and perception is termed the "primary retribution" (*mūla-vipāka*) and "sentient beings. This proceeds from the root to the branches.

It is also called "flowing with the current," meaning that the faculties flow outward toward external objects and become ensnared within the realms of the senses. Once the faculties and objects are fully present, they await the striking [of consciousness].

However, this seems difficult to understand. It is likely because one is obscured by dullness and agitation; "agitation" refers to scattering. Therefore, it is further termed "dullness and scattering.

Alas! What, indeed, are dullness and scattering? They cast me into the vast expanse of birth and death, where I have been tossed about through long kalpas, enduring the ultimate limits of suffering, yet remain unable to cast them off or dissolve them. This causes my present, daily activities—...
It is as if one were beneath a covered basin or tossed amidst a whirling gale, such that there is not a single moment of clarity or stillness.

This is neither the fault of Heaven and Earth, nor is it a malevolent influence from ghosts or spirits. Upon investigating the reason, it must be that what should be bright in me has instead become dark, and what should be still has instead become turbulent.
Man is called the most spiritual of all things, yet the power over this turbidity and dissipation lies elsewhere, not within oneself.
Thus, that which is selfless yet spiritual becomes buried and neglected; its original luminosity fails to manifest, and its original stillness fails to abide.

All of this is governed by dullness and distraction. For one who aspires to gather in the dissipated mind, if they cannot govern dullness and distraction but instead allow themselves to be governed by them, then the work of gathering will ultimately be difficult to accomplish. Therefore it is said: "If you wish to gather in the dissipated mind, first investigate..."
The reason why dullness and distraction arise is thus clarified. Once the reason for their arising is clear, it becomes evident that the power over dullness and distraction lies here and not there.

Yet, the reason for their arising is not easily understood; if one can understand it, then by means of the emotions one returns to the mind, and by means of the mind one returns to the nature—seeing it as clearly as the grain of wood in the palm of one’s hand or the reflection in a mirror.

Eyebrows and eyes. From this point on, one rides upon the nature to govern the emotions. It is like escorting the Son of Heaven to command the feudal lords; who would dare resist his orders? Therefore it is said:
"To follow one's nature and govern the emotions—this cannot be done by one who has not seen their nature. Again it is said: "Hearing the Way is easy; clarifying the Way is difficult. And again:
"When the Great Matter is not yet clarified, it is as if one had lost one’s parents; when the Great Matter is already clarified, it is as if one had lost one’s parents. Truly.
This is a maxim for all ages. Unless one is insane or deranged, who would not believe and enter into it? If one acts according to this, one’s efforts will not be in vain;

in the end, one returns to that which is "attained through non-attainment. Thus, what are called dullness and distraction are designated as concentration and wisdom, rather than being called clarity and stillness.

This is because the Sage wished that people would not forget the work of restoring their original nature. This is called "flowing against the current," for it indeed flows against the [natural] tendency toward non-existence.
Illuminating the flow [of consciousness], one enters the ocean of the *dharmatā*. Thus it is said: "By following along with ignorance, all states of existence (*bhava*) arise;

if one does not follow along, all states of existence are abandoned. This principle is so manifest that even a person of the utmost dullness would surely understand it clearly if shown the general outline of its contraries and correspondences, let alone a wise person.
Furthermore, if one frequently feels drowsy and sleepy after eating and drinking, this must be severed.
One must not indulge the mind. One must certainly treat it with the antidote of dispersive movement; then it will become clear. Once it has become clear, one may even sleep deeply.
The method for treating distraction is the same. This is because in the daily lives of sentient beings, when they are not dull they are distracted, and when they are not distracted they are dull.
Alternating between dullness and distraction, and distraction and dullness, they have exhausted themselves in this manner since beginningless time.

Furthermore, all illnesses arise from dullness and distraction; therefore, one who skillfully treats dullness and distraction finds that a hundred ailments are lightened and diminished, and they do not easily grow old.
To investigate the reason for this: it is simply a matter of exercising mastery over dullness and distraction so that they do not belong to them, but rather belong to oneself.
When one desires to wake, one wakes and cannot be made dull; when one desires to sleep, one sleeps and cannot be made distracted. Only then—
Test this before and after eating and drinking; ultimately, clarity will not be found in that which is immediately clouded or scattered.

Through *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight), one remedies clouding and scattering. When clouding and scattering return to their source, the so-called virtue of luminous stillness arrives without being summoned.
If you ask about the nature of the essence, I shall speak of it to you again only after you have forged your clouding and scattering into meditative concentration and wisdom.
It is not too late (shown to Lu Jigao). The dragon is the sovereign among scaly creatures;

it likewise possesses its own hierarchy of ruler and minister, as well as male and female. Even amidst the depths of the clouds and the density of the mountain crags, [it maintains these distinctions].

They appear and disappear, coming and going; for the most part, they are impermanent. Therefore, while we dwell here, in all our daily activities—whether sitting or rising, defecating or urinating, or even in the impure words spoken by those who are naked—we ought to exercise caution in every instance. By doing so, we shall protect and sustain our faith.
This is the natural law; it must surely not deviate from it. To act contrary to this, and yet be able to dwell long without demonic hindrances—such a thing has never occurred.
Alas! To reside here in such a secluded and sublime place and receive these pure blessings is truly like spending a mere moment that equals a hundred years.
"Should one not be self-reverent rather than self-important? (To the Dharma companions at Tanzhe). "Recently, human lives were implicated;
today, the śarīra is present before the assembly. Tell me, who has the merit and who the guilt? Dao Kai remained silent and contemplative.
The Master rebuked him, saying: "Darkness Maiden! Goddess of Merit! Use them well, and your blessings will be boundless. (At Xiyunju, to Dao Kai).
The wind stirs the myriad things; springs flow within the earth. When trees move, one knows there is wind; when things are moistened, one knows there is water.
Why must one wait for the eyes to see the wind and the springs before knowing them? The luminosity inherent in the human mind originally has no interior or exterior;
it does not belong to birth and extinction, and it is spiritual without a self. The eye relies upon it to perceive forms, and the ear depends upon it to [perceive sounds].
The ear hears sounds; the nose relies upon it to discern fragrance and stench; the tongue borrows from it so that flavors are not obscure;
and the two faculties of body and mind depend upon it for there to be sensation and cognition. Jishi said:
"Each and every one of you possesses a True Person of No Rank at the gateway of the six sense organs, emitting a great radiance that illuminates heaven and earth, yet none of you recognize it."

"Yet you grasp at me to seek the truth; how deluded you are! Changsha said: "Those who study the Way do not recognize the Real, simply because they have long been identifying with the conscious spirit.
On the lineage of Linji, it is held that that which is vividly manifest and spiritually lucid at the gateway of the six sense organs is itself Buddha-nature;
there is no need to seek it elsewhere. Changsha further [taught] that which is vividly manifest and spiritually lucid at the gateway of the six sense organs...
The "consciousness-spirit" (shishen) is pointed out as such; Buddha-nature is without self yet numinous, whereas the consciousness-spirit possesses a self and is obscure.
Master Ji was an ancient dragon in the ocean of Dharma and a master-carpenter of the Chan school—could he not have distinguished between Buddha-nature and the consciousness-spirit?
Changsha and Yangshan feared his sharp and formidable faculty, calling him "Tiger Cen"—could they also not have distinguished between the consciousness-spirit and the Buddha?

Is it the nature? These two points constitute a double barrier. Since the time of the Sage has long passed, people—regardless of whether they are wise or ignorant—do not even know the difference between black and white or beans and wheat.
They constantly mistake the conscious spirit for Buddha-nature, and denigrate Buddha-nature as the conscious spirit.

Claiming that "this is it and that is not" or "that is it and this is not," they style themselves great spiritual teachers (*mahākalyāṇamitra*). If they cannot yet distinguish between Buddha-nature and the conscious spirit, how much less can they [discern the ultimate truth]?
"A dwarf and a blind rooster! Even the ten thousand Buddhas do not recognize good from evil. He speaks at random and without restraint, caring neither for whether people like it or dislike it;
he only wishes for the fundamental principles (*gangzong*) to be clear so as to open the eyes of gods and men—even if it costs him his life.
Yantou said: 'Simply understand the fundamental principles; originally there is no substantial dharma. This is the talon and fang of Master Huo’s Dharma cave."

Furthermore, one does not rely on the Buddha-nature or the conscious spirit (*vijñāna*) for awakening; rather, one takes the fundamental tenets (*jǐngzōng*) as one’s own responsibility. Students should reflect upon this.
For when the fundamental tenets are thoroughly understood, demons and heretics are naturally restrained without the need for laborious fortifications; thus, the ancestral temple is secure of itself.

What is called "the true Dharma" refers to the exposition of principle, the exposition of phenomena, the unimpeded interpenetration of phenomena and principle, the unimpeded interpenetration of phenomena and phenomena, and the exposition of...
The Patriarch came from the East. He rejected forms and obliterated the mind; he pointed directly at the human mind, so that by seeing one's nature, one becomes a Buddha.

Whether he expounded the Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of the scriptures, or spoke of the seventeen hundred recorded机缘 (ji-yuan), all were the actual Dharma. Therefore it is said: "The entire Great Canon of Teachings."
This is the paper used to wipe a sore or tumor. These one thousand seven hundred cases of karmic conditions are a tangled skein of vines.
Nevertheless, if the fundamental principle (*jǐngzōng*) is clearly understood, then all those various phenomena are the inherent radiance of one's own nature.

Why is this? Because there is no phenomenon outside of the mind. An ancient worthy said: "When the mind is luminous, one first perceives the light of nature. Viewed from this perspective, when seeing forms, one [perceives them as such].

The eye is for seeing forms; when it comes to perceiving the nature, one takes the mind as the eye. When the mind perceives the nature, it is like wind wandering through the great void, or like a spring moistening the vast earth.
To say that there is a subject and an object is incorrect; to say that there is no subject and no object is also incorrect.
Why is this? It is because wind and the great void cannot be grasped or touched; moisture and earth cannot be distinguished or separated.
Yet, it is not that wind and the great void do not exist, nor is it that springs and earth do not exist.

Since Shiguang has already resolved his mind to seek unsurpassed bodhi, if the established principles are not clear, he will be deceived by the teachings when studying the scriptures, and he will be deceived by the ancestral school when investigating the lineage.
The teachings and the sects are both supramundane, pure dharmas; yet they were all unable to deceive Shiguang.
How much less could food and drink, men and women, sounds and colors, wealth and profit—the myriad wonders and strange phenomena within the arena of honor and disgrace—fail to deceive Shiguang?
Now tell me, what is the fundamental principle (綱宗)? It is that which Linji, Yunmen, Moshan, Fayan, Dongshan, Miyin, and all the masters of the various quarters transmit to their disciples.
The fundamental principle is like a general’s military tally; when the tally is held in one’s grasp, the more troops one has, the better.
But if the tally is dropped from the hand, not a single soldier will obey orders. Therefore, once the fundamental principle is clarified—

The Buddhas and Patriarchs may either give birth to or destroy [beings], for the pivot of their spiritual capacity lies within themselves; how much more so for humans, devas, māras, and those outside the teachings?
If one does not clarify the fundamental principles of the doctrinal schools (*kyōka*), then both principle (*ri*) and phenomena (*ji*) will fail to achieve samādhi;

thus, all words, phrases, and various doctrines are termed "ignorance regarding what is known" (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*). If one does not clarify the fundamental principles of the Chan school (*zenka*), then one cannot wield the tongs [of liberation].
Strike the student and kill their thieving mind. If the thieving mind is not killed, the ancients called it "the stinking falcon’s cloth robe.

You must know that the wisdom of the *dhāraṇī* of revolving [all phenomena] of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is not something for those of shallow knowledge, dull wits, or commoners to devote their attention to;
only those with the great mind can bear its responsibility. This *dhāraṇī* of revolving is precisely the fundamental principle of the school's teaching.
It is called "ear. From the very beginning, light shines forth. If one does not know the *svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī* (the revolving dhāraṇī), then the mind is not clear and is plundered by emotions.
How can one, in such a state, perceive the nature with the eyes? This nature is not difficult to see; the difficulty lies in being unable to respect oneself.
If one can respect oneself, then in all actions one will naturally not dare to be negligent. Although people of both high and low station have recently been called "discussants," [they remain so].

Among those who practice Chan and lecture on the Way, none are able to contemplate with profound depth or long-term foresight; they all generally act with mere expediency, seeking only a verbal liberation and nothing more.
Consequently, regarding the distinction between the conscious spirit (*vijñāna*) and Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), out of ten people, nine fail to discern them.

Since they cannot distinguish between the conscious spirit and Buddha-nature, how could they possibly understand the teachings concerning "following one's nature" versus "following one's emotions"? They simply cannot.
It is clear: if one follows one's nature, there is nothing that is not wondrous; if one follows one's emotions, there is nothing that is not coarse.
Why is this? Because following one's nature means that in every instance there is no "self," for it is the spiritual essence that employs all affairs.

Following one's emotions means that in every instance there is a "self," for it is the deluded consciousness that employs all affairs. Furthermore, if one has not yet seen one's nature while following it, how can one truly follow it?
It is like a person who, being thirsty, cannot see water; what water could they possibly drink? Only after one has seen their nature can they follow that nature.

Once they can follow their nature, then all seeds of defiled habits and their active manifestations from time immemorial—regardless of whether conditions are favorable or adverse—will naturally and spontaneously dissolve.
Therefore it is said: "For one who sees their nature, habitual tendencies are extinguished without being extinguished; they are not cultivated."

The ancient masters said: "If you recognize the master’s staff, I shall give you the master’s staff; you may then at will pick out the clouds and hang from the moon, parting the weeds and observing the wind.
If you do not recognize the master’s staff, I shall seize it from you, forcing you to lean on your fence and grope along the wall.
This is the very model for following one's nature and following one's emotions; it is also [the core] within the essential tenets (*jōsō*).
Regarding "attaining that which cannot be scrutinized": if one fails to scrutinize, then one will not distinguish between Buddha and Mara.

Furthermore, if one does not obscure their inherent nature, they will initially attain the utilization of their original radiance. Attaining the utilization of this original radiance is called "mystery" (*mi*).
By means of this mystery, being able to scrutinize and guard against demons and externalists is called the "seal" (*yin*). Caoxi [Huineng], because of Hui-ming’s question, said: "This..."
"Is there a hidden meaning (samdhāya) beyond this? Caoqi replied, "The secret is right with you. If Shiguang had asked about the ten thousand Buddhas, Wanshou would have said:
"Xuefeng breaking the sand pot is the hidden meaning; Linji’s dried-up dung-club is the hidden meaning; Xuefeng’s rolling ball is the hidden meaning;
Caoshan’s wooden snake is the hidden meaning; and Miaoyan of Mount Huangbo..."
"The water buffalo" is an intentional phrase (*samdhāya-bhāṣita*). Master Danchang’s "falling into the character" is an intentional phrase.
As for "Shiguang," if one claims that such expressions as "breaking a sand pot" are words devoid of meaning, this reflects the views of demons and heretics in recent times.
If one claims there is a separate path of meaning, tell me: what, after all, constitutes that path of meaning? If you cannot penetrate through this...
When [the wind] has departed, the tree moves yet one does not perceive the wind; the earth is moist yet one does not perceive the spring. This can be understood.

Wind and spring are metaphors for the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*); movement and moisture are metaphors for the consciousness-spirit (*vijñāna*). A metaphor is merely a small representation of an object.

If you can contemplate the elephant and grasp its essence, then as for the consciousness-spirit and the Buddha-nature, let them be left to whatever names or titles are assigned. Thus it is fully realized.
There is no fault. If the mind-as-it-is has not yet been attained, then the phrase will not be alive. If the phrase is not alive, one cannot wash the light of the Buddha-sun.
Now tell me, where does the Buddha-sun hang? *Pah!* To remove the overturned basin and seek illumination with a candle—to cut off one’s head and seek to live is sheer stupidity.
(This indicates the initial light.)

Read by Hanshan Deqing of the Ming Dynasty.

The Dharma discourse states that, fundamentally, it is from non-action that affairs arise; this is brought about by meager merit and proceeds from meager merit. Because one lacks clarity regarding *prajñā*, they are called "fools.
Such fools invite the retribution of the animal realm. Animals are not far removed from the hungry ghosts (*preta*), and hungry ghosts are not far removed from [the hell realms].
Hell is not far away; this is descending from the heights. If one ascends from the depths to the heights, one rises from hell to the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*);
from hungry ghosts to the realm of animals (*tiryagyoni*); from animals to a person of poverty and low status;
from a person of poverty and low status to a person of wealth and nobility; and from a person of wealth and nobility to one who studies Prajñāpāramitā. By means of this...
Contemplation: Descending from the high is nothing more than following delusion; ascending from the low is nothing more than following *prajñā*.
Yet *prajñā* and delusion are fundamentally not two separate things, being merely like waves and water.

Lately, in this peaceful world, there has suddenly arisen this great calumny, great doubt, and great peril. Although the factions of the heterodox have arrogantly usurped power, it is nonetheless by virtue of principle [that we respond].

Furthermore, when we reflect upon it, this is precisely where our daily path—both mundane and supramundane—has been obscured. Our social interactions have not been sufficiently clear, and we have all remained mired in the pit of mediocrity.
Our anxieties are not deep, and our considerations do not reach far; because our anxieties are not deep and our considerations do not reach far, we willingly sit within the pit of mediocrity.
The ultimate reason for this is that our roots do not value Prajñā (wisdom). Therefore, without cause...
This has invited such perilous doubt. Now that we have traced the roots and investigated the source, we know its origin.

If one does not feel an equal sense of urgent pain and sacrifice one’s head, eyes, and marrow to adorn *prajñā*, then whether conditions and circumstances are favorable or adverse, they shall serve to smelt and refine *prajñā*.

Through successive lifetimes, one will always be at the vanguard of the seed of Buddhahood for transcending the world, and always be at the vanguard of loyalty and filial piety within the world. As...
This is remorse; to resolve one's will in this manner is right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*).

If it is not thus, one belongs to the faction of the heterodox, is not a member of the Buddha’s retinue, and lacks the seed of loyalty and filial piety. Furthermore, among the adornments of Prajñāpāramitā, the single matter of carving the Tripitaka is most earnestly approved.
Whether one has discernment or lacks it, this is directly and easily seen; there is no need for my words to show it to you, my disciples.
When Emperor Yuan of the Liang dynasty was in Kuaiji, he was twelve years old and already possessed a great love for learning. At that time, he suffered from scabies;
his hands could not be clenched and his knees could not be bent. He would shut himself in his private quarters behind a screen of ramie cloth, sitting alone to avoid the flies.

He would pour sweet wine from Shan-yin into silver bowls and occasionally take sips of it to soothe himself. Following his own inclination, he read the histories by himself, consuming twenty scrolls in a single day.

Having never received formal instruction from a teacher, he might not recognize a single character or understand a single word; yet he insists on valuing himself highly, showing no sign of weariness or fatigue.
Zhu Jian of Yiyang was a man whose family had long resided in Jiangling, but later moved to Yangdu. He was devoted to the study of the Classics, yet being poor, he lacked the necessary funds.
For several days he did not cook; instead, he would occasionally swallow paper to fill his belly. Having no woolen blankets for the cold, he would lie down embracing his dog.
The dog, too, was famished; it would rise and go out to steal food. When Zhan called for it, the dog would not come, its piteous howling moving the neighbors. Yet, he did not abandon his practice.
He ultimately completed his studies as a scholar and served as the Administrative Assistant (Lùshì Cānjūn) of Zhènán. He was honored by Emperor Xiàoyuán. Alas!
If even one who is of imperial descent and accustomed to the leisure of childhood can achieve such things, how much more so should those among the common people who hope to advance themselves?

Furthermore, there was one whose poverty reached the very marrow of his bones, yet he still swallowed paper to fill his belly and never abandoned his studies. Now, I— (Note: The provided text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)
Cao Ji has received the spiritual favor of the Elder Dajue; his home mountain extends throughout the ten directions, and he may sustain himself with food and clothing until the end of his days.
Yet, he does not spare even a moment of time, instead indulging in gluttonous sleep and engaging in baseless chatter to waste his days.
Compared to Emperor Yuan of the Liang dynasty or Zhu Zhennan, he is like a small sparrow matched against a great phoenix. Moreover, as for those worldly studies—

The retribution of this single lifetime is no more than a bubble on water or a shadow in the sky. One must exert oneself with diligent effort, casting aside the physical body beyond concern, and treasure one's learning like pearls and jewels;
one must surely strive until success is achieved before ceasing. We of our class have transformed our appearance and discarded our robes.
Severing worldly attachments and transcending the mundane, one seeks unsurpassed *bodhi*. If it is not achieved in one lifetime, one must take rebirth;

if it is not achieved in that rebirth, one must continue until infinite births have passed. Only upon its achievement does it truly begin. Yet my resolve falls short of that of Zhu Daosheng of the Liang dynasty;
it is like seeking a child from a stone woman or searching for flames within thick ice—how could such things possibly be obtained? Lately, our distance from antiquity has grown ever greater.
Customs grew increasingly corrupt. Those who had left the household life formed groups and traveled in bands, roaming through prefectures and hunting for districts.

Among them, those of the highest caliber believed that mountains and rivers could nourish the mind of the Way; thus, they spent their entire lives greedily gazing at these sights without ever feeling satiated.

Those of middle standing carried half-fans and broken gourds and wore a single heavy robe of patchwork; they considered such a state to be "cultivation. As for those of the lowest sort, there were still those who could not be tolerated.
Regarding the term "superior" (sheng): it refers to what is called Chan and lecturing. One does not know what kind of flavor they possess.
Furthermore, there is a certain breed of wild fox-demon offspring who, having memorized one or two fragments of cause and effect, immediately claim, "I am proficient in lecturing.
Having learned a few words of talk that lack any firm foundation, they immediately claim, "I understand Chan. Tracing this back, the corruption of the Dharma has reached such an extreme.
In this regard, for the most part, when one first becomes a teacher, the initial thought is certainly not genuine; they have left the home life for the sake of birth and death.
When one first becomes a disciple, that initial thought of leaving the home life is likewise necessarily not genuine.

Since both the superior and the subordinate are thus insincere, how could there be a teacher who is not genuine yet able to instruct a genuine disciple? How could there be a disciple who is not genuine...
And yet, how could one possibly draw near to a true and authentic teacher? Observing this, it is only natural that the ancestral Way has declined.

Had I been fortunate enough to leave home as a *śrāmaṇera*, I would have resided in a famous mountain; furthermore, I would have had the opportunity to draw near to various great elders at Mount Qingliang.

Through being perfumed by them in the morning and scorched by them in the evening—amidst their casual shouts, rebukes, and the application of the whip or the rod—I would have transformed ordinary sentiments into wisdom.
[The light] shifts defiled habits into pure habits. All that one reads should be the sacred writings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

If one cannot cast aside the physical form to let the Way prevail within oneself, then small accumulations will become great, and drops will form the sea; thus one will penetrate the great matter of one’s own person and repay the Buddha’s profound kindness.
In such a case, being alive for even a single day is not as good as dying early by a single day. (From the *Yan Shijia xun*, "On Cultivating Learning and Hearing").
The five signs of decline in the heavens are not yet sufficient to be considered suffering; the eight difficulties in the human realm are likewise not yet sufficient to be considered suffering.

However, having fortunately attained a human birth, to receive a female body is itself suffering. Therefore, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas regard the female body as a pit of lethal poison and a den of venomous snakes.
If one unfortunately stumbles at the edge of this pit of lethal poison, their life of wisdom is instantly severed. Evil...
To share a lodging by misfortune within a snake’s den, once its venom has entered the heart, is difficult to cure even for Lu Ban or Bian Que.
For this reason, the virtuous of old said: "It is better to be a poor and lowly man than to be a wealthy and noble woman. Why is this?
The female body is the root of suspicion for the world and the medium for slander; therefore, [one should seek] mountain retreats and places of practice. Village.

The ruins of the vihāra were restored; sometimes meditation was practiced and lectures were given. Disciples of the Buddha gathered there, and the thunder of the Dharma shook the heavens while the light of wisdom shone forth.
The Buddhas looked upon them with compassion, and spirits and deities provided protection. Even poor and lowly beggars who came and went in search of food encountered no obstacles.
All who saw them gave rise to hearts of pity and conceived thoughts of providing for their needs. For instance, there was a woman who entered the site of practice for a brief moment. One...
All who see or hear of this do not inquire as to the intent behind its arrival; instead, they immediately give rise to doubt and engage in conjecture.
Once people have given rise to doubt, slander arises from that doubt; from slander, calamity accumulates.

Consequently, the radiance of the site of practice (dojang) is suddenly extinguished, the thunder of the Dharma is silenced, and the monastic community is no longer revered by the people. It is like a poisonous fruit, which bears three seeds upon a single branch.
It is through nourishment that they are brought to completion. Viewed from this perspective, a poor and lowly man is ten thousand times superior to a wealthy and noble woman;
of this there is no doubt. Therefore, when a woman studies the Way, she must first examine herself, whether in body or in mind.
"What kind of mental activity led to the reception of this body? For what reason does this body provoke the suspicion and slander of others?
By investigating these two points until they are clear, one will know that in a previous life the mind was full of lustful thoughts, and thus this body was received.
Since this body exists because of lustful thoughts—wherein the lustful thought is like a flower and the body is like its fruit—if one desires no fruit, one must first cut off the flower.
Although sentient beings have heavy karma and deep habitual tendencies, they knowingly commit transgressions;

for this reason, they find it ultimately difficult to escape from the pit of lethal poison and willingly slumber forever within the den of a venomous serpent. It is not only women who are unable to turn over and struggle forth.
A man of such noble bearing still regards this world as if ascending a spring terrace, showing no thought of weary detachment.
If you truly wish to study the Way and seek to transcend birth and death, upon hearing my words, you must surely weep with tears streaming down so uncontrollably that you cannot stop yourself.

If you hear these words and yet act as if you have not heard them, I know that your future rebirths will be in the wombs of donkeys and horses, or among pigeons, doves, birds, and sparrows—your single shoulder already burdened with the weight of such a fate.
There is indeed a burden to bear. Nevertheless, how could I bear to sit idly by while witnessing your success or failure?

I cannot refrain from giving rise to a single thought of benevolence and acting as a means for you to escape suffering. Among all such means, there is only one practice—contemplating the body—that is most essential.
First, contemplate your own body: why do skin, flesh, sinews, and bones exist? Why are there tears, saliva, blood, and veins?
Whatever is moist, by what cause does it exist? Whatever is warmth, by what cause does it exist? Whatever is movement and transformation, by what cause does it exist?
By observing in this way, the path of arising gradually matures, and the path of maturation gradually arises. Once this is fully understood—
The solidity of my body arises from the perception of earth; its moisture arises from the perception of water; its warmth arises from the perception of fire;
and its movement arises from the perception of wind. When each of these returns, in turn, to that which it was perceived from, this is what is called the "poisoned pit."
The den of the venomous snake—where, ultimately, shall it be placed? If one can penetrate and escape from this, why not take the five-colored filth as a broad and long tongue?
What is so wrong about preaching the Dharma to deliver sentient beings?
Is it that every man possesses three heads and six arms, while women must necessarily lack such power? Having read these words, I shall weep bitterly and apply myself with diligent effort.
Go and do it. If you do not, I, Xue-ren, shall act on your behalf to seek words for you; this too will have its own consequences.
I usually reveal these teachings to women very rarely, but because Xue-ren has entreated me repeatedly, I have written this down as a legacy for you. To transmit it to others for practice:
those who wish to transcend birth and death must first understand suffering. If suffering is not understood, one cannot avoid mistaking it for pleasure.
Regarding pleasure: once one has mistaken suffering for pleasure, there is ultimately no turning back; lost in delusion after delusion, when can liberation be expected?
Why is this? It is because not recognizing suffering is the first layer of delusion, while mistaking suffering for pleasure is the second layer of delusion.
Because they delight in this and do not turn back, this is the third layer of delusion. Thus, delusion follows upon delusion, and in the end, it is never resolved.
Furthermore, the suffering of women is more profound and grave than that of men.

If one were to analyze their suffering in sequence, even if the great earth were used as a tongue and empty space as a mouth, it could not be fully exhausted. For this reason, [the suffering of] women is not addressed first.
Know suffering. If you can thoroughly uproot the root of suffering, then how could the branches, twigs, and leaves ever grow again?
But tell me, what is the root of suffering? Suffering is not far away; it is simply this very body of yours before you.
If you can directly see through this body, then when all manner of disagreeable things come upon you, there will be no need for great effort to dispel them; they will naturally [fall away].
The fire that burns the heart is extinguished without being struck down (both sections demonstrate this regarding women).

After Great Mirror [Huineng] attained enlightenment, he immediately said: "Originally there is not a single thing; where can dust and grime settle? After Oxhead [Zhizang] attained enlightenment, [he said]:...

It is said that the wondrous virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are all contained within the source of the mind, and the hundreds of thousands of samādhis do not depart from this very place.
Both of these great elders were masters of the lineage for a thousand ages; one was thus, and the other was so. Are they the same or different?
If they are the same, their two statements appear to be contradictory; if they are different, since both are great elders who have awakened to the mind, how could they not be the same? And yet—
Huangbo further said: "If you can grasp neither of the two ends, then you may escape the forms of suffering and pleasure.
What Huangbo says here simultaneously refutes the words of the two great elders. Viewed from the perspective of emotional sentiment:
The words of the Three Elders seem difficult to comprehend, yet when understood through principle, they have never failed to accord with one another. As for the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha:

if spoken of in terms of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), not even a single speck of dust can be established; if spoken of in terms of non-emptiness, there is no phenomenon that is not fully contained within it.
When speaking of it in terms of both emptiness and existence, it is called the "empty-and-non-empty Tathāgatagarbha. For the most part, it is so designated.
This means that although there are various [manifestations], in truth, each person’s original face is precisely this.
By means of this face, it may be empty, it may be existent, or it may be both empty and non-empty; thus, it merely receives different names.
Yet, ordinary beings are deluded by this face, and in a flash, they give rise to the three delusions; sages awaken to it, and instantaneously realize the three *tathāgatagarbhas*.

Furthermore, as for the three delusions, they are what are known as the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), the delusions of the sands of *saṃsāra* (*rajas*), and fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*).

Because of the delusions of views and thoughts, one is obstructed from the empty *tathāgatagarbha*. Because of the delusions of the sands of *saṃsāra*, one is obstructed from the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*.
Because of fundamental ignorance, one is obstructed from the *tathāgatagarbha* that is both empty and non-empty. My friend, Master Nian, said:

His eminent disciple was named Xingzang (Treasury of Nature). Some who instead title him Yuzhen (Embodiment of Reality) likely do not realize that this "nature" possesses three treasuries (*trikosa*).
If the meaning of "embodiment of reality" were to be correlated with the Three Treasuries, it would correspond only to the *tathāgatagarbha* of non-emptiness;
both the empty *tathāgatagarbha* and the empty-and-non-empty *tathāgatagarbha* would be omitted. It is by this that I know.

Regarding the "Treasury of the Nature of Characters" (*Zixingzang*): it refers to those who do not know their own nature. Some say that even Dajian (Huineng) stated, "Originally there is not a single thing.
Does this mean he mentioned one while omitting the other? I replied to him: "Dajian pointed to one corner, desiring that people would infer the other three by analogy.
I have changed [the title] to 'Following the South' and titled it 'Containing and Storing,' for within consciousness there is the principle of awakening."

And regarding the meaning of non-awakening: thus, when a person cultivates the three contemplations to perfection, then the afflictions of view and thought are severed, the delusions of the "dust-sands" are shattered, and the fundamental ignorance is ultimately uprooted.
Therefore, severing, shattering, and uprooting are in accord with the principle of awakening within the *ālayavijñāna*;

they do not conflict with it. To conflict is to be in a state of non-awakening. This so-called "non-awakening" is the gate of conflict; it follows along with ignorance while moving contrary to awakening.
This is the meaning. Therefore, it is called the Gate of Contradiction. The south represents the position of empty luminosity; it is a metaphor for the awakening of the mind.
If you, my son, can truly follow my words and practice them yourself, then the three Tathāgata-garbhas can be realized through sitting meditation (this demonstrates the Nature-garbha).
When a white blade shakes one’s chest, the eyes do not even look back at a stray arrow; this is because circumstances have their moments of urgency and calm.
As for honor and disgrace versus life and death, these matters do not concern two different people; rather, one must carefully examine what is appropriate regarding their urgency and sequence.
If one can decide directly and immediately, then all worldly conventions will be eliminated of their own accord, without the need for further cleansing. (Instruction to Disciples)
To hold onto antiquity while governing the present, and to possess a mind that subtly understands form—this is truly because the workings of the mind are impermanent and must rely upon a basis.
Thus, if one stagnates in existence, every encounter becomes discordant; yet if one relies on the numinous spirit, there is perfect illumination without obstruction.

When illuminating the body, it is seen as a convergence of the four great elements; when illuminating the mind, it is likewise composed of the four aggregates. By understanding this convergence, attachment to the body naturally dissolves. Once dissolved, [all delusions vanish].
This illumination. To illuminate the mind with this: the four aggregates are impermanent; being impermanent, they have no master; having no master, there is no tree.

Leave it entirely to the shifts of cold and warmth; fundamentally, there is neither flourishing nor falling. Once you have contemplated and mastered this principle, when encountering conditions and touching objects—whether at the critical junctures of favorability or adversity—maintain a firm and refined resolve.
To endure through them, even at the cost of life and with bare skin, is true cultivation. As this cultivation gradually matures, one comes to understand form.

It is precisely the mind. Since form is the mind, the mind does not obstruct the mind; it stands alone as solitary luminosity. Upon encountering conditions, it achieves fulfillment; it opens up things and accomplishes tasks.

It is precisely wisdom that directs compassion, so as not to sink into withered stillness; it is precisely compassion that directs wisdom, so as not to be stained by the dust and turmoil of the world.
Practicing in this manner, from the subtle to the manifest, one traverses the fifty-five stages of the true path of Bodhi—this is not the four dhyānas or the four formless attainments.
They are worthy of being compared. Yan Yuanping did not forget his lord even in death;
what he had cultivated throughout his life remained with him. Zhang Xuyang cursed the rebel even while alive and did not change even after death.
Thus, it was only natural that he clenched his fists until his nails pierced his flesh and gnashed his teeth until his gums bled. As for us practitioners of Zen:

They did not penetrate it; this was simply because the two masters lacked the resolve. Had they possessed such resolve, the realization of the Way could have been accomplished within a single lifetime (instruction for disciples).
The mind’s direction is not constant; its governance depends on the person. Therefore, those who govern their minds with virtue and the Way are unaware of profit and utility;
those who govern their minds with profit and utility are unaware of benevolence and righteousness. Tracing this back to its origin, even in the case of virtue and the Way, profit and utility—
The starting points for seeking profit differ; yet none transcend one’s own mind, for it is only that the objects of their aspirations vary.

If one directs the mind toward the Way and its Virtue (*moralò*), then robbery, plunder, defamation, and humiliation are all merely stages on the path. If one directs the mind toward profit and utility (*gònglì*), then honor, fame, and imperial favor are entirely but harbingers of alarm.
When the mind is submerged by these harbingers of alarm, the spirit and soul are constantly disturbed; how much more so when one encounters robbery, plunder, defamation, and humiliation?
At that limit, there is something attained. Therefore, for one who studies the Way, encountering objects and conditions that are contrary to one's wishes is the greatest fortune.
If, amidst this great fortune, one fails to give rise to awakening and reflection, but instead drifts along with the environment, this is called "obscuring the mind.

For one who obscures the mind, even if they sit daily at the same table as sages and worthies and engage in fellowship with them, how is this different from a blind man wearing the bright sun upon his head?
This is indeed a great night. It is simply this: do not deceive your own mind. The mind is itself numinous and sagely.
When one dwells within inconceivable circumstances with this numinous and sagely mind, it naturally dissolves like lingering snow meeting spring;
why wait for thunder to split the earth before it melts away? A poem says: "The stones of another mountain can be used to grind jade. If one uses jade to grind...
Jade is difficult to fashion into a vessel precisely because both its parts are so smooth and lustrous that the whetstone has no effect upon them.

Thus, when one dwells in a state of sublime tranquility, the mind and its objects forget each other. In this forgetting, the light of awareness is lost. Even if a strict teacher or a virtuous friend should offer earnest and clear instruction, it only serves to increase one's familiarity with such negligence.
Once this familiarity is established, it is like a pampered child who fears neither his parents; since the mind is devoid of fear, reverence [is lost].
From what do these arise? From what can one obtain the benefit of being without reverence [for worldly gain] and without fear [of worldly loss]?
Therefore it is said: "The spear before the face; the arrow behind the head. The spear before the face is easy to dodge; the arrow behind the head is difficult to prevent.

Furthermore, as the ways of the world decline, the tradition of teachers and friends has long been in a state of collapse and lacks vigor. As for what are called strict teachers and virtuous friends, how easily can such persons be encountered! One who is able...
If one takes the inconceivable realm as the ground for teachers and friends, then wherever one goes, there will be no one who is not a venerable teacher or a virtuous friend.
When emotional consciousnesses float and sink, they cause the four great elements to increase or diminish;

yet when the light of wisdom is uniquely revealed and one turns back toward tranquil emptiness, even if there are lingering obstructions from the past, there is nothing to stir them up—how then could they inflict harm? (Both shown to Zhongfu during his illness.)
In the households of men, there is iron upon their necks and waists; it was not cast by the Way or Righteousness, yet how difficult is it to bend or stretch.
Once their bodies are bent, the light of the mind cannot break through, like clouds covering the moon, obscuring the spirit in its gloom.

Thus, amidst the distinctions of right and wrong, and within the realms of the favorable and the unfavorable, the high and the low, they are unable to stand forth with independent integrity. Knowing the truth, they willingly embrace ignorance; when a single breath does not return, all becomes profound darkness.
To achieve this for a thousand ages, the lingering spirit drifts on; the hope of emergence is rare—how can one not grieve?

Why not kick over the mortar and pestle and suddenly sever the root of emotion? Whether benefit or harm, whether adversity or favor, let only the luminous mind shine forth clearly, viewing all things as equal to drifting clouds.
If one day this vow is fulfilled, one may laugh and roam upon the home mountain—is this not a source of joy? (Shown to He Zhiren)

The distinction between the holy and the ordinary is inexhaustible; the reliance and the supported are endless. Rising and sinking undergo ten thousand transformations, and sentient and insentient beings ultimately cannot be known through intellectual cognition nor exhausted by calculation.
Yet, all of them take names and words as their essence. Why is this so? It is because wherever there is a name, there must be a meaning;
wherever there is a word, there must be a significance. Thus, upon hearing the names "water" and "fire," one immediately perceives moisture and heat.
They arrive without waiting for an invitation. Upon hearing words of praise or blame, joy and anger likewise arrive without waiting for an invitation.
Knowing that both are thus, one realizes that the ordinary and the sage, the provisional and the real, are in truth external to names and words and cannot be apprehended.
Alas! What kind of thing are these names and words, yet upon which the provisional and the real, and the sage... rely?
In all cases, these constitute the very substance [of discourse]. Therefore, while dwelling in one's chamber, if a single word is spoken well, it will be responded to from a thousand li away;

if a single word is spoken poorly, it will likewise be responded to from a thousand li away. Viewed from this perspective, regarding the establishment of names and the formulation of speech, if one does not rectify their source and ensure a thorough understanding of the underlying principle, there is nothing better than not establishing them at all, so as to avoid leaving behind calamity. Hence it is said: "Names and Speech."
This is the very juncture between delusion and awakening; how can one not be careful?

Some take Zhaozhou’s "Mu" (No) as their *huatou*. After many years have passed, they come to believe that whether in life or death, in favor or adversity, thought is itself the *huatou*, and the *huatou* is itself thought; there is nowhere it is not a single, unified whole. Others, having heard this...

He laughed heartily and said, "If one can truly bring the 'critical phrase' (*huatou*) to a single thought and consolidate it into one whole, one's countenance will naturally differ from that of ordinary people.

A radiance of clarity and serenity like a bright breeze or a clear moon will shine from between the eyebrows, causing even oxen, horses, chickens, and dogs to feel joy upon encountering such a person—how much more so for humans, who are the most spiritually gifted among all things? These sorts of words should be spoken only to the foolish."
The Way cannot be discussed with those who possess mere intellectual knowledge. Generally speaking, as for the secret of Zen meditation:

if one’s mind-ground truly becomes a seamless whole through both favorable and adverse circumstances, then awakening will occur within days or nights. People today who study the recorded sayings and encounters of the ancients are like blind men groping an elephant;
their hands lack sensation, so how can they know whether the elephant is fat or thin? Alas! Such people rely on fame and reputation.
To offer worship [to worldly deities] is like a terminal illness; it is to entrust the great matter of birth and death to the space between a horse’s hooves.
As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "When one commits a great falsehood, one falls into the Avīci Hell. Is this not what that refers to? (Shown to my disciples)
Ordinary people repay the virtue of their parents by offering the three sacrificial animals while they are alive and presenting ten thousand cuts of meat when they are dead;

this does nothing more than emphasize their black karma. Alas, the world is spiritually blind and it is ultimately difficult to instruct them in the correct principle. For now, we must follow their customary practices to satisfy their immediate desires.
The sages and worthies, knowing that such habits are not easily transformed, temporarily sink or float along with them, while secretly refuting [false views] through reason.

Their emotions were secretly regulated and harmonized. After a long period, their strength became sufficient and their habits transformed spontaneously; those who underwent this regulation even forgot how it had come about.
Therefore, the five rites were made uniform: in times of celebration, ordinary people did not offer congratulations, and in times of mourning, they did not offer condolences.

This is the bitter plight of the sages. Nevertheless, were it not for the supreme light of compassion to illuminate their dark spirits, those who remain obstructed would ultimately be left without rescue.
How could this possibly be the fundamental heart of a filial son or a loyal minister?

Now, if one wishes to illuminate the dark and subtle realms, nothing is better than for a filial son to purify his own three karmas and, for the sake of the deceased, to uphold the verses of Vipaśyin Buddha;
this is the most concise and beneficial method (to show to the disciples).
Now, ritual (*li*) is the backbone of the person. If the backbone is not upright, then though all other parts may be numerous, what is there to speak of?
Since the Great Awakened One appeared in the world, from Kāśyapa onwards, although the religious teachings have branched out, the principles of ritual have remained one and the same.

Yet, with the great masters having passed away, the established codes have fallen into neglect; those who merely follow in their dust do not recognize the fundamental structure, nor do they employ it as the foundation for uprightness.

Fundamentally, we have vied only with the superficial and ornate; as for what is called the "trunk," it has been entirely broken and snapped. You all should contemplate repaying the Buddha’s kindness by exerting your strength in this regard.

Whenever you see those who are latecomers and do not yet understand the great principles, you must earnestly and compassionately encourage and exhort them, so that their trunks may be upright and their roots and flowers flourish, and their roots may be firm and their trunk robust.
Do not show favoritism through indulgence; rather, you should love others [by guiding them toward the truth].
Virtuous One, for this reason, those who live far apart and those who dwell nearby shall meet at dawn and dusk;

it is essential that they maintain their ranks with propriety rather than negligence, observing the proper order between seniors and juniors and adhering to ritual precedence according to etiquette, never allowing themselves to act according to their own whims. This old man has wandered through rivers and lakes, his footsteps covering half the world.

In every place I have encountered many things that moved me, and thus I have hastily composed these words. This applies not only to those who have left the household life, but also to those who remain at home.

How could it be that this alone is merely neglected? My attendant Mìzàng served me with great diligence; yet, even regarding the titles and administrative regulations he encountered, there was still much that was diffuse and inconsistent—how much more so for other matters!
Confucius said, "It must be that names are rectified. For if names are not correct, then positions will not be fixed;
if positions are not fixed, then ritual cannot be established. If a human being dares to neglect ritual, they already act improperly; how much more so for one who acts as a Buddha?
"If you disciples do not rectify yourselves in this way, what is the purpose of shaving your heads and donning the dyed robes? (Addressing the monastics of both the black and white robes.
Yuan Shi asked, "The late Master Lu was a great lay practitioner of our time. He had been diligent in the Great Way for many days and nights.
Now that he is advanced in years and afflicted by illness, why do you say he was merely reciting the Buddha's name, holding mantras, and investigating the Patriarchs?"
If both the karmic capacity and the conditions fail to gain strength, then a lifetime of diligent toil will be nearly wasted in vain. For what reason do they fail?
I, your disciple, harbor deep doubts and distress regarding this matter; I beg the Master to provide instruction so that it may serve as a mirror for my future cultivation of the Buddha-vehicle.
Your posing of this question not only directly expresses your own doubts, but also profoundly encourages both the clergy and the laity.

Indeed, there is nothing more formidable than the calamities and blessings of life and death; nor can truth and falsehood escape notice when one is heedless. This venerable one has been a bastion of the Dharma-gate for many years;
whenever he encounters the crux of profit or loss, he harbors no worldly reservations, knowing only to protect and cherish the Great [Dharma].

Regarding the Dharma: were it not for having firm internal insight and, moreover, the power of vows from many lifetimes—wherein the hidden and the manifest support one another—who could possibly reach such a state?
Furthermore, the desire for fame is something even the worthy cannot suddenly forget; yet now, you lie prostrate with illness.
He asked abruptly; he answered suddenly. It was like a thunderclap in a clear sky, or the roll of thunder from a drought-stricken earth.

This can be discussed with those of wisdom, but it is difficult to speak of it to the common crowd. You should remain silent and contemplate this deeply; you will surely come to know for yourself the purpose of this old man’s actions.

Have you not heard of him who spent twenty or thirty years amidst green mountains and white clouds, rinsing his mouth with stones and resting his head upon a stream, embracing stillness in silent meditation?
If the thieving mind has not yet been emptied, it constitutes a great hindrance to all. I asked him thus, and he answered thus: "Is there a thieving mind? Is there no thieving mind?

Had there been a thieving mind, he certainly could not have answered in this way. Had there been none, he would truly be practicing mindfulness of the Buddha, upholding mantras, or engaging in Chan meditation;
yet in these three, he has gained no power. I pray that you will reflect upon this again deeply, lest you yourself [be deceived].
[Seeing] (Answering Wu Yuanshi):
There is a great body and a small body; the mind is likewise. If one takes the great body as one's body, then one can lift up heaven and earth and regulate the myriad things.
If one takes the small body as one's body, then when capable, one may manage a single household; when incapable, one cannot even do so.

I have not even had leisure to attend to my own body, let alone to matters of fame, achievement, or worldly affairs. Now, the "Great Body" (mahā-kāya) is something we inherently possess, yet some are deluded and fail to realize this.
The "Small Body," however, is a mere provisional combination of the four elements; being a provisional combination, it is not inherently existent.
Since it is not inherently existent, one instead stubbornly clings to it without transforming it. Consequently, when one perceives objects of desire, the Great Mind is immediately obscured.

How obscured! The Great Body is lost. Now, as for the Great Mind: its wisdom encompasses the myriad things without toil; its subtlety penetrates the primordial before forms arise, yet it is not a beginning.
For where there is a beginning, there is birth; where there is birth, there is extinction. Only where there is no beginning is there no birth;

where there is no birth, there is no extinction. Its radiance pierces the ten voids; its spirit reaches across the three periods of time. Abiding within the square inch of the heart, it encompasses all of space.
One enters the vast void through a mustard seed; thus it is said that those who speak of Chan while speaking only of emptiness are but the vulgar among speakers.

Nevertheless, compared to those who take five feet to be their body and a square inch to be their mind—who recognize but a single bubble and turn their backs on the entire tide, or who prize a small hillock while forgetting Mount Tai—they are far superior. Life after life, I have deeply lamented the passing of time. Thus...
Night following day, he exerts himself to compensate for his dullness. By ascending the steps of written words, he investigates the heart-essence of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
When the principles are refined and wisdom unfolds, he takes his own profound ignorance as charcoal and fans it with the wind of shame and remorse.

As the fire of faith blazes fiercely, being both courageous and constant, he then casts his narrow mind into a great mind and transforms his small body into a great body—just like throwing a flake of snow into a furnace.
To cast remaining ice into a red furnace, or to throw it into the spring sea—what difficulty could there be? (This is shown by Yusheng).
Although the Buddha-dharma is great, it is greater than the minds of sentient beings. If one is separated from the minds of sentient beings, then that greatness has no foundation.
Viewed from this perspective, "greatness" is merely what sentient beings conceive of as great themselves. Therefore, one who gives rise to the great mind becomes a great person;
one who does not give rise to the great mind falls among the ranks of petty people. Now that you have given rise to this great mind, it is vital that you maintain it constantly.
Thus it is said: "To establish a mind that is not constant leads to misfortune. If it is constant, then its auspiciousness is immeasurable. (Shown to Yuanxin)
The subtle words of China do not transcend the Six Classics; the Great Dharma that came from the West surely does not go beyond the Tripitaka.
As for the texts of Zhuangzi and Laozi, they too must be read; this was the endeavor of the broad-minded and accomplished gentlemen of antiquity.

Therefore, throughout the generations, there have never been those who failed to exhaustively study the classics until their hair turned white, nor those who did not refine the Dharma by sitting before lamps; though these pursuits are sought through paper, they remain constant.
"Ten years of labor with ink and brush are not equal to seeking it within one's own mind and nature; a single morning can match them.
When Wang Anshi went to visit Zhou Maoshu, he did not see him on his first visit, nor did he see him on his second.
Anshi said angrily, "I can seek it for myself in the Six Classics; why must I humbly seek it from another? From then on, he read his books until dawn.
He slept little; whenever he felt drowsy, he would chew stone lotuses to dispel the fog.

When his learning had reached full maturity and he entered the great administration, he considered himself such that even Confucius and Mencius were not to be held in high esteem, and that bringing a ruler to the level of Yao and Shun was no difficult task.

He took pride in himself as a man of the world, and when all the worthy and talented men presented their abilities and strategies, none met with his approval; he merely indulged his own obstinacy and dismissed them all.
Examining his original resolve, it was not that his ambition was not great, his learning not extensive, or his mind not far-reaching;

yet in the end, he ruined the vital energy of the Song dynasty and brought upon himself an unseemly reputation. For the most part, although one’s scholarship may be profound and vast, if one has never once attained a wondrous realization of the Dharma of the Mind, it is like a student of a master craftsman who, though not lacking in knowledge of the compass, square, circle, and straightedge for determining squareness, roundness, curvature, and straightness—
Though one may have clear understanding, because the rhythm of speed and slowness has not yet responded to the hand, one cannot avoid the affliction of injuring the hand.

Rules and compasses determine squareness and roundness; this is the method (*dharma*). The subtlety of speed and slowness is the mind (*citta*). To adhere to the method without having the subtle realization of one’s own mind—that such a person could become a great vessel has never occurred.
This holds true regardless of whether one follows Confucianism, Daoism, or Buddhism: first, there must be the subtle realization of one’s own mind.
To be extensively proficient in various books is called "pushing open the door and knocking down the mortar"—a natural marvel.
When applied to transcend the world, it is called the Supreme Vehicle; when used to govern the world, it is called the Way of Kings. This is true learning and true talent.
Next in order is to proceed from the broad to the concise: the broad is study, while the concise is the mind. This is yet another level. As for...

Though one may read extensively, it will be of no use when the critical moment arrives. It is like the "Dragon of Duke Ye": from afar, its head and horns appear perfectly formed, yet when a severe drought strikes and one desires rain and thunder, there is no way for them to manifest.
Therefore, some first practice conciseness and later seek breadth; among the various patriarchs of the Chan school, seven or eight out of ten followed this path.
Others, from ancient times to the present, have all been masters of the exegesis schools who first sought breadth and later practiced conciseness. Ten out of ten [of these latter]...
This is merely one or two examples. Since this is the case for the Buddha, it is generally so for the followers of Confucianism and Daoism as well.

To speak briefly: when this mind loves others, it is benevolence (*ren*); when one practices benevolence with appropriateness, it is righteousness (*yi*); and when one accords with the principles of righteousness, it is ritual propriety (*li*).
To be unhindered in the adaptive transformations of ritual is wisdom; to be sincere, reverent, and diligent in that wisdom is faith.
Viewed in this light, the wondrous function of these five virtues originally resides within one's own mind, rather than in books. Furthermore, consider the path of the non-arising of the single mind.
Whether one is a monk, a Laozi follower, or a Confucian—if, at this very moment, one is vast and open, free from doubt—then among Confucians one is called a true Confucian;
among followers of Laozi, a true Daoist; and among Buddhists, a true monk. Otherwise, it is as if all sages have emerged and great thieves have arisen;
with the stolen goods present and the evidence established, the crime is such that execution is unavoidable. Who would dare to pat the "big breast"? (i.e., who would dare to claim such a position?)
To deceive children is to mislead them; therefore, in assessing a person's capacity through their learning, one must apply the axe according to the specific wood.

Taking the physical constituents of the person as an example: the skin, flesh, sinews, bones, and various solid obstructions constitute the earth element (*pṛthivī-mahābhūta*); phlegm, saliva, [and so forth...]
The blood, pulses, lymph, and excretions constitute the water element (*āpas-mahābhūta*). The pervasive warmth and heat throughout the body constitute the fire element (*tejas-mahābhūta*).
That which moves, turns, assists the limbs, and enables locomotion and function constitutes the wind element (*vāyu-mahābhūta*); some refer to this as movement and rotation.

All of these are the power of the mind. What does it have to do with the wind-element? One simply fails to realize that when a person suffers a stroke, they cannot lift their hands when they wish to lift them, nor can they move their feet when they wish to move them. Does it mean they lack the power of the mind?

Why then do their hands and feet remain perfectly intact, refusing to obey their commands? This is because the conditions for the wind-element are lacking. These four elements, when combined, constitute the body.
If they do not coincide, where is this body? You, members of the Ministry of Population, must examine this with great care:
Are the four elements of my own body the same as or different from the four external elements? As for the external four elements: that which one treads upon underfoot is the earth element;
the water of the nine rivers flowing before one's eyes is the water element; and that which is burned daily in the hearth or the lamp...
The heat and warmth of the sun above, as well as all solar radiance, constitute the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*).
The long river sending off travelers’ sails, which fly as if full of wind, the swaying of forest trees, and the gathering and dispersing of duckweed, constitute the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*).

This is distinct from the "Ministry of People" (the physical body). If so, from where does this body of the Ministry of People arise? It is because my four internal elements must interact with the external four elements to be formed.
These four great elements, when analyzed, are called the five elements; when synthesized, they are called the four great elements.

From antiquity to the present, there has never been a single person who was not born through the influence of the five elements. How could the Ministry of People alone possess this body apart from the four great elements?
Since this is the same as for the Ministry of People, the internal four great elements are identical to the external four great elements.

If these were indeed the external four great elements, how could there be any person of intelligence who would identify the earth they tread upon, the waters of the nine rivers, the fire within the hearth, or the wind at the treetops as their own body? Even the most foolish person [would not do so].

The ignorant do not reach this level, let alone those of high intelligence in the Ministry of People. If one can roughly grasp this point, the characteristics of the body will immediately become light.
Once the characteristics of the body are light, one has already kicked over the nest of birth and death.
When even birth and death cannot move one, how could other things—honor and disgrace, love and hate—possibly move one? This is the worldly truth for a student of the Way.
A method for seeking advantage within [this] was found. Indeed, by following it, what further trouble could there be?
Only the principle of the four aggregates (*catvāri skandhāni*), when compared with the four great elements (*mahābhūtāni*), is subtle upon investigation and examination.

When the Minister of the People encounters circumstances and conditions therein, and thoughts of aversion or attachment arise, he should contemplate clearly from where this thought arises. If it arises from a self, then before encountering conditions...
At that time, how could it not arise? If it arises from the object, then even a non-self cannot arise.
If it arises through the conjunction of both ends, one first examines the arising from the self and finds it impossible; one examines the arising from the object and finds it impossible.

How can there be an arising through the conjunction of two impossibilities? At this point, Minbu had a sudden realization. Although it cannot be called "complete enlightenment," [it was a moment of insight].
It is so. One may rescue half [of beings] from the sea of birth and death. What are the four aggregates?
That which perceives and grasps external objects is called sensation (*vedanā*). What are external objects? They are precisely those objects encountered when meeting with conditions.

This sensation cannot be found apart from these external objects. Since sensation does not exist, how can perception (*saṃjñā*) arise? Since perception does not exist, mental formations (*saṃskāra*)...

Furthermore, from where would it come? Since volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) do not exist, from where would consciousness (*vijñāna*) come? It is because there is feeling (*vedanā*) that perception (*saṃjñā*) exists;

to calculate, deliberate, and conjecture is called perception. When the nature of good and evil within perception is not yet settled—suddenly shifting toward good and suddenly shifting toward evil, moving back and forth without certainty, and unable to reach a definitive resolution—it is called volitional formation.
Volitional formation refers to the process of flux. Suddenly, one becomes distinct and reaches a definitive resolution.
To distinguish between what is good and what is evil without any doubt is called consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Although these four [aggregates] function differently, when one investigates their origins, it is necessarily because there is perception (*saṃjñā*) due to feeling (*vedanā*), volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) due to perception, and consciousness due to volitional formations. This is not a forced correlation;
rather, it is the natural tendency and the natural principle. That I, this poor monk, have spoken such incoherent words from the outset was nothing more than an attempt to teach.
The dregs of one's household are not yet the livelihood of a patch-robed monk. For instance, when an ancient worthy asked a monk, "To say 'this very mind is Buddha' is to place a head upon a head;
to say 'Buddha is apart from the mind' is to cut off one's head and seek life.
If you, Minister of the People, can gain a clear understanding of this, do not rely on the testimony of others. If you can penetrate it directly yourself, naturally there will be no trace of [doubt].
Even a shadow of doubt is not it. This is the livelihood of a patch-robed monk (*śramaṇa*), yet it is still not the very core of a patch-robed monk’s being.
Tell me, what is the core of a patch-robed monk’s being? Before the Five Elders’ Peak, clouds come and go;
casually touching the nose of Minister Min (shown to Minister Min).
The gravity of the name of the Dharma exceeds that of great treasures. Great treasures do not surpass the utmost value of a single lifetime;

however, the name of the Dharma allows one to attain meaning through its name, to realize principle through its meaning, and to practice the Way through its principle without obstruction. By means of this unobstructed ladder, [one ascends].
One can then ascend directly to the shore of the Way (mārga). To attain the shore of the Way is what is first called "virtue" (de); thus, virtue is "attainment. Alas!
The Way and its virtue are without antiquity or modernity, yet they encompass all ages. Therefore, as for those who attain them—even a commoner is not destitute;
yet if one is unfortunate enough to lose them, even a sovereign of the world is not enlightened. Moreover, official rank is but a palanquin for the mediocre person.

"Live in seclusion! Furthermore, the name given by the Dharma is a "Dharma-relative," while the name given by the secular world is a "secular-relative. These two cannot be spoken of as being on the same level.

This is because secular relatives and names end with the exhaustion of one's physical life; when one is reborn, they take on a different surname. How can one be constrained by the names and surnames of this present life?

Therefore, for those who have attained the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), long kalpas are but a single moment, and within that single moment, there is both transgression and merit.
Form and shadow are clearly visible before our eyes; it would be as if we had not been reborn. O Sanding, do not abandon yourself. Strive on! (To Sanding).
Though an iron bowl is hard, when struck, it rings out with a resonant sound—clear, bright, profound, and far-reaching, reaching the ears so that the mind becomes empty.
In the Guiwei year of the Wanli era, I parted from you at Nanchan Temple in Yunxian. Last year, on the slopes of Mount Qingliang, suddenly...
I have received your letter. Upon opening and reading it, I know that you have attained a glimpse of clarity within this very gate.
I am greatly pleased. Among those who have personally approached me at Nan Chan, there are quite a few;
