yet, during these past five or seven years, not a single person has sent word to speak of such a realization of the essential meaning. In the early summer of the Wuzi year, you again joined Jian in being disinterested.
During a moment of profound silence, I requested further instruction from the lay practitioner Fu of Liaocheng in the Gaopu Studio.
Reflecting upon it, the scenes of past and present appeared as clearly as images in a suspended inch-long mirror.

Furthermore, on the first day of the fourth month—the very day you were born into this world—you were accompanied by many virtuous companions, and amidst the fragrance of incense and the light of lamps, we all offered our prostrations to the Water with one voice, though in different mouths.
Repentance! It washes away the defilements of past lives and cleanses the dust of this world. To transform sin into merit and ignorance into wisdom is a truly great matter.
You should also know shame within yourself and not fail your own spirit. Exert yourself with diligence and take awakening as your goal.
Thoroughly understand your own mind and become a "Li Longmen" of this Dharma-ending age through the tip of your brush.
To manifest the luminosity of one's own mind, to adorn the Triple Gem, and to repay the profound kindness of the Buddha:
in general, regardless of whether one's faculties are sharp or dull, if the aspiration is sincere and one’s diligence is fierce, one will swiftly attain the Way.

However, if the aspiration is not sincere and one’s practice is not fierce, then even if one’s natural talent is transcendent and one’s learning is exhaustive, it will only serve to increase intellectual views and nourish the conceit of a self.
It is simply this: those who are merely honest and straightforward are far more numerous than you.

You travel to the four quarters and wander alone across ten thousand *li*, casting your shadow alone in guesthouses, not for any other reason than that your parents are at home and your wife and children are below;

the expenses for food and clothing are matters that cannot be delayed, so you devote your entire spirit to this wandering life, refusing to decline hardships in order to seek out some provisions to satisfy their sweet needs.
This is the essential point, and it is also the great juncture for one who is a son. Do not be indolent;

do not let your youth go to waste or betray the daylight, thereby causing your parents grief and making your wife and kin bear anxiety. This very thought is the samādhi of compassion within your own mind;
it is the light of the Tathāgata illuminating the world. As long as this light does not grow dim, whether you emerge from Māra or enter the Buddha-state, it is all your Way.
Wherever you travel or reside, you should likewise provide clothing and food for your parents, making them abundant and pure as an expression of your utmost devotion.
Furthermore, you should encourage your parents to give rise to great faith, establishing firm conviction within the Buddha-dharma.

Regarding the Sahā world as a land of toxic miasma and the Land of Ultimate Bliss as a place of peace and joy, you must look toward every moment and every day, hoping only that one day you may be born in that land.
"Father, you have drawn near to Amitābha and served the bodhisattvas of the nine grades.
That you are able to provide such offerings for your parents is something that even the filial piety of Zeng could not be said to equal. Do you not see Jianmo?
Within a single year, his two sons died one after the other, followed by the death of his wife; in a state of distress upon the roads, he carried four coffins back south—this was Fu of Liaocheng."
Master Ai’s daughter, as well as Jiansi and Wenqing of Jinsha, were all kinsmen within our Dharma gate;
they have all suffered such heart-rending and disagreeable events. From a worldly perspective, this is indeed lamentable;
yet from the standpoint of the Dharma-eye, how can one know that those who have passed away were not Bodhisattvas manifesting these scenes of impermanence to cause you [to realize it]?
The young man Cao was struck with terror and realized that the world is not solid. This may yet be unfathomable;
on the day you return home, you should soon inform your parents of these circumstances so that they too may be moved to fear and develop resolute faith in the West.
How is this different from beating the drums on a battlefield? Drums are used to bolster the morale of the soldiers, and banners are used to unify the gaze of the multitude.
Thus, taking impermanence as the signal drum and banner: a sentient being with faith, a person of superior faculties, perceives the essential point and acts without waiting for the day to end;
hearing the sound they awaken, seeing form they attain clarity—this too is a model for those who are utterly blind.
How could awakening come only by waiting for the movement of lips and the stirring of tongues to expound the "Zen of words"? The time for my departure for Mount Emei is pressing;
I imagine I shall not linger there for long. When I first struck the iron bowl and it made a sound, that was already the "cannon-fire" of the Dharma for my journey.
You all heard the sound reach your ears, yet you failed to realize it—then, on the day I return from Mount Emei, your progress will be profound.
There is no progress; it cannot yet be determined. As you have heard, so you have heard. You should reproach yourself and not follow the worldly flow.
Take care (all have heard).
I have issued this solemn command to you for reasons that are profoundly far-reaching; it must not be treated with negligence, nor should you fail to reflect upon it deeply.
The meaning of "solemnity" (yán) is exceedingly vast; I shall briefly cite two or three instances to demonstrate it to you. Be solemn in mind through awakening; be solemn in body through virtue;
be solemn in both mind and body through inquiry and study. If these three are not neglected, you will grasp the essential framework of all things that ought to be treated with solemnity.
I have written these precepts for you, my son. Your father sent you here with instructions for you.
Although you are currently young and do not yet understand the reason why, once you have grown up, you will surely come to know it. Alas! When a tree is first planted, it is only a foot high;
yet after many years, it forms a lush and spreading shade. (Shi Xingyan)

Sentient beings recklessly engage in conceptual constructions that shroud and obscure their original mind; therefore, amidst the functioning of the total embodiment, they harbor doubts and are unable to employ it.
I bent one finger and asked Ruwen, "Do you see? He replied, "I see. I asked, "Do you see anything outside of this?"
He said, "I do not know. I sighed deeply in admiration. After a long while, he showed me, saying:

"When this finger of mine bends once, there is not a single dharma among all the holy and the ordinary, nor among all that is dependent or primary, that can extend. Not only does this bending occur thus; it is so for every dharma.
Just as when a single thought arises, the entire realm of empty space arises together with it; there is not even a space the size of a mustard seed that is empty."
A gap that can accommodate extinction—extinction is also like this. Therefore, Vimalakīrti said to Maitreya: "All sentient beings are suchness.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī replied to Vimalakīrti: "Householder, I come with the characteristic of not coming.
If there were an initial coming, I could not see you, householder, now. From this it may be said: non-coming is not coming, and coming is not [coming].
It is clear that they will not return. Only those who thoroughly understand their own minds will gradually break through emotional views;
once they have attained a single dharma within this Dharma-gate, all dharmas will be fully realized (as if hearing it for the first time).
From antiquity to the present day, those who have generally failed to achieve realization in the Way have often done so because they could not bring their own body and mind under control.
Consequently, birth-and-death, love, and hatred intermingle and cause turmoil; the spiritual citadel is muddied, and not even for a moment can one find clarity and tranquility.

This is entirely no better than being summoned by birth-and-death and the formation of love and hatred. Though one may rush about across lakes and seas in search of the Truth, [if the mind is not settled, all efforts are in vain].

They seek secret instructions for the purpose of regulating body and mind; these may be things perceived through the eyes or heard through the ears, transmitted from head to head and relied upon with forced manipulation.
Furthermore, there are those who, having attained some slight experience in stillness, mistake it for the ultimate goal.
Throughout one's long years and all day long, one merely dandles the eyes of a ghost and stirs up the vapors of rice and gruel.

One’s own body and mind have, in the end, not been rectified by even a hair’s breadth. Even when faced with times of upheaval and exile, or amidst fields of opposition and compliance, right and wrong, the cycle of birth and death remains vast and unyielding.
Hatred and attachment fill the breast; they flutter and sway about, making the center of one’s being feel as if pricked by thorns. This—
It is because one does not know the source of one’s own body and mind. Since one does not know the source of body and mind, the obstacles presented by this very body and mind are no small matter.
If one proceeds in such a lackluster manner, how could one ever hope to thoroughly awaken to and fully realize the Great Way?
I dare say that throughout their daily lives, from birth until death, they have not even dreamed of true peace and ease. Why is this? Because they do not know.

If one perceives the source of the body, one sees that there is a body; because one sees that there is a body, one undergoes the burdens of the body. If one does not know the source of the mind, one sees that there is a mind;
because one sees that there is a mind, one undergoes the toil of the mind. Master Sengzhao said: "Among all forms of toil and exertion, none precedes the possession of consciousness."
"There is no greater affliction than having a body. How could this deceive me? Now, speak of the source of this body and mind.
This physical frame manifest before you is nothing more than a combination of the four great elements. This present, clearly discerning, deluded mind—this very point—is it?
However, this is merely a conglomeration of the four aggregates. Sentient beings, due to their delusions, falsely take this body to be the self and this mind to be the mind.

For kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they have fallen into the abyss without ceasing; changing heads and faces like fire passing from one piece of wood to another, their proliferation continues without end.
A man of great character who sincerely studies the Way, why not exert his full brilliance? Beat your breast and judge for yourself; resolve upon a single, determined will.
Immediately, push aside the body as the four elements and push aside the mind as the four aggregates.

Encountering conditions and touching objects from morning until evening, maintain this continuously without interruption. Whether in joy, push them away in this way; whether in affliction, push them away in this way. Push! Push!
Pushing forward and withdrawing, when one's practice becomes mature, suddenly body and mind become vast and open, empty yet luminous.
Upon reaching this state, what ultimately can be called "body and mind"? What can be called "birth-and-death," "love," or "hatred"?

If De-xiu can truly shoulder this burden, he will not only have the potential to attain Buddhahood, but there will also be a path for him to study the Way of the Immortals; you may take it for granted that his realization is complete.
Within the Chan school, they likewise do not admit this. When De-xiu heard these words, he could not help but doubt whether [the masters] had become Buddhas or immortals;

yet upon entering the Chan school, he found that all such things were merely secondary matters. Little did he know that as for the "uppermost pivot" of the Chan school, even the Buddhas have not yet seen it in their dreams.
But tell me, what is this uppermost pivot? It is where the Buddhas of the ten directions reside.
Where are they all? They are entirely within the wombs of donkeys and horses (pointing to Hu Dexiu).
That all sentient beings perceive the body as something obtainable—this is called ignorance. That one recognizes cognition and awareness as the mind—this is called ignorance.
Now tell me: while ignorance is manifest before you, where is Prajñā? I rely on the great assembly to assist in reciting "Mō."
He recited the *Prajñāpāramitā* and circumambulated the sacred site three times. Now tell me: when Prajñā manifests before one, where does ignorance reside?
If Jiangruo can, within this very sound, realize that the past mind cannot be found, and the present and future minds cannot be found—Ei!
The flowing water before the gate is forever inexhaustible; infinite fish and dragons sing along.
*The Partridge (A Requiem for Layman Shen Shaojiang)* Since the passing of Confucius, Mencius alone has been the one who fully expounded his teachings. Why is this so?
It is because Mencius attained the heart of Confucius. If one asks how to seek the heart of Confucius, one need only seek it in Mencius.
Those who seek the mind of Mencius need only seek it within themselves. Once one’s own mind is attained, the minds of Confucius and Mencius are attained.

How is one’s own mind to be sought? It should be sought within daily life. Although human desires are numerous during daily life, they do not go beyond the adverse, the favorable, the deluded, and the dissipated.
What is meant by the "adverse"? All things that are contrary to one's will are [the adverse].

This is called "rebellion. To act in accordance with the Way is the opposite of this. What is meant by "obscurity"? It refers to encountering matters concerning the principles of the Way or hearing words concerning the principles of the Way, yet failing to respond with awe and exert oneself;
instead, one follows along with worldly habits and neglects them—this is all termed obscurity. What is meant by "indolence"?

It is to read the books of the sages and worthies without internalizing their meaning or putting them into practice; upon seeing virtuous people or gentlemen, one fails to exercise self-restraint, allowing the mind to wander toward the realm of desire.
When the divine mind soars aloft that one does not give rise to the thought of returning of its own accord, this is universally termed "indolence.

If you, sirs, can resolutely apply yourselves with vigor at these four critical junctures, then governing the universe, rectifying the common people, achieving merit for your time, and leaving a fragrance for a thousand ages will not be difficult—how much less so the attainment of a single degree before your eyes? Yet, to seek this [state beyond] indolence...
Regarding the mind, what is most important is knowing where it arises. If it arises from the Way and righteousness, exert all your strength to cultivate and fulfill it;
if it arises from that which is contrary to the Way and righteousness, exert all your strength to restrain it. The essential point of such restraint lies further in first awakening to one’s own mind.

If one’s own mind is not awakened, though one may forcibly constrain it, it will ultimately be difficult to uproot its source. Once the root is not uprooted, if one’s diligent practice slackens even slightly, the sprouts of human desire will burst forth.

However, it is difficult to suppress. You must, at every moment—whether dressing or eating, whether engaged in food, drink, or sexual desire, whether welcoming guests or attending to visitors, or even when defecating or urinating—in all your activities, examine this mind:

does it arise from yourself, or does it arise from external objects? If it arises from yourself, does it arise from within the body, or does it arise from outside the body? Does it arise from the body...?
[Question: How is it that the five viscera are not seen to arise outside the body? If they were to arise externally, they would have no connection whatsoever with oneself;
it would be like another person eating food—I certainly would not be satiated by it. If they were to arise from external objects, there would be no "self" to respond to them.

Since the mind is fundamentally non-existent, if there is no self to respond yet objects can still give rise to the mind, then why [does a puppet not feel pain] when bells and chimes are struck beside it?

Do you not see that which gives rise to the mind? Although the mind is illusory and unfathomable, appearing and disappearing without fixed time, it does not exist outside the realm of "self" and "other.
If one seeks the mind apart from self and other, it is like splashing waves in search of water. If one identifies self and other as the mind, it becomes like mistaking a thief for one's own son.
Neither is it the mind when separated from them, nor is it the mind when identified with them; ultimately, it is as [it is].
"What is this mind?"—ponder this deeply. Through true accumulation and sustained effort over time, one day there will be a sudden, expansive awakening.
Then, the efficacy of Mencius’s "seeking the lost mind" will be realized without even needing to look to Mencius himself (from the *Instruction to Disciples* on "Seeking the Lost Mind").
The Collected Works of the Elder Zibo, Volume Five;
The Collected Works of the Elder Zibo, Volume Six.
Read by Hanshan Deqing of the Ming Dynasty.
The Dharma says:

"That which you perceive and that which is like empty space both pervade the worlds of the ten directions. One cannot select space to set it apart from perception, nor can one select perception to set it apart from space.
For space and perception necessarily exist in mutual dependence; therefore, it is said that 'space and perception are undivided.'"

"Space exists but has no substance; vision exists but has no cognition. Space does not exist of itself; it must depend upon form (*rūpa*) to be manifested. Therefore, it is said that "space exists but has no substance.
Vision does not arise of itself; its arising depends on the dust of space. It suddenly illuminates an object, like a mirror reflecting an image, initially devoid of discrimination.
Therefore, it is said that "vision exists but has no cognition. This belongs to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). If it slightly involves cognitive awareness, it falls into inference (*anumāna*).
It is measured (shown to Cigong).

Before joy or anger has manifested, the nature is fundamentally complete. Once joy or anger has manifested, what is expressed does not exceed [the bounds of that nature] and does not deviate from its unmanifested state.
This is what is called harmony. If there is even the slightest partiality, it is called disharmony. When there is harmony, auspiciousness gathers in abundance;

when there is disharmony, ten thousand transgressions arise in profusion. When auspiciousness gathers in abundance, one shares the same spiritual lineage as the Buddhas, Patriarchs, Sages, and Worthies.
When ten thousand transgressions arise in a surge, one shares the same habits as all manner of evil beings.

Once these habits have become deeply ingrained, even if one were to take heaven and earth as a furnace, yin and yang as charcoal, the Creator as the laborer, and Vairambha winds as the bellows, it would still be difficult to refine and transform them.
Thereupon, the Great Awakened One borrows the waters of emptiness to wash them away; for such is the nature of sentient beings.
Those who are biased and perverse do not go beyond the matters of food, drink, and sex. When these are accorded with their proper order, they become auspicious;

when they are not accorded with their proper order, they become faults and perversities. Faults and perversities summon only suffering. When there is suffering, the spirit becomes terrified and the soul and spirit (hun-pei) become disordered.
Yet one fails to realize that when joy and anger have not yet been aroused, one is identical to our Buddhas and Patriarchs. Therefore, to be perverse in the face of anger is a grave error.
Those who are arrogant become asuras; those who are deluded and foolish become animals; those who are stingy become hungry ghosts; and those who are evil become denizens of hell.
Only gods and humans are fortunate, and this is solely due to the ten wholesome actions and the five precepts. These are what are called the six realms of existence.
Yet, even if one is a god, if one does not awaken, one may fall to become a human; and even if one is a human, if one does not awaken, one may likewise [fall].

They regard these as mere possessions. If such are the manifold obscurations, there has never been one who sought to restore their true nature without first cleansing them with the water of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Yet they fail to realize that there are three [types of delusion]: first, the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*); second, the afflictions like grains of sand (*rajas-aṇu*); and third, ignorance (*avidyā*).
All beings possessing blood and breath suffer because of these three; thus they fail to attain the Path of the Sages, failing to penetrate the principle and failing in their practice.

If one does not achieve integration, one will not be proficient on the Way. When one penetrates [reality], there is nowhere one cannot reach; when one achieves integration, there is no circumstance that can obstruct one.
When one is proficient, one unifies both emptiness and existence without being burdened by them. Such wondrous function is thus spontaneously perfected in each and every instance.

Now, within the daily lives of us people, likes and dislikes accumulate by the billions, and the mountains of "self" and "other" are as high as peaks. To follow these tendencies brings joy and delight.
If one opposes this, one becomes abruptly displeased. Once joy and anger arise, the *lingtai* (the spiritual terrace) immediately becomes obscured.

When the *lingtai* is obscured, upon seeing forms, one is deluded by form; upon hearing sounds, one is confused by sound. Whether it be fragrance or stench, sweetness, bitterness, astringency, or smoothness, or even the shadows of the good and the bad—all these arise from sensory dust triggering cognition.
When cognition is deluded, it becomes perverse. Being perverse is to deviate from the True. [It remains] as a single, round mass.
[It is] clear. The six consciousnesses are shattered; since they have become consciousness, one reckons the body as the self. Men and women deceive one another; food and drink nourish one another.
The waves of emotion surge vast and wide; their turbulent flow is never constant. Upon this stinking skull, within the pit of delusive thoughts, one produces all manner of foul secretions.
Heaven cannot cover them; earth cannot support them. Bound in obscurity for long kalpas, the physical form undergoes transformation and ascends.
Sunk in ten thousand states of being, its suffering is so intense it is difficult to describe. If a person were bitten by a mosquito or a fly, they would still twitch and remain ill at ease;
can one whose mind remains unmoved upon hearing of such extreme agony be called the most sentient of beings? To speak of the essential point:
All intense suffering begins with non-awakening. Because of this non-awakening, one falsely clings to the existence of a body within that which has no body;
one falsely perceives the existence of a mind within that which has no form. Once one perceives the existence of body and mind, one fails to realize that what is solid is earth.
That which is moist is not perceived as water; that which is warm is not perceived as fire; that which moves is not perceived as wind;

sensation is not perceived as being caused by objects; perception is not perceived as being caused by sensation; mental formations are not perceived as being caused by perception; and consciousness is not perceived as being caused by mental formations.
Thus, one is firmly attached to the eight dharmas of subject and object. At the critical junctures of death and birth, honor and disgrace, gain and loss, there is but a slight [awareness].
When one commits an offense, the soul and spirit tremble with terror; the hair stands on end and the bones grow cold. This is due to nothing other than a failure to understand.

[One realizes that] solidity returns to earth, moisture returns to water, warmth returns to fire, movement returns to wind, sensation returns to objects, perception returns to sensation, mental formations return to perception, and consciousness returns to mental formations. Once these powers are returned to their source, what was unconscious becomes conscious.
However, at the very moment of returning to the source, tell me: where, after all, do the so-called body and mind usually reside?
If one penetrates this point through and through, then ten thousand adversities can be transformed into auspiciousness, and disharmony can be transmuted into harmony.
The body will pervade the eight directions without affliction, and wisdom will encompass all things without toil. This gate of contemplation takes emptiness as its path.
A journey of a thousand *li* begins with a single step. Emptiness is not the Way; the Way is one’s own home mountain. Now tell me: when the impoverished son returns home, whose tune does he sing?
Heh! When cutting a lamp, one does not borrow another’s strength; there is more than enough light to illuminate the ten directions.
(Shown by Yuan Guangkongguan)
"When standing, one should be as if waiting upon a great guest; when in a carriage, one should be as if attending upon the Most Honored One.

These two lines from the *Book of Documents* can be recited without moving the tip of the tongue, spitting them out whole. While such a respectful demeanor is indeed good, it has not yet reached the pinnacle of beauty.
*Pah!* A single radiance of mind is forever unclouded; amidst a pack of tigers and wolves, there is nothing but spring breeze. (Shown to Wu Yuanshi)
Spontaneous and all-pervasive knowing is the light that originally has no dependence. When conceptualization suddenly arises, subject and object stand in stark opposition.
Now, if all sentient beings wish to restore this light of non-dependence, they must establish great resolve and give rise to the great mind from within the state of dependence;
otherwise, the original light will not easily be restored. Why is this? It is because knowledge that depends on conditions is limited merely to the span of six feet.
Beyond six feet, separated by a single sheet of paper, one becomes abruptly insentient. Not only is one unaware when separated by a membrane beyond six feet;
even within those six feet, regarding things such as the hair, body hair, nails, and teeth, one remains unaware once they are cut away.
If we, like us, seek the Unsurpassed Way, should we not do so by employing this consciousness that spans the six feet?
Is it that you seek what is not to be used? If you seek by employing this [knowledge], how could the six-foot-tall wisdom of the Buddha possibly seek it?
If you do not seek by means of this, then we would be like wood or stone if we were to discard this knowledge while seeking the Unsurpassed Way.
If this could be sought, then all insentient things would be able to seek the Way. Therefore it is said:

"The student of the Way does not recognize the Real, solely because they have recognized the spirit of consciousness from of old. This spirit of consciousness is merely the six-foot-long awareness of the physical body.
To seek [the Way] outside of this is further to sit in the difficulty of insentient things seeking the Way. Thus, I have investigated this with great pain (shown to Master Bu).
If the mind is not nurtured by principle, then what it perceives will lack spiritual efficacy; it is like a fish that is not nurtured by water—the growth resulting will not be that of a dragon.
The Perfected Person knows these two factors must mutually nourish one another for the work of cultivation to be completed.

Therefore, they serve every dust-mote world without weariness in their diligence, yet they follow the single truth without becoming intoxicated by quiescence. Nevertheless, from the very beginning, they do not rely on emptiness or stillness.

If you act for yourself alone, you cannot avoid being burdened by this seven-foot frame. If you do not take luminous awareness as your own mind, you cannot avoid being dragged along by攀緣 (pān-yuán, objective attachments).
Because of emptiness and stillness, death, birth, calamity, and fortune come upon you unexpectedly, like clouds striking a rock.

Because of luminous awareness, likes and dislikes, the public and the private, are inverted, like wind wandering through space. If you truly have the aspiration for the Great Matter, [you must realize this].
If these two [the ruler and the subject] become negligent and fail to feel urgency; if they feel urgency but lack constancy;

or if they remain constant yet fail to transform themselves—then the succession of the past and the opening of the future will cease, and the seeds of the sages and worthies will be severed. Should this occur, then heaven, earth, and the myriad things will all lose their refuge.
How could such a thing be possible? (To the monk Shifa Zhong:
In the past, in the city of Vaiśālī, there was the layman Vimalakīrti who taught the Dharma while ill and delivered immeasurable multitudes.
Now, can the Master of Tonglu likewise teach the Dharma while ill and deliver immeasurable multitudes? If he cannot deliver immeasurable [beings],...
The multitude was thus turned by the illness. The Buddha said, "If one can turn things, one is identical to the Tathāgata.
I then remarked, "If one can turn the illness, one is identical to Vimalakīrti. If one cannot turn it, then Vimalakīrti’s nostrils are in Daguān’s hands. Nevertheless, tell me:
does this illness exist within the four elements of solidity, warmth, moisture, and motion? Or does it exist apart from these four? If...
Regarding this illness arising from solidity, warmth, moisture, and motion: solidity belongs to the earth element; moisture belongs to the water element; warmth belongs to the fire element;
and motion belongs to the wind element. Since these four each have their respective domains, does this body truly exist or not?
If it exists, then the illness must have a locus in the elements; if it does not exist, where then is the root of the illness? Master, take advantage of this moment.
One must thoroughly investigate where the root of illness lies; then, whether it be birth, death, or neither birth nor death, there is nothing particularly extraordinary about them.
Whether it be life itself or death itself, there is nothing that is not a good thing. Alas! Since the body is the very foundation of suffering, what need is there to speak further?
To whom does the illness belong when the four great elements disperse? (Shown to Layman Xiang at Dongyuan during his illness.

Now, a bell does not strike itself; it strikes because it is struck by another. A person does not lead themselves; they ring because they are made to ring. One does not hear for oneself; one hears because of hearing.
Thus, it requires the union of three before there is ringing, and the union of five before there is hearing. This is the common condition of all people. How much more so for you!
One does not know that apart from the three, there is no sounding; apart from the five, there is no hearing.
Since each of the three lacks sounding and each of the five lacks hearing, how could the combination of the three and five produce sounding and hearing?

Now, if the combination of the three and five results in neither sounding nor hearing, then as for this "sounding-sounding" and "hearing-hearing," is there truly sounding and hearing, or is there truly no sounding and hearing? At this point, one becomes thoroughly enlightened.
Once this is understood, delusion will exhaust itself without needing to be pursued to its end, and the Real will accord with itself without needing to be sought after.

When delusion is exhausted and the Real is accorded with, if one examines its efficacy, it is not because the great circle acts as teacher, nor because the striking acts as practitioner, nor can it be led by any person.
Thus, when we enter the state of non-arising through the conditions of arising, from what source does this efficacy arise? Yet, if one seeks this efficacy...

When a bell is struck, if the person were not there, the bell and the striking could not produce sound on their own. Conversely, if the bell and the striking were not present, the person could not cause the bell to ring.
Examining this through successive reasoning, if one seeks the efficacy in the bell and the striking, there is no efficacy without the person;

if one seeks the efficacy in the person, there is likewise no efficacy without the bell and the striking. Since both the agent and the object lack inherent efficacy, efficacy itself has nothing upon which it depends.
When merit is without dependence, it is called "merit without merit. The former sages termed this "inner succession" (neishao).
Merit that involves effort is termed "outer succession" (waishao). Alas! When the three are obscured, there is "sounding"; when the five begin to be obscured, there is "hearing.

If sounding were not an obscuring of the three, and hearing were not an obscuring of the five, then in the very act of sounding and hearing, there would fundamentally be no subject or object. Therefore—
To preach the Dharma without speaking—how could the Dharma ever be exhausted? Should one encounter conditions yet fail to realize them, then root and object will inevitably clash;
because of this, one loses the light of insight and cannot avoid falling into the cycle of continuity and mutual dependence. Therefore it is said: "You should listen in this manner."
One should not listen in such a manner. However, Master Po, though a high-ranking official by profession, was free and unimpeded in his preaching of the Dharma.
He was like a luminous pearl rolling about, moving freely across a golden platter; its course could not be gauged by the four corners.
Had he not attained the samādhi of the non-attainment of phenomena and the samādhi of the non-attainment of principles, he would have been unable to avoid [entanglement].
As soon as the seams of his mouth open, he is left bewildered by the facts and principles. Some may deride Dongpo for his "literary Chan," claiming his sermons are rife with conceptual obstructions;
yet I know they have not even dreamed of meeting Master Dongpo (as shown in his *Inscription on the Bell at Fayun Temple for Yuan Yi*).
Now, if a bell is suspended but not struck, or if it is struck but there is no striker, then the bell and the striking cannot produce sound together.
It is only when these three factors coincide that the bell finally rings. Thus, before the bell has rung, one does not hear it by oneself; one must rely upon the ringing for it to be heard.
If we consider the ringing, the hearing, and the preceding three factors, then hearing does not occur until five things have coincided. If even one of these is missing, hearing will not take place.
One can hear; this may be known. It is only after the five [senses] have combined that there is hearing. When there is hearing, does that hearing truly possess hearing?
Or is it without hearing? If it possesses hearing, then hearing should be fivefold. If it is without hearing, then how is it any different from a wooden puppet?
Only when there is hearing yet no hearing is there nothing that is not heard. When there is nothing that is not heard, then hearing has no location. Since hearing has no location, then the eye and...

The nose, tongue, and body are all capable of hearing; how could it be that only the ear can hear? If this were so, then at the very moment of hearing, hearing itself would fundamentally be without hearing.
Since hearing is fundamentally without hearing, to claim that there is sound or no sound is an error.

Alas! The multitude are in a state of turmoil; they bind their ears and yet are able to hear. When the great sphere resounds, or when a reclining scholar strikes the instrument, can one say there is no hearing?

However, without the merit of being drawn forth by a person, these two would be useless. Even if they rely on a person to draw them forth, if those two were not subtle, what merit could the person possess?
By inferring this through mutual dependence, neither has any merit. Because they have no [independent] merit, there is nothing they do not accomplish as merit.
Thus, the great circle and the mark of the broad, long tongue cover the entirety of the ten voids and preach inexhaustible Dharma; yet it is not by means of the eye.

I have heard this. Who can grasp the profound meaning? Furthermore, as for the "lying person" and the "person with a tongue": is it the tongue itself? Or is it not the tongue? If it is the tongue, then the tongue does not strike the tongue;
if it is not the tongue, then the tongue cannot reach everywhere. An ancient worthy said: "To call it a bamboo stick is to encounter it;
not to call it a bamboo stick is to turn one's back on it. Now, when we investigate the characteristics of the tongue, it is precisely these characteristics of the tongue that are overturned.
It has become nothing more than a bamboo rattle. Viewed from this perspective, it cannot help but obstruct and block people throughout the world.

Therefore, those who ask the frontier guards whether they may pass have not yet crossed the barrier. Those who are accustomed to passing through the barrier naturally walk with their arms swinging; would they ever deign to ask again?
If one has not yet crossed the barrier, how can saying "hearing is not listening" be considered hearing, and saying "listening is not hearing" be considered listening? What is the meaning of this?
Is it not like carving up empty space, contending over its volume and disputing its fatness or leanness?

(Shi Yuan-yi) That which is called the six directions—up, down, and the four quarters—is termed the "six realms" (*ṣaḍ-dig*). That which are the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind are termed the "six faculties" (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).
To hold that the directions are absolutely unchangeable and the faculties are absolutely inviolable, and thus to call oneself a "multitude," is to be ignorant of the birth of the directions.
Within the directionless, the root arises from the rootless. Even if one were to know this, could the directions and the roots then be changed?
Could the fruits not be disordered? Nevertheless, it is only the Sage who dwells within the directions yet is not changed by the directions;
he relies upon the roots yet is not moved by the roots. Thus, he can invert up and down, reverse seeing and hearing, and point to the earth as heaven.
To point to heaven as earth, to see forms with the ears, and to hear sounds with the eyes—these cannot be achieved through non-action (this demonstrates the principle of contemplation).
"When birth and death have ceased, quiescent extinction is bliss. This half-verse was composed by our Great Hero when he manifested his parinirvāṇa at the Twin Śāla Trees.
Since ancient times, various masters have offered many interpretations; some explain it according to the *śrāvaka* teachings as the cessation of birth and death, while others...

There is the arising-and-ceasing and tranquil-extinction of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao); there is the arising-and-ceasing and tranquil-extinction of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao); and there is the arising-and-ceasing and tranquil-extinction of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

In the Treasury Teaching (Zangjiao), one necessarily negates the waves of arising-and-ceasing, taking the stillness of stilled water as bliss. In the Shared Teaching, one takes the realization that the waves are themselves the water as bliss.
In the Distinct Teaching, one takes the convergence of the waves into the water, the water returning to become the waves, and the state of being neither wave nor water as bliss.

This is what constitutes joy. In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), a single wave is such that there is no water that is not a wave, and a single drop of water is such that there is no wave that is not water.

To find joy in the fact that where there is neither wave nor water, there is nowhere that is not wave or water—this being so, when one takes up a single object and realizes its universal correspondence with all phenomena, they all fully embody the essential intent of the Four Teachings.
It depends entirely upon whether the person is skillful or unskillful in their mastery, and skillful or unskillful in their application.
It is simply a matter of skillful application. The Daoist of Penetrating Observation is not like this; he has a separate path for his own emergence.
I ask those with the karmic affinity to quickly take up this recommendation. What is "When birth-and-death have ceased, my finger extends"?
What is "To dwell in quiescent extinction is bliss, my finger retracts"? Extension and retraction are both my finger; yet they are also apart from my finger.
Neither identical nor separate; yet it is both identical and separate. There are sinews within the eyes and bone within the bone.

If a man of keen nature can bite through this, then the Buddhas of the three periods of time shall become his slaves and servants, and the patriarchs of successive generations shall become his oxen and horses for him. If he cannot bite through it, then [it remains as it is].
It is well to turn toward the Great View (Daguān). Seek a clear understanding beneath the staff of chestnut wood. Be careful, be careful! (To Zhīrěn):
This body is originally nothing but blood, flesh, sinews, and bones, along with mucus, saliva, lymph, vital warmth, and the moving winds.
It is through the gathering and temporary conjunction of these that this appearance arises. If you can recognize and thoroughly penetrate this appearance, you will attain the true body.
The excellence of the True Body is neither born nor does it die; it is pure, dry, and clean.

It is not like the physical body, which undergoes birth and death, possesses illness and suffering, and experiences both diligence and indolence—all such various sufferings are brought forth by this impure body of flesh and blood.
One should constantly, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, contemplate and examine within the body, specifically upon the five viscera.
Below the five viscera and within the five viscera, investigate each one individually: where is the liver? Where is the lungs?
Where are the intestines? Where is the stomach? What is stored within the intestines? What is stored within the stomach?
Observe these until you see them clearly and can visualize them with clarity. Furthermore, you should observe [the body] from the feet up to...
The knees: how many joints of bone are there? From the knees upward, how many joints of bone are there?

From the front of the chest to the crown of the head, one observes them in various ways. What constitutes the diaphragm? What constitutes the throat? What constitutes the head? And what is within the head?
Examining again and again, scrutinizing from top to bottom, each part is seen as clearly as the lines on the palm of one's hand, as if in a mirror.
When you face [this truth], it is clear and distinct. Naturally, all sufferings will gradually subside and attachments will gradually dissolve;

these are all the wondrous contemplations of the body. Therefore, it is said: "Contemplate the body and grow weary of its form. This body is a seed of suffering. Fools cling to it, but the wise truly loathe it.
Believe this deeply, believe this deeply! Do not neglect it, do not neglect it! If you neglect it and do not rely [upon it]...
I have applied myself with diligent effort and used all my strength in contemplation. Presently, various ailments pursue one another; once dead, a human body is difficult to obtain again.
My most sincere wishes, my most sincere wishes! All that has been described above constitutes the contemplation of the body, not the contemplation of the mind.
If one were to speak of the merit of contemplating the mind compared to contemplating the body, its merit would surpass the latter ten thousandfold. [This begins] at dawn this morning.
Coming and going, managing all manner of affairs, one is so busily occupied that there is no rest.
With hesitation and affliction in the heart, one does not know how many times one has risen within a single hour. At night, in dreams, there are chaotic and confused visions;
sorrows, joys, partings, and reunions do not differ in the slightest from those of the day. For this reason, the human spirit is withered and exhausted. If one could...
Discern this mind: from where does it arise? Examine it until you understand clearly. Then all roots of suffering will undoubtedly be uprooted and severed.

When first beginning the observation, first observe this discriminating mind that distinguishes between good and evil. Is this deluded dreaming born from external objects, or is it born from within itself?
If it were born from external objects, it would not arise when I am without perception; if it were born from within itself, [it would arise even when there are no external objects].

When the object does not contact me, this mind does not arise. Furthermore, this mind takes the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) as its root. Because there is the aggregate of feeling, there is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).

Because there is the aggregate of perception, there is the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Because there is the aggregate of mental formations, there is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

These are called the four aggregates. "Aggregate" (*skandha*) has the meaning of accumulation. However, when these four aggregates are thoroughly analyzed and broken down, the aggregate of feeling [is seen to be empty], and the other three aggregates naturally [follow suit].
It is not produced. What is the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*)? To experience an object is called sensation. There are six kinds of objects: the eye takes form as its object;
the ear takes sound as its object; the nose takes fragrance and odor as its object; the tongue takes flavor as its object; the body takes the sphere of touch as its object;
and the mind takes the reflections of the five spheres as its object. Therefore, there are six sensations corresponding to the six objects.

Thus it is said. When the single [false] reception is thoroughly destroyed, all receptions are consequently eliminated. Therefore it is said: "By observing the body through the four great elements, one immediately attains the true body;
by observing the mind through the four aggregates, one immediately attains the true mind. The true body has no birth or death; the true mind has no good or evil.
Although it is said there is no good or evil, this is not like wood or stone, which are utterly devoid of cognition. It is rather like a bright mirror: when objects come...
Self-illumination: although beauty and ugliness are distinguished, fundamentally there is no mind that illuminates.

If you can perform this contemplation, not only will you enjoy merit, longevity, peace, and happiness in the present life, but it will not be difficult for you to become a Buddha or an Ancestor. My words are not false. Give rise to a fierce faith! If my words were false, my tongue shall rot.
If you do not believe me, you shall suffer the consequences. May all holy ones and ordinary beings bear witness!
These words are truly fearsome, truly fearsome (addressed to Layman So-and-so).
Now, the habits of killing, stealing, lust, lying, drinking alcohol, and eating meat have no inherent nature from the beginning. Because they lack an inherent nature, they cannot awaken themselves;
one must wait to encounter conditions before awakening to their lack of nature. Once one awakens to this lack of nature, one can then tread upon both hatred and love.
This is the field where one encounters the realm of birth and death. When this awareness is not obscured, it is like a wind-extinguishing jewel cast into the great ocean;

the waves gradually subside. This is what is meant by the "five habits returning before they have gone far. For anyone who is a child of the Buddha, it is vital to know this first when receiving the precepts at the outset of their practice.
To know this is called the "precept of nature" (dharmatā-śīla); not to know it is called the "precept of phenomena" (vyañjana-śīla). As for nature and phenomena...
If it is ice and water, fundamentally there is no difference between them. When melted, it is called water; when frozen, it is called ice.
Therefore, if one first knows the precepts of nature (xingjie), then all precepts of phenomena (shijie) are such that there is no phenomenon that is not of the nature.
This is just like knowing that ice is water; then there is no ice that is not water. Zhitán, Zhitán, that you have given rise to this mind is truly rare. This is the initial aspiration.

It is like the first day of the third month, which eventually reaches full completion. Although this is so, Jñānasāgara, if you have not yet known the precepts of nature (*dharmatā-śīla*), you should for now observe the precepts of phenomena (*dharma-śīla*).
Through the long-term accumulation and cultivation of these precepts of phenomena, the nature of awakening will eventually be opened.

As for the precepts of phenomena, there are the fundamental precepts of phenomena, the śrāmaṇera precepts of phenomena, and the bhikṣu precepts of phenomena. Jñānasāgara, you should receive them first.

The five fundamental precepts provide the foundation for the subsequent precepts. As for the five fundamental precepts: first, not to kill living beings, and so forth (the conferral of the *Jītán* precepts).
In early spring, the lay practitioner Zhengguang offered firecrackers as an offering to the Triple Gem. Consequently, he had three attendants test the fire;
each one produced a sound like a thunderclap that shatters the heat. Suddenly, I recalled the Buddha’s instruction to Rāhula:
"When the bell is struck, it has sound; when not struck, it has no sound. This is merely what ordinary minds conceive. If one were to listen with the eyes...
Thus, when it is struck, there is never sound; when it is not struck, there is never no sound.
For example, whether a firecracker is set off or not, "sound" and "no sound" are both merely dualistic expressions. If one cuts off these two extremes while sitting, how could there even be a middle?
You, the great assembly here before me, listen to the sound of this firecracker with this very awareness, and then this sound is none other than Old Master Dadao.
"Chinese. This refers to the mark of the broad and long tongue. Nevertheless, it can be discussed with those who know how to speak of such things;
as for those who do not know how to speak of them, they have not even dreamed of it (he burns a firecracker and shows it to the assembly).
If one sleeps without dreaming, and if there truly were no self, then who would be the master of the inhalation and exhalation?
If you claim there is a self, where is this self located? Failing to understand how dreams are made, one suddenly finds oneself at a loss as to their origin.

One must earnestly set aside all external conditions, such that a single thought lasts for ten thousand years and ten thousand years are contained within a single thought; only by seeking this point of origin can one properly deliberate upon this matter.

As for this matter: if one comes with a spontaneous impulse and departs when that impulse has spent itself, yet wishes to use a mind of discursive thought to speculate upon it—even if one were to possess some partial understanding—it would all be like casting a net into the wind; it is merely laborious toil with no gain.

Since you, Master Nian, have come from afar and have already shown your concern for many days, I dare not disregard your sincere intention; therefore, I have waited specifically until the people were quiet.
I ask you this myself: You should reflect that old age and sickness come without appointment; time cannot be toyed with.

When one attains fame and fortune, it is no different from wearing flowers in one's hair in a dream. When one loses fame and fortune, it is no different from the flowers worn in a dream being withered and fallen by wind and rain.
One sighs at how easily the flowers fade and then awakens; having awakened, one looks back upon the flowers worn in the dream.

When flowers wither in a dream, upon waking, who is it that wore them? Who is it that saw them wither? When one awakens and knows who wore them and who saw their withering, who again is it that knows this?
Pushing the inquiry back to the time before there was a "self," from where did this "self" suddenly come?
Now that the "self" exists, I am unable to turn things; instead, I am ultimately turned by things. Ultimately, where does the root of this sickness lie? If you investigate...
When the root of illness is extracted, it is well to wear flowers; it is well for the flowers to wither. It is well to have delusive thoughts with eyes open;
it is well to dream with eyes closed. It is well not to dream; it is well to see the Wayman; it is well not to see the Wayman.

It is well to praise the man of the Way; it is also well to slander the man of the Way. If one does not apply restraint, neither the Confucian, nor the Daoist, nor the Buddhist has any share [in the Way].
This is the truth. Yet, if one is heavily shrouded by dark karma, one will simply lack the faith to believe it.
If one's dark karma is light, who would not feel pain upon seeing these words or hearing them? (To Shi Ma Xinfu:

Throughout thousands of sutras and ten thousand treatises, it is taught that [the enlightened state] is free from body and mind. Therefore, to perceive the existence of body and mind is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*);
to see no body or mind is precisely great wisdom (*mahāprajñā*). Alas! Ignorance and wisdom are fundamentally not two separate things; it is merely a matter of whether one follows one's own emotions.

When body and mind manifest before one and emotional attachments dissolve, body and mind become vast and empty. When body and mind manifest before one, birth-and-death and afflictions arrive without waiting;
when body and mind are no longer perceived, nirvana and bodhi are realized immediately without seeking. (This reveals the compassionate heart.)

Among the great burdens of human life, none exceed those of body and mind. Therefore, after the sages first brought their own bodies and minds under control, they subsequently opened up things and accomplished affairs.
It is like moving a jar from outside [the house]: once the jar is moved, not only one jar can be moved.

Even if there were hundreds of thousands of jars, one could command others to transport them; there would still be surplus strength remaining. Why then trouble oneself with carrying them? People differ from this:
they are like those whose bodies are confined within a jar, yet who wish to move the jar. Even a single jar would be difficult for them to move, let alone many jars.
Furthermore, in governing the body and cultivating the mind, one must first strive to exhaustively understand the beginning and end of both body and mind; only then...
One can indeed cure it. However, if one attempts to treat it recklessly without investigating its beginning and end, one will ultimately fail.

Now, the body is coarse and easy to investigate, whereas the mind is subtle and difficult to investigate; therefore, one first investigates that which is easier by practicing the contemplation of the body as separate from itself.
Once this has gradually matured, one then investigates that which is subtle, and then even the mind will not be difficult to investigate. What is the meaning of "body"?
The body takes "aggregation" as its meaning. What is the meaning of "mind"? The mind takes "adherence" as its meaning; thus it is said that "to leave" (li) is to "adhere" (li).

Viewed from this perspective, one must first aggregate the five elements and the four great constituents before the body is subsequently formed. When the object has not yet appeared before one, [the mind does not arise].
Thus, the mind cannot exist independently; it must necessarily be stimulated by an object before it has something to which it may attach.
The verse of Viśvabhū Buddha says: "One borrows the four great elements to form a body; the mind is originally without birth, arising only because of objects.
This accords perfectly with the principle that the body exists after the aggregation [of elements], and the mind exists only after attachment. Yet ordinary people do not [perceive this].
One may master the subtlety of written words and language, yet be obstructed by those very words and language.
Thus, that which was penetrating becomes blocked; that which is blocked cannot penetrate. If you understand this well, what obstruction is not penetration, and what penetration is not subtlety?
The Lamp of Wisdom comes before you; I speak to you: you must exhaustively investigate the reasons for the beginning and end of body and mind. Therefore...
However, once you have attained it, the cultivation of body and mind will be like bending the ring finger: the only difficulty lies in being unwilling to bend it.

If one is willing to bend it, what is there that cannot be done? Zhideng encourages you: from this day forward, whenever you encounter the winds and waves of honor or disgrace, hold fast to the helm and maintain yourself with firm resolve;
do not allow yourself to be turned by external conditions. Then, while the body remains, you shall be free [from suffering].

Regarding the burden of birth and death, the mind possesses it yet remains free from the partiality of likes and dislikes. If one is cautious and embodies this principle, then even ten thousand jars may be moved with ease. (Shown to Zhideng)
The fire of hunger can be extinguished by food; the fire of desire is difficult to uproot with forms.

This is because one is no longer hungry when satiated by food, whereas there is no principle of satiety regarding forms. Although these two differ in their ease or difficulty, both arise equally from ignorance.
Thus it is said: "If ignorance is not destroyed, one returns to hunger even after being satiated. Desire, in the end, is difficult to satisfy. For this reason...
Observe this: all sinful karma necessarily has ignorance as its mother; all merit and wisdom arise from the clarity of one's own mind.
To clarify one's own mind, one must further take Prajñā as its mother.
Now, if there are those who view this mother as a stranger and yet consider themselves not ignorant, are they not the most foolish among the foolish?
There are those who can shatter jade disks worth a thousand pieces of gold, yet cannot help but let out a cry when their cooking pots are broken.
This is the distinction between having a mind and being without a mind. Therefore it is said: "To die with resolute indignation is easy; to meet righteousness with composure is difficult.
Is resolute indignation not having a mind? Is composure not close to being without a mind? Confucius said: "Examine the beginning and grasp the end; thus one knows life and death."
Regarding this doctrine: among all calamities and blessings, none are more profound than life and death. If one understands this doctrine, then calamity and blessing are but minor matters.
What is meant by "tracing the origin"? It is knowing why life arises. What is meant by "summarizing the end"? It is knowing why death occurs.
If one knows why life arises, what is there to rejoice in regarding life? If one knows why death occurs...
Then what cause for grief is there in death? Nevertheless, the sentiments of the multitude are clouded by the notion of a self (*ātman*);
this delusion is innate and has become so firmly established that it exceeds Mount Sumeru in its solidity. If one does not attain the Way, it is not easy to shatter such stubborn attachment.
When I read the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, I came upon the passage where the Tathāgata asks Subhūti: "If a good man or a good woman..."
"Suppose, Subhūti, that a person were to take this trichiliocosm and grind it into a mass of fine dust. What do you think? Would that multitude of atoms be numerous?
Subhūti replied, "It would be very numerous. At these words, I could not help but set down the scroll; hot tears flowed down my cheeks. For what reason?
I felt ashamed that since beginningless time, I have stubbornly clung to the notion of a unified whole, reckoning it to be truly existent, thereby exhausting myself.

The compassionate heart of the Perfect Man is so thorough and meticulous that he could shatter the trichiliocosm to clear away my clouds of delusion and strip away my attachments and stinginess—no different from melting lingering ice in the spring sea or touching a flake of snow to a red-hot furnace.
This kindness and this virtue are so profound and great that they are difficult to repay. Now that I have realized the oneness of all things, I place it within the trichiliocosm.
Within this, there is as if nothing exists; how much more so can the world be shattered?

When the Tathāgata says that the world is composed of subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*), this is identical to Zhongni’s [Confucius’s] "tracing back to the origin. When he says that the world can be shattered, this is identical to Zhongni’s "summarizing the end.

Yet, because those of the Black and White schools practice Confucianism without mastery of Confucianism, and practice Buddhism without mastery of Buddhism, they have failed to achieve a comprehensive synthesis.
Alas, how lamentable! Now, a jade disc worth a thousand pieces of gold may be shattered, yet one cannot help but let out a cry when a cauldron is broken—this is the nature of emotion (*qing*).

To know that the great trichiliocosm can be shattered and that minute dust particles can be joined to form a world—this is the nature of principle (*li*). Emotion involves the self and is thus obscured.

In principle, it is that which is without self yet possesses spiritual efficacy. Elder, I pray that you take this "Holy Incense" from this day forward as your vanguard, taking as your primary concern that which is without self yet spiritually efficacious.
In this way, you may not fail the profound compassion and earnest exhortation of the Tathāgata, the Sage. May you, Holy Incense, exert yourself with great diligence.
Now, evil has no magnitude, and goodness has no depth; yet when one acts with intention, the offense is great while the merit is slight. Why is this?
It is because one commits evil through ignorance; even if their transgressions are as vast as mountains, the gentleman examines their lack of intent.
One must still grant them leniency. Thus, among all things, there is nothing that is not better when free of intentional mind (*citta*). To perform good with an intentional mind entails attachment;
where there is attachment, there are limits. Only those who are without intentional mind act rightly; their initial merit is then equal to empty space.
Viewed from this perspective, even performing good with an intentional mind is inadmissible, let alone performing evil with an intentional mind.

The *I Ching* has a mind in its prohibitions; the *Laozi* likewise has a mind in its prohibitions. Yet, when one observes their images and examines their lines, it is not as if they have no mind from the start.
The *Laozi* also dares not take precedence over the world; that it "dares not"—is this not surely having a mind?
Therefore, there is both the state of having a mind and the state of being without a mind; only the sage utilizes them skillfully, such that there is no situation into which he cannot enter.
Were it not for the sage, not only does the state of having a mind entail error, but even the state of being without a mind is never free from error.
If this is so, how should a beginner cultivate their practice? Only one who can discern this may proceed to read the *I Ching* and the works of Laozi.
Now, one knows autumn when the leaves of the *wú* tree fall, and one knows spring when the *jiā*-tube ashes move.
Are the leaves of the *wú* tree and the ashes of the *jiā* tube not visible things? Are spring and autumn not likewise invisible?
Yet, if one relies solely on visible objects, that which is invisible will ultimately remain unseen. If the Sage did not use visible phenomena to perceive that which is invisible...
If this nature were thus, then nature would ultimately remain invisible. Now, if nature is invisible, then that which I inherently possess is entirely lost.
If that which I inherently possess is entirely lost, then even if I wish to stand within the Great Completeness and employ its functions, it will ultimately be impossible to alter this state;
the Way will also nearly come to an end. If the Way comes to an end, then [the principles of] Heaven and Earth and the myriad things...
If things exist, then heaven, earth, and the myriad things are all external to the *Yi*. Even the most ignorant would not believe this;
yet by this I know that nature has the substance of nature, nature has the function of nature, and nature has the appearance of nature.

What is meant by "substance"? It is that from which function emerges. What is meant by "function"? It is that from which appearance emerges. What is meant by "appearance"? It is that which is manifest and can be encountered.

These are the phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*). The conditions of suffering and pleasure, as well as goodness and evil, are these phenomena. That which is luminous and unclouded before the conditions of suffering and pleasure have even encountered [the mind] is the function (*vṛtti*).
Both the external phenomena and the function—whether they be manifest or luminous—all lack any source of origin; this is the essence (*tattva*).
Former sages held that while nature (*prakṛti*) is neither good nor evil, the emotions (*citta*) are good or evil; yet they did not realize that...
Nature is devoid of inherent nature, yet it possesses the functions of good and evil. Function is devoid of inherent nature, yet it manifests the appearances of good and evil.
If an infant falls into a well and a heart of compassion arises, this is the emotion of goodness.

In the interval between when this emotion is about to arise and when it has not yet arisen, it cannot be approximated by the presence or absence of auspiciousness or misfortune; rather, one fails to recognize it as the mind and consequently—
They identify the mind as the nature (xing). Consequently, the study of the nature and destiny (xing-ming) has become obscured and lost its clarity.

Even regarding the hexagrams and lines of the *Yi*, there are those who claim that the hexagram embodies the nature while the lines embody the emotions (qing); this, too, is a case of identifying the mind as the nature.
Now, there are sixty-four hexagrams, and within them the conditions of good fortune and misfortune are fully present yet not yet manifest.
Because they are fully present, they are not non-existent; because they are not yet manifest, they are not existent. Since they are not non-existent, they cannot be called "nature" (xing);
since they are not existent, they cannot be called "conditions" (qing). Since they can be called neither nature nor conditions, may we not call them "mind" (xin)? Thus, [the hexagrams are] six...
The fourteen hexagrams are the abodes of the mind; the three hundred and eighty-four lines are the expansive display of human emotions.

Thus, although the internal and external states of emotion and the mechanisms of fortune and misfortune are ever-shifting and irregular, they do not transcend the boundaries of the "inner" and "outer," nor the odd and even nature of the lines.

The inner represents the near and the intimate; the outer represents the distant and the estranged. Fortune approaches the good; misfortune approaches the evil. This distinction between the near and the distant...
The possession [of qualities] without self is the mind (*citta*). The possession [of qualities] with form is emotion (*qing*).

Now, as for the mind and emotion, the Way of the *I Ching* reaches its ultimate here. Yet that which is called "nature" (*xing*) prior to the mind cannot be approximated by the hexagrams or their lines.
However, to seek it apart from the hexagrams and lines is like seeking water apart from the waves. Nevertheless, as it is said:
Why is this? It is said: "This is not within my knowledge. One who knows it is not one who merely knows. For what reason?
It is because the nature does not know the nature, just as the eye cannot see itself.
Although religious traditions are divided into sects, they do not transcend the Buddha’s words and the Buddha’s mind.

Those who transmit the Buddha’s mind are called *chongju* (patriarchs), while those who transmit the Buddha’s words are called *kyoju* (founders). If one transmits the Buddha’s mind yet contradicts the Buddha’s words, it is not the true school.
If one transmits the Buddha’s words yet fails to clarify the Buddha’s mind, it is not the true teaching. Therefore, it is said: "Rely on the sūtras to explain the meaning."
To deviate from a single word of the sutras is to be at enmity with the Buddhas of the three periods.
To know that the body is lovable is one kind of knowledge; to know that the body is unobtainable is another. The former knowledge is established because the body is perceived as obtainable;
the latter knowledge is established because the body is perceived as unobtainable. The former knowledge is like a preceding step; the latter knowledge is like a succeeding step.
If the preceding step does not arise, how can the succeeding step be moved? The preceding step follows upon the succeeding step; step by step, they appear as if uninterrupted.

Prior awareness continues into subsequent awareness; this knowing and knowing appears as if indestructible. For one who begins their practice of contemplation at the initial stage, this awareness must not be neglected.

Painstakingly investigate until you know the source of knowing; once the source is known, knowing ceases of its own accord. When knowing ceases, it illuminates the myriad things; without effort, there is nothing that is not penetrated.

This very state of effortless ease is also called the virtue of *prajñā*. This virtue is constantly manifest before one, whether encountering adversity or favor, like snow being doused by boiling water.
Entering death and simultaneously giving birth, sovereign and inconceivable—this cannot yet be spoken of; one will know it for oneself upon reaching the end.
The tongue-board shakes and the heels turn; the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma revolves. Look back at the precious life and conceal it;
wait until you have attained its use before you may show the object (to the steadfast sage).

When a man’s family does not know how to respect themselves and becomes arrogant, there is no limit to what they will do. If they do not respect themselves, then external things become important while their own person becomes insignificant;

if they are not arrogant, then external things become great while they themselves become small. Thus, that which is heavy and great is treated with contempt by them, while that which is light and small they accept without refusal.
Indeed, as for that which is most heavy and most great—whether it belongs to the old or the young, the wise or the foolish—it is beyond all discrimination.
Fools! Who is it that does not possess [this]? It is merely because of slight fame, petty profit, fleeting glory, and trivial rank that they have been deceived and led astray.
Everyone’s original mind-light illuminates throughout the three periods of time (to Shi Mazishan).
Understanding is like fire; contemplation is like fuel. Without fuel, fire does not transform; without fuel, fire does not transmit.

Therefore, when an ordinary person of great resolve takes this very mind of burning affliction and suddenly opens the fire of perfect understanding, and takes this very mind of birth and death and gradually accords with the fire of understanding—just as an ordinary person first enters the stage of faith and proceeds through the ten stages of faith, completing the work of overcoming birth and death, they finally ascend to the first [stage].

Abiding in the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), one accomplishes the practice of non-arising and non-ceasing; it is only then that one first attains effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*). This meaning has long been obscure;
how could others possibly know it?
A man of raw iron who wishes to investigate and clarify this matter—regardless of whether he is wise or foolish—need only possess a resolute mind, and immediately, right here, [he shall attain it].
It is attained. Alas! At the moment when the dawn is breaking and during the interval between arising and ceasing, the head and face suddenly appear, yet as soon as one moves the eyes, they are lost.
Therefore it is said: "Within the shadows of the colored clouds, a divine immortal appears; holding a red silk fan, he covers his face.
One must urgently turn one's eyes to look at the immortal; do not look at the fan in the immortal's hand."
The light of the mind is fundamentally limpid; its wondrous substance is free from entanglement. Yet, by arbitrarily generating cognition and views, one loses that essential brilliance.

Consequently, visual consciousness clings to form, auditory consciousness clings to sound, olfactory consciousness clings to fragrance, gustatory consciousness clings to flavor, tactile consciousness clings to touch, and mental consciousness clings to phenomena.

Racing toward objects and flowing outward, each eventually forgets its return. Little do they realize that the five consciousnesses are but a single awakening; it is only the six [sense-faculties] that burn fiercely.

It is known. If the six [sense-faculties] are not ablaze, what fault is there in that awareness? Therefore it is said: initially abiding within the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), the superficial dust has not yet arisen;
later, falling into the realm of the cognitive faculty (*manas*), external forms remain hidden. Thus, while the awareness is complete, this [perception] is deficient.
One who is able to awaken can perceive that which arises from the depths: the pain at the juncture of favorable and adverse conditions, and the field of right and wrong, honor and disgrace.
With clarity and steadfastness, one observes all gain and loss as clouds striking a rock or wind passing through trees—utterly free of obstruction.

Only then does one begin to live up to being a true man and fulfill the standard of one who has left the household life. Were one to fail in this, life would be no better than death. To preserve [this integrity]...
If you realize this, that which was deficient becomes complete. When the deficient is made complete, even defecating and urinating are all Buddha-activities;
how much more so the offering of incense and tending the fire? (To Chan student Quan).
Han Xin and Bai Qi—whom among these ancients and moderns has not been acclaimed as a great general? Yet they were merely able to fight others, but unable to fight themselves.
To fight others is easy; to fight oneself is truly difficult. Fighting others is like grasping an object with one's hand; fighting oneself is like eye gazing into eye.
Contemplating such a state, how can one bring down the hand [of mastery]? Through long contemplation, one enters it. Suddenly—
The eighteen realms are swept away by the army of Māra; the five aggregates are overturned like a nest. Finding one moment of peace and permanence, one becomes a person of non-action for long kalpas.
Such a hero—compared to Han Xin and Bai Qi—is not merely like a gnat matching the Great Peng in size.
Truly white! Truly white! The day passes while practicing the perfection of vigor; yet the eighteen realms are not yet empty, and the five aggregates remain thick and heavy. Fatigue...
The ailment of my heart’s membrane has not yet healed; the dream of life and death has not yet awakened. How could I dare to follow along with worldly ways and live a life of mere expediency?
(To Di Mingshu) When a man sets his will, he must take up the practice from hardship. Success in one's vocation comes through difficulty.

The venomous poison of vanity and the lustrous pearl of serenity remain unchanged through wind and frost, ever fresh as the years accumulate. One expands the breast and mind beyond the realms of love and hate.
A Barrier. To store one’s spirit at the juncture of flourishing and decline; to honor wisdom in one’s conduct; to conceal a jade tablet while its luster remains;
to seek fellowship with those of antiquity and establish the principles of the One Mind within. Then Mount Kunlun may be uprooted, yet a fist-sized stone cannot be toppled.

If you can truly achieve this, you shall not have disgraced this meeting. As for those who block the light of the sun and moon beneath an overturned basin, exhausting themselves amidst wind and clouds—

To contemplate this within the seclusion of the inner chambers, yet be able to raise one's voice amidst the clusters of vermilion cassias and spread one's wings above the yellow dust—how could such a thing be possible? (Presented to Yunfu).
Ordinary people know to value life, yet they do not know the way to nourish it; thus, they are burdened by their very lives.
The Perfected Person knows the way to nourish life, which is rooted in non-birth; therefore, they can view life as non-birth, and through non-birth, they give rise to life.
In such life, there is no burden of material things. Alas! The eyes are burdened by forms, and the ears by sounds.
Accumulation. As for the mind being burdened by the seven emotions and five desires, one might still say, "Throughout my life I have been happy and free from burdens.
Little do they realize that this state of "freedom from burdens" has itself been a long-standing accumulation. This is because the desires of the multitude are heavy and their spirits clouded;
they sit through their transgressions without realizing it. It is like a drunkard lying in the midst of mud and mire; someone wakes him up and says, "This is mud..."
"It is muddy; it is no place for lying down. The drunkard stared with wide eyes and said in anger, "In my entire life, I have never understood drinking.
Why do you falsely accuse me? Today, everyone in the world suffers from the malady of the drunken man; how could there be anyone who is not drunk?"
And how could one not speak with them?
