Regarding the four—teaching, principle, practice, and fruit—these are the models for both the black and white ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

Just as with the black and white ordinary beings, there is no one who does not fall into the net of heterodoxy and the Lesser Vehicle unless they take these four as their model. "Heterodoxy" refers to those outside [the Buddhist fold].

The Way is this: on a small scale, it is the Two Vehicles; the teaching is the Perfect Teaching; the principle is the Perfect Principle; the practice is the Perfect Practice; and the fruit is the Perfect Fruit.
It is like the four Vedas and the five sciences, which are the teachings of external paths; it is like the Āgamas and other such teachings.

These are the teachings of the Two Vehicles, such as the *Avataṃsaka*, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, *Awakening of Faith*, and *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* teachings; these are the Final Teaching, the Sudden Teaching, and the Perfect Teaching.

Therefore, to give rise to the mind [of awakening] within the provisional or inferior vehicles is the seed of the provisional and inferior; to give rise to the mind within the Perfect Teaching is the seed for attaining Buddhahood.

Furthermore, there are three types of Buddha-nature: the Buddha-nature of the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*), the Buddha-nature of the cognitive cause (*vidyā-hetu*), and the Buddha-nature of the resultant cause (*phala-hetu*).

The Buddha-nature as the direct cause (*nidāna-hetu*). Although I inherently possess this Buddha-nature as the direct cause, it must necessarily await the Buddha-nature as the revealing cause (*vijñapti-hetu*) to open it.

While the revealing cause is able to open the Buddha-nature as the direct cause, it in turn must necessarily await the Buddha-nature as the conditioning cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) to stimulate and develop it.
Now, that which is the Buddha-nature as the conditioning cause is nothing other than the principle elucidated by the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). This Perfect Principle, in...

That which pertains to the stage of ordinary beings is called ignorance (*avidyā*). When it is incited by the fire of the principle of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*), this ignorance—by the power of being incinerated by the fire of the principle—is transformed, within a state of neither-knowing-nor-perceiving, into non-dusty wisdom (*araja-jñāna*);
this is termed the Buddha-nature as the cause of realization (*vidyā-hetu-buddhadhātu*). Once this non-dusty wisdom has reached the culmination of true accumulation of merit, [it is perfected].

This is called the unimpeded wisdom of the vajra. The unimpeded wisdom of the vajra is called the wisdom of suchness (*yathābhūta-jñāna*); it is not the wisdom of conventional measurement (*pramāṇa-jñāna*).

While the wisdom of conventional measurement can open up things for others and accomplish worldly tasks, thereby guiding those of beginner capacity, the wisdom of suchness is a wisdom that does not exist apart from reality.
Wisdom itself is fundamentally without effort; reality does not exist apart from wisdom. Because they accord with one another, there is no subjectivity; thus, wisdom and [reality]— [...are non-dual.]
Principle is like spring water; wisdom is like a swimming fish. The water has no pride in nourishing the fish, and the fish has no pursuit of delighting in the water.
Fish and water forget one another, yet they are nourished and swim together, naturally sharing in all things. Thus it is with the ordinary person at the stage of the initial mind.

Just as with gold, silver, copper, and iron, so it is with the teaching, principle, practice, and fruit. They are like a great furnace of a smith: gold, silver, copper, and iron must be melted and transformed therein.
If one does not rely upon a mold and pattern, yet desires to produce the images of Buddhas, patriarchs, sages, and worthies, it can never be achieved.

Therefore, the teaching must have a teacher; when the principle is opened, it becomes perfect. When the principle is perfect, practice is not biased. When practice is not biased, [the fruit is attained].

The ultimate fruit is fully perfected. Now, the *Avataṃsaka* is rich in its literary expression; the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is profound and subtle; the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* is esoteric and minute; and the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā* (or *Arya-bodhicittotpāda*) is concise and complete.
These four Dharma-treasures should each have one lot drawn from. Having washed the body and rinsed the mouth, place the lots before the images of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
With robes and cap neatly arranged, pray with a sincere heart: "I, disciple [Name], shall approach the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as I did in the past."
Regarding the causal conditions: whichever sūtra’s conditions have ripened, one shall take it up with the hand of faith. Whichever lot is drawn, that is the sūtra one has obtained;

one shall uphold it for as long as life lasts, never daring to be indolent. After thus upholding the sūtra, if the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are slightly opened, one must by no means seek private salvation alone, but vow that from the light of a single lamp, ten million lamps shall be transmitted, and from those ten million lamps, ten million more shall be transmitted.
This is for the sake of the inexhaustible. This beginner ordinary person relies upon the model of teaching, principle, practice, and fruit.

Yet, just as the First Patriarch came from the West to point directly to the human mind and see one's nature to become a Buddha, the mortar of teaching, principle, practice, and fruit was already shattered and kicked over by that old toothless barbarian.
Now I ask you, Layman Lei Yu: what is the mortar of teaching, principle, practice, and fruit?
The mortar has already been kicked over by the old barbarian. Amidst the ordinary course of daily life, amidst thunder and rain, in whose dwelling will it settle?
One day, the Song official Zhu Yan asked the lecturer-monk Yijiang, "After this body dies, where does the mind reside?
Jiang countered the question, saying, "Before this body has died, where does the mind reside? Yan—
Suddenly he attained realization and presented this verse: "The four elements need not be realized after death; The six sense organs are empty while in use.
It is difficult to present speech or silence to the Master; It lies only within ordinary speech and silence. Jiang nodded in approval.
At Mount Tianchi in Wumen, when they first met, Jiang also asked about thunder and rain at the outset. [He said: "In daily life, one is able to discern."

"Where, ultimately, does the mind reside? He asked this repeatedly, pressing him again and again, yet amidst the thunder and rain, there was no answer. The following morning, he took his leave at Tianchi (Heavenly Lake).
Even today, the wind and moon at Tianchi remain as they were; but as for the koan of the inquiry and the pressure, one does not know if it remains as it was.
If it did remain as it was, how could there be such diligent accumulation and long-term effort without the mass of doubt being shattered?
Furthermore, two letters arrived during the thunder and rain. In them, Governor Wang requested instruction.
Although the Governor was not yet deeply versed in the principles of water management, he found it inconvenient to compose a formal letter to seek further guidance.
Nevertheless, even though no letter was written, the Governor’s bodhicitta had already been awakened prior to words and characters. This awakening prior to words and characters—
"Mind" refers to the very mind of the Patriarch’s direct pointing that came from the East.

If you can believe in this directly and without doubt, and your functioning becomes vast and penetrating, then heaven, earth, and the myriad phenomena will all be within the grasp of the Governor-General’s hand.

How much more so for a single province like Western Shu—would it not receive the abundant Dharma-benefit bestowed by the Governor-General? After Song Zhu Yan presented this verse: [Verse omitted as per instructions] After Song Zhu Yan presented this verse:
Before long, he established transformation among many people, awakening immeasurable faith in both the black and white [realms].
Layman Leiyu, if you can not forget the wind and moon of Tianchi at the Wumen Gate, then how could the wind and moon of Mount Emei possibly be above those of Tianchi?
An ancient worthy said: "If a person recognizes the mind, there is not an inch of land upon the great earth. Daguan then said: "If..."
When a person recognizes the mind, there is no wind or moon outside the mind. Master Xiu said: "The wind moves and the heart shakes the tree;
clouds arise and nature gives rise to dust. If you clarify today's affairs, you darken the person of original nature. Da Guan further said:
"Master Xiu sees only the sharpness of the awl-head, but does not see the squareness of the chisel-head. Da Guan sees only the squareness of the chisel-head, but does not see the awl."
Touli, I venture to ask you, King Zhi, Tai, and Chengdu Shijun: tell me, between Master Xiu and Daguan, which is the hen and which is the rooster?
If you can discern this, then the nest and mortar of doctrine, principle, practice, and fruition will not be overturned; yet even if they are not, it does not matter.

If you cannot discern it, then the nest and mortar of doctrine, principle, practice, and fruition shall surely be overturned, and you may take it that this very body will be brought straight to its end.
There is no place to rest. The verse says: "On Mount Emei, amidst wind and moon, and by the Heavenly Pond, In how many places is there joyful song, and in how many places is there sorrow?

When one realizes that outside the mind there is no separate dharma, All circumstances—whether adverse or favorable—are my teachers. (Entrusted to Layman Lei Yu, with a request to transmit it to Wang Zhitai.)

Once, while conversing with Yutai, the subject of the fundamental principles of the Chan school arose. I then cited the case where the faculty of awakening is unobscured from beginning to end, such as when Imperial Preceptor Wang interrogated Venerable Lang.
Or again, like the monk who questioned Qinglin; their exchanges were seamless and resonant, perfectly fitting.

Yet Venerable Lang could not clarify this point, and although Xueqian stepped in to turn the wheel for him, he was nonetheless unable to avoid having his faculty of awakening obscured from beginning to end. Regarding this moment of encounter—
At this juncture, the interaction between host and guest is like two mirrors reflecting each other’s light; it is pervasive, pure, and leaves no room for anything else.
Were one to entertain even a hair’s breadth of deliberation, it would be like a single speck of cloud appearing in the vast clarity of the sky.

This state cannot be understood through the duality of self and other, nor can it be understood as having mind or being without mind. It responds the moment it is touched; how could it be reached by discursive thought? It is luminously alive.
To receive a blow is to be of the same class as a wooden puppet. This is not a matter of pure insight;
it is the mastery of mature *banyo* (maintaining), where the scales are held in one’s own hand and the freedom to kill or give life belongs to a man of independent spirit.

Even with the cleverness of Zhang Liang or the strategic brilliance of Huaiyin, one ends up ten thousand *li* from home, the handle already in another's hands, and the power to kill or give life resting upon another’s heels. Wave after wave...
The earth turns away from such people. In recent times, it is difficult to find even one or half of one among this sort;
how much more so for those who truly lack strength? This makes one all the more sorrowful. Tell me, how can one find joy?
Sitting with head covered against the rustling night rain, tears fall in the spring breeze beyond measure of grief. Wild fox spirits abound, spreading across mountains and fields.
Meeting people everywhere, he blinds their eyes; giving them the "real Dharma," he truly lets it leak away.
Preaching the Dharma without rule, he grows increasingly sorrowful (from "Sitting in Quietude to Show Zhonglai").
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa asked the Buddha: "All sentient beings perceive the beautiful as beautiful and the ugly as ugly;

the Buddhas likewise perceive the beautiful and the ugly with perfect clarity and without confusion. Why, then, is it that while sentient beings are characterized by deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*), the Buddhas are not?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "All Buddhas possess only the conventional designations (*saṃvṛti-saṃjñā*) current in the world."
Within this, no attachment arises. Yet all sentient beings, within their conceptualizations of proliferation, give rise to false attachments;

thus they are turned about by the beautiful and the ugly. The Buddhas are like mirrors reflecting objects; though images interlace, what hindrance can there be? This is but the dregs of the teachings.
It is not so under the gate of the patch-robed monks (śramaṇas). Who would go into the womb of a donkey or the belly of a horse? Not so.

This Avalokiteśvara is none other than Samantabhadra. If you have sufficient faith, you have the potential to enter hell; if your faith is insufficient, you have the potential to join the ranks of Māra.
If you wish to cut off both sides and become a man of liberation, then morning after night and night after morning—where can such a body and mind possibly dwell?
Your every action and withdrawal never departs from the Mountain of Knives (shown to Zhonglai).
In the world there are two kinds of kinsmen: one kind is profound and nourishes the seeds of the Way;
the other kind is profound and increases evil habits. If one possesses wisdom, even kinsmen of evil habits can nourish the seeds of the Way.
If one's power is not yet great, one must cause what is raw to become ripe, and what is ripe to become raw. Herein lies the failure to see clearly.
If one does not exert effort in practice, one will suffer the burden of falling into ruin for a thousand lifetimes and ten thousand kalpas. Take, for example, the single matter of female beauty:
parents marry them off, originally desiring to continue the ancestral bloodline; this is a virtuous rule of the name-teachings (mingjiao) that the world cannot do without.
Yet there are those who, despite already having sons and daughters, do not sever their lustful desires, taking this as their pleasure and remaining mired in attachment until death, never awakening.
Alas! A dignified man can have his entire life brought to ruin by this foul orifice of excretion. Once the mind is deluded by desire, ten thousand principles are thereby obscured.
You were originally born from your parents; yet upon hearing the words of women, the words of your parents never again enter your ears.
This transgression is often committed even within the relationship between ruler and subject; as for brothers and friends, it goes without saying.

Sensual desire deludes people; it is so poisonous that it overturns the great moral principles. Not only does it increase evil habits, but it also entangles the spiritual consciousness—when will one ever be liberated from it?
An ancient sage said: "It is better to stay near a venomous snake than to be intimate with female beauty.
A venomous snake may harm one, but only this present body; the fetters of female beauty, however, are difficult to untie even through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Only...
The kinship of the Dharma grows ever more abundant and beneficial; it nourishes the seeds of the Way until the fruit is ultimately attained.

Through enlightened teachers and virtuous friends who do not speak of worldly affairs but investigate only the True Principle, one uses the numinous waters of Prajñā to alternately irrigate the faculty of hearing.

This perfumes and nurtures the *vidyā-hetu* (enlightening cause), so that the *dharmatā-hetu* (true cause) gradually becomes manifest. By persevering thus for a long time, when a single thought accords with reality, the Great Matter is completed. Life—
Transcending death is supreme; the net of worldly dust is instantly cast off. Like a fish with scales entering the sea, one is forever free from the affliction of the net.
Such is the benefit provided by Dharma friends and kinsmen, yet worldly people do not regard it as significant. Such is the harm inflicted by those who are kin in the cycle of birth and death.
The people of the world all regard this as important. For those who truly study the Way, one must possess the discerning eye regarding this;
one must know what is good and what is evil. If one does not know good from evil, one is either a seed of hell or surely a kinsman of Māra.
Such a stream of being would be startled even by a dream—how much more so when sitting shoulder-to-shoulder and knee-to-knee to discuss the Way! Come, let us speak of this further.
This principle should also be observed with great care. Even if one has no personal faults, one may still employ this method to transform others;

compared to painting Buddhas, constructing temples, or relieving the poor and uprooting suffering, its merit is even greater. Why? Because it causes the Dharma lineage to flourish and the True Teaching to be practiced.

The True Teaching shall prevail; the winds of Māra shall be extinguished. The seeds of Bodhi shall pervade every dust mote and fill every land, like the return of spring to the great earth, whereby all things come to life.
Those who will attain Buddhahood in the future, accompanied by their retinues to propagate the great Dharma transformation, must surely be those nurtured this very day.
Alas! With little exertion, one reaps great merit. A man of resolve must not fail to seize this opportunity. (Shown to Zhonglai)

The Sage has fundamentally no fixed mind; sentient beings have fundamentally no fixed habits. Therefore, there is nothing among vipers, snakes, scorpions, and centipedes that is not a partial manifestation of the Great Being.
Bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas are none other than the original nature of sentient beings. If the Sage possessed a fixed mind, how would he differ from wood or stone?
If sentient beings possessed fixed habits, then Buddhas and Patriarchs would never be able to continue their lineage. This is so.

Therefore, whether appearing with divine heads or ghostly faces, as ordinary forms or sacred countenances, through hundreds of thousands of skillful means, Avalokiteśvara acts universally according to what is appropriate.
Each and every manifestation arises from the field of the Bodhisattva’s compassion. It is like a sliver of moon in the sky, its reflection appearing upon ten thousand bodies of water;
how could it ever be fathomed through thought or discrimination? To awaken to this is to realize that the Bodhisattva appears wherever there is need.
When a person of the worldly truth enters into my Dharma, it is like a man drowning in the great ocean who has his hair-knot exposed;
a spiritual friend takes hold of him, just as one would pull someone by their hair-knot. You must exert yourself with all your strength; otherwise, you will surely sink.
Even if a thousand Buddhas were to appear in the world, they would find it difficult to rescue you. (Addressing the assembly.)
I have heard that regarding the thirty-two marks of a Tathāgata, each individual merit is for one's own enjoyment;
however, the merit of the light from the *ūrṇā-kośa* (white tuft of hair) between the brows is not for personal use. This compassionate gift is enjoyed by descendants without end.

Therefore, when a donor offers even a drop of water or a thread, at the moment it is about to be received, one should contemplate this *ūrṇā* as perfectly illuminating the Dharma-realm, wherein the reflections of both the holy and the ordinary appear within its light.

Within this, both the giver and the recipient appear within the light; subject and object are entirely absent. The three spheres are empty in essence, yet the distinction between self and other is not obscured.
Practicing contemplation in this manner, all conditioned phenomena become unconditioned. (Receive the white robe and prostrate before the Buddha.)
The Buddha-dharma is fundamentally ordinary, yet the world seeks it through the extraordinary; therefore, people often fail to grasp the Buddha’s mind.
Thus it is said: "The ordinary mind is the Way. This ordinary mind is inherently possessed by all sentient beings who possess breath and blood;
how could it wait for transmission from Buddhas and Bodhisattvas before existing? If one must wait for transmission from Buddhas and Bodhisattvas...
Regarding "existence after death": in the daily lives of worldly people, circumstances and conditions—whether adverse or favorable—are manifold;
they take what is wrong to be right and what is right to be wrong, burning with incessant discrimination. What kind of mind is this? It is precisely the ordinary mind.
It is simply that sentient beings do not know how to use it well, and thus manifest the strange and perilous minds of the three poisons. If one were skilled...
When applied, the wondrously perilous minds of sentient beings' three poisons are themselves the ordinary minds of the Buddhas.

Nevertheless, because sentient beings are habituated to these wondrously perilous states, when they suddenly hear the teaching that "ordinary mind is the Way," they naturally find it impossible to accept.
This is because their habitual patterns are so deeply rooted in the ordinary. Therefore, one must rely upon the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to...
When the sublime atmosphere of precious stands and rare treasures is proclaimed to transform their inferior minds, the spirit of bearing the burden [of enlightenment] arises.
Once this single mind has arisen, they further reflect upon their former inferior state, regarding it with contempt and revulsion.
Toward the ordinary mind, they then experience great wonder and marvel, deeming it something never before heard and something never before attained; thus, they transcend [the mundane].
A person of great capacity, knowing this to be so, further employs the "manner of the cat and the white ox" to fan the flames and transform their heart of astonishment and wonder.
When one reaches this point, the sentiments of both the holy and the ordinary are exhausted, and the ordinary mind opens. To employ that which has opened is called the "Great Function.
As for the term "function" (*jī*), it refers to illumination that is not obscured by its activity, and activity that is not obscured by its illumination. Now, as for illumination...
When function is not obscure, it is called "true illumination. When function is not obscure and illumination is present, it is called "great function.
Thus Linji said: "How can one ask about that which flows on without ceasing? Describe to him that true illumination which is boundless. One who is free from marks and names receives no transmission;

once the 'blow-off-the-hair' sword has been used, it must be sharpened immediately. Regarding "once the blow-off-the-hair sword has been used, it must be sharpened immediately," this refers to transformation.
This is what is meant by "exhausting [the source].

Once a single atom of the subtle engages in movement, auspiciousness and misfortune arise crosswise. If one can penetrate and illuminate that which precedes the subtle, then calamity and fortune will burst apart and fall away.

However, sentient beings have become habituated to delusion and defilement as their very nature; thus, it is ultimately difficult to turn their faculties. If those faculties could indeed be turned, their habitual defilements would gradually be released, just as in the case of practice.
If defilement could never be resolved, from where would the Buddhas of the past and present have come?
Since the sages of the past and present attained the Way based on concrete evidence, even though habitual defilements may be long-standing, there must necessarily be a cause for their removal.

As for those who, knowing there is a cause for removal, yet willingly follow along with habitual defilements—such people, the Old Man Yama himself will not let them pass; there is no need for others to trouble themselves.
I share your concern. This "subtlety" (wei) does not exist outside of the four phases of movement; therefore, observe it through these four phases.

The subtle is fundamentally non-existent, so how much less could there be movement? What are the four phases? They are: the state before subtlety, the desire for subtlety, the state of actual subtlety, and the state after subtlety has occurred. Thus it is.
If a single atom were truly existent, how could it be designated as an "atom" by depending upon the four phases [of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing]?

Nevertheless, when one contemplates the atom through these four phases, the atom is found not to exist. Thus, at the moment of engaging with movement, regarding objects that are agreeable to the mind, one experiences joy;
regarding objects that are disagreeable to the mind, one becomes impatient. This joy and this impatience, when examined through the substance of the four phases, are indeed existent.
Regarding these two: if one cannot contemplate them as having this duality, yet contemplates them as having the essence of this duality, then these two become habitual.
This is because such contemplation has arisen through habituation. Thus, the power of this contemplation is strong, while the power of the two is weak.
Thus, whether one attains power or fails to attain it, the observer knows the victory or defeat for themselves. Therefore it is said: "Understanding is not difficult, but practice is difficult;
practice is not difficult, but reaching the end is difficult; reaching the end is not difficult, but forgetting [the end] is again difficult.

Thus, only those who can employ [the mind] through forgetting will find contemplation realized at every turn. Furthermore, regarding the path before, the path in the midst, and the path after, there are two ways that are compliant and one way that is contrary.

Regarding the practice of truth and delusion, there are points one must understand. What is meant by "deluded conformity"? It is when that which is originally pure suddenly gives rise to the mountains, rivers, and the great earth.
What is meant by "wondrous conformity"? It is to trace back upward, so that conditioned emotions return to their original nature. What is meant by "reversal"?
It is when the nature is restored and one feels compassion for those of the same essence, launching the vessel of mercy to rescue and deliver all beings. These two conformities and one...
This is contrary [to reason]. Sages appear in the East; sages appear in the West. Sages appeared in antiquity; sages appear in the present.
Those who regard them with contempt and do not believe in them are all celestial Māras and followers of external paths; they are not sages.
Indeed, karma has never failed to be true, and the mind likewise has never failed to be true. The truth of karma is the truth of the mind;
the truth of the mind is the truth of karma. Apart from truth, there is neither karma nor mind; outside of mind and karma, there is also no truth.
Consider this: all sentient beings within the seven inverted realms of existence are, by their very nature, those who have realized the truth in the present moment.

Yet, because they are unaware while engaged in daily activities, they give rise to arbitrary conceptualizations within that very realization; thus, those who have realized it remain unaware during their daily lives.
Little do they realize that, even amidst this unawareness of daily life, there has in fact never been a moment when [realization was absent].

It is not that there is no direct realization. Just as the mind does not know the body, the body is fundamentally the *dharmakāya*; and just as the body does not know the mind, the mind is fundamentally wisdom (*jñāna*).
The *dharmakāya* is like a mirror, and fundamental wisdom is like its light. Light exists in dependence upon the mirror, and the light in turn illuminates the mirror;
yet fundamentally, there is nothing that can act. What thing is not true? Now, some say that because the mind does not know karma, karma is independent; [but] karma...
If one does not understand the mind, then the mind likewise has nothing upon which it depends; one then claims that both sin and merit are empty and that the self cannot be apprehended.

Yet, one fails to realize that the emptiness of sin and merit is merely a reflection of those who await their non-emptiness, and that the unapprehendability of the self is likewise a reflection of those who assume the self must be apprehended.
All of these arise from the ripening of passionate desires and the cultivation of intellectual truths; when spoken, they seem—
Awakening is that which remains deluded even when facing objects. It is like the "Wondrous Dharma" of the *Lotus Sūtra*. "Dharma" refers to all phenomena;

"wondrous" means to thoroughly penetrate beyond all phenomena, wherein from the outset there is no separate reality. Thus it is said: "Borrowing my mother-in-law's robe to bow at my mother-in-law's birthday."
It is further said: "Delusive thoughts have no inherent nature; how could they know karma? Karma also has no inherent nature; how could it know the mind?
The mind does not know karma, yet that which it preserves is without self. Karma does not know the mind, yet that which it preserves is fundamentally empty.

Being without self, the emptiness of what is preserved is not obscure. To know and then be able to act is to have non-arising in daily life. To know but not be able to act is to be bound by attachment in daily life."
Hatred. In daily life there is no birth; though the Yin and Yang be skillful, they cannot exert the power of molding and casting upon me. In daily life there is love and hatred;
though the faculties and their objects have no inherent nature, there is nowhere that does not shake my essence. When the essence is shaken, the six realms are disturbed;
when the six realms are disturbed, one loses the One. When the One is lost, the head becomes confused; when the head is confused, the mind becomes coarse. Therefore it is said: "The mind is coarse."
He strikes his head in confusion. Furthermore, although Confucius’s mind did not die, he lived naturally in his daily life;

yet because Yan Hui’s mind could neither live nor die, he was unable to command belief through silence, to encompass all through comparison, or to stand before the people as a vesselless leader whom they would follow.

Generally, when returning to daily life, the one who returns must know the people, and the people likewise must know the one who returns. Because both know each other, subject and object arise in opposition;
the living become dead. Therefore it is said: "When there is a self, the self exists within heaven and earth; when there is no self, heaven and earth exist within the self."
I was born because of desire; therefore, one who possesses desire cannot avoid being born. Once born, one cannot avoid dying.

Throughout the world, those who seek long life fundamentally regard birth as a blessing and death as a calamity; thus it is said that nothing is more intense than the calamity and blessing of birth and death.
This is likely because they do not know that I am the Goddess of Merit and the Maiden of Darkness, and that I can maintain a single-minded focus.

They will not arise; they will surely flee together without waiting to be driven out. Thereafter, they share in the fortune and misfortune of the world, yet neither fortune nor misfortune can burden them.
Such as these are called the True Cause. Those who act contrary to this are called the False Cause.

Furthermore, those who recklessly calculate that there are phenomena external to the mind, and who cannot realize that the myriad things return to themselves, are called Non-Buddhists (Tīrthikas). Viewed from this perspective...
As for this: when the external mind is absent, there is no arising; where there is no arising, there is no ceasing.
Thus, arising and ceasing, movement and stillness, penetration and obstruction, tranquility and change, separation and union, darkness and light—all are fundamentally one brilliant essence.
The six objects reflected therein flow away and do not return. Taking them near, within the mind itself, they constitute birth and cessation;
taking them far, among external things, they manifest as light and darkness, day and night, and the many cycles of antiquity and modernity, cold and heat.

Yet for those whose celestial mechanism (*tianji*) is profound, awakening to a single speck of dust and tracing it upward causes all remaining attachments to be pulled out at once. Therefore it is said: "With seeing as the condition and light as the cause, darkness becomes non-existent."

When seeing does not arise from ignorance, then all dark appearances can never again obscure it; this refers to the faculty of the eye detaching from its stickiness and entering [the state of liberation].
As for the faculty of the mind, its cognition depends on dharmas; without dharmas there is no cognition.

When it knows itself without depending on dharmas, then all signs of extinction can never again delude it. Alas! If those who crave long life were to thoroughly awaken to this principle, then their suffering—
I regret my former actions, for I fled from the capital to travel to Yan.
One who has reached the top of a hundred-foot pole may tremble at the touch of a great log, yet one upon the vast earth walks with composure even upon a single footboard.

Why is this so? The bamboo pole is fundamentally not empty, and the ground is fundamentally not real. It is because all sentient beings, within that which is neither empty nor real, falsely conceptualize emptiness and reality.

The Prince of Pigu said: "When there is one thing, there is one principle; 'yi' (義) means appropriateness. For example, earth is appropriate to be solid, water appropriate to be moist, fire appropriate to be hot, and wind appropriate to be moving.
If that which is solid were moist, that which is moist were hot, or that which is hot were moving, it would not be appropriate."
This is not so according to principle. Solidity can become moisture; moisture can become heat; heat can become motion; and motion can again become heat.
Heat becomes moisture, and moisture becomes solidity. Thus, that which is appropriate can become inappropriate, and that which is inappropriate can become appropriate.
It is like the beginning and end of a wheel: how could there truly be a starting point? Therefore, earth, water, fire...
Wind is also called the "four wheels. However, although these wheels cannot be traced to their beginning or end, since they are composed of iron on the outside, what else could the wheels consist of?
(Discrimination of Principles)

Dreaming represents delusion, while awakening signifies enlightenment; thus, the paths of the sage and the ordinary person are separated. Upon investigating their origin, one finds it is nothing other than not having reached the fundamental source.

Therefore, it is said: "Upon reaching the source, emotions are forgotten; when the mind is known, its substance is unified. Viewed from this perspective, when emotions have not yet been forgotten, there is no need to use emotion to forget emotion.
Why? Because emotion ultimately cannot be forgotten [by itself]. Once the source is reached, emotions do not need to be intentionally forgotten, for they vanish of their own accord.
It is forgotten. If the essence has not yet merged, there is no need to seek its merging. What is meant by "the essence merging"? It is the non-conceptual realization of identity.
If this is so, it is clear that knowing the mind is itself reaching the source, and reaching the source is itself knowing the mind.

Therefore, for one who reaches the source and knows the mind, although they appear the same as the multitude amidst the chaotic turmoil of the dream-state, they understand that the nature of these objects is non-existent, and they know the mind.
There is no external [reality]. One dreams more and more deeply until, all at once, the conditions of the dream are suddenly severed; the reflection of awakening is likewise empty.

Therefore, this is not the same as being deluded while awake. If one has not yet fundamentally attained [realization] and the mind remains ignorant, then even if that person is as loyal, trustworthy, and incorruptible as Boyi and Shuqi, their emotional attachments will be as firm and difficult to shatter as Mount Sumeru. This is what is difficult to break.
This clinging is called the "mark of a unified whole. This mark of a unified whole is a festering sore for all sentient beings;
even if one's parents or wife should slightly touch this sore, the eruption of ignorance is as fierce as a raging flame, let alone when touched by others.
The Sages know that this mark is difficult to shatter, and thus they regard it as Mount Sumeru—though it is solid and superior to anything else.
Indeed, yet when compared with the trichiliocosm, even Mount Sumeru is but a grain of rice in a great granary.

Therefore, the Sage shattered the trichiliocosm into minute particles so that sentient beings might know that even that which is as solid as Mount Sumeru within the trichiliocosm can be reduced to a multitude of minute particles; how much more so, then, [the rest].
This wretched body of mine, a mere lump of flesh—how could it remain long without being subject to decay? Furthermore, this world cannot possess its own inherent substance;
it must be formed by the aggregation of a multitude of subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*). Yet these subtle atoms likewise lack self-nature;
they must exist only when the world is broken down. Therefore, when one views the multitude of subtle atoms through the lens of the world, the multitude of subtle atoms...
It cannot be apprehended. When one observes the world through the multitude of atoms, the world cannot be apprehended.

Since both the world and the multitude of atoms cannot be apprehended when observed in relation to one another, then where, ultimately, do all the dual retributions of the environment and its inhabitants—of both sages and ordinary beings—rest?
A verse says: "A rabbit conceives and gives birth to six dragons; not only to bring rain, but furthermore..."
It becomes wind; seizing the opportune moment, it can snatch away and turn things upside down. A single slice of spring light melts ten thousand flowers.
*The Collected Works of Old Man Zibai*, Volume Six;
*The Collected Works of Old Man Zibai*, Volume Seven.
Ming Dynasty: Han-shan Deqing reads the *Fayu* (Discourse on the Dharma).
Earth, water, fire, wind, space, seeing, and cognition—along with awakening, hearing, and knowing—are called the ten great elements. When one investigates their ultimate source, however, they are...
The ten great elements do not exist apart from the *ālaya-vijñāna*. "Ālaya" means "to contain and store.

This consciousness is able to contain and store both the principle of awakening and the principle of non-awakening, as well as the two divisions of the seeing and the perceived (*darśana-bhāga* and *nimitta-bhāga*).

Furthermore, the five great elements—earth, water, fire, wind, and space—are established based upon the perceived aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of this consciousness. The five great elements of seeing-consciousness, hearing, smelling, tasting, and cognition are likewise [established].
Therefore, consciousness is established by differentiating its aspects. Furthermore, this consciousness is fundamentally without substance;

it exists as the essence of the originally unmoving wisdom (*acala-jñāna*). Why is this? Because this unmoving wisdom is fundamentally without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). The meaning of being without intrinsic nature is difficult to clarify throughout antiquity and the present.
This principle was revealed almost exhaustively by the Great Being (Bodhisattva) Zao Bo in his *Huayan lun* (Treatise on the Avataṃsaka). However...
The minds and consciousnesses of scholars are coarse and superficial; though they have read this treatise, those who truly comprehend its meaning are as rare as the horn of a rhinoceros.
Although I am not clever, I shall attempt to explain it. Generally speaking, regarding this wisdom: there is no wisdom outside of wisdom.

To fully comprehend whether this wisdom has an intrinsic nature or lacks one—and that wisdom does not know wisdom, nor whether it has an intrinsic nature or lacks one—to fail to understand this is precisely what is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
Ignorance (*avidyā*) pertains to arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*). Ignorance having no intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) pertains to non-arising and non-ceasing (*anutpāda-anirodha*).
Because arising and ceasing and non-arising and non-ceasing appear as one yet are not one, and appear as two yet are not two, these two are combined to form the *ālayavijñāna*.

The aspect of awakening (*bodha*) within this consciousness pertains to the category of the non-arising and non-ceasing portion; the aspect of non-awakening (*abodha*) within this consciousness pertains to [the category of] arising and ceasing.

It is subsumed within the cessation of the constituent elements of breath. Furthermore, because there was originally no distinction between awakening and non-awakening, and because fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) is without dependence or externality, it must necessarily follow conditions through fundamental wisdom.

Within the arising of conditions, when pleasure reaches its limit, suffering arises; when suffering reaches its limit, one contemplates the source; when contemplation reaches its limit, the mind opens.
Only then does one come to know that this extreme suffering of mine has originated from an ultimate bliss, and that this ultimate bliss itself has originated from a state of dependence.

When there is dependence, self and others stand in opposition and shake one another, thereby producing suffering and pleasure. Now I have realized that while there is present dependence, fundamentally there was originally no dependence.
Within this state of non-dependence, even pleasure cannot be found; how, then, could there be suffering?

Looking back upon the dream of self and others shaking one another, it is like laughing at the delusions of a dream while awake; though the residual habits of the dream remain, they cannot persist indefinitely.
[This] is excluded. Because that which I have realized is without dependence, without objects, and without self—vast and yet spiritual—it cures the residual habits of dreams.

It is like the spring sun shining upon lingering snow; how could the snow remain for long? Viewed from this perspective, the principle of the non-awakening of the eight consciousnesses presupposes dependence.
Therefore it is said: "Fundamentally pure and fundamentally unawakened; from this arise deluded thoughts. Thus does this [delusion] originate.

The meaning of consciousness is to awaken within the realm of dependence; therefore it is said: "That which is capable of delusion is not itself that which is deluded. How could they remain eternally identical?
Since they are not identical, one cannot avoid the arising of suffering when pleasure reaches its peak. Only when suffering reaches its peak does one seek the wisdom to transcend suffering.
Emerging from the wisdom of suffering and entering [into it], one directly and thoroughly understands that conditioned existence is like ice and unconditioned reality is like water.

Although their substantiality and obstruction differ such that they seem not to be identical, there is no ice apart from water and no water apart from ice. Thus, when ice manifests, there is not a single drop of water;
when water manifests, there is not a hair’s breadth of ice. From this point on, by means of this thorough understanding, one circulates through the five [aggregates].

In this station, where roots coil and joints interlace, one places body and mind amidst the midst of birth and death, fortune and calamity; one stakes one's life and nature upon the winds of favorable and adverse conditions.
Grinding crosswise and refining uprightly, refining uprightly and grinding crosswise—once this grinding and refining have continued for a long time, one’s practice will not fail its purpose.

Body and mind shatter and fall away, and the gate of birth and death opens. Riding the wheel of compassion and wisdom, one floats and sinks throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Transmigrating through the three periods of time and the ten directions, if those with icchantika-nature were not to ride this wheel, I would not attain Buddhahood.

Furthermore, this seventh consciousness (*manas*), as the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of consciousness, conceives of itself as the internal self. Moreover, the seventh consciousness serves as the source for the subtle objective-image division (*nimitta-bhāga*) that follows the six consciousnesses.
Therefore, although the two types of karma—projecting (*ākṣepaka*) and completing (*paripūraka*)—are separated by lifetimes, they do not lose their efficacy. Thus, the six...
The verse on consciousness states: "Drawn and fulfilled by the power of karma that summons rebirth, the seven consciousnesses are merely its source.

When moving the body or initiating speech, it alone is supreme. Furthermore, these six consciousnesses are the coarse aspects (nimitta-bhāga). As for the first five consciousnesses, they are all aspects of the eighth consciousness;
these aspects are themselves the functional divisions (vibhāga), not aspects of further aspects. These various consciousnesses are to be wondrously mastered."

The Dharma-realm and dependent origination are both devoid of intrinsic nature; they are the unmoving wisdom. Nevertheless, it is difficult to first give rise to faith and initiate the mind [of enlightenment], whereas it is easy to realize and initiate the mind.

This is because the initial giving rise to faith and initiation of the mind values cognitive engagement with conditions (*yuan-zhi*), while the realization and initiation of the mind relies solely upon direct, manifest knowledge (*xian-zhi*).
Once, while looking into a mirror, I saw my own reflection. In what form do I appear? In what form does the reflection appear as well?
Thereupon, I investigated that which is able to assume my form: ultimately, what thing is it? When I am in a state of anger, it is angry; when I am in a state of joy, it is joyful.
I first sought it within the six sense organs, then sought it within the nine apertures, and finally reached the five viscera and six bowels. Eight...
Within the fourteen thousand pores, long and short are sought, internal and external are sought; both the refined and the coarse are manifested.

Only that which is capable of manifesting these manifestations possesses the six sense organs and nine apertures throughout the pores of the entire body. These organs have the emptiness of the organs, and these apertures have the emptiness of the apertures.
The pores possess the voidness of the pores; their form is matter (*rūpa*), and their voidness is emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

If one can manifest this manifestation, it belongs to the unity of emptiness and matter, and thus becomes one with emptiness and matter. Then emptiness and matter do not know emptiness and matter. Why is this?
This is because one does not know one. If one were to know one, then "one" would be the object known, and "knowing" would be the subject; this would constitute duality.

Where, then, would the meaning of "one" reside? I have sought in every way for its defining characteristics, and only now do I realize that from the very beginning it belongs neither to emptiness nor to form.
Since it belongs neither to emptiness nor to form, how can it be sought through categories such as internal or external, ancient or modern, distant or near?

Indeed! Although one is able to seek through this capacity, if it is not vast and open, then even though this capacity is refined regarding emptiness and form, it is in fact coarse compared to that which precedes the seeking through capacity.
Therefore it is said: "If one uses knowledge to know stillness, this is not knowledge without conditions."
If one knows by means of self-knowing, it is still not a knowing that lacks an object; yet it is neither a knowing that knows quiescence, nor is it a knowing that knows itself.
Observing this very point, that which seeks the "prior" cannot possibly be exhausted through intellectual consciousness, nor can it be reached through effort.
Only those who have realized non-arising know this for themselves.

Once there was a monk who spent his entire life attending to the affairs of the monastic community, thereby delaying his own spiritual cultivation. One day, a messenger from the realm of ghosts arrived to arrest him.
