Yet the eyes of the multitude sleep upon forms, the ears sleep upon sounds, the nose sleeps upon fragrances and stench, the tongue sleeps upon flavors, the body sleeps upon tactile objects, and the mind sleeps upon mental phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). Once asleep, they sleep forever; for long kalpas they do not awaken.
Awakening: When the faculties and objects stand in opposition, consciousness wavers between them. Whether the eyes are open or closed, though there is waking and sleeping, in reality it is all sleep.

Only the enlightened one realizes that awareness arises from the objects and that characteristics exist because of the faculties; yet this awareness is fundamentally without knowing, and these characteristics are originally without form.
Thus, the opposing faculties and objects vanish of themselves without waiting for the contemplation of emptiness. Therefore, it is said: "The wild mind is suddenly..."
Cessation is itself bodhi; *bodhi* means "awakening. Alas! Originally there was one refined spirit, which divided into six harmonious combinations.
Through accumulated attachments, these became solidified, each remaining untransformed. Taking sleep for wakefulness and suffering for pleasure, they dwell in inverted dreams.
If the thunder of Great Awakening does not resound, those who sleep will never awaken. And so, let them awaken!

This term "awakened" (*xing*) is designated in dependence upon sleep; before one has fallen asleep, where does this awakening reside? If you say it resides in the objects (*viṣaya*), then the objects are not the awakening.

If you say it resides in the sense organs (*indriya*), then since the organs themselves are the awakening, what constitutes their root? If you say it resides in the awakening itself, then the awakening would not be awakening.
Jiang, come forward; I shall tell you how to investigate this awakening through three stages. Once you know where the awakening resides, then when the cold comes...
The heat departs; the heat departs and the cold comes. Both are merely the opening and closing of your eyes. Furthermore, whom do you call "asleep," and whom do you call "awake"?
Nevertheless, only after one has been able to transform sleep can one then be made awake. If you are unable to transform your sleep, then let Jiangsheng go to make you awake.
Let Jiangsheng strive for this! (Instruction to Jiangsheng on Sleep and Wakefulness)
Now, wood possesses the nature of fire, yet it cannot burn itself; it must rely on the friction of a fire-drill and tinder for smoke to first arise.
Although the smoke is not fire itself, it is the vanguard of fire. If the drilling does not cease, fire will surely follow the smoke and arrive.
Once the fire has arisen, the wood is consumed and turns to ash. Alas! Wood initially arises from earth and ultimately returns to earth.
This is the natural course of events. The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is like the nature of fire within wood; the various Buddhist scriptures are like the tools for drilling and kindling.
If these are present but the right person is not found, the fire will ultimately never ignite. Once the fire is ignited, the wood burns.

Sentient beings, by means of the Buddha’s scriptures, kindle the fire of contemplative insight to burn away the wood of the five aggregates; they ultimately return to the land of their original nature.
This is precisely the analogy for returning to one's true nature through the very passions.

The Buddha’s world is distant, and the Patriarchs have not appeared. As the kalpa has turned turbid, practitioners who first establish their resolve—even though they do so for the sake of transcending birth and death—mostly end up failing in the end. Generally speaking, where does the illness lie? It is not in sounds, forms, wealth, or profit;
it is not in the seven emotions or the six desires. It lies solely in this single, stinking physical shell of the person, which cannot be... [broken].
Broken. A single point of deluded thought that cannot be penetrated through inspection is immediately enslaved by the demon of birth and death.

From beginningless time, whether as a celestial body, a human body, or the bodies of animals and ghosts—whether with feathers, fur, scales, or shells—one has changed heads and faces within the sea of suffering, rising and sinking without a moment’s rest.
Now tell me: what is this demon of birth and death, and these various bodies of celestials, animals, and humans?
Is it given to them? Or do they summon it themselves? In truth, it all arises from not a single point of clinging mind (*parāmarśa-citta*).
This clinging mind may seem no great matter; yet, consider the "Yellow-Faced Old Man" (the Buddha): during his causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*), he gave away gold and even his royal head countless times.
Even when he was about to realize the fruit (*phala*), he further underwent various conditions of malice and rebellion, facing ten births and nine deaths.

Risking one's life and enduring hardship, disregarding hunger and cold, and paying no heed to profit or harm, one knows only that this single point of攀緣心 (pān-yuán-xīn—the攀緣心, or "clinging and seeking mind") is not yet extinguished;
the harbinger of calamity is no small matter. One must certainly see through it before it can be resolved. What kind of entity is this single point of clinging and seeking mind?
Not only does the Yellow-Faced Old Man (the Buddha) fail to subdue it, but even those who are diligent and brilliant disregard their own peril and ruin until they finally bring it under control.
"Attaining submissiveness. From antiquity to the present, there have been no few heroes and sages who assisted kings and aided their lords, achieving great accomplishments amidst tears and spittle.

Their fragrant names endure for a hundred generations and they receive offerings of blood; yet, none among them were able to penetrate this point of the攀緣心 (攀緣心, *pán yuán xīn*—the攀緣心, or "clinging and seeking mind").
Since they could not penetrate it, how could they ever attain submissiveness? Therefore, in the assembly of the Prajñāpāramitā, Subhūti and the multitude of devas and humans...
Previously, he raised a question: "How does one subdue the mind? How should one abide? Setting aside for a moment the matter of abiding, how exactly is this mind to be subdued?

This pivotal mechanism does not reside in the Buddhas, nor in the Patriarchs, nor can it be transmitted to you by learned masters or Dharma teachers. The Buddhas, Patriarchs, and learned masters can only...

I shall provide you with a secondary strike as an auxiliary condition. If you wish to see through this mind and attain thorough enlightenment, it is like a strong man bending his arm—it depends entirely upon oneself and requires no external force.
Even if there were the entire Great Canon of the Holy Teachings, they would merely be secondary remarks.
If Mengxiu truly wishes to resolve this matter of birth and death, you must decisively exert yourself in this regard.
A spirit of total self-sacrifice, even unto death. If this mind is not awakened, putting on clothes is merely donning fur and skin;
eating food is merely consuming urine and excrement. To awaken this mind, one must know how to reproach oneself;
otherwise, being obscured by the demons of indolence and torpor, one will ultimately never reach the place of awakening attained by the ancients. As Qianfeng told the assembly: "The Dharmakāya..."
"There are three kinds of illnesses and two kinds of lights; only when one has penetrated each of these can one be said to be practicing.
Yunmen came forth and said, "Why does the person inside the hermitage not know what is happening outside the hermitage?
Qianfeng could only respond with a hearty laugh. I venture to ask Master Mengxiu: what is the essential meaning of Yunmen’s statement? And what is the significance of Qianfeng’s laughter?

Regarding benefit and harm, if one can discern a bit of good and evil at the point where these two elders debate, then what is called "subduing the mind" is like raising dust with a following wind—what difficulty could there be?

If you let this pass by without seeking thorough penetration, then as previously stated, within the sea of suffering you will change heads and faces, sinking and floating without end. O Mengxiu, I ask you: among those with feathers, fur, scales, and shells, who shall escape?
"Proceed step by step from the very beginning. Shiyi said, "The three realms of suffering and a single retribution last for five thousand kalpas;
when will you emerge with your head? (Shown to Kang Mengxiu).

At the Śūraṅgama Assembly, the Buddha told Ānanda: "All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have experienced the continuous succession of birth and death because they do not know the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure and luminous nature. They employ various false thoughts; these thoughts are not real."
Therefore, there is cyclic existence. O virtuous ones, this section of the sutra contains two lineages: first, the lineage of the four noble ones;

second, the lineage of the six classes of ordinary beings. If one does not truly discern this critical juncture, it can be taken for certain that ten people moving their minds and feet will have five pairs of errors.
The eternally abiding true mind, the essence of nature-purity and luminosity—this is precisely the [lineage of the four noble ones].
The bloodline of the sages. Because this perception is not true, there is cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). This is precisely the bloodline of the six classes of ordinary beings.

The four sages are the Buddha, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas. The six classes of ordinary beings are devas, asuras, humans, animals (*tiryagyoni*), hungry ghosts (*preta*), and those in the hells (*naraka*).
These ten are also called the ten *dharmadhātus*. As for the term *dharmadhātu*, "dharma" refers to...
They are combined together, yet their realms are each distinct. All of this is because the initial resolve of sentient beings is unequal; thus, the fruits they induce are also different.
If one is a person of great *icchantika* nature, they simply do not give rise to a single thought, turning their body to join their father.
This is a matter of great importance; it is settled once and for all. To utter the single word "Buddha" is already defilement.
Now tell me: where do the ten realms of existence find their place? My speaking in this manner is like adding a handle to a bowl—it is like chewing food to feed others;
my heart is not at ease. Nevertheless, even though you are not yet a person of the icchantika class, you must still follow the established rules.
To tread within the square and act accordingly is not a great error. Therefore, practitioners of the Dharma-ending age must clearly understand these two lineages of blood;
only then can there be a discernment of the good and the bad. Otherwise, everyone is merely a person with a human head and a bull’s ears, speaking the gibberish of ghosts.

That I, a poor monk, and you, a virtuous one, have gathered here in this place is surely due to karmic conditions from previous kalpas, and is not the result of our present intellectual consciousness.
"O virtuous ones! From this day forward, you must certainly take the Four Noble Ones as your lifeblood; do not take the six classes of ordinary beings as your kin.
You must take the Four Noble Ones as your lifeblood, and you must necessarily give rise to the heart-mind of the Four Noble Ones.
Now tell me: how is the heart-mind of the Four Noble Ones to be aroused? To discern emptiness in a single thought—this is the lifeblood of the Śrāvaka."
To immediately realize that the essence of thought is empty—this is the lineage of the Pratyekabuddhas. Immediate thought is immediate emptiness; immediate emptiness is immediate thought.

When emptiness and thought are distinct and clear—this is the lineage of the Bodhisattvas. But tell me, how is the lineage of the Buddhas to be received? It is an ordinary matter, like seeking it within the womb of a donkey or the belly of a horse.
What is so extraordinary about the lotus on the jeweled throne? O worthy ones, only when a single thought is analyzed into emptiness...

This connects the bloodline of the Śrāvakas. I do not know, O worthy ones, when you encounter conditions and circumstances, whether at the critical juncture of adversity or favor, can you analyze and realize emptiness in a single thought-moment?
If in a single thought-moment it is empty, then the mind accords with emptiness. Once the mind accords with emptiness, [the practice is complete].
To speak of such a physical shell as this—at such a critical juncture—to again call it "love and hate," O worthy ones!
This state of affairs does not even exceed the lineage of the Śrāvakas, yet they are already transcendent regarding love and hate;
how much more so for Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Buddhas? I, too, have a few idle and simple words to offer, merely to help you, worthy ones, in ascending the mountain.
The toil of this [practice] is such that the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of sentient beings are base and inferior;

they respond with a bond like glue or lacquer as soon as matters pertaining to the six realms of mundane existence are raised. They feel a natural affinity for these things, embracing them with a vibrant spirit and a flavor in their discourse like drinking fine wine.
Yet, whenever matters pertaining to the four classes of noble ones are raised, they either fall into dullness or distraction.

In confusion, one strives with effort to urge others to recite the Buddha’s name one more time, to prostrate to the Buddha one more time, to read two more lines of scripture, or to serve two more spiritual teachers and virtuous friends. Yet, before long, the spirit becomes weary without being expected to do so;
within the mind there is a sense of prickling like thorns, such that the body feels constrained and the heart feels no joy.
This is for no other reason than that your world-transcending mind is slight while the karma of worldly toil is heavy. Now, all of you gentlemen are preeminent men;
how could you be compared to the ordinary? Nevertheless, from this point forward, you should each treat the Dharma-lineage with profound reverence.
Do not allow the shadows of love and hatred at the gates of the six sense faculties to wound the source of the bloodline. If you do not...
Fortunately, this exists. All of these are merely human heads and ox ears; what more is there to say?

When I, this poor monk, speak these words, the Buddhas of the ten directions, Śākyamuni Buddha in the hall above, the Dharma-protecting *gāralas* within the mountain temple, and the Bodhisattva Weituo who responds to the three continents, all see from afar with their divine eyes, hear from afar with their divine ears, and realize them through their knowledge of others' minds. O virtuous ones!
This is no trivial matter. If you overlook it, not only will you suffer great calamity in the present, but you shall not escape hell in the future.
Furthermore, tell me: when a single thought has not yet arisen, do hell and heaven exist or not? To say they exist is to fall into the slander of reification;
to say they do not exist is to fall into the slander of nihilism; to say they both exist and do not exist, or neither exist nor do not exist—these all fall into error.

"Accusation and Counting. This has nothing to do with you, Mr. Zhang or Mr. Li. According to the Vinaya, we shall interrogate you on your offense and proceed accordingly; we take no account of whether you admit it or not.
If you wish to emerge from this class of slanderers, you must understand: "The water is so swift it leaves the moon behind; the mountain is so high it does not obstruct the clouds.
(Shown to Ding Nan-yu, Miu Zhong-chun, Wu Kang-yu, and Yu Zhong-fu.)

Huang Shan Gu of Yuzhang once sighed that students run after the branches while neglecting the source. Therefore, he used the karmic conditions of the patriarchs to startle them into wonder and draw them toward it, saying:
"The meaning of the Patriarchs' coming from the West—apart from this, there is no way to enter. He did so by means of the verses of the Seven Buddhas.
Consequently, they overlook it and fail to investigate it. Little do they realize that if one sets aside the verses of the Seven Buddhas, Zen would have no source.

Furthermore, from where could the various streams of Zen possibly have originated? While the verses of the Seven Buddhas may seem capable of being explained through intellectual meaning (*artha*), the karmic encounters (*jiyuan*) of the patriarchs seem difficult to explain through such meaning.
Those who believe the meaning can be explained will ultimately be unable to transcend emotional consciousness; whereas those for whom the meaning cannot be explained...

It is not something that can be entered through conscious intellect; one must investigate it and awaken to it. Once awakened, there is awakening forever, for then everything is resolved and all matters are settled.

This is because those who do not understand the Seven Buddhas’ Verses find that even their intellectual interpretations cannot provide a point of entry. Even among the karmic conditions of the Patriarchs, there are instances where they could be understood through intellectual interpretation.
Generally speaking, the method of studying Chan is that the Dharma has no fixed nature. It is, for example, like a great general employing [his strategy].

In warfare, there are times when one conquers the enemy through the orthodox (*zheng*), times when one conquers the enemy through the extraordinary (*qi*), times when one conquers the enemy by employing both the extraordinary and the orthodox together, and times when one conquers the enemy by employing neither the extraordinary nor the orthodox.

Yet students must insist that the intent of the Patriarchs’ coming from the West lies in their recorded encounters (*jiyuan*) and not in the verses of the Seven Buddhas. How is this different from a general who insists that victory can only be achieved through the extraordinary?

To oppose the enemy when one truly cannot overcome the enemy—is this not folly? If a student can indeed refine and investigate the verses of the Seven Buddhas, they will finally realize that Chan is not external to these verses.
If, despite investigating the kōans of the various patriarchs, one still fails to attain awakening, I fear such a person may not even equal those who simply uphold the verses.
Throughout the thousands of sutras and myriad treatises, there is nothing else; they do nothing but explain how to transcend the body.

This is merely mental hearing. Like such students, they cannot free themselves from the obstacles of bodily and mental grasping; thus, they cannot awaken to or enter into the ancestral机缘 (ji-yuan) of the verses of the Seven Buddhas.
This is what is called "Yue Gong’s painted dragon. If a true dragon were to appear before them, I know they would surely drop their brush and flee in terror.
Therefore, I exhort both those who have left home and those who remain at home who are resolved to sever birth and death. To cut [through this]—

Regarding afflictions: if one can faithfully uphold the verses of Vipaśyin Buddha, and through long-term cultivation bring them to maturity, then the obstacles of grasping within body and mind will eventually be dissolved.
Furthermore, when the grasping of the body is eliminated, nirvāṇa manifests before one.
When the mind’s grasping is extinguished, bodhi manifests before one. These two are what the teachings call the "two fruits of the transformation of the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*):
namely, transforming birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) to rely upon nirvāṇa, and transforming afflictions (*kleśa*) to rely upon bodhi. Alas!
Since birth-and-death has been transformed into nirvāṇa and afflictions have been transformed into bodhi—at such a moment as this, I [am no longer...]

"What matters is this: since I am already free from all concerns, I may mount the wheel of compassion and wisdom to transport all those who possess such concerns back to the land of total non-concern.
This is not only the aspiration of the Layman of the Mountain Valleys, but also the fundamental vow of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, Laozi said: 'I have a great affliction, which is that I have a body. If I had no body, I would [have no affliction]...'"
"What is the affliction? he asked. Again it says: "To possess a sharp awareness and yet walk the Great Way—this is to fear only the act of bestowing.
Furthermore, when Yanzi’s mind was in a state of equanimity and he sat in forgetfulness (*zuowang*), it is said: "He cast off his limbs and discarded his intelligence.
Is casting off the limbs not the meaning of Laozi’s view that the body is an affliction? Is discarding intelligence not the meaning of Laozi’s view that the mind is something to be feared? (3)
The teachings of the Sages all instruct sentient beings to speak of detachment from body and mind; how could this apply only to the Śākya clan?
Vipaśyin Buddha—this means "Self-Mastered Awakened One. If one has not yet detached from body and mind, then wherever one goes there will be obstruction.
Once body and mind are detached, then wherever one goes, is there not self-mastery? (The Verses of the Seven Buddhas shown to the assembly.)
I respectfully hear that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the past, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the present, and all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the future,
have all embraced all sentient beings of the ten directions and the three periods of time through six modes, without leaving anyone behind.

I have not heard that one can gather and sustain sentient beings by smelting the crown of the head, burning the arms, plucking out hair to fumigate the nose, sleeping upon needles, or reclining on thorns.

Yet, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* contains accounts of burning the arms and incinerating the body; the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* includes the practice of burning a finger to repent for transgressions.
In the *Lotus Sutra*, the elephant is used as a metaphor; once the meaning is grasped, the metaphor is forgotten. In truth, it does not lie in the burning of arms or the incineration [of the body].
This is the body [of the teaching]. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* points out, it is truly for the purpose of repenting one's own sins; it is not something used to delude foolish men and women.

What are the six types of inclusion? First is "sudden inclusion" (*tun-she*). This refers to how all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, from their first generation of the mind of enlightenment, regard all sentient beings as their parents and, according to their capacity, directly benefit and include them through all manner of pleasant things.
To take them up is called "sudden inclusion. Second is "superior inclusion. "Superior" means preeminent or supreme.

This refers to when Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, having already resolved their minds [on enlightenment], give rise to a heart of respect toward their parents and, through various skillful means, exhort them to practice wholesome dharmas, making offerings to them at appropriate times and knowing how to repay their kindness.
Furthermore, they teach their wives, children, and kinsmen to practice wholesome dharmas, causing them to...
As for their superior advancement: sometimes the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas manifest as vidyārājas or noble cakravartins to gather in the people.

They transform them through the Dharma in accordance with the law, without inflicting unjust punishment. They benefit them through both material wealth and the Dharma, teaching the people according to their capacities to cultivate wholesome dharmas;
this is called "superior gathering. Third is "gathering by taking," which refers to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas...

The Bodhisattva always gathers in sentient beings by means of two kinds of methods. First, he always employs a mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*), benefiting all sentient beings with material wealth so that they may be freed from poverty.

Second, he always employs a mind of compassion (*karuṇā*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī*), benefiting all sentient beings with the Dharma, uprooting evil and false views and instructing them to practice the true Dharma.
This is called "gathering through attraction. "Evil" refers to the ten non-virtuous actions (*daśākuśala*).
The three of the body, the four of speech, and the three of the mind—these are called the ten unwholesome actions (*daśākuśala*).

"Perversity" refers to such practices as plucking out one's hair, fumigating the nose, sleeping on needles, lying upon thorns, cauterizing the crown of the head, burning the arms, and the precepts of cattle and dogs; these are called wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

"Long-term gathering" refers to how the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas gather in sentient beings over a vast period of time, teaching and transforming them for a long duration until they attain maturity; this is called long-term gathering.
Fifth is "gathering in a short time," which refers to how Buddhas and Bodhisattvas gather in sentient beings so that, through their instruction, those beings attain maturity in no long time;
this is called gathering in a short time. Examples include Sudhana, the Dragon Girl, and the butcher Viśākhā. Sixth is "gathering later."
This refers to how Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, following the aforementioned five types of gathering, gather sentient beings such that they can attain maturity within this very lifetime;
this is called "subsequent gathering" (*paścād-āvarjana*) or "final gathering.
Whether one is a monastic or a layperson, anyone who aspires to emerge from the ocean of suffering of birth and death should examine each of these six modes of gathering thoroughly and with clarity.
Rely upon them and practice accordingly; naturally, the Buddha’s knowledge and vision will open through this, and contemplative practice will be perfected through this.

If you do not follow the bequeathed teachings of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas regarding what is known and what is practiced, then even if you were to sacrifice bodies and lives as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and undergo various difficult and painful ascetic practices, they would all constitute the work of Māra. Why is this? Because the Buddha’s knowledge and vision would not be opened.
Therefore, because the Buddha’s practice was not [merely] about achieving external feats, the Buddha and Māra are like ice and water: where there is no ice, there is water;
where there is no water, there is ice. Thus it is said: "A difference of a hair's breadth results in worlds as far apart as heaven and earth.

Furthermore, while refining one's crown, burning one's arms, and offering rice to the Sangha are certainly virtuous deeds, they are not equal to contemplating the body through the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and contemplating the mind through the four aggregates (*skandha*). Body and mind...
Contemplating ripening: transforming birth and death into nirvana, and transforming afflictions into bodhi.
Comparing one who merely bears the name of "monk" but lacks the reality of a monk to [a true monk], their superiority and inferiority are as clear as black and white.

The Buddha said that those who call themselves disciples of the Buddha, yet do not understand the Buddha’s words nor practice the Buddha’s conduct, are called "shaven-headed laypeople. Therefore, feeding such shaven-headed laypeople is equivalent to feeding ordinary people.
If those such as beggars and the like were truly so, they would not yet know how to transform birth-and-death into nirvana or transform afflictions into bodhi.
They falsely take this suffering body as their practice and delude ignorant and foolish sentient beings; how could these be anything other than demons or heterodox teachers?
(Regarding the sixfold summary showing the renunciant and the householder:
Although sentient beings possess innate spiritual awareness, they are unable to employ it simply because they do not yet know that it exists. Once they know that it exists, [they can employ it].

In daily life, one is thus able to find harmony solely with oneself. Generally speaking, those who possess this knowledge know that the body is transformed by the body, and they know that the mind is transformed by the mind;
therefore, while abiding within body and mind, they possess more than sufficient liberation. Hence it is said: "To know existence is for existence to perish;

to know non-existence is for non-existence to fail. Since this is the case for both existence and non-existence, how could transgression and merit, or fortune and misfortune, exist independently of the nature?

Generally, those who study Buddhism may master the Dharma-nature school (Xingzong) while failing to master the Dharma-characteristics school (Xiangzong); they thus constantly remain lost at the entrance to the path of semblance-prajñā (xiangsi banruo).

Or, they may master both schools while failing to master the Chan school; this is like Duke Ye’s painted dragon, which so perfectly mimicked the dragon’s form and appearance that it seemed truly alive, yet ultimately could never bring forth thunder and rain.
Such individuals fail to discern the distinction at the entrance to the path of semblance-prajñā.

This is clear. It cannot help but draw upon various non-Buddhist classics and force them into conformity with Buddhist scriptures. Furthermore, the single flavor of the Nature School (Xingzong) is empty, vast, and spiritually penetrating;
those mired in the dust and toil of worldly life, upon encountering even a small ripple of its waves, feel their hearts immediately soar beyond restraint.

It is just like reading the *Zhuangzi*, which causes one’s spirit and soul to wander far beyond the surface of this turbid world. Within this state of emptiness and exhilaration, one receives [the teaching].

Once used, if one considers this to be the ultimate limit, one will never seek further progress. Whenever one encounters the blows and strikes of a true teacher (kalyāṇamitra), one immediately regards them as creating trouble.
If this malady is not eliminated, one will ultimately become a natural outsider (t’ien-jan wai-tao).

This is because those who are utterly unable to distinguish between good and evil on the path of training their habits lack proficiency in the Dharma-characteristics school (Lakṣaṇa-yāna) and have their eight consciousnesses (vijñānas) in a state of confusion.
If you do not know which consciousness is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), which is inference (*anumāna*), which is false cognition (*abhūta-parikalpa*),
and which consciousness encompasses all three types of valid cognition; nor if you do not know which consciousness is transformed into wisdom (*jñāna*)—
then even if you are thoroughly proficient in the Seven Schools and Eight Gates of the Nature School (*Xingzong*), it will merely be like filling yourself with a painted cake.

How could one who is hungry ever obtain satiety? If one has not reached ultimate realization in the Chan school, then such karmic occasions as Yunmen’s “beating the Buddha to feed the dog” and Nanquan’s “slaughtering the cat”—even a Bodhisattva of the Tenth Ground would, upon hearing such extraordinary matters, inevitably give rise to great doubt and terror.
Since ancient times in this land of China, there have always been those who have privately regarded these as [mere] Buddhist scriptures.
All of these individuals have extracted the essential threads from the *Zhuangzi*, *Laozi*, and the Six Classics to establish their own distinct schools.
If such people were to seek a clear understanding within the school of Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), how could they have made such erroneous statements as to incur the ridicule of later generations?

This is just like those followers of the scholastic tradition (*yixue*) who, perhaps giving rise to slander against the Chan school, formulate words to reject it; in all cases, their foresight is simply not far-reaching.
The mind clings with heavy attachment; because it does not penetrate through the sphere of sensory consciousness, one falls into this error.

For instance, regarding the present body, if one is ultimately not clear according to the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school (xiangzong), and fails to know where this body will fall after death, then one’s recognition of others remains unbroken.

If you do not break through the delusion regarding others, you will be deceived by them. Within the realms of food, drink, and the male-female relationship, you will naturally be unable to maintain mastery;
you will simply perceive what is desirable. Once you perceive what is desirable, this mind becomes distracted. When the mind is distracted, the body is deluded;

even if a living Buddha were to instruct you with ear-to-ear and face-to-face teaching all day long, he could not transform you. This is because this mind and this body have both become a single entity.
This mass of desire—wherein lies any empty space capable of receiving the *amṛta*? It is not at all difficult to discern and break through this body.

If, before birth, the eyes did not grasp forms, the ears did not grasp sounds, the nose did not grasp fragrances or stenches, the tongue did not grasp salty or bland flavors, and the body did not grasp tactile sensations, then the mental faculty (*manas*) would have no dependence.
Since the faculties have no dependence, how could the objects have any dependence? [And thus] object and consciousness...

It is without dependence; it is quiescent and extinguished in the present moment. When this quiescence manifests, all conditions—whether favorable or adverse—are suddenly transformed into the constant radiance.
By inferring from this, one's present body is nothing more than a shadow of the five sense-objects that fell away at birth.
If horizontal conceptualizations are not eliminated, one merely becomes this lump of flesh. Alas! During life, there were shadows of the five sensory objects;
because consciousness could not penetrate them, they coalesced into this present lump of flesh.

If this present lump of flesh is again not penetrated by consciousness, then this lump of flesh will continue to proliferate and evolve without end. Therefore, regardless of whether your faculties are sharp or dull, within the three realms—
Within the twenty-five states of existence, one must seek a way out from the very beginning;
this can only be achieved by scrutinizing the lump of flesh until it is completely shattered. Once this lump of flesh is seen through, the root of the affliction of birth is uprooted.

Once these roots have been pulled out, one is entirely free from entanglements. Having attained this freedom from entanglements, even such acts as coughing, spitting, or swinging one's arms are all pure Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*).
With the light of this Brahma-conduct, one illuminates those demons and heretics;

they will naturally lose heart and be struck with terror, finding no leisure but to take refuge [in the Dharma]. Nevertheless, to see through this lump of flesh is a difficult matter. If, however, regarding emergence...

The minds of people in this world are unsettled in their views and clouded by indecision; how could it be easy to transform them? Furthermore, the texts of the Abhidharma school (Xiangzong) lack a tradition of flexible adaptation and lineage transmission;
the more one studies, the more one becomes bound. Therefore, [one must look] toward the Nature School (Xingzong) and the Chan School.
They do not come together in harmony. If one has attained a thorough understanding of the School of Characteristics (Lakṣaṇayāna), then all external texts are likewise entirely the Buddha-dharma.

Thus, an ancient said: "If a person recognizes their own mind, there is not a single inch of soil upon the great earth. Since there is not even an inch of soil, what are external texts other than the mind?
I often see many such patients; therefore, I do not begrudge the trouble of pulling at the branches [to guide them].
The extension of this vine is as follows (shown to the disciples).

The utility of the Tripitaka Teaching lies in its urgency to transform ordinary beings. The utility of the Shared Teaching lies in its urgency to transform the inferior habit of clarifying emptiness by means of destroying form.
The Separate Teaching is urgent in transforming the narrow consciousness of those who follow the Shared Teaching. The Perfect Teaching is complete from beginning to end; I am like this.

This is the fundamental intent of the initial approach. Those who follow the *Tongjiao* (Common Teaching) speak in narrow terms; their severance of delusions stops at *jian-xi* (view-delusion and thought-delusion), and they merely excel in the skillful cessation of form (*rūpa*).
The efficacy of the *Biejiao* (Distinct Teaching) is extraordinary and does not conform to the standard of the *Tongjiao*; it involves the severance of twelve grades of *wuming* (ignorance).
The *Yuanjiao* (Perfect Teaching), however, severs them perfectly. Whenever one reads the inner scriptures, one must not fail to apply the principle of the "six stages of identity" (*liu ji*).
When both are fused, one is clearly aware and never deluded; there can be no doubt that this avoids the errors of demons and externalists.
If one deliberates upon this in detail, the essential meaning of the "Treatise on Non-Transmigration" will be understood by more than half. (Shown to Wenlang.)
Venerable assembly, today is the thirtieth night of the twelfth lunar month. Amidst the color of plum blossoms, a new year is added;
amidst the sound of firecrackers, the old year is diminished. I ask that you each still your discursive minds and listen attentively as I, Ciyun, speak two sentences of plain talk.

Generally speaking, life and death are matters of immediate concern. It is merely that the distractions of wealth and honor, or poverty and low station—whether in the bustle of activity or the leisure of idleness—obstruct one’s realization.
Even at the height of worldly glory, among humans one cannot surpass a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), and in the heavens one cannot surpass Maheśvara.
Yet when their merit is exhausted, the five signs of decline appear; their kinsmen grow weary and turn away, their majesty and power fade, and the Mara of Death stands before them. He...
Is it not that you must forcefully establish yourself as the master? You have enjoyed many days of deluded blessings;
yet, how can you withstand the insentient force of impermanence? When the time comes for you to depart directly, how will you differ from an ordinary person?

Ciyun sees those before him—those with heads held high and shoulders squared, with clever tongues and sharp teeth, speaking with such fluency—who do not all devote their hearts and minds [to this task]?
They take fame, achievement, wealth, and honor as their ultimate goal. Whether sleeping, waking, dreaming, or imagining, they insist on fulfilling their desires before they will rest.
Even other sovereigns, such as the Wheel-Turning Kings and Maheśvara, ultimately serve as nothing more than such examples.
Why do you exhaust your spirit and energy, rushing about in a frantic pursuit, only to bring your life to an end? Furthermore, there is another class who cannot be ensnared by wealth and status.

He cherishes idleness as his ideal and cultivates his sentiments in noble refinement. Little does he realize that between heaven and the human realm, there is nothing more idle than the divine immortals (*shenxian*):
they travel back and forth riding upon the winds, covering ten thousand *li* in an instant; wherever their will inclines, there is nothing it does not fulfill.
Once one has repaid their debts and fallen into the cycle of birth and death, all former supernatural powers, transformations, and various states of ease become utterly useless.
One must undergo suffering according to one's karma, sharing the same lot as pigs and dogs, repaying karmic debts.

O Great Assembly, those who previously enjoyed wealth, honor, and leisure have met with the night of the thirtieth day of the year; even they have reached such an end. As for the poor and lowly who were always busy—how much more so!

How much more so when it comes to this? This is the very model of suffering and joy within the triple world. Furthermore, you do not know that there is also suffering and joy outside the triple world.
Does the assembly believe me? If you say you do not believe, how can you dare to disbelieve the sincere words of the Buddhas?

The Śrāvakas have severed the delusions of views and thought, are forever liberated from the defiled body of the fragmented existence, and exercise the six supernormal powers with ease in the unconditioned.
One passes straight through mountain walls; one’s body is transformed and one’s nature is changed. If one recites [the name], it is accomplished immediately—how joyful this is!
Yet, there still remain sands-of-dust ignorance and fundamental ignorance; one cannot avoid the death and rebirth of transformation.

Regarding the Buddha-nature, one has not yet attained thorough, penetrating realization. One wallows in the turbid wine of quiescent extinction, facing a blank wall when encountering matters, like a withered log.

It is like a corpse; how could this not be suffering? This is the suffering and pleasure beyond the three realms, which obscures the Buddha-nature and prevents one from enjoying the samādhi of true quiescence.

How much more so within the three realms, with this putrid, precarious, and fragile body, and these deluded thoughts born of karmic bonds—clinging to wealth and status as if they were tears and saliva; truly, it is like having blood inside one's skin.
A man with sinews in his eyes—upon hearing such plain words, how could he not feel a burning heat in his face and realize his error?
He must seek a way to escape this trap. Great assembly, there is a matter that is both most ordinary and most extraordinary.
One simply does not know for oneself. What is "extremely ordinary"? It is that which all people inherently possess, which is fundamentally manifest from the beginning.
It is merely because one is sealed by emotions and locked by consciousness that one cannot enjoy its use. What is "extremely extraordinary"?

Without departing from this foul and impure body, and right within the den of afflictions and karma, to give rise to a segment of firm and resolute faith, with courageous and diligent effort. To benefit—
Regarding harm, defamation, or praise, disregard them briefly without attachment. Once you have resolved this matter with such a spirit, you may then meet a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Confide your innermost thoughts and sincere heart to him; he will certainly not辜负 (betray) this single point of your sincerity, and will surely point out to you the method for finding the path to life.
Accept his words directly and immediately; do not engage in speculative deliberation, nor do you "sell" [your practice].
To fabricate with cleverness is like a newborn infant who thinks only of milk, unaware of whether its mother is beautiful or ugly, noble or lowly.
A man who practices Chan must be likewise; for when a person is not in their true nature, the mind is not pure.
One must by no means engage in such matters. If one truly possesses the resolve for this, one should bind oneself to the original *huatou* (critical phrase).

Without regard for days or months, one should persevere with constant and subtle diligence until it manifests vividly before one—this being a single, seamless state that cannot be shattered by contact.
When the pass of emotion is severed and the functioning of consciousness ceases, at such a moment, you will find not even a single atom of hatred or attachment within your breast;
how much less could there be birth or death upon this physical shell? At this juncture, summon all your brilliance and courage, risk your very life to press forward, making awakening your sole goal.
If your true mind does not retreat, the Buddhas of the ten directions and the devas of provisional rank will [protect you].

The Eight Classes of Beings, including the Nāgas, will surely bestow compassionate protection and secret empowerment. Suddenly, you will attain thorough penetration; the Great Matter will be resolved, and mastery over both killing and giving life will be yours at will.
It is not an impediment to propagate the Dharma through wealth and status, nor to uplift the common world by manifesting noble refinement.
If one insists that wealth, status, and leisure are obstacles to the Way, this is merely binding oneself with no rope—there are many such "dead knots. Once you have truly reached this stage, even...
Without departing from this stinking skin-bag, one is a flesh-and-blood Bodhisattva. Together with all beings, one extracts nails and pulls out wedges, transforming the mundane into the sacred.
One strides boldly upon the crown of Vairocana and spreads transformation at the gateway of present affairs.

With a roar, one strikes down the thieving mind of those heroes who falsely claim to practice Zen; with staff and shout, one knocks away the habitual tendencies of the ignorant man. If it were thus...
This is so. It is not merely for one’s own realization; it is also for the sake of others. Is this not truly extraordinary?
O Great Assembly, what is the fundamental *huatou* (critical phrase)? Zhaozhou asked Touzi: "When a person has died the great death, how is it that they come back to life?
Touzi said: "Night travel is not permitted; you must arrive by the break of dawn. Tell me, what is the principle here? If there is anyone who understands this, please come forward and express it.
Look! If you fail to realize this at all, each person will simply follow their own whims. The verse says: "A single moment of ignorance clouds the numinous spirit;
Obscured and submerged, how many thousands of lifetimes have passed? Upon the putrid shell of a corpse, one discriminates beauty and ugliness;

At the gateway of illusion, one gives rise to love and hate. Deeply mired in deviant paths, who understands the peril? Drifting through the sea of suffering, one knows not to awaken. Do not say that these words are idle chatter."
The essential point is for all of you to emerge from the pit of fire (addressing the assembly on the eve of the New Year).
Now, the five desires are like an overturned basin that obscures the light of the mind; if one can lift it away, there will be eternal dawn for a thousand ages—is this not a source of great joy?
Therefore, as for the virtue of preserving life, nothing compares to the merit of inheriting the light. Indeed, when the sun sinks, the moon inherits its place.

When the moon sets, the lamp succeeds it. If there were no subtle light that shines forth of its own accord in places where the illumination of the sun, moon, and lamp does not reach, then all forms of darkness would forever shroud me.
Therefore, the purpose of establishing the lineage records (*zongpu*) lies in the precious succession of this luminosity.
From Kāśyapa down to the Patriarchal Founder in China, all have cast aside the ineffable mystery.
Within the space between his robes, bowl, verses, and hymns, those of superior natural talent immediately attained wondrous mastery, their clarity shining forth inexhaustibly.

Furthermore, he may be compared to the lamp of infinite light; yet it is only the single branch of Jibei that has flourished with such exceptional brilliance, appearing as though no other school could rival it.
Nevertheless, the lineages of Yunmen, Dongshan, Guiyang, and Fayen have also produced individuals who were all extraordinary and magnificent.
Furthermore, one is not like those "yellow-mouthed" beginners of the Chan school who merely grasp at black and white distinctions.

One must maintain the five precepts with precision and clearly understand the three categories of pure conduct (*trisaṃvara*). As for the five precepts: they are non-killing, non-stealing, non-sexual misconduct, non-lying, and non-intoxication.
As for the three categories: first is the *saṃvara-śīla* (precept of restraint). "Law" (*lǜ*) here refers to legal code; it carries the meaning of prohibition.
"Rite" (yi) refers to ritual procedure; it carries the meaning of a formal standard. One who upholds these precepts must:
first, not praise oneself or disparage others for the sake of gain or support; second, not be intentionally stingy or refuse to give to others;
third, not strike or revile sentient beings with a mind of anger; fourth, not slander the Mahāyāna sūtras. By upholding these four dharmas, there shall be no [transgression].
Because one does not abandon evil, it is called the *saṃvara-śīla* (precept of restraining discipline). Second, regarding the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precept of gathering virtuous dharmas):

this refers to all wholesome dharmas performed by body, speech, and mind, as well as the three types of wisdom—listening, reflection, and cultivation—and the myriad practices of the six perfections; because there is nothing that is not gathered and collected, it is called the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas.

Third, regarding the *sattva-anugrāhaka-śīla* (precept of benefiting sentient beings): this refers to being able to embrace and sustain all sentient beings. It is that which is capable of such embracing.

The practices are precisely loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). Loving-kindness is called "affectionate mindfulness," for it is able to bestow happiness upon sentient beings.

Compassion is called "pity," for it is able to extract suffering from sentient beings. Sympathetic joy is called "rejoicing," for it celebrates all sentient beings as they leave suffering behind and attain happiness.
Equanimity is called "neither hatred nor affection," for it constantly keeps in mind that all sentient beings equally attain this state of neither hatred nor affection. By means of these—

These dharmas encompass all sentient beings; therefore, they are called the "precepts for gathering sentient beings. Now, regarding the five precepts and the three clusters [of pure precepts], they are both refined and comprehensive, leaving nothing out.
As for their refinement, the five serve as the foundation of all precepts; thus, these five are called the "root precepts.

As for their comprehensiveness, there is no good quality they do not include; thus, these three are called the "three clusters of precepts. Therefore, one may uphold the five without upholding the three, but...

They lead others toward the realms of humans and devas, yet it is difficult for them to succeed the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Thus, they may refrain from killing but fail to release captured creatures; they may refrain from stealing but fail to practice giving;
they may refrain from sexual misconduct but fail to teach others to uphold the precepts; they may refrain from false speech but fail to speak with loving-kindness or preach the Dharma;

they may refrain from intoxicants but fail to encourage others to abstain from drinking. This is called the five precepts of the lower grade. To act in the opposite manner is called the middle [grade].

Regarding the grades of the five precepts: if one can maintain the five precepts and the three clusters of pure conduct (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*) simultaneously without transgression, this is called the superior grade of the five precepts. Alas!

When not a single thought arises, the five precepts and the three clusters of pure conduct are perfected in both ordinary beings and sages. Once a single thought arises, the five precepts and the three clusters of pure conduct...
Before entering the Way, one may not have even heard its name; or, having heard its name, one may not understand its meaning and intent;

or, though understanding its meaning and intent, one may be unable to maintain it due to heavy karmic obstructions caused by defilement. Only during the course of the Way or after attaining it does one do so;

yet the Way has degrees of depth, such that one may maintain it fully or partially, as clearly stated in the teachings, which need not be cited here at length. Furthermore, for those at the initial stage of mind, this is called "the hair."

Regarding ordinary persons on the Path: even if they encounter the winds of sensory objects—whether favorable or adverse—their consciousness is as flickering and unstable as a tuft of swan down dropped upon a broad highway;
when a slight breeze suddenly arises, it drifts and shifts without fixed direction.

Therefore, those who are determined to transcend suffering and uphold the five precepts must, if they do not make a grave and solemn vow to sternly restrain their consciousness, find themselves easily swept away by defilement and fall into ruin whenever they happen to encounter the winds of sensory objects due to the power of active mental formations.

The pure shore is difficult to ascend; therefore, the ancients, knowing their own defilements and habitual tendencies were thick and heavy, made great and solemn vows beneath each and every precept to support their resolve for the precepts, ensuring it did not waver or drift.
Now that you likewise know that fleeting glory is precarious and fragile, [you must likewise uphold the precepts].

Perceiving the signs, they act: casting off their caps and shaving their hair. From the nobility down to the commoners, and from the commoners seeking the Truth, may they, life after life, never again receive a mixed body;
may they always be born as men with all six sense-faculties complete, and with merit and wisdom following their vows, may they forever be bhikṣus.
After severing the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), one emanates bodies and disperses shadows to purify Buddha-lands and bring sentient beings to maturity.

How could such precepts and vows (*śīla-praṇidhāna*) be easily generated? Once one has received the precepts, if one does not bind the mind with the rope of vows through the fear of evil oaths, the precepts are indeed difficult to maintain.

Because vows are truly difficult to generate, if the precepts are urgent while the vows are lax, the precepts will belong to the realm of arising and ceasing. When both the precepts and the vows are urgent, [they transcend this].

The precepts themselves are without arising or ceasing. If one can uphold these precepts that are without arising or ceasing, then the five precepts and the three clusters (triskandha) will naturally remain unviolated amidst the favorable or adverse winds of sensory objects, occurring spontaneously.
Should you worry that the three clusters are too vast to maintain, you must first hold the five precepts with precision and gradually uphold the three clusters.
If the five precepts are not held with precision, the deities of the precepts will become angry; for each single precept there are five deities, and for the five [precepts] there are twenty-five.
The twenty-five deities of the precepts follow the practitioner like a shadow follows a form, protecting the one who observes the precepts without departing for even a moment.
If the observance of the precepts is not refined, these deities will likewise never fail to be indignant.

Two follow and one opposes; this is the fundamental principle of delusion and enlightenment. If these fundamental principles are not clarified, then understanding and practice will lose their standard.

In the fifth year of the Dazhong era of Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty, Hongbian of Jianfu Monastery in Jingzhao was summoned for an audience. The Emperor asked him, "What is meant by 'sudden realization'?"
"What is meant by 'gradual cultivation'? He replied, "Sudden [awakening] refers to the self-nature, which is of the same rank as that of the Buddha.

However, because there are defiled habits from beginningless time, one must employ gradual cultivation as an antidote to cause the functioning of that nature to arise in accordance with it. It is like a person eating rice: one does not become full because of a single mouthful.

The Emperor was pleased and conferred upon him the title Chan Master Yuanzhi (Perfect Wisdom). These two—sudden and gradual—are the "one accordant and one contrary" that serve as the seal of the fundamental principle.

Generally speaking, sentient beings originally possess no suffering-feeling (*duḥkhā-vedanā*). It is because their nature transforms into emotion that turbidity and agitation arise, and from this, the myriad phenomena are produced.

Once turbidity and agitation have arisen, clarity and stillness lose their true essence. Once clarity and stillness are lost, turbidity and agitation deepen daily. As turbidity and agitation deepen, there is nowhere they do not reach.
Thus, when a single thought flickers up—if that thought does not abide in the ten grave evils of the superior grade, it will instead [abide in the intermediate or inferior grades].
If one does not abide in the ten evils of middling stinginess, then one abides in the ten evils of minor delusion.
If one does not abide in the ten evils of minor delusion, then one abides in the interval between the fulfillment and deficiency of the five precepts.

If one does not abide in the interval between the fulfillment and deficiency of the five precepts, then one abides in the realm of practicing the ten wholesome deeds with suspicion and jealousy. If one does not abide in the practice [of the ten wholesome deeds] with suspicion...
The realm of the ten wholesome deeds lies in the heavens where the ten wholesome deeds are purely cultivated.

Although these six [realms] differ in their ascent and descent, and each is intersected by suffering and joy, they all exist because the fundamental nature (*xing*) transforms into emotion (*qing*). Now, the original nature is fundamentally wondrous;

when it transforms into coarseness, it is termed the "lower ordinary" (*xiàfán*). Coarseness inevitably flows toward turbidity; turbidity inevitably leads to suffering. When suffering reaches its extreme, one must necessarily contemplate the source.
It is like a person at the moment of death who does not call out to their parents, but must wail to Heaven and strike the earth;

when the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas encounter this state of fundamental thought, they then infuse them with the Buddha-nature as a causal condition. Once this infusion has matured, one attains liberation.

Through liberation, one is able to realize that the faculties and their objects are devoid of self-nature, and thus discern what constitutes "self" and "other. This state of being without self or other is such that even in the time of Yao, it was no different.

It increases; it does not decrease even under the reign of Zhou. Yao was able to resolve the defilement of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), whereby human desires diminished daily and the principles of Heaven (*tīnglǐ*) were perfected daily.
It is like the return of the sun to the great earth: as one part of ice melts, one part of water manifests before us.
When ten parts of ice are melted away, ten parts of water manifest before one. Once the water has manifested, the ice can no longer be found;
this is called the first reversal. The nature of water is pervasive and interfused: it is square when in a square place, and round when in a round place.
It can serve as the spiritual moisture for the six directions, and it can become the frost and snow of the three winter months. In the heavens it becomes rain; on the earth it becomes a spring. In...
Flowing, it becomes a river; contained, it becomes a lake; receiving, it becomes an ocean. Though its names are manifold, in reality, it is nothing but moisture.

Because it resides within vessels of various shapes and sizes, yet the vessels cannot obstruct or retain it, it is like the Sage of Wondrous Enlightenment who divides his body and disperses his reflections to enter all realms of existence.
He awakens the deluded and brings them to enlightenment; he transforms suffering into joy; there is no task he does not accomplish. However—
There has never been any accumulation [of obstruction]. This is called "wondrously conforming. It is also called "conforming to the nature to give rise to function.

Within this conforming-to-nature arising of function, there are those that are contrary yet incomplete, those that are contrary and about to become complete, and those that are contrary and already complete.

If one cannot forget that which is already complete, then the function of conforming to the nature will necessarily fail to accord with that nature. Only the function that accords with the nature [truly fulfills it].

Only then can one be free from the entanglements of wondrous phenomena. When [the Buddha] went to the Great Penetrating Wisdom-Conquering Buddha (Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū), he sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas without attaining the Buddha-way.

Yet, as soon as he sat upon this seat, the Buddha-dharma manifested before him; it was because he had forgotten [all conceptualization] that he was able to give rise to the functioning that accords with the nature of reality.
Within this single "contrariety," there are the four dharma-realms—the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, Bodhisattva, and Buddha—which are not equal.

Generally speaking, the śrāvakas regard suffering and its origin as defilement and take delight in cessation and the path as purity; the pratyekabuddhas regard the cycle of transmigration as suffering and take delight in the reversal of that cycle as bliss.
Although the bodhisattvas possess distinct and diverse types of realization, they all rely upon the six perfections and the ten pāramitās.
[Other Buddhas] purify Buddha-lands and bring sentient beings to maturity. The Buddha, however, is not so; he suddenly clarifies one's own nature (*svabhāva*).

Although one may be an odorous and vulgar ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), when confronted by the clash of favorable or adverse conditions, one can respond by following this single flavor of one's true nature. It is like a dragon using water, or a tiger using wind.
If one asks whether this is called "having a mind," [the answer is no], for even before the thought of the dragon or tiger has arisen, the wind and clouds arise spontaneously. If one asks...
Is it not because he is without mind? Were it not for the subtle dragon and tiger, wind and clouds would not arise. Old Pang said: "The affairs of daily life are no different;
they simply accord with me of their own accord. At every turn there is nothing to be grasped or rejected; everywhere there is no discordant tension. Who designates 'red' and 'purple'?
Mountains and hills are free from even a speck of dust. Spiritual powers and wondrous functions are found in carrying water and hauling firewood. Yunmen asked Da...
The assembly asked, "Is it the wood that carries the man, or the man that carries the wood? Master Xiaoshou was carrying firewood out to the market when the load suddenly fell to the ground;
he attained great enlightenment immediately and composed a verse: "It falling to the ground is no other thing; Spreading across all directions, it is not dust.
Mountains, rivers, and the great earth— The entire body of the Dharma King is revealed. Furthermore, Grand Master Lu Xun said to Nanquan, "Master Zhao [Sengzhao] was truly..."

How strange! To understand that heaven and earth share a single root and all things are one body—Nanquan pointed to the peony flowers in the courtyard and said, "When people see this one flower, it is like being in a dream. Alas! Lord Ye’s painting of dragons was not for lack of dedication.
When the True Dragon appeared before him, he immediately cast down his brush and fled in terror.
If Zibo had seen Nanquan speak in such a manner, he would have given him a slap and said, "Have you ever seen the several rows of white hairs on the back of the Master's head?

When Fashu came forward, Zibo—whose nature could not tolerate being tied up with trivialities—took up the essential principles of two direct and one reverse approaches for the sake of Shu Lang, while simultaneously invoking the ancient worthies.

A few instances of karmic conditions. Furthermore, regarding my own playful display of our family style, when I acted as a substitute for Lu Xuan to deliver a further word, it was nothing more than this:
"Mingshu Lang has not gone far up the mountain; he is bidding farewell to his aged mother.

If one does not comfort the hearts of Mingshu Lang and his mother with the matter of one's fundamental nature, would that not be the behavior of a mere child? Nevertheless, this matter of fundamental nature is not for those who are not heroes through and through.

It is likewise not easy to take this upon oneself. For now, let us use the Three Refuges to cultivate the causes for the transcendence of both mother and child, and the Five Precepts to nurture the seeds of the human and celestial realms.
As for the Three Refuges: by taking refuge in the Buddha, one shall not be deluded; by taking refuge in the Dharma, one shall not suffer from spiritual hunger;

and by taking refuge in the Sangha, one’s food shall surely be pure. Therefore it is said: "Food that is not of right livelihood is insufficient to sustain the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom. The Five [Precepts]...
Regarding the precepts: by not killing, one attains longevity; by not stealing, one attains prosperity; by not committing sexual misconduct, one attains purity;

by not speaking falsely, one attains credibility; by not drinking intoxicants, one attains wisdom. These five have superior, middling, and inferior levels. The superior level governs the mind; the middling level restrains the body;

the inferior level refers to those who, though having previously received the precepts, are in fact guilty of violating them in name only. One should carefully deliberate upon these superior, middling, and inferior precepts and choose for oneself with diligence.
(Shown to Zhu Qiuan). Now, the multitude are devoured by desire;
only the sage can devour desire. To be devoured by desire is to lose oneself and pursue external objects;
to be able to devour desire is to have nothing that does not turn [in one's favor]. Therefore it is said: "If one can turn desire, one is identical to the Tathāgata. The multitude...
When a person encounters the realm of desire, they perceive only the object and fail to perceive themselves. Only the sage possesses no desire within desire;
thus, he can wondrously transform all things without being entangled by them.
The spirit of worldly dharmas is not ultimate; it is not what I transform, and one can never enter its inner precincts. How much less so for supramundane dharmas?
Generally speaking, when entering worldly dharmas, one does so while still carrying emotional attachments, and thus one may attain their essence.
But as for supramundane dharmas, if one does not enter by transcending emotion—then even if you exert yourself with bitter toil until the end of time, you will never have an entry.

Therefore it is said: "Investigate apart from mind, intellect, and consciousness. If one does not investigate apart from mind, intellect, and consciousness, then whatever one investigates is merely mind, intellect, and consciousness.
The ancients called this "a thief using the master's house as its own"; not only will the house be destroyed, but in the end, disaster cannot be avoided.
Hanhanzi said: "I have read the *Zaopo lun* (Treatise on the Date-Palm and the Cypress), and thereby come to know Qingliang’s commentary on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Although it is refined and profound, it does not equal the expositions of Li Fangshan. There are no tracks or paths to be found;
yet for those with deep celestial faculties, taking that which cannot be sought as their vanguard, they investigate ceaselessly until suddenly entering [the truth], whereupon they laugh and sing."

Within the pavilions of Maitreya, those who roam above the immeasurable oceans of lands and have attained the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena are not lacking among the generations from the Tang through the Ming dynasties; such were Puan Xu and Ying Shaowu.
However, because their fortunes met with varying degrees of success or obstruction, those they attained remained either hidden or manifest according to the times—just as it was with Chuanzi.

Had you obtained Jia Shan, you would have ultimately sunk into obscurity amidst the misty waves. Now, the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* represent the beginning and the end of our Great Hero’s fundamental intention.
Regarding the commentaries on those great scriptures, there is Qingliang for the *Avataṃsaka*, and Fangshan for the treatises;
yet as for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, since it constitutes the culmination of the *Avataṃsaka*, if it had not been entrusted to the hands of Tiantai, then the *Xuanyi*...
Who, then, is capable of this? There is the Venerable Jiyin of the Song dynasty, who composed a treatise on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Within the three turnings and nine parables, he used written words to cast forth the wondrousness that is not transmitted—like a lustrous pearl in the night.
They roll, turn, slant, and collide within the golden basin; one cannot fathom their direction. What can be ascertained with certainty is that they do not leave the basin.
The basin is a metaphor for written words; the pearls are a metaphor for the ineffable subtlety. Someone might say:
"If the subtlety cannot be transmitted, and since it cannot be transmitted, who would know its subtlety? Yet, having known the subtlety, [one does not...]
If it can be attained through words and language, then how could words and language alone be external to the wondrous?
If words and language were indeed external to the wondrous, then words and language could not transmit it; yet the wondrous can be transmitted.
If the wondrous can be transmitted while words and language cannot, then the coarse becomes increasingly refined, and the refined...
The latter is increasingly coarse. "Son, go and inquire about this for me. The dull-witted son replied, "The subtle refers to principle (li); the coarse refers to phenomena (shi).
Principle is like water; phenomena are like waves. If one were to insist that written words and spoken language are not sublime...
The wondrous is not words or language; it is like seeking waves apart from water, or seeking water apart from waves.

If you, my son, awaken to this analogy of waves and water, then you will understand—without waiting for me to tell you again—the distinction between the refined and the coarse. Tiantai established the six stages of "being thus" (*liu ji*):

the six are the waves, and "thusness" (*ji*) is the water. There are those who, deluded by the waves, claim that the waves are not water; there are those who, deluded by the water, claim that the water...

It is not that the waves are not [the water]. To say that the waves are not the water is for the ordinary person to willingly fall into the pit of non-distinction, remaining forever deluded and unable to emerge.
To say that the water is not the waves is for those of shallow realization to inevitably sit in the trench of neglecting the Sage.
This is why my Tiantai school establishes the doctrine of the "six identities" (*liu ji*). The six identities are:

identity in principle (*li ji*), identity in name (*ming zi ji*), identity in practice (*guan xing ji*), identity in semblance (*xiang si ji*), identity in partial realization (*fen zheng ji*), and ultimate identity (*jue jing ji*). Now, identity in principle means that it is shared by both the holy and the ordinary.
Identity in name means that one has heard the names [of the teachings] and understands their meaning. Identity in practice means that one is able to rely upon...

This explains the "practice of realization" (pratipatti). "Similar identity" (sādṛśya-ekayāna) means that by relying on this practice, one attains a state of identity with the water of the principle of similarity.
"Partial realization identity" (praveśa-ekayāna) means that one is able to enter the first stage (bhūmi), attaining identity with the flowing water of the true Dharma.

From this point onward, through the stages up to Equal Enlightenment (samantaprabhā), one achieves Wondrous Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi); this is called "ultimate identity" (niṣṭhā-ekayāna). Therefore, know that outside of these six [aspects of] identity, there is no identity to be attained.
To know that the six external objects are identical, one finds that even the six [faculties] are unobtainable. One who can know in this way is said to possess "perfect understanding" (yuanjie).
Based on perfect understanding, one initiates practice; this is first called "perfect practice" (yuanxing). When practice is perfected, how could that which is realized not be perfect? Alas!

The Tripitaka, Shared, and Distinct teachings all flow from the Golden Mouth [of the Buddha], yet they are not named the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao); only the Flower [Adornment Sutra] is so designated.
Yan Fa-hua [states]: "The various sutras of the Supreme Vehicle are called the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao). This is because the capacities of sentient beings differ.

For instance, the time of the *Avataṃsaka* was not the time of the Deer Park, nor was it the time of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. How could the Tathāgata, a holy being, possess different intentions or different words?
This is like the establishment of the 'Six Identities' and the arrangement of the 'Five Stages,' which collectively signify that while principle can be realized suddenly, phenomena..."

It must be eliminated gradually; therefore, it does not rely upon the five stages. If one does not first achieve sudden enlightenment into the perfect principle, then the practice remains within the realm of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).

Only when the habitual defilements accumulated since beginningless time have been completely refined away can the essence of the fruition ever be realized. If the refinement of these habitual defilements does not begin with sudden enlightenment into the perfect principle, then the practice belongs to the category of the conditioned.

It is not that the perfect practice is separate from the six identities; it is simply that the six are the very identities. Outside of waves there is no water; it is simply that the identities are the very waves. Outside of water there are no waves.
Thus, both the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* employ images to convey their meaning. Those who can grasp the meaning while forgetting the image may point to the waves and call them water;
they may point to the principle and call it phenomena; they may point to the subtle and call it the coarse; and they may point to the coarse and call it the subtle.

It may be refined; yet, if one has emerged from the mire of the elephant but fails to grasp its underlying meaning, then even if one reappears at the Stone Gate of Mount Fangshan in Qingliang, I can do nothing for such a person.
If one were to use rope as a net, it is uncertain whether the lives of creatures on land and in water would escape;
but if one uses money as a net, the flavors of both land and water will be exhausted. Now, flavor does not exist apart from the tongue, and the tongue does not exist apart from the body.

The body exists because of the mind; without the mind, it does not exist. Thus, one who indulges in lust is transformed into a woman, and one who indulges in violence is transformed into a fierce tiger.
For when the mind undergoes change, the form cannot help but change as well. Is this not proof that the mind can give rise to the body?
If a person can truly obtain the tongue through flavors, the body through the tongue, the mind through the body, and the nature through the mind, then the nature is obtained.
Then what constitutes the object, and what constitutes the self? Therefore it is said: "That which belongs to the category of blood and breath must possess cognition;

all that possesses cognition must share the same substance. It is also said: "Nature is nearly the same [in all beings]. Yet the scholars of the world do not understand nature, and they arbitrarily claim that my own nature and the nature of things are different.
Thus, they lose their sense of taste because of flavor; they lose their body because of the tongue; they lose their mind because of the body; and they obscure their nature because of the mind.
If one is oblivious to their nature, then there is nothing that does not become emotion; thus, they are driven by physical form and cannot employ the form for their own purpose.
Once they are employed by the form, they do no more than exhaust the desires of mouth and belly—how could they know what is called "nature"? If Mr.
Liu were to recommend this [insight], then abstaining from killing would not be difficult. (Exhorting Mr. Liu to Abstain from Killing)
