Read by Hanshan Deqing of the Ming Dynasty.
The Dharma-teaching sages recognized that the three obstacles constitute a great affliction; therefore, they established the method of *kṣamā* (repentance) to wash them away.

Once the three obstacles have been washed away, the light of the original mind becomes perfectly round and full. When the light of the original mind is perfectly round and full, one benefits both self and others, such that there is nowhere one does not reach.
It is accomplished. What are the three obstacles? They are the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), the obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*), and the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*).
What is the obstacle of afflictions? The fundamental mind is without deficiency; yet, because one does not know it in daily life, this very point of ignorance constitutes the obstacle of afflictions.
Because of this ignorance, one commits unwholesome acts, which is the obstacle of karma. Once unwholesome acts have been committed, Heaven, Earth, and the spirits will certainly...

One must loathe them. Once loathed, they must be eradicated. When eradicated, one settles upon the offense and establishes the confession; death shall certainly not be pardoned—this is the retribution for obstructions.

If the single mind does not arise and the myriad virtues are not obscured, one opens up things and accomplishes affairs; the merit is supreme and free from entanglement. This, moreover, arises from awakening through non-knowing.
Non-knowing originally has no self-nature; non-knowing itself becomes wisdom. Using wisdom to govern habituation, once habituation is exhausted, [liberation is attained].
When the spirit is whole, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished through non-action; this is provisionally called "sagehood.
Now, as for the nature of water: is it permanent, or is it impermanent? To the devas and humans, it appears as lapis lazuli;
to hungry ghosts, it appears as fierce flames; to fish and dragons, it appears as their dwelling place; and to those in the human world...
Thus, one regards it as a flowing wave. Because it is impermanent, if one abandons the lapis lazuli, the fierce flames have no place to abide;
if one abandons the fierce flames, the cave-dwelling has no place to abide; and if one abandons the cave-dwelling, then the flowing wave likewise has no root.
The worldly afflictions (*kleśa*) that people use daily are, for the sage, nothing other than liberation. Are these afflictions and liberation truly one thing? Or are they truly two?
Consider this: first, affliction and coolness are not the same; second, one must abandon affliction to seek coolness.
It is like trying to find water apart from the waves—how could it ever be possible? Suppose there is a person here who wishes to perform great Buddhist works through worldly toil (*kleśa*);
if they do not yet understand my teaching, they will ultimately fail to escape being driven and enslaved by that very toil.
You are the master. As the master, how could you not receive this command?

You should contemplate this deeply. Indeed, the ordinary and the sage are impermanent; awakening and delusion seem different. Yet, if one observes the present state with clarity, it is fundamentally devoid of even a speck of dust.

Nevertheless, because the root of emotion has not been uprooted, one is shrouded by the enclosures of love and hatred. Having wandered through long kalpas, one merely exhausts oneself in vain. One inherently possesses the pearl within one's robes, yet remains unaware of it.
This treasure, once pointed out and broken open, yields inexhaustible wealth and joy. The *Sūtra on the Eight Awakenings of the Great Men* is concise in diction yet superior in principle;
its style is profound and subtle. Regarding the single moment of delusion in sentient beings, the Tathāgata, the Great Man, wonderfully expounds the eight awakenings.
If sentient beings with the karmic affinity obtain even one awakening, they will surely transcend the sea of suffering—how much more so for those who attain them all! —Li Jizi, Grand Chancellor Lu.

Jizhi was by nature prone to excessive reflection. He followed his habitual patterns without awakening to their consequences; he did not realize that excessive reflection harms the spleen, and when the spleen is harmed, the earth becomes barren.
Since all things take earth as their mother, how could the child alone remain free from affliction when the mother is ill?

Thereupon, [the Master] commanded him to receive and uphold this sutra, desiring thereby to assist his awakening and transform his reflections. When reflections are transformed, there is no self; and where there is no self, all are one.
When things are identical, there is no "thing. Once both object and self are forgotten, who is it that can think, and what is it that is thought?
When both subject and object are stilled, a single moment of delusion gives rise to the eight perceptions. This is Ji-gao’s elixir for prolonging life; how could I not treasure it?
(Shown to Lu Ji-gao while he was holding the *Sūtra on the Eight Great Persons’ Perceptions*).
Now, as for the seven emotions and the eight awakenings: are they truly one, or are they truly two? If one follows the seven emotions, waves arise in the sea of suffering;

if one follows the eight awakenings, there is stillness on the mountain of nirvana. Thus, the Elder of Great Awakening, out of compassion for those wandering in transmigration, took that which sentient beings daily employ without awareness and opened it up into the eight awakenings, desiring thereby for all beings—
Birth. A single awakening is an eternal awakening. It is like dividing the light of a single lamp; the lights are inexhaustible.

Yet this light becomes seeing when it is in the eye, hearing when it is in the ear, smelling when it is in the nose, tasting when it is in the tongue, sensation when it is in the body, and cognition when it is in the mind.
Therefore it is said: "Divide one refined clarity into six harmonious combinations. Just as when the one mind does not arise—now tell me, what of the eight?

Where does awakening reside? It lies within the brilliance of the black and white. If you can directly discern good from evil, then what difference would there be between the eight perceptions mentioned in the sutras and one who attempts to paint蛾眉 (yumei—butterfly brows) upon a primordial chaos (hunchun)?
Originally, this is the forerunner of the mallet that hammers away at dullness and distraction; it is that which the Buddhas of the three periods have transmitted to one another in succession.
It depends entirely upon how it is employed. If employed skillfully, it will dispel dullness and distraction in a single instant and support *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* within great quiescence.
It will cause mountains and rivers to fall back into the ground where they never began to exist, and it will wash away body and mind into the realm of non-attainment, severing the fetters of desire.

This sharp sword serves as the sustenance for the life-force of this numinous body; it manifests the valor of the person of the present moment. The mind roams before the Primordial Sovereign (Xiangdi).
Originally there was a divine pearl, its radiance held within the palm; it was never any other treasure, yet who could offer a price for its worth?

Realizing the Buddha-body through the ordinary body, one constructs the Ultimate Truth (Paramārtha-satya) by relying upon conventional truth (Saṃvṛti-satya). Its merit fills the void, and its blessings are immeasurable. Truly...

For the practitioner, when a single breath of dullness or distraction is cleared, that very breath is the Buddha; when a single thought of dullness or distraction is cleared, that very thought is the Buddha.
Alas! Within this vast and boundless sea of suffering, all beings possessing breath and spirit harbor an enlightened soul.

They emerge and submerge their heads in such numbers that they cannot be counted. Suppose there were a single person who, beneath the hammering wheel, could maintain even one breath and one thought free from dullness and distraction, achieving one breath and one recitation of the Buddha’s name—if one were to observe this with the Buddha-eye, its merit would truly be inconceivable;
how much more so for those who practice for many days! Indeed, it is essential for people to value self-reflection.
If you can reflect back upon yourself, then regarding your own state, from birth until death, has there ever been a single moment of stillness amidst your dullness and distraction?
Therefore it is said: "If a person sits in stillness for even a brief moment, it is superior to building stupas of the seven treasures as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Those stupas will ultimately turn to dust, but a single thought of a tranquil mind achieves perfect enlightenment. Even if you do not apply this skillfully, you will at least not lose it to negligence.
This is a field of merit for humans and devas. Therefore, those who are wise, noble, eloquent, and capable should propagate and extol it; those with power should protect and provide for it.

At every site where a *daochang* (meditation hall) is located, all should assist in its promotion with an impartial mind. (This refers to the "Furnace for Eliminating Dullness and Distraction" meditation hall.)

Longevity and early death have no fixed signs; their signs depend solely upon the mind. If the mind arises, then fortune and misfortune can be managed; if it does not arise, both the ordinary and the sage are cut off at the root.
Therefore, to cast a short life into one of longevity is like molding earth into a clod—whether it succeeds or fails depends entirely on how I act.
Thus, if one holds the mantra with a superior mind (*adhimukti-citta*), there is nothing that will not be accomplished; if one holds the mantra with an indifferent mind, [it will merely be...]

It may rival Heaven. Yet, if one holds the mantra with a narrow and inferior mind, one will ultimately fail to obtain its efficacy; it merely plants a cause for the future. (This was taught to Yuanxin as he held the mantra.

Once the Dharma is established, those who do not follow the Dharma cannot stand. However, if one does not cast their emotions into the fire of wisdom, then the Dharma and the emotions will stand side by side.
Generally speaking, the intention of the Sage is nothing more than to transform the emotions, rather than transforming the Dharma.

Generally, phenomena belong to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), while mental states belong to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Thus, by means of the imagined, one enters the dependent;

by means of the dependent, one enters the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*); by means of the perfected, one enters the broken earthen bowl; by means of the broken earthen bowl, one enters the poisoned drum;
and by means of the poisoned drum, one enters the ocean of the samādhi of profound compassion. Then, the crucible and hammer of ordinary beings and sages lie within.
"A dry dung-scrapper" does not reside within the Dharma; thus it is said: "The myriad phenomena preach the Dharma for others, while I merely listen idly.
Fali offered this recommendation, thereby beginning to repay the master Shitou’s remark that "the road is slippery. (This was shown to Fali.)
Characteristics are fundamentally impermanent; they follow the influence of habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) and conform to it.

Therefore, when the past karma of good and evil perfumes the mind, it evokes the retribution of present suffering and pleasure, just as a seal impresses its mark upon clay; once formed, it is difficult to alter. This discussion primarily concerns ordinary people.

If one is a practitioner, then the length of their cultivation cannot be fixed. Even if there are karmic deeds created in previous lives that ought to result in retribution of suffering, because they now exert themselves with diligent effort in the present, their transgressions will not overcome their merit; thus, suffering is transformed into joy, and a short life is changed into a long one.
This is often seen with our own eyes, and the evidence is not lacking. Furthermore, upon reading the records of the Great Dhyāna Master Sengcan of Nanyue...
The Master bestowed the essential instructions of the mind in their entirety. His certification was clear and evident, as bright as the sun and stars, so that I no longer harbored any doubts.
He said: "A beginner practitioner has not yet attained the stage where phenomena revolve according to the mind; they may only practice by closing their eyes and forming mental images.

Once this becomes thoroughly proficient through long practice, all dharmas will shift and transform in accordance with thought, as easily as bending or extending a finger—there is nothing difficult about it. Therefore, the Great Bodhi..."

Śākyamuni. Even those of the Two Vehicles, lesser sages, and seers possessing the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*) are able to effect transformations within phenomena, such that the non-existent appears as existent and the existent appears as non-existent.
Viewed from this perspective, if one perfumes the mind with the contemplation of the provisional (*parikalpita*), then every phenomenon is provisional;

how could transforming them be difficult? If one perfumes the mind with the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), every phenomenon is empty; one rolls away existence and enters non-existence. Thus, the marks [of phenomena] vanish.
It is unattainable. What is premature death? What is longevity? What is sin? What is merit? When the mind is perfumed by the Middle Way, existence and non-existence are transcended;
yin and yang cannot ensnare it, and divine wisdom cannot fathom it. Regarding its verbal manifestations, they may be transformed and yet they may not; they may not be transformed and yet they may.
They may not be contrary and yet they may; they may be contrary and yet they may not. It is like a divine night-luminous pearl, perfectly...
They swirl and shift across the golden platter; though one were as sagely as Zhongni or as keen-sighted as Li Lou, who could determine their direction?
Therefore it is said: "With the appearance they arise in the mind; with the appearance they perish in the mind. Whether there is appearance or no appearance, arising and ceasing depend upon the mind.
For one who has realized the mind, at the threshold of birth and death, coming is like putting on a garment, and going is like taking one off.
Pants. (Regarding the characteristics of the discourse: This is a brief account of not forming views of attachment or aversion.

Sō Kaishū visited the Master and asked, "For what purpose have you left the household life? He replied, "I have left it to seek liberation from suffering. The Master asked, "By what method do you seek liberation from suffering?
He replied, "My faculties are dull; I simply practice the recitation of the Buddha's name. The Master said, "When you recite the Buddha's name, are you always..."
"Is there an interruption? He replied, "When I close my eyes and sleep, I immediately forget.
The Master rebuked him with a thunderous roar, saying, "If you forget as soon as you close your eyes, practicing *nien-fo* in such a manner, even ten thousand years of it will be of no avail.

From this day forward, you must ensure that your *nien-fo* continues without interruption even within your dreams; only then will you have the possibility of escaping suffering. If you cannot practice *nien-fo* while dreaming, you will remain in forgetfulness."
When he finished, as soon as he opened his eyes, he rose up wailing and weeping bitterly. He went straight before the Buddha and prostrated himself until his head bled.
He recited [the name] either a thousand times or ten thousand times, exhausting all his own strength, and then ceased. He performed this twenty or thirty times in such a manner.
Within the natural state of great slumber, the Buddha is never absent.

Furthermore, those in this world who practice mindfulness of the Buddha may do so for twenty or thirty years, or even for the duration of their entire lives; yet when the time of death arrives, it proves useless.
This is because they lacked the mindful thought while in the dream-like state of life. Human life is like being awake, and human death is like a dream. Therefore...
Those who attain Buddhahood through mindfulness while dreaming will naturally remain undisturbed at the time of death (this demonstrates mindfulness).
The Dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha is the most simple and convenient. However, those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha nowadays lack firm resolve;
therefore, though thousands or hundreds of people recite the Buddha’s name, not even one or two among them achieve success. This single phrase of the Buddha—everything...
Bodhisattvas, all devas, and all humans who are born in the Western Land—there are none who do not cross the sea of suffering by means of this single phrase, "Amitābha Buddha.
However, whether the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha is genuine or not is a critical point for examination;
it is verified directly through the two states of joy and affliction. Thus, the genuineness or falsity of the mind can be clearly distinguished. Generally speaking:
A person who sincerely recites the Buddha’s name remains, amidst both joy and affliction, necessarily with every thought-moment uninterrupted.
Therefore, neither affliction nor joy can disturb them. Since neither affliction nor joy can disturb them, they will naturally feel no fear or terror when confronted by the states of birth and death.
Nowadays, when people recite the Buddha’s name, even the slightest pleasure or displeasure reaches them...
[If you] put Amitābha Buddha behind your head, how can you expect the spiritual efficacy of nianfo? If you practice my nianfo according to this method,

and at the critical juncture of hatred and love you do not lose sight of this phrase "Amitābha Buddha," yet fail to experience its benefit in your daily life and fail to be reborn in the Western Pure Land at the time of death, then my tongue-root shall surely [be cut out].
"Rotten! If you do not practice according to my Dharma, then the efficacy of reciting the Buddha's name will have no spiritual response. The fault lies with you;
it has nothing to do with me. (He addressed the assembly regarding the recitation of the Buddha's name.)
The consciousness of sentient beings has long been mired in the dust and toil of worldly existence, such that they do not know how to return to their fundamental source.

If one wishes to accord with the enlightened nature even amidst this dust and toil, it is appropriate to rely upon provisional means of sustained concentration; these methods are not of a single kind.

Yet, how could there be anything superior to the secret causes of all Tathāgatas—the *dhāraṇī* of total retention? Why is this so? Because teachings adapted to the sharpness or dullness of faculties and tailored to varying levels of capacity are not ultimate.
One need only maintain this mantra; regardless of whether one is foolish or wise, all shall achieve the unsurpassed, most profound, and rare [attainment].
This is because its secret cause is inconceivable. If a bodhisattva, with faith, contemplates and observes the words of the mantra they uphold, [they shall likewise succeed].
Every word and every phrase is clearly perceived by the faculty of hearing; mind and ear are held in mutual harmony without any confusion.
Even within the state of sleep or dreaming, they are not forgotten. To recite it even once is superior to reciting it a hundred thousand million times;
it can extinguish the eighty-four thousand afflictions and give rise to the eighty-four thousand fruits of the Path. All its merits are most rare and inconceivable.

As for the measure: because this mantra is the merit of the original vows spoken by the Tathāgata King Blazing Radiance, when a Bodhisattva maintains the mantra, they should perform nine prostrations to the Tathāgata King Blazing Radiance.
With palms joined and kneeling in the *brahmāsana* posture, they should recite it one hundred and eight times daily.
One should complete the recitation in a single breath, for it is possible to fix the mind upon the breath. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "As for its recitation..."
It is like a needle: it means that one should maintain it within the mind without even a moment’s interruption.

Throughout the twelve periods of the day, except for when speaking with others, one may maintain it from the first moment of waking until just before sleep; one may maintain it while walking, while standing, and while sitting.
One may hold it while lying down; one may hold it while eating or drinking; one may hold it while attending to defecation or urination. Therefore, the recitation must not be interrupted.
The primary method is to hold it silently with the mouth closed, ensuring that the sounds are clearly distinct. This constitutes the true holding of the mantra.

One shall obtain peace and happiness from the four great elements, and merit and wisdom will increase. Whatever one aspires for, one will surely attain according to one's wishes. When holding the mantra, one should...
Form the vajra-fist with both hands; let the upper and lower teeth meet, and place the tongue against the center of the upper gum.
Keep the eyes fixed on the nose, and following the nose, observe the heart; from the heart, observe the navel. With one’s entire vital energy, remain silent and merge with the mantra.
This is the bridge for truly entering the nature of mind through the method of effortless contemplation (*anābhoga-dhyāna*). May all who see or hear this [attain realization].
Receive and uphold this with joy; maintain it with firm resolve throughout the duration of your life, following it with faith and without opposition. Cherish it and circulate it widely;
such a person is a true child of the Buddha (demonstrating the holding of the mantra).
Dwelling in a cramped room, even a single inauspicious word will be answered from a thousand *li* away. When likes and dislikes accumulate in the mind, the ultimate public good is obscured.
Among the myriad things that flourish, although there is order between the noble and the humble, and the large and the small do not correspond, as for what is called "life":
There has never been one who was not equal in this regard. Thus, if one restrains their emotions and guards their sounds to honor the life bestowed upon them, they become a gentleman (*junzi*).

If, however, they indulge their passions and let loose their voices, failing to treasure that which was given to them, they become a petty person (*xiaoren*). Now, to treasure life is to value the preservation of the body;
to value the preservation of the body is to value the regulation of emotions and the carefulness of speech. These three things can only be accomplished by a gentleman.
Now, as for form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and phenomena—why are these all termed "objects" (*viṣaya*) and not termed "mind"?

It is because these six obscure and delude the fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), just like dust falling into the eye: not only does it cause the four directions to appear displaced, but even when one extends one's own finger, one cannot see it.

Therefore, they are named "objects. Furthermore, "objects" are termed the "perceived," while the "faculties" (*indriya*) are termed the "perceiver. When both perceiver and perceived are present, that is the mind.
It is not called "mind" (citta), but is called "consciousness" (vijñāna). Mind is not far from its essential nature, whereas consciousness is very far removed.

Therefore, the practitioner who knows the Way uses the mind to investigate the sense organs and their objects; the organs and objects are like lingering snow, while the wisdom capable of this investigation is like a furnace fire blazing intensely.

Yet, if one throws a fragment of snow into it, how could one worry that it would not melt? If one pushes against the sensory objects (*viṣaya*) and investigates the origin of their union and separation, once that origin is grasped, the sense-faculties (*indriya*) will likewise be uprooted along with the objects.
When the faculties are uprooted and the objects are shed, the nature of phenomena is revealed as being free from both emotion and designation.

Once one's nature has been restored, then upon the field of honor and disgrace, life and death, gain and loss—through thousands of moldings and ten thousand refinements—one’s practice becomes profound and one’s contemplation mature.
When this is further permeated by great vows and guided by the light of wisdom, the duties of a Great Man are complete.

Third, they develop the mind to practice dhyāna for the sake of their retinue; this mostly belongs to the development of the mind of an animal. Fourth, they develop the mind to practice dhyāna out of envy to surpass others;

It has been over three hundred years since Dongping broke the mirror; it has been over four hundred years since Longtan blew out the lamp.

Descendants of later generations have become lost regarding the True Eye, claiming that the mirror and the lamp were extinguished, yet they do not realize that while walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, one emits ten great rays of light—the lamp has never been extinguished.

The light of the mirror and the lamp are eternally quiescent; clarity and the illusory reflections are both like the *tathatā*. Their illumination is inexhaustible.
It is called the lamp of inexhaustibility; its reflection is infinite, thus it is called the mirror of inexhaustibility.

It is used daily without being obscured, shining brightly within the space between the mind and the eyes. Yet sentient beings are deluded and do not know this; therefore, there are the teachings of the Sūtras.

Thus, all sentient beings, in their daily activities, appear and disappear within the pores of Samantabhadra, inside the radiance of Vairocana, and within the pavilions of Maitreya, upon the sword-blades of Mañjuśrī.

Only after reciting "Mahāprajñāpāramitā" three times may they enter the water. For Prajñā is the mother of all Buddhas; thus one should recite it.

As for their mother, her children—regardless of how many there may be—all follow after her. Generally, those who do not understand Prajñā cannot give rise to great shame and remorse, nor can they discern the underlying causes.
Why is this? Because their wisdom-eye is unclear and they fail to distinguish between the beautiful and the ugly.
What is meant by giving rise to great shame and remorse? One should reflect thus: "This body of mine is defiled and turbid..."
I am worthy [of this], yet my realization of the ground is not thorough, and my conduct is meager and thin. How can I befit such a pure bath?

From amidst the cold clouds of deep mountains and from places where snow ages and ice withers, firewood was hauled and transported, transforming cold into heat. Considering myself, what [merit do I possess]?"

When the time of death arrives, it is certain that among those nine people, ten will be found in a state of frantic confusion.

As for the Dhyānapāramitā, its text consists of ten fascicles and contains ten major chapters; it was expounded by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai.
The ten major chapters are: first, the General Meaning of Dhyānapāramitā; second, the Explanation of Dhyānapāramitā; third, the Clarification of the Gateways to Dhyānapāramitā;
fourth, the Discernment of the Sequence of Dhyānapāramitā; fifth, the Distinction... [text continues]... of Dhyānapāramitā.
1. The Dharma-mind of the *dhyānapāramitā*; 2. The sixfold differentiation of the preliminary practices (*pūrvaprayoga*) for the *dhyānapāramitā*;

3. The explanation of the cultivation and realization of the *dhyānapāramitā*; 4. The manifestation of the retributive fruit of the *dhyānapāramitā*; 5. The exposition of the arising of the teachings through the *dhyānapāramitā*.

The ten sections bring together the *dhyānapāramitā* as their ultimate resort. Within the sixth major chapter, "Discriminating the Expedient Means of the *Dhyānapāramitā*," two types of sons are cited:
first, external expedient means; second, internal expedient means. Regarding internal expedient means:
Furthermore, two grandsons were born. First, the cause is clarified, which merely gives rise to internal and external roots of goodness. Second, the nature of the roots of evil is verified.
The seventh major chapter is the "Chapter on the Cultivation and Realization of the Dhyāna-pāramitā," which cites four types of sons:
first, those who cultivate and realize mundane dhyāna; second, those who cultivate and realize both mundane and supramundane dhyāna; third, those who cultivate and realize the supramundane.

Regarding the signs of meditation (*jhāna-nimitta*): there are four types of cultivation and realization that are neither mundane nor supramundane signs of meditation; one type of cultivation and realization is a mundane sign of meditation, which further gives rise to three "grandsons":
first, the four dhyānas; second, the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*); and third, the four formless attainments (*catasra ārūpya-samāpattayaḥ*).

Furthermore, there are two types of cultivation and realization that are both mundane and supramundane signs of meditation, which also give rise to three "grandsons": first, the six doors of skillfulness (*ṣaṭ-kauśalya-mukha*); second... [text fragment].

The sixteen stages of special excellence (*ṣoḍaśa-viśeṣa*), the three types of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*), and the three modes of cultivation and realization of supramundane meditative signs (*dhyāna-nimitta*) give rise to two grandchildren:

first, the outflow-free [wisdom] of counteractive application (*pratipakṣa-anāsrava*); second, the outflow-free [wisdom] that takes principle as its object (*tattvālambana-anāsrava*). The outflow-free wisdom of counteractive application gives rise to nine great-grandchildren: first, the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*).

1. The eight recollections (*aṣṭa-smṛti*); 2. The ten perceptions (*daśa-saṃjñā*); 3. The four and eight liberations (*catasraḥ-aṣṭau-vimokṣāḥ*); 4. The five and eight spheres of mastery (*pañca-aṣṭau-abhibhv-āyatanāni*);

How could this be the way a Perfected Being (*tathāgata*) maintains his mind? The "Dullard" (Hanhanzi) remained somber for a long time and said, "How could I dare not obey your command? Thereupon, he climbed the tall pine tree to...
"Ox and horse. "The tall pines and the withered grass recede;

all dharmas are non-arising. What does this mean? The mind is not of itself the mind; it gives rise to cognition through the objects of sense. The objects are not of themselves the objects; they [arise] through..."
The mind establishes objects; from objects, cognition arises. Does cognition exist because of this? The mind establishes objects; do objects exist because of this?
Since both mind and objects are non-existent, who is there to act as their common cause? To claim they arise without a cause—how could such a thing be possible?

By this I know that mountains, rivers, and the great earth are fundamentally unarisen. To say they have arisen is merely a conceptual construction of the deluded mind; it is not the truth. Therefore it is said: "By means of..."
Principle governs emotion, like spring dissolving ice;
a thousand years of darkness in a chamber can be illuminated by a single lamp, yet the light of that single lamp can be extinguished by a slight breeze. Is illumination or darkness truly permanent?
If illumination and darkness were permanent, then that which perceives them would not be permanent. One who understands this may [be called a sage].
By reversing day into night and night into day, one who can thus treat day as night and night as day is fundamentally free from day and night.
There is no alternation between light and darkness; those who speak of such alternation have merely followed the advent of their own conceptual discrimination.
If discrimination does not arise, where would light and darkness be? How tragic! Light allows for seeing, while darkness does not; this is what is called being driven by sensory objects.
Consciousness: If consciousness were able to govern objects, then light and darkness would reside here and not there. Therefore it is said:
"If one can transform things, one is identical to the Tathāgata."
The nature of fire is without self; it depends upon various conditions. To seek the nature of fire outside of its conditions—how is this different from one who seeks water apart from the waves?
Since the nature of fire is thus, how could the other six elements be any different? Alas! Is the Way far away? It is not so.

In every encounter with phenomena, there is reality. Is the Sage far away? To embody this is itself the divine. Now, when encountering phenomena we cannot realize their reality, and when embodying them we cannot manifest the divine, it is because the nature of discriminative consciousness has not yet been extinguished and the wisdom that perceives the absence of objective dust has not yet been clarified.
Light and darkness give rise to day and night; day and night give rise to cold and heat; cold and heat give rise to past and present.

To be detached from the single thought of my present moment, all those things would be like a stone woman giving birth to a child. Thus it is said: "The ten ages of past and present, from beginning to end, do not depart from this very thought.
And again: "When seeking the mind, it is utterly unattainable. Nevertheless, though it is utterly unattainable, it exists—yet as if it did not.
If that which can be attained is unattainable, how could it possibly exist in isolation?
That within the *tathāgatagarbha* there are no consciousnesses is the word of the ancients; I, however, do not hold this view.

Within the minds of ordinary people, one does not allow for the existence of the *tathāgatagarbha*. For what reason? Because both the mundane and the sagely are each independent. It is, for example, like a single...
Regarding the bending and extending of a finger: when it is precisely bent, what is there of extension? When it is precisely extended, what is there of bending?

One is manifest before one’s eyes while the other is not; they are certainly not the same. Yet, as for the entire substance of the finger itself, it is fundamentally without superiority or inferiority.
Therefore it is said: "The lion roams alone, without a companion."
Outside of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) there is no form (*rūpa*); outside of form there is no emptiness. Emptiness and form exist through the faculties and emotions.
If one observes them from the perspective of external emotions, then where could emptiness and form possibly reside? Therefore it is said: "Emotion is the mother of transformation;

the myriad things are all its children. When the mother perishes, the children follow; this is the natural course of things. Someone may ask: "Form can be transformed by emotion, but how could emptiness possibly be transformed? The Master Hanchan replied: "Emptiness..."
Matter exists by waiting for emptiness; when matter transforms, it perishes into emptiness. This is the inevitability of principle. Why do you alone harbor doubt?
If the Dao did not give rise to emptiness, where would that which possesses form be placed? If the human mind were not empty, from what source would infinite goodness emerge?
Therefore it is said: "Emptiness can contain; that which can contain is great; that which is great has no exterior. No...
Externally, it stands alone. That which stands alone does not increase because of Yao, nor does it decrease because of Zhou;
yet Yao attained it, while Zhou lost it.
Nature transforms into emotion; emotion transforms into things. If one can trace back upward from this, what thing is not nature?

The five elements generate one another and also mutually overcome one another. The world prizes life and loathes such overcoming, yet it fails to realize that outside of generation there is no overcoming, and outside of overcoming there is no generation.
Therefore, the adept understands that generation itself is overcoming; hearing of death, they are not confused, for they know that overcoming is generation.

Those who remain in office do not satisfy the people’s expectations for advancement; those who leave office harbor thoughts of remaining. Those who stay have the sentiments of those who would depart; those who depart have the hearts of those who would stay. All of these are delusions.

Now, to leave office without resolution is to fail in one's loyalty; to remain in office without decisiveness is called the great delusion. Alas! If this great delusion is not eliminated, then even though—
To dwell amidst secluded crags and deep ravines—how is this any different from being in the marketplace?
One who sees water but cannot cross it does so because they lack a raft; one who sees the sky but cannot tread upon it does so because they lack wings.
However, rafts and wings both consist of wood, and wood grows from the earth. Viewed from this perspective, one sees that the earth itself cannot cross over nor tread upon.
Those of antiquity who understood this were thus able to float across the vast ocean without a raft and traverse the great void without wings.
I do not depend on myself, yet I depend on things; things do not depend on themselves, yet they depend on me. Both depend upon one another, yet things and self remain in opposition.
Therefore, those who expand their lands see things and forget the self; those who disregard fame and honor see the self and forget things.
One forgets, while the other does not—how different from both forgetting? Only those who forget both can [attain it].
Objects serve themselves and others.
Birds can fly; fish can swim. Yet, without space and water, their wings cannot unfold and their tails cannot move.
Thus, wild horses gallop across distant outskirts, and long winds roam through the great void; if there were no ground upon which to extend their feet, how could they exert their power?

To treat them as if they were [ordinary] people is to be perilous indeed. Therefore, when a gentleman deals with petty men, if he cannot ensure that each finds their proper place of utility rather than being discarded, what benefit does the gentleman’s hearing of the Way bring to the world?
To wait until desire is already ablaze before beginning to treat it—how is this different from attempting to extinguish a fire of piled firewood with a single cup of water?
One must act while the condition has not yet arisen; that is to say, before one is deluded, one is inherently luminous, and before one is moved, one is inherently still.

It is simply a matter of being cautious. For when luminosity reaches its limit, illumination arises; when stillness is exhausted, movement begins. Illumination becomes the harbinger of delusion, and arising becomes...

Because movement induces [delusion], the Sage foresaw this and prescribed the medicine of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) to treat the maladies of dullness and agitation. Once the illness is cured and the medicine discarded, that which was originally luminous and originally still is no longer termed "luminous" or "still"; rather, it is called: [The following passage continues: "...the state of the Tathāgata. This is what is meant by the statement: "The nature of all phenomena is ultimately empty and quiescent; there is no arising and no ceasing. It is also said: "The nature of all phenomena is eternally quiescent and originally extinguished; there is no birth and no death. Furthermore, it is said: "The nature of all phenomena is eternally tranquil and originally pure; there is no defilement and no purity. And again: "The nature of all phenomena is eternally unborn and originally unceasing; there is no coming and no going. Moreover, it is said: "The nature of all phenomena is eternally non-arising and originally non-ceasing; there is no bondage and no liberation. And yet again: "The nature of all phenomena is eternally non-existent and originally non-apparent; there is no existence and no non-existence. Furthermore, it is said: "The nature of all phenomena is eternally non-dual and originally non-differentiated; there is no oneness and no otherness. And finally: "The nature of all phenomena is eternally non-conceptual and originally non-discursive; there is no thought and no non-thought. If one can thus understand the meaning of these various statements, then one will know that the mind-nature is fundamentally luminous and fundamentally still. It is not that it becomes luminous and still through the practice of cultivation; rather, it is simply that its original luminosity and stillness have been revealed. Therefore, it is said: "The nature of all phenomena is eternally luminous and eternally still; there is no cultivation and no realization. It is also said: "The nature of all phenomena is eternally luminous and eternally still; there is no practice and no attainment. Furthermore, it is said: "The nature of all phenomena is eternally luminous and eternally still; there is no path and no fruition. And again: "The nature of all phenomena is eternally luminous and eternally still; there is no cause and no effect. Moreover, it is said: "The nature of all phenomena is eternally luminous and eternally still; there is no teacher and no disciple. And yet again: "The nature of all phenomena is eternally luminous and eternally still; there is no Buddha and no sentient beings. Furthermore, it is said: "The nature of all phenomena is eternally luminous and eternally still; there is no samsara and no nirvana. And again: "The nature of all phenomena is eternally luminous and eternally still; there is no cause and no effect. Moreover, it is said: "The nature
As for "concentration and wisdom," it is because one does not wish to forget the merit of restoring one's original nature.
Food, drink, and sexual desire—these are what all people crave. Yet, those who are able to turn back from their cravings ultimately reach a state of desirelessness.
Ah! Only those who are free from desire can labor for the world and bring peace to the world.
The body is not my own; those who possess it are deluded. To destroy delusion, nothing is better than wisdom. Wisdom does not arise in vain; it must arise from a love of learning.
If one learns and is able to discern the truth, how could this state be reached without wisdom? Therefore it is said: "Learning is not itself the Way," yet it is sufficient to destroy delusion.
Once delusion is destroyed and wisdom is opened, one can finally enter the Way.
One who can take ill is one who is already ill; from where could illness arise? It is because one cannot take ill that I am thus ill.
Yet, among all illnesses, none is greater than the arising of the mind. Once the mind arises, there is nowhere it does not reach—not only illness, but everything. Therefore it is said:
The eye is afflicted by forms; the ear is afflicted by sounds; the mind is afflicted by the self. Only for one who has forgotten the self is there no affliction from which to suffer;
such a person can then provide medicine for the ailments of the world.

The pine tree is originally silent; when the wind enters it, waves arise. Copper is originally not a mirror; when a mirror is formed, clarity arises. That which is insentient is dependent upon that which is sentient.
That which is soundless is also dependent upon that which has sound. Without clarity, one depends on clarity;

yet clarity is itself non-clarity, sound is itself soundlessness, and sentience is itself insentience. Therefore, it is said that they are "dependent. As for that which is "independent," all such things lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Because it is established solely by one’s own mind, those who realize that the mind is without self remain unaffected by the realms of fortune and misfortune; though they dwell within them, fortune and misfortune cannot delude them.

There is nothing that is not spiritual. That which is not spiritual is the mind. When the mind exists yet is able to be non-existent, how could non-existence possibly intoxicate it? Non-existence—*wu*.
It cannot be intoxicated; there is that which cannot be obscured. It can overturn heaven and earth and bring existence and non-existence to all things. Is it the spirit? Or is it not the spirit?
Carve wood into the shape of a fish; its belly is empty and void. Strike it with an object and a sound emerges from that which is nothing. That which is nothing can produce sound.

If there is no fruit, how can it exist? Sound does not arise from nothingness; yet, if sound has no fruit, how can it exist? Alas! To cite one category as an example for all: what thing can delude us?
Among those with form, none is greater than heaven and earth; among those without form, none is greater than empty space. There is the Way.
This is because one knows that both of those are but reflections of one's own mind; thus, one perceives emptiness as non-empty and form as non-form.
The dragon is the sovereign among scaly creatures, so who would not submit to it? Yet, if the sovereign has desires, then humans can fatten it.
That which is fattened are dogs and pigs. Now, if a dragon can likewise be fattened, how could it be a true dragon?
"To be alertly aware, yet to fear only the performance [of conditioned deeds]—these are the words of Laozi. The Great Mirror of Caoxi, however, said:
'When the mind arises in response to objects, how can Bodhi grow? This, too, suggests that having awareness does not deviate from non-awareness."
Is it old age? Is it Cao? Are they the same? Are they different? I cannot know this; I entrust it to the descendants of Fumo and await those who come after to discern it.
Suppose there are now one hundred people here, speaking with different mouths yet with a single voice, such that those who listen might suspect it is but one person. Alas!
That their mouths differ is due to what their emotions have moved; that their voices are identical is what issues from their nature. May I venture to ask about this nature?
He replied: "Before sound and prior to mind, only one who is without thought can achieve resonance with the Truth.
When people of the world see a painted bird, they consider it unreal; yet when they see a flying bird, they consider it a real bird.
Little do they realize that humans borrow the five elements to form a body. If one analyzes it, the body is found not to exist—how much less could there be a 'person'? As for this person..."
Since [the true] does not exist, how could a painted bird or a flying bird alone possess existence? Therefore it is said: "The true depends on the false for its existence;
when the false is forgotten, the true follows in being forgotten. If this is so, what is the true and what is the false?

When a straw dog has not yet been displayed, it is adorned with brocade and embroidery. Once the sacrifice is over, herd boys trample upon it. Now, as for the straw used to make the dog, the amount of straw does not increase;
when the dog reverts to being straw, the amount of straw does not decrease. Viewed from this perspective, the "dog" is merely a name; in reality, it is only straw.
Some might see the straw and think it is firewood, or see the dog and think it is a domestic animal. Yet, a dog can guard [the house].
A thief can transmit fire; a thief can kill a person; fire can burn a mountain. One phenomenon causes another, ten thousand phenomena cause one another, extending to infinity.
Ultimately, this cannot be known through intellectual cognition. Therefore it is said: "When a single wave stirs, ten thousand waves follow."
The purpose of study is to destroy ignorance. Suppose there were a person here who does not use study to destroy ignorance, but instead uses study to satisfy their desires;
viewed from this perspective, it becomes clear that the Sage established his teachings fundamentally to treat the ailments of the masses.
If the medicine now produces illness, then the Sage’s skill has reached its limit. Therefore it is said: "The finest clarified butter (mṛtaka) has become a poisonous drug."
Beans are contained within a jar; when spring arrives, they are able to sprout. A person remains amidst desire; when awakening arises, dreams can be eliminated. Therefore it is said:
"Only after there is great awakening does one know that there was a great dream. Now, this so-called "great dream" refers to both dreaming and waking together.

When dreaming is awakened to, the dream is eliminated. When waking itself is awakened to, the waking state is eliminated. Only when both dreaming and waking are eliminated is it called "great awakening."
Zhuang Zhou dreamed he was a butterfly; the butterfly dreamed it was Zhuang Zhou. This speaks from the perspective of having a mind.
I, however, say: I dream that I am the mountains and rivers; the mountains and rivers dream that they are me. This encompasses both having a mind and lacking a mind.
Alas! That which is capable of having mind and capable of encompassing both having mind and not having mind—is it a dream?
Or is it not a dream? All things are fundamentally tranquil; it is only man who creates clamor. If man did not create clamor, what affairs would there be in the world?
Thus, the one who governs the world by simply hanging his robes and wearing his cap does not act out of a state of having mind.
A single basin of water and a single fist-sized stone are sufficient to encompass Mount Tai and the vast ocean. Why is this so? Greatness is not great in itself;
it is great only in relation to smallness. Smallness is not small in itself; it is small only in relation to greatness.
When greatness depends on smallness, the heavens and earth can be contained within a mustard seed. When smallness depends on greatness, even a pore of the skin can accommodate them.
It is empty space. Empty space has no form; even a single hair can contain it, let alone the heavens, the earth, and the myriad things. Therefore it is said:
"A hair’s breadth is not minute, for it accommodates all within its narrowness; empty space is not vast, for it contains all extensively without limit."
One plants pines so that cranes may dwell there; one raises cranes so that they may serve as substitutes for the wind.
Thus, when Liezi ascended lightly on the wind to roam beyond the Eight Wildernesses and returned to find his former dwelling gone, he still considered himself to be beyond the Eight Wildernesses.
Therefore it is said: "The Way is neither existent nor non-existent; how can it be sought through spatial location? The Way is neither distant nor near."
How could one doubt this by means of coming and going? Only those who neither seek nor doubt are either of superior wisdom or the most ignorant.
The mind consists of the true mind and the deluded mind. The true mind illuminates objects without arising; the deluded mind, however, is stirred up and pulled along by objects.
This is so because in the true mind, things and self are one and the same; the sages cannot increase it, nor can the commoners decrease it. In the deluded mind, however, objects are manifold:
some take the conditioned as objects, some take the unconditioned as objects, and some take the partial perspectives of the various schools of thought as objects.
Thus it is said: "The mind is originally without arising; it exists because of objects. Whether beyond the six realms or within the six realms, [it is all thus].

The cage is emptied. Furthermore, Laozi regarded the body as a great affliction; yet, while he maintained that when the body is free of affliction there is no [suffering], he did not state the underlying principle of how this comes to be.
To say, however, that "the four elements are borrowed to form the body," makes clear the reason why there is no body [once they are dispersed].
Now, the mind is fundamentally not weary; it is the form that burdens it with weariness. If the body is cast off, there is nothing capable of wearying the mind. The mind...
Is there a fruit [of this]? An ancient said: "For one who has perfected the spirit, the mind will even abandon it—how much more so the body?
Therefore it is said: "When the mind exists, sin and merit have a master; when the mind is forgotten, the master is absent. Although sin and merit exist, who shall be their master?"
My mind has not yet been stirred; do not construct pathways of meaning.

Therefore, to exhaust all the world’s sophistry and exhaust all the world’s principles is like using a net to catch the wind or shearing the hair from a tortoise. Nevertheless, those who act well leave no footprints;
those who speak well possess no power of the tongue. To speak thus and to act thus is called "speaking without speaking" and "acting without acting."
To act without acting, and to speak without speaking: though words fill the world, fundamentally there is no speech;
though conduct pervades the world, fundamentally there is no action. Therefore it is said: "Without acting, one arrives; without speaking, one is believed."

The multitude believed that height could not exceed that of heaven and thickness could not exceed that of earth; thus they said, "Heaven is high and earth is thick," and that nothing could equal them.
Yet they did not realize that although heaven and earth are high and thick, they too possess the magnitude of form.
Now, if form were separated from the formless, from what would form originate? If the formless were separated from form, by whom would the formless be made manifest? To be "made manifest" means—
This refers to the identity of existence and non-existence.
Courage that is not righteous is called violence. Benevolence that lacks clarity is called inversion. Inversion means that the small harms the great.
Only when benevolence appears as non-benevolent does it accord with the Way.
The moon reflects in the autumn waters; spring adorns the countenance of flowers. Even those of the utmost stupidity have never seen these sights without being pleased.

Yet they fail to realize that apart from one's own mind, the water has nothing to be clear, the moon has nothing to be bright, spring has nothing to manifest, and the flowers have nothing to flourish.
One who understands this may be spoken with regarding the general outline of how the mind accords with things as they are.
Master Daosheng gathered stones as his disciples and discoursed with them on the essential meaning of *nirvāṇa*. All the stones nodded their heads in agreement.

Now, stones originally have no minds; how could they have ears? To have neither mind nor ears, yet to nod in assent at the thought and to receive it through sound—was this nodding and receiving due to the mind, or was it due to the ear?
One who sees desire and forgets the body is one for whom desire is more important than the body. One who sees the body and forgets desire is one for whom the body is more important than desire.
For a person whose desires are heavy, what is the use of great talent? Only the sage utilizes desire as a means to its end.
In the end, this leads one to be without desire. One who values the person is naturally able to forget desire; for the body is the root of desire and the mind is its master.
If one cannot forget the mind, then the body remains subject to desire. Therefore it is said: "Only by forgetting the mind does the body have nothing to which it is bound."
A snake can become a dragon; the common people can become sages. Today, the common people fill the world, yet those who ascend to sagehood are so few.
Alas! Wind moves above, and custom is formed below; it depends entirely on how one inspires and rouses them.
If the one who inspires and rouses them is not the right person, then even if sages filled the world, they would be as if non-existent.
"The young child plays with his own shadow, unaware that he is being toyed with by the shadow. This is the word of Tanzi. I, however, say:
"The shadow toys with the young child, unaware that it is being toyed with by the child. Tanzi’s words can be sought through conventional meaning;
my words are difficult to reconcile through logic. As for Tanzi and I—who comes first and who comes after? Who is wise and who is foolish? I cannot distinguish between them. Moreover—
I entrust this to one who lacks the power of discernment.
Having read the *Zhuangzi*, I realized that Zhou (Zhuangzi) was not a follower of Laozi. Having read the *Mencius*, I realized that Ke (Mencius) was not a follower of Zhongni (Confucius).
For what reason? Laozi did not engage in disputation; Zhou excelled at disputation. Zhongni spoke of human nature.

Life is active; to say that nature is dead is to distort the truth through disputation. To be dead is to lack spiritual efficacy. To distort the truth and lack spiritual efficacy are the great flaws of even the wise.

A sheep does not know a donkey; a donkey does not know a horse; a horse does not know a dragon. To say a donkey cannot travel a hundred *li*, or to say a horse... [is likewise a failure of understanding].
To say that one cannot travel a thousand *li*, or that a dragon cannot undulate through the nine heavens, is to judge others by the limits of oneself.

If one were permitted to judge others by one's own standards, then the Way could be attained through mere human effort. Why then, if the ruler is supreme, would the minister not be able to present it to him?
And if the father is supremely compassionate, why would the son not be able to transmit it to him? Therefore, it is said: "One must not judge others by the limits of oneself."

Exhaustion. The Way cannot be attained through force. Only by relinquishing oneself and exhausting others can one reach the point where nothing remains unfeeling; there is no Way that cannot be attained in this way.
When the sun rises high, the masses of darkness vanish of their own accord; when the clouds thicken, the brilliant sun loses its clarity. Now, suppose there is a person here who—
With the water of non-arising, one douses the fire of craving; yet it scorches the spirit and consumes harmony, never ceasing.
One contemplates it by day and dreams of it by night; thought upon thought, dream upon dream, accumulating years into kalpas, where ten thousand ages pass as a single breath.
Some call this long, others call it short; whether long or short, existent or non-existent—only those who have transcended conceptual thought truly know.
This is it. From Mount Min to Stonehead (Shitou), one descends from the high. Mount Min is as if in the heavens; Stonehead is as if in a deep abyss.
When there is water in the heavens, fish and dragons dwell therein. When there is land within the abyss, people and things find their lodging therein. As for those above—
One does not prepare defenses against flooding because the land is low, nor does one worry about the scouring of water because it stands high;
this is destiny (*vidhi*) and karma (*karman*). Therefore, it is said that while one’s wisdom and vision desire to remain in the world, the force of karma constantly shifts one from land to land.
When the man sees the woman, he is joyful; when the woman sees the man, she is likewise joyful. Although the man and woman are distinct, their joy is never anything other than one.

Alas! Within the very inception of this joy, there exists that which is not entangled by joy itself. If a person can understand this, then such joy is precisely what is meant by "the thoughts being without deviation" (*si wu xie*).
Frugality can accumulate blessings, yet it can also accumulate calamities. If one practices frugality in common with others, that is not true frugality; blessings will surely accumulate.
If one practices frugality toward others but is not frugal with oneself, calamities will surely accumulate. Therefore it is said:

"One who practices frugality in common with others, though they may starve to death, feels no resentment; one who practices frugality toward others but is not frugal with oneself, though they may be warm and well-fed..."
It is not that they do not cherish it.
If one were young and did not grow old, grew old and did not fall ill, fell ill and did not die, then those who live would have no means [to end their lives].
If one were born and did not become young, became young and did not grow old, grew old and did not fall ill, then those who die would likewise have no means [to depart]. Alas! Death is—
Life is the medium for death; life serves as the medium for death. It is like a revolving wheel: from where does its beginning arise? Therefore it is said:
life is fundamentally without birth, and death is fundamentally without dying. It is merely that some experience birth and death arbitrarily.
The people of Wu delight in *lú* fish and water-mallow (*chén-cài*), while the people of Yan delight in camel’s milk and cow’s milk, water-mallow and donkey fish, and cow’s milk and camel’s milk.
Although their flavors differ, their preferences are not of two kinds. To the *lú* fish and water-mallow, the multitude considers them fresh;
to the camel’s milk and cow’s milk, the multitude considers them rank. Alas! If the tongue-root did not move and consciousness did not taste flavor, it would be like the rain falling from heaven.
Ambrosia. When the earth yields sweet and fertile produce, who does not know how to relish it?

Whether one treats it with public fairness or private partiality, both arise from the mind itself. If treated with public fairness, the whole world rejoices; if treated with private partiality, the whole world is incensed.
Joy gives rise to fortune; anger gives rise to calamity. One may know that fortune arises from impartiality, yet fail to use impartiality to extinguish private bias;
this is because one wishes to intoxicate the mind.
To restrain one's desires is not difficult; it is only self-respect that is difficult. If a person can maintain self-respect, even high rank and generous emoluments cannot move them.
If they can truly manifest such unwavering clarity until they reach a state where movement is free from desire, they are close to being a sage.

In antiquity, there was a woman of integrity who said, "It would be better to starve to death than to live having lost my integrity; to live having lost my integrity is like being dead. She subsequently died of starvation.
Therefore, the world looks up to his enduring legacy as one gazes at the moon in the cold sky;
it is as bright as the clear blue heavens. Suddenly, clouds arise. Within my pure and tranquil mind, thoughts arise abruptly. Do these thoughts arise of themselves?
Is there indeed something that causes them to arise? To arise and yet be able to return, to emerge and yet be able to go back—this is what it means to arise and yet not [be lost].
Returning to wander in foreign lands, solitary and suffering, from morning until night, one finds no moment of peace. It is like a long wind driving the clouds;
though the clouds have no mind of their own, they cannot help but drift aimlessly because the wind causes it to be so.

Therefore it is said: "The winds of sensory objects are vast and sweeping, withering the forest of merit; the fires of the mind blaze fiercely, burning away the path to the mountain of awakening. The mountain...
Above there is heaven; who can see it?

Food and drink, for human beings, serve merely to sustain their lives. Suppose there is a person here who does not use food and drink to sustain life, but instead harms themselves—this is surely the fault of a lack of moderation.
If one can exercise moderation in eating and drinking, [one will avoid such harm].
On a small scale, it can provide for one person and one family; on a large scale, it can provide for the whole world. Therefore it is said:
"The wise are able to harmonize the five viscera; when these are full and utilized, they can harmonize the world—this is no exaggeration."
In antiquity, there were those who possessed the strength to uproot mountains and the breath to swallow the world.

While a person stands upon the earth with their mouth on the surface of the earth, they are able to uproot a mountain. Since the mountain is earth and the mouth is also earth, this is called "uprooting earth with earth.
That the earth swallows the world is not contrary to reason. Conversely, although such expressions exist, they are merely exaggerations of heroic prowess.
The world compares a beautiful woman to a fine flower and a fine flower to a beautiful woman;
yet they fail to realize that in comparing a person to a flower and a flower to a person, that which performs the comparison is neither the flower nor the person. Therefore it is said:
"Circumstances and conditions have no inherent beauty or ugliness; beauty and ugliness arise from the mind."
The Hu horse yearns for the north wind; the Yue bird nests on the southern branch. Southerners know how to sail boats; northerners know how to ride horses.
Although humans and things differ, their constant principle is one. Thus, it enables the farmers to yield and defer within the Hall of Distinction.
To place scholars among the plow and the hoe—though they may grow accustomed to it after a long time—is ultimately not their natural state.
For this reason, the Sage does not teach the world by means of what is contrary to its nature; he teaches it through the Middle Way, simply following that which is constant.

What is constant endures; what endures persists for a long time; from long persistence arises greatness; and in greatness, nothing is left unexhausted. Why, then, resort to what is contrary to the constant?
The fragrance of the peach and plum blossoms is thick and rich; wandering bees gather without being summoned, and when the flowers fall, they disperse without being sent away.
Yet one fails to realize that while the flowers have their periods of flourishing and withering, the tree itself undergoes no change.

Since the tree undergoes no change, who knows that today’s falling petals may not be the very foundation for tomorrow’s thick fragrance? Long ago, there was a man who was just then receiving the seal of a high minister.
His prestige shook the world. He then inscribed a poem upon the walls of the guest hall, saying:

"The frost-covered pines and snow-clad bamboo at Zhongshan Temple—here I shall retire in my old age, spending the remainder of my life. Alas! How many hands and eyes does the Great Compassionate Bodhisattva possess?
Indeed, not even a single speck can deceive him; there is truly a reason for this.
With eyes open, one sees mountains and rivers; with eyes closed, one dreams of mountains and rivers. What is seen with eyes open is regarded by the world as real;
what is seen with eyes closed is regarded by the world as unreal. Yet they do not realize that as for reality and unreality, there is no dust apart from the mind.
If even dust does not exist, how much less so mountains and rivers?
One who can predict whether it will be cloudy or clear by hearing the sound of a bell possesses ears more acute than those of ordinary people.
One who, upon seeing a thousand horses pass by once, does not forget their colors and markings possesses eyes more keen than those of ordinary people.

Therefore, the world regards them as individuals of supreme intelligence. Nevertheless, when acuity is combined with non-acuity, and clarity with non-clarity, what constitutes true acuity and clarity?
Is he truly intelligent? Or is he truly unintelligent? An ancient person once said: "The ears of worldly people are not lacking in acuity;
yet their hearing is deaf toward the scriptures. The eyes of worldly people are not lacking in clarity; yet their vision is blind toward the scriptures.
If this is so, then his ability to predict fair or foul weather and his skill in distinguishing the colors of horses—how can these be considered true intelligence?
It is clear, indeed.
Mencius spoke of the goodness of human nature; Xun Qing spoke of its evil; Yang Xiong spoke of the mixture of good and evil in human nature.
Now, to speak of it as good or as evil is to divide the one into two; to speak of the mixture of good and evil is to combine those two into one.
First. Alas! That which is called "nature" is neither one nor two, yet it is both one and two. Who can divide it? Who can unify it?
By this I know that those who attempt to divide it or those who attempt to unify it are all like those who add legs to a snake.
I have read the works of Mozi, and only then did I realize that he was not fundamentally at odds with Confucius.
I have also read the works of Yangzi, and likewise realized that he was not one who would refuse to pluck out a single hair for the sake of parsimony.

To claim now that Mozi opposed Confucius or that Yang Zhu was stingy regarding a single hair is to say that neither of them read the books of Yang and Mo. Yang and Mo are already long gone, their bones having rotted away, yet...
The decayed ones lodge themselves within books; yet, without reading those books, they follow the mere lip-service of others to recklessly denigrate them.
Even if Yangzi and Mozi were not dead, upon hearing such words of denigration, would they not have clapped their hands over their mouths and fallen over in laughter?
The ten habitual tendencies and six modes of interaction are the accumulation of evil states of mind; when their fruit ripens, retribution manifests as the means by which causes are requited.
Conversely, the possession of the ten titles and the full flourishing of myriad virtues are likewise the accumulation of wholesome states of mind; when their fruit ripens, they requite those causes.

Thus, when evil accumulates, one suffers; when goodness accumulates, one experiences joy. If the single mind does not arise, what fault can there be in the myriad dharmas? If a person understands this...
In this regard, one would not even dare to rely upon goodness, much less dare to commit evil and willingly endure suffering. Therefore it is said:
although goodness is beautiful, evil is certainly not good. If goodness does not rely upon evil, then there will be no resources for practicing goodness; if evil does not rely upon goodness...

This would mean that goodness could exist without a teacher. Now, suppose there were a person here who insisted that the world could only begin to be well-governed after every petty person had been completely eliminated—could this possibly be the heart of a sage?
Fire overcomes water; water must become boiling broth. Water overcomes fire; fire must become cool.

Therefore, in the *Yi* hexagram of *Tai* (Prosperity), the valued authority rests with the superior man (*junzi*), yet it also ensures that the petty man (*xiaoren*) each obtains their proper place. However, the Sage does not find cause for concern in *Lin* (Approaching), but rather in *Dazhuang* (Great Strength).
This is because when one reaches the state of *Tai*, one maintains firm adherence and dares not advance further. Alas! It is not that his anxieties are shallow.
Who among those who contemplate the distant can know this?
Having read the *Yi*, I then realized that the sixty-four hexagrams have no fixed nature; therefore it is said: "They circulate through the six voids."

High and low are not constant; thus, their natures and dispositions, their aversions and preferences, their portents of misfortune and signs of good fortune, revolve without beginning and transform without end.
The "unmanifested" state of the *Zhongyong* is identical to the "unstruck" state of the *Yi*. The "manifested yet perfectly modulated" state is identical to the "already struck" state of the *Yi*.

Some call it the "central," some call it "harmony," some call it the "Way," and some call it the "Change. As for the "central": it refers to that which is not obscured when unmanifested and is fully realized when manifested.
As for "harmony": it refers to that which does not deviate from the unmanifested when manifested. This is what is called the "Prior Heaven" [state].
The Way. That which follows heaven is called the *Yi*. Therefore it is said: "That which transcends form is called the Way; that which is below form is called the vessel.
Once the vessel is formed, the *Yi* operates within it. To seek the *Yi* apart from the vessel is like seeking the hexagram lines apart from the trigrams;
how could such a thing be possible?
In deep mountains and vast marshes, dragons and snakes are born; among flourishing clans and great lineages, both good and evil emerge.

If one does not obtain a person of merit and wisdom to serve as their leader to exercise restraint and conversion before calamity strikes, then the disasters of extermination and death will inevitably be unavoidable.
Therefore it is said: "A single minute particle entering the realm of movement creates the momentum of this collapsing mountain."
Thus, while misfortune has not yet arrived, one does not recognize it as a blessing; only when calamity strikes does one look back and realize that days free from trouble were truly a great blessing.
How could one wait until one necessarily obtains ten thousand *zhong* of grain before considering it a blessing?
Those who are diligent in good do not know how good is accumulated; those who are complacent in evil likewise do not know how evil is accumulated.
Because they do not know how good is accumulated, their blessings are unsurpassed; because they do not know how evil is accumulated, their calamities are unsurpassed.
This is truly because ignorance arises from negligence, which is the beginning of disaster. Once one knows...
Diligence is the ladder to blessings. Therefore it is said: "To be negligent is to darken the mind; to be aware is not to darken it.
When one brings the thoughts of the human heart into order, feverish afflictions will naturally wash away, and one will gradually enter the realm of cool serenity.
If one suddenly fails to maintain composure, then manifold sufferings will arrive uninvited. Once they have arrived, they are difficult to dispel;
how much better it would be to maintain composure before they arrive, thereby exerting little effort while reaping great benefit? Therefore it is said:

"While the devas are in the midst of their pleasures and the asuras are in the midst of their rage, these states all arise because the mind’s deliberations are not maintained in composure, and one is thus shrouded by them. When shrouded, the fundamental mind becomes obscured. This is not...
For one who is intelligent yet impulsive, how could the mind and its deliberations be easily brought to order?

To transform consciousness into wisdom (*vijñāna* → *jñāna*) is something that none can achieve unless they have perfected their understanding and are refined in *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Now, there are three aspects of Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*):

the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*), the revealing cause (*vibodhana-hetu*), and the direct cause (*samyak-hetu*). If the conditional cause is not clarified, the revealing cause will not arise. As for the revealing cause...
It is unarisen. The primary cause (正因) is difficult to harmonize with. To "harmonize" means to return [to the source].

Suppose there were a person here who wishes to restore their nature but neglects the cause of realization (了因), or who wishes to activate the cause of realization but neglects the causal condition (緣因).

It would be like desiring seedlings without grain, or desiring cooked rice without seedlings; how could such a principle exist? Although Wenshi spoke of transforming consciousness into wisdom (轉識成智), [the sequence must be maintained].
Yet he does not explain the reason why consciousness is transformed into wisdom (*jñāna*). Because this reason is not clarified, there is name without substance. Someone said:
"I venture to ask for the reason why consciousness is transformed into wisdom. He replied: "If you can investigate the *Vijñaptimātra* (Consciousness-Only) treatises of the Śākya school?
If you can fully comprehend the principles of the *ālambana-hetu* (object-condition), *parigraha-hetu* (sustaining-condition), and *hetu-hetu* (causal-condition)? [The questioner] said: "Not yet."
Indeed, you will be able to do so. Alas! If you truly can achieve this, then the reason why consciousness is transformed into wisdom lies with you, and not with Wenshi.
The discourse in the *Wen-shih* (The Origin of Writing) concerning the transformation of consciousness into wisdom merely states that it is accomplished; it does not state how it is accomplished.
If the explanation of how it is accomplished is not clear, how can the meaning be refined? Only when the meaning is refined can one enter the divine and bring about its practical application.
Nevertheless, the meanings are manifold; how could they be easily explained? Nature transforms into consciousness, and consciousness has many varieties.

They are called the storehouse consciousness, the transmitting consciousness, the discerning consciousness, and the consciousnesses that see forms, hear sounds, smell odors, taste flavors, feel tangibles, and cognize phenomena;
these are collectively termed the eight consciousnesses. Only the storehouse consciousness contains the first five; it is a transformation of the fruit, not a transformation of the cause.

As for the sixth and seventh, they are transformations of the cause, not transformations of the fruit. Nevertheless, those seven consciousnesses all undergo transformation while seated, not while walking.
That which is "active transformation" (*pravṛtti*) is solely the functional capacity of the *vijñapti-mati-vikalpa* (the consciousness that discriminates phenomena).

Why is this? Because it is fully equipped with the cognitive objects (*ālambana*) and the mental factors (*caitta*). "Inference" (*anumāna*) refers to that which accords with principle; it means knowing through deductive reasoning.

When one knows without erring from the sacred scriptures, it is called "inference" (*anumāna*) because it follows the same track. If it does not accord [with principle], it is not a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). As for "direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*), it is fundamentally without... [text fragment ends].

Discrimination is the illumination of objects without thought. Therefore, for those who aspire to transform consciousness into wisdom, if they do not precisely discern the consciousness of phenomena (*dharma-vijñāna*), the explanation of how consciousness is transformed into wisdom will ultimately remain obscure. Thus I say:
The *Wenshi* speaks of its accomplishment, but does not speak of the means by which it is accomplished.
Although I read the *Wenshi* and, while appreciating its refined and pure prose—both brilliant and expansive—its refinement is such that it lacks variety.
Purity leads to clarity, yet it is free from the habits of the mundane world; its brilliance is so radiant that it cannot be obscured.
Vastness encompasses the broad, profound, and far-reaching; it is not something that those of shallow understanding can fathom.
