Nevertheless, while these qualities—refinement, purity, radiance, and vastness—are manifest, that which is coarse cannot be refined, cannot be purified, cannot be made radiant, and cannot be made vast. How could it be otherwise? For refinement, purity, radiance, and vastness... [are inherent].

How could that which is so vast and expansive be something that can be manifested? It is by this that I know that that which cannot be manifested is that which has reached the utmost subtlety and density.

Therefore, its description says: "The sagely wisdom leaves one bewildered; even ghosts and spirits cannot discern it. It cannot be contrived, it cannot be brought forth, it cannot be measured, and it cannot be divided.
Those who force a name for it call it Heaven, they call it Fate, they call it the Spirit, they call it the Mysterious Union, and they call it the Way."
This is what is meant by "keeping it secret.
Hunger and satiety have no fixed law; therefore, satiety can cure hunger, and hunger likewise cures satiety.
Not only can hunger and satiety treat one another, but life can treat death, and death can treat life. If death were incurable, then the succession of lives would not exist.
The Way has ceased. If life were truly incurable, then those who live would never die. Yet now, that life must inevitably end in death is what all the world perceives together.
By this, I know that life is fundamentally without birth, and death is fundamentally without dying.
As for the claim that nothing in the realm of fortune and calamity is more profound than life and death—how could one know this?
The *Prajñāpāramitā* comprises eight sections totaling over six hundred scrolls of magnificent prose; like the winds of heaven or the surging waves of the sea, its sounds emerge spontaneously.
The accomplishment of the text through a mind of non-activity may be called the mother of wisdom that gives birth to the sages and the red furnace that refines the ordinary.

Thus, the Great Being who propagated the Dharma condensed the magnificent writings of the eight classes of scriptures into the Heart Sūtra; though its characters number no more than three hundred, it contains the essential points of both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings.

All has been fully prepared. Perhaps one might further bind the *Śrī-mahāyāna-prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* into a single phrase, so that those who seek refinement through returning to simplicity may practice until their transformative minds attain penetration;
then, with both self and phenomena empty, they will ascend to the other shore before even lifting a foot.
Nevertheless, though the understanding of the two emptinesses may not yet be refined, how easy would it be for the mechanism of entering the spirit and attaining its function to manifest?

A beginner practitioner should first seek a thorough understanding of the emptiness of the self (*ātman-śūnyatā*). One should reflect: "The existence of a 'self' is rooted in the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
If one is separated from the five aggregates, there is fundamentally no self. Furthermore, is that self formed by their aggregation, or is it formed by their dispersion?
If it were formed by aggregation, then since aggregation must inevitably lead to dispersion, how could the self be a true self? If it were formed by dispersion, then the self would be non-existent."
Five: Seek through their gathering and dispersal; ultimately, there is no self. This is called the emptiness of the self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). As for those five [aggregates]:

first, they arise through the transformation of consciousness alone. Consciousness is like an illusion or a dream; if one observes it with refined discernment, the phenomena produced by consciousness are non-existent.

This is called the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Second, once understanding is established, one gives rise to practice based on that understanding. One should do so at the ground of hatred and love, honor and disgrace, and in the fields of death and birth, gathering and dispersing.
To practice with vigor means that it lies not in understanding, but in action.
Reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, I first realized the Sage’s intent of bringing all phenomena back to oneself.
As for those ancients who had already attained this, they said: "If a person recognizes the mind, there is not an inch of earth in the great world," and again: "Now, when I see a tree..."
"The tree does not see me; what do I see? I see the subtle excellence of the *Śūraṅgama* script, its details exhaustive and its refinement consummate, surpassing all others in its singular majesty.
These are the words of Mei Shan.

The mouth and belly burden others; the male organ brings much trouble. How few are those who, by these means, destroy their own persons, ruin their states, and bring about the extinction of their families?
Yet, it is not difficult to control them once one has grasped their mechanism (*jī*). To forcibly restrain them without grasping their mechanism is not only useless, but can even lead to madness.
What, then, is this mechanism? Alas! It is at the moment when the mind has not yet arisen, when the mind is about to arise, and when the mind is in the very act of arising.
At the moment of birth, when the mind has already arisen—how precarious, how precarious! To whom does the fruit belong?
If one knows this, then the mouth and belly will lose the skill of the long snake and the great boar; the male organs will lack the ferocity of a wildfire consuming the mountains.
The Master of the Laozi venerates spontaneity (*ziran*). Now, spontaneity is simply another designation for non-action (*wuwei*).
Non-action refers to the absence of laborious contrivance. If this were so, then when the Sage established his teachings, whom would he have intended to instruct?
Why? Because if good is spontaneous, then evil is also spontaneous; thus, there would be nothing that is not spontaneous. If this were indeed the case—

Thus, regarding the common people’s aspiration for worthiness and the worthy’s aspiration for sagehood, the theory that one begins from forced effort and eventually reaches spontaneity is a great contradiction of Laozi’s [teachings].
Therefore, Laozi speaks only of the end while neglecting the discourse on the beginning; such a doctrine has been practiced.
Thus, the teaching of transforming evil through perfuming toward goodness will be like engaging in battle without being able to achieve a complete victory.
Indeed, from beginning to end, it is a single path. Therefore, the common person aspires to the worthy; the worthy aspire to the sage—this is the perfection of the beginning.
The sage aspires to Heaven—this is the perfection of the end. To perfect the beginning means to govern the emotions with principle; to perfect the end means to restore one's original nature.
When one returns to one's original nature, that which was previously called "the single thread" becomes clearly manifest before one. What further matter could there be?
Reaching this point, one knows it is spontaneous; both are merely brandishing sticks to strike at the moon.

Among those who exhaustively elucidate the Way and arts of the entire world, is it not the Śākya school? Regarding that which lies beyond the six realms, the ancients preserved it but did not discuss it;

regarding that which lies within the six realms, they discussed it but did not debate it. It was not that it could not be discussed—it was feared that such discussion would terrify those within the six realms.

It was not that it could not be debated—it was feared that such debate would contravene the intent of the Five Constant Virtues. Now, the Śākyas reach far back to exhaustively investigate that which lies beyond the six realms, distinguishing it with absolute clarity.
There is a refuge. It reaches through the six directions of the universe, clearly delineated without confusion.

This allows those of lofty brilliance to make transcendent strides beyond the world, while those who abide in the ordinary are spared from striving for unattainable hopes. Therefore, the three realms are analyzed into nine stages, and the four types of sages are unified under the Single Vehicle.
Beyond the six directions of the universe, there dwells only that which does not undergo further existence. Within the six directions...

Internally, all are the dwelling places of sentient beings. That which can rely [upon them] is called the "direct retribution" (正報), while that upon which they rely is called the "circumstantial retribution" (依報).
Whether one is a sage or an ordinary person, there is nothing that arises without a cause; all are brought about by taking the initial aspiration as their ground.
Among them, some take dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as their ultimate goal, while others take non-arising (*anutpāda*) as their ultimate goal. Only the Buddha alone—

The person [of realization] is such that they can realize non-arising through dependent origination, and while abiding in non-arising, they do not obscure dependent origination. They negate and illuminate;
they preserve and dissolve. It is like a night-bright pearl upon a tray, rolling, turning, slanting, and crossing at will, moving with sovereign freedom beyond the reach of conceptual thought.
Therefore, their vision reaches far and penetrates near, as clearly as seeing the patterns of lines on one’s own palm or the reflection of eyebrows in a mirror.
This is the eye. Therefore I say: among those who have perfected the Way and its arts throughout the world, is it not the Śākya school?
When the Master Hanzhan was bathing, he showed his back to Kuangshishi and said, "Do you see the mark of the broad and long tongue?"
He said, "I do not see. Alas! Seeing arises from non-seeing; when one is skillful in returning to non-seeing, how could it be that only the back has a tongue, or the eyes have ears?
Even down to the pores and the hair, there is nowhere that does not involve seeing.
As for "a single thread," its original source is not remote; it lies within our daily activities. That one uses them daily yet remains unaware is because external objects burden them.
Little do they realize that objects are not objects in themselves; they become objects only in relation to the self.
If I can forget the self, how could objects stand independently? Therefore it is said: "Only for those who have forgotten the self, not only can objects not burden them, but objects..."
Furthermore, it is for the sake of transformation that we speak thus.
A basin of water—how does it differ from the vast ocean? To call it a "basin" or to call it an "ocean" is merely a matter of mental perspective (*qing*).
If this perspective is forgotten, then even the ocean does not exist; how much less so the basin? At such a time, that which manifests clearly before one is the basin.
"Ah, the sea! That which informs me by its deep redness is glowing charcoal; that which informs me by its drifting whiteness is flying snow.
Though red and white differ, their informing of me is one and the same. Color is the precursor to the five sense-objects; if the precursor can inform, then the others [will follow]."
How could one not inform you? Nevertheless, though all possess eyes and ears, even down to the faculty of intention, how could they possibly grasp the ultimate meaning?
To see by depending on light is called the way of the common multitude; to see without depending on light is called the way of the sage. Now, as for the owl—
The owl can catch fleas and lice at night and discern the tip of an autumn hair, yet by day it stares with wide-open eyes and cannot see even a hill or mountain.

Thus, it sees because of darkness; in light, its vision fails. Furthermore, tigers, wolves, cats, and dogs see equally by day and night; how do they differ from those whose vision does not depend on light?
Alas! If tigers and wolves see only when conditions are met, then the Sage also sees only when conditions are met—and likewise sees when there are no conditions.
Thus it is said: "The sage dwells within the realm of light and darkness; he opens up things and accomplishes tasks, yet light and darkness cannot burden him.
When one calls out to a sage, the sage responds; when one calls out to the common people, the common people respond.

Commentators say that the response of the sage is called *wei* (yes), while the response of the common people is called *a* (yes). Now, both *wei* and *a* are responses, yet they differ in their nature.
The latter is emotion (*qing*). The former is nature (*xing*). Nature and emotion are not far apart from one another; hence it is said, "Natures are similar, while habits lead to divergence.
Since that which is near can be practiced to become distant, why should that which is distant alone be incapable of being practiced to become near?
By this I know that nature is fundamentally not constant, and emotion is likewise not constant. If nature were constant, from what could emotion arise? If emotion were [constant]...
"Permanence. What does its nature illuminate? It illuminates that which is perfect; perfection is clarity; clarity is awakening. Guishan said: "It unifies all virtues and is fully complete;
it dispels the darkness of the multitudes and shines alone. Therefore, it is named Perfect Awakening (Yuánjué)."

In the waters there are *jiaolong* (dragon-eels), and on the mountains there are tigers and leopards; thus, woodcutters dare not enter, and fishermen dare not bathe. This is because they perceive the presence of these creatures.
To know that such creatures exist and thereby avoid them is not as good as forgetting the self. When one forgets the self, one also forgets the creatures.
Thus, the ancients were able to keep company with snakes and tigers, for both had forgotten each other. How could this be otherwise?
He said: "Wind, rain, and mist—are they one or three? If one calls them one, then wind is fundamentally not rain, and rain is fundamentally not mist; mist is not either of the two.
If one calls them three, then if it were not mist, wind and rain would have no foundation. Therefore it is said: 'When mist clears, it becomes wind. Not so.
Awakening is the manifestation of rain. Three is one, and one is three. Three is one; what existence is there in the three? One is three;
even one is fundamentally non-existent. One who knows this may be spoken with regarding the principle of the single mind and the threefold contemplation.
One may dig into the earth to obtain spring water; one may part the clouds to see the sky. The earth and the clouds are metaphors for emotional states (*qing*);
the spring water and the sky are analogies for the fundamental nature (*xing*). Now suppose there is a person here who wishes to make the earth solid and the clouds dense.
To indulge them without restraint not only harms one's life, but ultimately leads to the destruction of one's nature.
When Mencius refuted Yang Zhu and Mo Di to clarify the Way of Confucius, everyone considered this to be truly so; yet, do they truly know Mencius?
If they did, they would realize that Mencius was not merely refuting Yang and Mo, but was refuting those who attached themselves to Yang and Mo and thereby blocked the path of Confucius.

He was a man of the Way. Nevertheless, while the school of Confucius could not easily be expanded, as for those who were able to expand it—I have read the various works from the time of Zhongni [Confucius] onward—and it is only perhaps Wen Zhongzi who might continue the lineage of Confucius.
Beyond this, there may be others capable of continuing it, though I cannot know of them.

When lice and nits appear on the human body, one becomes angry that they are biting them and immediately rubs them to death. One fails to reflect that the Great Way constitutes the body, while lice and nits are the heavens and earth;
the heavens and earth constitute the body, while lice and nits are the myriad things. A human being is merely one thing among the myriad things.
If a person can trace back to their own origin, they will know that apart from the Great Way there are no heavens and earth, and outside of the heavens and earth there is nothing.

Among the myriad things, that which we call "human" is distinguished only by its spiritual intelligence. If one examines it from the perspective of the physical body alone, how does a louse differ from a human?
If one were to feel it as something as minute as a hair-tip, who—unless they have forgotten their own origins—could bear to do so?
The Ancient Sovereign asked Qingxi, "Is your mind truly within? He replied, "The mind is inside the body.
The Sovereign said, "If it is truly within, can you see your five viscera and six bowels? He replied, "I cannot.
The Sovereign looked grave and questioned him again, "When you are in a room, do you see the things within the room? He replied, "I do. Now, you say that the mind is within the body.
Yet one cannot see the objects within the body; thus, the dharma and the analogy contradict each other, and this is not logically tenable.

When joy is exhausted internally, it inevitably rushes outward. Little do they realize that the internal depends on the external, the external depends on the latent root, and the latent root depends on light and darkness.
Upon reflection, one sees that the internal depends on the intermediate space, and the intermediate space depends on the point where it meets its corresponding object. As for the meeting...

Wherever there is conjunction, it serves as the basis for all non-attachment and dependence; thus, through pervasive conceptualization and arbitrary clinging, one establishes the seven points based on conditions and dependencies.

For those of profound spiritual capacity, when the internal is thoroughly understood, the external is likewise exhausted. If one part is deficient, both are lost; how then could one avoid the trouble of having to repeatedly refute and eliminate the remaining points before achieving realization?
The eight [objects] can be returned; they are all merely external objects. Only that which is able to see these eight cannot be returned; it is the essence of seeing.
Observing it from this perspective, it is clear that the essence of seeing is fundamentally wondrous, pervading all things without entanglement. Suppose there were a person here.
When conditioned by light, one sees; when not conditioned by light, one does not see. Is this the fault of the essence of seeing? Alas!
When clarity and cognition do not arise, the five fundamental faculties are wondrous; thus the eye can hear sounds, and the ear can see forms.
If joy and anger were constant, once one was joyful, one could never become angry; and once one was angry, one could never become joyful.
Because they are inconstant, when one is in the midst of joy, if one suddenly hears news that is disagreeable, one immediately becomes enraged;

and when one is in the midst of anger, if one suddenly hears news that is agreeable, one immediately becomes delighted. Therefore it is said: "Joy is not joy for its own sake; it is enslaved by external things."
Thus they rejoice. They do not become angry of their own accord; they become angry because they are enslaved by external things. Alas! External things are the masters and I am the slave.
I cannot control my joy or anger; I am made to rejoice and be angry by external things. How is this different from a slave who enslaves his master? For man is the most spiritual of all things.
In the end, one cannot employ things, but is instead employed by them. Is this not tragic? My body is most minute;
it does not even measure six feet. Within the great transformation of the universe, what difference is there between these six feet and a single bubble on the great ocean?
Yet that which this body relies upon is still vast. For within this most minute body, there are eight [thousand] pores.
There are fourteen thousand [parasites]. Within a single pore, one parasite presides over them all.
When I am hungry, they are hungry; when I am satiated, they are satiated. If I do good, they all receive blessings; if I do evil, they all suffer calamity.
Therefore, for those who are intent on nourishing life, life must not be taken lightly. If one wishes to live again, one must first nourish its master. Who is the master? It is the master of life.
Ah! Can that which presides over life truly give rise to life? Therefore, only one who is without self can nourish life.
Since that which presides over life is itself without self, does life truly arise? One who understands this may be spoken to regarding the Way of nourishing life.
The wise elder used seven similes to illustrate how the five desires are of no benefit to human beings. Thus he said:

"The five desires become more intense the more one obtains them, like adding fuel to a fire, causing its flames to blaze even fiercer. There is no joy in the five desires; they are like a dog gnawing on a dry bone.
The five desires increase contention; they are like birds competing for meat. The five desires burn people; they are like grasping a torch against the wind."
A torch [of fire]. The five desires harm people like treading upon a venomous snake. The five desires lack reality; they are like what is obtained in a dream. Desire does not last long;
it is borrowed for but a moment, like a spark struck from stone. When a student reflects on this, [desire] is also like a hostile thief.

Alas! When a single atom stirs, the five desires arise. The five desires harm people; thus these seven analogies are composed. One who can skillfully contemplate a single atom [will understand them all].
Thus, within the provisional construction of causes, one understands that the five desires have no point of origin from the very beginning. For what reason?

Whether the five desires have not yet arisen, are currently arising, or have already arisen—one scrutinizes them with refined precision across these four temporal movements—and not even a single atom exists;
yet that which precedes even a single atom remains exactly as it was.
A fish in water does not know the water; a person within the mind does not know the mind.
If a fish could know the water, and a person could know the mind—would the fish truly be a fish? Would the person truly be a person?

Therefore, that a single drop of water can become the clouds of the six realms, and a minute speck of dust can contain the lands of the ten directions—is this not the work of neither dragons nor sages? Who else could accomplish such a thing? I...
By this we know that it is not difficult to be a dragon; it is for fish to know the difficulty of water. It is not difficult to be a sage;
it is for people to awaken to the mind. Therefore it is said: "The multitude are those who use [it] daily yet do not know it."
Heaven and earth may be said to be vast, yet they cannot be placed outside of empty space. Empty space may be said to be inexhaustible, yet it cannot be placed outside of my mind.
Therefore, when one observes things through the mind, there is no distinction between great and small among objects.
When objects burden the mind, the mind is unable to awaken. Only one who is able to awaken realizes that there are no objects apart from the mind.
Therefore it is said: "All phenomena have no substantial essence; I declare them to be nothing but mind. Not perceiving a 'no-mind,' one gives rise to conceptual discrimination."
Characters accumulate to form phrases; phrases accumulate to form chapters; chapters accumulate to form sections; and sections accumulate to form treatises.
A treatise is that which can explain the "reason why" things are as they are.

If the explanation of the "reason why" is not clear, then every character, phrase, chapter, and section is like wood gnawed by insects—accidentally forming patterns. Do the insects have any intention to gnaw them? It is simply the insects.
Since there is no mind, how could there be any principle (yi) residing within the text? Principle is the transformation of the mind.

For example, when joy and anger have not yet been manifested, it is simply called "Centrality" (zhong). Once they have been manifested, it is called benevolence (ren), righteousness (yi), propriety (li), wisdom (zhi), and trustworthiness (xin).

Benevolence has its own appropriateness; righteousness has its own appropriateness; propriety, wisdom, and trustworthiness likewise each have their own appropriateness. It is like spring having its own appropriateness.
It is warm. In summer it should be hot; in autumn it should be cool; in winter it should be cold. If it is not cold in winter, it is said that it is "inappropriate.

Therefore, the convergence of these various meanings, being orderly and without confusion, is called *li* (principle). To act according to principle and reach nowhere without success is called *dao* (the Way).
To proceed along the Way until reaching the place of ultimate rest is called *de* (virtue). As for virtue, it is like "attaining."
Characters form phrases; phrases form chapters; chapters form sections; and thus they constitute a treatise.
When I read the *Hongfan*, I realized that Jizi was a sage. Yet the sage did not hold office while Zhou held the throne.

The fall of the Shang dynasty can already be known from this. Jizi spoke of the five blessings and the six calamities, stating that only those who revere Heaven and love the people will have the five blessings respond to them from Heaven;
conversely, those who act otherwise will have the six calamities respond to them. Viewed through this lens, the principle of retribution is evident.

Regarding the principle of cause and effect: even before the teachings of Śākyamuni had spread to the East, those in China who sought to govern the world never failed to regard this matter with solemnity.

To claim now that the discourse on cause and effect and the proclamation of retribution are merely the techniques of the Buddhists to delude the ignorant, and that they are not fit to be spoken of by a gentleman—alas! This argument not only incurs sin, but...
Even among the Śākyas, this is what even Kǐzǐ would have found loathsome.

A painting of flowers and birds on a screen is not without its power to please the eye; yet, if one wished to make them fragrant or cause them to sing, I know that even a sage as divine as the Great Yu could not achieve it.
Suppose there were a person here whose wisdom could not encompass his own body, and whose strength...
One cannot bind a single chicken, clothe it, and crown it, and expect it to move about with the grace of bowing and yielding;
though this may be pleasing to the eye, what difference is there between making it govern the people above and making it paint flowers or depict the singing of birds?
Water within a cauldron cannot be heated without fire; seeds within the soil cannot sprout without spring. Ignorance within the mind cannot be destroyed without study.
Today, those throughout the world are not lacking in study; yet what they study concerns worldly desires rather than the destruction of ignorance.
Consequently, the world loses the Way, and the Way loses the world; thus, the world and the Way are in mutual ruin.

The custom of mourning has been fanned into being and has not yet ceased. Alas! If it continues to be fanned without ceasing, there will come a point where the consequences can no longer be described.
The stench of *eranda* (Ilan) is the most foul odor in the world; yet, if it is perfumed with *candana* (sandalwood), it can become [fragrant].
Regarding "fragrance": it is said that those who are utterly ignorant can never be taught. How is this different from the *eranda* tree, which can never be made fragrant?
If the *eranda* were to encounter sandalwood and be perfumed by it, it too could become fragrant; why then should those who are utterly ignorant alone be incapable of being taught?
The difficulty lies merely in teaching them without weariness. If one can indeed teach without weariness, then even metal and stone [can be transformed].
It can be penetrated. Although a person may be utterly foolish, they possess innate awareness and perception.

If one takes that which is innate and perfumes it with the fragrance of instruction, and after a long time it reaches maturity, then even the foul odor of that utter foolishness will be perfumed and transformed into fragrance. Therefore it is said:
To teach without weariness—only a sage can do this.
One night he dreamed that the earth split open; he wished to flee from it. Fleeing forward, he feared the front would split; fleeing backward, he feared the rear would split;
fleeing to the left or right, he feared those sides would split. At that moment, he had no plan for escape, yet his urge to flee could not cease, and he was filled with terror.

Ten thousand things emerge. When spring snow strikes the window, one suddenly awakens from a spring dream; yet the ground before and behind the bed, to its left and right, remains as it was originally.
It was never actually split—those who insist it was split are merely engaging in pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*). That which remains as it was is the dependent nature (*paratantra*).

Alas! Although the parikalpita (imagined nature) may be forgotten, the paratantra (dependent nature) is not. It is like the persistence of the awareness of a dream even after one has awakened; since this awareness is the basis of the dream, if that basis is not forgotten, can it truly be called awakening?
Fundamentally, there is only touch. To realize that touch has no inherent nature is what is called "wondrous touch. When one is moved by the perception of touch, it remains merely touch;

the wondrous quality is then lost. Therefore it is said: "Wondrous touch proclaims clarity. If this were so, then the mark of the broad and long tongue would not reside in the mouth, but would manifest throughout the body.
How much less would it be limited to the body alone? That which depends on the body is touch; since touch has already entered the wondrous state, [the mark] pervades all.
As for these stages, every sound and every form is the mark of the broad and long tongue;
nevertheless, were it not for listening with one's heels, how could such sounds be easily grasped?
To stand upright and walk is what is called being human. One who can stand upright can likewise lie horizontal. It is not that there is something inherently upright that is not upright;
how else could one be upright when upright or horizontal when horizontal? He who understands this may be spoken with regarding the resemblance of human nature.
When one’s strength is insufficient, fear arises; when principles are not clear, doubt arises. Therefore, those who speak grandly to deceive others are those who fear others.
To harbor doubt at every turn and to claim that nothing exists when there is something is the result of a lack of clarity. When the mind lacks clarity, there is no sovereign within;
having no sovereign within, one claims, "I can see and I can hear; I am cleverer than the masses. This is not the mark of a fool.
To thus deceive oneself—is evil not carried to this extreme?
When Mencius looked down upon kings, dukes, and great officials, was that "looking down upon" intentional or unintentional?
If one possesses a mind, it is not that one can despise others; rather, it is oneself who is being despised. Since I am without a mind, what need is there for me to despise anyone?

When kings, dukes, and great officials encounter a person who is without a mind, they will be so preoccupied with forgetting their own power that they have no leisure even to despise them—how much less would they wait to do so?

Only then would one cause them to submit. Therefore it is said: "If a drifting tile strikes a person, that person does not become angry; if an empty boat bumps into a person, that person likewise does not become angry.
This is because they know [the objects] have no intention. Thus, the gentleman cherishes the Dao and wanders at the gates of the feudal lords.
If one does not respond with an empty mind, there is nothing that will not happen.
A favor must not be accepted recklessly; if it is accepted, one should reflect on the origin of that favor: did it come because of my being loved, or did it come because of my being pitied?
Love arises from respect, while pity arises from compassion. If it is respect, what virtue do I possess that would merit it? And...
When one treats others with reverence and compassion, having already become a man, one stands upright between heaven and earth.
To cause others to pity me while I cannot pity others—how can this be the way of a true man? Therefore it is said: "When gifts are substantial and words are sweet, they are what the Way-man fears."
The peony is popularly called the "King of Flowers," for it is merely out of respect for its rich and magnificent beauty.

Little do they realize that when the pine tree takes root upon white stones, amidst the biting cold of wind and frost, it creates clouds and waves among the myriad trees, causing those who hear it to linger and be unable to depart, thinking the first tide of the sea has begun to roar. This, indeed, is the sound of the pine.

It causes the dusty mind to be swept clean away. Just as the roar of thunder can suddenly awaken the hibernating creatures, the ringing of bells and chimes can give rise to the human aspiration for the Way.
Speaking from this perspective, how could the splendor of the peony ever possess the wind of the resilient integrity of the pine?
The plum flower deceives the snow with its fragrance; the snow deceives the plum with its whiteness.

Each relies upon its own excellence to deceive the other, yet neither can prevail, so they engage in an unceasing, drunken battle. Alas! When a celestial wind suddenly arises and the snow swirls away as the blossoms fly, where then is that which each relied upon?
Therefore it is said: "Those who rely on their strengths to deceive others cannot endure in the end."
In the ocean there is a great fish that bears ten thousand mountains upon its back. Upon these mountains there is a great beast whose tail spans a thousand li.
When people hear of this, they do not believe it; let us now verify it. Without the four elements, the great earth would not exist.

Without the three elements, the great waters would not exist. Without the two elements, the great fire would not exist. Without even one element, the great wind would not exist. Thus, as for the earth...
Water floats upon water; water floats upon fire; fire floats upon wind; wind floats upon space; and space floats upon the mind.
Now, as for this mind, it is that wherein the myriad things are one body and where things and self share the same root.

Speaking from this perspective, even the *jiaoming* insect could carry Mount Tai, and ants could withstand thunder and rain. Fish are large enough to bear ten thousand mountains upon their backs, and beasts...
Great in size, with a tail trailing for a thousand li—what more need be doubted?
The multitude cherish wealth and honor while loathing poverty and lowliness; thus, burdened by wealth, honor, poverty, and lowliness, they remain unaware even unto death.
Little do they realize that wealth, honor, poverty, and lowliness are fundamentally one and the same path, and upon this single path...
To force oneself to love something or force oneself to hate something—how could this possibly be the Way? Therefore it is said: "The Way has substance, while emotions have none.
The sages attain this; the common people lose it. Alas! For one who has attained it, even though birth and death stand before them, they are made into a single thread;
how much more so the matters of wealth and honor versus poverty and low station!
The root of death lies in the existence of a self (*ātman*); the root of the existence of a self lies in non-self (*anātman*).
If this is so, then the existence of a self is merely a branch of non-self. One who is skilled at reversal seeks the root by means of the branches;

it is like catching a turtle within a jar or searching for an object inside a bag. What difficulty could there be? Nevertheless, all people are habituated to the notion of a self, and [it is difficult to realize] non-self.

The self arises from habituation; having matured, it can give rise [to further habituation], and having arisen, it can reach maturity. Were it not for one of great wisdom and supreme courage, how could this be easily mastered?

The existence of a self and the non-existence of a self are like the bending and extending of a single finger: while the bending and extending are impermanent, the finger itself neither hides nor manifests. Now, there is a person...
In this regard, when one observes the bending and stretching [of the fingers] while forgetting the substance of the fingers themselves,
then that which could not be added by Yao nor diminished by Zhou will ultimately be lost.
The sages and the common people are originally of one and the same light. However, the sages do not rely on the illumination of the sun, moon, or lamps;
they directly employ their original light to illuminate themselves. Therefore, even while dwelling in the midst of darkness, that darkness cannot obscure them. The common people are not so;
though they inherently possess this original light, they fail to employ it, instead depending upon the illumination of the sun, moon, and lamps before they can begin [to see].

One can see this: it clarifies that as soon as light fades, the appearance of darkness manifests before one. At such a time, one cannot even see the fingers of one's own hand, let alone see the heavens, the earth, and the myriad things.
The vast ocean has no bounds. When ice freezes to a depth of a thousand feet, if the sun returns for a single night, the ice will produce a faint sound;
then the ice shall turn back into water, and this can be awaited with certainty. I observe the hexagram Fu (Return): a single yang line arises beneath five yin lines.

Though it seems that yang cannot overcome yin, the mechanism of change resides in the yang and not in the yin; thus, instances where yin does not overcome yang are many. It is like the beginning [of spring].
When a Bodhisattva resolves their mind [on enlightenment], they immediately attain perfect awakening. For sentient beings are born amidst the fires of the five desires;
once their minds give rise to coolness, who but one who is supremely wise and a great hero could reach this state?

Thus, the cause encompasses the ocean of fruition—just as when layered ice first begins to melt, one knows that it will soon return to water. That the fruition penetrates to the source of the cause is because ice cannot exist apart from water.
This is because they share the same substance. Alas! Ice and water appear distinct; thus, the obstruction of solid matter and the fluidity of penetration are vastly different.
Yet, there is no water apart from ice, and no ice apart from water. One who understands this may be spoken with regarding the great purport of the *Avataṃsaka*.
Laozi held that the five notes can deafen the ears and the five colors can blind the eyes; that even a slight awareness can delude my lack of knowledge.
Yet he did not realize that the ears and eyes have no inherent existence—they exist only because of the body—and that cognition likewise has no inherent existence—it exists only because of objects.
Alas! Since body and mind already exist, there will inevitably follow birth and death, honor and disgrace, likes and dislikes.

There is nothing to which "is" and "is not" do not reach. Therefore, the Greatly Awakened Master taught the world to contemplate the body through the four great elements and to contemplate the mind through the four aggregates.
When these eight appear before one, then both body and mind are found to have no existence at all.
Since body and mind are non-existent, that which is called birth and death, honor and disgrace, like and dislike, and right and wrong, are like flakes of snow flying into a red-hot furnace.
How could such things possibly exist above that? Nevertheless, although the attachments of body and mind have been resolved, the eight [afflictions] have not yet been washed away.

Therefore, one is further instructed to contemplate the four elements through the four objects, and to contemplate the discriminating mind through the preceding objects. This is for those whose spiritual faculties are as profound as the heavens.

One immediately realizes that the four external sense-objects (*viṣaya*) are non-existent within the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). The four great elements and the four sense-objects are likewise non-existent.
When the external objects before one are absent, the discriminating mind is also non-existent; when the external discriminating mind is absent, the objects before one are also non-existent.
Subject and object wash away each other; things and self vanish into nothingness. At this moment, there is a body without a body, and a mind without a mind.
The mind [of enlightenment] is clearly manifest before one. Only then does one realize that though the physical form fills the eight directions, no great affliction can entangle it;

though wisdom encompasses the myriad things, no feverish distress can incinerate it. It drives the wheel of the Four Great Vows and mounts the horse of the Ten Great Vows, flying through the boundless and grinding away at both form and emptiness until all sentient beings on this broad earth are suddenly elevated to the stage of awakening. This is the Great Being (Mahāsattva).
This is the ultimate task.
The mind is fundamentally without self yet is numinous; therefore, it cannot be sought by means of a "self," nor can it be sought by means of a "non-self.
If one seeks it with a self, since it is already without self, would that not be at odds with it? If one seeks it with a non-self...
Since it is already luminously present, how could one not be at variance with it?
Since it cannot be sought through the notion of a self, nor can it be sought through the notion of no-self, would it then follow that the self ultimately cannot attain it?

If this were truly the case, not only would the multitude be deprived of the steps for aspiring toward sagehood, but even the merit of the sages in "continuing the past and opening up the future" would be obliterated. Yet, as for that [reality] itself—
It cannot be sought through existence or non-existence; it must be attained through the convergence of conditions. Therefore it is said: "Attained through conditions, it is forever free from loss.
As for these conditions: if people are perfumed by the conditions of the ten evil deeds and the five heinous crimes, then the manifestations of the Avīci hell will appear before them.
Even so, if they are perfumed by human conditions, or perfumed by the conditions of Śrāvakas and Mahāsattvas, then [the corresponding results will manifest].

The manifestations of the nine realms are as clear as the sun and stars; yet were it not for the Buddha alone, who perfumes them with the conditions of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), they would be unable to manifest their peerless and wondrous characteristics.
Viewed from this perspective, since the characteristics of the nine realms manifest in accordance with conditions and karma, if there is someone here who can follow conditions and karma and ascend...
When one offers this [sincerity] upward, then that which is spirit-like and without self will arrive without waiting for an invocation.

Those who revere Confucianism find fault with Buddhism and Daoism; those who revere Daoism find fault with Confucianism and Buddhism; those who revere Buddhism find fault with Confucianism and Daoism.
Since all claim to find fault [with one another], yet they know there is a malady but cannot treat it—this is either ignorance or delusion. Someone said: "I venture to ask."
The method for treating illness is as follows: to study Confucianism and be able to grasp the mind of the Master Kong; to study Buddhism and be able to grasp the mind of the Śākya-muni;
and to study Daoism and be able to grasp the mind of the Lord Lao. Then the illness will heal of itself. This is the excellence of this method.

This is something that has been donned by me and for which there is evidence. If you, sir, can simply accept it with faith and put it to the test, you will come to know that what I have donned does not deceive you.
Furthermore, Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism are all merely names; they are not realities.
Reality is the mind. The mind is that which is capable of being Confucian, capable of being Buddhist, and capable of being Daoist. Alas!
Is this capacity for being Confucian, Buddhist, and Daoist possessed by each of them individually, or is it shared among them?

Furthermore, regarding the manifest and the unmanifest, the dependently arisen and the non-arisen, and the named and the nameless—do these coincide or not? Only by knowing this can one truly understand.
The three schools speak with one path; where they differ, it is in name, not in spirit.
Suppose there were a person here who could read the books of the Four Treasuries, yet lacked a concise grasp of them—what would be the use of so many volumes?
Conciseness is the essence of the mind. The mind is the sovereign of all transformations; if one cannot trust it, one merely exerts oneself over decaying bones and dregs.
This is a deluded confusion. Someone asked: "May I venture to ask about the 'mind-as-such' (xinsuo)? I replied: "When it is in the eye, it can see; when it is in the ear, it can hear.
If one gives rise to thoughts or stirs up mental activity, that is emotion (qing), not the mind (xin). Alas! Only those who have clarified the mind can restore their original nature."

In antiquity, there were battles of the Way, battles of virtue, battles of benevolence and righteousness, and battles of wisdom and courage. The battle of the Way is fought without mind; the battle of virtue is fought by cherishing gratitude;

the battle of benevolence and righteousness is that by which one brings peace to the lives of all under heaven; and the battle of wisdom and courage is that by which one strengthens and fulfills one's will.
There are also those who engage in "battles where the very nose is lost"; they cannot face the enemy without a mind, for if they do so, they will surely be defeated.
If one has the mind to confront [the adversary], yet confronts them, one will be defeated. If one fears defeat and does not dare to confront them, one is likewise defeated.
Alas! Only Yunmen and Deshan were generals skilled in warfare.
In the *Yijing bilu*, it is recorded that the Master said, "Your nature is rigid. When you encounter various circumstances one day, how will you endure them?
He asked again, "How can one come to endure them? The Master replied, "If you perceive your own self as vast, you will naturally be able to endure. He asked again.
"How can one realize that one's own self is great? One must then be able to endure it. The Master says: Heaven and earth are great, and thus they can encompass all things;
empty space is great, and thus it can contain heaven and earth; my original true mind is great, and thus it can contain empty space. The Master further said:
"The reason a person of great character cannot tolerate others is none other than being obstructed by external things; it is simply that they have become deluded regarding themselves."
Having realized the true mind, one naturally becomes humble. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "The void arises within Great Awakening, like a single bubble emerging from the ocean.

The minute dust-motes of all worlds with outflows are all produced dependent upon that void. When the bubble ceases, the void was originally non-existent; how much more so the various realms of the three existences?

Great Awakening and the true mind are fundamentally neither existent nor non-existent, and cannot be described by such forms. As soon as one is deluded regarding this mind, [the world of phenomena] immediately comes into being.

It is like empty space and the world. Therefore, when a sage dwells within the realm of birth and death, fortune and calamity, yet birth and death, fortune and calamity cannot burden him, there is nothing particularly extraordinary about this; it is nothing more than not being deluded in one's mind.
Although this mind exists within the midst of daily life, the multitude do not know it. This lack of knowledge is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*). As for ignorance, it means:
The true mind is inherently present, yet we fail to recognize it. Instead, we obscure this mind and give rise to the world of empty space, clinging to it with stubborn persistence.
Within the three realms, everything is but a single mass of emotion; everyone dwells within this emotion. To speak words that transcend emotion—how difficult!
For example, Bodhidharma encountered six poisons, and Master Huisi of Mount Nanyue encountered more than ten poisons. This was because these two elders spoke with no intent to steal;
thus they attracted so much excellent support and offerings. It was their "stealing mind," yet it was also their "non-stealing nature."
To remain within the realm of emotions yet act according to one's nature—since antiquity until the present day, there has never been one who has not suffered harm from demons and heretics.
Nevertheless, as time goes on, the greater the harm, the greater the radiance. Therefore, the gentleman always suffers loss, yet always gains advantage.
The Master called to him again, saying, "Raise your fist. He raised his fist. The Master asked, "Who raised this fist?
He replied, "It was this mind that raised it. The Master asked, "Suppose this hand were gone; where would your mind be?"
Again, he was at a loss for what to do. The Master said, "I tell you that you must investigate this for yourself right here. If you cannot investigate it out, it is truly a misery.
Still unable to understand despite his further seeking, he requested the Master’s instruction. The Master said, "People are all foolish about this;
they spend their whole day lighting a lamp here, and then go to someone else's house to beg for fire."
One who cannot forget profit will necessarily be unable to bear resentment.
One should reflect from where this body comes to be and from where it departs; thus one comes to know from whence it arises.
Then one knows from where it has departed. The *Yi* says:
"The multitude of dragons without a head brings good fortune. This is the image. If one contemplates this image and grasps its meaning, then life resides within oneself.
Since the living one is already within me, then the dead one is also alive. Reaching this point, who is the intention and who is the form?
Therefore it is said: "If a person recognizes their own mind, there is not an inch of earth in the great earth. I, however, say: "If a person recognizes their own intent."
Unexpectedness originally has no form. Where there is no form, there is no object. Where there is no intention, there is no self.
When there is neither object nor self, what does the gentleman have to fear? To preserve objects and preserve the self—the gentleman finds this largely undesirable.

There are many gentlemen in Song, yet each merely possesses their own head. This "head" is the mark of the self (*ātman*). If each were without intention, without necessity, without stubbornness, and without self, [there would be no conflict].
This refers to Wang Anshi. Both he and those who attacked him were gentlemen.
To ensure the vessel of the mind is sharp, nothing is better than sweet serenity; to ensure the vessel of the body is sharp, nothing is better than being diligent in leisure.
The body is within the mind; therefore, the mind can move the body. When the mind is within the body, it cannot move it.
Why is this? It is like a kite in the wind: the wind can blow the kite up.
But if the wind were inside the kite, the kite would be large and the wind small; the small could not blow the large. The mind is neither inside nor outside.
Therefore, it can encompass both the internal and the external. If it possessed internal and external [dimensions], how would it differ from the internal and external themselves?

Since it is no different from the internal and external, naturally the internal and external cannot operate upon the internal and external. If the internal and external could operate upon the internal and external, [it would be no different from them].
Gold may be traded for gold; water may be washed with water.

The mind possesses cognition, while the vital breath (*qi*) lacks cognition. The four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are transformations of the single vital breath; the single vital breath is the return of the four great elements.
Thus, Zhuangzi said: "When the vital breath gathers, there is life; when the vital breath disperses, there is death. Life and death, birth and death, do not exceed this.
It is merely the gathering and dispersing of the vital breath (*qi*). Those who have attained realization know this to be so;

therefore, in the interval between birth and death, they never rejoice in life nor fear death. Otherwise, this five-foot body would be able to confine and limit this boundless and infinite spiritual luminosity.
It is like a person using their hand to move a brush; only then can the brush draw. The adept, by means of the drawing, infers it back to the brush;
from the brush, they infer it back to the hand; from the hand, they infer it back to the mind; and from the mind, they infer it back to that which is without self yet possesses spiritual efficacy.
When there is no self, there is no external. The external is that which depends upon the internal. Since the self has no external, the internal is also exhausted.

When the internal is exhausted, the external cannot exist independently. Once the conditions of both internal and external have withered away, there is neither internal nor external, and that which is capable of being both internal and external manifests before us.
As the *Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* says: "All sentient beings realize perfect enlightenment. This refers to this very state.
It is said:
the mind does not exist of itself; it exists because of objects. This is the mind that is a shadow following the conditions of the six sense-objects.
If one cannot investigate and thoroughly understand this mind, then the originally present, numinous, and luminous mind will never manifest before one. It is like floating clouds.
It is not yet pure; the blue sky is not revealed. Furthermore, when worldly people discuss the body, they instead speak of the mind in a confused manner;
when they discuss the mind, they instead speak of the body in a confused manner. For this reason, as for the body, the mind, the head, and the brain, they ultimately remain unclear.

If the body, the mind, the head, and the brain were clear, then one would realize that the body of birth and death is the Dharma-body, and that the mind of afflictions is the Bodhi-mind—no different [from their true nature].
It is merely a matter of bending and extending one's own fingers.
Humans are ghosts with form; ghosts are humans without form. To say that humans and ghosts possess two separate minds is illogical;
it is simply a distinction between having form and lacking form.
A student must first sever sensual desire. The path for severing sensual desire does not have many branches; it simply requires being able to discern one's own true nature.
Once this is achieved, even if the beauty of Xi Shi or the loveliness of Zidu were before one’s eyes, they would naturally be forgotten.
However, recognizing this is clarity; being able to forget it is courage. If one is clear but lacks courage, then defiled habits will proliferate, like oil soaking into flour;
once it has entered, it is not easy to extract. Now tell me, how can the physical body recognize and break through it?
First, one should investigate what existed before my birth: did this body exist as a result, or did it not?

If it existed, why was it necessary for my parents to unite in sexual intercourse to bring it forth? If it did not exist, then since it was originally non-existent, how could this body suddenly emerge from nothingness?
Investigate in this manner. If you investigate without ceasing, then this body will suddenly be thoroughly penetrated and understood.
Once one’s own body is thus understood, the bodies of others are likewise understood without needing to be analyzed further. When both one’s own and others’ bodies are thus dissolved, tell me:
what thing can then serve as the subject or object of lustful desire? If you investigate in this way, yet fail to achieve such understanding—
Having deconstructed one's own self, one should next contemplate the time when the parents unite. Does the mother’s mind move first? Does the father’s mind move first?
Do the minds of both parents move simultaneously? Or do the minds of both parents not move? If the minds of the parents do not move, then both are devoid of mind.
If there is no mind, there is no self. If there is no self, who gives rise to lustful desire? If the minds of the parents move simultaneously—simultaneously...
It is one. Being one, there is neither subject nor object; thus, even a lustful mind cannot move it.

When the parents’ lustful minds move first and then last, the former is not the latter, and the latter is not the former; fundamentally they do not depend upon one another, so the lustful mind likewise has no movement.
This is an inference based on principle, not a conceptual calculation of the emotions. Furthermore, at the time of the parents’ union, I have no lustful mind; the body is merely a causal condition.

"No. I had a lustful mind, yet my parents did not engage in sexual union; thus there was no causal condition for a body. A body exists only when the three factors—the cause, the condition, and the self—conjoin.

If a body were to exist through the conjoining of these three, one could calculate by alternating back and forth how much belongs to the father, how much to the mother, and how much to the 'self. Pushing it back and forth, pushing it away..."

Push it forward. Push until you reach the point where emotion is exhausted and wisdom is finalized; then, whether the body exists or does not exist, you will know it for yourself without waiting for another to ask.
To know is clarity; clarity is freedom from delusion; freedom from delusion means that both Xi Shi and Zi Du are merely the vanguard before my state of desirelessness.
Furthermore, that which is without self yet numinous is the *xing* (nature); that which possesses self and is obscure is [the ego].
This is emotion (*qing*). Nature (*xing*) transforms into emotion. Nature is boundless; emotion is likewise boundless. When emotion returns to its source, it is fully restored to nature.
Emotion is boundless; nature is likewise boundless. It is like the vastness of water and the abundance of ice: as the ice thickens, the water deepens.
Scholarship is not a matter of many heads; it is simply a matter of exhausting the spirit and reaching the ultimate limit of numbers.
To exhaust the spirit means that there is no self, and thus the spirit is fully realized. To reach the ultimate limit of numbers means that although there is a self, the obscure cannot obscure me.
Because numbers cannot obscure me, the one becomes many, and the many become one; this resides within me and does not reside in the numbers.
Just as the physical form is a temporary composition of the five elements—is this not a numerical phenomenon?
As for the mind, it does not arise when the body is formed, nor does it die when the body perishes; thus it can be considered the master of numbers, while numbers are but its servants.
With ordinary people, however, it is otherwise: the master becomes the servant, and the servant becomes the master. Some might say that the Chan school knows only the nature (xing) but...
"Knowing destiny. The Daoist school knows only destiny but does not know nature; this teaching is not comprehensive. "Spirit" refers to nature, and "number" refers to destiny.

There has never been one who could exhaust the mysteries of spirit without being able to reach the limits of number, nor one who could reach the limits of number without being able to exhaust the mysteries of spirit.

If there were those who exhausted the mysteries of spirit but could not reach the limits of number, they are the followers of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). [Those who] reach the limits of number and..."
Those who cannot exhaust the spiritual are the Earth Immortals (*dìxiān*). As it is said: "There is a thing prior to heaven and earth; nameless, it is fundamentally silent and vast.

It can act as the lord of the myriad phenomena, yet does not wither along with the four seasons. Is that which can act as the lord of the myriad phenomena not the spirit? Are the myriad phenomena not numbers?
Furthermore, there is the teaching that the mind governs both nature and emotion. Everyone in the world knows of this teaching, yet they do not know its [true] meaning.

The true meaning is rare indeed. Now, the emotions (*qing*) are the waves; the mind (*xin*) is the current; and nature (*xing*) is the source. If the external flow lacks waves, yet one abandons the current, the source will likewise be difficult to find.
However, this teaching is not clearly understood because of a failure to examine the emotions and the mind.

This is due to the neglect of the relationship between the mind and nature. That which responds to things without being entangled is called the "mind. That which responds to things while being entangled is called [the emotion].
As for emotion (*qing*) and nature (*xing*): that which responds to objects and that which does not respond to objects, yet remains eternally empty and numinous, is what is meant by "nature.
Viewed from this perspective, emotion is the mind (*xin*). Because responding to objects entails entanglement, it can only be called emotion and cannot be called the mind. The mind is emotion.
Because responding to objects is without entanglement, it can only be called the mind and cannot be called emotion. However, external nature has no response.

It is a matter of responding or not responding; it is merely a question of being burdened or not being burdened. If this is so, then emotion is nature, the mind is nature, nature is the mind, and nature is emotion.
There are three names, but no three realities. These are merely provisional words used to provide a description.
Yet when one reaches the point of ultimate truth, it is utterly beyond what language can describe or even approximate. Therefore it is said:
One must practice authentically; one must awaken authentically. In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, there is a sword within the royal treasury.
This sword is lustrous, brilliant, and pure. Not only does it slice iron like mud, but it can also reflect a person’s beauty or ugliness.
Is slicing iron like mud not sharpness? Is reflecting a person’s beauty or ugliness not clarity? Being both sharp and clear—is this not the most precious treasure in the world?
My mind judges right from wrong. Its sharpness is like that of a sword in a treasury; its clarity in reflecting the beauty or ugliness of things is as bright as the mirror of Qin.
Yet, if one encounters objects of desire, then that which was sharp becomes dull, and that which was clear becomes obscured.

Therefore, a great man must always ensure there is nothing within his breast and no desires before his eyes. When there is nothing within the breast, the mind can encompass the vast void; when there is nothing before the eyes—
If you desire it, then with the eye you may exhaustively penetrate that which precedes all forms (*xiàng*). Although knowing it is easy, practicing it is difficult.
Again, he drew a divination stalk and obtained the number five. The Master said: "Now, five is the number of non-self (*anātman*). To have a number while being without self—"
To calculate without self is to exhaust the spirit and reach the ultimate limit of calculation; to reach the ultimate limit of calculation is to exhaust the spirit. Why is this so?
It is like when the four directions are just determined, the center is determined; and when the center is determined, the four directions are determined.
There has never been a case where the center comes first and the four directions follow, nor where the four directions come first and the center follows. Viewed from this perspective, it is clear.
Not only is there no self in the center, but there is likewise no self in the four directions. It is only that the multitude are muddled and fail to perceive this;
their principle is obscured by emotion, leading them to claim that the four directions are inherently the four directions and the center is inherently the center.
Little do they realize that to seek the center outside the four directions, or to seek the four directions outside the center, is no different from seeking hair on a tortoise or horns on a hare.
Furthermore, the body is like the center, while earth, water, fire, and wind are like the four directions.

Therefore, if gold, wood, water, or fire possessed a self (*ātman*), they would not necessarily require the gathering of soil to form their substance. If soil possessed a self, it likewise could not serve as a resource for the other four elements.
Thus, soil does not constitute itself; it forms its substance by borrowing from the four elements. The four elements do not constitute themselves; they [exist] because...
The earth is that upon which things depend. Just as the body is not itself the self, yet can be returned to the four great elements;

and just as the four great elements are not themselves the four great elements, yet can be borrowed to form a body; so too, the center is not itself the center, but must borrow the four directions to constitute the center;
and the four directions are not themselves the four directions, but must rely upon the center to constitute the four directions. Alas! He who understands this teaching—

Thus, the single principle disperses into ten thousand phenomena, and the ten thousand phenomena converge back into the single principle. It is like seeing eyebrows and eyes in a mirror, or observing the grain of wood in the palm of one’s hand;
what cause for doubt could there be? Now, the "Middle" (madhya) refers to the principle of non-self (anātman), while the "Four" refer to the four matters of non-self.

The reason being this: external phenomena lack principle, and external principles lack phenomena; it is just as with external ice [which lacks the principle of water, and the principle of water lacks the phenomenon of ice].
There is no water; externally, there is no ice in water. Therefore it is said: "If a person recognizes their own mind, there is not an inch of earth upon the great earth.

Zibo, however, says otherwise: "If a person understands the principle, let the myriad things clamor as they will; I alone enjoy tranquility, with neither affliction in adversity nor vexation in prosperity.
This is like [the sequence] two, four, six, eight, ten; these are derivative numbers, not the fundamental number.
Earth, water, fire, and wind cannot be mixed even by the slightest degree. It may seem as though there is a self;

yet, since the body is composed of these four elements, those four elements themselves are without a self. Therefore, one knows that if the body possessed a self, it could not return to the four great elements.
If the body can never again return to the four great elements, then human beings would have birth but no death. Furthermore, solidity, moisture, warmth, and...

The four directions are like movement, and the center is like the body. Therefore, when there are the four external directions, the center does not exist; when there is the external center, the four directions likewise do not exist.

When there are the external solidity, moisture, warmth, and movement, the body certainly does not exist; when there is the external body, solidity, moisture, warmth, and movement likewise do not exist.
When the student is undecided regarding victory or defeat in the fields of food, drink, and sexual desire, they must be fierce.
When one cultivates this contemplation, the water of natural principle naturally deepens day by day, while human desires grow shallower day by day.
When those who possess a self yet remain deluded exhaust their attachment to gain and loss, only then can those who are selfless and spiritual be fully realized.

He asked again, "Is it possible for a single body to exist across three lifetimes? The Master said, "It is. This is simply because while the body is one, the lifetimes are three, just as when a person walks.

There is a road. The road extends for a thousand *li*, yet only one person travels it. To say that because the road is a thousand *li* long, there must also be a thousand people upon it, is the talk of a fool.
Yet this body is not merely a physical frame subject to birth and death or gathering and dispersal; it is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Now, the Dharma-body perceives a thousand ages in a single instant and ten thousand kalpas in a single breath; how could it be limited to but one life across three periods?
Is that all? The old man tells you: "One body throughout the three periods of time. This is a secret indication of the principle that one has never died;

it must not be neglected. You must take this to heart and value yourself highly. Should you encounter circumstances of supporting the collapsing or subduing the fierce, shoulder the burden directly and do not attempt to evade it.
The two sat in stillness; their minds were both clear and bright. Clarity implies freedom from disturbance, and brightness implies freedom from obscurity.
When there is neither disturbance nor obscurity, how could there be a mind that awaits external conditions? When a joyful object suddenly appears before one, a joyful mind arises;
when an unpleasant object appears, an unpleasant mind arises. If a joyful mind were an inherent part of my own nature, then in the face of an unpleasant object—
"Manifest before you. It is merely joy; how could it become a mind of non-joy? The Third Patriarch said: "The capacity arises from the object, and the object arises from the capacity.
If you wish to know these two aspects, they are fundamentally one emptiness."

A person must be able to roll through the midst of right and wrong, as well as calamity and adversity. If one cannot roll through the midst of right and wrong, calamity, and adversity, how can there be a true person?
Therefore, genuine gold must be forged by fire; a true person must be tempered by circumstances.

Yanzi cast off his limbs and body, thereby externalizing his physical frame; he set aside his cleverness and intelligence, thereby emptying his deluded mind. When the deluded mind is emptied, the true mind is revealed;
when the physical frame is externalized, the Dharma-body is perfected.
"Departure" (*li*) is the symbol of the mind. If one contemplates the elephant and grasps its meaning, then that which is empty yet luminous resides within oneself rather than in words and language.
If all words and language flow forth from this emptiness and luminosity, they will naturally manifest the patterns of heaven and possess wondrous mechanisms.
The Venerable Li of the Tang dynasty frequently used the meaning of *namo śrī* to illustrate this principle.
The Master Zhi often laughed at him, thinking that the Elder did not distinguish between Chinese and Sanskrit.
Little did he know that the Elder alone had grasped the essential principle of the *dharmadhātu* of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai*) in the *Avataṃsaka*.

Since this is the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena, it is perfectly permissible to explain Chinese terms using Sanskrit, and likewise to explain Sanskrit terms using Chinese. This is because they are both explained through the conventions of worldly writing.
It is permissible to explain worldly scriptures by means of supramundane scriptures;
it is permissible to clarify virtuous speech through unwholesome speech, and likewise to clarify unwholesome speech through virtuous speech. When words clarify, the meaning is attained.

When the meaning is attained, one reaches that which is empty yet luminous, and constantly serves as a sovereign for all things—whether defiled or pure, good or evil, Chinese or Sanskrit, right or wrong, beautiful or coarse.
Evil! All are but subjects and servants; all are merely the samādhi of speech. Alas! The mind is fundamentally empty and luminous, yet the world neglects it and fails to investigate it.
All these are my own manifestations from previous lives—body and mind obstructed rather than empty, obscured rather than luminous.
One clings to them with stinginess and refuses to let go. Little do they realize that that which is obstructed and obscured can become empty and luminous once it is released.
It arrives without waiting to be sought. Viewed from this perspective, regarding the saying "playing with the elephant to grasp its meaning":
if one’s worldly desires are not shallow and one’s celestial mechanism (*tianji*) is not profound, the elephant is not easily played with, nor is the meaning easily grasped.
Furthermore, I urge you to study the *Platform Sutra*, which was spoken by the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi. Initially, Caoxi was illiterate and did not know written words or speech; yet, upon hearing—
Upon hearing the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he attained sudden and great enlightenment.

He subsequently traveled to Huangmei, where he received the robe and bowl, and returned to Lingnan to transmit the Mind School at Baolin Temple on Caoxi. From that time forth, the world referred to it as Caoxi.
His *Platform Sūtra*—reaching from the two schools of Nature and Characteristics—woven them like warp and woof, interlacing them in myriad forms, as if one long practiced in the art of writing.
This is one who has attained the samādhi of language. It is merely the verification that one’s own mind is empty and luminous. Humans are the most spiritually gifted among all things;
knowing this yet failing to seek it with earnest effort while seeking elsewhere—can such a person truly be called the most spiritually gifted among all things?
A great man merely attains the pivot (ji). There is no more or less to the pivot; it is only because its applications differ that it appears as if there were more or less.

Nevertheless, the pivot of the preceding manifestation is the very pivot of the subsequent manifestation, and the pivot of the subsequent manifestation is the very pivot of the preceding manifestation.

If one calls it a single pivot, then the preceding manifestation is not the subsequent manifestation; yet if one calls them many pivots, then the preceding manifestation... [is not different from the subsequent].

The mechanism that follows after is preceded by the external image; yet the mechanism itself has no distinct mechanism. Because it rides upon the times and responds to things, there arises the distinction between the image preceding and the image following.
