The Collected Works of Old Man Zibo, Volume Ten.
Read by Deqing of Mount Huan in the Ming Dynasty.
The Dharma Words of Shiyuan:
A Further Account of Grand Master Yao at Chongguo Temple. He inscribed his own portrait, saying: "Having seen through the banana tree and the staff."
"Disciple, in the midst of the ordinary, you have thoroughly revealed your refined elegance. At times you shake the whisk made of tortoise hair until even empty space laughs and nods its head.
When the Master speaks of the *bājiāo* staff, he refers to the 'body. If I were to see through this, then the mind would be free from entanglement;
when the mind is free from entanglement, there is clarity; and when there is clarity, the nature can be seen. For one who sees their nature, even tortoise hair [can serve as a whisk]."

He considers this to be "brushing away" (fù). With this brushing away, one can become heaven and earth; rolling up and unrolling the great void, bending and extending the myriad phenomena—all resides within oneself and not in the Creator.
This was Yao’s own eulogy. Zibo, however, was not like this: "The *bājiǎo* staff is but turtle fur;
life and death, vertical and horizontal, his spirit and intent are bold. Whether saint or commoner, their souls and gallows fall; the fragrant breeze blows them down."
"Peaches on the treetop. The Master asked Fu Yao, "What is the excellence of Old Man Laozi? What is the deficiency of Zi-bai?
If you cannot distinguish between their strengths and weaknesses, you are a man with no pearl in your eye. Nevertheless, Zi-bai knows only the heavenly ordinances and earthly righteousness;
as for Old Man Yao, if he can leap out of this cage of 'ritual propriety,' I will grant him thirty blows."
“Strike! If you cannot leap out, thirty blows—no single blow shall be spared! Zibo looked left and right and said, “Where is Old Yao?
He then opened his eyes wide. The Master said, “If he is not here, let him pass; if he is here, only then may he take the blows on his behalf.”
He asked again: "Does human nature exist while one is in the mother’s womb? Or does it only come into being after birth, at the very moment one lands on the ground?
The Master asked, "Do you say that nature has boundaries? Does nature have past and present?"
He spoke again: "The nature is boundless; it has neither past nor present. The Master said:

"Since the nature is both boundless and beyond past and present, how can one establish a discourse on whether the nature exists or does not exist while in the mother’s womb, or a discourse on whether the nature exists or does not exist after birth?
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "It is pure and fundamentally so. Why, then, do mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? This is the fulfillment.
This is Maitreya’s question to the Tathāgata. Now, that which is fundamentally pure is like water; the mountains, rivers, and great earth are like ice.
Water is permeable and flowing; ice is obstructed and solid. If one suspects that what is obstructed is not what is permeable, can one say that ice is identical to water?
Yet, apart from water there is no ice; can one say that ice is not water? Furthermore, he asks regarding that which is said to "suddenly arise."
"What is the meaning of this 'sudden'? The Master said: "The sudden is not something that can be reached by the functioning of the mind.
If one insists on investigating the principle behind why it is sudden, then the sudden might seem measurable by the functioning of the mind. Nevertheless, because Buddha-nature is impermanent."
Water can become ice; because all phenomena are external to the true and eternal, they cannot establish themselves. Thus we know that ice can return to water.
Furthermore, there are those who possess a self yet are deluded, and those who lack an external self yet are spiritually luminous.
Consequently, one who possesses a self yet is deluded cannot be found. The Sage, knowing this, first causes things to merge with himself, and only then does he open the way for things.
Success in affairs means there is nowhere one does not achieve penetration. Why is this? It is simply because by regarding oneself as external to things, one finds no "things" apart from oneself;

and by regarding things as external to oneself, one finds no "self" apart from things. When one regards oneself as external to things, then the things that open up objects and accomplish affairs have never been anything other than oneself.

When one regards things as external to oneself, then things do not need to be gathered together for the self to be complete. Yet, though one knows this principle, if one cannot put it into practice, then [the goal] is mostly lost.
If the stains of habitual tendencies are not eliminated upon arising, one may practice but will not realize [the truth]; thus, the innate spirit will ultimately never be fully restored.
If one realizes [the truth] but cannot remain free from attachment, then the functioning that accords with the nature will never manifest before one. Therefore it is said:
"Where there is a great capacity, there must be a great function."
When water becomes extremely cold, it turns into ice; when the cold passes, the ice returns to water.
When the nature (*prakṛti*) transforms into emotion (*kleśa*), and emotion becomes excessive, the yin reaches its limit. All seeds of defiled habituation belong to the yin.

When one illuminates the nature to achieve cultivation, the force of defiled habituation gradually diminishes of its own accord, while the functional power of pure seeds also gradually increases. There are six stages of the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*); [only...]
The "diminishing of power and augmenting of capacity" is a tool for the beginner to navigate the critical junctures of daily life, whether in accordance with or contrary to the Dharma.

However, were it not for the assistance of a sense of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) in supporting one's resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), this transformative process could not otherwise take effect.
The Master asked again, saying: "That which can be grasped in your body is merely skin, flesh, sinews, and bones.
That which is moist, warm, and moving cannot be grasped. That which can be grasped is called the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*);

that which cannot be grasped is what is termed water, fire, or wind. These are collectively named the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). There are primary four great elements and secondary four great elements."
The primary four great elements are that ground you habitually tread upon, the water you drink, the warm food you eat, and that which animates all things.
The secondary four great elements are the skin, flesh, sinews, and bones of your body, along with moisture, warmth, and motion. Yet, the secondary do not exist apart from the primary;
at the outset, it is by borrowing the primary that the body comes to be. If there were a body that did not borrow the primary, [it could not exist].
If one relies upon it, the body will inevitably perish; this principle is very clear. Yet, the multitude is bound by their emotional calculations and cannot use reason to subdue emotion;
thus, they cling to the habits of the body, which are not easily eliminated. The Sage uses the mind to employ the body, whereas the multitude burdens the mind with the body.
One who uses the mind to employ the body is like the mouth spitting out foam—once spat out, one does not know how many times it has been done.
The Thousand Bubbles Star is like the immortal Zhou Dian, who manifested many bodies from a single body.
Those who burden the mind with the body calculate that skin, flesh, sinews, and bones can be grasped as "my body," yet they do not realize that in the end, these are not truly theirs.
This body was originally not mine, and in the end it shall not be mine; how then can that which exists in the interim be mine? When a sage possesses this body, he does not possess it as his own.
Therefore, when the time of death arrives, earth returns to earth, water returns to water, fire returns to fire, and wind returns to wind. Thus, with this—
As for that which is borrowed, one returns it; what fear or dread could there be? Death occurs precisely because of this lack of fear;
then the single point of luminous clarity remains as stable and firm as Mount Tai—how could it become clouded or disturbed?
Therefore, death afflicts only that which is borrowed, and does not afflict that which is undisturbed. Moreover, since this single point of luminous clarity still exists, it is naturally so.
The dead do not truly die; they again borrow the great elements of earth, and take the fundamental elements of earth, water, fire, and wind as their bodies.

Thus they die and are born again, and are born and die again, undergoing millions of lifetimes while the karmic mechanism does not cease. Although this explanation is correct, [it remains incomplete].
However, you do not yet know the reason why the reflected shadows of the six sense-objects constitute the mind.

As for the primary and secondary elements (*mahābhūta*), even if one were to borrow and return each component, it might seem as though they are clearly understood; yet, when observing how these objects are gathered back into oneself, they ultimately remain two separate fragments.

If one can thoroughly investigate the mind that perceives these reflected shadows, then the numinous clarity will finally coalesce. Furthermore, there are varying degrees of depth in this coalescence of numinous clarity.

Just as one attains the fruit of Arhatship by severing the delusions of views and thought, and attains the fruit of Bodhisattvahood by severing the delusions of the sands of dust, it is only when the fundamental ignorance is completely severed that one first attains the fruit of Buddhahood.
Therefore it is said: "The principles of the mental factors are subtle and wondrous; even Confucius and Laozi were unaware of them."
Master Mokhyang often said:
"If ginseng is infused with milk, it becomes diluted; if infused with wine, it becomes thin. As the distance from antiquity increases, human hearts become turbid;

thus, what was once considered strange is now taken as normal, while what is truly strange is regarded as the constant state of affairs. When those who uphold the tradition of emulating the ancients see this, they regard it as a fabrication.
It is only natural that [the people] have such strange eyes.
Some say: "The nature of the people is mostly violent; the Sage guides them with benevolence (*ren*). The nature of the people is mostly rebellious;

the Sage guides them with righteousness (*yi*). The nature of the people is mostly licentious; the Sage guides them with ritual propriety (*li*). The nature of the people is mostly ignorant; the Sage..."
The Sage leads people through wisdom. The nature of the common people is prone to delusion; thus, the Sage leads them through faithfulness.

It is not that the nature of the people is violent—that they could be led toward benevolence (*ren*). It is not that the nature of the people is rebellious—that they could be led toward righteousness (*yi*).
The nature of the people is not licentious; they can be led by means of ritual propriety (*li*). The nature of the people is not ignorant; they can be led by means of wisdom (*zhi*).
The nature of the people is not deceitful; they can be led by means of good faith (*xin*). If this is so, then those who are violent can be led toward benevolence (*ren*);

those who are rebellious can be led toward righteousness (*yi*); those who are licentious can be led toward ritual propriety; those who are ignorant can be led toward wisdom; and those who are deceitful can be led [toward good faith].
To govern them by means of trustworthiness is to govern them; it is not to guide them. Governing them is like Gung governing the waters; guiding them is like Yu guiding the waters.
Therefore, when one acts contrary to their nature, success will not be established; when one accords with their nature, the work continues to completion.
If their nature is inherently violent and one attempts to guide them through benevolence, I know that even if a sage were to be reborn, his way would be difficult to implement. For the most part...
Habit can be rectified, and nature can be guided by the Way. Therefore, violence is a matter of habit, not of nature.
To clear forests to hunt tigers and rhinoceroses, or to enter the water to grapple with crocodiles and dragons—what the world considers bravery is not true bravery.
To be able to apply the principle of supreme impartiality to subdue private, biased emotions, prevailing without being defeated—that is true bravery.
Someone said: "Suppose there were now an infant on the road about to be trampled by oxen or horses;

anyone who saw this, regardless of whether they were wise or foolish, would surely feel a sense of alarm and would all wish to drive away the oxen and horses to save the child. Yet, when it comes to a state with a weak ruler—"

In one's chamber there is a beautiful wife, yet one who plots for the state while desiring that chamber only harbors resentment toward the ruler and the husband, wishing that they not suffer the calamity of their innocent children.
Alas! What kind of mind is this? It is simply the mind that wishes to preserve life;

yet by slightly indulging in what is desirable, one’s discernment is suddenly lost—how can it come to such an extreme? Therefore it is said: "Not seeing what is desirable keeps the mind from being disturbed."
Now, skill and the Way emerge from the same source yet bear different names. Thus, for one who is proficient in the Way, skill is also the Way;
for one who is not proficient in the Way, even the Way is but skill. If this is so, are the Way and skill truly one, or are they truly different?
Now, as for afflictions and bodhi, turbid waves and clear water, emptiness and form, and doubt and faith—are these one thing or two things?
If one does not observe them suddenly, the three delusions will be vast and pervasive; yet if one turns back and investigates them, the three virtues are manifestly present.
This is not something that can be entered by toiling the body or exhausting the bones; it is valued in the deluded mind itself.
When birth suddenly occurs, exhaustively investigate its origin: Is it drawn by sound? Is it drawn by form? Is it contrary or favorable? Is it life or death?
Follow the place where the mind arises and embody that very moment; push it to its limit and exhaust it to the source.
Does it arise from oneself? Does it arise from another? Does it arise from the union of both? Examine this with unceasing persistence and with firm, penetrating rigor until—
In the power of wisdom, there is no application of effort; the faculties of the mind have no ground upon which to be planted.

Transcending attachment, one’s spirit becomes brilliant—like a starving dog gnawing at a dry bone: to chew it minutely yields no flavor, yet to abandon it leaves one desolate. One chews it, chews it, and chews it again.
Suddenly, both the vigor of the spirit and the dry bone—the subject and the object—are severed. Only then does one no longer doubt that emptiness is not different from form.
Defilement is not different from faith; afflictions are not different from bodhi; sentient beings are not different from the Buddhas.
Alas! One who can cast away their life can kill; one who can sever their attachments can enter the Way. Even if a sage were to be reborn, he would not alter these words of mine.
The mind’s operations are not constant; they depend entirely upon what it relies upon. Thus, if one relies upon the ten evil deeds, the hells appear;
if one relies upon stinginess and greed, hungry ghosts appear; if one relies upon ignorance and delusion, animals appear.

Relying upon the five precepts, one perceives them in human beings; relying upon the ten wholesome actions, one perceives them in the heavens; relying upon the four noble truths, the path of the śrāvaka is accomplished;
relying upon the twelve links of dependent origination, the fruit of the pratyekabuddha is attained; and relying upon the six perfections...
Thus, when a Bodhisattva’s compassion is vast, they rely upon the Supreme Vehicle (Agryayāna), whereby the fruit of Buddhahood is perfected.
Conversely, if one relies upon the Six Classics, one is called a Confucian; if one relies upon the Hundred Schools, one is called a member of the Hundred Houses.

To compare those who rely on the "Names and Forms" (Xingming) of Han Fei or the "Art of War" of Sun Wu to the distinction between animals and hungry ghosts (preta), or between hungry ghosts and those in hell—[the former are vastly superior].
Third, if one examines what they rely upon, although both are not good, this retribution is not caused by their own minds. Alas!
Man is the most intelligent among all things; if that which he relies upon were good, then what difficulty would there be in attaining sagehood? Yet [consider] Han Fei and Sun Wu.
Having already become a human being, it is unfortunate that what one relies upon is not good;
if one leads the world with slaughter, then one will take the hells as one’s gardens and pavilions, sporting there for long kalpas—I know that one cannot escape this. Someone may say:

"Legalism and names are used to remedy the deficiencies of virtuous teaching, while military force is used to slay the few to save the many; both are arts of benevolence. Why do you condemn them both?"

[The Master] refuted this. [The disciple] replied: "If we examine the scriptures that transcend the world and verify them against the classics that govern the world, there has never been one who was skilled in practice without having heard the Great Way.
As for being truly skilled in its application, none but a sage could achieve it."
Now, when all is vast and traceless, what is auspicious and what is inauspicious? Since yin and yang cannot be confined within a cage, how could calamity and fortune be distinguished by their gender?
Alas! When there is even a slight capacity for cognition, the myriad things come into being. Thus, by observing the lines and images (*xiang*), one may infer good fortune and misfortune;
by listening to sounds, one can determine auspiciousness and inauspiciousness. If this is so, then with a single mind—
Once life has arisen, how could the Three Collections and Six Classics serve as anything more than mere traps and snares?

Now, the deep mountains and profound abysses are what dragons, crocodiles, tigers, and rhinoceroses rely upon; great wealth and high positions are what those of noble lineage and illustrious status rely upon.
Yet neither dragons, crocodiles, tigers, and rhinoceroses, nor those of noble lineage and illustrious status, can escape their own afflictions.

This is because they merely trade upon their reputation. Nevertheless, one who has transcended the world cannot be seduced by wealth and honor; one who has transcended wealth and honor cannot be humiliated by poverty and low status. Alas!

To rely on purity to stand aloof from the world, and to trade in distress thereby harming one’s life—is this true fame, or is it not? If such is the case, then even dragons, tigers, and rhinoceroses will not act with violence toward them. Wealth— (Note:

Noble lineage and glory do not lead to greed; yet those who are exceedingly violent and greedy—could they not be those who have cast aside the world and forgotten wealth and honor?
Indeed, that honor brings disgrace and profit invites theft is something everyone easily understands. Yet, it is the fame that invites jealousy and the virtue... [that invites resentment].

This invites slander; the Way invites censure. Is this because one's knowledge is not yet authentic? If it were truly authentic knowledge, how could it be easy to know—unless one has truly trodden its threshold? How difficult it is to know!
All under heaven admire wealth and honor while loathing poverty and low status; all detest hunger and cold while craving satiety and warmth.
Yet they fail to realize that were it not for the foundation provided by poverty, low status, hunger, and cold, from whence would wealth, honor, satiety, and warmth ever come?
When drought reaches its extreme, water arrives; when flooding reaches its extreme, drought comes. Therefore, the sage observes the hoarfrost and knows the ice is coming;
he examines what is to come and knows what has passed. If this is so, as long as one has not yet reached the extreme, it is still possible to prepare for it.
Once the extreme is reached, the extreme does not turn back; what benefit would preparation then provide?

Generally, when one acts upon things before they have come into being, a single act brings ten thousand things to completion; and when ten thousand things are completed, that single act is not diminished.
If it were diminished, what benefit would there be in those ten thousand things? Because it is not diminished, it is called "benefit."
Now, that which summons birth and death is the body; that which summons likes and dislikes is the mind. As for this birth-and-death and these likes-and-dislikes, the sage suffers from them deeply.
Because he suffers from them, his suffering is itself free from anything to be suffered. Ordinary people do not suffer from them; therefore, they merely suffer from their own suffering.
Suppose there were a person here who, although unable to immediately eliminate that which summons [birth and death], knows that summoning is the source of suffering.

The go-between exists because of one's knowledge; as the go-between becomes more distant, one's knowledge becomes more remote. Thus, those who know that the go-between is remote, though they have not yet attained the perfection of a sage, begin their journey toward sagehood from this point.
Now, as for being awake and dreaming, or day and dream: are they Heaven or Man? In terms of Heaven, they are called day and night;
in terms of Man, they are called waking and dreaming. Therefore, one who understands this may be considered Heaven, and may also be considered Man.
If this is so, it is clear that Heaven and Man reside within me, and do not reside in the Creator.
I have often contemplated what else might exist above heaven; I have contemplated who it is that supports me beneath the earth.
I pondered it, I pondered it, and I pondered it again. When my thoughts reached their limit, they could no longer issue from the gates of my mouth;
how, then, could they ever be expressed through words or defined by form? Nevertheless, true sorrow is voiceless, and true kinship is beyond sentiment.
Thus, when sounds, appearances, and emotions arise, heaven and earth seem vast while the self seems minute.
Now, the honorable dream of disgrace; the wealthy dream of theft; the hungry dream of eating; the thirsty dream of drinking; the brave dream of cowardice;
the cowardly dream of bravery; a person from the south dreams of a boat; a person from the north dreams of a horse; and those with profound celestial mechanisms dream of mountains and rivers.
Clouds and atmospheric phenomena differ according to what beings prefer; thus, their dreams are each distinct.

Therefore, the Perfected One (Zhiren) understands this and knows that heaven and earth can be reversed, mountains and seas can be shifted, and birth and death can be treated as a game. Hence it is said:
"One who awakens to Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra) may succeed to the rank of the Buddhas and Patriarchs."
Someone asked me, "Why does the Monk of the Cloth Bag smile so much? I replied, "I fear people will find it strange.

When the questioner heard my words, he took them to be a deception and did not believe me. This is because he does not understand that those who plan great matters must have far-reaching concerns, and those who travel long distances must carry heavy burdens.
The Monk of the Cloth Bag and the Great Master Fu of Shuanglin were both emanations of Maitreya.
"This person is indeed so. This elder is the future Buddha; he serves as the East Palace attendant to Śākyamuni. The matter is no small one.
If you do not contemplate it deeply and plan for the long term, then when the time comes, regret will be of no avail. The questioner said, "I have heard your words."
"If you have told me this in such depth, I, your humble servant, am dull-witted and my consciousness is clouded; I have not yet been able to grasp it. I beg you to explain it to me in detail.

I replied to him, saying: "Do you know? When the Great Being Fu (Bodhisattva Maitreya) established the Dharma-wheel, and Bagua Heshang faced people with a smile, they did so because they foresaw that their transformations in the Sahā world would be complete and the Dragon Flower Assembly was about to begin. If one does not cultivate in advance..."
This is the cause for the *prajñā* of sentient beings and the condition for binding the world in joy.

Thus, when the time comes for one to attain Buddhahood, if the capacity for resonance is mired in ignorance and sentient beings abound in anger—since ignorance renders hearing the Dharma fruitless and excessive anger prevents the practice of universal compassion—[the teaching will not flourish].
These two are the grave responsibilities of the Sage. If these grave responsibilities are not contemplated, what is the purpose of attaining Buddhahood?

Furthermore, speaking in terms of ten parts of sentient beings, those who can read are few, while those who cannot read are many. They rejoice when things accord with their wishes and become angry when they do not.
Therefore, the Wheel Repository (Lunzang) is entrusted with the Sage’s broad and long tongue, and the Laughing Face (Xiaomian) is bound to form the conditions for joy. If this is so—
In this regard, all six sense-faculties are eyes; whether in accord or in opposition, all are the springtime.

Therefore, those who see the *Wheel Treasury* (*Cakrakośa*) with their eyes, those who hear the *Wheel Treasury* with their ears, those who touch the *Wheel Treasury* with their hands, those who contact the *Wheel Treasury* with their bodies, and those who take the *Wheel Treasury* as an object of their minds—whether they praise it with their mouths or revile it with their mouths—all cultivate the cause of Prajñā within the *Wheel Treasury*. Since this has been cultivated, that will be perfected. Thus, [it is] spread...
The laughter from the sack is but the hero’s feigned ignorance. Fudaishi’s construction of the wheel repository is the net of the eminent man.
Therefore I say: those who plan great affairs must have far-reaching schemes; those who travel long roads must have heavy baggage.
The questioner was moved to tears and offered his thanks.
Generally, those who laugh well must also weep well; those who run well must also stumble well.
For this reason, Fei Lian and E Lai both met their deaths prematurely. Han E and Qin Qing were renowned throughout the world for their skill in singing.
If this is so, then the laughter of the Monk with the Cloth Bag was not merely laughter, and the sorrow of Qu Yuan was not merely sorrow. By this, I know Maitreya.
One may preach the Dharma through laughter; the Grand Master Sanlu attained the Way through sorrow.
As for Zhong You, who died with his collar-strings tied, such death is not true death. Is the death of Fei Lian and E Lai not likewise true death?
Before the window stands a pine tree; in the sky hangs the moon. The wind stirs the reflection of the window. One who does not understand this, seeing it at night, suspects it to be a ghost.

Terrified, he lets out a cry and begs his neighbors for help. They explain to him, saying, "This is no ghost. It is simply the moon shining through the window and the wind stirring the shadow of the pine.
Why do you fear so falsely? Though the terrified man hears these words, he remains fixated on the suspicion that it is a ghost.
When dawn arrived and the sun rose, he went out to examine it for himself; he could not help but burst into laughter, only then realizing it was no ghost.
Alas! A shadow at the window: when seen at night, one immediately suspects it to be a ghost; when seen by day, one does not consider it a ghost.
A shadow is not dual; there is but one person who sees it. How could it arise and subside of its own accord?

Indeed, the ten directions, the environment and its inhabitants, and the three periods of time are like shadows within a window. Ordinary beings see them as existent; those of the Two Vehicles see them as empty;
Bodhisattvas see them as mind. Thus it is said: "If a person recognizes their own mind, the great earth is nothing."
A Square Inch of Earth.
In my youth, I knew only the faults of others and was unaware of my own. As I grew older, although I knew the faults of others, I also came to know my own.
After a long time, I knew only my own faults and was unaware of the faults of others.
Water is not clear by itself; it is people who clarify it. If people do not clarify it, the water remains clear by itself. This is analogous to how the mind is not enlightened by itself;
it is people who enlighten it. If people do not enlighten it, the mind remains enlightened by itself. Alas! Even if it is not enlightened [by others], can it be called "ignorance"?
The mind possesses four virtues: permanence, bliss, selfhood, and purity. Permanence means there is neither arising nor ceasing; bliss means there is neither like nor dislike;
selfhood means there is no governing master; and purity means defilement cannot adhere. Thus, one who attains permanence does not age even when heaven and earth perish.
To attain bliss is to transcend amidst the convergence of all sufferings. To attain the Self is to create the myriad existences while remaining without a mind.
To attain purity is to dwell within the five turbidities while remaining clear and cool. Although there are these four, do they exist apart from the mind, or do they exist as the mind itself?
Or do they exist as both distinct and identical? Once these three [distinctions] are resolved, the four virtues may be discussed.

One day, he suddenly felt his body and mind transcend the mundane. From evening until dawn, this bliss did not fade. Yet, upon encountering adverse circumstances, he was no longer in that state of transcendence;
for the illness lay in his perception. If one does not perceive pleasure, then one likewise does not perceive suffering. Alas!
If awakening is harmful to such an extent, how much more so is non-awakening?
Now, to obtain food when hungry, to obtain drink when thirsty, to obtain wealth when poor, and to obtain office when wealthy—these four things:

When one first attains it, the joy cannot be described in words; how much more so when the ignorant attain wisdom, the wise attain forgetfulness, and through forgetfulness they attain the mind—how could such bliss be described in words?

Now, among those who do not look upward for food, there are none other than slaves or servants. Therefore, if a household has ten people who look upward for food, its appearance will certainly not be destitute.
If a household has a hundred people who look upward for food, its appearance will certainly be distinguished from the masses.
As for a household with a thousand people looking upward for food, or ten thousand people looking upward for food, it is like the moon among the stars; its radiance and vastness can be known.
Alas! Generally, those who look upward for sustenance do so merely because their material wealth is sufficient;

they fail to realize that one who possesses the wealth of the Dharma can extensively save the sentient beings of ten thousand ages. Thus, the radiance of such a person is so universal that it cannot even be compared to the moon among the stars.
Viewed from this perspective, worldly wealth may provide for physical life, but it cannot provide for that which is beyond [the mundane].
Birth exists; where there is birth, there is death. Where there is death, there is exhaustion. Without birth, there is no death; without death, there is no exhaustion.
If this is so, then while the virtue of those who rely on material sustenance (birth) is subject to exhaustion, how could the grace of relying on the non-arising (non-birth) ever come to an end?

Therefore, those who look upward for food from others do so because they themselves cannot sustain their own life. Since they themselves cannot sustain their own life, how could they possibly sustain...
When humans are born, they are like oxen and horses that cannot sustain themselves; they must rely upon others before they can live.
Therefore, those who do not look upward for food are called "slaves" (*nubi*); this is to honor them, not to despise them.
Thus, when the ancients reviled those who study the mere letter of the teachings, calling them "slave-boys" (*nu'er*) and "slave-girls" (*bi-zi*), there was indeed good reason for it.
Some say: "There are differences between ordinary people, sages, and worthies, but there is no difference between the Way and sages or worthies. I, however, say:

"There is no difference between ordinary people, sages, and worthies, but there is a difference between the Way and sages or worthies. Therefore it is said: "All sages and worthies are distinguished by means of the dharma of non-action (wuwei)."
Some say: "The Way (Dharma) is discourse; it is a path. Yet they fail to realize that where there is discourse, there is sound; where there is a path, there is travel.
Sound is not the Way, and what can be traveled is not arrival. That which is neither the Way nor arrival—this is the Way that is not a way.
Or perhaps one might love painted flowers while not loving living flowers. Someone laughed at this and said, "To love the artificial and not love the real—is this not foolish?
The man replied, "Living flowers are what the Creator has transformed; painted flowers are what my own mind has created.
The Creator is but a reflection within my mind. You take that which is born from a shadow to be real, whereas I take that which is born from the mind to be so."
"It is a matter of convention. Am I not so? Are you not so? Only when there is someone who knows can a distinction be made.

Now, suppose someone contracts a disease of lust and cannot cure it; as the illness becomes critical and he is on the verge of death, even a skilled physician stands with his hands folded, unable to help.
I then asked the patient, "From where does lust arise? He replied, "Lust arises from the mind.
I asked again, "From where does the mind arise? He said, "I do not know. I said, "If you do not even know the mind, how can lust arise?
If lust does not even arise, how can illness arise? The patient was bewildered and did not respond. From evening until dawn, he remained in doubt, unable to resolve it.
When doubt is heavy, lust is light; when lust is light, the affliction diminishes. Suddenly one awakens to the mind’s lack of arising.
What we call lust and illness are like the fur of a tortoise or the horns of a hare—how could they possibly be real?
Alternatively, you may have been investigating the koan of Zhaozhou’s “The Cypress Tree in the Courtyard” for many years.

You have even claimed to yourself that you have attained some realization. One day, I questioned you: "Regarding your investigation of the koan 'The Cypress Tree in the Courtyard,' since it has no rational path, how did you attain it by claiming there is no rational path?"
I have once sought out the head and eyes within the four states of joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure to see what it truly is that can experience joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure.
Furthermore, when one is in the midst of joy, where is anger? When one is in the midst of anger, where is joy?
When one is in the midst of sorrow, where is pleasure? And when one is in the midst of pleasure, where is sorrow? Thus I have sought them morning after morning.
He sought it at evening; he sought it by day; he sought it for months; he sought it for years; he sought it for many accumulated years.
One day he found its head and face, and only then did he realize that when one is joyful, it is not another person; when angry, it is not another person; when sorrowful, it is not another person;
when happy, it is not another person—it is always I myself. Whether I am joyful, angry, sorrowful, or happy, it is I who seek it out; none of these states are anything other than me.
Although these are indeed the manifestations [of the mind] once it has been aroused, when it has not yet been aroused, where would the four—joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure—be?
If one understands this, one may speak of joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure; and if one understands joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure, only then may one speak of the state before they are aroused.
Alas! Can the state before arousal truly be spoken of? Or can it truly not be spoken of?
However, those who speak well do so by speaking through non-speaking; when speaking is non-speaking, why should it not be permissible?
Are sound and form truly obstacles to the Way, or are they truly not obstacles? Those who claim otherwise merely use their cleverness to bore through the truth.
Yet true knowledge has been lost. One fails to realize that the wind whistles through ten thousand pines and the moon illuminates a thousand peaks.
Is it sound? Is it form? Does it obstruct the Way? Or does it not obstruct the Way? Since this does not obstruct it, how could the elegant singing of a beautiful lady alone obstruct the Way?

If this is so, how could sound and form possibly obstruct the Way? It is people themselves who obstruct it. That people obstruct the Way and yet, conversely, slander [the senses]—how can they be blamed?
Sound and form—how are they different from old man Zhang drinking wine and old man Li becoming intoxicated?
The dragon delights in the abyss; the tiger delights in the forest. Although their habitats differ—one aquatic, the other terrestrial—they both delight in that which can shelter their forms.

Little do they realize that the dragon has no desire and the tiger has no malice; even if the dragon coils upon land or the tiger emerges during the day, who could possibly harm them? It is only humans...
The reason they are confined is that the dragon’s jaw contains the night-shining pearl, and the tiger is capable of devouring humans.
Some may think: "The height of heaven is due to its own height; the thickness of earth is due to its own thickness; the brilliance of the sun is due to its own brilliance;
the fullness of the moon is due to its own fullness; the light of a lamp is due to its own light. Little do they realize that these exist apart from my own mind.
In that case, Heaven would lose its lofty brilliance, and Earth would lose its vast thickness.

If this were so, then the brightness of the sun, the fullness of the moon, and the light of the lamp would all be but the colors of my own mind. Alas! If a person can understand this, may they be spoken with regarding the Way of Heaven and Earth?

Equanimity is the cause of suffering and pleasure; suffering and pleasure are the fruits of equanimity. These three feelings rely upon one another, never ceasing for a moment, like a waterwheel drawing from a well, revolving without beginning.
Suddenly there is hatred, suddenly there is love; suddenly there is love, suddenly there is hatred. When hatred and love suddenly reach their end, the appearance of equanimity manifests.
When sudden adversity or favor strikes, that appearance of equanimity is immediately lost; once lost, it gives rise to love and hatred. Therefore:
The clarity of non-feeling (*vedanā*) is like the moon shrouded by clouds; its light cannot manifest. When feeling is exhausted and the clouds clear, the original moon shines forth brilliantly.
This feeling cannot be dispelled through lack of effort, nor can it be driven away through effort. Without effort, how could feeling empty itself?
With effort, one instead provides a basis for the ground of feeling. Examining this from every angle, there is no way out logically. If this is so—

If this is so, then is it not the case that receiving [the teachings] can never be in vain? If receiving them cannot be in vain, then sentient beings would be cut off from the ladder to Buddhahood, and the Buddhas would block the path for saving beings.
This would result in the dual affliction of both the holy and the mundane; what benefit would there be in studying the Buddha?
The Way of Heaven commiserates the negligent; the Way of Man prizes the meticulous. The negligent, in relation to others, do not compete; in relation to time, they lose advantage.
The meticulous, in relation to others, excel in competition; in relation to time, they gain much advantage.

Those who compete and gain much advantage may indeed achieve victory in the present moment, yet this is not necessarily beneficial for what lies beyond. Conversely, those who do not compete and thus fail to gain advantage...
Although one may suffer defeat before one's eyes, it is not necessarily without benefit for the life hereafter. Furthermore, since man does not prevail over Heaven, how could defeat ever be constant?

Ordinary worldlings, at the outset, have no vision of the Truth. Regarding various adversities and favors, hatred and love, and impermanence—whether that which I hate is loved by others, or that which I love is hated by others—all of these are delusions.

Yet, to abandon delusion in search of truth, or to leave the waves in search of water, has never been possible. Therefore it is said: "Delusion and enlightenment, truth and falsehood, are like the bending of an arm."
Extension. Originally, there is neither front nor back. For one who awakens, the delusory is itself the real; for one who is deluded, the real is itself the delusory.
Thus, that which can bend and extend is the arm; that which can be real and can be delusory is the mind.
Therefore, know that the arm cannot be confused by bending and extending, and one who has realized the mind cannot be constrained by delusion and awakening.
If one views all objects of desire as perilous precipices, then the causes of defilement become the resources for purity.
If one does not give rise to longing or admiration for sublime objects, then the causes of purity become the openings for defilement. Therefore it is said: "Objects are neither defiled nor pure;
only for those who are diligent do they become objects of contemplation wherever they encounter them."

Without earth, water has no means to float; without earth, water has no means to support. One may quietly ponder the contributions of these two, yet in the end, one cannot reach a definitive resolution.
Only one who can reach such a resolution may be considered a teacher.
The world knows that wealth and honor and poverty and lowliness exist and are not non-existent. Yet, regarding heaven and hell, some resolutely claim they do not exist.
Little do they realize that since wealth, honor, poverty, and lowliness both exist and are not non-existent, why should heaven and hell alone be non-existent and not present?
By nature, I am stern and narrow-minded. If someone rarely opposes me, I become abruptly displeased; yet, once the matter has passed, I forget it immediately. Alas!
Though I may forget it, how can those who have been offended by me ever forget it? If this is so, then...
"I have forgotten it, but others have not. It is not yet forgotten. One must forget both self and others before one truly forgets.

Now, those who see what follows but do not see what precedes cannot be spoken to regarding spring; those who see what is below but do not see what is above cannot be spoken to regarding the sovereign.
Thus, oxen and horses know their herder but do not know their master; fish and birds know spring."
Yet they do not realize it is winter. They fail to understand that were it not for winter, how could there be spring? Were it not for the master, how could there be the herdsman?
It is simply that they do not reflect. Therefore, reflect upon it, reflect upon it; then even ghosts and spirits will communicate with you, let alone the master and winter.
Alas! A person who does not reflect is no more than a head of cattle or a horse.
Indeed, all phenomena are the mind. Because one has not yet awakened to the fundamental mind, phenomena are able to obstruct me;
but if one awakens to the fundamental mind, I am able to transform phenomena. Therefore, the sage condenses ten thousand kalpas into a single instant and extends a single moment into a thousand ages.
He disperses a single phenomenon into myriad phenomena, like a sliver of the moon in the sky whose reflection appears upon ten thousand waters. He rolls up the myriad phenomena...
It is a single entity, like a reflection dispersed across a hundred rivers, all encompassed by the single moon. This is not produced by supernatural power;
it is simply the nature of my own being.
One who does not eat sugar does not know sweetness; one who does not eat vinegar does not know sourness. If this is so even for sweetness and sourness, how much more so for the Great Way?
Indeed, when the single mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault. When people and things converge, they are fundamentally vast and empty. If it is thus—
This is because the myriad fragrances are not color, and the overflowing abundance is not sound. Therefore it is said: "Sorrow and joy arise from one another;
though one looks at them with wide-open eyes, they cannot be seen; though one listens with a tilted ear, they cannot be heard."

The character "Patience" (Ren) constitutes its meaning. By piercing the heart with a blade, it causes those who understand the characters to know that at the moment of encountering any matter, thoughts must not be allowed to arise lightly.
If a thought arises that is not in accord with principle, one should immediately draw the sword of wisdom to pierce it.
Thus, evil thoughts are extinguished and the virtuous mind grows. When goodness is pure and transformative, one is close to the Way.
Patience is such; how could one not be on guard?
I asked the Prince, saying: "Zhong You rejoiced upon hearing his own faults, and his good reputation has been inexhaustible.

Why is this so? He replied: "It is because only one whose mind is empty can receive what is good. Although Heaven and Earth are vast, it is emptiness that can encompass them. Emptiness is enduring; thus, it is only fitting that his good reputation should be inexhaustible."
Good and evil are impermanent; love and hatred have no fixed abode. Therefore, the common people may aspire to be worthy sages, and worthy sages may aspire to be holy ones.
Joy can become anger, and anger can become joy. If these four were constant, then the teachings established by the sages would only increase the ignorance of the world.
That which encloses the five viscera is the physical frame. That which presides over the entire body is one’s own mind.

While the physical frame can be seen and the five viscera can be known, as for one’s own mind—not only do others fail to know it, even knowing one’s own mind is like using one’s own eyes to look at one’s own eyes.
Thus, when there is a slight movement of cognition, the object immediately gives rise to the mind. Suppose there is a person here:
He summoned the masses of the ignorant and incited them to rebellion. In his suppression of the rebels, he relied not on sincerity but on deception.
Not only was the rebellion impossible to suppress, but it was from this point that the world began to lose its trust in the ruler’s word.
I have never seen a person of such great ignorance as this. It is like a thousand-foot layer of ice that, upon being warmed for a single day, immediately melts into a vast, unfathomable expanse.
If a person considers their bones base and their spirit dull, they will not dare to aspire to the Great Way.
Yet they do not realize that scaly creatures can become dragons and feathered creatures can become phoenixes. Goodness and evil are not fixed; clarity and turbidity have no master.

If one exerts oneself in goodness without ceasing, one approaches one's true nature. To approach it is to be in accord; to be in accord is to undergo transformation; to undergo transformation is to become empty; to become empty is to become numinous.
Now, as for that which is empty yet spiritual: is it sought within the mind, or is it sought outside the mind? If it is sought within the mind, then the handle is in one’s own hands;

it is clear that it does not belong to the Creator. If this is so, then how could there be any fixed constancy regarding the nobility or meanness of one’s bones, or the clarity or turbidity of one’s vital energy (*qi*)?
It depends entirely upon what one has cultivated. Therefore it is said: "Natures are nearly alike; it is practice that makes them different."
This is because they are distant from it. It must be that their bones are base and their qi is turbid, rendering them incapable of becoming sages; these are those who abandon themselves.
Having already abandoned themselves, even if they were to spend their entire lives in the company of sages, they could not be perfumed by them—how much less so by those who are inferior?
Human beings are the most spiritual among all things. Even a child five feet tall can learn and speak;
yet, when it comes to identifying what this so-called "spirituality" actually is, even great scholars and aged monks have never failed to be confused and mistaken. Therefore, it is said:
In every matter, the ordinary is never at fault; yet upon meeting, as soon as it is raised, confusion arises. Tell me, where does the root of this ailment lie?
For thirty years I have been speaking to break it open for you.
Heaven created the sun and moon, not to illuminate for those who would burrow and climb over walls; Earth provided the rivers and lakes, not to create obstacles for carriages and horses.
Yet, the traveler’s aversion to danger and the thief’s aversion to light are no less than the enmity between the states of Wu and Yue.
If Heaven were to abolish the sun and moon, and Earth were to block the rivers and lakes, then both would have no cause for regret. Alas!
If Heaven abolished the sun and moon, the myriad living beings would lose their sight; if Earth blocked the rivers and lakes, the ten thousand things would wither in heart.
Therefore, Heaven does not abolish the sun and moon because of the wickedness of thieves, nor does Earth block the rivers and lakes because of the treacherous nature of travelers. Zhong...
The Ni did not avoid the matter of right and wrong because she was moved by the illness of Huan Tui’s worthiness.
Someone said, "Your Way cannot be practiced simply because there are so many who slander it. He replied, "That my Way cannot be practiced is not the fault of those who slander me;
the fault lies in my own lack of sincerity in cultivating the Way. If one were sincere, one would move all things."

It must indeed be vast. Nevertheless, in the past there were those who awakened to the Way upon hearing the sound of someone begging for meat, and who recognized their original mind upon seeing peach blossoms.
Were these a dead pig or an insentient tree more wise than I?

To possess even a slight awareness is the beginning of destruction. To be vast and empty of self—who knows it when it is destroyed? To know through non-knowing is not to be oblivious to right and wrong.
Is this something that can be destroyed? Or is it something that cannot be destroyed?
Someone asked: "When Master Rong of Niutou had not yet met the Fourth Patriarch, the hundred birds brought flowers and celestial beings presented offerings.
After he had seen him, the flowers and birds did not come and the sounds of the celestial beings ceased. Why was this? He replied: "Ghosts and spirits revere virtue but do not understand the Way.
If they understood the Way, who would not be a sage? How then could there be a distinction between flowers and birds, and celestial beings?"
Now, as for the principle of Heaven (*tianli*) and human desire (*yuyu*), are they like a speck of dust and the great earth? Are they truly one, or are they truly two?
If they were one, then all people would be sages. If they were not one, then the sages’ establishment of the teachings would be of no benefit.
Therefore, we know that when ice is water, the ice does not exist; and when water is ice, the water does not exist.
Furthermore, if water does not exist as a separate entity, then principle does not obstruct phenomena; if ice does not exist as a separate entity, then phenomena do not obstruct principle.
When phenomena do not obstruct principle, one traverses the ten realms while remaining eternally quiescent. When principle does not obstruct phenomena, knowledge encompasses all things without toil.
Being without toil, there is no teaching that is not imparted; being eternally quiescent, there is no Way that is not unified. That the Way is without non-uniformity is like...
Flowers bloom in spring; the Teaching is without that which it does not bestow. It is like spring being present within the flowers.
Are they one? Or are they two? Someone may say: "Blessed is he who walks in the right path; calamity befalls him who follows the perverse. Is this so? Alas!

If it were not so, then the sun and moon could be made to fall, and the rivers and seas could be made to wither. Yet today, the sun and moon remain in the heavens, and the rivers and seas remain as they are.
Is this so? Or is it not so? In the past, there were those who pointed to a deer and called it a horse, or identified a tortoise as a soft-shelled turtle; the world condemned such acts as unjust.
Today, however, people point to a deer and call it a qilin, and identify a tortoise as a dragon; the whole world acquiesces to this. How lamentable!
Now, when the wind drives the clouds or water turns stones, how is it that they possess power despite being without intention?
When emotions cloud one's nature and habitual practice deludes one's knowledge, it is likewise as if there is nothing acting upon them, yet they act. Is this intentional, or is it unintentional?
Why is their power so resistant that it cannot be restrained?
The yang-sui (sun-focusing mirror) takes fire; the fang-zhu (moon-focusing vessel) takes water. Thus, when facing the moon, water pours forth; when facing the sun, fire ignites.
Now, as for water and fire, do they truly arise from the sun and moon? Do they truly arise from the fang-zhu and yang-sui? Or do they truly arise from the concave basins?
If they arise from the sun and moon, then why does water not pour forth and fire not ignite from the fang-zhu and yang-sui? If...
When fire is produced from various flint-sticks, why does it not ignite unless directed toward the sun or moon? To understand this is to be able to discourse on spiritual transformation (*shenhua*).
Among all things with form, none is greater than heaven and earth; among all things without form, none is greater than—
The Great Void encompasses all that exists and does not exist, yet nothing is greater than one's own mind. One's own mind is like the light of a mirror;
both [the world and its phenomena] are reflections within that light. Therefore, for one who perceives the light, reflections leave no obstruction; but for one who clings to the reflections...

Then the fundamental light is perpetually lost. When the fundamental light is perpetually lost, the function of light is not manifested. When the function of light is not manifested, the grasping at shadows does not dissolve.
How could there be one who perceives light within the shadow? To such a person, how can one speak of the light of one's own mind?
Now, the physical form is the shadow of the mind, and the shadow is the reflection of the form. Suppose there were a person here who, seeking to depict a shadow, desired it to be true;
yet they would fail to realize that even if it were truly depicted, it would still be but a shadow. How could that which gives rise to the physical form ever be depicted with brush and ink?
Someone said: "What thing is not the mind? It is only because of discrimination that the mind becomes things. If one simply does not discriminate, every single thing is the mind.
Therefore, a horse looks at its own reflection and is not startled; a fox sees its companion and does not doubt. This is because there is originally no dualistic perception."

Fire is visible; this is fire as a phenomenal characteristic (*lakṣaṇāgni*), not fire as an essential nature (*dharmatāgni*). If it were fire as an essential nature, it would be omnipresent and thus invisible.
Therefore, that which is seen when fuel is transmitted and not seen when it is not transmitted is fire as a phenomenal characteristic, not fire as an essential nature. Now, as for what is said:
The nature of water is moisture; the nature of fire is heat. This is merely using their inherent natures as metaphors for the meaning.
To observe a person with the eyes of the world is insufficient to fully comprehend that person. Why is this so?
Beings in the hells perceive the sixteen-foot golden body [of a Buddha] as being like the leg of a black elephant. If even the Buddha appears thus to them, how much more so will others?
If there is a self, then I am within heaven and earth; if there is no self, then heaven and earth are within me.

Consider, for instance, the bodies of each person present here: ultimately, by what cause do they exist? If one investigates their origin, before the emotions of the parents have moved, the red and white essences would certainly not flow;
what body could then exist? Once the parents' emotions have moved, the four great elements follow that stimulus.
Birth: The essence is not material form; it resembles form yet is not form. This non-material form grows spontaneously, and thus this body comes to be.
Observing it from this perspective, the cause is the movement of the parents' passions, and the condition is the union of the two—red and white.
When one exhaustively examines the causes and conditions of the body, they do not exceed these. As for the cause of the mind, however, it resides within oneself and not in the father.
Mother: Although my parents have united, if I were devoid of aversion and attachment, why would they have intentionally cast me into their womb?
Inferring from this, it follows that the mind arises because of an object; thus, the object is the cause for the arising of the mind, and the reception of the vital energy is likewise a condition.

The power of the mind is unfathomable. To test it by seeking fame and achievement is to test it through existence. Next, to test it by forgetting both body and mind is to test it through non-existence.
Only when one can remain unswayed while testing both existence and non-existence does one become able to wondrously transform all things and attain spiritual transcendence.

Therefore it is said: "Those who are capable of being heroes but have not yet reached the level of sages and worthies, do so because they cling firmly to the 'mind with form' (sacitta); thus their undertakings succeed."
Indeed, it is only those who are heroes capable of becoming sages and worthies who can master both existence and non-existence. Alas!
If even the master of existence is difficult to establish, how much more so the master of non-existence? As an ancient said: "The two dharmas of existence and non-existence encompass all phenomena."
It is not that they exist independently of the primordial state of being and non-being, yet they employ both being and non-being—how could one possibly express this?
A pure vase with a few scattered blossoms, petals falling from the fading red of the unarisen; a dot of rouge upon the surface of the water—this too is the path of deep spring.
Apart from the mind alone, there is not a single dharma that exists; it is impossible for there to be a dharma separate from the mind.
If one knows this, then whether living in a golden palace or dying in the mud, using a coarse mat as a coffin—what difference is there from Mount Li? Mount Li was the site of the Qin Emperor’s tomb.
To carve stone ten thousand *zhang* deep—its bones nearly reaching the heavens—may indeed be called a profound burial. Yet, with such a deep and secluded tomb, one may be plundered to enrich others.
Viewed from this perspective, who among us would value being entombed in a Qin-style coffin smeared with mud? Therefore, the man of great attainment forgets his life even before he dies.
Before birth, one forgets death; planting trees in the void, how could spring have a limit? Flowers bloom and fruits form; the fruit occupies the great earth.

If "non-birth" (wu-sheng) can be known, is it known by means of knowing? If one knows non-birth through knowing, then there is knowing; if one knows non-birth through not-knowing, then there is no knowing.

If one knows non-birth by having knowledge, then since birth already exists, how can one know non-birth? If one knows non-birth through not-knowing, yet it is called "not-knowing," who is it that knows non-birth?
If one knows that there is no birth, it is still the same as having knowledge;
if birth has nothing upon which to stand, one is called a "walking corpse. If death has something to carry, one is called a "debt-demon."
The earth element is composed of four gross particles (*mahābhūta*); water consists of three; fire, two; and wind, one. Therefore, that which has more particles is substantial and heavy;
that which is substantial and heavy has weak power. Only the mind is devoid of even a single particle; thus, its power is inconceivable.
"Particles" refers to visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility.
Among the parts of a single body, nothing is more intimate than the skin; therefore, when a needle pierces the skin, one feels a piercing pain that is difficult to restrain.
Yet the intimacy of the skin does not equal that of the flesh; the intimacy of the flesh does not equal that of the bone; the intimacy of the bone does not equal that of the marrow;
and the intimacy of the marrow does not equal that of the heart. Hence it is said: "When the mind arises, seeds are planted."
The various dharmas arise from this. Today in the world, people do not regard only those who are kin as kin; on the contrary, they regard those who are not kin as kin.
Consequently, those who truly practice kinship will ultimately find no kin at all. Alas! The mind creates heaven; the mind creates hell.
The mind creates sages; the mind creates the multitude. As for the vastness of heaven and earth and the breadth of the myriad things, all are the fabrications of the mind.
Yet those in the world who are renowned as intelligent and wise, if asked from where their bodies and minds originate, none know how to explain it.
If one does not feel sorrow over this, what else is there to be sorrowful about?
Now, joy and anger are without constancy, much like shifting earth with a board or trowel; yet human sentiments are stubbornly persistent, falsely entangling themselves in grief and joy.

Thus, those who were as bitter enemies as the states of Wu and Yue may become as affectionate as husband and wife through a single word of accord, while those who have been as close as family may turn their backs on kindness and forget righteousness over a single matter of discord.
Throughout the vast expanse of past and present, people are generally deluded by this. Only those who possess the Way truly understand joy.
One may cause another to be angry, and one may cause that anger to turn into joy; both are impermanent and should be viewed as identical to reflections in a mirror.
Therefore, though likes and dislikes alternate before one, the mind remains ever at ease.

When not a single thought arises, solitary luminosity shines forth in perfect clarity. Yet, when the six sense-objects act as overgrown weeds and thickets, the original wondrous nature loses its true essence.

Consequently, the waves of emotion become vast and surging, and the fires of karma burn fiercely; the decaying dwellings of the three realms are all subjected to burning and drowning. Only those who penetrate and perceive their own minds can escape this.

Cognition does not arise in isolation; it must depend upon objects to emerge. Objects cannot exist independently; they must rely upon cognition to manifest. Upon repeated investigation and inquiry, one finds that both are quiescent and extinguished in their very place.

Thus, when the divine pearl is held in the palm, its light does not come from without. To realize phenomena is to eliminate the notion of a "true" self, yet this does not involve the conceptualization of active functioning.
The Forty-Eight Vows: These are the vows made by the Tathāgata Amitābha when he was the Bhikṣu Dharmākara, in the presence of Lokeśvararāja Buddha.
If one were to attempt to fathom them with the conceptualizing mind of sentient beings, even a single vow would be difficult to bear, let alone all forty-eight.
Yet, if one examines them through the lens of ultimate principle, they are like empty space.

The boundlessness [of space], the height and thickness of heaven and earth, the vastness and multiplicity of the myriad things, the sage and the commoner, those with knowledge and those without knowledge—all do not transcend my own mind.
Therefore it is said: "Emptiness arises within Great Awakening, like a single bubble emerging from the ocean.
The minute dust-motes of worlds with outflows all depend on emptiness for their birth. When the bubble ceases, emptiness is fundamentally non-existent; how much more so [the worlds]?"

Regarding all those within the three realms of existence, when viewed through this lens, the vows issued by the Dharma-treasury and the words of the Tathāgata’s certification—whether verified through principle or applied to phenomena—are as clear as the sun and stars;
what further cause for doubt could there be? Furthermore, the habitual customs of sentient beings are vulgar and base, and their consciousness is not lofty or brilliant;
they recklessly conceive of the six-foot physical frame as the "self" and the heart within the square inch of the chest as...

The mind—whether noble or base, wise or foolish, in honor or disgrace, in favor or adversity—exhausts its spiritual power and depletes its deliberations, manifesting ten thousand forms from birth until death without a moment’s rest; it is simply that one has not yet been able to pierce through this body and this mind.
Therefore, the Greatly Awakened Sage, out of compassion for them, gave rise to a vast vow to illuminate [the truth].
Expand the mind and its objects so that all sentient beings may open wide the eye of clear wisdom and attain the body that is no-body and the mind that is no-mind.
When there is no body, great affliction ceases forever; when there is no mind, toil and exertion are suddenly emptied. Thus it is said: "Nothing is as great a calamity as having a body;
nothing precedes toil and exertion more than having intelligence. Such being the case, the body that is no-body has a form that fills [the universe].

The eight extremities are the mind that is no-mind; it illuminates all things to their ultimate depths. Humans are the most spiritual among all beings, yet regarding this vast body and expansive mind, they remain in profound ignorance.
Confined to their fetid physical shells, they fall into the dream of deluded thoughts, failing to realize it even for a hair’s breadth.
On the contrary, they are astonished by the Bhikṣu Dharmakara—truly are they not enlightened? How could they be so?
Daguan had not yet seen the tree when he dreamed of the wisteria; Zhuang Zhou knew himself as a man when he transformed into a butterfly.

Yet the wisteria has no consciousness, whereas the butterfly possesses consciousness. To have no consciousness is to be without emotion; to possess consciousness is to possess discernment. To be without emotion is necessarily to be without feeling; to possess discernment is necessarily to have causes.
Entering a dream without feeling, and being conditioned by one another through discernment—one does so because of this dream, and the other likewise.
Regarding dreams: although there is no difference between one dream and another, their origins are not the same. Only one who knows the origin can fully understand the dream.
Now, the Way within man is like space within a valley. As for the valley, a thousand calls elicit a thousand responses, and ten thousand calls elicit ten thousand echoes;
this is because space exists therein. Man is the most spiritual among all things; yet if he is provoked by evil words, he immediately becomes agitated.
Yet, when one is angry, if they are encouraged with pleasant words, they will immediately become joyful. A thousand provocations bring a thousand angers;
ten thousand encouragements bring ten thousand joys. Now provoked, there is immediate anger; long ago encouraged, there was joy from long ago.
Viewed from this perspective, it is not that the valley can respond to every thousand calls or the void can echo every ten thousand cries. To know this is to understand anger.

Anger and joy, joy and joy; now and now, ancient and ancient. It is not that there are no subtle joys, angers,nows, or ancients, but rather that there exists one who cannot be burdened by these joys, angers, nows, and ancients.
If such a person exists, then when they encounter whatever may come, their response will be inexhaustible.
Master Moguang often said that when sitting in meditation in the Hall of Stillness, his mind was so vast and empty it might serve as a metaphor for the great void.

Yet, as soon as he heard a sound, a thought would suddenly flash through his mind, and he felt his heart become slightly constricted; thus, the measure of the great void no longer remained. For this reason:
What is attained within stillness is difficult to apply to the world; if one applies it to the world, one loses it.

Therefore, it is said that it cannot be sought within stillness, nor can it be sought within movement. It is appropriate to transcend both movement and stillness, yet not abandon their functional utility.

It is further said: "Movement and function operate within a single void; stillness and silence pervade the realm of myriad transformations. Although one may understand this through intellectual realization, it is not easy for those who have not yet attained its practice to reach such a state.
To love life and hate death is common to all things, both human and non-human, for their cognitive awareness is equal.
Since this equality of awareness ultimately leads one to attain sagehood, it is said that those with a mind can all become sages. Refraining from killing is not out of fear of retribution;

it is simply that one does not dare to eat the flesh of a sage. If tigers and wolves knew this, would they ever again harm living beings? Humans are the most spiritually gifted, yet they are addicted to killing.
It does not stop there. Such a person is no different from a tiger or a wolf.
Can light destroy darkness? Can darkness obscure light? Light can indeed destroy darkness, yet in doing so, the light itself is destroyed.
Darkness can obscure light; yet darkness obscures itself. Why is this? If light were not darkness, its function would not remain;

if darkness were not light, its power would not be established. Therefore it is said: within light there is darkness, yet it does not encounter darkness; within darkness there is light, yet it does not behold light.
Does the thought-fruit have arising? Does the thought-fruit lack arising? If it has arising, then arising does not give rise to arising.
If it lacks arising, then non-arising does not give rise to non-arising. If this is so, then a single, subtle thought-moment is indeed the ladder to non-arising.
Generally speaking, as for adversities: when alive, they do not exceed slander and verbal abuse; when dead, they do not exceed mutual killing and execution.

If one can contemplate that the body does not truly exist and view the mind as an illusion, then what harm can slander and abuse cause, or what benefit can killing and execution add? Therefore it is said:
"If a true practitioner of the Way does not perceive the faults of the world, the single mind will not arise, and the myriad dharmas will be without blame.
These were the words of the Third Patriarch. Even those who have "cast off their white robes" and "driven away the crows" [monastics] are generally able to speak of this;
yet, as for the non-arising of the single mind, even venerable elders with thick eyebrows may find it difficult to attain, let alone those below them.
Master Zibo was unable to treat waking and dreaming as one and the same; thus, when his eyes opened he was awake, and when his eyes closed he was dreaming.

Waking and dreaming rushed past each other without a moment’s rest. At times, even within a dream, he would investigate the state of being awake; at other times, even while awake, [he would fall into a dream].
One investigates the objects within a dream. Although the waking state and the dream state differ, the objects do not transcend the categories of adverse or favorable.

Pushing this investigation further and further, as days turn into years, suddenly both waking and dreaming are found to be empty. Then, the one who is able to wake and the one who is able to dream laughs merrily and mocks Master Zibo, saying:
"When you open your eyes, you search for me; when you close your eyes, you search for me. You search..."
"I have finally found you! You are like a rat trying to enter a cow's horn. Now that I have leaped out of the cage of waking and dreaming, how can you possibly deal with me again?

Master Zibo, enraged, shouted, "Even if you were to hide your roots beyond the realm of waking and dreaming, it would still be boasting of a dream within a dream. Thereupon, he did not answer and fled. Now tell me—how about that?
"Where has he fled to? An ancient worthy said, "A shrimp cannot leap out of its basket.
Indeed, that which has already passed is like a dream within one's waking state. Is it truly existent? Is it truly non-existent?
If it exists, then even the wondrous power of the Creator could not cause it to manifest immediately. If it does not exist, one still calculates upon it.
If one cannot forget, then even the most foolish person will not forget a beating received yesterday; only those who possess the Way can forget it.
As for rhubarb and ginseng—the spring and autumn among medicines—there is not even a peddler or a kitchen wife who does not understand them clearly.

It is like a case of illness where one has committed an offense regarding food: although the *dahuang* (rhubarb) is bitter, one must certainly take it because its bitterness can purge accumulated toxins.
Now, suppose there is a person here who uses harsh words and perilous schemes to subject me to various forms of entrapment;
if I can accept these with equanimity, the accumulation of my narrow-minded habits will dissolve daily without my even realizing it. If this is so, then it is like *dahuang*.
It is not necessarily a land other than that of human beings.
Take thought as the eye; it perceives the beginning and end of the body.
Hearing is the beginning of thought, and thought is the end of hearing. Thought is the beginning of cultivation, and cultivation is the end of thought.
Cultivation is the beginning of realization; realization is the end of cultivation. Realization is the beginning of liberation; liberation is the end of realization.
Like a revolving wheel, may the King’s vows be inexhaustible. Like a great white ox pulling the chariot of the Supreme Vehicle, how could its transport ever come to an end?
Those who prize beauty do not know there is profit; those who prize profit do not know there is fame;

those who prize fame do not know there is the body; those who prize the body do not know there is the mind; those who prize the mind do not know there is nature; those who prize nature do not know the nature of no-nature.
Speaking from this perspective, for a snake to become a dragon, or for an ordinary person to become a sage, it is simply a matter of what one prizes. Therefore:
"Still further," means that one may communicate through emotion, yet cling to it through principle. Only that which has nothing to which it clings is called "Perfect Enlightenment.
Once it is perfect and enlightened, what more could be added? Therefore it is said: within the Tathāgatagarbha, consciousness is not permitted.
If there is consciousness, the Garbha is destroyed; once destroyed, there is leakage—leaking into the Lesser Vehicle, leaking into external paths, or even leaking into the hells.
All these begin with consciousness.
When the eyes close, one immediately dreams; while dreaming, one seeks awakening, believing that one has already awakened. Thus, all people and environments appear before one without exception.

Little do they realize that what they call being awake while awake is still within a dream. Only upon suddenly attaining great awakening does one finally know that the state of being awake within a dream was never truly awake from the beginning.
If this is so, then dreams arise from the mind; where there is no mind, there are no dreams. Awakening arises because of dreaming.
There is no dreaming and no waking. By this, I know that even a slight movement of consciousness is never without its object;
yet when the mind is vast and empty, there is no object that is not the mind. Dreaming and waking, mind and object—they are like water washing water, or gold striking gold.
To loathe the dream and seek the waking state, or to suffer the waking and seek emptiness—this is what is called "seizing the hair and rushing to the yamen. Who [is it]?

He acts as the master of the discourse on litigation. "Wisdom" (智) and "Advancement" (進) constitute his full name; the other perfections are all titles. First one uses concentration to move [the afflictions], and subsequently one uses wisdom to uproot them.

This is because the mountain of afflictions is firm and solid—without the power of concentration, it is insufficient to shake it; the roots of ignorance are deep—without the light of wisdom, it is insufficient [to eradicate them].
This serves to illuminate their lack of a fundamental basis and penetrate their lack of substantiality.

When Zhou Chu set his will upon slaying the dragon, he did not perceive that the water could drown him; when Li Guang set his will upon shooting the tiger, he did not perceive that the rock was solid.
When Shangqiu Kai believed in the benefit and had no doubt regarding the harm, he entered and emerged from fire without fear.
One sees that fire can burn; likewise, when falling from a height, one does not see that the height itself is dangerous.

It is for this reason that I know water is fundamentally not what drowns, stone is fundamentally not what is hard, fire is fundamentally not what burns, and height is fundamentally not what is perilous.
Yet, some fear drowning and dare not enter the water; they fear hardness and dare not shoot at stones; they fear heat and dare not approach the fire; and they fear danger and—
Those who dare not fall are all those who have submerged themselves, hardened themselves, burned themselves, and endangered themselves. Alas!
