To know this is to be able to enter and exit the realms of life and death, fortune and misfortune, without harm.
Generally, any bodhisattva who wishes to attain Buddhahood must take the Four Great Vows as their fundamental discourse.
To practice while abandoning these is the way of the Lesser Vehicle. Someone may doubt this, saying: "Whether afflictions are severed or not depends solely upon myself;

however, sentient beings are infinite and the Dharma gates are immeasurable. Since one's power has strengths and weaknesses, and realization varies between the ignorant and the wise, how can these [vows] possibly encompass them all?"
Is it not so? It is simply that people lack a constant mind. If the mind were truly able to remain constant, then even the kalpa-stone could be worn away and the vast ocean could be exhausted;
how much more so for other things! Furthermore, as long as afflictions (*kleśa*) are not severed, the wind of wisdom will not blow strongly;

if one’s learning does not reach its full extent, the thunder of the Dharma will not resound far. Thus, in the *I Ching*, the hexagram "Constancy" (*Heng*) is composed of thunder and wind—*leifeng heng*. This is because there is nothing like thunder to startle the ignorant.

Hibernation: Without wind, there would be no way to stir the myriad things. Now that the dark hibernation has awakened, it is able to stir them once more; if this were not constant, what else could it be?
If one is not constant, even sorcerers and physicians cannot act; how then could they engage in purposeful activity?
Zhuang Zhou held that among fish, none is greater than the Kun or the Jing; among birds, none is greater than the Peng;
and among men, none is more colossal than those of the Land of Longbo. These three are considered the greatest of all sentient beings in the world.

Yet they fail to realize that even the Bodhisattva Yingchi harbored doubts because he could not see the Buddha’s crown—doubts that arose from searching upward through the ten directions to their very limit.
Even if [the Buddha] were to expand himself to the size of thirty-two Ganges-sands of worlds, the crown of his head would remain as it was before.
If this is so, then what the Zhou dynasty called the Kun, Peng, and the Lord of Longbo are no different from the *jiaoming* insects or ants.

Yet some do not believe my words because they consider them too vast and grand; now, let me substantiate them. For smallness and greatness arise from having something upon which to depend; that which depends on others arises...

Regarding the existence of the mind: just as when the single mind does not arise, both object and self are transformed together; even that which is sought without dependence cannot be found, let alone that which depends on conditions.

People, driven by the needs of their mouths and bellies, use money as a net to exhaust the flavors of the tongue-root and bind themselves in cycles of retributive resentment. Thus, [it leads to] suffering.

When the Prince was about to die, he still greedily craved the bear’s paw; in the end, he had no leisure even to eat it before he was assassinated. Alas! If this was so for a son toward his father, how much more so for those who are preyed upon?
The human mind is impermanent, just like water; it conforms to the shape of its vessel and has no fixed essence from the start.

When encountering an object of desire, the mind becomes greedy; when encountering an undesirable object, the mind becomes angry; and when encountering an object that is both desirable and undesirable...

Hesitation and indecision give rise to delusion in the mind; thus, at the very moment of delusion, greed and hatred have no ground to stand upon, and at the very moment of hatred, delusion and greed have no source.
If objects do not touch the mind and the mind does not stain the objects, then these three—greed, hatred, and delusion—converge to become the constant light.
Nevertheless, this convergence is not in vain; for if one has not yet realized that both mind and objects are [empty],...
The mind is like the eye that cannot see itself, or the hand that cannot grasp itself; how could its realization be easy?

When ordinary men and women do not understand the principles governing life and death, the hidden and the manifest, they become filled with resentment whenever they encounter such matters, believing that once dead, one never returns to life.
How many are there who thus willingly accept an untimely death? Little do they realize that death is indeed... [the fruit].
If one were not to be born again, then the diligent efforts of sages and worthies toward doing good would be no better than the common wisdom of ordinary men and women.
Sages and worthies know that birth must be followed by death, yet they are not burdened by life; they know that death must be followed by birth, yet they are not deluded by death.
This is why they practice goodness without weariness. If, however, death were truly final and there were no rebirth, then the deeds of Jie and Zhou [the tyrants] would be justified.

Who could possibly take the place of him in repaying such debts and responsibilities? From this we know that Yao and Shun’s practice of goodness was certainly not mistaken, while Jie and Zhou’s practice of evil was surely due to great folly.
Judging from this, when even ordinary men and women find themselves unable to endure certain conditions and die with a willing heart, it is the lingering influence of Jie and Zhou.
Someone asked the Leather Ball Master, "Is form itself emptiness? The Leather Ball Master replied, "What do you call 'form'?

Is it the great heaven and earth, or is it the myriad things? If you take heaven and earth to be form, then outside of heaven and earth, neither the *parikalpita* (imagined) nor the *paratantra* (dependent) exist.
If you take the myriad things to be form, then outside of heaven and earth, where would the myriad things reside?"
How could it be attained? Now, as for "universal imagination" (*parikalpa*), it refers to the arbitrary conceptualization of form where there is no place for form.
When the conceptualization of form is dissolved into emptiness, one then arbitrarily conceptualizes the shadow of form. Yet, one does not realize that external form is itself empty.

Once the conceptualization of form has been dissolved, to again conceptualize the shadow of form—how is this any different from the original conceptualization of form? Generally, sentient beings do not understand their own minds. The mind...

Regarding external phenomena, one may give rise to the view of form (*rūpa-dṛṣṭi*) or the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*). Emptiness and form are impermanent; according to what one perceives, one makes calculations.
For example, ice and water are originally not two separate things, yet suddenly they become ice, and suddenly they become water.

Amidst this sudden impermanence, the multitude calculates that ice is solid obstruction and calculates that water is fluid penetration. Those who calculate it to be solid obstruction are fundamentally deluded.
This is the very root. Those who calculate based on "interfusion" (yōtsū) likewise lose sight of its branches. For fusion has no inherent nature;

it receives its designation only in dependence upon substantial obstruction (shitsugai). Substantial obstruction likewise has no inherent nature; it establishes its name only in dependence upon fusion. Now, names are merely guests; they are not the reality.
Today, the world venerates the guest and loses the reality, regarding it as clumsy to seek emptiness apart from form, while [failing to realize that] one clarifies [emptiness] through form itself.
Emptiness is skillful; clumsiness is clumsy, and skillfulness is skillful. Sentient calculations arise recklessly, forming ten thousand kinds of nests.

What is seen and heard takes up residence therein, like cotton clinging to thorns or glue being poured onto lacquer. From beginningless time until this very moment, they do not seek entry by transcending emotion, but only follow emotion to inquire about the Way.
Thus, the Way transforms into emotion; therefore it is said: "Emptiness and form are like children, and emotion is their mother."
The Mother said again: "Sentiment is the mother of transformation. She said further: "Sentiment is the mother of existence and non-existence. You ask with sentiment; I answer with sentiment.
This is because I respond to sentiment with sentiment; the sentiment resides in you, not in me. If you were to forget sentiment, only then would you know that I did not answer you with sentiment.
As long as you have not forgotten sentiment, even though I transcend sentiment to respond to you, you [still perceive it as such].
This refers to the "sentiment" (qíng). If you understand this, then the principle that form is identical to emptiness resides in you and not in me.
Piquiuzi said:
"That which is most manifest yet invisible is sentiment. Therefore, those who possess deep feelings and profound countenances..."
Father and son cannot fathom one another; that which is most hidden yet not difficult to see is the nature (*xing*).
Therefore, for those who have realized their nature, there is no mutual suspicion among sages or commoners. Today, throughout the world, people indulge their emotions while neglecting their nature;

thus, a father gives birth to a son and suspects him, and a son is born of a father and suspects him. This is because indulging in emotions causes habitual tendencies (*xi*) to drift far apart. It is like Fuxi... [text continues].
A certain person was born ten thousand generations ago, while King Wen and Confucius were born ten thousand generations later. Confucius did not doubt the Duke of Zhou;
King Wen did not doubt Fuxi. This is because they did not neglect their nature; thus, natures are "nearly the same. Therefore it is said:
when all people view things through the Way of communicating with the divine, then at the moment of opening up things and accomplishing affairs, they do not give rise to [doubt].

The mind is universally benevolent; it accords with righteousness without the need for constraint; it clarifies propriety without formal decorum; it possesses wisdom that is never deluded without the need for expedient adaptation;
and its trustworthiness remains unerring without the need for oaths or covenants. This is due to nothing else: it is simply the natural course of following one's inherent nature.
To respond to things without being shaken by them is called "quiescence" (jì). To be unshaken because there is fundamentally no arising is called "cessation" (miè).
Responding to things while remaining unshaken, despite the absence of arising, is called "quiescent cessation" (jìmíè).
Now, that which can only encompass a single body is deluded knowledge (*mṛṣājñāna*); that which can universally encompass all phenomena is true knowledge (*bhūtajñāna*).
Deluded knowledge apart from true knowledge is like waves apart from water; true knowledge apart from deluded knowledge is like water not being identical to the waves.

Yet, what is the point of there being "true" and "deluded" knowledge? It is because knowledge is fundamentally devoid of true and deluded; it is only because people take themselves to be real [that such distinctions arise].

It is merely one's own delusion. For those of profound innate capacity, when they know that delusion is not separate from the True and know that it exists [within it], then delusion naturally reaches its end.

Once delusion has reached its end, how could the True exist independently? Alas! When the attachments to the true and the false have withered away, fundamental awareness shines clearly amidst the activities of daily life.
It is like spring blossoms: if one does not seek them out, their brilliance is already manifest.
If you set your mind to grasp it, the flower-spirit has already departed. Therefore it is said: "It does not leave its original place and is eternally profound and still;
yet when you seek it, you know it cannot be seen. Viewed in this light, fundamental awareness is full and ever-present;

it is only because the minds of the multitude are coarse and lack refinement that they remain oblivious to it in their daily lives. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "When the essence of the mind abandons hearing, hearing..."
The so-called "dust of sound" left behind all returns to its fundamental wondrousness. Therefore it is said:
"All floating dust and the various changing phenomena of the vessel-world melt like ice in boiling water; in a single thought, they transform into supreme awakening.

Now, the Buddha’s words are fundamentally ordinary and commonplace, just as the earth is solid, water is moist, fire is warm, and wind is moving. The meaning is inherently thus; why wait for [anything else]?
Only by gouging out the fundamentally subtle mind can one finally attain clear penetration.
Nevertheless, while ordinary demons may enter the heart and lungs, even those of worldly wisdom and eloquence find it no easy matter to enter, for to them the Buddha’s words appear commonplace.
The lotus petals lock the stamens; the stamens lock the seed; the seed locks the core. It is through these three locks that this treasury is preserved.

Were it not for this treasury, those who are born again and again without end would almost cease to exist. Therefore, one who understands this holds all that is inexhaustible in the palm of their hand.
Once all is held in the palm, then whether saintly or ordinary, foolish or wise, whether giving life or taking it—this is the handle.
It does not reside in others; how could others perceive it? Not only do others not see it, but even one’s own self finds it difficult to see. It is like knowing the secret through secrecy;
if it were no longer secret, it would cease to be a secret. Therefore it is said: "That ghosts and spirits can be known refers to matters occurring after death."
What is constant brings peace; what is different causes alarm. Alarm leads to doubt; doubt leads to a lack of a guiding principle.
Without a guiding principle, one is dazzled by transformations and shaken by the interplay of the firm and the yielding. Therefore, the constant is the sharp instrument for shattering doubt.
As for why birds are able to fly and fish are able to leap, everyone sees this;
yet as for why the eyes are able to see and the ears are able to hear, no one is able to realize it for themselves.
Thus, though one sees throughout one's life and hears throughout one's life, one never understands what it is that hears and sees. How tragic!
Who does not know that what rustles and whistles is the wind? Who does not know that what flows with a murmuring sound is water?
Yet, when suddenly houses are overturned, thatch is torn away, and islands are swept away while counties are submerged, one does not know the source from which these things arise.
If one can know that source, then even if whirlwinds topple mountains and floods reach the heavens and soak the earth, one will never be startled.
The sense of shame and aversion, as well as the habit of shamelessness, are like those of the states of Wu and Yue: when Wu is strong, it annexes Yue;
when Yue is strong, it annexes Wu. This is the natural course of events. It is the same for a student whose understanding of principle is not yet settled and whose resolve is not firm.
Whenever one is suddenly confronted by a matter, if one is neither aware nor conscious, habit will take advantage of a lapse in principle and descend with a single stroke;
thus, the ruler’s principles are defeated.
Laozi said: "The superior man, upon hearing the Way, practices it diligently; the mediocre man, upon hearing the Way, is as if it exists and as if it does not. The inferior man...
When scholars hear of the Dao, they laugh at it greatly. If they did not laugh, it would not be fit to be called the Dao. I, however, say:

when the superior scholar hears of the Dao, he laughs at it greatly; if he did not laugh, it would not be fit to be called the Dao. When the scholar of middling capacity hears of the Dao, he diligently practices it.

When the scholar of inferior capacity hears of the Dao, it seems as if it exists, yet as if it does not. Perhaps some will consider Laozi to be right and me to be wrong; but this is not only because they do not understand—
In my heart, I did not even realize I had grown old.
Master Liang stayed at Heyuan Temple after crossing the river; Yan Yanzhi and Zhang Xu, admiring his virtue, lingered there in his company and would often sigh, saying: [text continues]

An Tai vomited forth pearls and jade before him; Sengbin and Sengliang vibrated with golden sounds behind him. These pure discourses and wondrous lineages, which were on the verge of extinction, have been restored.
Alas! Without Bole, a fine horse would forever be trapped at the salt wagon; without a discerning knower, even a Perfected Man [would remain unrecognized].
Thus, throughout one's entire life, one might never hear of them; they are as vast as the azure ocean—how could there be only a single pearl?
They are as towering as Mount Tai—how could there be no extraordinary trees? Our Great Awakened Sage governs the nine realms as sovereign and dwells within the great chiliocosm as his kingdom.
Amidst this mountain of wisdom, loftily precipitous, and this ocean of teaching, vast and surging, extraordinary trees and divine pearls cannot possibly be contained within a single carriage.
It can be measured with a bushel; one is able to know its quantity. Yet, when the wise see it, they call it wisdom; when the benevolent see it, they call it benevolence.
One’s own mind is pure and vast, like still water and a clear sky; there is no metaphor that can fully describe its ultimate state. Once this ultimate state is attained, all else...
One wishes to forget oneself; yet as soon as there is even the slightest movement, good and ill gather without being summoned.
Once good and ill have gathered, profit and harm fill the foreground, and the mind that fears gain and fears loss floats and sinks within the chamber of a single cun.
What is called the "pure and expansive self-mind" has already been buried. When the self-mind is buried, the myriad affairs have no master; one sees only what is desirable.
Desire means to joyfully wish to obtain; seeing that which is undesirable, one feels a sudden pang and finds no pleasure.
Once the light of the mind is obscured, the clouds of manifold darkness arise.
I have heard that for one who skillfully employs their mind, even the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds are all broad highways to Bodhi;
yet for one who does not skillfully employ their mind, even the three studies and the six perfections are all enemies of Prajñā. Viewed from this perspective, it is clear.
Green mountains and white clouds are not necessarily places of seclusion; the purple highways and red dust are not necessarily places of clamor.
It depends entirely on how the person encounters them. Thus it is said: "I am merely tuning my own mind; it has nothing to do with you."
When Lady Gongsun performed the sword dance, one could not discern whether it was the sword dancing upon my hands or my hands dancing with the sword.

Sword and hand were mutually forgotten yet mutually employed; even with sage-like wisdom, they could not be fathomed or discerned—how much less so for those who have not yet forgotten the distinction between self and object?
Therefore it is said: "In skill, there is neither great nor small; that which can enter the divine realm is what matters."
This is to share the same merit as the Creator. Viewed from this perspective, whether it be the great heavens and earth or the small myriad things, every object is a hand, and every hand is a sword.
How could an enemy find entry? One who understands this can be spoken with regarding the truth found in every encounter; to embody this is to be divine.
The Way does not reside in the mind; desire does not reside in things. When the mind arises, the Way is lost; when things are discarded, desire subsists of its own accord.
Therefore, those who fixate their minds to seek the Way are wounded; those who carve away things to restrain desire are mad.

It is like attempting to save one's life by cutting one's own throat, or fleeing from one's shadow while clinging to one's form. Were a young child to see this, they would surely pity the injury and laugh at the madness. Now...
The world is now taking those who are wounded and mad as its guiding compass. Where, then, can the Way be made clear? Where can desire be brought to rest?

Ming Dynasty: Han-shan Deqing reads and comments on the *Heart Sutra* Exposition.
Prajñāpāramitā means "wisdom that has reached the other shore"; it is not something that can be reached by those who are ignorant. There are three kinds of prajñā:

these are the prajñā of the true mark (dharmatā), the prajñā of contemplative observation (vipaśyanā), and the prajñā of words and letters. The prajñā of the true mark is that which is inherently possessed by every person.
The mind is the contemplative wisdom of prajñā; it is the luminosity of the mind. If one can attain realization through this, the light of the mind will shine forth brilliantly.
Whatever words or phrases one utters—whether in long compositions or short verses—will suffice to serve as a lamp of illumination for ten thousand ages, used to dispel the darkness of ignorance.
Therefore, it is called the Prajñā of Words and Letters.
The Mind is the structural framework of this great sūtra; just as a human being, though possessing five viscera and a hundred bones, has the mind alone as [the core].
It is the master.

The *sūtra* explains "constancy" (*chang*) and also explains "the path" (*lu*). As for constancy, neither celestial Māras nor external paths can obstruct or destroy it; as for the path, it pertains to both the ordinary and the sage.
All [who seek liberation] must follow this path.
When the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara practiced the profound Prajñāpāramitā, he clearly perceived that the five aggregates are all empty,
and thereby transcended all suffering and affliction.
Avalokiteśvara is an alternative name for Guanyin. Having realized his own mind, this Bodhisattva uses the light of contemplative observation to profoundly shatter the poison of delusion;
because this differs from the partial and shallow [realization] of the Two Vehicles, it is said that he "practices deeply.

Now, this "poison of delusion" refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), which serve as the root-stump of all myriad sufferings and the foundation of a thousand calamities. Sentient beings have yet to empty these.

Thus, they are entangled in suffering and distress like silkworms spinning cocoons; within the boiling water of a hundredfold cauldron, their heads emerge and submerge, with not a day that the threads are severed.
Since the Bodhisattva has severed the threads of the aggregates (*skandha*), he attains the dual fusion of emptiness and form, and wisdom and compassion operate in tandem.
Whether in terms of phenomena or principle, it is like the cook Ding dissecting an ox: nothing meets the edge of his blade. Therefore, he is called "one who acts with mastery.
Śāriputra, form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form. Form is itself emptiness; emptiness is itself form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
Śāriputra, son of the Śāris, was a disciple of the Buddha. His wisdom and eloquence were preeminent, and his discernment surpassed all his peers.
Yet, he had not yet realized the true emptiness of the Mahāyāna and remained intoxicated by a dry, nihilistic stillness. Therefore, the Tathāgata called him by name and addressed him, saying:

"That which I call 'clearly seeing the emptiness of the five aggregates' does not refer to an emptiness that is separate from the aggregates; rather, it is the emptiness within the aggregates themselves."
This is emptiness. Do not misunderstand this. The five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

As for "form," speaking in broad terms, it includes everything from the vast void of heaven and earth to mountains, rivers, grasses, and trees—without distinction between large and small, whatever can be seen.
All these are called "form" (*rūpa*). To speak of it in immediate terms, it is this present, solid body of flesh and blood.

"Feeling" (*vedanā*) refers to that which, from beginningless time until death, arises from perceiving objects through seeing with the eyes, hearing with the ears, smelling with the nose, tasting with the tongue, touching with the body, and cognizing with the mind—all of which are produced by inhaling external sensory data.
"Perception" (*saṃjñā*) refers to the mental deliberation upon what has been felt, evaluating it as good or evil, excellent or inferior.
Regarding honor and disgrace, right and wrong: "conduct" refers to deliberating upon impermanence, yet its flux remains unsettled;
"consciousness" refers to deliberating with clear comprehension, reaching a definitive judgment free from delusion. These five, when taken together, are in truth but a single thought-moment;
when analyzed individually, they are the differentiation of five functions.

Śāriputra, all these phenomena have the characteristic of emptiness: they are neither produced nor extinguished; neither defiled nor pure; neither increasing nor decreasing. Therefore, in emptiness there is no form;
no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. There is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind. There is no form, sound, odor, taste, tangible object, or phenomenon.
There is no realm of the eye, and so on, up to no realm of mental consciousness. There is no ignorance, nor is there any extinction of ignorance.

"Illuminating exhaustion: there is not even old age and death, nor the exhaustion of old age and death. There is no suffering, no accumulation, no cessation, and no path. There is no wisdom and no attainment.
The Tathāgata considered that for Śāriputra and all sentient beings, residual doubts had not yet been exhausted; therefore, he once again raised up and revealed this to them.

It is said: Once the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are empty and the luminosity of the mind is alone revealed, with drifting clouds cleared away and the full moon suspended in the sky, then birth-and-death, defilement and purity, increase and decrease—all are like snow falling upon a red-hot furnace. Therefore, after awakening to true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), it is not only that the five aggregates are fundamentally empty;

even the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), and the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), as well as suffering (*duḥkha*), its origin (*samudaya*), its cessation (*nirodha*)... [are likewise so].
The Way is likewise like the fur of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit. Nevertheless, ice does not melt of its own accord; it dissolves only when spring returns.

Frost does not dissolve of its own accord; it vanishes only when the sun rises. So it is with the five aggregates, up to the eighteen elements and the twelve links of dependent origination—these dharmas are likewise so.
Ice and frost are like the *prajñā* of contemplation; spring and the sun are like [the state when] the ice and frost have already melted away.
Once the ice and frost have dissolved, what need is there to mention spring and the sun? They are no more than discarded straw dogs. Therefore it is said: "There is neither wisdom nor attainment."
Because there is nothing to be apprehended, the Bodhisattva, by relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, has no hindrance in the mind.
Because there is no hindrance, there is no fear; far removed from perverted dreams and delusions, one attains ultimate Nirvāṇa.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time, by relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Ti. Alas! This light of non-attainment is not only that upon which Bodhisattvas rely to be unimpeded; even all Buddhas rely upon it to attain Bodhi.
The light of the Buddha and the Bodhisattva is not dual, yet there remains a vast distance between their respective excellences.

Why is this so? If one investigates the origin of light, there is in truth no distinction of superiority or inferiority. Because light shines with extreme intensity, its extreme illumination gives rise to delusion;
thus, when awakening recognizes delusion, that delusion is extinguished. One whose numinous awakening is perfectly complete is called a Buddha.

Although light is perfectly realized, as delusive habits are gradually eliminated, the path of awakening remains distant; such a one is called a Bodhisattva. Speaking in terms of the fundamental light, it is not...

The deluded thoughts of sentient beings are themselves the very state of attaining Buddhahood; yet for one who has not yet attained Buddhahood, if there were no deluded thoughts, there would be no gateway through which to enter awakening.
Therefore it is said: "All sentient beings fall into birth and death because of their deluded thoughts."

One also enters and exits birth and death due to deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Those who fall into birth and death because of deluded conceptualization are ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Ordinary worldlings do not realize that this body is the root of manifold sufferings, nor that this mind is the mediator for the thief of sensory objects.
Letting it go or not letting it go, they sport among the six sense organs and the six sense objects, like a fly stuck in saliva, lingering in the putrid froth.
Until death they remain unenlightened. It is through deluded thoughts that one undergoes birth and death;

yet, upon encountering the clear instructions of a spiritual friend or reading the scriptures of the Buddhas, patriarchs, and sages, one finally realizes the fault of being like a fly stuck in spittle. Thereupon, one suddenly feels a surge of indignation and resolve.

Therefore, for those who have not yet realized awakening, these fragments of deluded thought must absolutely be made firm and solid.
There are certain foolish ordinary people who mistakenly interpret the intent of the Buddhas, Patriarchs, and Sages; they see it said that there is no self and no person...
"Sentient beings have no self that lives; do not harbor intentions, compulsions, fixations, or egos.

Whenever he encountered others, he would discourse loftily and argue with vehemence, believing himself to have attained enlightenment. Such a person is truly pitiable. Moreover, as for you, here and now—every day...
When applied in the intervals [of practice], the seven emotions, the six desires, and the three poisons of ignorance are like snakes and scorpions;
who would dare to touch them? If one is unfortunately touched by them, there is none who does not suffer their sting and bite.

Since you have not yet eliminated even a fraction of this internal toxic vapor, how can you speak of such grand matters? If you wish to eliminate this toxic vapor, you must take the "Cooling Medicine."
This is the medicine that has finally been obtained: the medicine of cool serenity. It is not the liver of the dragon or the marrow of the phoenix;
it is not the *sudarśana* or *vaikrāntaka* minerals. Rather, it is precisely what was mentioned above: this fragment of deluded thought which must be made firm and solid.
If one can indeed make this resolve firm and solid, then the seven emotions, the six desires, the three poisons, and ignorance will gradually be transformed into the light of *prajñā*.

This is clear. Although visualizations are numerous, to speak of them in essence: first is the visualization of emptiness (*śūnyatā-bhāvanā*); second is the visualization of the provisional (*prajñapti-bhāvanā*);

When the visualization is perfected, it is like the bright moon floating in the sky and the vast heavens being a single expanse of azure; though the puddles at their feet reflect the ocean and rivers, each casting its own shadow and radiating its own light.

When the middle visualization is perfected, one transforms emptiness and molds existence, moving with ease like the bending and stretching of an arm, turning according to the mind without deviating from the whole body.

The visualization of emptiness cures the poison of *dṛṣṭi* (views) and *kleśa* (afflictions); the visualization of the provisional cures the poison of the *rajas* (dust-like) and *avidyā* (ignorance) of the sands; the middle visualization cures the root.
This is the poison of fundamental ignorance. Alas! These three poisons are the greatest poisons in the world.
Aside from the Buddha, who could avoid being harmed by their venom? The poison of the skin harms prajñā; the poison of the flesh harms liberation;
the poison of the bone harms the dharmakāya. Therefore, the King of Physicians from India prepared a great divine prescription using the medicine of the contemplation of emptiness.

One treats the poison of the skin with medicine of provisional conception; one treats the poison of the flesh with medicine of intermediate conception; and one treats the poison of the bone with medicine of ultimate conception.

Although these conceived medicines are threefold, they do not transcend a single thought-moment (*ekacitta*). Therefore, one who realizes the emptiness of this single thought-moment immediately accomplishes the virtue of *prajñā*.

Although the thought-moment is empty and void, it does not abandon the manifold existence of phenomena; thus, one immediately accomplishes the virtue of *vimukti*. This is the characteristic of the non-duality of existence and non-existence.
That is: emptiness and form are neither identical nor separate; in a single thought-moment of correspondence, one immediately realizes the virtue of the Dharma-body.
One must reach the stage of non-obstruction and the realm of fearlessness. One must directly eliminate all three delusions;
if even a hair’s breadth remains unexhausted, even a Bodhisattva would still sink into the hindrance of awakening, let alone an ordinary person. Therefore it is said: "If residual dust still..."
All phenomena are learning; ultimate clarity is the Tathāgata. It is further said: "Because of clarity there is seeing; because of darkness there is non-seeing.

When clarity arises from itself, then all appearances of darkness can never again obscure. What is meant by "because of clarity there is seeing" does not refer solely to the clarity of the three luminaries (sun, moon, and stars);
it refers to emptiness, to the provisional, and to the middle—all are due to clarity. If one were not dependent on clarity, one would be isolated.

Light radiates spontaneously; when the sentiments of ordinary and sage are extinguished, what more need be said of "the three contemplations within one mind" or "one mind within the three contemplations"?

Yet, until one reaches the point of total penetration—through and through—one must not depart even a single step from this light of wisdom.
It is so. If one proceeds with one's back turned toward the light, one will certainly fall into the pits of eternalism and nihilism;
such a downfall is certain. Therefore, know that the Prajñāpāramitā is a great mantra of spiritual power, a great mantra of illumination, and the unsurpassed mantra.
This is the mantra of the unequaled; it can eliminate all suffering. It is true and not false.
Therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā mantra is spoken. The mantra is recited as follows: *gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate.*
*Bodhi svāhā*. How magnificent is the light of the mind!
Its wisdom cannot be known; its consciousness cannot be cognized. Neither yin nor yang can encompass it; neither existence nor non-existence can describe it.
It shatters obstacles and dispels darkness; among both ordinary beings and sages, none can equal it. Thus it is called the Great Divinity.
It is indeed fitting that this be called a mantra, a great mantra, an unsurpassed mantra, and an unequaled mantra. Now, within the Prajñāpāramitā there are both exoteric and esoteric aspects.
From the time of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva until the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, these are termed the "exoteric exposition of Prajñā.
From the words "Know therefore that Prajñāpāramitā... up to [the attainment of] bodhi... [is the esoteric aspect].
"Ti sa bo he. This is called the secret discourse of Prajñāpāramitā. Furthermore, regarding mantras: it is like adding the incantation of the *gonglo* (wasp) to the *mingling* (caterpillar).
With focused mindfulness, one’s voice becomes like that of the wasp, continuous and unbroken; then the insects are permeated by this influence, and without knowing how, they transform into wasps.
Thus, the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, through the manifestation of both the exoteric and esoteric, permeate all beings with compassion.
All sentient beings are thus; therefore, all sentient beings do not know how they are transformed by this. Alas! The Buddha’s grace is vast and great—who knows how to repay it?
Yet the True Dharma hangs like the autumn wind, and the Way of the Patriarchs has fallen into desolation. Beholding a dull-witted youth such as myself, [I am filled with concern].

My Way and virtue are empty and meager; they are insufficient to move others. It would have been sweet to have gone before the court of Qin, crying out until my voice was spent, yet who was there to relieve Chu by remitting the annual tax on "no-clothes"?
(Heart Sutra)
The Heart Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom.
Now, wisdom and ignorance are fundamentally not two distinct things; the far shore and this shore are originally of the same source.

It is named "The Perfection of Wisdom" (*Prajñāpāramitā*). "Sutra" (*sūtra*) is a title that remains unchanging through all ages;

because it is the most primary, who could abandon this and seek unsurpassed *bodhi* elsewhere?
When the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara practiced the profound Prajñāpāramitā, he clearly perceived that the five aggregates are all empty, thereby transcending all suffering and calamity.
Sentient beings have never ceased to be bodhisattvas; it is only because they do not realize that both persons and phenomena are empty that they are ensnared by suffering and calamity.
Therefore they are called "sentient beings. If one realizes this without obstruction, who would not be a bodhisattva?
Śāriputra, form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form. Form is itself emptiness; emptiness is itself form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.

The reason for specifically calling him by name and addressing him at this point is to state that the emptiness realized by the aforementioned Bodhisattvas is not the partial emptiness of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), nor is it a dull emptiness (*jaḍa-śūnyatā*), nor is it a nihilistic emptiness (*uccheda-śūnyatā*); it is simply the emptiness that is identical with form (*rūpa*).
Since form can be identical with emptiness, emptiness can likewise be identical with form; therefore, it is said: "Form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not..."

They are different in appearance. Among the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is but one. Since form and emptiness can be mutually identified, the same applies by analogy to the remaining aggregates.
Therefore it is said: "Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so."
Śāriputra, all these phenomena have the characteristic of emptiness: they are neither born nor extinguished; neither defiled nor pure; neither increasing nor decreasing.

Therefore, within emptiness there is no form; no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. There is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind. There is no form, sound, odor, taste, touch, or phenomenon.
There is no realm of the eye, and so forth, up to no realm of mental consciousness. There is no ignorance, nor is there any extinction of ignorance.

The exhaustion of ignorance is clarified; even up to old age and death, there is neither old age and death nor the exhaustion of old age and death. There is no suffering, accumulation, cessation, or path.
There is no wisdom and no attainment. Because there is nothing to be attained.

Calling him by name once more at this point, the Buddha addresses him because he fears that his habitual tendencies toward the limited and narrow are so deep-rooted that it will be difficult for him to ultimately traverse the ocean of the Mahāyāna Dharma of the two kinds of emptiness.
Therefore, he clearly proclaims and reveals [the truth] to enlighten him: "The mark of the emptiness of all phenomena."
It is like solid ice that has already melted into water: in a square vessel it becomes square, and in a round vessel it becomes round;
touched by the wind it can produce the sound of waves, and reflected on the earth it can take on the color of the sky;
in rivers and lakes it can float ten thousand bushels, and during a great drought it can become clouds.

The rainbow-like [nature of reality] is such that there is nowhere one does not find spontaneous liberation. Furthermore, square and round vessels serve as metaphors for the objective realm before us.
This objective realm naturally possesses arising and ceasing, defilement and purity, increase and decrease—just as when water turns to ice, it is nothing but solid obstruction.

If the student understands this, then the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and the four noble truths (*catvāri āryasatyāni*) will all become clear at a glance. Although...

However, an object cannot empty itself; it must rely on illumination to be emptied. When the object is empty but the wisdom remains, it is like the medicine persisting after the illness has departed—it is ultimately not the fundamental essence.
One must wash away the medicine as well to completely exhaust all defilement. Therefore, it is said: "Without wisdom, there is also no attainment."
Because Bodhisattvas rely on the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), their minds are without hindrance.
Because they are without hindrance, they are free from fear and far removed from perverted dreams and delusions; they attain ultimate nirvana.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time, by relying on the perfection of wisdom, have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Therefore, one should know that [the perfection of wisdom is supreme].
The *pāramitā* is a great divine mantra, a great illuminating mantra, an unsurpassed mantra, a mantra equal to the unequaled.

The mantra is as follows: *gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā*.
"Hā! Alas, how profound is the difficulty of transforming those whose habits of the partial and inferior vehicles have become so heavy!

The Bodhisattvas rely upon it; with minds free from hindrance, they attain Nirvana. Even the Buddhas of the three periods of time have likewise attained unsurpassed Bodhi by means of it.
Fearing that they might still harbor alarm or doubt and fail to penetrate its depths, he further commanded them, saying:
This Prajñāpāramitā is a great divine mantra; it is a great illuminating mantra; it is the unsurpassed mantra; it is the unequaled mantra.
"Divine" means its majestic spiritual power is unfathomable. "Illuminating" means there is no hidden darkness it does not penetrate.

It is the life-force of wisdom. In the Sanskrit language it is *prajñā*, which here translates as "wisdom. In the Sanskrit language it is *pāramitā*, which here translates as "reaching the other shore.
This means that one who possesses wisdom illuminates and shatters the afflictions (*kleśa*), does not drown in the waves of emotion, and transcends birth and death with ease.
It wondrously accords with that which is primordially possessed; this is what is meant by "ascending to the other shore. The mind is used as a metaphor for this scripture.

Just as a person’s body, though it possesses the hundred skeletal parts and five viscera, has the mind as its master, so too, although the text of this scripture is concise, it is the heart of the magnificent writings of the six hundred fascicles.
A "sūtra" (jing) is that which is constant and unchanging throughout antiquity and the present; it is a path upon which people may tread and advance.

As for the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, it means that this Bodhisattva, by means of the aforementioned wisdom, perfectly illuminates both emptiness and existence, realizing them to be entirely without obstruction.

Master Zhao said: "If illumination does not lose its emptiness, then one engages with existence without being encumbered; if emptiness does not lose its illumination," [then one remains within emptiness without falling into nihilism].
Thus, one contemplates emptiness without becoming intoxicated; by embracing both existence and non-existence, one transcends both form and emptiness.

It is for this reason that one can exist and can be non-existent, and can be empty and can be material; hence, it is called "sovereign mastery" (*svatantra*). As for sentient beings who cling to existence, even the followers of the Two Vehicles still cling to non-existence;

each is biased toward their own particular view and cannot achieve universal penetration, and thus they lack sovereignty. Furthermore, there is a vast difference between wisdom (*prajñā*) and mere cleverness.
Cleverness (*prajñā*) arises from external objects, whereas wisdom (*jñāna*) is born from the fundamental mind.
Therefore, while cleverness is subject to arising and ceasing, wisdom has no dependence; thus, it is non-arising and non-ceasing.
"When practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*" refers to the contemplative wisdom cultivated by this Bodhisattva, which is not partial or shallow like that of the two vehicles. It is...

This is the profound *prajñā*. Because it is profound *prajñā*, it is able to illuminate thoroughly that form and emptiness are fundamentally not two different things, but are originally one true reality (*dharmatā*).
It is only because ordinary beings do not understand this that they see form but do not see emptiness; and because those of the Two Vehicles are biased and attached.
One may see emptiness and not see form, just as it is with the waters of the Ganges: fish and dragons regard them as their lair; devas and humans regard them as lapis lazuli;
those in the human world regard them as flowing waves; and hungry ghosts regard them as fierce flames. These four views are nothing more than the products of their own mental projections.
Only one who has awakened to the mind realizes that such views do not exist at all. Since form is thus, so too are sensation, perception, and the other aggregates.
The formations and consciousness have never been anything other than this; therefore it is said: "Feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are also like this.
When one clearly perceives that the five aggregates are all empty, then all suffering and affliction come to an end. Ordinary people are deluded and inverted;

they do not realize that this body is a provisional combination of the four great elements, yet they cling to it as being real. Consequently, they rejoice when they hear of birth and grieve when they hear of death, failing to understand that this body—

It is the emptiness of form itself, yet it does not preclude engagement with the world. This "emptiness-characteristic of all dharmas" refers to the illumination of the emptiness of the five aggregates.

To explain this by means of the stages prior to the Path, during the Path, and subsequent to the Path is not necessarily the case. Why?
Because when a practitioner illuminates the five aggregates with wisdom, form is severed in its emptiness; the sentiments of ordinary and sage alike are exhausted.

The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are identical to the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*). The twelve bases are identical to the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*).

Because the faculties and dispositions of sentient beings differ, the Buddha established his teachings according to their respective capacities. For those who are deluded regarding the mind but not regarding form, he taught the five aggregates.

For those who are deluded regarding form but not regarding the mind, he taught the twelve bases. For those who are deluded regarding both mind and form, he taught the eighteen elements. This is the essential point.

To speak of it in brief: the three categories of aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) do not transcend matter and mind. There is no ignorance, nor is there the exhaustion of ignorance;
even unto no old age and death, nor the exhaustion of old age and death. There is no suffering, origin, cessation, or path; there is no wisdom, nor is there one who attains.
This means that when a Bodhisattva illuminates this with wisdom, within this true emptiness, not only are the aggregates, bases, and elements fundamentally non-existent, but...
Emptiness. Even the circulation of the twelve links of dependent origination is empty; it is not only the circulation that is empty, but its cessation as well.
It is not only the cessation that is empty, for suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—all are empty. It is not merely these various phenomena that are empty.
Furthermore, this very wisdom that can empty the aggregates, bases, and elements, as well as the wisdom regarding suffering, its origin, cessation, and the path, is likewise unattainable.
This is because, since the objects [of cognition] do not exist, the subject cannot stand alone.

Although there are differences in skill and deficiency between the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas regarding the twelve links of dependent origination and the four noble truths, to speak in summary: within true emptiness, these things do not exist. Bodhi...
O Bodhisattva, by relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, the mind is without hindrance.
Because there is no hindrance, there is no fear. One is far removed from inverted dreams and delusions, and attains ultimate Nirvana.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time, by relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. This refers to this sutra.
Sentient beings revere it alone; they cross the stream of birth and death to ascend to the other shore.

Even the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, whether at the stage of partial realization or ultimate perfection, must necessarily rely upon this. This is intended to praise, exhort, and circulate this sutra so that all sentient beings may [attain liberation].
One should advance in practice by relying on *prajñā*, so as not to be deluded by demons or externalists. Yongjia said: "The great man wields the sword of wisdom;
the blade of *prajñā* has the brilliance of a vajra. It does not merely destroy the minds of externalists from afar;
it has long since struck down the courage of the celestial Māras. Generally speaking, those with the aspiration for world-transcendence possess such power and such spirit.
The longing of the clouds is such an intense state of mind that it is like a great mass of fire;

it would be well to let all things be enveloped by it so that they are instantly reduced to ashes and smoke. Otherwise, upon seeing even a slight object of desire, the sentiments of children will arise.
Some say: "The Master’s commentary on this sutra does not distinguish between cause and effect, nor does it arrange it into topical sections;

The five periods are not uniform; they do nothing more than refine the emotional dust of sentient beings and cleanse their views.
If emotional dust is exhausted and one's view is correct, then even that which does not accord with ancient regulations is in fact in accord. Why do you speak so much?
Therefore, know that the Prajñāpāramitā is the great divine mantra, the great illuminating mantra, the unsurpassed...
This is a mantra; it is a mantra without equal. It can eliminate all suffering; it is true and not false.
This is likewise a praise of Prajñāpāramitā and a testimony to its efficacy. The spirit is subtle and wondrous beyond the measure of all things; if it could be measured, it would not be spiritual.

When there is clarity, one responds perfectly to all phenomena without being entangled by them; when there is entanglement, there is no clarity. "Unsurpassed" means that there is nothing higher than this;
if there were something higher, it would not be supreme. "Peerless" (wu dengdeng) means there is nothing with which it can be equaled.
It is perfectly complete and full, such that nothing can surpass it. Guifeng said: "It is pervasive and pure, with no space within to admit anything else."

Who could equal him? The above constitutes the explicit exposition of Prajñā. Now, there are three aspects of Prajñā: namely, the letter (vyañjana), contemplation (vipaśyanā), and the true nature (dharmatā).
Indeed, without the letter, there would be no means to give rise to contemplation; without contemplation, there would be no means to discern the true nature;
and without the true nature, the Bodhisattva would have nothing toward which to aspire as the ultimate goal. What is this ultimate? It is realization.
It is said that there are varying depths of realization. At the shallow level, one severs the afflictions of views and thoughts, as well as those like grains of sand.

At the deep level, one completely uproots fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), proceeding directly to the state of wondrous enlightenment before coming to rest. Although the three contemplations are unified within a single mind, they are cultivated concurrently and in tandem.

However, in severing the afflictions of views and thought, the power of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) predominates; in severing the *rajas* and ignorance (*avidyā*), the power of the contemplation of the provisional (*upāya*) predominates;
and in severing fundamental ignorance, the power of the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*) takes precedence.

Now, if one has clarity regarding the ground of insight (*darśana-bhūmi*) yet does not cultivate the practices of contemplation (*bhāvanā-caryā*), how is this different from having a field without plowing it? Even if one cultivates the practices of contemplation, if the ground of insight...
I do not understand. It is like a blind man walking along a path; he is not only unable to return home, but I fear he will fall into pits or ditches.

If a person fears birth and death and loathes afflictions (*kleśa*), there is nothing like contemplating the body through the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and contemplating the mind through the four aggregates (*skandha*).
Now, the principle of contemplating the body through the four great elements and the mind through the four aggregates is the very heart-exposure of the Tathāgata.

"Cutting out the gallbladder" points to a skillful means (*upāya*). It is hoped that sentient beings, upon this very stinking physical shell and within the midst of攀緣 (*pán-yuán*, objective conditions), may immediately realize through wondrous awakening that this body and this mind are originally but the one true reality (*dharmatā*).

Yet, when sentient beings wander through birth and death and revolve through the realms of suffering, it is truly not because of sounds, forms, wealth, profit, food, drink, or men and women that they are obstructed; rather, it is simply that they are unable to...

By observing the body through the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the mind through the four aggregates (*skandha*), one perceives that there is a body to be grasped and a mind that can be obstructed.
When there is a body to be grasped, birth and death manifest clearly; when there is a mind that can be obstructed, hatred and attachment blaze forth.
When birth and death are thick and hatred and attachment are deep, the originally inherent light of wisdom is buried and obscured. How could the Buddha and sentient beings ever be two?
Indeed, the Buddha is no more than a person who is free from birth and death, and free from love and hatred; whereas sentient beings possess birth and death, and possess love and hatred.

Regarding the contemplation of the body as the four great elements: whenever a practitioner walks, stands, sits, or lies down, they should, with a mind of purity and cleanliness, turn their gaze back upon this body.
Skin, flesh, sinews, and bones fundamentally belong to the element of earth; blood, vessels, tears, mucus, saliva, and fluids [belong to the element of water].
The fundamental element is water; warmth belongs to fire; movement belongs to wind. When one examines and observes this with discernment, what of it exists for me?
Yet now, you grasp at it perversely and refuse to let go, recognizing it as real. How is this any different from two ghosts contending over a stinking corpse?

If one contemplates in this manner for a long time, the practice will become deep through accumulation; the place of arising will gradually mature, and the place of maturation will gradually give rise [to new arising]. This continues until the refinement is complete.
One must not neglect the single word "refinement" (*lian*). If one is not truly a person who has mastered the matter of birth and death, when circumstances of adversity or favor encounter them—

One would then be unable to carry even this burden. Regarding the contemplation of the mind through the four aggregates: first, one contemplates the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) to investigate from where it arises.
One pursues this inquiry to its conclusion: does it arise suddenly without cause, or does it arise dependent upon an object?

If it could arise without a cause, then while the preceding object has not yet been encountered and the fundamental mind is tranquil and luminously penetrating, how could there be what is called "delusive thought"? If it arises dependent upon an object...
When birth occurs, the external objects before one shift and change, and the mind likewise shifts and changes. How could this shifting and changing mind be my true self?
If it were my true self, then heaven and earth would be established by it, and all phenomena would take it as their root.

If it were subject to shifting and changing, how could it serve as the foundation for heaven and earth or the root of all phenomena? Therefore, know that what undergoes shifting and changing is merely a shadow of grasping conditions.
Listen! Now, the true mind is such that when sensory objects arise, it does not arise; when sensory objects perish, it does not perish.

It illuminates things without being entangled by them. Thus, the verse of Vipaśyin Buddha says: "Taking the four elements as a borrowed body, The mind is fundamentally unarisen, arising only due to objects.
If the external object is absent, the mind is likewise non-existent; Sin and merit are like illusions—they arise and then perish. This verse was spoken by the World-Honored One.

"Compassion" (*maitrī*) is the complete presentation of the guiding principle that dependent origination is non-arising. If one can realize this, then the subtle essence of the *Heart Sūtra* is exhausted within it.

Now, "dependent origination is non-arising" means that the mind does not arise of itself; its arising must be through objects (*viṣaya*). Objects do not manifest of themselves; their manifestation must be through the mind.
Because it does not arise of itself, the mind has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Because they do not manifest of themselves, objects have no [intrinsic nature].

This is their nature. If the mind and its objects have no inherent nature, then non-arising is manifest before one. If the mind and its objects have no inherent nature, then dependent origination is not abandoned.
As it is with the mind and its objects, so it is with all phenomena. This principle is what is called the "Dharmadhātu" (Dharma-realm) in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is termed "true reality" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Some may say: "This sutra takes the deconstruction of characteristics as its primary tenet and the discourse on emptiness as its ultimate aim;
how could it possibly speak on the same track as the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*?

Now, it is an established statement of the ancients that both the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* manifest the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*), whereas this sutra secretly discourses upon true reality. This is not a mere speculative fabrication of one who is not lacking in integrity.
This is like carving [into wood]. Alas! Sentient beings harbor doubts and fail to comprehend this principle. Within formlessness, they falsely perceive the existence of a body;

within mindlessness, they falsely perceive the existence of a mind. They do not realize that the body which is no-body has a form that pervades the Dharma-realm, and that the mind which is no-mind is a spiritual illumination that shines upon all things.
Indeed, how could this body and this mind be anything other than sublime, profound, and wondrous? It is precisely...
In the midst of my daily life, at every moment when responding to conditions, it has never failed to be luminously clear. The Old Man of Dongshan’s *Avataṃsaka* says:
"The Buddha-dharma is present in the midst of daily activities—in wearing clothes and eating food, even in defecating and urinating;
yet the very moment you raise a thought or stir a mental movement, it is no longer so. Layman Pang said: "The affairs of daily life are no different; they simply accord with me of their own accord."
"Supernatural powers and wondrous functions / Are used to carry water and haul firewood. However, regarding this principle, there are those who have attained awakening but not yet practiced;
those who have practiced but not yet perfected it; and those who have realized it and enjoy its fruition. Now, suppose there is someone here who has attained a slight degree of awakening.
They do not practice at all, yet they claim to have already attained realization; thus, they turn their heads away from both cultivation and realization.

When the last day of the twelfth lunar month arrives, their ignorance reaches its peak, and they are left with nothing but a sense of shame and regret. I, your humble servant, do not venture to join the ranks of those who debate doctrinal tenets.

However, because the Layman Haiyang recently inquired about this matter, I could not help but write this spontaneously according to my own thoughts. Therefore, I have not sought formal authorization from the Triple Gem.
This is also a verse for the empowerment of proof: *gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā*.
This is the esoteric teaching of Prajñāpāramitā. Since it is called "esoteric," this humble servant does not dare to offer a forced interpretation.
Regarding the Heart Sūtra:
this single text is the divine artifice of the sages, worthies, and heroes of both the mundane and supramundane realms.
Therefore, those who grasp its essential meaning may govern the great trichiliocosm and rule over all under heaven, as skillfully as a clever child herding sheep with a whip and commands.
Within this interval, there is nothing that does not find its proper place. To investigate its essential pivot, one finds the single phrase:

"The five aggregates are seen to be entirely empty. This is, moreover, the very heart of this sutra. Suppose there were a person here whose ambition lies in hearing the Way and who desires to bring universal benefit to all;
yet they abandon this book to seek it elsewhere—this is what is called walking at night while discarding one's torch: such a person is either a fool or a madman.
Thus it is. Generally speaking, the failure of the Way to be clarified and the difficulty of governing the world both take root in the notion of self (*ātman*).

Once this notion of self is established, one encounters objects of desire and immediately feels joy and pleasure toward them. When such pleasure fails to satisfy one's inner aspirations, one suddenly becomes angry.
By this means, the celestial mechanism is blocked; by this means, likes and dislikes become biased. Consequently, the innate wisdom...

The light of wisdom has been utterly submerged. Observing this through the lens of daily life, love and hatred wage war within the spirit-mansion (*lingtai*), while emotional consciousness (*qingshi*) floats and sinks amidst honor and disgrace.

Observing this through the lens of past and present, from the mutual slaughter of the Seven Hegemons and Five Barons to the gains and losses of the Han, Tang, Song, and Yuan dynasties—whether their conduct was entirely virtuous or not—it cannot be compared with [the state of true wisdom].

When it comes to speech, if there is no martiality, disorder cannot be settled; if there is no wisdom, the state cannot be preserved. To summarize, neither of these transcends the mark of selfhood (*ātmagrāha*).
Consequently, true nature becomes daily obscured, delusive thought becomes daily thickened, simplicity becomes daily diluted, and the ways of the world become daily degraded.
Thus it is said: "To govern the state with wisdom is a thief to the state; to govern people with a sense of self is a thief to people."
Enemies. Now, as for thieves and enemies, even if one’s parents were to bestow them upon their children, the children would certainly not be able to carry out [the parents’ intent].

Not only would they be unable to do so, they would surely turn their eyes against them and attack them. The Tathāgata knew that the poison of the *ātman*-view (*ātmagrāha*) infects the world and its harm is exceedingly great;
therefore, he opened up form and mind from a single thought-moment, and from form and mind, he opened up the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). From...
From the dust of form, the twelve bases (*āyatana*) are opened; furthermore, from the five aggregates (*skandha*), the eighteen realms (*dhātu*) are opened.

This causes sentient beings to realize that both attachment to the body and attachment to the mind are fundamentally rooted in the mark of self (*ātman*). The root of this mark of self, moreover, arises from ignorance (*avidyā*).

As each member conditions the next, suffering and its accumulation arise in succession; therefore, when one penetrates the origin from which ignorance arises, the true nature spontaneously becomes luminous.

When one penetrates that form and mind lack intrinsic nature, then not even a single thought-moment can be apprehended. When one penetrates that the five aggregates lack intrinsic nature, then form and mind likewise cannot be apprehended.
When one penetrates the origin from which the twelve bases arise, it is like the cook Ding dismembering an ox.
The ox is no longer perceived as a whole ox. When one contemplates this present body through the twelve bases (*āyatana*), not even a whole body can be found.

One who understands how the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) arise realizes that the two dharmas of form and mind are analyzed externally into the six objects (*viṣaya*), internally into the six faculties (*indriya*), and in between, they are clearly and distinctly perceived through the present discernment.
Know this in your heart. Furthermore, when analyzed, it is divided into the six consciousnesses.

Were it not for the Great Benevolence and Profound Compassion of our Buddha, how could the root of the self-identity, the source of poisonous harm, and the defilement of manifold sufferings be so easily uprooted and so easily cleansed? To cleanse these defilements is like cold waves washing over rocks;

to uproot them is like the *vajra* breaking through objects. If one washes them incessantly, the rocks will surely eventually change; if one breaks them [with the *vajra*], they will certainly be destroyed.
Once things have come to an end, they must necessarily be empty. A stone may easily be worn through; when things are empty, the self is discarded. This is what is meant by:
"If one is deficient, both will surely be lost. When both object and self are forgotten, the original mind naturally reveals itself. Therefore it is said: "The numinous light shines alone."
It is utterly detached from the sense organs and their objects. As for this light: if it illuminates the supramundane, the path of awakening may be ascended;
if it illuminates the mundane world, the ancient Way may be restored. Therefore, I say that the *Heart Sūtra* is a divine artifice for both the mundane and the supramundane.

The Prajñāpāramitā section consists of eight titles and comprises more than six hundred fascicles in total. Among these, this sutra alone is the pivotal key to the six hundred fascicles of its magnificent prose.
Furthermore, the pivotal key of this sutra is the single phrase: “To perceive that the five aggregates are all empty.
This perception that the five aggregates are all empty is, in turn, rooted in the two dharmas of form and mind. As for these two dharmas of form and mind...
Furthermore, this initial stirring of a single thought is rooted in the true mind (*tathatā-citta*). This true mind is originally clear and tranquil;
it fundamentally lacks roots, sense-objects, things, or self. It stands alone prior to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and is entirely devoid of sensory stimulus.
Thus, as for the origin from which this single thought stirs, even those of great wisdom and lofty brilliance, when they inquire into the source of that stirring—
"Since its birth, there has never been anyone able to repay it. I, your humble servant, have also harbored this doubt for a long time.
How could there be a Great Master capable of dispelling my doubts? Even if I must offer my own flesh as a gift, I would accept it with a willing heart."

The Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra states that there are no phenomena apart from the mind; this is the Tathāgata’s truthful word. Just as there are no waves apart from water, such is the urgent analogy of the sages.

Yet, because sentient beings have been defiled by the habitual tendencies of names and words since beginningless time, they are difficult to transform; thus, upon hearing of the ordinary, they cling to the ordinary, and upon hearing of the holy, they cling to the holy.

O Holy One, when one hears of existence, one becomes attached to existence; when one hears of non-existence, one becomes attached to non-existence. Upon hearing of birth and death, one becomes attached to birth and death;

upon hearing of nirvana, one becomes attached to nirvana; upon hearing of the world, one becomes attached to the world; upon hearing of the multitude of atoms, one becomes attached to the multitude of atoms. Thus, the original mind immediately vanishes.
Driven by names and words, they cling to them and forget their original source, thereby burying their own true nature.

Therefore, at the assembly of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the Tathāgata preached the *Vajracchedikā Sūtra* to destroy the multitude of atoms within the world, and to destroy the solid habituation within those atoms.
Once this solid habituation is destroyed, the habit of atoms is eliminated; one is lost and two are forfeited. When both "one" and "two" are lost, [the ultimate is revealed].
The original mind is thus suddenly revealed. Therefore, the Sixth Patriarch said: "When you do not think of good and do not think of evil, which one is the true face of Elder Ming?
This old master points directly at the state beyond the emotions of good and evil, indicating that one must realize this which is neither good nor evil.
This state of being neither good nor evil has many names: it is called the original nature (*prakṛti*), the true mind (*bhūtamanas*), and the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
It is said that these are "original enlightenment" and so forth. Therefore, those with profound innate capacity are not defiled by names and phrases;

they are able to awaken to that which names and phrases cannot reach, even while relying upon them. Thus, this sutra uses the multitude of world-dust particles as a basis for the Tathāgata’s skillful means:
by means of the world-dust particles, he refutes the world as being merely nominal and lacking substantial reality; and by means of the world, he refutes the world-dust particles.
The multitude possesses names but lacks reality; ultimately, both name and reality are non-corresponding.

When emotional attachments dissolve and the fundamental nature is restored, one is immediately identical to the Sixth Patriarch, who, through the emotions of good and evil, awakened to the original face that is neither good nor evil; there is from the outset no difference between them.
Observing it from this perspective, if one cannot immediately awaken to the fact that names are merely designations and thus remain unstained by those names, then not only in this world...

The elements (*dhātu*) are themselves a single composite phenomenon; the multitude of atoms (*paramāṇu*) is likewise a single composite phenomenon. Why is this? Because their conceptual attachments have not yet been shattered.
Therefore I say: "To lose one is to forfeit both. Thus, you members of this assembly have gathered here on the shore of Lake Mǎo to form the karmic conditions for the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
This is not a matter of plucking sprouts from the ground; rather, it is because [they] have, throughout many lifetimes, been intimately close to various Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Therefore, they encounter this unexpectedly. A man of the Way remains detached from the world, having no initial longing for anything else. Now, at this late hour and in profound stillness, amidst the light of a white candle, he does not spare his verbal karma.
Regarding both mundane and supramundane dharmas, he lowers what is high to meet what is low, employing various metaphors to explain them in detail.

I have analyzed this portion of the sutra in detail. Although the faculties and capacities of the various classes of practitioners differ—some may gain entry upon hearing a Chan master’s brief remark, while others may find no such entry—the one who understands shall, from this day forward, progress from the coarse toward the subtle.

Once you have attained mastery, you will necessarily enter the divine. Once you are able to enter the divine, then all names and phrases, the atoms of the world, and the virtues and evils of the holy and the ordinary—all their handles will be in your own hands. How could those names and phrases ever turn you?
Those who do not yet understand must resolve this from this day forward; only then will you not have failed this chance encounter with me here at Yaofeng. Furthermore, I am old and ill.
One does not set a date with others; the flowing light cannot be grasped or toyed with. In both worldly and world-transcending dharmas, one must each exert effort.

The conceptual calculations of sentient beings do not allow for "this" without "that," nor "sage" without "ordinary person. Therefore it is said: when the sentiments of sage and ordinary are exhausted, the true permanence is revealed in its essence.
Now, though the world may be shattered and fine dust may be reconstituted, the world and the fine dust have never, from the beginning, existed as separate entities.
It is eternal. Yet, amidst this state where eternity has never truly begun, sentient beings reckon the world as one and reckon atoms as many;
they hold that what is not one must be many, and that what is not many must be one. They indulge in these calculations without awakening, from time immemorial.

As for today, dying here and being born there, or dying there and being born here—if one investigates the reason for this, it does not go beyond the failure to empty the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*) and the consequent clinging to whatever one encounters.
Therefore, the Tathāgata said: "A unified whole (*ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa*) is ultimately ineffable. Yet ordinary people greedily cling to such things.
If sentient beings of sharp faculties were to claim that a world exists because atoms combine, would that world truly exist?
Ah! If one were to shatter the world into subtle atoms, would those subtle atoms truly exist? Alas! This lies in self-awakening;

it does not lie in the value of verbal exposition. Therefore, in this sutra, the Tathāgata raises the mainstay of non-arising amidst the midst of dependent origination—this is the true, profound, great compassion.
Now, when one shatters the world into a multitude of subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*), do those subtle atoms truly exist?
When one reassembles the multitude of subtle atoms to form a world, does that world truly exist? These two states act as subject and object to one another, mutually washing away each other;
how could the relationship between the one and the many require the stirring and rinsing of celestial winds and ocean waves before it is cleansed? Therefore, one who is skillfully adept—
As for that mind, though it dwells all day long amidst the one and the many, the one and the many cannot burden it.

One who acts contrary to this cannot withstand such burdens. Therefore, this sutra says: "That which is called a 'unified aggregate' is not actually a unified aggregate; it is merely named a unified aggregate.
Yet ordinary people greedily cling to such things because they do not comprehend that the one and the many are impermanent. This is the essential point.
This is because guests have no fixed nature. If one can penetrate this truth, then even a "unified whole" (*ekapiṇḍalakṣaṇa*) has never failed to be a Teacher of Gods and Humans.
Su Changgong once said: "The sound of the mountain stream is itself the broad and long tongue.
I would say: "A unified whole is itself the broad and long tongue. Some may consider Changgong right and me wrong; others may consider me right and him wrong.
To consider Master Chang’s view as incorrect is what is called "not speaking of dreams before a fool.
Whether one analyzes the world and the multitude of atoms through their mutual interplay, they are merely names and words; both lack intrinsic nature.

To say that the world exists because it combines with the multitude of atoms, or that the multitude of atoms exists because they fragment the world—both are the deluded projections of sentient beings.

This is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Yet, this horizontal construction is not without its cause; it arises initially from the fact that one’s engagement with phenomena is not refined and one’s penetration of principle is not thorough.

If phenomena were refined, one would be able to realize that there is no principle outside of phenomena. If principle were thoroughly penetrated, one would be able to realize that there are no phenomena outside of principle.
If there is no principle outside of phenomena, do phenomena truly exist? If there are no phenomena outside of principle, does principle truly exist? Therefore, [this] nature...

When the school of principle (*li*) is not yet perfected, the school of characteristics (*xiang*) begins to become refined. When the school of characteristics is not yet perfected, the school of nature (*xing*) begins to become complete.
