Because refinement is itself completeness, there is no thought within refinement. Because completeness is itself refinement, there is clarity within completeness. Because there is no thought, one accords with the same reality through phenomena.

Because there is clarity, one illuminates the principle more fully through phenomena. Such enjoyments bring fulfillment to both self and others; however, they are easier to understand within the stage of the cause.
It is difficult to realize while in the causal stage; once realized within the fruition, it is easy to realize but difficult to forget. Alas!
To enjoy it during the causal stage yet forget it upon reaching the fruition—this is something that those who wear fur and horns cannot achieve.
Now, regarding the four views of self, person, sentient being, and life-span: originally, they were but a single view of self.

Through successive and transverse conceptualizations, they eventually became four views. If one observes with the eye of wisdom, then the one mind does not arise; since even "self" does not exist, who could have the view of self?
Once the view of self is uprooted, the remaining views will naturally become empty without needing to be dispelled. Furthermore, as for the view of self...
The view of a self (*ātman*) is the act of forcibly positing a master where there is no master. The view of a person (*pudgala*) is the state of being dependent upon the "self" for one's perception;

it refers to the failure to engage in reflexive illumination, instead following emotional discrimination. The view of a life-sustainer (*jīva*) is nothing more than the thought of craving life and fearing death.
Viewed in this light, the four views described in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* do not actually exist within the sūtra itself.
This occurs precisely within the midst of our daily activities, amidst the fluctuations of favorable and adverse circumstances; what does it have to do with the Buddha?

Nevertheless, had it not been for this old fellow Gautama, who skillfully broke through the obscurations, this vast expanse of the universe would never have seen the dawn of enlightenment throughout all eternity.

The Buddha asked Subhūti: "If someone were to grind the trichiliocosm into a multitude of fine motes of dust, would that multitude of motes of dust be called many? Subhūti replied: "It would be very many. By this, I know Subhūti’s intention:
he considers it not merely many, but upon careful observation and examination, it truly exists only as a name and lacks substantial reality.
Therefore it is said: "That which is not a multitude of atoms is called a multitude of atoms. Furthermore, the meaning of a "world" is likewise a name without reality.
Therefore it is said: "That which is not a world is called a world. For atoms have no inherent substance of their own; they must exist by the shattering of a world.
A world likewise has no inherent substance of its own; it must be formed by the aggregation of atoms. Thus...

When one views the world through the lens of atoms, the world appears while the atoms do not. When one views atoms through the lens of the world, the form of the atoms appears while the world does not.
If one calculates them as many fragmented forms, then many fragmented forms appear; if one calculates them as a single unified form, then a single unified form appears.
"Many fragmented forms" is simply another name for atoms, and "a single unified form" is merely a different designation for the world.
If the capacity of the practitioner is such that they achieve sudden realization, then both the manifold aspects and the single unified aspect are merely names without reality;

thus, the conceptual attachments to "one" and "many" will naturally exhaust themselves without waiting to be swept away. Once these attachments to "one" and "many" have been exhausted, the luminous mind of one's inherent nature will manifest clearly before one.
Therefore it is said: "When the sentiments of ordinary and sage are exhausted, the essence reveals the true permanence. Furthermore, this...
Sentient emotion arises based on a single condition, which is called "one. Sentient emotion arises based on many conditions, which is called "many.

Sentient emotion arises based on the ordinary, which is called "ordinary. Sentient emotion arises based on the noble, which is called "noble. Thus, the notions of one and many, or ordinary and noble, do not exceed the horizontal conceptualization of a single sentient emotion.
This is also called "pervasive conceptualization" (*parikalpa*) and also called "the perception of the characteristics of external objects" (*viṣaya-nimitta-saṃjñā*).
It is further said that the "reflected shadows conditioned by the six sense-objects" are all alternative names for this very state of mind.
Guifeng categorized this section of the meaning as "realizing the Dharma-realm. How profound! How flavorful indeed!
Now, where there is contraction, there is expansion; where there is gathering, there is dispersal; where there is union, there is fragmentation—this is the natural law.
Therefore, the Tathāgata called to Subhūti and said to him: "If, in a trichiliocosm..."
"It could be crushed into minute particles. Would this multitude of particles be many or few? Subhūti, receiving the Buddha’s instruction, replied, "Very many.
To crush the great trichiliocosm into minute particles and compare them with the mental capacity of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), they would be more numerous than one can count.
Yet, from the perspective of what the Tathāgata knows, they would be fewer than one can count. How could it be otherwise?
If the Tathāgata did not know the number of atoms, would he then wait for Subhūti to determine it?

This is because the Tathāgata already anticipates that although all sentient beings differ in their faculties—some being dull and others sharp—they have never differed in their grasping of the world as a single, unified whole (*ekaghanasaṃjñā*).
It is only those of sharp faculties who, upon hearing that the world can be broken down, [realize its nature].

When they are reduced to subtle particles, it does not depend on Subhūti’s statement that there are many particles; rather, these very particles are not a multitude of particles, and are merely designated as "a multitude of particles.
Only then does one realize that a world is certainly not a single, unified whole (*ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa*).

For sentient beings of dull faculties, it is necessary to wait for Subhūti to secretly shatter their attachment to the multitude of particles, so that they may subsequently understand that a unified whole is [merely a conceptual construct]. First...
Fundamentally, there is no world; it is only through the aggregation of many subtle atoms that a world first comes to be.

Since a world exists only because it is formed by the aggregation of a multitude of subtle atoms, then at the very moment this single unified aggregate abides, its abiding is fundamentally non-abiding and its aggregation is fundamentally non-aggregating.
How could one wait until the world is shattered into a multitude of subtle atoms before this single unified aggregate is finally destroyed?
Furthermore, Subhūti, I and the Tathāgata have taken this world and shattered it into fine dust, and then joined those fine dust particles back together to form a world.
Thus joining and shattering, repeatedly piling up and overturning, those of superior and middling faculties have already realized that the world is fundamentally non-existent;
it exists only when fine dust particles are joined, yet even those fine dust particles are non-existent, existing only when the world is shattered. Up to this point—
This, then, is the attachment to the notions of "one" and "many," which does not require the contemplation of emptiness before it can be shattered.
Yet, because those of inferior faculties find it difficult to awaken, Subhūti again took up the trichiliocosm and declared, "It is not a world; it is merely named a world.
He spoke thus to reveal and enlighten them, saying: "If a world were truly existent, it would be a unified mass (*piṇḍa-grāha*). The world...
If the elements were a unified whole (*ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa*), then the Tathāgata would have previously taught that a unified whole is precisely not a unified whole;

it is only nominally called a unified whole. Why is this so? It is because the Tathāgata and Subhūti, out of compassion for sentient beings whose attachments are difficult to shatter—who relish this body and reckon it as substantially real—have explained this in detail to turn back those of inferior faculties.
Because their grasping at existence and their conceptual understanding were not yet exhausted, the Tathāgata called out to Subhūti and addressed him once more, saying:
"That which is a 'unified whole' (saṃghāta-lakṣaṇa) is inexpressible; it is only ordinary people who greedily cling to such things.
Did Subhūti not already know that what is a unified whole is, in fact, not a unified whole? Why would he wait for the Tathāgata to speak again before he understood? It was simply that...
The Tathāgata, through Subhūti, deeply rebukes those of inferior faculties who cling to the present body, falsely asserting it to be substantially existent and indulging in attachment to it.
Alas! First, the world was shattered into subtle atoms; then, those subtle atoms were examined and found to be non-existent.

Since atoms do not exist, the world has no substance. Therefore, Subhūti, he first breaks the attachment to multiple atoms rather than first breaking the attachment to a "unified whole" (ekapiṇḍa-saṃjñā).

For once the multiple atoms are refuted, the attachment to the unified whole is refuted without even needing to be addressed. Why? Because the many constitute the one; when the many are refuted, the one lacks substance.

Once all emotional attachments are exhausted, both the world and its minute particles are nothing other than the pure Dharma-realm. What object could one point to as being the "world" or "minute particles"?
If a student understands this, only then will they truly understand the bitter heart of our effort—the Father and Son Tathāgatas’ exhaustive overturning and analysis.
If you know this, then the solidity of the trichiliocosm... [is seen for what it is].
To shatter it into minute particles and then recombine those particles to form a world— how is this different from unrolling a sheet of paper or the gathering and dispersing of floating clouds?
On the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*:
I once read the *Buddhapiṭaka* (Buddha-śikhara) Sūtra. Regarding the investigation of the mind in its seven locations, I initially harbored doubts.
Subsequently, my state of doubt suddenly vanished, and I first realized that the Tathāgata’s mind is none other than my own mind. My own doubts were precisely those of Ānanda.
Thus it is. Once my doubts have been dispelled, how could Ānanda still harbor any further doubts?

Generally, among students, when discussing the analysis of the "seeking of the mind" in the seven locations, everyone says that the first location is not difficult, while the others are difficult. Little do they realize that where there is an "internal," there must be an "external";

where there is an "external," the "hidden root" is established; where the "hidden root" is established, the "intermediate space" is established; and where the "intermediate space" is established, the "opening" is established.

When the eyes are open, one sees light; when the eyes are closed, one sees darkness. If one stands and opens the eyes to see light and closes the eyes to see darkness, then one stands according to where they are joined.
To stand according to where one is joined is to stand with non-attachment to all things.

If this is so, then the initial argument concerning the internal [self] is the most egregious of the six [positions]. Once its egregiousness is exposed, the remaining factions will extinguish themselves. Furthermore, sentient beings...

This is because the attachment to the notion that the mind resides within is particularly difficult to break. If the attachment to the mind being internal is broken, how could the others be difficult?
It is for this reason that I know students consider the [subsequent] six stages difficult, rather than considering the first stage difficult.
This is truly because you have not undergone the hardship of diligent practice.
Now, when one clarifies the mind, what mind is being clarified? Is it the true mind that is being clarified, or is it the deluded mind?

If it is the true mind being clarified, since there is no delusion apart from the truth, whom else would you instruct to clarify the true mind? If it is the deluded mind being clarified, as for this deluded mind...
Is it that there is a mind which can be made clear by means of clarity? Or is it that there is no mind which can be made clear by means of clarity?

If there were a mind that could be made clear, then Ānanda would have identified the one capable of investigation as the mind; yet the World-Honored One directly rebuked him and did not grant his request.

That he rebuked him and did not grant his request was not a refusal. The World-Honored One’s intention was to hope that Ānanda would turn his faculty back upon himself to reflect, and thus illuminate this capacity [to investigate].

Does the mind that seeks and investigates reside within these seven locations, or does it not? If it resides within the seven locations, then as you investigate the location of the mind in each place, it is found to have no location whatsoever.
If it does not reside within the seven locations, then since both the sense organs and their objects are absent, upon what could the mind depend?
This is because when Ānanda sought the mind through the investigation of these seven locations, his inquiry was not thorough; thus he presented [only this incomplete account].

Answer: This is not yet understood. As for those who claim to be able to investigate thoroughly, they indeed search through the seven locations and find nothing there. However, what is this very mind that knows it is nowhere?
If one initially calculates that the mind resides within the seven locations, then because it depends on the sense organs and their objects, there are two [factors].
Since investigating them reveals nothing exists, I have no further doubt regarding that. But as for this present, immediate capacity to know that nothing exists—what is that, furthermore?
"What is this thing? This 'thing' is a name. Compared to the previous 'thing,' it is one level deeper.
The previous 'thing' was the mind that exists in dependence upon the sense organs and their objects; the subsequent 'thing' is the mind that exists apart from the sense organs and their objects.
Although one may directly investigate it and find it has no location, that which knows there is no location must necessarily be my own mind. Thus Ānanda said: "I, by means of..."

That which is capable of investigating to the ultimate limit is the mind. Yet, it is not realized that the mind which has not yet undergone investigation through the seven locations is a mind that "has a location.
Once the investigation through the seven locations has been completed, the mind that "has a location" has long since been understood to have no location at all.
Furthermore, the mind that "has a location" relies upon an existing object to possess cognition; the mind that "has no location" relies upon non-existence.
To exist and yet have something to rely upon, and to have a mind that exists while relying upon something—Ānanda has already forgotten this.
Yet he still regards as "mind" that which relies upon non-existence while existing; this is why, although the Buddha rebuked him, Ānanda’s mind did not ultimately die away.
Even when one is detached from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and inwardly maintains a state of profound seclusion, it is still merely a portion of the dharma-dusts.
Because it is a separate reflection of an object, Ānanda’s mind found some degree of acceptance;
yet, he was ultimately unable to accept it fully because he had not realized that these objects and their reflections are merely different names for that which has no location.
If Ānanda had truly known that these objects and reflections are fundamentally states of non-existence that arise through being drawn forth—initially...
When there is no inherent nature, that which discriminates this reflection further transforms into the wisdom that perceives no external objects (*anartha-jñāna*).
Now, as for this wisdom that perceives no external objects, it leads one from the state of an ordinary person to that of a sage, and from delusion to enlightenment.
If this wisdom were lacking even slightly, then all sentient beings would ultimately be unable to attain Buddhahood. Therefore, is it not fitting to title this chapter "Illuminating the Mind"?

The *Buddhāvatamsaka-sūtra* states: "Because of clarity, there is seeing; because of darkness, there is non-seeing. When clarity arises spontaneously from within, then all appearances of darkness can never again obscure it.
Having realized this, I first understood that Confucius and Laozi were not of the same Way, but rather shared the same transformative function (*huà*).
From then on, my faith grew ever more earnest, and I truly came to aspire to attain Buddhahood for myself. Yet, how could this light wait for...?
Is it that [the Buddha-nature] exists only upon attaining Buddhahood? It is, in fact, present before us in our daily lives, never failing to shine with brilliant clarity.

It is only because the attachments of deluded calculations regarding light and darkness have not yet been eliminated that one can see when relying on the dust of light, but cannot see when not so relying;
thus, the aspect of darkness may appear obscure. If the attachment to light and darkness were to cease, one would see even in the midst of the great night.
It is no different from the bright day; yet within that bright day, the light itself does not increase. During the Jiajing era, there was a person who transcribed the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Because his sincerity was steadfast and ultimate, delusive thoughts did not arise and emotional attachments did not emerge;
he was able to transcribe the sūtra in a dark room as if it were broad daylight. I dare not keep this to myself, but wish to share it with the world, and have thus entrusted it to Siming.
Li Sheng recorded this:

At the very beginning of the faculties and their objects, the fundamental radiance is inherently and spontaneously perfect. Within this perfection, even a Buddha cannot find a foothold, let alone ordinary sentient beings.
Because this radiance is fundamentally devoid of a nature of permanence, it is momentarily unawakened to, and thus transforms to give rise to the faculties and objects; the radiance becomes ensnared.
Among these, that which is so named is consciousness (*vijñāna*). Now, there are six types of consciousness: that which resides in the eye and governs forms is called visual consciousness;

this continues up to that which resides in the mind and governs phenomena, which is called mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Furthermore, the seventh consciousness is also termed "mental consciousness," yet it differs from this [sixth] consciousness;

it is merely a case where the name is the same while the substance is different. Generally, for all sentient beings, [the sixth consciousness] does not take the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) as its primary objective domain.
It draws forth [the mind]. Consciousness does not arise in its entirety. If the six sense organs did not exist, even if consciousness were to arise, it would have no basis for support.

Therefore it is said: "The objects possess the functional activity that attracts the mind; the organs possess the capacity to provide a basis for consciousness. Mind and consciousness differ in name but are identical in essence; do not conceive of them as distinct. Alas!
Speaking from the perspective of the initial encounter between the organs and their objects, the brilliance of Yao and Zhou was neither increased nor diminished.

Once the sense organs and their objects are established as such, Yao and Zhou are separated by a distance as vast as that between heaven and earth; it is simply that Yao attained them while Zhou lost them.
This is like the seeing depending on light to perceive, where darkness results in non-seeing—this is precisely what it means for the sense organs and their objects to fall into a trap.
When ignorance does not arise spontaneously, this is precisely the state of the vast and empty roots and objects. Furthermore, "sinking" and "vastness" are fundamentally not fixed dharmas.
If one receives the熏炙 (xūnzhì—infusion and heating) of the Buddha-nature as its conditional cause, then at the very beginning of the roots and objects, the original light will become perfect;

in the end, there will surely be awakening and understanding. Understanding leads to practice; practice leads to final realization. Even if one has attained understanding but does not practice, [the habituation continues].
It will never be extinguished. When habituation is not extinguished, it is difficult to detach from the faculties and their objects.

If one can practice according to understanding, not only will the faculties and objects be utterly detached, but the faculties and objects themselves will all return to their original radiance. This matter is easy to speak of, yet most difficult to grasp;
if grasping it is already difficult, how much more so is practicing it? Yet, if one can simply practice, why worry about not attaining realization? Once it is attained, of itself—
Yet, the aspiration one makes is vast and great. This is truly because of compassion that shares in the same essence and kindness that accords with the nature of reality;
being both great and independent, how could it be confined to the small? Such as the Four Great Vows and the Ten Kings of Vows, all are made out of a deep sense of shared essence.
The mouth of a practitioner is narrow and small; I cannot exhaustively expound them for you in a single breath at once. I have merely written this down to serve as a preface.
Mao: Chengzi, you ought to know what is good and what is evil. Strive with diligence and advance toward enlightenment.
Because seeing depends on illumination, seeing itself is not the condition for illumination. Since illumination is not the condition, how could darkness be the condition?
By this I know that when there is the light of the sun, moon, and lamps, one sees the myriad things; when there is no light of the sun, moon, and lamps, one does not see the myriad things.

Judging by this principle, such a thing is impossible. Why? Because when one perceives darkness before one's eyes, since the darkness is already in front, the subject and object are distinct and clearly separate;
there is no mutual interaction between them. When comparing darkness to light, light is likewise the same.
Generally, one perceives objects by means of light; when the light fades, they are no longer seen. Therefore it is said: "Perception depends on light, and in darkness, non-seeing occurs.

However, if one perceives objects without depending on light, then even though all manner of dark forms appear before one, my perception—which requires no external condition—is fundamentally luminous from the start.
Therefore it is said: "When clarity arises spontaneously, then all dark forms can never obscure it."
Nevertheless, while an owl may catch fleas and lice by night and discern the finest hairs of autumn, it closes its eyes by day and cannot see Mount Tai;
yet cats and dogs can see both by day and by night. If they see both by day and by night, how do they differ from that vision which is without dependence?
Now, cats and dogs see when their faculties are complete and do not see when their faculties are incomplete; only the Sage has faculties that are entirely complete.
They see it as well. They see it when the faculties are incomplete. They see it even at the crown of the head; they see it on the feet, the back, and the abdomen.
There is not a single one of the eighty-four thousand pores throughout the four limbs and entire body that they do not see. Therefore, the Bodhisattva of Great Compassion—
There are eighty-four thousand arms of the mudrā; each arm has a hand, and each hand has an eye.

This is because writing cannot exhaust speech, and speech cannot exhaust the intended meaning. Thus, the Sages established symbols to fully express that meaning. It is like the body of a single person, which possesses six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*);
that upon which these six organs depend is called the six objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). Now, in the assembly at the Śūraṅgama [Samādhi], the Great Awakened Sage—

Among the six sense faculties, we briefly take up the faculty of the eye as an example. By means of the objective conditions (*viṣaya*) of light from the sun, moon, lamps, or fire, consciousness is aroused;

where there is consciousness, there is seeing. This is deluded seeing. True seeing does not depend upon such objective conditions of light, but is that which is fundamentally illuminating and all-pervasive without exception.
Since this is the case for one faculty, it is so for all the others. Thus, Linji said: "You all..."
"O people! Upon this lump of red flesh, there is a True Person of No Rank who dwells within your six sense organs and is able to radiate a great light.
If you give rise to the thought of trying to comprehend him, he is no longer the True Person."
Scratching an itch with the hand, one speaks of subject and object. Grasping the topknot with the hand, the body does not leave the ground.

Taking the sight as the cause and light as the condition, the sight is like my hand and the itch is like the condition of light. Observing it in this way, subject and object are distinct; they arise spontaneously from non-illumination.

Independent and without dependence, it does not arise from its own lack of clarity; its essential principle is inherently in accord with reality. Yet, arbitrary conceptualization suddenly arises, revolving through a thousand turns in mutual causation;
cause upon cause is inexhaustible, and consciousness is difficult to fathom. Only those who have attained the true Dharma-realm are not deceived by consciousness;

those who have attained "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*) are not deceived by mental discourse. All of this is based on examining and illuminating through function; were it not for the king of geese discerning the milk, it would truly be impossible.
[Ananda] asked:
"It is difficult to understand. Light and darkness alternate with one another, yet the essence of seeing is fundamentally serene.
When I do not see, why do I not see the place where I do not see? If I were to see that non-seeing, it would naturally not be that [darkness]."
The aspect of non-seeing: if one does not see the ground of my non-seeing, it is naturally not a thing;
how could it not be you? The Master said: One day, Chan Master Dahuì asked Attendant Lǐ, "If you call it a bamboo stick, you encounter resistance;
if you do not call it a bamboo stick, you turn your back on it. What is to be done? Lǐ was unable to answer, so he instead said, "I hope that the Venerable Master will act as a witness for me."
Using skillful means to point the way, Dahui said to him, "You are a man from Fuzhou. Let me offer you a metaphor:
it is like taking a choice grade of lychee and peeling away the skin and shell all at once, placing it right at the edge of your mouth with your hand—yet you simply do not know how to swallow it.
As Daguan was reading Dahui’s Recorded Sayings by lamplight, he reached this passage and could not help but [break into laughter].
A laughable thing! You all, tell me: what is there to laugh at? If you can realize it, there is no need for Daguān to waste his words.
Since you cannot realize it, let this old man explain this passage of scripture for you; it will not do any harm.
It is just like when the Tathāgata acted out of his "old woman’s heart" for Ānanda—how is this any different from Dàhuì peeling away the skin and shell to reveal the name?
I offered him a piece of lychee, placing it right at the lips of the attendant who served the ritual; yet he simply did not know how to swallow it.
For the most part, if one does not reach the ground where intellect is exhausted and emotion is withered, one will certainly be unable to take this matter up.
But tell me, what is the appearance of intellect being exhausted and emotion withered? *Pfft!* The clay ox returns from afar at midnight, trampling through the ten thousand peaks ahead.
Qingyun: From that awakened clarity, there arose a clarity that was itself an awareness; having lost its essential lucidity, it became adhered to delusion and emitted light.

Therefore, at present, when you are free from darkness and free from light, the essence of seeing does not exist; when you are free from movement and free from stillness, the substance of hearing is fundamentally absent; there is neither penetration nor obstruction.

The nature of smelling does not arise; it neither transforms nor remains still. Tasting has no point of emergence; it neither separates nor joins. The perception of touch is fundamentally non-existent; it neither ceases nor arises.

When you thoroughly understand where these rest, you need only refrain from following the twelve conditioned characteristics—movement and stillness, union and separation, stillness and transformation, penetration and obstruction, arising and ceasing, light and darkness.
By uprooting even one of these, you will detach from the sticky attachment and settle inwardly.

Prostrate in submission to the primordial truth; it awakens the radiance of the fundamental source. This radiant nature, once manifested, causes all other five-fold adhesions to be uprooted and perfectly liberated.
This knowing and seeing does not arise from external objects, nor does the clarity follow the sense organs; rather, clarity is manifested by relying upon the organs.
Thus, the six faculties function as one another. Ānanda, do you not know that in this assembly, Aniruddha is without eyes?
Thus they were seen: the dragon Baddhananda heard without ears; the goddess of the Gaṅgā smelled fragrances without a nose;
Gavāmpati perceived flavors with a different kind of tongue; and the Śūnyatā-deva felt touch without a body. They were made to appear momentarily by being reflected within the light of the Tathāgata.
Yet, being of the nature of wind, their bodies were originally non-existent. This is how it is for those who have attained the extinction samādhi and the śrāvakas who have reached tranquility.
In this assembly, Mahākāśyapa has long since extinguished the faculty of the mind; he possesses perfect, clear understanding that does not depend on mental ideation.

Ānanda, if your faculties were now to be completely uprooted, their inner luminosity would radiate forth, such that these superficial objects of perception, as well as the physical world itself, [would vanish].
All manifested forms are like ice melting in hot water; they should, through mindfulness, be transformed into supreme awakening.
The Master said: "The numinous light shines in stillness, pervasive and pure. There is no room within for anything else; that there should be any dharma external to this is impossible.

Whenever sentient beings perceive dharmas as existing outside the mind, it is all due to the arising of a fleeting thought. When a thought arises, there is immediately a self; when there is a self, there is..."

There are limits, and thus there is the internal and the external. The internal refers to the sense organs and consciousness; the external refers to the environment and its conditions (*niśraya-vipāka*).
The environment and its conditions are insentient; the primary retribution (*samyak-vipāka*) is sentient. Because these exist, there arises the notion of "I" and "mine.

Although the three subtleties and six coarsenesses differ in their sequential order of arising, when traced back to their origin, they are fundamentally one single, perfect, and eternal Buddha-nature. By means of this...

After sentient beings give rise to thoughts, they remain entirely unaware of this; they are stuck to the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) takes its seat therein.

They become attached to the subject and the object—the "subject" being the six sense organs and the "object" being the six sense fields. These boundaries between the organs, the objects, the subject, and the object are strictly defined.
Consequently, the visual consciousness presides over forms, the auditory consciousness presides over sounds, and the same applies to the other four. This is what is meant by "due to that."
Awakened clarity: there is clarity within clarity, which is awakened clarity. This awakened clarity is the true mind; this clear awakening is the deluded mind.

This deluded mind is simply the true mind turning in confusion; it does not arise as a separate deluded mind apart from the true mind. Since it is confused about the truth, it loses its essential lucidity;
it clings to the unreal and emits light. The sense organs and their objects are that to which one clings; consciousness is that which clings. It is, for example, like this:
Visual consciousness cannot arise of itself; it must be triggered by the two objects of light and darkness.

As soon as this consciousness exists, if the external objects were absent, the consciousness would ultimately not exist. Therefore, for one who perceives phenomena outside the mind, there must be external objects;
where there are external objects, there is deluded consciousness. Once deluded consciousness exists, the six sense organs function in their proper sequence, without the slightest error.
All of this is due to being shrouded by the obscurations of emotional consciousness (*qing-shi*).

If one can, in this very moment, illuminate this single thought-moment (*nien*) as originally lacking the characteristic of arising—that is, that the thought is fundamentally non-existent—then since even the thought itself does not exist, how could there be external objects (*qian-chen*)?
Those who possess external objects as obstructions simply cannot, at this very point, directly penetrate and break through this thought. Thus, Qingliang said: "Ten ages..."

From antiquity to the present, from beginning to end, nothing departs from the present moment of thought (*citta*). The boundless oceans of lands and the distinction between self and other are not separated by so much as a hair’s tip.
For where there is thought, there is self and other; where there is thought, there is past and present. Since it is already improper to think of another as "one," how could there be "two"?
Viewed in this light, heaven and earth, the myriad things, and all sentient beings do not transcend my single thought. Furthermore...

The Tiantai Master Zhiyi said: "A single thought-moment possesses the three thousand [realms]. This means that when there is thought, the three thousand are present; when thought ceases, the three thousand vanish. This refers to the time of non-thought.
A practitioner who has truly given rise to the bodhicitta should, at the very moment a thought arises, realize it is ungraspable.
When contemplating the breath, one illuminates the ten voids. Thus, this section of the sutra initially addresses nothing more than the delusion of the true mind into a deluded mind;
because there is a deluded mind, there are sense organs and objects; because there are sense organs and objects, there are boundaries.
Because there are boundaries, one cannot exercise spiritual penetration through mutual interaction. This is explained from the perspective of delusion.

If one is free from both darkness and light, and the substance of seeing no longer exists, does it mean that seeing itself has vanished? If seeing had vanished, one would be nothing more than a wooden puppet.
That seeing arises because of light and darkness is merely the consciousness that responds to objects. To have seeing apart from light and darkness—
This is the illumination of the true mind. At this critical juncture, it is precisely the root of delusion and awakening.

If one awakens to it, the consciousness that responds to objects is itself true vision. If one does not awaken to it, the illumination of the true mind is itself the consciousness that responds to objects.
It is not that there are two separate things; it is only because of delusion and enlightenment that there appear to be these two states. As it is with one faculty, so it is with all faculties.

When the true mind gives rise to illumination, it does not depend upon external objects to arise. Since its arising does not depend on objects, this is an illumination that is independent and detached from things.
Being independent means that there is no dharma outside the mind. If there is no dharma outside the mind, I do not know what else to call it.
Acting in this way constitutes the roots and objects of perception. Thus Yunmen said: "The entire earth is a single eye of the śramaṇa.
This intention of Yunmen is precisely what the Sūtra says: "Now, when all your faculties have been completely uprooted, their inner luminosity will radiate forth;

thus the superficial phenomena and the world-receptacle, along with all their changing manifestations, will melt away like ice dissolving in hot water, and in an instant they shall transform into the Unsurpassed [Buddhahood]."
Sentient awareness. The vessel-world (the physical environment) is insentient; sentient beings are sentient.
How can sentient beings awaken to the Way so that the entire insentient vessel-world is also transformed into supreme sentient awareness?
This aperture—where it is located is unknown. If one finds this aperture, one may say that the insentient vessel-world attains Buddhahood. One may also say...
It is also possible for sentient beings not to attain Buddhahood; that is to say, taking the head as the tail and calling the tail the head.

When the scales are held in one's own hand, who is it that bestows praise or censure? Reaching this point, it is also possible to say that while the six sense faculties do not exist, there is nonetheless seeing and hearing.

It is also possible to have the six sense-faculties while lacking seeing and hearing. The aforementioned words of Yunmen possess a place of illumination; when there is illumination, there is function.
Even if one understands the purport of the sutras, it remains merely a single act of illumination. As for the place of function, it depends upon the person.
That the six sense-faculties are used interchangeably is not particularly extraordinary. If one understands through conditions and realizes it through them, the resonance is swift.

This phrase is precisely what you have been using all along. Although this section of the scripture describes how delusion arises from the Truth and how one returns to the Truth through delusion—manifesting a multitude of functions—it is nothing more than the ordinary, everyday affairs of our own lives.

Those who are deluded call it something extraordinary; yet, as the ancient masters said: "The numinous light shines alone, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects. Such talk is merely...
This is spoken for those who have not yet awakened the mind. If there were even a slight glimpse of insight, upon hearing this they would surely snort with laughter incessantly.
Since it is called "spiritual radiance," it is vividly alive. To speak of it as being thus utterly transcendent or not transcendent—yet fundamentally, it has no boundaries or shores.
This physical shell is no more than three or five feet long; by means of these three or five feet, [it manifests all].
Place it within that which has no boundaries or shores. Now tell me: is this utterly transcendent, or is it not?
If you say it is not utterly transcendent, how can this six-foot physical shell encompass the spiritual light that has no boundaries or shores? If you say it is utterly transcendent—
Right now, the great assembly is none other than sitting in a nest upon this very physical frame.
Although this nest is only five or six feet long, unless one is a truly heroic man of genuine spirit, do not even attempt to lift it up;
let alone speak of whether it is utterly transcendent or not. If it were indeed so, what would ultimately be good? The single retribution of the three paths of existence.
Five thousand kalpas have passed; when will the head emerge?

True mind and reality cannot be sought as a single entity, yet they are attained through multiplicity. Furthermore, they cannot be known through a pervasive body, nor can they be measured by non-pervasiveness.
Thus, they transcend both unity and multiplicity, and transcend both pervasiveness and non-pervasiveness. Therefore, they are able to be one and yet able to be many.
"Much. It is capable of being pervasive and incapable of being pervasive. Now Ānanda has not realized the true mind; he merely clings to objects and makes arbitrary calculations.

Therefore, the Tathāgata, knowing the locus of his ailment, dispenses medicine according to his capacity. To speak of it ultimately, there is no real meaning whatsoever, nor is there any fixed method. As when he questioned Ānanda:
'If [the awareness] were entirely pervasive, then when you prick [your body], it should be felt everywhere. Since you prick only one spot, [it is not pervasive]...'"

It is logically impossible for the substance [of the body] to possess multiple sensations while being devoid of consciousness. The Tathāgata challenged Ānanda’s calculation regarding the location [of sensation] with this intent:
if one touches a single limb and all four limbs perceive it, then that which is touched would know, and those not touched would also know;

thus one could say that the one being touched is not being touched. Why? Because since the three limbs not touched possess cognition, the single limb that is touched may likewise be considered as such.
No Emphasis. *The Collected Works of Old Man Zibo*, Volume Eleven;
*The Collected Works of Old Man Zibo*, Volume Twelve.
Ming Dynasty: Han-shan Deqing reads the verse of Vipaśyin Buddha.
Now, if one contemplates the external elements of solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion, this body is fundamentally not "mine. It exists prior to the external objects of perception.

Contemplating this, one sees that this mind originally has no place of birth. When observing it from the perspective of external objects and the mind, both transgressions and blessings are fundamentally without a master.
Thus it is said: "One borrows the four great elements to form a body. How could the Tathāgata’s great compassion deceive me?
Huang Tingjian of the Song dynasty, styled Shangu, was once approached by a nobleman who sought a calligraphic transcription of a composition he himself had written, using silk as payment.
Shangu laughed and said, "What is there of value in the writings composed by Tingjian? Only the poems of Hanshan serve as the means to cool the burning house of this world.
He then transcribed them for him and further instructed him, saying, "Although the poems of Hanshan are excellent, their source derives from..."
The verses of the Seven Buddhas have flowed forth from this source; thus, wherever Shanguo found pleasure in his travels, he inscribed these verses most frequently.
Among the verses of the Seven Buddhas, those of Vipaśyin Buddha are especially sublime.

The reason for this is that among the thousand Buddhas of the past, it would not have been possible to bring their lineage to completion without this Buddha; and among the thousand Buddhas of the present, it would likewise not be so without him.
None can achieve its beginning; to achieve both the beginning and the end truly depends upon this verse.

Therefore, for those who read, recite, copy, uphold, joyfully expound, and disseminate the verses of Vipaśyin Buddha, all the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, together with their supernatural powers, manifest the mark of the broad and long tongue to praise that person’s merit as being no small amount. Vipaśyin Buddha—this...
It is said that all are the sovereign awakening. Alas! All are the sovereign awakening. All obstacles to non-sovereignty have from the beginning not originated from anything else;
therefore it is said: "The mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction.

It is only that the Buddhas skillfully employ their minds, such that there is nowhere they do not attain sovereignty; whereas sentient beings do not skillfully employ their minds, such that there is nowhere they do not [fall into bondage].
It is not an external obstruction. Yet this obstruction does not descend from heaven, nor does it arise from the earth, nor is it bestowed by humans.
Because one perceives a self-body (*ātma-śarīra*), death, birth, honor, and disgrace arrive. Because one perceives a self-mind (*ātma-citta*), likes, dislikes, and afflictions (*kleśa*) arrive.
Indeed, death and birth, honor and disgrace, likes and dislikes, and afflictions all stem from this self-body and this self-mind.

It is the fundamental source. If there were a courageous man capable of pulling up its roots and blocking its source right away, then the obstacles of sentient beings would never have been anything other than the liberation of the Buddhas.
The *Sūtra on the Eight Great Persons' Awakening* states: "The mind is the source of evil;
the body is the thicket of transgressions. By this, I further believe that what Shangu said regarding the poems of Hanshan—that they are a "fertilizer"—is indeed true.
This is the means for cooling the burning house; its source flows from the verses of the Seven Buddhas. There is no deception here. Someone asked:

"The source of evil is withered and the thicket of transgressions is empty; is there a Way? He replied: "Borrowing the four great elements to form a body—the mind is fundamentally unborn, arising only because of external objects.
If one can read and recite this half-verse, reciting it and reflecting upon it, reflecting and attaining clarity, and through clarity...
Once you have attained realization, you will know for yourself whether the source of evil has been dried up or not, and whether the thicket of transgressions has become empty or not;
this is not something that can be conveyed by my words alone.
Now, the mind is the source of evil, and the body is the thicket of transgression. All that possesses vital breath and blood must possess consciousness;

is not vital breath and blood the substance of the body? Is not consciousness the mind? Alas! As for this body and this mind, no one knows what strange monsters they are, yet they poison sentient beings in such a manner.
There is a saying: "The practice of cultivation has no other technique than this: if one can simply act with self-restraint, one will naturally attain [liberation]."
One’s own body and mind are thus understood. Yet, how can one attain this very body and mind? Is this not a matter of no small significance?

For this reason, the Sage takes pity on them and establishes great skillful means, enabling ordinary people of the broad earth to transform the source of evil into an ocean of compassion, and to transform the thicket of sin into a grove of merit.
They realize that form is not form, and they understand that the mind is not mind. It is not...
As for form, it fills the eight extremities without entanglement; as for that which is not mind, its wisdom encompasses all things without toil.
Such wondrous function is none other than that expressed in the verse of Viśvabhū Buddha. Viśvabhū Buddha means "The All-Pervasive Enlightened One.
This pervasive enlightenment stands resplendent and solitary within the daily activities of sentient beings, from the very beginning free of obstruction.
An obstruction. Yet, for the Buddhas, it becomes an object of free enjoyment; for sentient beings, it becomes an obstacle.
Tell me, where does the root of this sickness lie? *Pah!* When all the beings of the great earth attain perfect enlightenment, the Buddhas of the ten directions fall into hell.
Now, the root of affliction has no foundation; it is rooted in body and mind. This is why Yanzi cast off his limbs and discarded his keen faculties—to uproot the source of affliction.
Laozi also said: "I have a great affliction: that I possess a body. If I did not have a body..."
What cause for concern could there be? From this it may be said: the body is the stake upon which hunger, cold, honor, disgrace, birth, and death depend.

If one contemplates the body through the lens of solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion, then the stake of suffering will fall without even needing to be pushed over. The mind is the stake upon which likes and dislikes, right and wrong, depend.
If one contemplates the mind through the lens of the identity of self and others as sharing a single root, then the stake of toil, likes and dislikes, and various poisons [will likewise collapse].
Nor does it wait for being pushed before it falls. Alas! Once the two posts have fallen, body, mind, and emotions wither away. Solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion are themselves the *dharmakāya*.
That which is capable of liking and disliking is the poison of conceptualization; that which is free from such likes and dislikes is non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
With the fish of non-conceptual wisdom swimming in the ocean of the boundless *dharmakāya*, the water does not wait for the fish to forget itself—the fish forgets itself spontaneously.
The fish does not wait for the water to be forgotten; the water, too, forgets itself. When fish and water forget one another, they float and sink with ease within a state of pure clarity.
Thus, both the fish and the water serve as intermediaries for the primordial image (*xiangxian*). May the Layman Pochen exert himself toward this end.
Viśvabhū Buddha—this is translated as "Sovereign Enlightenment" (*svayambhū*). "Enlightenment" (*bodhi*) and "sovereignty" (*svayam*) are mutually designated according to essence and function.

For where there is enlightenment, there is sovereignty; where there is sovereignty, there is enlightenment. Thus, the essence and function of the Sage are perfectly integrated: nothing coarse is not subtle. Where there is subtlety, there is oneness;

where there is oneness, there is no dependence; where there is no dependence, there is no exteriority. Where there is no exteriority, things and self share the same root, and heaven and earth are one.
The essence does not discard the great for the sake of the small; the essence does not discard its function. As for the faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*):

the faculties do not establish themselves independently; they are established by means of the objects. The objects do not establish themselves independently; they appear as guests by means of the faculties. If they are established by means of the objects, do the objects truly exist?

If they appear as guests by means of the faculties, do the guests truly exist? Once these two points are resolved, both self and phenomena are silent and still. Therefore it is said: "Silent and still..."
The realm of myriad transformations functions within a single void; thus, the faculties do not obstruct the objects, and the objects do not obstruct the faculties.
When the great function is complete, there is no trace. Where there is no trace, where are "self" and "other" to be found? To know this is called awakening.

That the faculties and objects do not mutually hinder one another is called sovereignty. If it is so, then the faculties have never truly existed as faculties, and the objects have never truly existed as objects.
Dust. The sage skillfully employs his mind; therefore, he is autonomous and awakened. Ordinary people do not skillfully employ their minds;
thus, what should have been autonomy and awakening instead becomes the obstacle of lack of autonomy. From this, I know that one should contemplate the body by means of the four great elements.
There is the function of the body, yet no characteristic of a body; by observing the mind through preceding objects, there is the function of the mind, yet no grasping at a self.
Therefore, this half-verse is truly the hexagram-line for breaking through birth and death, and the King of Physicians for treating the diseases of the mind.
Now, at the very origin of body and mind, there exists that which is neither body nor mind. It is profoundly still, perfectly complete, and exists alone.
Fuxi obtained it and drew the trigrams; Confucius obtained it and supplemented the *I Ching*; Laozi obtained it and composed the two chapters [of the *Daodejing*].
Our Great Awakened Elder obtained it at the assembly on Vulture Peak, where he held up a flower and smiled before the assembly of humans and devas.
A hundred thousand [beings], sages and ordinary folk intermingled, yet only those of the Kāśyapa clan attained it.
From that time, through the lineage of Ānanda, down to Bodhidharma, Dajian (Huineng), Nanyue, and Qingyuan, they all attained it in succession.
Thus, there are thousands of transformations and myriad changes: ghostly faces and divine heads;

some take compassion as their samādhi, some take wrath as their samādhi, some take ascetic practice as their samādhi, some take speech and written words as their samādhi, and some take the staff, the shout, or the smashing of a sand bowl as their samādhi—extending even to rolling wooden balls and grasping wooden snakes.
The accounts of such deeds as slaying serpents, subduing tigers, and rebuking dragons are too numerous to cite.
These various samādhis, encompassing both mundane and supramundane dharmas, interact and transform one another, causing all sentient beings to employ them in their daily lives without realizing it.

Whether they realize it or not, those who do not realize it are called ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), while those who do realize it are called sages (*ārya*). Alas! Sages and ordinary beings are originally and fundamentally one.
It is simply a matter of knowing or not knowing; this is what distinguishes the ordinary person from the sage. Viewed from this perspective, both knowing and not knowing depend on oneself.
Why, then, are those who know so few while those who do not know so many? Where does the fault lie?
It is truly because since birth we have reckoned the body and mind as the "self," yet that which exists prior to the body and mind is profoundly still and perfectly round.
Full. Wondrous things are free from entanglement, yet one turns away from them in ignorance and remains unaware. Once unaware, one is forever unaware.

Thus, though all have received the same endowment since the time of Bhīṣmagarjitasvarakalpa until the present day, they remain utterly bewildered and lack realization. This exhausts the efforts of the Sages, who pull from the right and guide from the left;
through hundreds of schemes and thousands of methods, they apply every artful means until their skills are exhausted, yet there is still no awakening at all. The ancients called this—
It is only fitting that these people are called walking corpses and roaming flesh, or "daytime ghosts.

I, Viśvabhū Buddha, did not withdraw my vow because sentient beings are difficult to save; I spoke this verse to ensure that ordinary worldlings at the stage of common ground may together ascend to the Unsurpassed.
Now, as for the "Unsurpassed," it refers to the primordial state of body and mind, wherein there is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, its light—

It penetrates through all eternity; its wondrousness transcends all existence. Its majestic spiritual power is unfathomable. To attain it is to become a sage; to lose it is to remain an ordinary person.
If this is so, the distinction between the ordinary and the sage does not lie beyond the nesting burrows of body and mind.
For those who can overturn and shatter these, liberation is boundless; for those who cannot overturn and shatter them, obstacles persist for long kalpas. Indeed, birth and death have no root.

The body is taken as the root; yet likes and dislikes have no fundamental basis. The mind is taken as the basis. If one can contemplate the body through the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), where does the body exist?
If one contemplates the mind regarding preceding objects, from where does the mind arise? Knowing where the body exists, the body exists yet is without entanglement.
Knowing how the mind arises, the mind exists yet does not arise. When the body exists without entanglement, what can birth and death obstruct?
If the mind exists yet does not arise, what hindrance can there be in responding to objects? What obstacle can there be to birth and death? Thus, the wheel of vows turns perpetually;
responding to objects without hindrance, the sun of wisdom remains ever-bright. Nevertheless, for a beginner on the initial path, one should not take the recitation of verses as a ladder or a vessel.
Thus, the ocean of suffering is difficult to cross. Furthermore, there are differences among those who uphold these gāthās—superior, middling, and inferior.

Those of superior capacity possess profound and subtle celestial faculties; they attain awakening upon merely touching the verses. Those of middling capacity must persevere for a long time before their minds are opened. Those of inferior capacity proceed by reading and reciting;
through recitation they come to uphold them, and through upholding them they become proficient. Once proficiency is attained, they may enter [the path] in this very life, or else...

Through many births one may attain entry; once entered, one is fundamentally the same as others. Upon reaching the highest realization, there is no difference. Viewed from this perspective, there is no distinction between sharp and dull faculties;
all who are able to believe can escape suffering. For what reason, then, do you willingly abandon yourselves to ruin?

Some, burdened by poverty and low status, are unable to uphold the verses; others, burdened by wealth and nobility, are unable to uphold the verses. Whether in poverty and low status or in wealth and nobility, though there be honor or disgrace—
It is not equal; suffering is of no two kinds. Furthermore, the passage of years cannot be toyed with; old age and sickness do not wait for an appointment with anyone.
When a single breath does not return, one immediately becomes another world. All manner of karmic offenses are what you yourself have created; you cannot avoid following them.
Following you without ever leaving, they are like a shadow following a form. Whether in the heavens, among humans, or within the great void of space, there is nowhere at all for you to escape.
If one could escape from these states, then the intelligence of all Buddhas, Patriarchs, Sages, and Worthies would not equal the folly of an ordinary person.
Borrowing the four elements to form a body, the mind is fundamentally unborn, arising only because of external objects. As for the affliction of birth, there is nothing...
Greater than birth and death are the afflictions of birth and death; only the Perfected Person (*zhiren*) can transcend them and remain free from entanglement.
Those below this level—who would not be burdened by them? Furthermore, birth and death are rooted in having a body.
As Laozi said: "I have a great affliction, which is that I have a body. Therefore, the world-transcending sages revealed this verse to awaken such people. This body—
It is formed by the aggregation of the five elements and exists through the combination of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
What are called the four great elements are earth, water, fire, and wind. Why are these four called "great"? Because they pervade everywhere, they are termed "great.
When these four great elements are within the body, they constitute flesh, skin, tendons and bones, blood vessels, and phlegm and saliva.
It serves as lymphatic fluid, as heat, and as movement. This present body before us is nothing more than a composite of these elements.
Having been so composed, sentient beings fail to realize it is not solid; they stubbornly cling to it as "self.

Therefore, at the threshold of death and rebirth, when faced with the critical juncture of gain and loss, their minds become dazed and confused; though they devise a thousand schemes and ten thousand plans, they do nothing but seek to preserve it.
Regarding this physical shell: one must realize that this body exists through the influence of earth upon its skin, flesh, sinews, and bones;
through the influence of water upon its blood, vessels, and fluids; through the influence of fire upon all its heat; and through the influence of wind upon all its movements.
Therefore, the wise do not wait for a leisurely moment to cultivate this contemplation, but constantly practice it within the midst of daily life.
Contemplate this: skin, flesh, sinews, and bones originally arise from earth; blood, vessels, and fluids originally arise from water; heat and energy originally arise from fire;
and movement and transformation originally arise from wind. These four great elements are shared by all sentient beings and every creature possessing breath and vitality.
Why am I so deluded as to stubbornly and falsely grasp them as my body? This contemplation pervades [all things].

Whether turning, looking up or down, advancing or retreating, bending or stretching, one should always maintain focused concentration without interruption. Gradually becoming pure and proficient, one suddenly attains awakening and realizes:
"Where is this body? Thus, those of old who attained realization said: "To bring one's head close to a white blade is like cutting through the spring breeze.
Furthermore, all the various afflictions of birth and death are like arrows, and my body is like a target. Having awakened to the nature of this body, it becomes firm.
Moisture, warmth, and motion each return to their respective sources. When the target itself no longer exists, who is there to receive the arrow? Therefore it is said:
"The body is provisionally formed by borrowing from the four great elements. Now, as for the mind, there is the true mind and there is the deluded mind.

The true mind is that in which there is no distinction between the sage and the ordinary person, and in which there is nothing to be added or subtracted. It is vast, numinous, and luminous, pervasively and perfectly full—this is its original state.

There is no birth; how could there be death? Fundamentally there is no coming; how could there be going? Transcending birth and death and severing coming and going, it is not separate from daily life;
it is profoundly still and ever-present. It cannot be attained through a mind that grasps at existence, nor can it be sought by a mind devoid of thought.

Only those who can divine its mystery and illuminate its brilliance may approach it. If this mind is not awakened, though one’s attire be as elegant as a scholar’s, one is nothing more than a walking corpse.

Flesh. Man is the most spiritual among all things. If one does not feel a sense of awe and dread regarding this, nor experience a sudden awakening of self-reflection, then one is either deluded or possessed by demons.
The deluded mind arises in response to external objects and is constrained by them;

thus, it rejoices when encountering favorable conditions and becomes angry when encountering adverse ones. Hatred and love entwine, drowning the luminous mind (the *lingtai*). Once this state is accepted by the heart, resentment...
It does not immediately release; joy does not immediately transform. These are all deluded minds.

The true mind, although responding to objects, cannot be burdened by them, just as a bright mirror reflects images: though it distinguishes between the beautiful and the ugly, it originally has no mind [of its own].
The deluded mind, however, exists because of objects and is thus burdened by them. Therefore it is said: "The mind is originally without arising; it exists because of objects."
Viśvabhū Buddha—this means "the one who is awakened to all sovereignty. Since he is awakened to sovereignty, what thing could possibly act as an obstruction?
Yet for those who are not yet awakened, they cannot avoid becoming stalled in a single path: when seeing form, they are obstructed by form;
when seeing emptiness, they are obstructed by emptiness; and when suddenly there is a body, they are obstructed by the body. In this momentary state...
Yet, when there is a mind, one is obstructed by the mind and obstructed by the body; one is obstructed by birth, old age, sickness, and death, and obstructed by joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure.
Thus, while revolving within a single light, one falsely establishes separate positions. Once these positions are established, total lack of mastery arrives:
birth is pressed by old age, old age is pressed by sickness, sickness is pressed by death, and joy is [pressed by sorrow].
Anger is driven by distress; anger is driven by sorrow; sorrow is driven by joy. "Driven" (po) refers to mutual impulsion. Alas!
If birth were fixed and permanent, old age could not drive it; if joy were fixed and permanent, sorrow could not drive it. Because they are impermanent, their flow cannot be halted.
Only those who possess the Way realize that the body is impermanent because it is composed of the four great elements, and they realize that the mind is impermanent...

Because the preceding object arises, one realizes the four types of impermanence. Because the body depends [on conditions], one realizes that the body is impermanent. Because objects exist due to the mind, one realizes that objects are impermanent.
By using "one" to wash away "four," the four have no place to stand. By using "four" to wash away "one," the one has nothing remaining.

By using "objects" to wash away "mind," the mind was originally non-existent. By using "mind" to wash away "objects," objects do not remain of themselves. When "one" and "four" mutually wash each other away, both mind and objects are simultaneously eliminated.
Forgetfulness. To manifest a single body as infinite bodies, while the physical form remains unimpaired and the mind focused on a single thought, yet its concern pervades all things;
the inner core is fundamentally tranquil. From the state where all is not self-mastered, one enters the state where all is self-mastered.
For one who attains this, a single kṣaṇa can transcend vast kalpas. If one has not yet attained it, the banner of liberation becomes nothing more than a walking corpse or a lump of flesh. Wisdom.

The "ford" (jin) is translated as the turbulent waves of the sea of suffering. From antiquity to the present, even the most eminent heroes and geniuses have been unable to break through this pivotal mechanism.
Though their achievements may tower over the ages and their fame illuminate ten thousand generations, they have no connection whatsoever to the matter of one's own fundamental nature.
Thus, when born, they are deluded by birth; when aging, they are deluded by old age; when ill, they are deluded by illness; and when dying, they are deluded by death.

Death is delusion. At times of joy, anger, sorrow, and delight, one experiences joy, anger, sorrow, and delight while deluded; thus, delusion follows upon delusion, and there is no day when delusion ceases.
Man is the most spiritual among all things, yet his spirit does not awaken. To continue delusion with this very spirit is the root of all dark karma (*kṛṣṇa-karman*).

Even if mountains were as high as they are and oceans as deep as they are, there would never be a time when they could be shaken or exhausted; how can those who possess even a modicum of self-reflection fail to feel dread?

Furthermore, spiritual clarity is like water that flows through and connects all things; delusion is like ice that obstructs and blocks. When there is flow and connection, one is square when in a square and round when in a circle.
When there is obstruction and blockage, one remains fixedly square when in a square and fixedly round when in a circle.

To have no stagnation in being square or round is called "vitality"; to have fixedness in being square or round is called "death. Therefore, the sage dwells within the square and the round, yet remains neither square nor round.
Nothing can obstruct it. Because it is unobstructed, it is able to penetrate the sentiments of all under heaven.
Ordinary people are not so; seeing the square, they are deluded by the square; seeing the circle, they give rise to attachment to the circle.
Thus, with the sage, one is dead yet alive; with ordinary people, one is alive yet dead. Therefore, the sage is called a "living person," while ordinary people are called "dead."
Thus, when one observes this, how many among those born as humans since ancient times have truly attained [enlightenment]? To become a sage is not difficult;
the difficulty lies in attaining spiritual penetration (*tongling*). If one can attain spiritual penetration, it is not only that one's own body and mind become spiritually attuned;

on a grand scale, it extends to the vast multitude of the void, heaven, earth, and all things, and on a minute scale, there is nothing—from a single blade of grass, a speck of dust, a single hair, to a single strand—that is not [penetrated].
How wondrous! As for the Tripiṭaka and the Six Classics, the various schools of philosophy, and even the crafts of the hundred artisans—there is nothing he does not master.
Thus, his physical spirit is so penetrating that no matter can obstruct it; his mental spirit is so penetrating that no principle can hinder it.
He transforms birth, old age, sickness, and death into unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*; he turns anger, joy, grief, and pleasure into the realization of *mahābodhi*. This is *nirvāṇa* and *bodhi*.
It is attained through body and mind; if there were no body and mind, by what means could the two fruits be realized? Therefore it is said: "This body is a mountain of defilement;
this mind is an ocean of various poisons. Once one realizes that the body has no self, the mountain of defilement is immediately a mass of merit.
To realize that the mind is like an illusion is to see that the ocean of various poisons is, in fact, the nectar of *prajñā*. Man is the most spiritual being among all things;
yet, failing to value himself, he willingly becomes a dead man rather than a living one. How truly lamentable!

This half-verse consists of only fourteen characters; yet within it, the Great Canon and its seventeen hundred koans, the essentials of the Nine Classics, the Two Treatises, and the Hundred Schools are all fully contained.

If you were to expand and expound upon it—even if the Great Earth were used as ink, Mount Kunlun as a brush, the celestial winds as a hand, and empty space as paper—it could never be exhausted. Therefore:
He said: "The Buddha-dharma possesses inconceivable power. Since it is called 'inconceivable,' how could it be known through the speculative conjectures of sentient beings?
One should simply believe with earnestness and uphold it; then, in the end, one will naturally awaken and enter [the truth]. Now, faith is sincerity, and sincerity is oneness.
When there is oneness, my mind in upholding this verse has nothing whatsoever to which it clings. If one continues in this way for a long time,"
Then, the arbitrary conceptualizations of body and mind will suddenly burst apart. At that moment, birth and death are cast as nirvana, and afflictions are transformed into bodhi.
These two are called the "two fruits of the transformation of the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*):

namely, transforming birth and death to rely upon nirvana, and transforming afflictions to rely upon bodhi. However, the mental consciousness of ordinary beings is coarse and restless; they ultimately do not...

One must be able to restrain [the mind] in a single place. Therefore, it is necessary to proceed from reading to recitation; through recitation, one maintains [the text]; through maintenance, one becomes focused; through focus, one becomes unified.
When unified, one approaches transformation. Through approaching transformation, one will then ride upon conditions to enter the state of non-arising.
When the Daoist Daguān was once bestowing the verse of the transmission of the Dharma by Vipaśyin Buddha upon others, he would invariably say:
"Recite it a hundred, a thousand, ten million times, and its free and spontaneous enjoyment will manifest before you. Vipaśyin Buddha means "the All-Pervasive Sovereign Awakened One.
To deeply investigate its purport, the essential point is simply to shatter the attachments to the body and mind of sentient beings. Therefore, it is said: "It is borrowed..."
The four great elements constitute the body; the mind is fundamentally without birth, yet it exists because of objects.
Observing this, one sees that from beginningless kalpas until today, all sentient beings have been unable to attain mastery amidst birth and death, or amidst hatred and love.
This is truly because, upon seeing a self-body, the characteristics of the body become an obstruction; and upon seeing a self-mind, the characteristics of the mind become an obstruction.
Obstruction. Alas! The characteristics of the body obstruct outwardly, and the characteristics of the mind obstruct inwardly.
With one movement and one stillness, the internal and external obstruct each other; there is not a single moment of a state of transcendence. How lamentable this is!
Yet within this very state of obstruction, for the Sage in his daily life, the body fills the Dharma-realm—like the moon reflecting in myriad waters—and wisdom encompasses all things—like a mirror.
It illuminates all beings; it arrives without haste and pervades everywhere without exertion. Dongpo’s "Record of the Hall of Great Compassion" (*Dabei ge ji*) is a commentary on this verse.
Its summary states: "Great Compassion is a manifestation of Avalokiteśvara. Why should one alone doubt Great Compassion?
If one infers from Dongpo’s intent, then if the mind's thoughts are not tranquil, its response to things will necessarily be chaotic."

It is not that Dongpo did not know that movement is stillness and form is emptiness; rather, it is because Dongpo’s capacity was limited to his own station, whereby he could only realize the state of the principle as it is inherently present.
He had not yet reached the stage where, being without a body, one manifests many bodies, and being without a mind, one’s wisdom reflects all things.
Such a stage is that of a Great Bodhisattva; how could it be easily attained? Nevertheless, observing Dongpo...
If you fully comprehend the intent of Sōgi, then what you perceive will be free from delusion.

Taking this undeluded vision as your foundation, push forward with sincerity through the realms of hatred and love, and at the critical juncture of birth and death; eventually, there will surely come a time when you reach the stage of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
The *Śāstra on the Eight Arousals of the Great Men*:

Now, awakening and non-awakening are like the clenching and opening of a hand. The Sage, knowing this to be so, takes the very awareness that sentient beings fail to recognize in their daily lives and unfolds it into the eight arousals.
When one awakens, it is like the clenched fist returning to being a hand; once the hand is restored, [the state of awakening is complete].
Thus, one may lift and guide the four modes of birth and transport the three periods of time; one may bind the vast void like a mustard seed and crumble the great earth into fine dust.
There is nothing that cannot be accomplished and no application that does not prove effective—all this is the power of the ten fingers.
If the hand were to form a fist, the ten fingers would be bent and unable to extend. If they cannot extend, how could there be such efficacy as described above?

Therefore, the fist is a metaphor for non-awakening, while the hand is a metaphor for clear awakening. Viewed through this lens, when Buddhas are not awakened, they are no different from sentient beings;
when sentient beings suddenly awaken, they are no different from Buddhas. It is like bending the fingers to form a fist, or extending the fingers to reveal the hand.
As for advancing and retreating, or yielding and asserting, the mechanism lies in the mind and not in the fists or hands.
Yet while the fists and hands are visible, the mind is invisible; only the sage, by means of the visible, perceives the invisible, and is thus able to employ the invisible to govern the visible.
Therefore, that which is visible serves as an instrument for the sage’s benefit. And...

This does not constitute a harm to the sages. Yet, because the common people regard only what is visible as their own possession, that which is invisible becomes increasingly distant and remote. Therefore it is said: "Natures are similar; habits make them divergent.
If one were suddenly to realize that what is visible is none other than what is invisible, then the knowledge that was previously unconscious in daily life would not only be opened...
These constitute the eight awakenings; from them, ten million awakenings may be opened.

This knowing of non-knowing is called the eighty-four thousand samādhis among the Buddhas, yet these same eighty-four thousand samādhis are called the eighty-four thousand afflictions among sentient beings.
Alas! Are these afflictions and samādhis truly permanent, or are they truly impermanent?
If there were permanence, sentient beings would ultimately find it difficult to attain Buddhahood. If there were impermanence, then even all Buddhas could become sentient beings;
just as the Buddhas can return to the state of sentient beings, why then should sentient beings strive to seek Buddhahood?
For anyone who recites and upholds this sutra, if they truly realize this "knowing" that is currently present yet unknown in their daily lives, the Tathāgata shall open it for them.
There are eight types of awakening. I have realized the vastness [of reality] through these eight awakenings;
thus, the eighty-four thousand modes of awakening reside within my daily activities, not in the verbal teachings of the Buddhas. Therefore, I say: the fist can be seen, but the mind cannot be seen.
If that which is invisible cannot be exhausted by means of quantity, how could the explanation of the twelve links of dependent origination—

namely, the twelve factors of dependent arising: ignorance, volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and aging-and-death— be so?

Birth, old age, and death. Not understanding one's own mind is called ignorance (*avidyā*). Once ignorance has arisen, there must necessarily be conditions; this is called volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
Following conditions, there must necessarily be discrimination; this is called consciousness (*vijñāna*). Once consciousness has arisen, there must necessarily be false conceptualization.
