This false conceptualization has no actual substance; it exists only as a hollow designation, which is called name (*nāman*). The body exists as a solid mass due to all that results from false conceptualization.
A single entity is what is called "form" (rūpa). Although the explanations of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) proceed sequentially, they constitute a single link [of dependent origination].

The mutual encounter of the sense faculty and its object is called "contact" (sparśa). Contact is the experience of sensation, which is called "feeling" (vedanā). Feeling inevitably leads to attachment, which is called "craving" (tṛṣṇā).

To crave without relinquishing and to reckon things as permanent is called "clinging" (upādāna). Clinging while grasping at reality is called "existence" (bhava). From existence, there arises birth (jāti).
Birth leads to old age; old age leads to death. From ignorance to old age and death, these are called the twelve links (*dvādaśāṅga*).

These twelve links constitute the den of birth, death, and affliction for all sentient beings, yet they are also the blissful land of *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa* for all Buddhas. It depends entirely upon how the practitioner treats them.
Now, as for the twelve links of dependent origination: it is said that conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations arise; conditioned by volitional formations, consciousness arises;
conditioned by consciousness, name-and-form arise; conditioned by name-and-form, the six sense bases arise; conditioned by the six sense bases, contact arises;
conditioned by contact, feeling arises; conditioned by feeling, craving arises; conditioned by craving, clinging arises; conditioned by clinging, becoming arises; conditioned by becoming...

Conditioned arising: because of birth, there is old age and death; these are called the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda*). Now, ignorance (*avidyā*) and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) belong to the past.

Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the end of the past and the beginning of the present. Name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), and craving (*tṛṣṇā*)—these five members belong to the present.
Grasping (*upādāna*) is the end of the present and the beginning of the future. Existence (*bhava*)...

Birth, old age, and death—these three links belong to the future life. Furthermore, regarding ignorance (*avidyā*), there is ignorance that deludes one regarding principle, and ignorance that deludes one regarding phenomena.
Ignorance regarding principle refers to the failure to comprehend the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Within the wisdom of universal radiance (*samantaprabhā-jñāna*), there is fundamentally no distinction between past and present, or ordinary beings and sages, nor between body and mind. This very lack of comprehension is termed ignorance regarding principle. As for ignorance regarding phenomena...
"Clarification" refers to grasping at the body—a provisional combination of the four present great elements—and the mind—a horizontal aggregation of the four aggregates—thinking, "This is my body;
this is my mind. It is precisely this attachment and discrimination that leads to joy when things are favorable and to affliction when they are adverse.

This grasping at objects is called ignorance regarding phenomena (*vastu-moha-avidyā*). Therefore it is said: as long as ignorance regarding principles (*tattva-moha-avidyā*) is not destroyed, one can never reach the fundamental source;

as long as ignorance regarding phenomena is not destroyed, one can never forget emotional attachments. Because one does not reach the fundamental source, one fails to awaken to the fact that the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is primordially present.
Because one does not forget emotional attachments, one falsely clings to the fact that the form-body (*rūpakāya*) is primordially non-existent. This clinging...
It does not cease. Based upon it, one performs deeds of good and evil. When these deeds are completed, they are called *karma*. When *karma* ripens, it is called the fruit.
When one experiences suffering or pleasure, it is called retribution. This is an exposition based on the single branch of "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*).

As for consciousness (*vijñāna*), it is drawn toward the experience of the fruit of retribution by the power of volitional formations; it discriminates and enters the womb. The false arising of hatred and attachment is termed consciousness. This consciousness enters the womb.
Thereafter, while within the mother's womb, it acts as the master of the red and white [elements]. At this stage, no physical form can be seen;
there is only its name, and thus it is called "Name" (nāma). "Form" (rūpa) refers to the union of the red and white elements.

Upon reaching the fifth week, it is called the stage of "Name-and-Form" (nāmarūpa), meaning that the sense organs and limbs appear to exist but are not yet complete; thus it is called "Form. Following this stage of Name-and-Form comes the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana).

Upon reaching the sixth seven-day period, it is called the stage of hair, body hair, nails, and teeth. Upon reaching the seventh seven-day period, it is called the stage of the possession of faculties (*indriya*).
This refers to the opening and expansion of the six sense-faculties, which possess the function of entering the six sense-objects; therefore, they are called the six entrances (*āyatana*).

These two stages are both fully present within the womb. As for the stage of form, the stage of hair, body hair, nails, and teeth is situated between the stages of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and the six entrances.

"Emergence" (*āyatana*) refers to the period after emerging from the womb until the age of three or four. Although the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) confront the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*), one is as yet unable to discern them;

thus, because the perceptions of pleasure and pain have not yet arisen, this stage is called "contact" (*sparśa*). "Feeling" (*vedanā*) refers to the period from ages five or six up to twelve or thirteen.
Due to the contact between the six sense objects and the six sense faculties, one is then able to experience the qualities of the external objects, such as their being pleasant or unpleasant.
Although one is able to discern objects, one has not yet given rise to a mind of lustful craving; this stage is merely called *vedanā* (feeling).

*Tṛṣṇā* (craving) refers to the period from ages fourteen or fifteen up to eighteen or nineteen, when one craves various excellent and wonderful requisites as well as the objects of sexual desire, yet is still unable to pursue them extensively and universally; this stage is merely called *tṛṣṇā*. *Upādāna* (clinging), however, begins from age twenty...
After [the stage of] *nāmarūpa*, craving and desire increase further; one rushes in all four directions toward the objects of the five sense-fields (*pañca-viṣaya*), never reaching satiety.
Therefore, this is called "grasping" (*upādāna*). Although these five members differ in whether they occur within the womb or after birth, they collectively belong to the present.
Grasping marks the end of the present and the beginning of the future, as was previously distinguished; here it is briefly clarified again. Some say that because of this rushing pursuit...

Regarding the various objects: when one gives rise to wholesome or unwholesome karma, it accumulates and exerts a drawing power that will produce the fruits of the three realms of existence; this is called "existence" (*bhava*).

The three existences are the existence of desire (*kāma-bhava*), the existence of form (*rūpa-bhava*), and the existence of formlessness (*ārūpya-bhava*). These three existences are also called the "three realms.
"Birth" (*jāti*) refers to being reborn from the wholesome or unwholesome karma of the present life into the six destinies and four modes of birth within future lives; this is called [birth].
Regarding birth, aging, and death: after having received birth from a previous life, the body composed of the five aggregates matures and then decays; therefore, it is called aging and death.

Alas! These twelve links of dependent origination cannot be clearly penetrated by those who lack the three types of supernormal knowledge, nor can they be fully illuminated by those who do not possess the five eyes.
Who is able to reach this state? Nevertheless, if study does not examine names, and names do not scrutinize meanings, how can meanings ever be refined?
If meanings are not refined, one will ultimately find it difficult to enter the divine. If meanings do not enter the divine, then practical utility will lack verification.

When practical utility lacks verification, although one may seem to have attained awakening during discourse, one will remain deluded when confronted with actual circumstances. Therefore, at the very first touch of the mechanism of birth and death, or fortune and calamity, [one fails].
Consequently, one loses mastery over oneself, leading to the ruin of reputation and the loss of virtue, becoming a laughingstock for all time and causing the world’s faith to recede.
Viewed from this perspective, if one does not take it upon oneself to follow the Buddhas, Patriarchs, and Sages, one will not even hear the name of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination;
how much less could one examine names and scrutinize meanings, penetrate the essence through refined understanding, and thereby achieve practical application? Furthermore—

The Grand Historian (Sima Qian) was renowned for his vast knowledge of antiquity, yet he remained hesitant and uncertain regarding the retribution of the three periods of existence; how much more so, then, for other matters?

Had Sima Qian been able to examine the names and scrutinize the meanings of the twelve links of dependent origination, understanding them with single-minded clarity, he certainly would not have made such erroneous statements concerning the retribution of the three periods and incurred the ridicule of later generations. Alas, what a pity!
In the *Eight Consciousnesses’ Rules*,
the first five consciousnesses take real objects as their domain; they are direct perceptions (*pratyakṣa*) and permeate all three moral natures.

This refers to the first five consciousnesses. Among the three types of objects, they perceive only objective entities (svabhāva-viṣaya). Among the three types of valid cognition, they are exclusively direct perception (pratyakṣa).
They are compatible with all three natures (trividha-svabhāva).

"Nature-object" (*svabhāva-viṣaya*) refers to various objective forms that serve as objects of cognition; they do not carry names or designations and thus possess the self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the object.
"Characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to blue, yellow, red, and white; "name" (*nāman*) refers to the designations of long, short, square, and round.

"Direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*) means a direct and clear apprehension of the object, without giving rise to conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*). The nature-object belongs to the objective realm, while direct perception belongs to the mind. [These] are the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
These are the natures of good, evil, and the indeterminate. All three natures are universally applicable because the nature of the five consciousnesses is not constant or uniform.

If one speaks of the objective realm (*viṣaya*) in terms of sense organs and objects as subject and object, it is constituted by eight factors; this falls within the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), as in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Thus, there is no such objective realm; yet this realm manifests before one, as clearly reflected in a bright mirror, serene and lucid, without the arising of discrimination.
This is what is called the "true realm. Although the two natures of good and evil are present within the five consciousnesses, they remain without discrimination.
And illumination arises from this; therefore, it is pervasive.
The three faculties of eye, ear, and body reside in two levels.
The three realms are divided into nine levels. From the hells up to the six heavens of the desire realm, all constitute the single level of the desire realm.
The realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) consists of four stages (*bhūmi*). The formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) consists of four stages; together, these constitute nine stages.

The desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is called the stage of the five destinies’ mixed habitation; it possesses all five consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). The first dhyāna heaven is called the stage of joy and bliss born of seclusion;
this constitutes the second stage, wherein there are only the three consciousnesses of eye, ear, and body, and lack the nose and tongue.
Regarding the two consciousnesses: because there is no solid food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) from the third dhyāna stage upward, the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*) are entirely absent.

[The mental factors present are] the ten universal (*sarvatraga*), the five object-specific (*viṣayapratiniyata*), the eleven wholesome (*kuśala*), the two intermediate (*aniyata*), the eight great (*mahābhūmika*), and greed, hatred, and delusion (*lobha-dveṣa-moha*).
Regarding these two lines: it is said that among the mental factors (caitta) associated with the five sensory consciousnesses, there are five universal factors;
the correct number of object-specific factors; eleven virtuous factors; two secondary afflictions; eight major secondary afflictions; and six root afflictions.
Now, there remain only the three—greed, hatred, and delusion—and the three general mental factors, totaling thirty-four. All of these are spontaneous and non-conceptual.
The five consciousnesses equally rely upon the pure material sense organs (*rūpa-indriya*).
Regarding these "pure white material organs," this refers to them in their ultimate sense (*paramārtha*). Only the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) can perceive them.

That which falls within the realm of physical form is the ephemeral organ (*tuccha-indriya*); how could it possibly illuminate objects? It is because the ultimate organ exists that the [consciousness] is able to take objects as its conditions.
It is said that the five consciousnesses arise based on the same dominant sense organs (*indriya*).
Regarding the phrase "nine conditions for seven and eight, with favorable proximity":
the nine conditions are space, light, the sense organ, the object, attention (*manasikāra*), discrimination, reliance on the defiled and pure, reliance on the fundamental, and reliance on the seeds.
My son, visual consciousness arises by means of nine conditions; auditory consciousness proceeds from only eight, because it excludes the condition of light;
olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses possess only seven, because they exclude both the conditions of space and light.
The three combined and the two separated observe the sensory world (*viṣaya*).

The three consciousnesses of nose, tongue, and body apprehend their objects through contact; the two consciousnesses of eye and ear apprehend their objects at a distance. "Observation" refers to the perceiving aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), which is the subjective faculty of cognition.
"The sensory world" refers to the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), which is the perceived object.
The foolish find it difficult to distinguish between consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the sense faculties (*indriya*).

This refers to the Śrāvakas of the Hīnayāna who follow the Dharma of the ignorant; they do not know that both the faculties and consciousness each possess seeds and manifest activity (*samudācāra*), and thus they mistakenly believe that the faculties and consciousness arise from one another.
Not understanding the seeds and manifest activity of the faculties, they think that the faculties can only serve as a guide for consciousness.

Regarding seeds and manifestations: it may be said that the sense faculties serve as the conditions for the arising of consciousness; however, it cannot be said that they give rise to consciousness, because consciousness itself possesses the seeds capable of producing it.
Since the followers of the Hīnayāna have not yet destroyed the cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa), they lack full understanding of phenomena;
therefore, it is difficult for them to distinguish [between these two].

The contemplation of emptiness through the transformation-aspect is exclusively the subsequently-attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*). Even within the state of fruition, it still cannot directly express the ultimate truth.
The Buddha possesses both fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and subsequently-attained wisdom. Fundamental wisdom is real wisdom; it can directly take True Suchness (*tathatā*) as its object.
Subsequently-attained wisdom is provisional wisdom; it can only comprehend the conventional, but cannot directly take True Suchness as its object. This refers to the stage of fruition.

The Buddha has already destroyed the delusions of views and afflictions and is able to employ his six sense faculties interchangeably. He transforms and gives rise to objective images (*nimitta-bhāga*), yet further contemplates the emptiness of those images.

Because he does not recognize the first five consciousnesses, as well as the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, he mistakenly identifies [his realization] as subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

He does not realize that subsequently attained wisdom is obtained from fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Although the Hīnayāna possesses both "conformity to principle" (*yathābhūta*) and "conformity to phenomena" (*yathāvastu*), [it lacks this].
The two wisdoms differ only in name; how could the latter truly be "subsequently attained wisdom" (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*)?

Even within the state of Buddhahood, subsequently attained wisdom does not fully express the ultimate reality (*tathatā*); how much less so while on the causal path? "Expressing" (*quan*) means "to accord with.

Fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), and therefore it directly perceives *tathatā*. Subsequently attained wisdom arises from the material sense faculties (*rūpīndriya*) and is conceptual (*savikalpa*); therefore...
They are unable to directly perceive the principle of non-conceptuality.

In the Hīnayāna, *anātman* (non-self) is taken as *tathatā* (suchness). By severing the discriminative attachments of the six consciousnesses, one is able to employ the six sense organs interchangeably, considering this to be the direct perception of *tathatā*.
The verse says: The Buddhas of the Small Vehicle and the Fruit-Head [Sravakas] possess only names in theory and logic; they are deluded by names and do not know their true meaning.
Doubting the Great [Vehicle], they give rise to contention. The five consciousnesses share a single awakening; thus, the eye could hear and the ear could see forms.

This is truly not the fault of the original faculties, but the fault lies with the one who discriminates. Therefore, when seeing and thinking are destroyed, the six faculties immediately function interdependently.
That minor [teacher] did not know this; he had not yet investigated the seven, eight, or five [doctrines]. When the three [truths] became clear to him, his arbitrary calculations naturally collapsed.
Having discarded the old dharma upon its refutation, he returned to the Mahāyāna with sorrowful reverence. Kumārajīva was his first teacher;
suspecting that Kumārajīva also possessed great discernment, once he realized the Great Principle, he again took Kumārajīva as his teacher.
When perfect luminosity first arises, it becomes the untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*). The three types of transformation bodies cease the wheel of suffering.
The first five consciousnesses follow the eighth consciousness in its transformation;

within the state of Buddhahood, the eighth consciousness transforms into the pure white untainted consciousness, while its associated mental factors (*caitta*) become the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), which suddenly manifests before one—hence the term "first."

When [the seeds] are activated, the first five consciousnesses immediately become untainted (*anāsrava*). Regarding the three types of bodies: they are the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
The thousand-fathom Great Transformation-body is for Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas in the four stages of application (*prayoga*).

The sixteen-fathom Small Transformation-body is for Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas in the three stages of equipment (*sambhāra*) as well as for those of the Two Vehicles and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), appearing according to their respective types.

The transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) universally benefits those of the three vehicles and equally moistens those in the six realms of existence, thereby bringing to rest the wheel of suffering for sentient beings.
The first eight lines clarify that which is with outflows (sāsrava); the latter four lines clarify that which is without outflows (anāsrava).
The sixth consciousness is described in its verses as possessing the indeterminate capacity to perform both wholesome and unwholesome deeds.
It functions across the three natures, the three types of valid cognition, and all three objects; its cycling through the three realms is easily understood.

They are all equally applicable to the three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; the three means of valid cognition—direct perception, inference, and non-apprehension; and the three types of objects—images-only, those with a substantial basis, and those that are neither.

Regarding "inference" (anumāna), it refers to knowing through analogy. Regarding "non-apprehension" (anupalabdhi), it refers to what exists in thought but lacks objective reality; it is an inference that fails to reach its mark.

The objective realm of "conveying the essential nature" (sabhāga-nirbhāsa) is of two kinds. When the mind takes the mind as its object, the intermediate image-part (nimitta-bhāga) arises from both ends;

because it arises conveying the essential nature, it is called "true conveying of the essential nature. When the mind takes matter (rūpa) as its object, the intermediate image-part arises solely from one end—the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga);

because it arises through transformation while conveying the essential nature, it is called "semblance conveying of the essential nature. The "solitary shadow" (kevala-chāyā) is also of two kinds. First, there is...

Substantial independent images (*dravya-kevala-pratibimba*): the seeds and manifestations of the five sense organs all arise by depending on a substantial basis. There is one type that is a non-substantial independent image (*adravya-kevala-pratibimba*):

the objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*) transformed [by consciousness] when perceiving flowers in the sky, rabbit horns, or the past and future. These are shadows of the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) that have already passed away;

they depend solely on the past five sense objects and on the shadows of the five sense objects arising through transformation in the future, but do not depend on the five sense objects currently present.
Furthermore, the six consciousnesses of a previous life grasped the shadows of dharmas to form the form-seed (*rūpa-bīja*) of this present life;

now, in this life, one again gives rise to shadows based on that form, which constitute the seeds for receiving a body in a future life. If, in this life, one can employ the six consciousnesses to practice contemplation and shatter [these seeds]...
Once self-grasping is eliminated and one no longer seizes upon mental objects (*dharmārambaṇa*), one will no longer receive a body of segmented existence (*paricchinna-śarīra*).
The cycling of the six consciousnesses through the three realms is manifest and easy to understand;
however, the fifty-one associated mental factors (*caitta*) are subtle.

This phrase indicates the number [of categories]. The two phrases concerning "nature" (*prakṛti*) and "realm" (*dhātu*) establish the names. It is intended that sentient beings, by means of the names, shall elucidate the meanings;

by means of the meanings, they shall realize the principles; and by realizing the principles, they shall achieve practical application. This achievement of practical application is explained in terms of the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
One employs function to embody the Way; one embodies the Way to establish virtue.
Good and evil are distinguished and assigned according to the occasion.

When the six consciousnesses encounter wholesome objects, they associate with wholesome mental factors; when they encounter unwholesome or neutral objects, [they associate with their respective factors].
Because it is associated with unwholesome and neutral mental factors, it is said to be "individually assigned. This is merely a neutral object of perception.

As for the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), however, even when unwholesome mental factors arise together with a wholesome mind that is vigorous and powerful, they are transformed into wholesomeness.
The natures, realms, and feelings constantly undergo transformation and change.

Regarding the six consciousnesses, they are constantly shifting and altering across the three natures, the three realms, and the five feelings— namely, sorrow, joy, suffering, pleasure, and equanimity.
The roots, such as faith and the others, are generally connected;

likewise are the six root afflictions, the twenty secondary afflictions, the eleven wholesome factors, and the others—the five universal, the five object-specific, and the four indeterminate—making fifty-one in total.
These are also connected by way of their nature, realm, feeling, and so forth, as they shift and change.
When moving the body or uttering speech, it alone is preeminent.
At the time of moving the body or uttering speech, its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is the most excellent among the eight consciousnesses, because it pertains to sentient beings.
The power of karma that draws forth and fulfills acts as the牵引 (qīnyǐn)—that is, it draws forth and initiates.

"Fulfills" means to bring to completion. This refers to the six consciousnesses being able to create karma and attract its fruits, thereby initiating the stage of the Ground of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).

The Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). Because of the abandonment of the conceptualized grasping at self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-vikalpa*), this consciousness is transformed into the untainted (*anāsrava*) at the first moment of mind in the First Stage; for it has abandoned the two types of dualistic clinging to self and phenomena that involve conceptualization.
The innate [afflictions], namely the non-conceptual grasping at self and phenomena,
are co-nascent with birth; at this time they have not yet been severed, remaining as entanglements and latent tendencies because the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) have not been abandoned.
After the Ground of Far-Going (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*), it is purely untainted (*anāsrava*). Its observation is perfectly luminous, illuminating the great trichiliocosm.
The "Far-Going" is the seventh ground. Prior to this ground, this consciousness arose with a mixture of tainted and untainted states.
Upon reaching this ground, however, the two innate obstacles (*kleśa-āvaraṇa* and *jñeya-āvaraṇa*) never again manifest, and it becomes purely untainted, associated with the mind.

It also transforms into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation, brilliantly and perfectly illuminating the great trichiliocosm. The seventh consciousness, characterized by its "substantiality-with-attributes" and being obscured,
encompasses both the phenomenal (sentient) and the fundamental (noumenal).

The seven consciousnesses take the "object with substance" (*saviṣaya*) among the three types of objects as their cognitive support. Among the three natures, they possess only the nature of being obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).

"Obscured" means that it veils the true nature; because it pervades the mental states of the six consciousnesses, its basis is the eighth consciousness. Thus, it pervades both the mental states and their basis.
Therefore it is said that the image-part (nimitta-bhāga) arises from both ends.

The seventh consciousness takes the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) of the eighth consciousness as its internal self. The seventh consciousness is mind (*citta*), and the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) is also mind;

thus it is said that "mind takes mind as its object," which is truly a case of "carrying the essence" (*sabhāva-sadṛśa*). The eighth consciousness is its essential nature (*svabhāva*); therefore, the seventh...

Since consciousness takes the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses as its internal self, the seeing-division of the eight consciousnesses is precisely the fundamental locus of the seventh consciousness.

When the seeing-division of the eighth consciousness perceives form, it is the seventh consciousness perceiving form. Because form is not real, it is said to be "apparently with a substantial basis" (*sadravya-sanimitta*).

Question: Regarding the "associated with the substantial" (*sābhisvabhāva*), it arises by being associated with the substantial natures (*mūla-svabhāva*) of the eight consciousnesses. However, what is the object (*ālambana*) of the seventh consciousness?

The eighth consciousness is able to store all things; it stores the entire root-body (*indriya-kāya*) and the receptacle-world (*bhājana-loka*), and it is that which is grasped and stored through the attachment to self (*ātma-grāha*).
Once the eight consciousnesses possess objects, one must ask whence these objects arise. They arise from the six consciousnesses;
thus, it is known that the seventh consciousness originally has no independent substance or position, and its objective aspect (nimittabhāga) is produced from the two heads—the sixth and the eighth.
To hold that the measure of the self is non-existent according to conditions is incorrect.
This consciousness, regarding the two types of non-conceptual grasping at self and phenomena, is spontaneous and continuous; therefore, it is said to "grasp at the self according to conditions."

The universal [mental factors] consist of the eight; the object-specific ones, the five; and wisdom (*prajñā*) is common to both. Among the great afflictions, greed, delusion, self-view, and pride are associated with one another.

Regarding the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), there are only eight; the universal ones are five, and the object-specific ones are the same as those for wisdom. As for the root afflictions, they possess all four types.
It is precisely greed, delusion, views, and pride that are [the afflictions].
They constantly and thoroughly deliberate, following along with the notion of a self.
The first five consciousnesses are neither constant nor thorough; the sixth consciousness is thorough but not constant; only this consciousness is both constant and thorough.

Through inference, reflection, examination, and measurement, one clings to the perceived portion of the eight consciousnesses as the self; therefore, it is said that the mark of selfhood follows along.
Sentient beings are perpetually mired in confusion day and night; the four delusions and the eight major afflictions arise in conjunction.
Once one clings to the eight consciousnesses as the internal self, sentient beings will perpetually dwell in the long night of birth and death without realizing it;
for [the mind] arises in conjunction with the four delusions and the eight major afflictions. The "four delusions" refers to the four root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*).
The six evolving consciousnesses are called the basis of defilement and purity;
all eight consciousnesses together constitute the evolving consciousnesses. When only the six consciousnesses engage in contemplation, then all the consciousnesses evolve together;

therefore, the term "evolving" is specifically applied to the six consciousnesses. The seventh consciousness is called the basis of defilement and purity because the six consciousnesses possess discrimination.
The seven consciousnesses are without discrimination; yet there is discrimination that arises based on non-discrimination, because non-discrimination is proximate to the insentient.
Regarding the nature of equality in the initial moment of the Ground of Great Joy, I constantly suppress the practice of effortlessness.
Within any given stage (*bhūmi*), the three minds of beginning, middle, and end are fully present; these correspond to the entry, abiding, and emergence [of meditative concentration].

At the initial mind of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*), this consciousness severs one portion of ignorance and is thereby transformed into the outflow-free state, becoming an analogue of the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*).

This is because it shifts within the causal stage. As for effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*), in the eighth stage, the two types of non-conceptual clinging to self and phenomena are completely severed;
hence it is said, "I am constantly crushing [them]," which constitutes the true wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*).
The six consciousnesses reach the eighth bhūmi and transform into the *suvicāraṇa-jñāna* (the wisdom of wondrous observation).

How is it that the seventh consciousness transforms into the *samatā-jñāna* (the wisdom of equality) at the initial moment of the first bhūmi? It is because the six consciousnesses transform into the *suvicāraṇa-jñāna* after the completion of contemplation;
at the time one first initiates contemplation, they transform into what resembles the *suvicāraṇa-jñāna*.
The Tathāgata manifests the Body of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*), which is the object for the capacity of Bodhisattvas on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Within the state of Buddhahood, he manifests ten kinds of bodies of enjoyment for others; the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages are precisely those who are the objects of this manifestation.
The nature of the eighth consciousness consists solely of the five omnipresent mental factors that are non-obscured.

Within this consciousness, during its causal state, among the three moral natures, it is exclusively of the non-obscured indeterminate nature (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). When it takes an object as its condition, its aspect...
Its mental associates consist solely of the five universal factors (*sarvatraga*).
Regarding its realms and stages, it arises according to the karmic power of others.
Within the three realms and nine stages, this consciousness arises according to the wholesome or unwholesome karmic power of the six consciousnesses. Because...

Because the eight consciousnesses are of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*), the followers of the Two Vehicles do not understand them; due to their deluded attachments, they are able to engage in debate with the Master.
This consciousness is most subtle, which is why the Śrāvakas who follow the teachings of the Two Vehicles do not believe it exists, relying only on—
The first six consciousnesses receive perfuming and maintain the seeds; when [the afflictions of] view and thought are severed, these are grasped as the wisdom of suchness (yathābhūta-jñāna).

When the six sense organs function interchangeably, this is grasped as the wisdom of phenomena (yāvadbhāva-jñāna). Because ignorance has not yet been entirely destroyed, the masters of the Mahāyāna treatises have repeatedly debated and argued to prove the existence of this consciousness.
The vast and boundless Threefold Treasury (Tripiṭaka) is inexhaustible.
That which can maintain the seeds without loss is called the "capable store" (ālaya). That which receives the perfuming of both the defiled and the pure is called the "stored-in" (ālaya).

That which the seven consciousnesses grasp as a self is called the "clinging store" (ālaya). Because the essence and function of these three stores are profound and expansive, ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle do not comprehend them.
The profound depth has seven waves, with objects acting as the wind.
The eight consciousnesses are like a clear and still abyss; because the preceding seven consciousnesses grasp external objects as the wind, waves arise.
It receives perfuming and maintains the seeds within the root-body and the vessel-world.

This consciousness is able to receive the prior perfumings of both the defiled and the pure, and it is able to maintain the seeds of the root-body and the vessel-world. "Roots" refers to the six sense-faculties;
"body" refers to the internal world; and "vessel" refers to the external world.
Departing first and arriving last, it acts as the sovereign lord.
This consciousness alone is the master of the collective retribution;
before the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*), it merely abandons its storehouse nature, and after the Vajra Path, the ripening fruit (*vipāka*) becomes empty.

The eighth stage is the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*). When this consciousness first reaches this stage, it immediately abandons the grasping at the grasper, the grasped, and the storehouse-consciousness.

Following the Vajra Path, it enters the state of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Regarding "maturation" (*vipāka*): it matures through transformation, matures over time, and matures as a different category.
After the Vajra Path, one severs the ignorance of the characteristic of arising (*utpatti-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*) and the seeds of maturation.
The "son" (the practitioner) is emptiness itself.
The "Vajra Contemplation Wisdom" is the name of this wisdom; it signifies that its firmness and sharpness are capable of destroying all ignorance (*avidyā*).
When the emptiness of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing—and the emptiness of karmic maturation—is realized, then even the slightest flicker of a single thought is the emptiness of ignorance.
The Great Perfect Circle arises simultaneously and shines universally throughout the lands and atoms of the ten directions.
When this consciousness reaches the stage of Buddhahood, it is transformed into the supreme, untainted pure essence, termed the "Stainless Consciousness" (Amala-vijñāna).
Simultaneously with its arising, it is associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) and universally illuminates the perfectly luminous worlds of the ten directions.

*A Brief Explanation of Consciousness-Only* (*Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-saṃkṣepa*): Now, to probe the profundities of yin and yang, to encompass the essence of creation and transformation, to penetrate the source of the vast chaos, and to shatter the primordial浑沌 (hunchun).

The aperture of the primordial unity (*dhun*) transcends both Confucianism and Daoism, standing alone in its loftiness; it crowns all other schools with its profound depth. To abandon the doctrine of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) and seek elsewhere is simply impossible.
For by negating the existence of external objects, consciousness is distinguished from the mind’s emptiness; by negating objects, there is nothing that exists outside of consciousness.
By distinguishing [consciousness] from emptiness, it is not the same as a barren extinction. Thus, it levels the pits of nihilism and eternalism, and blocks the cycle of birth and death.

This path clearly manifests the Middle Way and establishes the definitive principles of Hetuvidyā (Logic). It is beyond the reach of Māras and heretics, and is followed alike by both ordinary beings and sages.
Now, consciousness consists of eight types, distinguished as mind-kings (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*).

Were it not for wisdom that is empty yet spiritually alert and a discernment that is wondrously transcendent, how could one easily peer into its inner precincts? Regarding the *ālaya-vijñāna* and the others, I have roughly investigated their origins and presented them directly.
When the illumination of True Suchness (tathatā) reaches its limit and turns back into obscurity, it becomes conjoined with both the arising-and-ceasing and the non-arising-and-non-ceasing;

this is called the "witnessing-of-self-witnessing" division (*svasaṃvittisaṃvedana-bhāga*). It is like a person who has been awake suddenly falling into a stupor and speaking in a human voice: though one hears them speak, one cannot understand clearly. Can one say they are awake?
Yet, because they cannot understand clearly, can one say they are in a stupor? That they still hear the human voice—this is what is meant by being both "stuporous and awake."

These two aspects are intertwined; they are the very gateway between delusion and awakening. During such moments, if someone calls out to one, the darkness follows the awakening; if no one calls, the awakening follows the darkness.
Once awakening follows darkness, one is unable to discern external objects and does not even dream, remaining merely in a state of profound obscurity.
This is called the *svasaṃvittibhāga* (the self-verifying portion). At such times, there is no distinction between subject and object; it is a state of dark, silent unity.
Yet it remains alone. After a short while, one suddenly dreams of various forms of sorrow and joy, suffering and pleasure.

From the perspective of that which is capable of observing, this is called the *darśana-bhāga* (the seeing portion). That which is the object of observation is the *nimitta-bhāga* (the image portion). Someone may ask:

"Do these two portions—the seeing and the image—arise sequentially, or do they arise simultaneously? I respond to him: "Regarding the two portions of seeing and image, as for their arising sequentially..."
Within direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), non-conceptualization is not admitted; as soon as conceptualization arises, direct perception ceases.
This is called "antagonistic arising," wherein the subject and object are no longer identical. These four parts are the very foundation of the eight consciousnesses;

therefore, those who are intent upon this school must not fail to apply their attention to them. If these four parts are thoroughly penetrated, then the framework of the eight consciousnesses will be fully understood. Reflect deeply on this.
This is half [of the explanation].

Now, the eight consciousnesses and four divisions constitute the fundamental framework of the *lakṣaṇa* (characteristics) school. The ālayavijñāna, the manas-vijñāna, the *vikalpa-vijñāna* (discriminating consciousness), and the five consciousnesses of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body—these are called the eight consciousnesses.
The *sākṣāt-svasaṃvedana-bhāga* (the division that witnesses the witnessing of itself) and the *svasaṃvedana-bhāga* (the division that witnesses itself).

The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*)—these are called the four parts (*catur-bhāga*). To speak of their fundamental nature: the eight consciousnesses and their four parts originally possess no distinct substance;

they merely arise as various manifestations when True Suchness (*tathatā*) follows conditions (*pratyaya*). Indeed, the principle of True Suchness following conditions is most difficult to comprehend.
This is because True Suchness is pure and fundamentally free from any taint; how, then, could it suddenly give rise to the following of conditions? Regarding this—

If one investigates this without ceasing, one will suddenly awaken and enter [realization]. Regarding what are called the eight consciousnesses and four divisions, there will be no need for even a slight amount of verification;
one will then be able to understand the texts on Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*) with perfect clarity. Therefore it is said:

"If one penetrates the School of Nature (*xingzong*) but does not penetrate the School of Characteristics (*xiangzong*), then what is seen by the School of Nature is still not yet complete. If one penetrates the School of Characteristics but does not penetrate the School of Nature, then what is seen by the School of Characteristics..."

Furthermore, one may not yet have attained thorough mastery. Even if one has a comprehensive understanding of both nature (*xing*) and characteristics (*xiang*), yet has not awakened to the Chan of Bodhidharma, it is like Lord Ye Gong’s painted dragon:
while its head and horns appear perfectly lifelike from a distance, it is utterly incapable of bringing relief to a severe drought or raising thunder and rain.
Therefore, those who are resolved to transcend the world and shoulder the burden of the Dharma must cultivate themselves in nature, characteristics, and Chan.
As for this school, how could I dare not apply my utmost sincerity and focus my attention upon it? Now, the names and meanings within the School of Characteristics (Xiangzong) are numerous;
were it not for one whose mind and intellect are subtle and profound, who investigates exhaustively and with meticulous care, it would truly be difficult to clarify them.

For now, I shall select the general outlines and briefly discuss and annotate them, merely providing a rough understanding for the uninitiated. In essence, the *ālaya-vijñāna* encompasses the preceding [faculties of] eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.
The five consciousnesses should be treated together for exposition; they seem easier to clarify.

This is because both the *ālaya-vijñāna* and the first five consciousnesses belong to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and both are transformations within the superior grade of fruition. As for the seventh consciousness and the sixth consciousness, however, all three grades are present.
The three grades are as follows: the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) is the inferior grade; the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) is the middling grade; and the Ultimate [Path]...
Because it is of the highest grade, it functions among the seven [consciousnesses] and the six causes. Someone may ask:

"If the first five consciousnesses accomplish the category of mind associated with outflow-free [wisdom] (*anāsrava*) to manifest in the present body and benefit sentient beings, why was it stated earlier that the eighth consciousness accomplishes the outflow-free state?

It is because when perfect luminosity first arises, it is the category of mind associated with the eighth consciousness that accomplishes the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*); therefore, its first five faculties...

Regarding the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) transformed by the eighth consciousness: since the fundamental consciousness that performs the transformation has already become untainted (anāsrava), the five sense organs (indriya) it transforms must likewise naturally become untainted.
Once the five sense organs that give rise to them have become untainted, then the five consciousnesses (vijñāna) produced by them will consequently become untainted;
how could there be any doubt about this? Someone might ask: "If it is said that the eight consciousnesses are transformed into the four wisdoms (jñāna), why then do you say..."

"Are they associated with the categories of mind? He replied: "The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, fascicle ten, states: 'These four categories collectively encompass all conditioned merits (*saṃskṛta-guṇa*) of the Buddha-ground.
These are attained respectively by transforming the impure categories of mind associated with the eight consciousnesses—the seventh, sixth, and five sensory consciousnesses.
Although wisdom (*jñāna*) is not itself a consciousness, it relies upon the consciousnesses; since the transformation of the consciousnesses is primary, it is so described."

It is attained through the transformation of consciousness (*vijñāna-parāvṛtti*). Furthermore, in the state with outflows (*sāsrava*), wisdom is weak and consciousness is strong; in the state without outflows (*anāsrava*), wisdom is strong and consciousness is weak. To encourage sentient beings to rely upon wisdom and abandon consciousness, it is said that "consciousness is transformed into wisdom.

Regarding the meaning of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) in the Mahāyāna, it is said: "That which 'bears its own aspect' (*sākāra*). There are two distinct meanings for both "bearing" (*dharana*) and "own aspect" (*svākāra*).

As for "bearing," there are two meanings: 1. It refers to the cognition bearing the aspect of the object. 2. It refers to the cognition bearing its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Regarding "own aspect," there are also two meanings: 1. It refers to the aspect of the object itself. 2. It refers to the aspect of the cognition itself. Thus, the term "bearing its own aspect" encompasses these fourfold implications.
There are two types: first, direct grasping (*sākṣāt-parigraha*), wherein the cognizing mind directly grasps the essence of the object while cognizing it;

second, transformational grasping (*pariṇāma-parigraha*), wherein the cognizing mind transforms and gives rise to a "reflected part" (*nimitta-bhāga*) while cognizing it. That which is directly grasped is called the actual object (*bhūta-viṣaya*). That which is transformed and given rise to...
This is called the "provisional object" (*prajñapti-viṣaya*). What is a provisional object? It is the reflection of the actual object. What is a reflection?

It refers to the first five consciousnesses directly grasping the actual object; they engage it spontaneously and without being accompanied by names or phrases, occurring within the realm of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

It is like a bright mirror: when an object approaches, it reflects immediately, yet originally possesses no mind. As soon as one perceives beauty or ugliness, the direct perception has already ceased. Thus...
This falls into the category of inference (*anumāna*). I understand that these are merely shadows of provisional objects, which are the objects of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Furthermore, when the perceiving mind manifests and perceives its own *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect), this too is a provisional object. Now, within the school of Sthiramati, it is falsely claimed that the five untainted (*anāsrava*) sensory consciousnesses can perceive *tathatā* (suchness) while still in the causal stage;
yet they fail to realize that for the five consciousnesses to become wisdom (*jñāna*), they must necessarily depend upon the transformation of the eighth consciousness.
This constitutes the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Subsequently, the five consciousnesses are transformed into the all-accomplishing wisdom (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).
Why is this wisdom referred to here as "subsequently attained" (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*)? It is because it is attained subsequent to the fundamental wisdom.

This is because the five consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness both belong to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and thus they transform together at the level of the fruit. That [other view] maintains that within the causal state, the five consciousnesses have not yet transformed into wisdom.

If it can take True Suchness (*tathatā*) as its object, how could it not be non-delusory? Even though consciousness is transformed into wisdom within the fruit [of Buddhahood], it is merely able to illuminate the conventional;
it cannot take True Suchness as its object. Master Huihu said: "If even within the fruit itself it does not yet fully express the Truth, how much less so within the cause?"

Read by Hanshan Deqing of the Ming Dynasty.
Regarding the origins of the Engraved Tripitaka:

During the Jia-long era, Yuan Fenhū lamented that the Great Dharma was nearing its decline and that the monastic community lacked foresight, failing to reflect upon the achievements of the Tang and Song dynasties.
In this era, there are no fewer than twenty sets of woodblocks for the Tripitaka throughout the realm.

From the Yuan dynasty down to the Ming, the Tripitaka blocks at the Southern Capital (Nanjing) were frequently printed, yet they have already become blurred and are no longer very clear. Furthermore, having been worn out over the long years, they are decaying.

Although the blocks at the Yanjing (Beijing) are complete and robust, and the characters are clear and brilliant, because they are located within the imperial palace, printing them is not permitted unless by imperial decree.
I respectfully submit that I dare not act on my own authority. Furthermore, worldly affairs are impermanent; how can order and chaos be predetermined?
It would be better to replace the palm-leaf manuscripts with bound volumes. If so, the cost of printing will not be high and the books will not be scarce.

If the price is not high, printing will be easy; if the books are not scarce, they will be easily disseminated. Even if the world passes through periods of turmoil, they will surely not be entirely consumed by fire or destruction. Thus, [the Dharma] shall endure.
"The Dharma-treasure shall endure forever, and the life of wisdom shall remain firm. It is like sowing extensively but harvesting sparsely;

though one may encounter famine, one will not come to die of hunger. When the Chan practitioner Famen heard these words, although Master Ben considered his own strength to be weak and unable to plan for this, this aspiration remained vividly within his heart and liver, never daring to forget it for even a moment. As for...
In the seventh year of the Wanli era, I arrived from Mount Song and hung my monk’s staff by the Qingfeng Brook.
It was not far from Dayun Temple, where there resided the elder master Yungu, a preeminent figure among the white-browed monks of the Buddhist gate.
At that time, Ben Gu served as Yungu’s attendant. I visited Yungu at Dayun Temple and found Master Ben there as well. Subsequently, we discussed the carving of the Tripitaka.
I considered that thirty thousand pieces of gold would not suffice to complete this undertaking. For sentient beings regard wealth as their very life;
how easy would it be to beg for such things? Generally speaking, when ordinary people’s lives are harmed—even among parents, brothers, or wives—there are those who feel displeasure.
When one from beyond the world begs for the lives of human beings, who would be willing to grant them? I said:
My child, why do you not see that it is so grand? I fear only that your resolute mind is not sincere; if it were sincere, what need would there be for concern regarding failure?

Moreover, this magnificent Great Ming dynasty is not inferior to the prosperity of the Song and Yuan dynasties. As for the Song edition of the Tripitaka, there are still those who have transcribed and carved it;
the Yuan edition, too, exists in no fewer than ten or more sets. You must strive to produce one yourself; do not be self-disparaging, my son. This old man [speaks thus].
Though I am not quick-witted, I venture to serve as the banner and drum for the engraving of the Tripitaka. The banner is intended to unify one's eyes; the drum is intended to unify one's ears.
When the eyes are unified, they become clear; when the ears are unified, they become acute. This acuity and clarity are what sentient beings inherently possess;
it is merely because they lack the Great Dharma to permeate and open their minds that, though these faculties exist, they cannot be utilized. You, sir—

It is said that for sentient beings, wealth is as dear as life; for this reason, it is difficult to beg for. Yet they do not realize that those who hold wealth as paramount have truly not yet awakened their intelligence.
Once intelligence is awakened, one immediately knows that this body is a phantom and lacks solidity, and that this mind arises and ceases without constancy.
Having realized this, one would joyfully offer even one's own head when asked; how much more so [other things]?
"What external thing is this 'adú' (this money)? Thus, those such as Fǎběn transformed weakness into strength and turned narrowness into breadth;
they regarded the undertaking of carving the Tripitaka as a strong man bending and extending his arm, showing no sign of difficulty at all. Yet, even so, the project had not yet been carried out.
When Mìzàng Kāigōng came to inquire about the Dharma from the Old Man (Zhào), he was consequently entrusted with the matter of carving the Tripitaka. Kāi—
The Duke said, "If one were to change the palm-leaf manuscripts (vaṃśa-patra) into bound volumes (pustaka), they would lack reverence; would this not be improper?
I refuted him, saying: "Gold and jade are revered, yet they cannot sustain life. Although rice and wheat are not as revered as gold and jade, they can sustain life.
Even if the palm-leaf manuscripts were revered, if one does not understand their meaning, then one merely honors them."
What benefit is there? Even if the scripture were not held in high esteem, if it were easily produced at a low price, its circulation would surely be widespread.
Among those who reach this universal and all-pervading realm, could there not be one or two individuals who understand its meaning and intent?

Furthermore, I have heard that our Dharma is like a drum smeared with lethal poison; when it is struck and its sound resounds among the multitude, regardless of whether they possess intention or lack it, [they are affected].

For those who do so, their life-faculties (*jīvitendriya*) are severed. If this is the case, not only will those who honor and make offerings gain great merit, but even those who disparage and slander [the teachings] will ultimately surely obtain benefit.
Furthermore, in the Sahā world, the method for saving sentient beings prioritizes the "gate of refutation" (*chedana-mukha*), with the "gate of inclusion" (*saṃgraha-mukha*) following next.
Even those who treat the scriptural volumes with contempt shall first fall into hell and undergo extreme suffering.
Suffering leads one back to the source. Returning to the source means knowing the cause for falling into hell. Knowing the cause leads to reforming one's faults.
Reforming one's faults allows one to transform what was despised into that which is honored. Therefore, if they cannot be gathered through persuasion, they must be broken [of their transgressions].
Because they are broken, they come to see hell; once they have seen hell, they will long for heaven with painful intensity. This arises from faith in heaven.
Thus, one may honor the Buddha with faith today, yet tomorrow treat him with contempt; this is merely a matter of turning one's hand over or under.
This old man only wishes that all sentient beings might despise the Buddha-dharma and fall into hell, so that through the suffering of hell they may give rise to the Bodhicitta.
"If this were the case, by changing the Indian-style palm-leaf manuscripts into bound volumes, the mark of the broad and long tongue would remain ten thousand times more magnificent than before.
Why are you so lacking in wisdom? When Daokai heard these words of mine, tears fell from his eyes as he knelt and made a vow, saying:
"I respectfully accept the Master’s command. If there should be someone who provides thirty thousand ounces of gold to carve these printing blocks for the Tripitaka..."
As for this, Daokai vowed to offer his head, eyes, marrow, and brain as an offering to these people.

From this day forward, even if the printing blocks were incomplete, he would open his heart without dying. Viewed from this perspective, both the Dharma Master Daokai and this untalented old man, as well as all the present patrons who have carved the Tripitaka, are all emanations of Yuan Fenu.
A Call for Scribes to Copy the *Avalokiteśvara-utpatti-kathā*:
Now, the Sage has no fixed body; he takes the bodies of sentient beings as his own body. It is like a sliver of moon in the sky whose reflection appears upon ten thousand waters;
whether it is seen or not depends on whether the water is clear or turbid—it is not that there is no moon. Thus, our Great Being Avalokiteśvara...

Through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation, one enters samādhi. Initially, within the process of hearing, one enters the stream and forgets the object, thereby attaining two forms of excellence and accomplishing the thirty-two transformations.
These enable the water of the minds of all sentient beings to become clear and pure, so that they may, according to their conditions, behold the moon.

Judging from this, there is originally no distinction between Bodhisattvas and sentient beings; it is simply through the perfuming of hearing, contemplation, and cultivation that [the difference arises].

One immediately attains entry into the stream and forgets all objective referents; this is the perfect, wondrous response. Yet, when one is perfumed by greed, hatred, and delusion, one follows along with ignorance and flows downward into the various realms of existence.

For this reason, Bodhisattvas take pity on sentient beings as being of the same essence as themselves; employing the methods they have personally verified, they rescue and heal the multitudes of living beings.
Harnessing great compassion, they manifest divided bodies and dispersed reflections, benefiting others according to their respective types. One day, the venerable Master Qing of Dianyuan...
He was on the verge of death when he dreamed of Avalokiteśvara, who exhorted him to contemplate the Buddha of his own nature (svabhāva-buddha). Thereupon, he recovered.

Inspired by this, he resolved to commission ten thousand images of the Great Being (Mahāsattva) to offer as universal worship, thereby repaying the Bodhisattva’s kindness. His faith entered the stage of mental cultivation (manobhūmi), and his inner sentiments were manifested in these words.
I saw him with tears streaming from his eyes, and he spoke these words. Moved by this, I have composed this account.

Now, when a pure practitioner of meditation takes a grave illness as water and is able to behold the cool moon of the Bodhisattva, a Daoist of penetrating insight who hears such words will immediately realize it without doubt;
thus taking non-doubt as water, they likewise see it. May all those who seek purity...
Faith. If each and every one of you can simply cast it down directly without doubt, then the cool moon of the Bodhisattva will be seen everywhere.
Although the karma of sentient beings is heavy, not doubting is difficult; for now, head toward rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss through the second gate.
Together we behold Amitābha and hear the sound of the unsurpassed Dharma. Furthermore, this is the most expedient place among all the Universal Gate [Practices].
Regarding the origin of the iron alms bowl—how great is the Buddha’s bowl! Its arrival dates back to a remote past. The Buddhas of the past are beyond counting; as for the Buddhas of the present...
All [the Buddhas] personally held it. Future Buddhas will not eat without a bowl. If even the Buddha cherished it so dearly, how much more so should a bhikṣu?

Since we are far removed from the Buddha, the precepts and Dharma have declined; among the śramaṇas and sons of the Śākya, those who live as householders are many, while those who beg for food are few.
Furthermore, those who do beg for food generally carry gourds and do not know how to hold a bowl. In the famous monasteries and sacred temples wherever they are located...
They merely engage in public lectures. An sits in meditation and gathers the assembly; though there are thousands upon ten thousands of hands, not one is seen holding an alms bowl.

Now, the bowl is the vessel of the Sage’s measured capacity. It measures both self and object, like a box receiving its lid, or like the pitch-pipe of the Huangzhong, responding to the vital breath without fail.
Thus, through food and drink, one harmonizes the mind; when the mind is harmonized, things are transformed; when things are transformed, goodness expands.

Reaching afar, it benefits those beyond the boundaries; reaching near, its grace is spread throughout the world. Thus it is said: "When one man perfects his virtue, the Way permeates the great chiliocosm.
Now, the alms bowl is that which benefits oneself and others, the very vessel upon which the Great Dharma depends; how could it be a trivial object?

Yet today, those of us who have the misfortune of being called sons of the Buddha do not eat from the alms bowl, nor do we drink from the alms bowl, even as we tread upon the traces of the Lotus-Face (Avalokiteśvara).

The root of the bodhi-body was destroyed; the false was used as ornament to confound the true, and the void was relied upon to construct deceptions. As perverse winds fanned each other, the pure and upright were slandered.

Thereupon, the illusory son Kai, pained by the shifting of the True and Semblance Dharma eras and lamenting that the flow of the teachings had grown daily more superficial, proceeded to search through the Vinaya-piṭaka and carefully examine the protocols for the alms bowl (*pātra*). He concluded that while adhering strictly to antiquity would not accord with human nature...
To follow one's own whims would deviate from ancient models. An earthenware bowl is fragile and easily damaged; gold and silver bowls are extravagant and contrary to the Dharma.

Only the iron bowl is sturdy and simple, difficult to destroy yet easy to procure. Yet, in the age of the Final Dharma, the mental conduct of bhikṣus is coarse and flighty, and the times are perilous;
therefore, it is uniquely appropriate for them. Alas! When Rāhula washed his bowl, it shattered into five pieces; from this time on, the Vinaya...

It was divided into five schools, and their tenets were not uniform. The pearl of the precepts was lost from the hand; bhikṣus did not uphold the Vinaya, and bhikṣuṇīs did not observe the Eight Respectful Rules.
They carried standard-sized alms bowls while wandering through wine shops or entering brothels, engaging in all manner of domestic scandals.

The Tathāgata foresaw this with his transcendental knowledge, for he had long lamented such decline. To this day, the ordination platforms are overgrown with weeds, and the robes and alms bowls [are neglected].
I am left in a state of desolation, no longer even knowing what a *pātra* (alms bowl) is. Alas! Having become a son of the Buddha, one ought to repay the Buddha’s kindness.
Within this repayment of the Buddha’s kindness, there are further matters of urgency and leisure. Were it not for an eminent monk (*yingsha*), who could discern what is timely?

Master Kai, realizing that among the vessels of the Dharma none is more important than the *pātra*, resolved to have five hundred iron bowls cast. He shall seek them through alms as circumstances permit; if he relies upon me...
As the imperial spirit’s meritorious labors reach completion, I pray above for the Sage’s long life and offer blessings below for the well-being of the people.

I only wish that the True Dharma may flourish and prosper, that the winds of Māra may be utterly extinguished, and that the lineage of those who hold the Dharma-vessel may remain unbroken through ten thousand ages.
The Origin of the Feast for Monks at the Dinghui Hall of Qixia Temple:
The Buddha-Dharma is the study of the mind. Yet, those who propagate and sustain the Buddha-Dharma are the monks. Therefore, one who disparages the monks does not merely disparage the Buddha;
they disparage their own minds. Now, as for this very mind: from it the sages and worthies are born, and by it heaven and earth are sustained.
Its radiance is vast and great; its spiritual wondrousness is perfectly penetrating. It neither dies nor is born; it has neither present nor past.
It is manifest within the midst of daily life: one cannot enter it when approaching it, yet one cannot discard it when departing from it. It is present when one sees with the eyes.
It is known through the mind. When the objects of the senses have not yet presented themselves, it exists perfectly and independently. Artisans who attain it perfect their skills;
sages who attain it complete the Way. It is not difficult but easy to perceive; one enters into profound resonance with every event, yet people treat it with disdain.
Therefore, people use it daily without realizing its significance. Formerly, when Chan Master Daguan Ying was traveling on pilgrimage, he arrived in the region of Wu at a somewhat late hour.
He sought lodging at a Vinaya monastery, but the master refused him entry. The Master rebuked and reproached him, saying:
"The Tathāgata has spoken these words; have you not heard them? 'If householders do not welcome visiting monks, my Dharma shall perish.'"
Viewed from this perspective, Master Ying was a man of the Way who could not remain for even a single night; why then would he have been so incensed?

From this, I know that the single act of feeding the Sangha possesses the greatest merit: on a grand scale, it nurtures the seeds of Buddhahood; on a small scale, it widely plants the causes of fortune. Now...
