My illusory body grew haggard and my strength waned. Fearing the cold, I wore skins and drank cow’s milk—nine [skins] in total.

I am a deer. Having consumed the remains of a hundred catties of cow’s milk, I have secretly felt shame and remorse. I have presumptuously claimed the status of a son of the Buddha, yet I have not cultivated my spiritual practice;
my wisdom does not overcome my delusion, leading me to this heavy punishment. Yet I still rely upon the physical form of this furred species for my livelihood.

If I do not lean on the Buddha’s compassion, reciting the inner scriptures with my mouth while harboring fear in my heart, the flower of my transgressions will find it difficult to wither, and the fruit of my merit will lack fragrance. Thereupon—
He first donned a deerskin and immediately made a vow: for every skin, he would recite one copy of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

For nine skins, he would recite it nine times, repaying the debt of milk with but three. He vowed that those cows and deer, by the power of this merit, might be liberated from their animal state and be reborn in the realms of humans and devas—noble, exceptionally brilliant, with both merit and wisdom profoundly deep, never forgetting their past lives, always mindful of the roots of virtue, and even offering up their livers.
Discarding his own brain and exhausting his life, he has exerted the utmost sincerity. He piteously reflects upon my kindness, forgetting his own needs for the sake of himself;

he upholds the Buddha-Dharma to illuminate and broaden the realms of humans and devas. Supporting the rising and suppressing the falling, even if space were to come to an end, his vows would remain inexhaustible.

Taking merit and wisdom as a vessel, he carries all beings across extensively. May all who possess knowledge ascend together to the other shore. I, [Name], am now fortunate to have a healthy and strong body, with vigor as [before].

Formerly, having forgotten his original vow, he was like one in the Brahma-world. Thereupon, he swept and cleansed the hall, hung up the image of the Tathāgata, lit lamps, and burned incense, exhorting himself with diligence morning and evening without daring to grow weary or exhausted.
With his mouth reciting the sublime Dharma and his mind focused on its sublime meaning, his body became like a lotus flower;
the three karmas were purified. He performed repentance for the transgressions of killing oxen and deer and other animal sins, as if hot water were dissolving them away.
Ice. Through present karma and past causes, may it be transformed by mindfulness into supreme awakening. In birth after birth, may I be their teacher and the ox-deer be their child.
Manifesting in the forms of humans and devas, may I destroy the heterodox and assist the orthodox, turning the Great Dharma Wheel and shaking the Great Dharma Thunder.

Throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, within the oceans of lands as numerous as motes of dust, may my vows pervade every place where sentient beings dwell, filling them as completely as space.
It is full. Although there is noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), one cannot, even by distinguishing a hair’s breadth of form at the limit of form, find it at all;

therefore, the filling of form is itself the filling of emptiness. Furthermore, as when ice is abundant, water is abundant, mud is abundant, elephants are large, or water is deep and moisture is deep, I make this vow:
may the ox and the deer be like a boat, and I be like the bright moon; with the boat carrying the bright moon, may we return to dwell in the Unconditioned (*anāsrava*).
I have received it. I am overcome with shame and trepidation. I respectfully beseech the Three Jewels to bear witness.
This is the humble draft of the monk Benkong for the purpose of providing a meal for the Sangha at the Western Hermitage.
Regarding the nature of the public and the private: when one forgets oneself for the sake of others, it is called "public"; when one forgets others for the sake of oneself, it is called... [private].
In the public sphere, one may act without striving yet not be great; in the private sphere, one may act without striving yet not be small.

Therefore, if one gives even a single needle with a broad mind, the resulting merit and virtue are immeasurable; whereas if one gives a thousand pieces of gold with a narrow mind, that merit and virtue is likewise limited.

Viewed from this perspective, the accumulation of blessings and the gathering of virtue—how could these be the prerogative of only the wealthy and noble? Even the poor and humble [are capable of them].
Is it that they are incapable? It is simply a matter of whether their intention to give is broad or narrow. About a hundred paces west of Tongjiang Bridge, there is the Huayan Hermitage.

This was established when the Grand Councilor Lord Lu and the Minister of Justice Lord Wang donated their stipends to purchase a ruined hermitage as a place to provide meals for monks under the guidance of the Venerable Benkong.
These two lords, Wutaishan and Yanzhou, were manifesting in the bodies of lay officials.

"If this is the case even for a visiting bhikṣu, how much more so for us? The Buddha said: 'If a resident bhikṣu does not rejoice upon seeing a visiting bhikṣu arrive, it is a sign that my Dharma is about to perish.
Now, joy and lack of joy are clearly distinguished by whether they pertain to the public or the private.
If we merely have a roof over our heads made of grass, let us earnestly take the Buddha’s admonitions as a warning to our hearts; then, though the Dharma is on the verge of extinction,"
Furthermore, its further flourishing may be expected. I, Benkong, urge you all to persevere.
This is a memorial submitted on behalf of the great assembly to cease the rain and pray for clear weather.
I have humbly heard that when the single mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault; when the three words move Heaven, the five blessings arrive in their entirety. Now, at this time...

The torrential rains have continued unceasingly; the fields are gradually submerged, and the hundred grains are on the verge of rotting. The common people have lost all hope for survival, while the Sovereign is filled with anxiety and alarm.
As the sorrow of death spreads across the vast seas, the ditches and gullies are nearly filled, yet life has not yet been extinguished.
In this moment of deep reflection upon the calamity of the floods, there is no affliction visible to the eyes, yet within the heart there is a sign of radiant grace bestowed.
Therefore, sentient beings do not covet, for floods have no source; sentient beings do not harbor anger, for droughts have no root. It is only after emotions shift that misfortune and fortune arise;
it is only after the mind moves that one becomes subject to yin and yang. Now, we [the practitioners] possess the method to eliminate calamities and the means to block the source.

We look up to rely upon the majestic spiritual power of the Triple Gem—the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha—and apply ourselves with utmost sincerity to the three objects of veneration: sovereign, parent, and teacher.

With utmost sincerity, we collectively contribute our pure resources to prepare this modest offering. We burn incense, recite sutras, and perform repentance rites, while simultaneously washing away the transgressions of self and others, as well as the sins of the high and the low.
We prostrate ourselves with the earnest wish that the High Heaven will look down upon us, remit our unforgivable punishments, and bestow blessings that are easily sought.
May a celestial wind suddenly arise, sweeping away all traces of the dark forces without exception; may a brilliant sun instantly appear, so that all things are brought into equal harmony.

Shining together under one sky, we pray once more that the sagacious sovereign’s years may exceed those of heaven and earth, and that the blessings of his ministers and assistants may equal the majesty of mountains and rivers.

May the winds naturally fail to rustle the branches and the rains fail to break the clods of earth. Within the entire realm, even among the neighboring hamlets, let there be no distinction made between the old and the young.
Sharing Peace and Well-being.
An Exhortation for the Painting of the Portraits of the Sixteen Bodhisattvas.
Now, as for form and its shadow, they have never existed without being mutually dependent; nor have they ever failed to arise through mutual dependence.

There is none. Thus, at the very beginning of existence and non-existence, there clearly exists that which comes into being without depending on another, and that which ceases to exist without depending on another.
Yet worldly people merely toil amidst the forms and shadows of existence and non-existence, drifting along until they forget their way back.

To take the real as false and the false as real—this is where manifold afflictions arise. The Sage takes pity on this and establishes skillful means based upon the very nature of the real and the false:
that from the formed one may enter the formless, and from the existent and non-existent one may enter that which is neither existent nor non-existent.
Upon entering and fully realizing this, that which was previously called "preservation" becomes vividly manifest before one's eyes.
Although the form is near to existence and the shadow is near to non-existence, what is near is easier to enter.

Therefore, the Sage transforms his form yet leaves his shadow behind, so that those of future generations throughout the world may, through the shadow, attain the form; through the form, attain the mind; and through the mind, return to their original nature.
It is also like passing from existence into non-existence, and from non-existence into that which is not non-existent.

Suppose there were someone who vowed to reproduce the images of the sixteen arhats, filling more than thirty halls and distributing them throughout all the famous shrines within the world to offer them worship—like a crescent moon in the sky whose reflection appears upon ten thousand waters.
If some might thereby recover their original nature, then would not those who give rise to such a mind be [truly practicing the Way]?
How great is his great compassion! Those who explain this hold that the shadow is not equal to the form, the form is not equal to the mind, and the mind does not resemble the nature (*xing*).

Why, they ask, not simply reveal the nature? What need is there for the shadow? This is because they do not understand that from the coarse one may attain the refined, and from the refined one may enter the subtle.
If this were so, it would be clear that the coarse serves as the vanguard for entering the subtle. — *Daguan* (The Penetrating View).
Upon hearing this, the practitioner was delighted and magnified the teaching in order to widely exhort those who understand the Way, so that together they might accomplish this supreme undertaking.
*Memorial for Soliciting Funds for the Permanent Endowment Land of Zifu Hermitage at Lugou Bridge*
To the east of Lugou Bridge is Zifu Hermitage. Within the hermitage, the elder Chan master Shouxin excavated the earth and discovered a spring;
the water resounded like thunder, causing everyone to be startled. Before long, the sound ceased, leaving only a cold, clear flow. The source of its origin was unfathomable in depth.
The elder Chan master drew from it and distributed it universally to those traveling to and fro who were parched and weary; however, the rope was short while the well was deep.
He considered that [the previous method] could not last for long. He then hewed wood to make wheels, joined the wheels to form hubs, and utilized what was functional to employ humans and animals.
The wheel is named Prajñā; the spring is named the Sea of Merit; and both humans and animals are called Bodhisattvas.

The intent of this old Chan practitioner is that the Bodhisattva employs the wheel of Prajñā to draw from the waters of the Sea of Merit, providing universal relief throughout the ten directions, regardless of whether one is noble or base, human or animal.
Whether possessing a mind or being without a mind, all who receive even a single drop shall be able to illuminate their own minds and together ascend to the other shore.
Reborn within a lotus flower, they will draw near to Amitābha. Upon hearing this, the Daoist Daguang was delighted; being delighted, he rejoiced in it.
He sighed deeply and said: "How magnificent is this wheel! Its rumbling is an ocean of merit; its movement up and down is impermanent, yet it is empty and never exhausted.
If one maintains the mind through ancient meditation and sustains it with inexhaustible power of aspiration, its operation will be without end.
How then can its merit be fathomed by thought or discussed by speech? Thereupon, he acted as the patron for one hundred and seventy people who contributed their resources to purchase the land.

Over four hundred mu of land has been provided to support the permanent endowment of the monastery, so that the wheel of Prajñā and the waters of the ocean of merit may moisten and nourish all beings, never ceasing throughout eternity.
I humbly pray that all who see or hear of this cause and condition will give rise to great joy and profound gratitude;
that they will resolutely burst open the sack of stinginess and greed to bestow wish-fulfilling jewels, thereby together accomplishing this sublime undertaking—would this not be most excellent?
Ah! I, Li Changzhe of Fangshan, have drafted this memorial to determine my future course before the image [of the Buddha].

I have humbly heard that whenever Buddhas, Patriarchs, Sages, and Worthies appear in the world, they invariably act in accordance with what is appropriate to the occasion. If they do not act in accordance with what is appropriate...
Then the spiritual pivot would not engage with things; regarding the teaching, the Dharma, oneself, and others, there would be no benefit whatsoever.
I have reflected upon myself: I set out from a desolate and cold place, renouncing the world in haste. Riding upon the void, I entered into reality; manipulating the false, I made it true.

As for this mind and these traces—every detail from beginning to end—though others may not know them, I myself am clearly aware of them. Furthermore, the wisdom-mirror of the Buddhas and Patriarchs... [is before me].

Throughout immeasurable kalpas past and immeasurable kalpas yet to come, all manifest immeasurable events are like a pond in autumn without ripples—tranquil and transparent across the three periods of time.
As a faint cloud passes through the sky, its subtle shadow is not obscured; naturally, all the good and bad of my life has been within this illumination.

Nevertheless, although my view is free from doubt, when it comes to the active functioning of delusive afflictions (*kleśa*), whenever I encounter conditions or confront objects, my wisdom is weak while my consciousness is strong, and I frequently fall into errors.
Reflecting upon my station in life, I have not yet reached a definitive conclusion. Why is this?

I consider that while my body and life are easy to relinquish, such an act would be of no benefit to the teachings and provide no assistance to the Dharma; were this the case, then staying [in the world] would be superior to leaving it. Furthermore, I reflect:
The ancestral path has fallen into desolation and decay. Unable to endure his kindness yet unable to sacrifice my life to repay his virtue, my heart finds no peace.

Under such circumstances, it would be better to leave than to remain. Thereupon, on a certain day of a certain month in a certain year, I went in person before the honored image of the Elder, burned incense, and set forth my intention, drawing lots to decide the matter. I humbly beseech the Elder not to withhold his compassion and to act for my sake.

Instruction: For the sake of the Dharma and for [Name], I have reached a definitive decision regarding my departure. How could I dare not obey your command? I am overcome with trepidation as I report this.
Regarding the monk Xi’s burning of his finger to compose a memorial for Tanchi Temple:
I lament those in this world who know only yesterday, who know only today, and who likewise know only tomorrow. If one were to...

When interrogated regarding the three periods of time, they say, "I do not know. Yet they fail to realize that the past life is simply yesterday, the present life is today, and the future life is tomorrow. Therefore it is said:
"Yesterday, today, and tomorrow" are called the small three periods of time; "the past, the present, and the future" clarify the great three days. Thus, one can perceive the present life.
Those who possess wealth and honor must have come from what they cultivated in the past; those currently poor and lowly must have been summoned by what they failed to cultivate in the past.

Yet, there are those who, despite having cultivated in the past, cannot enjoy the splendor of wealth and honor; and there are those who, despite not having cultivated in the past, cannot be burdened by poverty and lowliness.
In these cases, wealth, honor, poverty, and lowliness originally possess no increase or decrease. One must understand these two points.

Those who practice while remaining unaware that they cannot truly practice are called people of merit (*puṇya*). Those who know that they cannot practice and thus do not engage in any practice from the outset are called people of wisdom (*jñāna*).
Only the Buddha and the great Bodhisattvas possess both types of perfection (*dvaya-saṃbhāra*) from the beginning.
Tanchi Temple was formerly the place where the ancestral master Dao’an led the people of Xiangyang to cultivate wisdom and merit. Lately, it has fallen into decay.

It was in a state of ruin beyond repair. There was a Zen practitioner named Zhenxi who, though possessed of the will to restore it, reflected that his merit and fortune were meager and he had no means to move others.
He therefore used his finger as a candle, lighting it to make an offering to the Buddha, and vowed: "If my heart is sincere, this great undertaking shall surely succeed;
if my heart is not sincere, this great undertaking will be difficult to accomplish. I have heard that the monastics of Xiang all said, "Zen Master Xi..."
People burn their fingers to repair temples not for the sake of food or clothing; yet if such noble deeds have no end, the spirits will surely lack divine power.
On the twenty-fourth day of the fourth month, I visited Tanchi once again and happened to meet the Zen practitioner Xi.
Observing his countenance, I knew his heart was sincere, so I have written this to look up to and inform the ten directions.
A Preface to the Image of the Buddha Adorned with the Skull Ornament and Offered by Sthiramati:

I have reverently heard that when the seven treasures were offered as alms until they filled the voids of the four directions, though the resulting merit was boundless, it ultimately fell within the realm of birth and extinction.

Only when the entire body is sacrificed at once, becoming equal to a single mustard seed, does the light of wisdom reach its perfect limit and accord with the true and eternal. For this reason, the Bodhisattva of the Snowy Mountains...
One does not begrudge one’s humble body in order to obtain the Dharma from what remains after the physical form has been cast aside.

Good Wealth (Sudhana) did not let the distance of a hundred cities deter him from fulfilling his heart’s desire amidst the gathering of mists and waters. Had it not been for such profound concern and far-reaching deliberation, this vow would have been difficult to fulfill.

If you must exhaust your thoughts with utmost sincerity, the Way will be easily accomplished. Yet, if the mechanism of lust is not severed, flesh and blood will transform into things of putrid stench;

whereas if the habit of desire is suddenly dried up, skin and flesh become fragrant and pure pearls. Within the mind there are the coarse and the refined, and their application is distinguished by fragrance and foulness.

If one awakens to the beginning where not even a single thought has arisen, who can name them as "saint" or "ordinary"? One must painfully contemplate the four subtle elements (*catur-mahābhūta*) at the very moment they first borrow [existence].
At that time, the signs of male and female first appeared; thus, in the ocean of the myriad treasures, the śarīra alone is the sovereign, and the *dharmakāya* (the firm and solid) is its minister.

This is because the state of non-arising (*anutpāda*) has not yet been realized, while the delusions of dream-like dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) prevail. If one were to fully comprehend dependent origination, then even though the putrid and foul would not decay, and though heaven and earth might perish, the firm and solid would suffer no loss.
When one transcends the realm of emptiness, the śarīra remains ever-luminous. May the bhikṣus bow their heads nine times in reverence.

Within the midst of the sacred flames of the statues of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and the eighteen Arhats, thirty seeds of firm resolve and thirty spheres of cranial bone are offered as a gift.
May they rest forever within the void of the five viscera of the principal and attendant deities.
It is my wish that these disciples, throughout all their births and in every place, amidst the alternating cycles of ascent and descent, may...

The boundary where ordinary beings and sages gather together. While my views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) remain unsevered, I shall always serve the Triple Gem in the body of a bhikṣu—like a shadow following a form, like light reflecting in a mirror.
When the shadow meets darkness it vanishes; when the light is covered by dust it is obscured. Such is the vow of my heart.

May my diligent upholding be firm and dense, not like a mere reflection of light or shadow; may it become even more manifest where [delusions] are extinguished, and shine even brighter when sealed [in stillness].
Now that the afflictions of views and thoughts have been severed, may I propagate the Dharma among all diverse beings according to their kind, never daring to grow weary.
Furthermore, I pray that you grant me steadfastness and grant me the crown of my head. May all the merit and wisdom I have accumulated be dedicated as a gift to you, and to all sentient beings.
"Born with merit equal to the merit of a Buddha and wisdom equal to the wisdom of a Buddha, my vow is finally fulfilled.
I have heard that whether layperson or monastic, for every ten parts of merit and wisdom cultivated, the king receives four parts and the practitioner receives six parts. Why is this?"

Because the Emperor is the sovereign of the world, those who cultivate merit and wisdom cannot, if they do not rely upon the imperial favor and the virtue of his protection, ever attain even a hair’s breadth of merit or wisdom.

Therefore, those who cultivate merit and wisdom must never forget the grace of the Sovereign, the grace of their parents, the grace of their teachers, the grace of their benefactors, and the grace of their spiritual friends. As for those who neglect and forget such graces—how could they...?
Alas, it is difficult to cultivate merit and wisdom, yet this human body is easily lost; one's lifespan is not long, a hundred misfortunes converge, and ten thousand blessings naturally vanish.
Therefore, as I reflect upon my manifold debts of gratitude, my five viscera burn like fire, and with a heart of singular sorrow, I offer various vows on their behalf.
I humbly beseech the eternally abiding Triple Gem of the ten directions, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, and the twelve divisions of the scriptures...
Sutra. May the Venerable Kauṇḍinya and all the holy ones, ordinary beings, and spiritual protectors of the Dharma who possess divine intelligence, together grant their solemn testimony and alliance.

Furthermore, following this aspiration, may the present sagely sovereign’s virtue of Yao forever spread, and his sun-like brilliance of Shun shine eternally; may the four seas be pure and peaceful, and the myriad people delight in their vocations, being born into this very body.
My parents... light arises from decaying bones; I have awakened to the wandering souls. I prostrate myself nine times again. Overwhelmed by shame and pain, I respectfully submit this memorial.
Memorial for the Release of the Stag.
I have humbly heard the Tathāgata’s clear instruction that bhikṣus must not wear silk, cotton, or fine fabrics, nor leather boots, furs, or skins.
This is especially true for those who have long suffered from malaria, whose vital energy is diminished, whose physical frames are frail and weak, and who fear the cold in every movement and posture.
If one does not shield oneself with hides and leathers, then the river winds and nocturnal dew will likely be difficult to withstand. Thus, I have purchased several pieces of *jia* (monal) deer skin.

I have patched a strip onto the lower garment to provide some protection against my former ailment. Although the Vinaya contains provisions regarding what is permitted or prohibited, and what constitutes an offense or its maintenance, my inner mind remains ultimately uneasy.
I reflect deeply that, among the species of musk deer, one is dragged by black karma in life and finds no path to the gate of compassion after death;
their lives end in arrows and nets, and their hides are torn by knives and needles. Now that I am using a portion of its vital essence, in the future... [the fruit will ripen].
Ge Nan declined the request. "If one does not anticipate being transcended and delivered, there may still be no lack of opportunity for creating the conditions [for liberation].
Therefore, I shall use a single skin to serve as the mouth for reciting one volume of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

I humbly pray that, relying upon the compassionate power of the Tathāgata and the majestic spiritual authority of the *Saddharma*, the deer and others may have the clouds of delusion dispelled in an instant and ascend the path of awakening through Prajñā. May they know this themselves."
To become a Buddha is like digging a well and seeing mud; to make a vow to deliver sentient beings is for the impoverished son to obtain treasure.

In the prayer for rain, I respectfully hear that while the sages have no fixed mind and sentient beings have no fixed habits, when it comes to the matter of resonance and response (*ganying*), how could the capacity (*ji*) fail to respond?

Thus, the teaching arises. It is like a physician who has no fixed illness and an illness that has no fixed physician; it is through the mutual encounter of physician and illness that the subtle and the coarse are first distinguished.
Therefore, for an illness caused by cold, one treats it with a cold medicine; for an illness caused by heat, one treats it with a hot medicine.
Just as sentient beings have immeasurable illnesses, the Buddha, as the King of Physicians, likewise possesses immeasurable medicines. In the world, there is a state of extreme... [text ends]
Regarding the anxiety over drought, the Tathāgata does not withhold the response of his own power (*bala*). Furthermore, this power is not possessed by the Tathāgata alone;

there is also the power of the heavens, the power of the earth, the power of the noble ones (*ārya*), the power of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), the power of the dragon kings (*nāgarāja*), the power of the dragon kings' retinues, and the combined power of all other classes of spirits and deities. It is for this reason that it rains.
If one does not pray, there will be no descent [of grace]. If sentient beings do not move [the Buddhas], the Buddhas will not respond.

Yet among all Buddhas, there is one named Tathāgata Great Compassion Cloud-Born, who deeply pities the suffering of sentient beings during a drought. When the grain and sprouts do not flourish, there is no basis for rice and food;
when there is no basis for rice and food, the life-force of sentient beings is severed. Thereupon, Tathāgata Great Compassion Cloud-Born...

Come! I make this vow to rescue them. Therefore, wherever there is a severe drought, if one invokes the name of this Tathāgata, then by the power of the Great Sovereign Real-Force Samādhi of the Tathāgata, leading all sages and ordinary beings, various real forces will be applied in unison to transform parched lands into lush abundance and turn scorching heat into sweet rain. I pray that the clouds of great compassion may arise like...

Come! Do not fail your original vow; look down in response to the capacities of all beings. May the three types of grass and two types of trees, and all the hundred grains, be universally rescued from their parched withering, so that they may all attain lush growth and ripened fruit. Respectfully recorded.

Preface to the White Text of the Diamond Sūtra:
This sūtra arrived in the East and flourished during the Tang dynasty; continuing through successive dynasties, its brilliance was cold and its color pure, as bright as the sun and moon.

Reaching our Ming dynasty, although there have not been lacking those who spread its light and continue its flame, the true eye of the Diamond Sūtra has, as it were, fallen into clouds and mist. This is because...
I have constantly reflected on this reason: when one's learning prioritizes intellectual principles, it is called the "ignorance of what is known.

If this ignorance of what is known is not destroyed, one's own mind cannot manifest before oneself. When the self-mind cannot manifest, the mind follows after external objects, becoming entangled and unable to be untied.
To seek a mind that dwells nowhere while holding a view that there is something to dwell upon is to deviate from the analysis of the sutras;

it is like Xiao Tong’s solitary drooling, which merely seeps into the ocean of consciousness—how, then, can the sutra be made clear? If one wishes for the sutra to be clear, nothing is better than directly seeking the Buddha-mind.
If one wishes to seek the Buddha-mind, nothing is better than reciting the original text. One must remain in profound stillness beyond the subtle and mysterious, and apply steadfast refinement to...
The gateway between birth and death, and between the favorable and the adverse, is a succession of moments that never ceases. It is like yeast in curd, or malt in wine;
it is neither with mind nor without mind. Within the conditions of conditions, there is that which is suddenly accomplished.

Thus, Great Mirror (Dajian) was originally but a wood-seller from Xinzhou; he did not possess a long-standing cultivation of literary or philosophical principles, yet by chance he relaxed [his grasp].
Dān (Dānpó) heard this sutra and his mind was opened; he subsequently traveled to Huangmei, where he received the patriarchal seal and wore it as a sash.

To this day, throughout ten thousand generations, he is known as the Sixth Patriarch. Is this not a clear verification of the maturation of conditions through the cumulative influence of hearing the Dharma over successive kalpas?
Formerly, when Páng Yùn was lying on his left side reading this sutra, Dánxiá rebuked him, saying, "Is this not to treat the Dharma with contempt? Yùn then placed his left foot upon [the other].

It is merely the right foot. As I read the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) up to this point, there has never been a time when my tears did not flow down to my chin, nor have I ever ceased to clench my fists in grief and pain.
Now, having edited and divided the sections, I have carved the original text of the scripture. The intent of the Tathāgata spreads as vast as the clouds across the heavens;
may all who possess knowledge receive and uphold it through life and death, wielding the tally of Great Mirror Wisdom to unfold the legacy of Master Pang.
When applied, it is certain that curd will emerge from milk.
In the Preface to the *Shimen Wenzixian* (Stone Gate Prose Zen), it is said:
Since the Jin, Song, Qi, and Liang dynasties, those who studied the Way have vied with one another to obscure their eyes with gold dust; yet the First Patriarch came from the East.
Administering medicine according to the ailment, he pointed directly at the human mind and established no reliance on words and letters.
Yet later followers, merely catching echoes in the void and ignorant of medicinal taboos, proceeded to fortify all boundaries and construct words and letters outside of Chan.

Consequently, they demarcated territories and drew lines, dissecting the empty sky; those who study Chan do not strive for the essential meaning, while those who study words and letters do not strive [for the truth].

To understand the mind: if one’s grasp of the meaning is not refined, the mind may be understood but will not shine with brilliance. If one refines the meaning but does not understand the mind, then the words and letters will ultimately fail to penetrate the spirit.
Therefore, Baojue wished to employ the study of the "study-less" so that it might flow like the hundred rivers converging at the sea, inexhaustible.
He marveled that Master Min, like a Persian ship from the South Sea, reached the shore by means of the wind; his exemplary reputation remains fully preserved, and his model conduct is not lost.

Far-reaching! Alas! It is through reflection that one may understand. For Chan is like spring, while words and texts are like flowers. Spring resides within the flowers, and the entirety of the flowers is spring;

Upon returning from Caoxi, I fulfilled my vow to Mount Lao. In the blink of an eye, three seasons had passed; it was the year Wuxu (1098), when I entered the summer retreat at Longdong Huayan Temple in Xiangyang.
At that time, a man of pure reputation named Liu from Huanglongtan on Mount Lu brought [the following] to me:
When the compassionate letter arrived, I learned that Kuangshi had already departed for the Pure Land. I sighed deeply for a long time. Thereupon, I returned to Xunyang once more;

mourning for Kuangshi, I lingered there for several days. Again sitting beneath the Hall of Long Pines and walking along the courtyard paths, I beheld the mountain mists and lake fogs shifting in their ethereal transformations.
Unconsciously, I was moved to reflect upon the meeting and parting of my friends, past and present.
The nature of these things and the transformations of birth and death cannot both be determined as auspicious or inauspicious by the conceptualizing mind;
they are like the illusory manifestations of mist and fog—visible, yet impossible to grasp.
Now, fame and profit are what the multitude strives for, while the body and mind are what the multitude clings to. Yet, there is a subtle transformation...
It shifts its authority to the sovereign who grasps its pivotal power; thus, in this human world, regardless of whether one is wise or foolish, noble or lowly, none dare not obey its commands.
Only those who understand transformation before it is fully manifest can abandon what the masses struggle for and empty what the masses cling to;
only then can the sovereign that secretly shifts its authority no longer exercise its power. Even so—
Since the conditions and circumstances of the past and present are thus, what difference is there between the various states of rising and sinking— both within and beyond the six directions—
and the shifting, impermanent nature of mountain mists and lake fogs that come and go before, behind, to the left, and to the right of one's lodging?
Record of the Return of the Son of Firm Resolve:
In the year Wuxu, Grand Councilor Wang Jingfeng bestowed upon the lay practitioner Shizhai one "Firm Resolve" seed.
In the spring of Jihai, Ruan, the Vice Minister of the Board of War of Raoyang, dispatched Yuantong, the Master of Mazu Hermitage on Mount Wan, to deliver a sandalwood shrine.
[The Master] sat and made offerings to Zibo. Zibo then transmitted them to Layman Shizhai. [Shizhai] stored the "Solid Son" (jianguozi) bestowed by Grand Councilor Wang in the Guizong Monastery.
The layman said: "Grand Councilor Wang was without intention regarding the sandalwood shrine, and Vice Minister Ruan was likewise without intention regarding the 'Solid Son.
That both were without intention yet naturally received one another is like a magnet and a needle."
[They] looked at one another. [The disciple] requested, "I pray you, grant me a word to record this.
Zibo said, "That which is firm is not firm by itself; that which is the incense niche is not a niche by itself. If I say it is 'firm,' then firmness manifests before us;
if I say it is a 'niche,' then the niche is inherently present. If one says that firmness and the niche are two separate things, then discrimination has not yet been forgotten. Furthermore—
This means that both the solid wood and the incense chamber are not things external to the mind; thus, one can use principle to harmonize with phenomena.

Yet, this is not yet to touch upon phenomena and realize the truth. If one could indeed touch upon phenomena and realize the truth, then the ten directions and the three periods of time would all be the son of the solid wood, and the entire dharma-realm of empty space would be the sandalwood chamber. When Vice Minister Wang and Secretary Ruan perform such acts of giving, then—
"One giving is all giving. When a lay practitioner of the true fast (zhai) receives in this manner, then one receiving is all receiving;
one giving is all giving. Giving is fundamentally without giving; one receiving is all receiving; receiving is fundamentally without receiving.
Since giving is fundamentally without giving, giving has no end; since receiving is fundamentally without receiving, receiving has no exhaustion. Such giving—how is it different from empty space?

Wind arises; such is sensation. How does this differ from the reflection being received by the light of a mirror? Thus, while the kalpa-stone may wear away, both giving and receiving are inexhaustible treasuries.
Layman, if you understand this, then the Golden Wheel and the Dharma Wheel will turn together in daily life.

How could it be that only the "Son of Firmness" (the Bodhisattva) and the sandalwood shrine are capable of skillfully reciting verses? Pine trees, wind, water, and moonlight; tiles, rubble, briars, and thorns—all are thus.
This is none other than the broad and long tongue-mark of the Honored One.

In my hearing, both within and beyond this world, there are five kinds of vast sounds that can serve as the thunder for the five vehicles, following [the needs of beings]. *The Record of Bodhidīpa at Tanchi Temple* I have heard that in the mundane and supramundane realms, there are five kinds of vast sounds capable of acting as the thunder for the five vehicles, according to [the capacities of sentient beings].
It is appropriate to cause them to be struck with awe; all these issues flow forth from the power of the Tathāgata’s merit and Dharma.
For example, punishing the ten evil deeds and rewarding the ten wholesome deeds is the thunder that strikes those who ride upon the vehicle of humans and devas.

For example, realizing that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent and subject to arising and ceasing, while Nirvāṇa is tranquil, unconditioned, and peaceful, is the thunder that strikes those who ride upon the vehicle of the śrāvakas.
To awaken not through another, viewing the Śrāvakas as narrow-minded and realizing the Way through solitary enlightenment—this is the thunder that startles the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.

To rebuke the two vehicles, extensively cultivating the six perfections, never ceasing the bodhisattva practices, never abandoning the bodhicitta, and remaining untiring amidst immeasurable cycles of birth and death—this is the thunder that startles the Bodhisattva vehicle. As it is said:
It is said that this is the First Vehicle, the Victorious Vehicle, the Most Victorious Vehicle, the Superior Vehicle, and the Unsurpassed Vehicle.

This is the thunder that awakens beings of great resolve. These five vehicles are also called the Five Lamps of Bodhi; for while thunder can stimulate the faculty of hearing, a lamp can illuminate the faculty of sight.
When hearing is stimulated, one’s auditory capacity is expanded so that there is no distance too great to hear; when illumination is opened, one’s vision becomes penetrating.
Yet, in vision, there is neither center nor periphery. If this is so, then within a single atom and beyond the ten voids, there is nothing left unperceived by hearing or sight.
Because hearing leaves nothing unperceived, the ear can behold forms; because sight leaves nothing unperceived, the eye can hear sounds. Therefore it is said:
"When clarity is manifested by relying on the faculties, that clarity does not follow the faculties. Since clarity does not follow the faculties, how could it be otherwise?
The eye can perceive sounds, and it can also smell fragrances, taste flavors, feel tactile objects, and cognize mental phenomena.
Even the eighty-four thousand pores of my body can likewise see forms and hear sounds. Alas!

When a single faculty possesses the functions of all six faculties, who but one who is supremely clear-sighted and courageous—having reversed the flow of consciousness and made the six into one—could achieve this?
In the autumn of the Wuliangxu year of the Wanli era, the lay practitioner and Bodhisattva-official Wang Erkang, known as Jinniu Jushi, visited Tanchi Temple.
Beholding the traces left by Gu Yin, he could not bear its desolation; at that time, he composed the verse:
"A cold spring and ancient cypress stand alone, guarding the Tanchi. He then donated one *yuan* of his official stipend and instructed the monk Zhenxi to cultivate the land.
One mu of land may slightly provide for the brightness of the lamps before the Buddha. If there were ten like-minded individuals, then there would be the resources for ten mu of cultivated land;

would the light not then be more extensive and far-reaching? Furthermore, through this light, one's hearing might be extended, such that there could be those who offer bells and drums to perform Buddhist services—this is yet to be known.
In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, there is the phrase regarding the "poison-coated drum," and in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*...
There is a statement regarding the proof of permanence through the striking of a bell; this is also a commentary on the five kinds of vast sounds.

It depends entirely upon what a person hears and sees. If one hears and sees with the eyes and ears of humans and devas, then it is called the Bodhi-lamp of humans and devas, the sound of the bells and drums of humans and devas, and so forth, even for sentient beings of great resolve who hear with their eyes and ears.
Upon seeing this, he called him "the great-minded sentient being, the lamp of Bodhi," and "the sound of the Bodhi bell and drum. He further said: "Outside the mind there is no dharma.
If one can realize this according to the occasion, then whether taking it from what is near—the body—or from what is far—external objects—what dharma is not the lamp of Bodhi?
What is not the sound of the Bodhi bell and drum? When the man of Zi柏 heard the Layman’s impromptu speech, he was struck with wonder.
Thus it was. Yin was displeased that his beard and hair had not yet been removed, yet he interrupted my discourse.
I have recorded this briefly to serve as a pretext for seeking him out again on another day.
Record of the Tiankai Guxiang Hermitage in Fangshan County The Sage has no fixed body;
he takes the bodies of sentient beings as his own body. It is like the moon, which has no fixed reflection;
it appears as reflections because the waters of the hundred rivers are clear and still. On the nineteenth day of the fifth month of the Ren-shen year of the Wanli era, at Mount Zhuolu, the clouds...
While residing at Dongguansi, the abbot Mingliang and others repaired the stone surface beneath the seats of the Buddhas of the Three Ages within Leiyinku on Shijing Shan.
Beneath the stone was a stone casket, the lid of which was inscribed as follows:
"The twelfth year of the Daye era of the Great Sui, the year of Bingzi; the fourth month, the first day of the moon, Dingyi; on the eighth day, Jiazi, here [was this placed]."
Inside the casket were placed three grains of the Buddha’s *śarīra*. Wishing that they might remain for eternal kalpas, Mingliang and the others saw them and were both startled and delighted.
They then opened it to inspect the contents; inside was a small copper casket. Within the copper casket was a small gold casket.
Inside the gold casket was a small gold bottle about the size of a pea, which secretly contained the *śarīra*. Indeed, there were three grains, varying in size.
There were three types: one larger than a grain of millet, one the size of a grain of millet, and one finer than a grain of millet.

Furthermore, all over the exterior of the bronze casket, sacred relics were attached. Alas! From the Sui dynasty until the Ming, spanning more than a millennium, these śarīra and sacred relics have simultaneously reappeared.
How could this be a mere coincidence? Is it not because for many years floods and droughts have been unseasonable, and the frontier regions have been beset by many troubles?

Have the Buddhas and Patriarchs, out of their compassionate pity, manifested this rare phenomenon as a sign of gentle breezes and sweet rains to utterly extinguish the portents of foul and cruel violence?

Or is it that the Greatly Enlightened Sovereign has transformed his habit of anger into waves of compassion? Or perhaps it is brought about by the Holy Mother’s profound faith in the Triple Gem? Thus have I heard.
At Shijing Mountain, the Venerable Huisi of the Northern Qi dynasty carved the Great Canon into stone to perpetuate the Buddha’s life of wisdom.
This tradition was continued by Jingwan of the Sui dynasty and concluded with Yuanhuiyue.

When Master Wan passed away, one portion of his sacred relics was enshrined in a stupa behind Lingju Temple, while another portion was concealed within Leiyin Cave. These present-day śarīra relics must surely be...
This was preserved by the disciples of Master Wan. I asked Attendant Kai, "Is the Buddha-body pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm?
He replied, "The Buddha and sentient beings are fundamentally without distinction; how could it not be pervasive? I asked him again:
"Since the Buddha’s body is already all-pervading, are the *śarīra* relics also all-pervading? Kaifang hesitated for a moment. I raised my voice and shouted, "Have you not heard?
Formerly, a high-ranking eunuch ascended Mount Ayuwang on the Zhejiang coast. Before he had even entered the triple gate, he asked Master Xiaoweng, 'Where are the *śarīra* relics?
Master Xiaoweng pointed to a pine branch, and the branch immediately emitted light. If you understand this, then you will know."
Thus, whether the śarīra are full or not full, one knows for oneself where they fall; what more need I say?

Nevertheless, the great bell receives all in its emptiness and does not fail to resonate when struck; the deep valley is impartial, and every sound echoes therein. Therefore, the Sage has no fixed body.
The moon has no constant reflection; it appears when the water is clear. When the spiritual capacity awakens, the Sage responds.
This hall was established many years ago, yet it had not yet received a name. Only now, upon the arrival of the śarīra relics and their radiant presence, does it finally attain its name.
I and my two or three companions have all been able to dwell in faith within the light of the śarīra, and we have further gained the company of the brothers of Ren’an Cí.
To be the host for such fragrant food—how fortunate one could be! Indeed, the bones of sentient beings are foul-smelling, while the bones of the Buddhas are fragrant.

Yet, if fragrance and stench were fixed and unchanging, how could an ordinary person ever become a sage? How could defilement ever be purified? That I have named this hermitage after the fragrance of the Buddha’s bones is for this very reason.
To understand that all sentient beings are fundamentally impermanent from the beginning: it is because they follow along with ignorance that the six realms of existence are arrayed like stars.

If one does not follow along, whose bones would not be fragrant? May you ascend to the name "Fragrant Bones" (*Gandhasthūṇa*), attain the name through thought, and then forget thought by attaining its meaning.
When thought is forgotten, there is the forgetting of forgetting. If this is so, how could it be that only this chamber is fragrant with bones? [It extends] to the four directions and above.
Below. There is nothing that does not possess the fragrance of bone.
In the *Hand-Print Record* of Grand Minister Lu, it is said:

"Formerly, there was a king who practiced virtue diligently from birth until old age without ever flagging. However, at the moment his life was ending, he happened to encounter an adverse circumstance."

Regarding the object: as soon as a mind of hatred arose, his life ended because of it, and he immediately fell into the body of a python. By the power of his roots of goodness, although his body had fallen as a python, he knew himself to be a python;
yet, having no means to escape, he thought secretly to himself: "It would be fortunate if I could find a bhikṣu who would preach the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts for me;
then I might be able to leave this python body. At that time, a bhikṣu arrived at the place where the python was, but did not know [how to help him].

While the python was coiled within the forest, it suddenly heard someone calling out, "Bhikṣu! The bhikṣu was surprised; in this deep mountain wilderness, amidst such dense thickets of trees, who could be calling him?
He paused and looked around in all directions. Again the voice called out: "Bhikṣu, I am a certain king.

Because I harbored anger at the time of my death, I have now fallen into the body of a python. I pray that you, Great Virtue, will recite the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts for me and deliver me."
[The Buddha said: "They are liberated from suffering. The bhikṣu said: "That king was diligent in doing good from birth until old age without ever flagging;

he must surely be reborn in heaven upon death. How could he have fallen into the body of a python? The python replied: "Because my anger was intense at the time of my death. Anger is the master and goodness is its companion; the companion must follow the master."

Therefore, he fell into the body of a python. However, because of the power of his diligent practice of virtue throughout his life, had he heard the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, he could have escaped this python body.
Thereupon, the bhikṣu proceeded to recite the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts for him; the python died accordingly. How marvelous! The power of thought transforms and transcends the impermanent.
While alive he was diligent in virtue, yet at death he stirred a mind of anger; thus, good and evil arise from the new impulse of anger.

While undergoing the retribution [of his previous life], he heard the precepts for taking refuge; by the power of this new wholesome perfuming, his goodness continued to flow on. His anger was extinguished, the serpent died, and he was reborn in heaven.
How marvelous is the power of mindfulness! How divine it is! Observing this very case, one can know that there is no such thing as "great" or "small" regarding mindfulness.

If a thought arises from a wholesome cause, even if the matter is great and difficult to accomplish, one must certainly contemplate deeply and consider the long-term, employing myriad skillful means to carry it out with meticulous care.
If a thought arises from an unwholesome cause, though the matter be trivial, one must immediately and resolutely eliminate what is desired so that it does not come to fruition.
In this way, one will naturally receive a magnificent reward in both this life and future births, whether among humans or in the heavens.

His virtue surpassed that of his contemporaries; whatever he desired to do, there was nothing he could not achieve as he wished. Why was this? It was due to the power of his initial wholesome thoughts.
Therefore it is said: "One must be diligent in good and must overcome evil. When serving as the Grand Chancellor of Hugu, he had placed his faith in the Buddha throughout his life.
Upon reaching the point of protecting the Dharma, he remained detached from both slander and praise; if someone spoke ill of the Buddha, he would immediately regard them with love.

If one lacks faith, love turns into hatred; yet he knew only that the task of protecting the Dharma was of paramount importance, remaining entirely indifferent to matters of intimacy or estrangement, honor or disgrace.
Thus, even in the midst of a grave illness, his countenance remained clear and serene, and his spirit was undisturbed.
Before he fell ill, he used his left hand for purification, never employing it where there was defilement, using instead only his right hand.
Furthermore, when his illness became critical and he was no longer aware of the sun rising as morning or setting as evening, ten days passed.
Then, his second finger of the left hand and his thumb were pressed together so firmly, as if born that way, that they could not be separated.
Were it not for the power of his diligent and devout mindfulness, such that matters of life and death entered his breast, who could have reached this state? Alas!
Consider this: if the left hand were pure and the right hand impure, then within a single body there would be two hands, and purity and defilement would exist as entirely separate realms.
Judging by outward appearances, it might indeed seem so; yet when inferred through principle, this is clearly not the case. The hands themselves possess neither purity nor defilement;

purity and defilement reside solely in the mind. How could a single person possess two minds? Since a single person cannot have two minds, [the distinction between purity and defilement is likewise unreal].
If the mind is pure, it is free from defilement and impurity; thus, the fruit is likewise free from defilement and impurity.
How could one claim that only the left hand is pure while the right hand—previously considered impure—is not? For what reason?
Once the single mind is pure, then from the feet to the crown of the head, from the extremities to the center, and even throughout the eighty-four thousand pores, there is nothing that is not pure.
Regarding impurity, it is therefore said: "If the mind is pure, then the Buddha-land is pure. This is the word of the sages. I, however, say:
"If the mind is pure, then every pore is pure. Since every pore is pure, how could the mountains, rivers, and lands not all be pure?
If this is so, then this seal of the Grand Chancellor’s will surely remain unloosened even after death; his rebirth in a Buddha-land is certain.
"Indeed. Nevertheless, this may be discussed with the wise, but it is difficult to explain to the common multitude.

In the *wuli* year of the *Xinmao* cycle (1591), after I had finished copying the two sutras—the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*—the true forms of the Eight Classes of Deities were to be painted upon the niche."
By relying on its majestic spiritual power, it wards off misfortune and ensures that these two sutras are protected and remain unharmed wherever they may be.
Now, Master Yù of Línghán Temple in Zhuǐlǐ has arrived with a transformed image (*pariṇāma*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

Upon viewing it, I was greatly pleased and thus commissioned Dīng Yúnpéng of Zhāngshān to produce a faithful copy. Once installed within the shrine, its exquisite and intricate craftsmanship is truly magnificent and solemn.

How rare! As for the *Huayan bianxiang* (Transformation Tableau of the Avataṃsaka), although the holy and the mundane differ, its principal figures and attendants stand in solemn array, their dignified postures fully perfected.
In manifesting the Dharma through concrete phenomena, its profound intent is darkly yet brilliantly clear, like the moon reflected in autumn waters; it requires no words.
It causes those who see it to each perceive it clearly and without confusion. Among them are the eight classes of beings: such as the *asura*, which means "non-god";
the *garuḍa*, which means "golden-winged bird"; the *kiṃnara*, which means "doubtful human"; and the *mahoraga*.
"Mahoraga" means "great python. "Yakṣa" means "one who lives in suffering. "Vaiśravaṇa" means "one whose eye-organ is adorned with various colors.
"Kumbhāṇḍa" means "a ghost that causes nightmares. "Gandharva" means "seeker of fragrance. Each of these has its own king who governs immeasurable retinues;
they respectfully receive the Buddha’s command and protect the Dharma wherever they are. They possess innate, constant radiance, which is born..."
The Buddha is non-dual; yet, according to the conditions that influence and permeate them, the manifestations he displays differ.
Therefore, wherever a single thought arises in sentient beings, each has its own specific cause. For example: asuras are characterized by much anger, flattery, and deception;
garuḍas subsist on devouring living beings; kiṃnaras obtain food by playing music; mahoragas protect monasteries; yakṣas live by tormenting others; and vairocana...
The *kumbhāṇḍas* lead hosts of nāgas; they consume vital essence and bewitch sentient beings with nightmares. The *gandharvas* seek fragrances and perform music.
Such various beings receive different retributions according to their karma, yet these also depend upon the nature of their initial resolve.
Now, when all people—whether virtuous or non-virtuous—engage in the practice of daily life, the thoughts that arise are manifold. One should attempt to observe each of them one by one. This...
Is it the karma of an asura? Is it the karma of a garuḍa? Or even the karma of a gandharva?

Illuminating the place where these evil thoughts arise, one uses the fire of knowledge and vision, the wind of diligence, the forge of patience, the hammer of ethical discipline, the charcoal of meditative concentration, and the water of generosity—refining them through these various means to transform all the copper of defiled habitual tendencies.

If they were suddenly melted away without a trace, who would not belong to the lineage of the Tathāgata? Such being the case, even the eight classes of spirits and celestials, each perceiving the light, regarded it as the mark of the broad and long tongue;
how much more so those who uphold the Buddha and protect the Dharma, even at the cost of smearing their livers and brains upon the ground?
It is fitting that one should paint [this image] and offer worship to it.
Regarding the Record of the Great Compassionate Bodhisattva composed by Vice Minister Zhao:
"When the single mind does not arise, the hands and eyes are immeasurable. When a slight thought arises, the functions of the hands and eyes become divided. If they are immeasurable..."
The hand can see form; the eye can grasp objects. When their functions are distinguished, the hand can only grasp and the eye can only see.

Observing it from this perspective, the hands and eyes of Bodhisattvas and sentient beings are equal. Therefore, for those with two eyes and two arms, if the single mind does not arise, then the perfect functioning will be without deficiency.
For those with a thousand hands and a thousand eyes, if even a slight thought arises, then the sense-faculties and their objects [are divided].

They mutually limit one another. It is like an empty valley that has no mind; it responds a thousand times to a thousand calls and ten thousand times to ten thousand calls. Yet the caller grows weary, while the responder never tires.

Even an empty valley, though void and lacking sentience, still responds ten thousand times without exhaustion. If such is the case for that which is void yet not sentient, how much more so for the human being who is both sentient and void?
To call upon that which is sentient but not void leads to exhaustion; how much more so for that which is both void and supremely sentient, wondrously presiding over all things and standing alone?
How could it be otherwise? His hand-eye coordination is immeasurable; his various faculties function interchangeably—how can there be any cause for doubt?
Yet, there are those who harbor doubts and fail to believe, for they cling to the notion that the body is merely six feet tall and the mind is but a square inch.

They fail to realize that those who see only the small will inevitably lose the great, and those who see only the narrow will inevitably lose the vast. There is nothing greater than being bodiless; there is nothing more expansive than being formless.

Therefore it is said: It is not that there is no attainment of the formless body (*an-ātmabhāva*), for without it one cannot manifest the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of jewel-eyes and wondrous arms;

and it is not that there are no immeasurable hundreds of thousands of jewel-eyes and wondrous arms, for without them one cannot manifest the attainment of the formless body. Thus, it is the one who is without thought.

One can thereby realize identity. To realize identity means one can employ [the mind] perfectly. When employed perfectly, one engages in intense discrimination yet does not deviate from the identical essence.
If the employment has not yet reached perfection, then even if the body is like withered wood and the mind like extinguished ashes, neither constitutes true forgetting.
Only those who have attained true forgetting are like dragons: in the space of a finger-snap, they manifest impermanence; on a large scale, they may...

It fills the void horizontally; yet when minute, it can take a mustard seed as its palace. Since even the power of karma—the workings of those with desire—is difficult to conceive, how much more so for those free from desire?
Zhao, the Minister of the Court of Judicial Review at Mount Yu, cast an image of the Bodhisattva Mahākaruṇā in white copper;
its hands, eyes, and posture were exquisitely peerless in the world. When the Daoist Da’guan first beheld it—
He appeared joyful, a radiance manifesting upon his brow and countenance. The Junior Minister asked, "Does the Master find joy? He replied, "I do. Furthermore, he said to the Junior Minister:

"While the name 'joy' (yue) is indeed the same, the joy of the mind is vastly different. To rejoice in being a Bodhisattva and to rejoice in benefiting sentient beings—this is the joy that transcends the world.
To rejoice in fame and achievement, or to rejoice in rank and position—this is the joy of the mundane world. [The Master] was poor...
I am indeed lacking in wisdom. If you, sir, can bestow this precious image upon me, I shall cast it according to its form and take it as my teacher;
thus, your kindness would be great. How could I dare not inscribe this virtue? The Junior Minister said:

"When the Master returns to Tianmu, it would be truly magnificent if he were to bestow this image among the green mountains and white clouds. Relying on such a famous mountain and blessed land, the image may enjoy long-term security."
Furthermore, having obtained a master to preside over Tianmu, the Eye of Heaven now has its lord; it is that which the Bodhisattva possesses—this is my humble wish.
Shortly thereafter, the Daoist descended to Tianmu and heard that the Bodhisattva had still not arrived at Qian.
"Could it be that the Junior Minister, with the heart of an empty valley, responds to me? I, with the heart of one calling out, await this very image? Nevertheless, I...
Taking the Dharma-realm as the Celestial Eye and empty space as Great Compassion—if this is so, then although the image does not emerge from Mount Yu, it has never been absent from the Celestial Eye.
Although the Bodhisattva may reside at Mount Yu, the practitioner has never been outside the uplifting illumination of the Great Compassionate Father.
Fearing that one might forget what has been bestowed and subsequently leave no trace, I would fail the Minister.
This is the mind of giving. It was recorded because it obscured the original vow of the Way-man. Thus, regarding the "Text for Paying Homage to the Fifth Patriarch":
I have heard that past Buddhas could not achieve the realization of the Unborn Mind, nor could they attain the path of Supreme Enlightenment, were it not for the present... [text continues].
A Buddha of the past cannot obtain the mind of a Buddha of the future, nor can he achieve the path of unsurpassed enlightenment.
A Buddha of the future cannot obtain the mind of a Buddha of the present, nor can he achieve the path of unsurpassed enlightenment. Viewed from this perspective, I, the Elder Śākyamuni—
If one does not attain the mind of Kāśyapa Buddha, then one cannot attain the state of Buddhahood with a mind.

Maitreya likewise did not attain the mind of Kāśyapa, and thus he also could not attain Buddhahood with a mind. Nevertheless, since Kāśyapa did not attain Buddhahood with a mind, [how could Maitreya do so?]
Thus, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, when [the Buddha] held up a flower to show the multitude, only Kāśyapa smiled and received the intent. Was this, then, with a mind? Or was it without a mind?
If one can discern and distinguish this point, then previously it was Kāśyapa’s elder brotherhood; subsequently, Maitreya would not dare to claim the younger brotherhood.
If one cannot discern and distinguish it, then if one calculates it as "existent," it will always pierce the heart; if one calculates it as "non-existent," [it likewise does].

Thus, the thorns of [extreme] annihilation and permanence pierce the heart; the precipices of eternalism and nihilism have, from antiquity to the present, caused countless beings to fall by obscuring their vision.
For this reason, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas give rise to great compassion and manifest the great hand and eye, employing a single reality with manifold names and immeasurable skillful means.
According to what is appropriate for each occasion, they appear in the world as Buddhas, as Patriarchs, and as Bodhisattvas.
It is said: "Bhikṣu," "householder. It is like many dishes of a single flavor or many vessels from a single stalk.

One who recognizes this through penetration is said to have attained the reality; one whose recognition is not penetrated forgets the reality and clings to names—such as "Buddha," "Patriarch," or "Bodhisattva."
These are all merely names; they are not the reality. What is called reality is that which the ancient masters, from their rootless tongues, directly uttered as a message:
"Do you all wish to recognize your original mind? Each of you is presently manifest before yourselves. The numinous light shines alone, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects.
