One fails to realize that the author’s power lies in the self-nature and the penetration of the fundamental principle (*zongtong*). Through the ineffable wonder, he has cast away [reliance on] the three types of language.
Obscure! The tail and spine are impermanent; the birth and death of sages and ordinary beings are like a luminous pearl upon a tray, rolling and flowing with ease.
Even one as wise as the divine Yu could not fathom its direction.
Preface to the Scroll on Sacrificing the Body for Half a Stanza at the Snowy Mountains:
A single word from a sage is such that heaven and earth find it difficult to encompass or support; this is simply because the Great Way resides therein.

The body is a great affliction, yet this man was able, amidst thousands of crags and ten thousand ravines in the midst of ice and snow, to cast away this great affliction and offer up half [of his life].
Verse: Is it not the case that the one who has attained clarity and valor does not need to arrive?

Regarding this fascicle on the manifestation of the Great Being of Potalaka, those who have arrived do not reach him; yet the Great Being manifests his body. How could this be caused by those who arrive? My arrival causes his body to appear; how could this concern the Bodhisattva?

Repeatedly observing, one finds no ground for what appears. Within this groundlessness, sea, mountains, and clouds arise; her wondrous countenance is both compassionate and solemn, such that those who behold it shed tears.
The waters of the ocean may dry up, but these tears never cease. One who conceives such a thought enters the Universal Gate instantaneously.

With ears reaching across the waves and eyes hearing the roar of whales, one moves with perfect mastery through water, land, and air. Since pleasure has no root and suffering has no stem, they are both ultimately non-existent.
Preface to the *Collection of Records of the Victories of Siṃhalavana*.
This record of Siṃhalavana was obtained by the Purple Pine Recluse (Zibai Daoren) from the study of Shen Bohong in Wumen. Alas! Siṃhalavana has long been overgrown with brambles;

foxes and hares have gathered in droves, and under the bright sun and clear sky, they act as various malevolent spirits. The Lion— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "The Lion" (師子), which likely refers to the Lion-king (Siṃha) or the monastery itself, Siṃhalavana (Lion Grove).*
He was heedless of his own slumber; now that this assembly has emerged, the lion’s nostrils have been pulled and pained by it.
Pain leads to awakening; awakening leads to roaring. I ask you, the great assembly present here: tell me, when the lion is truly roaring, where do this pack of foxes and hares find their place?
If you can realize this, the Lion Grove will be restored in an instant—this I grant him.
He came into the forest and departed at his own will,
treading freely upon it. This *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*,

carved by Baosheng, takes the five dharmas, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the eight consciousnesses (*aṣṭavijñāna*), and the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*) as its central tenets, intended for bodhisattvas whose faculties are mature.
Directly clarifying that the substance of consciousness is entirely true, one suddenly accomplishes the function of wisdom.

Thus, when the Buddha preached this sutra on Mount Laṅkā, it was because the mountain is steep and lofty, overlooking the great ocean below, with its sides completely devoid of gates or entrances; only those who have attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) can traverse it.
This serves to symbolize the Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground, which cannot be reached through mere cultivation or realization. "Laṅkā" here means "inaccessible. If...
If that is so, then can all sentient beings never attain [liberation]? Nevertheless, the object does not exist as an object by itself; it becomes an object because of the mind.
The mind does not exist as a mind by itself; it becomes a mind because of the object. Since the object does not exist as an object, the object cannot be apprehended.

Since the mind does not exist as a mind, the mind also cannot be apprehended. When both mind and object are unapprehendable, the mountain of wisdom is without dependence, and the ocean of awakening...
Without moving from one's heels, one has already ascended the peak of Laṅkā; as soon as a thought arises, one enters the Tathāgata-garbha.
A monk asked Yantou, "What is it like when arising and ceasing do not stop? Yantou asked the monk, "Who is it that arises and ceases?
Those who read this sutra will truly find a turning point beneath Yantou’s words; only then can they come to accord with the Old One.
It is not too late for the Han to deliberate upon this sutra.

The title "Wenzi Chan (Zen of Words) by Old Master Dongpo" refers to that old rebel Dongpo, who used words as his green forest, appearing and disappearing before the mountain peaks and at crossroads amidst thickets of thorns.
In the midst, bow-recesses and poisoned arrows are hidden everywhere, waiting specifically for those unblinking, reckless men who would kill without hesitation.
Once they touch the trigger, knives and arrows are discharged all at once; corpses lie scattered and blood splashes, turning the azure stream crimson.

Tell me, do you think he is a thief or not a thief? Try to discern and examine him! If you can discern him, you will surely find that the boulders blocking the road from of old have become boiling cauldrons.
Like snow scattered across the page,
Zhao’s painting on this fan depicts the density of mist at dawn or dusk; whether the mountain forms are present or absent cannot be fathomed by the mind, much less captured by brush and ink.
It is exhausted! Yet, at the very inception of the luster of ink and the beginning of the path of the mind, there must necessarily be a "host" present therein.
Therefore, the adept knows that clouds, mist, dusk, and dawn are not constant; they are treated as being equal to the contours of mountains.

Thereafter, with every stroke of brush and ink, whether drawn horizontally or vertically, wherever the intention reaches, the brush follows. The host and guest ascend and descend, having no fixed positions from the start. The intention...
Is it the fruit of intention? Is the brush truly the brush? It was at the head of Milar’s fan that I found Master Zhao.
I inscribed this for the *Recorded Sayings* of Chan Master Shizi Duan while I was a guest at Mount Qingliang. One night, I dreamed of a monk wearing a lion’s skin, traveling from east to west.
The slanting sun hung in the sky; its light shone upon his face. Suddenly he opened his mouth, revealing a maw like a basin of blood and teeth like frost-swords.

In my dream, I thought to myself: "I shall become like him. Upon reading the *Recorded Sayings* of Master Duan, I was struck by how he had cast off all conventional molds, deploying the Great Function with such mastery that he followed no fixed rules—truly like a golden-maned lion leaping forth.
If one were to cast [a challenge] onto an open clearing, there is not a single beast among the hundred species that would not have its brain split upon hearing the wind of such a threat. Alas!

Since antiquity has long passed, those who serve as the talons and fangs of the Gate of the Patriarchs (Zongmen) are rarely encountered; for the most part, they are like demonic foxes and monstrous dogs—yielding, soft, and flaccid whenever they encounter anything desirable.
Wagging their tails to beg for pity and assuming myriad guises to flatter others, once they have satisfied those desires, even the Old Man Yama stands before them bellowing with rage,
yet they do not have time to look at him— how much less will they look toward the Way? As for producing "Eulogies on Ancient Cases" (songgu) based on karmic conditions,

and from these eulogies producing "Collected Commentaries" (pingchang), and from the commentaries circulating what are called "Secret Essentials" (biyao)— once these Secret Essentials circulate, then later...

Those who study this [Dharma] do not understand critical commentaries; if they do not understand critical commentaries, how can they understand ancient verses? If they do not understand ancient verses, how can they understand circumstantial encounters (*jīyuán*)?

If they do not understand circumstantial encounters, how can they understand their own minds? If they do not understand their own minds, how can they understand the intent of the Patriarchs? Now, circumstantial encounters are "living phrases" (*huòjù*):

life and death are exercised with sovereign ease, and their elevations and suppressions are unfathomable. They exhaust the paths of both ordinary beings and sages; they are the medicine for and the disease of right and wrong. If one is not...
For such a person, the Way does not travel in vain. Only one who has fully awakened to their own mind can take illness as medicine and medicine as illness;
kill while living, and seize while letting go. What is suppressed is elevated, and what is killed is brought to life.
They use the staff and shout as a broad and long tongue, and offer iron-nail rice and wood-shard soup as an offering. Roaring at the opportune moment, even devas and nāgas rejoice.

Yue! The souls of foxes and rabbits would wither away. If this is so, then those of today who claim their secret essentials are the orthodox transmission, yet treat the Way of the Dharma with arrogance and contempt—how can they avoid feeling shame before their teachers?
Postscript to the Works Composed by Master Mu Xuan’an:
In ancient times, there were those who cast gold to fashion Buddha images and made offerings to them. One day, a great thief carried them away and buried them deep beneath the earth;
the world knew nothing of this. Suddenly, with the passing of generations, the descendants of the one who originally cast the Buddhas...
They had all likewise dispersed to distant lands. At that time, from the depths of the heavy springs, a light suddenly reached the crimson heavens;
far and near in the four directions, there was none who did not behold it. Struck with wonder and alarm, they clamorously drew one another along to seek the source of the light.
Those skilled in water descended into the deep springs and recovered the golden image; they lifted it up and made offerings to it at Chao, Ling, Tang, and Yi.
The Inner Secretary Mu Konghui, styled Xu’an, authored numerous works that elucidated the profound mysteries of both Confucianism and Buddhism.
Although more than fifty years have passed since the Master’s passing, his legacy has now been brought to light through the memorial presented by his fellow provincial, Imperial Censor Fu Guangzhai.
Consequently, I too have been able to delve into the esoteric classics of Xu’an. Generally speaking, for a man to establish himself...
One’s resolve must not be shallow or mundane; it should not be intended merely for temporary display among worldly factions.

Rather, one should strive for what is profound and far-reaching, perfecting it through diligent cultivation. Even after a hundred generations have passed, there may arise others who share the same aspiration.
This is like casting a Buddha from pure gold: though it be buried beneath deep springs, its radiance will surely reach the crimson heavens on a future day.

To speak of this directly: the great thief conceals his image; though he is but a single individual, the worldly faction shields him from view, and there has been no generation in which his influence did not spread widely.
Thus Zhuang Zhou said: "Elevated words do not reach the hearts of the multitude, and sublime joys do not penetrate the ears of the common folk."
However, that which is accumulated through refined brilliance cannot be obscured even by Heaven and Earth, let alone by the private envy of human sentiment.
Regarding the scroll of Wang’s paintings:
one sees the painting but not the brush; one sees the brush but not the hand; one sees the hand but not the mind; one sees the mind but not—

Regarding that which precedes the mind: may it be called "seeing the seer"? If one borrows the painting to see the brush, borrows the brush to see the hand, borrows the hand to see the mind, and borrows the mind to see that which precedes the mind—may this be called "not seeing the seer"? Nevertheless, when the scroll is unrolled, clouds and objects appear in profusion;
when the scroll is rolled up, peaks and springs are desolate and silent. Now tell me: who holds the handle of this unfolding and rolling up? 畢 (End).
In whose hands will it ultimately fall? To attain such freedom—should you have doubts, there is Wangchuan Moqie (Wang Wei) whom you may consult.
The Chan practitioner Bababqi has transcribed the Avataṃsaka Sūtra in blood.

I have heard that the Avataṃsaka Mahā-sūtra is truly the fundamental wheel of Dharma. It concerns the Buddha and the great Bodhisattvas; it is not something that those of inferior capacity can withstand. Thus it is said:
"When dragons and elephants trample, it is not for donkeys to endure. From beginning to end, it is a single thought-moment;

past and present are one time. Cause and effect are one Buddha; ordinary beings and sages are of one nature. The ten directions are one land; the three realms are one essence. Throughout the periods of the True, Semblance, and Final [Dharma]...

There is one Dharma: from beginning, middle, and end, it is of a single limit, manifesting right where it is. It does not involve emotional understanding; it is fundamentally and spontaneously perfected, not something obtained through cultivation.
Therefore it is said that wisdom arises through the skillful means of samādhi-contemplation; delusion and awakening are revealed through this, rather than being accomplished through cultivation.

As for the permeation of compassionate vows, they pervade all in accordance with the nature [of reality], and their activity is likewise inexhaustible. Some may say: "The vow ends when its function is fulfilled."
If [this were] discarded, then how many complications would there be for the Buddhas of the past, who practiced the cause while carrying the fruit?

Nevertheless, when it is said that "in the One Vehicle there is no cultivation" and that "from beginning to end it is but a single thought-moment," this refers specifically to the essence of the fruit (*phala*).

If one is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one must first awaken to the fundamental essence of the fruit; only then may one emulate the model of the ancient Buddhas, walking according to the square and the compass, beginning with faith.
Next, one successively passes through the stages of practice, dwelling, and dedication (*pariṇāmanā-bhūmi*), perfectly purifying the defiled habits accumulated over many lifetimes.

When these habits are exhausted and the merit is perfected, the enlightened activities of Vairocana are complete. That the *Sūtra* begins with Sudhana’s inquiry into the Dharma and his universal study under fifty-three sublime friends reflects the concern of the Sage:
that writing cannot exhaust speech, and speech cannot exhaust the intended meaning; therefore, he established these images as a means of representation.

I intend for those who aspire to the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) to contemplate the image until it becomes manifest; to spiritualize and clarify it so that it is realized within their physical bodies without the toil of gradual cultivation.
This is like the *Lotus Sūtra*, which uses the image of the dragon girl attaining Buddhahood to embody the True Reality (*bhūtatathatā*).
Through the three assemblies and nine parables, it strikes from various angles again and again—how is this any different from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*? It is only that inferior ordinary beings...
To believe only in one’s own mind is to rely merely on the Buddha’s words; being turned by written characters, one buries one's original radiance and cannot directly experience it.
One becomes a servant to right and wrong, a slave to honor and disgrace, an enemy to death and life, and a partisan of likes and dislikes.

Thus, topsy-turvy, the master and servant exchange positions: the Great Function is inverted into deluded affairs and ignorance, and the Great Capacity is entirely reduced to delusion regarding principle.
...obstacles. When principle is obscured, every encounter with phenomena becomes an impediment; when phenomena are obstructive, one remains forever deluded regarding principle.

Thus, the *dharmadhātu* of the *Avataṃsaka* and the *bhūtatathatā* (real mark) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* exist in name only while their meaning remains obscure. When the meaning is obscure, principle cannot be realized; when principle is not realized, the Way will never be fully penetrated.
Since the Way is not penetrated, on what day shall one arrive at the home? If one does not arrive at the home, how can there be peace?

There is something to be attained. If there is no attainment, then one’s vision will necessarily be unsettled. When vision is unsettled, there is no distinction between the partial and the perfect, nor can the heterodox and the orthodox be differentiated;
such people are called those who rely on intellectual understanding. Since they lack even a share of this [realization], how could they possibly manifest realization and enjoy its fruition?
On Mount Lu in Xunyang, Yuzhang, there is Huanglong Monastery; the plaque for the monastery was bestowed by His Majesty the Emperor.
There was a monk of the monastery named Qi, who was resolved to pursue the Buddha’s One Vehicle (Ekayāna).

Reflecting that his innate capacity was not profound and his nature was dull and stubborn, he found it difficult to penetrate and awaken to the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Thereupon, he made a vow to transcribe the entire Great Scripture.

His intention was to dwell among green mountains and white clouds, transcribing and reading it morning and evening, and reciting it with prostrations, thereby washing away the transgressions of the past and present.
Regarding the gravity or lightness of karmic defilements: suppose one has possessed even a slight root of goodness from former lives;

by relying on the majestic spiritual power of Vairocana and being awakened by the perfuming influence of the *Avataṃsaka*, the Dharma-realm suddenly opens up and one enters the lineage of the Buddhas.

This is how Qi informed me. I praised him for his resolve and have thus compiled this general outline of the *Avataṃsaka*. I spoke to Qi once more, saying: "If you know that when you take up the brush and drink from the inkstone, you are facing..."
Upon a blank sheet of paper, those lines drawn horizontally and vertically—what are they? Are they time? Are they Buddhas? Is it nature? Is it lands? Even the limits?
Is it elephants? Is it mind? Is it manifest before one? Or is it not manifest? Alas! If one can comprehend this, [one will understand].
Then Mount Sumeru would be the brush, the great void would be the paper, and the vast earth would be the ink. If one were to write such a scripture as this, would it ever come to an end?

Or would it be truly inexhaustible? If you do not understand this, then even if you were to flay your skin for paper, split your bones for a brush, and draw blood for ink, you would still be far removed from the youth Sudhana; how much more so from his fifty-three noble friends? If you can...
It is close at hand. Qí, you must exert yourself in it. Qí, you must embody it.
This postscript to the Huang Shan Valley Collection:
this collection is like the water-purifying pearl; when cast into ten thousand acres of turbid waves, they become clear instantly. It is like the *maṇi* jewel, [relieving] hunger and cold.
One who encounters this in such an age shall find their illness immediately cured. Indeed, this elder did not merely honor what he knew or practice what he knew;
he was further able to cast aside his arms beyond conventional boundaries and let out a lion’s roar.
Observe how, at the critical juncture of honor and disgrace, and upon the path of life and death, he leaped about with sovereign ease, like a luminous pearl rolling upon a golden platter.
Within this, shadows cannot be retained; they are like reflections in water or the heavens shimmering within the vast void, their radiance having no fixed location.
There are those who falsely claim that the *Liezi* also contains Chan (Dhyāna) discourse. How could Chan have begun with its general introduction [to China]? This is not the Master’s own words;
it is merely the superfluous chatter of those who do not distinguish between what is good and what is evil. Although the words of the *Liezi* are indeed precise and subtle...
Those who have reached [the goal] may also proceed by way of the path of meaning (*artha*). However, in the case of *dhyāna*, it is not only that the path of meaning cannot provide access;

even if there were no path of meaning, it would still not be *dhyāna*. Only those who have attained thorough awakening to their own mind will find that they "build a carriage within the closed door" yet "fit the tracks upon leaving the gate.
Those who do not recognize what is essential and what is trivial, wishing instead to force-fit everything with rational principles, are what is called "grasping at and rubbing at empty space."
It would merely increase one's own toil. I know his family members, and thus I have appended these few words.
I praise Heshi for his endurance in transcribing the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* with his own blood.
Before he had yet pricked his finger, his finger filled the void; as soon as he pricked it, the blood flowed across the great earth. His finger was, indeed, the Vajra.
Blood is itself Prajñā; therefore, whether a transgression is light or grave, it can be extinguished by even half a character.
Whether merit is shallow or deep, it is fulfilled by merely taking up the brush. Nevertheless, while the Layman Dàn-ān was still in this world, he did not take this sutra as his regular practice;
thus, after his passing, though you possess the filial piety of Zēngshēn, your transcription of this sutra will ultimately be no different from that of the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā*.
The bloodline cannot be continued. If that were so, then the householder [is the lineage] of this sutra, and this sutra is the learning of you, the benevolent father and son.
How could it be interrupted by existence or non-existence? I have heard that Prajñā has neither past nor present, and the Vajra has neither inner nor outer.
Where there is past and present, there is extension and contraction; where there is inner and outer, there is intimacy and distance. Yet, one has not yet reached the skandhas.

That which is empty arises and perishes from moment to moment. When the passions and sensory objects cause one to cling with stubborn attachment, it is as if mosquitoes and gadflies were biting one’s skin, causing the hair on the entire body to stand on end;

or as if a grain of rice straw were in the eye, causing the four directions to shift their positions. How much more so when a warm finger pricks a cold needle—blood spurts forth; how could there not be pain?
Now, if one studies benevolence, it immediately flows into the form of calligraphy; once the ink is formed into characters, it reaches the level of phrases.
Gāthā: This single scroll is now complete. Examining its sincere devotion, how does it differ from the sacrifice of one’s entire body?

Seeing this, the Daoist Daguang was moved by pity and, further inspired by the profound sincerity of Xueren, felt he was not unworthy of Ziyi. He has written this and appended it to the end of the scripture, wishing that all who see or hear it may give rise to this same resolve.
In praise of the bells and drums:
The Sage possesses a body yet remains free from entanglement; he possesses a mind yet remains free from toil.
Because he is free from entanglement, a single body can manifest as ten million bodies. Because he is free from toil, a single mind can exhaustively penetrate all phenomena. As for ordinary people...
It is not so. Where there is a body, there is encumbrance; where there is a mind, there is toil. This encumbrance and toil have continued from the beginningless past until this very day.
Through death after death and birth after birth, through honor and disgrace, and through the myriad variations of likes and dislikes, one has undergone countless changes of form and appearance.
Feathers, scales, fins, and horns—there is no form one has not passed through. To have attained a human body and to be counted among the most spiritually gifted beings is exceedingly rare.
Yet, with such a rare body, if one cannot hear the Way and wash away the toil and burdens of long kalpas, how is one any different from horses and oxen?
Nevertheless, toil and burden are not easily washed away; if one wishes to wash them away, one must do so by means of this verse.

If one acts as a sea of fragrant water, washing away [impurities] over a long period until they are naturally eliminated, then all people may reach the state of a sage. Let the wise reflect upon this.
These are the "Chapters on the Way" by Bamozi.
Zhuangzi said: "Where does the Way reside? The Way resides in the weeds and wild grass. The *I Ching* says:
"That which transcends form is called the Way; that which follows form is called the vessel. Someone asked Zhaozhou, "What is the Great Way? Zhaozhou replied: [The weeds and wild grass].
"The Great Way penetrates Chang’an. Now suppose there were someone here who asked all three of these questions at once:
"Does Muzi’s discourse on the Way refer to the *Zhuangzi*? Or does it refer to the *Yijing*? I would respond to him: "Setting aside for a moment the *Zhuangzi* and the *Yijing*, I venture to ask:
regarding Zhaozhou’s phrase 'The Great Way penetrates Chang’an,' does it indeed speak of the Way? Or does it not speak of the Way? If one says it speaks of the Way, then his words..."

It can be known through wisdom and attained via the path of meaning. If one says that there is no difference between asking about the Way and answering about the Way, then for someone who, amidst two such questions, knows how to discern the good from the bad with unerring accuracy, the Way of the *Zhuangzi* and the *Yijing* becomes clear.
It is like the moon in the autumn sky, bright and utterly transparent. If you cannot discern it through inspection, not only will you have no means of emerging from Zhaozhou’s words;
even if you find it easy and straightforward, you are merely telling a dream to a fool.

Nevertheless, from the coarse one attains the refined, and from the refined one proceeds to the transmission of hearing. That which is coarse and that which is refined are indeed the precursors to the transmission of hearing.
[End of] the *Bāzhèngdào gē*.
The Han Dynasty’s Liu Hou (Zhang Liang) appeared like a beautiful woman; the Ming Dynasty’s Liu Chengyi likewise appeared like a woman.
Yet, when faced with great affairs and decisive moments, they were as clear as seeing one's own eyebrows and eyes in a mirror; none of their contemporaries could equal them.

Although Master Yongjia was a practitioner of austere meditation in the clouds beyond, his appearance was also gentle and refined. When the Venerable Jiyin of the Song dynasty first read his [Yongjia’s]...

Regarding the line in the *Zhengdao ge* that reads, "The great man wields the sword of wisdom," Jiyin remarked that this old master must have had a magnificent appearance, his majesty eclipsing ten thousand monks.
However, upon paying respects to his portrait, he discovered that his physical frame was lighter than his robes and his countenance resembled that of the young Vinaya Master Xuán.
He then sighed, saying: "One must certainly not judge a person by their speech or appearance; for throughout this old master's life..."
His practice was clear and manifest, and his intellect was sharp and keen; thus, his utterances were like knives and saws.

He was like a fragrant elephant that has snapped its tethering ropes of the five desires and departed with transcendent ease—truly a great man! Lately, as we have moved further from the Sage, [the teachings have become obscured].
The faculties of these people are thin and inferior. Generally speaking, those who are called "leavers of home" are all born in remote, cold, and ignorant regions;

their parents merely allow them to leave home and become renunciants so that they may bear heavy burdens for their children, or so that they may provide for their own personal needs for food and clothing, rather than coming to seek transcendence from the world.
Next are those who are fugitives, driven by the tightening net of the law. By means of me—
The monastic community has become a vast marsh and thicket, serving merely as a refuge for those who seek a fleeting livelihood; how could such people possess the aspiration to attain Buddhahood?
For over thirty years, I have wandered aimlessly across rivers and seas, my footsteps reaching every corner of the world.

In every place I have visited, I have observed that both the monastics in black robes and the Daoists in yellow caps are generally content with eating their fill and sleeping at ease. Their idle chatter lacks any foundation, and they commit every kind of depravity, defiling both the Buddha and Laozi.
It causes people’s faith to regress. Were an old man of a single night’s experience to behold this with his own physical eyes, how could he refrain from weeping and shedding tears?
You, Master, have the Dragon Gate within your chamber; if you do not employ it for the benefit of the world, you shall leave the household life to seek unsurpassed bodhi.
One must not remain downwind of Yongjia. Formerly, Lord Cui Zhao asked Chan Master Guoyi Qin of Mount Jingshan, "Can your disciple leave the household life?
Qin replied, "Leaving the household life is the business of a great man; how could it be something performed by ministers or generals?
Lord Zhao was deeply moved in his heart. Therefore it is said: "Examine carefully the ancestral tradition—what a lofty standard it is! This is truly the case today. Foxes...
Rabbits form herds, and dragons and elephants gallop away; thus, the Old Man Śākyamuni would truly be the head of a band of wine and meat drinkers.
Alas, how painful!
This concludes the scroll on Master Dachuanyan Feeding One Hundred Thousand and Eight Thousand Monks.

I have read the verses and postscripts of various lay practitioners (*gṛhapati*). While I rejoice that they possess the mind of one who pushes a boat downstream with the current, I grieve that they lack the hand of one who grips the rudder against the wind. Tell me, what is it to grip the rudder against the wind?

*Tu!* Right now, in the midst of the perilous waves of birth and death, amidst honor and disgrace, and at the moment of a headlong, raging gale, let the sincere heart remain unclouded—this is the myriad virtues.

If one is constantly diligent, taking a boat as one's life, then all will exert their strength to support it. If one takes the nation as a boat, then all will unite their hearts to cross over together.
All the various emotional barriers will melt like ice and crumble like tiles; all notions of self and other will be swept away like lightning and struck down like thunder.

Only then may one be permitted to go before those who have no "handle" (no conceptual foothold) and castigate the Buddha-dharma with yellow and black ink. Nevertheless, what about that single phrase for "leaving the body"? How would you say it?
"Who has bound and released this single iron chain? At the mountain peak, all Buddhas laugh as they pull it together.
The *Vajra-sūtra* (Diamond Sutra) and the *Vajra-prajñā* (Diamond Wisdom)—the hardness and sharpness of these two are known to all in the world. Yet, as for the hardness and sharpness of ignorance...
I have not yet examined this. Now, delusion is neither firm nor sharp; I shall first shatter it and first attack it.
Yet, my stubborn attachment to birth and death, and to likes and dislikes, is so solid it cannot be broken, and so keen it cannot be attacked.
For this reason, Vīradhvaja and Śākyamuni attained the Way before me. Nevertheless, because delusion is neither firm nor sharp, Prajñā—
It has no basis. Therefore, the Sage uses the diamond (*vajra*) as a metaphor for *prajñā*.
This is because the diamond can sever everything, yet nothing can sever the diamond; just as *prajñā* can sever all ignorance (*moha*), yet ignorance cannot sever *prajñā*.
This is said from the perspective of one who already knows existence. If one does not yet know existence, then it is ignorance.
Wisdom can sever ignorance, yet wisdom itself cannot be severed by ignorance.

Viewed from this perspective, how could there be any permanence in the relationship between ignorance and wisdom, or between a diamond and all other things? It depends entirely upon how that person applies their mind.
If one first understands that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) exist as the vanguard, then *prajñā* is like a diamond (*vajra*).
If, however, one does not know they exist and yet forcibly employs ritual practice to shatter attachments, then ignorance (*moha*) is like a diamond.
Thus, the single substance of the diamond can serve as a metaphor not only for *prajñā*, but also for ignorance. This sutra contains over five thousand words and comprises twenty-seven chapters.
If we are indeed able to skillfully employ our minds, then every word and every doubt shall serve as a go-between for contemplative observation.
Conversely, if it is otherwise, then every word and every doubt shall likewise act as an intermediary for ignorance. It is like the blue vine, which is originally a subject.
The Duke of Rong was originally a member of the monastic community, yet his conduct was such as this.
Whether he acted as a matchmaker or an intermediary out of mere suspicion based on words, I cannot know. Song Zhonghang’s seal script is peerless throughout antiquity and the present.
It is exquisitely refined and lively; its spiritual vitality flows and permeates like spring blossoming flowers.

It is eternally existent, yet there is no time when it is not so; thus one attains the state of eternal non-existence and eternal existence.
Following the "Aspiration Text of the Revolving Clouds," it is said:

Seeing demons and weeping ghosts is entirely the product of one's own clouded mind.

to practice is difficult. To stand and laugh upon the edge of a ten-thousand-fathom cliff—Hanshan and Shide both have no merit therein.
Postscript to the *Wubiquan lun* (On the Non-Transmigration of Things):

I have heard that only one who has entered the state of non-arising (*anutpāda*) truly understands the *kṣaṇa*. Thus, in the *Wushi jiaojiao jing* (Sūtra on the Fifty Calculations), a Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"My transgressions have been extinguished; why do I not perceive the mark of their extinction? The Buddha replied: "It is because your mind is still capable of turning [toward objects]."
“Does it arise? He replied, “If my mind did not undergo transformation and rebirth, I would be unable to converse with the Tathāgata.
The Buddha said, “When your minds undergo transformation and rebirth, do you perceive the initial mark of the mind’s arising? He replied, “I do not know.
The Buddha said, “Since you do not know the initial mark of the mind’s arising, how could you alone know the mark of the extinction of offenses? It is precisely this.”
By observing whether the mind shifts or remains unchanging, one finds that the marks of arising and the marks of ceasing do not transcend a single *kṣaṇa*.

How much less could the distinction between "thing" and "non-thing," or "transmigration" and "non-transmigration," possibly transcend it? By this I know that those who refute non-transmigration and debate non-transmigration are unaware of the *kṣaṇa*;
for them, the state of non-arising is still far off. To refute and debate so fervently—is this not like brandishing a staff and splashing water?
O Moon! Then I, too, cannot escape the reproach of being talkative.

"Spring is in the flower branches. If one must wait for such pointing out to perceive it, then it is no longer its true nature.
I have read the "Imitations of Hanshan" by the Elder of Ban-shan. It is as if I were beholding the moon upon autumn waters or the springtime of flowering branches;
without stirring a single thought of effort, joy arises. Is this truly heaven? Or is it not heaven? Let those with the discerning eye try to offer a recommendation.
Epilogue to the Text on Refraining from Killing and Releasing Living Beings:
Whether noble or base, our vocations differ; yet as sentient beings, we share the same spiritual essence. To rely on brute strength to slaughter life only serves to entangle one in evil habits.

To indulge the palate for a fleeting moment results in the binding of calamities upon the body for ten thousand kalpas. When the retribution for such pain becomes unavoidable, it cuts short the suffering that has no beginning.

Fundamentally, nothing is better than abstaining from killing. If one does not refrain from killing, then my own afflictions will be transmitted to other beings, and their afflictions will be transmitted to me.
These afflictions and transmissions multiply one another like the buckets on a well-drawing wheel, revolving without end. Reflect upon this repeatedly; it is truly terrifying.

Once this terror has arisen, one should regard all beings as oneself and regard oneself as others. For once the impulse to kill is stirred, it is not only those who commit the actual act of cruelty who suffer.
Spirit! In truth, you have already severed the root of your own life. Why harbor such thoughts? Why wait until a Buddha emerges from a pig's tusk to finally refrain from killing?
*An Inscription on the Transformation of a Buddha from a Pig’s Tusk in the Song Dynasty*
Every thing possesses a Buddha, yet every thing remains unaware. Because of this ignorance, they devour one another like buckets on a waterwheel, without end throughout long kalpas.
Out of compassion for these beings, the Buddha flows forth from the mortar of his compassionate teeth; the Buddha emerges from the mouth of the pig, his Brahma-mark perfectly complete.
It was shaped like a thumb and resembled the autumn moon; its radiance was vivid and manifest. Upon hearing or seeing it, one conceived a sense of wonder and felt great terror.
From that moment on, one would refrain from killing, becoming equal to those who have already attained non-killing. When I made this vow, the Buddha immediately appeared before me.
Neither form nor emptiness; neither ordinary nor holy. It emerges from within the ordinary and the holy. For this reason, every single thing is the Buddha.
Why, then, does the intoxication of karma cloud the Buddha-mind? Buddhas devour one another. May these waves of compassion flow into the teeth of all beings.

Like a single lamp-light dividing into hundreds of thousands of lamps—each lamp continuing to divide its light—the radiance remains inexhaustible. When beings behold the Buddha-light, it shines universally upon them all.
Regarding these true words concerning the three periods of time, all who see or hear them will cry out and weep, as if a pig were being slaughtered and felt the pain for itself;
by contemplating in this way, the habit of killing is immediately ceased.
Colophon to the Song Dynasty Embroidered Sūtra of Avalokiteśvara.
The Zen practitioner Lin Bai brought a single scroll of the Song Dynasty embroidered *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*. I bowed and read it.
Upon reaching the passage, "Upon hearing its voice, one immediately attains liberation," a sudden doubt arose, and my mind was unsettled. Then, seeing the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati...
Śāriputra, having heard the Buddha praise the benefits of Avalokiteśvara’s merit, Ajita took from his own neck a necklace of various precious jewels and offered it to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
The Bodhisattva was unwilling to accept it, but at the Buddha's encouragement, he finally accepted it.
He then offered one portion to Śākyamuni Buddha and one portion to the place of the Stūpa of Prabhūtaratna Buddha;
thereupon, his doubts suddenly vanished. Now, Prabhūtaratna Buddha is a Buddha of the past, while Śākyamuni Buddha is a Buddha of the present.
If there were no past, the present would have nothing upon which to depend; if there were no present, the past would become a mere annihilation. If there were no past...
If the present does not exist, how can the future be established? If the three periods of time are discarded, then one is ignorant of the *kṣaṇa*.
If one is ignorant of the *kṣaṇa*, then upon what shall the functions of all sages and ordinary beings, as well as the foundation of the primary and secondary realms, rely?

Viewed from this perspective, it appears that the Sage originally intended to directly reveal his essential teaching; however, considering that the capacities of sentient beings are dull and they cannot "spiritually clarify" it, he therefore established [these provisional teachings].
The imagery serves as a vehicle for the underlying meaning; if one contemplates it and grasps that meaning, the imagery is forgotten and one spontaneously accords with the truth.

Knowing this, those who currently read the sutra and those who contemplate its reading—though they may differ in wisdom—are both revolving within the light of quiescent extinction, with no separation whatsoever from the beginning.
This sutra is wondrous and beautiful, its spiritual radiance complete; every stitch pierces straight into perfect penetration.
This realm—each and every character penetrates and encompasses the truth of the Ultimate Way. From the Song dynasty until the Ming, six hundred years have passed;
yet the strokes and characters remain as sharp as blades, resonant as if newly inscribed. Were it not for a sincerity that pours forth from the very liver and gall, who could achieve such a state?

rocks are inherently not extraordinary; it was from Yu the Great that they first became so regarded. Up until the time of the Layman Dongpo (Su Shi), he not only ceased to regard rocks as extraordinary, but went so far as to treat them as the supreme offering.

Even if one’s realization were to surpass that of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, I know that such a person would still be affected by external circumstances.
The banner has fallen.

When the Old Man of Halfway Mountain recited the poems modeled after those of Han Shan hundreds of thousands of times, the flowers of the mind bloomed; fragrance floated through his nostrils. As fragrance arose from his nostrils, the fragrance was no longer...
As for "hearing fragrance": one who understands this well is like the old man of Mount Ban, whose tongue-root drags upon the ground;
even this is nothing extraordinary. After writing the *Eulogy on Maitreya* by Shengguan:

"The principle-water is like the sea, and my mind is like a fish. To nourish the fish with the sea—how difficult would it be for it to transform into a dragon? Furthermore, may I attain non-retrogression."

The Verse of Buddha Vipaśyin:
Ordinary people know that life is precious, yet they do not know the way to nourish and sustain life; thus, they are burdened by their very existence.
The Perfected One knows the way to nourish life, which is rooted in non-arising (*anutpāda*); therefore, he is able to view life as non-arising. Non-arising...

Thus they are born. To be born is to be burdened by nothingness. Alas! Suppose there is a person here whose eyes are burdened by forms, whose ears are burdened by sounds, and whose mind is burdened by the seven emotions and five desires, yet who still says, "Throughout my life I have been happy and free from burdens.
Little do they realize that their state of being "unburdened" has itself been a burden for a long time. This is because the desires of the multitude...
The mind is heavy and clouded; one passes through errors without even realizing it. It is like a drunken man lying in the mud;
someone wakes him up and says, "Mud is no place for you to lie. The drunkard stares with wide eyes and says in anger, "I have never in my life understood drinking;
why do you slander me? Today, everyone in the world suffers from this illness of the drunken man; how could there be anyone who does not?

if they recite them, they will reflect upon them; if they reflect, they will gain clarity; and if they attain clarity, they will achieve realization. What cause for concern is there that they will never eventually awaken?
Preface to the *Daśavidyā-śāstra* by the Venerable Pañjika-kīrti:
Now, even the most foolish person, if made to tread upon fire, fears being burned and boiled; though driven, they will not enter.

Yet the cauldrons and fires of the five desires burn and boil the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom of sentient beings—not merely for a morning or an evening—and yet people submit to them with complacency.

That one treads upon them without fear—is this not because they have lost their minds and gone mad? It is because they reckon this stinking skin-bag to be a pure vessel and reckon the mind of ignorance to be the root of life;
thus, they are unable to contemplate the body as the four great elements and the mind as the four aggregates.
Nowadays, when people are about to lie down to sleep, if their pillow is even slightly uncomfortable, they cannot rest;
they must settle it properly before they find ease. Yet, birth and death are matters of the utmost gravity for humanity, yet everyone remains complacent and takes no account of them at all.
Thus, they owe a great debt to the Elder Master Juefan.
Preface by Great Master Yuanming of Ba Song to Parting from Hu Qiangzhong at Shaoyang:
Within the light of purity, there is no cause for forced illumination. Where there is neither body nor mind, one recklessly conceives of having a body and a mind.

The mind is the source of evil; the physical form is the thicket of transgression. If the source is not blocked, how can evil ever come to an end? If the thicket is not cleared, transgression will surely never cease.

Although the mind may be devoid of good or evil and the physical form has not yet manifested as auspicious or inauspicious, the source of evil has from the beginning been the ocean of compassion, and the thicket of transgressions has from the beginning been the mountain of merit; it depends entirely upon the nature of one's mental application and conduct.

Alas! To possess a sense of self and, knowing it, fail to turn back from it—thus the torrent of evil flows unchecked. To possess stubborn attachments and, clinging to them, fail to release them—thus the mountain of transgression becomes lofty.
Only the one who possesses the Way realizes that the mind is not existent; thus, without needing to discard anything, love and hate naturally vanish.
He knows that the body is fundamentally non-existent; thus, without avoiding calamity, honor and disgrace naturally dissolve. Therefore it is said: "If a person wishes to know..."

The realm of the Buddha requires that one purify the mind like empty space, remaining far removed from delusive thoughts and all forms of grasping, so that the mind encounters no obstruction wherever it turns.
As for me, the Venerable Jiyin, though currently bound within the shackles of captivity—a place where nine out of ten die—I am able to transcend these conditions with self-possession;
thus, the anxieties and sufferings of birth and death cannot enter my breast.
[The Emperor asked: "What artifice has brought this about? If a great man lacks the will to govern the world, he ought to devote his full heart to transcending it.
Therefore it is said: 'Exhaust the mind to know nature; once nature is known, one can employ it.

It is like a dragon that can use water to form clouds and use clouds to bring rain; thus, it does not drown when in water, nor does it fall when moving through the clouds. For this reason, I [say]:...

it is not merely that grief and affliction cannot be found there, but one can even use them as a broad and long tongue. I now write this account to prepare "iron-nail rice" as an offering for the Zen practitioner Yuanzong.
If the Zen practitioner understands this, what regret could I have?
Preface by the Great Master Yuanming of the Ba Song Monastery to Hu Qiangzhong on Behalf of the Dharma-Master Yigan:

The Dharma fundamentally transcends emotional conceptualization; yet if one seeks the Dharma through emotion, the Dharma cannot be attained. To seek it while knowing it cannot be attained—this is the way.
Their delusions became increasingly profound. Take those such as Fan Pang and Kong Daohai; their character was lofty and their learning vast—they were truly extraordinary men.

Therefore, I value it. I present this as a preface to the "Hónglǎo’s Preface on Sending off Húshēng," and append these few words of colophon.
Colophon to My Reading of the Universal Gate Chapter of the Lotus Sūtra:

I was reading the Universal Gate Chapter of the Lotus Sūtra when I reached the passage: "If there are sentient beings who have much lustful desire, they should constantly mindfully recollect and pay respectful homage..."
"Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva can cause one to become free from desire. Unconsciously, he set down the scroll and sighed with admiration for a long time:

"The great affliction of sentient beings—no affliction exceeds that of lustful desire. If one can constantly maintain mindfulness of and pay respect to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, one shall indeed become free from desire.
The Buddha’s words are not false. Those in the world today who respectfully and mindfully recollect Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva..."
They exist within one's own being; yet how few are those who invoke the name and thereby become free from desire! Is it then that the Buddha’s words are also false? Alas!

Lustful desire and reverent devotion are fundamentally not two separate things. If one can truly and constantly keep the Bodhisattva in mind, then reverence will manifest and lustful desire will vanish.
If one invokes the name with even slight laxity, then lustful desire will manifest and reverence will vanish. It is just like this.
I have personally verified this many times regarding the depth or shallowness of these states and the maturity of one’s vital energy (*prāṇa*). The Buddha’s words are not false;
it is only because people lack constant resolve that they fall of their own accord into the net of doubt.
Bazhou Shuzong’s Letter on Listening to the *Lotus Sūtra* Song:

Now, the *Lotus Sūtra* consists of seven fascicles and over sixty thousand words. Although that which it elucidates comprises the three stages and nine parables—whether spoken directly or explained indirectly—it does not go beyond the single reality-mark (*ekadharmatā*).
This very reality-mark is clearly manifest and inseparable from our daily activities.
Within this, how is it that Master Lou, for over sixty years, traveled on foot with diligent toil seeking it yet could not find it?
And Changqing’s meditation cushion was worn through seven times, yet he sought it and could not find it. Viewed from this perspective, even by practicing and seeking, one cannot find it.
Seeking it while sitting, one likewise does not find it; thus, this true reality (*dharmatā*) cannot be found or sought within the four modes of deportment.
If this is so, then how could the clear fact that it is fundamentally present in daily activities not be more than a dream-like statement?
Furthermore, the Elder Yongjia said: "Without leaving this very place, it is ever serene; yet when you seek it, you know it cannot be seen. By Yongjia’s...

This is its entire manifestation. It is this ox: its head and horns are towering and jagged; it enters and exits through the gateways of our six sense organs.

Tansheng, a master of Chan, has always regretted being unable to manage this beast. Upon seeing this song for the first time, he immediately felt as though he had mounted the ox.
Although I have this aspiration, I have not been able to find anyone capable of writing it down to treasure it. Therefore, I have composed this "Pith Instruction on Seeking the Ox.
Whether in mountain forests or cities, amidst favorable or adverse circumstances, hold to this and investigate it. If you do not find the ox, do not cease until the end of your life.
The Purple Cypress Recluse (Zibai Daoren) laughed heartily and said, "Are you not like that blind cat who leaps over the fish platter in search of tofu?
When it comes to calligraphy today, if one sets aside my uncle Zong and seeks elsewhere, would that not be a mistake? Nevertheless..."
If someone asks where the great white ox-calf ultimately resides: "At the place where he brandishes his brush to write upon grass and grain;
listen closely to the sound of his hooves by the inkwell."

In the past, the Tathāgata did not abandon even the merit of threading a needle. This was truly because merit is not accomplished without the accumulation of goodness;
