Being able to ride upon the birth of conditions to enter the unborn (*anutpāda*), how is this different from obtaining [the fruit] by means of a flower?
Ah, spring! If this is so, then is the blessing of threading the needle not itself the flower? Now, the Grand Minister of Rites, Lu, has long cultivated his lofty virtue in the Green Fields.
Having reached the age of ninety, he does not yet decline from the occasion of threading the needle;
for the mountain master of all conditions, he spreads the flowers of frozen clouds, their fragrance drifting far and near. He may truly be called the rebirth of Anāthapiṇḍada. Alas!
I exclaim: "Excellent!

O you who shattered the bowl at Caoqi, when the single mind does not arise, there is no ground for sage or ordinary person; things and self share the same radiance. Therefore, the sages are not the same."
Yet this mind and this Way have never been anything other than identical. It is only because people cling to their emotions and forget their fundamental nature that they perceive differences.
Laozi was born after the Buddha; Confucius was born after Laozi. When I read the *Daodejing*, I do not see any words therein that are not those of the Buddha.
When I read the *Spring and Autumn Annals* and the *Analects*, likewise I do not see any words therein that are not those of the Buddha. Great!
When a sage appears in the world, he is fundamentally without a fixed mind; he simply takes the minds of the common people as his own.

Therefore, whatever can lead them toward goodness, he employs without exception. He is like a skilled physician who seeks only to cure illness, using ginseng, atractylodes, ginger, and cassia as appropriate to the case.
Even for strange symptoms and bizarre maladies, he does not avoid even arsenic, snakes, or scorpions.
In this regard, their failure is one and the same. The followers of the three later schools failed to comprehend the Sage’s original intent;
they engaged in mutual disputes of right and wrong, attacking and excluding one another without ceasing—a bloody struggle that was no different from taking up arms to cut down one's own kin.
I have heard that Lord Zhuang Quwei, a man of profound virtue in our dynasty, could not tolerate Caoxi’s single alms-bowl and harbored such envy that he could not contain himself. With his own hands—
Why shatter it? Why show people such a lack of breadth? Nevertheless, the Great Mirror originally takes empty space as his bowl, and heaven, earth, and the myriad things as the food within that bowl.
Whether it be rice and grain during a famine, or medicinal herbs during an epidemic, these are all but food within the bowl.
How could there be one who eats the food of food? For what reason? Because there is neither subject nor object. When there is neither subject nor object, then...
There is no dependence. To be without dependence is to stand alone. To stand alone is to have no ground upon which the mind can arise or the hand can be placed. Alas!
Were Master Qi to read this postscript from the Nine Earths (the realm of the dead), would he not be filled with shame? Nevertheless, tell me: what are the means of this Elder of Reconciliation?
Adverse or favorable circumstances and conditions are like the wind passing through a tree; my remaining life is not worth half a coin.
Cheng Kangbo’s Epilogue to the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*:
"The Venerable Old Man (Bodhidharma) directly pointed out that the daily afflictions of sentient beings are the Treasury of Great Radiance of Supernatural Powers.
The Twelve Great Beings, however, explained that the Tathāgata’s Treasury of Great Radiance of Supernatural Powers is itself affliction. From this point on, they were father and son."
Their feelings were at odds; the path between the sage and the commoner was severed. Kang Bo and Mr. Cheng, observing from the sidelines, could not restrain their bitter sorrow.

Thereupon, they resolved to transcribe this scripture by hand. Strokes accumulated to form characters; characters accumulated to form chapters; chapters accumulated to form volumes. Within a single *kṣaṇa*, Perfect Enlightenment was realized.
What had been discordant became harmonious again; what had been severed was restored to continuity. Father and son cried out in joy, clapping hands and receiving one another’s support.
An edict was issued, and the holy and the mundane gathered like clouds; it was as natural as water reaching its channel.

At that time, the Purple Crag Hermit (Zibo Daoren) happened to purchase a boat on the banks of the Min River, while Master Kang Bo manifested within the Great Treasury of Miraculous Radiance (*Prabhāsa-vyūha*) to present this offering to the Hermit.
At that moment, he did not receive it face-to-face, but rather enjoyed it from behind; this was enough to leave Mañjuśrī speechless and Samantabhadra stumbling. How much more so, then, for others?
Is it otherwise? Nevertheless, lice and fleas regard their own heads as Mount Kunlun; those who walk in cramped steps regard a puddle in a horse's hoofprint as the vast ocean.
Since smallness and greatness are not constant, who gains and who loses?

In this scroll of Zhou Shuzong’s calligraphy practice, there is a saying among Chan practitioners that to deviate from a single word of the sutras is to speak as a demon; yet to rely on the sutras to explain their meaning is to be at odds with the Buddhas of the three ages.
Among calligraphers, those who study the art of writing until they die within its constraints are called "slave-calligraphers. Observing Master Zhou Shuzong as he practices these various [scripts]...
In the shifting transformations of the calligraphic forms, the underlying principle (*dharma*) is occasionally revealed. It is like the moment thick clouds gather and thunder rumbles;

though the dragon is not yet visible, its head and horns briefly appear. One whose innate capacity (*tianji*) is profound may, through spiritual insight and clarity, perceive that the dragon’s head and horns do not reside within the brushwork of Shu Zhong, but rather lie in the very interval between my desire to grasp it and my failure to do so.
The Mountain Dwelling Poems of Chan Master Bashiwu say:
Do not say that dwelling in the mountains brings freedom; In recent years, there has been no day without worry.
By the bamboo, old women often steal the shoots; Among the wheat, children intentionally let their cattle loose. Nuts, locusts, and earthworms damage the vegetable sprouts; Wild...
A rat from Mount Zhuyi eats the heads of the grain; as soon as it acts thus, things do not go as intended. One can only let it subside within oneself and rest.
Now, the body and mind are the target for life and death, and for the good and the bad. If the target is not forgotten, the arrow will not cease; if the arrow does not cease—
If this were so, how could those who harm me ever come to an end? Nevertheless, those who harm me generally do not transcend the realms of the "intentional" and the "unintentional.

Therefore, the man of ultimate attainment abandons this [the intentional] and does not abandon that [the unintentional]. If one abandons this, that becomes masterless. When there is no master, the adversary acts at will;
how is this any different from shooting an arrow into empty space? For this reason, this old man takes the dissolution [of all things] back into oneself as his refuge.
Sudu: "How profound these words!
I have read Dongpo’s *Eulogy on Amitābha Buddha* and am struck by how its essential meaning is as clear as the sun rising over the great earth."
His light illuminates all without exception. How extraordinary was Master Chang! It is truly fitting that people of old called him the previous incarnation of the Fifth Patriarch, Master Jie.
Indeed, the deluded thoughts of Perfect Enlightenment are fundamentally not permanent; when these deluded thoughts exist within the Buddhas, they are named Perfect Enlightenment.

Perfect Enlightenment (Samantabhadra-vijñāna) resides within sentient beings; this is what is called "inverted perception. If sentient beings can skillfully employ their own minds, who would not be the Buddha of Immeasurable Life? What in this Sahā world would not be a pure land of lotuses? To insist that one must leave behind sentient beings to attain Buddhahood, or depart from the Sahā world to be born in a pure land, is merely a provisional city established for those of dull faculties. Now, let us inquire into this matter throughout the world: [The text continues with the following: ...if one does not know the nature of the mind, how can one realize the Way? If one knows the nature of the mind, why should one seek it elsewhere? It is like a person who, while walking on a road, suddenly sees a city before them. They enter the city, stay there for a while, and then depart. If they do not know the city was a conjuration, they will surely think it is real. If they know it was a conjuration, they will not cling to it as real. Thus, the Tathāgata’s teaching of the three vehicles is like a conjured city. Those of dull faculties, having heard the teaching of the three vehicles, take it to be real and do not seek the One Vehicle. Those of sharp faculties, having heard the teaching of the three vehicles, know it is a conjuration and immediately seek the One Vehicle. Therefore, the Tathāgata says: "If you wish to see me, look at your own mind. If you look at your own mind, you will see me. If you do not look at your own mind, you will not see me. Why? Because the Buddha is within the mind, not outside the mind. If you seek the Buddha outside the mind, you are seeking a phantom among phantoms. If you seek the Buddha within the mind, you are seeing the reality within reality. Therefore, the Tathāgata says: "The mind is the Buddha; the Buddha is the mind.

There is no other Buddha apart from the mind. If you know the mind, you are the Buddha; if you do not know the mind, you are not the Buddha. This is why the Tathāgata says: "To seek the Buddha outside the mind is to be far removed from the Way. Please, let us now inquire into this throughout the world: [The text concludes with an exhortation to practice and realize this truth.]
Upon entering the conjured city, everyone was delighted and joyful; yet when invited to the place of true treasure, there was none who did not knit their brows and depart. Why is this?
[This is] the postscript to the volume for the solicitation of funds to carve the Great Canon by the Chan practitioner [Name].
Now, the Great Canon is the Buddha’s word, and that which the Great Canon elucidates is the Buddha-mind. The Buddha’s words are like firewood.
The Buddha-mind is like fire. When the fuel is abundant, the fire blazes; when the fuel is exhausted, the fire cannot be transmitted.
Once the fire cannot be transmitted, its function of transforming the raw into the cooked and dispelling darkness to spread light will almost cease.
Therefore, the transmission of fire must depend upon fuel for the fire to have utility; the transmission of the mind must accord with the Buddha’s words for the mind to be free from doubt. I—
Once the mind is free from doubt, the Buddha-mind is one’s own mind. If the Buddha-mind is one’s own mind, then among all those who possess cognition and awareness, who is not a Buddha?
Nevertheless, sentient beings are fundamentally Buddhas; yet, alas, they do not realize this in their daily lives.
This is called fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*). It is like a person born blind: from the moment of birth until the end of a hundred years, they will never know the heavens.

The earth, the sun, and the moon—what things are these? Sentient beings are fundamentally Buddhas; yet they do not know them in their daily lives, which is called being "blind from birth" and is termed "ignorance" (*avidyā*).

Is this not so? When a person blind from birth finally encounters a skilled physician who extracts the cataracts from their eyes, then the vastness of heaven and earth and the brilliance of the sun and moon become clear and free of confusion. Such is the ignorance of sentient beings.
If one does not obtain the Buddha’s words, they serve as a golden probe to excise the cataracts of ignorance. Although the Buddha-nature is inherently present, how could one recognize it otherwise?
It is like fire, which has never been absent; yet if there is no fuel to transmit it, the fire cannot be utilized. Therefore it is said:
"The second stage of Earth gives rise to Fire, and the third stage of Heaven completes it. If the third stage were not completed, then—

Although fire exists, it cannot illuminate objects [if not ignited]. Likewise, although the *dharmatā-nature* (正因 *zhengyin*) of Buddhahood exists within sentient beings, if it is not perfumed by the *pratyaya-nature* (緣因 *yuan-yin*), the *vijñapti-nature* (了因 *liaoyin*) will not be opened.
If the *vijñapti-nature* is not opened, the *dharmatā-nature* will ultimately never be restored.
From this it may be said: the *pratyaya-nature* is the Buddha’s word; the *vijñapti-nature* is the realization of the Buddha’s word.
This is that which is to be expressed. The direct cause (*zhengyin*) is the self-mind inherently possessed by sentient beings.

Although this self-mind is inherently present, it cannot be utilized unless transmitted through the words of the Buddha. It is realized through the revealing cause (*lioyin*). Even though the self-mind is inherently present, it ultimately cannot be put to use.
This is just like fire being present, yet if one does not obtain fuel to transmit it, the fire likewise can never be obtained for use. This is so.
Therefore, those who aspire to employ their own minds must first clarify the Buddha’s words. Now, when one’s own mind is clear, there is nowhere it does not reach with clarity.
Thus it is said: "If clarity arises spontaneously from within, then all dark phenomena can never again obscure it.
Only a person whose mind is forever unclouded is capable of enlightening things and accomplishing affairs. It is for this reason that I know the carving of the Great Canon is essential.

How could it be that only ordinary beings may ascend to perfect enlightenment? In truth, amidst the governance of the world, this is a great opportunity for opening up things and accomplishing affairs.
Regarding the origins of the carving of the Great Canon, I, [Name], am now about to seek contributions from the four quarters. The Grand Historian [Name] has already composed a preface;
I follow after him to add this postscript, for I reflect upon how difficult it is to gather firewood—yet once the wood is gathered, [the work proceeds].

It has never been the case that fire does not transmit its heat. It has likewise never been the case that the Buddha’s words have spread widely while sentient beings remain ignorant of their own minds.
I shall now depart; may you proceed without hindrance.
*Commentary on the Exposition of the Lotus Sūtra:

Pouring Out the Sea* I have read Master Jie’s *Exposition of the Lotus Sūtra: Pouring Out the Sea*. Upon reaching the section on "The Whole Person is the Dharma," there was a sudden awakening; the mind became vast and the eyes transcended their objects.
This subtlety does not exceed the coarse, and it is truly not something that can be understood through discursive thought or discrimination. Now, the lotus flower is a metaphor for the marvelous.

This is the meaning of the Dharma. When a practitioner can contemplate the elephant and grasp its meaning, the elephant has never been anything other than the meaning; the coarse has never been anything other than the subtle. Furthermore, tell me:
when the person is entirely the Dharma, who is it that contemplates the elephant? *Tut!*
Written after the "Kōan of Harelana’s Questioning of the Twenty-second Patriarch," in the spring of the Wuli era, the year of Guisi (1613).
While staying as a guest at Biyun Temple in Yanjing, I was reading the *Fozu Tonggan* by lamplight;
upon reaching this passage, I could not help but close the volume and sigh. I then turned it over and reflected further: Harelana had been a *bhikṣu* in a previous life.
The Master went to the Dragon Palace for a meal. Upon surveying the assembly of five hundred, he found not a single person worthy of such a sublime offering;
therefore, he did not wish for his disciples to attend with him. However, the disciples failed to understand their teacher’s intention and vainly gave rise to notions of self and others.

The Master then reluctantly yielded to their feelings and took them to the gathering. Subsequently, because the five hundred disciples possessed meager merit and shallow virtue, they were reborn as birds.
The clan was moved by this kindness and followed his transformation. Alas! One who is among the most sentient of beings should not rely on emotional attachment rather than the illumination of wisdom;
yet here we see that even among the feathered tribes, they have been transformed. This is likely because they had reached the extreme of delusion before returning to awakening.

Nevertheless, though they awaken at this point, it would be far better to awaken prior to this—would that not be superior? At that time, Qizi asked: "Hegel... (Note: *Hele* refers to the name of the crane-hermit).

"How is it that the flock of cranes does not know its own past causes, while the twenty-second patriarch alone knows them? He replied, "When one has seen the Way, there is no distinction between superior and inferior;

however, regarding the reduction of habitual tendencies, there are degrees of depth and shallowness. This is because those with deep realization illuminate the boundless, whereas those with shallow realization shine only upon limited objects.
He asked again, "Hegeluo preached the Dharma for nine cycles of winter and summer, yet the flock of cranes was ultimately not liberated."
When Maṇa had finished reciting the verses, the flock of cranes immediately realized the state of non-arising (*anutpāda*). They flew away, calling out as they went. It is said:
The *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* states that because the Tathāgata’s physical and mental activities are supreme, those who hear the Dharma easily attain realization.

Judging from this, Maṇa’s power of the Way (*mārgabala*) far surpassed that of Hakkotaro. It is like striking a bell: if the mallet is large, the sound is grand; if the mallet is small, [the sound is faint].
The resonance was thus close at hand. Upon hearing this, Qizi leaped up, pressed his palms together, and prostrated himself in worship.

He then ascended the great peaks of Mount Mei to collect the works of the Elder Su. Whenever he composed essays, eulogies, or gāthās, he brought forth their unfathomable subtlety; his style was unrestrained, versatile, and transcendent.

That he causes others to enter [his realm] such that none may even glimpse its boundaries is because his attainment of the *dhāraṇī* of the languages of sentient beings and his samādhi were achieved long before the Great Hero beheld the morning star. Thus,

he is able to speak of "is" from the standpoint of "non-is," to speak of "non-is" from the standpoint of "is," and to speak of that which is neither "is" nor "non-is" from the standpoint of both "is" and "non-is."
Come! From the place that is neither "is" nor "is not," speak forth what is "is" and "is not.
It may be long; it may be short. It may be high; it may be low. It may be shallow; it may be deep. It may be near; it may be far.
Whatever is thus appropriate is all a settled view that remains unshakable for a thousand ages. The settled view is like a platter, and its words are like pearls.
A pearl rolling upon a tray: the tray contains the pearl, yet it moves crosswise, askew, curved, or straight, surging and colliding with complete freedom;

ultimately, its location cannot be measured. Should there be one who gives rise to the thought of measuring it, it would be like attempting to catch the wind with a net or containing water in a basket.
Those who know it is difficult to measure and thus resign themselves to not daring to measure it at all are even more mistaken. Could this not be the Master Dongpo?
Is it that having three heads and six arms makes one different from others? Or is it that having a furrowed brow and a prominent nose makes one no different from others?

It is simply that the obstacles of phenomena and principle prevent others from attaining [realization]; therefore, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished. Furthermore, regarding the obstacles of phenomena and principle:

It cannot obstruct others. Wherein lies its subtlety? Its subtlety lies in its being untransmittable. It is precisely this untransmittable essence that Confucius attained and became a teacher for ten thousand generations;
Laozi attained it and became a teacher for all beings; and Śākyamuni attained it and became a teacher to those who have no teacher.
Now, if there were someone here who could know the dwelling place of this teacher of those who have no teacher, then—
The wondrousness that cannot be transmitted was uniquely attained by him alone.
Postscript to Tang Xiuya’s *Song on Hearing the Lotus Sūtra*:

Now, the Dharma of the mind is fundamentally wondrous, making no distinction between the holy and the ordinary; yet, when it resides in a sage, the six sense faculties can be employed interchangeably.
Ordinary beings willingly remain in the folly of being shrouded by thick clouds, believing that the eye can only see and cannot hear, and that the ear can only hear and cannot see.

They fail to realize that it is because ordinary beings do not understand through their pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*)—mistaking a vine for a snake—that the six sense faculties appear incapable of functioning interchangeably.
When such pervasive conceptualization is eliminated, the dependent nature (*paratantra*) is revealed as fundamentally wondrous.

The faculties and their objects are ungraspable; subject and object are not severed. It does not involve emotional understanding or intellectual interpretation, but is realized in the manifest experience of daily life.

Thus it is said: "The Buddha-dharma is found in the midst of daily activities. Yet, whatever one does or whatever one undertakes, even the raising of a thought or the stirring of a single intention is still not it.
Our Great Hero, at the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, through three cycles and nine parables, spoke both horizontally and vertically to describe the wondrous Dharma; this may truly be called—
This fully exhausts the compassionate heart. Yet, in the end, it does not equal this song. The essence of the teaching is fundamentally wondrous;

it enables ordinary people of great capacity to realize the truth immediately upon reading this song. Although the *Lotus Sūtra* contains over sixty thousand words and its exposition of the wondrous Dharma is by no means narrow, all of those are "dead words.
Only this [song] captures the wondrousness of "living words," capable of enlivening the dead.
It is for the sake of livelihood. For example, it is like all earthenware, bronze, copper, and iron that, with a single drop of cinnabar, are all transformed into gold and white jade.

Or again, it is like the moon reflected in the autumn water or appearing upon a flowering branch in spring; its clarity, brilliance, and freshness—how could one wait for a pointing finger before knowing its wondrousness?
After writing "The Diamond Sutra:

Cutting Off the Stream," [I realized that] the Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa is one's own mind, and one's own mind is the Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa. As mind and crown mutually subsume one another, the eternal radiance manifests before us.
This is the pivotal moment when the Patriarch cut off the stream beneath these Five Milk-Peaks; it is like the Master using his pen for cutting off the stream to expound upon the *Śūraṅgama*.
Yan Daoyi was open-minded and refined, utterly transcending the mundane. Once it passed through the faculty of sight, the faculty of hearing became transparently clear.

Now, since the crown of the head cannot be seen by the eyes, how could the mind be known by intellectual consciousness? Nevertheless, the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements are all the crown.
Yet, the crown does not see the crown; when active manifestations suddenly arise, doubt is born in their application, pursued day after day.
[The text] ends with "Dingduo'er" (頂墮耳).

Regarding the *Record of the Pavilion of the Fivefold Compassionate Contemplation* (*Wucianguoji*) by Zao Bo, it is said: "Throughout the ten ages of past and present, beginning and end do not depart from the present moment; the boundless ocean of lands..."

Self and others are not separated by even the tip of a hair. Viewed from this perspective, the time before a single thought has arisen is called the "Source" (zong), and the time after a single thought has arisen is called the "Function" (yong).
Thus, the Source and the Function are merely like the bending and extending of a single finger.

When the finger has not yet bent or extended, the finger exists, yet it cannot be apprehended through sight or hearing; it is precisely when one points to the finger that its bending and extending are perceived.
At that time, the finger is hidden and cannot be identified by movement or stillness. If one says it is moving, bending is not the same as stretching;
if one says it is still, stretching is not the same as bending. Bending and stretching each exist independently;

therefore, at the very moment of stretching, bending cannot be found, and at the very moment of bending, stretching also cannot be found. Even at the very moment of both bending and stretching, the substance of the finger cannot be found. Not yet—
At the moment of bending and extending, even bending and extending cannot be apprehended. Only one who knows the fundamental principle (*zong*) can employ function (*yong*).
"Principle" refers to the essence; "function" refers to bending and extending. Furthermore, for one who knows the principle, emotions manifest throughout past and present;

for one who employs function, self and others are not separated. Thereafter, employing this love for others is called benevolence (*ren*); employing this appropriateness in managing affairs is called righteousness (*yi*).
To apply this to those above and below with regulated propriety is called *li* (ritual). To apply this to transform all things without obstruction is called *zhi* (wisdom).
To apply this with firm resolve, remaining without the slightest bit of hypocrisy at the critical juncture where life and death are exchanged, is called *xin* (faithfulness).
These five were never exhausted by the ancients; thus, people of today may still employ them.
To know this is to have understood more than half the essential meaning of the five kinds of compassion (*pañca-maitrī*).

Nevertheless, while the compassion of loving-attachment, the compassion born of the power of forbearance, and the equal and great compassion can all be attained through intellectual principles, the singular point of "true compassion" (*bhūta-maitrī*) is otherwise.

Unless one clearly awakens to one's own mind and remains unentangled by conceptual views and knowledge—just as when Lord Ye Gong painted a dragon and a true dragon appeared before him—it cannot be realized.
Previously, it was not necessarily that he did not cast down his brush and flee in terror.
Following the writing of the *Zhao lun*:

Now, the mind is fundamentally without abiding; that which has attachments is merely emotion (*qing*). Emotion is fundamentally without root; apart from the mind, it has no ground. Therefore, one must realize the mind.

Those whose emotions are fully understood realize that the nature is complete; when the nature is complete, the mind is empty. When the mind is empty, the great function is sovereign, like spring in the myriad things or wind in the thousand forests.
How could the vivid and transformative states of its roaring and calling ever be approximated by ordinary intellect or emotion?
The composition of Master Sengzhao’s *Five Treatises*, with its fundamental principle of "non-transmigration" and other works, is no different from spring bringing forth the myriad things.

The wind whistles through the thousand forests! Since it is able both to give birth to them and to stir them, there must exist that which precedes this giving birth and stirring—namely, the Spring, without which they could not have been born and the wind could not have stirred them.
Nevertheless, without the fundamental source, the four treatises would have no mind; without the four treatises, the fundamental source would have no body. For the body is the outer wall of the mind.
Furthermore, the mind is the outer wall of the nature.
This four-line, twenty-eight-character verse by Vipaśyin Buddha encompasses the entire Great Canon and penetrates the source of Chan; there is nothing it does not exhaustively reveal.

However, sentient beings are superficial and their anxieties are not profound; they are negligent in their resolve, seeking the light of dawn upon seeing the egg, or seeking grain in the belly upon seeing the sprout.
Therefore, although many read this, those who achieve its efficacy are few. I have held to this for fifteen cycles of winter and summer, maintaining it with diligence without ceasing.
Whenever I encountered adversity or favor, or when hatred and love were intermingled, [I applied this practice].
In the beginning, one must certainly take this verse as the vanguard; there are countless instances where it has overturned armies and slain generals.

Yet nowadays, when people hold [this practice] for less than ten million transgressions and find no immediate result, they blame its inefficacy and seek instead to hold what they believe will be effective. This is like digging a well.
I dug three feet into the earth and found no water. I moved to another spot and dug again, yet still there was no water. I changed locations once more, but in the end, I could not find any water;
my spirit was exhausted, and my thirst remained unquenched. If anyone has the resolve to uphold this verse, they will understand the parable of digging a well and maintain it without slackening.
If it does not produce a miraculous effect, then the old monk’s tongue shall surely rot.

The *Bāda rénjué jīng* (Sutra on the Eight Awakenings of a Great Man), appended to the *Huài* [section]. The phrasing and purport of this sutra are clear and profound, like the moon in the autumn waters; even one who is utterly foolish [would find it so].
Please point this out for me. I, Jiaoran, have already understood the meaning. However, as this scripture has been distant from antiquity for a long time, its circulation has also been sparse.
It was initially because a person from Dongchan Temple copied it out by hand in a single scroll. Although Dong has passed away, his eminent disciple Shinan has preserved it and shown it to me.
I read it hurriedly, and before I knew it, my mind opened and my understanding became clear. Thereupon, I commanded both the monastics and the laity to propagate it widely.

As for the subtlety of the eight awakenings (*aṣṭa-bodhyaṅga*), how could they exist apart from the very awareness that sentient beings daily employ yet remain unaware of? Is there some separate awakening distinct from this?

The Great Being, the Tathāgata, out of compassion for those who do not awaken, has taken the very awareness that sentient beings daily employ yet remain unaware of, and opened it up into the eight awakenings.
Those with the karmic affinity who manage to attain even one awakening can thereby shatter the darkness of the long night. This is like...
If one were to divide the flame of a single lamp so that it illuminates the entire world, how could its spiritual radiance ever come to an end?
Furthermore, the mind of a person is like a fish in water; yet does a fish in water truly know the water? So it is with people.
It resides within the mind. If one truly knows the mind, one is already a dragon; if a person knows the mind, they are already a sage. Thus it is said:
"The common people use it every day without knowing it. Alas! Man is the most spiritual among all things.
If, while alive, one does not know why one lives, how can one know why one dies when dead? To be ignorant once is to be ignorant forever.
If one never knows, then there is no knowing at all. That a human being should lack knowledge—how painful this is!
Thereupon, the Greatly Awakened Sage beheld them and lamented, saying: "How extraordinary! All sentient beings possess the Tathāgata within. I have already awakened first, yet they remain unawakened.
To be unawakened is to be mired in the long night of delusion, never contemplating for all eternity. How can I bear this? Thus...
The awareness that sentient beings employ daily without realizing it is opened up into the eight kinds of awakening (*aṣṭa-bodhyaṅga*).

Although there are shallow and deep stages with differing applications, in brief, from the entry of the ordinary person into sainthood, through self-awakening and awakening others, nothing remains unfulfilled.

This sutra contains a total of three hundred and seventy-one characters; its words are concise while its meaning is rich, its prohibitions and illuminations are profound and subtle, and it possesses the capacity to manifest existence while remaining non-existent.
Though it is non-existent, it can be possessed. To attain a single awakening is to suddenly wake from the great dream; how much more so for one who attains the eight awakenings? Alas!
Through awakening, sentient beings may become Buddhas, and ordinary fish may become dragons. During the Zhizheng era of the Yuan dynasty, the Great Master Xue’an Pǔ was renowned for his calligraphy.

everything is created solely by the mind. This verse is it. Thereupon, the entire family began to recite it. Later, they saw the deceased [in a vision], adorned with jewels.
Wearing a celestial crown, he vanished into the air and departed after offering his thanks. Su Shi heard this from Chan Master Foyin;

Foyin heard it from Fan Yaofu. When I read Dongpo’s "Gāthā on Breaking Hell," I regretted that his tongue was not sufficiently broad and long, so that the meaning of the gāthā he uttered was not fully expressed. Alas! This gāthā does not merely break hell; it [breaks] hell itself.
From the hells up to the hungry ghosts; from the hungry ghosts up to the animals; from the animals up to humans; from humans up to the asuras;
from the asuras up to the devas; from the devas up to the śrāvakas; from the śrāvakas up to the pratyekabuddhas;

and from the pratyekabuddhas up to the bodhisattvas—whether ordinary beings or sages, all are shattered without exception. Some may say that while there is no doubt regarding the destruction of the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals, [there remains doubt regarding others].
When [the Emperor] reached the point of refuting the humans and devas, as well as the four types of noble ones outside the realms, he feared it would not accord with principle. [The Master] replied:
"Although the four types of noble ones and the six classes of ordinary beings differ in terms of defilement and purity, they all contemplate matters of the future life.

For example, when Caoxi asked Huiming, 'Neither thinking of good nor thinking of evil—what is that original face? Ming attained great enlightenment at those words and subsequently succeeded Caoxi. [Cao]xi, at Cao..."
Within the words of the "Creek" (Gorge) verse, there is a point of entry; only then will you know that the "Verse for Breaking Hell" is the sword that slays Buddhas.

But tell me, where does the hilt of this sword now rest? "A single thought not arising, one sinks into the waters of death; The six sense-faculties so much as stirring, one encounters the surging waves.
When the paths of sage and ordinary are cut off, it is the place to turn the body around; Who knows that life and death lie upon the tip of the scale?"
Great wisdom arises from the mind; where in the mind can it be sought? It accomplishes all meanings, being neither ancient nor modern.
These four lines of verse do not establish themselves through mere phenomena or principles; they are the fundamental wisdom of Mañjuśrī and the differentiated wisdom of Samantabhadra.
The entire Avataṃsaka Sūtra is fully contained within them. Those who recite them are mostly able to give rise to wisdom. Why is this so?
Great wisdom is fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Great wisdom arises from the mind; thus, principle is perfected.
However, since wisdom has already arisen from the mind, the mind itself has been transformed into wisdom. Where, then, could one seek the mind?

If the mind were something that could be sought, it would mean that the mind could see the mind, which is logically impossible. Therefore, it is said: "Where in the mind shall one seek it? There is nowhere to seek it.
This is what is called "non-reliance. When great wisdom is non-reliant, it is horizontally without the external; when it is horizontally without the external, it is horizontally without dependence.
Is wisdom that is without dependence not perfected through principle? When principle is perfected, there is no obstruction to phenomena.

And thus the task is accomplished. Therefore it is said: "All meanings are accomplished. Although all meanings can be accomplished, if there were neither past nor present, then the task would not be accomplished either.
Without past or present, there is no place of abiding. Because there is no abiding, vertically there is nothing external.
When vertically there is nothing external, then vertically there is no dependence. This verse is by Venerable Uisang of Namsan Rock.
He served as an attendant. In his previous life, the attendant had been an ox; by virtue of carrying bricks to construct a temple, he obtained the retribution of becoming a monk.

However, he suffered from a lack of auditory faculty. After reciting this verse for a long time, his power of hearing was suddenly and completely restored, and he was thereafter able to memorize all the scriptures.
For this reason, this verse is called the "Verse of Wisdom" (*prajñā-gāthā*), for those who recite it are largely able to develop wisdom.
Therefore, Master Yuan of Wei-fu said: "The Buddha-dharma is present in the midst of daily activities; it is in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down; in drinking tea and eating meals;
in speaking and questioning one another; and in all that one does. Yet, when you raise a thought or stir a念 (nian), it is no longer it."

Fuyong said, "That has nothing to do with him. Old Pang said, "The food had reached the edge of my mouth, yet I was taken by him..."
He snatched it away. Fuyong then went down to eat. Old Pang said, "One phrase would have sufficed. Daguan now asks the virtuous teachers:

tell me, at the moment when the two mirrors reflect each other’s light, the sharp point of their wit flashes forth like a luminous pearl tossing and colliding within a golden platter—difficult to grasp at last. Is this what they call...?

"I am born with you on the same branch, but I do not die with you on the same branch. Now tell me, what does it mean to die together and be born together?
Understood. *Tut!* When two mirrors reflect each other’s light, do not attempt to deliberate. The Great Wheel of Dharma turns within the Wheel of Food.

Dongpo’s verse in praise of the Dharma states that the mind (*manas*) is the root. The four lines say: "The objects of the mind (*dharmāḥ*) are the shadows of the five sensory objects that have fallen away;
they are what the mental faculty apprehends. They are not real external realms. Why? Because the clear and discerning consciousness has a beginning and a middle..."

The latter three parts: the first part is close to the preceding five consciousnesses and still belongs to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). The middle part is the proper domain of the sixth consciousness and belongs to inference (*anumāna*).

The final part is close to the seventh consciousness and belongs to non-valid cognition (*aprāmāṇya*). Only that which is apprehended by the five consciousnesses constitutes direct perception and is the true object.
Since the sixth consciousness is not direct perception, it is nothing more than a shadow of the five sense-objects; therefore, it is called "dharma-dhātu" (mental objects).
It takes the Buddha as its essence. "Buddha" has the meaning of awakening (*bodhi*). It is that which is apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);

when present in an object, it is the true object. Therefore, it is called the *dharmakāya*. Yongming said: "Initially, while abiding within the direct perception of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), the floating dust has not yet arisen—this is precisely the *dharmakāya*.

Later, one falls into the realm of the cognitive faculty (*manas*) and the sense organs; external forms then conceal the original shape. 'External forms' refers to the floating dust. That which is so-called..."
This refers to the *dharmāyatana* (the sphere of mental objects). Formerly, when Layman Pang met Mazu, his previous perceptions were suddenly dissolved.
Since those perceptions were dissolved, what else could they be but the *dharmakāya*? Thus the verse says, "The wind ceases and the waves become still.

However, because the *dharmakāya* does not exist separately apart from the *dharmāyatana*, it is also said that "water has no water separate from itself. When released, it becomes rivers and streams; when employed, it is universally beneficial. This is the Mahāyāna.
The activity of a Bodhisattva does not merely consist of self-benefit; it also encompasses the benefit of others and flows on without stagnation.
When waters converge to form a pond or marsh, they remain solitary and good for nothing if not employed; this is the Dharma of the Śrāvaka’s Lesser Vehicle, which stops at self-benefit alone.
How could there be any efficacy therein that reaches other things? When the wind ceases and the waves subside, the waves are precisely the aforementioned seven consciousnesses.
It is as stated in the *Eight Consciousnesses’ Rules*: "The profound depth has seven waves; the objective realm acts as the wind.

"A single call turns the head back—do you recognize me? Vaguely, the moon through the vines becomes a hook. A son of a thousand pieces of gold, having just fallen into ruin, Has such boundless sorrow on his desolate path.
Regarding this verse by Tiantong: those who devote themselves to the study of the profound mysteries may perhaps find joy in it.

This clarity is manifest and spontaneously present; fundamentally, it is neither strange nor perilous. Some may despise it as being "stuck to the skin and bound to the bone," deeming it a lapse into ordinary consciousness (*vijñāna*).

when used by Bian Que and Hua Tuo, it can raise the dead back to life amidst laughter and conversation. If one is not...
Although that person possesses the Mo-ye sword, it is not as sharp as a hoe or as effective as a weed-killer.

The Vajra of the neighboring temple weeps most piteously; the eldest sister of the eastern village cries out her grievance.
If you say that this verse of mine is no different from that of Tiantong, then once you have understood Tiantong’s verse, it will not be difficult to understand mine.
I know that Zhaozhou has risen again and Miaoxi has been reborn; yet I fear even they would not have grasped it. How much less so those who come after?

How can there be two meanings for one and the same causal occasion? My brothers, *Note: This passage is a commentary by Dahui Zonggao on his own verse regarding the story of Zhaozhou’s dog.*

Since the Buddha-dharma came to the East, there have been no lack of individuals throughout the generations—exalted guests beyond the mundane world and eminent scholars within it—who have propagated its Way like the sound of a lute.
Yet, among them, only the Venerable Yuan of Mount Lu’s East Garden in Xunyang during the Eastern Jin dynasty possessed such profound concern and far-reaching foresight that his vision...

He stood out preeminently. He perceived that those who considered themselves monks did not understand their own school (zong), while those in secular life did not understand the transformative power (hua) of the Dharma;

thus, school and transformation were muddled, leaving both without a guiding principle. Consequently, he composed the *Jiazhai Chujia* (On the Laity and the Clergy) to explain the reasons why this was so, transmitting it for ten thousand generations so that those who follow the Dharma would each know their proper direction—like raising the sun and moon in the midst of the sky, or shaking the thunderclaps from heaven.
Within this great dream, who among those with eyes does not see it? Who among those with ears does not hear it?
Yet, in recent times, there are those among both the laity and the ordained who have not heard even the titles of these works until their deaths, let alone their meaning.

Alas! Since the Buddha departed, the time has been long; Māra is powerful while the Dharma is weak. Erroneous teachings run rampant, and correct words have fallen into ruin. I often reflect upon this...

Arriving at this point, I do not know from where my tears come. I have therefore instructed Master Qi to first transcribe the *Discourse on the Laity and the Clergy* (*Zaijia chujia lun*) and its biographies, so that those who are resolved upon our Way may study them with diligent hearts.
Laozi said: "Heaven and Earth are not benevolent; they treat the myriad things as straw dogs. The sage is not benevolent; he treats the common people as straw dogs.
Now, as for the nature of these straw dogs: before they have been displayed, they are adorned with brocades and silks and presented with music.
Once they have been displayed, some are discarded on the roads, while others are stuffed into cooking pots."

Enough. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "If one possesses the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span, then one is not a bodhisattva.

It further states: "If one perceives that there are sentient beings who can be saved, this is precisely the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, and the mark of a life-span.
Viewed through this lens, Heaven and Earth treat the myriad things as straw dogs; the Sage...
People treat the common people as straw dogs. This is not because they lack benevolence; rather, "lack of benevolence" is merely another designation for "egolessness.

How could the Sage not know that straw dogs are made from bound bundles of firewood? Furthermore, he decorates them with brocade and embroidery to demonstrate that what is "useless" is nevertheless put to use.
Now, regarding that which is useless yet used: the object itself may be non-existent, yet its utility is not non-existent.
Things are non-existent, yet their function is not non-existent. Although the heavens and earth are vast and the myriad things are numerous, from the very beginning there has never been a "thing.

To know that from the beginning there has never been a thing, yet the function of heaven and earth is not non-existent and the functions of the myriad things are each fully sufficient—this is the function of saving sentient beings without the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of sentient being, or the mark of life-span.
As for those who are eternally enlightened, how could they not know the benevolence that transcends benevolence—the great benevolence that has no bounds?
Mount Wan and Yongjia both attained the subtlety of the "special transmission outside the teachings"; their excellence lay in cutting off all reliance on language and written words.

One directly awakens to one’s own mind. As for the *Xinxin Ming* (Inscription on Faith in Mind) and the *Zhengdao Ge* (Song of Realizing the Way), they are like the myriad flowers of a thousand hues in the midst of spring:
are they language and writing, or are they not language and writing? Let those who are not constrained by conventional views try to explain this. Nevertheless, do flowers and fruits obstruct spring?
If flowers were to obstruct spring, it would be as reasonable to say that spring does not flower. To know [this] is to be unobstructed.
If one insists that spring must produce flowers, then spring is deluded. If spring were not deluded, would flowers and fruits obstruct it?
If this is so, how far apart are words and letters from the separate transmission outside of teaching?
It comes from nowhere; it swirls like thunder. Relying on emptiness, it can travel; striking objects, it produces sound. It stirs the myriad things, yet possesses sound without form.
Its coming and going leave no trace; this is what is called "wind. However, as it cannot avoid arising and ceasing, it is not the True Wind.
As for the True Wind, it does not rely on emptiness to travel, nor does it strike objects to produce resonance.
Fundamentally there is no coming or going; how could there be arising or ceasing? At Vulture Peak, the Buddha held up a flower and Kāśyapa smiled;
when Kāśyapa called out, Ānanda responded. Thus they missed it face-to-face, and the flagpole fell.

This continued until the Patriarch came from the West, where Shen Guang stood in the snow and the wind rose at Shaoshi, causing the grains on his jade tower to stand on end. Seeking to find peace of mind, he found that the mind cannot be grasped; thus he severed his arm.
Why is it that fresh blood lies in profusion, flowing into Caoxi until the Caoxi stream turns azure? Tiantong offers his verse yet remains silent;

the Third Patriarch speaks yet has no words. The *Xinxin Ming* (Inscription on Faith in Mind) is composed, as if empty space were being gnawed by insects; this is truly the great fanning of the True Wind.
The fire of wisdom blazes fiercely; whether one possesses a mind or is without mind, whether one is an ordinary person or a sage, if one touches it, it burns away the face;
if one turns one’s back on it, it freezes the Dharma-body to death. It causes those who can speak to roll up their tongues and those with wisdom to become fools.
Confucians lose what makes them Confucians, and Laoists lose what makes them Laoists. How great is this calamity that has reached our own homes! Recite [the name] once.
As for the Buddha, one simply needs to rinse the mouth for three days; all of this is brought about by the stirring of the True Wind (Zhenfeng).
Tiantong’s verse says: Do you see this single piece of True Wind? The subtle Mother of Transformation weaves at the loom of principle. She has woven an ancient brocade containing the image of spring;
Alas, what can be done against the Lord of the East leaking its secrets? This verse overturns and surges forth; it may cause either loss or gain to one's family reputation. There is... [text ends]
The female possesses the male; through the transformation of a true wind, it becomes ancient brocade. When the dung of a mule is picked up, it exchanges for another’s eyeballs.
A kind heart does not receive a kind reward; one who delivers charcoal in the snow is instead told that it increases the cold. Master Daguan cannot bear the bitterness.
He dictated a verse: "Do you see this fragment of true wind? The subtle Mother of Transformation sets her shuttle to the loom;

She weaves an ancient brocade containing the image of spring. Alas, what can be done about the Lord of the East leaking it all away? Then another person, who could not restrain himself, stepped forward and said:

This is a verse by Tiantong. For what reason did the Old Monk, under the bright sun and clear blue sky, drive away the plowman’s ox and snatch the food from a hungry man? The Master said, "I do not care whether he is Tiantong or not;
tell me, where is this old fellow's nostrils? When [the monk] could not speak, the Master said, "Then prostrate yourself and go drink tea. Come back again."
Within the true wind, it is not too late for realgar and yellow arsenic to distinguish white from black.

If one knows that there is resonance when the three unite and hearing when the five unite, then the construction of the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) will be eliminated without waiting for them to be washed away.
Therefore it is said: "The single word 'knowledge' is the gateway to all wonders. There was a reason for this in the sages of antiquity.
The eyes perceive sounds, and the ears behold forms and appearances. Thus, the distant is shown as near, and the obstructed is shown as unobstructed.
One may pass directly through mountains and walls, and traverse the void; there is no other path.

This beginning does not exceed the realization that there is dependence, yet one becomes deluded by that which is independent. Dependence is itself independence. Having known this, one is further able to practice it; therefore—

That which depends on conditions arises gradually; that which does not depend on conditions ripens spontaneously. When it ripens, there is transformation; when there is transformation, there is identity.
This is why one can manifest the near within the distant and manifest the unobstructed within the obstructed (as in Dongpo’s Inscription on the Bell).

When one is deluded regarding the nature and treats it as emotion, one cannot distinguish between water and oil. Only by awakening to the nature through emotion does one finally realize that water and oil cannot coexist.
If they were to coexist, water would bubble when it encounters fire, whereas oil remains tranquil when it encounters fire. That which is tranquil—
If fire and oil were one, they would be without opposition; thus, the oil would not know the fire, and the fire would not know the oil.
Only when the oil and fire do not know each other can they function for one another. Water, however, is not one with fire; therefore, it merely arises upon seeing the fire.
Fire is a metaphor for the objects that entice the emotions; water is a metaphor for the emotions that become stained by those objects; and oil is a metaphor for the discernment of those objects.
Wisdom. However, when external objects are present, emotion does not arise; when external emotions are present, wisdom has no ground. Now, emotion and wisdom are originally not two separate things.
When they are driven by external objects, they are called "emotion"; when one realizes that objects do not truly exist, it is called "wisdom."
Therefore, wisdom and emotion abide together like oil and water. When emotion contacts an object, it flows away like a torrent that cannot be turned back;

when wisdom comprehends an object, subject and object do not arise. Thus, wisdom is always one with principle, while emotion is always at odds with principle—just as oil is always one with fire, while water is always at odds with fire.
Being at odds constitutes enmity, and enmity must have victory or defeat. As for water, it does not...
If one wins by fire, one will inevitably lose and rise from defeat in the end. Viewed from this perspective, external objects possess no principle, and external emotions possess no wisdom.
When a student understands this, they will realize that the daily activities of Old Pang have no difference [from their own]; every single thing naturally accords and harmonizes.
Old Pang first set his body forth from the burning house; he submerged his family wealth in the Xiang River, and his wife and children gathered around.

Round and complete. Together forging non-arising, the faculties and their objects are serene and distant. The evolving consciousnesses are transformed into wisdom; the great matter of birth and death is uprooted in a single lifetime.

If one traces its origin, it does not exceed the thorough realization that the objects before one lack inherent nature. When the roots and consciousnesses are severed at the base, one rides upon principle to govern emotion.
Whether in adversity or favor, there is no interval; whether moving or still, they are as one. Knowing is thorough, practice reaches the goal, and naturally, one approaches the end of life.

[The Verse on Water]. Dongshan said:
"Greed, anger, and ignorance—how utterly ignorant they are! Fortunately, today we have caught them; when they move, we strike them; when they are empty, we beat them.
We entrust them to the Mind-King to examine them closely. For immeasurable kalpas they have remained unliberated. I ask you three: [what will you do?]"
"Knowing or not knowing? Shen Ding said: "Greed, anger, and delusion—truly there is no knowing. Throughout the twelve hours of the day, let them be as they may.
Walking, it goes; sitting, it follows. Entrust this to the Mind-King, for there is nothing to be done. From immeasurable kalpas past, one has been fundamentally liberated;
why need one further ask about knowing or not knowing? Regarding these two verses, some people appreciate Dongshan’s approach to daily life and its circumstances.
Whether in opposition or accord, forge your own mind with fierce and subtle hammering. Some reach the true state of great rest at Shending;
for them, whether coughing or spitting, waving their arms, joking, laughing, or reviling, everything is nothing other than liberation-samādhi.
Old Man Daguan now asks you, the assembly: where do you say Dongshan’s nostrils and Shending’s feet are located? You—
How dare one recklessly speculate? One must realize that Shending was not forged in the furnace and bellows of Dongshan;
how could he have attained such spontaneous ease otherwise? Dongshan did not strike Shending because he perceived a sign from the world.

From the moment you began striking me this morning until you pounded me this evening, I dare say that greed, anger, and ignorance have remained utterly unsubdued, as if waiting for the year of the donkey.
If you can discern and distinguish [the truth], I grant that you have understood the Buddha-dhyāna;
yet if it is the Patriarchal Zen, it is still ten thousand miles from your native land. If you wish to understand the Patriarchal Zen, you must take Dongshan Shending and place him behind your head.
Only when you find a way to turn around right before your own eyes can it be accomplished. Thus it is said: "It is merely the place where one used to walk;
yet upon meeting and raising [the matter], confusion arises. A man of extraordinary character has, from the beginning, his nostrils reaching toward heaven and his heels planted firmly on the ground.
Why is it that he acts like a thief, always harboring a sense of inner insecurity? When suddenly pressed by another, he immediately...

One worries that stolen goods might have no place to hide. If they are the sons or daughters of a virtuous family, even if others shake them by the thousand and sway them by the ten thousand, they will naturally not give rise to groundless alarm;
their minds will be as calm as the sea. Why can they be so stable? It is because they have never, from the beginning, stolen the property of others.
As the times have grown increasingly distant from antiquity, great men do not appear, and the Way of the Dharma...

The "slow slicing" (lingchi) execution is truly terrifying. Whether one is a layperson or a monastic, having acquired some intellectual understanding from the sutras and treatises, or having caught some of the pungent stench within the tangled vines of conceptual proliferation, they claim for themselves: "I have already seen through to the very source of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Thus, they presume to be honored as supreme masters where there is no Buddha. There is a certain class of blind roosters who follow after sounds day and night; suddenly, they collide with—

yet they cannot, in that very moment, give rise to great shame and remorse, weeping and self-reproaching. Instead, regarding such a person of true substance, they give rise to great arrogance.

"Regarding this matter, let me first ask you about seventeen hundred cases of tangled vines. Although these are the leftover soup and rancid rice of the ancients, if you can handle them, you will have no doubts.

Important.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Such intrinsic nature is like an illusion, like a dream, like a shadow, like a reflection; it is entirely unestablished.

While scholars all know that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are like illusions when it is stated directly so, the claim that even intrinsic nature itself is like an illusion—though one may have been intoxicated for a long time—is [rarely understood].

Regarding the ocean of meaning, there has never been one who did not harbor doubts. Furthermore, those who do not know pain and itchiness yet claim to have no doubts—such doubters certainly cannot understand what those who truly have no doubts can know.

Even Buddhas and Patriarchs stand in awe of such a true person of no doubt; how much more so others?
Is it otherwise?

"Retire. Let the fisherman stay and watch patiently; he too shall naturally obtain fish. Thereupon, he thought of Master Xiaodong of Haedong, who had come to China to seek the Dharma.
One night, while staying there, he was so parched with thirst that he looked around and saw a small pool. He cupped his hands to drink from it, and the water was exceptionally sweet and cool.
When he looked at it the next morning, it turned out to be a pit of skulls. While he was still retching, he suddenly attained enlightenment, saying: "The one mind is not..."

"Birth! All dharmas are without fault. He subsequently returned to Japan, where he produced commentaries on the *Avataṃsaka*, *圆觉* (*Yuanjue*), and other sutras, which circulated widely throughout the world.
Furthermore, when Kumārajīva was five or six years old, he followed his mother as she lifted the Buddha’s almsbowl.

He thought to himself, "My body is very small, while the Buddha’s bowl is very large," and unconsciously let out a cry as he dropped the bowl. When his mother asked him the reason for this, he replied, "Just now, I was born."
The mind is like a bowl that may be light or heavy. If one phenomenon is thus, all phenomena are likewise. What further cause for doubt could there be?

Yet those who study today, before even meeting a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) or Dharma teacher, first harbor doubts within themselves, saying: "Will this spiritual friend truly be able to awaken me?
"Will this Dharma teacher truly be able to instruct me? "Will this precept master truly maintain pure precepts himself?"
Alas! The gentleman seeks out excellence by examining even the finest hair, while the petty person seeks out flaws by examining even the finest hair;
yet the mind that seeks excellence is not as skillful as the mind that seeks flaws. With such a disposition, one cannot even become a good person in this world, let alone a son of the Tathāgata.
Master Duan’s verse says: "When ascending the platform to receive the full precepts, first of all, do not doubt the master. [He] plucked...
Take the sweetmeat and eat it; do not mind the horizontal branches of the tree (referring to the verse by Master Duan Shizi).

When I read the *Lotus Sūtra*, I know that one who attains the purification of the six sense faculties sees the forms of the three thousand great thousandfold worlds with their eyes, hears the sounds of the three thousand great thousandfold worlds with their ears, smells the fragrances of the three thousand great thousandfold worlds with their noses, and tastes [the flavors] with their tongues...
The flavors of a trichiliocosm are tasted by the body; the touches of a trichiliocosm are felt by the body;

the dharmas of a trichiliocosm are penetrated by the mind, as clearly as seeing fruit in the palm of one's hand. Nevertheless, though I know them, I have not yet attained their use because the six sense faculties are not yet purified.
If they were once purified, they would manifest before me—what cause for doubt is there? Alas! Who among those who employ these [faculties] does not [possess them]?
It exists. Because it is shrouded by views and afflictions, and obscured by the dust-like sands [of ignorance], it does not manifest before one.

When views and afflictions are severed and the dust-like sands are cleared away, the mind becomes like the mirror of Xuanyuan (the Yellow Emperor), penetrating through the ten directions; this is self-realized—how could it depend on the words of others?
Sōngp’o’s Praise of Avalokiteśvara says: When sentient beings fall into the eight difficulties, their body and mind are both lost;

yet there remains but a single thought by which they can call upon Avalokiteśvara. Whether in a pit of fire or on a mountain of blades, amidst fierce beasts and various poisons—when all manner of suffering gathers upon the body—the one who calls does not feel the pain.
If the caller were to feel the pain themselves, they would certainly be unable to call. If they have realized this...
"It is not painful. Why then call upon the Bodhisattva? Because sentient beings are bound by duality, a single body undergoes manifold sufferings.
If one can truly realize non-duality, that is Avalokiteśvara. Eighty-four thousand people will simultaneously arrive together to provide rescue. The commentary explains:
Now, as for the fragility of a single body, if the eight difficulties should suddenly converge, it will be difficult to survive; one may know then that both body and mind will be lost. However...
When both body and mind have perished, yet one is able to call upon Avalokiteśvara—is it the body? Is it the mind?

If it were either body or mind, they would be difficult to preserve, yet body and mind have long since perished. If it is neither body nor mind, then in knowing the pain and being able to call upon Avalokiteśvara, is there actually pain?
Or is there no pain at all? If there is pain, then body and mind have never truly perished.

If there were no pain, then body and mind would never have been lost. One who finds this difficult should investigate that pain by means of the body and mind themselves, and then investigate that pain apart from the body and mind. Between these states of identity and separation, one should observe and examine back and forth.
Once the location of the pain is clearly perceived, whether there is indeed pain or whether there is no pain will become self-evident, without the need for further seeking.
Guanyin merely seeks the location of the pain. This eulogy by Dongpo is subtle, profound, and transcendent; how could those such as Lu Zhi or Shao You ever hope to even approximate it?
I have observed that although Tiantong’s verse on the karmic conditions of Dongshan’s illness is indeed wondrous, [it does not reach this level].
Yet this is not as good as the following praise: "The four corners tread upon the earth. The verse says: "Cast down the stinking skin-bag;
Pick up and turn the red-fleshed ball. When the nostrils at the head are straight, The skull beneath is instantly dried. I say: If the skull is not dried, the nostrils are not straight;
if the nostrils are not straight, the dynamic of the meeting of arrowheads will naturally be blunted by no small measure.
Furthermore, another interpretation states that from the character "difficult" (難) up to "various observations" (種種觀察), all constitute *anumāna* (inference).

Regarding this eulogy by Dongpo, if one does not overlook the first character "difficult" within the commentary on "the skull forming in the basin," but instead applies diligent observation, then Dongpo’s eulogy will naturally provide entry.
The phrase "the skull directly dries up" refers to what is meant by "wisdom reaching its limit and emotion withering away. It is vital.

A human skull and the skull of a dead person are fundamentally no different. However, the skull of a living person has not yet withered in its emotional consciousness (*saṃjñā*), nor has it forgotten its cognitive inclinations (*jñāna*);
thus, it is called a "foul-smelling skull. The skull of a dead person is so called because both its emotions and its cognition have completely withered away.
The ancients called this the "Vajra Skull," which is precisely what is meant by the *dharmakāya*. For when both emotion and intellect have withered away, the self is forgotten;
once the self is forgotten, there is nothing that is not the Way. Thus it is said: "Is the Way far? It is real in every encounter. Is the Sage far?
Embodying it, one is immediately divine. The character for "embody" (*ti*) refers to *anumāna* (inference); the character for "divine" (*shen*) refers to *pratyakṣa* (direct perception).
Chew upon this with great care. Han Daibo commented on Xuedou’s verse: “A single rabbit lies across the ancient road; as soon as the blue hawk sees it, it seizes it.
Later hunters’ dogs lack spiritual nature; they vainly search for it at the old spot where the withered stump once stood. Xiangyan said: “Movement!”

To reveal the ancient path is not to fall into the trap of silent stillness. Nowadays, there are those who take "the non-arising of a single thought" for Buddhahood and "the non-emergence of joy or anger" for the Middle Way;

these are what are called those who seek the old site of a withered stump. If one can grasp a single instance and reflect it back upon all things—such that brightness and darkness, movement and stillness, penetration and obstruction, tranquility and change, union and separation, birth and death—are all as they were before any form had yet taken shape—if this is not so...
This Buddha is within this very midst; that which was once a single refined spirit has divided into the six harmonious aggregates, thereby becoming what is called the "external.
Thus, there are those who can hear the sound of hairpins and bracelets through a wall, and they have likewise attained entry.

Speaking from this perspective, the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) are all the ancient path of Han Daibo. To abide within the six sense-objects without being stained by them is precisely the [path] of Han Daibo.
It is also like the rabbit [in the moon]. Linji employed its essential function while changing its name, saying:
"Upon each of your bare flesh-balls, there is a true person of no station, who, at the gates of the six sense organs, emits a great radiance that illuminates heaven and earth."

That you all have been unable to realize these aforementioned words is because they were all ancient worthies and Zen elders who emptied their entrails to speak "old woman’s Zen" for the sake of those young novices of Zen.
If one were to act according to one's true nature, one could not reveal even a single fragment. Why?
Because the life-root of the Buddhas and Patriarchs has been severed; how much more so for sentient beings with feverish minds! Therefore it is said:
"The weeds before the Dharma Hall are ten feet deep; truly, they do not deceive me" (referring to Han Daobei’s case regarding Xuedou).
The *Song of Realizing the Way* by Yongjia says: "If you simply untie the soiled garments from within your own breast, who could boast of their diligent progress elsewhere?
These two lines of the song have deceived no small number of people throughout the world; it is not Yongjia's fault, for it is the people themselves [who are at fault].
