[The Master] asked, "I do not ask about the meaning of the teachings. What is the meaning of the 'separate transmission outside the teachings'?

Dongshan said, "Setting aside for a moment the separate transmission outside the teachings, what is the meaning of the teachings? Cao Shan said, "Yellow scrolls and red axes. Dongshan said, "These are the words that express [the meaning].
What is the meaning of the teachings? Cao Shan said, "The mouth wishes to speak, yet words fail; the mind intends to engage, yet thoughts vanish."
Zhimen said, "When the mouth wishes to speak, words fail; this is in response to having speech. When the mind intends to engage with objects, thoughts vanish;

this is in response to deluded conceptualization. What is the essential meaning of the teaching? Zhan was at a loss and did not know how to answer. Zhimen asked, "I hear that you, Minister, are well-versed in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, is that so?
Zhan replied, "I dare not say so. Zhimen said, "The Sutra says: 'Cultivating one's livelihood and engaging in productive enterprises are all in accord with the Right Dharma.'"
The Dharma. Now tell me, at the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, how many have fallen from their station? Zhan was utterly bewildered. Men shouted at him and drove him away.
Because of this, Zhan redoubled his resolve to practice Chan. Consider this through the lens of Yunmen’s function:
Yongjia merely said, "I simply untie the soiled garment from within my own breast; who can boast of diligence by looking outward? Was it not true that Minister Chen alone failed to do so?
Do you understand these two lines? If you do, then why do you see Yunmen as being like a wooden puppet?
It is because this master had not yet overturned the conceptual nest of doctrinal principles; instead, he was overturned by that lame monk.
One reaches a point where there is no place to sit; this is what is meant by "greedily gazing at the moon over the river while losing the oar in one's hand.
Such intellectual understanding relies on supernatural powers (*abhijñā*); though it may seem somewhat lively, it is fundamentally not the true nest of principle and can be buried and extinguished.
However, what is called "cognitive understanding" is faith based on supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), not faith that penetrates the Way (*mārga*).

Faith based on supernatural powers seems like awakening when it is explained, yet one is inevitably deluded when encountering actual objects. It is like quicksilver or silver: it cannot withstand fire;
upon the slightest touch of fire, it flies away. Faith that penetrates the Way is not like this. For example, Kāṇadeva exhausted [his opponents] with his eloquence.
A non-Buddhist practitioner. A disciple of this non-Buddhist practitioner resented Deva for having distressed his teacher.

One day, while Deva was walking in meditation amidst the forest, the disciple took a sharp blade and slit open Deva’s abdomen, saying: "You distressed my teacher with your tongue; I shall now distress you with my knife."
"Are you still capable of performing miracles? Deva accepted this with a smile and further comforted and instructed him in various ways.
Deva’s intestines fell to the ground. His disciples arrived, wailing in alarm. Deva instructed them, saying, "He has merely destroyed his own roots of goodness; what concern is that of mine?
I only grieve that he is consumed by the poison of his own anger and will surely fall into suffering in the end. My heart [is thus resolved].
If one does not feel anger toward those who harm them, then the suffering of that person’s fall into misery shall ultimately be taken upon oneself instead.

Only when one further washes their intestines and stomach with ambrosia (*amṛta*) will my mind finally find peace. Alas! The illuminating function of the Buddha—how could it be compared to the lecturers on mere doctrine?
How could one possibly distinguish between the strengths and weaknesses of the school of wild fox saliva?

Furthermore, there are those who so-called "lecture on the Way" or "study the teachings," yet they are even inferior to the lecture masters and the wild fox Chan. Thus it is said: "One blind man leads a multitude of blind men;
leading them, he causes the multitude of blind men to fall into a pit of fire. Therefore, I say that these two lines from Yongjia’s song have deceived the people of the world.
It is few. Nevertheless, if one is a true master of the Way, these two lines of verse are both the sword that kills and the sword that gives life.
Now, regarding those of lesser capacity in the *Avataṃsaka* and those who withdrew from their seats in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*:

the former considered that because the *Avataṃsaka* had not yet fully encompassed all capacities, it did not fully express its original intent; the latter considered that those who withdrew from their seats in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* were precisely those for whom the *Avataṃsaka* was intended.
This is a minor root [of understanding]. How could one alone claim that the *Avataṃsaka* is not perfect while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* alone is perfect?

Consequently, among the followers of these two schools, those who revere Qingliang (Chengguan) came to regard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* as incomplete, while those who revere Tiantai likewise regarded the *Avataṃsaka* as incomplete.
To them, I then said: "If you truly consider the *Avataṃsaka* to be for the sake of gathering in sentient beings..."

Not yet finished. At that time, when the Buddha preached the Great Sūtra, with the exception of the great Bodhisattvas, there were still the eight classes of beings and others who, because they had planted perfect causes in previous lives, were also able to hear the voice of Vairocana. I venture to ask:
besides these various species who heard the sūtra, are there other sentient beings who did not hear the *Avataṃsaka*? If there are such, why is this so?

One might alone suppose that because those of small capacity do not hear this sutra, the teaching has failed to encompass all capacities; or one might further claim that the departure from their seats in the *Lotus Sutra* indicates it is not perfect.
I venture to ask: apart from those who departed from their seats, are there still other sentient beings who have not heard the *Lotus Sutra*?

If there are such, then the "small capacity" of the *Avataṃsaka Sutra* is not necessarily anything other than the Perfect [Teaching]. As for those who have heard it, there is no reason to [doubt its perfection].
[The interlocutor] replied, "Yes. I further instructed him, saying: "Do you understand? If the *Avataṃsaka* lacked the 'lesser roots,' its perfection would be unable to bind [all beings].
If the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* lacked the 'non-retrogression from the assembly,' its subtlety would be unable to arrest [the mind].

Only when the perfect is accompanied by the lesser, and the subtle is accompanied by the ignorant, do we finally see that the perfection of the *Avataṃsaka* is not [merely] perfect, and that the subtlety of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is not [merely] subtle. Therefore it is said: 'To realize perfect enlightenment...'"
Those who abide in perfect enlightenment are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Those who seek to realize perfect enlightenment but have not yet attained it are Tathāgatas.
To know this is to understand Tiantai and Qingliang. Upon hearing this, the listeners were at a loss for words and withdrew.
Huayan said: "Such intrinsic nature is like an illusion, like a transformation, like a shadow, and like a reflection;

none of these are established. The nature of True Suchness (tathatā) is originally and spontaneously perfected. Yet, through non-awakening, it moves and flows according to conditions; therefore, in principle, it is not established."
Since the dependent and the imagined lack intrinsic nature, phenomena are not established.

When both phenomena and principle are unestablished, the obstacles of principle and the obstacles of phenomena are both eliminated without the need for effortful transformation. Once the obstacles of phenomenon and principle have dissolved, neither sages nor ordinary beings can fathom them.
Therefore, those of true character take the head as the tail and the tail as the head, yet their heads and tails remain perfectly orderly;
they possess mastery over both life and death. As I read the "Entrustment" chapter of the *Lotus Sūtra*, my tears flowed uncontrollably. Why is this? Because of the *Lotus*—

It is supremely subtle; sentient beings are supremely coarse. To cause each and every one of these supremely coarse sentient beings to comprehend and understand the supremely subtle Dharma—even for a great Bodhisattva, this is difficult.
Therefore, when the Tathāgata entrusted them with the propagation of the Dharma, he said:
"To transmit it [to others] is indeed a weighty task. This is truly so.
The *Lotus Sūtra* says: "To open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Its meaning is fundamentally clear; it has never been mysterious or subtle.

If one seeks it through mystery and subtlety, then the Buddha’s knowledge and vision will not be clear. For the Buddha’s intent is precisely that knowledge which sentient beings use daily yet do not realize.
When the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are opened, then with the eyes one sees forms, with the ears one hears sounds, and with the nose...
The nose smells fragrances; the tongue tastes flavors; the body perceives touch; and the mind clings to objects. There is nowhere that the Buddha’s knowledge and vision does not reach.
By this I know that within the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, sentient beings open up their own sentient-being knowledge and vision;

and within the sentient-beings’ knowledge and vision, the Buddhas open up their Buddha-knowledge and vision. Viewed in this light, both Buddhas and sentient beings originally possess no fixed essence.
It simply depends on the nature of the knowledge and vision he has opened up.

Ajita (Akṣayamati) wondered: "If sound can be heard with the ear, for what reason does this Bodhisattva alone observe all sounds with his eyes? The Buddha answered Ajita, saying: "All sentient beings receive..."

When one is beset by various sufferings and afflictions, if they single-mindedly invoke the name of Avalokiteśvara, Avalokiteśvara immediately perceives the voices of all who invoke him, and sentient beings all attain liberation. Ajita then clearly understood this without doubt.
Because sentient beings perceive sounds with their ears, there arises a sense of separation between self and others; thus, the eight difficulties converge and manifold sufferings arise.

To undergo an eon is called "capable" (neng). That the self undergoes the eon is called "the locus" (suo). Thus, the faculties and their objects are tossed about, and the fires of karma incinerate them.
If one investigates their origin, one finds that the ear serves as the ground for hearing sounds, while sound acts as the inducement for auditory consciousness.
Therefore it is said: "Objects possess the karmic function of inducing the mind. If one could truly perceive sound with the eye, then...

The faculties have nothing upon which to depend, and objects have nothing by which they can be depended upon. When one contemplates in this way, it is not merely that the distinctions between sentient beings and bodhisattvas vanish;
rather, the paths of both ordinary persons and sages are exhausted, and the roots of suffering and pleasure are uprooted. Yet these functions are not matters of intellectual understanding;
therefore, when encountering conditions or contacting objects—whether favorable or adverse—they all serve as the guiding steps for my entry into the Way.

Furthermore, Ānanda, there are four grave errors in taking "non-attachment" as the mind. When [the nature of] dependent designation is established, it has already been stated that non-attachment cannot be attained.
[The mind] is momentary yet continuous; it is momentary yet mutually dependent. This extends even to the point of dependent designation, at which time [non-attachment] has already departed.
"One is not attached to the three [aggregates]. To speak of "non-attachment" while remaining within the realm of conditioned existence (*samskāra*)—is this not the fault of the fourth grave offense?

Now, when the three [faculties] combine, one clings to the existence of sound; when the five [elements] combine, one clings to the existence of hearing. These are the ways of ordinary people. To discard the three...
To cling to "no sound" when there is no ringing, or to cling to "no hearing" when the five [senses] have ceased, is likewise the way of the common person.
Only those who harmonize with the Three and Five do not cling to existence; those who abandon the Three and Five do not cling to non-existence. This is not something known by the common person.
Having read Dongpo’s “Inscription on the Bell at Fayun Temple,” I attained great awakening to the *dhāraṇī* of the samādhi of language. Indeed, all literature is thus.
Characters and speech are all transformations of one’s own mind. To know that they are transformations of one’s own mind is to realize that when the three [elements] combine, there is resonance;
when the five [elements] combine, there is hearing. When the three are discarded, there is no resonance; when the five are discarded, there is no hearing. It is like drawing patterns upon water:
the formed pattern is water, and the non-patterned is also water. Combining is the mind; discarding is also the mind. Thus it is.
All are the mind. How could the mind grasp the mind? Could the mind abandon the mind?
Knowing it to be thus, one may compose poetry, one may sing songs, one may write prose, one may lament, and one may rejoice.
Words are like flowers; the self-mind is like spring. If spring obstructs the flowers, it cannot be called spring; if the flowers obstruct spring, they cannot be called flowers.
Flowers: they assist one another without obstruction; thus, the flower is itself spring.

If the flower can be identified with spring, then sensory objects (*viṣaya*) may likewise be identified with the sense faculties (*indriya*). How could it be that the faculties alone cannot be identified with their objects?
Since the faculties can be mutually identified, why should they not also function interchangeably? The inscription says: The ear sees and the eye hears; when silence resounds, it resounds.
The Teacher in the great, perfect void sits alone upon a high and broad seat; reclining like a man free from attachment, he neither leads others nor does he not lead them.
To both he says nothing at all, yet he speaks the Dharma of non-speaking. Although dharmas are inexhaustible, when questioned, he should respond with three.
"You should hear it in this way; you should not listen to it in that way. Furthermore, these several phrases consist of sixty characters in total.
If the characters are likened to flowers, the phrases are the spring. If the phrases are likened to flowers, the meaning is the spring.

If the meaning is likened to flowers, the principle is the spring. If the principle is likened to flowers, the mind is the spring. Thus, this composition by Master Sō (Sūshin) is rigorous in its diction and refined in its meaning. If...
Those who do not understand the wondrous nature of consciousness will simply regard this as paper flowers; how could there be any "spring" in them?

It was likely because Master Su Dongpo considered that through this, I have attained the realization of the meaning of the six sense organs functioning interchangeably, and that all six sense objects are the wondrousness of the Way.

If one does not reach the resonance of the "threefold union" and the hearing of the "fivefold union," and further extend this to the state where the "three and five are united yet there is neither resonance nor hearing," one will ultimately never [attain it].

It can be so obtained. Therefore, the bell is named after its master; this is to repay his virtue. If there is a master but no seat, or if there is a seat that is neither high nor broad, how can it be great?
To be called "great" implies having no exterior. If there is no exterior, then the reclining scholar cannot be found.

This striking of the bell while omitting the full tolling is not a matter of omission; it is actually a matter of inclusion. Thus, the tolling bears the name of the "gentleman" (shi) but lacks the actual substance of the gentleman.
If one does not fully relinquish human sentiment, the ultimate principle will never reach its finest clarity. This is because the person has usurped the role of the master-gentleman (shi).
If the master-gentleman is usurped while the person is not, one has still not reached the subtle excellence. Furthermore, this is followed by the usurping of that [subtle excellence].

It is a matter of humanity. When these three mutually usurp one another, then though the function remains, the merit is forgotten. Now, when the function remains, emotional attachments wither of their own accord;

when merit is forgotten, the path of righteousness naturally severs itself. When the path of righteousness is severed and emotional attachments have withered, one attains the preservation of the subtle essence of one’s own nature and life.
How could this be something achieved by those who are mired in obscurity or who cling to what is heard and what is proclaimed? I initially said: "Reading..."
Regarding Dongpo’s Bell Inscription: those who have attained great awakening to the *dhāraṇī* of the samādhi of language do not engage in frivolous speech, nor do they engage in false speech.

If there are those who can read my writing and understand the intent behind Dongpo’s composition of this inscription, then I am their second younger brother—just as I was to Master Dayuan (referring to Dongpo’s Bell Inscription).

Read by Hanshan Deqing of the Ming Dynasty.
The Buddha’s Praise of Śākyamuni Buddha:
I prostrate to the Peerless Honored One. How could primordial light arise or cease? It depends on its application or non-application; therein the tracks of the ordinary and the sage first diverge.

It is not for the sake of mere heat and affliction; when employed, it is entirely divine power. With thirty-two wondrous marks, each one complete with auspiciousness, he shall achieve his merit during the Bhadrakalpa.
He is neither three nor five; planting his feet upon blue lotuses, the wind of his compassion fans all things.
This flower, touched by the wind, tilts; the hair-ornament pearl likewise seems to fall. Amidst this tilting and falling, there is a profound intent difficult to express in words.
When thought does not arise regarding that very place, the Dharmakāya is suddenly revealed. If one contemplates in this manner, the offerer is a true child of the Buddha.
The Buddha Śākyamuni praises his wondrous countenance, which fills every place, like the springtime pervading all things. Beings suffer daily in their routines yet remain unaware;

suddenly they realize that merit and wisdom are inherently complete. The Buddha’s body is no body, yet it overflows the eight directions; we ordinary people, however, cling to a limited conception of the self.
Six feet in height; the Buddha-mind is mindless and penetrates all, while our human minds give rise to thoughts that obstruct everything.

Having realized that body and mind are like the horns of a hare, his majestic radiance blazes like the moon among the stars. Those who see him or hear of him find refreshing clarity; how much more so when both hearing and seeing are found to be utterly quiescent!
I prostrate to the Muni, the Unsurpassed Honored One. I pray only that the waves of your compassion may eternally nourish all beings.
Praise of Amitābha Buddha:
The Great Way is neither one nor two. How could there be many kinds of Buddha-lands?
It is because their ultimate vows were originally different that the resulting retributions are thus. Ten thousand billion lands to the west, the Lord of Transformation is named Amitābha.
Amitābha, because you made forty-eight vows in the past, you are thus supreme and transcend all; those born in your land shall all never regress.
If I were to make vows equal to yours, O Ancestor, I would truly be Amitābha’s own flesh and bone. Amitābha’s body and lifespan are incalculable;
ten thousand bushels of mustard seeds cannot serve as a metaphor for them. Compassion and wisdom do not arise from outside the mind; they are produced through one's own self-exertion.
Valor is also the power of the mind; observing thus, one understands it without doubt. I am indeed the first teacher of Amitābha.
Once the disciple has already emerged from the sea of suffering, how could the teacher fall into birth and death?

Entering the mountains to praise the Buddha image, one finds joy in the south; one regards [worldly pleasures] as mere worn-out sandals. Were it not for ultimate clarity, how could one perceive that and know this? Amidst the dark rocks and white clouds—
In the Jade Palace upon the golden altar, who is female and who is male? The compassionate father’s arrow of mugwort;
the Buddha image from his ascetic practices in the Snow Mountains.
Praise for the eyes: the eye does not see the eye; the mind does not clarify the mind. If the eye were to see the eye, the eye would not be my eye; if the mind were to clarify the mind...
The mind is not my mind. Who says that six years of diligent ascetic practice were required? At the moment the morning star appeared, he attained enlightenment upon a single glance.

If the Way could be awakened to, it could likewise be cultivated and realized; yet cultivation and realization are not the Way itself—the three studies and six perfections are merely expedient means and arduous toil.

Through permeation and cultivation in accordance with reality, the evolving consciousnesses are transformed into wisdom; wisdom becomes the emptiness of consciousness, and emptiness is itself the myriad dharmas. The myriad dharmas are themselves emptiness.

Though their distinct characteristics do not obstruct one another—taking the head for the tail or using the feet as hands—this may seem like a perversion, yet it does not destroy their original nature.
Perversely calculating without understanding, one perceives hands and perceives feet, clinging to every phenomenon as if seeing the eye with the eye or seeing the mind with the mind.

To see in such a manner is like searching for a needle in the great ocean; for ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, one will exhaust one's sinews and weary one's bones, toiling the heart and exhausting the will.

What benefit has there ever been? This is merely a skillful means (*upāya*) of Gautama, claiming that Buddhahood can be attained. If Buddhahood were something that could be achieved through effort, it would not be a true Buddha.

*Eulogy on the Śākyamuni Buddha Snow Mountain Image (with Preface)* Among all things born, the greatest suffering is that of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Birth and death originate from emotional attachment (*tṛṣṇā*). As long as emotional attachment is not severed...
Throughout ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, one repays karmic debts. I do not value your asceticism on the Snowy Mountains or your enlightenment upon seeing the stars;
I only admire how you severed all worldly attachments with a single stroke of the blade. Were this not the mark of a great hero?
How could one possibly grasp this within the palm of the heart? Thus, I bow my head in praise.

Originally noble and dignified, he now assumes the appearance of a lowly person. Perched upon a precarious cliffside, his countenance is like that of one who has died; both humans and birds have vanished from sight.
Snow covers the thousand peaks; all is vast and silent. Where could thoughts and perceptions arise? Why is this so? To treat a live horse with the medicine for a dead one.
*Ei!* Were it not for the bone-chilling cold, how could one catch the fragrance of plum blossoms upon the nose?
Eulogy on the Image of Śākyamuni Buddha Emerging from the Mountains:
How can the dragon-robe compare to the deer-skin cloak? At peace. Snow covers a thousand peaks; he alone is worth gazing upon.
Had it not been for the morning star startling his dream-eye, Would he have deigned to come and stir the waves of the sea of suffering?
Upon seeing the morning star, his eyes immediately blossomed like flowers; wherever he encountered people, he scattered sand and dirt. What was accomplished by six years of asceticism?
It only provoked the verbal karma of those from all quarters.
Praise of Vairocana Buddha at Cihui Temple I prostrate to the unsurpassed Vairocana Buddha. His radiant light blazes forth, pervading all things; Each receives it according to their own capacity.
The enjoyment of both the holy and the ordinary is complete and perfect. Even a louse or a flea does not begin or end with smallness; Nor is an asura necessarily [limited].
Regarding the Great [Vehicle]: it is simply because when a fleeting emotion arises, it is like attempting to traverse the vast ocean by means of a cow’s footprint.

Therefore, the Hero of the World established skillful means, casting this rare body in bronze as a model. Like the mid-autumn moon appearing from a cloudless sky, surrounded by a host of stars to increase its sublime brilliance, those who see or hear of it find ever-greater coolness; their feverish afflictions are instantly brought into the inconceivable.
Praise for the Buddha Vairocana of Mount Lu:
I prostrate to the Unsurpassed One of True Golden Color, Whose marks and signs are perfectly complete, beyond existence and non-existence.

With a broad and long tongue like the waves of rivers and the winds upon lakes, All who see or hear are filled with inconceivable wonder. Mount Lu is a supreme site of practice in this land of China; Now once again, the Radiance halts here.
O Venerable One, it is like a precious vessel holding a mani-jewel; though it rolls, turns, tilts, and leans, it never ceases.
If a deluded person were to observe it from a fixed perspective, how would this differ from seeking flames within layered ice? The mind of the wise is ever serene and profound;
therefore, the white tuft of hair constantly shines forth universally.
In praise of Amitāyus Buddha:
That which has birth must have cessation; that which has a lifespan must have a limit. That the Buddha is titled "Immeasurable" (Amitāyus) must surely have its reason.
Although the path to the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the West is exceedingly distant, those who merely recite the Buddha’s name shall certainly be born in that land.
The World-Honored One Śākyamuni proclaimed with his golden mouth: "It is definitively without error or delusion. Birth arises from non-birth; that which is non-born is beyond calculation.
That which is beyond calculation is the root of all calculation; it is the progenitor of the myriad things. All people possess this progenitor, yet failing to awaken to it, they do not perceive it."
Just as one suddenly perceives one’s own mind, arising and ceasing cannot be found. Based on this, one should give rise to a vow, like that of Amitābha Buddha.
Buddha after Buddha, vows succeed one another; light upon light shines without end. When this Buddha appears before one, doubt is like snow doused by boiling water.

Eulogy on the Stone Buddha Floating upon the Sea in the Wu Region (Preface sent to Director Cao Yuanzhong) As for the origins of image-making, none can be traced back further than King Udayana’s golden image and his sandalwood image.
As for the spiritual wonders of these images, none can be considered more miraculous than King Aśoka’s bronze image and the stone image in the Wu region. Indeed...
If it is said that "the golden Buddha does not pass through the furnace" and "the wooden Buddha does not pass through fire," then it is clear that the stone Buddha does not pass through water.

Yet, the stone Buddha of Wu emerged from and disappeared into the great ocean, floating and sinking amidst the surging waves; with his spiral hair and corded robes, he sat in the full lotus posture upon the azure lapis lazuli.
Manifesting this great marvel, fish and dragons gazed up at him with sorrowful devotion as he crossed the sea to enter Wu—yet he alone...

In response to the request of Mr. Zhu and his son, we observe from this that since the stone Buddha was able to cross the water, the golden Buddha crossed the furnace, and the wooden Buddha likewise crossed the fire.
From this, I know that there is no object that is not mind, and no image that is not reality. The mind can roll up and unroll all things;
its essence and its manifestations are unfathomable. Only those who possess both illumination and function in their entirety—such as [the Yellow Emperor]—

The earth and the pine branches both emitted light in response to the occasion; how much more so for my two Tathāgatas, Vipaśyin and Kāśyapa, who throughout immeasurable kalpas have shared a great karmic affinity with the people of Wu.
They have manifested these signs specifically to cause immeasurable sentient beings to conceive the thought of a spiritual response.
To think is to reflect; to reflect is to awaken; to awaken is to attain penetration; and through such penetration, one takes what is near at hand within one’s own person.

To seek these things from afar is to realize they are all one’s own mind. Yet, as for those in the four directions who are black or white—those who do not come to Wu—they have no opportunity to gaze upon them with reverence;
I lament this greatly. I therefore entrusted the gentleman Ding Nan-yu to paint their portraits so they might be transmitted.

Just as the moon in the autumn sky does not discriminate between a vast ocean and a puddle in a cow’s hoofprint, the two Tathāgatas will henceforth manifest their presence everywhere. In praise, it is said:
The golden Buddha does not pass through the furnace; the wooden Buddha does not pass through fire; the stone Buddha can pass through water.

Because of the power of vows made throughout many lifetimes, may all who see or hear [this] have merit and wisdom like spring flowers—without the need for artificial arrangement, each flower is wondrously beautiful in its own right.

Through its reflection, one attains the Buddha-mind; the Buddha-mind has neither center nor periphery. Though its functional application is inexhaustible, the suffering of delusion is exceedingly great.
Buddhas Vipaśyin and Kāśyapa fulfilled their vows to manifest wondrous miracles; they performed Buddhist rites upon both water and land, yet because of this, others were not permitted to know.
For all who offer worship, there is the assembly of the Transformation Buddha of the hells. In this assembly of the Buddha, the five aggregates are empty;

yet neither sin nor merit remains obscure. The prison cell is named the Hall of Blessings. Examine the name and its reality for yourself in detail. Through suffering, awakening and illumination arise; once awakened, self and others are forgotten.

Yao’s spring had no center or periphery; Shun’s virtue knew neither brevity nor length. Morning and evening he paid homage to the two images; piercing through the clouds, he beheld the blue sky. Fish and dragons looked up at his radiance;
tigers and rhinoceroses melted away their rage and arrogance. From the waters of Wu to the mountains of Yan, for fifteen months all was full.
In praise of the emanation of Maitreya:
with eyes like rivers and a mouth like the sea, his mind is as vast as the great void. When the long wind travels therein, the ground remains abundant; my own mind is thus.
What can turn it? Within this cloth bag, the holy and the ordinary are difficult to distinguish. Maitreya Buddha praised that the people of the world grieve much;
the Venerable One laughs much. Grief and laughter have their regularity; in their function, there is neither coarse nor subtle. With a relaxed mind, he lets his belly hang down.
The布袋 (Buddhabhadra) manifests both life and death; he gathers them in and releases them. Holy ones and common folk alike lose their footing.
A eulogy for Maitreya Buddha of the Shanyuntang:

His celestial countenance and sage-like features are wondrous beyond thought. Waiting until the Dragon Flower Assembly to see him will be too late. Utterly transcending the senses and their objects, he stands alone and pure.
Dewdrops: Sudden emptiness makes self and other mutually known. A smile upon the face is still not the ultimate marvel; the spring flowing from shoulders and back is truly wondrous.
With every prostration and every gaze, merit and wisdom increase; by constant intimacy with this, how could one fail to attain Bodhi?

Praise for the Self-Arisen Buddha of Huguo Temple (With Preface) Now, when an earthen ox plows the moon and a wooden horse neighs in the wind, the common folk hear of these things and are struck with awe. This image is neither of gold nor of stone;
it is composed of various materials. It was released upon the boats of Jingchu and secretly exchanged for the bones of the barbarians. It has reached [this land].

Those who possess wisdom are easily moved, while ordinary people are often deluded and difficult to inspire. Yet, this [teaching] dissolves my strife through true compassion and clears away the feverish afflictions of heat and vexation.
Although it does not occupy the rank of kings or lords, its virtue penetrates even before the Primordial Sovereign (*xiàngdì*).
In Sanskrit it is called *Buddha*, which means "the Awakened. When one is awakened, there is nothing that is not mind; when one is unawakened, what is there?
The mind is not a thing; what thing is not the mind? A single blade of grass can become a sixteen-foot golden body; what mind is not a thing?
A sixteen-foot golden body can become a single blade of grass. Alas! If one does not possess the person [of realization], the Way will not manifest in vain.
In praise, it is said:
When the river is clear, the moon is first seen; when conditions ripen, the Buddha comes of his own accord. If my mind-water were pure, the Buddha-eye would open suddenly.

If the defilements of one's own mind have not been emptied, one will resent the Buddha for lacking spiritual efficacy. It is like a sick person drinking sugarcane juice, yet perversely suspecting it to be the same as yellow bitter melon.
If one day illness is suddenly cured, how can vegetable broth taste sweet? If you pray to the Buddha and he does not respond, is it because the Buddha has favorites?
Simply examine your own mind; the fruit will reveal whether your sincerity is genuine or not. If your heart is sincere and penetrating, there is no Buddha who would not respond with compassion.

Maitreya Buddha praises all afflictions as the very source of joy. If there were no afflictions, there would be no joy; thus one knows that joy exists without affliction, yet ultimately, joy must have nothing upon which to rely.
I now bow my head to the Honored One Maitreya, whose smiling mouth is ever open. Equal [to all].

At the Gate of the Sea, seeing and hearing with sympathetic joy, one dissolves the notions of self and other; every pore of the body gives rise to spring. This spring does not arise from a mindless state;
through the maturation of wisdom and vows, one delivers sentient beings. If I were devoid of emotion, my mouth would laugh itself to pieces;
dare I ask whether the arising of the heart brings joy? Please observe the wooden man—birds do not fear it; though the wind blows and its hands move, it does not run away. —The Venerable One.
Who would not rejoice in such laughter? Such joy is generally of this kind. If one knows that there is nothing beyond this joy, then both joy and fear will naturally fall away.
When the sack is opened, the treasures are not many; meeting them, take whatever you can to stave off hunger and cold.
A Praise for the Withered Tree Maitreya Buddha:
Cast from raw iron, forged from gold, carved from jade and stone—these five forms of Maitreya, how do they compare to this withered tree?

There is no need for elaborate carving; the marks of virtue are perfectly complete, and his smiling countenance is immediately accessible. Wood does not smile; if it were to smile, it would no longer be wood.
To seek a smile from wood is like seeking the hair of a tortoise; to seek wood through its smile is like seeking the horns of a hare. These exist in name only, but lack reality.
Without substance and without principle; the path of logic is blocked. At a precipice a thousand fathoms high, if one can somehow grasp it, could it be anything other than Maitreya?
Maitreya Buddha holds a cloth bag in his hand. Praise:
When the mouth is closed, the tongue is hidden; when the mouth is open, the root of the tongue is revealed. At the moment of neither opening nor closing, where does the question lie?
If you know how to grasp it, I shall entrust this cloth bag to you; if you do not yet know how to grasp it, I will never give it to you, no matter how much you squeeze my hand.

The stone Buddha praises the boundless clouds and waves as a raft; together they ride upon the light to illuminate the Zhu family of Wu. Having repeatedly endured the fires of war, there was originally nothing [to be lost].

Beholding and hearing this, the flower of the mind blossoms. Where the flower of the mind blooms, its fragrance pervades the ten voids. Light has no center or periphery; it is suchness from the very beginning.
If a person has the karmic affinity to prostrate once, the three obstacles are instantly eliminated in a single instant.

When the obstacles are dissolved, the stone Buddha speaks the Dharma; with two mouths and one tongue, they cover all lands and worlds. Even when sentient beings defecate and urinate, [the Dharma] flows upon their tongues.
Who is it that awakens? Who is it that awakens? Who is it that awakens? The eye does not see the eye; seeing arises and ceases.
Saints and ordinary beings are treated alike under this command. The butcher of broad forehead is truly fierce; the boundless sea of suffering becomes a sea of wisdom.
With a single finger’s flexion and extension, the matter is easily resolved. Deeply holding this, go to Mount Emei; fish and dragons everywhere shall experience joy. Narrow...
Meeting Liu Sahe on the road, the roots of all transgressions are finally uprooted.
Maitreya Buddha praises that there is something within the breast; the belly is large yet narrow, this mind is equal to empty space; the chest is narrow yet vast.

Moving among herds of oxen and horses, entering and exiting the ranks of sages and commoners—how different is this from the wind passing through pines? How can it be any other than the moon piercing the water?
Having traveled for long, I suddenly sit; looking up, I gaze at the Milky Way. Since I feel no shame before the high-flying birds, how could I harbor envy for the swimming fish?
Praise of Vairocana Buddha and the Two Bodhisattvas Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, along with the Eighteen Arhats: Vairocana Buddha is the light of Vairocana;
its daily illumination is manifest. Because I had not yet realized it, the Dharmakāya seemed like a hidden treasury. Now that I have understood and attained maturity, [it is revealed].
When the merit of the myriad practices is forgotten, who is it that occupies the position?

To call a servant "lord" is the state of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva when sentient beings have not yet attained realization; everywhere they encounter, they act only out of emotion. Once realization is reached, emotion withers away—how could there be much love or hatred? This is the golden-haired lion.
Leaping and bounding without ceasing, he takes this as his seat. Not walking yet walking, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva manifests in ten thousand variations and a thousand differences.
His practice is neither right nor wrong; he enters into the perceptions of sentient beings, spreads the flowers of great compassion, and his elephant-like stride occupies the ten voids.
Trampling the three carts and slaughtering the butcher with his broad forehead—this son is the benefactor’s family.
First, Venerable Piṇḍola-Bhāradvāja held a branch of rattan in his left hand;
the rattan seemed to bend and stretch, yet his fingers appeared as if they had no sensation. He prostrated himself before the Venerable One.
The lamp of wisdom in the deep night personally received the Buddha’s prediction to illuminate that which is loved and hated.
Second, Venerable Kanakavatsa offered a staff with both hands;
though his outer hands were empty, he bent and extended his fingers, already acting for the sake of the one [who was to be saved]. If that one had not realized it, [it would have been in vain].
"I can do nothing about it. For now, I shall withdraw one foot; I will release them again for his sake.
Third, the Venerable Kanakavatsa brushed away the stumps with his right hand while his left hand remained empty.
He closed the兑 (duì) trigram and opened the 離 (lí) trigram; his mind neither went out nor returned. He treated all people with loving-kindness.
People suddenly treat my true self with indifference; they miss it right before their faces. Once gone, it is difficult to encounter again.

The Fourth Patriarch, Sūpinda, rests his left hand upon his knee—what is he contemplating? He clenches his right hand into a fist—nothing is seen being held. Though resting and clenching are two distinct actions, [the essence remains one].
A person has no dual cognition. When the mouth opens, it is not necessarily a smile; when the eyes widen, the eyebrows hang down.
Fifth, Venerable Nārada, I ask you, O elder:
by what cause and condition does this itching arise? Does it arise from within, or does it originate from without? If it originates from without, then it is the same as external objects.
"Itching was not present before; observe and examine this closely. The youth was transcendent.
Although the Venerable Sixth Bhadra held the beads in his hand, his mind was not there; his eyes looked elsewhere, clearly and without doubt. Dadian raised this as an illustration.
Han Yu was utterly ignorant of this. The Head Seat knotted his teeth [in protest], yet the rest followed suit in unison and pursued him.
The seventh, Venerable Kālika, had a round face and long eyebrows;
his spiritual wonders were immeasurable. His eyebrows formed the ropes of aspiration, and with those ropes he drew the Dharma-ship to ferry all who possessed the karmic affinity.
Emerging from this cauldron of boiling water, his face is like the moon and the sun, subject to the impermanence of waxing and waning.
The eighth, Vajraputra, has his shoulders bared and his arms crossed;
his *kāṣāya* robe girds his waist as he sits barefoot reading a scripture. His demeanor is carefree and elegant, his gaze commanding the respect of devas and humans alike.
Both humans and devas were filled with doubt: "Who is this venerable one who tramples upon such majestic deportment?

The ninth precept-holder, Venerable Bhoga, amidst the vast azure of the mountain clouds, uses a stone as his seat; seated in the lotus posture, he raises his right hand, pointing upward. In these woods and springs, there is no summer heat."
Holding a fan, he ponders the coolness; suspecting him to be a one-eyed dragon, his sharp wit is hidden in darkness.
The tenth, the Venerable Upārdhaka, narrows his eyes and stares upward.
With focused mind, he reads the sutras; his Sanskrit voice is resonant and clear. He does not permit listening with the ears; the characters are spread across white cotton cloth.
Wild geese fly across the autumn sky, drifting crosswise and intermittently; their shadows are disordered by the wind of wisdom.
The eleventh, Venerable Rāhula, gnashes his teeth in resentment—toward whom?
He resents the delusion of worldly people who recklessly cling to body and mind, not knowing how to relinquish them. His sword-like brows arch across the void.
The eyes reveal the mechanism of slaughter; by means of killing, one brings life to completion. The compassion of the Sage is profound.
The Venerable Nāgasena, whose body dwells beyond the clouds, gazes upon the human world from above.
Seeing the beautiful and the ugly therein, he lets out a cold laugh that dissolves all idleness—a laugh so intense it seems his jaw might fall off.
Holding up his fist and supporting himself, his caution was excessive; this is the folly of a sage.

(13) Because Venerable Kātyāyana received the sutra and left behind his staff, and later received the staff and left behind the sutra, he abandoned one thing and took up another, his mind never remaining still; furthermore, he gave away both the pearl and his body.
The fourth was Equanimity (Samatā). In this state, there is no external world. The Brahma-sound was clear and resonant.
On the fourteenth day, the Venerable Vanavāsī’s inhalations and exhalations became empty.

The mountain was neither different nor the same [as before]. Seeing the mountain, he prostrated at its feet; the mountain frequently displayed a smiling expression, as if saying, "I am in meditative concentration."
Within the boundless center of meditative concentration, he dwells in the sphere of infinite space. Concentration and wisdom are fused as one.
The fifteenth, Venerable Aśvaghosa, has a head like a swelling mass;
he clasps his knees and laughs heartily. His nose is curved and his eyes are askew; his eyebrows hang down and his mind is empty. This emptiness of mind is the absence of self.
How could there be love or hatred? In all my laughter and speech, I am the lamp of wisdom for sentient beings.
(Note 16: The Venerable Cha-ban-tog-ka—tree aged and vines withered;
his mind was like the great void; he forgot "I" and "mine"—the tree was then myself. With a movement of his left finger, it extended and contracted.)
For whom was dhyāna taught? The mark of the broad and long tongue—sound issues from the right side.
The seventeenth, the Venerable Kyung-woo, is this body, Song-un.
This body is Song-un; though ears and eyes remain, fundamentally there is neither seeing nor hearing. With hands joined, he offers the cup.
He appeared as if in a state of forgetfulness. Holding a willow branch dipped in water, he did not sprinkle it upon his companions.
Eighteenth, Venerable Piṇḍola: his robes did not cover his shoulders;
his feet were weary and tucked into sandals; his two eyes gazed upward as the light of the sun and moon was obscured by mist; and a staff rested in his right hand.
Merit is beyond left or right; the mind is not dual. How could its function be disparate?
Li Cigong painted this image of the Buddha who Welcomes and Leads to represent the late Layman Jiansu (also known as Shanyun).
Where is the Buddha’s body? It is perfectly complete everywhere. Yet in daily life one does not see it, buried by the dust of worldly conditions. Suddenly, he extends his hand.
Whom do you wish to receive? Layman Shanyun, this mind understands: during life one possesses virtue; after death one paints Buddhas.
With every stroke, there are lotus flowers; fragrant breezes waft gently. The Sahā world and Sukhāvatī—defilement and purity are impermanent; they manifest according to one's karma.
Truly difficult to fathom are the forty-eight vows of Amitābha; each vow accords with the capacities of beings. Take this single note to heart. O clouds of goodness, clouds of goodness!
How could you lack the merit of seeing and hearing [this teaching]? Cast aside your yellow caps and instantly transcend the ranks of the immortals, returning to the Land of Immeasurable Life.

Bowing deeply through life and death, the great lotus of the chariot—what hindrance could there be to walking the path? To be born is to be the mother of death; to loathe death and love birth is not as good as having no birth.
Where there is no birth, there is constant birth. With Avalokiteśvara as one’s friend and Mahāsthāmaprāpta as one’s companion, one wanders through the seven realms of existence.
One should know the gravity and lightness [of offenses], yet here [the text] is blurred;
this would be to do a grave injustice to Mr. Li.

*Eulogy on the Painting of the Taming Lion (with Preface)* A single roar of the lion causes the heads of a hundred beasts to split asunder; this is the height of ferocity. A single leap of the lion [causes the hundred beasts...]
All were delighted; this was the height of harmony. Only the tiger was not harmonious, for it killed innocent creatures.

The Perfect Man, knowing this to be so, therefore regulated and harmonized him, making him the leader of the hundred beasts. Thus, moderation between leniency and severity was achieved; he was formidable yet capable of harmony.
Like the sun in winter, it is warm and yet spring-like; thus the *I Ching* says: "The medicine for the absence of delusion (*amoha*) must not be tested.
The claws and fangs within the Dharma-cave are like a thunderclap in a clear sky; with every cry and every leap, there is both joy and sorrow. I am originally without mind.

The depth and shallowness of celestial mechanisms share the same root in life and death; clarity and obscurity, floating and sinking, form interlocking patterns like woven silk that are difficult to distinguish.
Even those with copper-colored pupils and iron eyes have already been cast aside by them.
Eulogy for the "Diagram of Sweeping Away the Elephant" (with Preface):
Now, regarding the fundamental and the differentiated: these two wisdoms are one mind. Yet, because there are differences in the depth of realization and attainment, there is a sequence of priority.

In terms of seeing one's nature, nothing is greater than the fundamental; in terms of treating the emotions, nothing is more essential than the differentiated. Thus, the ancients had this [simile]: [The text continues with the eulogy.]
The principle of life differs from the penal statutes for those who die with their branches; the transformative applications of light and darkness intermingle.
Nevertheless, when the Sage establishes symbols, his primary aim is to exhaust the meaning. If one grasps the meaning and forgets the symbol, then the symbol becomes a mere fishing trap.
If one attains the mind and forgets the emotion, then one attains that which is non-attainment.
The ten evils and the five heinous crimes, when traced to their source, possess an inherent nature; as for the myriad demons and strange apparitions, who can revert them to the state of rectitude?

One must fully comprehend that Mount Kunlun is not solid and that form and emptiness have no ground; yet when the white elephant appears before one, residual habitual defilements remain, which must be swept away.

Beneath the long pines, a basin of water reflects the void; host and attendant mirror one another, while sages and ordinary beings appear in their distinct gradations. The vast array of all phenomena is like the ocean-seal samādhi—within it, the male and female principles reside.
In praise of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva:
A thousand crags and ten thousand gorges are all layered with ice; All sentient beings are frozen to death. Last night, the plum blossoms bloomed upon the ridges.
Head! Swarming bees and butterflies embrace the spring colors; as snow melts in Ba and Shu, the flowing waters rush on. Infinite fish and dragons give rise to joy.
Great wisdom manifests before one, and the spring light returns; touched by it, body and mind are like ice melting away.

This light has once been the teacher of the seven Buddhas and is again the eldest son of Kāśyapa. Though there is no name by which to call him, he is Mañjuśrī; he is the most excellent among Sudhana’s [visits].
First, one sees it at the outset: once seen, it is amidst the misty waters of a hundred cities; the realms of favorable and adverse conditions are neither inverted nor topsy-turvy.
Returning home with empty hands and nothing at all, the Old Man of Qingliang strokes my head once more.
Praise to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva:
I prostrate to the Great Honored One, Samantabhadra, who in every Buddha-land acts as the King of Vows. He universally leads all living beings to return to the ocean of wisdom.
Its waves and tides are vast and boundless, unfathomable. His towering white elephant fills the void; it is like [the water] contained within a bowl.
The bowl is full of rice; once the rice is full, how could it admit even the slightest thing? When an elephant fills the void of space, where could one sit?
The Bodhisattva reaches this state and halts all discursive thought. Like a bell struck, its sound answers me: within the gateway of the ten thousand practices, there is great skillful means.

I pray that the King remains unmoving and eternally sovereign. Snow covers the cold crags as the Dharma-realm deepens; the *laṅ-laṅ* sound of the palm-leaf manuscripts rolls from the tongue in clear resonance.
I do not permit Gautama to hear this; the Ox-Head and Horse-Face [deities] know only their own biases.
I pay homage to the Great Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva of the Northern Terrace.
I prostrate to Mañjuśrī, the Honored One among wisdoms, who attains the fundamental source without departing from the myriad dharmas—just as a goldsmith does not abandon [the ore].

The vessel is discarded, and the golden essence alone is revealed. Sudhana beholds it once, but it is difficult to encounter again. He reaches out his golden arm and strokes the crown of [Manjushri’s] head;
this crown makes no distinction between the holy and the mundane. Pure and manifest, it cannot be seen.
Yet within that which cannot be seen, one beholds wondrous marks, like a sublime lotus flower emerging from the water. His wondrous countenance dwells amidst vast clouds of fragrance; all behold him.
All were filled with joy. Relying upon this king of beasts, the precious vase was carried with delight, as serene as if resting on a small table.

Yet one cannot help but pity humanity, the most intelligent among all things; who among those thus intermingled would not give rise to sorrowful attachment? Those with hearts who come here to pay homage to the Bodhisattva, having heard the roar of the Master, yield their excellence.
The roots of emotion accumulated over kalpas are instantly extinguished; amidst the mingling of dragons and snakes, there is constant sovereignty.
Who is the mother of the wisdom of wondrous observation? It is the Elder Ancestor of the Hundred Cities of Smoke and Water.
With sincere devotion, I rely upon the power of the Bodhisattva to utter these humble words in praise of his merit. How could the praise of the Bodhisattva’s merit ever be exhausted?

It would be no different from thunder crashing in a cloudless sky. To the majestic and wondrous Mañjuśrī, I pray that the light of your wisdom may forever shine upon me, as the drifting clouds vanish away.
The void is boundless; atop the peak of the Dipper, the moon is solitary and cold. All is contained within this pure radiance and wondrous stillness.
A flicker of thought arises, and one is separated by a thousand miles.
—The Bodhisattva Holding the Pearl praises [this].

Though the beads have been strung together, they do not move unless stirred; yet one who has grasped the subtlest nuances can turn the celestial sphere as swiftly as a flash of lightning. How many springs and autumns have passed?
The instruction given was not much. Hearing sounds within the ear, one falls back into confusion and error.

In praise of the crab and centipede by the Bodhisattva Mahākāruṇika: With many legs but few eyes, they scuttle sideways and dash straight ahead; how can their inner thoughts ever be understood? All other beings have but two hands.
The eyes, too, are but two. Abundant arts and manifold talents all arise from deluded thoughts. Although things and the self differ, their functional dependence is the same;

as long as distinctions between identity and difference are not forgotten, one shares yet does not truly share. I observe that Great Compassion arises through hearing and leads to awakening; sound itself has neither opposition nor compliance.

Upon hearing it once, one is liberated from the shell; this "shell" refers to sensory dust (*rajas*). When the dust dissolves, the sense organs are uprooted. There is no sequence of first and last, nor any distinction of beginning and end.

It functions spontaneously and pervasively, like many arms and many heads, each head and arm possessing eyes—like the clarity of autumn. This applies to all, regardless of whether they are wise or foolish.

All who heard of it or saw it were struck with amazement. I was enfeoffed as a Marquis and held my office constantly; yet I harbored doubts regarding his sage brilliance. [The deity] has forty-eight arms and eleven heads.

Each arm holds something, and each head lacks a left or right [distinction]. Holding symbolizes wisdom (*jñāna*), and grasping symbolizes compassion (*karuṇā*); thus, compassion and wisdom are brought into dynamic operation.

Illuminating all without exception, this light requires no external conditions; it cools the heat of affliction. With a single finger’s bend or extension, there is no distinction between center and periphery.
When one thinks of those sentient beings—be they maggots, crabs, or any other conscious being—the three poisons are difficult to dissolve. Thus, one invokes the name of Great Compassion.
Beholding the marks of great compassion, in the space of a single cough, one awakens to and enters the Unsurpassed. The Holy One of Immeasurable Life is the Sovereign of Great Compassion;

through the power of the vows of this sovereign and his ministers, they together rescue the deluded multitudes. Like an arm directing a finger, there is no distinction between self and other. This is the absolute center, free from all deviation.
The wondrous being is free from entanglement; this compassion free from entanglement is what all beings think of. If one seeks sons or daughters, the Great Master [bestows] sons and daughters.
Through love, faith arises; through faith, the mind attains penetration; through the penetration of the mind, love is uprooted—this is the divine power of the Bodhisattva.
Praise of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva:
I bow my head to the Greatly Compassionate One, Avalokiteśvara, who possesses great skillful means to extract beings from all sufferings.

If a person has many lustful thoughts, by constantly recollecting and revering him, they shall be freed from desire. When these words were first heard, their subtlety was not perceived; yet after savoring them for a long time, their wondrousness becomes clear.
It is boundless. From this point on, the mind-consciousness of sentient beings is coarse; they do not know the benefit of the Bodhisattva’s salvation from suffering.

The karma of lust has been practiced for no single day; it originally stems from beginningless time until the present. To wish to suddenly abandon it by reciting the name once—when sentient beings first hear this, who would believe it?
They do not believe because their faculties are not yet mature. When the faculties are mature, doubt will naturally not arise. This is the treatment of lust.

Since the gate of contemplation is thus, the gate of contemplation for treating anger is likewise. If a person has much anger in their mind, they should investigate from where this angry mind first begins.
If one wishes to extinguish anger without knowing its beginning, it is like cutting off a stream without blocking its source.
If the source does not flow, how can the blockage be cleared? If one has not grasped the beginning, how can anger be stilled?

I vow that those who universally recollect Avalokiteśvara shall, amidst all adversities and favors, hatred and love, rouse their indignation and exert themselves with vigor to strike away [these afflictions]. Once they have achieved victory in battle, there will be no doubt as to the result.
To harbor such a thought is called right mindfulness; to fail to harbor such a thought is merely wrong mindfulness. How could there be anyone who...

The spirits of all things respond. If one does not practice right mindfulness but practices wrong mindfulness (recite the Universal Gate Chapter), one must not consume poison and must not associate with the wicked.
Consuming poison will surely lead to an untimely death; associating with the wicked will surely cause one's goodness to decline.
Therefore, Buddhas and Bodhisattvas employ various skillful means; they use poison to counteract poison, yet the poison does not kill the person.
They use evil to counteract evil, yet the evil does not harm sentient beings. If one acts in such a manner, both good and evil lack a fixed nature.
If poison were not a wondrous medicine, the sages would surely discard it. Thus we know that Avalokiteśvara is skillfully adept at this samādhi;
he is able, through the path of the Universal Gateway, to rescue all sentient beings. That those who receive benefit must repay their debt of gratitude is the common understanding of sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva uses his staff to strike at the moon in the sky; if the moon in the sky were to feel pain, then the Bodhisattva would receive offerings (*pāṭha:

*bǎocǎo*). If sentient beings do not call upon his name when suffering, whom else could the Bodhisattva save? His compassionate majesty saves them from suffering, and they are moved by that suffering.

Birth. Suffering is the great compassionate father of sentient beings. If one claims that because the Bodhisattva’s power of vow is profound, all sufferings of the world are thereby transcended—such an observation is not a skillful observation.

Skillful observation takes the suffering of both the noble and the ordinary as fundamental. When a person suddenly realizes that the nature of suffering is empty, it is only then that the Bodhisattva truly appears.
At the time of this appearance, even the metaphors of lightning and fire are not equal. [Thus ends] the "Discrimination of Sounds."
The sounds are all visible:
from the first needle to the last, the thread is never severed; it is through pulling that completion is achieved. But how can there be completion?
Since completion is not established by effort, where does the pulling begin? If one can contemplate in this way, the embroiderer cannot be found.
May all people contemplate this well. The Bodhisattva has now manifested before you (in this embroidered image).

At the ancient bank of a cold stream, where slender willows and sparse bamboos stand, her skirt and sash flutter slightly as the mountain flowers drift with their fragrance. A single basket and a pair of carp;

the person is hidden within the boat. Whether one is discerning or ignorant, upon beholding her radiant countenance even once, the mountain of blades, the mass of fire, the poisonous drugs, and the boiling water [vanish].

All manner of myriad sufferings are suddenly and entirely forgotten; the feverish afflictions of sentient beings are inherently cool and serene. One immediately realizes that this was a deluded dream, like mistaking a servant for a lord.
It is a great labor for those supreme beings who, through their vast compassion and manifold means, used fish as drums whose sound shook the eight wildernesses.
Even for an icchantika, hearing the stench [of fish] would cause them to perish (like the fish-basket).

Amidst the three calamities, the nine untimely deaths, the eight difficulties, and the two pursuits, sin and merit are impermanent; perfect penetration is sovereign. If sin had a master, [it would not be so].
Merit cannot be cultivated; if merit were eternal, then sin could not be washed away. Both are devoid of power.

When compassion and wisdom are perfectly realized, it is as if seeing a single flower: spring has no boundaries. Clouds, peaks, and seacoasts; a dilapidated house and blue lotuses; misty waves stretching far and wide.
The Bodhisattva wishes to speak: (Sea Lake).
The spring mountains are turning green; peach blossoms are in full bloom. The Celestial Youth Mahāsattva hangs his seat upon the rocky terrace. A flower-branch parrot—
Peering from the side at the youth, he chants and responds in the original mode. Who can grasp this meaning? There are ears beneath the feet; within the ears are eyes.
Observing all sounds, the principle is abundant while the words are concise (Tian Nan).

Amidst the boundless waves of the ocean, clouds and mountains suddenly cluster together; fish, dragons, shrimp, crabs, monkeys, apes, and deer all listen to the sound of the tide from morning until night, sharing together in the merit of compassion.
Man is the most intelligent of all beings; beholding this, one ought to weep bitterly.

Even those of different species take refuge; you, however, remain merely in vain turmoil. This floating life is like a bubble on the water; in a single moment, our arms have crossed and our hair has already turned white.

A child does not fear the perilous; he plunges into the surging waves, repeatedly rising and falling. In an instant, the sense-faculties and their objects become empty, and the wondrous marks [of the Buddha] are as tangible as springtime flowers one might grasp.
Gazing upon the merging mist and fog, only the purple bamboos stand in somber majesty. Master Wu harbors transcendent thoughts; throughout the great earth, the plum blossoms are fragrant.
(Portrait of the Master of Plum Blossoms)
Sentient beings have suffering, which the Bodhisattva rescues. When the Bodhisattva was first in suffering, who pulled him out?

If there were yet another to pull him out, how could the pulling of that pulling ever come to an end? Suddenly, when wisdom is perfected and emotions wither away, the Bodhisattva speaks of the ocean moon, clouds, and mountains.
Whether it be fierce beasts, forests of swords, or pits of fire, or thunder, hail, and lightning—the drum of compassion—how could these sounds be distinguished [in its resonance]?
Whether saint or commoner, once it passes through the faculty of hearing, none shall not die. Therefore, Avalokiteśvara delivers sentient beings;
when the empty flowers fall as reflections, the spring light begins (Haimyue).
The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body—these five are fundamentally wondrous. Yet, in a fleeting instant, they give rise to clear perceptions; the five sense organs become like jars of glue.
All sounds, whether good or bad, are heard by Avalokiteśvara with his eyes. Sometimes it is not so; when he hears with his ears, he is no different from the common crowd.
Through hearing, one reaches the state beyond hearing; together they enter the ocean of the universal gate. Eye and ear share a single object; only the faculties differ in their nature.

What is realized is without distinction, yet upon returning to the source, the waves diverge into separate tracks. Where there is a subject, there is an object; when the object is forgotten, the subject also ceases.

When the subject is exhausted along with its objects, the merit does not belong to the subject; when the subject is exhausted and follows the transformation of objects, the merit likewise does not belong to the objects.
Ultimately, both are devoid of merit; the subtlety of compassion and wisdom is unfathomable. The two wheels crush the great night, like the rising of the bright sun.
His hands are already countless; how could his compassionate majesty have a limit? His eyes do not reside solely upon his face; they also emit light from within his palms.

If one infers by analogy from his hair and eyebrows, his hands and eyes exceed even this. When the world beholds such great compassion, it is struck with alarm; being alarmed, it becomes startled and bewildered.
Who would have known that the very one who is deluded is non-dual with the Bodhisattva (of Great Compassion)?
I have heard that the mind of a Bodhisattva is precisely the nature of sentient beings; sentient beings and Bodhisattvas are like two ladles sharing a single handle.
If one says that the Bodhisattva delivers sentient beings, this is entirely the delusory illness of people themselves.

If one says that sentient beings remember the Bodhisattva, it is like cutting off one's own head while seeking to save one's life. Tell me, how can medicine and illness both be eliminated so that the life-blood remains unbroken?
Guanyin manifested in the body of a bhikṣu and, at Mount Potalaka, exercised his true authority (the bhikṣu).

Through true contemplation, the attachments of both the holy and the ordinary are suddenly severed; great wisdom manifests before them, and the Bodhisattva is revealed. Through compassionate and loving contemplations, their benefit and grace are profound;
the three types of grass and two types of trees all receive its nourishment. Such merit is inconceivable; may all sentient beings gaze upon it with longing.
The manifold sufferings of sentient beings are fundamentally inexhaustible, yet how could the power of the Bodhisattva’s vows ever come to an end? This power of infinite vows—
The deliverance is inexhaustible. It is like a revolving wheel that seeks its beginning and end.

When sentient beings are rightly beset by the urgency of suffering, if they call upon the Bodhisattva with single-minded sincerity, the Bodhisattva hears the call and looks down with his eyes; the sufferer is immediately freed from all afflictions.
If a person knows pain and knows the absence of pain—that very absence of pain is the power of Avalokiteśvara. When one faculty enters the stream, all sensory objects are extinguished. Eight.
It is difficult to fulfill, yet one realizes perfect penetration and awakening (the Jewel Wheel).

The winds of heaven and the waves of the sea do not come into contact with the ear; yet one is able to use the eye to observe, whereby all sufferings melt away like ice. Thus, the thirty-two manifestations appear.

The fourteen fearlessnesses, together with the two conformities, are such that when the mind does not arise, no virtue is lacking. Should one slightly involve oneself in the dust of sensory objects, there will be traces upon the mirror.
When subject and object stand in opposition, one arbitrarily perceives estrangement and intimacy; using the mind to grasp the mind, the level ground sinks into the abyss.
Water does not drown people; it is people who drown themselves in the ford. This is simply water; the water does not extinguish anger. Among the eight difficulties, wind and fire are perilous;
they cut through things without form and display their power by borrowing material objects. If the external fuel is exhausted and empty, the force of both will come to an end.

As it is with wind and fire, so too is the nature of water. Those whose celestial faculties are profound know this and understand all things; yet if one cannot achieve spiritual resonance, how can they avoid error?
My words are exceedingly plain, yet seeking the wondrous in them is difficult to comprehend. If you reach the root and forget the branches, you will naturally understand from the very outset.

Suffering is the guide; do not loathe it. To abandon suffering and seek pleasure is like having a teacher but lacking the necessary provisions: one may inherit the light of wisdom yet fail in its realization. Both [the former and latter views] are ignorant of this principle.
When the white robe is held up, is the moon truly within the finger? (As in the story of Guan Tao pointing at the moon with his finger while wearing a white robe.)

Holding up the basket to show people, she enters the dust and wind. This one fish is presented amidst both light and dark; as soon as the Fisherman’s Son glimpses it, his teeth water with anticipation.
After the skeletal frame is lifted out, it is fresh once it emerges from the water. (The Fish Basket)
I prostrate to the Great Compassionate Avalokiteśvara. How may that which is sought lead to the attainment of the Way?
I pray only that the Bodhisattva will reveal this to me, so that by a mere snap of the fingers I may attain perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*).

If I should thus attain perfect penetration, I vow to deliver all beings—every living creature endowed with breath and consciousness—and lead them one by one into the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*). May the Bodhisattva, using his body as a vast tongue, reveal this to those present.
Regarding that which you seek: if you truly wish to attain my mind, my mind resides solely within your daily activities. When it is in the eye, it is in conjunction with the dust of form;
this continues up to the mind, where it is in harmony with dharmas. If you can thoroughly understand form and the other sensory objects, from where do these objects themselves arise?
If you know the place from which each object arises, the six sense organs will have no ground upon which to establish themselves. The organs—
The dust falls away, leaving a single, brilliant clarity; the solitary light shines afar, impossible to conceal.

A teacher who liberates all beings from suffering, he hears sounds with his eyes and preaches the Dharma upon the mountain. Where does Sudhana seek Avalokiteśvara? You should ask the person who first sought Avalokiteśvara.
This person seeks the Bodhisattva outside of themselves; it is like trying to split a single sturdy tree trunk into two pieces. Tánláng, this is the manifestation of the transformation body.
Lánggòng and Tánduān both emerged from my mouth. Had I not attained the Bodhisattva mind, how could I have conveyed this message for them?

Had the Bodhisattva not received my instruction, he would have sunk into the river of craving and never reached liberation. Now I sit upright within the stone niche; the melody of the pines and the sound of the spring are as still as white ash.

A flower blooms upon the withered wood, its fragrance extraordinary; the faculty of the nose— *Note: This passage appears to be a fragment of a poetic or gāthā-style composition, likely from a Chan Buddhist text, expressing the transmission of the Dharma between masters and disciples.*
The ear-consciousness is difficult to perceive (Stone Grotto).
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva can save from suffering; before one has become a bodhisattva, who saves from suffering?

Examining this through its coming and going, the merit of saving from suffering—throughout the beginning and end, no one is seen to possess such merit. If a person wishes to recognize Avalokiteśvara, they must understand this eulogy.
For a Bodhisattva, sentient beings naturally do not require rescue; it is as if taking up a snowball and pouring hot water upon it—it simply does not register.
Rather than engaging with it through the ears, one engages through the eyes; all sounds, whether present or absent, leave the six sense-faculties flourishing and vigorous.
A single stone, towering and majestic—whose nostrils are these? The sockets of the Great Being (the six sense organs purified).
I prostrate to the Great Compassionate Avalokiteśvara, who conceals his supreme form to manifest this youthful appearance. Surveying him from all sides, he stands some seven *zhang* or more;
even sentient beings with narrow experience feel fear. That which they fear is his body’s great height, for they do not believe such a being exists in the world.
"O person, it is because of people like you that I have spoken this verse, so that their feelings of fear may vanish on the spot and they suddenly realize that my body is vastly greater than theirs.
Please observe the Bodhisattva’s contemplation: if there were 'large' or 'small,' how could one contemplate?

Because the capacity to contemplate has neither largeness nor smallness, it is thus able to illuminate both large and small objects; this is just as when contemplating emptiness, one contemplates in this same way. Even if one contemplates..."
The same applies to heaven and earth. Even when one uses the power of contemplation to observe a mustard seed, it is entirely something understood by that which contemplates.
If the capacity of the contemplator is small, it cannot be large; how then could it further contemplate heaven and earth? If the capacity of the contemplator is large, it cannot be small.
Furthermore, one cannot even perceive a mustard seed. When I seek it with the wisdom of wondrous observation, I find that the perceiver is ultimately neither large nor small.
Since the perceiver is neither large nor small, even space and the heavens cannot be compared to it.
If these three great things are thus, how much more so the seven-foot form of an infant? Alas! Foolish children do not observe themselves; they pursue external objects and engage in discrimination.
A sense of dread arises. If a person can investigate these verses in return, they will surely laugh aloud; for while the truth is manifest [before them], they appear like a seven-fathom child.
Sentient beings have suffering, and Avalokiteśvara saves them; yet when Avalokiteśvara saves from suffering, he himself has no suffering.

If one who already possesses suffering could save others, such a principle has never existed from antiquity to the present. It would be like using fire from wood to boil cold water: the water becomes hot, but the fire itself does not.

Once moistened, when sentient beings fall into perilous difficulties and cry out in terror seeking liberation, who would know that the one who cries out within themselves cannot be bound by any suffering?
If those who cry out in suffering could be bound by it, then water might become hot and fire might become moist.
If a person encounters suffering and contemplates in this way, they will always find peace and joy amidst the boiling cauldrons and glowing coals. (Salvation from Suffering)

The Universal Gate is not far away; within the midst of daily life, the expressions of likes and dislikes are the countenance of Avalokiteśvara. If one can focus single-mindedly on this contemplation, then self and others are fundamentally identical.
Amidst heaps of fire and mountains of knives, all becomes harmoniously tranquil like spring waves. The moment one engages in discursive thought, the Bodhisattva withdraws her trace.
I look up with hope for deliverance from suffering. Turning my head westward while facing east, Sudhana could not restrain himself and suddenly ascended into the void.

Between ordinary people and sages, there is originally no difference in their minds; it is only through the improper application [of the mind] that one encounters rising or sinking. Water is like the moon reflected outside.
Clear yet not transparent, like the moon or external water; transparent yet incomplete, mutually not external to one another, yet capable of both illumination and purity.

The multitude is ignorant of this, and myriad sufferings gather upon their bodies. To realize that the body has no dependence—those things upon which it depends are all but spirit—is to observe sound with the eye.

Rescuing those adrift in delusion (like the moon in water), the wondrous peaks and verdant bamboos are the eyebrows of the Bodhisattva. These eyebrows preach the Dharma; who is able to hear them? One must simply observe with the eyes.
The mind is at peace regarding its objects; even mountain-blades and masses of fire are no different from *laṅkānaga* gems.
