Exterior strength with interior emptiness—spiritual yet selfless—I open the gates for those in the seven destinies and compassionately pull them from the three miserable paths. Taking wisdom as my sun, frost and snow are eliminated. I search for the mark of sin, but find none.

The beard of a woman; the six sense organs functioning interchangeably—where could one go that is not transparently clear? Where does this transparency reside? It resides within my pores. One pore is a single body;
Bodhisattvas as numerous as atoms fill the ten voids. Like the moon reflected in ten thousand streams, when Sudhana wishes to grasp it, it is everywhere.

The parrot mocks people. As for honor and disgrace, gain and loss—who lends them reality, and who possesses them truly? Honey has its center and its periphery; behind the crags there is no spring (the Bamboo Grove).
Beyond the water there is no mind. What is it that observes? If mind and matter are distinguished, then the observation of water is attained. When this observation is attained—

Form is empty within the Avīci Hell; throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, all is vast, profound, and harmoniously fused. When the defilements of both ordinary beings and sages are removed, the wondrous countenance is finally perfected.

Regarding the immeasurable and agonizing sufferings of the three miserable realms and the eight difficulties, one should constantly maintain this contemplation. As for the mountain of knives and the land of bliss, if one were to contemplate them as something else, [the truth would be obscured].
The Land of Bliss is a mountain of blades, while the waters of innate nature are vast and deep. In the surging waves of the sea of suffering, fish and dragons are in turmoil;

they are addicted to the five desires, and their hope for the source of craving to dry up must wait for a donkey’s year. Out of compassion for them, the Bodhisattva takes his own body as a boat and comes and goes across the ocean of desire.
Forming the conditions for purity, the eyes hear the sound of the waves; host and guest share the same mystery (the contemplation of water).
Amidst the boundless clouds and surging tides, how complete is that crescent moon! The Bodhisattva sits within this moon; all terror has long since been severed.

Fish and dragons look up at his brow and countenance; their appearance and disappearance have no fixed time. Constantly mindful of Avalokiteśvara, the sound of the waves enters the path with its wonders.

A hairpin and bangles fall across the wall; when they meet, who can provide the recommendation? If one can recommend the fish as being the dragon, guard against it manifesting as thunder and lightning.

Lightning compared to sparks from flint—how frantic! A thought arises and its radiance is already lost. Willow branches are inserted into a pure vase; tossed by the wind, they learn to sway up and down.
Round mats and auspicious *śaṅkhapuṣpī* grass—until what year will you sit? As long as the realm of sentient beings is not empty, I too shall kneel and work the mud.
If sound is heard by means of the ear, the faculty of the eye perceives it all in confusion (like the moon in water).
I bow my head to the Great Compassionate Avalokiteśvara; the sounds of all suffering are heard only by the eye. The mountain of blades and the mass of fire become liberation;
at that time, where can one find the clouds of delusion? The waves of the long river are as high as the Snow Mountains; if I am without mind, the water [is still].
In this world of restlessness, the rushing currents of all rivers are like flashes of lightning; among them lies a path leading to Chang’an.

Though the wind and moon of Chang’an are indeed fine, the flaming light atop one’s head burns the apricot trees early. Without relying on the thunder beneath the earth in the third month of spring, the hibernating dreams of sentient beings will never end.
Homage to the Most Victorious Avalokiteśvara, who acts as a noble guide amidst the mountains of suffering and calamity.

I have heard that Avalokiteśvara was once an ordinary sentient being. Because he encountered the Buddha Avalokiteśvara, who taught him to observe sounds with the eyes, the Bodhisattva received this instruction.
He then began to observe sounds with his eyes; however, when he attempted to give rise to the mind [of insight], he could not succeed. For many times, his countenance was filled with deep sorrow.

In contemplating sorrow and suffering, my insight was not yet thorough; as I contemplated for a long time, my heart suddenly split open. When the heart split, I knew myself to be cast away; knowing I was cast away, even my views were liberated.
When both knowledge and views were forgotten together, the eyes beheld sounds with clarity. What was once immeasurable suffering has now become the path of compassion and wisdom.
The path enters through the Universal Gate. Interchanging yet not interchanging. The sound of a hairpin falling against the wall—how many know the way?
Observing this sound, one’s roots of goodness are deep; seeing it, it gladdens my heart. I behold the voice of Avalokiteśvara, which constantly shines upon me morning and evening.
Through sound, I presented this meaning; thus I was able to cast my almsbowl into the needle.
Bodhisattvas and sentient beings are fundamentally no different from one another; by skillfully employing their minds, one may first attain perfect penetration. I have no doubt regarding this method.
In the vast void, the long wind moves with sovereign freedom; what thing could form a boundary? If one’s application is even slightly unskillful, doubts and delusions manifest crosswise.

Birth and death, honor and disgrace, the faces of demons and the faces of Buddhas—all these the Bodhisattva pities; he plucks away my veils and obscurations, so that I may suddenly return to original luminosity.
The light penetrates the three periods of past, present, and future. Like lotuses blooming upon an ice river, his arms cross as he walks slowly;

his feet do not touch the dust. The waters transform into lapis lazuli, startling both fish and dragons; they float and sink with no fixed place. Those with eyes are as if blind, while sounds are perceived as if by sight.
Is it not true that Vairocana was moved by Sudhana’s urgency? He lamented his own dull faculties.
Spring rests in the peach blossoms, red as if dyed with blood; spring resides in the Bodhisattva, whose compassion never tires. Leaning his left elbow upon the rock...
The right hand curls its fingers; only two remain extended. Between the two and the three, there is no abiding in either curling or extending.
If one seeks through abiding, this is called a "dead word. Where is the "live word"? The peach blossoms sway; the flowers themselves preach the Dharma. The Dharma pervades the Ganges.
Those who hear this will, with their very eyes, suddenly cast out the waves of craving.
Reciting "Avalokiteśvara" seven times and the Four Great Vows three times, the character "Pu" (Universal) appears clearly as it is grasped by the hand of faith; there is an eye upon the finger.

When the visual faculty perceives sound, it moves from what is intimate to what is distant; thus the manifold sufferings are stilled. Such is the nature of phenomena: they arise through conditions yet are unborn.

Upon the mountain of blades and the forest of swords, where agonies are difficult to endure, one gropes for a pillow in the dead of night; though Great Compassion manifests its form, one loses it before one's very arms can reach out.
Walking barefoot and on foot, Sudhana pursues a shadow; the parrot flies and cries, present yet unseen.

A willow branch obstructs his vision, leading him to claim that this is not real and that Putuo is the truth. A hairpin falls behind a wall; he enters through the sensory dust of sound. Sound can indeed expound the Dharma.
Form is the Great Master; do I have anything hidden? You must contemplate this with earnest attention.

The thirty-two manifestations, the vermilion of compassion and majesty—when Deshan held his bowl, the bright sun shed its radiance. Hearing the bell within the realm of the eyes, all suffering ceases its activity.
After the rain, the fragrant grasses are green; woven from grass, they become green jade. Seated in meditation, the jade is warm and lustrous; ten thousand anxieties need not be washed away.
This mind is like a clear, empty pool; defilement and purity forget their boundaries. Those who see it find their own thoughts naturally dissolve; as for excessive talk, it is not my concern.

The myriad phenomena expound this lofty discourse; how could the faculties of all listeners be fully equipped? Only those whose faculties are incomplete can skillfully hear the teachings of the myriad phenomena.
Blazing forth and never ceasing, the eye-faculty acts as a matchmaker, guiding in suffering sentient beings to find rest within the Universal Gate.
The pure water flask and the willow twigs were arranged before him;

though they bring cooling relief to burning afflictions, they possess no permanence from the start. How one employs them reveals their true measure, long or short. The Bodhisattva, knowing this, [proceeded accordingly].

That which is observed differs from the person; for the śrāvaka, it is an object of the eye, whereas for the person, it is an object of the ear. Hearing sounds with the eyes, the Dharma has neither shallowness nor depth;
the barriers of sentiment are severed, and both ordinary and sage sink into equanimity. Taking this as the gate, the gate encompasses empty space—both that which has form and that which is formless.

Forged within this realm, the transformations transcend artifice; even the workings of yin and yang find it difficult to rival their skill. A single hair contains many bodies; ten thousand apertures resound with the wind.
Sound becomes a Buddha-activity, the very essence of Great Compassion. With wisdom and compassion as the vessel, the power of one’s vows is inexhaustible. Even leaves serve as a mat.

The one of wondrous countenance sits cross-legged; the bending and extending [of the limbs] resides within the mind—how could it depend on outward traces? The green grasses grow thick and lush; how dense is the autumn light!

The eyes of sentient beings are poisonous, while the eyes of a Bodhisattva are compassionate. Compassion and poison are opposites; they are difficult to understand one another. When poison fills one and evil reaches its extreme, [it is impossible to perceive the truth].
When evil is extreme and sins are deep, myriad sufferings converge; only then does one call upon Avalokiteśvara. Avalokiteśvara is able to rescue.

Though the principle may seem difficult to penetrate, the faculty of the eye perceives sound, and a thousand calamities are suddenly dissolved. If sentient beings know this, they are identical to the Bodhisattva.

Sentient beings possess ignorance; Bodhisattvas possess perfect penetration. When both are observed with discernment, they are fundamentally neither different nor the same. The three miserable realms and eight difficulties involve endless suffering;
poisons, drugs, and mountains of knives arise when the mind forms attachments. When picked up, they are immediately employed; where they are employed, one encounters them.

If that [nature] were the self, it would be like calling a horse a dragon; yet here, in this very moment, it is taken up. Compassion and wisdom are harmoniously fused, transcending all contrivance and naturally hitting the mark.
Amidst the flowing waters of layered cliffs, the mark of his tongue covers the void; his preaching of the Dharma is inexhaustible, such that those who hear with their eyes are deafened by the sound.
Ten thousand kinds of affliction are but the pine wind in the sixth month; Sudhana falls asleep, facing west with his back to the east.
The function of compassion and wisdom is inherently complete within all sentient beings; yet because of the notion of "mine," that which is perfect becomes imperfect. Take suffering as your teacher.

One undergoes extreme suffering through deep contemplation. When this contemplation has accumulated over a long period, the mind opens and the spirit becomes serene; the faculties find their clarity and manifest, functioning without obstruction or conflict.
Like a luminous gem resting in a bowl, it moves with sovereign ease. Yet if one gives rise to a calculating mind, it will burn your eyebrows. The Bodhisattva takes pity on such people.
Expedient means are fully provided through hundreds of thousands of samādhis; the response-body is tireless, like a sliver of moon in the sky whose myriad reflections appear in the ponds.

Fundamentally there is no before or after—how could there be any discrepancy? Even the mountain of knives and the mass of fire are occasions for liberation; it is only that one feels fear and trepidation.

Suturing ox-hide with thread; a light breeze stirs ripples on the water. Exotic grasses grow in the mountain ravines; the Bodhisattva sits there in sovereign ease. His mind reflects upon the many sentient beings.
Five or six slender bamboo stalks stand by a vase where willow branches hang sparse. The great earth is fundamentally cool and refreshing; what heat and affliction could it possibly dispel?
Celestial winds arise at the edge of the sea; emerald bamboos rub against the void. Even the willow branches know how to dance; the water in the jar knows its own profound stillness.
If a woman wishes to become a man, she must first wither the mechanism of lust. When lust is withered and the mind is pure, one will surely become a great man.

In his youthful innocence, he severed the bonds of affection; throughout his life, he guarded the pearl of the precepts. Whether practicing Chan or studying the Way, demons and heretics could not disturb him.
Suddenly, he opened the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, hearing the flutes and pipes with his eyes. He entrusted this to Master Dong, the one with the long beard, who is diligent in his practice.
Why must one wait for a future life before emerging from the path of delusion?

If the six sense faculties are not fully penetrating, emotional attachments cannot be emptied. When emotions are forgotten and thoughts extinguished, the six faculties will naturally function interchangeably.
One performs many Buddha-deeds; for the most part, this is the power of a single faculty. Among the eighty-four thousand hairs, each is without distinction of superior or inferior.
Who says that the ear hears sound? Who says that the eye sees form? Between the holy and the ordinary, there is not an inch of ground to be found; how can there be a sequence of mother and child?
When not a single thought arises, the original radiance is ever manifest alone. Perfect penetration resides in vipers and scorpions; the Universal Gate belongs to snakes and tigers.
The Great Being possesses no merit—what is there to praise, and what is there to disparage?
Using the hand as eyes, taking the pearl as sound; the void is the obstructing bone, where diverse forms are unborn. By springs and rocks, pure and secluded, this jade-like countenance is lodged.
Seated in the half-lotus posture, the bending and extending are naturally at ease. The parrot seeks food; Sudhana hides from the stubborn.
When called, he would not come; when unbidden, he would immediately return (holding the pearl).

Using the surging waves as rafts, they drifted together along the edge of the sea. Though others vied with one another to request [the pearl], it was granted only to the house of Zhu. The fish and dragons wailed piteously.

The aquatic creatures have lost their father; now that they have become human, we sigh with emotion. Humans take pity on the soft-shelled turtles and crocodiles, praying to the Buddha for his secret grace.

May all those born from moisture find their minds opening like the flowers of enlightenment. The human mind and the Buddha-mind reach the same fundamental source without distinction; may fish and dragons come to know this.

Sighs and idle clamor arise; yet the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are one. A jade stone is originally without flaw. As the conditions at Wumen matured, the site of Tongxuan became auspicious.

Though the two alms bowls were broken, the spiritual presence of the Two Honored Ones remains far-reaching. Those who have seen or heard of them are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Whether they disparage or praise—
Who beats the poisonous drum? With mind or without mind? The drum is truly its own fang and claw; the deluded child does not understand.

Striking the grass to startle the snake—the snake suddenly sheds its skin. Amidst slanting wind and rain, within a flash of lightning, the Master of Thunder reveals and conceals. The nostrils of the stone image.

Now high, now low; like a mountain collapsing amidst snow-tossed waves, a skiff moves upon the surface of paper. Neither on land nor in water is there peril; the holy and the ordinary are but one carriage.
Carrying a heavy load to travel far, he cradles a lute—whether it makes sound or not. When Zhaozhou was granted tea, it had barely passed his lips.
Waves like hemp seeds (The Two Stone Buddhas of Wuzhong).
I bow my head to the Great Compassionate Avalokiteśvara, who performs the Buddha’s work through sound.
When all sentient beings undergo suffering and cry out in bitter pain, you immediately hasten to their rescue. Like the pure moon at the edge of the sky, wherever there is water, it appears therein.
Pervasive entry: Water is the heart of sentient beings’ intense suffering; the moon is the power of a bodhisattva’s skillful means.

Whether on mountains of knives and trees of swords, in boiling cauldrons, or drifting and falling into lands of black winds and demons—when the life-faculty of sentient beings is about to be severed, the bodhisattva compassionately and exhaustively restores it for them.
Or when they encounter famine, cold, illness, or pestilence, and mother and child disregard one another and are torn apart—the bodhisattva...

The body manifests as clothing, food, and medicine, causing people to rejoice and be restored to wholeness. Although sentient beings may undergo the suffering of ignorance, they do not awaken upon seeing it through words and language.
The Bodhisattva secretly employs the water of ambrosia to wash away the obscuring clouds, so that suddenly all is penetrated and understood.
The mundane and supramundane dharmas are like fruits held in the palm; clearly and distinctly perceived, they are never again deluded.

The majestic power of the Bodhisattva responds immediately to one’s invocation, yet ultimately, it all depends upon the power of my own mind. If my heart’s anguish were not genuine, the Bodhisattva could not save me from suffering.
The fourteen fearlessnesses, the two kinds of following, the thirty-two transformations, and all other merits—if these were separated from me...
With a heart of piercing urgency, how could outward seeking ever provide relief? I have also closely observed this piercing pain; though I sought it with all my might, I saw no such thing.
Seeking it within the suffering of suffering, there is nowhere to find it. If suffering had a fixed location, how could it ever be extinguished?
Now that I cry out to the Bodhisattvas, all places of suffering become joy. Thus one knows that both suffering and pleasure are entirely impermanent. [The multitude...]
Birth does not understand birth, whether in accord or in opposition; honors and insults swirl about as dreams grow ever denser. Though I call out and cry many times, I do not wake.

I only pray that the Bodhisattva will have pity on my folly; through secret influence and empowerment, may I awaken the moment I am called. Once awakened, body and mind are like flowers in the void; love and hate, birth and death, are like a brush made of tortoise hair.
To know this thoroughly is to lose the path of "perfect penetration" (yuan-tong); for the Bodhisattva, there is no ground upon which to stand.

Standing here, I have no choice but to become a horse-herder’s wife; yet, by using the hook of desire to lead others across the many sufferings, it is like using poison to counteract poison—once the illness is cured, the poison is likewise gone without a trace.
What harm is there in having a demon’s face or a deity’s head? Whether moving forward or moving backward, may all beings receive universal benefit.
Because of the One-Dou Spring at Fángshān, I was able to behold the body of the Bodhisattva with its excellent marks and signs. Furthermore, at...
Upon the stele at Cishou Temple, I once paid homage to the image of a Bodhisattva while begging for alms. In his hand, the Bodhisattva held a fresh bamboo basket;
within it, the fish appeared as if alive. The lotus flowers were radiant and elegant, complementing his majestic countenance, causing those who beheld him to conceive the thought of the Buddha.
Sandalwood and camphor are burned morning and evening; the fragrant smoke billows, enveloping the towers and terraces.

Such offerings of wealth and honor are beyond compare, and the dragon girl Sudhana is ever joyful. Yet only the parrot feels its heart is not satisfied, still claiming that this place is arid and difficult to dwell in.
Who would have known that in the Tuṣita Temple above, there too is Avalokiteśvara within his rocky grotto, amidst mists and incense?
How utterly desolate! Transcending it all, she finds no weariness in solitude (the Fish Basket Guanyin).
Before a Bodhisattva has attained the Way, how can they be at ease while traversing the world? Once they awaken to their own mind, liberation is no longer an obstacle.
Not a body, yet an inexhaustible body; the marks of compassionate majesty are not one. Without mind, it pervades all things; its refined illumination penetrates everywhere.

Body and mind are fundamentally in samādhi, yet sentient beings delight in inferiority. They perceive suffering within that which is not suffering, and seek pleasure within that which is not pleasure.
This is called inverted perception; it is difficult to enter the perfect, penetrating awakening.
Like a surging tide shaking Mount Dai, even a great ship dares not cross over. What can a bodhisattva do? [Only one whose] feet are cradled by lotus petals.

Coming and going like a goose feather, one floats away from all terrors. When dragons, crocodiles, turtles, and all manner of aquatic creatures behold one’s reflection, they give rise to hearts of compassion;
even the wheel of swords suddenly comes to a halt. Homage to Avalokiteśvara! Your wisdom and vows are vast and inexhaustible.
I have already taken refuge and paid homage; may all beings become like me.
Originally there was but one luminous essence, which, through delusion, became the sixfold combination. It is like water freezing into ice: obstructed and no longer flowing.
Mañjuśrī selects those who are ready; he is the foremost among the holy Bodhisattvas. When the sound is heard, the sound is immediately the mind, for the mind does not perceive the mind.
If the mind could perceive itself, the eye could likewise observe the eye. To understand this all at once is to be liberated from all suffering.

To open up things and accomplish tasks is the capacity of the Sage. Whether through the direct path (*nīti*) or through expedient means (*upāya*), they give rise to the non-arising according to conditions.
Within awe there is compassion, yet it does not encounter awe; within compassion there is awe, yet it does not meet compassion.

It is like mountains giving rise to clouds, like the moon appearing over water, or like spring bringing forth flowers—these three manifest together. It is through non-encounter that they are perfected, and through non-meeting that they become numinous. Only...

Accomplishment and spirituality—its power lies in non-action. The Great Compassionate One has a thousand hands; every hand has an eye. When compared with this wondrous form, how meager are [ordinary] hands and eyes!
The meager is the mother of the many, and the many are the children of the meager. Where the many and the meager do not meet, the wise understand for themselves.
To understand is to have no doubt. This very form is I; that I can doubt myself is the manner of entering the Way.
"The five colors blind the eyes; the five tones deafen the ears. Dwelling in seclusion among bamboo and stone, one transcends the concerns of body and world.

Within the midst of existence and non-existence, both form and sound can enter the path of universal penetration (*āyatana*). To investigate the reason for this is the merit of the "Eye-Avalokiteśvara" (the faculty of sight as the gateway to liberation).
Therefore, the three miserable realms and eight difficulties arise like clouds from myriad sufferings; whether in adversity or in favor, they are like a clear breeze.
The measure of this is like the pine tree:
the ocean of wisdom and the ocean of desire are from the outset without constancy. If the mind is skillfully employed, the ocean of desire emits light;

if it is not skillfully employed, there are glowing embers and boiling cauldrons. Taking the lotus as a boat, one drifts upon the Universal Gate; invoked, one responds, making no distinction between horse and ox.
The horse glimpses the shadow of the whip and gallops without waiting for a second command; the ox pulls the great cart, proceeding with sovereign ease wherever it goes.

Fish, dragons, birds, and beasts—the various species of water and land—are all reflected within the *Sāgaramudrā-samādhi*; there is no image that is not gathered therein. With the *śaraṇa* (willow branch) in his hand, he occasionally dips it into the surging waves of the clouds.

Those touched by its heat and distress find their hundred sufferings instantly extinguished. Taking the ocean as a chalice, fish and dragons rest within the palm; with eyes beholding the dragon’s roar, the sound of thunder resounds through the clear sky.

The fire of the mind already blazes fiercely; the winds of sensory objects fan it, withering its original wondrous nature. Amidst the perilous and strange eight difficulties, a mere duration of one meal feels like hundreds or thousands of kalpas.
Mutually startled by honor and disgrace, one matures black karma, exhausting that compassionate mother; rushing about, one creates only weariness.
I contemplate the great earth as if it were my only child. The suffering of not finding what one seeks is more urgent than fire burning one's eyebrows.

When the human world lacks heirs, the heavens share in the grief. Seeking out voices to rescue those in suffering, before the very sounds are heard, the moon of the Universal Gate is full, and my vows are likewise fulfilled.
Seeking a daughter, one obtains a daughter; seeking a son, one obtains a son. These are manifestations of one’s own mind.
As for the bodhisattva’s craving, however much it may be asked, the rosary in his hand and the young boys and girls turn about as they please.
I have encountered adverse conditions; the heat of affliction scorched my liver and lungs. I have met favorable conditions; joy welled up from the pores of my skin.
Originally, there is but one "I"; why should suffering and pleasure be so manifold? The world regards suffering as suffering, yet does not regard pleasure as evil.
Who would have known that suffering is never-ending? It is all because pleasure acts as the matchmaker. If this matchmaker cannot be dismissed, how can the root of suffering be uprooted?
Even when suffering and pleasure are exhausted, equanimity itself is a thorn. For these three reasons, Avalokiteśvara takes pity on sentient beings.
This is truly the source of all evils and the place where all sufferings converge. Thereupon, employing skillful means, I taught you to hear sounds with the eye;
by entering the stream, you attained perfect enlightenment, obtaining the thirty-two marks of response and the fourteen fearlessnesses, as well as the two kinds of compliance, superior and inferior.
To broaden the bodhisattva’s compassion and wisdom: when I was truly suffering, I experienced wild beasts and swords all at once;
the agony was unbearable, and I cried out, "O Bodhisattva! Suddenly, I wondered about my own pain: who is it that cries out? Who is it that calls?

In genuine pain one can cry out; yet in this case, both the pain and the cry are absent. To cry out falsely when there is no involvement—how is this different from dreaming of being bitten by a snake?

When one is in the midst of a dream of being bitten by a snake, the fear is unbearable and urgent; yet suddenly hearing a rat overturning a basin, one thinks: "What gain or loss does the snake have for me?"

Eulogy for the Buddha Fragrance Hermitage Sandalwood Avalokiteśvara Image (with Preface) If one analyzes sandalwood, there is not a single fragment that is not fragrant; if one divides the vast ocean, there is not a single drop that is not moist.
Sandalwood and the vast ocean take the mind as their mother; therefore, those who attain the mind can become the progenitor of all sages. The Great Earth Mother, relying upon... [text ends]
Since birth has already passed away, viewing it from the perspective of human emotion, it is like water rushing toward the east that cannot be turned back.
I have heard that the myriad things are one thing and the myriad people are one person; thus, the sage understands this and employs them in alternation.
If this is so, once this image has been brought to life, does the "life" upon which it relies truly pass away? In praise, I say:
If Mr. Feng has indeed died, this image does not exist; if this image still exists, where has Mr. Feng gone? It is like the eye perceiving sound:
the clear mechanism is within the palm of one's hand. If Mr. Feng possesses a spirit, do not neglect my thoughts.

Eulogy on the Manifestation of Avalokiteśvara by Wu Daozi (with Preface) In general, the subtlety of painting does not lie in what is easily visible; rather, it is precisely that which is invisible where the subtlety truly manifests, for that is difficult. Therefore, that which is subtle yet visible can emerge with ease, whereas depicting it from oblique perspectives is difficult—only those who possess profound insight [can achieve this]. When looking at it, it emerges as if from the side, appearing as if in a blur; this is not something produced by the painter’s flight of fancy or illusion.

How could one not feel drawn to it and become intimate with it? The ink may fade, yet its spirit remains! Therefore it is said: "To wondrously transform all things without being entangled is called the Divine (shen).

Where the Divine resides, even in the most decayed of objects, its vital energy touches the heart such that it seems impossible to conceal. This cannot— (Note: The provided text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)
As for "concealing": it enshrines the myriad things within its spirit; wherever it dwells, it acts as the sovereign. Wherever the sovereign resides, what thing is not its subject?
In the year Dingyou, I beheld the *Transformation of Avalokiteśvara* painted by Wu Daozi in the home of Grand Secretary Dong.
The thirty-two physical forms and their spiritual attitudes manifest in ten thousand transformations.
They are like a luminous pearl within a golden platter, rolling about with effortless ease; one can certainly not use a discursive mind to calculate their direction.
At times they appear mindless yet are not wooden puppets; at other times they possess thought yet do not cling to conceptualization. Such is their nature.
Can one not know this? The eulogy says:

That upon which wandering thoughts are寄托 (reposed) is neither coarse nor subtle. Guanyin is his master; he has transcribed my empty and numinous spirit. Every stroke, every line, captures it perfectly.

Dependent origination is non-arising. A single body contains manifold wonders; ten thousand mirrors reflect a single lamp. It is delightful yet difficult to approach; seeking to leave it behind, one instead falls into darkness.

To exhaustively investigate its source, one must remain in profound silence like a peal of thunder. One does not value what is heard by the ear, but should rather listen with the eye. The Universal Gate is deep and mysterious.
The path of the mind is difficult to ascend; the Bodhisattva takes pity on them. He divides his light and disperses his form to act as their guide.

He beckons with his hand and calls out their names, yet the compassionate mother’s voice chokes with grief as her child ultimately does not respond. Thinking of this, her heart is pained, and she weeps in vain.
Praise for the Skull Avalokiteśvara:

Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva never rests; all day long he contemplates his own body, continuing into the night. As he contemplates what has passed and what is yet to come, he beholds a skull—withered and dry, yet right before my very eyebrows and eyelashes.
At this moment, if Xi Shi were to come and pay her respects, the Bodhisattva’s mind would be filled with lust.
Do not arise; do not let him emerge from contemplation only to encounter a wild fox. Seeing him with his own eyes, joy arises in his heart.
*Tut!* Whether man or woman, it is all like this. Why must you give rise to thoughts of love or hatred?
Praise of Cundī Bodhisattva:

When the single mind does not arise, all functions are fully present. Though her arms and hands appear to be crossed, she remains transcendent and free from entanglement. For sentient beings, there is but scorching affliction.
Their spheres of activity are not uniform; they employ incantations to refine their habits, like lotuses blooming amidst the mud of desire.
This is the first of the eulogies for the Eighteen Arhats by Tang Guànxiū.
The ten directions are a single pearl; the three periods of time are a single thread. If the Venerable One has the intent, how could it be turned by merely pushing it?
As for the years of Daian and the devotion of Han Yu, how many inquiries were there? Establishing the Sangha was the response given in their stead.
The second leans his back against a withered log; who knows the passing of the seasons? A single nostril has fallen into whose house?
Selling off the sun and moon, he dispels the great darkness; ghosts who cling to the gloom are all in a flurry of startled amazement.

The third master contemplates all things as a mother gazes upon her child. The child, moved by the mother’s kindness, sheds his coarse skin and embraces her with affection; he clasps his hands together and holds fast to her counsel.
Two fingers point toward the heavens; a snail grows horns. Twin pagodas hang a lamp;
what is that object held in the fourth hand? Buddhas and patriarchs do not recognize it. The left hand rests upon the knee; the mouth is open enough to measure, yet silent as a thunderclap.
Sound exists even before it is sounded; if one listens with the ear, even Li Lou would lose his sight.

Fifth, outside the mind there are no phenomena; these clouds and mountains are this very mind. As for this body, its existence is contingent and difficult to trace; close your eyes in a mountain cave.
The very body is no-body; for those with the conditions to see it, who would not find it divine?

Suddenly, in the sixth [consciousness], one encounters a delusion—the Dragon of the Single Eye. Upon the fan, the green mountains and flowing springs are inexhaustible. He bends and extends his five fingers.
Two or three things are not fixed; one lets the mouth freely apply the yellow pigment to the black (arbitrarily revising).

Amidst the bells and chimes of a thousand peaks, the seventh [consciousness] has deep blue eyes that are clear and azure; no phenomenon can escape it. Grasping both hands together while resting the chin upon them, one fears they may not be secure. The throat is as deep as a valley.
When opened, it is shallow, no more than three inches deep; when closed and concealed, who can discern it?

Eighth, view the body as a cloud: how could the cloud be different from the body? The water in the bowl and the willow branch are the spring for all sentient beings; the old pines twist and coil about.
Wherever wind and rain reach, there are infinite dragons and serpents, displaying their transformations at will.
Beyond the ninth meal, I find leisure to study Buddhist scriptures; casting my gaze across the lines, I unroll and re-roll the scrolls—those white silk leaves bearing the tracks of birds.
A wild goose flies over the snowy peaks; its path is intermittent as it follows the wind. Its reflection remains in the wild waters.

On the tenth cubit of the pavilion, clouds rest upon the rocks. His hands remain in the void; his shoulders bared, he holds his staff while his eyes watch the flying goose. This is what is called the divine function.
Who would not possess this? Its presence or absence does not depend on wine; yet all who drink it become intoxicated.
This eleventh wooden boy has a body but no hands; he achieves success by relying on his teacher. The teacher’s hand is my own; its application follows what is appropriate.
Itching does not reside in the skin; it is removed by scratching. Who is it that fully understands this?

The twelfth [chapter] uses the eyebrows to preach the Dharma; both the mouth and the lips are at ease, unfolding and rolling as they please. Within the interval of long and short, they happen to serve as a measuring line.
Binding the void, placing a mustard seed within it; mountains and rivers are infinite.

With the tenth mouth closed and unable to open, who knows the teeth are missing? The root of the tongue flickers lightly, leaving matters of reward and punishment entirely to chance as one sits with arms around the knees.
Steadfast as a withered stump, half-asleep yet not fully asleep, he finds delight in this state.

Fourteenth: The single palm and five fingers bend and extend without constancy, like the wind playing with willow branches; how could the branches themselves exercise control? Whether called "bending" or "extending," [it is all movement].
The wheel of the cycle revolves from beginning to end; one’s dreams and aspirations are wearying. O Venerable One, why do you harbor anger?

The fifteenth Great Compassionate Bodhisattva possesses hundreds of thousands of hands and eyes; since all implements are fully prepared, why is his illumination not perfect? [He holds] the sutra-bead and the staff.
It simultaneously subdues delusive thoughts. If mindfulness has not yet arisen, one loses both at once.

At the sixteenth stage, one commands both Buddhas and demons; the handle is in one's own hands. Like a tempest of thunder and wind, whatever one wields is effective. Whether carried by donkey or horse, it bears the burden.
Giving and taking money side by side gives rise to the dualistic mind; empty space would then have boundaries.
(17) The two eyebrows are like the wind; the two eyes are like the ocean. The sutra is before one’s face, yet it seems to wait expectantly; in a single hair, there are mountains and rivers.
The succession of kalpas is beyond measure; whether one calls it distant or near, it is like the space contained within a jar.

Now that the eighteenth subtle atom has been split open, the beginning of the scripture appears before us. Though the words and phrases are not many, by observing them throughout the years, one comes to realize that they reside within oneself.
It does not reside in the sutras; both possess constancy. The ox-hide [satchel] beholds the stars.
Furthermore, the first of the Praises to the Eighteen Arhats.

A withered log has sprouted flowers; it is not that the ears do not see them. Both the forehead and the nose rise high; how boundless is the springtime! His movements of bending and extending follow a constant measure;
his mechanism is beyond suppression or exaltation. Three straight lines and two curves—his arms and shoulders are majestic and imposing.
The second head is a strange and wondrous stone; its hair is like willows swaying in the wind. One hand holds a pearl, which serves as a mouth; do not be startled by its wide jaw.
It possesses the general form yet remains detached, an inverted Buddha-head that vaguely resembles Deshan.
The third robe is cast over one shoulder; azure eyes are fixed upon the sutra. This sutra is most profound—a thunderclap amidst a great dream. Characters are not reality;
reality is not characters. With one foot alone hanging down, both hands move freely at will.
In the fourth vision, the Sūtra hung down with its head drooping; its shoulders and back swallowed its ears, and a spring gushed from within the earth. The paper remained still and clear.
Old Lu of Lingnan paused his firewood carrying to await the Dragon Treasury, his mind abiding nowhere.
Fifth, with both hands supporting his chin for fear of falling to the ground, his mouth agape and teeth bared, his eyes bulging while his mind was lost in sleep; his mind asleep, his body forgotten,
the rock could not exert its hardness, and the rock forgot my feet— what harm was there in sinking into it?

Sixth, when the single mind does not arise, I am the mountain cave and the cliffs; the waves are the patterns on my robes, and the spring’s murmur is the lush, precipitous peaks. Though my eyes are not open, light illumines the six directions;
brightness and darkness are both forgotten, for the essence of seeing is not mixed with anything else.
Seventh:
leaning a staff against the forehead, making the forehead the stand for the staff; one shoulder towers alone, while both feet pay the price.
The staff and the forehead are not the same—what merit do the host and guest have? Only the shoulders and feet strike at empty space.
The eighth [relic] was a lapis lazuli bowl, transparent both inside and out. Fixing my gaze upon it, Mount Wutai appeared before me;
white clouds unfurled and withdrew in hundreds of forms and thousands of moods. Thus, I buried it at the root of a pine tree to manifest its sovereign freedom.
Ninth: Drawing in the shoulders and clasping the knees—what indeed is being contemplated? That which I contemplate is the mind’s refined contemplation; having relinquished contemplation, one sits.
Whether the space be wide or narrow, it is all acceptable. The stone has no marks; even a blade sharp enough to shave a hair cannot hide from it.

The tenth arm holds a staff, and his hand further grasps a rosary; fearing that the mind might wander, he leans upon a scripture for his own amusement. As wild geese cry out across the autumn sky, the Sanskrit characters appear in irregular succession;
with these I offer praise to the Buddha, for I am an elder who has long known the truth.
Eleventh: "His hair bristling in rage. I consider this not to be so. To cut thatch grass one does not need an axe; with a single outburst of anger, all is cleared away.
Three bends and two stretches are the rolling up and unfolding of a single hand. Anger as a Buddhist practice is truly an uninvited friend.
Twelfth: Behind the head, boundless; resting upon high crags as a pillow. That which is grasped in the hand is a fan and a casket for subduing dust.
Clouds boil forth without intent, occasionally veiling half the face. Who would prostrate themselves? One simply does not see me.

The thirteenth face is as round as a shallow bowl; its five features are merged into a single cavity. It carves out boundaries and divides territories, where pestles float and blood flows. The lords of the various divisions have eyebrows that do not conform to the crowd;
when sitting, they obstruct the bends, and when walking, they trail the clouds.
The fourteenth:

If there were a back, the itching would be difficult to relieve; yet since there is no back, the scratching of the itch is not false. Through repeated investigation, the emotions withered and wisdom reached its limit.
When the pond was formed and the moon arrived, the Buddha appeared before his eyes.
Fifteenth: His brows are arched and his eyes are bright; with a single snap of his fingers, all is solemn. This very person is the tongue [of Dharma], whose teachings moisten both humans and devas.
Who would dare act like a tiger cub, with fangs and claws so sharp, yet possessing them without baring them? Even the jackals would avoid him in fear.

The sixteenth shoulder is long but useless; it may serve merely as a support for a staff. The knees are likewise vacant; what harm is there in supporting the scriptures? Do not disdain the length of the eyebrows;
they flutter across the rock cave without obstructing the eye’s vision, as clear and still as a cold pool.
Seventeenth: He clasps his staff and extends his fingers; it is not three, but only two. He hides his feet within his boots; when the boots are removed, his feet are refreshed.
His air is leisurely and detached, like that of Chao Fu and Yu Shu. His hair and beard appear as they were, and his nostrils are clearly exposed.

Eighteenth: The robe does not cover the chest. The mind is identical to empty space; who can strike when the fist is clenched? To open the mouth is to let the wind escape; this refers to the hand resting upon the knee.
The knee has no self or person; this refers to the knee supporting the hand. The hand originally belongs to the body.
