Eulogy on the Sixteen Arhats by Tang Guànxiū, Number One:
Venerable Pindola Bharadvāja. He holds a staff in one hand, with two fingers bent;
he rests a scripture upon his knee but does not look at it.
A staff pierces his tiger-like mouth; his remaining fingers are bent inward. By such means he is made a man—yet what can one call him?
His skull is extraordinary, swelling and yet hollowed out; beneath the crag, his twin eyes possess a radiance that cannot be obscured.
The second was the Venerable Kanakavatsa. With both hands forming a mudrā, he leaned a staff upon his shoulder, appearing like a withered tree.
Suddenly, his face opened wide; amidst his mustache and eyebrows, his eyes were sunken and his nose was upturned, as he held a single *khakkhara* staff.
Firmly grasped in his fists; with mind or without mind, it is difficult for brush and ink to depict.
The third, Vajraputra (Kanakavatsa), has a gaunt and skeletal frame;
his eyes stare wide and his eyebrows arch like swords. His right hand holds a fly-whisk, and his left hand rests upon his knee.
His bones are as withered as firewood; he has forgotten both self and others. His eyes are bared and his brows are knitted; meeting people, he buries them alive.
With his right hand he grasps the whisk, suppressing the male and elevating the female. Shoulders raised and feet together—this is the lineage of the dragons and elephants.
The fourth is the Venerable Subhūti. He sits cross-legged upon a rock; his right hand is clenched into a fist, and his left hand rests upon his knee.
His eyebrows are long, covering his face;

one hand is clenched into a fist while the other rests upon his knee. He sits with his feet stacked one above the other, as if ten thousand ages were but a single day, his facial features appearing somewhat broad.
His head was crowned with many peaks. When asked about the meaning of the Dharma, his two eyebrows covered his cheekbones.
The fifth, the Venerable Nārada, held a wooden boy in both hands.

Whenever he felt an itch on his back and could not scratch it with his hands, he used the wooden boy; with a single scratch from it, the itch would cease. When there was no itch, there was no itching.
Once the itch has been scratched away, I venture to ask the Venerable One: what is this itch like?
The sixth Venerable Bhadra, with a flat head and full cheeks, stared upward with wide eyes while his hands counted his prayer beads.
How many springs and autumns have passed? A hundred and eight cycles of day and night. Like a revolving wheel, the pearl turns; thus do the holy and the common experience birth and death.
The brain and forehead lack fullness; what is craved is but partiality. As the eye-light shoots into the void, the startled bird halts its flight.
The seventh, Venerable Kālika, sat in meditative repose upon a rock. His eyebrows were long, encircling his face, yet did not extend beyond the size of a shallow bowl.
His five sense organs each performed their respective functions; sounds, forms, fragrances, and flavors each followed their own natural laws. His body was less than one *xun* in height.
His eyebrows were over ten feet long; he used them as a tongue, rolling and unrolling them at will.
The eighth was the Venerable Vaśaravarta, who bared his shoulders and joined his hands, gazing intently at the scripture.

Upon the stone spread with the *paitā* (Bodhi) leaves, he cast his gaze across them and read. With arms crossed and shoulders bare, his mind was lost in thought. In the empty mountains where no one dwelt, the ancient trees were his only companions.
The wind played upon the new twigs, sounding as if they were both supple and snapped.
The ninth, Venerable Pāṭika, sat to one side. His face was turned half-way toward me. One hand held a fan and whisk;

the other hand had its three fingers bent and rested upon the handle of the fan, while his right hand formed a fist. As seen by the multitude, it was thus; however, I did not see it so, for he held the fan with his hand.
What, then, could there even be of a fist? One who contemplates in this manner perceives the clouds and mountains as my own elbow.
The tenth half-figure, Venerable Tāṭaka, holds a scripture with both hands; he draws in his neck and raises his shoulders, fixing his gaze upon it.
The shoulders rise high above the occiput; the eyes burst forth like the heavens splitting open. The sutras revolve within his double pupils, leaking forth a clear mechanism.
Wind and moon have no master; this troubles the venerable one. Whether it be dragon or snake, let us attempt to proclaim it phrase by phrase.
The eleventh was the Venerable Rāhula. With furrowed brows and glaring eyes, his hand pointed out whatever he intended;
when enraged, he was displeasing to behold. His twin eyes were like swords, their pupils flowing with fire like lightning flashing across a clear sky. He harbored every kind of perverse thought.
Pointing at it, it is immediately empty; the original radiance is uniquely revealed, like the sun in the midst of the sky.
The twelfth, Venerable Nāgasena, raised his fist to support his chin, opened his mouth to reveal his tongue, and seeing his own throat, burst into a great laugh.
The eyes move and the brows flicker; opening the mouth, the tongue is revealed. To awaken beings through sincerity, one raises the fist and makes gestures.
Behind [the practitioner], there are clouds and mountains, and flowing springs murmur. Without hearing them with the ears, my mind finally finds rest.
The thirteenth was Venerable Kātyāyana. Leaning on a staff resting upon his shoulder and cradling a scripture in his left hand, he lowered his head and gazed intently at it.

With his right hand, he held prayer beads to subdue his mind, ensuring it remained without distraction. The rosary rested upon his fingers and the scripture lay within the palm of his hand; he appeared as though he feared even the slightest lapse.
Leaning his staff against his abdomen and shoulder, he gazes at the sutras with his eyes; his mind roams ahead of the elephant.
The fourteenth was the Venerable Vanavasi; with the six sense-faculties inactive, he entered meditative concentration in mountain ravines.
The mind is like extinguished ashes; the form is like withered wood. The spirit is wondrous beyond all things; the blue cliffs are its flesh and bone. Who strikes the iron chime?
An echo transmits the sound through the empty valley. If you call out, there is no response; yet without calling, the eyes stare wide open.
The fifteenth is Venerable Ajita. With both hands clasping his knees, he opens his mouth and gazes upward, revealing all his teeth.
Having cast off several garments, his labor of clasping the knees is effortless;
his head is lofty and towering. Barely opening the seam of his mouth, the mark of his tongue is as if it could be sketched; he preaches the Dharma with his eyes.
Opening and closing are impermanent; light and darkness alternate. How could these affect this radiance?
The sixteenth was Venerable Cūḍapanthaka, who leaned against a withered log and wrote upon the void.

With a handful of *sō*-leaf fans tucked at his waist, upon which were painted the sun, the moon, ancient trees, and hanging moss, he repeatedly flexed and extended his fingers and questioned the Great Being: "Are you for me? Are you for others? He held a single-handled *sō* fan.
It was not until the wind arose that the boundless heat and afflictions were suddenly cleared away by its sweeping touch.

Bodhidharma praised the voyage across the sea to come eastward and proclaimed the transmission of the Buddha-mind; yet, though he severed his arm to seek it, it was utterly unattainable—a scene of sheer embarrassment.
Who has suffered such humiliation? Before the Five Milk Peaks, there was utter chaos; skin, flesh, marrow, and bone lay in a stench so foul it offended the nose.
Even now, upon smelling it, one still says, "I do not recognize it."

The Gandharva King Candana praises the path where non-arising cuts off all tracks and the gate of arising opens. The expedient means of the Sage are unfathomable in their transformations; he manifests a majestic and formidable appearance.
The pain of a compassionate mother—indeed, for all who have infants, they love them as if they were qilin or phoenixes.
In praise of the spiritual image of the Venerable Nāgārjuna:
I bow my head to the Venerable Nāgārjuna. Had he not appeared like the moon’s orb, the failure of Nātaprabha would be unbearable to hear.
Now tell me, how was it that this old fellow turned his body at the very end? *Pah!* Five thousand heterodox practitioners have gone to Buddhahood;
you yourself are simply sinking into hell.

Eulogy for the Portrait of Venerable Senghui of Kangju (with Preface) I have heard that when Sun Quan first beheld Master Hui, he doubted his appearance and attire. However, when he sought śarīra relics and they were proven efficacious, he subsequently erected a stūpa.
Alas! The human mind is full of doubt; this arises from the presence of desire. Where there is desire, there is calculation of profit.
Harm. When benefit and harm have not yet been decided, doubt arises from this. Yet one does not realize that when the single mind does not arise, ordinary beings and sages are equal;
its fundamental radiance is perfect and full—whence could benefit or harm come? Sentient beings are ignorant of this, and the Sage pities them.
Thus, from thousands of miles away, he carries a "night-light" [a jewel] to offer to others, yet people still cross their arms with drawn swords. How tragic!
The body is not mine; the mind, too, is impermanent. Beyond body and mind, what else could there be? Three times I invoke the Tathāgata, my blood and tears soaking my robes.
For whom do I hasten in grief over this eternal pain? Those who truly know you are rare; your virtue is immeasurable.

Śāriputra’s numinous spirit manifests without limit. Alas for me, a mere youth, who has unworthily entered the ranks of the Sangha. On the night of the Mid-Autumn Festival, I beheld his radiant countenance once;
his compassionate majesty flowed into me, quenching my parched heart. This feeling and this kindness shall not be forgotten, even through kalpas as vast as mustard seeds.

Inscription for the Portrait of Venerable Huiguo of Kangju, Sent to Master Han (with Preface) The Three Kingdoms was a gathering place for heroes, yet it was also a gathering place for the blades of war. Therein, the gates of compassion and *prajñā* had no entry.
Yet the Patriarch of Kang [Huiguo] arrived with a single staff upon the river; three times he invoked the name of the Tathāgata, his two eyes bled, and he cast in *śarīra*.

The vase radiates brilliance throughout the six directions, its grace extending for a thousand ages. At that time, among the sovereign and ministers of Wu, there were none whose hearts were not moved or whose complexions did not change;
they verified the principle through the facts and knew that the Buddha existed, free from doubt. Once the Six Perfections had been translated, [the Way flourished].
The gateway of *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing) opened; there was no distinction between the black and the white.
Those who attained the purity of the Dharma-eye and those who entered the subtle depths through meditative contemplation were beyond counting—all owe their first arrowhead to my Patriarch.

Now, the Great Master Hanshan Deqing, while exiled to the miasmic seas for the sake of propagating the Dharma, skillfully employed the Samādhi of Compassionate Mind to cause withered bones everywhere to bloom with spring. This is the sacred flower.

The lay devotee, moved by the reputation he had heard and filled with longing, specially commissioned a portrait of the Patriarch and sent it up to Caoxi to serve as a representation of the Great Master.
Alas! Since the Tang and through the Song dynasties, those who drank from the waters of Caoxi and attained the Way have appeared generation after generation without fail.
Lately, however, Caoxi has run dry; the rustling of its trees is desolate once more, and we must rely yet again upon Master Han.
Taking penal exile as a surging wave, the source of Cao was revitalized; the Patriarch Kang manifested his body in many forms, and the eyes within the skull were opened.
These things are difficult to compare even to the sands of the Ganges; how could one possibly fathom the depth of such merit with a conceptual, discursive mind?
The Daoist Daguang does not know how to steer against the wind; he only knows how to push a boat with the current.

For him, I offer this eulogy: Master Kang came to Wu; Master Qing was exiled to Yue. The Great Master Skull had diamond-like eyes protruding. Amidst the horrors of the miasmic sea, [he remained steadfast].

His bones trembled and his soul was startled; that the Great Master attained victory further moved him to feel the Sage’s brilliance. At Caoxi, the poison was so virulent that all who drank it perished, yet the Great Master drank it and exhausted all his hindrances.
Pointing his finger to grasp the *śarīra*, he lamented the greed of the former patriarchs: "To covet for oneself—how can such a heart not feel shame?

Though he incurred the offense of propagating the Dharma, his life was as fragile as a single strand of silk; he traversed the thousand-li miasma-covered ridges, his straw sandals covering every path.

The path of thunder is steep and precipitous, and the typhoon is at its height. The almsbowl and flask travel alone; the mark of the tongue is resplendent. In Nan Yue, ghosts and spirits clap their hands in broad daylight.
If I were without mind, the Bodhisattva would be but a shadow and an echo; because I have a mind, he responds to me. Master Kang was but a fool.

In the land of those who wear the *zhangfu* cap, who would not harbor doubts? At the Stone Head (Shitou) monastery, our innermost hearts were as cold as ice. Master Ding blew the fire; he transcribed the portrait of Master Kang.
Through the shadow he attained the mind; when the mind is forgotten, nature becomes dark and profound. Great function is impermanent; the bell is heard with the eyes.
Roots and objects, subject and object; gathering and releasing, dreaming and waking. Holding aloft a jade pagoda upon the summit of Mount Laoshan.
In Praise of the Footprint at the Guanyin Hall of Jiafu Temple on Mount Tanxia (With Preface):
Wu Zai took vengeance for his father’s disgrace and destroyed Yue; Goujian tasted gall and annihilated Wu; Wu Yuan overturned Chu; Shen... [text fragment]

Liu Baoxu wept at the court of Qin to restore the state of Chu; in all such cases, one must exert the mind and will, labor the muscles and bones, accumulate months and years, and forget both cold and heat before one’s wish can finally be fulfilled.

Now this practitioner, using the soles of his sentient feet to rub against the insentient stone, has worn a path through it until his two footprints are perfectly formed. When those who see them in the future perceive them, their hair and pores shall stand on end.
Shu stood there, tears streaming down his face. The habit of indolence and the light of diligence were like clouds dispersing to reveal the sun.
When comparing the accumulated mental power of Fu Chai and his four sons with the physical strength of this practitioner, how can they possibly be equal?
Moved by this, I offer this eulogy; not merely out of a desire to emulate the worthy, but hoping that everyone will be inspired to exert themselves through these words of praise.
From exertion arises constancy; from constancy, one achieves mastery. [The Commentator] says:
I prostrate at the traces of the practitioner’s two feet; the hairs on my body involuntarily stand on end all at once. The habit of beginningless indolence is suddenly eliminated;
the clouds of the celestial realm disperse, and the sun of diligence breaks forth. Thinking that this person had not yet passed away, I pay reverent homage morning and evening with earnest devotion.
O Great Being, with the mind fixed upon your holy countenance and the name being recited by the mouth, how could the bending and stretching of the physical frame be calculated?

Days accumulate to form months; months accumulate to form seasons; seasons accumulate to form years; and years accumulate to form kalpas. Such gradual accumulation is difficult to describe in its entirety.

A drop of water pierces stone through the power of the mind reaching its limit. It is like beginning the first step toward a thousand li, or like the growth of a hair-tip from a tree trunk as thick as two arms. Thus, it is achieved from the heel.
The *zhuan* (mortar) gradually wears away; though the *zhuan* is worn, my diligent effort has not yet ceased. The *zhuan* pierces through the great earth to support the soles of my feet;
though the earth is pierced, people do not see it. I alone understand this clearly, without doubt or hesitation; because of this, I am restless with grief and weep.
May I, from this moment until my final prostration, take diligence as my feet to tread upon the ground of awakening.

May adverse and favorable conditions be like snow cast into boiling water, or like a sharp blade cutting through fresh bamboo—solving itself at the first touch and vanishing upon contact with heat. May I always possess such mastery in every place and circumstance.
Furthermore, may all who see or hear of these traces find their momentary laziness completely dissolved like ice.
I praise myself for making a house out of stone; from the beginning, there has been neither success nor failure. Wind and dust betray my feelings; water and moonlight settle my debts.

The pearl of the mind is silent and still; the realm of the eye is like empty space. Wearing the robes of the fields, I stand in respectful silence; treading on one another’s feet, we perform these strange antics. Heh! Neither the Teachings nor the School are understood.
When one is first wealthy and noble, who can compete with them?
Some say, "You are too expansive," while I laugh at you for being so narrow-minded. Upon seeing the good, I rejoice; upon seeing the evil, I find no pleasure.

If good and evil have not yet been forgotten from your heart, how can you enter the state of non-attachment? Furthermore, you say, "I am clearly enlightened; having enlightened myself, I shall deliver the multitude.

You believe yourself to be a living Buddha, and day and night you give rise to such earnest devotion. I know that your views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) still remain, and that you have not yet ascended to the emptiness of dharmas (*dharmāśūnyatā*).
Preaching the Dharma while still harboring worldly emotions is to deceive the deaf and the blind. I have heard it said: "To know others is wisdom; to know oneself is clarity. As for you—
Regarding these two, what serves as the balance? E! To preach the Dharma with emotion—what is this "emotion"? Light and darkness intersect;
the agent alone knows.
If you were I, then all the various beauties and uglinesses of the mundane and supramundane worlds could not deceive you by even a single point. I—
If it were you, at every critical juncture of adversity and favor, at the crossroads of birth and death, you would pass like the wind through trees or clouds striking a rock.
Even so, this is not necessarily the true character of an old man. If one were to manifest that true character, one could guarantee that both ordinary beings and sages would lose their souls;
yet the "poisonous drum" remains silent. There are those who do not know where your feet are planted, searching for it in vain.
Look upward! Ultimately, from where did you arise? Simply say to him: "I smile at my own tracks, like a wild crane;
weary from flying over the front ridge, there is a tall pine tree."
If he is me, what remains of me? If I am he, where does he linger? To give rise to a mind of discrimination is to sever the flow of the lifeblood;
to not discriminate is the straightforward principle of the School. When withered trees bloom and stubborn stones nod their heads, one plants the weeds of the house;
the Spring and Autumn Annals are hidden within the skin. *Ei!* Do not say there is no wit when you meet—there is much!
There are few fish or dragons in the silver sea.
You, man of little merit, meddle too much; seeing someone, you immediately urge them to study Bodhi, yet you also know how to talk of others' long points and speak of their short faults.
The moon over Songjiang—Who can recognize it? Tonight it hangs bright and white against the azure void. Limitless fish and dragons are busy sucking at its reflection;
the river waves roll on, churning up muddy sludge. Old Hermit Ānāṃda stares with wide eyes into a cauldron of lime ash.

Inside the Crystal Hermitage is the lair of Li Lou. Within this dream, the spring surges are swift. Do not drink the water from a house of venomous insects. Whether you know it or not, the life-root is severed.
When the life-faculty is severed, where does one stand? Turning back to regain the body is like waking from a dream. All that gold is but empty space and bone.
At the peak of Niu-wei and by the side of Hsien-hua Rock, I do not shrink from the mists and clouds to visit this old man; such was the karmic connection of days past.

The clouds of floating jade are intertwined; the moon upon the golden tortoise shines. With the mark of the broad and long tongue, he speaks with clarity: "North of the River and south of the River, spring is fundamentally the same;
yet the peach is red and the plum is white—their colors are distinct. But tell me, what is it that is being distinguished? In whose hearth is there no smoke?
Let the wind blow from the side as it will; he remains utterly at ease.
I ask him, "Where is your home? He roams freely and unrestrainedly between north and south. At times he gazes upon the surging waves; at others he lets out a long啸 (shout) from atop the lofty ridges.

His obsession with mountains and waters is most profound; it is beyond comparison even to a terminal illness. Neither the Son of Heaven can make him a minister, nor can the feudal lords form a faction with him.
Life and death are viewed as a single thread; how could honor and disgrace be two separate thoughts? Yet there is another kind of clumsiness: failing to measure one's own weight.
Even the Buddhas and Patriarchs must be weighed on the scale. When the winds of circumstance blow favorably or unfavorably, let one’s conduct and withdrawal follow their natural ebbs and flows.

An empty boat crosses the swift current; fish and dragons depend on its overturning or upright position. Tigers and rhinoceroses are known for their ferocity; the clanging of a monk’s staff and rings resonates unevenly.

To be fastidious brings misfortune even in times of auspiciousness; to be dull-witted and ignorant may yet bring prosperity. When both head and tail are completely cut off, the central pillar is lost.

To love the good and hate the evil; to praise the praiseworthy and revile the blameworthy—every path one encounters leads into these attachments. To give rise to such thoughts is quickly to create an obstacle.

I recall in the past ascending Mount Ge Hong, where my staff turned back as the waters of Tian-shui swelled. At the River Bridge, black and white were arrayed; shaking my head, I ascended upon the bright moon.

The Marquis of Chen is none other than Samantabhadra; their pure radiance is fundamentally one and the same. As the evening bell tolls at Yongning Temple, how many times have I longed for his iron staff?
His lofty traces cannot be pursued, leaving me with a profound sense of regret. From the vast, clear sky he does not come afar; from amidst the azure clouds he seeks out your likeness.
Speaking freely, he recounted the past; holding it back, he offered it as a constant供养 (offering).
Among the Chan practitioners from all quarters, who does not have a karmic connection (生緣) from birth? Yet you alone remained silent at first—like the azure sky reflected within the water.
Without wind, the waves are naturally still; with shadow, the form is inherently present. If one calls this a monk, he possesses a faint beard and mustache;
if one calls him a layman, his eyes look through the Chan of the Patriarchs. If one says he cannot be named, why are there so many borrowed titles?

He habitually used the hammer of light and dark; with that hammer, he shattered the bottomless boat. But tell me, when the bottom of the boat is shattered, where does one find a place to settle and establish one’s life?
It is enough to let the fragrance of wisdom permeate the Dharma-realm; the misty waters of the Wu River remain as they were from the start.

Shaded by deep purple cypresses, the withered Chan practitioner rests; A single path of divine light illuminates the great thousandfold world. In this world, it is difficult to find a smile upon opening the mouth;
By the clouds, one may always sleep with the head resting on the flowing stream.
"You are I; a sliver of moon in the sky, its reflection reaches a thousand ravines. I am you; when wisdom is exhausted and emotion withered, the mud ox lets out a roar.
Now tell me, whose tune is this? *Pah!* When the clouds over the sea-mountain have vanished, the Flower Rock emerges;
before Guangde Hermitage, the spring waters run deep."
"You are I, yet you possess no awareness at all; I am you, yet delusive thoughts fly about in confusion. Joined, we are not one; separated, our doubts increase further.
Even with the brilliance of Nāgārjuna or the wisdom of Śāriputra, it would be difficult to discern this.

This person is by nature arrogant and unrestrained; his inner mind is muddled and unrefined. He disregards rules and standards, regarding profit and loss as a mere dream. He possesses quite a heroic..."
In his heart, he harbored no ambition for fame or achievement; thus, it was difficult to detain him within the mundane world. He was content only to roam freely among springs and rocks.

Furthermore, he possessed a certain air of arrogance, considering that Buddhas and patriarchs were of dull faculties and limited capacity, while even the "black slaves" and "white oxen" were fit to be his companions.
At times, he would cite the teachings to verify the essence of the school, or use the essence of the school to seal the teachings; at other times, he would treat thorns and rubble as [the path].
Everything is a treasure. Sometimes coral and agate are not worth so much as dung and weeds. A single tongue is unfixed in its praise or blame;
right and wrong are thrown into confusion. Where there is kindness, it is no different from enmity; where there is no feeling, it is accustomed to lingering.
Most especially, your moods of joy and anger are inconsistent; you are like an infant. I see that you deal with people without employing any stratagems;
when touched upon, you prattle on aimlessly, provoking others' hatred or affection while remaining yourself as foolish and simple-minded as ever.
You put on this single red Zen robe and feel joyful; yet if you were to be seen through by a single man of piercing gaze, I would watch you—[and you would be undone].
Not worth a single coin. Hehehe! Who can recommend this? The scales are in hand; one may suppress or exalt as one pleases. If you want someone to live, they live; if you want them to die, they die.
Morning offerings, evening offerings—anger and joy are ever-changing waves of consciousness. One must simply be able to die at once, right here and now, and steal away the calculating mind.
This is the true wondrous mark of this old fellow: a purple silk robe and an old monk’s cassock; looking at these two, which is superior? Sandalwood and dog dung are clearly present;
at the threshold of the ordinary and the sage, the path is not far. If you understand thus, there is no turning away or following after.
Flowing waters and green mountains are entirely unclouded; this very lack of obscuration is the lotus within the fire. Fragrance and light, the moon of precepts, are free from flaw or blemish.
*Praise for the Blood-Scripture Diamond Sūtra*
I prostrate to the Diamond Sūtra, the Prajñā that is most firm and sharp; among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), none can surpass it.
If a person sees even a single character, or hears a single phrase, or even as few as four lines, their merit is inconceivable.
Ink-inscription is not as good as silver; silver-inscription is not as good as gold; gold-inscription is not as good as blood.

In the Sahā world, in the land of China, there was a woman of great diligence who viewed her body as being like a bubble and understood that the mind is fundamentally an illusion. With a single thought of firm and steadfast faith, she [inscribed it with her own blood].
Having pricked the ten fingers until they bled, I have written down this unsurpassed treasure. May all who see or hear it suddenly empty the attachments of body and mind.
Wielding this vajra-sword, may they sever all hatred and love. Such wondrous benefit is not sought for the sake of human merit.
I dedicate this merit to the ocean of Prajñā, to bathe my body of five outflows and obtain a pure body of the seven jewels. As a *kumārabhūta* (vimala-kumāra), I sever worldly defilements;
having early encountered a teacher with the clear eye, I have awakened to the mind as a Buddha’s son and propagate that wondrous Lotus Sūtra, its sound shaking the lands of all atoms.

Whether without mind or with mind, there is no cultivation of the noble seeds through external conditions; how much less so for this scripture written in my own blood? How could its karmic fruit be in vain or deceptive?

The Bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya praised the jade palaces and golden gates as being equal to a speck of dust; he did not value wealth or status, but instead exerted his body for this purpose. The clouds and mountains stretch vast and azure.
Using stone as his bed, his mind is like empty space. A king among monks, clad in the robes of a field-laborer, his nostrils are high and noble;

he bears the Great Dharma upon his shoulders as a bridge across the sea of suffering. His head is perfectly rounded, the spiral curls long since removed; were one to seek even a single strand, it would not be found.
Snow touches the red furnace. I bow my head to Cunda, the patriarch of the bhikṣus, who continues the lamp of the Buddha’s mind, its light transmitted through eternity.
This light is not the moon; the moon has waxing and waning, but that which neither waxes nor wanes—the bhikṣu should explain it. To explain it, yet not hear it.

Having submerged myself in the clouds of delusion, I troubled others with my wooden-stone-like dullness; my loquacity startled the multitude, yet through that very shock, I suddenly attained realization. With willow branches I rescued the sick, and by untying the water jar I entered the depths of Chan.
Obeying the Tathāgata’s command, the sound of the spring resounds through a thousand peaks; with eyes beholding the True Commandment, I abide in the ultimate state.
In Praise of the Bamboo Staff: Whence has this "Gentleman" come? It accords with my long-held aspiration. When there is support, it supports; when there is nothing, it sustains.
Mount Emei and Mount Wutai—when the hand is as if holding the staff, and the staff does not hold the hand, one sees directly beneath. Do not run to either end.
In the eulogy of Han Shan and Shi De:
The elder brother holds a rosary; the younger brother grasps a broom. If one asks which is male and which is female, the clay ox bellows. Whether in mountain forests or city markets.
Together seek the unborn; grasp the image and meet the meaning. By casting off the coarse, one attains the subtle.
A verse on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: The Buddha told Ānanda, "When I do not see, why do you not see the place where I do not see?"
If you see that which is not seen, it is naturally not the characteristic of "not seeing. If you do not see the ground of my non-seeing, it is naturally not a thing;
how could it not be you? Chan Master Zhantang Zhun’s verse says: "The Old Barbarian [the Buddha] exhausted his grandmotherly heart;
for Ānanda, his intent grew even deeper. Han Gan’s horse neighs as it crosses the fragrant grasses; Dai..."
The bull of Mount Song lies resting in the shade of green willows. The verse says:
The azure dragon is accustomed to delighting in lying in the deep springs; the black pearl beneath its chin shines ever more brilliantly.
If one asks who is able to pluck it out, it transforms into the sun and moon to illuminate the mountains and rivers.
Once, Nanquan encountered the monks of the East and West Halls as they were each disputing over a cat. He addressed the assembly, saying, "If you can speak [the truth], I shall save the cat;
if you cannot, I shall put it to death. The assembly was speechless. Nanquan then killed it.
When Zhaozhou returned from outside, the Master brought up the previous conversation and showed it to him. Zhaozhou then took off his straw sandals, placed them on his head, and went out.

The Master said, "If you had been here just now, you could have saved the cat. The Verse says: The cat was lost; the master’s heart was grieved. Zhaozhou placed his sandals upon his head. If he had been there at that moment, He would have rescued the cat.

Had Nanquan not raised his blade, where would the straw sandals have displayed their charms? If you should meet those guests from the two halls and ask them about it, they all have straight noses and brows arched across their faces—they are all cats by nature.
The cat was not necessarily worth a thousand pieces of gold; it provoked even the Head Monk to feel moved. With a single stroke of the hand, it was cut in two;
he took away the blood-stained straw sandals.

Huangbo said, "You are all nothing but fellows who eat the dregs of wine. Do you know that within the Great Tang there are no Chan masters? At that time, a monk asked, "The various quarters gather crowds of followers; why do you say instead that there are no Chan masters? The Master replied, "I do not say there are no Chan, I only say there are no teachers. He then spoke this verse: All of you are nothing but fellows who eat the dregs of wine. Do you know that within the Great Tang there are no Chan masters? If you ask me why I say there are no Chan masters, I do not say there is no Chan; I only say there are no teachers. If you can understand this, you will see the true meaning of the Buddhas and patriarchs. If you cannot understand it, you will fall into the pit of views and attachments. If you can understand it, you will transcend the three realms of existence. If you cannot understand it, you will remain bound by the six paths of rebirth. If you can understand it, you will realize the Way of the Buddhas. If you cannot understand it, you will wander in the sea of suffering. If you can understand it, you will attain liberation from birth and death. If you cannot understand it, you will continue to revolve in the cycle of samsara. If you can understand it, you will see your own original face. If you cannot understand it, you will be obscured by delusion and ignorance. If you can understand it, you will manifest the great function of the Way. If you cannot understand it, you will be trapped in the net of conceptualization. If you can understand it, you will be free from all attachments. If you cannot understand it, you will be bound by all things. If you can understand it, you will be at ease wherever you go. If you cannot understand it, you will be troubled wherever you stay. If you can understand it, you will be like the sun and moon in the sky. If you cannot understand it, you will be like a cloud covering the heavens. If you can understand it, you will be like the great earth supporting all. Year after year, year after year, he consumes dregs of wine; lost in flowers and intoxicated by willows, his waves flow on. His two eyes have been traded away for donkey dung;
with a smile, as he departs, he offers you this cup.
One day, as the meal was late, Deshan set down his alms bowl and went out from the hall. At that time, Xuefeng was serving as the head cook;
seeing him, he said, "This old fellow, the bell has not yet rung and the drum has not yet sounded—where are you going with your bowl?
Deshan then returned to his quarters. Xuefeng reported this to Yantou, who said, "Great Deshan does not yet understand the final word. Deshan heard of this.
Upon hearing this, he ordered his attendant to summon Tou. He asked, "Do you refuse me, an old monk? Tou secretly conveyed his intention. The Master then desisted.
The following day, when the Master ascended the hall, it was indeed different from his usual manner. Tou went before the Sangha Hall.

Clapping his hands, he laughed loudly and said, "I am glad that this old man understands the final phrase. Nevertheless, it shall only last for three years. The Master indeed passed away after three years. He spoke this verse: Clapping my hands, I laugh aloud:
"I rejoice that this old fellow understands the final phrase. Though it be so, it shall only last for three years. The Master truly passed away after three years. The verse says:
Gusou dug a well and forced Shun to enter; Xiang hurriedly filled it with earth and stones. How tragic, O Shun! When will you emerge?
It was not necessarily the true thief who passed through the gate.
Furthermore:
Ringing the bell and eating a meal are matters of daily life; yet this old fellow was uniquely the first to receive his alms bowl.
Had it not been for Xuefeng’s personal penetration of the matter, Yantou would surely have been left utterly bewildered.
Furthermore:
With his white hair hanging down, he comes forth from the hall; holding aloft a single bowl, how extraordinary!
Had it not been for Yantou’s personal piercing revelation, his eyes would remain closed in sleep to this very day.
Chan Master Wuyin of Heishan in Jizhou addressed the assembly, saying: "To study and learn is called 'hearing. To sever learning is called 'the neighbor.
To go beyond these two is called 'truly transcending. A monk asked, "What is truly transcending?
The Master said, "Heishan knows how to beat the drum. The monk asked, "What is the True Truth? The Master said, "Heishan knows how to beat the drum. Furthermore...

A questioner asked, "If you say 'this very mind is Buddha,' why do you not ask what it means to say 'neither mind nor Buddha'? The Master replied, "Heishan knows how to beat the drum. The questioner asked, "What is the matter beyond this?

The Master replied, "Heishan knows how to beat the drum. He then offered this verse: Heishan knows how to beat the drum; Heishan knows how to beat the drum. The matter beyond this is Heishan beating the drum. The matter beyond this is Heishan beating the drum.
Mount Kunlun is the pole, the Yangtze River the line; Mount Tai is the bait, to catch the leviathans. *Du!* How strange!
The peach-blossom winds and rains are fierce; fish and dragons alike are lost amidst the surging waves.
Chan Master Baoyun Shouduan went to visit Yangqi. One day, Yangqi suddenly asked, "Who is your preceptor?
The Master replied, "The Venerable Yuru of Chaling. Yangqi said, "I have heard that he had an awakening after falling while crossing a bridge."
"The verse you have composed is most extraordinary. Can you recite it? The Master recited it: "I possess a bright pearl, Long locked away by the dust of worldly toil.
Today, the dust is cleared and the light shines forth, Illuminating ten thousand peaks of mountains and rivers. Daofu smiled and hurriedly rose.
The Master was struck with astonishment and could not sleep all night. At dawn, he questioned Daofu about it. It happened to be the end of the year, and Daofu said, "You..."
"Did you see those who were performing the *ou-no* exorcism yesterday? He replied, "I saw them. Qiji said, "In this, you fall short by one move.

The Master was again startled and asked, "What is the meaning of this? Qiji said, "He enjoyed being laughed at; you feared being laughed at. The Master attained great enlightenment and composed a verse:
[Verse omitted as per instructions]
From of old, the likes of Bo Le and Jiu Fang Gao have caused even the price of a common hack to double;
yet they fear ridicule because their hearts harbor regret, falling one move short of the wild foxes and Cao.
Furthermore:
On the riverbank, greedily watching the high surging waves, one’s oar was snatched away by another; the solitary boat tossed by the wind had no master at all.
A single laugh reveals clearly the sword that governs both killing and giving life.
Verse: Xuefeng, you tiger!
When the light returns to illuminate itself, the mind has no fear. You tiger, who knows that the light is perfectly round? Most bitter is the monk becoming a different species;
once a human body is lost, when will it ever be restored?

The verse says: "Hearing the sound of hairpins and bracelets through a wall—outside the ear there is sound, yet this [sound] does not exist [there]. Apart from the sound, the existence of the ear is likewise non-existent. One should go before the lamp and examine the sound and the ear.
Among five-colored filth, one finds a single pearl."
A verse: Before the mountain of the five aggregates lies a stretch of emptiness;
when there is a self, it constantly turns its back on the Lord. When there is no self, where does it not encounter [the Lord]?
It plays at will upon the mountain of knives and the mass of fire, never failing that stretch of emptiness before the mountain.

A monk asked Zhaozhou, "The myriad dharmas return to the One; where does the One return? Zhaozhou said, "I am in Qingzhou, making a cotton robe that weighs seven catties. A verse says: The myriad dharmas return to the One; The One returns to the place of no-return. In Qingzhou, I am making a cotton robe; Its weight is seven catties.
When the time comes for it to be worn, It will naturally cover you from head to toe. If you wish to know its price, Go ask the people of Qingzhou.
The seven-pound robe was made in Qingzhou; half a month it sank into the river, and the fish feared the hook.
How strange that the azure dragon is ultimately different—once returned, where does he go to roam at ease?

Linji, in his ordinary discourses on the high seat, would say: "Within the lump of red flesh that you all possess, there is a true person of no station who constantly enters and exits through the gate of the face, illuminating heaven and earth.

Yet, none of you have been able to realize this. He then spoke a verse: The true person of no station Constantly enters and exits the face-gate; He illuminates heaven and earth— Why do you fail to recognize him?
The "True Person Without Rank" is a dried-up dung-club; one name for two realities, causing people to speculate. His own house naturally has a man of penetration;
how could he be like Han Lu chasing after a clod of earth?
Chan Master Fushan Fayuan retired to Huisheng Rock in his later years. There he expounded the profound meanings of the Buddhas and patriarchs and composed the Nine Baskets (*jiu dai*), which are:

the Basket of the Buddha’s True Dharma Eye; the Basket of the Buddha’s Dharma Treasury; the Basket of the Pervasion of Principle; the Basket of the Pervasion of Phenomena; the Basket of the Interpenetration of Principle and Phenomena;
the Basket of the Crooked and the Direct; the Basket of the Subtle Harmony of Both; the Basket of the Golden Needle and Double Lock; and the Basket of Even-mindedness.

The "Constant Reality" (Changshi) Band: Having already transmitted and recited [the previous teachings], the Master said, "According to the perfectly ultimate Dharma-gate, there are originally ten bands.
Now, these nine bands have already been explained for you all. Is there yet another band that you can perceive?
If you can perceive it intimately and clearly, then please come forward and explain it before the assembly. If you can explain it..."
"Clearly! I grant you the penetrating, ninefold, perfectly luminous eye of the Way. If your vision were not intimate and direct, your words would be inconsistent.
To act solely according to my words while claiming it as your own understanding is called slandering the Dharma.
When you reach this point, what will you do? The assembly remained silent. The Master rebuked them and departed. He then spoke a verse:
No sitting place; no sitting place. You must remember the five ranks and nine bands. The wind and rain have come at night, and the peach blossoms fall;
meeting one another everywhere, where can one avoid it?
Changshui asked Langye, "If it is fundamentally pure and still, why do mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? Langye replied, "It is fundamentally pure and still;

why do mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? He then spoke this verse: Fundamentally pure and still, How do mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? Fundamentally pure and still, How do mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?
The infant has long been orphaned and wandering in exile; meeting you unexpectedly on the road, I call out your name once.
Knowing the place where your mother’s heart breaks, even an iron-hearted man must let his tears flow.

Grand Master Lu Xun raised the *Treatise by Sengzhao* and said to Nanquan, "What Master Zhao calls 'the ten thousand things as one body' and 'heaven and earth sharing the same root' is truly extraordinary.
Nanquan pointed to the peony in front of the courtyard and said, "Grand Master, people of this day..."
Seeing this single branch of blossoms is like a dream. The verse says:
The dragon emerges and wields the brush—how could this be real? Floating clouds bestow rain, yet they further deceive people. To speak of dreams within a dream, those who understand are few;
Flowers fall before the courtyard—the spring has already passed.
The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "At all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts; yet do not attempt to extinguish these deluded minds.

Abide within the realm of deluded perceptions without applying analytical knowledge; and within this lack of analytical knowledge, do not discriminate between what is real and what is false. The verse says:
One’s own itching and pain one must scratch oneself; if scratching it wounds you deeply, do not lament. Green bamboos and yellow flowers are found everywhere;
from the south to the north of the Yangtze, the road is not far.
Cen Master Yantou Quanhuo encountered the suppression of the Buddhist monastic order and took up work as a ferryman on the shores of Lake Ezu.

He hung a wooden board on each bank; whenever someone wished to cross, he would strike the board once, and the master would dance his oars to welcome them. One day, a woman carrying a child approached him.

As she approached, he said: "I shall not ask about you presenting the oar and dancing with the paddle; but tell me, from where did this child in the old woman’s hand come? The Master struck her. The old woman said: "The old woman gave birth to seven sons; six did not meet with one who understands them. This one alone is not even worth keeping," and she threw him into the water. As soon as that foul mouth opens, one strikes with a sudden shove. The old woman, having no stratagem, reeks of blood and stench;
she casts her infant into the cold waves, provoking the fish and dragons of the four seas to clamor in turmoil.

One day, the World-Honored One ascended the seat. As soon as the great assembly had gathered and settled, Mañjuśrī struck the gavel and said: "Contemplate clearly the Dharma of the Dharma-King; the Dharma of the Dharma-King is thus.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One descended from the seat. The verse says: The World-Honored One ascends the seat; The assembly gathers and settles. Mañjuśrī strikes the gavel: "Clearly contemplate the Dharma of the Dharma-King; The Dharma of the Dharma-King is thus. The World-Honored One then descends from the seat.
The Elder Gautama possesses nothing extraordinary; it is the junior monk who must know that he is not the same. Meeting him within the inner depths, one can understand him thoroughly.
On Vulture Peak, who is the true master?
Furthermore:
When saints and ordinary people gather like clouds, it cannot be for no reason. If there is a matter at hand, why does his mouth not open? The Elder, knowing for certain, descends from his seat;
Mañjuśrī strikes with his mallet, causing others to speculate.
Furthermore:
A tiger crouching in the deep forest leaves no trace; as soon as its claws and fangs are bared, its majesty is lost. The hunter’s bow and arrows are ever-present;
in the instant the string rings out, life has already ended.
Furthermore:
When saints and ordinary beings gather like clouds, the occasion is no ordinary one. Sitting upon the seat, why not proclaim the teaching? Fortunately there is Mañjuśrī who knows how to gather it up;
thus the light shines at both ends—above and below.
At Huating in Xiuzhou was Chan Master Chuangzi Decheng, who had received the seal of his mind from Yaoshan. He maintained a close friendship with Daowu and Yunyan.
Upon leaving Yaoshan, he said to his companions, "I am by nature simple and rustic, and I delight only in mountains and waters.
Hereafter, should you know where I have settled, when you encounter a clever lecturer, send someone to point him out to me. Thereupon, they parted ways.
I arrived at Huating and traveled in a small boat, passing my days according to circumstances. Later, when I reached Jingkou, I encountered Jia Shan presiding over the assembly.
A monk asked, "What is the Dharma-body? He replied, "The Dharma-body is formless. The monk asked, "What is the Dharma-eye?
He replied, "The Dharma-eye is without flaw. I let out a laugh. Jia Shan descended from his seat and asked me, "How did you respond to this?"
In the monastic discourse, there must be something incorrect that causes one to laugh. I hope you will not withhold your compassion.
I said, "Venerable Master, you are equally one who has left the world, yet you have no teacher. Baoshan asked, "Where is it incorrect? I replied, "I shall certainly not say;
I request that you go to Chuanzhi at Huating. Baoshan asked, "What is this man like? I said, "This man..."
Above, there was not a single tile; below, there was not even space for the point of a锥 (a small awl). If he were to leave, he would have to change his robes before going.
Deshan then dispersed his assembly and went directly to Huating. As soon as Chuanzhi saw him, he asked, "Virtuous One, in what monastery do you reside?
Deshan said, "I do not reside in a monastery; where I reside is not like [an ordinary place]. The Master said, "What is it that is 'not like'? Deshan said, "It is not."
The Master asked, "Where did you learn this? Sansheng said, "It is not something reached by the ears or the eyes.
The Master said, "A single phrase that fits the head is a tethering stake for ten thousand kalpas. The Master further asked, "The line hangs down a thousand feet;
the intent lies in the deep pool. It is three inches away from the hook—why do you not speak? As Sansheng prepared to open his mouth, the Master struck him.
He attained a sudden and great enlightenment. He then nodded his head three times. The Master said, "The line on the tip of the pole is for you to play with;
yet, by not disturbing the clear waves, your intent is naturally extraordinary. Shan then asked, "When casting the line and throwing the hook, what is your intention, Master? The Master said:
A thread hangs over the green water; floating, it conveys a sense of both existence and non-existence. Shanshan said, "The words carry the profound yet there is no path;
the tongue speaks, yet it does not speak. The Master said, "Having fished through the waves of the river, at last the magnificent-scaled fish is encountered. Shanshan then covered his ears.
The Master said, "So it is, so it is. He then instructed him, saying, "In the future, you must leave no trace where you hide your body, and do not hide your body where there is no trace.
For thirty years I was at Yaoshan, and I understood nothing other than this matter."
"You have now attained it. Hereafter, do not dwell in cities or villages; go instead into the deep mountains.
By the side of your mattock, seek out one or two [disciples] to carry on the lineage, so that it shall never be severed. Shan then took his leave, looking back again and again.
The Master called out, "Śrāmaṇera! Shan turned his head. The Master held up his oar and said, "Take this."
It is said that he departed by overturning his boat and entering the water. A verse says:
The enmity between father and son is bound most deeply; Who knows the heart of one who capsizes his boat to end his own life? The moon upon the waters of Zhu Jing remains as it was before;
How many times have they passed in vain, the mind still unresolved?
Furthermore:
A pair of liver and intestines sliced away without remainder—Jia Shan still turned his head back in secret darkness. Where the wind is calm and the waves are still, the boat capsizes;
amidst the whistling of the duckweed and sedges lies ten thousand ages of sorrow.
Furthermore:
"I grant you fifteen blows; I regret that you do not know the mind. Last night was the moon over Huating; how deep or shallow was the Zhu Jing?
When the First Patriarch, Master Bodhidharma, first crossed over to China, he arrived at Jinling and met Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty.
The Emperor asked, "What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths? The Master replied, "Vast and empty—there is no sage. The Emperor asked, "Who is it that faces me?
The Master replied, "I do not know. The Emperor did not attain realization. The Master then broke off a reed and crossed the river to Wei.

Later, Emperor Wu raised this matter and questioned Master Zhigong. The Master said, "Your Majesty, do you know this person? The Emperor replied, "I do not know him. Zhigong said, "This is the Great Being Avalokiteśvara, who transmits the Buddha’s Mind-Seal.

The Emperor said, "I shall dispatch an envoy to summon him. Zhigong said, "Do not say 'Your Majesty summons him. Even if the people of the entire nation go, he will still not return. He then offered this verse: The Emperor asks about the one with the white hair;

Zhigong replies that he does not know him. He is the Great Being Avalokiteśvara, Transmitting the Buddha’s Mind-Seal. If the Emperor sends an envoy to summon him, Even the people of the whole land would fail to bring him back.
Master Xiao was no ordinary man; upon seeing him, he immediately scattered the dust before his face.
This left the Old Barbarian with nowhere to place his hands, so he broke reeds and hurriedly crossed the river ferry.
Mañjuśrī was at the assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, the gathering place of all Buddhas. He saw a woman sitting near the Buddha, having entered into samādhi.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying, "Why is this woman permitted to sit so close to the Buddha? The Buddha replied:
“You need only awaken this woman and cause her to rise from samādhi; you may question her yourself.

Mañjuśrī circumambulated the woman three times and snapped his fingers once. Even when he had carried her up as far as the Brahma Heaven, he could not bring her out despite exhausting all his supernatural powers.
The Buddha said, “Even if there were hundreds of thousands of Mañjuśrīs, they still could not bring this woman out of her concentration. Below here, beyond...”
"In twenty-four lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is the Bodhisattva Vimalaprabhā who can bring this woman out of her concentration.
In a brief moment, Vimalaprabhā arrived at the Buddha’s presence. The Buddha commanded him to bring this woman out of her concentration.
Vimalaprabhā then snapped his fingers once before the woman; she thereupon emerged from her concentration. The verse says:

Entering meditative concentration, one rests near the Buddha through others; traveling by land in carriages and horses, or navigating the waters in boats—Wang Ming displays his brilliance with a light snap of the fingers, yet even this is sorrow provoked by the absence of sorrow.

Xuefeng was once asked by Sansheng, "What does the golden fish that has passed through the net eat? The Master said, "I will tell you when you have emerged from the net. Sansheng said, "A teacher of fifteen hundred people and yet you do not even recognize the point of the question! The Master said, "The affairs of this old monk’s abbacy are many. He then spoke this verse: The golden fish has already passed through the net; What need is there to ask what it eats? If you wish to know its food, Wait until it emerges from the net. Then I shall speak to you. But if you still ask, I am a man of many duties. I cannot answer you. If you can understand this, You may be called a true successor. If you cannot, You are merely a person of empty talk. Do not seek it outside yourself; Seeking it is a great error. If you can see it within yourself, You will surely attain liberation. If you do not, You will remain lost in delusion. This is the Dharma of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; It is not something to be grasped by the intellect. If you can realize it in this very moment, You will transcend birth and death. If you do not, You will continue to wander in the cycle of existence. Therefore, strive with all your might! Do not let this opportunity pass. This is the essential teaching of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; It is not something to be found in books or words. If you can see it directly, You will attain the Way. If you do not, You will remain bound by views and attachments. Therefore, practice with diligence! Do not waste your life. This is the true path of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; It is not something to be sought through external effort. If you can awaken to it within, You will realize the nature of reality. If you do not, You will remain caught in the web of conceptual thought. Therefore, let go of all seeking! Rest in the natural state. This is the ultimate teaching of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; It is not something to be attained through striving. If you can let go of all grasping, You will enter the realm of non-duality. If you do not, You will remain trapped in the duality of subject and object. Therefore, abandon all effort! Be at ease in the present moment. This is the heart-essence of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; It is not something to be understood through logic or reasoning. If you can see it clearly, You will be free from all doubt. If you do not, You will remain mired in confusion and ignorance. Therefore, cultivate with sincerity! Do not follow after appearances. This is the profound Dharma of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; It is not something to be realized through intellectual analysis. If you can cut through all conceptualization, You will manifest the true mind. If you do not, You will remain bound by the illusions of the world. Therefore, practice with earnestness! Do not be distracted by external things. This is the direct transmission of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; It is not something to be learned from teachers or scriptures. If you can see it for yourself, You will attain the fruit of enlightenment. If you do not, You will remain a seeker in the realm of samsara. Therefore, awaken to your own nature! Do not look for it elsewhere. This is the final word of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; It is not something to be grasped by the senses or the mind. If you can realize it in this very instant, You will transcend all limitations. If you do not, You will remain subject to the laws of cause and effect. Therefore, let go of all attachments! This is the true Dharma of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; It is not something to be realized through effort or striving. If you can see it clearly, You will be free from all doubt and hesitation. If you do not, You will remain bound by the illusions of the world. Therefore, practice with unwavering resolve! Do not be distracted by external appearances. This is the final instruction of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; It is not something to be understood through study or reflection.

The Master said, "Ask. He then asked, "Does a great practitioner of the Way still fall within the realm of cause and effect? The Master replied, "One does not obscure cause and effect.

From the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, the "Universal Gate" chapter of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva: "Immediately upon hearing their voices, all shall attain liberation. The verse says:
When one is suddenly provoked to anger and draws a sword to strike a tree, the wood is severed and the head falls; mountains and rivers do not stand between them. When Mother Cai bit her finger...

When one follows [the path], the heart immediately suffers pain; though the journey there and back differs, the channels of blood and qi are not severed. When sentient beings cry out in distress, the Bodhisattva’s heart is grieved; he gazes upon them with eyes of compassion, and their suffering ceases.
Through this, one attains knowledge that patterns things; who would have known that the patterning of things is achieved? When the patterning of things is realized, the emotions are fully understood.
When things are fully understood and emotions are stilled, there is a path of liberation that opens. When putrid meat gathers flies, it is because there is no flavor;

one chews upon the unfathomable, and in that state of the unfathomable, one concentrates the essence and unites all strength. Like beans bursting from cold ashes, the spiritual mechanism is infinite. Observe those sounds.
That is itself liberation. Before one has contemplated this, ten thousand sufferings press in upon one another. If suffering were permanent, how could liberation be attained?
Now that liberation has been attained, it is clear that suffering originally has no bone, while liberation possesses sinew. There is no gate for opening things; water has neither bone nor sinew.
The great boat was able to prevail. Xu Xuan was struck with astonishment; Zhang Feng turned pale. The dragon pool was no longer visible—how could there be any value in a dragon?
In an instant, amidst flashes of lightning and thunderclaps, they cried out thus, and their faculty of sight was restored.
The Universal Gate is vast and great; those who have no savior find peace and comfort upon entering it.

Mañjuśrī asked the woman Āmradārikā, "What is the meaning of birth? The woman replied, "The meaning of birth is that which is born through non-birth.
Mañjuśrī asked, "How is it that the meaning of birth is being born through non-birth? The woman replied:

If one can clearly understand that the four conditions of earth, water, fire, and wind have never spontaneously attained any state of combination, yet are able to function according to their respective suitability—this is the meaning of "birth. Su further asked, "What is the meaning of 'death'? The woman replied:
"Dying by means of not dying is the meaning of death. She asked, "What is meant by 'dying by means of not dying'?

The woman replied, "If one can clearly understand that the four conditions of earth, water, fire, and wind have never themselves undergone separation or dispersion, yet can function according to their appropriate circumstances—this is the meaning of death. The verse says:

To realize that from the very beginning there was nothing: this "non-existence" is precisely what is appropriate. At this very moment of appropriateness, this is what is called the meaning of "arising.

If one does not realize that from the beginning there was nothing, defilement would not be appropriate. Although delusion and awakening are impermanent, the spinning of the pearl remains never obscured.
Kāśyapa, because of Ānanda’s question regarding what the World-Honored One had transmitted besides the golden robe, called out to Ānanda.
Ānanda responded, “Yes. Kāśyapa said, “Throw down the banner-pole in front of the gate. He then spoke this verse:
Beyond the golden robe, what transmission is there? To call for him would only cause him to topple the flagpole. Little substance and much emptiness—it was not that he had no choice.
Even Kāśyapa still lacked the ability to turn his own boat over.
At the beginning of the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month, when the morning star appeared, the World-Honored One suddenly said: "How marvelous!
All sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtue, and marks of the Tathāgata; yet, because of deluded thoughts and attachments, they are unable to realize it."
The Verse says:
Three times seven days of contemplation—how very busy! The foolish child is truly frantic within the burning house. Moreover, the gate is narrow and hard to avoid;
The old man’s heart nearly breaks many times over.
The verse says: When the youth heard the *shao* music, he departed;

on high mountains and flowing waters, few are those who understand the notes. The barking of dogs and the crowing of roosters—how much deeper is their melody! Try listening for a moment before the sound;
I fear there may be yet another "compass needle" therein.
In the *Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch*, a monk recited the verse of Chan Master Wōluén, saying: "Wōluén has skillful means; he can sever a hundred thoughts.
When confronted with objects, his mind does not arise; thus, Bodhi grows day by day. Upon hearing this, the Patriarch said:
"This verse does not clarify the ground of the mind. If one follows it in practice, it will only add further fetters. Thereupon, he showed them another verse:
Huineng has no skillful means; he does not cut off the hundred thoughts. When encountering objects, mental states arise—how could Bodhi grow?
The verse says: A bright mirror does not reflect images, yet it is said its light grows day by day. How can such a view be questioned? It is like trying to catch the wind or grasp an echo.

A bright mirror reflects myriad forms; their beauty and ugliness are clearly and without error revealed. Regarding this vision, one asks: can there be any length to the light of the mirror? Why is this so?

The Tathāgata has said that what is not a unified whole is called a unified whole.
Subhūti, that which is a unified whole is ineffable; yet ordinary people greedily cling to it as such. The verse says:

You simply tell me one phrase regarding the time before your parents were yet born. Xiangyan said, "Master, please speak for me."
Guishan said, "If you can speak it, that would be my samādhi; what benefit would it be to you?
Thereupon Xiangyan wept and took his leave, saying to Guishan, "A painted cake cannot satisfy hunger. In this life I shall no longer study the teachings;
I will simply become a long-wandering monk who prepares gruel and rice. He then departed and stayed at a hermitage in Nanyang to rest. After some time, one day—

He cleared away the filth and debris and struck the bamboo, then said with a smile, "The great compassion of Master Shouduan was greater than that of my own parents. Had he explained it for me at that time, how could there be a 'today'? He then spoke this verse: Clearing away the filth and debris, Striking the bamboo, he laughed.
"Shouduan’s great compassion Was a kindness exceeding that of my parents. Had he explained it for me then, How could there be a 'today'?"
Before parents were even born, the horns were already exposed; today, Guishan pays homage to Xiangyan. Do not find this saying lacking in clarity:
ten thousand miles of cloudless sky, the moon fills the heavens.

That the bed wakes while the person awakens is a principle made perfectly clear. The fundamental Dharma is thus: to give rise to a mind is already an error.
