A servant girl and a young slave have long endured toil; why does the master, in turn, treat them with such haughtiness?
To provoke the laughter of neighbors for no reason is a breach of propriety brought upon oneself by one's own past actions.

One day Zhaozhou asked Touzi, "After a person who has undergone 'great death' returns to life, what is it like? Touzi said, "Night travel is not permitted; one must arrive by dawn. He then offered this verse: Night travel is not permitted; By dawn, one must have arrived.
The great matter is not a matter of birth or death; It is simply the original face before the parents were born.

Having become a spirit through many years of aging, he has long boasted of his prowess; accustomed from of old to striking those who are unprepared, who would have known there was yet another "white-handed" thief?
Deep within, how could he ever let him go?
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "What is 'the mystery of mysteries'? Zhaozhou said, "How long has it been since you began seeking this mystery? The monk replied, "I have sought it for a very long time.

Zhaozhou said, "If you had not met an old monk like me, you would have nearly killed yourself with your own mystery. The verse says: The mystery within the mystery— How long have you been seeking it? Had you not encountered an old monk, You would have nearly perished in your own profundity.
Madam Meng San is exceedingly coquettish; her feet are small, and she tilts her head as soon as she walks. She has been married off to Old Wang of the neighboring village;
instead of being taught embroidery, she is made to fire the kilns.
Danxia returned from Shitou and went once more to Jiangxi to visit Mazu.
Before he had even paid his respects, he entered the monks’ hall and sat astride the neck of the sacred statue (shengseng). The assembly was startled and immediately informed Mazu.
Mazu entered the hall in person and looked at him, saying, "My son is truly natural. The Master then descended to the ground and prostrated, saying, "I thank the Master for bestowing this upon me."

His Dharma name was Tianran (Natural). When the Patriarch asked him, "Where have you come from? the Master replied, "From Shitou. The Patriarch said, "The path at Shitou is slippery; did it cause you to fall?

The Master replied, "If I had fallen, I would not have come here. He then offered this verse: The path at Shitou is indeed slippery; How many have stumbled and tumbled? I have come from there, yet I have not fallen; This is what is called the Way of the Buddhas.
Pushing through the grass to catch the wind, one goes and returns again. How could Shitou be the same as Zhaozhou’s barrier?
Without cause, opening one's eyes, one stumbles idly; the story of the staff has been passed down, its laughter never exhausted.
Chan Master Wuzhuo Wenxi of Hangzhou once visited Yangshan and immediately attained realization through a mutual accord of mind. Yangshan appointed him as the head cook (*diànzuò*).
Once, Mañjuśrī appeared atop a rice-pot; the Master struck it with his rice-stirring paddle and said, "Mañjuśrī is Mañjuśrī, and Wenxi is Wenxi.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī spoke this verse: "The bitter gourd is bitter from root to tip."
When the melon is sweet from stem to tip, one has practiced for three great kalpas, yet is still disparaged by this old monk. The verse says:
In drinking tea and conversing, what intimacy lies in the meaning? Who says that Mañjuśrī is the host? After our parting, how many times have we sung in mutual response;
Yet upon returning, it turns once more into dust before the eyes.

To the east of the city there was an old woman who had been born at the same time as the Buddha, yet she did not wish to see him. Every time she saw the Buddha approaching, she would immediately turn away to avoid him; nevertheless, wherever she looked toward the east or west, everywhere was the Buddha.

She then covered her face with her hands, but within the palms of her ten fingers, it was all the Buddha as well. A verse says: The old woman and the Buddha were born together, Yet she did not wish to see the Buddha. Whenever she saw him coming, she would flee; But wherever she turned—east or west—it was all the Buddha. She covered her face with her hands, And even within her ten fingers, it was all the Buddha.
One’s own joy and one’s own anger—when the fire of karma burns the heart, do not blame others.
If you wish never to see Gautama again, you might as well hide yourself within the nostrils of a golden statue.
A Verse on the Poor Son Finding His Kinsman:
Amidst the sound of war drums, father and son were separated for over twenty years; though fortune and misfortune are impermanent, this feeling remains unclouded.
Without cause, one morning, atop the Apricot Flower Tower, we drank lightly and sang softly; like kin of different surnames, we shouted for joy and indulged in pleasure.
Suddenly, someone announced: "Our parents have arrived at the gate. In that initial state of being lost and scattered, they appeared without a thought. All you children of the Buddha—

Deluded regarding fundamental wisdom, one drifts upon the ocean of consciousness like one who has lost their parents, left alone and exposed. If one contemplates this for even a single moment, the sun of wisdom suddenly shines bright;
all circumstances, whether adverse or favorable, become like a single hair cast into a great mass of fire, which one intends to pull out.

Losing body and life, clutching his topknot as he hurries to the yamen; rising by himself and falling by himself—suddenly the wine clears. That rising and falling was not caused by the wine. *Eulogy on the Two Demons Struggling over a Corpse:* The two demons quarrel over a corpse; One says it is mine, the other says it is his. They fight for the sake of a single piece of skin; Who knows who will win? The corpse lies there, neither male nor female; It is merely a bundle of bones and flesh. If you can see through this, Then you have attained the Way. If you cannot see through this, You are lost in birth and death. Do not seek the Way outside yourself; Seeking it elsewhere is like chasing a shadow. If you can grasp this in an instant, You will transcend the three realms. If you do not grasp it in an instant, You will wander through the six paths. This is the eulogy on the two demons struggling over a corpse.
Two ghosts struggle over a corpse; their affairs are not the same. Who can catch and bind the wind atop the ridge? Last night I borrowed lodging at Hanshan Temple;
only after waking did I realize it was a hollow continuity of emptiness.
The Verse: When Zhang Tianjue saw Yun'an, Yangqi gave a single laugh while Duan Gong was at a loss;
Zhenjing showed a single fit of anger while Wujin lost his advantage. These were the fangs and claws of the Dharma cave.

Joy and anger are without constancy, resembling a divine dragon that suddenly expands and suddenly contracts. All those with minds, during these moments of expansion and contraction, say, "The dragon expands" or "The dragon contracts.
Yet for one who perceives it in this way, the dragon has long since departed.
The verse states that the three poisons and four inversions are likewise all pure.
The Han dynasty’s great achievements arose from Huaiyin; had it not been for Xiao He seeking him out beneath the moon, it is certain this man would not have been employed in the end.
Meeting such a person, who else could truly be a connoisseur?
Verses on the Dharmakāya:
The *zhizǐhuā* (purple-rod flower) tipsy with wine reviles the lotus; It loses out to the lotus and pays it no mind. It vexes the *zhizǐhuā* to death—who will take its life in exchange?
The wind blows through the willows, as chaotic as tangled hemp.
One day National Teacher Huizhong called to his attendant. The attendant responded. He called him thus three times, and each time the attendant responded.
The Master said, "I thought it was I who had failed you; it turns out, rather, that you have failed me.
Later, a monk asked National Teacher Xuansha about the meaning of calling the attendant. Xuansha said, "It was actually the attendant who understood."
Yunju Xi said: "Tell me, does the attendant understand or not? If you say he understands, the National Teacher also said, 'You have failed me.
If you say he does not understand, Xuansha also said, 'In fact, it is the attendant who understands.
So, how do you deliberate upon this? Xuangjue questioned a monk: 'What is the point where the attendant understands? The monk said, 'If..."
[The monk] argued. [Xuedou] commented: "How can you respond in such a way? Xuangjue said, "You have not understood for long.
He also said, "If you can reach a resolution here, then you will see Xuansha. A monk asked National Teacher Fayan, "What was the meaning behind calling for the attendant?
Fayan said, "Go now; come back at another time. Yunju Xi said, "Fayan spoke in this manner."
To clarify whether the National Teacher’s intention was manifest or unmanifest: A monk asked Zhaozhou, "What was the National Teacher’s meaning when he called for his attendant?
Zhaozhou replied, "It is like a person writing characters in the dark; though the characters themselves do not take shape, the traces of the brushstrokes are already revealed. The verse says:
The attendant understands the response but not the meaning; those from all quarters understand the meaning but not the response.
A night-luminous pearl rolls within a golden platter; who can grasp it firmly right before their own face?
A Verse on Zhaozhou’s Barrier:
Though the roads of Shu are difficult, they may still be traversed; Zhaozhou’s barrier is perilous, beyond the power of ascent.
The Court of True Suchness is clearly before one's eyes, Yet how many of noble spirit have failed to pass through?
The Monk Pòzào Duò of Mount Song was once at a shrine on the slopes of Mount Song that was extremely efficacious.
In its hall there was only a single hearth, to which offerings were made incessantly from far and near; many living beings were slaughtered for sacrifice.
The Master struck the hearth three times with his staff and said: "Tut! This hearth is merely composed of clay and tiles. From where does the 'saint' come? From where does the 'efficacy' come?"
He rose. As he was thus slaughtering living beings, he struck [the hearth] three times more, whereupon the hearth stove collapsed and fell apart.
In a moment, a person in blue robes and a tall ceremonial cap came forward to bow and said, "I am originally the Hearth God of this temple.

Having long endured the retribution of my karma, I have now been granted the Dharma of non-arising by you, Master, and have attained liberation from this place to be reborn in heaven. I have come specifically to express my gratitude. The Master said, "It is so."
"You originally possessed this nature; it was not my own forceful assertion. Shen bowed twice and vanished.
Later, a monk asked the Master, "I have long served at your side, yet I have not received any skillful means. What principle did the stove god realize that he was immediately reborn in heaven?"
The Master said, "I simply told him it was composed of clay and tiles; I had no other principle to give him. The monk stood there reflecting.
The Master asked, "Do you understand? The monk replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Why do you not understand your own original nature?
The monk prostrated himself. The Master said, "Falling! Falling! Broken! Broken! Later, another monk brought this up.
He reported this to National Teacher An. The National Teacher sighed and said, "This son has realized that things and self are one and the same. He spoke in verse:
"The Buddha’s hearth and the sentient beings’ hearth— A single strike of the staff, and both fall away. The jeweled table bites the cat; The nests of the holy and the profane are secure."

Furthermore: "The stove does not attach itself to me; I myself attach myself to the stove. Relying on the Master’s striking to awaken me, I shall no longer fall into error. Although the stove has already fallen away, how could Heaven not be the stove?
This falls while that is established; whether it be 'white' or 'black,' there is no doubt regarding its function. Thus, both 'Heaven' and 'Stove' are the 'Divine Stove.'"
I bend and extend my arm; the hearth falls completely. When bowing to the Buddha, it does not fall. Who rises? Who falls? Rising and falling are at will.
This mastery over the myriad wonders—though one hearth has fallen, the Lord of Mountains lets out a cold laugh.
At Lingshan in Chaozhou, Master Dadian Baotong was visited one day by Han Yu, the Duke of Wen. The Duke asked the Master how many years he had been in the world.
The Master held up his rosary and said, "Do you understand? The Duke replied, "I do not. The Master said, "One hundred and eight [beads] for day and night.
The Duke did not comprehend this and returned home. On the following day, he came again; upon reaching the gate, he saw the Head Seat raising [the rosary].

[This concerns] the previous conversation. [The Master] asked, "What was the meaning of that? The Head Seat struck his teeth three times. When the Master saw that the Head Seat had responded to the previous question in this way, he also struck his teeth three times.
The Official said, "It turns out that the Buddha-dharma is not of two kinds. The Master asked, "What is the principle behind this?
He replied, "Just now, when I questioned the Head Seat, it was exactly like this. The Master then called out to the Head Seat, saying, "Is it you who acts in such a manner?"
"Is it so? "Yes," he replied. The Master then struck him and drove him out of the monastery.
The verse says: "A rosary of one hundred and eight beads to mark the years; The Head Seat caught the wind, his horse learning from the ox. Thirty strokes of the rattan drove him out the gate;
Master Han has a matter weighing on his mind."
Furthermore:
"Dadian’s skills were hardly many, yet he was caught in Han’s living net; though he calculated every way, escape proved difficult—how could the blind staff of Chaoyang have let him off?"
Chan Master Zongjing of Longxing Temple in Hangzhou first visited Xuefeng and secretly received the seal of his lineage.

Once, while in the monks' hall, he bared one shoulder to fasten the curtain. Upon seeing this, Xuefeng remarked, "In the future, you shall dwell as an abbot with a thousand monks, yet not a single one among them will be a true patch-robed disciple.
The Master repented his error and took leave to return to his native village, where he resided at Liu... (text fragmentary).

He went to the hospital. King Qian ordered him to reside at Longxing Temple, where there were over a thousand followers, all of whom were practitioners of the Three Studies engaged in lecturing and recitation;
it was exactly as Xuefeng had prophesied.
Though baring one’s shoulder may be a gesture of good intent, it was within the Weiyang Palace that Huaiyin was executed.
Year after year, on the day the flowers bloom, it causes heroes’ sleeves to remain drenched in tears.
The Verse on the Cūḍāmaṇi of the Wheel-Turning King:
For long the Night-Bright Jewel was hidden within the topknot; Thirst for desire dried up as he fought with great vigor. Returning from victory, he personally received it upon his crown;
Its radiance shines forth—not only illuminating the eastern quarter.
Verse by Chan Master Baizhang Huaihai: "Better to be the master of the mind than to be mastered by the mind.
Who cares about the gateway of likes and dislikes? Calling and shouting in a mess like tangled hemp—every household has its slaves and servants;
when used without doubt, I am the father."
The Ancient Chan Master Shuangfeng once received the seal of certification from [Master] Shuangfeng. Later, he arrived at Shishuang.

Shishuang wished to interrogate him regarding his realization, but had not yet found the opportunity. When the Master took his leave of Shishuang, Shishuang held out his whisk and escorted him to the entrance of the gate, calling out, "Attendant Gu!
The Master turned his head. Shishuang said, "To conceive of it is already an error; to grasp it is already a deviation."
"It is not that it is not so; yet do not form a conceptual understanding of it. Unless one knows 'that which is,' one cannot know it.
Go well, go well. The Master assented and then departed. Shortly thereafter, Shuangfeng passed away, and the Master succeeded him as abbot.
He then uttered this verse:
The young lord of Luoyang is intoxicated by luxury; he gazes not upon the green mountains, but only at the flowers.
If you can remain long enough to stay at this pine-clad temple, why would this old monk begrudge you a cup of tea?
Once, while Chan Master Zhichang of Guizong on Mount Lu was weeding, a monk who was a lecturer in the sutras came to visit him.
Suddenly seeing a snake pass by, the Master severed it with his hoe. The monk said, "I have long looked up to Guizong;
I never expected you would be such a coarse practitioner. The Master replied, "You are coarse, and I am coarse. The monk asked, "What is this coarseness? The Master held his hoe upright.

The monk asked, "What is 'fine'? The Master made the gesture of slaying a snake. The monk said, "If that is so, then I shall act accordingly. The Master said, "Setting aside for a moment acting accordingly, where did you see me slay a snake? The monk was speechless. A verse says: The head. He asked, "What is 'fine'? The Master made the gesture of slaying a snake.
[The monk] said, "If it is thus, then I shall follow it. [The Master] said, "Setting aside for now following it, where did you see me slay a snake? The monk had no reply. The verse says:
Meeting on the road, he struck once with his blade; one belt became two or three. To dwell in the mountains and bind the belly, there is no need for bamboo strips;
the poisonous vapor is extinguished this very moment.
Furthermore:
"The place of severance is the nature; the place of movement is emotion. A little snake bears a great spirit. The Buddhas of the ten directions are his descendants.
I tell it to those who pass by—who would be willing to listen?"
Chan Master Fǎhuì of Yángqí in Yuánzhōu was asked by a monk, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "A three-legged donkey prances about on its hooves.

The monk said, "Is it not this very thing? The Master said, "Elder of Húnán. He then offered this verse: A three-legged donkey prances about on its hooves; The whole world is filled with its tracks. If you wish to know the Buddha, Look at the Elder of Húnán.
Yangqi plays with the foal; the stone woman gives birth to a child—do you know it or not?
One day it pursues the wind for thousands of miles, yet upon its return, even a single day seems too late.

A monk asked Xinghua Jiang, "Before the Many-Sons Stupa, what did they discuss together? Jiang said, "One person transmits the empty; ten thousand people transmit the real. The verse says: One person transmits the empty;
Ten thousand people transmit the real. If you wish to know the matter of the ancients, Look at the moon reflected in the water.

Before the stupa, many sons discuss the profound mystery; Listening with ears, they transmit it through the eyes. Though there are ten thousand realities and a thousand truths, they do not realize them— Like a bride riding a donkey, led by her mother-in-law.
The Collected Works of the Elder Zibo, Volumes Eighteen and Nineteen.
Read by Hanshan Deqing of the Ming Dynasty.
Verse on the Lamp:

When the lamp first exists, there is no light; it is when I light it that the light first arises. If the light were already present within the lamp, then even without light, the lamp would not be dark.
There is one who understands this meaning; they can travel through the night without fire. Not believing, he asks Avalokiteśvara, who laughs without ceasing. The birth verse says:
"I know for myself that today I have emerged from my mother’s womb. Today, for what reason has the mother not come? Coming and going, I search for her but find no trace."
It is attained: a single branch blooms within the Land of Lotus Flowers.

When the verse on arising and non-arising is about to dawn, before the unarisen has arisen, one must first forget that which has already arisen. If that which has already arisen is not forgotten, the unarisen will ultimately never be known.

Within this, even a thousand demons and a hundred monsters are all fully known; outside the mind, there has never been so much as a single thread. When one realizes the source and forgets emotions, the affairs of birth and death are seen for what they are;
those who treat these as real are considered deluded.
In the *Night-Walking Verse*, when walking in meditation during the night, the front and back steps arise alternately. If the front step reaches the ground, the back step cannot yet rise;
if the back step reaches the ground, the front step likewise does not rise. Only when neither the front nor the back step touches the ground can one continue to rise without ceasing.
If one observes this with true discernment, how could the feet ever actually reach the ground? Since the feet do not reach the ground, one may likewise tread upon empty space and water.
If one can indeed tread upon empty space and water, who would not possess supernormal powers (*abhijñā*)?
Instruction for Disciples (with Preface). The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "The seed of the Buddha arises from conditions; therefore, it is said to be non-arising.

Now, non-arising does not mean falling into eternalism, and non-ceasing does not mean falling into nihilism. When one does not fall into eternalism or nihilism, what could possibly not be true? Thus, the *Saddharma*...
This refers to the coarseness of engaging with phenomena. Alas! How could coarseness and subtlety have permanence? It depends entirely upon how clear one’s own realization is.
Thus we know that if the ground from which conditions arise is not true, the fruit will ultimately be circuitous. Consequently, one remains far removed from the Buddha;
the great dragons and elephants have vanished, and among the ranks of both monastics and laypeople, there is no discernment between the heterodox and the orthodox, nor between beans and wheat.

He lacked discernment. With palms joined, he prostrated before the Buddha, yet his mind remained fixed on the fox. Having shaved his head to become a monk, his aspirations were rooted in worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Thus, he manifested a thousand manners and ten thousand forms that are beyond description; all this was due to the lack of a true foundation at the very moment he first underwent the tonsure and donned the dyed robes.
Whenever I reflect upon this, although I have wandered across rivers and lakes for nearly forty years, I have never once [been so].

I have lightly granted ordination and conferred names upon others; this was not due to a lack of compassion. Rather, I feared that such minor acts of kindness might actually harm the greater compassion.

Come, I shall speak to you: you must take this to heart. Whenever anyone sheds their white robes to leave the secular world, they must first examine the foundation of their practice (*yindi*) and ensure their resolve is genuine.
Only if there are no signs of ulterior motives or deviousness should one definitively undergo tonsure.

Or perhaps my whereabouts, whether near or far, are not fixed, and we have not been able to maintain contact through letters. In such a case, you may simply visualize the venerable elder’s meditative form and receive the name through the tonsure;
there is no need to be attached to formalities. You should directly bring this supreme cause to fulfillment. This "supreme cause" is none other than the seed of Buddhahood.

If one is not victorious due to causes, one belongs to the race of Māra. It is difficult to distinguish between Māra and the Buddha; let each of you be cautious of this. A verse says: A favorable cause is an evil cause;
True reality is hard to deceive. Above my head, the heavens are clear. I entrust this to the traveler returning with the spring tide and rain:
Upon your return, quickly board the ferry at the crossing.
A Verse on Awakening from a Dream:
To know it is a dream while dreaming is to be about to enter the state of awakening. To know it was a dream while awake is to be about to realize the emptiness of the self (*ātman*).
Since the self is empty, who could there be as male or female?

An Account of Staying at Shizhong Temple (With Preface) In the third month of the year Wuyiwei, the Venerable Zibo was on his way to Caoxi. Accompanied by two or three disciples, we stayed for two nights at Shizhong Temple by Lake Hukou.
The temple commands a magnificent site where mountain and water converge; upon our first ascent, all worldly concerns were completely washed away.

Now, the gathering and dispersing of those in this floating life are no different from bubbles on water or flowers in the air. Only the true contemplation of the adept views gathering as dispersing and dispersing as gathering;
thus, while lamentations and songs of grief are not ceased, the reflection that they are fundamentally non-existent remains unerring.
You disciples have therefore requested that I leave behind a verse to serve as the vanguard for the mark of the broad and long tongue. The verse says:
The stones upon Lake-mouth Mountain—how could they be merely tens of thousands? May passing vessels pause for a moment; every surface is inscribed with the *Dharmapada*.
A single verse upon each fragment of stone; Gautama reveals his smiling countenance. Travelers listen to these auspicious sounds; he alone grants favor to the faculty of sight.
Ten thousand apertures suddenly roar in fury; long waves thunder across the river plains. I shall give rise to a mind of realization; lightning already flashes across my brows.

Long have I admired Shizhong Temple, yet though I encountered monks at the temple, I had not seen them before. Turning the sutras is not difficult at all; with a snap of the fingers, one knows how many times it has been turned.
The journey of a thousand li begins with a single step; as I walk along, how could I dare complain of weariness?

I offer this *candana* verse. The one who offers is the fragrance; beyond the fragrance, there is no person. When the path of subject and object is severed, who receives this fragrance? A receiver is impossible.
How much more so for those who offer it! Contemplate fragrance in this way: fragrance is itself the Teacher. To receive fragrance as something external is like being a withered tree.
For this reason, fragrance is universally boundless, equal to the emptiness of the ten directions.
In the *Śataka-śāstra-vyākhyā*, it is said:

"If there were form within the visual consciousness, the dead person should see objects. If there were form within the consciousness and the eye followed the consciousness, the dead person would see objects as they do when alive.
How then can one be called 'dead'? If the consciousness departs and the eye follows the form, then the sense organs and their objects depart simultaneously."
Judging by the facts, this is not so. When one repeatedly examines the subject and the object, the one who is born does not perceive form;

how much less, then, can they perceive death? When principle reaches its ultimate limit, emotion naturally fades away. When emotion fades, consciousness becomes wisdom. To observe the sense organs and their objects with this wisdom is like water washing water.
In the Verse on Selecting the Immortal:
The view of a self is difficult to eliminate; even gold and stone become light. Why need one further aspire to learn the art of longevity? Try observing that parental affection is not truly existent;
only then will you see the lamp that illuminates the world through the dark night.
A Verse Presented to Zhou Shuye:
Spring breeze everywhere, flowers everywhere; I ask you, where is the root and the sprout? Before the eaves, pines bend;
a few rafters decay. Cast off the *kāṣāya* and start a household anew.
The Verse on Contemplating the Hub (with Preface) Laozi said:
"Thirty spokes converge upon a single hub; it is through that which is empty [the hub] that the utility of the chariot exists. He further said: "That which has form is taken as its benefit;
that which is formless is taken as its utility. I say: It is not only in the case of kneading clay for vessels, carving doors and windows, or fashioning spokes and hubs.
Indeed it is so. Examine your own body slowly: the ear has an outline, and because that outline contains a hollow cavity, the ear first becomes functional.
Is this not likewise true for the eyes, nose, mouth, and so forth?
Even one as dull-witted as a fool can understand the rest by taking a single faculty as an illustration. The verse says:
By observing the hub, one knows the body; by observing the body, one knows heaven and earth. This contemplation is excellent and vast; there is no ultimate principle that is not understood.
The ultimate principle resides in the fundamental mind, yet in daily life we lack deep insight. Thus, though it is used, it is not perceived; this is what is called being "one of the multitudes."
If one understands this directly and thoroughly, who would not be a Great Awakened Honored One? Since I myself have attained Great Awakening, how much more so those who are noble in the world!
To investigate the verse on delusion:
it is like a person who, while awake, suddenly gives rise to a state of being asleep. This sleep exists because of waking; therefore, it cannot be called waking.
Apart from awakening, there is this delusion; how could one person possess two states? Examine this back and forth with meticulous care: where is the root of delusion planted?
When you suddenly penetrate this point, your state of doubt will be resolved instantly.
The Gāthā of the Sandalwood Banner (with Preface):
Last winter, the master of Laoshan told me that a Mr. Wu from Zhenzhou had brought forth a sandalwood banner he himself had offered.
It was less than a foot in height; its surface was carved into a door. Upon opening this door and looking within, the space inside was as empty as the void, and suddenly a thousand Buddhas appeared.

The principal figures and their attendants are layered upon one another like a mound of piled-up millet; the eyebrows encircle Mount Sumeru, and the eyes are as deep as the great ocean—nothing is left unmanifested.

Its exquisite craftsmanship surpasses that of the spirits, leaving those who behold it utterly amazed. It is almost impossible to fathom with the intellect, nor can its depths be exhausted by the power of sight.
This evening, Mr. Wu visited me at Fanchuan, and before the lamp, we again discussed this banner.
He marveled, saying, "How could Heaven carve it with divine chisels so that within less than a foot, a complete world is contained?
I sighed deeply and said, "Master Wu, Master Wu! How can you know whether there is birth or non-birth? If you truly knew whether there is birth or non-birth," [he would not have been so amazed].
Then a mustard seed could be hidden within empty space, and cow hair could be contained within the vast ocean; how much more so this banner?
Furthermore, the *jiaoming* insect regards the wing of a mosquito as its world, and the snail regards a drop of moisture as a surging tide;
these are all cases where the small is taken as the large. Yet why should the large alone not be made small? Therefore it is said: "To take the small as the large—the small is not the large."
Externally, the great is treated as small; yet the great is not outside the small, and the small is not outside the great. If that is so, what small thing is not the great?
Since the great is not outside the small, what great thing is not the small? If the great is not the small, then within a single bean, the intervening spaces would be unfathomable.
If the small is not the great, then beyond the eight wildernesses, even the most distant would be near. This is truly because of the nature of the great and the small.
They arise from emotional perceptions. If emotions are forgotten, what could one not accomplish?

When Wenzi presented this, it was like windless Mount Lao suddenly giving rise to waves; such receiving of emptiness and responding to echoes—is this not like the dream of an ant building a palace? The verse says:
The wood does not exceed a foot in length, yet that which it contains is immeasurable. Whether ordinary or holy, male or female, they cannot be grasped through conceptual thought.

Just as when the mind has not yet arisen, its capacity encompasses empty space; within it, lands as numerous as motes of dust appear like reflections in a mirror. Once a single thought arises, one immediately falls into the realm of limitations.
The circumference of the wheel is known to be five feet; one discards the ocean to seek a single drop. Whether great or small, the sword stands erect; its sharp edge is difficult to approach.

If one does not forget the self, the heart will shatter and the body be severed. Wenzi exhorted him: "There is no going forth that is not auspicious. My words are ordinary; follow them and you shall obtain benefit.
The merit of this carving is dedicated to the Triple Gem. If one applies oneself with a virtuous mind, what skill is not a treasure?
This verse for the dedication of merit for one’s mother, written by Sun Zhong, states:
"This Dharma is most subtle and wondrous, and it is also most firm and solid. That which is subtle and wondrous benefits the father; that which is firm and solid benefits the mother."

When a filial son has not yet dipped his brush, the deceased is born into a favorable realm; how much more so when there are accumulated characters, sentences following upon those accumulations to form a section.

Each and every one depends on the power of the mind; whether living or dead, all are revealed in solitude. Yet people use them daily without realizing it, like feeling their own nose and suspecting it to be a drum.
The Crawl-and-Itch Verse:
Flowers in front of Nanquan’s courtyard; crawling on the back of Zibo. These two held up together, like a scholar viewing a male and female.
The Lice Verse.

Who knows of these swarms of lice and nits? They too can stretch out their heads and knit their brows. If one were to shake off the Dharma-body with a light toss, they would all be made to fly away like withered husks driven by the wind.

In offering verses before the portraits of the various patriarchs, the common crowd is muddled: they regard the portrait as false and the physical form as true. The wise are not so; they know that the physical form gives rise to the portrait.

One knows that the mind arises from reflections, yet the mind has no arising or ceasing; how, then, could there be past and present? Since there is no past or present, even "arising" does not exist, let alone "ceasing.
Non-arising is not permanence; non-ceasing is not annihilation. To speak thus and to investigate in this manner—this is true discernment.
In every shadow and every form, his wisdom and virtue are without deficiency.

When offering incense with a devotional mind, there is no incense apart from the mind, nor is there a mind apart from the incense. They are like the body and the hand: if a hand exists outside the body, it certainly cannot be one's own hand.
The body exists outside the hands; it is certainly not one's own body. Hand and body are without doubt, and the mind of incense is clearly manifest.

To offer this to the Patriarch, the Patriarch will surely joyfully accept it. Acceptance is neither a matter of phenomena nor principle; who could abide therein? Because there is no abiding, the merit of the donor [is inexhaustible].
How could there be any limit? Using this to offer to one's ancestors, there are none who do not transcend; using this to pray for the ruler, there are none who do not receive blessings.
To the common people, vision is but half-sighted; they perceive fragrance but not the mind. To the sages, the eye is wondrous; they see fragrance but not as fragrance. Only at our Caoxi is this so.
The fragrance of the mind is impermanent; neither of these two approaches succeeds. To achieve everything, one uses it as a "poison drum. Those who hear it lose their hearing;
having lost their hearing, they use their eyes to gaze at trees through walls. That which is produced by fragrance—whether acceptable or unacceptable—acts as the teacher for humanity.
He becomes the lord of hell. Fragrant! Fragrant! It is not sandalwood that bears this name; filial piety is the finger that points to it, its heat enduring for a thousand ages.
If one understands this with upright composure, they do not fail as a son; their fragrance continues without end, and its misty smoke remains thereafter.
In his verse on the Dharma-offering to the Sixth Patriarch, the Master says:
"Originally a wood-seller, how profound was his celestial faculty! Upon hearing a single phrase of the *Vajracchedikā*, he immediately awakened to his own mind."
Having already awakened to one's own mind, what further matters remain within the breast? Journeying afar toward Huangmei, he took up menial labor at the granary.

Using a stone to weigh down his waist, for eight months he worked as diligently as eating a single meal. When the rice was cooked, the mechanism [of mind and matter] fell into accord; at midnight, he entered the Patriarch’s chamber.

The secret transmission resounds like thunder; among the holy and the ordinary, it is as tumultuous as boiling water. The Master does not listen with his ears, but directly perceives through the eyes.
The multitude is not so; they neglect their ears and do not grasp the sound. Therefore, there must be a place of abiding, where subject and object stand in opposition.
One should simply abide nowhere; when the mind arises toward objects, there is no fault. Where there is no fault, there is no "non-mind. What further thing could there be to depend upon?

Though discrimination burns fiercely, it is like a horse seeing its own reflection; because one understands that it emerges from the body itself, one sees it at that moment without being startled or amazed.
If one sees the reflection of another object, why should the horse’s alarm be cause for doubt? Since no other object is seen at all, from where could this alarm and doubt arise?
To take one's own mind with one's own mind—this even the Buddha did not approve. For those who seek the Dharma apart from the mind, the water of Caoxi will never wet them.
How great is the contemplation of the Perfected Person! It must take sincerity as its foundation. When there is sincerity, the thieving mind dies;

when the mind dies, the nature is naturally numinous. Being numinous, there is nothing it does not illumine; yet phenomena and principle are both not established. Precisely through this non-establishment, one is able to accomplish all things.
It is like the deep winter when the myriad trees are frozen as if about to break; yet with the return of spring for a single night, their radiance is revealed without exception.

This is called "sincerity giving rise to clarity," not because the light of illumination is already perfect. My teacher has attained the heart of the Patriarch; that heart of the Patriarch lacks nothing.

Through great vows and compassion, there is no need for external cultivation or refinement. Their spiritual power is inconceivable.

The Dharma Master Fǎngsù and the Daoist Dūguān have exhausted their wits; their joys and angers are inconsistent, inviting both praise and slander. They rejoice when things go their way and are vexed when they do not.
From narrowness, they have long since expanded to breadth. Let us try taking this old fellow as a "poison drum": upon hearing its sound, whether in favor or against, one’s life [is at stake].
My faculties have declined; I only fear that praise and slander are not very frequent. The more there are, the better it is for the salvation of immeasurable beings.

Immeasurable sentient beings are like grains of millet; I, this old man of penetrating vision, am like a boat. With the boat, I carry the millet—whether much or little—and teach every single grain to reach the other shore.
When the wise person observes it in this way, they see that praise and slander are truly great skillful means. [They are] the drum of poison.
Transforming oneself into implements for saving beings, one rescues the multitude from hardships at the shore of the sea of suffering. Those who rescue others from hardship are kin even to strangers;
how could a wise person harbor malice toward their own kin? To hate one's kin is surely the mark of a fool. Fools who slander and revile should be met with compassion.
With a heart of compassion, upon hearing an evil sound, one should feel as if an infant were reviling its parents;

when parents hear this, their pity deepens even more, so how could they have leisure to give rise to anger toward the child? If a person hears slander and feels resentment, they should study the perspective of the enlightened observer (*daguan*) and cultivate this contemplation:
"May the slanderer not give rise to anger upon hearing it; what is there to envy in the clamor of praise? One must know how to respond to joy and anger.

They do not exist independently; they arise in mutual dependence, forming hatred and love. If either one is deficient, both are empty. This vast, penetrating, and ever-present radiance has neither interior nor exterior.

Since there is neither interior nor exterior, there is no distinction between far and near. Once far and near are discarded, past and present are lost. When past and present are lost, who is old and who is young?
Without birth and without death—this is the true Bodhisattva. I exhort the people of the world to recite my verse; it is superior.
To read the Great Canon a thousand times—how inconceivable is such merit! Fleshy pus is transformed directly into a mass of vajra;

a mass of vajra, indeed a mass of vajra! It cannot be kneaded into a ball, nor can it be broken by striking. Should one encounter the conditions to obtain it and employ it skillfully, one’s descendants shall forever be wealthy and noble.
A verse on the propagation of the Dharma:
In a dream I saw the sea, yet could not cross it. Standing alone upon the shore as the sun was setting, to retreat home the path was already too far;
to advance, there was no ground where my feet could find purchase. In ten thousand ways I wandered, finding it difficult to either advance or retreat. At this moment of true difficulty, who—?
The drum is struck; before the sound of the drum has ceased, the dream is already over. Upon opening one's eyes, how could there ever have been any affliction or suffering?

Furthermore: In the midst of waking, one sees the sea but cannot cross it; turning the head, the setting sun on the western mountains is already dusk. Moving forward, one is terrified by the surging waves.
The person, having retreated, has lost the way home. At this moment, there are a thousand hardships and ten thousand difficulties.

One knows not who can save one from suffering. Can anyone save one from suffering? Can anyone save one from suffering? Contemplate the body and mind with clarity: who is the source of fortune and calamity?

Fortune and calamity have always had their own separate gates. When the single mind does not arise, who is the master? Within the field of hatred and love, distinguish the false from the true. Upon the road of birth and death...
Distinguish the strands: wash water with water, join gold with gold. In daily life, be clear and skillfully interweave them—skillfully interweave them, skillfully interweave them!
Without heedlessly encroaching upon another’s crops, you break open the void as an old water-buffalo.
Inscription on the Wall at Jiaoshan for Elder Lun, Written by Su Changgong (Attached is Changgong’s Verse).
Su’s verse says: The Dharma Master dwells at Jiaoshan, yet in truth he never dwells. Whenever I come, I invariably inquire about the Dharma, and the Dharma Master remains silent.
It is not that the Dharma Master has nothing to say; it is simply that he knows no answer to give. Observe the head and the feet: they are one and the same.
Originally, one naturally wears one’s own cap and shoes. It is like a man with a long beard who does not consider his length to be a hardship.

Yet, once, when someone asked him about it, every time he slept he found himself at a loss; upon returning home, he looked up and down and discovered that for an entire night he had worn them nowhere.
He tossed and turned until dawn, intending to pluck them all out with tweezers. Although these words are vulgar and shallow, they nonetheless possess a profound significance. Hold fast to this.
He questioned the Dharma Master. The Dharma Master smiled and consented: "Suzi comes in such a manner;
the Dharma Master dwells in such a manner. These two are both white-handed thieves; they can speak fluently though they have no tongues."

This mind is fundamentally ordinary; it is because of the many wandering travelers [of delusion] that it appears otherwise. It is like a son driven mad by wind who puts his cap on his feet and his shoes on his head;
having taken suffering for pleasure, he likewise takes pleasure for suffering. Regarding matters of suffering and pleasure within a dream, let us ask: who could possibly arrange them with ease?
I myself cut off my long beard; I cut it and I know where I did so. Without cause, I doubted myself; like sparks from a flint or a flash of lightning, it vanished.

Had I not doubted myself, I would have followed others toward the realms of existence or non-existence. Suddenly meeting a person of clear vision, before a word was spoken, my heart already gave its assent.
A Verse on Viewing Peach Blossoms:
Old trees and new blossoms open for all to behold; these flowers are no different from their appearance last year. Who knows that it is the flowers smiling at human discrimination?
Their frequent flourishing and falling leave the tree’s very root in tranquil stillness.
Preface to the Reading of the Verses of the Universal Gate Chapter (Pumenpin):
The three poisons of sentient beings have become their habitual nature through long practice, like oil permeating flour; even if one wished to press it out, not even the divine Yu could do so.
Now this sutra says: "If there are sentient beings who abound in lustful desire, they should constantly maintain mindfulness and reverence."
"By reverently contemplating Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, one immediately attains freedom from desire and so forth.

Since it says "constantly mindful" and yet "immediately free," the force of the phrasing and its underlying principle are ultimately difficult to reconcile. If one savors this carefully: "constant mindfulness" means there is no interruption;
because there is no interruption, one only then "immediately attains freedom from desire. If this is the case, it is like using the waters of the Eastern Sea...
It is logically inevitable that one should rescue [others] from a fire of bundled firewood.
Nevertheless, though this is constant and requires reverence, who but those of great wisdom and supreme courage could achieve it? Furthermore, reverence and indolence cannot coexist;

if one’s understanding of the principle is not yet settled and the force of habitual tendencies is fierce, the principle will not overcome habit, resulting in defeat nine times out of ten—just like the case of the orangutan.

He drinks wine and utters angry insults. Amidst this anger and cursing, he is secretly driven by the turning of habitual tendencies; unaware and unknowing, he departs only to return again. The fragrance of the wine infects his spirit;
his spirit becomes intoxicated and his vital energy exhausted. The force of his cursing suddenly turns soft and warm as he draws the wine in with his mouth.
At such a time, one does not know there is gain; how could one know there is loss? One does not know there is death; how could one know there is a body? Therefore, I say:
those who can constantly mindfully revere and pay homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva transform the three poisons into the three virtues.
Were it not for great illumination and supreme courage, who could attain this? The verse says:

Reverently receive and uphold this sutra. This sutra is manifest before you; this sutra is manifest before you. Avalokiteśvara expounds the Dharma. To listen with the eyes is to begin in the profound;
yet one does not listen with the eyes, but instead hears with the ears. These profound and wondrous sounds become clouds of ignorance; these clouds bury the sun of wisdom.

The long section covers the *Drapo* (Raspberry/Cluster). Those who read this sutra take reverence as their foundation; it makes no distinction between old and young. Such is the nature of the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
Contemplate it in this way, and the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa will protect you with mindfulness, cherishing you as he would his own head or eyes, without weariness.
Verses on the Lack of Self-Nature in Mind and Objects:
The mind is not mind by itself; it becomes mind because of objects. Objects are not objects by themselves; they become objects because of the mind. It is because of objects that there is mind.
Whom do you call "mind"? Because of the mind, there is dust. Pointing out what is this dust? Once both are realized, the myriad dharmas penetrate the Truth.
A Verse Sent to Wucizheng upon His Return Home to Visit His Parents:
I venture to ask where this body comes from; the four elements are clearly but a mound of earth. Within it lies kindness that cannot be forgotten.
It is attained. As the west wind falls the trees and one crosses the Yangtze and Huai rivers, I show to the Zen practitioners that flowing water and the sound of pines are both tongues;
the true mantra revolves unceasingly through the ages. If you rely on your two ears, in the end it will be difficult to grasp.
Listen. To harmonize it, one must still require a human skull.
A Verse to Manifest Knowledge and Depart from Ambitious Resolve (with Preface):
Now, as for "ambitious resolve," that which is not ambitious serves as its mother. Suppose there is a person here who does not obtain it...
If a mother wishes to force her son, this is called "the son restraining the son," and the son will ultimately not submit; only by winning over the mother can one restrain the son. Thus it is said:
"When the copper mountain collapses, the bells of Luo respond; when the mother bites her finger, the son feels pain in his heart.
All these are instances of the mother summoning the son—how could the son fail to respond? Yongjia said: "Without leaving the present place."
Ever serene and profound—is it the son? Is it the mother? He who knows this is said to have attained the Mother.

If the heroic spirit can be dissolved, then even the sounds of music and dance may find their place; a single palm-leaf should be set upon Mount Tai and Mount Song. The ocean of desire, ten thousand fathoms deep, can never be measured;
the source of craving, a single drop, is ultimately inexhaustible.
A Verse for Offering to My Parents upon Entering the Lushan Stupa When my father was alive, I fled from him;
In bitter shame, I could not provide him with sweet delicacies. When my father died, I had not yet returned;
Who would cover his bones with but a single mound of earth? This shame and this resentment—when will they ever fade? Day by day, month by month, they accumulate into a mountain.
Mountains accumulate; even hills and great mountains eventually crumble at the end of a kalpa. Though the kalpa ends and mountains collapse, my grief remains inexhaustible.

Now, relying on the Buddha’s light, I write this sutra; the merit of each and every character is inconceivable. *Namo* to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, the king of all sutras, which is my own nature.
By this merit, I repay my deceased father: may his dark karma be instantly extinguished and he be born in the Buddha-land, where he shall behold the Buddha.
Having heard the Dharma and realized the true mark, it is like gaining the crest-jewel as a reward for merit in battle.

May my deceased father hold this treasure, illuminating the ten directions with boundless flames. My biological mother passed away before she could raise me; my heart’s longing remains fervent, as difficult to transform as stone.
I have no way to repay such supreme virtue; I rejoice that I have left the dust of the world to become a son of the Buddha. I reflect deeply upon the gravity of a woman’s karmic burden of lust;

it is so firm and difficult to uproot that it is like Mount Sumeru. Even Sumeru might be toppled, but lust is difficult to sever. To serve as a bridge across the ocean of suffering requires the power of a Sage.

Among all the sūtras spoken by the Buddha to deliver sentient beings, he always places the precept against killing first and the prohibition of lust second; he never places lust first and killing second.
O Śūraṅgama! Therefore, in repaying my mother’s kindness, I should rely upon this. Homage to the Unsurpassed Śūraṅgama Dhāraṇī!
May it extinguish my mother’s karma of lust like a celestial wind, such that not even a moment’s trace remains. May the pearl of her precepts be pure and its light flawless.
May she behold the Buddha, hear the Dharma, and realize her own mind. May all phenomena become entirely firm and stable. I make this vow equal to the nature of reality (dharmatā). May I behold...
Those who hear [this] shall all emerge from suffering; how much more so those who copy the sutras to repay their parents? If there were no benefit, my words would not be true.

I only pray that these two sutras enter this stupa, and that the stupa likewise remains forever without decay. May the wind-bells proclaim various dharanis and mantras, so that both those with minds and those without may attain realization.
Furthermore, I pray that when the time for such causes and conditions arrives, a great radiance shall be emitted to illuminate [all beings].
The Dharma-realm. Those who touch this light give rise to filial piety; through this heart of filial piety, they attain Bodhi.
One lamp is transmitted to a hundred thousand lamps; from those hundred thousand lamps, the transmission continues forever without end.

May the Buddhas bear witness to my vow, as well as the Dharma, the Sangha, humans, devas, and the eight classes of beings, and all who have resolved their minds in the assemblies of these two sutras, standing before the Buddha to recite various mantras and vowing to provide protection.

This sutra is like the protection of one's eyes; wherever I may be, I shall never be parted from it. I now entreat you with compassion to recite this mantra, so that it may likewise protect me as I transcribe this sutra.
When I attain Buddhahood, I shall repay your kindness just as I repay the kindness of my parents today.
The Verse on Crumbling Nails (with Preface):
When heaven collapses and earth splits, all things are startled; yet when hair falls out and nails wither, people do not perceive it.
If they were to perceive it, their alarm would be no different from that caused by the collapse of heaven and the splitting of earth. This principle is extremely subtle; reflect upon it slowly.
Contemplate this. Know it through reflection. Where there is knowledge, there is nothing that is not perceived. Where there is perception, there is nothing that is not startled by.

When one is startled, one does not neglect. When one does not neglect, one returns to the source. When one returns, the heavens are fundamentally not rent asunder; the earth is fundamentally not split; hair is fundamentally not shed;
and nails are fundamentally not withered. As the verse says:
The pivot has neither refinement nor coarseness; it is used by those who perceive it. As soon as one wishes to give rise to a thought, the pivot becomes a source of doubt.

Doubt leads further to non-awakening; when heaven cracks open, how can one know? Such is the case for the coarse; for the subtle, confusion deepens further. Roots and objects fall into vast desolation; the "Crushed Armor" (Sui-jia) guides us.
Chan Master Doufo’s Verse on Raising the Coffin:
A hundred battles for mountains and rivers; To bury the bones takes but a few steps. With a thousand bushels of beans chanting the Buddha’s name, The Buddha’s dream is shattered this very day.

When the sentiments of both ordinary and sage are withered away, the sense bases and objects suddenly fall away. As the coffin is raised, the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power manifests; the void joins its palms in celebration. Where shall this skull be buried?
The Dharma-body is suddenly and fiercely revealed. If the Buddha of the Beans possesses any numinous power, would he dare to overlook you face-to-face?
Although it is thus, tell me: now that the funeral rites of raising the coffin have been completed, is there still a path for manifesting one's true self? Heh!
From of old, there has not been so much as a hair’s breadth outside the mind; yet people labor their hearts digging the earth to bury others.
Chan Master Doufo’s Verse on His Hanging Portrait:
The great earth, mountains, and rivers—who is this? There is not a single dharma to be contemplated. At that moment, Doufo’s entire body is revealed;
Facing one another, how many can truly know? Heh! The peaks and ridges of the clouds and mountains are exposed; The flowing waters understand how to discourse upon the sutras.
A Gatha on the Staying of the Reliquary by Chan Master Doufo:
The path ahead of Anle Rock is not mistaken; The black and white robes swirl in a clamor amidst the mist and clouds.
One must know that where the reliquary now rests, The rain has cleared, and the groves announce the awakening sprout.
A Verse on Scattering Sand into the Hidden Stupa by Chan Master Doufo:
A handful of auspicious sand is scattered into the tranquil depths of the lake; The stupa remains hidden for ten million years, and its descendants shall ever flourish.

After finishing his bath, as he was about to enter the water and emerge from it, he recited a verse: "Wherein lies the center and the periphery? As soon as he paused to reflect, his entire body broke out in white leprosy.
He then showed this verse to Master Dao'an.
Master An suffered from an ailment in his feet. Zibo offered him his fingernails; as soon as they scratched the itchy spots, the root and its objects suddenly fell away into vast emptiness.
At that time, when asked about his foot ailment, he used his clever tongue to request that [the nails] be placed in a cabinet. This intention was quite ordinary, yet the wise cannot grasp it.

Questioning the Original Abode: A Verse Sent to Layman Zheng of Kunyan on the Theme of "Pure and Originally Thus" Questioning the Original Nature: The old karmic conditions of Langye and Changshui; Guests at the pavilion of Five Peaks and Twin Streams;
The seven pagodas and one pond adorn me.
When ten thousand people call out to an empty valley, the empty valley responds as one. If both the person and the valley were aware of these ten thousand sounds, both would possess a sickness.

The sickness lies in the moment the mind arises; quickly depart from the realm of person and valley. Whether receiving favor or enduring insult, they are like those ten thousand people; whether startled or responding to emptiness, it is all like the echo in the void.

A fleeting moment of joy or sorrow arises; alarm likewise quickly transcends the boundary. By means of my inferential cognition (*anumāna*), the principle of the person and the valley is naturally established.
Without needing to deliberate further on honor or disgrace, I am startled by the principle that the person and the valley are one and the same realm.

A bowl of gruel from the Chan hall is a gruel of the Way-mind; it surpasses drinking ginseng broth. How could rice have two different natures? You must know that it depends on one’s own heart and mind.

The petty person does not cherish their blessings and merely inflicts daily injury upon themselves. The wise feel deep shame and reverence, planting the fragrance of the sun within the field of their minds.
Showing the Layman Kuangshi:
Clearly, the great earth has never known dust; how could water and fire ever have been different from the truth? Under the lamp, one investigates in vain and departs with regret;
the person who came last night is still here this morning.

A Verse for Condoling with Lady Shen: Earth, water, fire, and wind exist everywhere; Meeting conditions, they falsely combine to form head and body. The person of realization understands this and leaves birth and death behind;
This is called truly attaining immeasurable life. When the honorable mother’s retribution is exhausted, she returns to her source; Earth, water, fire, and wind do not...

These may be mixed. To view them through emotion, there is birth and death; to infer them through principle, there is neither addition nor subtraction. The mountains are high and the waters deep, yet they do not alter their constancy.
Peach blossoms are red and plum blossoms are white, each a harmonious color. With every blooming flower comes another spring;
year after year, the brothers increase their weeping.
Next, the verse on the Inn:

This inn is a metaphor for the triple world. Like a sudden rain shower, guests disperse and gather in an instant. Having received the instruction on the principle of non-arising, what can one do for those whose eyes are clouded?
Facing it directly, they have no leisure even to look. When asked the way to Mount Tai, they simply walk straight out the gate.

In the verse of Duanfeng, neither past nor present can be found; who then seeks the limits of before and after? Neither birth nor Buddhahood can be found; who then establishes the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional?
Because there are those of inferior capacity, there are the precious desk and the rare regalia; because there are those struck by wonder, there are the dark-skinned dog and the white ox.

All follow the delusions of the multitude, saying, "This is black (the monastic) and this is white (the lay). The white derives its name because of the black; without the white, the black would have no meaning.

Yet, in the ultimate sense, between the black and the white, there is not a single atom of true reality. This applies equally to the prior and the subsequent, to the ultimate and the conventional; even the limit of words is likewise so.
When the ultimate limit is exhausted, there is nothing more; where can cessation be lodged? With the direct mind, words and thoughts cease; yet in a blink of an eye, one falls into deliberation.
A wooden man claps his hands atop ten thousand peaks; a stone woman smiles at the cliff’s edge as they gaze upon one another.
I show you the ancestral patriarchs' single plot of idle land; alas, their descendants are too lazy to till it. As days pass and years deepen, it has fallen entirely into ruin;
were it not for those of true bone, it would be in vain to turn it over again.

A Verse on Resting at the Ancient Rock: In human life, who reaches a full hundred years? In the blink of an eye, one arrives in the next world. Ephemeral glory is like a flower in a mirror; The sea of suffering has no boundless shore.
The struggles between Chu and Han for supremacy— What purpose do they serve now? Why not instead guard the city of the mind, Protecting this ground of luminosity?
The kalpa-fire burns it not; the turbid waters defile it not. The numinous mechanism governs the six gates, entering and exiting to release the true meaning.
I urge you to observe the rock cliff: the Buddha within the niche is none other than yourself. Were one not a great man indeed, it would not be easy to take this up and bear it.
Within this, even a single thread is not at all suspended. Who would not fear hot excrement being splashed upon them?
Shedding their fur and wearing horns, they turn their bodies; limping and hopping, they move with lively vigor.
The Verse on Observing Archery:
The void contains the traces of the arrow; the arrow pierces the void. It is difficult to distinguish whether the void and the arrow are different or the same in essence.

If one claims there is no path for the arrow within the void, yet clearly the arrow passes through the void. The profound void contains the arrow, making its traces difficult to observe; the arrow skillfully pierces the void, yet leaves no mark.
I have traced the traces [of the Dharma]. Even if an arrow in the sky were slightly obstructed, how could it be that both [the source and the recipient] attain perfect fusion?
Bathing in the azure clouds, I beheld the spiritual image of Kumārajīva in his meditation chamber;
a single ray of light shone from the East, and the Dharma was spread throughout China. Although the meanings vary in depth and the vehicles differ in size, all are the golden [Dharma].
This is what has been proclaimed by his mouth. As for the lineages of those who have translated the scriptures, they number no fewer than over a hundred families.
Yet, in terms of the refinement and elegance of their prose, and in their unerring ability to adapt to the capacities of sentient beings, none surpasses Master Kumārajīva.

Having long admired and yearned for his compassionate rain, I have privately wished that we might have been born in the same age so that I might once receive his alms-bowl and staff. In the spring of the year Wusi (1613) of the Wanli era, I stayed for two nights at Bi... [text truncated]
At Yunsi Temple, I was honored by the Venerable Master Yunzhuang, who provided me with a bath. Subsequently, I had the good fortune to behold the portrait of Master Shi in his meditation hall;
I prostrated myself three times and spoke this verse:
I prostrate to Master Kumārajīva, an ocean of the Prajñā of letters. Having bathed in the words of the Tathāgata, they flow fresh and pure throughout the Dharma-realm.
I am ashamed that, born in this degenerate age, I have had no leisure to follow his staff and bowl; yet as I gaze upon the shadow of the Venerable One, a profound sense of reverence arises within me.
Relying on the power of compassion, you have pulled me from the mire of ignorance and folly. You bathe me in the waters of wisdom and insight, moistening this seal of the true nature (*dharmatā*).
Without waiting for dry earth to be dug up, I sit sated upon the nectar of Prajñā; I make no distinction between sound and form, nor even the voices of oxen and horses.
Laughter and jesting, spittle and abuse, earth, stones, and all thorns—all these are the samādhi of speech.
At Yunzhuang and Baoshan, jade marrow gushes from beneath the pines; drawn up and led around the steps and terraces, it flows into the kitchen of Xiangji, where it turns cold into warm springs.
Mixed with various medicinal herbs, it was placed in a wooden basin while still hot; he directly fashioned it into a pool of fragrant water.

Out of pity for my weariness from traveling on foot and the accumulation of dust and grime upon my tattered robes, he cast me into its clear, cool waters, submerging both my head and my feet, as if within the ripples of a spring.
How much of the remaining ice can possibly be shaken away? When the subtle touch proclaims clarity, neither sense-faculties nor objects can be found;
it is like reaching out one's hand to feel empty space. How could empty space have bones? Yet Master Kumārajīva saw through it and laughed incessantly. "Alas! he cried to his young disciple.
Do not look at the eye with the eye; if the eye could observe itself, it would ultimately not be one's own eye. Although the eye does not observe itself, its own existence is not thereby negated.
If you can understand it thus, this basin is the broad and long tongue, appearing and disappearing as the sublime mark of the tongue.
Unobstructed by the mark of the tongue—this is called a messenger of the Tathāgata, also named Avalokiteśvara. If a person intends to bathe, they should first know this verse;
if they do not know it and waste water, who shall take responsibility for the merit or the fault?
The Collected Works of the Elder Zibo, Volume Nineteen;
The Collected Works of the Elder Zibo, Volume Twenty.
Translated by Hanshan Deqing of the Ming Dynasty. Reviewed.
The Five Constant Verses:
Homage to the Buddha Benevolent and Compassionate. Loving others as one loves oneself, If this mind is never obscured, Then the Tathāgata appears in the world.
Homage to the Buddha Righteous and Spirited. Loving others so they surely obtain what they need, Acting with no laxity when facing affairs, One attains perfect enlightenment on the spot.

Homage to the Buddha of Reverent Etiquette. In every matter, clarity is essential; the order of elders and juniors remains undisturbed. The World-Honored One is none other than you. Homage to the Buddha of Wisdom.
Transformation and adaptation proceed without obstruction; one upholds the upright and does not support the depraved, transforming suffering into blessings.
Homage to the Buddha of Faithful Mind. Truly there is nothing that changes; a single thought-moment and ten thousand years are always as one from beginning to end.
These five Tathāgatas are inherently possessed by every person. When used well, they are the Buddhas who radiate light; when not used well, they are the Buddhas who enter parinirvāṇa.
I pray that all beings, regarding death and birth, as well as the pleasant and the unpleasant, must always apply their minds with diligence; do not be turned by worldly passions.
When born, the Buddha does not die; when passing away, how could the Buddha be extinguished? This state of neither extinction nor birth—this is the ground of auspiciousness.
Wu Yuan and Shen Baoxu—initially, these two were inseparable friends. One set out to destroy Chu; the other set out to restore it. Yuan was indeed jealous of Baoxu.
"How could he have been able to destroy Chu? If Xu had been as jealous as Yuan, it would also have been difficult for Chu to survive. These two were like mirrors reflecting one another;

their fundamental radiance was never obscured, and the Great Function manifested before them. Yet they could not bear the burden, and when they contemplated advancing or retreating with a calculating mind, they were called 'wild foxes.'"
It is not of the lion’s lineage.

The verse on "the unchanging following conditions" begins with a single piece of gold from which all birds and beasts are fashioned; once the birds and beasts have lost their original nature, they contend with one another, dividing things into "self" and "other."
The wise see it and smile; the foolish see it and become angry. To smile is to despise its folly; to be angry is to assist its strife.
As I observe the people of the world, how many there are who assist in strife! Among ten thousand, not one smiles. I only pray that you may ride upon the Buddha’s light.
Wrath and laughter are both illuminated and shattered; in adversity and favor, he is ever sovereign.
Reading Dongpo’s eulogy on Shi Ke’s painting of Vimalakīrti:
"I observe that this Stone-Master is inconceivable; his supernatural power exceeds that of Vimalakīrti. He was able to take the past city of Vaiśālī..."
The chamber is such that all who gaze upon it see it as clearly as the palm of their own hand. The thirty-two sages do not engage in dualistic discourse;

from their mouths, the great rivers flow in surging torrents. The sick man has no words to answer Mañjuśrī; his ears burn, his face is yellow, and his mouth remains silent. Holy ones and commoners alike seize the opportunity to heap praise or censure at will.
In the end, who can truly discern light from dark? This ready-made fragrant meal is intended for a single satiation. Having eaten one’s fill, one beholds the wondrous.
Huiyan again seized him; the lion throne was over twenty thousand feet high, yet the Bodhisattvas were accommodated without crowding.
The square fathom did not expand, nor did the assembly diminish; they illuminated one another like lamps without mutual obstruction. I observe that Master Su’s skill is even more extraordinary:
he plundered the Stone Hermit from within a dream, and further placed Vimalakīrti behind his head, displaying his own words of sovereign spiritual power.
Rolling up or spreading out, speaking or remaining silent, bending or extending the arm—what effort does a strong man expend? Yet he causes onlookers to gasp and startle;
how is this any different from a butterfly caught in the wind and rain? Amidst the fluttering, they seek an entrance upon the paper, vying to find a high hall to avoid being swept away or drowned.
I laugh at myself, this old man, unable to restrain them: with a single blow of the fist, I knock down the Son of Mei-shan and seize the Dragon Pearl.

The radiance is even more wondrous; the sudden teaching covers the basin-like land and brings enlightenment to the nation. As the butterfly’s dream returns and spring first clears, the people within the city of Vaiśālī are finally able to speak.
This is the verse on hand-seals by Grand Chancellor Lu.
Now, among all calamities and blessings, none are more profound than life and death; yet the vanguard of life and death must invariably originate in old age and illness.
At the critical juncture of old age and illness, when one’s condition is precarious, even the courage of Mengben or the wisdom of Shun Yu could not be applied.
Now, as the Grand Chancellor stands at this moment of old age, illness, and peril, his spirit remains undisturbed and his hand-mudra firm.
He maintained [his composure]. Though old and ill, he could not be burdened by it. Gazing at his countenance, one saw that his expression was clear and luminous;
was this not a manifest proof of the steadfast vigor of his mental power throughout his life? The Daoist Daguān asked after his illness and witnessed these matters with his own eyes.
He spoke this verse of praise:
"The mudrā is firmly maintained; though seen by all, the beginning of the mudrā cannot be fathomed by the mind, much less beheld by the eye."
This cannot be seen; whether it is destroyed or not, the wise understand it clearly, while the multitude are struck with wonder.
At the Four Buddha Terrace of the Yuantong Hermitage on Longshan at Jintan, I inscribed these words:
"Though he still laments that his dwelling is too narrow, the four Buddhas share a single terrace, each finding contentment in one another."

Ordinary beings and sages are fundamentally the same; it is only through delusion and awakening that a separation is formed. Hehehe. Do you understand? The peach is crimson and the plum is white as spring reaches its midpoint;
the bright moon and clear breeze possess different moods.

A Verse on Nianfo for So-and-so (Composed before Age Fifty-eight): "How many years have you actually reached? Contemplate this with great earnestness. Once you have understood how many years there truly are, you will understand how to practice nianfo well.
It is better to understand while still alive; birth and death arise from the body—apart from the body, where else would you seek them?"
The two of them have not yet seen me; the lamp-light is like the break of dawn. Return home and investigate with care; do not take the wrong path.
Verse for the Birthday of Mother Ci-yin: Today Ci-yin is born;
The compassionate mother’s body feels light. Who shall turn the wheel of Prajñā? The sound of the Dharma from the Golden Wheel.
Able to hear through every pore, manifesting divine power in daily life; who would have thought that the tongue of compassionate sound was a thousand-fathom vajra gong?
To reveal the Stone Gate, the monk Gu Ni composed this verse:
"When coming there is nothing, and when departing it is the same; coming and going are clearly like the wind from a bellows. If only the departed spirits could know this..."
O mind, when the eyes open and close, what trace remains?
This verse shatters the mind of birth and death:
where does the presently manifest discriminating mind ultimately arise? If it arises from one's own mind, since there are no external objects, what would serve as its ground?

The object can give rise to conceptualization; how could the object itself conceptualize the object? Even if one claims they arise through mutual causality, the union of two such things cannot be established without difficulty.
Since their union is irrational, one ultimately falls into the view of spontaneity (*svabhāva*). The wise examine this with great care; the ignorant lightly overlook it.
In this regard, I have not investigated it extensively; the mind of birth and death is difficult to shatter. To Ji Chanren (with preface):
Master Zibo once read Dongpo’s *Eulogy on Avalokiteśvara* and most cherished the line where the one who calls out seems to suffer the pain himself.
Then one will certainly be unable to call out. Now, consider the peril of a Zen practitioner crossing a river;

while they may initially feel they have the power to repel the danger amidst the perils, as the waves grow larger and the winds rise higher, they will ultimately be unable to avoid being turned about by the wind and waves.
This is the honest word of such a Zen practitioner. Nevertheless, from this point on, one must remain honest even when facing adversity.
Regarding favorable conditions: when encountering the perils of wind and waves, one must exert effort to dispel them; if this continues for a long time, one may enter the stage of faith (*śraddhā*).
Therefore, I have composed this verse to leave behind for fellow practitioners, as a slight aid toward diligent progress.
A thousand waves and ten thousand billows leave a single boat in peril; how long can one merely struggle to sustain oneself?
If you inquire where the life-root is about to be severed, who among them is the Great Compassionate Teacher?
Verse on the Difficulty of Mother’s Kindness: My mother gave birth to me, yet I have no means to repay her; For long I have owed my mother this single debt of gratitude.
That I burn incense here at Yushan today Is to invite a wandering monk on behalf of my mother.

Verses on Dwelling in the Mountains: Dwelling in the mountains requires no great artifice; it is simply a matter of returning to a state of singular simplicity. After the rain, new ground is revealed; as the lamp dims, old soot is trimmed away.
Illuminating the mind, I turn over the *bǎiyè* leaves; supporting my feet, I protect the verdant moss. Having long severed the path of wind and dust, who would ask of the Great Plum?

The Verse on Contemplating Flowers: The hibiscus blooms upon the river; its flowers hold an autumnal gaze so wondrous. When the wind stirs them, one suspects they are looking back and forth. The traveler’s heart and soul are muddled with infatuation.

Do the flowers truly possess the traveler’s heart? Why does the traveler’s heart not reflect upon this? By contemplating the mind that contemplates, you will spontaneously realize that the flower is your teacher.
This meaning is indeed not shallow. When the mind opens, it yields its celestial mechanism.

If the verse on light and darkness were not set with a lamp, then darkness would fill the space before one. Yet, when the lamp is suddenly lit, the brightness is complete and perfect; the darkness was truly there as darkness.
