From what does illumination arise? If there is illumination, from what can darkness take form? Whenever one contemplates in this way, the faculties and their objects become serene and empty.
In this state of serenity, moisture has no center or periphery; when water freezes in the cold, its solid nature is difficult to remove, yet when ice encounters warmth, it melts away.

The fused characteristics are fundamentally suchness. Brightness and darkness, ice and water—these serve as analogies for the myriad things. Once a single thing enters [this state], every single thing becomes honey.

Though honey has its periphery and center, the Buddha finds it difficult to analyze; even analysis cannot reach it. When攀緣 (pān-yuán, the grasping of objects) naturally subsides, vision becomes penetrating and contemplation matures.
Birth and death, adversity and favor—these are but the carving of empty space. A thousand ages are but a single instant; who undergoes extinction, and who appears in the world?

Riding the wheel of wisdom and vows, one manifests both the provisional and the real. The provisional stops the crying of children; the real brings about one’s own completion. Light and darkness are my teachers.
How could I forget your virtue? Ice and water are my friends; how dare I distinguish between the fine and the coarse? My boat is moored at Nanxu; willow branches rest upon my elbow.
Within the Unconcealed Studio, at the mouth of the Zhenjiang sluice-gate, Qilang writes for me while Zhilang nods in agreement. All those traveling with us have fallen asleep.
A Dream of a Somersault.
An Ode for Soliciting Offerings of Lamp Oil for the Buddha at Huanglongtan on Mount Lu (with Preface):
Now, fire does not transmit itself; it must rely upon fuel. Fuel, likewise, does not burn itself; it must rely upon fire. Thus...
To say that when the fuel is exhausted the fire is extinguished is not the insight of a person of realization. Why?
Because while the fuel has an end, the fire is inexhaustible. If the fire were to have an end, then wherever there is fuel there would be fire, and wherever there is no fuel there would be no fire.
But now it is not so; for by using a *fangzhu* (a concave mirror) directed toward the moon and receiving [the water] in a basin, [fire is produced].

In a short while, the basin was filled with water. One might say that this water indeed comes from the moon; yet, if it were merely like the *fangzhu* (the "square-jade" lens), then the moon alone could not produce the flow of water.
One might say it comes from the pearl; but if the pearl does not depend on the moon, why would it not produce water even without it?
One might say that water arises when the pearl and the moon coincide; but this too is not so. At first, the moon and the pearl each seek their own [conditions].
Water. Water has no self-nature; how could there be water through the union of two absences?
The gentlemen of the world should truly regard the study of "investigating things to bring about the extension of knowledge" as not being beyond their capacity, and should examine it with patience.

When the fuel is exhausted, is the fire truly extinguished? Do the concave mirror and the moon truly unite to produce flowing water? If one examines this for a long time, [the truth will become clear].

When sincerity accumulates, clarity will emerge. Once one attains awakening and penetration, one will then know that that which transcends form has never failed to be an instrument, and that which is below form has never failed to be the Way. If this is so, then within the midst of my daily life—
Welcoming guests and attending to visitors; bowing, turning, bending, and rising; matters of right and wrong, honor and disgrace;
circumstances that are favorable or adverse; physical and mental toil or ease; dressing and eating; defecating and urinating; seeking clothes when cold and seeking food when hungry;
being joyful when things accord with one’s wishes and angry when they oppose them—one should also examine these calmly: are they the vessel, or are they the Way? They are the Way.
Is it not so? You must surely understand this clearly for yourself. At Huanglongtan on Mount Lu, there is a golden image of Vairocana Buddha.
"Vairocana" means "light pervading all places. Since his light already pervades all places, why rely upon a lamp?
For the sun illuminates the day and the moon lights the night; [the lamp] merely succeeds them.

As for this clarity—clarity regarding the inexhaustible—it is only the lamp that can provide it. The Sage desires that people grasp the meaning through the image, so that once the meaning is grasped, the image may be forgotten;
this is the final word of Great Awakening. O extraordinary man, why must you ascend Huanglong to behold a Buddha statue before you attain enlightenment?
You may do so right now, sitting together with your children in a circle amidst the light of candles and lamps.
After drinking at night and singing songs in joy, once one has fallen into a deep sleep and the effects of the wine have dissipated,
if one slightly opens their eyes from intoxication and slowly examines the light of this lamp— whether it arises from the oil, from the wick, or whether the fire illuminates itself—
if at this moment one suddenly awakens to the source from which the light arises, take it for granted that this drunkard need not undergo the cultivation of three great kalpas.

"Attaining Buddhahood in this very place" is a matter for the gentlemen of Xiangyang. If you do not regard the words of a man of profound insight as madness, but are able to adopt and listen to them, then the masters who transform beings like Huanglong will be as numerous as hemp seeds among you, patrons. The verse says:

At the Yellow Dragon Pool on Mount Lu, one begs for oil to make offerings to the Tathāgata. One knows not who possesses the karmic affinity to joyfully bestow pure wealth, purchasing fragrant and clean oil to light lamps that illuminate the Buddha’s altar.
Their radiance is forever inexhaustible; those who hear or see it find the flower of their mind in full bloom.
Oil also emerges from water; yet water and fire are naturally opposed. Their conflict continues without end until the water departs and the oil and fire remain together.
This principle is most subtle; know it and do not doubt the ways of the world. That which arises through conditions is itself non-arising; the Way and its vessel are fundamentally of one womb.
Countless Buddhas born from the womb all come forth from this radiance; may all those who offer oil be in accord with the heart-mind of Vairocana.
*Ten Verses on the Ten Scenic Views of Cheng'en Temple*, "Precious Lion Rock" (Bao Shiyan).
His tail brushes the blue sky and his head shakes the void; with a casual roar, he terrifies the hair-raising insects.
The old man Mañjuśrī rides him away, roaming through the dust-motes and lands throughout the ten directions.
The ox lies in the pond, not the azure dragon; he lies down with his white ox. Within the great trichiliocosm, all is gathered upon the tip of his horn.
Usually too lazy to trespass upon the crops of men, he finds abundance in clouds, sunlight, water, and grass.

The path to Thousand Peaks Hermitage lies in the void, not in the dust. Where the white clouds gather, the Chan practitioner lies in repose. When spring comes and the rain falls, the thousand peaks are purified;
from the treetops, the spring water flies forth as five new blossoms.
The Phoenix Bridge locks the phoenixes and dragons; fearing they will not return, the stone beam acts as a bolt to bind them forever.
If you should ask how many monks there are upon meeting them, ten thousand fingers stand in dense rows surrounding the inkstone pool.
The fluttering banners on the broad virtue-pole and the chiming of the bells—how could their harmony be the same? Caoxi spoke in vain, saying it was not because of the wind.
If fish and shrimp were permitted to be dredged from the level fields, today’s peach blossoms would be as red as those of old.
The Spring of the Five Eyes:

The five eyes are inherently complete within every person. When the ground of ignorance is shattered, the clear pupils emerge. If one were to use horizontal eyes to distinguish between the ordinary and the sage, one would have to use a rabbit’s horn to pick through the clouds over a distant hill.
On the Terrace of Nirvāṇa, set aside body and mind to inquire of fortune and misfortune; it clearly carves through the vast void.
Upon the Terrace of Nirvāṇa, on a clear autumn night, ten thousand miles of cloudless sky, the moon stands in its full splendor.

In the stupa courtyard of Master Chenggong, the precious grounds and empty groves hold many fallen leaves; the spiritual remains of my former teacher lie amidst the surging waves. Grasping my hoe, I intend to dig for the moon in the water;
it is better that I cast incense and pay homage at the upper terrace.
In the Xixin Pavilion, seeking the mind, no mind is found; this is the very method for washing the mind. All feverish afflictions are made cool right where they arise.
If travelers could understand this meaning, the faculty of their tongues would grow long through the pines, water, wind, and moon.
In the depths of ten thousand peaks, Guanyin’s Tomb opens its Universal Gate; how could such a spirit of the Way willingly remain shrouded by the miasma of the burning house?
Truly, this Great Being was the son of Emperor Yang; why did the qilin give birth from an ox’s womb?
The Verse on Illuminating Body and Mind:
If the body were identical to the mind, who would be the body? If the mind were identical to the body, who would be the mind?

If the body were identical to the mind, from where would birth and death arise? If the mind were identical to the body, where would afflictions reside? When body and mind are thoroughly penetrated, doubt does not arise. This is...
This body and mind are true *prajñā*. When *prajñā* manifests, body and mind are empty. Although body and mind are empty, body and mind remain;
this body is the true *dharmakāya*, and this mind is the true wondrous mind. The *dharmakāya* is fundamentally without birth and death;
sentient beings are deluded by it, and thus birth and death arise. The wondrous mind is fundamentally without afflictions; sentient beings are deluded by it, and thus afflictions arise.
Disturbed and agitated, as soon as one's own body and mind reach the water, waves arise. In the ordinary course of daily life, every single thing is present;

when meeting others, it is no mere play of children. If body and mind do not awaken, they are truly like dogs and swine. How much more so for a human, the most intelligent among the myriad things—if the Great Matter is not understood, one must feel dread and alarm.
Through long-term dread and alarm, the Buddhas take pity; they manifest transformed bodies to preach non-arising before one’s very eyes.
Those who meet morning and evening—who among them does not kindle the Buddha-lamp within their breast? Yet though the Buddha-lamp is lit, it does not illuminate oneself;
with eyes wide open, one walks as if in the night.
At first, entering the stream from within hearing, one loses the objects of perception;

like a veteran general who refuses to surrender, one carves out a boundary within the vast void. As frozen thunder emerges from the earth, awakening a lingering dream, there arises a distinct fragrance of plum blossoms.
The pig-verse:
Raising pigs to satisfy one’s appetite creates enmity through the bonds of craving. If the pig understood this meaning, it would not eat all day long out of sorrow.
If it were both sorrowful and fasting, would there still be pork for others? It is fortunate that the pig remains ignorant; thus, its fat flesh passes down your throat.
In the end you will become a pig; you must still repay the debt for the lard. This principle is indeed not false; I urge you to stop raising pigs.
If the firewood of words is subtle, the fire of contemplative insight has nothing to cling to. If the fire of contemplative insight is subtle, the firewood of body and mind will not burn.
The firewood burns and instantly becomes ash; as the ash flies away, body and mind are exhausted. The lamp of the profound true reality has radiance that is neither internal nor external;
it burns itself and burns others. One lamp transmits to a hundred thousand; those hundred thousand transmit endlessly, remaining forever like the break of dawn through all eternity.
Throughout the ten directions there is no time of night; the fuel of letters is merit. Therefore, the wise attain the mind through letters.
Apart from the mind, no phenomena exist; letters are the light of the mind. When this light illuminates the faculty of the eye, there is no form capable of confronting the eye.
Taking light as the sound of thunder, the ear-hearing and ear-consciousness are empty. Taking thunder as wondrous fragrance, the nose-olfaction finds nothing to grasp.
Taking fragrance as supreme flavor, the tongue-tasting is itself wisdom. Taking flavor as the object of touch, the sensation of contact leaves the body-faculty behind.
Where do birth and death reside? They are like a tortoise’s hair binding a hare’s horn. Taking contact as the principle of phenomena, the five sensory objects fall away like shadows.
Conditions are not causal conditions; they transform through the transformation of discrimination. Each shadow possesses its own three aspects: seeds, habitual tendencies, and manifestations.

Though they pass through thousands of millions of kalpas, the six sense faculties are further immeasurable; within the four modes of birth and seven realms of existence, their floating and sinking are difficult to count.

Seeds, habit-energies, manifestations, and so forth—perfuming, seeds, and reflections—are not in disorder. Because they are not in disorder, each has its own rule; therefore, it is named "Dharma-rule" (*dharmatā*).

I have composed this verse on the firewood of writing, titled "The Buddha-nature as the Conditioned Cause. May it perfume your understanding and realization, so that the lamp of the true mark may be transmitted forever.
Whether enemy or friend, may all enter the ocean of radiant light.
An Explanation of the Verses from the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* (with Preface):

There is no going in that which has already gone; there is also no going in that which has not yet gone. Apart from that which has already gone and that which has not yet gone, there is also no going in the "present process of going.

What meaning does this verse clarify? It is because that which has not yet gone serves as the cause for the "present process of going," and the "present process of going" [serves as the cause] for that which has not yet gone.
The present going is the effect of that which has already gone, and that which has already gone is the cause of the present going.
Observing it in this way, the present going cannot go by itself; it must depend upon that which has not yet gone in order to have going.

Since it must depend upon that which has not yet gone for there to be going, going fundamentally lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Once one realizes that going has no intrinsic nature, [one likewise realizes the same for] that which has not yet gone and that which has already gone.

It is so in all cases. For example, where there is a middle, there are two ends. The wise person thoroughly understands that these three times have no coming or going, yet they are not oblivious to coming and going.
That which has not yet gone is not called "going. That which has already gone is not called "going. Apart from what has already gone and what has not yet gone, who is it that goes while going?

Furthermore, apart from the very act of going, neither the already-gone nor the not-yet-gone can be obtained. Apart from these two, there is no intermediate state; it is impossible for such a thing to exist.
To claim that there are two heads in a single body is likewise impossible. With my discerning wisdom, I have investigated the coming and going of things;
like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit, they possess names but lack reality. When one sees through a single phenomenon, one has no doubt regarding all phenomena.

If one has doubts regarding all phenomena and has not yet fully understood even a single dharma, yet possesses roots of goodness, upon suddenly comprehending this verse, all sūtras will become as clear as looking at the palm of one's hand;
like the opening and closing of a clenched fist, one will attain mastery over their expansion and contraction.
The Verses on Radiance:
The Treasury of Immeasurable Radiance. Its applications vary according to conditions; if there were a fixed nature from beginning to end, how could every phenomenon be perfectly interfused?
Exhortation to the Youth.
Zi-fang’s suppression of Qin’s martial spirit was more than just a ten-thousand-foot rainbow. Once he was able to humble himself, he advanced his shoes before the old man at the Broken Bridge.
I have heard that when the elderly butcher sat in leisurely merriment with his guests, he would call out to a guest who must immediately kneel; yet the guest’s face showed no sign of anger.
Having knelt for a long time, he remained silent; the butcher then invited the guest to share a meal. The guest, filled with suspicion, ventured to ask the elder:

"For what reason do you kneel thus? The old butcher spoke slowly and deliberately: "When young, I passed the highest imperial examinations; I had never yet been humbled by poverty or low station. If I do not forget this [present state], I must kneel."
Throughout his life he never exhausted its use. After Zhang Liang presented his shoes, the Old Man of the Embankment’s bones had already rotted away;

yet to this day, hearing of his spirit makes one’s hair stand on end. The one who knelt was buried in yellow earth, while the Chancellor was entrusted to the flowing waters; such kneeling knows neither past nor present.
Those who hear this are without fail inspired with courage. This courage, when encountering sounds and forms, cannot be deluded by those sounds and forms. This courage governs the barbarians;
the barbarians dare not act contrary to it. I vow that with this courage, I shall maintain it daily without forgetfulness, so that in every place there is a Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Verses for the Midday Meal (with Preface) I have long suffered from an ailment regarding water and stone, which has not yet been cured. By chance, while my midday meal was not yet finished, the mountain and river scenery suddenly presented themselves before me.
Unaware that the faculty of the eye consumes form and the tongue does not abandon flavor, one laughs at oneself and deludes oneself, merely reciting these verses.
The tongue takes food as its sustenance; the eye takes form as its sustenance. The tongue and eye consume simultaneously; there is neither sequence nor non-sequence.
The mountains and waters abound with mist and clouds; the vegetables and rice are provided with salt and vinegar. Are these the same or different? Fundamentally, they are but one human affair.
To seek "subject" and "object" within this is like using one's own hand to rub one's nose: if there were a hand outside the nose, it would be another and not oneself.
This meaning is clear from the outset; why trouble oneself to seek it out?

When the verse of illness is shown to people of all quarters, those who were previously free of illness considered themselves cast from solid iron; yet when the day of illness arrives, how could they not become as soft as cotton wool?
As the four great elements increase and decrease in mutual conflict, no suffering fails to reach one. The Buddha’s knowledge and vision that one has practiced prove utterly ineffective when tested.

In the midst of illness, it is difficult to maintain mastery; at the moment of death, how could one not err? Once this error occurs, for ten million kalpas, one will be like a weight sinking to the bottom of the sea.
If you wish for its head to emerge, you must wait for a horse to grow horns. How could one find such a marvelous man? When ill, he remains as if not ill;
when assailed by alternating chills and fevers, his heart remains as calm as the sea. Though the wild waves rage against the heavens, his moist nature remains fundamentally unchanged.
This very state of non-alteration is understood as clearly as one's own palm; it is like the opening and closing of a fist, or the bending and extending of an athlete’s arm.
The sick man is like a weakling, while the healthy is like an athlete; when they compete for victory or defeat, even a fool can discern the outcome.
How much more so for a person of wisdom—how could they have any doubt or confusion regarding this? Knowing that the illness is empty and non-existent, prajñā suddenly manifests before them.
As soon as there is the slightest perception of suffering, prajñā immediately vanishes. How could the suffering of illness and prajñā ever have been two separate things?
Coolness and feverish affliction, in a single kṣaṇa, may suddenly reverse. Where does the root of the illness lie? Let the sick person seek it out for themselves.
Once they have found its root, the illness is cured, and they laugh aloud.
The Verse on Hearing the Bell:
If there is dust within the faculty, And if there is the faculty within the dust, Since faculty and dust have already intermingled, Subject and object would be mutually uninterrupted.
If there is no dust within the faculty, And if there is no faculty within the dust, Faculty and dust do not intermingle; Who is first, and who is later?
The true and the false each have their own paths; they proceed together but do not enter together. Upon entering, one realizes it all at once; before entering, there is only fragmented distraction.
This matter is no small thing; only the Great Hero can truly comprehend it.
Hymn in Praise of the Fourth Patriarch:
Homage to the Great Master Xinxing of the Fourth Patriarchate. From childhood he already knew how to seek liberation;

had it not been for his innate, numinous bone-structure from former lives, how could his profound concern and far-reaching deliberation have reached such a state? One morning, meeting the Venerable Can on a narrow path, a single blow struck him head-on and sent him flying.

Foul-smelling sweat. To fully understand the dual discourse of bondage and liberation: the *lienu* and the white ox-demon are constantly in their company; at the moment of departure, they receive the child of no lineage.
The impoverished household’s broken utensils are inherited by another. With much sentiment, they suddenly emerge from Huangmei, deceiving Niu-tou until his poverty reaches the very bone.
Among humans and devas, there is naturally a loss of reliance and protection; embracing their stolen goods and crying out in grievance, who can understand them? They carry flowers in their mouths...
Birds of a hundred species seek their tracks; how is this different from seeking fierce flames within layers of ice? I have long harbored a heart like that of a dog or a horse;

now, while still afflicted by illness, I bow my head once before your compassionate light. I pray only that our ancestors will pity us, the weak and lost, and frequently deliver us from the dream of birth and death.

A Verse in Honor of the Fifth Patriarch: I bow my head to the Great Master Ren of the Fifth Patriarch. He did not reckon with moments of leisure, but reckoned with long periods of time. Before and behind the mountain he planted pine seeds;

The pines grew tall, attracting cranes to roost therein. Though the cranes came, they did not understand how to ride them away. There is going and there is coming, yet it is not [a matter of] departing.
My concern is this: while long life is surely superior to a short one, it would be better than having neither birth nor death and remaining as such.

One morning, setting down my hoe, I prostrated at the foot of the bed; the Way of the Dharma could then be entrusted to me. The Abbot, weary of my age, permitted me to return; I simply questioned my mother, not my father.
This deceived my mother’s belly until it suddenly grew large, and the whole clan fell into a clamor, contending in their grief and resentment. My single body—

Solitary and without reliance, he dwells morning and evening in ruined halls and cold temples. Having given birth to a child who immediately understands the Way has no surname, he strikes at the head monk’s heart-disease.
The robe and bowl from the West are all handed over to him; the red egg roars as it carries out the Patriarch’s command.
The Buddhas of the ten directions shrink their necks; the hunting tribes of Lingnan possess vast supernatural powers.
They seek their livelihood amidst the ranks of hunters, while seven hundred eminent sages remain bloated with empty bellies. That the road to Shu is difficult to traverse is known to the world;
who would say that the transmission of the Dharma hangs by a thread? I often contemplate this in the deep night; worldly thoughts cause tears to moisten my black robes. Today, at the muddy harbor...
Passing by the riverbank, the grass before Liangni’s Mound remains as it was of old. With the west wind falling the leaves, the road ahead is difficult;
the affection between mother and child is broken from this point on. A Verse on the Holy and the Mundane.
A rabbit conceives and gives birth to six dragons; not only do they bring rain, but they also stir the wind. Seizing the moment, they can wield power and turn things upside down;
a single expanse of springtime light melts all the myriad flowers.

Verses on the Subtle and Manifest Profound Principle of the Innate Evil of the Tiantai School (also known as the Verses on Non-Nature) I bow my head to the Honored Ones of the Triple Gem throughout the ten directions—those of the future, the past, and the present. I now entreat you with compassion to bear witness;
may you grant your protection through both hidden and manifest power. The three periods of time are not separate from a single thought-moment; how could they exist apart from the three periods?
A single thought-moment is like a finger that can bend and extend. If one discards bending and establishes extension, the blood vessels are severed.

Defilement and purity likewise follow what is perfumed by conditions; as conditions vary, the two aspects of good and evil manifest. That which manifests and can be seen is called "cultivation" (*xiū*); that which cannot be seen is called "nature" (*xìng*).
Nature itself is not a [fixed] nature, for it is inherently non-awakened. This non-awakening is not separate from defilement and purity. To realize this is to understand.
Since defilement and purity are thus, what is there to be troubled by the bending and extending of a single finger? Bending and extending cannot be found apart from the finger;

likewise, how could defilement and purity exist apart from the mind? The mind is the fundamental essence, the source of both defilement and purity. Yet even this source is not a fixed nature; how then could it truly be defiled or pure?

Only through awakening the mind can one reach definitive resolution; through resolution, one first comes to know the subtlety of the Tiantai school. The subtlety of the Tiantai school lies in its doctrine of inherent evil (*xing-è*).
This "Samādhi of Inherent Evil" is the King of Samādhis, wherein all defilement and purity are simultaneously and freely mastered. All of this relies upon the power of the merit of inherent evil.

A blind teacher who fails to perceive the mystery of inherent evil abandons defilement and establishes purity, thereby destroying the essence of the Buddha. I, your disciple, look up to and rely upon [the Master].

The Power of the Triple Gem. This verse briefly elucidates the fundamental tenets of the Tiantai school. I further pray that all who see or hear it may together awaken to the nature of evil within sentient beings, thereby benefiting all conscious creatures.
A verse for offering milk-rice to the Buddha on the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month.
The Tathāgata attained the Way this very day. In the ultimate attainment of the Way, what is there to be gained?

We have not yet attained the Way today; in our non-attainment, what is there to be lost? Let the great assembly present here investigate this with deep pain. If you can penetrate through it, use your nose to eat the milk and curd.
Do not loathe this as reckless talk; every word and every character is the juice of lethal poison.

Verses on the Bee Touching the Paper Window (Two Poems) Even if it flies a thousand times or ten thousand times, the mind arises because of its objects; how could it possess true knowledge? Simply cast away both subject and object together;
without relying on arduous study, you will penetrate through to non-doubt.

When coming, there was never any obstruction; as soon as you wish to seek illumination, penetration becomes difficult. If you are willing to look back and see where it comes from, what path of coming and going would not be as vast as the heavens?
A verse shown to Xu Mengru:
When the head is turned and struck with a snap, there is therein no place for thought to dwell. Young Master Xu, recognize the place of return face-to-face;
only then will you believe that when spring comes, the branches are full of blossoms.

**Verses on Holy Wisdom (with Preface)** If it is claimed that the non-arising of thought is holy wisdom (*āryajñāna*), then one must realize the non-arising of thought; this realization is itself a form of knowing.
Does this realization involve thought, or does it not involve thought? If it involves thought, then thought exists, and it is certainly impossible to fathom that which is without thought.
Regarding "mindfulness": if mindfulness does not engage with objects, then since mindfulness does not engage, knowing (*jñāna*) is likewise fundamentally non-existent.

To say that realizing the mind has not yet moved is "sage-wisdom" (*āryajñāna*)—how is this realization any different from [the futility of] trying to grasp at space or counting someone's bones? Reflect on this.
Noble wisdom is luminously clear—cease further seeking. Beyond the mountains and rivers, there is no other spirit.
Only by searching for arising and ceasing right where you stand can you truly believe that there is still ice remaining in the red furnace.
When Master Lei was drinking tea, he recited this verse:
"Before the thought of 'I' has arisen, who is it that drinks the tea? How could one know that the tea does not consume itself? Within this, there is a separate path through the throat;
every drop must be made to become a dewdrop upon a flower."
A Verse on Hearing Rain at the Bābāja Hermitage:

It is truly as if it comes from the treetops over the deep springs; *Gung-gung*, the light peals of thunder rise from the crags and gullies. Why need one seek out secluded retreats beyond the mundane world?
In the city, the essence of forest clouds does not differ.
The sound of rain beating on the banana leaves—when heard, delusion and enlightenment are all too distinct. Only Lingyun was permitted to see the peach blossoms;
I dare say Panshan’s dream has not yet awakened.

The sacred traces of Lord Wan extend through a thousand peaks and ten thousand crags; the sound of flying springs resounds from mid-heaven. A path winds back along the cliffs to reach the secluded depths;
there, amidst flowing waters and peach blossoms, one may inquire after Lord Wan.
A Verse by Shi Yu-jing:
Who does not love the crimson flowers when spring arrives? Suddenly, the eastern wind rises in the vast void. One looks upon their lush beauty and then their withering;
this mind is everywhere empty and harmonious.

In these verses on the inverse and the conforming, lust, anger, and impermanence are all but this very channel. Encountering conditions, whether adverse or favorable, they alternate in multiplication and subtraction.
Following the teachings, one’s skillful means may overturn heaven and earth, yet how many times have we sought them out only to lose our old dwelling place?
Spontaneously composed in verse:
The power and profit of heaven and earth are the same; one judges the male and female by means of sin and merit alone. This old man of penetrating insight is uniquely clever and sly;
he is well-practiced at hiding his body within the horns of a hare.

A Verse by Chan Master Xiangjiao Tan of Xuanchou (with Preface) Tan was of the Niu clan of Wenzhou; his family had for generations practiced the craft of silver-smithing. While he was once scrubbing and polishing a silver pitcher, a realization arose within him. He subsequently left the household life and became a disciple of Chan Master Fayan Wenyi at Mount Tiantai. Later, he resided at Xiangjiao Monastery in Xuanchou. His verse reads: The Armory of the Zen School, Son of the Niu family of Wenzhou. While washing a silver pitcher, A realization suddenly dawned. He left home to follow Fayan, And finally attained the Way. Now he dwells at Xiangjiao, Where he guides the assembly. His teaching is like a great sword, Swift and decisive in its strike. If you wish to see it clearly, Look at this very moment. Do not seek it elsewhere— It is right here before you. If you can understand this, You will see the Buddha’s heart. If you cannot understand, You remain a common man. This is my humble verse, Offered to the assembly. May all together realize The ultimate truth. [End of Verse] (Note: The original text contains a lacuna following the phrase "While washing a silver pitcher," as the subsequent portion of the narrative is missing from the source provided.)
There was one who left the household life through a sudden realization; he was known as Chan Master Tan of Xingjiao in Xuanchuan.
How strange that the cowherd’s trade is refining silver! As the silver pitcher is ground, his entire body appears. His broad and long tongue is not so very large;
it is granted only to him to see it intimately.
When dealing with matters, one is stuck in stagnation and does not realize they have lost their way; I compose this verse:
"After the thief has passed, drawing the bow is already too late. To further laugh at the thief’s folly is even more deluded. When shall the bright mirror be free of obstructions?
Beauty and ugliness cannot deceive it; it belongs to no one who knows."
To Wang Yuanmei:
The Dharma-body has a mouth that can eat rice; the great earth is free of dust to obscure the eyes. You already know this matter from afar and have entrusted it to me;
I pray you will grant a word to seal my humble understanding.
Master Fanglu Daowang’s verse says:
"Before birth, he already spoke of the Avataṃsaka; at the moment of death, his habitual tendencies truly manifested before him.
To distinguish the tail of a Buddhist from the head of a Confucian is difficult—it is just like using a bamboo stick to test a deluded Chan practitioner."
Untitled (Twenty Poems) The sixteen-foot golden body serves as a sign for selling wine. One morning, utterly intoxicated, he sleeps like a cat.
Beneath the peony flowers, amidst the spring breeze, How much fragrance wafts along with the dew!
The wild mind has not yet ceased, like a monkey; day and night it tosses about this skull.
A single spark of the fire of ignorance burns it away—within the mass of purple smoke, one should turn back.
Do not wait until the flames consume you before turning back; while still strong and healthy, it is best to train the ox well.
When the skin has fallen away and the whole body is white, let the waters be distant and the mountains long, and wander freely as you will.
In this misty land by the water, he sat and entered dhyāna; Six *liǎozhū* of incense drifted through the heavens where flowers were scattered. Now his sacred remains have no place to be found;
Only the wind and rain, whistling and moaning, escort the traveler’s boat.
Treading through thousands of layers of empty green, The winding path of Caoxi locks the Buddhist palace.
If you wish to ask what was transmitted south of the ridge, It lies amidst the green mountains, white birds, and the sound of water.
A perilous beam a hundred feet high spans the emerald stream. When a traveler reaches this place, do not hesitate. The wind sweeps the spray like rain flying in the clear sky;
In the blink of an eye, one’s clothes are already soaked.
Suspended in space, its foundation is difficult to shift; strange rocks form its frame, and moss serves as its skin. Strike it with an unperforated iron mallet and it resounds;
for those in the lineage of Zen, there is no need for doubt—just go straight down.
The man of the Way has no place where he does not grieve at autumn; for what reason does he float his small boat under the moon?
Who can join the rhythm of the "White Snow" and "Yangchun"? At Shimen, the flowing water secretly meets him.
How many tall pine trees are in your house? They draw forth the celestial winds to form ocean waves. Let there be a thousand million bushels of feverish afflictions;
sitting here alone, they are completely extinguished.
Floating clouds do not initially stain the empty sky; their arising and ceasing shift from faint to dense.
If one could make the body and mind into a rabbit's horn, responding to all myriad things would be like a spring breeze.
A white heron carries a fish to the fishing rocks; the old fisherman does not engage in thought at all.
Where water and sky are vast and boundless, and one has forgotten all else—the sitter sits, and the flyer flies.
The myriad distinctions and thousandfold differences are all this one mind; who can melt the great earth into gold?
Amidst the entanglement of love and hatred, where it is difficult to dissolve, how many men have been submerged and lost!
Spring has arrived, and the flowers and grasses flourish in profusion. At the vermilion chamber and jeweled grove, one wanders with courtesans. The body of Vairocana manifests everywhere;
among those intoxicated, how many can turn their heads back?
In the empty forest, where does the bell toll at night? Treading upon the verdant moss, I knock at the gates of the Buddhist temple. There is no need to speak of the matter at this gathering;
we gaze at one another, squatting cross-legged in the bright moonlight.
The myriad distinctions and thousandfold differences are all without hindrance; where the mind is absent, one may forget everything encountered.
Although the six sense bases are like an empty village, when seeing a pig, how could one ever call it a sheep?
In spring, a hundredfold springs emerge from the treetops. Satiated by my meal, I sleep amidst the clouds; I never tire of listening.
Had Tao Qian known this intention, why would he have needed to wait until his strings were broken before playing the "no-string" lute?
The mother’s nipples are as large as bushels; the child does not eat them, but sees them and runs away. She drinks her milk from the breasts of another’s progeny;
before one mouthful is finished, she takes another.

The mark of the broad and long tongue covers the void; within its unfolding and rolling, the great earth, mountains, and rivers are contained. If one asks where humans and devas are situated, they are all accommodated within the mouth of Guizong, which possesses a fistful of space.
Whatever occupies my place is not me; when there is no "I," only then am I complete. Even if empty space were used as a metaphor, space comes after me, while I have existed before it.
Flowing waters and green mountains laugh at my folly; I am accustomed to crossing rivers and scaling steep peaks without tiring. For what purpose do I travel south and north?
The single thread of true principle the world does not know.
An Examination of the Mind through Verses (with two prefaces).
The Master Píqiú said: "When the single mind does not arise, there is no ground for doing good; how much less for doing evil?
Therefore, regardless of whether one is buffeted by the winds of favorable or adverse conditions, even if thoughts arise, though the mind may intend to restrain them, they do not emerge."
This is the principle. Whenever a wholesome thought arises, you should exert yourself to expand and cultivate it.
If an unwholesome thought arises, you should investigate whether this thought is greed or anger; greed leads to lust, and anger leads to killing. As for the transgression of lust—
There is no greater transgression than this; there is no calamity more severe than that of killing. Within my own pure and vast clarity, such an inauspicious thought has suddenly arisen.
If it were fortunate that this thought began but did not end, perhaps the transgression and calamity might be avoided.

But if, unfortunately, the thought arises and persists from beginning to end, at the very least it will lead to the loss of life, the ruin of one's reputation, and the corruption of one's virtue; at the greatest, [it leads to further ruin].
Then one falls into Avīci Hell, where the soul undergoes punishment; day and night, it dies ten thousand times and is reborn ten thousand times, making it extremely difficult to escape.
Furthermore, if one investigates the origin of this present body, it initially arises from the mixture of the father’s semen and the mother’s blood.
As for the present mind capable of discernment, its initial origin likewise lies in the time when the parents were in union. It is not...

Upon encountering the external object, one realizes it is but the mind; thus, one becomes deluded by the object. Therefore, when a male enters the womb, he conceives the thought that the mother is desirable;
when a female enters the womb, she likewise conceives the thought that the father is desirable.

Once this thought has resulted in the formation of a body, it is no longer called "thought" (saṃjñā) but is termed "mind" (citta). This impurity, formed from the mixture of semen and blood, is governed by the mind.

Thereafter, it is no longer called "impurity," but is termed the "body. Therefore, when men and women of wisdom understand and practice this contemplation, and after long practice have gained mastery, then even if the winds of sensory objects fan and stir amidst food, drink, and the relations between men and women, thoughts will naturally not arise.
Alas! If thoughts truly do not arise, then that which was previously pure and vast returns once more to enter into me.
It is finished. Therefore it is said: "Though this be an old, empty plot of land, only after one thorough weeding does one finally rest.
Only upon reaching this point can one speak of "plowing the field to earn one's meal," being free from shame in one’s heart.
If one has not yet reached this, the ancestral fields still belong to the management of others; how would I dare harbor such delusions? The verse says:
The foul stench of sexual union first brings about the formation of the body; within it, craving and lust constitute the consciousness-spirit (*vijñāna*).
If one can see through both of these, what hindrance could there be to turning the freezing cold into a warm spring?

The ancestral fields have been sold for many years; where can one seek the deed amidst the winds and dust? It is said that jackals, wolves, foxes, and hares now dwell there, where once the desolate thorns and brambles grew into a dense forest.
Xingchang Stabbed the Sixth Patriarch:
Xingchang stabbed the Sixth Patriarch, yet he was stabbed by the Sixth Patriarch instead. Who among the people of the world knows this? Is it not a matter of grievous injustice?
A Verse on Wisdom and Cognition.

The five consciousnesses grasp objective entities; this is called transformation due to causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-pariṇāma*). Since active discernment has not yet arisen, how could names and words reach it?

Simultaneously, the mental consciousness suddenly arises; the five [sensory] consciousnesses then become residual guests. Once the five have receded and the sixth has advanced, the sixth grasps only mental images (*pratibimba*).
Because cognition arises from objects, this cognition does not exist inherently. Because the appearance of objects manifests through cognition, this appearance differs from the empty sky.

Between clear comprehension and non-comprehension, consciousness (*vijñāna*) and wisdom (*jñāna*) diverge along separate paths. Consciousness is a false name for a thief; wisdom is the son who masters the household.

Blazing with intense discernment, my attachment to self and dharmas gradually dissolves. Entering the stream, there is nothing to be attained; as the object is lost, the subject is likewise forfeited.
When neither subject nor object has a place, the chariot rolls on without ceasing.

It is shown that within this, the affliction of the national thief lies in the intellect; the affliction of the mind-thief lies in the profound mystery. Only when one encounters the three-pronged fork does one see the thorn; it is the source of liberation from all sensory dusts.
Amidst the dragon pools and tiger-and-leopard dens, there is trepidation at the edge of the snow-covered pines.
To Runfu: The Sixth Patriarch was originally a woodcutter; upon awakening to the mind, he became a patriarch. What is this mind? To realize it is to transcend both past and present.
It is not only Śākyamuni who is thus; Confucius was likewise so. If you say you have not heard [this truth], then though you live, you are no different from the dead.
Furthermore, speak! Speak! What has been heard? At the outset, enter through faith; remain steadfast and never be indolent. The person of natural realization points the way;
follow it and proceed directly. Do not let your single mind waver or turn back. There are winds of praise and blame in the world—these are the emissaries of all Māras.

The more one encounters [obstacles], the firmer one's strength becomes; only then does one truly believe in practice. If even a single doubt arises, it brings calamity upon oneself without an intermediary.
Were it not for a man of heroic spirit, it would be difficult to hold the helm against the wind.
Verses on the Pure Land:
When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure; when the mind is defiled, this land is defiled. Since purity and impurity both reside within the mind, why seek the principle elsewhere?
Simply observe that before the mind has arisen, where could purity or impurity exist? If this contemplation is thoroughly penetrated, all transgressions will naturally be extinguished.
Without waiting for the lotus to bloom, fragrant light issues from the mouth. Homage to Amitābha Buddha! The Buddha is the awakening of one's own mind;

when there is awakening, deluded emotions do not arise. When deluded emotions arise, they create the conditions for killing the Buddha. Killing the Buddha leads to falling into hell, making it difficult to be reborn in the Land of Lotus Flowers.
If one can cause afflictions not to arise, Amitābha will come to welcome them personally. With a lotus flower as their womb, they shall never again become sentient beings.

Although reciting the Buddha's name is not difficult, it is difficult to break through the barrier of favor and opposition. Only when this barrier of favor and opposition is broken does one first behold the countenance of Amitābha.

The points upon which all people focus their attention are simply food, drink, and the concerns of men and women. What we, however, must urgently attend to is the cultivation of the mind; for this medicine, "stopping" (śamatha) is paramount.

This stopping does not depend on "contemplation" (vipaśyanā). Yet, this stopping alone is not entirely sufficient; stopping and contemplation must serve as each other's teachers. Revolving in this way, their wondrous interaction is inexhaustible.
This present mass of raw flesh—skillfully employed, it is not a burden from the start. Who would say that this stinking skull cannot be compared to the indestructible diamond?
Form and emptiness arise together and are no different; waves and water are merely "this" and "that. An ancient master once spoke thus, grieving for his disciples who had passed away.
When Yang did not recommend him, the white bones died for you; turning one's head toward Shilou is folly, and the humiliation at Huating where the boat capsized.
Birth and death are but equal playthings; once the mind understands this, what is there left to mention?
A Verse on Hearing the Drum While Eating a Water-Vegetarian Meal:

In the past, while eating a water-vegetarian meal for several months, I distinguished between lightness and heaviness. My body and mind were as if non-existent; the sounds of the drum poured through my six sense faculties.
Upon careful reflection on the reason for this, it was like a Taoist striking a drum: though the temple was still across the river, the sound reached from nearby.
Only then did I realize that thought does not arise; the path has been the same through all time. Distinctions of far and near arise from the mind; how could the Dharmakāya ever be obstructed?
Clouds in the six-cubit sky: when they arise, there is no boundary; their gathering and dispersing are from the start impermanent. Why suffer in vain with such arbitrary conceptualizations?
If these arbitrary conceptualizations are not eliminated, one will undergo birth and death for as many lifetimes as there are donkeys.
The Verse on Liberating from the Female Body:

When there is a body, there is the grasping at being female; when the grasping at a body ceases, that [grasping] vanishes of itself. Sentient beings have long been inverted, falsely grasping the body as solid and firm.

Through the contemplation of solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion, the female body and such are seen to be like a tortoise’s hair. If this contemplation reaches maturity, the lotus becomes the womb.

Furthermore, hatred and love are emptied; the mind is void and the objective realm is desolate. Subject and object, along with the dust of sensory emotions, are swept away. A young maiden donned the square monastic robe.

Through Zen practice and the study of the Way, she was forever free from the disturbances of demons and heretics. Zhenxiang deeply upheld this verse; in her female form, she attained transcendence right where she stood.
As the verse from Changru Temple says:

"Inversion and conformity have no inherent nature; they appear to exist only through arbitrary conceptualization. If one knows that joy is itself anger, then at every step is the ground of peace and bliss.
Thus it was shown to Wenlang.
The ghost fears the stubborn person; ignorance fears the stubborn wisdom. Through persistent effort, one naturally matures; suddenly, one accords with non-discrimination.

To demonstrate the cultivation of compassion, there is the self of sentient beings and the self of the Buddhas. When truth and falsehood are clearly understood, one suddenly transcends the path of birth and death.

The verse on light and darkness concerns arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-non-ceasing. The analogy of light and darkness is that one exists while the other does not; this does not accord with the *pāramitā*.
The analogy of light and darkness concerning arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-non-ceasing is that both exist yet do not encounter one another; only then does it accord with the *pāramitā*.
The Verse on Severing Lust (with introduction):

As for those whose words are pure but whose conduct is turbid, they preach the Vinaya with their eyes open, yet practice lust with their eyes closed. Although waking and dreaming differ, the root of lust remains the same.
Therefore, as long as this root is not uprooted, it is difficult to escape birth and death. In both this life and future lives, whether the eyes are closed or opened, [the affliction persists].

The faculties and their objects, the subject and the guest, interact in an endless cycle of giving and receiving. If one can remain such that not a single thought arises, the mechanism of lust will wither of its own accord.

From the perspective of ordinary beings, the arising of thoughts is the constant; the non-arising of thoughts is the change. From the daily life of a Bodhisattva, the non-arising of thoughts is the constant; the arising of thoughts is the change.

Both constancy and change are rootless, being merely perfumed by habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). When these are fully matured, they are called "constant"; when they are newly produced, they are called "change."

This is what is called "transformation. Although names may change, there is from the beginning neither difference nor identity. Therefore, one can perfume [the mind] with the fragrance of precepts, concentration, and wisdom without interruption;
thus, the pure function manifests before one. Yet, if one moistens it with the waters of greed, hatred, and delusion, the power of defilement becomes fierce.
Thus, the Venerable Jiyin, in his *Praise of Avalokiteśvara*, said: "Pity my heart; its clarity and power are not..."
At times, the seeds of manifesting formations emerge. This, my venerable sir, is one who has overturned the habitual molds of the beautiful and the ugly, and is thus able to utter words of truth.
Like clouds clearing from the vast expanse of the sky, the bright moon is revealed;
such is his purity and brilliance. The verse says:
Throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, I alone am the one who indulges in lust. For me, severing the mechanism of lust is not difficult;

yet lustful people fill every place, and their mechanisms of lust are suddenly difficult to sever. From moment to moment they mutually influence one another, growing without end. I have severed it, while others have not.

Cutting off and cutting off, the perfuming becomes ever deeper; defilement and purity each have their own source. When the source of both defilement and purity is exhausted, they are washed away; the root of precepts spreads throughout empty space.
Outside of emptiness there is no thing; where there is lust, there is no earth-treasury.
The Verse on Abstaining from Killing:

When one contemplates heaven and earth with the mind, heaven and earth are like elder and younger brothers. When one contemplates the mind through heaven and earth, things first differentiate as male and female.
From male and female arise strength and weakness; from strength and weakness arise combat and attack. When victory and defeat do not yield to one another, their mutual devouring knows no end.
Before one has exhausted [the depths of practice], one can still know how to transform. One must refrain from gluttony and rich, putrid food.

As for those who sleep while reciting the "Verses of the Reclining Buddha," they do not forget the stone; how could they lie upon a stone? It is not that the stone causes them to forget their sleep; rather, the stone itself possesses the mark of selfhood (*ātman*).

Who says that within the state of dual-forgetfulness, the wind from the nose blows through the trees? Since neither yin nor yang reaches there, the coming and going of the breath is difficult to describe.
Only those of original nature, upon hearing this, call it a peerless song.
A Verse on Hearing Thunder Before Rain: The thunder roars first, its booming sound reaching the ears. Thereupon, one investigates the hearer; yet the subject and object remain undecided.
Since that which is heard has no cognition, how could the hearing itself arise alone? If it were through their union that hearing occurs, a close analysis reveals this to be irrational.
Since neither the subject nor the object exists, what is it that unites them? Even if their union were to arise simultaneously, Nāgārjuna never permitted this.
If one could hear without a cause, then mountains and rivers would all be my ears; yet through repeated investigation of their causes, one ultimately finds they have no beginning.

From beginningless time, hearing has never been obscured; when hearing occurs, it leaves behind both self and other. The ancient master Xuansha once had this verse: "Within the drum there is no bell-sound;
within the bell there is no drum-intent. Bell and drum do not intersect; every phrase is without beginning or end."
Verse Six: The Function of the Six Consciousnesses.

Through the contemplation of the arising of phenomena (*dharmas*), the coarse characteristics of one's own stage are extinguished; their subtle characteristics then penetrate the divisions of the seven consciousnesses.

By contemplating the arising of phenomena through non-discriminative observation (*avikalpa*), and continuing this practice until effortlessness is achieved, one utilizes this state of effortlessness to forge [realization].
Vipāka. Once the vipāka has dissolved, one enters spontaneously; the five and eight consciousnesses revolve simultaneously. From this point, the noble ones' work is finished.
Boarding this effortless, sovereign vessel, they cross over the multitudes of beings amidst favorable and adverse winds and waves.

All such ultimate, manifold virtues as these arise from the power of the six consciousnesses performing contemplation; the other consciousnesses can only remain seated and cannot act. It is only the six [consciousnesses] that...
One who is able to act has never sat still; Old Zhang drinks wine while Old Li gets drunk. When told to others, who would believe it?

The three measures and three objects encompass the mental factors (*caitta*). For this reason, their function resides in the six [consciousnesses]. In the state of sages and ordinary beings, delusion and enlightenment, these six do not function.
The sky is always clear, yet the ground remains damp.
In waking and dreaming, Elder Zibo’s delusions abound; last night, with eyes closed, his dreams were many—thousands upon thousands of good and evil within the dream-state.
Upon opening one's eyes, when has there ever been even a blade of grass? The brain, marrow, heart, and liver are what sustain life; yet in a dream, someone takes them away for no reason at all.

One who has not yet mastered the realization of emptiness is stingy when it is taken. Having perfected their stinginess and greed with many clever schemes, they eventually reach the end of their stratagems and their anger erupts completely.
Yet the brain, marrow, heart, and liver remain perfectly intact. Take those who possess these organs and compare them to the state within a dream—regarding birth and death, and honor and disgrace.
I humbly permit you to sport at will.

This *Dafangguang fo huayan jing* (Avataṃsaka Sūtra), which holds the verses of the *Huayan*, is the fundamental wheel first turned by the Tathāgata; this wheel turns without departing from the four [truths].

The Gate: the turning of principle into phenomena, the turning of phenomena into principle, and the turning of both phenomenon and principle; the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena is most profound and mysterious.

When brought forth, it is used immediately without any trace of attachment. Without principle there are no phenomena; they are like waves and water. The mutual turning of phenomena and principle is likewise of the same nature.

If one subtly enters the fourth stage of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena, the previous three stages will ultimately not be free from their old molds. As long as one does not leave these molds, the emotions will not wither; yet if the emotions do not wither, [the mold remains].

Alas! Wisdom does not reach its consummation. When wisdom does not reach its consummation, awakening becomes an obstruction. When the winds of sensory objects are favorable or adverse, one lacks mastery.
Whether it be the obstruction of principle or the obstruction of phenomena, who is the demon? If awakening is not an obstruction, every matter is swift and easy.
If you can receive and uphold this sutra scroll, you will penetrate to the root of my verse. But tell me, where exactly does this root ultimately reside? The heat of affliction burns the heart.
Who has lit this fire? How could such refreshing coolness that penetrates to the very bones come from the heavens?
At Changsong Hermitage, the verse on the snow says:
"The bright moon is in the sky, yet veiled by clouds. When the veiling clouds thin and part, the bright moon is revealed; it is conjured as pear blossoms and willows.
Cotton絮: Spread everywhere across the mountains and rivers without a gap. White elephant: Do not stumble or break stride.

When treading upon favorable or adverse conditions, even the golden-haired lion’s brain would split from hearing this. In the third month, peach blossoms smile at passersby; here, the master can let his mind rest.
A verse on repairing the woodblocks of the Great Canon:
In three hundred and sixty thousand days of a hundred years, how urgent has been the toil and striving for worldly benefit!

If one were to compare a hundred years with long kalpas, those hundred years are no different from a single inhalation and exhalation. To manage such momentous affairs within the span of a single breath—who but one who is both wise and courageous could do so?
It can be attained. Its benefits and merits do not merely extend to this brief life; these supreme matters provide the resources for my liberation from the miserable realms.

An Exposition on the Contemplation of Equality: A Preface to Reading the Verses of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra The body that possesses a body is a gathering place for manifold sufferings; the mind that possesses a mind is entangled by ten thousand anxieties.

Only the body that has no body fills the eight directions of space with its form yet remains free from affliction; only the mind that has no mind encompasses all things with its wisdom yet remains untroubled.
How exhausting! Beings in their daily lives do not realize this. Their illness lies in being externally confined within the six-foot frame and internally lost within the square-inch mind.

If there were a wise man who realized that external confinement is no confinement and understood that internal delusion is no delusion, he would then take his single body as an infinite body, manifesting divine heads and demonic faces to assist the Dharma-gate;
and he would take his single mind as an inexhaustible mind, employing extraordinary means and strange expedients.

With wisdom, one penetrates the Buddha-dharma; by employing the broad and long tongue among the divergent paths of the hundred schools of thought, one causes them to return to the Great Way—this is what constitutes truly repaying the Buddha’s kindness.
The ten-fascicle *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is a single-edged sword; the entire ox is seen, yet no hair remains before the eyes.
If you test this blade of wisdom upon the horse of the mind, the ignorance accumulated over kalpas will vanish in an instant.
Reading Dongpo’s “Eulogy on Avalokiteśvara”:

When I was a guest at Shaoshi Mountain in those days, after finishing my meal, I went for a walking meditation. At the foot of a cypress tree, I saw a short stele carved with the form of Avalokiteśvara.
Above is a eulogy by Dongpo. Reading it was like a mosquito landing on iron; yet, savoring it slowly and for a long time, one day I suddenly attained complete penetration.
From then on, I let my mouth roam at will, speaking of it to others wherever I went. The Great Duke Su of Meishan—his search for the Buddha-mind has already ceased.
When the mind comes to rest, the light is naturally perfect; both phenomena and principle are vibrant and alive. Whether it be jesting or reproach, they are like a rift in the blue sky.
When the sky cracks, the field of vision becomes lofty; beyond the sky, the scenery is distinct. If you do not see this for yourself, you instead mock others for their perceived clumsiness.

I show Zhou Jihua that the ignorance of sentient beings blazes fiercely; by clinging to the body, they invite birth and death. The Sage, pitying their folly, teaches the four contemplations through one.
When the four are seen with clarity and without delusion, the single body cannot be found. This washes away the defilements of ordinary people; it is not the attachment of the Two Vehicles.
Furthermore, by means of the one, the four are dispelled; yet the four are likewise unattainable. When both the one and the four are non-existent, there is the wisdom of immediate non-arising.
It cannot be sought through calculation, nor can it be realized through sentiment. When both sentiment and calculation are completely severed, the physical mass is the adamantine body.
For example, it is like a hand forming a fist. One might perceive it as a fist, or one might take the fist to be the hand, or perceive the fist as the hand.
If the fist possessed the intrinsic nature of a fist, it could not be made into a hand; if the hand possessed the intrinsic nature of a hand, it could not be made into a fist.

The fist and the hand both lack inherent nature; how could the one who grasps them not be deluded? Although the fist and the hand have no inherent nature, the fist and the hand appear vividly as such.
Through this verse on the fist and the hand, who will recognize me when we meet? My self-confidence accords with the Buddha-mind; may the dragons and spirits reverently protect and uphold it.
May all who see or hear this together awaken to the principle of non-arising.
Regarding the verse on the discrimination of subject and object:
if discrimination exists because of an objective realm, how can that realm have any interaction with me? All ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle have not yet realized this.
Knowing: the faculties and objects are turbulent and have no way to cease. To understand that these two are merely names and words—how could the subject and object ever be two separate pieces?

Seeking a beginning or an end upon a revolving wheel only makes one laugh at Old Woman Wang of the Eastern Village. When this knowing is realized, one becomes a true child of the Buddha through cultivation;
even with afflictions not yet eliminated, one transcends the ten stages. This knowing is the Great Teacher of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; fools cast it aside.

The Master seeks the path of awakening; within the absence of subject and object, there is no fear of faculties or objects. Who knows that faculties and objects are the provisions for the path of awakening?
When ice is abundant and water is abundant, why need one have doubt? If sentient beings were made to lack "mine-ness," the lifeblood between the holy and the ordinary would all wither and be severed.

To deny cause and effect is to become a breed of demons; yet such people doubt that thorough knowledge is not their own kin. Who knows that within arising and ceasing lies the non-arising and non-ceasing?
In the single stream of consciousness, there is both identity and difference; I shall now speak these sublime verses. How different from the sun and moon suspended in the deep night!
While all people dwell within the light of suffering and joy, they remain unaware of it day after day—the fault lies with the blind.

When the King of Physicians suddenly plucks away the cataracts, that light was never originally separate from the eye. If one were to say that this light was bestowed by the King of Physicians, then one would have been seeing darkness all along.
What is this? To reveal and know it within the midst of various ailments:

during bitter cold and scorching heat, being a traveler who does not return home, consuming the hot and swallowing the cold—one knows this only for oneself; when objective conditions and circumstances clash and conflict.

One sustains oneself by swallowing the breath; if this is not done through principle, it is extremely difficult to dissolve [afflictions]. Whether encountering adversity or favor, honor or disgrace, these are fundamentally indifferent according to principle.
If one attempts to dispel them through emotion, they will become chaotic and endless. Joy belongs to Yang, while anger belongs to Yin; Yang is easily relaxed and unimpeded.

The yin-channels are constricted and submerged; they should be relaxed, expanded, and made permeable. When the face and eyes lose their luster, it is because the constrictions have become stagnant and turbid.

Poison takes advantage of this to act as a thief; the thief occupies the joints and sinews, causing pain that cannot be endured. If one investigates the reason for this, it arises solely from karma. Karma arises where there is no fixed ground.

The creator is mind alone. That there are phenomena external to the mind—this is what the Sage pondered. When the Great Master of Nanyue’s body suddenly became swollen, he sought life but could not find it;
he sought death but found no relief. As he rolled about without ceasing, his suffering reached its peak and his awareness became luminous; he realized that the illness was nothing but karma.

He realized that karma is nothing but capacity; tracing the origin of this capacity, he found it to be spirit without a self. His swelling immediately subsided, and he attained the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvajātismara*).
Past good and evil deeds passed before him like clouds over a marsh; not even the finest detail was obscured, as clear as seeing one's own ten fingers. "Noble sir! Noble sir! [he cried].
Lying ill upon a single bed, right in the midst of the pain, one’s consciousness becomes frantic; wisdom cannot cure it, and strength cannot subdue it.

With every "pain, pain, pain" of sensation, the duality of subject and object arises. I observe for him: when the sense faculties and their objects fall away into vast emptiness, the illness is then recognized as mere cognition.
He enticed me to enter; how marvelous, how marvelous! I entered as a thief and emerged as one. Within a single atom of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), every atom is clearly manifest;
self and other are without interval. By the supernatural power of Vimalakīrti, the eighty thousand teacher-seats were all contained within a single room; large and small were mutually accommodated.

The positions and divisions remain intact. Question: What is the fundamental principle? Master Duanlang takes up the brush; the brush is like a precious sword, leaving both sages and commoners speechless.
But tell me, how about the final word? Within the light of lamps and candles, they inquire after one another’s illness;
the pure, bright tea and rice are naturally fragrant.

An Inscription for He Yang’an (With Preface) Now, the mind has neither reality nor delusion, yet the names "reality" and "delusion" arise. This is because one is deluded regarding the mind that is devoid of reality and delusion, and thus the names "reality" and "delusion" cannot help but be established.
Furthermore, there are those who are deluded by these very names of reality and delusion and fail to seek [the mind itself].

In truth, people are busily occupied with worldly affairs until their hair turns white at the crown of their heads, yet they cling to mere names without returning to the source—how lamentable this is!
Now, things must have names, and names must correspond to things; name and object do not contradict one another.

However, for those whose celestial mechanism is profound, they take names as a ladder and ascend by means of them, ultimately attaining the reality behind them. Once reality is attained and the mind becomes clear, the true can be distinguished from the false.
What is meant by "the Real"? It is the numinous state that is without self, yet it manifests with blazing discernment without contradicting its fundamental nature;
this is the beginning of the Real. What is meant by "the delusory"? To flow outward toward external objects, becoming lost and failing to return—this is what is called the delusory.

Furthermore, the delusory body exists provisionally based on the four great elements, and the delusory mind likewise exists provisionally based on the four aggregates. Thus, the delusory body is full...

It is not five feet. The deluded mind circulates but does not exceed the body. Yet today the world competes to take that which is five feet as the true body, and that which does not exceed the body as the true mind. I do not know whether this is truly real or truly delusory.
I have heard that space is boundless; it is but a shadow within the Dharma-body. Thus it is said: "Space arises within Great Enlightenment, like a wave in the ocean."
It bubbles forth. I have heard that the sacred and the mundane, as well as their environments and inhabitants, are likewise without end; they are established based upon the true mind.

Therefore it is said: "Outside the mind there are no dharmas. Furthermore, because ordinary beings have long been deluded regarding the truth, the truth has given rise to delusion until it has become habitual.
Within this state of habitual delusion, one relies upon Buddhas, patriarchs, sages, worthies, teachers, friends, and kinsmen as conditions and causes to be awakened through the process of perfuming.

Based on the initial awakening, one cultivates and nurtures it. Amidst the alternating onslaughts of favorable and adverse "winds" of circumstances, and amidst the intersections of death and life, likes and dislikes, one employs courage to support clarity and clarity to sustain courage.
Thus, one advances with keen intensity and penetrates with refined depth. This is called using a mind of arising and ceasing to open up an understanding of arising and ceasing;
muddying the clay and carrying the water, one ultimately completes the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), wherein all is the arising of perfect understanding (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*).
This is the power of cessation (*nirodha*). When entering and abiding [in that state], the power is neither arising nor ceasing.
I feel compassion for you brothers, who dwell within the mire of worldly toil and its foul stench, yet are able to observe the perpetual fast and abstain from all flesh and blood;
you are truly lotuses in a burning house. Thereupon, he spoke this verse:
It arises because of objects and ceases because of objects; its arising and ceasing are impermanent, trading upon conditions.
From time immemorial until this very day, you have taken this for your mind, mistaking a thief for your own son and plundering your family’s treasure at all times.

Having lost the wealth of merit, one is as destitute as if washed clean. Turning one's back on the non-arising and non-ceasing, one follows along with arising and ceasing, taking the twelvefold dependent origination as one’s dwelling place.
With joyful attachment, one never thinks of abandoning it; within this failure to abandon it, a multitude of sufferings accumulate.
Like a shadow following a form, anger pursues one without ceasing; from kalpa to kalpa, it revolves like a water-wheel in a well, rising and falling without rest.

As for these various sufferings mentioned above, they originally have no foundation; through a single delusion of fundamental wisdom, the various realms of existence are illusorily produced, devoid of any locus of subject or object.

The establishment of a self and others, the clash of spears and swords, victory and defeat, and blood flowing so as to float the pestles—all these are created by one's own mind; apart from the mind, they do not exist.

Thus, observe the mind itself: what is this fundamental wisdom? By what causes and conditions does it manifest as the sense organs and their objects? Once [this is understood], its essence becomes clear and lucid.
Like a child finding its mother, those twelve links are all driven by merit; benefiting oneself and others, they are without end.
To illustrate this sequence of virtues with a verse:
"Beyond water there are waves, yet waves are never wet. If waves were actually wet, what wave would not be water? Fools do not understand this.
One perceives those wave-like appearances, undergoing a thousand transformations and myriad changes; surging and turbulent, they are impermanent, arising and ceasing in many forms.

Chasing after names and words, one is turned by external objects; burning with conceptualization, there has been no rest since beginningless time, as these forms change their heads and alter their faces.

Scales and shells, feathers and fur—whether among humans or in the heavens, rising or sinking according to one's karma—all these are but waves. Those who are deluded by the water mistake the waves for something other than water;
thus they are called fools. The wise are not so; they realize that the waves are nothing but water, and they penetrate the truth that all objects are but mind.

Fundamentally, there are neither ordinary beings nor sages; how could there be past or present? Spiritually luminous and without self, [the Buddha] is the ancestor of all living beings. Thus, one who knows the ancestor must necessarily be filial and obedient;
one who awakens to their own mind must necessarily revere and honor it. If one does not revere and honor it, it is like describing food that will not satisfy one's hunger.

Dry wisdom is useless. When encountering matters and facing critical moments, do not seek with deluded views and attachments; the jewel of the Dharma is in the palm of your hand—do not err and let it fall away.
The light of years is difficult to grasp; do not expect to escape old age and sickness. This humble disciple feels deep shame; may you not be oblivious in your daily life.

In response to the "Greeting to the Verse on Vigilance," there is a drum of lethal poison in this world. Whenever it is struck, it produces a sound; regardless of whether a mind exists or not, no one who hears it escapes being destroyed.
If no one were to strike it, the sound would likewise not exist. If there is hearing without sound, what is it that the hearer hears?
Therefore, regarding the poison-coated drum, whether it is poisonous or non-poisonous, even if one lies upon the drum, the poison cannot harm the person.
This is because, lacking the necessary conditions, even a Buddha cannot transform them. My drum is not like this; it is made of "Name."
Poison is smeared upon the names; these are passed along as drumsticks. One person passes them to a hundred, and those hundred pass them on endlessly.
With such endless sticks, one takes hold and strikes this drum. Whether they see it or not, none of those who hear it shall fail to die.
There may be someone who has not seen me, yet has merely heard my name. Who knows of the "poisoned paint"? If one hears its sound, the poison enters the ear.
That the poison enters but does not manifest its effects—this is absolutely impossible. You have already heard my name; how could you possibly avoid receiving the poison?
For this reason, although you died with a thieving mind, that mind having died, your nature was restored to life. When the nature is alive, who is not a Buddha?
It is by this that I know you have already been numbered among the Buddhas.

Verses in Mourning for the Librarian Faben (With Preface) Now, to cut one’s own thigh to save a stranger is not as good as cutting one’s thigh to save a parent; and to cut one’s thigh to save a parent is not as good as sacrificing the secular self to propagate the Dharma.
Why is this? That which sustains my body cannot prevent me from being born again; yet that which gives birth to me...
This body cannot prevent me from suffering. Laozi said: "I have a great affliction; it is because I have a body.
