If I had no body, what affliction would there be? It is only through the virtue of sacrificing the body to propagate the Dharma that, in the near term, I may transform this very great affliction into medicinal herbs, and in the distant term, I may forge the conditions of dependent origination to ultimately realize non-arising.
To take affliction as medicine is what the wise find sweet; to awaken through conditions is what the multitudes fail to perceive.
The wise find sweetness where the multitudes are muddled—like choosing milk from water. Were it not for one who is both clear-sighted and courageous, who could discern this?

You practiced *yoga* in your youth, but having subsequently encountered a great spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), you severed your *yoga* practice to follow the path of meditation (*dhyāna*). Although you have not yet attained realization in meditation, [you have nonetheless made this choice].

Cao, Jie, Zhuo, and Lun—though their instruction was not yet complete, they propagated the Dharma without slackening. It is a pity that while their resolve was abundant, their vital energy could not sustain it.
On the [day/month/year] of the Wanli era, as his life drew to a close, he still said to his fellow practitioners:
"In this life, I am destitute of wealth. Whenever I perform Buddhist rites, there are many difficulties and few easeful opportunities.

If, upon my next rebirth, I should obtain the body of a high official, then the carving of the Tripitaka will not be difficult. Alas! As a monk, one knows the poverty of monks but does not know the poverty of officials;
as an official, one knows the poverty of officials but does not know the poverty of monks. Monks are poor..."

The wealthy are poor in their official positions, while officials are poor in their leisure. That both of these groups are poor indicates that neither recognizes the mind nor penetrates the fundamental source.
Thus, when those in office undergo much toil and humiliation, they say it would be better to be a monk in pure leisure; yet when monks undergo much poverty and hardship, [they likewise lament].
They say that nothing is better than being a high-ranking official; yet they fail to realize that no toil is greater than having a mind, and no great affliction is greater than having a body.

Only by realizing that the mind is not the mind and understanding that the body is not the body can one illuminate all phenomena without weariness and fill the ten directions of space without affliction. Only then can one give rise to compassion for those of the same essence and... [engage with them].
An immeasurable multitude directs their wisdom toward the realm of non-existence, ultimately attaining the unsurpassed state;
that the transmission of the lamp remains unbroken is our primary duty. Thus it is said: "To weary of the suffering of birth and death is to lose the Way of the Buddha-Dharma.
Now, although your aspiration differs from that of the masses, if we judge it by our own original character, you have missed the mark in your progress. For as for the form...

There is gathering and dispersing; the mind has neither past nor present. Since that which gathers and disperses has already been transformed, how could that which is without past or present not remain?
You have served me as a compassionate father and have even died for the sake of the Dharma.
If I do not instruct you with the pain of following one's nature and the hammer-stroke of transcending emotion, to remind you of your true essence, I fear you will be buried and lost. Listen to me!
The verse says:
Forty-nine years before, forty-nine years after, he searched back and forth for birth and death, like seeing the Big Dipper at midday.

He grew weary of the Sangha and desired to become an official; yet you do not know that an official’s poverty is such that his stipend is so meager it cannot provide for him, leaving his entire family starving like dogs.
If one obtains wealth while serving as an official, it must have originated from greed. To perform Buddhist services through greed is to cultivate merit only to nurture calamity.

Fortunately, because of the vow to propagate the Dharma, he ultimately differs from the common crowd; though he may cast off this body to receive another, let him be careful not to lose the pearl of the precepts.

If the pearl of precepts is not lost, one’s place of birth will naturally be radiant and pure. What you aspire to shall ultimately be fulfilled; at the Nine Original Springs, you need no longer weep blood.
If I grow old but do not die, I shall await your swift emergence from the depths. If you do not obscure your original resolve, come to serve as the ox that plows the ocean of Dharma.
Having plowed the entire field of the Great Canon, one’s merit and wisdom begin to be boundless.
Even if a glowing iron wheel were to spin upon the crown of your head, risking your life to burn away [delusions] through the teaching is itself a favorable cause and condition.
Shi Wangmeng composed this verse:
"When a person sits in stillness, delusive thoughts come to disturb them. Though they strive with all their might to expel these thoughts, the delusions are never fully understood.
Not understanding that delusion is a thief, the thief will surely plunder my treasure. Once my treasure has been plundered, the master remains as withered and parched as before."

Human beings are the most spiritually endowed among all things; how could they be compared to withered and decayed matter? If one wishes to attain true stillness, one must first seek the source of movement within oneself.
This movement arises from me; this movement arises for the sake of things. If this movement truly arises from me, it would not exist unless things had already stimulated it.
This movement arises from objects; when objects are absent, the wooden man has none. To the ultimate degree, movement is sought through coming and going, yet neither object nor self can be found.
Since neither object nor self can be found, it is falsely claimed that they exist through conjunction. If two non-existents could conjoin, then water could wash its own water.
Just as water can wash away water, one’s own eye sees its own eye; the eye itself is able to see the eye. Observe this closely and reflect within yourself:

in both waking and dreaming, the enemies and kin encountered provoke joy or anger, yet there is no difference between the dream and the waking state. One rushes toward external objects like a starving rat overturning a basin.
Upon awakening, one knows these are not real; they are like illusions, bubbles, and shadows. This dream-body is likened to dew or a flash of lightning, fleeting and momentary.

When arms were exchanged between old and new, Confucius was moved to sorrow and the Bodhisattva moistened his robe with tears. Before Yanzi was offered as a guest, he sat in forgetfulness with even greater diligence; his limbs fell away and his senses were cast off.

Detached from clouds and the lunar orb, pure radiance fills all space, illuminating that which is beyond center or periphery. To observe sound with the eye is the universal gate of perfect penetration;

like a single moon reflected in a hundred rivers, it meets one everywhere. Yet I think of that Sudhana, who has gone forth in search but not yet returned—like seeking the moon by searching for its light.

The moon is shrouded by clouds and mist; the body is like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, a dewdrop, or a flash of lightning. Although this shell is a provisional combination, one should constantly maintain this contemplation.
Once this single contemplation is perfected, the other five will manifest spontaneously. When views and afflictions are dissolved, this body expands and contracts like a white cloud.
How could one be entangled by fetters? Walking barefoot, the heels possess the eye.

With ink-drawn verses, it is said that all things are fundamentally void; only humans disturb themselves. The single mind is fundamentally true, yet by chasing after objects, it falls into inversion. There are only objects and the mind.
Upon awakening, all is wondrous. Because one has not yet awakened, it becomes an enemy that causes frantic turmoil. Only the Great Awakened One is perfectly clear in daily life;

seeing objects, they are immediately the mind, and seeing the mind, it is no longer withered. Wisdom encompasses all existence, for this numinous constancy is ever-luminous. Thus, through form, one enters emptiness.

Discarding the mundane and the minor paths, one directly encounters emptiness and the coarse world; there are none among the multitude who do not understand this upon beholding the inked lines. I compose this verse to entrust it to the profound depths:
The gāthā of Mount Yi is neither vertical nor horizontal, such that neither ordinary beings nor sages can fathom it. Should a thought stir for even a moment, it will thunder at one’s side.
Verses on Upholding the Precepts (with Preface) The five precepts are called the fundamental precepts; they are indeed the foundation for humans, devas, sages, and ordinary beings alike.
Expanding upon these, they are termed the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera; expanding them further still, they are termed the two hundred and fifty precepts of a bhikṣu.
Regarding the precepts, all are rooted in the initial five precepts; therefore, they are called the "fundamental five precepts.
For any sentient being who possesses consciousness and is born, if they do not uphold even one or two of these initial fundamental five precepts, [they are not considered to have them].
One can never be born among humans. Therefore it is said: "If one's precepts are superior, one is born in a superior realm; if one's precepts are inferior, one is born in an inferior realm.

That which constitutes wealth and nobility versus poverty and lowliness within this vast expanse is by no means caused by a Creator; it is entirely what is fashioned by one’s own mind. An ancient said:
"If the five precepts are not upheld, the path to the human and celestial realms is cut off. Aha! The path to the human and celestial realms is cut off.
Furthermore, I ask you: toward what destination do you raise your feet? The verse says:

"If one does not uphold the five precepts, the paths to the human and celestial realms are exhausted. Where will you go when you raise your feet? Into the wombs of oxen and horses. To uphold the precepts is not difficult."
The difficulty lies in valuing the Way. If one can truly value the Way, what precepts would not be luminous? When the precepts are luminous, the roots are fragrant;

when the fragrance pervades the ten directions, both the ordinary and the sagely appear and disappear within that fragrant light. If the precepts are broken, every step is a path to death—a truth of which I dare not speak.
Awaken to this pain yourself.
*The Collected Works of Elder Zibai*, Volume Twenty;
*The Collected Works of Elder Zibai*, Volume Twenty-One.
Ming Dynasty: Han-shan Deqing reads the "Miscellaneous Sayings" and the "Account of Kuang-shi’s Sudden Death."
In this world, there are those whose years and aspirations are both at their peak who seek Bodhi; yet, if their aspirations are not fulfilled and they die suddenly, some may give rise to slander.
Quwuzi responded to them, saying: "The death of such a person is, in fact, the mark of the broad and long tongue.
One who skillfully listens to the Dharma realizes even at this moment that the realm is precarious and fragile—how much more so is this frail body? It is like Xuefeng pointing [at the mountain]."
[Zhaozhou] took the skull of a deceased monk and showed it to the assembly, saying, "This monk is truly real for you all.
Great Assembly, how will you take him up? Xuan Sha had a verse that said: "The divine light of ten thousand miles is the mark behind the head.

If this were so, then as for the sudden death of Master Kuangshi, how could there be a fixed pattern of "dead" or "not dead"? It would merely become fodder for the mouths of those who wear their hats backward (the ignorant).
"Ascend and depart.

"The *hun* and *po* spirits distinguish between the refined essence (*jing*) and the vital energy (*qi*) to form things; the wandering soul (*you-hun*) constitutes transformation. Thus one knows the nature and circumstances of ghosts and spirits. This is the [teaching] of Confucius.
These are his words, yet commentators differ among themselves. Some say that the *jingqi* (vital breath) is without consciousness while the wandering soul (*youhun*) possesses consciousness;
others say that both the *jingqi* and the wandering soul are without consciousness; still others say that both the *jingqi* and the wandering soul possess consciousness.
Thus, the traditions followed by scholars also vary accordingly. Nevertheless, the words of Confucius are like the sun and the moon.
When it is in the heavens, the blind do not see it; can this be the fault of the sun and moon? Thus, the intent behind Confucius’s formulation of his teachings includes three perspectives:
that which is conformative, that which is contrary, and that which is contrary yet returns to being conformative.

Regarding these, Master Yichuan and Master Huicang maintain that both the *po* (corporeal soul) and the *hun* (ethereal soul) are devoid of consciousness, whereas Dongpo and Shen Neihan maintain that both the *po* and the *hun* possess consciousness. Only Xin... [text truncated]

Jian claims that the *po* has no consciousness while the *hun* possesses consciousness; all of these [views] purport to comprehend the intent of Confucius, yet as their interpretations become increasingly facile, the intent of Confucius becomes ever more obscured.
What is meant by "following" (*shun*)? It is to proceed from one's inherent nature (*xing*) toward one's emotional dispositions (*qing*).

What is meant by "contravening" (*ni*)? It is to proceed from one's emotional dispositions back toward one's inherent nature. What is meant by "contravening yet following"? It is when the Sage regards himself as... [the source of this state].
To restore one's nature. If people do not restore it, then their passions will not be extinguished. If passions are not extinguished, then the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*) will blaze forth.
When the view of self blazes forth, greed and violence become insatiable, and strife and contention never cease.

Therefore, they are taught by means of the doctrine of restoring nature, so that those who follow the natural order may understand what is contrary to it, and those who act contrarily may understand what is natural. Thus, by tracing back to the origin and returning to the end, the discourse on death and life can be clarified.
Indeed. Those who follow along with delusion and do not know how to go against it indulge their passions and remain oblivious to their nature;
while alive they are *po* (souls), and when dead they become ghosts. Those who follow along yet know how to go against it awaken to their nature and govern their passions;

while alive they are *hun* (spirits), and when dead they become gods. The word *po* signifies "floating" (*bo*). As for this floating, it is because the multitude has not yet heard the Way, and thus they lack...
To go [to death] is not a matter of insentience; yet sentience has no self-substance and must necessarily rely upon the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*).

Therefore, among the multitude, those whose endowment is thick have strong vital energy (*prāṇa*), while those whose endowment is thin have weak vital energy. Thus, in life, they find lodging within things, and their strength or weakness follows accordingly;
likewise, in death, they must also find lodging within things, and their strength or weakness follows accordingly. This is as with Bo... [the case of] Bo... [is].

This is what is meant by being "possessed by a malevolent spirit. The gentleman is not so; once he has heard the Way, he knows that there is nothing outside the Way, and that there is nothing that is not the Way.
Therefore, even if he is honored as the Son of Heaven, he does not consider it a glory; even if he is humbled as a commoner, he does not consider it a disgrace.
Shun and Yu were like this. Judging from this, the teaching of the Yichuan (Cheng Hao) is incorrect. Xinjian (Wang Yangming).
In these treatises, gain and loss are roughly equal. Only Su Changgong and Shen Neihan approach the truth;

yet even Su and Shen were unable to precisely discern the beginning and end of the three states—favorable, adverse, and both favorable and adverse. Consequently, while their principles are complete, their practical applications remain somewhat superficial.
If affairs are abbreviated, the waves diminish; if the waves diminish, the water is deficient. Waves are a metaphor for affairs; water is a metaphor for principle (*li*).

Thus, when affairs are not harmonized, the principle ultimately remains unpenetrated. Therefore, I say: when the multitude indulge their passions and are oblivious to their nature, the *po* (corporeal soul) flourishes while the *hun* (ethereal soul) declines.
For the noble person (*junzi*), however, the *hun* predominates and the *po* is diminished, because they have heard the Way and are able to act according to principle.

This is because they are severed from their emotions. Thus, the *po* is the cause of the ghost (*gui*), and the ghost is the effect of the *po*. The *hun* is the cause of the spirit (*shen*), and the spirit is the effect of the *hun*.
When the essence of cause and effect is refined, the explanation of the *hun*, *po*, ghost, and spirit becomes clear—like seeing eyebrows, eyes, and ears in a mirror.
What room is there for doubt? As for the doctrine of the three *hun* and seven *po*, this applies to ordinary people; as for the *hun*...

To have much [of the physical] while having little *po* (the vital soul) is the mark of a gentleman. Only the Sage is without *po* and possesses only the Spirit (*shen*). Therefore, in his life, he cannot be burdened by living;
and in his death, how could he alone be subject to the burden? Thus it is said: "That which wondrously transforms all things yet has no mind is called the Spirit.
It is also said: "The Sage has no further [retribution]. This "no further" means that outside of his nature (*xing*), there is no further emotion (*qing*).
It can be cured. If there is even the slightest emotion that is not exhausted, it will ultimately never cease to exist. Therefore it is said: "Even a mote of dust remains for those still in training;
when clarity reaches its ultimate limit, one is a Tathāgata. It is further said: "All floating dust and illusory transformations should, upon a single thought, be transformed into supreme awakening.
Speaking from this perspective, the Book of Changes is profound and subtle; so too is the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
This is a scripture. How wondrous! How profound! Long ago, Zhang Wujin said, "Only after reading Buddhist scriptures did I come to understand Confucianism.

Thus, unless one exhausts principle and fully realizes human nature to reach the destiny of Heaven (*ming*), then regarding the discourse on the *hun* and *po* souls and ghosts and spirits, the depth of beginnings and endings, and the sequence of cause and effect—from the subtle to the coarse, from the coarse to the subtle—one must traverse thousands of twists and myriad turns.
To dismantle [dogmatic attachments], to unravel emotions and release fetters, to differ in terminology while agreeing on the underlying principles,
to affirm what is erroneous and negate what is correct, to induce doubt where there is none and to eliminate doubt where it exists—
this is the profound compassion of the Sage and the diligent toil of the gentleman. Students must not fail to understand this.

In the "Shi Yu Tai Fang Guang Shi" (The Stone of Radiant Light Showing Cosmic Tranquility), it is said that the arising of doubt and faith in the world does not arise from phenomena (*dharma*), but arises from principle (*li*).

Thus, that which arises from phenomena is deluded regarding principle; that which arises from principle is suspicious of phenomena. Viewed through this lens, one may believe in principle yet not believe in [phenomena].
Regarding phenomena: to believe in phenomena while not believing in principle is what is called "belief that is not true belief" and "doubt that is not true doubt.
Only when one believes in phenomena by means of principle, and believes in principle by means of phenomena—what more need I say?

As for the milfoil stalks at the Mausoleum of Confucius and the sandalwood trees of the Elder Xuanzang, phenomena are inferred through principle, and principle is investigated through phenomena; this is the relationship between the sentient and the insentient.
It is extraordinary. As clear as the sun and stars, this stone has six facets and sharp edges; its substance is lustrous and pure, radiating brilliance when reflected by the sun.

It originates from Mount Emei and is not found on other mountains. Commentators maintain that the six facets symbolize the Six Perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā), and the sharp edges symbolize diligence (vīrya).
It fulfills the Three Studies and governs the myriad practices; it embodies the myriad practices to subdue all habitual tendencies. These tendencies—
When cultivated, phenomena themselves become principle, and principle itself becomes phenomena; thus, the virtue of universal auspiciousness is perfected.
Now, Mount Emei stretches for a thousand *li*, its azure void meeting the heavens; its precipitous ridges and wondrous peaks manifest ten thousand forms of alternating concealment and revelation.
How could it be that these mere specks of stone possess all such virtues? One might say: "A single flower can reveal boundless spring; a spoonful of water can represent the full moon."
When the moon is full, it is so for that [moon]; how could this alone be otherwise?
It is as Wan Zhai said:
the Sage did not consider the long snake or the great boar to be a source of affliction, but rather considered his own person to be the affliction; his anxiety was indeed profound.

It is so. Like the Zhuangtai Terrace girdled by water or the Apang Palace reaching to the clouds, one may indulge in the pleasures of sightseeing to the utmost, yet die without being able to return—how lamentable this is!
Lang of Songling knew that the body is a source of affliction and did not value the pursuit of material well-being.
Because he did not value material well-being, everything he managed was merely sufficient for its purpose; thus his hall was not designed to be lofty, nor his inner chambers designed for luxury.
Truly, thatch and reeds are sufficient to shelter one’s form, and thick gruel and thin porridge are enough to stanch the thirst of the mouth.

With an ancient inkstone and ancient books, and with a simple heart and poor bones, one may find a profound richness in the humble glory of the Jin and Zhang families. The Purple Cypress Recluse (Zibai Daoren) happened to take refuge from the wind and rain here;
delighted by its rustic simplicity, he found it possessed the air of a country dweller. He titled it "The Studio Resembling Perfection" (Simowan Zhai) and wrote this to leave behind.
Jiaolu Sheng’s Commentary on the Thousand Character Classic says:
"The origin of painting is the state before painting; this state before painting is rooted in one's own mind. Therefore, when the mind desires to make one stroke, or desires to make two strokes,"
This extends even to painting ten million images; each and every image is alive and has never been dead.
What is meant by "dead" and "alive"? It is said: if one sees one image, one calls it one image; if one sees ten million images, one calls them ten million images.
This is called knowing death but not knowing life. Only those who know life understand that although the images are inexhaustible, they clearly realize that the pivot lies within themselves.
It does not reside in the painted lines. Take, for example, the sixty-four hexagrams and three hundred and eighty-four lines:
if each hexagram were fixed and each line were destined for death, then change and transformation would also have an end.

It is precisely because every hexagram is without constancy and every line is fundamentally alive that they circulate through the six voids; their positions above and below are not fixed, whether as emotion or nature, or as ghost or spirit.

Its coming and going are unfathomable; its concealment and manifestation appear like a mystery. To act before Heaven yet not oppose it, or to follow after Heaven yet accord with its timing—were one not to understand this vitality, how could one reach such a state?
Thus, Cangjie beheld bird tracks and awakened to the alphabet; the Brahmī and Kharoṣṭhī scripts did not require external stimulus for him to realize that characters arise from the mind.
Although the forms of these writings may be horizontal or vertical, their capacity to explain meaning remains unchanged.

In the beginning, they were not the same. Just as bird tracks evolved into the Great Seal script (Dàzhuàn), the Great Seal evolved into the Small Seal (Xiǎozhuàn), the Small Seal evolved into the Clerical (Lì), the Clerical evolved into the Regular (Kǎi), and the Regular evolved into the Cursive (Cǎo); once Cursive was reached, it returned almost to the state of bird tracks.

How is this different from the Central Indian script evolving into the scripts of the four regions, those four evolving into the Hu, and the Hu evolving into the Yi? Therefore it is said: "He who understands change is the one who originally established the system."
This is because those who follow after change are merely the masses. Nevertheless, at the beginning of creation, the few were sages and the many were ignorant.

If there are those who can awaken to that which was not yet painted by means of the painting, or attain awakening to the mind by means of the mind—alas! That which has not yet been painted is the mother of all paintings;
the mindless state is the ancestor of heaven, earth, and the myriad things. Once one knows the mother and further attains the ancestor, then the ignorant may become sages.
The sage can appear identical to the fool; hence it is said that "great wisdom resembles folly.

I have beheld the *Qianziwen* written by Jiaolu Sheng, wherein the strokes rise and fall, extend and contract, and undergo transformations with orderly regularity, yet do not remain bound by fixed rules.
Is this not indeed the skillful category of a calligrapher?

Regarding the explanation of the posthumous title "Xiao" (Filial): This refers to Zhou Xiao Hou of Jin. When he encountered a great enemy, he desired to risk his life in a single battle. A colleague urged him, saying, "The General’s mother is advanced in years.
If you do not prevail in battle, where will the Great Lady find refuge? Xiao Hou replied, "As a high minister, I must..."
He fulfilled his duties as a minister. Regarding the events of this day, since he was already a subject of the state, how could he have been concerned for his mother?

He subsequently died in battle. The court praised his loyalty and posthumously conferred upon him the title of Marquis Xiaokou (Filial Marquis). Viewed from this perspective, loyalty and filial piety are fundamentally one and the same path.

It is incorrect for scholars to treat filial piety as filial piety and loyalty as loyalty, interpreting them as two separate paths. Generally speaking, it is because one views things through the lens of the "self" [that they appear distinct].
To serve one’s parents with all one’s strength is called filial piety; to serve one’s ruler with all one’s strength is called loyalty.

When the mind harbors no divided intent, those who possess such loyalty and filial piety are merely given these names. Therefore, one who has realized the true nature of the mind understands that loyalty and filial piety are one;
one who pursues mere names erroneously clings to them as two.
I have just said that if a son is not firm, he cannot be filial; if a minister is not firm, he cannot be loyal.

Yet, when it comes to the critical junctures of honor and disgrace, life and death, if one does not take firmness as one's ground, one will be dazzled and deluded by them, having no leisure to maintain self-possession. However, firmness itself is also not... [incomplete]
This is easily said. One must first hear the Way. Having heard the Way, one’s insight becomes lofty and clear;

thus, one can understand that heaven, earth, the myriad things, the past and the future, are all reflections and echoes of my own mind. These reflections and echoes exist because of the mind, and the mind is manifested through these reflections and echoes.
When these reflections and echoes appear in the present, everyone perceives them and reckons heaven, earth, and the myriad things [to be external].
Regarding size: one calculates the void of physical forms as either existent or non-existent; one calculates the mass gathered within a single vessel as one's own body;
one calculates the reflection produced by the external environment as one's own mind. From this perspective, there is nowhere it does not reach.

How could it ever be exhausted through words? Therefore it is said: "The quality of hardness (*kāṭhinya*) is the very foundation of the nature and destiny (*prakṛti-dharma*) of the Five Constant Virtues."
The Old Man of the Moving and Still Leather Ball asked Huanglong’s disciple, Sun, saying, "In the ancients, they were still even while moving; where does the meaning of this lie?
Sun replied, "Stillness lies within movement. The Old Man pointed to the peony before his seat to test him, asking, "Suppose this flower is at its peak of fragrance and fullness—"
When they wither and fall, is this not movement? To say they are "fragrant and lush" is for them to abide in fragrance and lushness; when they wither and fall, they abide in withering and falling.
Since these two each abide in themselves, can they be called still? Two is not one, and one is not two. Two is two and one is one; one is one and two is two.
It is like seeing flowers bloom and fade within a dream, seeing them fade and then bloom, where blooming precedes fading.
Regarding the sequence of arising and ceasing: to claim that each exists within its own nature throughout a single lifetime—that is, that movement is itself stillness—is the talk of the ignorant.
The wise resolve that this is not so. Why? Because arising and ceasing, whether prior or subsequent, cannot be found apart from a dream.
A dream does not exist of itself; it must arise due to conceptualization (*saṃjñā*). Conceptualization does not exist of itself; it must arise due to the unmanifest (*avijñapti*).
Perception exists; yet before perception, it does not exist of itself. It must manifest through perception. Therefore, non-perception is the father of perception;
perception is the father of dreams; dreams are the father of flowers; flowers are the father of blooming and withering; and blooming and withering are the fathers of movement and stillness.

As for saying that stillness resides above movement, it is then the child of movement and stillness. To speak of a "child" is to abandon the root by going too far; how can such a thing serve as evidence?
Wherever one looks, one encounters the theater; why need puppets ascend the hall at night? Prosperity passes before the eyes as the three watches hasten by;
fame and profit pull at people with a thread that stretches long. Young children naturally vie to marvel and speak of it; even the short-statured man is likewise tossed about in vain.
"Sorrowful! When have you ever recognized your original face? For now, learn from the madman of Chu before this honored one.
This is a "puppet play" poem by Yangming. Master Zibo said: "Yangming’s viewing of the play—this play is also a teacher of the Way.
How is the joy of the common people any different from a puppet show? Thus, when King Mu of Zhou was enraged by Yan Shi, Yan Shi disassembled his puppets.

King Mu finally realized that he was not an immortal. Today, throughout the world, regardless of whether it be ancient or modern times, people may bow to one another in formal attire, or men and women may sit together in mixed company, conversing with transcendent ease.
Yet, if one were to momentarily let go of the mind and look back at this body of mine, by what means is it actually constituted?

Even if it must exist by virtue of the five elements (*pañca-dhātu*), these five elements are subject to constant cycles of production and destruction; how could they possibly [provide lasting stability]?
If even that which possesses a self is impermanent, how much more so that which is possessed? Contemplating the body in this way, one sees that the body is no different from a plaything;
is it not then like the work of the puppeteer, the Master of Marionettes (Yan Shi), who possesses the mark of the broad and long tongue?
I have heard of Zhuowu of Tiantai for many years, yet I had not yet had the opportunity to meet him. It was only upon reading the biography of Geng Ziyong that I first truly came to know Zhuowu.
Zhuowu said that you, Master of Tiantai, regard human relations as the ultimate; I, however, regard the Unmanifested [the *wufa*] as such.
"Among these, human relations are the ultimate [virtue]. For this reason, we held onto our respective positions and did not transform one another for nearly ten years;
only now have we begun to transform. This is how he described it himself. Now, human relations are like waves; before they arise, they are like water.

To hold that the waves are the ultimate is certainly wrong, but would it not also be wrong to hold that the water is the ultimate of the waves? It is simply because [the waves] have already manifested externally."

If [the state] has not yet manifested, then that which has already manifested would have no source. To insist that the unmanifested reaches the manifested might suggest that the unmanifested can be grasped;
yet one fails to realize that both the manifested and the unmanifested are neither graspable nor discardable.
If the manifested were graspable, how would it differ from seeking waves apart from water? If the unmanifested were graspable, how would it differ from seeking... [water] apart from waves?
It is water. Whether already manifested or not yet manifested, it can neither be grasped nor abandoned. Therefore it is said: "It cannot be grasped; it cannot be abandoned;
within that which cannot be obtained, one simply obtains it. If this is so, then Zhuowu’s [Zhang] Tiantai first clung to things and did not transform, until he transformed and no longer clung.
How is this different from a silkworm that clings to and abandons its cocoon?
"Or upon a mass of fire? An ancient worthy once said: "Dead water certainly cannot harbor a dragon, yet even living water is not the place where a dragon dwells.
This is spoken merely with respect to a *false* dragon. As for a *true* dragon, it is both dead and alive;
its presence depends on the dragon itself, not on the water. Now, as for the nature of a dragon: when dwelling in the void, it is like water; when striking a rock, it becomes stone.
It transforms into water; when it touches trees and forests, or touches fire, it does not turn its tail and transform [into those things].

Judging from this, if one says that emptiness can be grasped, then the Great Void would have something left over; if one says that emptiness can be abandoned, then there would be something outside the Great Void.
Emptiness is but the shadow of form, yet it cannot even be approximated through grasping or abandoning—how much more so for that which is greater than this? —Zhuowu.
Zhuowu—truly a dragon? Truly that which Lord Ye painted? To ask about the "original" (ben) is itself unaskable;
if it can be asked about, it is no longer the original. Why? Because the original does not inquire after the original. It is just like the original.
One may ask: "How is this different from water washing water or gold striking gold?
Nevertheless, the skillful questioner asks what has never been asked before, and the respondent likewise answers what has never been answered before. Long ago, there was a monk who asked Mazu:
"Beyond the four propositions and transcending the hundred negations—please, Preceptor, point directly to the meaning of the Westward Transmission.
The Patriarch said, "I am weary today and cannot speak for you; go ask Zangzhi. Zangzhi said, "I too have a headache and cannot speak.
He asked Hai to go, and Hai said, "I do not understand. The monk then went to see the Patriarch and reported the words of Zangzhi and Hai. The Patriarch said, "Zang..."
The head is black; the head of the sea is white. The monk also withdrew with an expression of shame. A Celestial Youth composed a verse on this karmic occasion:
"Stately, he sits cutting off the path of the tongue; One must laugh at that ancient sage of Vaiśālī. I find the flavor of this verse by the Celestial Youth profound.
Thus one knows that when Mañjuśrī questioned Vimalakīrti regarding the meaning of non-duality, Vimalakīrti answered with silence. This instance, however, involves both a question and an answer.
In the winter of the Renyin year of the Wanli era, the layman Zheng of Kunyan on Mount Tiantai once inquired of the Venerable Zibo regarding the purport of the "fundamentally pure" nature.
The Master said: "Layman, your karmic conditions have not yet matured; it will not be too late to inquire again once they have matured."
Alas! When a "night-light" is thrown at people, few fail to draw their swords. Reflecting instead upon the ocean of the hidden [teachings], I cannot help but clench my fists in frustration.

In the spring of the Gui-mao year, when the Chan practitioner Chong returned to Guoqing Temple, the Daoist Zibai had previously sent a verse concerning the "Original Pavilion" (Benting) to the Layman.
Furthermore, he entrusted Chong, saying: "Construct a pavilion for the layman at a place by the Guo River where the water, stones, and air are secluded and refreshing.
Name it 'Inquiring into the Source' (Wenben), so as to manifest the meaning of the practitioner not forgetting the layman's intent to inquire into the source."
As the sun sets, the drum hangs suspended;
the faculties of sentient beings are dull and their attachments are heavy. Though their ears and eyes appear to possess clarity and intelligence, their minds are in truth deaf and blind.

The Sage, knowing this to be so, could not have opened them through mere names and words. Thus, he employed names and words as a provisional means to lodge his methods within specific locations, manifesting them through images and objects.
This is what is called using emotion to broaden emotion, and using objects to seize objects. At first, one molds the self into things; in the end, one integrates things into the self.
However, the manifestations of suffering are manifold; if one does not experience them personally, it is not easy to know suffering. Once suffering is known, [one understands its nature].
One then infers happiness by means of suffering; although happiness is not yet perceived, its principle is found upon examination to be non-false.
By this, the power of faith becomes firm, and one practices without ceasing until the goal is finally achieved. The great significance of the suspended drum does not exceed this.

Although other contemplations employ various methods of detailed regulation and the sequence of cultivation from shallow to deep is clearly distinct and difficult to confuse, only those with the resolve to transcend suffering [should apply them].
If one applies effort without negligence, one will ultimately achieve profound mastery. Only then will one realize that true compassion is the original aspiration.

Regarding the three realms, it is said that within a single heaven-and-earth, there are four great continents: the eastern is called Zhōuzhōu (the Divine Continent), the western is called Hèzhōu (the Western Continent), and the southern is called...
There are four provinces and states. The northern one is called Luzhou, and its territory extends for several tens of thousands of *li*.

According to calculations based on the divisions of the Seven Luminaries (*saptarṣi*), it likewise has its own specific measurements in *li*. However, in the southern state, the human lifespan is only one hundred years, and wealth and nobility are not particularly exalted.
In the eastern state, the human lifespan is two hundred and fifty years, and wealth and nobility are highly esteemed; thus, it certainly surpasses the south.
There are many such states. Comparing the eastern states to the western state of Aparagoyānī, the people of the western state live for five hundred years;

their nobility, wealth, and honor further surpass those of the eastern states. Yet, when comparing the western state to the northern continent of Uttarakuru, there is a difference as vast as that between heaven and earth.
For the people of the northern continent live for a thousand years without premature death, and their wealth, honor, and nobility are likewise unsurpassed.
This is what is meant by "the ultimate. If one were to compare this to the Four Heavenly Kings, it would not even be like a vinegar-mite matching the Great Peng bird.

Even the wealth and nobility of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations, when compared to the joy and bliss of the First Dhyāna, is like a commoner offering the warmth of basking his back to a sovereign of ten thousand chariots.
From the heavens of the First Dhyāna up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception, the levels successively increase.
The superior is not matched by the inferior; there is a vast and profound disparity between them.

If one were to view the lifespan, wealth, and exalted status of the Non-Perception (Āsaṃjñisattva) realm with the divine eye of a Śrāvaka, it would be like an insect born in the morning that dies at night, wallowing in mucus and saliva.
Yet the people of the Southern Continent (Jambudvīpa) generally rely on their own wealth and status, wasting their years from birth until death without a thought for their impermanence.
One is deluded and restless, desiring dreams and never awakening for even a moment.

If one were to compare the three continents to oneself, the four kings' heavens to the three continents, and the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception to the Yāma and Trāyastriṃśa heavens, then would not those in Jambudvīpa—who pride themselves on their wealth, status, and nobility, and who regard a hundred years as an eon—be moved to sorrow? Therefore it is said: "Viewing the three [realms] with the Dharma-eye..."
The retribution of the realms, both the primary and the secondary, is no less than that of a prisoner in a dungeon; how could this deceive me?
Having read the *Suwen*, I have heard it said that Bodhisattvas of Prajñā can attain great mastery among all phenomena. Observing from this perspective...
In the Confucian tradition, he is the Sage Teacher of enlightened kings; in the Laozi tradition, he is the Perfected Man and the Divine Man;
in the Buddhist tradition, he is the Great Awakened One and World Hero; and among the hundred schools, he successively serves as their leader.

Those who each raise their banners and drums to proclaim themselves to the world are all manifestations of Bodhisattvas. When I read the *Huangdi Suiwen*, reaching its summary which says: "Those who merely maintain..."
The Pivot. Above, one guards the pivot; the movement of the pivot does not depart from its emptiness. The pivot within emptiness is pure and subtle;
its coming cannot be met, and its going cannot be pursued. One who knows the pivot knows the Way; such a person cannot be entangled by even a hair’s breadth [of attachment].
Unconsciously placing the scroll aside, I sighed deeply. This book—were it not for a sage, no one could have composed it. By this, I know...
One who attains its emptiness can regulate the wind; one who attains the wind can regulate the fire; one who attains the fire can regulate the water;
and one who attains the water can regulate the earth. Thus, the earth floats upon the water;
the water is sustained by the fire; the fire relies upon the wind; and the wind is borne by emptiness. Therefore, one who attains emptiness can bring all things to completion.
It is subtle. Being subtle, it cannot be sought through signs or omens, nor can it be met by welcoming or sending away.

If one is thus able to settle the spirit in emptiness and perceive its form clearly—discerning the parts, the channels, the vessels, and the depths of the internal organs—it is like standing within a hall and illuminating all things;
how could there be any confusion? Therefore, the skilled physician knows to maintain the vital mechanism and grasp its subtlety, his spirit roaming in the realm of non-being.
It is pervasive; there is nothing subtle that it does not examine. Earth consists of four elements; water lacks one; fire lacks another; and wind consists of only one.
Because the single element has fewer cumulative burdens, its functional power transcends the other three.

The solidity of earth, the moisture of water, the dryness of fire, and the movement of wind—all these are subject to partiality, and when they are not in harmonious equilibrium, they constitute a disease. Space, however, is not [subject to such conditions].
These four are that which is confined by the enclosure. Therefore, only one who attains emptiness (*śūnyatā*) can begin to master these four.
When the four have a master, it is like the people obtaining a ruler; there has never been a case where the world was not well-governed once the people obtained a ruler.

Nevertheless, while one may attain the subtlety of emptiness and thereby govern that which has form, one cannot thereby govern that which is formless. To be able to govern that which is formless is not merely to attain emptiness, but to attain the Mind.
None are able to do so. Therefore it is said: "Emptiness arises within the Great Awakening, like a single bubble emerging from the ocean.
This refers to those who have attained Prajñā, the Bodhisattvas.

The golden tongue and three eyes are manifestations of the mind’s own spiritual penetration; yet, following conditions, they form appearances. Thus, when the Venerable Master Jinshe cut off his tongue to present it to Emperor Wenzong of the Tang dynasty, his tongue continued to chant the sutras as before.
The Emperor marveled at this and subsequently posthumously conferred upon him the title "Venerable Master Golden Tongue" (Jinshe Heshang). This was because—
It is because when forged with fire, it becomes golden in color. Regarding the Three-Eyed Arhat, he has an eye on his left arm that perceives objects from afar;
many in the world marvel at this. Yet they do not realize that the human mind is fundamentally spiritual. Because it is shrouded by the five desires, its spiritual function does not manifest.
Now, the Great Compassionate Bodhisattva possesses a thousand hands and a thousand eyes, while the nine-headed ghost-car bird possesses a strange variety of emotions.
Viewed from this perspective, the difference between the sage and the ordinary person is merely like the bending and extending of a single finger. The finger is a metaphor for one's own mind;

bending and extending are metaphors for its function. Thus, while Avalokiteśvara skillfully employs his own mind, manifesting a thousand hands to grasp and a thousand eyes to illuminate, these too are but a single drop in the great ocean or a single grain of millet in a vast granary.
The ghost-car (guīchē) suffers such ugliness because it does not skillfully employ its own mind.
I reply: Alas! Nevertheless, when an earthworm is cut in two, both ends move; when a mosquito is bitten, its whole body trembles with alarm.
One who understands this may be spoken to regarding the distinction between the golden tongue and the three eyes.

The *Luyaya Yehua Ji* (Record of Night Talks on Reed Sprouts) states that from antiquity to the present, those who serve as historians have never failed to meet with human calamities; indeed, they invariably incur the punishments of Heaven.
For humans are the most intelligent among all things; though the worthy and the foolish follow different paths, they do not differ fundamentally in their essential nature. Their hearts—
In the subtle and hidden recesses of human conduct, even the wise are not necessarily free from a single lapse, nor is the ignorant necessarily devoid of a single insight.

For the most part, the worldly teachings used to examine the worthiness of men cannot discern with absolute clarity. Since they lack such penetrating insight, when they set pen to paper to comment upon others, how could they avoid error?
I have often observed that many Song dynasty Confucians fell prey to this ailment; only the Great Hero who has transcended the world is exempt.

Only then can one be free from obscuration. The reason for this is that these three fundamental delusions have been completely severed, and the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) have been fully realized.

The eye penetrates immeasurable worlds; the ear hears immeasurable worlds; and the nose, tongue, body, and mind—each and every one—are void, luminous, and all-pervasive, leaving nothing unilluminated.
It is like the constellation Xuan-yuan suspended in the vast emptiness of space, wherein the six directions, the four quarters, and the ten directions and three periods of time are all as one.
Not even a single speck of dust or a tiny grain of mustard seed escapes his clear penetration.

From the time of the Elder [Mahākāśyapa] downward, regarding all those in the world—whether wise or foolish, whether acquaintances near or far, and the shifting complexities of human relations—I cannot privately determine their merits or faults when it comes to matters that cause heartache or stir the mind.
For we who dwell within the cave of ignorance must surely have our errors and delusions. In the year Dinghai, I and Master Miaoyan of Luyaya sat by the lamp...

Having happened to engage with worldly affairs, I unwittingly spoke of the shortcomings of one or two associates. Thereupon, I reflected that since I am not a Tathāgata, how could I know there was no error?
I have written this to record my own transgression.
When Jiju composed his essay "The Subtle and the Obscure," he said that it is like wind upon a sail: the wind cannot be seen, yet the sail fills and the boat moves; this is something visible.
It is like a spring within the earth, by which the hundred grains are produced: the spring cannot be seen, yet the hundred grains flourish and bear fruit; this is visible.
It is like springtime in a flower. Spring cannot be seen, yet the flower can be seen. It is like the flavor of salt in water;
the water can be seen, but the flavor cannot be seen—it is only those who drink the water who know it. It is like the blue pigment within a color;
the color can be seen, but the blue cannot be seen. It is like the sun rising as it kisses the mountain, or the full moon facing the door. One—
Half is visible; although that other half is invisible, one knows with certainty that it is not non-existent.

It is like the place where space arises: this is precisely where form arises. This is a true statement. Yet, people see only the space and do not see the form because their minds are bound by attachment.
Eighth, if one realizes this one principle, then all others are equal. For example, when you compose a literary work, once it is called...
Regarding "timely writing" (*shiwén*): this requires that I go to others. If I were to wait for others to come to me, it would no longer be timely writing.
Yet, in my going to others, I must go while not going; only then is there nowhere I do not go.
Precisely because there is nowhere I do not go, even if people do not wish for me to come to them, they cannot help but do so. That people cannot help but come to me is because—
There exists that which is invisible. Nowadays, when people compose writings, what is visible is in abundance, while what is invisible is desolate.

If one can use the visible to serve as an introduction to the invisible—like a dragon amidst the clouds, whose head and horns, though not revealed, possess an inherent spirit within—then in all such cases, the false cannot mask the true, and the true likewise [cannot be obscured].
This is because one does not conceal falsehoods. Thus, the writing is like clouds, while the intent of my mind is like a dragon.

If one’s inner being is not empty and lucid, yet desires for the intent of one's mind to be as divine as a dragon, such a thing has never occurred. Indeed, the cultivation of the inner being consists precisely in governing the emotions with principle (*li*).
When the emotions are extinguished, there is a measure of emptiness, vast as the expanse of the azure sky; therein, literary expression naturally becomes elegant and brilliant.

This is what is meant by "using myself to approach others. Even if others wish not to let me approach them, it is impossible for them to do so. To restrain greed and violence, one cites the ancients as examples:

for the sake of the office (*guan*) and the family (*jia*), they treated these as public vessels (*gongqi*). Therefore it is said: "The Five Emperors made the world their office; the Three Kings made the world their family."

Alas! Among the people of today, those of the higher sort regard holding office as a source of disgrace for their families; those of the lower sort regard holding office as a means to become a wealthy patron.

With their ranks and titles serving as their green-banded banners, they openly raise their standards and drums, wielding spears like those of the long serpents and great boars to plunder and seize the common people.
This has become so habitual that it is considered the norm throughout the land, and no one deems it strange. Judging by this, then...
To treat those who bring shame upon their offices and families as the primary remedy for the times is indeed an excellent prescription.

When bandits take the green forests as their lairs and weapons as their power, they are easily captured; yet if they take official robes as their lair and noble rank as their power, they are difficult to seize.
Thus Zhuang Zhou said: "If the Sage did not die, great thieves would never cease. There is truly a profound reason for this. Nevertheless...

They rely on their power to plunder the living beings, and having grown fat on bribes, they conceal themselves behind the insignia of nobility. Above, they deafen and blind the ears and eyes of the sovereign;
in the middle, those of the same robe protect one another; and below, the common people dare only to be angry but do not dare to speak.
They fail to realize that the living beings are the very foundation of the state. To plunder the living beings is precisely what destroys the sovereign. Once the sovereign is destroyed, their rank—
To whom do positions belong? To whom do robes and caps belong? If this is so, then thieves will naturally exhaust their own haunts and naturally strip away their own power.
Alas! Man is the most spiritual of all things; yet, failing to become a sage or a worthy man, he willingly becomes a thief.
He must reach the point where his haunts are exhausted and his power stripped away, yet he never awakens. Can this not be called the height of delusion and the ultimate folly?
The Dharma King and the Human King have declared that when the Great Way was in a state of dream, heaven and earth were divided. Once heaven and earth were divided, the myriad things came into being.

As the myriad things arose, they received breaths of varying strength and weakness. If there were no sovereign to preside over them, the strong would oppress the weak, and the weak would suffer oppression.
The weak cannot coexist with the strong within the space between heaven and earth. Formerly, Yao offered the empire to Xu You;
Xu You loathed the very mention of it and washed his ears. Commentators have held that it was easy to be like Chao Fu and Xu You, but difficult to be like Yao and Shun.

Yao and Shun bore the responsibility of universal benevolence and were perfectly attuned to the sentiments of all things. If there were even a single thing that did not find its proper place, [they would not rest].
"Though one faces south in the joy of sovereignty, one cannot dispel one's sorrow. What kind of mind is this?

If those like Chao Fu and Xu You maintain the view of solitary excellence and enjoy the blessings of solitary excellence, regarding the world as worn-out sandals and viewing the physical body as a great affliction—treasuring the internal while disparaging the external—what kind of mind is this?
Master Mei held these two views and sought a middle way from the late Master Zibai."
Sheng said, "Between Yao and Shun on the one hand, and Chao Fu and Xu You on the other, who gained and who lost? Master Cheng responded, "Both gained and both lost.
Meixi Zi said, "Master, I truly do not understand what you mean; I beg you to reveal it to me. He replied, "Do you know of the mundane and supramundane dharmas?
In the *I Ching*, that which transcends form is called the Way (*Dao*); that which is below form is called phenomena (*dharma*)."
Therefore, those who preside over the Way are Dharma Kings; those who preside over the vessel are Human Kings. Yao and Shun were Human Kings;

the teachings they established revered Heaven alone, so whenever they faced affairs of state, they invariably invoked the Supreme Lord (Shangdi). Even those such as Chao Fu and Xu You likewise revered Heaven.
Only the Buddha, because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is boundless, established his teachings by taking that very nature as the boundaries of his domain.
The nine realms are taken as subjects and citizens. These nine realms are: hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, asuras, devas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas.
To compare this with the teachings of Yao and Shun or those of the sages Chao and Xu is like comparing a puddle in a cow’s footprint to the vast ocean.
Furthermore, while there is but one human king, there are four Dharma kings. Among them is the Dharma King of the Treasury of Teachings.
There is the Dharma King of the Shared Teaching, the Dharma King of the Distinct Teaching, and the Dharma King of the Perfect Teaching.

The Dharma King of the Treasury Teaching practices the contemplation of emptiness to sever the afflictions of views and thoughts. The Dharma King of the Shared Teaching practices the contemplation of the provisional to partially sever the "dust-like" and "sand-like" delusions.

The Dharma King of the Distinct Teaching, however, practices the three contemplations of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle in succession, thereby being able to sever the twelve grades of ignorance and realize [the stage of the First Ground].
When the three virtues of partial realization reach the stage of the Perfect Teaching’s Dharma King, they become the ultimate three virtues.

The three contemplations are cultivated simultaneously, and the three delusions are completely severed—namely, the skin-delusion, the flesh-delusion, and the bone-delusion—all severed without remainder.

One directly ascends to Wondrous Enlightenment and returns to non-attainment. Alas! This Great Way was once a dream, yet from it heaven and earth were divided; this is what is meant by "arising from purity."

It is pure and original by nature, yet suddenly gives rise to mountains, rivers, and the great earth. This is because there are small and large capacities for the faculties, and shallow and deep levels of delusion and awakening;
thus, the *xiang*, *tong*, *bie*, and *yuan* [teachings] must be established as four. Yet, when investigated, these four are one.
Therefore, the Sage possesses both hidden skillful means (*mingquan*) and manifest skillful means (*xianquan*). Judging by his hidden skillful means, [he regards] Yao, Shun, Chao, and Xu [as equal].

All of these are inconceivable. If one were to apply the standard of manifesting expedient means (*upāya*), then even Yao, Shun, Chaofu, and Xuhou would all be counted among the six realms of ordinary beings (*ṣaḍ-gati*).

The *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* speaks of seven destinies; therein, even those such as immortals and spirits are subsumed within the six realms of ordinary beings—how much more so, then, the cases of Yao, Shun, Chaofu, and Xuhou?
Indeed, the distinction between the ordinary and the sage, or between defilement and purity, does not exist apart from non-arising (*anutpāda*); they are all conditioned by causes and conditions.
They arise. Yet within this arising through conditions, the myriad paths differ; all are dreams, not awakenings.

If one can follow arising through conditions and enter non-arising, then both awakening and dreaming are awakening. Zhuang Zhou said: "Only after attaining great awakening does one know that it was a great dream.
One who has attained great awakening has neither waking nor dreaming; both are like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a hare.

People today frequently use the principles of the secular world to criticize those who dwell beyond its boundaries; this is because they have not clearly understood the paths of the Human King and the Dharma King.
If those who offer criticism were truly to understand both the mundane and supramundane paths, they would simply follow their own respective teachings. What cause for criticism would there then be?
One who rules over a territory is called a human king; one who rules through the Way is called a Dharma King.
Since territory has physical boundaries, there are those who are honored and those who are not; since the Way is without limit, there is nothing that is not honored.
Therefore, an iron wheel is not as honorable as a copper wheel; a copper wheel is not as honorable as a silver wheel; and a silver wheel is not as honorable as a gold wheel.
As for the wheels: although the Golden Wheel is honorable, it is not equal to the honor of Śakra and Brahmā. These are all honored based on the extent and breadth of their respective lands.
Only the honor of the Dharma King—from the ordinary person to the sage—encompasses both the non-existent and the existent.
It encompasses the ten voids without omission and governs the myriad existences without decay. Because the Way has no boundaries, there is nothing it does not revere.
Since there is nothing it does not revere, one cannot constrain it with the laws of a worldly sovereign.
Thus, those who rule without territory and are noble without rank are called "guests beyond the square" (fangwai zhi bin). Now, if people insist on using the standards of the world...
The rites and laws of the sovereign serve to bind those who dwell beyond the mundane world. When these means of binding prove insufficient, one then seeks to destroy and abolish their teachings.
Thus, when Huan Xuan of the Jin dynasty composed elegant prose intending to refute Master Huiyuan, Huiyuan utilized that very refutation to gradually expound his principles;
consequently, Xuan’s anger was instantly dissipated. How could this have been achieved by means of verbal contention? It was through principle.

This is because [the former] can be bent [toward the latter]. Thus, a human king takes benevolence (*ren*) and righteousness (*yi*) as his principle of governance, while a Dharma King takes nature (*xing*) as his principle.
Benevolence and righteousness are the goodness of the emotional dispositions (*qing*). The *I Ching* says: "That which continues it is goodness; that which completes it is nature.
