"How could it be possible that there is no other world? Kātyāyana replied, "Are these sun and moon now for gods or humans, for this world or for another world?
If there were no other world, then there would be no sun or moon. The non-Buddhist lowered his head in silence.
After such back-and-forth exchanges occurred several dozen times, the non-Buddhists’ spirits were withered and their wisdom exhausted;

they then took refuge [in the Buddha]. Someone asked the Buddha, "Kātyāyana and Pūrṇa both possess wisdom and eloquence; for what reason is this? The Buddha said, "Those two have cultivated the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*) throughout many lifetimes;

therefore it is said they have cultivated the contemplation of non-self. [The questioner asked,] "By cultivating the contemplation of non-self, how do they obtain wisdom and eloquence? The Buddha said, "Do you not see?"
"Bells and drums have no inherent intentionality, yet they respond to every strike because their interior is fundamentally empty. Upon hearing this, the questioner finally attained understanding.
During the Jiajing era, there was a Chan master at a hermitage beneath Xiangbi Rock in Wan County, Kuizhou, who was transcribing the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
One day at dusk, when the setting sun had already vanished, he was still writing slowly and without ceasing. His attendant reported, "The sunlight has been gone for a long time;
why do you not stop writing the sutra? When the Chan Master heard this, he reached out his hand, yet could not see his own fingers. Alas!
This fundamental radiance is ever-present; it makes no distinction between the ordinary and the sage. Yet, when a fleeting thought arises, the veil of darkness manifests before me.
Recalling the sincere devotion of my former years in a single hermitage, this light suddenly revealed itself as I was transcribing the scriptures.

Thus, I composed a verse: No fire at the tip of the brush, yet light is born in the night; Clearly and slowly, I write several lines of scripture. A solitary bird calls out once, its cry echoing through the green trees.

"The east wind scatters the fragrance of a hundred flowers. I have forgotten this verse. Recently, at Fucheng Hermitage in Wan County, the monk Xingxing came from Wu to request the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Hearing that I had transcribed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* at the Ink-Light Pavilion in Jian-su, he specifically visited me for two nights.
While by the lamp, we happened to mention this verse; I was suddenly struck with realization and thus re-composed it.
In verse it says: Ten thousand counties and the Wu Gate share one sky; In the scriptures, who comes after and who comes before?
Deep in the night, I casually raise an old case; This constant radiance appears once more.
Ding Ciyin of Songling mentioned the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, specifically the passage: "One should give rise to the mind without abiding anywhere.
The Master pressed him, asking, "What is meant by 'giving rise to the mind without abiding anywhere'? Mr. Ding was left bewildered. The Master said:
“You have questioned me; I shall explain it for you. Ding Sheng responded, “Yes, Master. The Master suddenly struck the desk once and asked, “Ding Sheng, did you hear that?

He replied, “I heard it. The Master said, “This is not [the state where] the mind arises from nothingness. He asked Ding Sheng again, “When you heard it, was it with a mind that heard, or without a mind that heard?
He replied, “It was without a mind that heard. The Master said, “This is not [the state where one] should abide nowhere.”
Shortly thereafter, the Master spoke another verse, saying: "The wooden fish is struck so often; Fearing the pain, it suddenly gives rise to anger.
If you knew the place where it feels pain, The golden-scaled one would pass through the Dragon Gate. (The name of Disciple Ding was Faling.)
If the pre-heaven (*xiantian*) were constant, how could the post-heaven (*houtian*) begin? If the post-heaven were constant, how could the pre-heaven return?

It is precisely because the pre-heaven is not constant that the post-heaven begins to unfold; it is precisely because the post-heaven is not constant that the pre-heaven can be restored. As it is said:
Before Fuxi drew the lines, was there not the *Yi*? Yet, had it not been drawn by Fuxi, the world would have remained unaware of it.

Reading Su Changgong’s commentary on the *Yi*, I came to understand that although the natures and emotions of the sixty-four hexagrams and three hundred and eighty-four lines differ, their underlying constancy is one and the same.
Why is this? If *Qian* possessed a fixed constancy, then it would ultimately...
It has become Qian; from what would Li have begun? If Kun were constant, it would remain forever Kun;
from what would Kan have arisen? Therefore, both Qian and Kun are without constancy, and from them Li and Kan are produced.

Extending this to one hexagram producing eight hexagrams, and one line producing sixty-four lines—if these were not rooted in non-constancy, their production would be exhausted. This is drawn from the distant perspective.
This is spoken with reference to all things. To take an example from what is near at hand, one’s own body has four limbs:
the hands and the feet. Counting the hands and feet together, they do not exceed twenty fingers. Examining a single finger, it can be bent and extended.
If the finger possessed a fixed nature, the path of bending and extending would be blocked. If bending and extending were fixed, the finger would ultimately...
One may no longer point [to them] as such. By this I know that the *Zhenyan* (Prior Heaven) *Yi* has no fixed constancy;
thus, the path of the *Houren* (Posterior Heaven) is inexhaustible. While the *Houren* *Yi* is without constancy, the way of the *Zhenyan* is fundamentally and inherently pervasive.
If nature (*xing*) were to possess constancy, from what would emotion (*qing*) arise? If emotion were to possess constancy, from what would nature be made manifest? It is only through nature...
If impermanence is understood, then the Way can serve as the vessel; if only emotion is seen as impermanent, then the vessel can be restored to the Way.
The Sage, knowing this, follows emotion to restore the nature, yet does not abandon the functions of the ears and eyes;
he follows the nature to govern emotion, yet fundamentally remains free from the burdens of "self" and "other. Thus, he opens up things and accomplishes affairs, employing manifold transformations.

Transformation: To cause all under heaven to be moistened by this transformation, so that emotions are dissolved and nature is restored, is like the spring sun upon the myriad things—there is nothing that does not undergo transformation;
it is like the severe winter storing away the myriad things—there is nothing that does not return to its source.

Yet, in the *Yī*, there are principles (*lǐ*) and phenomena (*shì*), as well as emotional nature (*xìng*) and physical nature (*qíng*), and the hexagrams and lines (*guà yáo*). These three share the same substance but differ in name. Why is this? It is because they reside in different locations.

This is because designations differ according to the occasion. If one can spiritually and clearly comprehend this, then principle may be treated as phenomena, and phenomena may be treated as principle;
in that case, why should nature (*xing*) and emotion (*qing*), or the hexagrams (*gua*) and the lines (*yao*), not be mutually interchangeable?

As for the numbers of the *Yi*, they are the emotions of the lines; as for the principles of the *Yi*, they are the nature of the hexagrams. When the numbers are clarified, then good fortune and misfortune, waning and waxing, [become manifest].
The pivot of this lies within myself, not in the Creator. When principle is fully realized, one rolls up the myriad things and conceals them within the One;
even the spiritual power of ghosts and spirits, and the subtle workings of yin and yang, can no longer mold or cast me.
The hexagram is named Dàyǒu (Great Possession). This is because a single yin line occupies the position of honor, possessing the three virtues of faithfulness, compliance, and honoring the worthy;
thus, the multitude of yang lines submit their hearts and naturally turn toward it. Hence, it is called Dàyǒu. Only the first nine (chūjiǔ) is situated far away and cannot communicate with the fifth;
therefore, it is as if there were harm. The second nine (jiǔèr), however, corresponds in position with the fifth; the yang is communicated through the softness [of the fifth]. As for the third...

Yang occupies a yang position; its power is such that it can communicate with the Son of Heaven. Furthermore, there is the upper nine (shang jiu) who, though hidden, assists it. Thus, for it to communicate with those above—is this not easy?
As for the fourth line, it is close to the fifth (the ruler), and the third is not one of forceful arrogance; therefore, it will exclusively attach itself to the fifth.
Moreover, the fifth knows for itself that being weak, it cannot stand alone, and thus it receives the upper nine to attach itself to. Once the fifth has done so...
Furthermore, it is able to accommodate both four and three, two; thus, the primary correlate specifically assists the five without wearying itself—this is indeed credible.
Viewed in this light, although the first nine occupies a remote position, its yin line is deeply imbued with the virtue of the five.
There has never been one who, having been graced by such profound virtue, did not harbor a desire to repay it.

By this I know that although there is one Yin and five Yangs, the Yangs submit to its sincerity, compliance, and reverence for the worthy; it is only fitting that they should willingly serve it. Is this not indeed appropriate?
I have observed the *Shi-he* hexagram of the *Yi* and thereby come to know the nature of human emotions; they are like water and fire.
For water does not cease until it reaches the lowest point, and fire does not cease until it reaches the void. Reaching the lowest and the void are the extremes of water and fire.
This is like the *Chiu-jiu* (First Nine) of *Shi-he*, who, resenting that the Six in the Second position (*Liù-èr*) has mounted upon him, seizes and bites her out of anger—starting from her skin.
It reaches the nose. Thus, the second six (the hexagram line) maintains itself through the virtue of extreme flexibility and finds its peace in the Way of Centrality and Rectitude;

it remains placid and does not take [the situation] to heart. However, this is ultimately not the fortune of the first nine. Therefore, the Way of Heaven diminishes that which has a surplus and commiserates with that which is deficient.
Furthermore, the evil of the third six is that the ninth four is mounted upon it; it also bites out of anger. This is...
It is not known whether the fourth and fifth lines are both as hard as adamant and difficult to bite through; nevertheless, the power of the third line is thereby exhausted.
Yet, the fourth and fifth lines do not wait for the exhaustion of the third line’s strength, but instead exert their combined force to bite it. Thus, as for the third line:
if it wishes to oppose them, its strength is insufficient; if it wishes to remain at peace, its heart is not content. It can only harbor malice.
And that is all. Thus, when the strength of the third six is exhausted, it becomes the blessing of the fourth nine and the fifth six.

Since both the fourth nine and the fifth six are firm and difficult to bite through, this in turn becomes the blessing of the third six. Yet, the third six does not realize it has obtained such a blessing.

They harbor nothing but malice; they may indeed be called foolish and base. If the fourth and fifth lines had truly known that the third line harbored poison, and having bitten it, were able to stop, then the fourth and fifth lines would have gained much merit as well. It is only the topmost (ninth) line that [remains].

To dwell at the end of the hexagram "Shi" (Biting) without knowing how to exercise caution, but instead making biting one's primary concern, means that all the calamities of biting will fall upon one who dwells at the end.
Is it not fitting, then, that such a person should bear the yoke upon their neck until their ears are destroyed? Alas! Only the gentleman contemplates the images to grasp their underlying meaning;
having grasped the meaning, he knows how to exercise caution. He upholds principle to subdue emotion; when emotion is subdued, principle becomes full. When principle is full—

Thus, one daily advances toward the realm of non-self. Therefore, when there is an offense, one is able to be patient and inclusive. To be inclusive is to be great; to be great is to have no boundaries.
When there are no boundaries, heaven, earth, and the myriad things can all be encompassed within it. How could this be the time for the hexagram *Shi Ke* (Trampling and Chewing)?
"I have no skill with which to ward it off.
Now, a well does not become a well of its own accord; it becomes a well through human effort. Therefore, although a well cannot be altered, it can be leveled.
Yet a well does not level itself; it is leveled by human effort. Viewed from this perspective, whether a well is leveled or not, whether a well is pure or not—"
Purity depends entirely on the person; what does the well have to do with it? Thus, the well experiences neither gain nor loss, while the person undergoes coming and going.
"Nearly arrived" means the jar has entered the well but not yet obtained water. "Before the rope is hauled up" means the jar has obtained the water but not yet emerged from the well.
It is like drawing water from a well with a rope: if one succeeds in pulling it out, there is merit and no misfortune;

but if one has not yet drawn it out and breaks the jar, there is misfortune and no good fortune. In both cases, the outcome depends on the person and not on the well; the well merely responds accordingly.
Furthermore, a hexagram does not exist as a hexagram in itself; it comes into being only after the six lines are combined. A line also does not exist as a line in itself;
it comes into being only after a single hexagram is divided. Thus, when the six lines are combined to form a hexagram, the mind is present while the emotions are absent.
When a single hexagram is divided into six lines, the emotions are present while the mind is absent. Now, do the emotions truly possess emotion?
The mind possesses its fruits; indeed, it does. However, when responding to objects with entanglement, it is called "emotion" (*qing*);

when responding to objects without entanglement, it is called "mind" (*xin*). Thus, emotion and mind are merely names. As for their reality, they depend entirely upon the person. Therefore it is said:
"It circulates through the six voids, moving up and down without constancy. That which is not constant is emotion; the "six voids" are—

This is the *xiáo* (line). The *xiáo* is a void position. That there is sudden good fortune or sudden misfortune is entirely due to the influence of emotional states. Thus it is said: "Good fortune and misfortune shift according to emotion.
If the single mind does not arise and the six voids do not roam, then one will be burdened by responding to external objects;

this would be utterly different from one who is free from such burdens. When one is complete [in this state], it is called a *guā* (hexagram). In a *guā*, there is no self, and the numinous resides therein. In a *xiáo*, however, there is a self.
Yet the ignorant dwell therein; the mind, moreover, dwells within the hexagrams and their lines. Thus, it can unify emotion and nature. "Unify" means to penetrate.
For one who skillfully employs the mind, emotions are penetrated and yet not existent; nature is penetrated and yet not non-existent.
This is why Laozi and Pang said: "I only wish to empty all that exists; by all means, do not reify what does not exist. There is indeed a profound reason for this.
"Stopping at the back so as not to perceive one's own body; walking in the courtyard yet not seeing the person"—these fourteen characters originally convey but a single meaning.
For it is because one has a body that one has a self; it is because of mutual dependence that the body has others.
When the body is no longer perceived, who is there to be called "I"? When the self is no longer a self, who is there to see another? Therefore, I say: these ten... [characters].
These four characters share a single meaning.
I understand the four lines of the hexagram Xian: if one responds with a deliberate mind, it will ultimately not be particularly brilliant or great.

If one listens to Heaven without a mind of one's own, then even that which has not yet attained radiance will become radiant. Alas! As soon as I give rise to a mind, my nature transforms into emotion.
Nature is without self and is spiritual; therefore, it can penetrate the emotions of the world. When emotions are penetrated, there is no undertaking that is not auspicious.
When they are not penetrated, there is a sense of self and stagnation; thus, when used to plan affairs, even what was auspicious turns into misfortune.
One day, the attendant Wen asked me about the meaning of the hexagram Xian-gen (咸艮). I took my staff and jabbed him in the foot; he let out a cry of pain.
I questioned him, saying, "Do you understand the meaning of Xian-gen? He replied, "I do not know. I then showed it to him again.
He said: "Do you understand? If you are not empty, then even if you respond, it will not be appropriate. If you do not bring [the mind] to rest, then even if you respond, you will not know [it].
It is only through resting that emptiness is supported; therefore, one's responses are inexhaustible. It is only through emptiness that stillness is supported; therefore, wisdom is tireless.
What is called 'universal stillness' (xian-gen) resides in daily life; it does not reside in speech or written words."
Zhijian said: "When the single mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault. Lushan said:

"If even a single atom stirs into the realm of movement, it creates the momentum of this crumbling mountain. I have long heard these words from the two elders, yet until now I never fully understood them.

However, upon reading the *Book of Changes* (Yijing) and reaching the Jian hexagram, I finally understood the words of the two elders without any doubt. This is because the hexagrams embody nature (*xing*), while the lines (*yao*) embody...
As for the sentiment: "If the one mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault," this is the meaning of the hexagram.
"If even a single subtle movement involves motion and stillness, it forms the momentum of a crumbling mountain"—this is the meaning of the individual lines (*xiāo*).

Generally speaking, when the one mind does not arise, there is no ground for good or ill fortune; once a single subtle movement involves motion, good and ill fortune arise. Thus, regarding the six lines of *Jiàn*, a single subtle [movement]...

Before one has yet entered [the path], the positions exist but the persons do not. Once there is even the slightest movement toward involvement, then both these positions and these persons come into being.
Li Zhangzhe of the Tang dynasty utilized the six lines of the *Jian* hexagram to embody the meaning of the progressive advancement through the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).
Indeed, from the first to the tenth of the ten faiths, all involve hearing the Dharma and attaining realization through a mind of arising and ceasing; it is by means of this realization that...

The initial stage of being stained still belongs to the realm of arising and ceasing; one has not yet entered the state of non-arising and non-ceasing. Upon reaching the first dwelling (the first bhūmi), one then partially attains non-arising and non-ceasing.

While reading the *Appended Statements* of the *Book of Changes*, I reached the passage: "In heaven, images are formed; on earth, forms are shaped; change and transformation manifest. This is the state of awakening.
The elephant and its form are both like temporary shelters found everywhere, yet they are not the "everywhere-ness" that manifests as elephants and forms.

If one were to attain this "everywhere-ness" that manifests as elephants and forms, then the manifestation of elephants and forms would be no more than the bending and extending of a single finger. Alas!
When gold has not yet been melted, it is merely a solid lump; when it has been melted, it is merely a liquid fusion.
Yet, if one seeks liquidity outside the lump, or seeks solidity outside the liquid, I know that even the divine and the sagely would be unable to do anything about it.
As I examined the *Yi* until reaching the hexagram Tai, I could not help but close the book and sigh deeply for a long time.
Now, during the times of Da Zhuang and Guai, the petty men were increasingly declining while the superior men were increasingly flourishing. Yet, the Sage alone found peace in Tai;
he did so because he considered that the petty men of the world could not be completely eliminated, and that one must not necessarily seek to oppress and drive them out.
If they are driven to exhaustion with no place to turn, their condition will inevitably lead to strife. Once there is strife, the outcome of victory or defeat remains undecided.

It would be better instead for the superior man alone to abide in tranquility and security, allowing him to constantly occupy the center and govern the destiny of affairs, while the petty man remains outside yet has a place to be settled.
Only then will the perils facing the superior man have no way to arise. Alas! The Sage—

This vision is far-reaching indeed. The gentlemen of later ages do not embody the intent of the Sage; as soon as they obtain a position of power, they invariably seek to drive out all petty men in order to fully indulge their own ambitions.
Yet they fail to realize that gentlemen and petty men, the heterodox and the orthodox, are fundamentally different—indeed, as distinct as heaven and abyss.
Nevertheless, they both share Heaven and Earth as their parents. As for Heaven and Earth toward their children, whether they be worthy or not...

How could Xiao not know this himself? He knows it, yet he tolerates him; for once he has brought him to life, to cast him out because of his unworthiness would be something even the hearts of parents cannot bear.
One should simply ensure that the worthy govern the destiny of others, while the unworthy obey their commands;
thus, the superior person does not lose the measure of embracing the vast, while the petty person...

Thus, they are also able to fulfill their natural inclinations. If one were determined to expel all petty men and employ only superior men, even if a sage were to be reborn, he could not carry such a policy into practice.
To know that it cannot be carried out and yet to force its implementation is to call one a person who rebels against Heaven.
If such a person were to obtain power and act according to their will, the vital energy (*yuanqi*) of the state would not fail to suffer great decline.
It is impossible that the common people should not suffer its bitter poison.
Inscription for the Stele Erected for the Mahā-vīra Hall at Renwang Temple in Fancheng.
I have heard that the Prajñā of the Western Regions possesses a single name that encompasses manifold meanings; yet in the Middle Kingdom, there is no single name with such multiple meanings.
For the sake of translation, the Sanskrit term was retained while the Chinese characters were abbreviated. Prajñā comprises both the lettered (textual) and the contemplative (insight).

There is the true mark (dharmatā). Third, although names may be identical, their referents differ; if one attains the reality, how could names possibly cause confusion? Furthermore, there are eight sections of Prajñāpāramitā;
among them, only the *Ratnarāśi* (or *Benevolent Kings’ Prajñā*) was first requested from Śākyamuni Tathāgata by King Prasenajit as a method for protecting the state and blessing the people.
King Prasenajit is also named Candraprabha (Moonlight); the sūtra requested by Candraprabha comprises eight [sections] in total.
It consists of over a thousand words, each of which is rooted in the Five Patiences (*pañca-kṣānti*).
The establishment of these Five Patiences is such that for any state or household, if they do not regard them as their vanguard, the seven great portents will arise one after another.

If these portents arise and they do not employ the Five Patiences to ward them off, then the altars of the land and grain (*shèjì*) will perish. Furthermore, in Sanskrit it is called *prajñā*, which here is translated as "wisdom" (*huì*). Indeed...
Since all inauspicious things arise from ignorance, a ruler who is ignorant loses his ministers; a minister who is ignorant is disloyal;
a father who is ignorant is not compassionate; and a son who is ignorant is unfilial. Jie, Zhou, You, and Li were the ultimate examples of ignorance.
Yao, Shun, Yi, and Hui were the foremost of wisdom. [The Temple of] the Benevolent King at Fancheng, Xiangyang Prefecture.

The temple was originally constructed during the Jingding era of the Song dynasty. It fell into ruin during the present dynasty, yet the three princes of Chu, Tang, and Xiang all remarked that there must be a specific significance for the temple to be named after the Benevolent Kings (Renwang).
Subsequently, they consulted eminent monks and scholars, who informed them that the name was derived from the scriptures.
Thereupon, they united their efforts to rebuild it. Coinciding with the ascension of the Shizong Emperor to the throne at the Han River, the name was changed to Renhuang (Benevolent Sovereign).
In the *Xinmao* year of the Wanli era, impurities befouled the site, and the Fire Dragon, enraged, bathed it in flames, reducing the halls and corridors to ashes.
Thereupon, the governors of the three provinces of Chu, Tang, and Xiang, considering that this temple had been established by our former kings, restored and rebuilt it together.
Alas! King Prasenajit was the sovereign of the Five Indias, yet he did not inquire after the supramundane Dharma.
He then inquired about the worldly dharmas that serve as the means for protecting the state and blessing the people.

If one has not planted the roots of goodness in former lives and possesses great wisdom, how could one take the worldly dharmas and thereby clarify the supramundane dharma? That the sutra is titled "The Benevolent Kings" is surely to honor their virtue.
Furthermore, the three kings—Chu, Tang, and Xiang—likewise all planted the roots of goodness in former lives and succeeded to the legacy of King Moonlight.
That the world treats this as a golden fortress—how could this be a mere coincidence? When the hall was completed, the Chan monk Master Qian came to pay his respects and asked me:
"It was a misfortune that the temple was destroyed by fire, yet it was fortunate that the successive magistrates of Chu, Tang, and Xiang did not neglect the will of their ancestors."
Furthermore, as we are rebuilding together, I venture to beg for a word from the Master to illuminate the virtues of the three former abbots.

I replied: "I am but a person of humble status and insignificant words; how could I dare to undertake this? Moreover, you are a man of Chu; it is as if you were carrying a cloth drum to the Gate of Thunder.

The Master remained somber for a long while, then led the abbot and the assembly to inquire again, saying: "In recording the history of a temple’s construction and restoration, there is nothing that should not be included."
As for a person: if one were to examine names and scrutinize reality to elucidate the profound purport of Prajñā, I fear that without the Master’s pen, it would not be fully realized.
I replied, "So be it. Now, there is no dharma outside the mind; the nature of words is detached [from reality]. Since the nature of words is detached, contemplation is subtle and profound.
Since contemplation is subtle and profound, that which is called "attaining accord without thought"—is this not the true mark (dharmatā)? What else could it be?
How great is Prajñā! A single name with manifold meanings. Confucius attained it and thereby governed the Six Classics and composed the *Chunqiu*.

Laozi attained it and the two chapters were produced. Mencius attained it and established his treatises. Wang Tong attained it and composed his own classics. Li Ao attained it and authored the *Fuxing shu*.
Xinxin attained it and proclaimed the teaching of "Innate Knowledge. Nevertheless, there is the True [Prajñā].
Prajñā. There is that which resembles prajñā, but true prajñā realizes that form is emptiness and realizes that emptiness is form.
Therefore, one does not perish in withered desolation, nor does one drift upon the waves of emotion. One practices through thorough understanding; thus, there is nothing to practice.
Because there is nothing to practice, when confronted by the impact of favorable or adverse conditions, habitual defilements are extinguished, yet I have nothing to practice.

It is like *prajñā* [semblance-wisdom], yet one understands it without refining it; neglecting cultivation to indulge one's views, so that when danger and doubt suddenly converge, understanding is lost and spirit is forfeited.
External circumstances seize the consciousness and emotions, leading to failure and the spreading of disgrace, leaving one to be laughed at for a thousand ages.
This is the fault of indulging in semblance-*prajñā*. Whether lay or monastic, if anyone has the aspiration for *prajñā*, provided they do not...

To be able to refine the ultimate meaning and enter the divine so as to achieve practical application is not only to betray the Holy One Kāśyapa, but truly to betray King Prasenajit, as well as the kings of Chu, Tang, and Xiang, who for generations established temples like impregnable fortresses. The inscription reads:

"The temple is named Renwang (Benevolent Kings); its origin lies with Candraprabha. With the establishment of the five stages of patience, all inauspiciousness is eliminated. From west to east, the Dharma..."
Its fame spread throughout China. In Fancheng, Xiangyang, there was a Chan monastery; it was first established during the Jingding era of the Song dynasty.

Having endured for a long time, three kings supported it when it was tottering, and successive descendants protected it so that its defenses became as firm as gold and moats. When the dragon ascended upon the Han River, the Benevolent Emperor changed its name.
Under the sky of Yao and the sun of the Buddha, its radiance shall shine for ten thousand ages. The single term "Prajñā" encompasses many meanings; let us examine them.

It is named "Examination of Reality. Its subtlety is ineffable. It is secretly present within you; yet to me, it appears coarse. Free from "self" and "what belongs to self," the verdant bamboos are True Suchness (*tathatā*).
When the Fire Dragon bathes them, the halls and pavilions turn to flying ash. The three kings built them together; they are the legacy of the Persians.
I pray that we, clad in the square robes of the Dharma, may keep the roots of our precepts pure. May the earth produce spiritual sprouts, and may spirits and deities offer their protection. *Brahma*.

The lands are firm and secure; morning and evening we pray for the Sage that his reign may endure as long as earth and heaven. May the fields of Shun bear fine fruit and the Bodhi-tree blossom with fragrance.

May the mundane and supramundane dharmas illuminate the eight reaches of the universe. May all who possess a mind suddenly forget their sense-bases and objects. As the spiritual flame blazes intensely, may we together penetrate the true and eternal.
Inscription for the Footstool (With Preface):
Now, the Great Way is without delusion and thus has no dreams. Dreams do not arise independently; they take delusion as their medium. To trace back the current and exhaust the source.

He thoroughly understands both the root and the branches; he follows the Way and does not turn back. Whether in abundance or in want, he remains steadfast. Therefore, the skillful observer possesses the whole world yet receives nothing;

though as poor as a starving beggar, he has more than enough. Thus, the petty man ceases his attempts to pry into the affairs of the superior, and the gentleman is free from the blemish of excessive seeking.
He establishes the Three Powers in this final age and brings forth great enlightenment amidst the layered obscurities.
Twilight. Those who emerge are like fish leaping into the spring sea; those who remain are like beasts aged in the mountain clouds. Rites and music are employed without conscious awareness;
daily activities proceed while one forgets their illumination. The public is forgotten by the private, and the private is forgotten by the public.

When public and private are mutually forgotten, it is as if the mind forgets the body. One does not perceive excess; who then awaits deficiency? From deficiency arises sufficiency; when sufficiency forgets deficiency, all is complete.

Only then can one contemplate sufficiency. Contemplating the sufficiency of the expanse, it fills the ten voids and is ever content; the expanse manifests the myriad existents yet is ever non-existent.
The earth floats supported by space; the water follows heaven wherever it reaches. The four seasons grant and take away; in a single thought, there is both female and male.
Flowers flourish in the gardens; grasses perfume the hills and mounds. Fish and birds move forward and retreat; those who find this state in sitting or reclining attain freedom in every head.
Those who lose it find themselves at odds everywhere. Black and yellow exhaust the power of their eyes;
likes and dislikes shake the light of their minds. They long for contentment yet cannot find it; contentment becomes the master of their desires. They long for the open hall, yet cannot...

The *xuān* (the incense burner). The *xuān* is my master; name and reality are difficult to deceive, yet the roots and objects are easily obscured. Thus, coming and going are impermanent, and guest and host are used interchangeably.
The coarse or the subtle depends on the person; the *xuān* serves merely as the vanguard. The inscription says:
When not a single thought arises, all sensory objects are without dependence; the radiance is boundless—how could it need to be bought with money?

When the seven emotions blaze forth, they obscure the original heaven. Like smoke and clouds arising and vanishing, one takes horses for ships, carrying all manner of inversions; how can one who is crazed and intoxicated ever attain clarity?

The objects of sound are manifold; one loses track of the dawn upon the pillow. Sound and form have no treasury, for the treasury consists only of the ears and eyes. The ears and eyes have no master, and the master is lacking.
Only for the one who is without self do all wonders cluster together; such a person is universally good toward all, standing alone and free from desire.
Inscription for the Foot-stand (with Preface):
I, a fool, have read the "Discourse on Overcoming Qin" (*Guo Qin Lun*). Therein I learned that Jia Yi advanced and withdrew heroes and applied the critique of "feminine" and "masculine" strength;
his intent was focused solely upon Qin, while he regarded all others as merely relying upon numerical calculations. Judging from this, Qin has already passed away [as a model]. Yet, it is not...

Contentment is paramount. As for such things as whipping up mountains or filling the sea in the hope of attaining longevity—if even the altars of the state (sheji) cannot be preserved for one’s descendants, how much less can anything else?
Yet, at Bo Lang, you failed to awaken to the significance of the escaping hammer.

Consequently, the likes of Chen Sheng and Wu Guang rose up with their staves, leaving the Qin dynasty in a state of ruin and disorder. Today, you, O Younger Master Lin, dwell here amidst the earthen steps and thatched roofs.

Wearing coarse clothing and eating simple food, he felt neither joy when leaving nor sorrow when staying. He refined his emotions through the wind and moon and cultivated his nature through poetry and the classics.
Within the four continents and beneath the six heavens, compared to what the Qin state boasted, [the latter] was but a grain of wild rice in the imperial granary.
Among the six heavens, there is a heaven called Tuṣita; this means "Contentment. Alas!
Ah! If one knows contentment, even a thatched cottage with earthen steps surpasses a palace of jade and golden chambers.
If one lacks contentment, though dwelling atop the Nine Heavens, it is as if one were in a ditch or ravine. Nevertheless, if there is a body but no mind, who would perceive honor or disgrace?
If there is a mind but no body, who would experience suffering or joy? Body and mind—these two are but a single retribution.
A traveler’s lodging: to claim it as one's own possession is to ensure that no affliction will fail to arrive.

If this is so, then even body and mind are not "mine"—this is the beginning of contentment; how much more so for that which lies beyond body and mind? Thus was it with the son of the ancient Yan family.

To cast aside the physical form and set aside the clever intellect is to accord with the Great Sameness (*Mahāsamatā*). In this Great Sameness, neither heaven and earth are "great," nor are motes of dust and a single hair "small.
Speaking from this perspective, "contentment" is named only in relation to "insatiability";
if there were no insatiability, then contentment would likewise be nothing more than a mere hair. Master Yunmen had the phrase that "encases and covers heaven and earth" and "severs all streams."
The sentence of flowing water; the sentence of following the waves and riding the currents; three sentences in one sentence—gain and loss depend on the person.
This is further sufficient evidence for [Master] Xuan’s inscription, which says:
Three phrases in one sentence: the person of great realization knows this for themselves. With a tongue that could lift up a carriage, his influence spreads like the wind and flows like water.
*The Inscription for the Chamber of the Qilin* (with preface):
The dragon is the sovereign among scaly creatures; the tiger is the hegemon among the thousand peaks; the lion is the king of all beasts. He roars...
Its roar shakes the multitude until their skulls split open; the phoenix flies and cries, and feathered creatures follow like clouds.

The nature of the qilin is not to accept fetters; benevolent and free from desire, it moves freely east and west. Freedom from desire approaches the quality of strength; benevolence approaches the quality of compassion.

Only when both strength and compassion are present are the principles of Heaven and Earth complete. By employing the nine and employing the six, one enters and exits with sovereign ease; thus is the Qilin.
When the qilin appears, a sage is born; when the qilin dies, the sage grieves. Alas! To be firm yet to save with compassion, to be majestic yet not fierce;
to be compassionate yet to overcome with firmness, to be broadminded yet not excessive—when these two qualities are not deficient, the virtue of the sage is perfected.

The sage was once but a man, yet through clarity, courage, and self-strengthening, he remained unbent despite a thousand humiliations, ultimately transcending the ordinary. Thus he dwells among the scaled creatures.

When a dragon dwells among feathers, it becomes a *huáng*; when it dwells among fur, its appearance changes. Thus, its conduct and concealment differ according to circumstance. Now, you have named your son’s chamber after the *qínlín* (unicorn).

You should reflect that at the beginning of human life, one is but a common, childish youth; mired in the obscurity of ignorance (*tún-méng*), one has not yet attained clarity. Yet, in a single moment, one may be enlightened to what is correct, and the numinous aperture shall radiate light.

By thus illuminating one's own inherent virtue, one realizes Buddhahood within the very mind. Though words may vary in their similarities and differences, the underlying meaning has neither center nor periphery. This is excellent.

When one contemplates, there is no scripture that does not pass through; when one does not contemplate, there is no scripture that is not a book. Books record names and surnames, while scriptures are eternally unchanging.

That which changes undergoes extinction; that which does not change is not born. In this unborn mind, neither annihilation nor permanence can invade. In the myriad crafts and arts, profundity is practiced at every turn.
As Lao Pang said: "In daily life there is nothing distinct; it is only I who happen to be in harmony."
When they are in harmony, even Buddhas and demons are brought into service; how much more so those others? The inscription says:
The dragon and the tiger each have their domain in water and on land; the lion and the qilin each follow their own path; the phoenix flies and sings.
Feathered creatures produce light; the qilin is born in the wilds. These auspicious omens accompany the sage-kings; such is the case with all things. Humans must exert themselves through self-effort.

Between the gentleman and the petty man, there is originally no fixed seed. Emotion and reason contend with one another; victory and defeat are as distinct as black and white. Thus it is on the island of Laṅkā.
On the island of the Brahma-river, the seagull pavilion soars into the void; its windows swallow the moon at dawn. This chamber bears the name "Qilin"; let this humble youth not be alarmed.
Buddhas and demons are held within one's grasp; govern the emotions with principle.
Inscription on the Spring of Buddha-Wisdom:

The wisdom of the Buddha is profound and vast; it can extinguish the heat of affliction. When one drinks from it, it enters through the eyes; yet a single stirring of thought leaves one withered and parched.

Beneath the azure stone, at the edge of the cloud-forest, its original state is serene and still—this can be realized through spiritual communion. To see the reflection and know the source: I alone am deluded by inversion.
Both [the worldly and the transcendental] exist, yet neither achieves ultimate efficacy;
there is no movement that does not accord with the Way. Epitaph for the Śrāmaṇera Peng (with Preface):
When Pengzi was young, he was a scholar. He held his brush and practiced the arts of the examination candidates, until he turned to the study of ancient prose, poetry, and rhapsody.

He refined his mastery of the arts of *yīng-yáng* (yin-yang) and the *chèn-wěi* (astrological and esoteric commentaries), reaching the depths of their mysteries. Furthermore, due to the manifestation of his past habitual tendencies, he came to know how to take refuge in and revere the Great Dharma.
Subsequently, while traveling and studying in the capital of Yan, he was moved by profound reflections upon the events he encountered; he thus resolved to undergo tonsure and ordination.

With his emaciated frame standing out in stark relief and suffering from a chronic cough, he braved the deep snow and showed no fear of the bitter cold as he ascended Mount Qingliang through thick clouds.
On the full moon day of the eleventh month in the Ximmab year of the Wanli era, he visited the Daoist at Miaode Hermitage and was thus able to fulfill his initial vow.
On the tenth day of the fourth month the following year, he passed away suddenly. Alas!
His secular age was thirty-two years, and his monastic seniority was one hundred and forty-five days. The Daoist lamented for Peng, saying that while his resolve was abundant, his life was short.
It was not permanent; thus, I have specially inscribed this epitaph. The inscription says:
Though his aspirations were not yet fulfilled, life and death underwent their change. His resolute single thought—once a vow is made, it must be accomplished. From antiquity to the present day.

How can day and night be distinguished? The distinction between day and night is merely the difference of a finger’s breadth. Between the buttocks and the spine, there is fundamentally no center or periphery;
yet when seeking their two ends, one takes yellow for black. Pengzi understood this and did not cling to the provisional as real; he took his vow as the hub.

The Great Wheel of Dharma was turned; his bones were interred at Jiafu. At the Chicken Garden (Kukkutārāma), the blossoms vied for beauty. Between the ancient Buddha and the new patriarch, who is to the left and who to the right?
If the Peng-bird possesses a spiritual essence, may it swiftly manifest its discernment here. May the three periods of time coincide, universally vibrating with pure and sublime sounds.
Epitaph for the Founder of Zifu Temple in Wanping County, Chan Master Shouxin Duan (with Preface) The Master’s name was Zhenduan;
his courtesy name was Shouxin. His clan was Chen, and his ancestral home was originally in Changzhi County, Luan’an Prefecture, Shanxi.

From the time of his birth, many auspicious omens appeared, causing the neighbors to marvel at him in astonishment. In his youth, he did not enjoy playing with toys; his character and physical bearing were preeminent among his peers. At the age of... [text continues]
12. He resided at Hongfu Monastery in Licheng County. Master Rui was his preceptor, under whom he received his formal training.
After a short time, however, he left and traveled to Mount Fowu and paid homage at Potalaka.

Subsequently, he went to Mount Wutai in Daizhou to visit Chan Master Erhu, who recognized his potential upon first meeting him and accepted him as a dharma heir. When he returned to his former [home],...
Mount [Name]. Upon hearing of him, the Prince of Shen held him in high esteem and invited him to reside at Zifu Chan Monastery, providing him with most diligent support.

One day, the Master said: "A man of great character, if he does not leave the household life, should serve as a minister of benevolence and righteousness to assist an enlightened sovereign, so that his grace flows far and wide.
If he leaves the household life, he should penetrate the depths of the religious teachings and reach the very source of the Dharma, propagating the legacy of the Buddhas and Patriarchs."
The Way enables ordinary people of this broad world to ascend to the state of sainthood with a mere snap of the fingers, thereby repaying the Buddha’s kindness;
only then would one not feel ashamed of being a man. Reflecting upon myself, I find that between these two [goals], I possess nothing at all.

Although the King of Shen was diligent and generous, remaining confined to a single region prevented me from widely providing food for those arriving from afar; ultimately, this was not my humble aspiration. Thereupon, I abandoned him once more and came to Yan.
In Shan County, Wanping, east of Lugou Bridge, he constructed a thatched hut with rafters gathered from the wild as a place for travelers from all quarters to rest their shoulders.
He also inscribed the name "Zifu" (Funding of Merit) upon it to show that he did not forget the Prince of Shen.
To the southwest of Zifu, the Master dug a large well and installed six square stone conduits, making this vow: "Regardless of whether one is monastic or lay, foolish or wise—"
Furthermore, all sentient beings who possess consciousness—whether they have drunk a drop of my water or eaten a grain of my rice—shall be born together in the land of Amitābha Buddha.
There, the Awakened One of Immeasurable Life shall personally bestow upon them the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), and they shall ascend to the stage of non-retrogression.

Nevertheless, because the Master’s nature was stern and cold, he did not delight in worldly honors; even when the powerful and noble came to his door, he would not deign to bend. Thus, from such-and-such a year...
In a certain year, donors became scarce and the monastic community fell into desolation.

The Master personally embraced this withered austerity, yet he welcomed those who came from afar with joy, never showing even the slightest sign of weariness. When some could not bear his distress, the Master said, "I simply wish to practice these gāthās;
through diligent toil and detachment, I shall not seek worldly acclaim. This is my lot, so why should I harbor resentment? Princess Wang Gong also heard of this.
The Emperor respected him and dispatched an imperial eunuch to replace his thatched roof and wooden rafters with gold and green-glazed tiles.

Just as the Master was fulfilling his aspirations by planting the banner of merit to pray for the longevity of the Sage Emperor and to invoke blessings for all living beings, in the twelfth month of winter in the twentieth year of the Wanli era, he told his disciples: "I shall depart tomorrow."
"Having accumulated years of diligent labor, you patrons have enabled me to accomplish this gateway of practice. After I depart, you all must unite your minds to maintain the monastery;
as long as there is no lack of food and gruel for those who come, I shall be as if still alive even after my death. When the appointed time arrived, he indeed passed away while sitting upright.
All the donors and faithful said that the Master had foreknown that his time had come, and they turned toward him with redoubled devotion. Thus the Master was born [into this world].
He passed away on a certain day of the [blank] month in the second year of the Jiajing era. He died on the [blank] day of the twelfth month in the twentieth year of the Wanli era.
His monastic seniority was fifty-seven years; his secular lifespan was seventy-three. Following the Indian Dharma, his disciples cremated his physical remains.
His bones were enshrined in a stupa on South Hill. The Daoist Daguān conferred upon the Master the posthumous title of Pǔ... (e.g., Pǔhuá).
Compassion. His stupa was named Yuanguang (Vow-Light). Alas! There is nothing more formidable than fortune and calamity, nor death and life;
yet Master Duan was not disturbed by them. He transcended and shed them all, such that great afflictions could neither detain nor hinder him.

Even those so-called heroes of antiquity who, wielding benevolence and righteousness, assisted sovereigns to establish great achievements and leave their fragrance for a hundred generations—when it came to facing [death]...
At the moment of death and rebirth, his body was so limp and cold that he became a laughingstock to the world.
Viewed from this perspective, was Master Duan not indeed a man of the Great Way? The inscription says:
All who possess consciousness are driven by desire; they arise because of desire and depart because of desire. Only the Master differs from this:
his coming and going are mounted upon vows, and his toil through birth and death is not for the sake of trading in desire. From youth until old age, he grows ever more vigorous as he ages.

Providing relief to all, from beginning to end without distinction, he erected a stupa on the southern ridge for the sake of all quarters: to provide food for the living and to enshrine the bones of the deceased.
Though Mount Yan may be worn away, his vow shall never end; may the monks' meals never cease, even at the moment of death.

My descendants cherish this memory and strive with all their might to sustain it. Like the waters of the Lugou River, which flow on long and without ceasing, my lord’s eldest progeny—whose mother was Lady Gongfei—heard of the Master’s virtuous reputation and took refuge in him with profound faith. If the Master possesses spiritual power, may he protect this noble donation.
May blessings and longevity be boundless; may ten thousand generations be established in peace. May this serve as a golden bulwark for the Buddha, with vast monasteries constructed throughout.

May the great disciples (nāgas and elephants) tread upon it, and may the light of the sun and moon shine ever more brightly. The heart of this rustic man is shallow and not deep; he has laid bare his innermost red core, and may the spirits and deities bear witness.
This inscription is engraved upon a firm stone. Heaven and earth share the same vital pulse. While forms undergo change and succession, the mind is without past or present.
Regarding the Bodhisattva of Great Compassion with many arms and eyes:

the world has harbored doubts about this Bodhisattva of Great Compassion. Seeing his numerous arms and eyes, people were struck with mutual astonishment; this was surely because they failed to examine the matter through reason.

If one observes this superficially through emotion, yet examines it with reason, then every person will be so preoccupied with their own self-assurance that they will have no leisure for doubt—how much less would they doubt the Great Compassionate One?
Consider my own single body: its eighty-four thousand pores are densely arrayed like a forest;
six feet in height is by no means narrow. When these pores are fully manifest, not even a single body can remain within them, yet a single body appears therein.
When [the light] moves forward, all the pores become hidden; as hiddenness and manifestation alternate, the one and the many remain distinct and clear.
At this very moment, is there not something that cannot be encompassed or bound by the numbers of "one" and "many"?
Like a circular wheel without end, responding to the myriad things infinitely—this Great Compassion belongs solely to [the Buddha], while I alone am without it. This...
This is emotion; it is not principle. Therefore, when responding with principle to the eyes, one can see through to that which precedes even the Lord of Images (*xiàngdì*).
When responding with principle to the ears, one can hear through to the sounds of mosquitoes and gnats beyond the eight wildernesses.
I often sit in stillness, and suddenly body and mind are both cast away; my ears and eyes become boundless, and all emotions of distance and proximity vanish.

Transformation. Once the dream of antiquity and the present has been shattered, one begins to find it strange that the arms and eyes of the Great Compassionate One are so few, yet people of the world still suspect them to be many—is this not delusion?
Nevertheless, people of the south do not believe in a tent for a thousand men, while people of the north do not believe in a boat of ten-thousand-hu capacity;
this is because they trust their own feelings rather than reason. Little do they realize the calamity [of such ignorance].

Fortune and misfortune, life and death, the vastness or narrowness of self and others, the succession of past and present, and the clarity or turbidity, the floating or sinking—all these exist through emotion (*qing*) but do not exist in principle (*li*).
If one can use principle to resolve emotion, then one may draw near examples from within oneself and distant examples from the external world.

"All are my own arms and eyes. If this is so, then in uplifting the four modes of birth and in having wisdom encompass all that exists, these matters were from the beginning not within the reach of mere valor or clarity alone. The inscription says:
The original single luminous intelligence briefly responds to the six faculties; responding without returning, it looks toward the flow [of phenomena] while losing sight of the source.

The Bodhisattva of Great Compassion taught me to contemplate the Ear-Organ (śrotra), not by means of hearing with the ears, but by seeing with the eyes through profound dhyāna. This profound dhyāna is unfathomable; the traces of both the "one" and the "six" are laid bare.

The embroidered straw dogs have already been displayed; do not begrudge them. One becomes the immeasurable, and the immeasurable becomes one. Phenomena and principle are neither established nor completed.

Compassion extends to all things, manifesting according to karma. My essence is fundamentally ordinary and constant; through the thirty-two transformations, light is emitted throughout the dust-motes and lands.
If one emerges with a mind, the Bodhisattva falls ill with madness. The Patriarch came from the East; Mei-shan was a man of rare talent.

The Record of the Hall of Great Compassion—gathering it together and letting it loose, rolling it up and unrolling it at will, the principle is thoroughly penetrating and unimpeded. Amidst the *guāngláng* groves, Elder Gao lets his ease run free.

Before bears, cubs, tigers, and leopards, he regarded them as his peers; they would enter in anger and depart in amusement, never once startled or alarmed. Having lived after Master Gong, I have come to know his *samādhi*.
From the Zen elder, I have learned that his speech was like brocade and embroidery, resplendent as spring flowers; the beauty of spring flaunts its myriad forms.
Those who do not observe skillfully seek spring by looking for its flowers; yet spring cannot be found there. They weep at the crossroads until their robes are damp with tears.
Texts and language are the radiance of the Way—why must they be rejected before one can claim to be unerring?

The Inscription on the Shao Stones: When the gaze is upright, the spirit coalesces. A cowherd was out in the fields when Confucius saw him; he realized that this man had heard the *Shao* music. Alarmed, he spurred his horse from behind, but by the time he arrived, the music had fallen into decay.
It was not heard with the ears; its resonance was silent and vast. From the beginning, there is neither ancient nor modern; how could there be near or far?
This is the heart of Shishun; its clouds join in lofty heights.

Ding Nan-yu’s "Jielü" reveals the essence of the primordial chaos (*hundun*), the very bone of Changxi. Nan-yu obtained it, yet Xiangwang could not recognize it; the Mysterious Pond was divinely revealed.

As the dragon soars through the colored brush, in the space of a single snap of the fingers, all Buddhas emerge like surging clouds. Adorning the Pure Land, they permeate and transform all sentient beings;
those who see or hear them attain liberation in that very place. Who compressed the great earth to form this single fragment of jade, encompassing the ten voids?
Manifesting all manner of wonders, he takes Mount Sumeru as his tongue; its praises could not be fully exhausted. His mouth is the great void, swallowing everything whole without emitting a sound.
The sons of the Ding family treasure one another like precious gems, regarding them as irreplaceable as the pupils of their own eyes.
Among these, the "Inscription on the Song-End Inkstone by Fu" states:
From heaven to man, from man to heaven; the color of the Great Antiquity, within which lies a dark spring. Clouds emerge therefrom without end.
Fish and dragons may sleep here; if one attains this, one’s transformation will be as firm as the eternal.
Inscribed upon the Ox-Lying Inkstone:
the mountain streams are inexhaustible, the spring grasses abound. Untroubled by hunger or thirst, one sleeps with a blissful transcendence. With Maoying as my whip, I ride forth.

A single cry sends a shudder through him; his neck and tail bend and stretch, his hooves and horns become supple or firm. Alas! The back of a crane is light and precarious, the back of a dragon is slippery;
returning home, the back of an ox is as stable as a boat.
Inscription for the Fuquan Inkstone:
Cultivating sincerity establishes it; faith penetrates metal and stone. When the monk’s staff was planted, the spring gushed forth; when he lay upon the ice, the carp emerged.
Its utility knows neither sage nor commoner; its names range from black to white. Its sweet and clear flavor is extraordinary—it is the very lifeblood of Master Fu.
The Inscription for the Gourd: It contains the emptiness of the ten directions yet does not become large; it holds the waters of the four oceans yet cannot be filled to overflowing.
It is a supreme vessel for quenching thirst and a wondrous implement for supplementing hunger. Even its remaining drops and leftover grains can satisfy dragons, snakes, tigers, and leopards.
The leopard is the worthy companion of the bowl. It alone stands tall in the high, clear, and sunny expanse of the hermitage’s inscription;

choosing this site for its dwelling, such was the auspicious omen. The wind passes through the sparse forest, and the waves of incense fragrance resound clearly. Having finished the meal, there is nothing more to do.
Reading the scriptures of India, I occasionally attained their profound meaning; body and world were entirely forgotten, and my original nature was revealed like the moonlight in a cloudless sky.
Strolling through the courtyard, my hempen robes felt cool and refreshing. The heat and vexation of the city felt like ten winters in a single hour.
Kings and lords seemed but a dream—how can they compare to this carefree wandering in my state of leisure?
Inscription for the Bamboo Gourd:
As for this object—firm yet possessed of joints, empty yet capable of containing; it elegantly divides the moon by the streamside, and idly hangs from the pines atop the crags.
May we grow old together, amidst ten thousand valleys and a thousand peaks.
Inscription for the Cloud-Canopy Hat (original text missing):
The hat upon one’s head, people do not recognize it; It is like a fragment of cloud covering the tips of pine branches. When the night crane returns, its nest can no longer be found.
Regarding Wubasheng’s Biography:
Wubasheng himself said that he was born at Qingcaotan (Green Grass Beach). This beach is the Songling of Gusu, which is today’s Wujiang.
I have associated with Wubasheng for a very long time; whenever there were moments when his movements and his state of withdrawal from the world were overlooked, I observed them.
In the midst of his voice, smiles, and countenance, as well as his habitual tendencies and movements, if one observes him closely, he seems not to be a man of Qingcao Beach.
This is because his nature is naturally transcendent and unrestrained; he cannot endure worldly affairs and is entirely unconstrained by the rules of conventional custom.
I once offered him counsel, to which Wuba replied with a laugh, saying: "Why do you not examine the name and scrutinize the reality? As for the name—"
To examine is to verify reality; when reality is verified, names are not empty. When names are not empty, the guest is identical to the host, and the host is identical to the guest.
Both things and the self are compelled by necessity to receive their forms within the space between heaven and earth. If one does not comprehend this, [one will remain deluded].

Then what could there be that does not involve dependence? Now, where there is dependence, there is entanglement. Where there is entanglement, vulnerabilities and fissures need no carving; they are beyond counting.
I have often observed the general outline of such dependence, and it does not go beyond the seven great elements: earth, water, fire, wind, space, sight, and consciousness.

"It has a great name but lacks substance. At this moment, allow me to ask you:
from within this great mass of fire, can you pluck out a single eyebrow for me? He replied, "I cannot.
Wubashela laughed heartily and said, "Although you have followed me for a very long time, you do not yet know me. Can such a thing as this be called 'knowing one another'? You did not...
Have you heard the verse by Nāgārjuna? "All phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another; they do not arise from both together, nor without a cause.
Therefore, it is said that they are unarisen. Contemplating this very point: if there is arising, then there must be a self; only when there is a self does there come to be a thing.
If one seeks to discern the relationship between name and reality, there is no reality external to the name, and no name external to reality. Therefore, I say:
the guest is the host, and the host is the guest. When the guest is the host, the host has never been a host; when the host is the guest, the guest has never been a guest.
Since the host has never been a host and the guest has never been a guest, then "I" and "things," and "things" and "I," are not distinct.

One must wait for the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) before [all things] become utterly vast and open. Therefore it is said: "Only the Sage is able to bring all things back to himself. If I possess a self, how could things be brought back to me?
If things possess their own nature, then those things likewise cannot be brought back. Thus, that which depends on conditions is manifest, while that which does not depend on conditions is hidden.

Solidity constitutes the interstices of earth; moisture constitutes the interstices of water; warmth constitutes the interstices of fire; motion constitutes the interstices of wind;
formlessness constitutes the interstices of space; illumination constitutes the interstices of seeing; and discrimination constitutes the interstices of consciousness.
None of these can exist without their respective "noses" (essential characteristics). If one observes these seven elements with one's own mind, then [the nature of] earth...
Water has never been moist; fire has never been warm; wind has never been moving; space has never been formless;

seeing has never been illuminating; and consciousness has never been discriminating. If this is so, it is permissible to say that the seven are one, and it is permissible to say that the one is seven.

If "one" were to be "seven," then "one" would never have been one; it would not exist in dependence on the hidden, but rather in dependence on the manifest.
By this I know that both the dependent and the independent are, from the outset, devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Is this not what is meant by the saying of Caoxi (Huineng) regarding the impermanence of Buddha-nature and the permanence of all phenomena? Therefore, I observe the nine apertures and the six sense faculties with my own mind.

It is said: "To know movement as movement is to destroy it; to know stillness as stillness is to ruin it.

"Is this out of suspicion or envy?

It is already complete, yet you still treasure it; moreover, you wish to wash away its coarseness while preserving its essence. But what kind of mind is this?
Yet you do not know that once the coarse has departed, is there indeed anything of the "essential" remaining? Ha ha!

Yongjia said: "The great trichiliocosm is but a bubble on the ocean; all sages and worthies are like a flash of lightning. How much more so the ordinary person?"
"Regarding Xi-ge: this is a matter of principle, not of emotion. A man of the Way should first illuminate the light of reason and use that power to subdue emotion;
do not allow emotion to obscure reason. Furthermore, Xi-ge’s physical form has its gathering and dispersing, its birth and death, and cannot be constrained.

Yet his coming and going are free, and he receives retribution entirely according to his karma. How can one know that the mechanism for his swift departure today was not [the result of] a different day?"

Is this not the mechanism for a swift arrival? However, I pray once more that amidst the entanglements of worldly conditions, you may kick over the pillar of emotion and thoroughly penetrate the ocean of principle.

When your wisdom and vows within that ocean of principle move the Buddhas and devas, may one or two sons of merit and wisdom emerge from within the compassionate and majestic light of the Buddhas and devas to console the grief of you, Hxigo. Furthermore—
He was appointed to the post of Jixie (補喜哥) at Jintang. Furthermore, it remains uncertain whether Jixie will return again; reflect upon this.

At that time, Taiquan and Zhuochen, along with two or three fellow practitioners of the Dharma, were likewise choked with sobs beyond restraint. Yet, as for Jixie—

The Dharma is preached through death; Vimalakīrti preached the Dharma through illness. Although ancient and modern, young and old differ, when examined through principle, they are fundamentally no different.
I do not know whether Master Xigao has heard Xigao preaching the Dharma. If he has heard it, he must weep.
The sound does not cease, yet the emotion does not violate principle. Faced with the immediate vicissitudes of life and death, favor and adversity, all are but my teachers.

I fear that because the feelings of Shi Guang and his son are so deep, you may soothe them with reason too slowly, or perhaps allow their emotions to persist, leading them to resent Heaven and blame others.
Therefore, I have first appended the character "hand" (shǒu). This is like urgently removing the firewood from the bottom of a cauldron of boiling water.

Third: Regarding the Great Buddha of Kuāng Mountain, it was first conceived in your mind; now that you have fortunately brought it to completion, you should maintain firm and steadfast right faith, and not allow it to drift toward heterodoxy.
Furthermore, you fair-faced young man, having suddenly become the parent of the people, your daily awareness is that upon which both humans and animals depend.

If you follow your true nature (*xing*), then benevolence, clarity, and courage are manifest everywhere; if you follow your emotions (*qing*), then the ox-heads and horse-faces of hell and the myriad habits of the animal realm are likewise manifest in every encounter.
Alas! Within the pure light, to give rise to thoughts without cause—how perilous and precarious this is! Indeed.
This is no empty word. Layman Wu, Layman Wu!
*Du!* It was at the East Meditation Hall of Lengyan, from the time I first met you, the worthy father and son, that I came to truly know you, the worthy father and son. Indeed, I knew you well.

The Master had those with the karmic affinity for Bodhi. Thereupon, he entrusted Junshi with the composition of a "Commentary on Protecting the Dharma" (*Hufa shu*) to be burned before the Vajrapāṇi deity;

Junshi accepted this directly without any doubt. Furthermore, when Master Xian and his son pursued the Master to Wangjiangjing, they encountered torrential rain pouring down, yet Master Xian and his son never showed the slightest sign of weariness. This was nothing short of extraordinary.
Those who witness this find it utterly impossible to remedy. Now, by good fortune, I have received orders to take charge of Xunyang. Xunyang was once an ancient seat of Chan;
yet recently, among the monastic community, whether they be residents or visitors, most merely eat their fill and sleep indolently.

It seems there are not a few of those who engage in idle chatter devoid of foundation. Alas! When the corruption of administering governance according to the times arises, the rule of benevolence and sincerity perishes.

When the governance of benevolence and faithfulness fell into decay, wisdom and courage were employed to rescue it. When the governance of wisdom and courage fell into decay, there was nothing that could be rescued for many years.
It was not until the time of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty, when the auspicious dream occurred and Mahāmaudgalyāyana came from the Western Regions, that [the Dharma] arrived.
Thus, by means of a single supramundane dharma, one rescues that which cannot otherwise be rescued; this is the natural course of principle and circumstance.
For when worldly dharmas reach their ultimate limit of change, if they are not rescued by supramundane dharmas, the transformation will ultimately never cease.

When supramundane dharmas reach their ultimate limit of change, if they are not in turn rescued by worldly dharmas, their transformation likewise will never cease. Therefore, when Kāśyapa, the Elder, was about to enter nirvāṇa—

However, among the followers of Confucius and Śākyamuni, there are not many in the world who are deeply sorrowful or far-sighted. Consequently, these two traditions have been unable to support one another to remedy their deficiencies;
instead, they inevitably disparage each other, causing those deficiencies to proliferate all the more. When the Daoist first came from Wumen to Nan-kang, he stayed...

and as for one who will succeed these two masters, it must be you, Junshi. From this day forward, regarding the transmission of [this tradition]...
When receiving excessive words, whether in the context of letters or correspondence, one must examine and contemplate them with great care.

one who acts for others with a feigned heart must first rely on indulgence. Virtue and achievement accord with one's nature; indulgence accords with...

When one accords with emotion, both illumination and function are obscured; thus, defiled habits are not cultivated away but deepen day by day. Alas! Within the three realms...

Sentient beings with heavy emotional afflictions (*kleśa*) will certainly not be reborn there. Therefore, although the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) and Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are superior to the realms of hungry ghosts and hell, and although the four *dhyānas* (the heavens of the Form Realm) are superior to the four *ārūpyas*, and although the Heaven of the Four Kings (*cāturmahārājakāyika*) and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven are superior to the [lower] four *dhyānas*, when observed according to reality, the superior realms must have heavier emotional afflictions than the inferior ones;
for the superior beings constantly dwell in favorable circumstances (*anukūla-viṣaya*), whereas the inferior beings do not.

Such a person constantly dwells in adverse conditions. Thus, when conditions are adverse, suffering is extreme; when suffering is extreme, one contemplates the root; when contemplating the root, one approaches awakening.

When one approaches awakening, the root of suffering and pleasure is understood without confusion. At the moment of this clear understanding, one suddenly pushes back beyond suffering and pleasure to ask:
where, ultimately, does the root of suffering and pleasure reside? Through long and persistent inquiry, sincerity accumulates. Sincerity...

Once one has mastered this play, then entering hell is also a good thing, and being born in heaven does not give rise to thoughts of wonder.

Thereafter, one must deeply lament that those of our same essence are sinking deeper into the sea of suffering and that the smoke in the burning house grows thick, incinerating the three realms and causing us to drift through the seven destinies.

While these Four Great Vows are not difficult to utter, the single word "forcefully" (or "strenuously") is the most difficult to bear. If one can directly take up this burden, [then the vows will be realized].

A practitioner of the Way must truly exert effort to shoulder this word "strength"; otherwise, one will frequently fail to rise to the occasion.

This is because sentient beings are habituated to the familiar while Buddhas and Patriarchs are habituated to the raw; when sentient beings are habituated to the familiar, their faculties become difficult to transform.
"Uproot! If my roots are difficult to uproot, then these shoulders would not be Vajra-shoulders. It is for this reason that one is turned about by profit and loss, benefit and harm.

"It is not broken. Why is it that one cannot carry it on one's shoulder? Such statements describe what is easy to say but difficult to practice;

therefore, Guishan reprimanded Yangshan, saying, "Jizi, do not merely have liberation through verbal understanding. Furthermore, the Buddha-dharma does not take meditative concentration as its essential requirement.

Furthermore, regarding the current state of the world, even among one's own closest kin and flesh-and-blood relatives, if they happen to offend one, one disregards them entirely and seeks nothing more than to cast them into death for one's own gratification. This—

this is the natural course of events. O practitioner, I hope that you will truly employ both wisdom and diligence.

This letter is addressed to Huang Shengxuan.
Recently, I received a letter from Wang Yutai, learning that you have already departed from Chang’an. I imagine there will soon be a day when you return home. Herein...

The Venerable Taichuan preserves the portraits of the various patriarchs of both the Flower Garland (Huayan) and Brahmanical (Buddhist) traditions and enshrines them within the Radiance of Samantabhadra on Mount Emei for eternal veneration.
These portraits were painted by Ding Nan-yu Yunpeng of Xin’an; their spiritual essence is imbued with compassion and their demeanor is profoundly serene.
This is truly a rare and sublime matter. I wish to compose a record of this, which must surely issue from your own hand.
Only then can one truly satisfy the aspirations of those who seek the Way. Xu Yanwen has now become a guest of the Nine Mounds (the realm of the dead), which brings heartache to all.
While the green clouds remain unharmed and Mount Yan remains as it was of old, the deceased know not where they have gone, and the living know not what awaits them.
Whenever I reflect upon this, sorrow and joy mingle within me. I do not know whether Shenxuan understands the intent of Dao Ren. As for Zhongfu’s late father, his loyalty—
Houmai transcended the mundane when he ceased his breathing; from the beginning, there was no confusion or disorder.

Although throughout his life he was unable to practice pure conduct, it can be inferred that the power of his loyalty and integrity produced this efficacy. Now, loyalty and integrity mean not to deceive; where there is no deception, one naturally lacks a thieving mind.
When the thieving mind is diminished, those instances in daily life where one deceives oneself will, without needing to be consciously alerted, naturally become few. Therefore:
He said: "It is simply that if one does not deceive the mind, the mind itself is numinous and sagely.

If the power of loyalty and sincerity is already such as this, how much more so for those who open up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*) and use that knowledge and vision to cure their habitual tendencies? Be cautious; the letter you previously sent considered the Buddha’s knowledge and understanding to be an obstacle."

"As soon as you know and see correctly, you may walk boldly across the world. If Linji were correct, then Shenxuan would be wrong;
if Shenxuan were correct, then Linji would instead be incorrect. There is another parable regarding this; Shenxuan should reflect upon it deeply. There was once a man of military rank.
While fighting with bandits, he was defeated. Retreating, he privately complained in anger, "It is because my martial arts are too many that I cannot defeat these bandits.
If I had no martial arts, I would not be hindered by them, and I could defeat the bandits.
When a Daoist master reads this passage, he will surely burst into laughter and fall over. Master Dahui of the Song dynasty often said to the scholar-officials:
