This is because intelligence and clarity belong to the category of non-valid cognition (*aparāmārśa*). Non-valid cognition refers to that which does not correspond to the ultimate principle (*tattva*).
The Buddha’s knowledge and vision, at its highest level, belongs to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); next, it belongs to inference (*anumāna*). As for direct perception:"

This refers to what is called "attaining without deliberation" and "hitting the mark without striving. As for *anumāna* (inferential cognition), although it arises from conceptual deliberation and comparative measurement, it accords with the authoritative judgment of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and is not false.
Using this to treat habitual tendencies, one ultimately enters into *pratyakṣa* (direct perception).
The ancients called this the "flowing True Suchness" (*tathatā*). This cannot be discerned by anyone who has not deeply penetrated the essence of the teachings.
Dharma practitioners often encounter scholars and officials who, upon hearing mention of "flowing continuity" (*liuzhu*) or "true suchness" (*zhenru*), immediately shake their heads and turn away.

They fail to realize that flowing continuity and true suchness are matters that even Linji and Dongshan did not dare to overlook. Thus it is said: "By means of words, one reveals that which is wordless.
It is also said: "Moving the countenance, one raises the ancient path; one does not fall into the trap of the silent mechanism. And again: "But..."

he began to speak recklessly, praising or disparaging the recorded sayings of the ancient worthies, and even judged that Jiyin was certainly not a monk who had attained enlightenment.

Sisi bowed his head and remained silent. Furthermore, there is another kind of person whose level of realization...

when it was said that Dongpo was speaking of principle (*li*), he would prick once; when it was said that this point did not involve the path of principle, he would circle it several times.

I am returning home with Yu Zhongfu and Xie Xiaoxuan; you should resolve to become a "stinking-vinegar-eating" fellow. The habits of a wandering monk must be thoroughly and gradually eliminated.

Regarding the character "Yu" (於): it must first depend on you to be so. You carry this character upon your head, yet you cannot endure the stench of fermented vinegar, nor can you digest the habits of a wandering monk.
To expect to manage the affairs within the family gate and have that household remain stable and harmonious—there is no such possibility.
Furthermore, when the ancients dwelt in favorable circumstances for long periods, they would say, "Even Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not come to protect and mind me."
Observing this, it is truly because when disagreeable matters pile up one after another, those who must face them reach the height of suffering;
they cannot help but become deeply anxious and far-sighted in their reflections. When anxiety is deep and reflection is far-reaching, the actions taken will for the most part possess righteousness.
Conversely, if one acts with reckless negligence born of impulsive emotion, the actions undertaken will inevitably lack righteousness.

These two gates were not newly established by Nanyue; they are actually derived from the two gates of True Suchness and Arising-and-Ceasing in Aśvaghoṣa’s *Awakening of Faith*.

Today, among those who study Chan, practice the lectures, seek rebirth in the Pure Land, and those so-called scholars of the Way—among these four types of people, is there not even one who studies with a sincere heart? They simply all refuse to take deep concern seriously.

Their considerations are far-reaching. Thus, their Chan is not the Chan of Bodhidharma; their lectures are not the meaning of the Tathāgata. They seek rebirth in the Pure Land while believing that the root of craving has not been uprooted;
they claim that even those who are merely superficial can be reborn there. As for their study of the Way, they do not investigate the original intent of Confucius at all.
Instead, they take the stale, rotten talk of Cheng and Zhu as their banner and drum, desiring to unify all people under heaven.
With their own ears and eyes, they see those who study Laozi or the Buddha as if they were enemies.

Little do they realize whether Confucius, Laozi, and the Buddha are truly three people or truly one person. Such judgments are made by those who, while conversant with both Confucianism and Daoism, have not yet deeply mastered the Buddhist scriptures;
they recklessly speculate, having never once touched upon the fundamental essence of these three traditions, and yet proceed to speak of them.
These Confucians talk of Laozi and talk of the Buddha; they are nothing but a pack of blind donkeys, everywhere drumming up the stench of vinegar.
If you encounter them on a narrow path and feel impatient in responding to them, it means you lack the capacity to endure the smell of sour vinegar.
This is the lingering habit of a wandering monk that will never be extinguished. As for my own nature, as soon as I hear this sour stench—

The name alone causes the soul to tremble ten thousand miles away; this is the habitual tendency of a wandering monk. When I first left home to become a monk, my own temperament was even more extreme than yours.
In recent years, I have deeply grieved that the Buddha’s kindness is difficult to repay, and I have bitterly regretted my own fierce and violent nature.

I have gradually treated it with the insight of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, yet it remains like sour, stinking vinegar; nevertheless, I have been eating it slowly. Such is the habit of a fierce and violent nature.
"I am about to depart with a painful ailment. If you, as one of these two types of people, cannot practice with such intensity, then the result you will achieve can be known.

When this old man spoke these words, my mouth was already in pain; furthermore, amidst the urgency of my departure, I had to speak at length despite enduring this agony because I did not know what thoughts would be stirred in you when you read these words of mine. Here—"
If you neglect this, then you will not be equal to even dogs or horses. "Ling-lang, ling-lang! I feel deep sorrow as I contemplate my instructions.

Both Wang Yutai and I are advanced in years; furthermore, both your elder brother and your younger brother are by nature free-spirited and unrestrained, such that they are unable to [fulfill their duties].
Regarding medicine: if Master Guang were not capable of bearing this burden, who else could? This is but the natural course of affairs. This old man thinks only of Master Guang;

if he were to obtain a son in his later years, then the lineage would have a successor. If one serves their parents without a successor, not only will there be no one to perpetuate the glory of the family line, but even the light of the Dharma lamp will find it difficult to continue its subsequent flames. This is a bitter [reality].
This occurs among humans alone, yet it also exists in the heavens. Thus it is said: "In the human realm there is the pain of a lineage being cut off;

in the heavens there is the sorrow of having no son. If Master Guang can accord with cause and effect, remaining directly free from doubt and instead taking this lack of affliction as a resource for contemplation, then the suffering of childlessness is, in fact, Master Guang himself. Suffering.
What else could there be? It is only feared that once one recognizes this truth, one cannot bear to pass it by; ultimately, one will be dragged along by the ropes of habituation.

When encountering the shifting heat and cold of worldly conditions, one will again—unaware and unperceived—suddenly give rise to immeasurable lamentations. It is precisely at the moment of such lamentation...
Wipe away the dust from your nostrils and seek some water and grass to eat before your parents were even born;
this sentiment of profound resonance is also the introduction to Master Guang’s state of non-birth.

These five turns—if you can place them in succession within your daily life, moving horizontally and vertically—constantly bring to mind this thought: "This is my original teacher, not thousands of miles away."
Externally, amidst these overlapping winds and waves, when someone sends a person to bring me something, you must ask yourself: "Does this person seek my fame? Do they seek my profit?
Do they wish for my well-being? Or do they not wish for my well-being? Is their heart sincere toward me? Or is their heart feigned toward me?
You must not neglect these six "ya" (yes/whether) questions; chew them over carefully. Perhaps, at the critical juncture of your likes and dislikes, you will find a way to resolve it.
The field is also one's true nature; it is not something extraneous. Master Guang, exert yourself!
In response to Yunfu:
Having received your letter regarding the visit to Yulin, as I read it slowly and closed the volume to reflect upon it, I realized that five years have passed since I crossed the river.

"Time passes with its cold and heat; you yourself feel as though the days drift by aimlessly. Within the True Dharma, you are no different from one who is deaf or blind, having nothing to present or demonstrate.

This result is truly painful. If you are struck with such alarm that it never ceases, and with such indignation that you advance with vigor, then regardless of whether evils are great or small, or sins heavy or light, they shall all be transformed by the Teacher and the Uninvited Friend.
But if your resolve slackens even slightly, or your effort becomes even a little lax..."
Then, for a brief moment, there is a state of refreshing clarity; this is surely not other than the vanguard of the three obstacles.
The Three Torches truly have the power to suddenly clear away the dust of the emotions. These words of an old and worn-out mind are remnants of what I could not previously bring forth;
I examine who it is that causes this—within that which was previously beyond expression, when ignorance suddenly obstructs the mind, occurring without one’s knowing or perceiving.

At that time, one complacently commits evil; once the evil has been fully committed, it is ultimately difficult to repent for its retribution. Ignorance obscuring the mind is the affliction-obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*);

complacently committing evil is the karma-obstruction (*karmāvaraṇa*); and the ultimate difficulty in repenting for the retribution is the retribution-obstruction (*vipākāvaraṇa*). These three obstructions are thus established.
It is like a source and its current; although the names "current" and "wave" differ, their moisture is one and the same.
The old man asks about the three torches: "One is just so. If you can recognize this, then calmly examine the three obstacles previously created by that [source].
Are they suffering or joy? If you reach the very root of suffering and joy without doubt, then the three obstacles are themselves the Three [Treasures].

This is the original face of the torch. I, an old man, cannot bear to withhold it from you. If you do not investigate that which precedes the "one," and fail to discern what is essential and what is trivial, you will be unable to turn yourself around in this very moment;
how could things go well? You must, within the Three Jewels, be willing to sacrifice your body and life to protect the Dharma.

It is like passing by the *Śūraṅgama* Sūtra and prostrating before the sacred image, yet seeing it covered with withered grass and tattered mats—[how can you remain indifferent? Do not [be like this].

When one’s entire body feels as if covered in bristling needles and sweat breaks out upon the forehead, this power of a single thought can eliminate the sins of the ten evils and the five heinous crimes.
Even a gift of a thousand or ten million pieces of gold does not equal the merit of this power of thought; it cannot be fathomed by ordinary intellect or worldly wisdom.
Provided that this power of thought can carry one from beginning to end, then even though you, Brother Ben, and Brother Kai may be separated by birth and death, [you shall be reunited].
There is a sequence of before and after, yet the intent of his heart is already clear. As for the matter of carving the Tripitaka, there will ultimately be those who take up the burden;

do not worry. Even this memorial from Direct Pointing (Kang Zhichu) is like the pines and wind by a pond and the moon over a pool during the three months of summer—it can it not cool the liver and lungs of this old man?
Convey my regards to Zhongchun; do not let your mind be troubled. This old man is now in his sixtieth year, yet I have not yet been able to... [the text ends].

Upon reading this letter, my heart was pierced with grief; I could not help but wring my hands in distress. Why trouble yourself with such distant thoughts? I only think that among you brothers, you have compared my appearance to a man digging for gold who sees only the gold and fails to see its owner. You must grant me great indulgence for this. Having written thus far, I send this letter. Please do not worry about me. I am currently staying at the residence of the Elder Master [Shen]xiu. I, an old man, am indeed like a congealed pus-bag regarding the realization of emptiness.
Yet, amidst this unconscious state, as I contemplate the scenes of your parents' time, tears well up to flow forth; though I strive to stop them, I cannot. For parents are the very root of you all.
If you both are willing to remember this root, then the emotions of discrimination will fade away. When emotion fades, the realm of non-self is reached without effort.

Look up; it is clearly manifest above you. This is none other than your three elder brothers. Although they were previously praised as the virtuous ones of the Yu clan, their failure to reflect upon themselves was even greater than yours.
Now that I, an old man, have clarified this for you, henceforth hold fast to the character "forgiveness" (shu).
If you can endure and become mature through both adverse and favorable circumstances, your future enjoyment of the Dharma will not be slight. — Juren.
Jurlang, do not consider my words as old and far-fetched; exert yourself with all your might. Second:
When a great man dwells within this vast expanse of the world, his fundamental task is inherently no more than this: to engage with the world or to transcend it.
It is merely for the sake of the world. If one is without intention regarding worldly affairs, even if one attains wealth and honor, what use would they be?
If such things are employed for food, drink, or the passions of men and women, this constitutes the creation of transgression; it is not true employment.
If one sets one's heart upon transcending the world, yet fails to restrain the body and mind and ultimately fail to study the Way of Nature and Life, then the Great Path will never be heard. Alas!

Humans are the most spiritually gifted among all things. If you fail to achieve anything in either the worldly or the world-transcending realms, and instead choose to compete with ignorant people in their ignorance, you will only compound your error.
Reflect on this, reflect on it! If you gain insight, you should gather up your worldly affairs;
there is surely another ground for cultivation. Do not neglect this.
Last year, when I heard of you from Lord Lu, I set aside all other matters and devoted myself solely to the diligent recitation of the Buddha’s name; this is the true essence of one's final years.

However, if one is supported by the favorable conditions of supreme purity, the mind of recitation will easily become continuous and dense. As for such favorable conditions of supreme purity, nothing surpasses—

This concerns the conditions of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. If a statue of the Buddha is placed before you and the sutra scrolls are arranged there, and you further obtain one or two members of the Sangha with whom to associate intimately morning and evening, then naturally these superior and pure conditions will be most excellent.

However, among the members of the Sangha, it is ultimately not easy to find such people; for even I, a poor practitioner, am a person who has wandered from east to west and north to south—how could I remain constantly?
To serve as an aid for purification, I have requested the artist Ding Sheng to paint this portrait of the Venerable Bhadra.
My intention is that it may assist you, my disciple, in your practice of nianfo on my behalf. I pray that you will listen to his teaching with your faculty of sight;
thus, all worldly entanglements shall be severed at once, and the true mind of mindfulness will manifest before you. This is what I, a poor monk, deeply hopes for from you, my disciple. [Year]...
Light flickers and vanishes; it does not abide for even a single kṣaṇa. How much less so for an old man with white hair! Yongjia said:

"One must practice with diligence day and night, for fear that conditions may diverge; how much more so if one is not diligent! Alas! The divergence of conditions confuses and disturbs right mindfulness.
Even those who have attained penetration are frequently buried by them, let alone those whose insight has not yet penetrated. I pray that you, sir, will not treat me with contempt.
It is fortunate that you have disregarded human speech as being inconsistent with reality. You have further elucidated the principle of the non-arising of phenomena according to Dong Yuanzai;

this is the very marrow of the patriarchs and Buddhas. Yet, in this degenerate age, among the tens of thousands and hundreds of thousands of people—both monastics and laypeople—one must seek it [with great effort].
Those who possess faith are rare to find. Now, you alone are able to believe and enter into this;

were it not for the latent seeds of spiritual potential (*gotra*) prepared from former lives, how could these conditions have been awakened by past causes? How is it that they now manifest and briefly appear? How joyful this is!
Your letter states that at first it was quite refreshing, but now it is no longer lively and seems as if it might be lost. Where does the fault lie? Since this is merely a brief manifestation...
The power of the incense has slightly faded and it naturally vanishes; there is no need for doubt. However, the words and phrases of the Chan (Zen) school must not be treated with casualness.
If you, sir, have entered through faith, I intend to open the pivot for you—this is what is meant by "the Duke of Lu nourishing birds with his own way of feeding them.
Long ago, Dou-shuai Yue asked Zhang Wujin, "Do you have any lingering doubts regarding the 'entanglements' of the Chan school?"
Wujin said, "The karmic conditions regarding Deshan’s alms-bowl have not yet been resolved. Doushuai raised his voice sharply and said, "If there is doubt here, how can there be no doubt elsewhere?
He went straight into the abbot's quarters without looking back. From this, Wujin became resolute in his investigation and subsequently attained great enlightenment.
If you, sir, have not yet penetrated two or three out of ten cases, you are still far from Wujin.
You must exert yourself to the utmost; resolve this in this very life. Do not allow doubt to linger within you, lest you bring about your own ruin in future lives.

Furthermore, your letter states that "wherever thoughts arise, the head is already in hand. May I ask you, sir: is it because the place where thoughts arise is fundamentally non-arising that one attains realization?
Or is it because one realizes thoughts are fundamentally empty that one accords with non-arising? If the place where thoughts arise is fundamentally non-arising, then one knows—

Regarding "non-arising": is it thought? Or is it non-thought? If one realizes thought, then one accords with non-arising; yet, as for this "realizer," does it mean realization through thought, or realization without thought?
If there is thought, one has already deviated from non-arising; if there is no thought, who then accords with non-arising?
If you can penetrate and transcend this without doubt, then even staying for many nights in a grass hut would not be the ultimate treasure-place. However, come...
This demonstrates how one should practice, how one should maintain [the path], and how one must wait for strength to become full before entering the field of experience for testing, and so forth;
you will know the proper timing yourself. Why wait for this poor monk’s prolixity? This poor monk does not begrudge his verbal karma in such a manner;
it is all merely adding a handle to a begging bowl. It is only for your sake that I have exerted great effort within both the *zong* (School) and the *jiao* (Teaching).
Regard him as an enemy; you must by all means raze his lair and destroy his dwelling.
It will not be too late to deliberate further with Ding Shuoyuan.
All matters of honor and disgrace, gain and loss, concern nothing but what lies beyond this life. Previously, Xing Laici of Xinyang troubled me by bringing eight points of conduct to present to you;
this was truly because he wished for you to contemplate gain and loss through these conditions.

To contemplate through such conditions and yet seek that which has no beginning—once that which has no beginning is attained, one can then board the vessel of the unoriginated and travel back and forth between honor and glory.
You have humbled yourself by crossing the ford of gain and loss, life and death; you have broadly guided all beings and established them on the further shore.
Unexpectedly, before long after your reply reached me, the rudimentary chariot of the Sage Emperor has arrived once more. This is truly Heaven’s way of bestowing great favor upon you.

It is not that I slight you, my worthy friend; I only ask that you take the strength to sustain yourself. Furthermore, I am but a reclusive wanderer beyond the clouds, truly indifferent to the world and seeking nothing therein.
Yet, that I am so earnestly concerned for you as I am—surely there must be some subtle intention behind this.

I hope you will regard the miasmic regions as a pleasure garden and the *diaodou* (military drums) as sights for your excursions; please take care of yourself and value your own well-being. As for me, this wanderer, should I ever...
Regarding my travels to Caoxi, I have not yet fully understood the details of their commencement and conclusion upon further inquiry.

In response to your question concerning the meaning of "stainlessness" (*vimala*) from Chen Wuyue: I am but a dull and ignorant person; how could I possibly be worthy of such an answer? Nevertheless, there are many explanations regarding the doctrine of stainlessness.
I do not know what kind of question you, the Layman, have asked. Now, Bo Yi and Shu Qi were considered stainless because they would not eat the grain of Zhou;
Zhonglian of Lu was considered stainless because he resolved people's perils and relieved the urgent distress of others, yet did not covet rank or emolument.

The son of the Yan family lived in a humble alley with a single bamboo bowl and a gourd for sustenance, yet he was transcendent and self-joyful, regarding this as being "without defilement" (*vimala*).

These are all cases of being without defilement within the mundane world. As for the Śrāvakas, they regard the physical body as a source of affliction and contemplate emptiness as being without defilement.

The Pratyekabuddhas, however, regard the initial non-existence of affliction as being without defilement. The Bodhisattvas, moreover, perceive that affliction is identical to the mind, seeing that the myriad phenomena are all true.
Stainlessness: For all Tathāgatas, stainlessness consists in non-apprehensibility;
from my own first patriarch Bodhidharma downward, the various Chan elders have taken a dried piece of excrement as stainlessness—this, moreover, is a supramundane form of stainlessness.
If you take worldly stainlessness to be the attainment of the ultimate meaning, then you yourself, beneath my feet, are capable of manifesting it; there is no need to trouble this poor monk.
If you take supramundane stainlessness to be what delights the mind, then if a śrāvaka dwells in this hut, the hut immediately deviates from emptiness;
if a pratyekabuddha dwells in it, the hut was originally not existent; if a bodhisattva dwells in it, the hut is simply one's own mind. If...

The Tathāgata dwells therein, yet the hermitage cannot be apprehended. Someone asked: "If the Tathāgata cannot be apprehended, is this not the same as the emptiness of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?
He replied: "As for the Tathāgata’s being unapprehendable, even all the great bodhisattvas are unable to fathom its limits;
indeed, even the Tathāgata himself cannot know it. How much less so the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas!"
How could it be fathomed? Regarding the realm reached by the Tathāgata, there is no place for any holy being or ordinary person to harbor a conceptual mind;

therefore, it is designated by the name "Ineffable. That this [Ineffable] should then be conflated with the emptiness of the Hīnayāna—were it even a man three feet tall driving away crows, anyone who heard of it would not fail to laugh until their sides ached.
This is the general purport of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*; I venture to present it here in brief.

As for reaching the summit of this hermitage, it shall be determined by one’s own high intelligence and clarity. If there is a future opportunity for us to meet and converse, I shall allow myself further time to seek your instruction.

Once you, Layman Lei Yu, have recovered somewhat from your illness, you should immediately recite the *Śloka on the Eight Consciousnesses* in silence. This verse is the skeletal framework of the *Yogācāra* (Dharma-character) school. The Yogācāra...

This constitutes the Five Treasuries of the Nature School (*Xingzong*). Just as when the mutual overcoming of the five viscera is not understood, the entire body cannot be properly nourished and maintained;

so too, regarding the principle of transforming consciousness into wisdom (*zhuan shi cheng zhi*), if the Characteristics School (*Xiangzong*) is vague and obscure, one can never achieve precise realization.

If this is not precisely realized, then even if one’s lofty discourse is fundamentally subtle—excavating the truth and stripping away the secrets—if one encounters an object and engages in a contest of wits, the function of illumination will fail to be brought forth.

He will not emerge. Furthermore, my arrival here at Chao-ling is no small matter; yet when sentient beings view it with their ordinary, mundane perspectives, they ultimately fail to conceive of it as something truly extraordinary.
Worldly affairs are not enduring, human sentiments are fickle, and one recklessly calculates them to be impermanent; such defiled habits are difficult to wash away.
You must therefore cause your spirit and soul to break forth in earnest, resolving to surpass metal and stone in steadfastness, so that you may emerge from this state.
A fleeting moment of complacency, and one knows that the time for the exhaustion of suffering has not yet arrived.

Among these, those who have recently begun their studies as practitioners of the Way, if they can remain unexhausted by the knowledge of change, then change cannot startle them and exhaustion cannot distress them. Alas!
This samādhi is not something produced by seeing a few [signs]; who then could employ it?

As for Zhao Qian, his fortune and misfortune were as intense as those between life and death; thus, even the most impoverished and lowly person, upon hearing they might attain life, rejoices as if ascending [to heaven].
O Heavenly One, when one hears of death, one grieves as if plunging into a deep abyss; yet all this is merely the product of emotional sentiment.

If one can follow their true nature (*xing*) to contemplate the realms of death and life, honor and disgrace, then not only will those realms of death, life, honor, and disgrace be unable to seize my resolve, but those very realms will secretly become my uninvited friends.
Therefore, a great man (*dàzhàngfū*), while living in ordinary times, remains free from the great suffering and agony of oppression.
At such times, one must exhaustively investigate principle and fully realize one’s nature;

otherwise, if one were to overlook and let slip even a single point, then when encountering unexpected circumstances in daily life and they intersect before us, my will would surely be entirely usurped by external conditions.
Thus, although Li Zhuowu could not have escaped with composure, he did so with speed.
"To die would be a blessing. Having said this, he finally raised his blade and took his own life. It is truly extraordinary that Sun Quan’s anger was thus appeased.
Now, as for matters of straightforward sincerity, they ultimately do not lead to the loss of body or life; at worst, one may simply be sent back to their rural estate.
Furthermore, it remains unknown how the Creator might use adversity to bring about my fulfillment. Viewed from this perspective, even the most extreme measures of cruelty...
As for those who plot to slander and entrap me, I fear it is the work of the Creator. If one attempts to comprehend such matters with the common mind of the masses, one will surely miss the mark.
One must instead employ the mind of the Buddhas, Patriarchs, and Sages, maintaining a humble heart and a tranquil spirit.
Study and comprehend this thoroughly. When there is a point where you can truly nod in agreement, then that which is without self yet spiritual will manifest its head and face.

If, at such a juncture, one does not believe the sages and worthies but instead believes the common crowd, I shall never hear the Way. As a human being, one is ashamed to be among the spiritually gifted;
how could it be that the Way is not heard? I pray that you reflect upon this deeply.

I have just received your letter; upon reading it, I too could not help but feel moved to sorrow. However, regarding those who intend to manipulate and arrange others, I fear their resolve may lack vigor and their stratagems may lack depth.
If they act solely out of a desire for straightforwardness, they will find no room to live while leaving a lingering aftermath in death.
This has been the common condition of all people from antiquity to the present. Therefore, when a gentleman encounters such a realm, he must proceed with caution.
If a sense of gratitude arises, you should not accept it; rather, you must deeply reproach yourself. This is because the perception of one's own faults arises from within one's own mind.
Thus, when self-reproach reaches its peak, only then will the perception of others' faults cease to arise in the human heart. I beg you once more to reflect upon this with deep earnestness.

Second: Throughout antiquity and the present, all matters of fortune and misfortune are fundamentally impermanent; yet, when one judges right and wrong by means of both heavenly principle and human sentiment, there is nothing that does not prove true.
If one judges human sentiment by means of heavenly principle, then public justice becomes clear. However, if one judges by means of human sentiment...
When the principles of Heaven are severed, private resentment becomes heavy. When private resentment is heavy, those both within and without will establish defenses and make arrangements;
their efforts in this regard will surely be thorough. Amidst such thorough preparations for private resentment, moreover, those harboring such resentment will be many.
How can one determine the mechanism of life and death? This is not something that human effort can secretly manipulate.
However, there is no principle by which a straightforward mind could harm life; even nature, in its aged wisdom, would be unable to bear it. One may perhaps observe the consequences later.

Third: Generally, the roots of calamity and fortune, as well as self and other, are rooted in that which has already been manifested. If one examines them through that which has not yet been manifested, then the roots of calamity and fortune, as well as self and other, originally have no ground.
That which has already been manifested is emotion (*qing*); that which has not yet been manifested is nature (*xing*). Therefore, by means of...
When one contemplates the affairs of fortune and calamity, self and others, there is a self that is increasingly obscured. When it is obscured, it becomes heavy;
when heavy, it becomes dense; when dense, it becomes deep; and when deep, it becomes accumulated. Once accumulated, it is difficult to discharge lightly.

Therefore, the cycle of retribution between self and others cannot be brought to an end even after hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas. This is an inevitable reality, yet the ignorant do not understand this principle regarding self and others.
Regarding the roots of misfortune and fortune, not only are they unable to be uprooted, one instead exerts effort to plant them; it is truly lamentable that one’s regret does not go deep enough.
Therefore, when Buddhas, patriarchs, sages, and worthies urge people to hear the Way and see their nature, they have no other intention than to cause everyone to sever the root of worldly attachment.
Once the root of attachment is severed, then as for the misfortunes and fortunes of the past—[they cease].

My affairs have all gradually transformed into wondrous functions. With the eye of wisdom of these wondrous functions, observing the misfortunes and blessings of all people, as well as their struggles over self and others, is truly not at all strange.
If you cannot open your heart and expose your lungs within today’s field of self and others to receive this teaching of wild decay, then you shall fall; you can do nothing but weep.
Reflect upon this, reflect deeply upon it. Furthermore, fame, achievement, wealth, and honor are rooted in this body. This body’s maximum lifespan does not exceed a hundred years;
yet within those hundred years, one enjoys wealth, honor, and pleasure while being beset by sorrow more often than joy.
Thus, the time spent enjoying wealth, honor, and pleasure during those hundred years is but a brief moment. Why suffer for the sake of such a short duration?

Regarding the sentiments of fortune and misfortune, or self and others, people have long been content to obscure their original nature. A person of realization observes right and wrong, or honor and disgrace, through the lens of this original nature;
they are no different from the subtle gathering and dispersing of clouds within the vast void. What leisure have they to harbor such concerns?
Amidst the many troubles of these present times, I, Wild朽 (Yexiu), do not begrudge my verbal karma as I provide various explanations to set your mind straight and clarify your inner disposition.
If one misses these compassionate hearts amidst the decaying speech of the wilds, then the kalpa of suffering for that straightforward mind will truly endure for a long time.

Alas! At the critical juncture of a great man’s nature, if you recognize this truly, then those who contend with your straightforwardness today and those who harm your straightforward mind are all your spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). If you have this...
"I see. What does it matter if one wears coarse clothing and eats coarse food? To resolve the great matter of birth and death—is this not joyful?
Your name is Fafu; you were born precisely for this very day."
Fourth: the power of devas, the power of the earth, the power of the Buddha, the power of the Dharma, and the power of the Sangha—all these are external powers.

Only the power of one's own mind is internal power. External power serves as assistance; internal power is the primary force. If the primary force is not vigorous, then despite much assistance, in the end...
One cannot transform misfortune into good fortune. Therefore it is said: "If one acts before Heaven, Heaven does not oppose them. It is also said:
"The power of one's own mind can overturn heaven and earth. If one believes this is no exaggeration, yet seeks external assistance instead, there is absolutely no such possibility.
Whenever ordinary people like me encounter calamities or harm, there is no other method than to simply believe directly that, apart from one's own mind, where could calamity or harm exist?
Whenever one encounters misfortune or harm, it is entirely created by one's own mind; consequently, one must likewise receive the poison from within one's own mind. This principle is most equitable.
Reflect upon this again and again.

5. It has been a very long time since we last met, and my longing for you is profound. I do not know whether, in recent times, amidst all the various realms of experience—whether intentional or unintentional, and amidst their manifold conflicts—you have been able to use the Great Compassion and Great Wisdom of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara to forge both the adverse and the favorable into one.
Regarding self-enjoyment samādhi: first, it is essential to know and penetrate this samādhi; second, it is essential that one's practice be firm;
third, one must certainly expect to realize it before ceasing; and further, once realized, one must be able to forget it. Only when one forgets it and yet employs it is its function fully perfected.
For a great man, what leisure is there to debate Confucianism, Buddhism, or Daoism? These have all already been exhausted by the ancients;
they are no different from dried grass dogs long since discarded. How could one have the energy to occupy oneself with them?

Nevertheless, if one’s own inherently existing mind of non-arising has not yet been thoroughly understood, then the texts of Confucius, Śākyamuni, and Laozi, as well as the most essential scriptures, remain of vital importance.
Furthermore, one must not fail to apply oneself with earnest attention to this matter.

Whenever I, this poor monk, am walking or sitting by beautiful mountains and waters, there is never a time when I do not encounter moments of excellence that expand my thoughts toward the vast and empty.

Moreover, I reflect on how those initial gatherings with Nangao, Shuoyuan, and Cunxu at Shitou were distant and beyond recovery. Recently, I have also had the opportunity to meet Zhao Qiansuo, yet his spirit is superior [to mine].
In principle, he cannot avoid being shaken by the winds of favorable and adverse circumstances; this is truly pitiable. His loyalty and integrity are no less than those of the ancients. Six.
To maintain loyalty and yet suffer dismissal is fate. It is precisely because one knows fate that one remains tranquil in the face of dismissal and feels no distress.
If, upon being dismissed, one harbors distress, was what was previously called "loyalty" truly loyal? Had the person been disloyal, I certainly would have known it.
This is wisdom (*jñāna*), not clarity (*vidyā*). It is only my lack of loyalty; within the mind of self, it is perfectly clear and unclouded—this is clarity, not wisdom.
Now, as for whether this upright mind is loyal or disloyal, only Heaven knows it, and only the upright mind itself knows it.
Moreover, when a person intends to place the upright mind in a state of death, it is fortunate that it has become a lay official.

This is a most magnificent blessing; why, then, should there be any cause for distress? When a great man repeatedly encounters dismissal and humiliation, he need not regard them as a source of resentment.
I pray that you maintain a straightforward mind and take up the burden of a great man yourself; in the end, we shall surely meet again at an appointed time. Last year, I sent a letter to Hai’ruo;
in that letter, I already stated that a person of straightforward mind will ultimately suffer dismissal. If you happen to meet Hai’ruo, please retrieve this letter for him.
Investigate this. Viewed from this perspective, being a lay official (*baiyi lang*) is not something that began today. With a direct mind, a direct mind—cease further hesitation.
When all conditions (*wan yuan*) have come to rest, joy is most profound. Let this be your parting gift: the entire earth is pure gold.
7. Since the twentieth day of the first month, I have received your letter, and my wavering mind has suddenly come to rest.
Before receiving your letter, because rumors were so rampant, even though I held a firm conviction, I was unconsciously affected by a slight dizziness; this is but the common nature of human emotion.
Simply maintain a straightforward mind toward your writing and correspondence; there is no need to strive with others to debate the distinctions between clarity and turbidity, right and wrong.
To engage in such debate is to lose sight of what is great. When the great is lost, one's capacity for broad-mindedness becomes narrow.

Furthermore, since departing from Chang’an with a straightforward mind, the distinction between clarity and turbidity, right and wrong, has never failed to become increasingly clear and manifest. Lately, there have also been those who act for the sake of straightforwardness...
As for those who wring their hands in distress: they should simply maintain a straightforward mind and place their body and mind in the realm of nothingness. When hunger comes, eat;
when weariness comes, sleep—this is enough. Should the habitual affliction of arrogance arise, one must view it with a single flavor as mere self-inflation.
Then the mark of self is no different from the realm of nothingness. Furthermore, tell me: at such a time, where would you place the habitual affliction of arrogance?
Do not neglect this; it is the daily meal of a true man of spirit. To seek anything else apart from this is to be a heterodox practitioner.
If one’s straightforward mind can truly see through this and apply it upon encountering circumstances, then— [The text continues: ...toward [the realization].
Those things which are considered treasuries of resentment by the upright mind are, in fact, all the very resources for the upright mind’s entry into the Way.
How, then, could there be any such thing as a treasury of resentment? Has there been any news recently from Tang Ruoshi? He too has been reflecting upon this lately.
Laozi said, "Honor and disgrace are both causes for alarm. Judging honor and disgrace according to Laozi’s intent, alarm is the same in either case. However, these...
These words are not for those who would mutilate their bodies or deafen their ears; such a severance is not easily understood. Only one with a straightforward mind may know them.
Once they have emerged again, only then will you be permitted to charge crosswise and collide head-on within both mundane and supramundane dharmas.
The west wind is at its height, and leaves fall from the empty woods. As the night deepens and all is still, how great is the longing for an old friend!
Do not resent others for the harsh winds and waves of the sea; outside of the mind, where could there ever be a cresting wave?
If the habits of arrogance are not eliminated at once, one will pore over Zen texts with meticulous scrutiny even when satiated by a full meal.
8. Generally, regarding human affairs and the events of the times, there must be karma that causes things to be as they are between what is agreeable and what is disagreeable.
Karma is precisely destiny (*niyati*). If one believes in circumstances but does not believe in destiny, then a hundred stirrings of emotion will arise. Therefore, the Perfected Person—
One knows that human sentiments and the vicissitudes of worldly events can seize one's resolve; therefore, one must first exhaustively investigate principle (*li*).
When principle is exhausted, vision becomes settled. Once vision is settled, the shifting transformations of human sentiments and worldly events cannot rob one of their resolve.

With resolve thus established, even if one has not yet reached the state of responding without a mind to the so-called alternation of life and death, honor and disgrace before one, [one remains steadfast].
Yet, if one maintains my intent, accords with principle, restrains the emotions, and applies effort without timidity, then the emotions will naturally vanish and principle will daily unfold.

As principle unfolds daily, the nature must be thoroughly penetrated; "thorough" means to the very limit. Therefore it is said: "Exhausting principle and fully penetrating nature"—this is a single path of discourse.
Previously, you repeatedly raised the matter of the "direct mind," as if there were some separate oral instruction not to be transmitted, using such bland talk merely to block people's way.
You set it aside without further inquiry; yet, when encountering matters that do not suit your fancy, you immediately find yourself unable to endure being treated with contempt by others.
To then wish to risk one's life and settle the matter of victory or defeat with another—how could this be the conduct of a great gentleman? Therefore it is said:
"I exist" means that I am within heaven and earth; "no-self" means that heaven and earth are within me.
If one’s upright mind cannot sincerely believe in the principle of spiritual no-self and instead forcibly constrains itself with the notion of self, then this darkness will never turn into dawn.
Reflecting upon this point, even I, a withered man of the wilds, still bring forth these words of detachment. I fear that within this detachment there may yet exist something that is not detached.
To Zhou Jinyu:
The lay practitioner has visited me three times; one may say he is most diligent. Yet, beholding my physical form is not as good as attaining my mind.
Now tell me, what is my mind? Horses neigh by the willow trees as the spring breeze warms; People face the *dharma-flower* as the moon of wisdom cools.
I am able to present this. Let us meet again before it is too late.

I send this to Miao Zhongchun regarding a man’s single journey through the world: ultimately, what matter is of the utmost importance? Even the section on performing repentance—if one acts according to one's own whims...

I shall resist this consciousness. It is better not to bow at all; yet once I have bowed, I have surrendered my very life, gouging out my heart and cutting open my gallbladder to wail in lamentation before the image.
When evil habits prevail, one must turn them back directly and immediately. Once turned back, there must not be even a moment’s interruption; for as soon as there is an interruption—
It is just like mercury that feigns death only to revive; it must undergo both horizontal and vertical smelting within the fires of favor and adversity.
Only when one reaches the point where death is truly realized can one be joined with Shen Ji'an.
The Buddhas and Patriarchs have said: "All sentient beings cross over birth and death because of mental conceptions (*saṃjñā*), and they undergo birth and death because of mental conceptions.
Now, those who have not yet attained the ultimate fruit claim that mental conceptions should be utterly eliminated;

this is because they do not understand that mental conceptions are both the thief and the son. It is like a sharp sword: if one grasps it to rob others, it is used as a weapon by a thief; if one grasps it...

Saving sentient beings is the functioning of the Way. It is precisely through these thoughts that one employs them to deliberate upon the Buddha-dharma—contemplating again and again, recollecting and reflecting back and forth, until one no longer knows how it came to be.

When the thoughts of sentient beings have been transformed into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, only then can one speak of the spontaneous manifestation of liberation. If you have not yet reached this stage, you must remain firm in your contemplation; do not [slacken].
A Brief Note on the Dharma of Overcoming Sloth. Reply: I, [Name], have received your gracious letter.

I am informed that your beloved daughter has recently passed away; while you celebrate her promotion, you are beset by much turmoil. At this time of intense heat, your emotions must be difficult to bear.
I, a humble man from beyond the clouds, am unable to alleviate your lifelong toil and suffering; I can do nothing but heave long sighs.
Nevertheless, I, this poor monk, also venture to offer congratulations to your Excellency. For all that gathers as myriad sufferings arises from craving;
once craving has perished, the root of suffering is already uprooted. Furthermore, the deceased no longer loves those who remain alive and has departed forever, yet the living still love them.

And so they weep for them. If weeping could cause them to return to life, then it would be appropriate to weep; but if weeping does not necessarily cause them to return to life, what benefit is there in weeping?
Formerly, there was a scholar whose son died, and his grief did not cease. Because he suspected that his intense sorrow might obstruct the Way, he asked Miaoxi:

"If a child dies and one’s grief is excessive, does it not obstruct the Way? Miaoxi [replied]: *Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "Miaoxi," indicating the response from the master is missing from the source.*
He said: "If one does not feel pain at the death of their child, they are like a wolf or a jackal. Comparing the words of Miaoxi with my own speech today, my words may seem unfeeling;
yet if one examines them to the ultimate conclusion, there may indeed be some道理 (principle) therein. May Your Excellency ponder this.

As for your future movements to the north, I imagine there will naturally be a settled course. However, I have further things to say. An official who presides over the Ministry of Justice (*Sikou*) must grasp..."

Regarding the handle of life and death, if one can exercise a single act of compassion and sacrifice a lifetime of toil to save even a few people who ought not to die, this too is an inconceivable merit.
Furthermore, if one can administer the prisons with humanity, then both spirits and men will be pleased and submit.

When spirits and men are pleased and submit, then yin and yang will be harmonious and compliant. When yin and yang are harmonious and compliant, then the harvests of the year will be abundant. The harvests of the year...
When grain is abundant, the people’s desire for life becomes weighty. When the people’s desire for life is weighty, it is easy to apply punishments and teachings.
If punishments and teachings can be effectively applied, they will greatly contribute to the way of governance. Why must one linger in hesitation?
Having long relied upon the Way, I venture to offer this exhortation. Whether it is appropriate or not is also a matter of laying bare my heart.
I reply: I have received your letter, Layman. Having read it twice, there is nothing among your doubts or observations that is not made clear. As it is said:
"If I am without mind, all else is understood. Alas! Is this mind so easily absent? Even if one could, in that very moment, [attain it]—
There is none. Nor is this the primary matter here. Furthermore, it is said: "To realize that afflictions are themselves bodhi.
This is certainly a source of doubt, and it further gives rise to great terror in the lay practitioner. In the past, Master Fayen Yi served Changqing for a very long time;
only later, upon seeing the venerable Dizang, did he finally reach full penetration. Changqing’s eminent disciples, Masters Zhao and Fang, were both dissatisfied with this.
Yan led the assembly and questioned him, saying, "Whose incense are you burning, Master? Yigong replied, "Dizang. Yan said, "How can you betray your former teacher?
Yan added, "I do not understand Changqing’s phrase: 'Among the myriad phenomena, the body alone is revealed. Zhaor said, "Ask me; I shall resolve it for you.
Yan asked, "'The body alone is revealed'—does this negate the myriad phenomena, or does it not negate them?"
Xiang Fang said, "I do not reject it. Master Yi pointed two fingers and said, "Two. I ask you, layman: since you do not reject it, why does it then become two?
If you say that a mind arises within non-rejection and thus falls into dualistic emotion, then it becomes two.
With such a perspective, you wish to grasp the nostrils of the Dharma-eye; this is like wearing the *guanzhangfu* cap while trying to convert the people of Yue."
How could it possibly be "just so"? If Master Fang does not strike it down, there will be a scene of total embarrassment. Thus, for you, layman, affliction is itself bodhi;
yet if he does not strike it down, you must simply resolve to face it. I do not know what plan you, layman, have devised to extricate yourself and leap over this field of embarrassment.
If a person truly knows that birth and death are of the utmost gravity, they must certainly settle this matter once and for all. Furthermore—

Severing in a single sitting all ordinary understandings that people commonly arrive at, swallow a flavorless pill—regardless of whether it has flavor or not, regardless of whether there is awakening or not.
Chew it daily without breaking it; add to this chewing monthly. Chew it monthly without breaking it;
add to this chewing yearly. If you cannot break it even after chewing for years, then even if you must leave this life unfinished, how could you fail in future lives?
If you break through this, you may enter and gain admittance into the Sangha. However, if you lack such resolve and such fortitude, do not bring it up at all.
Although you cannot set foot within it, you should nevertheless apply your spirit to searching through the essential inner scriptures;
once you have attained even a single point of understanding, the path will naturally become refined, and coarse, floating habitual tendencies will spontaneously [dissolve].
It is a clearing away. Once the coarse habits have been cleared away, the spiritual root (linggen) will naturally flourish and grow luxuriantly, nourished by the irrigation of the waters of Prajñā.
Only then can one seek a genuine fruit from the hands of a master; in the end, this will not be difficult. It is hard to exhaust my meaning with pen and tongue;
if we have the opportunity to meet in person, I shall take it up again, for it would not be a burden. Having completed this...

"You are all like insects and vermin; I too must exercise patience. If I am not patient, not only will the weeds before the hall grow a full ten feet deep, but you shall surely see Da-guan’s life brought to its end at the hands of you wretched karma-ghosts."
I said to Feng Kaizhi:

"How is it that before this sudden birth there was neither Buddha nor sentient being, and certainly no 'self' or 'other'? Yet, how is it that after this sudden birth, the faculties and consciousness of ordinary beings become mundane;
as soon as they are stained by the minor pleasures of humans and devas, they shift their original vows from many lifetimes past? [What of] those original vows?"

Now that you have moved away, it is not merely that minor pleasures will be difficult to enjoy for long; I fear that Ox-Head and A-p’ang already hold their cauldrons, boiling water, and glowing coals, waiting for you there for some time.

As for one’s original vow: since you call yourself a disciple of the Buddha, if you do not take it as your own responsibility to open up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, then nothing would be better than to dwell deep in the clouds and within layered ravines, finding contentment in leisurely seclusion. Why trouble yourself by [seeking fame]?

One’s feet tread upon the dust of the world; one provokes the yellow-headed barbarians and allows their eyes to glare with insolence. These words concern the distinction between our respective paths of renunciation and worldly involvement;
it is indeed thus. If one is a bodhisattva remaining at home, it is not so: where there are parents, one serves them as parents; where there is a sovereign, one regards the sovereign as paramount.
Should one not forget their original vow, then they may even take that sovereign and those parents as their golden ramparts and thorny defenses.
With manifold and skillful means, he protected and upheld the True Vehicle. He cast gain and loss beyond the waves of worldly emotion and transformed benefit and harm within the ocean of his vows.
His mind was like space; his bones were as adamantine as vajra. Through a thousand grindings and ten thousand twists, he remained firm and unyielding.
If one acts thus, the resolve to protect the Dharma will increase twofold, immeasurable sins will be extinguished, and immeasurable merit will grow. How [could this not be so]?

For this reason, one's original vow does not waver; it is because the roots of goodness grow silently and steadily. Therefore, when compared with the six realms of ordinary beings, evil is abundant while goodness is meager.
In this age of scant virtue, it is unfortunate not to have encountered the True or Semblance Dharma, but instead to have met the Age of Dharma Decline (Mappō).
Those who possess even a slight degree of spiritual capacity will find their hair standing on end upon slow and careful reflection. Beyond this, what further words need be said? Guest.
At the beginning of the year, I met the Master at Jixiang; we met again at Jinghai. After our parting, the Daoist practitioner fell ill in Xunyang for over a hundred days.
Upon the arrival of the new year, I traveled to Caoxi to pay respects to the Sixth Patriarch, and then purchased a boat to return east.
Suddenly, a momentous event arose: it was my duty to travel north to clear his innocence. Having sent letters to the various officials, I returned once more to the south. It happened that...

Furthermore, it so happens that you, Master, have arrived here. It seems that by the power of the causal conditions of our respective original vows, we have met as if by appointment, even though no such meeting was expected.
For a practitioner of the Way not to take the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision as his primary concern is to forget his original vow;

he would be a model for those who sever their own roots of goodness. For you, Master, not to take the Great Dharma—which is like a golden fortress—as your foundational wheel is likewise [to forget your vow].
"The appearance of the ox-headed *āpāṅga* as a plaything—my words are not false. Master, you should take your original vow to heart; do not neglect it. (2)

The previous draft was cluttered with coarse language; its narration stirred up dust, failing not only to illuminate the hidden brilliance of the former masters, but actually obscuring their true character.
If one were to attain the Bodhisattva’s mind, they would clear away the redundancies and refine the coarseness;
where the narration stirred up dust, they would blow it away with the celestial wind and wash it clean with divine rain, thereby bringing forth [the truth].

Revealing profound radiance amidst chaos and restoring the original essence after dispersion, you have caused our Venerable Dragon-Head to re-manifest the Samādhi of the Physical Body for a thousand ages and once again extend the mark of the broad and long tongue throughout the ten voids.
Thus, the flame of the Great Enlightened One shall never lack the brilliance of eminent monks, and the Garden of Awakening shall possess the light of the transmitted Mind-Lamp. I, this poor monk...

I have reflected upon this repeatedly. While there are many who can speak in your stead and never fail to do so, as for pruning the superfluous, transforming the vulgar, skillfully stirring the celestial winds and ocean waves, refreshing these withered bones, and restoring them to their original nature while cleaving open the hidden radiance—this cannot be achieved by any pen but yours.

Otherwise, the literary form will lack substance, and substance will lack literary form, such that the path of principle and phenomena would stray from its course. I pray only that you, Master, will consider my plea and uphold the precepts.

The Dharma Altar is that which sustains the life-force of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. It serves to shake off my sense-bases and their objects, to fortify the power of my wisdom and vows, and is the Great Dance of the Pen-Point Samādhi.
May it bring fulfillment to the Elder Fu, universally manifesting the form-body to benefit beings boundlessly. How fortunate!
This old man of Ngoc San City has never known illness before; yet suddenly it has arisen. When he encounters all manner of heat, it is like the conflagration at the end of an eon;
when it is cold, it is no different from the icy hells; and when cold and heat alternate, his suffering becomes even more intense than that.
When alternating bouts of cold and heat arise, they cause this old man’s fragmentary consciousness to suddenly fail to sustain itself. Thus, illness begins;

though it seems to emerge without cause, its arising must have a source. Generally, one traces illness back to karma, traces karma back to the mind, and traces the mind back to that which is "not-mind.
Once traced to this point, the one who performs the tracing encounters "not-mind" and comes to rest.

As for those who were cold and now feel cold, or hot and now feel hot, they cease to feel so as soon as [the illness] subsides; only those who from the beginning were neither cold nor hot remain as they always were.
Such words have never been leaked to those who have not suffered this illness. How would they differ from wooden shavings or iron nails?
I thank you for your distant inquiry, and I reply to you according to the truth.
I have received a letter from Wang Yutai and Zhongfu, which has greatly relieved my long-standing anxieties. However, in your letter you state that practicing Chan is not easy;
if one merely waits for enlightenment with the mind while indulging in greed and anger and neglecting the work of gradual cultivation, will this not result in a double failure?
One can only subdue it by following conditions. This implies that if you realize it through words, you are merely bending our school's tradition;
it teaches one to awaken to the mind as equal [to all things] and to let go of habitual tendencies. When I previously discussed this with Yutai, such a thing had never occurred.
I do not know where Yutai obtained this kind of understanding. If the true mind seeks to transcend birth and death, one must not deliberate with others.

One must attain it; one must personally seek a clear understanding for oneself. Although I am but a blade of grass within the School of the Gate (the Chan/Zen tradition), when it comes to the ground of insight (*dṛṣṭibhūmi*), I have never failed to rely upon the teachings of the Vehicle as my authoritative evidence.

During Śākyamuni’s causal stage, before he encountered Dīpaṃkara, his arduous cultivation over many kalpas would ultimately not have constituted the cause for Buddhahood. Only after encountering Dīpaṃkara did he achieve Buddhahood by uttering a single "Namo Buddha. This is so.

The principle is clear, pure, and easy to understand; it represents one aspect of the ground of insight (*darśana-bhūmi*). The Buddhas have designated this as the "great causal condition" (*mahā-kāraṇa-pratyaya*).

Yet, people nowadays give rise to views according to their own inclinations: some focus exclusively on seeking rebirth in the Pure Land, while others recite mantras and sutras, claiming that by "borrowing conditions" they can refine themselves and dissolve their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Little do they realize that if their ground of insight is not thorough, how could the Pure Land ever be intimately realized? As for the practice of recitation...

Reciting incantations and sutras—how is this different from pouring water onto ice? All such acts merely bind one to karma and provide no benefit whatsoever. An ancient master said: "Only after attaining awakening does one truly practice.

However, there are various interpretations regarding this so-called "awakening": there is awakening through understanding (*jie-wu*), awakening through cultivation (*xiu-wu*), and awakening through realization (*zheng-wu*).

Regarding awakening through understanding: it occurs when, through the long-term power of hearing and being permeated by the scriptural teachings, the mind gradually opens and becomes clear. Furthermore, it is said:

Regarding those who attain realization through understanding based on the penetration [of the teachings]: they have previously possessed the熏 (vāsanā) of hearing and have once attained a slight degree of comprehension, yet had not yet obtained actual experiential enjoyment.
Now, having emerged into this life, they may practice with some effort, whereupon their doubts are suddenly severed and experiential enjoyment manifests before them.

Regarding those who attain realization through direct awakening: their faculties are sharp and keen; without shifting for even a single kṣaṇa, their habitual tendencies dissolve along with their awakening, and they become Buddhas on the spot.

Now, although Yu Tai is currently unable to cultivate realization or attain awakening, he should nevertheless thoroughly study one section of the scriptural teachings in order to seek intellectual understanding.
Through the power of this cultivation, habitual tendencies will diminish of their own accord, even without seeking such diminution.

Nevertheless, this too must take realization as its primary goal; it has merely come to this point because one's efforts have not been sufficiently vigorous. Therefore, one should model oneself after the highest standards.

It is sufficient to attain the Middle Way alone. If one merely follows conditions to subdue the mind while utterly lacking the aspiration for enlightenment, then habitual tendencies will ultimately never be eliminated, and the path of Buddhahood will ultimately never be accomplished. Why is this?
Planting hemp will certainly not produce rice; thus, to take a lower standard as a model is not its true cause.
Reply to Layman Yuezi: I have received the honor of your letter. Having read it, how great is your ambition and how profound your anxiety! It causes my spirit to remain in constant distress.

That the Dharma and the Way are in decline, and that we of our generation are but vain and mediocre, is indeed as you have said. Reflecting upon my own dullness, I find that the Way does not overcome my habitual tendencies; my talent and understanding—
Nor am I very far from them; I have mingled indistinctly within the forest of black robes (*kṛṣṇavarṇa*), offering no benefit to the Teaching.

People suffer because they do not know themselves; if one can know oneself, then other delusive thoughts will naturally cease. Though I am dull-witted and not quick of mind, in recent years I have come to know myself somewhat:
my shortcomings abound while my strengths are insufficient. The world loves flattery, whereas I love straightforwardness; who can tolerate me? When people do not tolerate me...

Yet I am unaware of this myself. To take a square and cast it into a circle—how could it not be placed upside down? Moreover, my coarse and boisterous nature remains as before, and my stubbornness and license do not shift.
Those who know me think that there is nothing else within my breast, so they find it unnecessary to compare; those who do not know me [view it otherwise].
Considering me to be arrogant and lacking in evidence, they regretted not having cast me into death immediately for their own gratification.

For this reason, I, being dull-witted, ought only to feign madness and pretend to be deranged. Whether in mountain forests or cities, I shall eat my fill and sleep at ease, merely prolonging this life.
I am merely failing to repay your lofty friendship; how can I not feel shame? Your Reverence is advanced in years, yet I, Zijin, have been a guest for many years.
I have been unable to provide you with delicious food and drink, nor have I been able to attend to you in person during our acquaintance.
For long I have harbored grievances while starving on the ruins of my old mountain, my single body bound in fetters thousands of li away. Among all those who know me, how could this be...?
Is it not a pity that some hear of this yet do not act with urgency, or see it yet feel no pain?

Judging from this, one must ask whether those previously mentioned who claimed to know Prince Zijin truly knew him. Thus it is said: "It is not easy to know one another; it is only easy not to know one another.
Nevertheless, there may be those who deeply understand Prince Zijin, yet lack the power to act; while those who possess such power may not necessarily [share his insight].
We know each other well. It is truly true that Master Zijin’s destiny was fated to be one of misfortune.

I have kept this hidden, brooding over it in the intervals between my meditation and recitation, and even the green mountains and white clouds turned pale at the mention of it to this old man; how much more so for those with feelings?

Furthermore, Master Zijin lamented that both worldly and world-transcending dharmas were simultaneously perishing and could not be sustained; in his indignation, he desired to shave his head and don the monastic robes. However, as for the matter of shaving one's head—

If one's insight is not penetrating and one’s resolve is not firm, it is likewise not easy [to succeed]. Reflect upon this deeply. Sun Wu said, "Fewer calculations are not as good as more calculations;
how much less so having no calculations at all? I suspect that the words of Prince Jin (Zi Jin) would certainly not have been uttered lightly.
If Yu was not prepared with many calculations, how could he have acted so readily? Formerly, Duke Cui Zhao asked Chan Master Qin of Mount Jingshan, "My disciple has managed to emerge..."
"Shall I leave home [to become a monk]? Yan Junping asked. Huiqin replied with a stern expression, "Leaving home is the business of a great man; it is not something that generals or ministers can do.
When I first read this, I thought the Venerable Huiqin was merely relying on his own lofty character to disregard worldly fame.

However, upon verifying it for myself, I realized that this elder spoke these true words from a heart of absolute sincerity; indeed, he did not deceive me. For how could the roots of worldly emotion be so deeply entrenched? How could...
Mount Kunlun and Mount Sumeru may be compared; the surging waves of consciousness are like the surging waters of the ocean—how could they ever be equaled by the Min River?

Although the positions of general and minister are not for those who are not among the human elite, yet even one who lacks great talent and insight can still perform these duties if they act with focused resolve.
Only the path of renunciation is such that, relying on a brief lifetime, one seeks to uproot the emotional roots of kalpas of existence. Relying on...
With the forelegs of a mantis, one wishes to bale out the waters of the Cang and Min rivers; only by reflecting in stillness will one first know what is possible or not.
Gu Ziji considers my words to be mere excrescences, and laughs heartily as he cuts them away; I have no regrets.
Qingliang Dayaya is not to be equaled by any other famous mountains. If one could set aside worldly affairs for a moment to ascend it, what joy could be greater than this?

Furthermore, there are one or two matters concerning the Dharma that I am eager to discuss in person. The circumstances regarding Tanzhe have been detailed in Jianmo’s letter and are not repeated here.
If one is not proficient in the School of Nature (Xingzong) with Layman Shiguang of Linchuan, Wuzhou, one cannot avoid falling into the snare of the obstacle of phenomena (shizhang).

If one is not proficient in the School of Characteristics (Xiangzong), one cannot avoid falling into the snare of the obstacle of principle (lizhang). If one does not fully comprehend the School of Chan (Chanzong), one cannot avoid falling into the snare of "Lord Ye’s painted dragon. In recent times...

Black and white [views] alike lack the mind that is sorrowful and far-sighted. Thus, there is neither nature nor non-nature, neither characteristics nor non-characteristics, and neither Chan nor non-Chan.
Furthermore, regarding the three schools of Nature, Characteristics, and Chan, each has its own fundamental tenets, such as the Eight Teachings of Tiantai and the Five Teachings of Xianshou.
In all these matters, there is not the slightest point that can be disordered. How could it be that the Chan school alone lacks a fundamental principle?

If the Chan school were without a fundamental principle, then would not the statement by Yantou Quanhuo—that "the fundamental principle has been understood, yet there is originally no real dharma"—be considered reckless?
Master Huo was a dragon-elephant of the Chan school; how could he have acted so hastily?

It is only because people of later generations have coarse and floating minds and inferior faculties that they fail to understand the standards of the ancient worthies and the complete mastery of the masters.
If one were to know this, one would surely feel a burning heat upon the face; I consider such a person’s heart to be dead and incapable of revival.
Second: Once you have reached the fruit of the path, being able to set aside worldly affairs and devote yourself single-mindedly to pure practice (*śukla-karma*) is the primary principle.

However, I fear that if the principle of pure practice has not been thoroughly penetrated, one will inevitably undergo the defiled seeds of many lifetimes; with current practice thus hindered and frustrated, it will be difficult for one's actions to ultimately correspond to one's words. Great!

If you have set your mind upon the practice of pure karma, by all means do not grow weary or find it tedious. If you grow weary, your realization of the nature and characteristics of reality will ultimately fail to be lofty and clear.

To exert oneself in the practice of pure karma with such a lackluster realization is impossible; it can never succeed in subduing the seeds and active manifestations of defilement, nor in nourishing and activating the functional power of pure seeds.
It is like the story of Su Qin, who wished to rely on his verbal eloquence to obtain an official post, yet when he reached the gate... [text truncated]

My meager gold was exhausted, and I returned home hungry. Only then did I realize that I had initially left because of weariness with worldly affairs, and in the end, I had returned for the same reason.

Indeed, when one is weary of worldly affairs, one cannot contemplate deeply or look far ahead. When one cannot contemplate deeply or look far ahead, one will certainly be unable to grasp the intent of those who established these words.
If the intent of those who established these words is not grasped, then even if one’s belly is full of the *Shi* and *Shu*, it is of no avail.
Though one’s speech may flow like a rushing river, it is ultimately nothing more than dregs and lees. One might obtain an official post through such dregs, but can an official truly govern the world?
It is merely a matter of conforming to the times and occupying a rank. Thus, Xun Qing, driven by indignation and hunger, returned once more to search for the books stored in his home.
As for those who suspended their beams and pricked their thighs, who abandoned sleep and forgot food, they were only able to grasp the meaning of the scriptures after emerging from such toil;
only then could they fulfill their aspirations. If even those seeking fame and office were thus diligent, how much more so should it be for one seeking the supramundane Dharma?

Considering this, if one’s realization is not lofty and clear, it will not be easy to cultivate pure karma. Reflect on this. Furthermore, regarding the path of pure karma, among monks and laypeople in recent times—
It is a refuge for fugitives and runaways. The three lions should undergo profound self-examination and remorse. My old age is thus filled with such distress; it is not that I lack insight. Third:
Since our parting at Linru, nearly a year has passed in an instant. The light and shadows within the boat appear as solitary reflections; truly, this is but a single subtle atom.
Enveloping ten generations—if this is indeed so—then Da and Linchuan have never been separated from one another.

Nevertheless, regarding the critical juncture between the two "conformities" and the one "reversal," if one cannot yet cast off their arms [to cross over], then nature transforms into emotion, and emotion in turn becomes nature.
The explanation for why this is so must certainly be investigated with great urgency. Furthermore, it is because of this that those close to us, whether black or white, rely upon it.
This is merely a matter of circumstance. Otherwise, for a guest beyond the mundane world, to sever ties with things is to be lofty; to be stained by things is to be base.
This, too, is the natural course of events.
4. "The true essence of the teaching in this land resides in purity within hearing sounds. Hearing sounds is precisely the samādhi of letters;

this samādhi is also called the Prajñā of Letters, and it is also called the Buddha-nature as the conditional cause. It is like the example of carving the Tripitaka. This is what is correctly [meant].
This refers to the *pratyaya-buddha-dhātu* (the Buddha-nature as the condition). Generally, sentient beings habituate themselves to impermanence;

when this is perfumed by the *pratyaya-sattva-dhātu* (the sentient-being nature as the condition), the knowledge and vision of sentient beings manifest. When it is perfumed by the *pratyaya-buddha-dhātu*, the knowledge and vision of the Buddha manifest.
The perfuming agent is like the wind, and that which is perfumed is like a valley. In this Sahā world, [this is realized] not through words or samādhi.
He inspired the Buddha-dharma so that the Dharma could be practiced with peace. Fifth:

Amidst the urgency of his departure, there was nothing he failed to attend to; from this, one can know the depth of his devotion. This was not possible without having long cultivated the spiritual roots.
Furthermore, those who possess a profound resolve and regard fame and reputation as spit and snot are incapable [of such a task].

However, it is simply that I cannot bear to let even small virtues and minor conditions go to waste during the Shiguang era; my intention is not to neglect small virtues, but to ensure they become great by attending to their details.
As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "Because sentient beings have various desires, the Buddha employs various causes, conditions, parables, and..."
To guide them toward benefit is precisely this same intent. Speaking from this perspective, the only concern is that sentient beings lack various kinds of desire;

if they possess such desires, then the principle that "there is no water outside of ice" is established. Once this principle is established, the further concern arises that there may be little ice and much water.
Please reflect upon this deeply. Lately, among both the clergy and the laity, there are some who do not understand this meaning.

Although one may not discriminate between types of goodness, if one practices it with diligence, this results only in the retributive fruits of humans and devas, as well as the conditions for Māras and externalists.
