In the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), all manner of wholesome deeds are viewed as a burden; they are discarded like ashes for fear that they might burn the practitioner.
Therefore, regardless of whether a good deed is great or small, if one regards it directly through the contemplation of "mind-only," then virtuous conduct will invariably be spiritual. Indeed.
Thus, how could toil and weariness alone not be divine? This is addressed to the layman Wang, a wild man of the forest.

By nature he is frugal and upright, sparing in his desires for worldly things; his conduct is leisurely and unassuming, which serves only to further enhance the brilliance of the eminent and talented.

In these jests and discourses, I have failed to contribute to the profound transformation of the holy lineage. Though I have taken refuge in this solitary and pure abode, how could I forget the desolate shores?
Having briefly bid farewell to the white clouds, I now feel ashamed before the crimson cliffs. As I prepare to turn my staff and bowl back toward the world, I venture to inform you of my departure.
I beg you only to fulfill the nature of this ape-like creature and to illuminate its dog-like ignorance, so that it may return to its original state and forever offer prayers for your long life,
together with Mr. Lou.
Since our parting, many cycles of cold and heat have passed. Those who have departed cannot be pursued. Whenever I reflect upon this, Master Lou is never far from my sight.

Master Lou, Master Lou, you are but a being in this world of Saṃsāra with its defects. Because it is defective, one can never fully satisfy one's desires; because it is a pitfall, one can never truly escape.
Since it is so difficult to find what one desires, where could one go that is not suffering? It is so difficult to achieve liberation.

Detachment! What could one go toward that would not lead to being dragged down? Thus, the multitude forms the notion of attainment regarding the pit of defects and forms the contemplation of detachment;
it is like grasping at empty space—it only increases one's own weariness. Only the realized one knows that the body is not "mine" and that the mind arises in pursuit of objects;
therein, birth and death are empty without being rejected, and likes and dislikes are extinguished without being discarded.
Transformation: what was called a pit of defects is suddenly made into a land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).
Yet, if one possesses clarity but lacks courage, the dual attachments of body and mind will likewise not be easily dispelled.

Thus, when the ancients walked upon jagged ice and traversed the edge of a sword, it was because the gateway of birth and death is not easily shattered, and the pit of love and hatred is not easily escaped. Therefore—

There is this analogy: if one is unable to attain liberation regarding these two [extremes], then to discourse on the profound and speak of the subtle is what Mount Mui called "liberation through the mouth.

Unless one actually enters the water, a tall person is difficult to see. If Lou Sheng can truly bear not to betray the compassionate concern of the Way-man, he will surely find himself in a pit of defects;
there will come a day when the wish-fulfilling jewel within him emits light. The Way-man goes begging for food.

In Jiangling, I happened to encounter the Venerable Master [Name] of Your Noble County— an unexpected sound of footsteps in an empty valley. As the Venerable Master returns to the East, I append these words to urge him on,
entrusting them to Gu Rupi.
Generally speaking, among the various craftsmen and artisans, there is no principle by which one can achieve mastery in their art if they do not allow their own mind to die;
for if the mind does not die, it is impossible to reach the pinnacle of refinement. Why is this?

It is because when the mind dies, all former defilements lose their stubborn hold, and the original mind becomes fully realized, such that the spirit is no longer exhausted by its own exertion. However, this "death" of the mind must necessarily be preceded by...

It exists because of sensory objects (*viṣaya*). Since it exists due to preceding objects, if one could master the non-substantiality of objects such that the mind does not perish, such a thing has never occurred.
Furthermore, those who claim to master the non-substantiality of objects are merely like those who pretend to master them; they have not truly distanced themselves from objects.
All such cognitions and views that merely pretend to master objects are called "mercury-elixir" (*yao-gong*); just as silver flies away when it encounters fire, how could such things ever endure?
This is my concern for you. From this day forward, you must reach the realm of true penetration. Then, your fame, achievement, and very life shall surely fulfill your aspirations.
You must take pains not to辜负 (disappoint) the compassionate thoughts of the man who has attained the Way.

Regarding Master Ma Junhou’s statement that there are two kinds of rain—rain from Heaven and rain from man: that which falls without prayer is rain from Heaven; that which falls through prayer is rain from man.
This is the established teaching of the ancients. Furthermore, when a person prays to Heaven, it depends upon virtue and not upon rank; nor is this anything extraordinary.

This art is possible; it requires nothing more than sincerity. Within the Great Canon, there are three fascicles of the *Scripture on Invoking Rain*, which is a sublime remedy for drought, born of the Great Awakened Sage’s compassion and utmost sincerity.

Since Your Excellency already holds the common people in your thoughts, if your sincerity issues forth from within, its essence will penetrate heaven and earth, and rain can certainly be brought about. However, you must select those of pure precepts and conduct to perform the invocation.

A high monk was appointed to establish an altar and purify the ground, performing the rites according to the prescribed ritual manual (*ko*). As for the method of invoking rain, it was made a condition that rain must necessarily be obtained.
A monk from Longxing Temple was capable in his recitations and was quite sincere; his conduct was well-regarded by his fellow villagers, so he was respectfully invited to preside over the altar.

Furthermore, he was granted the rank of an official monk (*sengguan*) to assist and manage the proceedings. After the altar was established, another Chan monk was engaged to perform the rites night after night.

A single banquet of *yankou* (flaming-mouth) *houshi* (measures of food) was offered, with rain falling as the limit [of the efficacy]. This is because the origin of such severe drought must surely lie in what has been suppressed.
When that which is suppressed cannot be extended, one harbors resentment, and from this resentment, a rebellious and contrary energy arises.
When there is a resonance below, the heavens above must respond accordingly. If one does not rely upon the compassionate light of the Great Awakened One and exert the power of the spirits...
As for incantations and the local lords who guard the soil, if one humbles oneself and prays with devotion, then what is bent cannot be straightened and resentment cannot be resolved;

how then could rain be obtained? There are many kinds of resentment, which are difficult to describe exhaustively; yet by inferring from human sentiment, they can be fully understood through the mind.
I only pray that Your Excellency will greatly empty the spirit within your inner chamber and illuminate the innermost thoughts of this rustic man. Regarding everything within the altar...
All expenses and items for requisites shall depend solely on what is required by the presiding master of the altar.
At the various public offices, one should provide offerings for the sacred rank of the Tathāgata Great Compassionate Cloud-Born (Mahākāruṇika-megha-udbhava).

As for the orders issued to each province and county to prohibit slaughter, these too were all under the direction of Your Excellency. Furthermore, the prohibition of slaughter in most places is merely in name and lacks substance; even children and young students [are aware of this].

One cannot deceive with what is untrue, much less before the lofty and brilliant Heaven. This matter must also be proclaimed with expressions of deep sorrow and distress, so that it may be made known throughout the prefectures and districts.
This is of the utmost urgency, of the utmost urgency.
The Collected Works of Old Man Zibo, Volume Twenty-Four;
The Collected Works of Old Man Zibo, Volume Twenty-Five.
Read by Hanshan Deqing of the Ming Dynasty.
Poem (Five-Syllable Verse): Staying at Hongfu Temple, Recalling the Past The floating life is like lightning or dew;
how could there be the longevity of mountains and rivers? Mount Mojia rises high into the clouds, enduring as long as heaven and earth.
Who was it that spread such a splendid feast? At midnight, he wielded his bronze ladle; chasing the deer, he feared no peril; seizing the gold, he cared not for disgrace.
The Huo-tuo River flows on eternally, yet he lay his lodging beneath the peaks of a thousand mountains. He had no leisure to think of his own kin; his extravagant heart was like a vast marsh.
How lofty were his hegemonic achievements! Yet the path of rectitude makes it difficult to keep one's mouth shut. In this wild temple, the autumn wind is clear;
the bell on the stupa releases its lion’s roar. Before the lamp, I hear the grasshoppers; once more, I am moved to sorrow for the *púliǔ* tree.
In this mountain retreat, the bird-path winds and straightens; stretching afar, it leads into profound stillness. Withered pines perform the dance of dragons; strange rocks seem like standing monks.
Fragrant clouds soften the ground beneath one’s feet; the sound of the clear chime rings out clearly. An old monk smiles as he comes to meet me—a welcome beyond words, yet full of meaning.
Having stayed overnight, I may now depart from the hall; as a rustic, I have no fixed intent to come. How could I have an intention to go? Both coming and going are devoid of intent;

the white clouds know where they tend. A single path winds through the secluded bamboos; fallen leaves gather at the four eaves. Reflecting on this, the night dew is cold, and the grass insects chirp without ceasing.
**On the Azure Garden (Two Poems)** Without wind, the water is naturally still;
the still water reflects the vast void. The four banks are shrouded in mutual cool shade; how dense is the cover of the bamboos and ginkgos!
Swimming scales play at the treetops; the reflection of heaven appears inverted. The one who departs is likewise a recluse; those with such feelings find it difficult to exhaustively describe them.
The setting sun clarifies the deep blue garden; on the shallow creek, the orchid-wood oars stir the water.

I have chosen to dwell in the vast wilderness; here, in silence, there are no thoughts of the dusty world. At night, the distant bell is heard, its pure resonance pouring through my six sense-faculties.

By day, I read the scriptures of India, my mind wandering in a state of sublime clarity within the secluded window. A dog barks in the shade of peach blossoms; amidst the rippling waves of wheat, people pass to and fro.
I love most the clearing rain at evening; the empty forest is refreshed by the reflected light.
The Furuo Temple spans a cloud-bridge, while white clouds know no boundaries.
I break bamboo to make a light broom; though I sweep it several times, it closes again. The flowing spring strikes the rocks and roars.
Gazing at the peaks and ridges, their wonders stir my longing; yet, though I wish to go, I dare not hasten. An old monk acts as a bridge across the ford—will you fear coming and going?
The illness is bred by having a body; when the physical form falls, nothing remains but decay. Since the enlightened have realized this, what beauty or ugliness can there be in birth and death?
The sutras have ended and the stone chimes have also ceased; how could one hear the cries of roosters or dogs anymore?

Having risen from sleep in my quiet chamber by the Dragon Pond, still slightly drowsy, I wipe my eyes and step out through the meditation gate. The azure sky holds the high red sun; the light of the clouded mountains can be seen.
Leaning on the railing, I listen to the flowing spring. Upon the bridge, who is my companion? Beside the cliff stands a strange rock; facing me, the rock seems to dance.
The patch-robed monk standing nearby does not restrain it, yet he conceives jealousy toward the stone. You are originally a mindless thing; how could you understand the profound path?
In the past, Master Daosheng instructed you; now I intend to strike it down with my mallet. Between this one hatred and one love—tell me, who is the source of fortune and calamity?
To realize this is to attain the Buddha-mind; if you do not understand, you remain a great blockhead.

When he left Xiapei to pay his respects to the son of the Marquis of Liu, Zhang Liang, his spirit for striking down the Qin was like a ten-thousand-fathom rainbow. Yet, when he could suddenly humble himself, he advanced his shoes before the old man at the Bridge of Yi.

The old man grew angry and ultimately refused him entry. Yet he advanced again with the same resolve as before. Had it not been for one of heavenly and earthly capacity, his plan to repay the House of Han would have been too remote.

Once his merit in assisting the Han was accomplished, he transcended all and walked away with a casual wave of his arm. Having departed into the green mountains from which he never returned, he fulfilled his oath to the Red Pine (Chisong).
Mooring at Xiapi on a moonlit night, I suddenly heard the sound of flowing water. I still suspected that you, Master, were there; my feelings of gratitude were boundless.

Dwelling in the mountains by the Tanzhe Stream, where the crags and woods are deep, how could one hear the voice from the empty valley? When the frozen clouds suddenly thundered, who else but you would have had such a heart as the sun and moon?
Before the stupa, he releases radiant light; this illumination knows neither past nor present. The old man does not fail him; his influence exceeds all bounds.
If he can indeed not fail the old man, wherever he may be, he shall remain as distant and sublime as ever.

Baek Inam said: Who would say the mountain path is perilous? To me, I feel the mountain path is secluded and profound. In the empty forest, fallen leaves rustle; from the broken cliffs, cold streams cascade.
The winding trails are difficult to remember; amidst the leisurely clouds, one occasionally lingers. Towers and pavilions lean against the rocks; pines and cypresses grow old like coiled dragons.

Wiping away moss, I read the fragmentary inscriptions. How could Master Yuanyang have been among the common crowd? Through his five essays, he awakened to the essence of past and present; through his six matters, he put to shame the lords and princes.
The perilous peaks serve as its host, while jade-white snow floats in the magnetic bowls. The lotus-drip water-clock drips without ceasing; the board for the game of chess remains unfinished.
A mournful song, he departs trailing his staff; at the close of day, he cannot bear the autumn.
Sitting in meditation at night atop Shangfang Mountain, I observe the present circumstances:
upon my head I wear the hat of an ancient; in the night zazen, the pine needles weep with dew. Joyfully intoxicated by the vast expanse, I imagine this is the habit of many lifetimes.
Clouds lock the gates of Tuṣita; a person comes, parting the clouds to enter. How many tiers of jade ladders are there?

Grasping the iron ropes with urgency, one lifts the eyes to see the towers and terraces, where overlapping peaks and ridges rise steeply. The resonance of the bells pours through the azure void; the pure spring water is drawn by the Way-farer.
The water ended and the path was exhausted; meeting one another, we could only join our palms in reverence. After the tea, he brandished his fly-whisk, yet his profound discourse allowed no leisure.
Before the moon on Mount Zhongyan had set, I took my leave with a long bow. Greedy for sleep, I feared only the break of dawn; who would have cared again for wet clothes?
Sentiments for the Layman Jingguang Hua at Yintang on Tanzhe Mountain:
The paths of the world are full of rugged precipices; I dwell idly in these mountain ravines. Coming and going, there are only white clouds; Heaven and earth are likewise my thatched hut.

When thirsty, there is a spring from which to drink; to soothe hunger, pine needles serve as sustenance. As the bright moon rises over the eastern peak, I leisurely open and read the palm-leaf scriptures.

Upon realizing their essential meaning, I suddenly lose the sense of self; with an empty mind yet a full belly, I let go of the mediators of birth and death. To forget one’s own abilities—how could this be unique to me alone?
It is like an ancient precious mirror: when free of dust, its light naturally returns. Sitting by the pines for a long while, in a single moment, one becomes six.
The celestial waters were originally not far away; how could they not be the Five Indias? My traces of travel are difficult to retain; who will strike the *zhu* to offer me tea?
Though our meeting may yet be expected, mountains and rivers obstruct my sight. My restless longing knows no end; I unroll this scroll to entrust my thoughts to these few lines.
Rising at dawn on Xiao Peak, I find the heat of summer unbearable;
leaning on my staff by the shimmering stream, I happen upon a secluded shade where a gentle breeze stirs the fragrance of the forest flowers.
Fresh lotuses float upon the dews; idle clouds rest upon Xiao Hill. The distant mountains are already clear, and the far waters are likewise vast.
The sleeping gulls startle and then settle again; I and my self are both forgotten. In silence the flowers briefly fall; the water flows steadily, its murmur echoing through the corridors.
Though there is a mind that accords with sensory objects, it remains as the King of Dharmas. To inquire about the meaning of the West’s arrival, the reflection falls upon the empty hall.
At sunset, one returns from Longtan;
fame and profit are not the misty peaks. They draw people forward without refusal to travel far. Springs and rocks are no mere fine wine, yet they intoxicate me so that I know not how to return.
A wild laugh resounds from deep seclusion; the setting sun sinks behind the pine ridges.

Sitting in meditation at night in the Long Pine Hall, I settle beneath the trees in the courtyard. The grassy path is far removed from the dusty world. Sometimes birds converse with one another; no one comes to knock at the gate.

The sound of the river mingles with the rustle of pines; having finished my meal, I listen to the murmuring flow. As habitual tendencies are gradually washed away, the spirit-mansion seems to draw near to stillness.
Xu Xun was skilled at posing difficult questions, and Zhi Dun’s answers were never stingy. Do not ask about the moon over the city tower; at Xunyang, it shines upon the emerald coves.

Dwelling in the mountains, I already cherish the peaks and springs, which are inherently sublime; what need is there for artificial adornment? Beyond vegetarian food and drinking water, the white clouds can bring joy and solace.

I am ashamed of my own meager virtues as I speak freely, yet I secretly aspire to conduct that is perilously steadfast. Deer disperse and then gather again; I forget the classics and then think of them once more.
Longtime friends lament that the distance between us is too great; who else can we share the chewing of purple *zhī* fungi?
In midsummer, I have brought Jue-sheng to receive food amidst the lotuses on Mount Feng, idly taking our meal with this "rice-bag" (the practitioner).
Here we enjoy the cool breeze together: clouds and cranes nest in the lofty pines, while fish in the pond sport in the clear water.

If there is a mind, how can one attain the wondrous? If there is no thought, one falls into stagnant stillness. Ancient sages did not prize prior consciousness; simplicity is the very beginning of wisdom.
Crows returning to their roosts dot the evening smoke; with staff and sandals, my heart yearns for my native village.
Jue sheng was surprised that I had composed two rhymes on the difficult and rare *jiang* and *dong* tones, which were hard to follow;
I responded with these two verses:
A bright pearl is hidden within an old oyster, Floating and shimmering in the harbor of Wumen. One day, who shall cleave it open? Its perfect radiance shall shine upon the Buddha’s neck.

To discourse on the sutras, no tongue is needed; to point directly, one uses only the staff. Reclining with head high upon a crumbling cliff, the sound of pines and waves replaces the daytime lecture.

The pine-window does not prize crimson curtains; it constantly takes the clouds as its alleyway. When the rain ceases, the thousand mountains grow cold, and the flowing springs descend according to their natural course.

Woodland crows clamor as the evening sun sets; across the azure sky, a rainbow floats. Villages see cattle and sheep returning home; from where does that evening bell toll? Human life is but a brief sojourn;
when buried beneath the earth, there is no distinction between the wise and the dull-witted.
Inscription for Master Long’s Meditation Chamber at Guxiang Hermitage:
Painting of Plums Ten thousand trees are frozen to death; The withered branch flaunts the colors of spring. Midnight chill within the Zen chamber; A bright moon hangs by the side of the branches.
It is as if a dark fragrance floats; the faculty of smell cannot discern it. Zhi Lang has just returned from his meditative absorption; his emaciated form lies across his ribs.
To whom can this intention be told? The icy spirit finds its own kind. Salt and vinegar are not what he hoped for; in his final years, he shall ultimately dwell in the Buddha-land.

Lamenting that there is no one with whom I can share my thoughts, I see this body as a well beside a mound. I use my life-force as a rope to draw water; after long use, it will surely snap—who in this world understands this?

To those who have attained the Way, I owe a debt of gratitude; they constantly warn themselves whenever a thought arises. Birth and extinction are fundamentally of one essence; by seeing the form, one immediately knows the shadow.
The past and future differ, yet remain the same; clamor and silence are neither hot nor cold. The sound of the刁斗 (diāodǒu) drums never ceases; the power of the śramaṇa’s contemplation is fierce.

Before death, one indulges in the turbidity of movement; how could sentient beings transcend their dullness? The pure dust of Master Yuǎn—now that the Master has passed away, who shall maintain this order?
I lament that although Daochao once beheld my shadow in the past, he truly did not grasp my mind. Though seeing my shadow planted the seeds of cause, only by attaining my mind can the Way be sought.
Birth and death are no trivial matters; the spirit must be tranquil so that darkness cannot invade it. If one does not possess the very bones of the Way, how could one avoid drifting and sinking?
These five obstacles are difficult to overcome; that single sound is easily lost. Fresh graves are covered in lush grass, and the pines in the wind offer many mournful songs.
Who possesses the Sūtra of Firmness to play this lute of non-arising?

I mourn Master Suanan; Qixia has long been secluded and still. The springs and rocks gradually brighten and clear. Through the power of his vows, he shed the blood of his heart, and the Chan monastery finally became magnificent.
The colors of the green mountains do not age; the azure waters flow without obstruction. Yet how can one truly harmonize with his tongue-mark and virtuous countenance through mere sight or hearing?

When the Master arrived in the following spring, he donned his robes; when the Master departed, even the monkeys shed tears. I am ashamed that I merely recognize the Master, yet am unable to support him as he leans toward ruin and decline.
The Dharma-beam of the Southeast has snapped; the sea of suffering is vast and difficult to cross. This humble disciple gazes at the white clouds, and how many times have tears moistened my fur?
Chángsōng Guàn: Reciting by the West Wind At dawn I sit upon the courtyard steps;
The falling leaves do not cease. It is not yet that the west wind rises high, Yet the thousand forests seem to have shed their hair.
The bhikṣu Linlincheng sat upright, far and near; though he was without mouth or tongue, how could there be toil? Wondrous sounds issued from his hands. His disciples gathered like white clouds;
who would dare to neglect hearing the Dharma? Using the eye as the faculty of hearing, the realm of sound was utterly transcended.
Tall pines stubbornly thrust their heads forth; at night’s stillness, they hang the bright moon. Myriad sounds are hushed and do not clamor; the moonlight fills the Zen hermitage.
Passing morning and evening in leisure, what rewards or punishments are there to be seen?
Parting at Mount Yan to See Master Wuyuan as He Takes Up Residence at Shaolin Temple:
The green mountains do not grow old easily; how short are the white days! Leaves fall upon the Golden Terrace; who can move with either haste or ease?
The four springs are clear and deep; the five mounds are filled with autumn clouds. To draw from them requires no deliberate intent, yet they provide rain to relieve parched lands.

If one does not employ them skillfully, even what is correct may turn back into its opposite. Once the tree for the almsbowl has grown to a man’s embrace, the fragrance at the Emperor’s seat shall never dissipate.
The rafter-wheel has long lost its master; rewards and punishments require clear judgment. When the Patriarch’s command is fully upheld, Pāpīyas must bare his left shoulder.

Like a *jiao-ming* insect alighting on a mass of fire, or a swallow, a sparrow, and an autumn crane all within an egg—when the mind does not arise directly beneath, both sages and ordinary beings alike submit.
Spontaneous Verses Composed at Bāzhuān Hermitage:
Who would say this city is noisy? My dwelling is like a deserted valley. At dawn and dusk, the sounds of roosters and dogs I mistake for mountain waterfalls.
Cloud-like rocks are arrayed across my courtyard; a gentle breeze stirs the sparse bamboo. My old acquaintances are busy with worldly affairs—who is there to bathe with me in the ocean of Dharma?

Shimonsi Temple I love Shimonsi Temple, a place of pure vastness overlooking the river. Its practice is as deep as the moon reflected in the water; its Way is furthered by the aid of fish and dragons.

The shadows of sails disturb the secluded windows; the sound of oars stirs my tranquil meditation. Even if the Nanshan and Mount Emei were to exchange places with it, they would never be able to replace it.
Reading the Lotus Sūtra in a single room atop a deep mountain peak, even woodcutters cannot find me. As the long day passes in leisure without end, I alone turn the Lotus Sūtra;
reciting it myself and listening to it myself, I ask who else appreciates this sound? Upon careful and repeated investigation, I find that fundamentally there are not two minds.

How is it that the sense organs, objects, and consciousnesses—each having its own cause—leave me with doubts difficult to resolve? I sought a decision from the white cloud peaks, yet the white clouds did not answer;
they merely change with the season, shifting between sun and shade.

The waters bend at the Brahma River; the midday breeze is clear. A light boat glides over shallow ripples of white spray. My host has gone out on a journey and not yet returned. Sitting amidst the emerald grass, it grows soft beneath me.
With tea in hand, for whom shall I sip? With a mind full of intent, toward whom shall I unfold it? Moved by the fleeting waves of youth, I must strive together with the bright sun.
Why must one gaze upon the vast blue sea to call its waves and surges "boundless"? Mount Kunlun and a mere hillock—when the underlying principle is realized, there is neither hidden nor manifest.
Islands arise like mounds of earth; ponds are valued for their winding turns. When the water is clear, the shadows of trees appear; across the shore, clouds unfurl and roll away.
In the midst of the central flow, a monastery was constructed; thorns were first cleared away. Fish and birds recognized the incense and lamps; children grew accustomed to the wholesome practices.
Wang Youcheng of Wanchuan entrusted his official rank to springs and rocks; now there is the Master of Qu’a, who has sought out this secluded choice within the Buddhist realm.
The Wayman happened to dine here; fine rain moistens the green moss. Where will you steer your boat next? In the northern garden, there are few chickens or dogs.

Passing through Shizhong Temple, the Changjiang waters are not shallow; the mountains at Lake Mouth are not deep. Amidst the clouds and rocks, there is much wondrous artistry; one suspects it was born from a mind skilled in painting.
I, together with two or three companions, took turns gazing at the spring forest. How different it was from a painted scroll! Laughter broke forth as empty sounds arose.
Between artificial hills and true mountains, the forms could finally be discerned one from the other.
Passing over Kuānglú and Qīxián Bridge, I recall my former travels to Éméi.
Amidst the blue clouds of Éméi, the Bā River flows down from heaven; a thousand li are traversed in a single day.
Now I have come to the north of Mount Lu; its peaks and ridges rise and soar in hidden majesty. The Jade Abyss overflows and must spread forth; how resonant are the Three Gorges!

Tired from my journey, I sit by the bridge’s side; the sound of tinkling pendants rings out clearly. Hearing this, my mind becomes solitary and pure; the tongue-mark of Avalokiteśvara is long and vast.
How many cross the flowing stream? Yet in their shadows they behold the compassionate light.
Wind-blown dust reveals the wind; dust and water-moon are one. Taint and purity are but the mind alone. Try looking at the mirror within its case: its radiance is serene, still, and profound.
One morning, I ascended a high tower; the myriad phenomena were illuminated equally. Whether beautiful or ugly, not even the most minute detail was obscured;
there was never need for weary deliberation. My mind has become like this; how could I fear the encroachment of the winds and dust?

As for the discarded staff of *jaṭila* wood, from what did it arise? Its roots were entrusted to the rocks of Mount Emei; by chance it was cast away on this mountain. What gain or loss does the Venerable One experience therein?

Furthermore, when observed through the four sense-objects (*catvāra āyatanāni*), one finds upon investigation that it has no inherent substance. How much less so for this staff alone! All phenomena share the same essential function.
Presented to Mazishan: On the embankment hang drooping willows; Beneath the embankment, the grass is lush and green. In moments of casual, pure wandering, One’s writings are all exquisitely wondrous.
Without relying on the labor of carving or polishing, They are naturally and spontaneously refined. If one asks whence this comes: It arises from having no afflictions within the breast.
Presented to Jiao of Mingyue Temple:

This ancient temple rests upon Lingyan Mountain; situated in the deepest recesses of the lake and peaks, its subtle dust is inherently difficult to approach, for its mind is remote and fundamentally beyond involvement.
Liushui excels in refined conversation; Baiyun loves coming and going. When the sutras are finished, I sit beneath the pines, regulating my breath to clear worldly cares.

The bright moon hangs high in the sky; upon the empty bed, I assume the *kijutsu* posture at will. Do not resent the "green and white eyes" (favoritism or disdain); body and life are equal to drifting fluff.
Occurring While in the Mountains: The gruel is finished and there is nothing more to do; I take up my staff and seek out the secluded depths. Beneath the crags I listen to the flowing water;

its cool clarity seems to speak to whom? The weather is cold and the tea is not hot; the mist is thick and the day does not break. This is originally a land of dragons and serpents; yet, in its vast emptiness, I forget all fear and anxiety.
Our conversation has not yet ceased; as evening falls, it is difficult to remain for long. When the moon rises, we shall surely return again—why need one harbor hesitation?
[Preface to] A Visit to Tianning Temple:
I have read the *Deciding Doubts* (*Jueyi lun*) by Li Zhangzhe of the Tang dynasty. From this, I know that that which is accomplished through non-action is Heaven. Responding...
To be amidst things without becoming disordered is tranquility (*ning*). Thus, there were ancients who styled themselves "One Who Is Tranquil Amidst Agitation" (*ying-ning*);
this is also of that nature. In early spring, I took two or three dharma companions to visit Master Li at Mount Fang. Thereafter, we returned to Qingliang.
As the ice on the Hutuo River was about to melt, I lingered and did not cross. Resting briefly in the meditation cell of Master Yuan of Tianning, I composed this:
The years of one’s life cannot be retained; how can teeth and hair be relied upon? Having been young, one must inevitably grow old; the force of the passing waves is difficult to stop.

Where there is no birth, there is no death. That which has an end must have had a beginning. The willows by the riverbank dream of awakening; the peach blossoms still harbor a sense of shame. With whom shall I roam the sacred grounds?
Sipping tea, we shall discourse on the *Zhuangzi*. With a single roar, I shall depart through the gate; my inspiration for the thousand peaks is now fully aroused.

At Mount Fangshan, by the Vajra Spring, a man afflicted with impotence and unable to endure long-term labor took a single sip of the Vajra Spring water. His physical frame immediately became firm and strong;
he viewed life and death as equal and regarded suffering as a field of joy. Through this contemplation, which has long been matured, both body and mind are now entirely cool and serene.
I bid farewell to the mind-opening adept who travels to Mount Wutai and Mount Laoshan;
from Wutai to Laoshan, they are both near and far. Near, they exist within a single kṣaṇa; far, they are boundless and shoreless.
The thought arose to pay homage to Mañjuśrī; it was like a flash of lightning across the vast void. In the blink of an eye, all has already sunk away; the lines on my palms can no longer be seen.
The autumn is high and the air is cold; fallen leaves stir boundless emotion. Gazing afar at the solitary cloud drifting in the distance, it makes one’s longing and attachment increase.

While reading the sutras, I once spread lotus flowers; their pure fragrance pervaded the dry land. Amidst the bowing and rising of now and then, even a thousand li are no more than a thread's breadth apart.
The Great Being welcomes me with a smile, tea served in crystal bowls; the breeze from my nostrils stirs waves of blossoms, as fragrant light sways through the halls and palaces.
There is no missing the point; the arrowhead’s pivot is sharp. He turns his head toward the empty, precipitous peaks.

Under the moon he reads his books; the sky is high, the autumn dew cold. His fellow companions have all retired to rest; the oil is sootied and the lamp is dim. He borrows the bright moonlight to read.

Having found companions at the very beginning of antiquity, my mind was naturally satisfied as I realized the underlying principle. Closing the scroll, the night was already deep; pure light filled the mountain caves.

Passing through Longmen, the quiet chambers lie along a winding path of sheep-gut steepness. Deep forests conceal the meditation halls; once arrived, I sat by the gate, where overlapping peaks rise like clouds.
A hollowed tree trunk, three hundred feet long, serves as a raft; stones are piled to bridge the void. Cold spring water flows in winding curves, its droplets falling into the kitchen.
Yesterday, I saw upon the monk’s head the sound of rushing water as it came on in haste. We looked at one another and laughed, clapping our hands—a scene Wang Wei finds difficult to describe.
Only those who are mindless can realize the ultimate meaning and transcend the dust-sealed world.

Ascending Mount Qingliang on a spring day, I have recently entered a secluded valley. Grasses and trees, having received sufficient seasonal rain, flourish and smile toward me; red, yellow, and purple hues mingle with the green.

Brandishing my halberd, the sun is hard to turn back; the flowing spring rushes away with great speed. Just as I was thinking of Master Qiu of the Eastern House, who sighed by the river that he would not return, I visited the Elder Li at the place where he composed his treatises early in the spring.
I have long admired the refined character of the eminent Elder Li; having questioned him on the Dharma like the child Puyizi, I shall depart from here for the West.
The green mountains do not change their hue; the white-footed monk offers verse in response. Human generations pass like flowing water; Yunyan presents his wondrous form.
Lotus flowers encircle the meditation hall; the palm-leaf scriptures give rise to thoughts of the Buddha. Spring snow covers the four fields; the dark ford washes away the five hindrances.

The Avataṃsaka was first expounded by the Buddha; the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra truly elucidates it with great clarity. I regret that my birth was so late that I had no leisure to attend upon you with handkerchief and staff.
Yet I still rejoice in serving the Venerable One, as the dragon and the elephant advance together. The night is cold and the mountain path is secluded; staying for two nights dispels my melancholy.
Shangpu Ya, I am no man of antiquity; you are a stone of primordial antiquity. The distance between now and then is vast indeed, yet in a single day we have come to know one another.

Because I grieve for the decline of the world’s ways, I seek out companions from a thousand ages past; alas, I must journey to Mount Emei. I shall not have the leisure to remain by your side for long.
At the edge of the clouds we parted; pouring out tea, our sorrow was profound. I dare aspire to a heart like the bright moon, always illuminating my consciousness as I walk.
Feeling moved at Fènglín Monastery:
In the past, people relied upon cold crags; tigers and leopards were their constant companions. A single mind surrendered to silence and solitude, appearing as still and formless as the Primal Chaos.
The ancient tree knows nothing of spring; birds are not startled by the woodcutter’s axe. Suddenly, as the sunlight returns, white clouds transform into a vermilion garden.
I, old and wishing to cast down my staff, have already grown wings upon Mount Emei.

When eating vegetables, do not disdain their bland taste; within that blandness, the flavor is profound. What is long-lasting can endure for a long time, and through endurance, one withstands the frost of the years.
Others say that fine meats and broths are delicious, but I cherish the fragrance of the vegetable roots. As Su Dongpo once said: "A man of great character must try them."
Simplicity nourishes lofty brilliance; extravagance muddies the light of the mind. Frugality can establish a household; waste leads toward licentiousness and ruin.
Listen to these words from my cold tongue, and the world may also find peace.

Sitting in the mountain hall at night, the empty chamber is clarified by the Buddha-lamp; the cold moon shines upon the monk’s *pāṇḍukambala*. Looking up and down within the vastness of heaven and earth, even the metaphor of the "ice pitcher" falls short.
A faint cloud thins as if about to vanish; wild birds gather on snow-covered branches. The winding ridges alternate between light and shadow; the flowing spring is frozen, yet does not weep.
We sat together until the break of dawn. The practitioner repeatedly requested to enter. Since what each delights in is difficult to harmonize, how could the waters of Canglang be familiar to an ox?
An Autumn Night Staying at the Jixian Hermitage in the Meditation Chamber of Master Hong (whose style name is Dazong):

Scattered clouds disperse across the azure void; a crescent moon hangs in the sky like white silk. Listening alone to the chirping of grass crickets, I find deep resonance with the profound mysteries left behind by the sages.
By relying on the coarse, one attains the refined; the refinement of transformation merges with the eternal Way. To behold it directly is like gazing upon a thousand peaks;

how could words ever reach it? In the empty window, the coolness has just begun to rise; sitting wrapped in my woolen robe, it is truly pleasant. Yellow leaves drift in the autumn wind; who will sweep them up again in the night?
In the single-sound hall of Tanzhe, the three realms are like a temporary lodging;
how could a bhikṣu dare to cling to them? His coming and going resemble solitary clouds; his footprints are difficult to trace.
I stayed but a single night beneath the tree; lingering longer would have led me into bondage. These carved beams and painted rafters—how could my lingering regard for them not have been a mistake?

In this degenerate age, social customs are corrupt; though they shave their hair and beards in vain, men and women remain intoxicated by great desires, finding pleasure only in food, drink, and sensual delights.

Though you may wear the *kāṣāya* and travel on foot through all directions, if you have not investigated the fundamental reality of your own nature, you will remain mired in deluded silence and scorched by the fever of affliction.
When the demon of death suddenly arrives, in your panic, where will you find refuge?

At Shengshou Monastery in Wujiang: I love the mountains of Wujiang; I take my cup and wander freely among their seclusion. I also love the waters of Wujiang; gazing at the flowing stream, I leisurely reflect upon my own mind.

Within the city lies an ancient temple, yet its inscribed steles lie buried and forgotten. By chance, I read the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*; from the era of the Red Bird (the Three Kingdoms) until the present day.
The Buddha-lamp was severed yet reignited; staff and shout resounded like thunder. The Zen tiger, Old Xiatang, once occupied this grove.
Ruined steles are embedded in new walls, stirring the verses of wandering poets at every turn. In recent times, were it not for Master [X], it would have nearly been overrun by thorns.
How can you abandon us and depart? It causes my breast to ache all the more. Is it the mountain that is noble because it is high? Is it the water that is noble because it is deep?

If one is free from desire even in a mere inch of space, then the marketplace is itself a cloud-topped peak. Vastly departing from the ground of suffering—who could understand casting off the hairpin and the sash?
Inscription for the Two Springs (with Preface):
While I was visiting Guanghui Temple, I beheld a spring whose waters were profound, clear, and crystalline. A sense of joy arose within me, and my feverish afflictions naturally vanished.
Therefore, I named it the "Spring of Joy. Upon further inspection, I saw another spring, its waters gurgling as they poured from the mouths of dragons.

If one is a great dragon of withered dhyāna, roaming the ocean of awakening amidst surging waves of wisdom, yet remains undisturbed by the nature of its clarity and purity—moving yet inherently still—one may be said to resemble the state of meditative concentration; this is called the Spring of Dhyāna-Bliss.
Subsequently, whenever eminent men and noble scholars pass by Guanghui, they all give rise to joy and enter into dhyāna.
Delighted! May I not fail the intention behind the names of these two springs?
At the Spring of Joy, where a stream flows among a thousand peaks, how bright it appears at first sight! Joy arises spontaneously; together we shall accompany the mountain moon at dawn.

Scoop up the water to reveal wondrous touch; directly beneath, there is nothing that is not understood. The night is still and the bells and chimes have ceased; pure sounds pour forth from the dense bamboos.
Furthermore, one hears the remnants of the bowl being rinsed, which stirs the wandering fish to circle about.
The merchant rejoices upon seeing profit; the farmer is glad when he receives rain. In the empty mountains, ten thousand sounds fall silent; the old monk remains mute, with nothing to say.

Though their pleasures differ, who can judge which state of mind is superior? A cold wind blows through the thin clouds, and the waves of emotion for both the mundane and the holy are thoroughly penetrated.

Passing by Master Gong’s meditation cell, I broke through a thousand feet of ice. A square-chamber hermitage was formed amidst the clouds; fishermen and woodcutters ceased their coming and going. Heaven and earth shared the same gaze;
not a sound of clamor or laughter was heard, only the resonance of flowing water. The mountains were deep and travelers rare; as the night grew still, the bright moon rose.
Grasping our sleeves, we discuss our pure hearts; forgetting artifice, we merge with the Great Mystery. To brew the tea of Tiger Hill, I have already joined you with my crane-knee staff.
Where does the distant bell stir? At this moment, who claps their hands? Human life is like a bubble; do not let afflictions grow long.
Highly erect is the banner of diligence; together we transcend the net of ignorance.
*The Jewel-Bead Spring (with preface)*:
During the Jiajing era, there was a Chan practitioner of unknown origin. Moving like drifting clouds and flying birds, his footprints filled the heavens.
[The Master] went down and took a liking to Jingshan in Hangzhou. The mountain has Lingxiao Peak, which rises higher than all the surrounding ridges.
With little stone and much soil, it is suitable for cultivation; however, due to a lack of water, those who dwell there cannot remain long.

This Chan master prayed to the dragon deities, and one day, a spring gushed forth, filling his cupped hands. After three days, the pool was so deep and abundant that it could satisfy the "dragon-elephants" [monks]. (Wanli era)

In the second month of spring in the *wuchen* year, he came from Hangzhou to Mount Wutai; having related the beginning and end of his journey in this manner, I have thus composed these verses for him:

Cold currents surge from the mountain’s summit, Pure and cool, far removed from the mire. At midnight, amidst thin clouds in the void, The icy wheel [of the moon] is reflected in the vast blue waters.
Whoever tears open the patched robe, divides the jade to pour into the cauldron. As the glowing coals first boil three times, the flower-foam and bright pearls appear together.
Try pouring it into a porcelain bowl; with a single sip, the dream of meditation awakens.
At Fuyong Monastery, among the thousand peaks, there are flowing waters; in the azure pond, there is the bright moon. Seated upon soft clouds of incense, what is lacking in this heart?
The beauty’s autumnal thoughts run deep; will she deign to rest by the mountain crags? The deer go forth and return again; the solitary wild goose vanishes into the horizon.
The night dew fills the city with cold; lamps illuminate the Buddha-land. Within the mirror, the floating *stūpa* is renewed; mountains and rivers fortify the Chan hermitage.

Passing once more through Loufan Temple, the Great Being is about to be born. From the precious ground, a spiritual spring wells forth; those who drink from it, whether noble or base, alike find all their calamities extinguished.
One morning, golden fungi sprang forth; on the day the Buddha was born, a great radiance shone. For a thousand ages the thunder of the Dharma has resounded, its tongue-root as firm as solid rock.
At Loufan, the teacher’s village, you and I grieve over these old traces; at Mount Lu, the autumn wind blows high, and Donglin is truly desolate.

The spring of wisdom has not yet run dry, yet the dust and soil have accumulated over the well of excellence. We stand together, scratching our heads in hesitation; the cry of the distressed wild geese hastens our aging hair.

How could we dare to receive the light of the Sage, which divides its flames to illuminate even the barbarian lands? All the more so for those born in the Central Kingdom, who have from the beginning been bathed in the moisture of the Dharma.
My strength in the Way having declined, I am unable to achieve brilliant renown.
At the mountain inn of Xuangang, I part from my fellow practitioners of the Dharma, Ningwu;

we happen to dine together at the Shanshan inn. My fellow practitioners diligently maintain right mindfulness, looking back upon their own bodies and minds; how can these differ from a flash of lightning?
A hundred years are like morning dew; when the sun rises, the flowers close. Honor and disgrace are but dust upon a mirror, vainly staining its original radiance.
The autumn wind urges on my horse's hooves; as I depart further and further, my longing knows no satiety.

Passing through the Cool Grove of the Cemetery to show a certain Zen practitioner the beauty of a courtesan wandering in the flower grove: who would not praise it? White bones scattered amidst the wild grasses—seeing this, who would not sigh?
Throughout the course of a hundred years, the beautiful and the ugly are distinguished by the times. When those who sighed were still alive, their countenances were so radiant;

yet when those who offered praise are buried in yellow earth, their bleached bones are but a single thread. The Buddha taught the *Strīsamādhi*: within this very body, one accomplishes the contemplation of the objective realm.
The bhikṣu dwells in the śmaśāna, gathering his mindfulness and wearying of the segmented body. As he contemplates a single branch of a flower, he penetrates the boundlessness of spring.

Passing beyond the Huayan hermitage by the flowing waters and green mountains, he clears away the weeds to polish the mirror of his mind. Although the Dharma-realm has four layers, once it is understood, the ordinary can become the sacred.
The wind strikes the iron chimes in the cold; the moon rises, making the pine-window pure and clear. Do not say that old paper is thick; the power of your drilling and study must be firm.

Once a single speck of dust is suddenly split open, the entire Great Canon is instantly and completely realized. For now, let us speak of the deepening springtime; the apricot blossoms are at their peak.
How long can this fleeting life last? Who realizes that the body is but a disease?
*On Driving Away the Drought-Demon (with Preface)*:
While traveling to Xingshan Temple, I beheld the withered wheat seedlings and knew that the drought-demon (*mò*) was the malevolent spirit at work. I therefore composed a poem to drive it away.
I shall await the fulfillment of the rains as my proof.

The sprouts and wheat look up to the sweet spring; the infants hunger and long for their mother’s milk. Having come from Qingliang, I have long been separated from the company of those afflicted by the fever of suffering.

Traveling through the land, I beheld withered and parched fields; drought spirits gripped their charcoal axes, rejoicing in the dryness to indulge their lustful habits. All living beings have lost their father. For the people, food is as heaven itself;
the wheat is withered—upon whom shall they rely? O Sage of Great Compassionate Awakening! May your clouds pour down rain to nourish what is rotten and decayed.
Famous from near and far as the sound of thunder, the wicked and arrogant fall into dark suffering.
By chance I have attained long life, remaining only carefree; there is nothing to which I am attached. Mountains and rivers are likened to gray dogs; birth and death are equal to wild horses.
The prowess of Cao and Liu lasted but a brief moment; fortune and decline vanish in the blink of an eye. I yield to those beyond the world, who paint the void with adamantine clarity.
*Pentasyllabic Regulated Verse:
Inspired by Feelings at Kaohua Temple*

The establishment of this victory began in the Sui and Tang dynasties; the transmission of its lamp has defied the count of frosts. The banner is high and the script ancient; the stele lies prostrate, its mosses and lichens deep green.

When rain falls, the golden visage weeps; when flowers bloom, the iron cauldron is fragrant. Having once ascended here with feelings of lamentation, I find the locust trees cold as they lock in the slanting sun.
With disheveled hair, I receive my food amidst the lotus ponds of Mount Furuang;

with disheveled hair, I dwell beneath the long forests. A pure song accompanies the azure channels; the water flows while the reflection of heaven remains. The wind is still, yet the sound of the bamboos is empty.

The path emerges from the tips of the clouds and pines; the mind roams the primordial realm of the Supreme Sovereign (*xiàngdì*). Who from the upper reaches sends offerings? Fragrant rice and fish from the pond.

Guests are many, yet the pavilion is small; my desires are few, for this place is ultimately secluded. Forgetting artifice, one returns to the fundamental source. Sails and masts vie amidst the azure waves; sun and moon race across the blue heavens.
My ears lodge beyond the sound of the river; my mind roams before the Primordial Sovereign (*Xiangdi*). The path of awakening opens amidst the world; I ascend to gaze upon the stone gate.
At twilight (two poems): The wind falls the leaves of spring; moss grows on the steps after the rain. Before the gate, the twin trees grow old; beyond the bamboo, a single sail unfurls.

The high towers swallow the sinking sun; the *Cetiyavana* grove hides the mirror-like terrace. Gazing from afar, my feelings remain unfulfilled; the nesting birds urge me to return home. At twilight I moor at the riverbank;
the lamps of neighboring boats float upon the water. The ground is so high I suspect it borders the Dipper constellation; as the heavens grow dark, I halt my boat.

The spring warmth has begun to thin my clothes; the river’s clarity inspires me to cast myself into this journey. In these foreign lands, all are but transient travelers; yet the local tongue confirms that I am indeed in Suzhou.

Amidst the snow, I harbor thoughts of solitude within the empty mountains; the continuous gloom of rain and snow deepens. The cranes grieve as their nests are broken by the trees; the monkeys fear the cave entrances will be sealed shut.
It is difficult to distinguish the grasses and trees; the mountains and rivers appear as if identical. Who can clarify this meaning? At evening’s clearing, the bell sounds from above.

At Tanzhe, listening to the spring on New Year’s Day: today marks the beginning of the year. Warmth first arises in the cold valley. Beneath the pines, the sky floats; at the edge of the clouds, the sound of the chime is heard.

Suddenly turning away, I bid farewell to the secluded ravine; this destination leads toward the vast blue sea. My Way is cold as the autumn wind, yet the ripples of the waves bathe the sun in brilliance.
Dwelling among the mountains deep within ten thousand peaks, where can the traveler seek you? A broken cliff can block the path, yet the flowing water naturally composes its own song.
White hair gives rise to empty thoughts; the green mountains chill the worldly heart. Who would have known that within the city, by broad daylight, one might snatch at gold?

Passing Bogoonsa Temple, a single stroke of the oar brings me to this Zen abode. The mountain stream and peaks are fresh with spring rain. Sleeping clouds hang across the ancient steps; a neglected statue lies prostrate in the desolate ruins.
Broken steles obscure the Tang inscriptions; from the empty beams, a Song manuscript is found. All who travel together are dharma companions—who can now uphold the lineage of this gate?
An old monk at the Moonlight Pond passes his leisure: by the clouds he hews this spring. Its depth cannot be measured; from antiquity to the present, it remains only serene.

The reflected image in the stream gazes at me; Containing the void, the earth presses against the heavens. In the cold night, all sounds are stilled; How many times has the bright moon waned and waxed?
I stayed this autumn night in the meditation quarters of Attendant Ben, the place where I dwell.
Throughout the long days, few are the tracks of men. The water and moon exist in all four seasons; The clouds and mountains number in the tens of thousands.
A yellow monkey steals the purple yam; a white crane perches upon the green pine. In the stillness of night, I sit alone; before the lamp, whom can I follow?
*Traveling to Zhanggong Cave (with Preface)*:
In the late spring, I traveled with two or three companions to Zhanggong Cave and Yunütan. On the boat, I read the works of Master Zhi.
Preface to the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra*: Wearied, I opened my eyes and suddenly beheld emerald green floating before the boat, its ripples reflecting upon my desk.
At that time, those of lofty discourse constructed clouds of elegant refutations, while those of open mind responded as if pouring from one vessel into another.

Subsequently, leaving the boat and leaning on my staff, I followed a path of woodcutters and entered. Upon arrival, ancient pines flanked the road and tall bamboos were painted with dark ink, amidst which stood strange rocks.
Emerging from the chaos, the clear spring drips with a resonant sound; the source of the immortals is secluded and sublime, leaving no leisure for one to attend to it all.

At times, I have composed brief miscellaneous records of these matters. Although there is no chanting of the Dharma like that at the Kukkutārāma or Mṛgadāva, this too is a fortunate encounter of our time.
Gentle ripples sway the shadows of the trees; the breeze favors the lightness of a single sail. Within my gaze, a thousand peaks display their splendor;

by my path, a single stream flows clear. Noble discourse dispels the long days; I search out hidden treasures to entrust to my secluded sentiments. The Peach Blossom Spring is near at hand; I often ascend it with my dharma-companions.

**Miscellaneous Verses on the Northern Garden** In leisure, with nothing to do, I gaze upon the flowers to suit my secluded sentiments. The bird’s path gives birth to the bright moon; the fish’s course merges with the Great Clarity.

I often seek out monasteries among the azure mountains; in this turbid world, I leave no name behind. Beyond the clouds lies the one who understands me; from the front peak comes the sound of bells and chimes.
Mooring on the Xiang River at dusk, where my boat has come to rest: Vast and desolate, the ancient ferry lies to the west. Clouds shroud the moon above the river; rain dampens the traveler’s clothes.
My traveling companions speak a foreign tongue; the lamps on neighboring boats flicker dimly. My native mountains are separated by a thousand li; their distant reach brings nothing but sorrow.

Dwelling among the crags, I attend to my affairs where the valley hides amidst heaped clouds; The cold spring flows without ceasing, and the thousand peaks forever lock in their verdant hue. Even in the sixth month, it is as if autumn;

the struggle of ants startles heaven and earth, Yet men remain empty while horses and oxen run wild at will. Whether in mountain forests or within cities, when the mind comes to rest, one finds harmony with all.

Taking my leave to bid farewell to Master Han: The Great Way has long been desolate and overgrown. This song of parting is sung by the eastern sea. My tracks shall extend ten thousand li; The ferry for crossing over is now but a faint memory.

In broad daylight, my liver and entrails ache with bitterness; Upon the green mountains, my kin and flesh are fragrant. Meeting is immediately followed by parting; I wipe away tears that would soak my robes.
He reveals to his father the silent ground of the hero: where worldly vanity holds no deep account. Myriad species of fine flowers bloom; ancient trees stand alone at a thousand fathoms.
When the path ends, wondrous wisdom arises; when words are exhausted, one attains the self-mind. To be enfeoffed as a marquis upon the western seas—white bones bartered for gold.
Passing by Layman Xing Kuangshi, I visited his residence this morning;
along the way, I treaded through mists and clouds. To realize the principle, the flower does not wait to bloom; when the pond is dug, the water has its limit.

The stone bridge facing the door is perilous; the mountain fortress borders the river, slanting away. Having finished my meal, there is nothing left to do; by the empty window, I turn the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Accompanying the attendant Miao Zhongchun, we stayed at Hongfu Temple (with preface).
Long ago, when Chan Master Tanshi ascended Mount Nanyue, it was as if he were returning to a familiar place. Thereupon, he dug into the earth and discovered a skull. And...
With his ceramic bowl as his sole possession, he eventually founded a temple named after his three previous lives.

When I, a poor monk, accompanied two or three companions past Hongfu Temple, we looked around in hesitation; it was as if we were visiting an old haunt. Yet, I did not know where the skull of my former life lay.
Nevertheless, though this is no longer a skull but a ceramic bowl, the former body of Dashi was the wind and moon of Mount Nanyue.
The master remained faithful to it. From the Tang dynasty until our Ming, its decline and restoration have occurred countless times.
Now, the temple monk Cifeng Chao has once again exerted great effort to restore what had fallen into ruin, while this poor monk and two or three companions [have joined him].
Hindered by rain, I was granted leave for two nights. In the morning, the Master requested a poem to be inscribed upon a stone;
I thus composed this to seal our karmic bond across three lifetimes. It was the eleventh day of the sixth month in the summer of the Wuli Bingxu year.

I stayed for two nights at Zhongliu Temple. My movements and seclusion were shared by my attendants. In this Chan dwelling, the water reflects the moon; the Buddha-lamp illuminates the fish and dragons.
Stones mourn the traces of heroes; clouds bury the footprints of past and present. With infinite thoughts on decline and prosperity, I ask the ancient planted pines.

At Laoshan Haiyin Temple, the Beaded Forest preserves its ancient remains. The Son of Heaven bestowed sacred scriptures upon it. Bird-paths hang above the crimson cliffs; the monks’ hall rises amidst white clouds.
Fish and dragons dwell beneath the steps; the mundane world is divided from the sea’s edge. Who shall continue the Buddha’s flame? Only the incense of the mind is perfumed morning and evening.

When the Brahma-river suddenly gives rise to emotion, every single thing becomes an obstacle; when the mind is empty, every matter is as it should be. Though birth and death are indeed great, coming and going are entirely under my own control.
To store water, one need not trouble the vast ocean; to block the wind, one need not employ the Great Void. All things are available for use—what object could possibly delude me?

By My Boat at Shimen Temple, an Ancient Monastery In this land of marshes, one is separated from the dust and clamor of the world; on all four sides flow the waters, and a solitary peak rises alone above the clouds.

Silent sounds proclaim the realms of existence, while the Elder’s sūtras are arrayed in written text. As my boat arrives within the depths of twilight, the sound of the bell is heard following the drum.
Spontaneous Compositions (Four Poems) Breaking reeds, he comes to the First Ground;
The fisherman sleeps, his head pillowed on the waves. The pagoda bells chime idly of their own accord; The monk’s dream awakens, and he forgets all karmic conditions.
Wells and hearths are the lairs of fish and dragons; wind-blown dust is the sky of water and moon. Though not seen with my own eyes, the clarity of their reflection remains as it was.

Dwelling in the mountains requires no great artifice; I simply come with a single flavor of rustic simplicity. After the rain, new ground is opened; when the lamp grows dim, the old soot is trimmed away.
Illuminating the mind, I turn over the palm leaves; cushioning my feet, I tread upon the green moss. Having long severed the path of wind and dust, who would inquire after the Great Plum?
Seated upon the grass at the White Cloud Temple, I weigh matters in leisure: gain and fame are not my concern; the passing years leave others in a frantic rush.
I eat my fill of pine pollen; smoke drifts with the fragrance of cypress seeds. If this lingering scent may be relied upon, then the Way belongs to the lords and kings.

As for me, I am a man apart from the world; I intend to spend my final years in these empty mountains. The pine wind is cool even in the sixth month; the moon over the pool is bright as ever through the ages.
The yam tubers are plump after the rains; the white clouds need not be swept away. When I arrived, the path was already forgotten; wishing now to depart, whom would it be good to ask?
At Shaolin I met Gao Zhu, and at Chuanchuan I met Xiangyang again;

parting from you once more, how many frosts have passed? Meeting again, our hair is equally gray. Our traces are like clouds gathering and dispersing; on this road, the way is sometimes low and sometimes high.
Frequently ill, I have come to know meditative contemplation; lacking talent, I am weary of worldly bustle. Tonight’s moon at Shaolin must once again shine upon the eastern corridor.
Autumn Day at En Temple with Various Dharma Companions, Black and White:
Autumn comes to the Golden Mouse [Temple]; The west wind carries the sound of falling leaves. The willows along the embankment still bear their green; The grasses by the pond still hold their azure.

Broken steles obscure the eras of antiquity; in this empty mountain, I lament the ways of the world. My companions are all fellow practitioners of the Dharma—who among them can explain the state of non-arising?

I chant of the wind: Heaven and Earth rely entirely upon it; ten thousand things are unrestrained in their surging and turning. Shaking the trees, one hears only the sound; pushing through the clouds, no form is seen.

The swallowing and spitting forth possess true power; coming and going, they are fundamentally without sentiment. In this singular display of wonder, the sound of a *ghaṇṭā* is sent forth from the empty mountains.

At Wolong Hermitage, the temple is hidden by dense green trees; the path winds through deep white clouds. The mountain retains the colors of a former dynasty; many people here possess the hearts of antiquity.
Floating dust cannot be seen; flowing water knows its own sound. With eyes full of intent toward the east and west, I inscribe this poem hoping to seek it again.
An autumn night spent at Shuiyue Hermitage; at dusk, mooring at the Fishing Terrace.
Sitting, I listen to the lament of the grass insects. The waters are vast and heaven and earth cannot be distinguished. The hall is finished, and the moon comes of its own accord.
Having already awakened from the dream of the plantain and the deer, I shall not allow the seagulls to grow suspicious. The people on the opposite shore are like grains of millet;

ascending this height, my worldly thoughts are reduced to ashes. The Bodhisattva Saṃgha dwells eternally within the Nārāyaṇa Cave, taking refuge in the lush green peaks above. The mountain is so high that the sun seems near; the sea is so vast that the sky appears low.
Islands screen off the Middle Kingdom; waves and tides limit the foreign lands beyond. Returning once more, fearing I might lose my way, I brushed away the stones to leave this brief inscription.
In this chamber of the Golden Wheel, I am bound by the affairs at hand;
I dwell beneath the golden pagoda. From time to time, the sound of bells and chimes is heard. I plant seedlings not for the sake of alms, but weed the grass as a substitute for walking meditation.
Spring waters reflect the azure sky; clouds and mountains stand green before my door. Who was it that slew the snake to seize its nature? Wiping away the eyes of delusion, I realize non-arising.
In this new autumn, I think of Master Kai-lang;
meeting autumn early amidst these travels, the lingering rain cools the woods. Even small fish still gather in joy; yet the attendant, alas, would rather forget.

Do not say that a thousand mountains separate us; you must know that a single pulse extends far. The wild mind will eventually cease of its own accord; with tears in my eyes, I prostrate before the fragrant altar.

Inscribed at Zhanggong Cave: Exploring Spiritual Traces at the Clear Dawn. Singing as I walk into the verdant heights, the mountain radiance opens the eye’s horizon; the sound of the spring waters dulls the machinations of the mundane world.
The path ahead is not difficult to traverse; this fleeting life cannot be relied upon. Clouds do not penetrate the cave entrance; thus, my way in and out remains free from confusion.

Inscribed at the Jade Maiden Pond, where tall pines shade the road on both sides: This secluded excellence permits me to seek it out. How could ancient trees know the passing of years? The clarity of the pond reflects this very mind.

Traveling together as fellow practitioners of the Dharma, we listen to the warbling of birds until their sounds fade away. As the sky grows deep and shadowy, approaching the hour of You (the Western Quarter), the sound of flutes and pipes is occasionally heard.
At Layang Village, I have entered the summer retreat;

mindful of my attendant, I find no other business in my leisure. My iron bowl holds clear spring water; its mirror-like surface reflects the color of the heavens. My meditative mind is empty of worldly ties.
Human life is already brief; how could these illusory forms remain forever firm? We have met, yet it is difficult to know one another fully; Master Kai-lang has not yet returned.
I visited Yuan-an, Layman Mu, at Duobao Temple to pay my respects.
Amidst the dust, he opened the path to awakening. I came to visit this excellence, ascending the heights at night. The palm-leaf scriptures remain as they were; who now seeks the lotus flowers again?
Your traces are cast upon the official robes of rank; your name has fallen among the jeweled groves. A single moon in the vast blue sky—this is the heart of the Master for all eternity.
Written by Chufuer at Bietanzhashan, addressed to Master Zuo, the Abbot of Jiafu, and his fellow practitioners.
From how far has the numinous pulse come? How many times have I crossed this deep stream? The clouds and mountains were suddenly severed, and the heavens and sun instantly reopened.
The Way is so great it can never be hidden; its fame is so lofty it cannot be buried. As he walks among those of noble station, the empty greenery surges up to form towers and terraces.

Presented to Wang Taigu at Lüdi: I encountered your Highness on a journey; your refined bearing stands far beyond the common crowd. Your family is like leaves drifting upon flowing water; your inner mind is like clouds over distant mountains.

You still carry your sword as one who follows the way of chivalry, yet you find solace only in the composition of literature. How much better it would be if we both cast these aside together, to meet with you for a single moment beyond this world.

Consoling Xu Jue: His thoughts of returning home have not yet ceased for long; we have gathered together at the snowy peak. Clouds and mountains are ever before our eyes, yet wife and children no longer weigh upon the heart.

Under the moon, we seek through Chan contemplation; in leisure, we practice the Sanskrit chants. I further pity his former habits of unrestrained indulgence, now forged into the needle of Great Compassion.
I visited Kuoxiansi Temple but did not meet Master Fangliao;
I have come from afar to this misty monastery. Pine trees line both sides of the path, the green mountains bear the colors of antiquity, and the flowing water produces its own natural sound.
Upon the rocks, the traces of a deluded dragon; amidst the woods, the cry of a frightened dove. The Western River lies far away; who will console my feelings as a traveler?

Having ascended the summit of Mount Tiangmu and traversed every rugged path, the ground suddenly levels at the central peak. Clutching at vines, I once more venture through peril; sitting upon a stone, I watch the clouds arise.
Those with desire are naturally envious; the Way is spontaneously realized by those without such intent. Together we shall ascend the highest peak, and once more feel this body is light.

For Feng Yuanfu: In his study, fleeing the dust—is this not true reclusion? To nurture one's essence lies within the common people. The lake water in the ink-well is azure; the autumn mountains behind the brush-stand are green.
Mist and clouds permeate my refined thoughts; wind and waves mingle with the sound of reading. Throughout the long day few people arrive; one hears only the calls of secluded birds.

The boat reaches Shimen (Stone Gate), where I pay homage to antiquity at Yunxi (Bamboo Creek). Black winds bend the reeds, yet the Stone Gate remains open. A single stream floats jade-like amidst the waters; A solitary grove embraces two peaks.
The Buddha’s arm toiled as a bridge across the ford; the boat and oar deliver one to the Chan palace. At year’s end, I explore these ancient traces; a song of sorrow rises as the cold mist thickens.
[Two Poems on Dwelling in a Shell-like Abode by the Brahma River] In this watery land, the Chan courtyard is vast;
a small boat may not be taken lightly. The ripples of the water sway the reflections of the pavilion; the pine breeze learns the sound of the tide.
The small fish is ever fearful with its meager knowledge; the dragon sleeps on in ignorance, yet to wake. Do not say the city is near; across the shore, the distant mountains are green.
At leisure, I sit by the pond and pavilion, riding the moonlight to play with the murmuring stream. Vulture Peak floats above the heavens; the fisherman’s boat is moored beneath the trees.
Birds clamor as they discuss the Dharma; dragons emerge but have not yet returned to their cove. Those who seek out secluded depths have already grown few;
the wattle-and-daub gate need not be closed. Mount Luoji sends forth its transmission;
dwelling in vast serenity, one knows not its depth. Who can share this single search? With ears that hear the clouds of heaven and earth, and a heart of sage-like stillness held within.

The green mountains remain where the House of Han once stood; the sun casts its shade upon the shrine of Han. How can one bear these tears of parting? They fall like spring rain upon the Seashell Peak.
Accompanied by several lay practitioners, we ascended Ink Light Pavilion.

The place is secluded, with no neighbors nearby; by the time we arrived together, the day had already grown dark. We startled the birds nesting in the clouds as we passed through them, and the moon followed us into the secluded pavilion.
The nearby waters are fit for contemplation; the empty windows allow one to transcribe scriptures. Fishermen’s boats hasten an early crossing; the wind is cold and the night waves reek of raw fish.
I rejoice that Zhongfu has entered Tanzhe again; I rejoice that you have arrived in the mountains.
A single break in the clouds at Yunmen reveals the seal. Listening to the spring, body and world are exhausted; sitting upon the rock, thought and word are empty.
The bright moon rises from the eastern sea; incense burning, I pay homage to the Great Hero. On the path of today and tomorrow, staff and sandals shall emerge from a thousand peaks.

On an autumn day, I ascend Xuanmu to view the sights, accompanied by noble companions. Clutching at creepers, I visit the Buddhist temple. A light rain falls across a thousand mountains; for several years, my solitary traces have been cast here.

Amidst the misty green, the sparse chime rings out; The ripples of light illuminate the distant peaks. Who among the travelers of mist and clouds would welcome a guest? Only Master Zhigong comes to see me off.

Passing through Baoyuan Temple at Jurfu, I am moved by the thoughts of this new autumn as I wander upon this sacred ground. The setting sun shines upon the city’s outskirts; Horse tracks encroach upon the azure moss. Cicadas cry out from the ancient locust trees.
The short stele bears the lion’s aperture; the lofty talent is like a phoenix’s down. On this day, as we support what has faded, it is necessary for Xuandu to come.

May we together strive: when the Master of Lectures visited Hongshan Temple and raised his blade with no desire to cut, what was the intent behind that severed foot? The Dharma rain moistens the ten thousand mountains; the clouds of compassion shade the ten thousand leagues.
The clear spring remains as it was of old; the white blood flows on unto this day. Ancient steles are lost amidst the wild weeds—who will now accompany me with staff and sandals to seek them out?
Staying overnight at Longxing Temple in late autumn:

Entering the temple, the mists and clouds are ancient; golden cords lock the Brahma palace. The translators of the scriptures are no longer seen; the alms bowl for consecrating water has become empty.
The grass by the river where the漂母 (Piaomu) fed me; the pines atop the tomb of Marquis Han. With the night deep, who sits with me? Hard to bear is the autumn wind. Shown to Wu Kangyu:
This life is but a morning dream; both favor and disgrace are equally non-existent. When will the three oars find rest? When will I leave these thousand peaks?

The image within the mirror of heaven and earth; the world and self are but mud upon the tip of a nose. Departing on, the spring journey grows distant; amidst the smoke and flowers, the subtle mechanism is revealed.
In response to the rhyme of Prince Songch’ang at Wonchang Temple:
To cross over, alas, there is no boat; yet one may linger by the famous grove. The rain has ceased upon the pavilions; the Milky Way floats through the thin clouds.

When the water is still, the moon is clearly reflected; when the mind is empty, the environment is naturally profound. With the lamp of wisdom shining through the night, there is no need for sorrow at the setting of the sun.
Reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* at night, I was moved:

the carriage and cap increase the marks of the human condition, while pines and springs chill worldly sentiments. A minor office is as heavy as the Five Peaks; the Great Way is as light as a single hair.

The rocks are pure, yet clouds arise in weariness; the windows are empty, yet the moon shines ever brighter. The remaining sutras have not yet been fully translated—where does the sound of the dawn bell come from?
Master Chekong of Lukye-p’ing maintains lofty integrity;
dwelling in seclusion, he is indifferent to worldly affairs. On idle mornings he observes the color of cranes; on tranquil nights he listens to the sound of the spring.
