Walking the Path, my single body is hale; translating the scriptures, my two eyes are clear. I feel ashamed that I joined the community so late; I beg for a patch of ground to settle beneath the shade of pines.

In the deep clouds of the secluded valley, there is a sense of the Pure Coolness; One wonders how many stories high the pavilions must be. A woman in crimson skirts sings under the night moon; A monk in black robes is intoxicated by the autumn wind.
The sounds of roosters and dogs now pervade the place; how could the tracks of monkeys and apes be the same? I reflect upon Minister Zhang, whose single wrath purified the dragon palace.

Beneath the lamp, I recall Master Hanshan, who once dwelt here as a young monk; he recorded the passing years amidst ice and snow. Having already mastered the skill of slaying dragons, he still practiced the meditation of subduing tigers.

The Dharma-thunder resounds through the Ten Stages; a rain of flowers scatters among the various heavens. Having spent two nights with a mind emptied of worldly burdens, I intend to tune the strings of my parched *tóng* zither to its ultimate pitch.
Dwelling in the mountains, I rejoice that the snow has cleared;
within a single chamber amidst ten thousand peaks, who is there to seek out Master Yuǎn? The snow obscures the path of the woodsmen; the frost seals the palace of the ant-king.
Illuminating the nature, I know it is not defiled; without thought, I first accord with the ultimate sameness. Having finished my morning gruel, the sea-sun rises over the eastern peak.
A single drop of spring water holds the memory of my dharma companions;
the path is cut off amidst a thousand peaks. Suddenly Yunmen breaks through the seal: how many layers of fine mountains there are! Wild grasses naturally form their own clusters.
The stony path leads to the treetops; a cold spring emerges from within the cliffs. Among the fellow practitioners below, who could have the fortune to follow along here?
In midsummer, I traveled with fellow practitioners to Shangfang Xiyu (Joyful Rain on the Upper Peak).
[Two Poems] The road begins upon the level fields; the azure cliffs appear as if carved by hand. There is heaven at the summit, yet no ground upon which to press further.

To avoid the world, clouds are not merely pale; with the cessation of artifice, the waters naturally become clear. Arriving together we encounter a fine rain, as the bells and chimes announce a new clearing of the skies.

Having built our cottage near the blue heavens, we dwell on high where the terrain is naturally secluded. Birds sing in the trees beneath the steps; dragons emerge from the springs within the caverns.
The mountain moon is white throughout the night; pine-clad clouds brush away the summer heat. From afar I know that within the city walls, one cannot sleep upon pillow and mat.
A Five-Syllable Heptameter Verse on Passing through Master Zhilang’s Studio of Serenity.

The seclusion of this place aids the stillness of the mind; the emptiness of the pond awakens one to the world’s bustle. Looking back, neither of these truly exists, yet we insist on calling it "constant radiance.

The reflections in the windows of the pavilions, the fragrance of pines and springs within the mirror—mountains amidst the clouds never grow old, and for whom does the moon upon the water provide coolness?
The heavens break as fish blow the waves; the book is cast aside and the traveler lies upon his bed. In coming and going, the mind remains unstained;
in clamor and silence, all paths are forgotten. Do not disdain the small thatched cottage; within the dust and wind lies a separate place of practice.
The Collected Works of the Elder Zibo, Volume Twenty-five;
The Collected Works of the Elder Zibo, Volume Twenty-six.
Read by Hanshan Deqing of the Ming Dynasty.
Poem (Seven-Syllable Old Style):
At Fishhook Peak, the House of Han lost its deer, and all vied to pursue it. Upon the river, a single strand of line suffices for mountain and water. In my dreams, dragons and snakes battle fiercely.
Intoxicated! Beyond his sheepskin robe, what does he desire? Casting his fishing rod at random, he transforms into a perilous peak; hanging from the moon and propping up the clouds, it never bends.
Have you not seen how one leisurely cast of the line by the waters of the Wei yielded a fish that lived for eight hundred years, sustaining all things through its vital energy?
What has this Master accomplished with his single cast? For ten thousand ages, he causes people to look up to his lofty footsteps.
Last night I stayed south of Taiping Bridge over the Xujiang;
tonight I sleep south of Taiping Bridge. South of the bridge and north of the bridge are but a single stream;
how could one stream ever hold two boats? If the weather should be fair at dawn, I shall go from the mountain above Gushan to visit [the Master].

The Immortal. The immortal was originally an ordinary woman. When the passions of the ocean of desire withered and the bonds of craving were severed—once the serpent of craving was severed, she became a dragon, flying freely and soaring alone in transcendence.

The wild crane among a thousand peaks; the Daoist’s crane at the edge of heaven. The valedictory essay winner for three years; the sparrow within its cage. The wild crane at the edge of heaven flies with sovereign ease;
the satiated sparrow in its cage gladly accepts its confinement. The pine-clouds and the court robes—their ailments are not the same. How many people know that one can be ill?

Taking medicine, I laugh at myself for having studied the art of slaying dragons in my youth; now that my skill is perfected, it is useless and utterly abandoned. With my alms-bowl, staff, and *kāṣāya*, I travel everywhere;

with a willow branch for rinsing my mouth, I chew it every morning. Within this bitterness there is a flavor, refreshingly cool; the livers of dragons and the lungs of phoenixes pale in comparison to this stillness.
Banchuan asked Yuexie Linlang:
"Juesheng, I ask about the moon at the edge of heaven—has it ever experienced separation? From Mount Yanshan to Wumen, how many times have we witnessed its waxing and waning?"

Sometimes they are born upon the sea; at times they vanish amidst the forests. Their radiance appears and disappears; would they ever allow themselves to be muddied by the clouds of delusion? Have you not seen it?
Within the *xiāo-sì* (Pine Monastery) by the side of the Chang’an road, incense burns as one sits in the open air beneath the moon suspended in the sky.
Last night, eighteen eminent monks gathered; the clouds and moon are boundless—whence do you come again? And have you not seen it? The ineffable mystery is scattered everywhere.
Thrust! Who can pick up the pearls scattered across the ground? This state of mind cannot be grasped through the metaphor of emptiness; one must exert effort to shatter that very emptiness.
To the lay practitioner Lian’an, who has come to Southern Min.
The man of the Way feels self-reproach that his mind is not yet empty; he pities you for your distant journey, his heart filled with anxiety.

Once gone from Zhangzhou, it is four thousand li; one knows not how many treacherous ridges you must traverse. At the head of the Fen Water Ridge, the path is narrow as a thread; servants call to one another, evening and morning.
Where do the cold clouds resound with the cries of monkeys and gibbons? The sun and moon do not hasten the graying of our double locks. It is said that at Liangshan...
Pine trees thick with frost; the roots of the pines embrace the rocks, their mossy hues deep. My silent vow shall not be betrayed, as constant as a river.
Let me not be denied the chance to brush my hair amidst the thousand crags.
On the walls of Zhaozhou’s Bolin Temple, water is painted.
In painting water, how could there ever be the characteristics of water? If there were such characteristics, how could one paint the form of water?
The numinous hall (*lingtai*) is devoid of things, profound and clear; with a confident hand, wind arises and sweeps into waves. Behold them rolling on, yet listen—there is no sound.

Day after day, the billows stretch for thousands of miles. Within this, it is not necessarily that fish and dragons are absent; their heads and horns remain hidden, awaiting the roar of thunder. You do not understand; I shall paint it for you.
If the thought of painting does not arise, the painting will never be completed once it has begun. It is like the return of spring to the great earth:
how could every branch, red or white, possess intention?
Seeing a monk returning from the South to the eternal abode of Qian-nian at He-lin Temple, I reflect:
you, my teacher, have died for the sake of this permanent residence alone. Even mosquitoes and gnats, though minute, still cling to life;
how could a human being not cherish it? Moved by grief for the deceased, I compose this poem. Do not say that these are but decayed bones.

That which is known: how many times, under the bright moon in the bamboo grove, did the souls of the departed wail with choked sobs? Though the famous monastery has not yet been restored, how could I forget it in my heart?
Since my heart does not forget, the Way remains present. Most pitiable is that when the bitter autumn winds and rains have ceased, your teacher shall come and go upon the ridges of this mountain.

At Lingfeng, gazing at the spring, the mountains and waters have no intention to flaunt their spiritual wonders. Yet as travelers distinguish them, profound thoughts arise. Before these profound thoughts first arose through discrimination, who could have known the spiritual wonders of the mountains and waters?
Within this very state there is naturally a place of excellence; it is not that having a mind makes it so, nor is it that lacking a mind makes it otherwise.
At the moment of mind, I wandered upon the Spirit Peak; the peak did not speak. In profound silence, there was the sound of thunder, as if my ears were about to fall away.
The giant tortoise bore me on its head as I seemed to fly off; leaning my staff upon the clouds, where could I go?

Dwelling in the mountains, do not say that the forested clouds are but a "transformed city. How many who meet here have lightened their worldly ties? The green mountains do not know how to grow old with man;
white hair alone knows how to follow the passing years. The myriad realms are originally empty, yet the mind creates obstructions; when the One Reality is without dependence, this is the Way.
Only then was it completed. If Chang’an should ask about the excellence of Kaixian, tell them: after the meal, listen idly to the sound of the waterfall.
During the midsummer, I joined various dharma companions to pay homage to the five hundred arhats at Duobao Temple.
Just then, a Chan practitioner was kneeling before the statues reciting the Lotus Sūtra; I listened quietly, [the sound] like cold mountain springs flowing.
The sound of the water rushing past enters my ears; the spirit-mansion is clear and translucent. Joyfully, I compose this verse:
The white sun comes to attend the meditation of the Subduing Tiger; with whom can one share the dyeing of the monk’s robe? Amidst wind and dust, there is a path that leads to the ground of the mind;
amidst water and moon, no one asks about the sky of nature. In vain I imagine the Xuan-an hermitage turning over the *Bai-ye* (Palm-leaf) scriptures; from afar I know the thunder and rain protect it.
At Kintetsu, amidst the cool pines, I listen to the cold waves; the root of passion for ten thousand kalpas is washed away in a single moment.

Reciting my reflections, I mingle my petty, wild songs with those of the butcher; suddenly, in an instant, I am intoxicated by the clarified butter (amṛta). Within my breast, the sun and moon shine without end.

All is exhausted. The afflictions of external wind and dust have been dispelled. Tigers and leopards have always been but dogs to the mountain temple; who among kings and lords realizes they are slaves to profit and fame?
With leisure on a morning, what is there to divert oneself with? After the meal, one leans alone against a catalpa tree to gaze at the clouds.

The stone steps winding through the Tianqi Meditation Hall cannot be counted; deep within the chaotic peaks lies the hermitage. Water falls from hollowed logs amidst the clouds, and the monks dwell upon high crags where the field of vision is empty.
Desiring to complete the remaining sutra, they wait for the moon; having spontaneously composed half a verse, they pause for a moment.
Chanting in the breeze. Returning, I did not realize the mists and clouds had grown dark; at the mouth of the valley, I first heard the evening bell for meditation.
Two Poems on Stirring Emotions:
Mountains upon mountains, waters upon waters—one must know that the paths of delusion and awakening are not the same. Within the field of profound stillness, [I am] like a louse...
Tiger! On the roads of Chang’an, horses are like dragons. White clouds naturally disperse to return to the green peaks; who shall take the bright moon to hang in the azure sky?
If one could prevent the noble from dying, let the peach and plum trees laugh at the spring breeze.
How could such seclusion exist amidst the dust and wind? Ten thousand ravines and a thousand crags lock away but one small mound. White hair does not need planting yet grows all too easily;
red cheeks one wishes to detain, yet they are hard to keep. One seeks the tracks of flying birds within the void;
the aged monk has no heart for wandering beyond the mundane world. I ask my old friend: in the dream of the槐 kingdom (huánguó), at the fifth watch when the frost is cold, will you awaken?
"Who has taken this lapis lazuli lamp and cast its icy orb down to the lower realm? The old Chan master picks it up and hangs it in the empty hall.

Though its rising and sinking depend upon other powers, from the beginning, both within and without, it has been luminous by its own nature. Before being lit, the golden countenance remains cold and dim; as soon as it is ignited, the precious seat becomes even more radiant."
Resplendent! Do not compare it to the dragon-candles; they do not illuminate the human king, but illuminate the Dharma King.
Beyond Laṅkā Island, the solitary peaks on every side give rise to clouds and mist;
boundless fish and dragons stir within the waters and heavens. One wishes to dispel the myriad errors—do not trouble yourself with questions.

Answer: A single phrase dissolves both the center and the periphery; there is no need to fortify defenses so that men find it difficult to reach. Yet, if one harbors no seeking, the ground is naturally impartial.
When the great sun of wisdom grows ever larger, what need is there for worldly affairs? With the sutra unfinished, one sits with knees tucked, watching the gulls sleep.
A Poem on the Waterfall at Kaixian Temple, Left for Zhongjian’s Travels:
Faintly and thunderously it descends from the heavens; Layered white clouds cannot obscure its brilliance. There is no place to cut or shape it with blade or ruler;

It is accustomed to riding the wind and manifesting as rain and thunder. Upon reaching the sea, it must ultimately encompass the sun and moon; Having left the mountains, how could it ever consent to be stained?
Dust and grime, he carries on the tip of his staff toward all quarters; he rolls up fish and dragons and carries them back home.

Listening to pines, the mountain waters and scenery—worldly sentiments are empty. Incidentally listening to the pine wind, it is yet more extraordinary. Without a dream, one wanders through heaven and earth.

Externally: Having a body, how could one fall within the cycle of birth and death? A name renowned since antiquity is a burden to the mind; when the Way resides within, what prevents one from reaching the very marrow of poverty?
Zhi Ying abandoned his gourd on the riverbank because it annoyed his ears, yet did he know that this sound was the Great Compassionate Elder?
Mooring my boat at the eastern bank of Shimen, I visited the sacred traces of Jiyin and concurrently reminisced about Chan Master Chang of Guizong on Mount Lu.

Having traveled the entirety of the rivers and mountains, my inspiration remains undiminished; I have briefly moored my small boat to the east of Shimen. May the rains and dew of the Golden Wheel [the Buddha] descend upon the thousand...
Ancient: The jade calendar and spring breeze come from the Nine Palaces. One need not worry that one’s hair turns white overnight;
having already realized that body and mind are originally empty, what hindrance is there between city and mountain forest? With bottle and staff drifting, he visits the Sleeping Dragon.
The winding mountains and waters are wondrous beyond measure; misty waves and azure skies grace the monastic halls. There is a path through the stone gate, yet one must rely on boat and oar;
though the golden ground is empty, none await the sound of the meal bell. Rain assists the stream’s voice, swallowing it in silence;
clouds drag the ocean’s hue, sharpening the void. Returning once more, I ascend the Laṅkā Pavilion; leaning against the railing, I sing long as I gaze toward Mount Zhurong.
Spontaneously composed: Having readied myself for the world, I have returned to hide on Half-Peak. A small thatched cottage is tied together east of Tiger Creek.

Fully realizing that the mark of self has no place of rest, the conditioned mind is directly rendered empty in this very moment. Flowers falling and blooming are dreams of success and failure; bubbles arising and vanishing are...
No trace remains. Should you encounter me and ask of my life’s affairs, I shall lie flat upon my belly and sing aloud amidst the vastness of the Great Clod.

At the Ink Radiance Pavilion, I have chosen a secluded dwelling beside the Dragon River; bamboo beds and mossy paths hold few human footprints. On idle mornings, cranes perch upon the tips of pine branches.

Standing still, in the quiet night when the moon is high and cloudless, mountains and rivers arise in my dreams as thoughts stir; the honors and disgraces before my eyes are empty by their very conditions.
Having finished copying the sutras while burning fine incense, I still perceive the dense ink-fumes from my ceramic inkwell.

Sitting at night in Yiwentang, the faces of old travelers in the dust of the world pass by. Having come here to lie high among the ten thousand peaks in leisure, let the myriad joys of the worldly path take their course;

how could the single piece of a meditative mind find such idle ease? The empty greenery has feeling and lingers for the bare feet of the monk; amidst the scorching heat, no dream reaches [the senses].
Green Mountains. Let the sugarcane juice do as it pleases to dispel the summer heat; by the stones, listening to the spring, one cannot yet climb.
Ascending Yueyang Tower, I recall Master Lü the Immortal:
I have heard that the Master would become intoxicated upon this tower, allowing others to call him a horse or even a cow. In this turbid world, who has the fortune to see him in his true green hue?

The eye attains its purpose at the blue waves where white gulls dwell; A single sword of cold radiance makes the celestial gates chill; A half-bowl of bright moonlight finds the autumn of Lake Dongting.
Mount Junshan laughs that I have come so late to ascend; I know you shall join me in wandering from dawn to dusk.
Early I crossed the Jialing River and ascended Mount Jinping; the sun rose over the long ridges as a rainbow spanned the sky.
Across the river, mist-shrouded trees mark the ancient land of Cancong. Perilous peaks seem on the verge of falling, yet are embraced by the roots of pines;

the vast dew has just begun to fade, leaving flower shadows empty. The colors of the mountains and waters are no different from those of former dynasties; yet the garments and caps still bear the traces of the wilds.
The wind of humanity; the white gulls wonder at my late arrival. They come and go, flying and calling amidst the brocade waves.
On a winter night at Ink Fragrance Hermitage, I miss Master Fanglu, who has built his home in a river village far from the dust of the market.
Seeking one another morning and evening, there are only those who till the soil. By the water’s edge, I practice seated meditation within the mirror.
A shadow walking under the moon, a body within a dream; Yellow leaves need not be swept by a youth, White gulls are uniquely intimate with the wild monk.
Having spent long days writing books, I know this has become a vice; I wish to visit the meditation hall for a time to nourish my spirit.

In this new autumn, who could have foreseen whether my traces would go or stay? In these grottoes and ravines, I am suddenly startled to find summer has turned to fall. My Buddha-nature rejoices in following the clouds with ease;
my Zen mind is too weary to vie with the flowing water. To be poor in body while dwelling beyond the mundane world is my constant lot; to suffer little illness amidst leisure is my blessing.
Supreme. Let the paulownia leaves fly by the tens of thousands; for the man of the Way, there is nothing to give rise to sorrow.

This poem was written upon passing through Cishou Temple, moved by the afflictions that disturb the meditative mind. How strange that years and months have been wasted on empty rhetoric! Before a single thought arises, the light is already gone.

When the consciousness of the senses arises, one does not know suffering. Carrying a jar to water the garden—do not say it is clumsy; storming a city or building cloud-stacked towers—these are but vain wonders.
How can these compare to sitting with robes draped over one’s shoulders in a stone chamber? When the mind is clarified, there is a distinct principle.
In the azure garden, the thatched gate is left unbarred by white clouds; whether coming or going, there is no need to ask the master. The square inch of the mind is a lofty mirror of a thousand ages;

myriad conditions are empty and still, like the sound of a single bell. A coolness arises in the liver and lungs from the lotus-drip water-clock; fragrance wafts through the curtains and beams from the *baidūrya* [lapis lazuli] incense burner.
Leaves rustle in the wind. May my iron bowl pour forth the waters of Samādhi; may they scatter as nectar to drench the world.
Hearing the sound of autumn, I am moved;
whether dwelling, walking, or sitting, do not suspect the birds. Because I crave this secluded excellence, I linger once more. Smoke and mists have never belonged to man since antiquity.

In this world, the stony rapids are uniquely able to wash away the traveler’s sorrows. How many layers of cloud-peaks lie beneath the steps? Why does the autumn color on the crags seem to arrive so precociously?
The boat hidden in the stone ravine—who would betray it? In the stillness of the deep night, contemplation serves as the medium.
In the late spring, I passed through the bamboo courtyard to visit the layman Jiansu.
The shadows of ten thousand bamboos sweep across the ripples of the water; the wilds are vast, the breeze gentle, and the scent of ripening wheat fills the air.

Those of our generation have long been prone to indolence and eccentricity, yet our host is so open and unpretentious that we have come to forget ourselves entirely. Within the pavilion, the chessboard remains as the waning moon strikes it; beyond the pond, the mountain peaks stretch on and on.
Half the hall. The gulls know nothing of the affairs of the dusty world; they fly here and there, watching people in their haste.
Passing through Yangxian and Shushan to pay my respects to Su Changgong, who came from Huangzhou and spent his final years here.
Amidst green mountains and flowing waters, he was separated from the winds and dust of the world. His mind, like the sun and moon, could not escape its course.

His reputation for slander filled heaven and earth, yet he could not save the poor; through several cycles of exile, his life seemed like a dream. His writings endure through all eternity with a spirit as fresh as spring.
In the clear autumn, where can one find a place worthy of lamentation? At a desolate shrine on a hill in Shu, my soul is moved to sorrow.

Meeting many while dwelling in the mountains, they mostly urge me to cease my pursuit of the immortal way; yet traveling on foot, it is ultimately difficult to reach the end. A sliver of moon hangs in the sky, its light unceasing;
a thousand peaks face the door, their green hues ever floating. Upon the stones for leisurely repose, I inscribe yellow leaves; by the clouds to quench my thirst, I drink.
Azure streams flow; in my decline, how can I bear to hear these words? Moved by such sentiments, I linger for a while.
Having traveled to Caoxi, I found temporary rest at Changsong Guan;
I have chosen a secluded dwelling within the city. Where bamboo waves and pine clouds meet, a grass path leads through. To practice tranquility, why need one depart from the myriad things?

Transformation follows conditions; responding to them, one does not obscure the dual emptiness. Before the lamp, who is this traveler in the green robe? Under the moon, one often hears the bell of the White Society.
The debt of the road remains unpaid even now; at Caoxi, he pays homage to the bowl and watches the dragon descend.

Passing the hermitage of Layman Tao, I did not meet him; he lies high upon the green mountains, severed from the dust of the world. The wattle gate remains closed all day, covered in verdant moss. Clouds join the hue of the trees, darkening the interior of the chamber;

bamboo leads the sound of the spring, arriving through the empty air. No ordinary bird dares to inscribe its mark upon this ground selected by the Buddha; where, then, has the Master gone to find his wine?
At the Immortal Terrace, we met, yet had no time to explore lofty discourse; gazing idly at the dark-faced monkeys, I was filled with melancholy.

Feeling moved by the early winter, the scorching heat has not yet ceased when the cold arrives once more. It drives the hair upon my head into a mass of snow. All matters of joy arise from amidst busyness.

A mistake! One’s sorrowful thoughts should open up within stillness. If birth and death were to favor the noble and honorable, then the Way and its Virtue would surely be seen as equal to dust and soil.
When reason and emotion are as clear as black and white, there is no need to speculate about poverty or prosperity, longevity or early death.

Paddling through the night at Shimen, parting the weeds to gaze upon the wind—how could this be by mere chance? A journey of a hundred cities across vast distances is but the unfolding of past karmic conditions. The moon over the central stream is deep yet shallow;
the clouds and mountains on both banks are severed yet joined again. All disciples vie to boast of sitting upon the celestial throne, while a single sail seems to float within a mirror.
Hanging in mid-air, the stone gates and bells move in concert. How does listening with the ears compare to listening with the eyes for the profound?

To show the King the vastness of the universe, his lofty ambition is majestic and his hair is not yet gray. Let no man betray the good light of his time; at the break of dawn, a single thought buries the spirit.

All worldly dust is transformed into the fragrance of virtue during the day; worldly pleasures have always been honey upon a blade. This fleeting life is as swift as frost upon the tip of a blade of grass.
There is a path to transcendence that lies not beyond the heavens; it is clearly manifest in daily use, never concealed.
Sitting in the night, I heard the two young men, Yu and Miu, discuss the path of friendship and the killing of life;
though the resentment of an enemy may not be deep, the betrayal of a true friend is most difficult to restrain.

One must firmly maintain vows of diligence beyond the kalpas, constantly reflecting before the lamp upon a heart of lamentation. Worldly conditions and karmic ties are not true kin; the spiritual seeds of the gate of compassion are what truly matter.
The True Cause. This time I have lost my *bodhi* seeds; the vast ocean of suffering is boundless and difficult to find.
When Tang Fengchang Ning’an came to visit me, we discussed the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. I rebuked him, for I felt that many Chan practitioners are insolent.
He departed without bowing, so I composed this verse to mock him.

Why have you traveled so far from Yunlin to seek me out? You have trodden upon my verdant moss; can this truly be called "appreciating the music"? Last night’s dream of the plantain-leaf deer was no auspicious vision;
the fire-bulls of antiquity were merely intended to repel a grave invasion. With many karmic ties and a shallow worldly existence, I hold my precarious rank lightly;

surely lofty words alone cannot still the hearts of the multitude. Since we have met, there is no need to harbor further thoughts of pride; a single rebuke from Wang Sheng is worth a thousand pieces of gold.
In reply to Vice Minister Liu:

One need only purify the mind until it is as empty as space; why must you visit Master Yuan frequently? If one treats public affairs as if they were private family matters, then the worldly mind will become identical to the mind of the Way.
You must know that once death has come, there is no room for high or low; from antiquity, floating clouds have been easily dispersed.
From beginning to end, he always laughed at his own leisurely life as being of no use; he would wander east and west, gazing upon the mountains and waters.
He stayed at Zhao Hua Temple on Fangshan (with a preface).
Now, that which is most spiritual and excellent is man; that which is most venomous and fierce is the tiger. When a man encounters a supreme man...
He laughed heartily. Seeing the elder, the tiger became docile and submissive. Was it man or tiger? Was it tiger or man?
Surely there must be those who understand such words. I have long heard of the elder’s reputation; now, having joyfully beheld his portrait, I compose this verse.

A thousand peaks lie silent and desolate; the path is long and arduous. In the moss-covered grotto of the Elder, the striped tigers roar. On the frosty cliffs behind the ridges, the clouds remain frozen;
in the sun-facing groves and valleys, the snow has just begun to melt. The radiance of his teeth clarifies the ocean of Dharma like the moon over the pines;
the mark of his tongue roars with the celestial wind like the night surging tide. Since Miaoyan cast down his brush, who else has continued to wield the pen for the *Saṃpuṭa-sūtra*?
Together with Attendant Fu and General Wang, we pay homage at the Great Image on Fang Mountain.
From of old, heaven and earth have been its rocky grotto; the wondrous form stands majestic, facing south alone. Ten thousand ages of lamp transmission rely upon the sun and moon;
a single hair radiates shadows across the rivers and mountains. Wild birds descend from the void to offer flowers; the azure dragon emerges from the water to listen.
Intoxicated by the Dharma, I turn my head to see white clouds sealing the mountain peak. With whom can I share the realization of this merit?

Reflecting on my own state, I have wandered through rivers and lakes for many winters. I do not study the madness of Chan, nor the eccentricity of the madman of Chu. White hair has an enemy that urges me on.

Old age: the green mountains laugh at the busy toil of men. When passions are extinguished, how could one merely cast oneself into emptiness? To sever habitual tendencies, one must practice contemplation and forgetfulness.
With staff and sandals drifting freely wherever they may rest, where攀緣 (pān-yuán) is stilled, that is one’s true home.
Incidentally composed:
Coming from afar to the water’s surface to seek traces of the past, my Way-learning is one with that of Nāgārjuna in India. Beyond sleep and sitting, I cast aside antiquity and the present;

amidst laughter and talk, I distinguish the ordinary and the sage. Once the book is finished, the price of paper rises all at once; when the principle is penetrated, the literary composition reaches ten thousand heights.
O Hero of the World, there is yet another aspect of your carefree elegance: death and life enter your heart as if in a dreamless sleep.

Dwelling amidst the mountains, you have never perceived the dust and turmoil of the world; wild deer often accompany your Dharma-body. In the vast blue sea, you alone remain at ease beyond the clouds.
Guest: The green mountains laugh coldly at those within the world. Six dragons on a decaying rope can never travel far; two mice on a withered vine are easily separated by a broken neighbor.
If kings and lords were to understand this truth, they would likely cast off their caps before the break of dawn.
On an autumn day, I stayed with Master Tongcheng at NanTai; the vermilion steps wind and turn, the path long and arduous.
In the urgency of my inspiration, who would have known the toil of staff and sandals? The bright moon fills the terrace, its hue mingling with the snow;
white clouds span the valley, mistaken for the surging tides of the river. The golden urn truly permits the concealment of the true bone; the precious verses are able to bring about transformation.
A venomous dragon! My Way has now fallen into profound desolation. For whom do I shed tears that dampen my black cassock?
Having woken from sleep, I read the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*;
in stillness upon my grass mat, I lie with the clouds. Dreaming awake, the moon at the eaves is perfectly full. As the thought arises to eliminate anger, anger only increases further.

Blazing! When the mind arises to abandon delusion, delusion only increases further. To neither establish existence nor non-existence is not yet the ultimate subtlety; to forget both person and phenomena simultaneously is still not the primordial source.
The ultimate Way is empty and void—who would dare to compare it? Once one engages in deliberation, one has already fallen into the two or three extremes.

In humble reply to the esteemed Vice Minister Wansisi, who has long since lost his heart for worldly affairs and offers this as a jest: Who in this world can truly be called a friend? The clear pool is surely the lair of the azure dragon;
The grand mansion is ultimately no more than a nest for the wild crane. After a meal, one need only sit or lie at ease; Once a poem is finished, why must one toil over it further?
*Pondering.* I know from afar that Great Fan delights in the passing scenes; In this stillness, I fear he has not yet cast aside his refined seclusion.

*On the Occasion of Events at Ink Fragrance Hermitage, Shown to Yuan Guang (Two Poems)* After the rain, who is it that takes up the short staff? Daosheng, wrapped in his fur robe, moves with ease. The azure sky is boundless as the clouds first appear.

Severance. The bright moon constantly comes; the water never fails. To inquire into the Dharma, one must transcend the path of the intellect; seeking through fragrances is ultimately but the trace of conditioned activity.
Within my house, there is a separate place for penetrating the source: it is firmly binding the clay ox to the pine tree atop the ridge.
The Way lies in following conditions to dispel delusions; calling it "ox" or "horse" are but idle names. A plum must meet the snow to compete in its whiteness;
a bamboo only reveals its clarity when facing the wind. When the mirror is free of dust, its light is naturally full; where there is a path among the clouds, the deer always travel.
If you should encounter me and ask for the temple before the mountain, the cold, clear flowing water mingles with the sound of the chimes.
At Ink Fragrance Hermitage, Shown to Guanglang (Two Poems) Before the village and behind it, all is misty waters;
year after year, the rice and grain are abundant. The mossy path is silent and desolate, for no one comes;
in the clear and vast autumn sky, the moon passes first. The Three Maoshan peaks lie far away, and I long remember them always; having just composed this half-verse, I am alone.
I hummed this to myself. I love most the distinct melody of the zither of non-arising; yet upon Mount Long, the sound of the stone chimes is frequent.

Out in the wilds, amidst the whistling wind and falling rain, Master Zhi has not slept since nightfall. If human life were such that one never grew old, why would the moon be disparaged for its incomplete orb?
My karma lies in these fine mountains where I am content to be a guest; once the Way is realized, one severs attachment to all affairs.
Grasping at objects—exhausting the spiritual essence may not necessarily be deluded wisdom, yet how can it compare to the fragrant couch where dhyāna has not yet been reached?
Amidst leisure, my thoughts stir as I show this to Guanglang:
the fiery calamity of the burning house dries the lips; who is there to partake of the sugarcane juice filling the bowl? From now on, attain the wondrous through following the flow.
Entering. To face the world without a mind has been difficult since antiquity. Beneath the water, red flowers sway on both banks; before the wind, green bamboo dances in a thousand stalks.
If the passage of years could be made to remain forever, who would ever be willing to hang their crown at the Northern Gate?

At twilight, aboard a boat on the Xiao and Xiang rivers, I return from ten thousand miles with staff and sandals light. Having boarded this vessel, I find myself able to sit and practice walking meditation; the sound of the oars and the shadow of the sails provide material for my poetry.

The hues of the water and the brilliance of the mountains answer the traveler’s longing. To lament the ancients amidst the misty waves is truly a source of regret, yet the gulls, having forgotten all artifice, remain naturally at ease.
No cause for alarm. At dusk we moored, knowing not where we were; beyond the clouds, the distant sky and moon shone bright.
While observing the summer retreat in the northern garden of Jintan, I also recall Hou Tie’an’s pleasure in the cool breeze—why need one dwell alone at Fufu?
The serene charm of water and wood is the same in both places. In this world, all alike prize the "fat horse."
The price is set; in the forest solitude, the sick monk is left to his indolence. Moss patterns form characters as cranes pass by;
moon shadows are swallowed by fish, yet they do not understand emptiness. I further recall the dream atop the Danxu Pavilion; drifting fragments of cold clouds meet upon the ridge.

From my boat on the Ji’an River, I gaze upon the towers and pavilions of Bailu Academy, a single expanse of water in the center of the stream. The white egrets flutter through the mist, having known how many frosts.

Though the green mountains on both banks remain silent, for a thousand autumns those with yellowing hair have looked up to their lingering fragrance. Smoke rises from the Buddhist temples as they burn dragon-brain incense; ripples shake the study lamps as they pass by.
A traveler’s journey: Do not say that the day of ascending will never come; my straw sandals have trodden through the very bowels of the Prefect.

Recalling my youth, I was mixed among those who slaughtered dogs for the sake of profit in the spring and autumn of history; who would have thought that I would don the black robes to become a bhikṣu? I feel ashamed that my habits of chivalry remain uncast off.

Exhausted, one truly cultivates; only then does joy arise as progress continues without ceasing. In tranquil meditation, clouds and rocks serve as a bed and seat; in preaching the Dharma, the pines and wind take the place of the tongue.
With nothing left but this idle body, what need is there for anything else? Amidst overlapping mountains and rivers, one wanders freely at will.
The Dharma King Xī (Nandirāja) was born from the primordial source;

he extensively inquired into the Dharma. Pine and bamboo surround his meditation chamber; his coarse robes rustle as he stays far from the marketplace. A single strike of the clear chime cuts through the dream of worldly dust;
A few fragments of white cloud leave the Way-mind at ease. The soaring birds in the heavens must surely look up with admiration; The green moss beneath the steps does not...
May this be deleted. Who comes at night to the Golden Ground to inquire of the Dharma? Together we share the lamp-light to illuminate the mountain of ignorance.
In the mid-winter month, I miss Jue;
summer has passed and winter arrives, and old age is easily startled. In this world of heaven and earth, who else can comfort my inner feelings? Flowers do not obtain dew and ultimately wither.
Form: Pine must rely on the wind before it has sound. Let the Way come naturally; it has been honored for a thousand ages. Leaving home is as light as a single hair.
When we meet, I wish to ask about the Yellow River: since childhood, how many times has it been clear?
A Visit to Chan Master Guifeng at Dajue Temple:
Having traversed streams and mountains, I arrive at this sacred abode. In the empty grove, fallen leaves cover the steps and thresholds. He passes his days in leisure, burning aloeswood incense;
His merit surpasses our own as he prizes the crest-jewel. Great news hangs from the rafters like palm-leaf scriptures; The crow-watches are observed upon the waters.
Lotus. Ordinarily, when the meal is finished and there is nothing else to do, I scoop up cold spring water myself to wash my alms bowl.

I visited Yuan Kunyi with a sense of resonance, intending to gather *pinghua* flowers; I have traveled here many times. Suddenly, it is once again the clear autumn of Taoyuan. The empty crags are desolate, the pines and cypresses sighing.
Old age. Vast and desolate is the watery realm, where orchids and *du* reeds grow in seclusion. Purple fortifications cut off the wild geese; dreams drift beyond the clouds.
On green mountains, a scattering rain brings sorrow to the traveler. Mooring my boat, I seek the windless tree—yellow leaves fly about, never ceasing their fall.
Delighting in this place, I have just passed through Longquan;
for a time, I shall lodge my staff and bowl upon this mountain. Amidst the distant peaks, I seek out the rock-cave hermitage; within the shadows of the tall pines, the clamor of the world is stilled.
Amidst the sound of flowing water, the moonlight is cold. The sacred bones are not to be sought outside the self; the divine pearl is shared within the palm.
It is worth looking upon. May we meet again so as not to betray one another; from of old, the morning flower and dew are easily withered.

Having happened upon this mountain, I have grown weary of the wind and dust and thus closed these gates. My heart is pure and cool, like a cold pool; I trim the pines and let the moon through the wall.
Above, I lead water to move it toward the corner of the thatched roof; there are only Zen texts to pass the long days, and no human tracks reach these green mountains.
Let those who know me not laugh at my clumsy means of livelihood; in this vast and boundless universe, how few are truly at leisure?
Waterfall (Two Poems) Whose thousand-fathom lengths of white silk are drawn forth? Hung high upon the clouds, never to be withdrawn.

Having realized that the source from which it comes is far, How could one be willing to confuse its roots with the common current? Let the skillful hand try as it may, it would be hard to cut; Grant me this leisurely mind to share in its flow.
Casting myself down, from here I shall surely return to the great ocean; I wait to see the waves splashing against the heavens as they surge.

Wishing to cast myself into the blue sea to become its billows, how could I dread the difficulty of the thousand-fold mountain paths? The resonance steals the sound of the chime-bell, two swords grow cold;
the light swallows the moonlight, a single brazier grows chill. The silver river pours downward outside the azure sky; the jade tree hangs solitary amidst the emerald void.
Amidst the mountain curtains, how many times has the celestial wind failed to blow it away? It remains to accompany the monk’s leisure within the cloud-filled ravines.
On this autumn day, one pays homage at the Qingliang Pagoda;

through the shifting mists of successive eras, how many frosts have passed? The sacred relics within the stone casket are preserved by themselves; the reflections of the pearl grove fall as the heavens hang down.

The canopy covers the jeweled stupa as it rings out from the empty space, its banners crowding the air. Its grace extends across heaven and earth, while the dream of returning fades away. Spring returns to the rocky valleys, and the fragrance of the molded clay rises.
Coming once more to pay full respect, my grief and lamentation increase; beneath the falling leaves of the high autumn stands the old Hall of Shadows.
Miscellaneous Verses Written in the Mountains (Two Poems) In the Mahāyāna, why must one sever all attachments?
For a minor hermitage, one must likewise stay far from the marketplace. To practice meditative concentration, I gaze at the bright moon by the water’s edge;
To dispel idleness, I look upon the blue sky amidst the trees. If there is desire within the mind, the mountains are not tranquil; Only where there is no seeking in this world is it true peace.
Self-secluded and solitary, I marvel that our mutual understanding makes my plans for home so slow.
The nesting peaks lie desolate, locked in heavy mist; the wilds are vast and the wind high—a grand spectacle. For whom do you laugh and talk amidst the quiet of the Ox and Cow constellations?

Leaning on the railing, I feel the blue heavens draw near; who below could know the leisure of the white sun? Mountain hues stretch across the void, falling beyond the curtain; the ocean tide roars at the gate as I sit.
A chill in the mid-spring. Ascending these heights, my "madman's" enthusiasm remains unspent; with a bowl of tea, I sing a dirge for the hardships of the traveler’s path.

*Verses on Dwelling in the Mountains (Two Poems)* In leisure, I gather broken flax to mend my sleeves; how could I trade springs and rocks for fleeting splendor? Light shines through the jar-window of Dongshan.
The moonlight scatters incense across the altar above the world; in dreams, the hero Bai Qi toils in vain.
Since antiquity, haughty lords have laughed at Fuchai, who in the depths of winter flaunted his wealth and nobility—digging ice from his own ponds and boiling tea for himself.
Vast and boundless is the sea of suffering, now surging with waves; there is no better plan than to escape into Chan—this is the highest strategy.

The worldly path has already alarmed my heart, yet it does not die; fame and office remain but a dream, while my hair has already withered. Because I am content with plain white congee, I have forgotten its bitterness;
yet I find strange how the verdant moss shares in my solitude. That joy reaches its peak is simply because poverty has reached my very bones; even Yao and Xu were not permitted to yield the vanguard.
In praise of Dharma Master Xiufeng of Yongqing Temple:
From a young age, you knew to cease worldly entanglements; with your jar and bowl in hand, you retired in quietude to Mount Funiu. The bright moon possesses its own light and cannot be obscured;
white clouds, free from burdens, easily linger on. Do not startle the wild monkeys, for they are but Zen tigers; how could their seizing of prey ever differ from that of other beasts?
Seagulls. For years I have preached the Dharma, wearying the waters and rocks; for whom do the waterfalls cascade from the precipice?

The matter of "inviting the recluse" regarding birth and death is no light affair—how strange that these deluded people do not startle themselves! Ten thousand *li* of golden wealth exhausts the mouth [of the seeker].
The belly is full; with a head of white hair, one strives for fame and merit. Does Master Yan truly value the skill of "slaying dragons"? Why must Master Tian needlessly learn the barking of a dog?
Sooner or later we shall return to the temple beyond the clouds, where at night deep we shall read the *Lamp of the Dharma* by the pine-fire.

Ascending Luyaya in the Snow (with Preface) I was residing at Lêng-yen in Wu-chung when I suddenly dreamed of ascending a mountain. Its ridges were layered and its peaks were heavy, with ten thousand pines reflecting the snow.
Upon waking, I recounted this to Attendant K'ai and said, "From now on, I shall style myself 'Pine-Snow' (Sung-hsüeh). K'ai replied, "I pray that you..."
Xuesong opened his writing brush. Kneeling, he made his request with great persistence, and I finally granted it. Now, having ascended Luya to visit Master Miao, I encountered a heavy snowfall;
it was exactly like that dream scene from years ago. Moved by this, I composed this verse.
For several years I have traveled through rivers and lakes, staff in hand; in a single moment, the weeds and brambles have been transformed into a pure abode.

Tigers crouch upon the crags, closing off the paths of the world; springs fly from the treetops, entering the celestial kitchen. Often I am troubled by the need to burn leaves to brew tea, yet I still love gazing at the mountains while being too lazy to read books.
Once in a dream I came here to share a meal from the same bowl; as for the pines and snow today, what can they possibly be like?
In conversation with the host of Luya on worldly affairs, I was moved:
The cloud-roofed house is vast and silent, heavy with ice and snow. Before the lamp, with tea and wine, we discuss heroes. If the barrier of emotion is not broken, how can there be no loss?
Meeting on the paths of the world—is this not difficult? We share a drink, yet I pity that our sorrows are not shared; Though we lie upon the same bed, our dreams need not be the same.
The same. Over these years, how many matters have caused me grief? I entrust them all to the wondrous contemplation of Gautama.

I send this method of grain-avoidance to the Layman Yuan Liaofan, Water斋 (Water-Zhai), and the Mount Hua-yue Hermit. You, Master, have already attained the ability to abstain from grain; I know for certain that the ranks of immortals in heaven will increase.
Relying on this, how could I begrudge the flickering light of human life? The jade elixir constantly swallows, moistening liver and lungs; The golden cinnabar can turn white hair back to black.
The green mountains are not far away—we shall surely meet again; A new young man has been added to my circle of true friends.
The Dragon’s Beak (With Preface).
Before Mount Rìguāng, there is a ridge with jagged peaks that hangs over the side of a ravine; its form is like that of a coiled dragon, hence it is called the Dragon’s Beak.

A thatched hut has first been built upon this peak; I rejoice in its purity and vastness. Furthermore, two practitioners of the Dhyāna of the Second Dhyāna were reciting sutras here—one the *Saṃpuṣpita-garbhā* and the other the *Padma*.
As I descended from the Brahma-Immortal Peak, I happened to hear their clear and resonant voices, and thus composed this verse.
The bird-path winds and turns, difficult to ascend; herein, the clarity and vastness satisfy the secluded heart. Shaded peaks are draped in emerald, as spring clouds pass by;
reflections fall upon the empty pool as the sea moon rises. Mountain herbs are more than sufficient to fill the clay bowl; the practitioner especially delights in hearing the Lotus Sutra.
As the cool, dripping sounds reach within his parched entrails, let him not mistake the Precious Place for a conjured city.
The scriptures were transcribed at Qu’a;

as my humble cottage was already in disrepair, there was no need to clear away the thatch. Moreover, separated by green mountains from the bustle of the capital, the wild monk often arrives of his own accord, shrouded in clouds.
How could the host, who protects the Dharma, know of such toil? A solitary lamp flickers with the red shadows of falling flowers; a thousand bamboos stir in the wind, surging upward.
Cuitao. If those of noble station could but arrest the passage of time, how could Yao Chao and Zhong You have been content to lie amidst the brambles?
An Account of the Ritual at Shijing Mountain on an Autumn Night to Pay Homage to the Sacred Remains of Master Wan (With Preface).
All beings possessed of blood and breath necessarily possess consciousness. Possessing consciousness entails desire; possessing desire entails birth; and possessing birth entails...

There is death. Only the Perfected Person (*zhiren*) can use non-arising (*wu-sheng*) to treat human desire. When desire is emptied, knowledge is not abandoned, and its wondrous function becomes boundless.

During the Sui dynasty, Master Wan read the *Vow Text* of the Great Master Nanyue Huisi and, knowing that the era of the Final Dharma was drawing to a close and the three calamities would suddenly arise, perceiving that all treasuries of the Dharma would eventually perish, he sighed deeply and said:
As there are heaven and earth, one cannot do without the sun and moon; as there is activity and rest, one cannot do without clothing and food;

and as there is human life, one cannot do without the Buddha-dharma. Yet, while the sun can illuminate the day, it cannot illuminate the night; the moon can illuminate the night, but it cannot illuminate the day;
clothing can shield a person from the cold, but it cannot prevent the season from being cold; and food can sustain a person...

It cannot cause years not to suffer from famine; only the wondrousness of the Buddha-dharma can ensure that heaven and earth endure through all eternity, that all beings forever dwell in perpetual dawn, and that there is no affliction in birth and death, even to the point of transforming the ordinary into the sagely and turning darkness into light.
Realizing that all life is non-arising, he employs the power of his great vows to universally deliver all beings throughout the myriad existences.
How inconceivable is this vast and sublime excellence! He then engraved this upon stone as a scripture to prolong the life of the Buddha-dharma until the time of Maitreya.
Fearing that with the passage of time and the shifting of ages, the cliffs and ravines might change, he enshrined both the relics of the Buddha and his own skeletal remains therein.
I concealed them within various stone caves and filled this mountain with them, so that the great treasury of the Dharma might endure without destruction for eternal kalpas.
Moved by the Master’s profound concern and far-reaching foresight, I have composed this with tears.
On a moonlit night, I visited Master Wan at Green Mountain. In the stone hall, we faced the thousand peaks in silence. Every petal of the lotus was his heart’s blood;

every line of the palm-leaf manuscripts surpassed the artistry of Nature. His sacred bones may be buried, yet his name remains imperishable; the Dharmakāya is beyond form, its function ever-pervasive.
How could one bear to carve out a chamber upon the azure cliffs again, to enshrine the scriptures and demonstrate their inexhaustibility?
Questioning the Bamboo Pavilion:

An Occasional Verse Cane in hand, I seek this "Gentleman" deep within the forest. In the empty pavilion, who else remains to dispel the dust and clamor? The green mountains cannot bear to dwell here for long;
Why need the flowing waters be heard alone? Hair like frost is difficult to turn back to black; Profit and fame are no match for wine.
The family is in darkness. Shu-tuo rises from meditation amidst a thousand peaks; holding his jade scepter upside down, he sweeps away the white clouds.
A five-character quatrain gazing at Fangmao and the various mountains from Xiao Hill.
There are waves here that can incline the ear; why need one necessarily have a thousand-foot pine? Incidentally resting upon these fragrant herbs, the spring mountains face the distant void.

Chanting of snow as it emerges from the valley, the secluded clouds grow fine; they form flowers across the great earth, casting deep shade. They overturn the dreams of peach and plum blossoms entirely; this purity and whiteness is the mind’s original nature.

I prostrate before the stone pillar of pride, as lofty as Mount Sumeru; it can only be bent by one who possesses great self-weight. How could the Honored One, who has transcended desire, come here again and again to present offerings?
[The Spring for Washing Robes]
By the pines, I trim the emerald mists; by chance, they form a cassock. Worn for long, how could it ever be stained? I idly let it float upon the ripples of the waves.

The flowing stream reveals a stone path beyond the tiered peaks. Supporting my staff, I head toward the deep ravine. Seated in *paryaṅka* amidst the sound of water, I gaze tranquilly at the falling, icy cascade.
Fellow practitioners of the Dharma sat scattered about a pine ridge. Suddenly, Shuzong floated a small boat into the shade of the willows;
it truly possessed the air of a solitary wild goose vanishing into the void.
He composed this verse: The spring waters stretch on boundlessly; In what direction does the boat head? Deeply hidden within the flowers and willow shade, At sunset, one forgets to return.

A tree-meditator in the empty mountains, a wooden elder; sitting upon a rock, he knows not the passing years. Without a mind to record time, the wind-swept branches retain their full tongue-like form—his iron *kāṣāya*.

Heaven fashioned this robe of merit; in what year was it bestowed upon the Chan master? Wearied by its weight, he cast it away at the edge of the clouds; there it was buffeted by the wind and scorched by the sun.

In your hermitage, miscellaneous verses: the bamboo is still as the rain has just ceased; The breeze is gentle and the birds sing with vigor. My writing finished, I fall into a solitary sleep; Dreamless, my thoughts wander through the river city.

In the moonlit courtyard of the *bājiāo* (plantain) hut, one might mistake it for the edge of a ravine; the scaly stones seem ready to give birth to clouds. Who would have thought that amidst the clamor of the dusty world, one could dwell in such seclusion reading the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*?
The Island of Laṅkā.
The torrential ravine cuts through the azure mountains; the flying bridge spans where ancient trees slumber. Where I lean upon my staff at dawn, clouds drift across the sky reflected in the water.

Inscribed on a Painting: The waters bend and the mountains repeatedly merge; Spring’s chill leaves the flowers weary to bloom. The Xujiang River comes and goes once more; The person returns within the painted scene.
Inscription for the Stone Chamber in Bamboo Grove:
Where is there no green mountain? A single mind extinguished is difficult; a single mind extinguished is easy. With wisdom, one transcends ten thousand layers of barriers.
—The Lecture Hall Platform.
The Venerable One’s physical form was empty; where could his faculty of taste have rested? The pines and winds, along with the flowing waters, exhaustively expound the meaning of non-arising.

When the First Patriarch faced the wall in his pavilion and did not preach the Dharma, to whom could this mind have been transmitted? After Shen Guang’s three prostrations, the five lamps were suspended throughout China.
Three Poems on Qianzi Dang Green mountains dot the treetops; Slanting sun shines upon the creek’s bend. I ask of Qianzi Dang: The blue waves are cold through the long night.

In my gaze, the waters rise high above the boat; Yet I suspect they fall into the void of heaven. Having reached this level ground as flat as a palm, Human voices are transmitted like echoes in a mirror.
Upon seeing water, the mind is immediately understood; encountering mountains, the eye is instantly opened. Having exhausted all my lifelong skills and stratagems, what else remains to be harbored?
A sharp sword, a sharp sword—daily cutting through mud, its edge gradually blunts and is set aside. If one were to grind it on sand and stone, it would cut iron as if slicing water.

Sitting in Meditation at Night: Sitting in meditation on the empty steps, all is silent; pure discourse cuts off the ladder to delusion. Looking back toward the treetops amidst the clouds, I did not realize the moon had already sunk to the west.
Clouds fall upon the rocks.
Flying back, I observe the world; fallen here, I am unaware of spring. I wish to pluck it and take it away, yet fear startling those who dwell beneath the forest.

Gazing at the Jade Terrace, I immediately conceive of the singular peak’s beauty beyond the clouds. Standing like jade, one never tires of gazing upon it. Sitting here for but a moment, the six voids and the square inch of the heart are fully encompassed.
Inscription for Wan-yu-an (Ten-Thousand-Jade Hermitage):
Who took the Kunlun Peak and, with a single axe, split it into a thousand or ten thousand fragments? Scattered and strewn across the Tianmu Mountains, they remain peerless through all ages.
The Stone of Dharma Exposition.
Beside the clear, pure mountain stream, beneath the cold, solitary rocks, the Great One, Honored among the Multitude, speaks the discourse of non-arising.

At Shaolin on the cliff, the single transmission was passed when an arm was severed; at Wuyú, the blood flowed high. In the end, who will perform the three prostrations? Amidst the clouds and snow, they reach to the waist.

Showing the place where Layman Kuangshi held up a book to display it: "The spark from flint and the flash of lightning are slow; as soon as one attempts to give rise to a thought to answer, does the wind through the pines know or not?
*Singing of Pines in the Mountains*
The summit is solitary and peaks are still; for many years its green has not changed. How many times, on nights of a fine moon, have I leaned on my staff to listen to the sound of the waves?

Heaven has revealed this stone, which reaches deep into the clouds; in its profound obscurity, who can recognize it? One does not see the people of antiquity, but one sees only the stone of antiquity.
The Kun Mountains and Mount Kunlun are most towering and vast; with a flying sword I severed their peaks and placed them upon my desk and mat, where smoke and clouds darken morning and evening.
Crossing the Yan River rapids.

The sails are full and the passenger boat is light; it has long been known for its reputation of nourishing virtue. Such a moon as this night’s is difficult to encounter; to see the moon is to see the Master.
At Lion’s Roar Terrace, those who fly dare not fly, and those who run dare not run. Sitting cross-legged in the vast expanse, one listens silently to the lion’s roar.
The spring of joy has craving as its root of affliction; when craving is exhausted, afflictions are empty. When the mind is like this water, who would not have a joyful countenance?
Deep and clear, it flows from the precipice.
All things begin with water; the six passions begin with movement. If the single mind does not arise, then purity and depth reside in daily life.

The dewy spring flows coolly as I am accustomed to resting upon it; this quenching of thirst is not through physical drinking. Though I do not crave eternal life, my heart-mind is profoundly cool and refreshing.
Master Lang’s Rock:
Master Lang did not die at first; they said he died because no one knew of Lang. Try looking at Master Lang’s Cliff: it lies crumbled—whom does it contemplate?
The Alms-Bowl Peak.
Who extends the golden hand, smiling as they rest the jade bowl? With joyful intent they bring it forth; the source of merit shall never be exhausted.
Originally a deep spring, water flows from the crevices of stone; beholding it, my heart becomes serene. Who scoops up the water to rinse their teeth, drinking it all dry from the heavens above?

I laugh at the Stone with Crossed Heads on Veda Peak; how can it compare to Vajrapāṇi Peak, where the Great Compassionate One stands solemnly by its side? Grasses and trees increase in majesty and spirit.
Once again I visit Huanghuadong.

Leaving my horse, I ascend the perilous peaks; I know not how many times I have circled and turned. The azure crags open to reveal stone chambers, where we together hear the mingled chimes of the flowers.
I present this to Liu Shanyou of Longquan Pass regarding Wumeng Peak and Sane Peak.
Though the distance between them is not great, the moment a thought arises, Pu-er’s robe smiles upon the wild vines.
Miscellaneous Verses from Er’an:
The crane understands the monk’s speech; the fish vie to await the sound of the *brahman*. As the bright moon rises over the sea gate, from where does this sound of reading come?
Cold Rocks.
Its source comes from beyond the clouds; how could it have undergone fewer than ten million turns? Reclining drowsily upon a cold crag, a single roar startles the celestial palaces.
Tired while traveling through green jade, one encounters green jade once more; joyfully wishing to sit for a moment, purple and azure dragons coil and writhe, bursting forth to rend the clear clouds.
At Huxin Temple, I recall Layman Jianguang Zhao:
The bright moon rises over the sea; Vast clouds drift across the empty sky. A clear light shines upon my humble gate; I must wait for the sound of the celestial wind.
The words of the Layman Dàn'rán:
"White clouds have no mind of their own; where there is expectation, there are traces. How much better it is to have no expectation! Following the wind, they are not unsuitable for any place."
Ascending Tiger Hill:
I love the clouds of Tiger Hill; they come and go without intention. Travelers sigh over the feats of the hegemon; the carved jade walls abound with subtle rhymes. (II)
I love the moon of Tiger Hill; its pure radiance remains ever-clear and limpid. Through tens of thousands of layers of sorrow and joy, it shines universally without discrimination.
(III) I love the rocks of Tiger Hill; they nod their heads as the sutras are expounded. Since Master Sengsheng departed and did not return, they have long harbored the seclusion of white clouds.

Spontaneously formed within my breast are a thousand bamboos; beside my brows lie ten thousand acres of wu trees. Their pure sounds constantly color my ears; when hearing ceases, even the hawks and fish are reached.
(The second verse.)

I pray that you preserve these bones of a dog or a horse, striving to repay your compassionate kindness. May it be like the waters of the Xiang River, nourishing the parched earth and moistening the world once more. To Layman Haitong:
Encountering this late winter at the High Pavilion, the mists deepen over the mountain streams. You should diligently uphold even half a verse, until you ultimately realize the mind of Haitong.
Gazing from the Hall of the Dark Emperor toward Shimen Temple, I recall Tang Suichang:
Red fish dart across the emerald ridges; white birds dot the green forests. Both Chu and Yue are but initial stages on the path; who among those we meet can truly appreciate this music?

When Kaixian opened the Dragon Pond, the earth split and the pond was first formed; when Heaven opened, the waterfall first hung down. If the old dragon were not there, what thing would give rise to clouds and mist?
Sitting in the Cypress at Yuansu Hermitage.
The wine-drinker peers beneath the curtain; Yun sits in meditation at the foot of the cypress. Were it not for the hand of Wang Moqie, who else could have captured the true likeness of Yuan Zhen?

In the Azure Pavilion, ten thousand bamboos hold the verdant mist of the void; the square pond holds the azure current. A small bridge leads to the separate garden; white clouds embrace the rocks in profound stillness.
While reading the *Miaoshan-zhi* at night, I read the *Miaoshan-chuan*. How many are there who are unborn? In the end, those who merely look on see the flowers fall for another year’s spring.
Foxiangzi said: "Observing the meaning of this poem, if one were unborn, then one would not die; yet since one has already been born..."
Thus it is. To desire to cast oneself into immortality is to fear that such a principle does not exist. If one wishes for longevity, one must first forget life.
This is because when life is forgotten, the medium for death is severed. If one can attain the state of non-birth, then even the doctrine of "forgetting life" falls into the background.
Whether ten thousand years are made into a single year, or ten thousand years are made into a single day, or [three hundred and sixty...]
Ten days constitute one year; or, a mere instant may be reckoned as a long kalpa. These are all matters concerning what follows after thought.

If one can trace back and ascend from this, then even "thought" itself will not exist. How could the so-called years, months, days, and kalpas be anything other than calculating the growth of hair on a tortoise?
The Collected Works of the Elder Zibai, Volume Twenty-Six;
The Collected Works of the Elder Zibai, Volume Twenty-Seven.
Translated by Hanshan Deqing of the Ming Dynasty. Review.
Poem (Heptasyllabic Quatrain): Sitting Amidst the Snow at Longhua, Presented to Master Zhen of Rui’an The ground leads from the bustling capital into the empty mountains;
Fine flakes of jade descend, chilling the myriad wells. Surrounded by tea bowls and incense burners, we grind [the dharma].
He sat. Six dragons without heads lay upon the clear pool.
At dawn, he passed by the natural old Chan master’s quarters; the old Chan master, not yet having had enough sleep, lay there peacefully and drowsily.
I compose this verse to present to you:
The crimson sun shines upon the eastern window across the sea and sky. Reclining high upon the bed and pillow, all things are forgotten. Who is it that comes as a guest within the realm of dreams?
My delight in wandering and enjoying the Lotus Land is especially great.
In Nan-yu of Zhen-zhou, Wu Kangyu’s dream has always been that things are but bubbles upon the water.
Who can discern the autumn hair in a mirror? Meeting and parting—do not let one another fail.
Beyond the gate, the long river flows day and night.
Presented to the Abbot of the Tzelin Hall at Longquan Temple in Tanzhe:
His coarse cotton robes embrace a profound stillness; He has traversed the Dragon Canon to answer the Imperial Court. In these deep mountains, peach blossoms naturally bloom late;
On every branch, red and white flowers abound with the ancestral meaning.
A Gift for Master Jingzhu of Zheng’an upon His Recitation of the Lotus Sūtra In days past at Mount Kuanglu, I once beheld you; Upon the Yellow Dragon Pool, we paused but briefly.
Now, meeting you again within the Yan Mountains, The Great Lotus of the carriage opens from beneath your tongue.

As if ascending Mount Emei, soaring into the crimson heavens, alone among the emerald peaks; I hear it said that from of old you have dwelt everywhere in auspiciousness. With wings outspread across ten thousand *li*, you pursue the white elephant;
at dawn, crossing the Qiang lands, the flower-like ripples of the waves are sparse.
Presented to Master Jingyuan Xiou:
The solitary crane dwells in silence, long perched upon the paulownia tree; Ordinary birds, male and female, clamor amidst the thorny thickets.
When the whirlwind rises thirty thousand li high, Its pure resonance effortlessly pierces the crimson void.

At Longquan, Nian Zhongchun observes that the morning dew and the wind are so intense they form frost; even as summer approaches, the ice and frost still cloak one's garments. Among men there is no trace of the heat of summer;
on the five peaks, the diligent practitioner walks with few lapses.
I inform my companions:

in the sixth month, weeding the fields, the water is like boiling soup; the farmers' shoulders and backs are all covered in sores. Once the monks have finished their meal, they are free from worldly concerns;
they wave their fly-whisks as they lean idly against bamboo windows amidst the clouds.

The moon hangs from the West Terrace Peak as the earth enters the cold void, and the heavens hang inverted. Ten thousand lovely lotus blossoms grace the monastery; here the sovereign’s emerald carriage once lingered.
Beneath the pines, the thousand officials stand as the moon is at its zenith in the west.

Moved by the feeling of cool serenity, I enter this coolness out of sorrow for the afflictions of heat. White-haired *dhūta* practitioners are amidst the fragrant brow-paint. It must be that the autumn is deep and the frost and dew are cold;
white clouds and the bright moon accompany the meditation cord-bed.
The second verse:
Green curtains of light mist amidst the purple roads; An eastern breeze overnight sweeps away the withered red.
Everyone we meet says that spring has departed, Who would have thought the spring is even more intense in these cold crags?
The attendant Kai welcomed [the Master] from Qingliang to Pengcheng and showed him this;
under the bright sun and clear sky, you have arrived. Yet, you still suspect it is a dream and are filled with startled doubt. You must know that human life is like morning dew;
dwell but once within the light of the Man-shi room.
The second verse:
Cold clouds layer upon layer as ten thousand peaks deepen; who can take this bright pearl to comfort the distant heart? I only fear that Master Zhi’s feelings have not yet been glimpsed;
in his dreams he grasps his sword, yet this is the mark of a true知音 (zhīyīn—connoisseur).
Inscription on the Ten Thousand Buddhas’ Cliff at Luyaya Mountain:
A vast cliff of azure, the ancient womb of the Buddhas— With diligent toil, ten thousand Tathāgatas were carved forth. The cold spring flows day and night without ceasing;
May their nostrils and mouths, in one voice, call for an early return.
To Lord Lu Taizai:
Yellow dust has not yet settled, yet again there are green mountains. The flowing spring beneath the steps goes away and never returns. Let it reach the sea and become a mighty wave;
It yields to the secluded stone that cradles the clouds in leisure.
Prime Minister Lu offered this precious sash as a gift to Qingliang, to whom I composed this verse:
A single word, slightly askew, surpasses the precious sash; At ease, it makes even the old Mañjuśrī laugh. The golden ramparts and moats of our Way remain as ancient as the mountains and rivers;
For now, these eight pieces of jade shall serve as a substitute for my almsbowl.
The ancient halls of Shuangfeng Temple stand desolate as the gate and path open; twin peaks like swords flank the incense altar. At nightfall, flowing waters respond to solitary melodies;
beyond the clouds, a Chan practitioner feels a deep pang of sorrow.
At Longquan Temple, the autumn waters of the tea-drinking grotto flow again after having been cut off; the sun-facing ravines turn back toward the pearl pavilion.
Who is it that pauses for rest upon the stone by the clouds, sipping seven bowls of dragon-ball tea beyond the kalpas?

Embracing all my dharma-fellows, I wonder how many layers of clouds and mountains lie within my gaze. I hear once more the flowing water and the pines in the wind; how can I bear the suffering of human entanglements?
The dust of chariots on the south and north roads has not yet cleared from my dreams.
Showing the Great Way to Zen practitioners:
Who cannot walk the Great Way? How could one know it obstructs one's own body and mind?
If both are pushed back until no ground remains, then everywhere there is the sound of white clouds and flowing water.
Ascending the Dharma Hall of Xuanmu with Zhu Yangu, I composed this on the spot:
The Azure Cloud Tower looms faintly amidst the misty heights; Ten thousand miles of lakes and mountains are gathered in a single glance.
As we stroll hand-in-hand past the place of Chan recitation, The falling leaves upon Fan Peak evoke a sorrow beyond measure.
I visited the abbot’s quarters of Master Zhantang at Wutai Mountain’s Tongwadian;
the sparse trees lean against Vulture Peak. At Xiantong, the bell for sutra lectures has long been silent. I feel even more pity for the wind and frost that age the Tongwadian;
I fear that should I come again, it may not be easy to meet him once more.
Passing by Baoyuntang, I recall Yinyang;
pounding snow and striking ice, he did not fear the cold. How many times must he have lingered amidst the deep frozen clouds?
Last night, facing the moon alone before the front peak, I wonder: can it compare to that at Huating?
On Mount Qingliang, I yearn for Grand Councilor Lu;
amidst layered cold clouds, who dwells there? In this world, there is no path by which we may be acquainted. Waiting for you in vain, I depart with a long sigh;
willows and peach blossoms bring spring everywhere.

Lamenting the Boundless Teacher, the peach and plum trees fall in profusion as cold clouds lock the sky. The cassia branches are broken by the autumn wind, a sound too painful to hear. Do not let the lingering fragrance drift to the bottom of the ravine;
let it follow the flowing stream out beyond the village ahead.

While lying ill at Chángsōng Guàn, I recall the Elder Báiduān, that dragon among the monks of the Song dynasty. Observing him upon the seat of Perfect Penetration (Yuántōng), he let out a single shout, wrapped his waist-cloth, and departed;
though a million beings, gods and men alike, pursued him, he did not return. His resplendent light illuminates the ages. While lying ill...
Xunyang. Not far from Nengren Monastery, yet I have not yet had the leisure to pay my respects at the sacred traces. First, I compose this verse to release my long-accumulated longing:
In the city, who asks after the white clouds? Under the moonlit night of the tall pines, I alone think of you. The young masters of the Five Tombs, their sharp wit—
Separate. I encountered a poor scholar who had severed all ties with the crowd.

To visit Master Chao at Wanshan Temple, I entered the distant peaks. The auspicious clouds have dispersed and the ten thousand pines stand empty. I have heard that the Sagely Sovereign personally inscribed [the temple’s name].
Ink. Amidst the purple and azure of a world of pavilions and terraces, passing through Wanshou and Longyan, he divined a site for his dwelling among the layered cliffs;
his plan was not in vain. There is a path leading to Xiangxian—do not hesitate. What is this sound of the spring and color of the peaks?
When things have just returned to life, the mind has already lost its emptiness.
Written at Tàipíng Temple in Huán for the Layman Zhuófán:
Sitting with legs crossed, three prostrations—what mind is this? Not seeing, one turns it into seeing even more deeply. Mountain colors and river sounds are on your tongue.
Appearance. Even across a wall, one still perceives the pure tones.
Chanting over painted waters, the azure ocean surges within the gaze; where can one find dragons and fish amidst the startled waves? At the Jade Tower, one only feels a chill arise.
Millet. He then calls his children to build a brazier on the ground.
Of the two swords of the Double-Sword Peak, which one does he take to pierce the crimson heavens? At times its radiance brushes the tip of the Dipper. If only the old monk could pick it up!
In practice, worldly sentiments are severed without a trace.
He declined the gift of purple robes to yield them to Master Han;

for thirty years he has wandered through rivers and seas. With a mere fragment of a patched robe, he passes the spring and autumn. He feels self-reproach that his poor bones cannot yet don the full vestment.
