Purple. To bestow these upon a person of high character brings even greater merit.

Passing the Heavenly Flower Mound of the Mother, one seeks a dwelling for the immortals by the Phoenix City. The waters wind around the Heavenly Flower for more than ten li; if one were to ride the vital energy upon the locks, [the journey would be swift].
Bones. Even the seagulls understand poetry and the classics.
At Yufeng, one hears that there is a profound depth; at Yufeng, once one has traveled to the end, it is even more difficult to find. Petals of peach blossoms drift away with the current.
It is merely that one does not hear the songs of the hidden birds.

Sending off Sun Zhong to go to his lodging at Xin'an—whether a man becomes a dragon or a snake is never constant; it depends solely on what his will is directed toward. If his will is set upon the Way, [he is a dragon].
If one seeks virtue, one must first take the awakening of the mind as the primary goal; if one’s ambition lies in fame and achievement, one must first take mastery of the arts as the ladder.
Once these two orientations are settled, the spirit and consciousness will coalesce within, and the wandering mind will abide of its own accord.
What then could one not accomplish? Now, while you are amidst the sweltering heat, traversing rugged terrain to reach Xin’an, you cannot cover a thousand *li* in a single day.
A village where ten years pass in a single night—where then does one’s resolve lie? You must exert yourself!
In summer, steaming springs bubble everywhere; a thousand peaks flank the road, yet the heat is strangely concealed within. I pity you as you depart like a fish leaping into a boiling cauldron;
simply contemplate non-arising, and you shall find coolness right where you are.

Observing the trees on the artificial mountain in the northern garden, there are high peaks and short stumps, rare among those of the world. The trees suppress the mountain while the mountain supports the trees—a case of the deluded supporting the deluded. Those that are high remain high, and those that are short remain short;
yet within this, there is also a natural spontaneity of its own.
Passing through the plum orchard, I visited the layman Jiansu, but I did not meet the host;

nor did I meet the bamboo, yet first I encountered it. Along the winding path, the subtle breeze resounds from the void. If one were to listen to this melody with a deliberate mind, the faculty of hearing would be blinded and the faculty of sight deafened.
Occasionally I produce fine wine; when it intoxicates others, I do not crave it myself. Those who pursue profit and fame die of intoxication yet remain sweetly complacent.
If this floating life were truly like a spring dream, would I feel shame upon returning from my slumber?
Mooring for the night at Louze Temple on a winter evening, I send this to Meditation Master Mei:
At twilight I moored my boat to inquire of the charnel ground; The moon fills the cold void, and the waters are deep and clear. There is no need to trouble the faculty of speech to preach the Dharma;
How could the faculty of hearing possibly grasp the profound resonance?

Visiting Louze Temple Again How could my return here be merely a simulation of the immortals' travels? I love most of all the spring waves where white gulls bathe. I laugh at myself for wearing black robes instead of being a prime minister;
Yet I seek to find a noble rank within this garden of awakening.
At Louze Temple, where does the bell ring?
Amidst mists and clouds, the dawn bell tolls. The traveler’s countenance is once again in a hurried rush; a single sail, filled with wind, approaches the Wu River.
The melodies of the singing and piping from the tower-ship differ from these.
While wandering in the garden, I was moved by the thought that the "Wave-Subject" (the dragon) once failed to don his *kāṣāya*; he instead begged for a garden pavilion to serve as a resting place.
This left the master with no choice but to employ his ingenuity, using a thousand pieces of coarse matting to substitute for a fence.
At Tangshan Temple, I pay homage to the Great Master Chan Yue;
I sought a man of high attainment deep within Tiantai. Time and again I ascended the heights, yet found no one. Returning instead to Tangshan Temple, I looked out:
the pond was clear, its reflection manifest, wondrously penetrating the divine.
Second: On a tranquil night in Zhejiang, the moonlit peaks are all my teacher Guan Zilong;
he has painted forth the infinite forms of the Tathāgata, leaving no trace behind in any water throughout the world.
Returning across the Red Ford Ridge, I recall Tang Yiren;

having stepped into the thousand peaks, he went forth and returned again. The ancient path through the mountains is covered in mossy green. Whether the red fish appears early or late, it remains hidden in the Dragon’s Treasury.
One must believe that Tang’s vows shall never turn to ash.

Spontaneously Composed While Sitting at Night I often pity those in this world who have leisure; even to open a smile is increasingly difficult. Having awakened from sleep, I don my robes—who is there to sit with me?
Only the lute of insects and the drum of frogs amidst the bright moon in its quietude.
Lamenting how, in years past, we gazed together at the clouds and the idle moon; tonight the bright moon shines upon Qu’a. Who would have thought that this time it would be a final parting?
The moonlight over Mount Yan fills the pine and ivy.
Sitting at night in Qu’a, I miss Xiūláng Dàochéng;
with no worldly achievements, he has returned to the green mountains. Who else will pity you as you depart and do not return?
On this moonlit night by the lakeside and riverhead, the heat and humidity must make your journey through the vast distances all the more difficult.

Passing the pagoda courtyard at the precipice, one travels to the very end where the mountains cease and the waters run out. The sheer cliffs stand like walls, filling the heart with sorrow. Who would have known there is another path leading to the heavens?
Even for monkeys and apes, it is a place they cannot roam.
For over thirty years I have kept the death-gate at Gaofeng Pagoda; how could my soul and dreams ever fall upon the green mountains? As I depart, my white bones have no place to be hidden;
I cast them onto the tongue of the Golden-Haired One to rest there.
I tell you, Layman So-and-so:
do not seek my mind within your own mind. Vast and boundless as the blue sea, it would be difficult indeed to find.
If fish and dragons were to hear this news, infinite winds and waves would all sink into the depths.
Three Poems on Viewing Lotus Flowers by the Pond How many red and white lotuses are there? Master Yingzhai has cleared the ripples. Wishing to speak in the breeze, to whom can he entrust his words?
Maoshu in his day loved only the "Elder Brother."

The dense trees, though heartless, screen out the sun’s glow; the gentle breeze, as if possessing intent, softens the fragrance of the flowers. On this wave, I am further permitted to sit with my head resting on my knees;
were it not for this profound seclusion, who could provide such guidance?
Sitting in the shade of trees for a moment in the sixth month, a breeze from the lotus flowers comes across the water. I ask the traveler on the streets of Chang’an:
perhaps the sugarcane syrup does not necessarily cool one’s heart.
Moved by a dream, I feel the ocean of suffering is vast and deep, where one floats and sinks again. That my parent has drowned therein is most heartbreaking;
though I have sought to rescue them many times, I lack the power, as I stand at the riverbank, tears filling my breast.
The Dharma-flower Peak:
this flower does not bloom when sages are hidden; once it blooms again, the sage emerges. A gentle celestial wind arises in the great void;
its fragrance and light are boundless as they honor the Buddha-Sun.
In mourning for Chan Master Mou of Wujiang:

A solitary city, a single expanse to the east of Lake Tai. Who would have thought that such a hero would emerge from Wujiang? He sat firm, cutting off the paths where both sages and ordinary folk can go;
his descendants weep for eternity at their exhausted journey’s end.
Lazily wandering through the world, I refused to stay; now come to this cliff, I am too lazy to leave again. After meditation, I lie with my fist as a pillow upon the green moss.
Within, there is a mind—whom shall I speak to?
The most excellent spring has never run dry despite long-term drought; it rains as clouds and disperses on its own. How can the springs at the foot of the mountain compare to those upon the peak?
Their source is solitary and lofty, surpassing all others.
Visiting the Temple of Su Shi at Daxian Village on Mount Wutai:

The ancient temple stands desolate, its gates locked amidst ten thousand peaks. I have traversed the cold clouds in search of his lingering traces. With sincere reverence, I bow again and cannot bear to part;
I laugh at myself, for my appearance is still that of the old Chan-liao.

Evening at Longtan: At the cliff’s edge, I await the moon as the heavens are hushed; atop the rocks, I listen to the spring as ten thousand cares vanish. I laugh and ask my two or three companions who came with me:
"Who is it that finds delight within this state of both being and non-being?"
Flying Cloud Spring:
A single crevice in the azure cliffs pours forth a cold current. I wish to investigate its source, yet my resolve remains unfulfilled. Let not the celestial winds carry it away;
let it merge with the great ocean to become its tide.

Three Poems on Passing by the Abandoned Lengyan Temple A new painted pavilion rises amidst ten thousand flowers; A jade maiden leans upon the railing as spring unfolds in the heavens. A single bright moon hangs cold outside the curtain;
In the deep night, it once shone upon those who sat in meditation.
I once beheld this famous garden in its full splendor, when young gentlemen roamed in springtime, intoxicated by the fragrant blossoms. Now, in this Deer Park, the flowers have no master;
there is only the cuckoo crying upon the branches.
In years past, I roamed here where flowers were boundless; today I return, yet the flowers are not seen.
I suspect that Master Zhi, weary of such splendor, has not permitted them to remain amidst the mists and clouds.
On a boat upon the Chu River, I am moved by Master Dumen’s exposition of the general outline of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
Master Dumen of Jingnan, Xijian: Every word speaks from the heart, never resting in emptiness. If one asks where the *Laṅkā* resides:
In every head and every object, there is a solitary peak.
Spontaneously composed upon hearing of the scenery at Qili Tan from Linlang:
The wind drives the blue sail across the distant emerald stream; The sound of springs on both banks requires no effort to hear.
If one asks whether people are there now, The green mountains fold together like a single hair.
In late summer, traveling from Mount Qingliang through Lianyang, I ascended Wanghu Pavilion.
Below, the lake’s radiance; above, the pines of the mountain. Who is this reclining on a high pillow within the void? A great wind sweeps in—whence does it come?
In spirit and dream, I still suspect I am amidst icy ravines.
The Brahma-river and the conch-shell hall are clearly distinguished as one single shell; how different from this hall situated amidst misty waves!
Those who come in leisure to pluck reeds and ascend to this place stand alone in the vast, desolate expanse, chanting their own songs.
Passing through Benou, I pay my respects at the site of Su Changgong;
where have the sun and moon within his breast hidden? I hear that Benou was the place where he passed away in a seated posture. Who can now collect his remaining words and fragments?
For a thousand ages, the rivers and mountains shall rely upon their radiance.
At Chōsōkan, I encountered snow;
every tree was covered in blossoms, all of a single hue. Branch after branch was leafless, yet shimmered with abundant light.
Though it is said that human tracks have vanished since morning, there is still the neighbor to the east busy delivering charcoal.

Two Poems on Inspiration The surging waves and billowing clouds turn not their heads; The Magistrate has thus built the Locking-the-River Tower. It is not certain that those in scarlet robes shall remain masters forever;
Who atop the pagoda will ever open their eyes?
The Bodhisattva of Fragrant City was formerly named Lin; flowing waters and pines like surging waves chant the Brahma-sound.
It is surely because this mountain’s scenic splendor is so fine that one might easily obscure the heart of the Great Official.
In mourning for Master Jiao of Miaofeng:
A golden-winged bird soars through the void on ten-thousand-mile winds; entering the wondrous through the Gate of Having is shared by the ancients.
The moon at the bridge of Zhuling’s *Zhi Guan* hangs not upon Tiantai, but upon a distant peak.
Miscellaneous Verses:
My hair grows ever new in its various grays; the flowing waters, vast and surging, further sadden the spirit.
Only the bright moon flows on without ceasing, illuminating this reclusive man tonight at his thatched window.
Exhorting Daecheon (Daechun) Yi San-u to seek birth in the Pure Land:
the transition from the heat of affliction to coolness is not at all mistaken. What harm is there in thorns and lotuses meeting? How many who encounter them know how to return home?
At twilight, the sound of the bell escorts the setting clouds.
Lamenting Penglang’s gaunt, skeletal frame as he ascends the Five Terraces, he shaves his beard and hair, severing all worldly dust. Having left the mountains, he is not seen;
having entered the mountains, he departs. This vexes Mañjuśrī, whose tears fill his cheeks.
In the Yintang Hall of Tanzhe Mountain, I bid farewell to all my dharma companions:
"Within a dream are green mountains; within a dream is this body. How can one bear the parting from those near and dear? There is no need to wait until after awakening to observe hatred and love;
Only then does one truly believe in the 'seventh dust' of the tortoise's hair."
Yiwen Hall Rejoices in Clear Weather:
Last night, wind and rain filled the mountain clefts; From the treetops, the sound of a hundred cascades surged forth. Infinite fine mountains were entirely shrouded by clouds;
Who would have known that tonight they would appear so majestic once more?

Beyond the gate of Hong’en Temple, within the depths of Qianfeng Temple, a single lamp shines; its one light illuminates the three periods of time across the golden cords. The old Chan master, having finished his meal, has no further concerns;
he listens in stillness to the surging waves of the pines, transcending all love and hate.

Passing through Zhaokeng Temple, circling back, green mountains enclose the Brahma palace; before the steps and behind them lie the tracks of the Elephant King. I know well that his transcendence of the world is not without its foundation;
the fragrant clouds of the Dharma rain cannot be counted as heavy.
The Great Compassion Hall: Minister Lu was dispatched by imperial decree to return home;
the Holy Sovereign’s radiance shines upon him. Leaning on the void with a single laugh, he forgets the myriad affairs of state. One who has eyes in hand should know the resonance;
hearing sound within the ear—how could it be merely the constant?

Second: His golden body stands over seven feet tall; he has supported heaven and earth without regard for toil. It was only because the Sovereign took pity on these withered bones that he released him back beyond the clouds to listen to the sound of the pines.
Passing through Tongguan, the yellow mule was no different from the blue ox; why must the frontier guards act as enemies on the road? Heading west toward the Qin Pass, we go together;
to whom shall this divine pearl be cast in the great night?
Under the Moon at Hongfu Temple in Pengcheng, I Long for Zhongchun:
Before Mount Panma, the moon shines with perfect clarity; The misty waves stretch far and wide, a single sail glides lightly. This pure radiance is no less than the night at Jintai;
In this meditation chamber, few are those who wear the southern cap like Miu Sheng.

Ascending the Horse-Playing Terrace, he shook his beard with a laugh as fire consumed Xianyang. Dressed in brocade, he sang long songs on his return to his native land. Need one ask where he once brandished his spear?
Now only the withered autumn grasses bear the cold frost.

Seeing Zhongchun return south in haste to attend his father’s funeral, the wind-whipped trees sigh along the road for a thousand li; two rows of blood-stained tears soak his hempen mourning clothes. As I see you off, my heart is heavy and words fail me;
how could I hear the cries of the *guì* bird atop Mount Yan?
A Summer Day’s Visit to Qingquan Temple:

Within the temple is a clear spring, and beyond its gates are the mountains. The ripples on the water and the empty mountain verdure both produce a sense of chill. I alone pity the Hall where the Great Being translated the sutras;
at twilight, foxes and hares pass to and fro of their own accord.
An Inscription for Su Dongpo’s Yellow Pavilion at Pengcheng:
A solitary city stands against the surging tide; Time and again, turtles and dragons dance within its moats and ditches.
The First Emperor once sought the Zhou tripod here, Yet he could not match the loftiness of the Yellow Pavilion’s intent.
Inscription on Master Fuyan’s Lion Peak:
For a thousand days and ten thousand days you did not roar; now that I have come, you immediately let out a cry of fearlessness. At midnight, wind and thunder shake the crags and valleys;
among the hundred beasts in the deep forest, there is none that is not startled.
Together with the sons of the Dharma, we gaze at the moon from the Golden Mountain;
the green peaks on both banks hold fast the golden turtles. Upon the rocks, we watch the surging waves as the moon rises high.
Beyond the clouds, a single sail flies on without ceasing—clearly, it is like a swan’s down crossing a mirror.
Accompanied by my fellow disciples, we passed Guangling and stayed overnight at Shangfang Temple;

there we arranged our parting beneath the moon, seeking out the secluded depths as we knocked upon the gates of the Buddhist monastery. The aged Chan master remains within the realm of my dreams and spirits. Need one inquire about the path for tomorrow morning?
The peach blossoms along both banks display colors that differ from one another.
Inscription on the Avalokiteśvara Pond at Shangfang Monastery:
The Great Being has, for no reason, misapplied his mind; He does not contemplate form, yet he contemplates sound.
If cold currents were to enter apart from sound, One would seek a single needle amidst a thousand-fathom billowing tide.

Reading the "Record of Peach Blossom Spring," one knows how deep the peach blossoms line both banks. For what reason did the fisherman seek it out? This time he has gone forth and lightly betrayed the secret;
he has truly brought ruin to that single heart of earnest caution.
In Wang Xizhi’s Hall for Sunning Books of the Jin Dynasty, the blood and heart of ancient sages remain. Who would allow them to be consumed by bookworms or gather further dust?
Knowing that there is no day of returning from the Southward Crossing, I offer these to the Tathāgata to turn the Wheel of Dharma.
To Xu Rūdōng, Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, upon his leave to return to the mountains:
The Canglang River has seen many autumns of toil and hardship; A single heart of sincere loyalty remains unrequited. I happened to seek out the "White-footed" one at Shuanglin Temple;
As we discussed emptiness, he still dreamt of his spring fields.
Mooring for the night beneath the walls of Yixing City, misty waves and azure peaks shroud the sky in a drizzling rain. A solitary city lies within the mountains and waters;
desiring to seek out the profound depths of seclusion, I halt my oars at twilight and hear only the sound of the bell.
Lament for Master Nantang: Showing the way while embracing utter poverty, his bones chilled through;
moreover, he has suffered successive bereavements. When the Bodhisattva heard this, he too was moved with grief. Who on the river would be willing to abandon the "boat of wheat"?
His descendants stand tall and firm upon Nantang.
I have heard that the Qin authorities have issued strict prohibitions against field meditation.
If I were such a demonic monk, how could I begrudge my remaining years to defile Your Majesty’s sagely wisdom? I would simply request a single stroke of the blade to manifest the national laws;
what harm is there in realizing the state of non-arising at the very point of pain?
Mooring my boat beneath the Shrine of Su Changgong on Mid-Autumn Day, dew moistens my kerchief as I rest by the waterside.
The snow rises to the level of the Bronze Coffin, and the moonlight is fresh and bright. There is no need to exchange song and laughter for coins or cloth;
in this leisurely state, who is there to grant an opening for speech?
The paths of carriage and cap differ from those of pine and clouds; Mount Shuangshan rises high above the pines of the Grand Master. From where does this gust of celestial wind come?
It sweeps away the surging billows, echoing through the azure void.
Passing through the Le-zai Garden, one sees skulls;

do not say they are many here. The entire Dharma-realm is Mount Vaipulya; look further at whose tombs stand by the roadside—how many times there have been laughter and joy, and how many times songs of sorrow.
Inscription on the Reverse of the Stele for Marshal Yue Wumu at Jinshe Temple (The stele contains the phrase:

"Accompanied monks to the quarters to pay homage to the Golden Immortal") For what reason does the General pay homage to the Golden Immortal? Hongren’s refined loyalty and his own were originally of one source.
Had he not possessed the true skillful means of killing, How could he have severed the worldly entanglements?

The elder rose from meditation as subtle clouds vanished and the heavens were washed clean. Rising from concentration, he practiced walking meditation amidst the moonlight; to whom could he tell of this boundless splendor?
Before the hermitage and behind it, the green mountains lie in layers.
The Elder Amṛtānanda read the *Deciding Doubts* treatise;
Sudhana did not shun toil, visiting fifty-three teachers until the silence was hushed.
Had it not been for the Elder Li of those days, how could Gautama have possessed even a hair or a pore?
To the virtuous friends of Da-xian Village:
All people in the world resent the busyness of daily life; they are tossed about in dreams and forget upon waking.
What is real and what is false? Let us all together examine this matter in detail.
Early Spring Visit to Master Li of Fangshan; Returning from Qingliang, Inviting Grand Councilor Lu—Specifically Composed These Two Quatrains:

Eating yellow rhizomes for food and wearing hempen robes, A bowl of long Chinese cabbage is better than sprouted tea. If those who know me should ask about my life in the mountains, [The answer would be as above.]
Incident: Rising from meditation before the cliff, he sweeps up fallen blossoms.
(II) The five peaks have held ice and snow since ancient times; spring fills the universe, yet its cold cannot be restrained. The Old Man of the Man-chamber departs in vain.
Chamber. I knew from afar that you would not have disappointed those who came to visit;
now, having paid my respects to the Venerable Elder Li of Fangshan, I am returning to Dingxiang. On the road, [there is] a preface:
For many years I have admired the Tang Dynasty’s Venerable Elder Li, yet because I have been occupied with my studies, I have not had the leisure to visit his remains.
Record. On the third day of spring in the Renchen year of the Wanli era, he took his three sons—Kai, Jiang, and Cai—from Mount Qingliang to pay a special visit to him in audience.
Thereafter, he raised his whip and returned to Mount Qingliang; spring snows fell in profusion, and the myriad mountains were shrouded in jade.
I reflect back upon the elder’s voice, countenance, and smile; I lament that I was not born at the same time as him, so that I might serve him with a handkerchief and fly-whisk.
Moved by this sentiment, I compose this verse:

For ten years I have yearned for his lofty character like one parched with thirst. In spirit, I have sought his traces of the Way upon the mountain ridges and plains. Spring snow falls in profusion, covering the south.
North. Where shall I lean my staff against the cold pines?
Three Poems on Passing through Shengshou Temple:

Beyond the city walls, the green mountains slope down on both sides; The meditation hall is silent, locked away by mists and clouds. Before the Buddha, whose lamps and fires shall there be to attend them?
Picking [the teeth] clean, one obtains pure light that illuminates ten thousand households.
If one waits for the flowers to turn red before viewing them, boundless springtime will be swept away by the evening breeze. One must fix the gaze beyond heaven and earth;
holding the fishing pole across the world’s oceans, one discerns the fish and dragons.

For what reason do the willow branches betray the spring light? Bees and butterflies swarm across the low wall. I fear only that the east wind, jealous of the flowers’ smiles, will let a horse’s hoof tread upon the crimson fragrance for a thousand miles.
Seeing off Wei Juechu by the Yangjiang River at Fuyang: When parting from you here, the moon over Lanxi was still faint. The bright moon, being without intent, can illuminate both places;
Yet at the ferry crossing of Qiantang, it stirs longing in the heart.
Passing Qili Tan, the mountains and waters of Fuchun stretch on infinitely. Who was it that donned a sheepskin robe to hide within these depths?
Had Liu Lang not summoned him back, where would later generations have sought his traces?
Seeing the *zhizihua* (shrub rosebay) in the North Garden, I am moved:
Before the flowers were seen, they have already fallen; There is no difference between before and after the rain. Bees and butterflies flutter to and fro;
A stretch of springtime light is obscured by my own eyes.
At the midnight hour of autumn, I heard the sound of a layman from Fayan Hermitage reciting the sutras at Shishi Cliff.
The light rain had just ceased, and the night air was cool; I sat cross-legged upon a rock on the mid-slope, using it as my bed.
Suddenly, I heard the resonance of sutra recitation beneath the pines—a pure chime striking through the waning moonlight.

Inscription on the Temple Wall Repairing the temple brings disaster to the pines within. When the temple is finished, the pines depart and the cranes' nests become empty. Nothing can be done but to leave these green pines behind. (Note: The Master traveled to Mount Heng and passed by this temple.

Encountering the temple in ruin, the local people cut down the temple trees to repair it. He then inscribed this poem. Upon seeing the poem, the district magistrate halted the felling and had the verse engraved upon stone.)
Having attained long life, he transformed into a dragon.
Sitting in meditation on a secluded mountain at night, who would have known that the bright moon would shine upon the cold spring? Unprovoked, he lost his companion; the monkeys looked on.
A call! In a flash, body and mind are once again as they were.
To the layman Jiue-mi:
Your hair is like snow, your bones like thistle; if you ask for the path to longevity, it turns ever more remote. Lust and killing—first sever their very roots.
Severance. The Pán-táo peach resides only in the sprouts of one’s own mind.
To console Master Fù:
layered green mountains abound with ancient trees; a solitary hermitage is loftily established amidst pines and vines, leading deep into seclusion beyond the edge of a pond.
On the road, the layman lies alone upon an empty bed, clutching his ailment.
He pays homage to the Reclining Tathāgata at Mount Xiangshan;
with both legs stretched out long, he simply sleeps. Who knows that the waves of suffering are surging like a flood to the heavens? To study together, do not ask about the Twin Śāla Trees.
A Dream. How many times in the depths of spring has the cuckoo cried?

Coming here to hide, I recall the three men of former days who secluded themselves to practice dhyāna. The crane perches on the pine treetop; the dragon dwells in the abyss. I have come once more in my old age to seek this excellence.
Trace: Do not worry that the broken hearth will produce no smoke.
When the Old Man of Fengtou ascends the Dharma platform, the smiling faces of ten thousand valleys and a thousand crags open wide. If preaching the Dharma were to trouble the tongue...
Signs: Rainy flowers entice the celestial deities to come.

I have traveled extensively across the nine pines, the five sacred peaks, and the three mountains to inscribe this ordination platform; yet among these, the pine trees here have no peer. When the clouds vanish from the saddle-shaped peak, they completely cover the altar.
It emerges: wind and moon, dragons and snakes dance without ceasing.
At the hermitage of the Elder of Daxian Village, he embraces all his dharma companions from Jiangnan;
before the steps and behind the buildings, nothing but green mountains. The mossy path is desolate and far from the marketplace; those who come and go share the same dusty heads amidst the winds.
I reply: How can it compare to listening to the murmuring stream beyond the clouds?
At the Three Sages Temple by the willows on Mount Emei, I parted from Wenqing and Zhongfu in the capital of Yan;
the willows hang low and silent, their sorrow beyond measure. Since time immemorial, the Wood Deity has been difficult to serve.
Master, do not weary of the sounds of wind and rain amidst your leisure.

At the beginning of a dream, you once saw the Lion Master in your sleep; his elegance and refinement were naturally beyond compare, yet he covered himself with nothing more than a single piece of skin.
The Head: At ease, he roars through ten thousand layers of clouds.
At Tanzhe, I miss Miu Zhongchun;
at Gushui and Longquan, there is but a single cloud. Who can perceive his coming and going as he leaves the flock? Only the vast blue ocean remains at night.
The Moon. Its boundless pure radiance cannot be divided.

On the winter of the fourteenth year of the Wanli era, the lay practitioner Wei Zhongguang visited me at Mount Tanzhe. (With Preface) [End of] "Burning Firecrackers. Lay Practitioner Wei Zhongguang. In the winter of the fourteenth year of the Wanli era, he attended upon me at Mount Tanzhe. Jia... [text continues]
At Fusi Temple, in the second month of the following year, I again bid him farewell there. Zhongguang was fond of setting off firecrackers; hearing that I did not like them, he desisted.
I said to Zhongguang, "The Yin energy at Tanzhe has accumulated for a long time, and the Wheel of Dharma has not turned."
"It would be right to scatter them by shaking them apart with the sound of firecrackers. Zhongguang was greatly pleased and burned bamboo until dawn.
The sun’s disk returned its course, and a harmonious atmosphere gathered. Did Zhongguang provide some assistance? Moved by this, I composed this poem.

Since we parted amidst the sound of firecrackers, how many times has the peach blossom bloomed at the valley mouth? In this place where the sky of Yao and the sun of the Buddha shine once more with brilliance, do not spend your fleeting life away at the wine cup.
In the meditation quarters of Biyun Monastery, a single scene of spring blossoms possesses a charm all its own.
When the practitioner catches sight of it, the myriad conditions of existence vanish into emptiness.
Most exquisite is this night of pines, springs, and bright moon, as its fragrant essence wafts throughout the palace of the Brahma King.
How many long pines stand in the house of the Lord of Chángsōng Pavilion? They draw forth the celestial winds to form ocean waves.
Let there be a thousand million measures of feverish affliction; sitting here within, they naturally vanish.
The recluse of Mount Ganyan returns from Mount Tai;

in all affairs, everything is secluded and profound. The celestial maidens scattering flowers—how could they be as effortless as the butcher of the whole ox? Amidst clouds, who else can share the appreciation of waters and woods?
Leaning on my armrest, I am without intent, facing the seagulls.

The Chan master Dao Wujin sat until his rush cushions were worn through countless times; it is said that his worldly ties have long since turned to ash. Deep in spring, flowers lie in profusion by the crags;
a hundred birds cry out in vain, unable to call him back.
Up above, Master Bieshou Yu, Shaozong, and the Celestial-Grace Bodhisattva—everyone at Mount Emei is a traveler from afar.
In our parting, our courtesy was as intimate as that of bone and flesh. Turning my head toward the layered white clouds, the scenery along the Ba River is like spring within a cavern.
On a Rainy Day at Xishuanglou on the Brahma River:
Winding ponds and willows in the breeze, Floating pavilions amidst mist and rain. Who can use half a verse to tether the horse of the mind?
At night, fish and dragons gather in the water-moon palace.
At Fanchuan in Qu’a, the cold is such that it could melt gold and stone;

the snow falls in vast drifts, not only upon perilous peaks and lofty ridges. Along the myriad bends of the Qin roads and the Ba River, one gazes upon the sprouts of reeds and the clouded trees as they are encased in ice.

He showed the King that throughout Jiangnan and Jiangbei there are nothing but monasteries; yet only the Dragon and the Spirit have the deepest vow, for they are willing to cast away their very lives in this place.
It is like the blind turtle meeting the floating yoke, or planting a wooden pin in a mustard seed, or casting a needle into the sea.

Accompanying Zen Master Daguang, his staff and bowl drifted lightly across ten thousand mountains. Amidst the winds of external circumstances—whether favorable or adverse—his single mind remained at ease.
If one were to follow his traces like the moon reflected in water, it would be as if carving emptiness to create the visage of the Way.
Traveling by boat, I observe the scene before me:
on both banks, fine mountains remain evergreen; a single stream flows with boundless azure.
The square sail catches the wind, its white spray flying into a thousand peaks and ten thousand crags.
To the Scholar Li Pei of Jiahe:
Since our parting at Wutang, several autumns have passed. Ten thousand miles of clouds and mountains bring sorrow to both lands.
Only the moon over the River at Wumen— Its clear light does not follow the waters eastward.

Washing the inkstone in the pond—washing the stone, washing the head, and seeking the source. The ripples of the water shimmer; the ink-blossoms are springtime. With a single mind pure and white, one dwells in a cloud-roofed house.
How many such people are there in this world today?
Moved by Feelings While Gazing at the Moon from Hōke-shō:
In this desolate mountain, the night air is crystalline; How could a single cloud arise across the vast sky?
Unaware that I stand within the pure radiance, I still ask others to point out the moon’s brilliance.
Wandering Lake Tai—how could one have obtained such a wondrous journey throughout one's life? With high winds along both banks, the fallen leaves are sparse;
upon the single expanse of water, thousands of sailing sails drift, as ripples fly across the mirror of the blue sky.
Presented to Layman Zhao Yiguang:
Meeting unexpectedly on the road, he calls out, "Have some tea. The staff held in his hand has eyes to distinguish dragons from snakes.
Who would have known that after this chance encounter in the autumn wind, Sparse plum blossoms have bloomed once more in the southern lands?
Ascending the Wenshu Pavilion atop Mount Niushou, I recall the past as I stroked the tall pines from this high tower. The stupa’s imposing form rises sharply amidst the cloud-filled ravines;
a solitary laugh rings out beyond heaven and earth, its traces lingering faintly within the void.
Ascending the Fishing Platform with the three sons of Li and Shen of the Wei dynasty:
How high this Fishing Platform reaches beyond the clouds! The Tung River has cast its single thread for ten thousand ages. The waters are cold and the night is still; fish and dragons sleep.
Who will listen to the Master’s song of the purple mushrooms?
At Huayan Ridge, the vermilion pillars and painted beams lock away the mundane peaks; along the winding paths across the precipitous ridges, a way remains open.
One volume of the *Avataṃsaka* has strayed from its ancient melody, yet dragons and serpents once here received the true wind.
Lamenting Master Sŏnsim of Sŏngju Hongje Temple:
As the setting sun and returning birds head toward the riverbank, I find rest amidst the roar of the surging waves. The great tree has been toppled by the wind with no warning;
Passing this place once more, my sleeves are moistened with tears.
Chan guest of the prophecy:
the jeweled stupa soars into the void as flocks of birds clamor. From where has this extraordinary creature come, able to fly and wheel? A pair of iron wings were fashioned by Heaven itself;
in my dreams, they once startled the spirits of swallows and sparrows.
At Lingyan, I passed through the old haunts of Layman Fu;

there, he indulged in wine and wild song, questioning the butcher about his dog. In the Zen quarters, he would drink himself into a stupor by day and challenge others to play with dice. The mountain streams and peaks have not changed from the paths of old;
in the empty courtyard, one reads the Buddha’s scriptures while partaking of fragrant offerings.
Inscription for Master Yong’s Meditation Chamber:
Dragon Offering Spring Who would bind reed mats atop ten thousand peaks? In the deep ravines, cold springs flow day and night.
Ever since Master Yong returned to his seclusion, The old dragon has finally withdrawn its jade essence.

Climbing Fuhu Cliff, how could it be to seek the traces of the Subduing Tiger? It is to behold the multitude of peaks arrayed at the base of the crag. Laughing, one divides the four elements into a thousand reflections;
on every mountain peak there is frozen pus.

At the Spring of Joy, the bird-path winds and turns; how many layers does it encircle? I imagine the Dragon Palace, where the cold spring moistens my parched throat. I call for my servant to try hewing stones from the edge of the clouds;
even the plum trees by the roadside have served their purpose in quenching my thirst.
Ten Poems on Passing through Huaimai Hermitage The mountain forests are pure and originally free of dust; how could mud and lime ever bury this body?
It would be better not to die within one’s mother’s womb, thereby sparing the people of the world from being vexed by one’s presence.
Try looking before your parents were born: could there have been a physical form leaning by the tree? It is simply that the Head Monk lacks clarity;
his stench of flesh and grease scorches the earth and perfumes the heavens.
The skull is ultimately empty from the very beginning; though emptiness may be buried, it leaves traces of emptiness. I wonder, what kind of view does our Master hold?
Without cause, he seizes upon forms and obstructs the wind.
Pervading the void of space, it never tires of heights; why must you dig into the earth to bury it on a mountainside?
You should know that the eyes of the world are not so great as to begrudge a leather bag being thrust upon you.
The great affliction has always been this physical body; it is better to bury it so that no dust may arise.
With green mountains and white stones as one's coffin and outer shroud, one becomes a living-dead person amidst idleness.
Birth and death have never been two separate paths. Being buried alive does not necessarily mean one is stifled by foul odors. Let it fill the void of empty space;
ten thousand households and a thousand gates stand high everywhere.
With nostrils piercing the heavens, he cannot be hidden; dragged and pulled by others, he grows ever more frantic.
How much better it would be to bury him while still alive—this would be superior to a horned sheep hanging from the treetops.

Burying the body is not necessarily superior to burying the mind; directly beneath, there is no birth, cutting off past and present. Whether in mountain crags and valleys or in the marketplace and court, all are great recluses.
Why, then, does my teacher hide away in the depths of the clouds?
Why must one bury oneself amidst green mountains? If one is simply without mind, the myriad realms are at ease.
How strange that this old Chan master makes such a fuss, standing at a double barrier deep within the white clouds.

From of old, those of lofty reputation have faced no light burdens. Drinking from the ox’s trough, he remains pure in the highest reaches of the stream. Before my Master has even passed away, you have already buried him;
you are now walking upon the very crown of the heads of Chao Fu and Shou Yi.

The moon mourns the cypress tree whose roots were planted by hand at the edge of the clouds; how many years have passed since it was first rubbed and brushed by wind and frost? What began as a mere sprout is now seen with the eye to have grown into a trunk of girth.
The King of Yue’s arrogance led him to underestimate the worthy man of Wu.

Passing by Tanyang Pavilion, I heard that Tanyang had already attained the Way and become an immortal; he ascended to the clouds and heavens upon the white sun. Who is it that regrets having followed him so late?
With hair turning white and thinning, I read these old verses.

Moved by these reflections, I have examined this mind for twenty years; it makes no distinction between purity and defilement, drifting freely as it may. When we meet, do not speak lightly of the rules of the craft;
were it not for the green pine, who else would appreciate its sound?
Since the time Jian Kui, the Chan practitioner,
served as a disciple of Tan Yangyi and parted from him, I have felt a kinship with my fellow robes. While the discourse on truth at Shaoshi was truly peerless,
I did not expect that in recent years you would favor soaring upward, exchanging liberation for mere carefree wandering.
Answering the Zen Guest:
With a staff of sorrel, you enter the pavilion in the spring breeze; Within this heart’s affairs, we need not guess at one another. On whose tower does a flower-like maiden stand?
Weary, she leans against the balustrade, her hand resting upon her cheek.
To the monk Ge Wan of Southern India:
Having heard that your compassionate heart reaches even the insects, you once tamed a dragon without relying on supernatural powers. When we meet, do not ask about matters of the road;
at the edge of the mountain pass, spring is deep and the snow has not yet melted.
On Buddha’s Hand Cliff, the vast and boundless triple world is entirely lost in confusion. Though Confucius and Laozi possess power, their strength remains slight;
were it not for Gautama extending his great hand, who could lift up sentient beings as they sink into ruin?
Though the roads of Shu are difficult, they may still be traversed; the pass of Zhaozhou is perilous and cannot be climbed.
With eyes wide open, one clearly sees the Zhenru Monastery—how many of the most brilliant spirits have yet failed to cross?
Passing the Hanging Pearl Pagoda, the clear stream winds around the towers and terraces. The golden ground is empty and still, utterly free from even a speck of dust.
I have heard that the birds of the old forest by the lake, finding no branch left to roost upon, have also flown here.
I was invited to attend a lecture by various scholars at Longguang Temple, to which I replied:
After rain falls, the empty forest gives rise to midday coolness; In the Hall for Washing the Mind, high discourse is held among those in scholar’s robes.
I know from afar that this Way has now been firmly established, And does not belong to the side-tracks of the Chan school’s staff and shouts.
I intend to accompany Master Kai to Mount Lu to pass the summer;
a thousand-fathom precipice flanks the Dragon Pond, where long pines and solitary rocks bring a chill. At Kaixian, who will be my companion to escape the heat?
I shall lie watching the flying waterfalls cascade from the edge of the clouds.
Who has taken up the golden shears to laboriously cut and shape these flowers? With reverent hands, they are offered to the Tathāgata.
Though they do not rely on the power of the spring breeze, every branch, red and white, blooms in its proper succession.

Spontaneously Composed in Two Verses The wild ox’s nostrils have always reached toward heaven; In its coming and going, it has never been pierced. Fresh and bright water and grass suffice for its needs;
As for the timing of its departure, do not pity it in vain.
As the pine needles catch fire, the flames first surge upward; one after another, they rush toward the light, vying to travel north. Before the night grows deep, the smoke has vanished;
returning home, everyone laments that the divination was without efficacy.
A Gift to a Certain Zen Practitioner:
With a sharp axe, he lightly severed his own finger-tip; Within a grove of a hundred flowers, all worldly ties were stilled.
Now, as this is presented upon the banks of the Xiang River, The fresh blood flows forth as a stream of emerald water.
Staying overnight at Wenshu Temple, I recall the Chan Master Fenglin and bid farewell to my fellow practitioners.

The wind has risen high overnight; the white grasses are desolate and chilling. The solitary paulownia tree remains empty, yet the phoenix has already flown away. Moonlight like water clears the dreams of men;
as we gaze upon our cups and tea, our thoughts are stirred.
Moved by these reflections, my hair shows every trace of frost. The southern bird and the northern swan both feel all the more sorrow.
Having traveled the rivers and lakes for thirty years, I buy a boat; the number of guests is as usual, boundless.
I wish to visit the nobleman’s villa, so I first inform him of this:
the sky was overcast for several days, but today it is clear. With my staff in hand, I leap with joy as I walk through the southern garden. My host awaits me by the pond with a smile;
we gaze at one another over our tea bowls as fragrant waves arise.
Together with King Fanglao, we visited the estate left behind by my deceased son;
grieving for him, we faced the sunset, mists, waters, and a desolate tomb. There were also those who came to sweep the white clouds. Today, leaning on the railing, we shared tea together;
the sound of falling leaves in the thinning trees is unbearable to hear.
Do not say that tomorrow each will be under a different sky; though the streams and mountains differ, the moon is impartial.
If you can keep the water of your mind always like a mirror, the pure radiance will be before your eyes everywhere.
I visited the aged Chan master Wan-yan;

three logs were arranged in the shape of the Chinese character "san" (品) for a fire. The hermit, wrapped in coarse wool, found warmth in abundance. A thousand crags were covered in snow, cutting off all traces of human presence;
only the plum blossoms could console the solitude.
In the Wei-xiao Hall of Yi-hao Temple at Huating, peach blossoms by the marshes turn red year after year.
How many times have I laughed at the spring breeze while still under the influence of wine? These years, do not inquire about the assembly on Mount Ling;
at midnight, my chanting lingers on as the temple bell tolls at dawn.
The Sangha bought crabs to provide for the lay donors; hearing this, I was moved.
For years you have横行 (roamed wantonly), forming swarms by day upon the sea sands and fields. This morning you were seized to serve as matchmakers;
now, amidst the hundred-boiling cauldrons, you vainly cry out to Heaven.

How joyful it is to meet you, Layman Wang, who tells me that Zhongnan has tens of thousands of peaks; with the spring rains now falling, there are thousands of cascades. I wish to build a thatched hut in the deepest recesses;
is there perhaps a sunny slope where one might settle even amidst the cold and damp?
Spontaneously composed:
My old mountain remains unchanged in its vast, azure solitude. Ten thousand ridges wind and turn, imbued with a grand vital energy. I laugh at myself that my weeds and wilds have not yet been buried;
even from within the void, my horns still stand tall and proud.
On a winter day at Gēfēng Terrace,
Mount Éméi must pierce ten thousand layers of heaven. Having endured frost and ice to reach the ultimate summit, when likes and dislikes strike like wind passing through trees,
the Elephant King’s path is naturally transcendent.
The asura of the Sudarśana Spring used the Sea of Wine as his vessel; however, the wine failed to ferment, whereupon he became greatly enraged. "How can this spring be so clear and sweet?
A single sip causes one to forget all sufferings!"
Before the Peak of Primeval Antiquity, I recall Governor Xu;

facing one another, we sit in desolation as profound thoughts arise. From here, Deer Spring lies beyond layers of clouds. I have further heard of the affairs within White Buddha Mountain—upon whom shall these names of imperishable fame be inscribed upon the azure rocks?

Two Poems on Cooling Off at Xiao Gāng Cooling off, the breeze from lotus flowers meets me everywhere; How many layers of green mountains lie within my gaze? I marvel that autumn has arrived so early at Xiao Gāng;
The stifling heat cannot reach here where the shade is so thick.
It is difficult to spend the summer retreat atop Mount Wulao; by day there is no heat, yet by night one suffers the cold. Though dwelling in the city during the sixth month, my mind roams here;
even the stones scorched and the metal melted are all but idle.
In Commemoration of Master Yang Cihu, Three Poems I have once read the works composed by the Master.
Bright stars and clear moonlight illuminate his Chan abode. Tonight, my head and face are fully revealed;
He knows me as a fish in the waves of Cihu.
The second:
That man is no true hero; as soon as a thought arises, he is clouded. Look at the bright blue sky by day:
from time immemorial, it has never had a single speck of cloud or mist.
Third: The lake of compassion remains ever pure today; who would say that the Master has passed from life to death? From where does the wind arise to stir the waves?
Still resounds the unceasing sound of the sutras being expounded.

Spontaneously Composed on an Autumn Day In my youth, I galloped past Handan on horseback; A knight-errant hearing of this wind, his very hair and bones grew cold. After the meal, the day is long and there is nothing to do;
I cut away fragments of broken clouds to mend my tattered robes.
Spring excursions:
across the bank, peach blossoms are stained crimson with blood. Whose dog barks amidst the sound of the water?
Had it not been for the rain passing by and the spring river widening, I would have knocked on the thatched gate to ask about Little Emptiness.
The old monk of Huangyan grew weary while walking by Kaixian Waterfall; dozing off, he knocked over the water from his pure jar, which transformed into a long rainbow of thousands of fathoms,
its gurgling sound resonating unceasingly through antiquity and the present.
As I see you off for the South Sea, I often hear that the winds and waves there are vast; until one has attained emptiness of body and mind, one should not travel.
Your small boat flounders like a mustard seed upon the waves, and I worry for you amidst the clouds of wealth and youth.
Passing through Zhaozhou’s Bailin Temple, the flowers and trees are withered and the spring colors faint. The ancient pivot of the pines before the courtyard—now who would dare to pick it up again?
Boundless beings among devas and humans have received the intent and returned home.

Inscription on a Painting of a Thousand Pines and a Broken Ravine with a Severed Flying Bridge: Beneath the pines, who is there to inquire of Old Pang? The flowers fall, yet do not follow the flowing stream out;
Who would have known that within these depths lies the springtime light?

Sitting at night on Mount Lu, clouds swallow the waterfall; now it exists, now it does not. Returning to the brocade pavilion, the day has already ended. With two or three fellow practitioners, we sit comfortably in conversation;
the sound of the *ghaṇṭā* resonates together with the murmuring of flowing water.
Spontaneously Composed Under the Moon:
In the still night, cloudless and with the moon at its zenith, Where does this pure radiance not find its equal?
From the south of the Yangtze to its north, across the halls and pavilions, How many minds hear the temple bell at dawn?
Staying overnight at the Lingyin Mountain Hermitage, I was moved by these reflections:
Nine li of ancient pines connect to the Flying Peak; From the emerald crags, clouds and waves roar like the Dharma-thunder. Monkeys and birds are needlessly startled by the axe and chisel;
Each time I ascend this place, my heart is filled with sorrow.
Ascending the Xuanlan Pavilion in Danyang, the pines are stunted and the mountain views obscured. Once they reach a thousand feet, they will naturally open up and allow passage.
On a clear autumn night at West Ridge by South Lake, viewing them under the moonlight, they appear even more extraordinary.
To Wu Yuanshi:
A single fragment of solitary light is fundamentally perfect and bright; as soon as the mind arises, it is already separated by a distance.
Seeking it upon paper is all the more laughable—how could a painted dragon ever possess spiritual intelligence?

In dreams, one knows that joys and sorrows are empty; how could the realms within waking life be real? Constantly examine waking and dreaming with subtlety, and you will be at ease at the critical juncture of adversity and favor.

The stages of the path for revealing the secret treasury and practicing the hidden function are such that as soon as one’s cleverness is exposed, one has already deceived oneself. Since one cannot yet depart from active mental formations even in moments of clarity,
how could one avoid being dazed and deluded within the dream?
In this year of contemplation, my inner thoughts follow the flowing stream; once they reach the vast blue ocean, they never return. Only the numinous mind remains, unattached to anything;
amidst the winds of circumstances—favorable or adverse—it is ever tranquil.
Recalling Sun Zhonglai, who followed me past the Patriarchs’ Hall in search of Venerable Lanrong;
leaning on his staff, with whom did he inquire after the bamboo chamber? A thousand peaks of empty verdure stain one’s robes.
The flower-offering birds have departed without trace, yet they cause the Way of Yanling to become even more fragrant.

A single slab of cold jade spans the azure stream at Yubian Bridge, leaving behind the Gate of Deliverance. When travelers reach this place, they are suddenly struck by autumn. Do not let it fly away into the human world;
as rain and as clouds, may it never turn its head back.
At Chengtian Temple, I recall the past with a poem:

Where can one inquire after the Luo family amidst the dust and wind? By the head of the Eight Virtues Pond, I behold the flowers of awakening. The clusters of orchids beneath the courtyard are now silent and desolate;
Only the *Gensheng* remains, able to dispel delusion and error.
At Mount Emei, seeing someone off on a journey to Mount Qingliang:
The paths of ice, snow, wind, and dust are not the same. Stepping out the gate, one’s staff becomes a dragon. Where does the peach-blossom wave arise this morning?
Fragrant clouds, flake by flake, join the Five Peaks.

Two Poems on Crossing the Eighteen Rapids A lone reed-boat drifts all day amidst the verdant heights; Just as one rapid is passed, another begins. We enter straight into the deepest reaches of the remote mountains;
Yet Caoxi still lies to the southwest of the ridges.
Green mountains on both banks, the moon fills the river. The boatman, greedy for sleep, does not ply the vessel. At such a moment, the flavor of things is as pure as this;
the Dharma verses are difficult to proclaim with the mouth.
At the hermitage temple, we part;
the Southern Palace’s horses neigh as willows sway in the warm spring breeze. Facing the *tánhuā* (dharma-flower) and the moon of wisdom, the air is cool.
I know not where we shall meet again after this parting; a single sail drifts faintly across the vast blue waves.

Dwelling in the mountains, I wrap my belly with three thick strips of bamboo; who among these mountain-dwellers is full, and who is hungry? How many times have I wandered alone along the desolate mounds?
I do not learn from Caoxi to roll in the mud of right and wrong.
In a boat on the Wu River, the yellow plums have not yet faded when the red plums appear again; the song at Zhinshui has ended as I arrive at Jishui.
If Donglin were a place where one could plant my staff, I would wash away the dust of the world in the cool waters of Chongming Spring.

Passing through the pass, he carries clouds across the snow-capped ridges from the south; when will the flowing waters and green mountains return? Why must the frontier official strike his weary horse?
There is nothing in his bag to attract the dust.
I happened to sit for a moment beneath a tall pine tree; it has been three hundred days since I reached this dusty world.
Who would have known that before a single thought arose, there was but a hollow, suspended block of mossy stone?

Inscription on a Landscape Painting of Mount Laṅkā I have previously beheld the peaks and springs of Shandai; what I see now is even more wondrous. Cloud-tossed waves and empty verdancy are both inexhaustible;
let people at leisure debate whether this is but the ashes of a kalpa.
Mooring for the night at Xingzi, the waves lashed against the Zhu Embankment as I passed the foot of Nankang City. For those traveling by boat, life was as fragile as a single strand of silk.
If Xin’an had not produced Master Zhu, who would have built this embankment by the lake?
Passing through Nanxiong, I leave behind the noble and virtuous;
coming from the south, how could it be merely across a thousand ridges? All day long, mist and clouds accompany the traveler’s journey. Who can explain that the Zhen River flows westward?
Only the broad and long tongue of the Buddha can preach non-arising.
Ascending the Dharma-pulpit of the Second Patriarch, where the Ancestor preached the sutras in years past; where the falling flowers and the wind of wisdom were ever pure.
Now, amidst the desolate halls and pavilions, only the Fenglong Peak remains unchangingly green.
The Chan practitioner Mansu has labored in the monastic groves for ten years; like a sunflower in June, his heart is a single, focused point.
As clouds pass over Longquan and the autumn rains cease, the cold current flows on—mostly sounds that break the heart.

Spending the Night in the Autumn at the Zen Quarters of Attendant Ben At the beginning of autumn, after long rains, a sudden new clarity breaks through. The cloud-houses are vast and silent; a sliver of moon shines bright. A crisp air presses upon me, and I cannot sleep.
As I walk in meditation, who else is there to listen with me to the sound of the spring?
Awakening from a dream, a dream is spontaneously formed;
as I traverse peaks and springs, my兴致 (zìxìng) is thick. Ten thousand pines are lost in a single stroke of the bell. Upon awakening, the empty verdure is still enough to be cupped in the hands.
As soon as the mind stirs again, the path of interest is exhausted.
Inscription on a Painting of a Fine Hardwood Tree, Presented for the Longevity of the Vice Minister of Justice, Wang:
Cattle and sheep dare not lie in its shade; rising high from the earth, it overtops the myriad groves. Firm and upright, it does not change with the autumnal air;
being without sentiment, how could it ever betray its original heart?
On an autumn day, I visited Duobao Temple and reminisced about Lord Chen Pingjiang, Duke Mu Wenjian:
Fish and dragons remain unchanged amidst the old waves and tides; Duobao Temple supports the clouds, its grandeur standing in silent solitude. Where can one seek the traces of Chen and Mu?
Broken steles and crumbling monuments lie amidst the withered grasses.
At the ancient cypress trees of Aifuku-ji, the fragrant leaves are lacy and their emerald shade spreads wide; how many times has the wind passed through them, pouring forth clear sounds?
The jeweled ground before the eaves remains as it was, yet there are no longer the birds that come at dawn to announce the break of day.
Ascending Mount Zhongtai at night, I gaze afar from the summit of Lion Peak; turning my body, I soar straight up into the azure clouds.
With a long cry resounding beyond heaven and earth, the wind rises atop the five peaks and the moonlight grows cold.

Delighted by Attendant Yao’s inquiry into the Dharma, the white-footed monk of the Black Terrace smiled as he recalled his former ascent to the rank of Pillar Historian. Burning incense, he asked about the Mahāyāna: "The Buddha-nature has always been without distinction between noble and base;
any man with resolve immediately attains spiritual penetration."

Two Poems on Passing Through the Ancient Zhuyuan Hermitage at Heli Forest Deep clouds cover the groves of emerald bamboos; a small thatched hut is enough for peace. Let the golden sun scorch the stones as it pleases;
this old Chan monk, wrapped in his fur robe, still finds the cold unbearable.
The second:
On the green mountains, there are ten thousand bamboo stalks; when hearing the rain, one comes to lean against the railing. Suddenly, the sense organ of hearing cannot be found;
the Master shouts, shattering delusion and stubbornness.
Entering Xiangyin from ancient times, the waters of the Ba River flow on like a stream of characters. The waters of Xiangtan emerge even more profound and secluded;
thirty-six bends come as they go—none knows who shares the same boat.
On Recalling My Feelings: What need is there to speak of world-surpassing fame and glory? To those of this age, my worth is as nothing.
Who knows that there is another way to pass the imperial examination, One that lies not within the ink and paper of literary composition?
Occasional Occurrences on a Boat in Yangxian:
Coming and going amidst the dust of the world, my two temples are already white with age. The green mountains laugh coldly at the toil of mankind.
In a lifetime of mere mediocrity, what has been accomplished? A single slice of time vanishes within a dream.
I show you that among monastic robes, this *kāṣāya* is difficult to wear; dragon-embroidered robes and sable furs are not necessarily superior.
If one’s intention to be a monk is not yet resolved, what need is there to shave the head and dwell amidst the mists and clouds?
Two Poems on Crossing Mount Dayu Empty-handed I left the ridge, a mere woodcutter; With a bowl in hand, I returned to join the Patriarch’s lineage.
The nostrils point downward as before; China has become a thicket of tangled vines.
A yellow plum bowl beneath the red plum grove— Who carries it across the ridge at midnight? Countless fine mountains remain silent in their greenness;
How can one investigate this single phrase within?
To Zen Master Benlai:
Before and after, a thousand peaks go and come; how many times have my wax-soled sandals worn through the green moss? Now I am too weary to travel to various quarters;
after my meal, I lie upon the stone terrace amidst the clouds.

Passing by the Hall for Reading by Zhang Wénxué, amidst flourishing trees, bamboo groves, and flowing streams, I find myself even more enamored by the pure breeze that brings midday coolness. Before joy or anger has yet sprouted, who is the master?
Fragrant clouds, slice by slice, drift across the long corridor.
I weep for Master Qiānsōng;
throughout the vast universe, all is a foreign land. In this age of semblance, the banner of the True Dharma has been struck down in shock. Gazing south toward the river plum, my sorrow knows no end;
deep within the thousand pines, the cold fragrance falls.
Gazing at Mount Xie, no labor of needle and thread is needed for shoes to form themselves. Ten thousand ages of surging waves cannot bury them.
If there were someone in the world capable of wearing them, they would yield to this man of boundless capacity who has come.
Lamenting Mu Yuan’an:
How strange it is that Old Master Yuan’an has awakened! The spring light has leaked away, and the tree-tops are empty. I am ashamed of my own single tongue of red lotus;
there is no place left for me to lightly brandish this blade of eloquence.

Traveling by boat through the Nine Rivers, willows sway in the spring breeze as I inquire of the path ahead. Ten thousand li of passes and mountains stretch north and south; a single moon shines over the river waters.
At this moment, my thoughts exist within, yet they are not there.
The Collected Works of the Elder Zibo, Volume Twenty-seven;
The Collected Works of the Elder Zibo, Volume Twenty-eight.
Read by Hanshan Deqing of the Ming Dynasty.
Poem (Heptasyllabic Quatrain):

Ascending the Pagoda at Huayan Temple on Wujiang What need is there to inquire of Emperor Han Wu about the ashes of the kalpa? Now the old dust of the vast ocean remains. Who shall light the pagoda lamp upon the Wujiang River?
Above. Directly, the sleepy eyes of fish and dragons are opened.

Sitting cross-legged in an empty hall at night, the empty hall is as clear as water; the spiritual mechanism is vivid and clearly transcends all emotions. One hundred years consist of thirty-six thousand days.
How could one obtain even a brief moment to walk upon this ground?
I compose these verses for the Three Dukes, the Observers, and the Tenth-Rank Official:

In autumn, the wind moves through the sparse shadows, chilling the windows; At night, the clear fragrance draws one into the depths of the sitting hall. I cherish all you gentlemen who are able to embrace [this virtue].
Section. Not because of frost and dew did he lose his original resolve.

At Heilin Temple, it has long been said that the pines preach the Dharma with the sound of waves; there is no need for the old monk to weary his tongue. Who would have thought that one morning they were all cut down?
All is exhausted. How many times have the cranes returned at night to seek their nests?
Sent to my fellow practitioners of the Dharma in Wujiang:
"The bright moon of Wujiang was once shared with you; now, ten thousand *li* away, I journey toward Shu. Send these words to the flowing waters of the Long Bridge."
The Way: Do not hasten the white-haired old man of this dusty world.
Sent to Zhongchun:
Depart for Emei, more than ten thousand *li* away; turning your head toward the Eastern Sea, what is your intent? Simply take your parents' bones and bury them on level ground.
The earth; wherever one goes, the green mountains are good for composing books.

Presented to Yao Guobin, the Pillar Official, returning with a single chest of frost. Who would have visited him when he was ill in Dongchang? A fragmentary reflection on the Fen River nestles upon the ridge.
The Moon: its light never ends across a thousand li of passes and mountains.
I mourn the Great Teacher of the Trichiliocosm;
the water of his eight virtues is most cool and refreshing. Those who drink from it can extinguish the madness of feverish afflictions. On the high tower of non-duality, the clouds disperse.
All is exhausted. Ten thousand dragon-elephants grieve all the more.
At Lingyan, I rejoice that General Wang and Attendant Fu have arrived;
I sweep away the dust and advance toward the white clouds. Amidst the empty mountains and flowing waters, I hear them within stillness. Above the ninefold heavens, many people dwell.
Few indeed; how could their number ever match that of you two masters?
At Foxiang Monastery, we passed the Qingming Festival. Outside the gate, the willows hung low and were a vibrant green. It was no wonder the dawn orioles sang so unrestrainedly.
Severance. The broad and long tongue-mark sweeps the wind with ease.

At the summit of the Eastern Terrace, the wind is high and the white sun is cold. Layered clouds and mountains are viewed from before the railing. Deep into the night, one leans against the southern tower.
Pillar Inscription: Delightfully beholding the vast blue ocean surge with jade orbs, I inscribe this upon the Jade Maiden’s Pool:
Her ethereal form is fragrant and pure, inherently free from dust; It is not that she must bathe her body in the pool, But rather that Master Shan detests the stillness.
Silent. Adorning this secluded and sublime place to draw in travelers, one pays tribute to Xuan’an;
the peach blooms red and the plum white—what a fine spring scene! Who would have thought that the eastern wind would rage in the dead of night? Master Xuan’an was not one for mere silence.
Silent. The flavor of the vegetable roots endures long through ancient and modern times.

Beyond Xuanyan’s thatched hall, spring birds cry out as the flowers grow deep. Can one find a mind of tranquil dwelling within this thatched hall? Once the flowing river has passed, it does not return.
Returning, how many times have my sleeves been drenched with tears as I face the wind?
To Jiang Shihua:
In this burning house of affliction, how can one dwell long? My hair has turned to snow, a laborious task to dispel; yet the old mountain from which I came is not far away.
Far away, within the great lotus robes of the chariot, lie pearls;
they manifest dignified grace as flowers fall and bloom through many springs. This body is like a dream and like dust; at dawn, it gathers and disperses with the eastern wind.
Urgent. The color of the red spots on the moss is not fresh.
To Fu Gongsu (Four Poems). The hibiscus by the river faces the morning breeze;
The hue of its color is especially deep amidst the first mist. The pleasures of the human world are truly worth enjoying.
Laughter. Song and pipe, towers and terraces, are reflected in a mirror.
White hair has never feared anyone; upon the heads of lords and kings, the morning frost is fresh. When returning home, do not say the mountain passes are far;
with a single thought turning the light back, the frozen earth becomes spring.
The sun and moon rise and set without ceasing; the hair upon my temples shines like snowflakes in a mirror.
How much better it would be to wave my sleeves beyond the dust and clamor, idly passing this life alongside woodcutters and fishermen.
The flowing waters rush on, murmuring day and night; who among those of this fleeting life can no longer feel their heart tremble? The green mountains remain constant while men grow old;
the lute-songs along the purple thoroughfare can no longer be heard.
I show Master Han the snowy hue within Mount Luoji; his embroidered robes are beyond the clouds as he polishes his cap. Master Han also understands how to listen to the bells and chimes;
having exhausted all sounds and dust, he attains the eight returns.
To Layman Tie'an:
The mountain colors of Tianxiong are like those of Wuyi. You broke your promise and entered my dreams. It is no wonder that Vimalakīrti was constantly ill;
with no wild geese to carry a letter, who could have communicated?

Two Poems on Traveling to Hai-men The mountain sovereign’s imperial assembly has been heard of since antiquity; Today, seeking its source, I arrive at Hai-men. I send word to those upon the Jie-shi cliffs as they travel:
Do you still have the Kun fish of the North Sea who map their course southward?
In the green mountains, companionship is best for forgetting artifice; the spring waters and peach blossoms are all one crimson hue. The Peng bird laments its own feeble wind-power;
the minnow first returns toward the eastern sea.

Seeking refuge from the heat at Xiao Gao, one does not recognize the kinship of profit and fame. How many people in the world have been ruined by it? At every place where pines and springs abound, one can find respite from the heat;
why then would one begrudge walking with bare feet through the wind and dust?
Spontaneous Compositions (Eight Poems) A Dharma Hall is opened amidst the misty waves; Carriages and horses can never tread upon the emerald moss. Pure chants cannot be confined by bamboo fences;
The sound of the *ghaṇṭā* flies out from the water and clouds.
On the mountain peak lies a hundred-mu bowl-shaped field; I have heard that eminent donors have held it for many years. Today Yunju has gained a new master;
when the fine scented rice is exhausted, may you show us your compassion.
How many bends does this single stream of the Xiang River take? On both banks, the peach blossoms have not yet turned crimson. Do not say that the spring chill makes the willows timid;
even they can dance upon the misty waves when riding the wind.

The mountains and waters of Jianchang surpass those of Linchuan; even if Wang Wei could not paint them all, behold the Great View formed by the wind, which blows directly toward Little Western Heaven.
In the late autumn of the Patriarch’s Grove, the *juehua* flowers wither into emptiness; the *śāla* trees stand desolate, locking away the Brahma Palace.
The solitary birds, as if pitying the seamless stupa, break heart several times as they cry out into the western wind.
Looking out in all four directions, heaven and earth are entirely clear and bright. A single sail hangs over ten thousand li of the long river. Not many roads lie ahead from Xunyang;
the Five Elders' peaks part the clouds as emerald dyes the sky.
The wild waters stretch six or seven li back and forth; In a small boat, two or three people, some dark, some light. After the rain, the misty waves are naturally moistened;
Returning home, the pure song is fresh under the moonlight.
At dawn, the golden phoenix sells its crimson fragrance; Each blossom, bashfully containing the luster of dew. Form arises from emptiness, and emptiness becomes form;
In vain you boast of the light and graceful body of Feiyan.

Hearing the chimes, the long embankments and short shores are cut off from mist and waves; it is as if the Dragon Palace were hidden within the *bìluó* vines. The wind is warm and the sound of the chimes flies on, nearly breaking off;
who can understand this lingering resonance while listening to the fisherman’s song?

A Spontaneous Composition at Fanchuan in Qu’a during Summer In the three months of the dog days, heaven and earth are like a single steamer. In quiet contemplation, I imagine myself atop a cold pine by a mountain stream. The frozen clouds seem to penetrate my pores;
Yet this is not as good as observing a long fast before a painted Buddha.

Rowing a Boat on the Brahma River (Two Poems) A gentle breeze rises by the embankment of green willows; Red lotus feet vie to startle the jade-green basin. Who rows a small boat across the mouth of the stream?
Fragrance wafts and wafts, carrying a light chill.
Without applying rouge, her allure is already profound; she pities herself as her complexion reflects upon the surface of the pond. One must know that beyond this there is no mark of emptiness;
why should the brocade of Shu be hindered from floating across the water?
Revisiting Kuangde Hermitage on a spring day, the flowing waters and peach blossoms belong to the Great Being’s home. Here the man of the Way once floated upon the star-raft;
now, idly blowing the flute by the White Ox Pond, I return as the sun slants toward evening.
Cishou visited Master Laosheng but did not meet him;
he traversed a thousand crags, reaching the moon amidst the wind and dust. He went once more to seek the man within Naradong Cave. Do not say that he would not enter even if the door were open;
where the fragrant clouds rise, he reveals his entire body.

Passing through Yuhé Guānyīnsì, a single path leads through autumn clouds to the wild weeds. I inquire about the traces of the Sui and Tang dynasties amidst the misty waves. Who will come again to restore the legacy of Master Xiáng?
On horseback, I chant the "Five Thies" song as I travel.
A Guest at Dongyun Monastery:
On the Occasion The attire of official rank and the misty pines differ in their nature; How can the clamor of flutes and drums mingle with the sparse temple bells?
With a single long cry of laughter, I depart the mountains; Wild cranes have never had a fixed track.
Upon hearing the words of Master Xing, the Xianling Palace was moved;

the source of the immortals is close to the Rui-zhu Palace. When the clouds have cleared and the moon is centered upon the celestial altar, the dew on the pines causes the cranes to spread their wings, once again moistening one’s sleeves.
Meeting you here, do not laugh at the density of the wild mists.
Passing by Xiyun Temple, I am moved:
Ten thousand *li* to Mount Emei, gone and yet returned. Ancient steles, devoid of characters, are washed of their green moss. Whose wisdom-life shall continue that of Master Wan?
Tears fall upon the green mountains, staining them with the ashes of the kalpa.

The flowing spring at Mount Nanyue’s Guanyin—how could this be a sound of the mundane world? When delusive thoughts fly about, one cannot hear it. Try for a moment to set aside the faculty of hearing;
beyond the clouds lies another path leading to clarity.
The mirror is empty;
within the mirror is the springtime of flowers in the void. Before the mind has arisen, one returns to the Real.
If one were to allow bees and butterflies to swarm about, I fear the East Wind would surely grow resentful.

I hope you will universally proclaim the mark of the broad and long tongue that covers the void; within the inhalation and exhalation of Buddhas and sentient beings, the sound of bracelets heard through a wall becomes the handle for life and death,
while coolness and burning affliction distinguish the male from the female.

The twin pines of the Venerable Hall coil and spread across the waists of ten thousand peaks; In the still night, a gentle breeze mimes the roar of surging waves. Hundreds and thousands of dragon-like and elephant-like beings pay their respects in succession;
Rolling up the curtain, I joyfully behold the lofty phoenix-head peak.

The ordination platform has coincidentally been completed; who would record that it was built of gold? A dead horse could have drawn Yue Yi here. Upon a precipice, a platform is erected to transmit the Buddha’s precepts;
the equipment of the Great Hero [the Buddha] is as vast as frozen clouds and thunder.
Entering the winter retreat at Yongci Temple, I present this to Master Miaogong, the host of the reed sprouts:

The depths of the eternal forest are unfathomable; where tigers and leopards dwell, How could one need to expel them when the Way is so lofty? Dread peaks stand in a circle for listening to dhyāna and contemplation, While winding streams flow in loops as one studies the Sanskrit script.

Master Shoushou of the Chan Hall passed away when the grass was knee-deep; together we traversed the barrier of life and death. Now his sacred remains are interred in the empty mountains. A single incense offering flies as a memorial within the autumn wind;
amidst the sound of flowing water, the shadow of the stupa is cold.
