Spontaneous Verses at Fuyong Pavilion A small boat passes by the head of the White Ox Creek; The sail is full as the wind drives the flower-like spray. The mist is so deep one knows not where it returns;
From time to time, the sound of singing reaches the painted tower.
I composed this while waiting for Wang Taiyu as he ascended Maoshan, yet he has not yet returned.
In every place, the eastern wind plays with the willow branches; my traveling companion has still not reached the Three Maoshan Peaks. At the mouth of the Huayang Cave, spring is nearly spent;
it brings grief to the traveler whose path home is so far away.
Mooring overnight in Wu, a cool breeze arises as the duckweed stirs in the autumn wind. Ten thousand *li* of sky, cloudless, a single empty mirror. Where shall this lone boat be moored tonight?
Amidst the clear, shallow waters of the Wu River, beneath the bright moon.
The Ruined Garden of the Wu Family (Two Poems) The lineage of Fenyang preserves the elegance of Jin;
Amidst the misty lakes and mountains, I am moved by past excursions. Today, who is the master of these pines and vines?
Fragmented clouds and waning moon lock the river pavilion.
A golden palace was built to house the lovely maidens; for how many years have they been lost to the nightmares of weeds and the delusions of flowers?
Looking with sorrow upon the former site of song and dance, cold mist rises from the ancient locust trees and sparse willows.
Staying at Huanglongtan on Kuangshan, I send this to the Elder Chan Master Yian of Bin yang:
High up amidst the emerald mists he dwells in leisure; A thousand feet of flying cascades, ten-thousand fathoms of peaks. On a moonlit night, for whom does he sing the "White Snow"?
From afar I hear its pure resonance falling through the pines.
An old man in the mountains:
green peaks encircle him as the path winds and turns. Running water, pines, and wind are cold even in the sixth month. This ninety-year-old forgets day and night;
when awake, he views things only as he did in his dreams.
Seeking Master Ze at Mount Gesheng, my path lies across a severed ravine leaning against cold pines;
Layered peaks and ridges embrace the Buddhist temple. Before I have crossed the bamboo bridge, the clear chime of the gong has ceased;
An aged Chan master leans on his staff and smiles as we meet.

Mooring my small boat at dusk by the western marsh, I anchor in a solitary village as the day fades. What thing blows across the void? The clouds in the heavens. Lying down, I watch the moonlight shine upon the shallow waters;
who is it that points from afar to the crystal ripples?

I recall my mountain dwelling, where weary bare-footed monks toiled amidst the winds and dust; Just since we parted from the green mountains, autumn has turned to spring again. Layer upon layer, deep clouds hang over the cottage by the crags;
In its solitude and emptiness, it remains locked, long without a person.
I visited Zheng Chunhuan but did not meet him;
the scenery within the city walls of Huzhou is truly unique. Half the households dwell amidst misty waves. In lamentation, where has the immortal recluse gone to his drunkenness?
The thatched gate is desolate and silent, sealed by water and clouds.

Bestowing upon the Indian monk a journey of a hundred thousand leagues spanning several years; at the riverhead, he taught with clicking of the tongue to subdue the dragon. When the day arrives in the Five Indies, the sun shall be white;
the moon sets slanting toward the west as the midnight bell tolls.
The great Chan master of the vast square ascends the mountain;
a single sheet of white clouds reveals the profound treasury. Though family blemishes may be many, be careful not to broadcast them. The true countenance of the old Chan master of Song Valley:
the colors of Mount Taihang are naturally azure and vast.
With Layman Zou Nangao:
A solitary pine stands tall at the head of the great river; day and night, waves and billows toss his boat away.
Several times the wild crane circles as if about to descend, yet the wind-whipped branches remain ethereal and cannot detain it.
Passing toward Guangfu Temple in the city, ten thousand clusters of clouds and mountains embrace the Buddha’s palace; its jeweled eaves and ornate ceilings are now overgrown with weeds.
As the evening sun sets upon the hamlets north of the city, the sound of bells drifts through the breeze several times each day.
At Tanzhe, I miss Miao Zhongchun;
at Gukou Longquan, there is but a single cloud. Who else can see you as you come and go, no longer part of the flock? At night, there is only the moon over the vast blue sea;
its boundless pure light cannot be divided.
In the capital of Yanjing, the various voices of the lay devotees have fallen silent;
a single moon sinks toward the west. Who can depict that which has not yet been born? Chang’an does not lie beyond the realm of springtime;
how few among us recognize the vanity within our dreams?
Parting from my attendant at Nikkō-ji yesterday, the western mountains were already falling into decay; the words of our parting linger in the empty hills.
The dust of travel swirls along two diverging paths, yet the azure sky above cannot be moved.
On the Stone-Milk Spring:
The stone-milk hangs high, its age uncounted in autumns; From mid-air it falls, a clear cascade of cold currents.
I know from afar that this flow shall return to the vast blue sea, Raising great clouds and surging waves to bathe the mighty vessel.
In my dreams I long for solitude, yet regret that there is no one with me on this ten-thousand-bushel vessel; amidst the shifting waves, it is difficult to remain even for a moment.
Who knows that the man on the shore holding his fishing rod has, through many instances of setting suns, let his robes grow damp with tears?
I show these novices my sincere heart, piece by piece, for all people’s sake; yet they cannot endure my painful blows and harbor a bellyful of resentment.
I only fear that once they leave this gate for thirty li, their hearts of hatred will ultimately turn to dust upon the water.
I entrust this to Master Ben, the abbot of Zifu Temple at Lugouqiao, who has spent ten years braving life and death in his resolve.
Whether meeting with adversity or favor, do not harbor any shifting emotions. Wait until the deep winter has passed and spring arrives of its own accord;
then the myriad flowers of a thousand hues will all bloom together.

Living in the Mountains (Two Poems) Walking alone, I have not yet desired to sleep; The cool night air, the bright moon, shine upon the pines and the spring. A single bowl of fine tea, and the darkness finally subsides;
Treading through the void, there is another heaven.

White clouds have no intention—this is the mind of the man of the Way. Flowing water leaves no trace—this is the footprint of the man of the Way. When both mind and footprint are forgotten, existence and non-existence are equalized;
who, then, can recognize white clouds and flowing water?
A Preface to the Parting from Grand Councillor Lù (with an introductory note):
Since my childhood, I have known the name of Grand Councillor Lù. It was only after I had donned the white robes [becoming a monk] that I first met him at Dàshèng Temple in Jiāshàn.
Tracing back from the present, twenty-two cycles of winter and summer have passed. I once met the Grand Minister;
his coming and going were inconsistent, and his gains and losses were intermingled, such that he could not be fathomed by ordinary sentiments.
It was as if Vimalakīrti used his protracted illness as a broad and long tongue to preach the Dharma-gate of Non-duality. For indeed, illness and non-illness constitute duality, as do death and life.

To speak of gain and loss as two is dualistic; to speak of honor and disgrace as two is dualistic; to speak of old age and youth as two is dualistic; to speak of the ordinary and the sage as two is dualistic.

To realize that sickness is itself non-sickness, death is itself non-death, honor is itself non-honor, old age is itself non-old-age, and the ordinary is itself non-ordinary—this is called the Dharma-gate of Non-duality.
If one can enter this, then even amidst heaps of fire or mountains of blades, all shall be cool and refreshing.
The Ground of Compassionate Patience (*maitrī-kṣānti-bhūmi*). Only the Grand Chancellor has long entered this Dharma-gate;
thus, he is able to move with sovereign ease amidst the transitions of birth and death, honor and disgrace, and emergence and withdrawal.

I am twenty-two years younger than the Grand Chancellor, yet he has honored me by not regarding my youth, poverty, or illness, but instead entrusting me with our bond of righteousness and principle. Now, as I am about to part from him and depart for Jinyang:
I have not yet had the opportunity to meet you in person; moved by this thought, I compose these verses:
Spring passed while you were in the Vimalakīrti chamber with your illness; summer arrived and you were at ease in the Vimalakīrti chamber. Now that we part, I know not where you will go.
In this floating life, opening one’s mouth to laugh is beset by many hardships.
Master Xie Taichu, the Silent Patriarch, has bestowed upon me ten thousand layers of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* commentary;
cold clouds embrace the desolation, and though the sun is high, I am still too weary to stretch my waist. Who can deliver these ten scrolls of the *Śūraṅgama*?
A single stick of incense is a blade amidst laughter.
One must be self-accepting yet self-reproachful;

do not disparage the extraordinary as an obstacle to the sacred spring. When great function confronts the opportune moment, it does not manifest before one. I am ashamed that my poisonous mind has not yet reached its end;
I have deceived men and women, causing them to fall into trivialities.
Sitting alone in the mossy grotto by the Prajñā Spring, all myriad thoughts are empty. A solitary stream pours down from the layered peaks. Let dragons and elephants gather like clouds;
for offering to the Buddha and watering the flowers, its use is inexhaustible.
Climbing Haizang Tower on a moonlit night, I miss my dharma companions in Jiangnan:
Above my head, the azure sky and mountains on all four sides; A single tower towers high amidst the verdant mists. I cherish these empty windows most during cloudless nights;
The overflowing pure light I behold all alone.
Awakening from sleep, I show the Way;
the gruel is finished, and I am just now pitying myself as I wake from a dream. The sun is high, yet I still snore and sleep; my son Kai has already learned to follow this indolence.
Stretching out his legs, he has inadvertently torn through his trousers.

Having personally attained self-acceptance over many years, my footsteps have traversed mountains and rivers. Though I have visited the Five Peaks and Mount Qingliang, I have no desire yet to return. Yet I laugh at this very day as my mind attains self-acceptance;
let the dragon-elephants as numerous as the sands of the Ganges climb and scale as they will.
Preface to the Bestowal of the Name "Zhitaí" upon the Newly Tonsured Chan Practitioner (With Preface).
An ancient said: "To know others is wisdom; to know oneself is clarity. When Master Mǎ was dwelling on the mountain...
The hunter Shigong was chasing a deer past him when [the Master] asked, "Where is the deer going?
The Master said, "How many deer have you shot with a single arrow? Shigong replied, "One deer. The Master said, "I am not like that. Shigong asked, "How many deer does the Master shoot?
He replied, "A whole herd. Upon hearing this, Shigong was struck with awe. The Master, seizing upon his state of wonder, enlightened him.
[The Master] said, "You can shoot a deer; why do you not shoot yourself? Gong then turned his bow around and shot himself, saying, "I simply have no place to apply my hand.
The Great Master said, "This fellow's ignorance of a thousand kalpas has been instantly melted away like ice.

If this is so, one truly knows that it is easy to know others, but difficult to know oneself. For a person to be able to know themselves is like using one's own eye to see the eye itself. If [one cannot do this],..."
For one who is not among those who have attained the Middle Way, it is truly not easy to speak of Shigong’s state where there is no place for the hand to descend.
A Chan practitioner named Changke gave me the courtesy name Zhitai.

Because his tonsure was pure and cool, I sincerely hope he will not forget the virtue of the old man Mañjuśrī, as well as that of his preceptor. Nevertheless, if Zhitai can know this for himself, then...
One may stop at this platform; one may stop at this platform. This grace shall not be forgotten. How long is human life?
To know this in old age and turn back [from worldly affairs]—if one cannot do so by the shores of empty stillness and solitude, in a place where ice withers and snow ages, to fulfill one’s resolve.
This is not the way of a true man. Zhitai urges you on:

those who reach seventy years of age are rarely encountered in this world. I envy you, grown old yet emerged from the dust of the mundane. Wherever the sword of wisdom is raised, the roots of worldly passion are severed;
whether departing or staying, never forget the springtime of Wuding.
Visiting Tanzhe Temple again after ten thousand *li* to Mount Emei, I return once more. The Dharma rain and fragrant clouds pervade the nine realms.
Who would have thought that this place of thorns from years past now has towers and terraces emerging from the empty mountains?
The clouds have cleared, revealing Shimen Mountain;

here, the mountains and waters are like Lady Xi Zi, cradling a pipa with her face half-concealed. Had she been seen by the winds and currents of the deep pool, who would not have been struck with wonder this morning when the clouds finally vanished?
Daliao An, Layman:
On Mount Wuyi, the old mountain greens remain unchanged. My ten-volume lecture on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* remains unfinished. Ashamed of myself, I speak thus and eat my own words;
I simply send this single verse to Yanling.
Master Dàowáng Fānglù once spoke of his past life as a practitioner of Huáyán;
at the moment of death, that habitual tendency indeed manifested before him. It is difficult to distinguish whether he was a Buddhist in tail or a Confucian in head;
it is just like using a bamboo stick to test a deluded Chan monk.
Gazing at Conggu Mountain from my boat on the Xu River, I have learned that attaining longevity is indeed a marvel;
yet who knows that while the body remains, its shadow must follow? How much better it would be simply to learn the state of non-arising!
Since I am already free from birth and death, I naturally transcend them.
Once I was a fledgling within the purple cypress nest; the harmonious sounds [of that time] were altogether not like this.
Today, as I once again present this single volume, the traces of blood soak through and permeate the coral.
The springtime craftsman fills his belly and plants everywhere; I take up my brush to depict a single branch in bloom. Who can appreciate this music without strings?
Far away across the Double Path lies the plum of Mount Yǒu.
Autumn of the Dingmao year. While reading the carved edition of the *Zibai ji* (Collected Works of Zibo), my disciple Yuanguang participated in the labor of proofreading.
Whenever he encountered passages where [the Master] had offered a sudden, inspired turn of phrase, he would break into tears.
Consequently, I composed two quatrains and appended them at the end, without considering whether the wording was skillful or crude.
Song of Aspiration for the Sangha:
O friends, have you not seen that within the great mass of earth and beyond it, all that possesses form is but gathered foam? The wind sweeps across the vast blue ocean.

Utterly withered. Since the bark no longer exists, what can the hair rely upon? From now until antiquity, how many generations have passed? Searching through the rise and fall of dynasties, one is moved by much lamentation:
the splendor within the mirror is but frost upon the grass. When the sun rises, where does its floating light finally remain? The Great Way has been lost.
Benevolence and righteousness give rise to folly; the ignorant and wise are distractedly divided into "self" and "other. The Seven Hegemons and Five Barons were arrogant with the air of slaughter.
The madman of Chu lamented for the phoenix and censured Confucius. Li Bo-yang, why do you act thus? To discard the ornamental and grasp the substantial is still a fragmented approach.

If you wish to return to the true and simple heart of Pangu, people of this age may not necessarily understand how to follow you. You exhaust the hundred schools and investigate the various doctrines, yet those who follow side paths crowd together.
Households increase while confusion deepens; those skilled in both civil and martial arts seek fame through war. In the end, there remains nothing but a thousand-year-old resentment.
Since the time of Qin, it has been unspeakable: the power of mountains and rivers, the blood of pestles.

Although beauty and ugliness are viewed differently, when one reaches the ultimate, even a thousand calculations and ten thousand deliberations regarding status and rank bring shame before the ranks of the ancients. From antiquity to the present, all is but a single dream. Cold and heat...

Competition over grooming one’s hair makes it turn white more easily; how can this compare to the merit of shaving the head to pay homage to the King of Emptiness? The karma of the King of Emptiness is a noble inheritance. Amidst the turbulent current of birth and death, he provides oars and rudders.

Those with the karmic affinity need only clap their hands to board the vessel. When not a single thought arises, the coarse and the subtle are equal. How could the water of the well of death conceal a dragon?
With a single shove from the Great Spirit, the silt and sand are cleared away. The hundreds of thousands of samādhis all originate from the mind-source. Transversely...

Holding up and brandishing [the staff], he maintains the family tradition. There are some people whose eyes stare wide open; their hearts are like fire as they seek immortality. Who knows that life is the medium for death?

Once the medium is established, it is difficult to undo; even if medicinal herbs succeed, what is achieved must inevitably decay. Since decay is certain, such cultivation is not something to be understood.
In my youth, I laughed at those who studied to ascend to heaven; how many times have I sold off this one piece of refined spirit?
Many calculations lead to victory; few calculations lead to defeat. Calculating and re-calculating, one finds joy as a monk. The five aggregates and the body-mind are like water and its waves;

when both holy and ordinary are cut off, there is no obstruction. With one flask and one bowl, the mountains and seas are vast. Clouds drift and birds fly as they sing their hymns at will. May you become monks! May you become monks!
From life to life, from birth to birth, continue the ancestral lamp. Take the Four Great Vows as the hub and the Dharma as the wheel.
The wheel crushes and severs the love and hatred of sentient beings. Du Hongjian and Wang Qinyi wished to become monks while alive, yet died breaking their vows.

To be honored as a state councillor is not as noble as being a monk. The realized one knows for themselves the nature of liberation and bondage. Amidst the bends of green mountains and the curves of blue waters, when the wind comes through the pines and bamboo, it enhances the countenance of the Way.
If you should meet someone and ask about the affairs of being a monk, you must believe that being a monk is no ordinary matter.

Casually. Calling out to the birds and singing, one lets go of the human realm and transcends this floating life. Whether in city or mountain forest, one walks wherever the feet lead. Aside from putting on clothes and eating, there is nothing else.
Before the meal, there is nothing before one’s eyes to which the mind can cling. Clouds at the edge of the pines; beneath the pines, stones.
Leaning my staff as a pillow, I sleep crosswise, wasting away the white days. Let the flowers and birds announce the passage of time for me. My snoring is like thunder as I sleep most deeply.

Suddenly waking, I take up my iron bowl and sing wildly as I leave the valley—how truly joyful! Gazing toward the smoke, I beg for alms in the village ahead. Once full, who would distinguish between fine or coarse?

Amidst the coarse winds and dust of the mundane world, the realms of experience differ; hatred and love swirl in confusion, difficult to sever. To those who have passed the examination of an empty mind, I yield:
when encountering circumstances, whether good or foul, why such vexation? Whether you know or do not know, it is all in vain delusion.

The traces of the Xiao and Liang dynasties are overgrown with lush grass; the two wheels of the sun and moon are cast like balls. The children who once rode bamboo horses now have hair as white as silk. Poverty and lowliness, wealth and—

To associate with the noble—looking at this with cold eyes, there is no front or back. This madman merely sells his own high reputation; amidst the light of equality, he harbors aversion and suspicion.
He does not wear a straw raincoat, but instead dons a sheepskin robe; on the banks of the Seven Li Rapids, he has brought such waste upon himself. This very light—

Seeing and not seeing—daily life is majestic and grand, like a flash of lightning. Even if it were Śruti and Li Lou, exhausting all their keenness of hearing and sight, they would still be separated by a single thread.
To seek the Way is easy; to realize the Way is difficult. How many who meet it will truly surrender their hearts and livers?
At the slightest thing that offends the mind, anger arises. I am willing to show you this divine pearl. Once you obtain this pearl, the Great Matter is finished. I was originally...
Who is born that must again grow old? Amidst the sound of flowing water, one chants *li-luo*; within the shadows of the setting sun, one calls to the returning birds.
Stop, stop, stop! Rest early; the ancient trees among a thousand peaks are sufficient for pure seclusion. Do not wait until you have flown so high that you are weary before descending;
once your feathers have fallen, the Way is difficult to cultivate.
A Song on Planting Trees for Master Hu-yueh of K'ai-shan Have you not seen the old monk of K'ai-shan, known as Hu-yueh?
When Master Lo saw him, he did not dare treat him with negligence. He bestowed upon him the name "Lake-Moon" (Hu-yueh), and this was not without reason:

his clarity and purity reside within his person, while his physical form is outwardly simple. Amidst the mountains of the lake, in a cave by the moon, he goes back and forth from morning until evening.
I come and go without ceasing. Seeing someone cutting down a tree, I immediately wail in grief; kneeling before it, I beg that you do not fell it.
To preserve even a tiny branch is as vast as the difference between heaven and earth. To damage one branch of mine is like plucking out my own hair. If you wish to cut it down, do so all at once.
To this old monk, watching such a thing is like having my own bones severed. I pray that you will suddenly give rise to the Bodhi-mind, sparing it to serve as a majestic gateway for the Zen grove.
In summer months, travelers find coolness on both sides of the road; when winter comes, wind and snow find it difficult to bury them. Furthermore, a divine breeze arrives from beyond the heavens;

the rustling of trees and the sound of a spring flow right before one’s face—*duh!* A man who understands how to turn himself around at the face of this *duh* can, with a mere snap of the fingers, cast off the emotional dust of both ordinary beings and sages.
A Song for the Layman Juebo: Last year’s flowers fell and bloomed; this year’s flowers fall and bloom next year. How many times have flowers blossomed and fallen?
Who can fathom that which existed before birth? Before birth—painfully investigate to the ultimate limit! At that very moment, death and life, hatred and love, are transcended.
Pure! The flowers of awakening bloom everywhere upon the Bodhi tree; their fragrance fills the ten voids, and the faculty of hearing receives it.
Each illness sings its own song:
what are the five elements and the four great constituents? They resolve cold and heat, and resolve the cycles of birth and conquest; wind, cold, water, and dampness intersect one another.
Racing along! The root of the emotional mind has not been uprooted, and one encounters its delusions. Having encountered its delusions, how many times have you sought it out and found nothing at all?
A single piece of empty luminosity blocks the gate of the mouth; though there are a thousand words and ten thousand phrases, they cannot be uttered.

The Foal of the Horse! The Buddha of the Sun’s Face! The Buddha of the Moon’s Face! Dongshan shares the same rules with us in the dark. Behold his portion—who else knows it? Seize and turn back the stubborn mind; it is red.

Bones standing bare, white bones standing bare; following the teaching, the five eyes find it difficult to perceive or recognize. Yet, one grants permission to the lineage of the tabby cat and the white ox.
They leap and bound idly within the furnace of cold and heat. Do you not see? Peach blossoms are red, plum blossoms are white;

as soon as they receive the spring light, their colors deepen. Last night the east wind passed over the low wall; this morning, the ground is strewn in empty disarray. The flourishing before one's eyes—how can it...
How many are there? Two rats gnaw at the vine; one falls, yet another rises. In the mirror, the hair at my temples has turned gray.
This is the news of death approaching for the person within. The news of death: if I were not here, the medium of birth would not enter. To whom can I speak of these ailments?

How many sons of man heedlessly neglect this! How they heedlessly neglect it! The Iron-Faced Lord Yan can weave his nets; for the three realms of suffering, a single retribution lasts five thousand kalpas.
Even if one manages to emerge from them, it will ultimately take great effort. Furthermore, have you not seen how high-soaring wealth and nobility shake heaven and earth?
Yet when the hair turns white, gold cannot buy back youth. On the southern mountains and northern ridges, graves lie piled up; it is said that the *pángāo* weeds now pierce through them.
Within the eye, the simpleton can fall ill; in a dream he picks up a broken earthenware basin, yet upon waking it is but a handle for discussing Chan.
He responds with the winding branches of a pine tree as they come to hand; the celestial wind blows specifically through his grasp. With a single clap of thunder, his head suddenly lifts high.

A Song of Peach Blossoms: Do you not see the peach blossoms bloom? Do you not see the peach blossoms fall? When they bloom, how fragrant and lush they are; when they fall, how desolate and silent they become.

Who knows that, fundamentally, there is no difference between them? It is only human sentiment that fluctuates between abundance and scarcity. Along the green paths to the south and the purple roads to the east, there is no end to the crimson of the peaches.
Li Bai: A person in the Jade Tower is drunk and cannot be awakened. In a dream, he administers the government of Nankuo Prefecture;

he knows not where the dawn oriole is singing. Upon waking, the red sun hangs in the azure sky. Recalling the matters of honor and disgrace upon the pillow, they are like the horns of a rabbit or the hair of a tortoise—whom can we rank as superior or inferior?
Ancient and modern, joy and sorrow, movement and stillness, clamor and silence—all are but a single horizontal line. Yao and Shun were but birds in their nests.

From flowers reflected in a mirror; amidst the deep spring winds and rains, one idly blows the flute. How could a cowherd have a heart of sorrow or joy? If he has a heart that listens, his heart is as if plucking [the flowers].
Peach blossoms open; peach blossoms fall. Their opening and falling are unrestrained by impermanence. The practitioner lies among the crags and gullies.
Above the gully, to the east of the cliff, there are especially many verdant cypresses and gray pines. A long wind suddenly wanders through the Great Void.
Emptiness. Cloud-tides roll, resounding through a thousand peaks; the faculty of hearing is washed clean of all sound.
I have lost myself, and my traces are gone. With no trace, who am "I"? As the setting sun goes west, the bell tolls of its own accord.
If the drumbeats within the bell could be intermingled, how would one break through the darkness at dawn? Peach blossoms fall; peach blossoms are red. Discriminative emotion is empty.
The metabolism is the same. I am the true flesh and bone of the Tathāgata; how could I dare deceive the world with false words?
To show this, I sing the "Song of Contemplating the Body as Like a Seal":
Have you not seen it? Who among those like flower-like women does not cherish them? It is only because their faces are tender that they fear the wind. How many times have they hidden themselves...
Avoiding the peach blossoms by the bank, one does not see the Prince of Wu’s warships carrying Xi Shi, drifting upon the midstream while flaunting her beauty.
One morning, when the troops of Yue passed through the Spring Circuit, Gusu was lost amidst a casual laugh. This lump of flesh brings ruin to all;
throughout ancient and modern times, countless have perished in the dust. I, the old monk, possess a spell for subduing demons; it is not for those who lack heroism.
Understanding consciousness, one should constantly take this mind to observe this body: "What, ultimately, is this body? Observe it today; examine it tomorrow.
Search it thoroughly from within and without until you are exhausted. It is skin wrapping flesh, and flesh encasing bones; horizontal tendons and vertical veins interlace with one another.
Examine the three *jiao* and five viscera in minute detail: worms such as *rāji* and *krimi* are regarded as the Land of Ultimate Bliss, pus is taken for gruel, and excrement for water.
For the sake of food, one remains intoxicated all day, imagining oneself to have attained something. Yet when the retribution for one's life is exhausted, this illusory body is consumed by fire;

it vanishes entirely, carried away by the wind amidst smoke and flames. That which is able to observe is my mind; that which is observed is my body. Between the observer and the observed, how could there ever be distance or intimacy?
It is like the rivers and mountains of Wu and Yue, which the ignorant, lacking wisdom, mistake for one. Observe this long, observe it.

As his strength gradually fails, he trembles; a single ray of divine light shines upon the latrine pit. Amidst the writhing maggots, he longs for longevity, yet this place of foul stench is unbearable.
Competing for fame and vying for profit—who thinks of stopping? For ten thousand taels of gold, they purchase a beautiful face.
It is said that their elegance shall never die; how tragic, these karma-demons and lecherous sprites!
Unknowingly, the east wind arises in the dead of night, yet they still claim that the springtime is always thus.
Song of the Paper Coat: Do you not see the six-liang robe in the heavens? Or the palace brocade gown among men? Their delicate textures interlaced are indeed beyond compare;
yet how can they rival the sublime flavor of the mountain rambler’s path? The western wind rises—whom does it not fear? Its piercing chill assails one like a flying arrow.
In solitude, one sits amidst a thousand crags; at such a time, let the cold clouds spread freely over the roof tiles of the hermitage.

When night is half spent and the moonlight through the window is white, even an attendant cannot distinguish blue from red. Mistaking the cry of a frosty monkey for a disturbance to my meditation, I suddenly strike him with my staff right before his face.
Curved! Curved! Straight! Straight! When the sentiments of ordinary and sage are forgotten, it is difficult to fathom; the shuttle of the Mother of Transformation weaves on without end.

Accomplished! What need is there to compare its color with fine silks? Worn while walking, it is light; worn while sitting, it is warm. Whether sitting or reclining, it is always at hand to be rolled out or tucked away.

Let the eight winds rage as waves and storms as they will; how could a man of the Way change the countenance of a Bodhisattva? Hanging from a pine branch or drying in a corner of the eaves, even if a thief sees it, he will not seize it.
In the depths of winter, it alone brings comfort to the old monk’s breast. This single piece of empty luminosity is enough to suffice.

To depict this is difficult; moreover, the appearance of the "Paper-Robed Wayfarer" was truly extraordinary. How free he was in coming and going through birth and death! Yet he was sternly rebuked by Caoshan.

To harbor such strange notions is to obscure the profound essence. Old Zhongfeng also wore a paper robe; whether held horizontally or wielded vertically, there was nothing he did that was not excellent.
He preached the Dharma from within his robes with a voice like thunder—those who are naturally deaf have simply dulled their ears.
In recent years, worldly customs have grown ever more debased. Foxes and hares form swarms, recklessly tunneling and excavating; willow catkins and reed flowers obscure the eyes.

Those who possess the radiance of liberation willingly accept their own bondage. Zibo Sheng, seeing this, could not bear it: "If it is contrary, let it be contrary; if it is favorable, let it be favorable."
The face of the Yakṣa Bodhisattva is impermanent; through the transformation of an ignorant lad over kalpas, he awakens to the Heart-Seal (Citta-mudrā).
He takes no account of whether your Qingzhou robe weighs seven catties, nor does he care if your hemp tunic lacks four ounces. This single life-force is equal to a mote of dust:
what is rewarded is punished, and what is punished is rewarded.
In Commemoration of Xu Wenqing, Grandee of the Court of the Imperial Stables:
Why need one go to the Ten Thousand Peaks to escape the summer heat? This empty hall is tranquil, yet abounds with mountain delights.

Whirling winds and torrential rains pass in an instant; From the ridges and gutters, streams of water pour forth. Who could have brought these myriad valleys and thousand crags here? Yet they arrive so casually, right within the city walls.
The center opens. Autumn thunder rumbles as the Dharma drum resounds; infinite weary lives return from within a dream. Do you not see that when the gate opens, the green comes of its own accord?
Where one looks, the red is like a painted adornment. To know non-form through form, the fragrance of lotus buds lingers amidst the dust and wind.
Not many days later, Xu Yanwen hurriedly packed his bags to pay homage to the Sage. Suddenly, news of his death reached us—an unexpected blow. All is empty.

Understanding not yet deep, tears fall in profusion. The boat ahead is the very eye of the boat behind. Do not say, "He has died; I have nothing to do with it. Suddenly, it arrives right upon one's own head.
Like a flash of lightning or a spark from flint, mere lamentation is in vain. Following along with ignorance, one gives rise to the various realms of existence (*bhava*).
Heroes vie in battle over the beautiful and the ugly. If one does not follow along, one departs from all realms of existence. How could the Buddha’s hand ever be different?
With my own hands, I gaze upon the peony, contemplating the arrival of Compassion;
where has the Master gone before the flowers have even bloomed? Even as they bloom, he still does not return. Should a night of wind and rain suddenly fall—
Born, it is pitiable—its lovely, seductive beauty adorning the dark moss. Have you not seen that wealth and honor, poverty and lowliness, are fundamentally one and the same?
The blossoming and falling of flowers are but empty clamor. Before the sprouts have even emerged, try to observe them; though they wither and fall, the solitary root alone thrives in warmth.

Song of the Whip-Mirror: Do you not see the peach and plum blossoms? Fresh and tender, their red and white petals branch after branch have not yet been swept away by the wind. The young lord halts his whip and restrains his horse to gaze;
in an instant, a single petal drifts upon the clear, shallow water. By the river’s edge, the current flows on and does not return. How regrettable that such a crimson countenance!
Day by day it gradually decays. Following the teaching, take up a mirror and contemplate the skull; it would make the foolish heart laugh to death with its lingering attachments.

Furthermore, one does not see that even the most beautiful countenances of Pan An and Song Yu, once a single breath ceases, become discarded and cast away. The bronze mirror knows to whom it will fall;
it does not reflect the young man, but reflects the old woman.

A Song of Mountain Dwelling: Reaching the Peak of Vision. Reaching the peak of vision! What the multitude loves, he does not pity. Withdrawing from the clamor, he entrusts himself to the restless one;

in his carefree madness, he finds sole delight in the forest springs. Raising himself up and walking forth—there is no great error. His nostrils are solitary and precarious, refusing to be tethered by a rope.
The worldly path is rugged and the journey difficult; calculatedly, seclusion in the wilds is the superior choice. Generally speaking, it is better to withdraw than to advance.
Being prudent in one’s coming and going leaves no lingering entanglements. Clad in rags yet harboring treasures, how could one be considered foolish?

When others do not know me, I am truly noble. Dwelling in the deep mountains, I dare not seek mere ease. Tilling with fire and the hoe, I pass through the cold of winter. After the meal, by the empty window, I pay homage to the Buddha.

A Letter: How many times have I borrowed the light of the bright moon to look? Leaving the scroll unfinished, I fold my two feet together. The resonance of water and the sound of pines do not entangle my ears.
Suddenly, a single sphere of perfect clarity appears before me. The moment a thought arises, it is no longer seen.

A nail in the eye, a wedge behind the head— It would not be easy for even Lün Bian to extricate himself from this. Whether the response is slow or swift, let it be at ease. If you let it go, it remains as it is.
Two stakes; the handless man understands the fist. With a light blow, he shatters Zhaozhou’s barrier. The ancestral seal of the Five Houses falls into his grasp.
The mastery of life and death, wielded at will—is this not something ordinary? On Mount Luoxiu, the rock is solitary and hard; the bird-path hangs in the void, eternally still.
Ten thousand valleys and a thousand crags are connected by a single thread. Longquan is secluded and deep, with many pools and caves—a place where one may dwell. May it be so.
Washing the mind: on the path of awakening, all is desolate and the transmission of the sound has been lost. Foxes and hares form packs, howling in the bright daylight;
beneath the emerald palace of the setting sun, autumn gloom descends. Do you not see the inchworm? It bends and it stretches, yet it lacks great utility.

When the azure dragon hibernates for three winters, upon emerging from the water, the clouds and thunder naturally follow one another. As for the pursuit of mist and clouds—do not raise them in vain. From antiquity to the present day...
He draws upon the example of Yaoxiao and Shuqi. Lan Zan of Mount Heng sleeps while resting his head on flowing water; though imperial edicts repeatedly summoned him, he could not be roused.

Such is this family tradition: do not let it leak outward. If you can penetrate this meaning, even kings and dukes will find themselves outshone by your own inherent nobility. Cast away fame and office, and study the path of suffering and emptiness.
Banchuan asked Yuexie Linlang:
"Juesheng, I ask about the moon at the edge of heaven—has it ever experienced separation? From Mount Yanshan to Wumen, how many times have we witnessed its waxing and waning?"
Sometimes born upon the sea, sometimes vanishing amidst the forests; its radiance appears and disappears, yet how could it be muddied by the clouds of delusion?
Do you not see, within the Xiao Temple by the side of the Chang’an road, where incense is burned and one sits in the open air as the moon hangs in the sky?
Last night, eighteen eminent men gathered there; the wind and moon are boundless—whence did you come? And do you not see the ineffable wonder being cast about in disarray?
Cast down! Who could gather the pearls filling the ground? This sentiment is difficult to illustrate with the metaphor of empty space; to shatter empty space, one must exert great effort.
*Song of the Two Cypress Trees at Qingliang Temple*
Have you not seen the ancient Qingliang? Its towering peaks pierce the clouds through many autumns. Suddenly, before the window, a divine breeze arises;
the emerald waves roar and call, chilling one's very entrails. At this moment, who can grasp its essence? Through countless kalpas, the dust of worldly passions has been utterly cleared away.
Majestic and vast is this ancient spirit-platform; it fills all of empty space, leaving no room for anything else. What a noble tradition! Do not follow the deaf.
This floating life is like a dream, and a dream is like emptiness. The splendor of today and yesterday is but a frantic display in a mirror. I urge you: do not betray the true host.
The achievements of Huaiyin and the strategies of Liu Hou—in the end, they were all merely wasted effort. After the peach-blossom rains of the third month...
Look! Withered red petals cover the ground in a pitiful mess. Generals of Great Command, Lords of the Five Ranks—your glorious names have fallen without cause into the rivers and lakes.
How can they compare to the cypress trees beneath the embankment of Qingyuan? Such "elder" and "younger" brothers are without peer in this world.

And do you not see the high-pitched phoenixes? Coming and going, they cherish this nest; its fragrant leaves are delicate and their resonance uniquely marvelous. Listen quietly as the waterfall washes over them.

The sprout of the mind. Worldly customs gradually grow thin; truly, this is pitiable. How many people harbor deluded thoughts as they fashion coffins? Though encased in golden walls and jade enclosures, all must ultimately decay.
How can wooden planks ensure long-term preservation in the grave? Do not be short-sighted; do not seize upon mere convenience.

Summoning servants and shouting at slaves, you parade yourself as a "fine hero," straightway claiming that even the blue sky may be deceived. But the blue sky calculates better than you! It spreads its great net, leaving nothing to chance.
He delves into it; at the end, each case is resolved. How much better it would have been to turn the light back upon itself in those years!
Let this clear shade remain for later generations to feel its gratitude. To Zhang Chuntang.
With a sincere heart, I seek a kindred spirit beyond the clouds; barefoot, I search for the mind of faith amidst the dust. For twenty years I have endured the bitterness of frost and snow;
with a heart of anguish, for whom do I chant this verse? For whom do I chant it? At Wumen, the wind and moon are my truest intimates.
This true intimacy does not depend on life after death; a single ray of divine light pierces through past and present. Hearing of my travels, he sent me a pair of sandals—ten thousand miles away.
Mist and clouds arise from beneath his feet; mist and clouds are all the heart of mutual understanding. Departing, I miss you—how could there be any self? How could there be any self?
In a mere flash, emotion arises and we are no longer close. I pray that you will protect and mind me as if I were dead.

When a dead man sits cutting off all攀缘 (pān-yuán—clinging conditions), even withered wood and cold ashes are not enough to compare with him. Suddenly, the spring light returns to the great earth, at every single point.
Every place is fragrant and purple; whatever the hand grasps is a medicinal scripture. I ask you, where do you leave your commentaries on the scriptures?
I only pray that dragons and spirits will always protect and uphold them, universally serving as a potent remedy for all sentient beings.
A Song of Lady Jiang’s Chastity:
Who could rival Xiang Yu for his fierce might? He acted with unrestrained cruelty, setting fire to Xianyang. The smoke and flames reached the heavens for three hundred days;
Yet he looked upon them as if in jest, remaining unharmed. Surely his entrails were cast from forged iron, Or else he was like wood or stone, devoid of feeling.

His thoughts were stirred by the memory of parting from Lady Yu; when his song ended, his heart was so grieved that his tears fell like rain. Furthermore, he could not see the Great Magnanimity of Han Gaozu, renowned throughout the world.
Embracing his illness with groans, his soul was on the verge of breaking; he could not bear to let go of Lady Qi, yet she died without regard for him.
They stroke their beds and gaze at one another, tears falling in profusion. These two men—how rare it is to find such as they, whose spirit swallows the world!
They treat heroes like mere children; whether one is noble or base depends entirely on them. When they encounter Lady Yu or Lady Qi, it is no different from wrought iron being cast in a furnace;
square, round, curved, or straight, they submit to the hammer and tongs. They are also like a reed mat, yielding to whatever shape is required. Chu...
The Hegemon King and the Han Gaozu—how can their great magnanimity and fierce prowess be reckoned? At the gateway of desire, they both surrendered;
even at the point of death, they lingered on, still looking back with longing. Yet they were not equal to Lady Jiang of East Jiahe City, who maintained her wifely virtue as firm as metal and stone.
For fifty years atop a high tower, she remained unchanged, dwelling there as if for a single morning or evening, like a withered tree.
A tree leans against a cold rock; as the springtime slips away, my heart is as if dead. Only its pure integrity remains unchanging, its enduring influence forever steadying this degenerate age.
Wandering through Shanjuan Cave.

By nature eccentric, I have loved springs and rocks throughout my life. I have traveled across the mountains and rivers of the world, searching for wonders and exploring the extraordinary for many autumns;
there is no Buddhist grotto or immortal source I have not known. There is no such place I have not known. Yet the secluded spirit of Shan Juan is even more exceptional.

Fragrant mists at Mount Kongtong constitute a realm apart; carved crags and etched peaks are adorned with clouds and smoke. The stone fields and vermilion furnaces remain as they were of old. The Immortal...
Once a person departs, they do not return. The figures of people stand in dense rows, solemn as if alive. Tourists grasp them and play with them; how much sentiment there is!
The transformations wrought by the Creator are indeed difficult to fathom. Yet, by investigating through the Way, they may be understood.

It is because these tourists do not awaken to the mind that they instead give rise to emotional attachments outside of the mind. Once emotional attachments arise, they follow conditions and drift along; when will they ever cease? This mind...
The clarity and vastness are fundamentally boundless; through ignorance of this, joy and sorrow arise without cause. Sitting by a spring or upon a rock, one immediately feels delight;

grasping the wine cup and singing aloud, one compares oneself to an immortal. In a mere moment, the inspiration is exhausted and one returns to worldly toil; a single fragment of secluded sentiment turns into a web of entanglement.
How about directly awakening to the mind that has always been present? With a hand of faith, one grasps earth and it all becomes gold.

The entire great earth is but a single eye; one knows not where a needle could be placed therein. If there were even a single needle that could be contained within it, then outside this mind there would surely be something.
If there were something, how could there be no love or hatred? Once love and hatred arise, one becomes deluded regarding true consciousness. My love for the mountains—
Water: from the beginning, this has never been interrupted. Having traversed famous mountains, one remains untainted by dust; having gazed upon rivers and mountains, what color remains?
With nostrils reaching toward the heavens, one may be as lofty and independent as one pleases. Whether departing or staying, there is neither the realm of non-existence nor the realm of existence.

Who knows who can recommend the essential meaning herein? At Guoshan Temple, one pays homage to the King of Emptiness. Having finished paying homage to the King of Emptiness, one exits the Dharma Hall; the thousand peaks close together once more.
The setting sun. A solitary boat drifts into the distance, toward who knows where. Mooring for the night amidst the misty waves, the expanse stretches ten thousand li.
I sing this "Song of Resolute Firmness" to present to Xiangzi:

"That which possesses form may be firm and enduring, yet only Heaven and Earth remain; even the calamities of water, fire, and wind will ultimately sweep them away. This, then, is the Tathāgata’s truth."
I say: this is not a casual deception. Though the affairs within heaven and earth are many, the scenes of ascent and descent are darkly consumed away;
each has already passed and is no longer reckoned. Yet honor and disgrace still tug at human sentiment; when sentiment does not wither, one rejoices in spring and grieves in autumn.
From antiquity to the present, it has always been thus. One does not consider that heaven and earth are not eternal; one merely—
Whatever one desires can all be preserved; yet when the cycles of heaven and earth reach their end, even they collapse. In this fleeting moment, what have I to do with honor or disgrace?

Though spring flowers are lovely, they must inevitably wither; though one’s countenance is beautiful, it must inevitably fade. Have you not seen how the head of Han Zhongli Manqian turned white as he stole the peaches?
Cold and heat hasten the years, from which there is no escape. There is only one thing that can be escaped: the Great Way of Heaven and Earth.
There is no death for one who destroys others; do not seek it in deep clouds or distant ravines. It is not apart from the place of daily activities before you.

When wearing clothes and eating food, do not let it pass by. To give rise to a thought is already to have gone astray at the outset. When the single path of radiance transforms consciousness and emotion, [this is it].
Changing head and face, it is he who acts. In a flash, awakening to the nature of consciousness, this is itself the Vajrāsana.
All myriad things belong to birth and extinction; only this seat is eternally firm and solid. Were it not for the heroic great man, who could occupy it and find peace?
To find peace—to find peace! You, named Rujian (You-Jian), do not let your life pass in vain. This song of mine flows from the mouth; it is not [a deliberate composition].
Reflecting on this, bystanders read it and laugh at my madness; only you have firm faith and do not doubt. Morning and evening you chant and recite, passing the time.
Passing the time—where is the fragrance of the profuse spring blossoms? One does not taste them with the nose, but tastes them with the mouth.
I sing of the white hemmed robe for the sake of Feng Kaizhi:
This color is no different from the *bentāli* flower; Coming and going through the dust of the world, it remains unstained by mud.

May you let this mind be like this color— A single point of solitary brilliance, ever vivid and clear. Furthermore, like the sun and moon piercing the dark heavens, It ascends and descends through the universe without limit.
Traces of its presence remain. When this robe is worn, it never turns inside out; may your body always remain bright and pure. When the north wind blows snow, the heavens feel no cold;
furthermore, it serves as a yellow-cotton quilt for the common people. This robe is also like the clouds over the green mountains:
rolling up and spreading out at will, it becomes a sweet rain. All that is withered and parched receives its grace, and even insentient things give rise to hearts of joy. With you...
We have gathered for no very long time; I know your mind is but lightly stained by dust. As we part, I leave you this monk’s robe-cowl;
may you always keep your spirit alert and vigorous. May your faculty of hearing remain as firm as an iron scroll, never turning back; when we meet again, may your face still bear the look of spring.
Amidst the black and white, his character is extraordinary; demons and outsiders look upon him with their hearts trembling in fear. I am departing; you must remember this:

the shadows of clouds and the light of heaven are all my own state of mind. On idle mornings and quiet nights, do not harbor mutual recollections. Do not harbor mutual recollections; sever all emotion and consciousness.
A single point of solitary clarity is ever-present and distinct. This color is no different from that of the *bentāli* flower.
May your mind be like this color. Hehehe. Du du du. To the very end, what news of its radiance? Bai bai bai. Hei hei hei.
Your pulse. Lanzan’s Song Presented to Zeng Jinjian:
I have heard that your residence is on Mount Heng; In your comings and goings, you always follow monkeys and cranes. In your leisure, you further understand how to play with the murmuring streams.

"Yuan! It is far superior to contending in the dust and wind over games of chess and gambling. Furthermore, I have heard that there is one named Lanzan at Mount Heng who knows nothing but putting on his clothes and eating his meals.

While sentient beings are drifting and sinking in the sea of suffering, he hides away by the crags and pays no mind at all. A man of spirit, having entered this world, what purpose does he serve for sentient beings?
One who is a withered sprout or rotten seed lacks the great root; such a person is fit only to be beaten to death."
To feed a dog! Under heaven, all is the King’s domain; yet you alone hide yourself away, indulging in indolence.
If the whole world were to follow your example, who would deliver sentient beings from their downfall? This malady of laziness, if not eradicated, causes harm that is no small matter.
From this day forward, such a wind must not be fanned. Have you not seen how a sovereign’s indolence leads to the ruin of the state, and a man’s indolence to the ruin of his household?
There will be no prosperity. Lazy farmers lead themselves to starvation; lazy silkworm-women find their cocoons inevitably stiffen and die.

You, man, have no foresight; you are solely accustomed to the habit of idleness. Once the malady of laziness is established, there is no medicine to cure it. In your entire life, you have accomplished nothing.
Have you not heard how the Tathāgata rebuked laziness as a venomous serpent? It darkens the spiritual palace (the mind), and its suffering is boundless.
Sinking and surfacing within birth and death—how few are able to behold the *udumbara* flower! Now that you have returned, Lazy Zan (Lanzan) must surely be an old acquaintance of yours;
convey these words to him with earnest diligence: from this day forward, do not use "laziness" as an excuse.

Upon hearing these words, if he still does not reform and continues to greedily cling to his independence like a pine and its clinging vine (*shōra*), I shall give him a single blow of my fist and kill him. I dare guarantee it.
For long kalpas there shall be no debt of sin; yet I fear that your strength is insufficient, lest you be knocked down by Lan Zan.
A total defeat will be heard throughout the world, bringing laughter to the mouths of your descendants.
Zi-fang’s Mountain Song:
Clouds upon Mount Pengcheng, waters beneath Mount Pengcheng—gathering and dispersing, floating and sinking. Human generations succeed one another through endless beginnings and ends.
Have you not seen how much of life is granted by the Great Mass? The Yellow River flows eastward without turning back; its splendor passes away.

The eyes perceive the frost of heaven; who can win a hundred battles for mountains and rivers? The struggle between Chu and Han was but a weary dream; what more is there in these mere puddles to boast of?
The world says that you, Master, perceived the signs early on; you cast aside the seals of nobility like withered grass. Transcending all, you entrusted yourself to roam with the Red Pine (Chisong);
in the end, how could you be troubled by the likes of Han Xin and Peng Yue? This is based on the traces of the Master; how could one know [the rest]?
The Master’s mind dwells on retribution for Korea; fame and achievement are not what he delights in. Qin has perished and his life's task is done; why linger, refusing to depart?
Furthermore, one does not see that fame and achievement and long life are not far apart; to discard the former and grasp the latter is a shallow understanding.
I know that the Master’s celestial mechanism is profound; a mere grain of medicine or a feathered pen are things he no longer cherishes.
Having ascended this ancient temple, I composed this song, casually casting my ink traces upon the misty vines. Do not laugh, Master, at these many affairs;

the ambition and spirit of a man are difficult to grind away. If they are indeed as unyielding as the azure mountains, then though rivers shift and valleys change with no fixed course, only you, Master, remain.
A single mind constantly enhances the beauty of this mountain.

Regarding the song of the dragon and the snake: have you not seen that dragons and snakes are fundamentally impermanent? If a dragon has desire, it becomes a snake; yet a snake can be free from desire.
The king of scaly creatures. Though the desires of worldly people are indeed many, food, drink, and sex constitute the six afflictions.
If one compares food and drink to sex, sex is yet the spearhead of desire. Regarding the great magnanimity of the Han High Ancestor and the fierce ferocity of the Chu Hegemon:
he burned Xianyang with a single fire yet felt no sorrow in his heart; when bidding farewell to Lady Yu, how soft was his sentiment! As for the merit of Huaiyin...
The noble one endured execution; when the Lady Qi was about to be put to death, she hesitated in bitter anguish.

One who can lightly overturn the ocean of desire—how many such true men have there been in the world since antiquity? As for Xi Shi, what kind of being is she? She had no great power to topple a city or a kingdom.
Had she been kept by Yue at that time, even Yue’s hegemony over the feudal lords would not have been certain. Furthermore, have you not seen the five hundred immortals?

A skilled driver of clouds, coming and going across the void, far surpasses all others; yet as soon as he hears a single note from a palace maiden’s song, his divine powers are entirely consumed by the fire of desire.
Su Qin, holding the Han envoy’s staff, swallowed felt and ate snow until his life was nearly extinguished;
though life and death could not be guaranteed from moment to moment, he still took pleasure in the birth of a son by a Hu woman. Such is the difficulty of severing desire—it is truly hard to sever.
"One capable of severing desire must be a man. Even for a man to sever desire is already a great difficulty; how much less shameful is it for a woman to lose her integrity?

Though these words seem contrary, their intent is most poignant. Every character is distinct, as if my heart were bleeding. Whether man or woman, one who can sever desire is truly a hero of this world.
To uphold human relations and rectify the ways of the age—if one is not a hero, how could they possibly accomplish this? *Rao*.
To possess the talents of the Duke of Zhou or Yi Yin, yet fail to sever desire and remain in perpetual delusion—this is truly laughable! It is truly laughable!
Many fine men are lost in the apertures of urine and excrement; they spend their efforts adorning this stinking skin-bag, looking at one another and all praising it as "wondrous."

Little do you realize that this body is a composite of the four great elements, and this mind is a gathering of the four aggregates. If one contemplates these four sets of four, where can one seek body and mind?
How could there ever be a limit to the ocean of afflictions? Dragons and snakes emerge and submerge amidst clouds and mist; at the gateway of human desire, thunder and rain are deep.
Who will be the first to casually undergo this transformation of the bones?
A Song for the Pultong Stupa at Longchonsa Temple on Guril-ryeong Peak Do you not see it?
To the east of Nongseong and to the west of Longcheon, A tiered stūpa leans against the clouds and rainbows. The mountain is high;

the sacred bones cause the scales of creatures to grow, The earth yields precious gems; phoenixes and peacocks dwell there. The old master Byeokcheon’s vows and practice were firm— Like Mount Emei and Mount Potalaka.
All circulate together. The pearl of the precepts is perfectly pure, its light drinking in the sun. One hundred thousand and eight thousand acts of merit are performed.

To realize this mind is not a matter of a single lifetime. Throughout the ten directions and three periods of time, with such sincerity, who would have thought that this skull has no place of attachment?
Among the assembly of monks at Mount Qingliang, I once dwelt on Golden Pavilion Ridge. Returning again, I vow to establish a banner of my resolve. How pitiful—this one...
A heart of singular kindness. Shenlang merely split open the liver and lungs of a donkey. Master Zhao’s *Meaning of Nirvana* [states]: "Skin and flesh are connected without a point of severance.
Master Daosheng exhaustively declared him to be his former incarnation. Having come and gone among the white clouds for how many years? At the time of his death, he manifested a great capacity;
sitting upright in the lecture hall, he recited the name of Amitābha. Before ten breaths had even ceased, his spirit departed alone. The lotus...

An infant is born within the kingdom; a guest of the Chan school is truly hard to find. Heaven has bestowed a piece of primordial, undifferentiated substance. Whether morning or evening, one must be diligent with the *huatou*.
Picking medicinal herbs amidst the forest, one suddenly enters meditative stillness. As the red sun sets, there is no knowledge of returning home.
Amidst a pack of tigers and leopards, the body is left behind. Grandchildren look up in hope for their father’s return; lamps and candles are sought, yet the bird-path is lost. Ancient.

By the mountain stream, amidst the settled pine smoke, a foolish child sees it and cries out to the blue heavens: "Why have you not returned home for days on end? Instead, you lie with tigers in the deep forest.
Once awakened, he forgets what he has realized and still says, "In this brief moment, there was not even a single instant [of realization].
You fellows, why do you needlessly trouble the old monk? What a fine opportunity for a nap that you so disrupt the stillness! Of these three elders, who can express it? He yields.

Amidst the playful clamor with the leather ball, the family’s hidden shame is overturned and left nothing behind. A vast resonance and radiance form an eternal melody. When Qi undergoes a transformation, it reaches the level of Lu;
when Lu undergoes a transformation, it reaches the Way. From the coarse to the refined, a standard for conduct is established.

Flowers fall and flowers bloom, yet the spring is not counted; year after year, those in black and white come to offer sacrifices. This site of practice was difficult to establish at its inception; its history spans countless years.
In a fierce battle against the Qing at Han-yen Rock, who knows the pain of gun wounds and sword slashes? At that time, how many lives did the leaders risk?

Among those who assisted in the fight, both old and young, monks and laypeople died violent deaths—truly lamentable. That today the great assembly may enjoy peace and security is due to their sacrifice.
When hungry you eat and when thirsty you drink, all is warm and full. Such kindness—do not forget it! Lifting my head toward the void, there is a Bodhisattva;
whether one’s conduct is good or evil, he knows it all. I urge you: do not act like a fool. I have composed this song; its meaning is most beautiful.
I only fear that we shall forget our origins. When the origin is forgotten, the root is severed and the branches wither. What has been achieved by the hardships of those who came before?
Speaking of this, my very liver and gall are rent asunder. To know gratitude and repay it requires a hero. Spring comes and the peach blossoms bloom outside the temple;
the lingering petals, both old and new, are the blood of the deceased.

A Lament for Master Yan Ziling (with Preface) From the era when the winds of purity were washed away, down to the heroes who seized the empire from their horseback, men of profit, utility, wisdom, and valor caused waves to shake and dust to fly.

Ruler and minister harbored mutual suspicion; one morning they were noble and wealthy, and by evening they were executed and exterminated. Yet those who rushed toward such power remained as numerous as before.

The moth’s flight into the flame—how tragic! When Your Excellency placed your feet upon the Emperor’s belly, you cast off your ceremonial cords and stirred up a pure wind that extended to the likes of Li Ying and Fan Pang.
You did not exchange your principles for life or death; this is the enduring legacy of the single strand of fishing line at Tongjiang.
Now, having fortunately passed beneath the shrine, I have composed this brief verse to offer my lamentation for Your Excellency.
The poem says:
Three times summoned, yet he could not bring glory to the Master; once retired, yet he could not diminish the Master’s loftiness.
Since glory and loftiness are external matters, the Master cannot be defined by them. Only that the mountain is high and the water is long—this alone allows one to gaze upon the Master.
With a look of melancholy upon his brow, he walked away.
(The "Song of the Bronze Calf," left behind by Master Han at Longmen):
To the west of Fusang and to the east of the Black Waters, the vast expanse is imposing and majestic, the color of the sea is dim and hazy, with wondrous crags and extraordinary gullies.
Amidst winding streams and towering peaks, deep within the mists and clouds, where surging waves shake the void, there dwells a beautiful woman in a silent meditation hall.
I once knocked upon the gate; as if a drumstick striking a bell, she responded without hesitation, and as soon as I questioned her, she granted me passage. There I beheld this azure calf.
Carrying the immortal master upon my back, I unroll his scrolls without ceasing; my mind rests in profound serenity, while my spirit wanders to the primordial state of chaotic unity.

My traces correspond to the period after the separation of heaven and earth. Having long received your venerable teachings, Elder, I now behold these objects and think of you, my heart truly filled with deep anxiety.
Sitting at Night on Shangfang Mountain, Thinking of Sun Zhonglai:

The bright moon is in the azure sky; Flowing waters are by the emerald mountains. Between the pure radiance and the cold resonance, I listen in stillness to the interval between existence and non-existence.
That which I long for is the beautiful woman who has not yet returned. The time of darkening shadows is indeed difficult to wait out; in an instant, my hair has turned gray.

I have built a cottage deep within the pines and creepers, situated moreover by a bend of the clear stream. A light boat drifts upon the white waves, where the fishermen are mostly soft-natured and unruly.
Having departed, they return once more; for the fish with their flower-scales, life is no small hardship. Joyfully exchanging it for turbid wine, one drunken stupor forgets ten thousand cares.

Clapping hands, one calls but cannot wake them; their wandering spirits roam idly between rivers and seas. The winds and waves are unfathomable; one should strive to reach the other shore as soon as possible.
A Warning to the World: Alas for the people of this world! How short-sighted are their calculations! They seek only to satisfy the present moment, utterly neglecting the eternal.
The physical form is subject to decay, yet the true light is ever sovereign. That which does not perish must surely undergo rebirth; once born, one must repay the debts of karma.
That this present life is not as one wishes is the result of causes from the past. Though there be distinctions between the noble and the lowly, how could the mirror of karma ever grant a reprieve?
When the form is upright, the reflection is surely beautiful; when the face is ugly, the reflection is surely strange. Youth is like the spring flower; once it has bloomed, will it not wither?
I constantly observe the withered things; why wait for them to fall away before attaining awakening?
Alas for the monks of Lingyan Temple!

Do not say that leaving the household life is good; dwelling in the mountains is free from worldly distractions, yet as the years pass, my suffering increases more and more. To whom can I open my mouth and speak?
The mountain slopes are withered; the mountain fields are emaciated. From these withered and emaciated lands, how many pecks of harvest can there truly be?
Guests coming and going are forced to be supported. What else is there to provide for such excessive demands? Moreover, after three years, there have been two further years of famine.

Every day one swallows hunger like a starving dog. Speaking of this, tears fall like rain. It would be better to leave the mountains and go begging for alms. One turns back to reflect upon the ancient monasteries of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
The forest—how difficult it will be for it to be abandoned all at once to the wild thickets. Do you not see that at Lingyan Temple, both the large and small meditation halls have fallen into ruin?
The old monk has gone out begging for food and has not yet returned; we know not where his bleached bones shall be interred. The sound of the flowing spring is difficult to bear to hear.
Who would say that Lingyan possesses the four supreme excellences? The pines and winds now sing this heart-rending dirge. Even a wooden puppet, hearing this, would be moved to tears.
Tears fall. A Lament for Master Jie of Suanan at Qixia (with Preface).
That which the Master has attained is attained through non-attainment; thus, though he encounters loss, he has never truly lost anything. By means of this—
Because he had never once faltered, all those who adorned the Pure Land and brought majesty and splendor to the monastic groves saw their every aspiration fulfilled.
Even if the clouds and mountains could be ground away and the Min River could be exhausted, the Master’s virtuous countenance would remain ever full.
That he has now abandoned us and passed away—how can there not be sorrow? Therefore, I compose these words of lamentation, which say: [The lamentation follows.]
The Master came, using compassion as his hook; the Master departed, and life and nature merged into the wondrous.
The green mountains are the Master’s bones; the flowing waters are the Master’s smile. My grief is profound—may you cast your light upon me. The Dharma-beam has broken—who can now emulate it?
With these humble words and this incense, I offer my single requiem.
A Song Climbing Fangshan:
Have you not seen the Elder Li of Fangshan in Jinyang? He loved the tiger that carried his scriptures and had no need for a horse.
At the head of Daxian Village, Gao Shanu, upon seeing this supreme man, was able to dismount. Alas! The ways of the world have declined; this culture has ultimately come to an end.

I, Jia, have long heard the fame of your carriage and capes, yet my own ancient refinement has already declined. The ancestral Buddha hall of the Ma family has long been desolate within its earthen chambers.

The Elder has departed and does not return; who shall now wash the light of the Buddha-sun? I am ashamed that this humble youth was born so late. How could I dare to succeed to the black robes at the Twin Trees?
Yet, seeing the worthy, I think of emulating them and do not shrink from toil; I have sought mountains and inquired of waters, knocking upon the profound portal. I, once...
Hearing the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the model and standard of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, one encounters the fourfold dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) that is difficult to conceive.
Who could wield the brush without hesitation? It is like the hundred rivers vying to reach the sea, where the waves of ten-thousand-li clouds manifest in brilliant patterns.

Furthermore, it is like the spring light upon all things; whether vast or minute, thick or thin, all are spontaneously free. The principle-dharma-realm (*li dharmadhātu*) is likened to water; when water freezes...

It is like the phenomenon of ice: mutually forming and mutually destroying, contracting and extending. Though it unfurls in a thousand ways and rolls up in ten thousand volumes, it never departs from the finger.
This is the most difficult to awaken to. As for the latter kind, every matter is without restriction and not a jumble of confusion;

it is handed over to Mañjuśrī and Ajita. When the verse at Dangyang was produced, its value increased in weight. The ox of Huaizhou, the elephant of Jiazhou—Zhang San eats grass and Li Si swells with gas. Furthermore...
Furthermore, empty-handed he grasps the hoe; light and dark intermingle as he displays his skill. Amidst daily life, he reveals his true form. Holding the brush and facing the paper, why such haste?
Five cycles of stars and frost have passed, and the discourse is now complete. The world’s tradition says that celestial maidens all soar into the void.
Furthermore, I have heard that when the Elder first arrived, he carried his scriptures in a sack across perilous and dangerous terrain.

For a single night, wind and frost shook the forests and valleys; ancient pines were uprooted, and the spring water tasted like nectar. To this day, the mountain monks look up to him for sustenance against hunger and thirst.

How could we ever forget the profound virtue of this Holy Master? Daguan Han emerged from the moss-covered grotto. In early spring, he joined companions to descend through the cold mists. Worn-out straw sandals have been trampled into the earth many times.

Layered snow covers the ground; I have come for a trial visit to Mount Shenfushan. With broad brows and bright eyes, he ascends the peak; his lips are crimson and his cheeks purple, his beard unlike any other.
Standing seven feet and two inches tall, he is a true hero who has opened the ocean of the Dharma by heaven’s decree. With deep sincerity, I bow twice, unable to bear parting;
as I walk away, I turn my head back, and the mist and clouds grow ever heavier.
A Song for Dwelling in the Hut (With Preface):
I have heard that after the Elder of the Great Ultimate (*Tàijí Lǎrén*) first awoke from his dream, the two polarities (*liǎngyí*) began to move.

Since then, among those that stand alone or stand in circles within the vast expanse of the Great Mass (*Dàkuài*), there is only the mountain. Within Zhendan, Mount Kunlun is the ancestor; its height reaches three...
Lofty! It honors the Five Peaks with its extraordinary majesty and robust grandeur; its spiritual wonders rival those of Penglai.
Today, it surpasses Kunlun, eclipses the Three Emei, and outshines the Five Peaks, such that Mount Konglu alone stands preeminent.

This is because the mountains of Konglu are pure and profound, as well as simple and beautiful. Being pure, they stand aloof from defilement; being profound, their mysteries are unfathomable; being simple...
Thick! Refinement is remote from flattery. If people find something in this, it must be for a reason. Upon hearing this, the "Dullard" (Hanhanzi) sang this song:
"Pure, indeed, and fundamentally unstained; Profound, indeed, and difficult to fathom. Dull, indeed, yet possessing capacity; Refined, indeed!"
How far-reaching is this charm! Why should he alone possess these four virtues? I hold him in high esteem. Have you not seen Master Cheng’s "Song of the Spring"? Behold:
by the high mountains and winding crags flows a stream; shrouded by mist and hidden by clouds, it is unseen by men. The bare-footed monk has exhausted his search...

I, You, happened to recognize it. Leaning on my staff, I paced back and forth, unable to bear leaving. Spring! Spring! Spring! How mysterious it is! It seems as though it wishes to speak, yet its voice is incomplete.
Again, one does not see the purity of Bo Yi or the cleanliness of Chao Fu; if this spring were used as a metaphor, it would be difficult for me to find satisfaction.

After Master Cheng finished his lecture, he came to pluck at his tongue; like a dark dragon bringing rain to moisten the parched earth, he causes one to long remember Lord Xumi, who labored in the mud and brickwork within the lair of dragons and serpents.
Song of the River Water:
The river water suddenly rises; The river water suddenly subsides. Rising and subsiding— By whom are they sent?
The water of the mind is originally clear, yet suddenly anger arises. Once anger acts as the mediator, that which is called "joy" requires no further introduction.
They accord with one another spontaneously; this matter is very easy to understand. Alas, why is it that we are deluded in every encounter?
Rising and falling without a medium, the wind-singer plays his game: puffing and swelling as he comes, silent and still as he goes.
As he comes and as he goes, whose command is it? A commentator says: "Only after the existence of Yin and Yang do movement and stillness arise. Wind, oh wind! You are Yin and Yang."
Before judgment, all is vast, clear, and penetrating; this is the Elder of Chaos. May I venture to ask what preceded this Elder? It is said:
"The Great Ultimate (Taiji) is the Infinite (Wuji). Alas! What could have been named before the Infinite? Some say:
"After the Infinite, the names of Virtue first arose. The simpleton clasps his knees and sings: "Name and reality—they are mutually dependent!"

Exhausted! What is called the "Ultimateless" (wuji) is merely the painting of colors upon the Great Void. Joyful! Angry! When the single mind has not yet arisen, are they indeed different or indeed the same?

Once joy and anger have already manifested, there is that which depends and that which does not depend. One who knows existence and non-existence—does this truly accord with reality or is it delusion?
If one can analyze this, then the rising and falling of the Yangtze River will be as vast as the sea.
