How noble! How poor! How honorable! How lowly! All are but children riding bamboo horses in the spring breeze. To know this is to understand where the wind begins:
it lies within oneself, not in external things. An ancient person once spoke a verse: "The great earth, mountains, and rivers—who is their master?
There is not a single dharma to be conceptualized. Before the lamp, joy and anger arise and fall of their own accord. I venture to ask the West [the Buddha].
"Neighboring one knows what the other does not know. Alas! Last night the bells and drums resounded everywhere; they shattered the skull, yet no one knew it.
The Layman Leung-yu of Yen-shan, sent on an embassy to Chu, pays his respects.
Have you not seen the Xiang River and the Xiang Mountains, rare wonders beneath heaven? Misty waves and empty emerald hues shine upon one another. A single sail vanishes into the distance.
Yet as he heads deeper into the recesses, he shakes his head in sorrow, realizing that the human world is but a dream. Jia Yi and Han Yu have both passed through here;

before me lie these secluded wonders, stirring thoughts of returning home. Failing to appreciate such fine mountains and waters, one knows from afar that this path has not yet reached its subtle depths.

Furthermore, one does not see Làn Zǎn, who sleeps soundly with his head upon a stone pillow; his meditative mind is as clear as water, never ceasing, while amidst a thousand peaks, he perceives only the truth.

The warmth of the yam fire—how could one know there are kings and lords in this world? You, having received the King’s command, depart from Mount Yan; the autumn wind blows gently as your temples turn white with age.
The Min River and Lake Dongting stretch far and wide; tigers, rhinoceroses, fish, and dragons circle day and night.

One awakens to the existence of the mind and perceives the existence of the body; for no reason, the clear mirror suddenly gathers dust. Yet its light, illuminating the present and shining through antiquity, remains sovereign; thus we meet.
How many can employ their true nature? Do not say these words are bland and tasteless; within this flavorlessness lies boundless spring. High Mount Zhuling has long been silent and desolate;
before the Return-of-Geese Peak, thorns and brambles abound. Foxes and hares form packs, laughing and then wailing;
to drive them away and clear the way requires the toil of a fortified wall. On the eve of my departure, I offer you one more cup of tea; two rows of hot tears moisten my black robe.
Passing once more by the garden of the Layman Dàn-ān, I am moved:

What need is there for the waters of the Cangshang Sea when one has a ladleful? What need is there for the rocks of Mount Tai when one has these stones? The meaning of these stones and this water is profound;
Who else, besides the white clouds and green grass, can recognize them? Who else can recognize them? Who else can recognize them? I have heard it said that the Master himself [inscribed]...
The Encampment: Every flower and every tree was planted by my own hand. Though I came here without intention, it was as if the Master had come to greet me.
From the Collected Works of Old Man Zibo, Volume Twenty-Eight.
The Collected Works of Old Man Zibo, Volume Twenty-nine.
Ming Dynasty. Read by Hanshan Deqing.
Songs.
The Song of the Leather Sack:
This leather sack has neither beauty nor ugliness; its empty form has never been able to be opened by external means.

It is simply that human sentiment has not yet dissolved, so a thousand fragments and a hundred shards are divided into pure and defiled. Do you not see? Before the skull of the old Yuan-sha, the Vajra lies prostrate.

Exhausting one's spirit, one cannot support it; it causes people to constantly grieve and lament in the night in vain. Cen Dachtong displays his family style: "The thickets and obstructions are originally empty.
Once pressed by a single blow, there is no way to plead one's case; karmic obstacles remain as barriers that do not pass through. These two Chan masters have direct paths of mind;
with blood-stained blade after blood-stained blade, they show no shame. The public case is clear—please try it for yourself.
Contemplate this: when cold ashes crackle with the sound of beans popping, one knows the depth of gratitude. Once this barrier is penetrated, it is no longer difficult;

one may walk with arms flung wide, acting as one pleases, even if stubborn and unruly. Provided that there is no "old food" (preconceived attachments) within the breast, let the medicine and the illness naturally resolve themselves in every way.

The sentiments of sagehood and ordinariness are instantly severed; dwelling neither in the middle stream nor on either bank, you must know that dead water does not harbor dragons—look amidst the lightning and thunder.
A chaotic mess! Look at this chaos! Look at this chaos! In the end, his whole body breaks out in stinking sweat.
Life and death intermingled amidst an air of nonchalance—generally speaking, he loses out to the man of true substance.

A Song for Sending Off the Attendant Jing’an to the Capital to Cast a Buddha Image (With Preface) The Venerable Jing’an was about to cast a copper image when he suddenly took his leave of me to depart from the mountains. I asked him, “What is the purpose of this journey?
He replied, “I am going to cast a Buddha. I said, “If a Buddha can be cast, then emptiness could be made blue or yellow. If you know that [the Buddha] is like clay...”
The Buddha does not cross over water. Does a golden Buddha not cross over the furnace? It would be better to cast the mind as a Buddha;
then great waters reaching the heavens cannot drown it, and the kalpa-fire blazing intensely cannot burn it.
Is this not magnificent? Why use molded bronze for it? The Master said: "I have heard that ice can become water, and color can become emptiness. Earth and wood—"
Copper and iron can both be apprehended by the eye; are they not, then, forms? If this is so, the mind has no shape or segments, and emptiness has no boundaries;
emptiness is the mind, and the mind is emptiness. As for this emptiness and this mind—who could possibly conceive of them through thought?
What is wrong with casting copper into the form of a Buddha? An ancient worthy said: "If a person understands..."
He attained the mind [of realization]. There is not an inch of earth upon the great earth; since there is not even an inch of earth, what can one point to as "copper"?
I said, "Excellent! You may go. Then I composed a song to encourage him. The song says:
The kalpa-fire blazes forth, turning heaven and earth to ash; Vairambha winds howl and strike, causing the third dhyāna heaven to collapse.
Casting bronze to form a Buddha—this cannot be destroyed; Its eternal radiance shatters the gloom and dust of a thousand ages. On this journey, autumn deepens and the season grows cold;

Upon returning, the peach blossoms must surely have withered away. The Elder Mañjuśrī calls out to me again and again; Within dreams, the springtime splendor easily fades. Have you not seen the wild geese?
The tiers of the stupa rise high into the clouds; the treasures of the Dragon Storehouse are rare and difficult to hear. Do not casually waste your years;
cease this quarreling with words over old age and illness. Hehehe! Do you understand? How much suffering is there in flaying one’s skin and piercing one’s blood?
How could it be that the ancients saw nothing? Walk by their side and contemplate them deeply from time to time.

When the Bodhisattva Daowuchen visited Qinsui, he found the scenery in harmony with his vision; when he traveled afar to Tanzha, he returned alone. The white clouds suddenly dispersed—how could they not?
It is bearable. Not far from you, your righteousness is complete. Life is the harbinger of death—what joy is there? Death is the mother of life—what difficulty is there?
To realize this and transcend it is to remain steadfastly at ease amidst all movement. If you, sir, have understanding, you will be liberated while suspended between going and coming.

The Song of the Red Zen Robe, together with the attendant Kai, is truly like a single great mass of fire. Upon contact, who would not die instantly? Only those whose life-root has long since been severed can wear it everywhere as a banner.
It is also like the moon on the eighth day of the lunar month; black and white are intermingled, making it difficult to distinguish.
Discriminating: within a withered, decaying skull, the dragon’s roar is released; layered dark clouds give rise to a clear radiance.

Do not say that what has been worn through is no longer beautiful—Huālín once demonstrated this to Minister Pài. His second coming was not dependent on Avalokiteśvara; the old monk stands upright, directly facing the wall.
Have you not seen how Niǎokuǒ picked up [a feather] and blew upon it casually? The attendant knew it immediately before his very eyes.
Returning. On a bright and warm day, one sits draped in this. All things are either interchanging or non-interchanging;

there is a reason for Caoxi and Shaoshi. One who is not a true knower will not nod their head. Whether it be the Five Ranks or the Three Falls, these are all garments to ward off the cold for sentient beings.

Even a butcher slaughtering pigs recites the name of Amitābha. When the holy and the ordinary face each other, they vainly offer their separate accounts. Vainly they offer their separate accounts—silver.
A basin holds the snow-moon, with a heron hidden within. Who can discern its beginning and end here? It may be entrusted to a wooden child or a stone woman.
It may be entrusted; it is neither silk nor cloth. Its brilliant radiance is revealed everywhere.
One who wears it sits peacefully amidst wind and snow, no different from having a brazier set around them. A brazier set around them—can you see it when you throw snow into it?
If you do not see it at all, you will remain in a state of vague obscurity; if you do see it, there is no need to seek out affairs and labor over them.
I sent these condolences to Chen Neihan Liangzhou:
When I ascended Mount Lu, I visited the gentleman at Donglin. Not many years have passed since our parting, and the gentleman has attained a high rank in the imperial examinations.
The dream of the yellow millet was not yet complete when I suddenly heard that he had already abandoned the world. Flowers must eventually fall; human life must eventually end.
Once flowers have fallen, they bloom again; once a person has died, they do not rise again. To whom can this sentiment be told? There was a renowned scholar from Lei-yang.

Thus, people are startled by their own [condition]; impermanence knows no distinction between self and other. Even if one lives for a hundred years, it is nothing more than a matter of priority and sequence.
O noble ones, noble ones! Gazing at the clouds in the void, our longing grows. The spring of wisdom shall never run dry; when will this choked voice find its end?
Watching the Release of Firecrackers, I Sing:
Do you not see? Wealth and honor are what people delight in; poverty and lowliness are what the world loathes. From antiquity until today, who has ever had a fixed limit to their rise or fall?
Only those who have attained the Way regard both glory and disgrace as mere illusions. [Consider] the Emperor Gaozu of Han and the Hegemon King of Chu, vying for power...
How lofty and majestic was the aura of Feng Qi! Yet when viewed with the correct eye, it is all but empty. Chang’an and Pengcheng are both desolate.
The tomb of Yan Yifu and the grave of Xiao He—thorns grow deep there, where foxes and hares lie asleep. The mountains and rivers remain unchanged, yet their meritorious achievements have vanished.
Why must one necessarily undergo much toil and hardship? It is far better to be like an old man in the forest. Within his breast, he harbors neither honor nor disgrace.
Like white clouds that come and go without intent, he wanders freely among springs, rocks, and city walls. At times he loves stillness; at times he allows himself the clamor.
Transcending directly, one realizes it is not a matter of concern. Ten thousand sounds are silent; the night moon is cold.

Why not gaze together at the flowers and fireworks? Sounds delight the ears; colors feast the eyes. Amidst this profusion of sound and color, who can awaken? Constant radiance leaves both arising and ceasing behind.
A thousand peaks are still and desolate; the mind is like a valley. Furthermore, we do not see Minister Zhang or Eunuch Feng; their brilliance shines forth.
Splendor and nobility are boundless; yet in a single morning, when merit is exhausted, one is like frost upon the tips of grass.

Since the sun rises, has it ever witnessed a single drop [of permanence]? It was so in antiquity, and it is so now. Upon meeting, who is the truly extraordinary man? Listening to the cannon’s roar and observing the blossoms, one pierces through worldly sentiments;

hanging one's cap from a rocky cave, one seeks out the lofty gentleman. Proposing the Great Function, hearing the "poisonous lacquer"—with a snap of the fingers, the root and dust become a spark of flint. One undergoes spiritual transformation.
It is just like ice trapping a fish; when the yang returns, the whole world is filled with joy. To study non-arising is to be without death. Birth and death have always arisen from one another:
if there were no birth, there would likewise be no death. This solitary luminosity shines clearly through the ages.
To understand this, one must be a hero—one who has completely severed all traces of worldly emotion, like a majestic elephant shedding its bonds and chains. Let it loose!
Transversely, one does not allow oneself to be pulled or dragged by others. When people listen to the cannon, I too listen; when people gaze upon flowers, I too gaze.

Within this, there is a distinct and profound mystery: beauty and ugliness intermingle before the mirror of wisdom. A single mind, limpid and still, is likened to a cold pond. The water of this cold pond is clear to its very bottom;
nobility and poverty, wealth and meanness are like bubbles and cataracts. Amidst this bustling and clamorous world, what expectation can there be? It is all lost.
I rest my head upon a stone and sleep in harmony with the clouds.
A Song in Illness (with Preface). By the Hermit Píqiú.
Regarding the four kings who contend for superiority yet remain unsubdued—some employing fire as a tactic, others... [text fragment] ...or... [text fragment] ...or... [text fragment].
Earth was used to dam it, yet the two generals of Water and Wind repeatedly stirred and surged against it; the great battle raged without ceasing.

Consequently, Yin and Yang failed to harmonize, coalescing into the disease of cold phlegm. Seeking medical aid from Lu Shan and Bian Que, and trading their arts with Hua Tuo, all were made to draw back their hands, saying:
"This disease is rooted in the beginning of Chaos and manifested at the stage of the Great Ultimate."
Later, [the Master] realized that it was necessary for him to attain realization himself; he possessed the consciousness required to achieve this, something of which we could not provide a remedy.
The hermit Píqiú heard of this from the side and laughed at it, subsequently composing a song based upon it.
The leather-ball practitioner embraces phlegm and fire; coughing up cold saliva morning and night. The four elements clash and are not easily harmonized;

with every inhalation and exhalation, there is no constant master. To realize this principle is truly blissful. To speak idly of heaven and earth as one’s coffin and shroud is merely the talk of Zhuang Zhou from within a dream.
On the path of non-arising, they are difficult to grasp. Since there is no arising, how could there be [death]?
Death. All bending and stretching is but illusion. Heaven and earth are likewise nothing more than a stinking skin-sack.
Why begrudge the drops of pus within that sack? Ten million kalpas are but a single instant. How dull is the gate of Mount Nanyue!
Created by the mind, karma gives rise to calamity; wearying oneself, one loses one’s original nature. Do you not see that when a single thought does not arise, even the Buddha is an illusion? Since—

Birth gives rise to awareness, and awareness gives rise to emotion; within the eternally quiescent light, one undergoes trials and tribulations. Apart from Perfect Enlightenment, there are no six realms; were the six realms abolished, there would be no Three Vehicles.
When the crux of increase and decrease is not understood through principle, the King of Physicians prepares medicine merely to cleanse and wash away [delusions].
The "Ball of Skin" practitioner’s single body is light; this single body is light, as agile as a dog. The Protector of the State clamors incessantly, his mouth never ceasing. His appearance—
Whomever I meet, my heart and liver are revealed; even the merit of moistening the grass has been achieved. Stop, stop, stop! My hair and bones have transformed.
The Great Being Mañjuśrī has not yet finished his ride; now he shall ascend only Mount Emei. Amidst the ranks of the elephant kings, he leaps beyond their shackles and cuffs.

Furthermore, I did not see that the two practitioners, who were most fond of one another, were absent; before the lamp, they paid off my debt for brushes. Writing line after line, they recorded my medical prescriptions.
The "Leather Ball" practitioner remains ever-undecaying; ever-undecaying, he is supremely free. In the depths of Fángshān, he seeks the springtime light.
Whether it be giant peaches or common apricots, who would steal them to sell? Lately, Master Sūn’s medicine has become expensive; it blows away like the wind, drifting and falling.
Fresh blossoms lie unexposed to the sun; as it is with the person, so it is with all things. Through the mechanism of phlegm and fire, the myriad dharmas are made manifest.
Let not the Creator be angry at this leaking of the true secret: in whose garden are the apricots not red?

The simpleton scrapes firewood; how well he scrapes the firewood! How vigorously he scrapes it! Who would dare forget the dignified bearing of the ancients? It makes no distinction between old and young, nor between the wise and the foolish.

At the sound of a single wooden rattle, one descends from the meditation seat. Descending from the meditation seat, observe the transformation: in an instant, the head is changed and the face is renewed.
Everyone gathers around a single broken mat. Fluttering along with the crowd, they exit the gate and travel far away. One step high, one step low;
suspended alone on a path where birds fly, the way is crooked and treacherous. A whirlwind of cold air assails the heart and belly; the sun shines upon jagged ice that is as slippery as mud.
Reaching deep into the clouds, they pause for a moment to rest. The heavens are cold and the earth frozen; it is difficult to stand for long. Finding a withered stump, they steal a moment’s joy.
Light! Who would have known that the heart becomes damp when struck by rain? Having collided with it, let it be heavy; place it upon one’s shoulder and descend step by step.

On high ridges and steep peaks, the turns and twists are vexing; several times the feet stumble, and the heart is filled with fear. Not having experienced it oneself, how could one know the suffering?
Time and again people seek ease and indulge in indolence, waiting until they must personally undergo such an ordeal. From this day forward, may you know [the truth].
Interact with one another. Eat hot rice; sleep in a warm pit. You must also turn back the light and reflect in private:
"If we all did not labor together, how could we enjoy such pure blessings? Stir the firewood vigorously; stir the firewood well. Dwelling in the mountains, do not indulge in idle clamor.
Since you, monks, wish to refine away dullness and torpor, stir a piece of firewood without giving rise to vexation.

The attendant Kai and the attendant Longquan—whose names were Daokai and Longquan—were there. White clouds fly away and then fly back; the mountains are deep and remote, wearying those who come and go.
The Way of the Patriarchs is desolate, gathering dust; the hoofprints of sheep and horses cover the green moss. The udumbara flower withers and fades.
Opening it once more: How many times have I scratched my head, yearning for Huangmei? From the turning wheel and the hammer, the timber for the ridgepole and beams was carved out.
Exhausting all one's strength in the late age to support what is collapsing and tilting—I reward you with this special gift of seven cups of tea.
A Casual Song on Mount Zifang (Revised Version) Clouds upon Mount Pengcheng,
Waters beneath Mount Pengcheng— Their gathering and dispersing, their floating and sinking, Their decline and prosperity cannot be counted.
Have you not seen? How long can human life endure within heaven and earth? The Yellow River flows eastward without turning back its waves.

Splendor passes before the eyes like frost at dawn; who can win a hundred battles to seize mountains and rivers? The rivalry between Chu and Han was but a weary dream; what more is there in these mere puddles to boast of?
The world says the Master perceived the signs early on, casting aside the Marquis’s seal as if it were withered grass. Transcendent!

Thus, he entrusted himself to the company of the Red Pines to roam; in the end, how could he have been troubled by Han Xin and Peng Yue? This is based on the Master’s outward traces; who knows the Master’s heart?
The Master remained to repay his debt to Han; fame and merit were not what he delighted in. Qin was lost and his life’s task was finished; why linger and hesitate not to depart?
Furthermore, do you not see that fame and longevity are not far apart? To discard the former and grasp the latter is a shallow understanding indeed.
I know that Your Reverence’s celestial faculties are clear; you have ascended as an immortal and departed in flight, free from all lingering attachments.

Because I climbed this mountain, I composed this song, casually casting my ink traces upon the misty vines. When Your Reverence hears it, what will you say of me? The spirit and vigor of a man’s resolve are difficult to grind away.
That which is truly difficult to grind away are only the mountains and waters; rivers shift and valleys change according to no fixed course. Only Your Reverence remains...
A single mind constantly enhances the beauty of this mountain.
When I lament Master Xubai, my birth is originally empty; when the Master passes away, the One Reality is without dependence. Being originally empty, there is birth.
Yet there is no arising. Without dependence, there is cessation that is not cessation. Arising yet without arising—the Master is no different from me;
cessation yet not cessation—I am no different from the Master. Master and I reach the ultimate limit: like flying snow upon a glowing furnace.

Within this lies a profound meaning; who else shall awaken us to it? I now weep for my Master—not the weeping of sorrow. If the Master possesses a spiritual essence, may you discern this humble thought of mine.
The swallows have moved their nests to avoid the songs of the Buddha;

I, Yu, dwell in the purple garden of Attendant Censor Fu. Because I am deeply moved by the current state of affairs, and further observe that the local customs favor force, boastfulness, deception, and slaughter, I have remained here for a long time, hoping to transform them through my influence. One day, while performing my prostrations before the Buddha, I heard—
There was a "wu-wu" sound. Upon looking, I saw that the swallow nest atop the Buddha’s head had moved its construction to a side eave.
I could not help but feel a sudden misty sorrow. For nearly three months I have stayed here, and during this time, doubt and faith have fluctuated morning and evening without constancy;

yet the swallow recognized sin and merit, avoiding the Buddha to relocate its nest. Thus, it has greatly assisted my work of transformation. How much more so, then, would a feathered creature [be moved by the Dharma]?

While their worldly desires have lightened and the gap for the numinous spirit still remains, it is not as if the human mind were so depraved and obscure that its original nature were entirely obscured.
Moved by this, I composed this song out of lamentation.
Who says that winged insects are foolish? Winged insects are not inferior to humans. Year after year they build their nests upon the central beam;
this year they have moved themselves to dwell upon the side rafter. They labor greatly to provide for the sacred images of the Master, yet I fear they may incur the sin of defilement.

Reflecting on this closely, it is truly pitiable. Among those that fly and chirp, who understands the subtle workings of fate? Humans alone are the most intelligent, the foremost among all things. [Yet] they are foul-smelling...
Suddenly entering the period of meditation, I value this unusual bird for its extraordinary nature. Though its form is obscure and its understanding slight, it places its faith in the Triple Gem.

If you should hear the sutras and awaken to your own mind, you, a winged creature, may become a vessel of compassion. A vessel of compassion. As the crimson sun sets, how many times have I waited for travelers at the ferryhead?
Amidst the waves of ignorance, you act as a bridge. Only then will I believe that a winged creature is superior to humans.
I have come to this azure garden to read this song. Within its verses, there is much bitter flavor and toil. Do not say that these murmuring words are merely the ocean waves of idle chatter;
they are urgently intended for all people to cross over the river of craving. This present connection is not without cause; it is solely because the swallow has composed this piece.
Viewing it from this perspective, the bird is my teacher. How could I dare not transmit the teacher’s kindness and virtue?
At Luyashan, while reading the *Fahua lun*, I recall the attendant Kai.
Have you not seen how the Northern Emperor raged with fury and a cold wind arose, as azure clouds and crimson mists raced across the Great Void? Upon the wooden seat in the forest...

When I rise from sleep at the crack of dawn, a single expanse of jade and snow shines beyond my door. Longing for the person of my heart, I am weighed down by profound melancholy. A solitary wanderer drifting through life, I lean on my staff;
the earth is frozen and the mountains are ice, while plants and trees wither. The tracks of beasts and the traces of birds are entirely invisible.

Beneath a bright window, I sit reading the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-śāstra* by the light of incense, seeking to dispel my weariness. The paper grows weary and the characters grow old, yet my initial clarity of mind remains undisturbed—a state beyond mere thought.
The measure of his dwelling is hidden where the ox sleeps; his essence is tranquil extinction, his waist is radiant light. The three circumambulations and nine metaphors are but skin and hair.

If you should meet him and ask about his horns, ten thousand valleys and a thousand crags lie far upon the snowy path. Hardly has he blinked than he is gone; his gait is like the wind and like lightning.
It vexes one beyond measure that though one waves the whip to call him back, he will not return. In the dens of bears and cubs and the lairs of leopards, there are many pits and ravines. Thorns...
The thorn forest is the realm of afflictions; hatred and love entwine to bury one’s own self. The sprouts of reeds are pure and superior, distinct from the wind and dust.
Sooner or later, return and sleep upon the dewy ground. Return! Do not bring companions with you. The path of the minds of sentient beings in the burning house is perilous;
even those sharing a single bed and blanket still harbor mutual suspicion. How much more so for those immeasurable men lost in the mists and clouds? These immeasurable men never find rest.
Coldly observe the lords and kings as they cultivate dark karma; until death, they never hear the fragrance of wisdom and insight. Vast and boundless, when will the sea of suffering ever dry up?
Furthermore, one sees those born in the heavens still subject to falling. How many days can human wealth and honor last?

Though spring flowers are beautiful, how could they remain fresh forever? In the end, they wither as the winds and rains rage. Fuchai was arrogant; Goujian suffered humiliation. He lay upon firewood and tasted gall.
Dare I laboriously seek retribution? Now, as for the old mountains and rivers of Wu and Yue, year after year we see only the lush green of the spring grasses.

How can these compare to the seven fascicles of the wondrous *Lotus Sūtra*, which one frequently turns and reads in a pure chamber amidst the deep clouds? To turn and read them repeatedly is to sever the habits of delusion;

thus the assembly on Vulture Peak has never once dispersed. In this bustling marketplace where ordinary beings and sages intermingle, the *dhūta* practitioner is accustomed to the smile upon the holding of the flower.
Such is the nature of things; there is no artifice. To set forth the whole matter openly—how could one conceal it?

It is simply that the emotional views of sentient beings run deep, so that even the supreme flavor of *amṛta* turns into poison. Opening the door for the attendant is quite vexing; with staff and sandals fluttering, where will you fall?
The customs of Qi and Lu are lofty, and the falling leaves are cold. How could one endure the long watches of night without a padded robe? It is well that you have returned;
listen to this sutra, and together let us watch the celestial flowers fall before the eaves.
Song of the Azure Green Pavilion (With Preface) In ancient times, there were those who regarded profit as a malady;
they used fame as medicine to treat it. When fame became a malady, they used life to treat it; when life became a malady, they used oblivion as medicine to treat it.
Yet they failed to realize that profit does not profit itself, nor does fame... [The text continues with the realization that these things are interdependent and lack inherent self-nature.]
Names are such that arising does not arise by itself, and forgetting does not forget by itself; all exist only in mutual dependence.
Thus, white, black, red, and green originally possess no color, yet some perceive them as colored—is this not because they have forgotten their own profound clarity and become intoxicated by green?
Master Zibo, accompanied by two or three disciples, went to inquire after the illness of Mr. Di at the Zhanlüe Pavilion. Juefeizi stepped forward and said:
"The Great Master has arrived. Shall we not administer the medicine? Master Xian shivered with laughter and said, "Red, green, white, and black;
sounds and forms; even food, drink, men, and women—the myriad things, whether refined or coarse—are like a profound stillness that is never obscured.
Which of these is not a fine medicine? Juefei said, "If that is so, why do you not say 'the six are profound,' rather than saying..."
"Danzhu. The Master said, "Writing does not exhaust speech; speech does not exhaust meaning. Did the Sages establish images to exhaust meaning?
Now, an 'image' (xiàng) means 'resemblance' (sì). Therefore, 'lù' (green) is actually 'liù' (six).

When Jiǔfāng Gāo appraised horses, he disregarded their dark and yellow [coats] and sought instead their spiritual majesty. If you now cling to the dark and yellow, then what is called spiritual majesty—"
This is hidden. The song says:

"Profound indeed, green indeed! Male indeed, female indeed! If it were not for the person of such caliber, how could they easily return as one? To possess a conscious awareness would belong to the realm of deluded thought;
to be withered and devoid of consciousness would be to rank with wood and stone. Yet, if one further probes and reflects, [the truth] becomes even more..."
To gain is to lose; were it not for one of clear and lucid insight, who could discern this?
*Song for Máo Shān, Seeing Sīdēng Return to Sōnglíng (with Preface)* Dīng, a youth of Wújiāng, had studied Confucianism from his early years.
Having failed repeatedly in the examinations, he eventually abandoned them and sought the Way of non-birth (*amṛta*). Once [he had found it],...
He was about to shave his head when his son sought out his father and found him in Yunyang.
Wailing, the son said to his father, "Though my family is poor, I can provide you with thick gruel and rice; how can you bear to abandon our native land and depart for a foreign region?
Ding Sheng laughed heartily and said, "The three realms take names and words as their substance; names and words arise through the transformation of causes and conditions. This floating life—"
Within the transformations of causes and conditions, there are myriad manifestations: son and father, kin and stranger, honor and disgrace, death and life.
These are like a rope made of tortoise hair or a staff carved from a rabbit’s horn—tying the wind or picking at the moon;
how can they be taken as real? My young disciple, go forth! Do not fail in the great matter of your father. Thus spoke Master Zibai in his vigor.
The words of Mr. Ding express his sorrow for his son’s sincere filial piety; he presents him with a bundle of *máo* grass and sings:
Upon the moon over the Jiang River in Wu, This evening it shines upon Mount Mao. The clouds atop Mount Mao Escort you back to the Jiang River in Wu.

Human life is but a brief dream; whether circumstances are adverse or favorable, they bring nothing but sorrow and joy. Try observing when the mind has not yet arisen—what is lacking, and what is complete?
The clouds of Mount Mao and the moon over Wujiang—the affection between father and son is ultimately difficult to sever.

It is truly difficult to sever. Yet in the end, even love and attachment must come to rest. Do you not see that after five generations, there is no celebration for joy nor mourning for death? Let it be so.
For the sake of the Way, the frost-white hair vanishes in an instant as it follows the blade. Last night, my headache grew into five peaks;
having attained the Way and returned, I row the ferryboat, carrying both the hateful and the kin within the state of non-self.
Sitting at Night in Buddha Fragrance Hermitage:
Tonight I sit before the Buddha Fragrance Hermitage; tomorrow morning we part upon the banks of the Laishui River. Tonight the bright moon shines upon those who sit;
next night the bright moon will shine upon those on their journey. The traces of travel come and go without fixed destination, yet the bright moon is ever present wherever one is.

We recognize each other; we have always recognized each other. The barking dog and the crowing rooster announce the news. If the moonlight were something that could be grasped and played with, would the immortals of the sea be willing to shed their bones?
Shou Zhongjian seeks the Buddhist song of Master Li:
Human affairs are ultimately difficult to fulfill; the passage of years cannot be detained. Right and wrong plunder from all sides, leaving me without any freedom.
How could it be that only now is this so? I fear the ancients were much the same. Yet, if one can but hear the Way, one consigns life and death to the flowing current;

how much more so regarding honor and disgrace, which are no different from clouds drifting across the void. Have you not seen how when a pig rubs against a mountain of gold, the gold shines all the more brightly?
The petty man and the superior man each have their strengths. The petty man harbors evil and thus forgets goodness; the superior man harbors goodness and must necessarily forget evil.
In the end, both good and evil reach no place; this is naturally the Hall of Joy for the superior man.
When one man is joyful, the world is at peace; when one man is sorrowful, the world is in hardship. Crimson peaks and azure waters further the Way-seeking mind; exchanging a golden hairpin for wine—
The Prince and Duke are cold; furthermore, Li Misun is not seen. Master Li is a Buddha. Before the Chongxue Shrine, by the Hudu Bridge, his traces remain faintly visible even in the bright moonlight.
A mountain monk is originally a guest beyond the mundane world; with his bamboo staff and straw sandals, whom does he seek to know?
Yet it is said: "Seeking afar for the Buddha of Master Li, how could one fear the rugged precipices of the seven gates?
The Preface to the *Fengtou Ge* (Song of the Phoenix Head):
In years past, a mendicant monk begged for alms in the capital. The various high officials and nobles vied with one another to feed him. Among them was...
Those who are young and have not yet undergone the capping ceremony are colloquially called "phoenix-heads.

Lately, while they were nursing their illnesses on Mount Fang, these phoenix-heads came from no great distance to provide food for this practitioner; now, however, they have already been capped. Alas!
When the Brahmin returned with his hair white, his neighbors said, "The man of old is still here. The Brahmin enlightened them, saying, "I am indeed the man of old, yet I am not the man of old."
He was a man. His neighbors were all astonished by his words. Moved by the phoenix’s head, the practitioner did not fear the ruggedness of the crags and valleys;
he reverently obeyed his master’s command and provided food for the practitioner in the deep mountains, whereupon he composed this verse.
The phoenix head of old; the phoenix head of today. Who says the phoenix head of today is the phoenix head of old? Those who come have not yet arrived; those who depart cannot be detained.
Since coming and going are neither existent nor non-existent, one sees the phoenix head within the eye. Alas for the people of this world!
Face-to-face, one is ignorant of the phoenix-head; the phoenix-head follows upon the phoenix-head. Transverse calculations flow like a rushing torrent, surging onward with no way to turn back.

Without wind, they strive to overturn their boat. The Great Awakened One could not bear to look on; he lowered his hand to pull up the deluded ox. Like a luminous gem cast into the darkness for a man.
Who among those clutching their swords is not an enemy? Alas for the people of this world! Who recognizes the phoenix-head?
On the scroll of Master Chetian at the Jingye Hall:
The old monk, with no further affairs, personally brushes the bamboo desk by the window; a single scroll spread out horizontally is no ordinary thing.
Leisurely. Where does the misty tide and empty verdancy end? Have you not seen the solitary village on the broken bank, rich in flowers and plants, their fading beauty envied by mountain ghosts?
Nor have you seen a single idle cloud drifting across the azure sky, where a thousand li of ships and barges appear like a row of fish tails.
With towering waves and high winds, the sails fly past one another; turtles and crocodiles emerge and submerge like ants. Behold, such is the nature of life!
A speck of dust, so light. Playing with danger, how many can achieve a successful conclusion? Upon half a peak, the stones lie heaped. Spring has passed; the secluded branches hold their buds.
Like a lady of Wu about to break into a smile, one watches the setting sun, unaware of regret. Before the tombs of former kings.
Behind the royal tomb, the autumn rain falls desolately, nearly breaking one’s soul. When we meet, do not ask about matters of male or female;
gain and loss are as identical as the clouds over the Valley Mouth. Present and past—willows grow from the elbows. Wealth, nobility, and fame are not mine to possess;
let the Creator toss them about as he pleases. With earnest care, I embrace the broom of non-arising. The owl and the screech-owl, the phoenix and the peacock, the qilin and the incense...
The elephant shares one jar; the long pines bear heavy snow as the crane’s nest tilts. Who knows that this shatters the fisherman’s dream? Amidst the mist and clouds, the dragon palace is hidden.
The bells and chanting resound, shaking the vast void. Hearing these sounds, how many can enter the stream? In ten thousand kalpas, the root-faculties and sense-objects melt away on the spot.
Wielding the tip of the brush, relying on contemplation and observation—who can discern what exists before thought has arisen? The entire platter is set forth.
Held out for others to behold—only then is one a hero or a great man. Heh! Heh! Heh! Do not let it leak away. The setting clouds and solitary wild goose both vanish;
the hue of the waters and the luster of the mountains hang like a single mirror. To pierce through to heaven, there is yet another secret beyond the reach of ordinary sentiment.

A Song of Qingliang Temple on Wanhua Mountain in Jingle County Have you not seen Qingliang Temple deep within Wanhua? Where mountains wind and waters meander in pure beauty. In the past, a recluse cultivated his mind here;
For how many years did he know only of millet soup and bean leaves? Suddenly, thorns and brambles have transformed into towers and terraces; The blue lotus...
The Tathāgata sits majestically upon the precious throne; in an instant, he suddenly lets out a lion’s roar. The brains of Māra, heretics, and demonic beasts split asunder.
Once the Sage has emerged, the world becomes like a wilderness of weeds; foxes, wolves, and jackals howl like thunder. Jade palaces and golden pavements lie prostrate beneath oxen and horses.

Who that beholds this would not feel sorrow? I pity those of the past whose heart-blood has withered away; though they exhausted their strength amidst the weeds and brush, they built only a humble hermitage.
Not even five hundred lifetimes have passed since then—how could one bear to see this and not provide support?

Furthermore, have you not seen that the fame of the Prince who spread the gold endures for long, and that the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada exists in every direction? Read my song and believe my words; this is it.
The worthy donor of Jetavana sighed deeply and lent his hand to rectify this; his descendants shall surely attain many victories. Hehehe! Who is the wise one?
When not a single thought has yet arisen in Qingliang, ten thousand flowers bloom and the six gates are fragrant.

If a person hears this and awakens to the Great Function—awakening to the Great Function, do not give rise to doubt. Though karma be heavy, it is ultimately difficult to savor; one must cultivate weary detachment. Weary detachment...
The two characters "renunciation" (厭離) are the command of the sages and worthies; when ordinary people hear them, they treat them as mere chaff. Only heroes possess a different disposition;
upon meeting, they immediately pledge their commitment to one another. If animals lack the mind of renunciation, how can they become human beings who uphold the constant patterns of ethics?
If humans lack the mind of renunciation, how can they hear the Way and emerge from the ford of suffering? If one does not loathe wealth, one will be entangled by wealth.
Kill it! Do not remain apart from form; you are bound by form. Since beginningless time, killing and binding have caused a lack of weary detachment (*nirveda*).
O friends, if you wish to traverse the dusty road of saṃsāra, washing the mind and cultivating weary detachment is the true secret instruction.
Song of the Mei Mountain Range:
Have you not seen how high the Mei Mountain rises, reaching the very limits of the clouds? A dense, swirling mist blankets it for thirty thousand *li*.

Who could endure the deep coolness of its summits? Even in the sixth month, snow falls and a chill pierces the skin. Silver hooks hang there; too weary to wipe them, they are left to dangle as they will.

Possessing the wind-bone (spiritual majesty) of one approaching full maturity, this old man of Nanheng’s tune is not the same. Sometimes he may enter, sometimes he may exit; manifestation and concealment—how could they have constancy?
It is like a single hand grasping and then opening again: the deluded person sees it as having opening and closing.

Once you have realized that all within the world is without hindrance, the waters of the Ba River flow over the stones; in a dream, one needlessly distinguishes between far and near. Where is there [any such distinction]?

In the green forest, birds suddenly cry out; upon awakening, the white elephant is still the lion. This is the joy of the mountains; sounds are but fetters. Why must a great recluse give rise to attachment?
Going and staying are like idle clouds, freely rolling up and unfurling. Let people laugh at me for having no sharp edges or corners.
With a sheepskin from Wuyang and a single fishing rod, I play with a marble within a bottomless bowl. Floating in the air or falling to the ground, it leaves no hindrance behind—how perfectly so!
Turning his gaze askance and sideways, he looks out upon the high autumn winds as the summer heat fades away. The mountain paths and rocky peaks stretch far into the distance;

with graceful gait and staff in hand, the traveler crosses the perilous passes of Han. Two or three fellow practitioners, all with their robes tucked into their satchels, move along—one descending, one ascending.

Turning his head toward the pines, they appear like figures in a painting. With weary feet, they sit together in a circle beneath the trees; before them, a carpet of yellow leaves enhances the clarity and vastness of the scene.
Sitting, he rises again; passing through deep and winding places, the flowing water is cool and clear, utterly free from the dust and vulgarity of the world.

Yet I am reminded of the many stratagems of Huaiyin (Han Xin), where the *diaodou* drums of Chen Cang resounded through the empty valleys. Caught by surprise, with no time for preparation, he lacked the strength to roll up the Central Plains in a single sweep.
The hero is not seen; we hear only his name in vain. A dark monkey cries beneath the moon amidst the mountain hues. Now is the past, and the past is now.
The traveler fears to hear the sound that breaks the heart; it leaves me with nothing to worry about in my breast. Like a drifting duckweed on rivers and seas, I float and sink as I please.
Passing through Loufan Temple, I am moved by reflection.
Have you not seen how the Five Barbarians threw China into chaos, tearing asunder the social order? Ruler and subject devoured one another like vipers and scorpions.

The Jin dynasty became as precarious as a stack of eggs; treacherous heroes usurped power and displayed their prowess. Whether old or young, they could not bear to speak the truth; even flesh and blood were cast adrift.

Leaving behind the overgrown wilderness, the Central Kingdom was partitioned among the dog-like and sheep-like tribes. Stench and filth filled the earth—who would report it? Benevolence and righteousness were both abandoned;
the Seven Classics and Two Treatises became mere waste paper. Valuing "excellent weapons" and martial prowess, the air was thick with the arrogance of slaughter.

It was asserted that mountains and rivers could be governed from horseback. The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas took pity on these people; they forged the stubborn into the virtuous, raining down compassion like a deluge. (Gu Yin)

Longfei succeeded to the Buddha’s legacy; Loufan underwent a tiger-like transformation, illuminating all classes of beings. He established edification according to circumstances, following the needs of the times;

both noble and base followed his influence as he enlightened the ignorant. Yao Qin and Shi Le awakened to their original resolve; the common people, submerged in the mire of suffering, were delivered through this grace.
Furthermore, the golden branches of the extraordinary well were seen to excel beyond the ordinary; they radiated light as if to manifest the auspicious omen of *tathāgatagarbha*.

The three types of grass and two types of trees were all equally moistened by its dew. Yet how could the sound of the drums reach the ears of the *icchantikas*? One threw his whip to cut across the current, narrowing the Yangtze River;

the fierce and arrogant ones looked back in fear while indulging in devouring others. When the army set out, Master An admonished [Fu Jian] time and again, but Fu Jian leaned against the carriage rail and feigned sleep. (1)

The morning troops disperse and the hegemonic enterprise is empty; for a thousand ages it will be a source of ridicule, truly a mere plaything. Gales and torrential rains, the clanging of *diaodou* drums;

the common people can do nothing but rely on their wood-gathering and firewood-cutting livelihoods. Mount Lu is high—its five peaks are steep and majestic, where mists swirl and the seated posture remains firm.
The five articles and six matters surpass those of Chao Fu and You Zhou. When the Emperor issued his decree at Xunyang, it was not granted.

Upon hearing this wind of integrity, what greedy or weak man would not become resolute and clear-sighted, dissolving their baseness and stinginess? His merit in benefiting the world has been high since ancient times;

yet even Li Ao of Changli and Ji Shui harbored suspicion and resentment. A black silk cap—Heaven is above! Do not rashly cast aspersions upon a person’s character; do not be so reckless. Such recklessness brings human calamity.
The heavenly punishment is as clear as the palm of one's hand. I urge you: do not play with ornate rhetoric. It withers the pure and damages the simple;

when such writing becomes the standard for rulers, right and wrong are inverted—truly a matter for lamentation. It drives the *luan* and *feng* birds into the ranks of the *chi* and *xiao*. It leads the younger generation to emulate the frivolous.

Whether it be short verses or grand compositions, they are merely spread about by the lips and tongues of the fickle. Great gentlemen of broad vision naturally possess their own insight; would they ever deign to follow children in cultivating dark karma? Study!
Zuochi and Liu Yimin, at Mount Kuang in Xiangyang, drew near to his pure fragrance; with a single word or a single verse, they sang in response to one another.
Their radiant influence is sufficient to dispel the darkness of ten thousand ages. The frontier winds are fierce, piercing the bones with cold;

with staff and sandals, he wanders gracefully seeking out famous springs. White grasses and yellow clouds, the ancient hall is chill; the noble traces of Master Huiyuan have faded into desolation. The lotus water-clock, the stone chessboard—[at] Dong...
The Linbaixia remains empty, its name alone surviving. I, a mere youth, am ashamed that my cultivation of the Way is sparse; sitting by and watching its rise and fall, I find it difficult to sustain.
With a mournful song and tears streaming down my face, I drag my staff away. The Huo-tuo River rolls on, its sound enough to provoke sorrow.

A Long Song to See Off the Venerable Master Zhan of Huanglongtan on Mount Lu as He Travels for Study (With Preface) The ancients who set their wills upon study were certain to achieve success in it. Those of today, though they likewise set their wills upon study, have yet to achieve such success.
Is it that the perception and awareness of ancients and moderns differ? It is likely because the learning of the ancients was single-minded.
Be single-minded and diligent; be diligent and constant; be constant and reflective; be reflective and clear-sighted; be clear-sighted and act accordingly.
Regarding these six matters, do not dare to be indolent for even a moment, and your learning will be perfected. Now you are about to travel to study in the four quarters;
if you can maintain these six principles with constancy, then the ancients will not be far away. I offer this song as a parting gift. Thus it was composed.

The staff for a long journey; in decisive battle, one has always valued risking death; in decisive study, one has always valued self-exertion. One who risks death when facing the enemy possesses a resolute spirit;
where there is such resolve, the enemy shall surely perish. One who exerts oneself without ceasing will surely achieve success in learning. Why worry about failing midway?
Thesis: Therefore, when the ancients were dedicated to study, frost and ice would naturally form upon their faces in ordinary moments.

They entrusted both the beautiful and the foul realms to the void, leaving nothing to obscure the light of the mind within their square inches. When the light of the mind is unobscured, wisdom arises spontaneously;

once wisdom has arisen, there is no principle it does not penetrate with clarity. When principles are clear, examining the teachings brings them into natural accord, and speech emerges spontaneously in harmony with the Buddha’s wisdom. This is the Buddha’s wisdom.
Since there is a ladder to the dark heavens, I know that you have reached this point without falling into delusion. Returning home, you dwell in seclusion by the Yellow Dragon Pool;
barefoot, you have traversed the western peaks of ten thousand mountains. Meeting under the moonlight, we discuss our past; now I realize that my words were entirely true.
There is nothing unreal; it is simply groundless and utterly chaotic. These are not spears and banners meant to delude people;
they are intended to flaunt our own lack of a root.
Ascending Mount Tianmu and Mount Jing, I compose this.
The wealth and nobility of the heavens are envied by those in the human realm; the wealth and nobility of the human realm are spat upon by those in the heavens.

From of old, only the person who has attained the Way has seen through both heaven and humanity. With a single staff of chestnut wood resting across his thin shoulders, he explores remote mountains and waters for years unknown.
Who casts these two orbs of sun and moon? How many times have the blue seas and mulberry fields shifted and changed? Have you not seen Mount Kunlun?
The belly of the Kun mountain rises up; it flies to Zhejiang and is called Tianmu. A single branch sways toward the Eastern Sea.

Like a furious horse galloping that suddenly halts and bows its head, the two paths wind and turn where clouds and mists deepen. Five peaks crouch and sprawl, clustered like the stars. This is what Heaven has wrought.

That which is hidden in the earth awaits a person to emerge before its fame can begin to spread. When the Master first received the offering from the dragon deity, the deep pool overflowed and became a site for the practice of the Way.

When the Way was perfected and virtue had grown thick, he moved the Son of Heaven; kings and lords hurried to his side, providing him with a golden fortress. One must believe that in opening a pond one need not wait for the moon;
once the pond is completed and filled with water, the moon shines of its own accord. Furthermore, have you not seen the trees of the secluded crag, having endured all...
The severe frost has not yet met with spring; in a single moment, the warmth of the sun suddenly returns. Tender flowers and fresh buds cluster together in profusion.
From the Tang dynasty until the present day, how many times have the mists and clouds, the courts and markets, drifted in and out? For what reason does the eastern wind shake the temple bells?

Withered red petals drift in the stream, leaving the human heart pale and weary. Dragons and snakes have no permanent dwelling. An old man upon the mountain, eighty years of age, [meditates] through the night.
He pierced the Buddha’s face and shook the family’s reputation; when the True Command is manifest before one, how could he yield it to another?

The tracks of the white hare, the tomb of the numinous rooster—his merit in warming his feet was great, his courage in heralding the dawn. How could he be merely a human among the spirits of all things? Encountering conditions, he failed to sow the seeds of Bodhi.
In the pond for releasing living beings, golden lotuses bloom; a wondrous fragrance occasionally perfumes the pavilions and terraces. A gentle breeze idly blows through the pines upon the rocks.

Within meditative concentration, one is first startled by a sound like thunder. As for sound and form, cease from false conjecture; what the eyes hear and the ears see cannot be grasped as it truly is.

Since these two are identical in their dharmic nature, there is no great power required for an ordinary person to become a Buddha. It is strange that this dull-witted fellow is clouded by the defilements of karma;

amidst the clear blue sky and bright daylight, he gives rise to doubt. The stone knows how to roar; the conch shell knows how to live. Sentient and insentient beings are governed by a single mechanism.
Try pulling the stone down with a light line: moving horizontally or vertically, it reaches everywhere. When the conch has died, it returns once more.
Born into a cauldron boiling at a hundred degrees, one travels by a separate path. If a person understands the news here, they may let the kalpa-fire and the Vairambha winds cook them as they will.
For now, I shall take the small to illustrate the great; once this is realized, every single thing is fundamentally not obscure.

As for the Zen of the patriarchs of past and present dynasties, who well understood the application of means and what was beneficial or harmful—when Zhaozhou said, "The dog has no Buddha-nature," and we encounter this and bring it up, who can speak of it?
No illness. One morning, having thoroughly overturned [the world] all at once, he saved the wretched life of Gautama.

This one great matter—though one were to employ dukes and ministers, take it for granted that they would know how to handle it, yet they could not manage it. It is not that Master Qin deludes people; his emotional ties severed, he yields to the master of true character.
Zhang Liang’s schemes and Huaiyin’s merit—the struggle between Chu and Han is but a spring dream. Where do the flying sands go?
The sounding of the knife and the drum: upon waking, one laughs at how both have become empty. The appearance of obstruction is fundamentally pure;

the boundless oceans of lands are a mirror of void clarity. If even a single atom stirs, Mount Tai collapses. From ancient times to the present, there has been a flurry of grasping at the handles of hatred and love. It would be better to realize this early.

Rest directly here. A thousand heads and ten thousand threads are entrusted to the mountain stream. When sitting in meditation by the moonlit brook, the cloudless sky and the temple halls are naturally pure in autumn.
Alas, the ancestral Way has grown increasingly desolate; foxes and hares swarm together, running wild in broad daylight. What are these three robes and earthen bowl?
They are no different from the brothels and wine shops where prices are weighed and compared. There is nothing more excellent than this place of water and mountains; atop the very peak—just a moment.
Ascending, one gathers all that is beautiful. The surging waves of the Zhejiang River meet the tide at Haimen. The tongue-mark of Guanyin drags along the bedding.
Old Dahui is compassionate and kind; Baiyun even permits a red skirt to sweep it clean. If travelers marvel at being lost in the smoke and flowers, I dare say the Master has not yet heard the Way.
The delusion lies within me, not with others. Adverse or favorable circumstances trap the faculties and sense-objects; only by completely detaching from them can one be liberated.
The faculties and their objects are revealed in solitary radiance; wildflowers and weeds are all in spring. Let us wander for a while, though we cannot remain long.

Who will follow me to the headwaters of the Two Streams? With a single lamp reaching dawn, we speak of days gone by; as we part at Pingyao, our feelings are even more profound. A man of spirit—would he ever idly tread these paths?
May the printing blocks of the *Lotus Treasury* be preserved forever. Entrust them to the mountain spirits to guard and uphold them well. Ten thousand...
The Ancient Stūpa of the Fearless for the Common People.
A Song by Nu-ge (with Preface).
I have heard that among all things that float and sink within birth and death, it is emotion alone that constitutes their burden. Therefore, one who has not yet transcended emotion...
This person understands that one is not a slave to others, yet remains a slave to oneself; how does this differ from Dong Xi who made the ugly Madou her servant?
Thus, I have spontaneously sung this song:
"Have you not seen how Emperor Xiao of the Liang dynasty sought to become a slave to the Buddha, prostrating his five limbs upon the mud? To this day..."
The lowly crowd laughs at the mouth; who knows that within lies a far-reaching design? Again, consider Zhang Zifang: when he offered his shoes at the Qi Bridge, people called him mad.

As a youth, he did not disdain bowing to the white-haired; thus the powerful Qin was overnight brought to ruin. Life and death are indeed great matters for man, yet when compared to the difficulty of overcoming the mighty Qin, they are but this and that.
It is not the Retainer of the House (Liu Hou) whom one laughs at, but Emperor Liang of the Liang dynasty. West.
The appearance of the generous is ugly, while that of the ugly woman is beautiful. Alas for the eyes of the world! What do they see as deficient? They praise the distant and slander the near in vain.
For kalpas of dust they feel no sorrow, yet they grieve for a mere moment. The slow become swift, and the swift become slow. Zhang Liang destroyed Qin to avenge the state of Han.
The affairs of Qin’s downfall are now complete; transcendent, I entrust myself to the company of Chi Song. With flowing waters and green mountains, heaven and earth are vast.
Among the great afflictions of human life, none surpasses the body itself. Is the word established by Laozi not indeed true?

Having realized that this body is a great affliction, one who forgets the self to serve the Buddha is surely no ordinary person. I urge you, while the vital energy of the night is clear and bright, to carefully examine these two [matters].
The distinction between the distant and the near lies in the depth of one’s resolve, as held by Xiao and Zhang; how different this is from the contrast between the azure sky and the yellow dust!
The multitude sees the small and fails to see the great, treating an anthill and a dragon peak as equal beneath a single headcloth.

Furthermore, they fail to realize that the eye is a slave to form, the ear a slave to sound, the nose a slave to fragrance and stench, the tongue a slave to saltiness and acidity, the body a slave to touch, and the mind...
They are slaves to their objects of perception. Chao Fu and Xu You were slaves to the pursuit of fame.
Yao and Shun were slaves to the world. Laozi was a slave to the Three Jewels. Confucius was a slave to benevolence and righteousness.
Śākyamuni was a slave to sentient beings. This old fellow Daguan was a slave to nothingness. Tall, he is a slave; short, he is a slave; beautiful, he is a slave; ugly, he is a slave.

A slave. In antiquity you were a slave; now you are still a slave. Before the Great Way was distinguished, who were "you" and who were "I"? All that falls within the realm of signs and traces is a slave.
Alas! In this turbid world, things are overturned and inverted: you do not consider yourself a slave, yet you call me a slave.

It is like fish and dragons in the water, who divide their territories and carve out boundaries, strictly distinguishing between what is different and what is the same. Little do they realize that if one seeks fish and dragons apart from the water, where can the fish and dragons be found?
The source from which they arise. It is like the great earth, where the small mounds and Mount Kunlun are distinguished by their height and depth relative to the ground.
A blind man laughs at another blind man—ha ha ha! Do you understand? If you know this, you may come and cross the sea of suffering together.

A Song of Summer Retreat at Leshang Village Leshang Village, Leshang Village—where the earth is vast and the sky seems low, and the wild colors are deep azure. Verdant trees are sparse, casting shade by day;
emerald vines emit light when the moon rises at night. Leaning against a clean desk, facing a bright window, I murmur the chapters of the Buddha after my meal.
The breeze of wisdom sweeps suddenly, rolling away the clouds of delusion; the single wheel of spiritual discernment shines boundlessly.

Rejoicing in the long summer, though in a desolate forest and a remote place, how could a wandering traveler seek out my traces? With water for the bowl and incense from the burner, my soul and dreams are cooled.

With whom can I sit cross-legged to indulge in this secluded ease? Have you not seen the path of honor and disgrace? Anxious for gain and fearful of loss, the worldly bones are startled. With hair turning white and thinning, who can understand [this state]?
Cease! To let your breath break in vain with empty weeping—though sons and grandsons fill your eyes, on the road to the Yellow Springs there is no eye to see.
You created your own sins; you must bear them yourself. Regret that in life you failed to cultivate merit.

Beneath the shade of compassion, the green dragon hall—how many years have been spent in its cultivation? From the pavilion of hearing, it covers and hangs over the Jade Hall; a single petal of red floats down.

The azure sky, morning and evening, one diligently performs their devotions; amidst the sound of the iron chime, the deceased are delivered. The Right Vice-Minister’s villa has been converted into a monastery;
for a thousand years, the Wang clan has made this Wǎngchuān their home. Alas for past and present, they have misdirected their efforts—neglecting to accumulate pure karma while amassing yellow gold.
Though the snow on their heads is white, it cannot be spent away; the towers and pavilions of song and dance have turned into brambles and thorns. The tomb of King Wu of Wú. Qi.

At Wangling, year after year, one records but empty names; the golden coffin and silver outer casing belong to wealthy patrons. Travelers visiting these ancient sites stop their carriages in vain for lamentation.
How can they compare to Layman Fu of Liaocheng, who begot a son for his father to continue the transmission of the lamp?

A Song of Fangshan: The marvelous wonders of Fangshan are few in all the world. Its myriad peaks serve as beams and rafters, with the blue sky as its roof-tiles. On all four sides, emerald cliffs lock in the luminous void;
their innermost depths are difficult to depict. The paths for birds are perilous; one must clutch one’s staff and grasp the hanging vines to avoid falling.
Error. Those in the lineage of Chan who wish to penetrate the barrier of birth and death must advance further from the top of a hundred-foot pole.

Even if they risk falling to their deaths, the perilous crisis is exhausted; tiger dens and dragon palaces are all stilled and extinguished. When facing objects with no mind, the square inch of the heart is at ease. To leap across a precipice requires a hero.
When Old Yan sees such people, the karmic mirror is clear and their offenses are difficult to assign. From the beginning, they have never fallen into any trace.

In the midst of the omens, Lord Deng crushed the leg of a colt. According to rank and according to the distinction between self and other, Danxia’s burning of the Buddha should also have resulted in death;
who knew that disaster would strike those with such fervent hearts? The head monk’s eyebrows and whiskers must surely fall out. Is it not a grievance? Is it not an injustice?
When life and death are at stake, one does not distinguish between patriarchs and Buddhas. Donkey dung meets and exchanges eyes; a night-glow pearl is turned into—
Objects by the roadside. Do you not see, deep within the clouds, the sound of the Tuṣita bell clashing like a sword? The "white-handed old man" understands how to turn things around.
When light and darkness interpenetrate, to whom can one speak? Whether speaking or not, whether knowing or not—by the clouds, the old tree’s branches obstruct the way.
How many times has its gaunt shadow stretched across the moonlit night? Mistaking it for a snake, one drives away the crows. Not yet a *li* away.

Dripping and trickling down, each drop makes a sound; where can one seek it? Since one sound is thus, ten thousand sounds are the same. With the eyes one listens to the pure tones of the primordial flute.
The music of the Chan school is naturally simple and plain; it does not belong to the scales of *gong* and *shang*, nor is it distinguished by clarity or turbidity.
The sages are far removed and false views run deep; how can these myriad demonic followers ever attain awakening? As it is with the flute, so it is with the zither. Ziqi—ten thousand...
Long buried in the Yellow Springs, it is difficult to imagine him being roused by the clapping of hands; how could Boya bear to tune his strings again?

Upon the high mountain there is flowing water—since when did this thing called "One Peck" begin its fame? We have heard that during great droughts it becomes clouds and sleet; the three plants and two trees experience sorrow and joy.
Within the single universe, water is visible, yet before they have merged, the waves are even more perilous. If one speaks of it...

When the dragon departs, the water immediately dries up; when the nature of emptiness becomes the true water, it turns into a hollow pit. To contemplate in this way is called right contemplation; demons and heretics will have their hearts and gallbladders turn cold upon hearing this teaching.

Since it is so for the one great [element], it is so for the three great ones and all others; all things share the same root—do not deceive yourself. Upon sudden awakening, consciousness transforms into wisdom.

Within the causal stages of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, one distinguishes the levels of attainment. In the gates of contemplation, whether moving against or with the flow, exert yourself with earnest diligence. Year after year...
One should cherish this light and not let it go to waste. O Honored One who fills the place of succession, Patriarch of the Dharma-character school!

You bestow the rain of Dharma upon the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; the palaces and halls above are truly resplendent. The dragon-elephants of former times have formed their ranks; beneath the cold crags, strange grasses grow green. One should not listen to talk of rise and fall;
even within the Gate of Emptiness there is still waxing and waning. How could human generations be free from decay and glory?
Emperor Gaozu of Han and the Hegemon King of Chu contended for supremacy over mountains and rivers through a hundred battles; look now, where are they?
The dragon towers and phoenix pavilions lie in ruins amidst the weeds. One laughs at Huaiyin [Xiang Yu] and yields to Liu Hou [Kang]. Whether one succeeds or fails, by whom is it caused?
It is simply because that first move was wrong; the board is full, yet the game is not yet over. A remarkable man—how could he not be swift?
Yet with eyes wide open, he lets a woman sell his wares. How many who meet him claim to be heroes, but when the matter comes to its end, they all suffer defeat.
At dawn after a dream of spring, one hears the singing birds. From antiquity to the present, how many such matters have there been? Last night the east wind passed over the short hedge.
The wall. Scarlet petals fill the ground; who gazes upon them? A pillar is first erected. Old Huayan: the Dharma-realm is profound and subtle—try to investigate it!
The first three can be known through study and understanding, but the last one has always lacked a head. The calamity reaches descendants and never ceases;
Heaven opens its eyes as the Forest Elder distinguishes green from black. The Ball-of-Leather Daoist forcibly offers testimony—this too is his own creation.
Returning, I find myself overturned. The mountain of my dwelling is fine; it suits me whether walking or sitting. Peak and crag face one another like blossoming flowers;
the moss upon the stone steps smiles at the hooves of horses. I look coldly upon the travelers clutching iron chains—those who ascend, those who descend.

Its fragrance has flowed since antiquity and cannot be grasped. I, old and infirm, do not make appointments with others; do not wait until the moment arrives to shed tears in vain. Because there is this body.
To invite honor or disgrace is due to having a mind that gives rise to likes and dislikes; the ocean of suffering is vast and difficult to cross.
Therefore, one must directly regard both as being like a city in the sky—how could one fear taking the wrong path on the road to Fangshan?

The elder brother sings songs of the sheep that give birth to tigers; the dog gives birth to an ox. To point out a deer as a horse—who is to be blamed? For the most part, human sentiments are full of reversals;
the waves and ripples cannot necessarily convey the whole truth. Where power lies and where profit resides, people debate with blood-stained mouths while their true hearts remain obscured.

How much more so when repaying one another with a cup of wine; how could he not then be willing to pour out his very liver and lungs? Have you not seen that of all things possessing form, only Heaven and Earth are the greatest?

They encompass all existence without discarding even the most minute. As summer passes and winter comes, and as things flourish and perish, they have never possessed a conscious mind to act as a governing rule.
As for Brother Cash (Kong-fang), the Noble of Power and Splendor (Shi-yao-bo), their majesty and fortune have been exceedingly brilliant in recent years, yet even their own flesh and blood—
Meeting on a narrow path, life and death, honor and disgrace, all serve at their whim. Confucius, Laozi, and Śākyamuni—the three elders of heaven and earth—are most transcendent among the multitudes.
Yet even they have now reached the exhaustion of their skill; as we gaze upon one another in this seated assembly, tears fall in profusion.
Green becomes yellow, white becomes black; the straight becomes crooked, and the crooked becomes straight. Rites, music, poetry, and books pass away.
The wind in the ears; five thousand and twelve radishes. Director Kong Fangbo; the brilliance of Shi Yao’s elder brother.

Heroes, each towering over the other. Proving the present as the past, and the past as the present. Relying upon divine power, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished. I laugh at myself for never having been content with my lot.
I regard my two brothers with indifference, as if they were mere soil or dung. My peers all say, "Just follow the times. But my nature and destiny are firm.
A narrow disposition does not approach the ultimate nature of life; it is as worthless as a mere coin. Cast it east or west, trusting in past karma.

If there is truly a living mechanism within one’s heart, how could there be no clear sky above one’s head? Amidst mountains and clouds, within the dust of the world—wherever one goes or stays, there has never been a fixed track.
Whether noble or commoner, lord or duke, view them all as one path. What sorrow or joy can there be in the fluctuations of circumstances? Thus it is said:

Easy to speak, difficult to practice; at the critical juncture of likes and dislikes, one battles through the cold of winter. If the mind itself is not yet understood, one must grind and polish it by force.
Yet, until the very end, the root of emotion is not easily abandoned. Break the alms bowl, snap the staff; when a single breath no longer comes, everything is cast away.
Only a stinking corpse remains. Let the maggots emerge and rot it like a sauce. Rotting like a sauce—there is no silver sarcophagus or golden coffin.
Two things. On the mountain peaks of both north and south, there are many burial grounds. Who among the living is not a craftsman of power and profit? What I have said is quite correct;

I fear that singing it might offend my elder brother’s sensibilities. If my elder brother will from now on turn his light back upon himself, the clouds of delusion shall be melted away to reveal the mirror of the mind.
When the mirror of the mind is bright, one gains self-confidence: that former pursuit of power and profit was truly a source of guilt and transgression. One should take this thought as...
Expand upon this: your elder brother’s direct lineage is entirely that of Yao and Shun. Furthermore, one sees that there is no constancy to either the noble person or the petty person;
demons and Buddhas are as indistinguishable as snow and hot water. To seek snow again within the melted water is no different from a "stone woman" searching for her father and mother.
Such words are very easy to understand, yet people fail to comprehend them because they are disturbed by their desires. Try to observe when not a single thought has arisen.
At that time, what is large or small regarding the daily use of body and mind? Suddenly, one attains sudden enlightenment; the child finds the mother.

In a state of vigorous ease, the natural disposition is spontaneously harmonious. Life and death, even in times of upheaval, are treated as mere trifles. This single thread of affection knows no left or right.

From the beginning of the ten thousand ages to their end—only when the principle is realized as I have explained it will it be understood. If you do not follow my words and seek another path, let it be so; even the Buddha would have to pay homage to it.
A shout! Jishui Huanzou says: "Separated from Jishui by a distance, one gazes toward Jishan.
Beneath Jishan, who has built this hermitage? Before the hermitage, the ancient path is covered in verdant moss."
Complete. Only the white clouds are permitted to wander to and fro.
A Song of Mountain Dwelling left for Chan Master Long of Doushuai Temple.
Spring in the Mountain Dwelling: The atmosphere is permeated with the fragrance of flowers and trees; a solitary bird calls out once, awakening the morning dream. It casually summons [the soul].
Awakening to the person as they truly are:
A summer dwelling in the mountains. Amid thunder and rain, dragons and snakes vie in their transformations; beyond the door and before the steps, clouds and waters are deep.
The Chan practitioner lies in a daze beneath the tall pines.

Autumn Dwelling in the Mountains. Upon the rocks, I cut clouds to mend my patched robe; let the west wind blow its leaves away as it pleases. In the gardens, the taro and chestnuts have already been gathered in full.
Winter Dwelling in the Mountains. Snow covers a thousand peaks and ten thousand peaks; deep in the night, I sit alone in my thatched hut by the earthen brazier.
The morning is warm and sunny.
Sent to Master Han, a song for Guanyin:
How large is the stone boat’s cabin? It is wide enough for you and me to sit together. It has been three years since we parted; we have not met.
I have seen it. When has it ever been separated from the Upper New River? Yet, lacking a boatman to hold the helm, I sought out the Elder Guanyin of the Universal Door.
This Elder Guanyin is no different from me; now I am entrusted by Guanyin to Guangcheng. Guangcheng, too, is no different from the cabin of the ship.
