My public life, morning and night, is filled with joyous emotion. This emotion resides before the Emperor of Elephants (the Ultimate). Through a thousand grindings and ten thousand trials...
Observing with compassion, Guanyin has specially manifested her body as three old men; for many years they have steered this boat for you.
Once this boat has been steered to a place of safety, what need is there to fear winds and waves lashing against the heavens? Waves lashing against the heavens! Waves lashing against the heavens!

One forms karmic connections within the shipyard of the precious vessel. I have heard that the treasures of the South Sea are most numerous; has your public vessel filled with these many treasures? The boat...
If we do not meet again with full weight, what is the intention of my elder brother Guanyin? What is his intention? What is his intention?
At Mount Jufeng, the sea moon shines as clear as a mirror, shattering the unmanly nature of Zhilang.
Pang Degong’s Song of Xiangyang:

Master Pang of Xiangyang was, in his youth, neither strictly restrained nor did he shave his white hair, yet he was not vulgar. While the world rushes about in pursuit of things, I alone have cast them aside;
I have more than enough, while they lack. Beneath the trees by Deer Gate there is moonlight; on Tiger Creek there is no wind for my boat.
I stayed overnight above. I did not recognize the fisherman who was there at the time; I simply admired Changkang’s painting of the Golden Grain.

Now I have closed my mouth and no longer speak of it. Master Pang was a man of unbending integrity. When people from the east or west asked the old man about him, he would say: "A bright lamp illuminates the ornate hall.
Whether in five-character or seven-character verse, these are but a child’s play; three lines or five lines are likewise merely coincidental. Such is my nature.
Not drinking, yet understanding intoxication; it is just like the spring breeze playing among the myriad flowers. For forty years we have shared the same affairs;
in old age, what need is there to distinguish between the foolish and the wise? The ancients neither dwelt nor perished; I now neither act nor cease.
I entrust this to the wandering people of the world: they are but a speck of dust, born and dying in waves. There is no pool for washing ink and no tomb for brushes;
I offer this merely as a plaything to delight you.
Singing by the Min River, he wears not the indigo robe but the black cassock. Amidst the clamor of the world, he yearns for solitude.

When mountain and stream are brought upon his staff of wisteria, how could one find leisure to waste away one’s white hair? The hair is white; like snow covering layered peaks, such a state of being is difficult to attain. Let it be as it may.
Scorching afflictions are transformed into cool clarity; this Sahā world is no different from a land of lotuses. Simply entrust both hatred and love to the Min River.
From within the Dragon Hall Temple, the dragon first emerges. The dragon first emerges—thousands upon thousands of mountains are shrouded in ink-black clouds.
A shooting star collides with an old bhikṣu; his skills are useless, and he can only weep in vain.

Singing by the ancient stream, one descends directly through a thousand peaks and ten thousand crags. A single rain in the mountains sends waterfalls cascading for a thousand li; as they flow into the deep recesses, they become still and full.

Branching out, the pools spread level, reflecting the distant sky. Do you not see? With a source far-reaching and a current long-lasting, emerging from heights, it ultimately returns— [To the Sea] (implied by context)
"The great ocean produces waves and surges. Although these words are commonplace, when one grasps the meaning, the words are forgotten; the principle is fundamentally profound and distant.
Furthermore, one does not see that the Dharma-body expressed through speech has anything coarse or subtle. When words are forgotten and the meaning is grasped, all is True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Amidst the layered white snow and the sound of flowing water, even if one listens with ears pricked, it is as if there were nothing. From the Grand Chancellor down to you gentlemen, whether speaking coarsely or subtly—
Like insects gnawing through wood, by chance forming characters; whether with mind or without mind, the path is exhausted. The flowing water chills as white clouds emerge.
The Daoist of Far-Reaching View travels vigorously on foot, searching everywhere from north of the sea to south of heaven. Having eaten his fill under the green mountains, he lies beneath the pines;

the sound of the spring, stifling against the rocks, hastens the awakening from a dream. When the dream awakens and the eyes open, heaven and earth are vast. What need is there for greetings of cold or warmth?
Dwelling in a place of no peace, I happened to come to Jingchu to beg for alms. In the corner of a bamboo desk within a Chan hall of pure practice, a practitioner smiled and showed me this scroll.
With the sound of the spring washing away my turbidity from both ears, I felt as if my body were amidst the mist and clouds.
When shall I clear the brush and bind a hut in this Chan hall? The sound of the stream is truly the broad and long tongue; what need is there to labor with the mouth’s clamor to preach the Dharma?

The tonsured monks sing at will of indulgence and stubbornness. Indulgence and stubbornness! The sages are far removed, yet they have no sense of shame. These tonsured monks, the Six Groups and the Seven Groups, eat their fill and wander about engaging in reckless prattle.
Some cling to the Buddha; others cling to the Patriarchs. "The Buddha and the Patriarchs—these are the footsteps we, our own kind, should follow."

With the nature of a sheep yet the skin of a tiger, they roam everywhere. Their transgressions often trouble the government officials; yet the officials do not understand, giving rise to groundless suspicions.

Jade and stone are burned together as one, leading them to conclude that there are no *lingzhi* (spiritual fungi) in the monastic groves. Thus, even in three-family villages or seven-li inns, [they find nothing but the like].
Good and evil, the wise and the foolish—these may all be verified. To examine names and scrutinize reality, true circumstances are difficult to conceal.

To the good, grant incense; to the evil, grant the sword. When rewards and punishments are clear, the treacherous cannot escape. It is impossible to confuse black and white by even a hair’s breadth. The Gate of Emptiness is vast and wide, its inhabitants numerous;
thorns and the wutong tree each have their own place. A phoenix perches on thorns; an owl gathers at the wutong. Phoenix and owl possess their own respective spirits.

It is extraordinary! Do not let your dwelling cause you to lose sight of the true nature of things; how could an owl ever produce the song of a phoenix? The Buddha’s knowledge and vision value the precepts and discipline:

to turn one's back on them brings misfortune, while to uphold them brings good fortune. If those who are monks do not cease from consuming pungent and fatty meats, the Tathāgata calls them "shaven-headed soldiers.
Whether in cities or among mountain forests, famous monasteries and authentic temples are as numerous as fingers to count; yet for nineteen out of twenty, they have fallen into ruin.

78. The disciples of Shushan Shimen wept bitterly. They traced the origin of their sorrow and the cause of the temple’s ruin: it was not because of those with yellow caps, but because of those with shaven heads.
If those with shaven heads would but guard the pearl of the precepts, the field of merit would naturally yield a great autumn harvest.
With the rice of true reality, the meal is like snow; chew through one grain and the wild mind ceases. Where the wild mind ceases, that is original Bodhi; its light shines back upon itself.
Without fullness or deficiency—such is the Sangha. Who would not revere them? When one reveres the Sangha, the mind of the *dāna-pati* (donor) likewise becomes upright.
When the minds of monastics and laypeople shine with light, it is inexhaustible. Shushan and Shimen exercised the True Command; when the True Command is exercised, gods and ghosts weep.

At such a critical moment, even Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot intervene. Chen Yingzhong was a dragon among men. Tiantai’s teachings and contemplations have the masters Yongming Yanshou and Zhiyi. Shanglan Chang...
Lao Shiying’s examination: The profundity of the religious teachings is that of the Elder Juefan.
Ascending Nalanda Cave, he was moved by a sense of resonance.
Do you not see? Before the Great Simplicity was carved, at the beginning of Chaos, there was neither self nor other between the sentient and the insentient. In a fleeting instant—

I contemplate from whom this was born. Flesh, bone, mountains, and rivers have become obstructive barriers. The Nara Cave is profoundly deep and dense; its depths are empty and luminous, unfathomable.
I hear it said that a divine monk once entered therein, leaving his pack and hat behind at the edge of the clouds for a thousand ages.
Hearing of his wind-like influence, I too have come; my emotions stir with melancholy as I linger amidst the secluded crags. I am ashamed that my own views still remain within me. Bodhisattva.
The gate of existence is not opened; proceed directly upward. Do not engage in discrimination. Both ordinary and holy beings are, in essence, nothing but dry dung-sticks.

If you allow yourself even a moment of deliberation right before them, a wedge shall be driven deep into the back of the stone man’s head. Viewed from this perspective, cease external seeking. Eyes and sounds, ears and forms—the skull is cold.
A single expanse of constant radiance, neither form nor non-form: heaven and earth are contained within the tip of a single hair. Furthermore:
One does not see that Vimalakīrti’s room, barely ten *hù* square, could accommodate hundreds of thousands of teachers’ seats.
If you say this old fellow was merely displaying supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), you are clearly mistaken due to being drowsy. Who does not possess such wondrous function?

Do you remember eating your rice and wearing your clothes? It is simply that this man is no true hero; he leaps beyond the golden-haired lion and turns into a dull dog. When the wind blows through the grass—*fu*.

Originally there was no thief; it was merely the sound of barking at a shadow that would not cease. Yet when a great robber plundered the master of the house, the knife of affliction rang out and he fled into hiding.
Drunk on the wine of karma, on what day will you sober up? Amidst the bustling vanity of the world, all are intoxicated.
Light furs and fat horses pass the time; these ailments bring grief to those who know you well. Let others be as they may; each must manage their own affairs. Such is the nature of a macaque.

The frantic square is treated with pain; at the gateway of likes and dislikes, the forest trees are deep. How could there ever be fixed rest above or below? When whipped from behind, it immediately turns its head;
when scolded away or called back, it dares not resist. Even while the rope is still held in the hand, the Zen elder mockingly laughs at the ugliness of this madman.
To clarify the Way is easy; to tread the Way is difficult. Having practiced the sentiment of water in the pond, how easily can it be dried up? It is not so.
Exert yourself with all your might. When speaking, it seems like awakening; when acting, one is deceived. When the words reach this point, tears fall like rain;

every drop flows from the liver and lungs. Rarely does one encounter a person of such caliber. Let not a sorrowful person speak to another who is sorrowful. Since there is bitterness, there must be sweetness.
When the Yin is exhausted and the Yang returns, the mouth of the cave dries up. In leisure, one bakes one’s back while mending a hempen robe. How peaceful!
I know my body is amidst layered peaks; at night, I hasten toward them, forgetting human affairs. Upon ten-thousand-li waves and mists, the sea moon rises.
Were even kings and lords to know this realm, they would surely regard fame and office as worn-out sandals.

The Song of the Leather Sack: How strange are these four great elements! Truly they are my affliction and harm. They labor ceaselessly to provide what is required; every thought follows after what is loved.
Not for even a brief moment have they shown pity or compassion; how can one thus forget such immense ingratitude? It is precisely because I wish to urge them forward toward purity...

In vain, it conversely invites fluctuations of diligence and indolence. One truly wishes to forget such things in the realm of nothingness, yet is unaware that one has shifted into states of love and hatred.
In youth, I relied on my parents for support; in maturity, I depended on teachers for instruction. By day, they employ me like horses or oxen;
by night, they cloud my spirit like insects or stinging wasps. Climbing the mountain, my breath comes in gasps.
The spirit grows weary; crossing the waters, my feet grow cold and my waist aches. Only when in motion do I feel a momentary sense of ease, yet as soon as I turn my gaze, it is already gone.
There is no time for stillness. Just as I wish to rest upon this subtle impulse, suddenly a thousand streams and ten thousand branches surge forth.
My grace and virtue increase daily, while your transgressions and faults decline daily. From this day forward, recognize this enemy for what he is, and let me act with total freedom.

Whether you leap into fire or throw yourself from a cliff, I shall never be surprised or alarmed by you. Whether you are struck by arrows or pierced by spears, how could these ever again be obstacles for you?
I only wish that every person would transcend such sentiments; then what need would there be to distinguish between the nine lotus realms and the three worlds?
If you allow even a single thought to be deluded by them, you may rest assured that you will have to repay your karmic debts in a future life.
At Shimen, amidst many magnificent pavilions, we sip tea and sing of the moon through the night.
Where is the bright moon? This very night, I have finally beheld you. I ask the bright moon, but the moon feigns deafness;
its clear radiance is profound and still, as if coyly silent. Who knows that this silence holds a deeper meaning? The bright moon has no mind, yet it understands.
We meet one another wherever we go, from the edge of the sea to the ends of the earth. When the faculties and their objects are utterly detached, the moon becomes our companion.

If this bright moon were subject to waxing and waning, how could Shi De and Han Shan have granted us their approval? Li Bai raises his cup and asks the bright moon; the bright moon at Shimen Gate, in turn, questions me.
I have no answer, so I point to the rivers and mountains—the rivers, mountains, and bright moon are where I always dwell. My mind...
The moon is the month, and the month is I; I and the moon together mock the cold and heat. Lu Tong’s seven bowls gave rise to a pure breeze;
I, having sipped three cups, inquire after Wu and Chu. Where are the King of Wu and the Marquis of Chu now? On the remains of the Zhangtai Terrace, empty boats drift in dreams.
The snow melts and spring waters arrive from Ba and Shu; I test-roast the Luoyue Dragon Ball tea once more.
As the soup bubbles in the earthen stove like the roar of thunder, a single cry from the frozen ravine causes me to forget my self.
A Song of the Water-Moon at Wenchang Bridge in Linchuan Have you not seen the moon upon Wenchang Bridge?
How many times has it been full, and how many times has it been waning? That the moon wanes and waxes is not without intent;
One must know that black hair turns to white. If white hair could never turn back to black, Then there would be no distinction between the noble and the lowly.
In the end, the bones are buried. Whether it be a golden coffin, a silver inner coffin, or a woven reed mat, once the bones have decayed, they must all ultimately vanish.

Furthermore, look not at the waters beneath Wenchang Bridge; the passing waves flow away once and never return. One knows not how many times flowers have bloomed and fallen; the flowing stream carries the flowers away, whether near or far.
Carried near, the flowers sink in the river before one’s eyes; carried far, the flowers begin to wither upon reaching the eastern ocean.
Though divided by distance, all are but lingering crimson. Why do you sing such mournful songs beneath the trees so late? O moon, o flowers—what things are you?
Your waxing and waning, your flourishing and falling, are indeed subject to constraint. When one probes both ends, emotion naturally withers; when emotion withers, wisdom likewise comes to an end.
When wisdom ends and emotion withers, look closely with your own eyes: the bright moon and flowing water are like boiling soup. Like boiling soup. (Text)

The Chang Bridge is broken; it ought to be adorned with *fu* and *fu* patterns. The *fu* and *fu* of Wenchang’s merit are supreme. As a ford and bridge for ten thousand ages, how rugged and steep it is! How rugged and steep it is!
At the gateway of profit and loss, one must cherish the clearing away of attachments. When attachment is cleared and principle is penetrated, the ford and bridge are established.

Let the head [of the bridge] rest at the bottom of the water; there is no need for sorrowful depression. When the moon is bright upon Wenchang Bridge, the Dharma-food is scattered everywhere; there is no need to beg. May you be taught thus.
Once full, one forgets a hundred hungers. When the skull awakens from its dream, the mind is no longer the Buddha.
Wandering atop Mount Aofeng, I lament Master Luo Jinxi;
Yunfeng is like a flower, and Gongru is like spring. Spring returns, yet the flowers naturally lose their spirit. The lofty mountains and flowing waters have been thus from the beginning.
How different! Wind and moon are boundless, yet they lack a master. Once the master has departed, he does not return. Why do you laugh at me for coming to visit so late?
The plum blossoms have fallen away, and wavelets float upon the water. A single sail, filled with wind, leaves a distant trace. The boat stops at the foot of the mountain as I gaze toward the peak.
A bridge spans half the sky, crossing over the precipitous cliffs. I have heard it said that those who walk across Lónggōng Bridge look up at the azure [sky].
Reclining upon the Celestial Bridge, his body and mind already perceive all things as equal to empty space; how could empty space ever undergo increase or decrease?
Turning his body on the bridge, first east and then west, those below look on in astonishment at his instability. Master Luo sings with a grand voice that halts the drifting clouds;
its resonance fills heaven and earth—who could conceal it? The song falls entirely into Magu Spring, where the spring water transforms into wine, the very remedy for sorrow.
Sorrow has nothing greater than profit and fame; profit and fame, moreover, have the body as their key. When the body is forgotten, afflictions vanish and the spirit begins to be whole.
When the spirit is whole, the winds and dust are themselves the Kunlun Garden. Why must one seek the sister-in-law (Cigu) deep within the clouds?

One is instead laughed at by Mazu as being mired in the mundane. The inner thoughts of Lord Luo are dissected within his song. The deity Mārīcī presides over the Northern Dipper; she possesses a single body with many arms.

The hands move freely in all directions; what need is there for them to grasp external objects? If the mind has purpose, the two hands labor in vain; if the mind is free from purpose, a thousand hands are naturally harmonious in their wondrous function.
As for this wondrous skill of Master Luo, who can transmit it? If you could transmit it, I ask you: do you have a recipient?

If there is a recipient, then apart from the mind there must be a dharma; the sense organs and their objects would stand in opposition, and the spirit would run wild again. Body and mind would instead become a nest of right and wrong, and profit—

It is said that birds and sparrows contend over beauty and ugliness; yet the *jiaoliao* (sparrow) finds peace with its body on a single branch. Would one dare to emulate the *wuya* (crow) by opening a foul mouth?
If the foul mouth is not opened, then the good mouth is opened. When words are spoken, they never deviate from principle.

Whether speaking horizontally or vertically, the myriad apertures resound like the wind of heaven—how could this arise from a mind? Without a mind, where are the roots and objects? What "this" and "that" could there be? Whether departing or coming, do not [cling to them].
A wild guess. Did Master Luo not attain this meaning? He secretly transformed non-attainment into the spring thunder. When the spring thunder emerges from the earth, all hibernating creatures awaken;
once awakened, the dreams of the three families naturally return. Have you not seen how the descendants of the Confucian, Buddhist, and Daoist traditions harbor crosswise afflictions?
Master Luo’s single laugh is like a spring breeze; it blows down the stakes of ignorance all at once. Xiangjiang San.
The moon releases peach blossoms; how many fair-faced women are there on both banks? Do not say that Master Luo has gone and will not return;
the ancient path through the cloud peaks is no one’s to sweep.
Song of Awakening (with Preface)
The ancients said that awakening to the Way is difficult; I most certainly do not agree. I have composed this song merely to vent my subtle thoughts:
Have you not seen the oxen and horses? They love only to sleep soundly and do not care for being beaten. When the grass is lush and the water is fine, their spirits are all the more joyful.
Hooves and horns are parched with hunger and difficult to provoke; fish in the water, birds in the trees—alike in their flight and concealment, whether great or small.

To long for the deep pool or choose one’s tree is most difficult to evade; the startled crossbow and the alarmed hook are too clearly manifest. Furthermore, have you not seen those who have attained the highest disregard the carriage and cap?
They dwell in bitter devotion to cloud-cloaked valleys, pines, and springs. Like the solitary orchid in the empty valley, its fragrance is its own; in the end, it need not follow the crowd.

The Pure Wind Unfurls. Only those of middle capacity find pleasure in the scholar’s robes (*jin-shen*). They revel in sights and sounds, their spirits fresh and new. When the banquet at the Jade Grove concludes, their shouts are like thunder.

Returning home with wine upon them, the candles have already grown dim. The hardships of the farming family; the joys of the farming family. Their suffering and happiness rise and fall according to the abundance or scarcity of the harvest.
Most exquisite is the fragrance of the late-ripening rice in the western wind, as they pour out the turbid ale and share it with their fat ducks. The magpies on the southern branches.
The sheep of the vast ocean—Sū Wu must have tasted them in Cold Pond. Since the opening of the horse market thirty years ago, the teeth of General Pofu have turned entirely yellow.
Between humans and things, there are distinct hierarchies; when joyful, they raise their voices, and when sorrowful, they weep. Do not say that humans are noble and things are base and insignificant;
before a single thought arises, all exist independently. When nature undergoes transformation, it becomes emotion; thus, hatred and love intersect.

The principle is not easily clarified. One must know that conceptual thought is itself fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). If one seeks water while abandoning the ice, how could the Buddha ever be realized?
Linji’s staff and Deshan’s shout—these are the fierce methods of the buffalo-headed and horse-faced guardians. Nobles, commoners, dukes, and marquises are all viewed with a single eye;

whether ordinary or holy, they are all subject to this cutting and carving. This very thing is a truly wondrous art: it sweeps away the clouds of delusion and suspends the sun of wisdom for all. Together!

All things reside within the pure light; yet to the blind, it remains pitch black. Even with further skillful means to open the path of awakening, one searches within and without for the mind and finds no abiding place.

This non-abiding mind is identical in both self and others. Yet, through the blazing intensity of attachment, distinctions arise from joy and anger. Joy and anger arise, yet they have no inherent nature from the start.
Once separated from the sensory objects (*viṣaya*), there is nothing to grasp. The wise person suddenly realizes that both subject and object are empty. *Beng* (a sudden burst/awakening).
He brought forth the Mirror of the Primeval Age from Xuanyuan; when used casually, it distinguishes the beautiful from the ugly. It brings an end to the very life-force of Gautama.
Awakening to the Way is easy; the difficulty lies in the person. If a person is truly resolute, winter can become spring—as Mengzong wept for his bamboo, and the shoots sprouted forth.
Even a dull-witted snake-slave can ascend to the Truth; this fills the world. Old Monk, with a single tongue you have spread slander everywhere, creating seventeen hundred tangles of complications.
Now all are cut off and scattered by the wind. Who cannot eat their meals and wear their clothes?
What joy or sorrow is there in life and death, honor and disgrace? Seeing ghosts at a desolate grave, one no longer gives rise to doubt—this is truly the Golden-Haired Master.
My son, here is a song about the broken straw sandals,
offered as a parting gift. Having trodden across a thousand cliffs and ten-thousand fathoms, try to see it when the tip of the foot has not yet been lifted.

Saints and commoners alike strain their ears; like thunder and lightning, swift is the call to diligent exhortation. Do not be indolent or weary. Cherish every fraction of a moment of this fleeting life.

Exhausted by the toil of traveling back and forth between the northern frontier and the southern border, one harbors a thousand regrets for failing to realize the Great Matter. Furthermore, one has never even seen the Old Dharmatrāta.
Holding a single sandal, he passed through Hantuo; meeting him at the summit of the ridge, it was indeed the Real One. The opening of the coffin at Xiong’er Mountain is even more of a fabrication.
How does this old fellow’s straw sandal compare? Wandering through clouds and mountains with the *bìluó* vines.

Even if one possessed the thousand hands and eyes of Great Compassion, they would surely be made to grope for waves within a fire. Another matter: do not try to divine it again; coming and going is like a bouncing ball.
Rolling on and on. Old Uncle of East Village is my closest friend; several times we were laughing, yet it turned into crying. When delusive thoughts arise, there is no need for conscious awareness;
walking aimlessly at one’s ease is most truly simple and plain. If you leave the great earth to seek your own footing, how is that different from leaving a stone to search for its raw jade?
If you deliberate upon honest speech, you will lose your wooden comb and ask instead for a hoe. This is the upward path.
There is a path to travel; it deceives the simpleton who brings himself to grief.
Ascending Mount Jing, I sing of Old Zibai.
Old Zibai! With a single staff of bamboo, he probes the wonders and mysteries. Only those places within the Middle Kingdom not yet sealed off [are his domain].

There is no superior water or beautiful mountain that I have not visited; yet this mountain alone I have never ascended. Now that spring has arrived, I have reached its summit and struck upon the gate of Chan.
Five peaks coil and settle among the heavens; two paths wind and turn amidst ten thousand valleys. Tang Guoyi was titled the First Patriarch.
Clearing the brush and cutting through the thorns, he opened up this land; the lamp’s transmission endures through eternity, its wisdom-light cold and piercing.
Dragon and elephant follow one another in succession, vying for every step. This "board-carrying" fellow cannot be bound; whether saint or ordinary person, all are swept away.

Even if one could turn back from the edge of a sword, one would already have been laughed at by me as a mere fabrication. O Grandson of the Dharma King! You are like a phoenix—how could you chase after a mountain fowl in vain?
A tumultuous whirlwind rises ten thousand *li* high; who in this world can control worldly honor and disgrace?

One morning one departs as a general, by evening one enters as a minister; yet when a single breath ceases, none can rely on such status. The meritorious deeds that once tore open the heavens are now clouds before one’s eyes; will King Yama lightly pardon such transgressions?
Do you not see how Liu Bang left his arm behind to enter the thousand peaks, no longer serving a sovereign but attending to Master Chi Song? Not so.
These fine flowers have not yet fully blossomed; suddenly, an autumn wind rises through the halls and pavilions.

At Tiger Hill, the landscape surges like a sea, its towering peaks piercing the clouds; green pines and white stones remain far removed from the dust and clamor of the world. Deep within the misty vines lies the site of a former dynasty.
In the temple, when the wind clears, the sound of bells and chimes is suddenly heard. Once, I cast aside my staff to pay homage to the Great Awakened One;
the golden walls of the hall radiated brilliant light. Who was it that burned aloeswood in the precious incense burner? Clouds of fragrance swirled about, settling upon my monastic robes.
Today, seeing this painting in your home, the magnificent events of those years appear as if they were only yesterday. How much of human life’s prime can there be? Throughout the long years...
Pleasure is not to be sought in abundance. Have you not seen that when the King of Wu was at his zenith, his power was already at its extreme?

When he marshaled his troops in the Middle Kingdom, who dared to oppose him? Yet after his failure at Huangchi, he returned late; the mountains and rivers of Wu bore a look of shame. The dreams of heroes last but a moment.
The palace flowers of level ground have turned into thorns. The Sword Pool now belongs only to wandering travelers; there remains only the Fish-Intestine Sword as his companion.
A withered bone. Furthermore, one does not see how Goujian attained his ambition and crossed the Qiantang River, with beautiful Wu women filling his boats.
Though the dragons and serpents desired them, they dared not seize them; the King of Yue carried them back to his native land. Even now, Kuaiji remains as it was.
The rustling bamboo arrows mark the passage of human eras. The House of Wu flourished; the House of Yue declined. When Yue was at its peak, Wu was defeated.

The rivalry between Wu and Yue was but a single dream; their karmic spirits have for a thousand ages settled their debts of vengeance. Since the carriage ahead has already overturned, let the one behind take it as a warning.
A single thought turning the light back toward oneself is not far away. Although the great and small differ in scale, there is always a principle that remains constant.
A Divider Line. I have composed this song with profound intent. You should remember the critical juncture of favor and adversity.
When Wu and Yue contended for supremacy, it was already a thing of the past; how much less would I, my friend, contend over trivial vapors? Frugality and diligent labor are my fundamental practice;
the profound inner scriptures clarify my mind’s resolve. Let others stir up waves and storms on every side; with a single incense offering, I shall repay Heaven and Earth. To dispel [distractions].
The spring light unfolds this painting; Tiger Hill has been transposed into the study hall.
I inscribe this song for Master Mou’s meditation chamber, admiring his dwelling:
it is lofty, vast, and far removed from the dust of worldly affairs; amidst the deep, secluded cliffs, deer and roe alike find their home.
Late. White clouds embrace the secluded rock; how can it be said that there is nothing to know? The bright moon lingers over the clear spring; how could there be a time for coming and going?
Xuedou strokes his chin—few are those who can appreciate this pivot. I drag my staff out of the mountains;
the solitary pine and fragrant orchids draw forth what I long for. What I long for lies within the subtle distinction (*li-mei*). Once separated, it cannot be spoken of.

This is called seeking. When it is subtle, it cannot be grasped by thought or mental inference. Since it cannot be sought or inferred, heaven and earth are but a single finger, and the myriad things are but a single horse. That is I, and I am that; since I am that, what is there to think about?
A Song of Viewing Flowers:

Come to view the flowers; come to view the flowers. Flowers bloom and fall through many cycles of joy. Human wealth and status are just like this—how many among those who view the flowers have their own "flower of the mind" blooming?
When the flower of the mind blooms, form is fundamentally empty. From the beginning, the flower of wealth and status has been but a breeze.

The brilliance and fragrance amidst the wind—how could they differ from the horns of a rabbit or the hair of a tortoise? Eyes see forms; ears hear sounds. Within this field of sound and form, love and hatred abound.
To flourish brings joy; to suffer humiliation brings grief. Vast is the shore of suffering, so difficult to ascend.
Behold the flowers! Behold the flowers! Cold and heat press upon us, hastening our aging. From now on, let the feverish afflictions be transformed into purity.
Cool! Do not let this coolness bring about the affliction of heat. Flowers are the mind; the meaning is most profound. How many who meet them are true connoisseurs?

Within the ranks of Mañjuśrī, one knows how to turn the body around. In every dust mote and every world-system, all is pure gold. Flowers obstruct the eyes; the eyes produce flowers. What is clearly fundamental becomes, instead, a deviation.
Whether objects and conditions are good or foul, they exist nowhere outside the mind. Heaven and earth, the human realm—all are one.

A flower. Go to see the flower. Go to see the flower. Do not dwell upon the existence or non-existence of ordinary beings and sages. From the beginning, the provisional manifestation of the flower’s form has been most wondrous.

Having already released it so it may bloom, you then gather it back together. I ask you: by whose power do you hold the handle? When viewing the flower, let the meaning of the song not be taken lightly.

A Gift to Dai Shengzhi: Have you not seen Master Dai? Though short and small in stature, his spirit and courage are bold. He fears neither the surging waves of the Min River nor the towering heights of Mount Lu.

With an air of haughty confidence, he drives his lone reed-boat; how carefree and soaring is his intent! He lightly cuts through the lairs of dragons and freely seeks out the dens of tigers and leopards.
Beneath the long pines, I bow to the aged monk. The aged monk bears no seal, yet his waist is slender. For what purpose does Dai Lang act?

He dares to draw from the profound source to nourish the sacred sprout. Once this sacred sprout has emerged, it reaches ten thousand fathoms; a celestial wind suddenly arises, brushing against the highest heavens.
It is said that the fragrance of the rice flowers pervades the ten voids; how could one refuse the toil of securing the Great Dharma as a golden fortress? And have you not seen Dai?
When robes are worn out and gold exhausted, everyone who encounters such a person cannot help but laugh. Who knows that this is the mechanism by which humiliation leads to vindication?

With one's talents and character towering like peaks, one must await the thunderclap. If one remains coiled in the mud without the will to soar toward the heavens, what difference is there between a man’s living and his dying?
Furthermore, have you not seen how Goujian avenged Wu by bitterly tasting gall, and how Mengming accepted his punishment without turning back? [He] smashed the cooking pots...

He burned his ships to resolve the battle in a single engagement; the men of Jin held their ground firmly and dared not emerge. It has been ten years since Master Dai left me; when we meet again, our hair is startlingly gray.
His spirit is no longer as it was when we gazed upon the Yellow River; even carrying a cart, he still labors at the summit of the Yangchang Pass.
I reproach myself for being but an old man who understands emptiness; unaware, I drank in my tears alone for a long while. The youth of spring and the ancient paths do not return;
Dài Láng, as you go hence, do not begrudge your own decay. The mountain colors of Lúshān remain ever green; the surges of the Mín River roar forever on.
When the flame of glory one day burns the apricot blossoms, even three inches of black gauze will not be unseemly. May you come again to Wǔlǎo.
Gazing at Fan Lake. Do not say that the affairs of my heart have not been exposed today.
The Collected Works of Old Man Zibai, Volume Twenty-nine (End).
